Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā

The Great Sub-commentary on the Path of Purification

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Saddhammaraṃsimālī [M 1.0001][V 1.0001] yo, vineyyakamalākare;

Vibodhesi mahāmoha-tamaṃ hantvāna sabbaso.

He who possesses the garland of rays of the good Dhamma, having completely destroyed the great darkness of delusion, caused the lotuses, which are the beings to be trained, to blossom in the lotus pond.

Ñāṇātisayabimbaṃ taṃ, visuddhakaruṇāruṇaṃ;

Vanditvā nirupaklesaṃ, buddhādiccaṃ mahodayaṃ.

Having paid homage to that Buddha-sun—the disc of supreme knowledge, the dawn of exceedingly pure compassion, the great mountain of sunrise, completely free from defilements.

Lokālokakaraṃ dhammaṃ, guṇarasmisamujjalaṃ;

Ariyasaṅghañca samphullaṃ, visuddhakamalākaraṃ.

(And having paid homage to) the Dhamma, which brings light to the world and is resplendent with the rays of virtue, and to the Noble Sangha, fully blossomed and like a lotus pond of exceptional purity.

Vandanājanitaṃ [V 1.0002] puññaṃ, iti yaṃ ratanattaye;

Hatantarāyo sabbattha, hutvāhaṃ tassa tejasā.

By the power of whatever merit is thus generated by homage to the Triple Gem, I, having become one whose obstacles are destroyed in every way...

Sampannasīlācārena, dhīmatā sucivuttinā;

Ajjhesito dāṭhānāgattherena thiracetasā.

Requested by the Elder Dāṭhānāga, who is endowed with perfect virtue and conduct, wise, of pure livelihood, and of steadfast mind...

Visuddhacarito nātho, yaṃ visuddhimanuttaraṃ;

Patvā desesi karuṇāsamussāhitamānaso.

The Protector, of pure conduct, having attained that unsurpassed Purity (Nibbāna), taught, His mind being urged on by compassion.

Tassā adhigamūpāyo, visuddhanayamaṇḍito;

Visuddhimaggo yo vutto, suvisuddhapadakkamo.

That Path of Purification which was taught—the means for attaining that (Purity), adorned with pure methods, and having a very pure sequence of terms—

Suvisuddhaṃ asaṃkiṇṇaṃ, nipuṇatthavinicchayaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, samayaṃ avilomayaṃ.

Perfectly pure, unmixed with the views of other schools, containing subtle and decisive meanings, and not contradicting the doctrine of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

Tassa [M 1.0002] nissāya porāṇaṃ, kathāmaggaṃ anākulaṃ;

Tantinayānugaṃ suddhaṃ, karissāmatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Relying on the ancient, unconfused, and pure path of exposition, which follows the method of the sacred texts, I shall compose the explanation of the meaning of that (Path of Purification).

Iti ākaṅkhamānassa, saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiṃ;

Vibhajantassa tassatthaṃ, nisāmayatha sādhavoti.

Thus, as I desire the long endurance of the good Dhamma and analyze its meaning, listen, O virtuous ones.

Nidānādikathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Introduction, etc.

1. Svāyaṃ visuddhimaggo yaṃ suttapadaṃ nissāya paṭṭhapīyati, taṃ tāva nikkhipitvā tassa nidānādiniddhāraṇamukhena nānappakārato atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetuṃ “sīle patiṭṭhāyā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Dhammaṃ saṃvaṇṇentena hi ādito tassa nidānaṃ vattabbaṃ, tato payojanaṃ piṇḍattho padattho sambandho adhippāyo codanā sodhanaṃ vattabbaṃ. Tathā ceva ācariyena paṭipannaṃ. Ettha hi bhagavantaṃ kirātiādi desanāya nidānapayojananiddhāraṇaṃ, visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissantiādi piṇḍatthaniddhāraṇaṃ[V 1.0003], sīle ṭhatvātiādi padatthasambandhādhippāyavibhāvanā, kiṃ sīlantiādi codanā, tato paraṃ sodhanaṃ, samādhipaññākathāsupi eseva nayo. Kasmā panettha vissajjanagāthā ādimhi nikkhittā, na pucchāgāthā. Pucchāpubbikā hi vissajjanāti? Vuccate – tadatthassa maṅgalabhāvato, sāsanassa ādikalyāṇādibhāvavibhāvanato, bhayādiupaddavanivāraṇena antarāyavidhamanato, upari saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammasaṅgahato cāti veditabbaṃ.

1. This Path of Purification is established by relying on a certain Sutta passage; having first set down that passage, [this work] is commenced with the words 'sīle patiṭṭhāya...' in order to explain its meaning in various ways, with the determination of its introduction, etc., as the principal method. For one explaining the Dhamma, its introduction should be stated first, and then its purpose, condensed meaning, meaning of individual terms, connection, intention, objection, and clarification should be stated. And the Teacher has proceeded in just that way. Herein, the passage beginning 'bhagavantaṃ kira...' is the determination of the introduction and purpose of the teaching; the passage beginning 'visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissanti...' is the determination of the condensed meaning; the passage beginning 'sīle ṭhatvā...' is the elucidation of the meaning of the terms, the connection, and the intention; the passage beginning 'kiṃ sīlan'ti...' is the objection, and what follows is the clarification. This same method applies also in the sections on concentration and wisdom. Why, then, is the verse of reply placed at the beginning here, and not the verse of inquiry? For is not a reply preceded by an inquiry? It is said: it should be known that the verse of reply is placed at the beginning because of the auspicious nature of its meaning; because it makes clear the nature of the Dispensation as being good in the beginning, etc.; because it dispels obstacles by warding off dangers and calamities; and because it summarizes the Dhamma to be explained later on.

Etthāha – kasmā panāyaṃ visuddhimaggakathā vatthupubbikā āraddhā, na satthuthomanāpubbikāti? Vuccate – visuṃ asaṃvaṇṇanādibhāvato. Sumaṅgalavilāsinīādayo viya hi dīghanikāyādīnaṃ nāyaṃ visuṃ saṃvaṇṇanā, na pakaraṇantaraṃ vā abhidhammāvatārasumatāvatārādi viya. Tāsaṃyeva pana sumaṅgalavilāsinīādīnaṃ visesabhūtā. Tenevāha “majjhe visuddhimaggo”tiādi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.ganthārambhakathā; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.ganthārambhakathā). Atha vā thomanāpubbikāpi cāyaṃ kathā na vatthupubbikāvāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sāsane hi vatthukittanaṃ na loke viya kevalaṃ hoti, sāsanasampattikittanattā pana satthu aviparītadhammadesanābhāvavibhāvanena satthuguṇasaṃkittanaṃ ulliṅgantameva pavattati. Tathā hi vakkhati “ettāvatā tisso sikkhā”tiādi. Sotāpannādibhāvassa ca kāraṇanti ettha hi ādi-saddena sabbasakadāgāmianāgāmino [M 1.0003] viya sabbepi arahanto saṅgayhanti vibhāgassa anuddhaṭattā. Tena tiṇṇampi bodhisattānaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyā sīlādayo idha “sīle patiṭṭhāyā”tiādivacanena saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tiṇṇampi hi nesaṃ carimabhave visesato saṃsārabhayikkhaṇaṃ, yathāsakaṃ sīle patiṭṭhāya samathavipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā taṇhājaṭāvijaṭanapaṭipatti ca samānāti. Atha vā “so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”nti sādhāraṇavacanena sātisayaṃ, niratisayañca taṇhājaṭāvijaṭanaṃ gahitaṃ. Tattha yaṃ niratisayaṃ savāsanappahānatāya. Tena satthu pahānasampadā kittitā hoti, tannimittā ñāṇasampadā ca. Tadubhayena nānantarikatāya ānubhāvasampadādayopīti. Evampi thomanāpubbikāyaṃ kathāti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā thomanāpubbikā evāyaṃ kathāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, “sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇacāro”tiādinā satthu thomanaṃ purakkhatvā saṃvaṇṇanāya āraddhattā. Sā panāyaṃ yasmā pucchantassa ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ byākaraṇasamatthatāya vibhāvanavasena pavattitā, āciṇṇañcetaṃ ācariyassa yadidaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbadhammānukūlaṃ saṃvaṇṇanārambhe satthu abhitthavanaṃ. Tasmā [V 1.0004] iminā kāraṇena evamettha thomanā pavattitāti. Thomanākārassa vuccamānassa kāraṇaṃ uddharantena paṭhamaṃ vissajjanagāthaṃ nikkhipitvā tassā nidānacodanāmukhena pucchāgāthaṃ sarūpato ca atthato ca dassetvā tassā pucchāya aviparītabyākaraṇasamatthabhāvāvajotanaṃ bhagavato thomanaṃ purakkhatvā yathādhippetadhammasaṃvaṇṇanā katā. Tenāha “sīle patiṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Tattha gāthāya attho parato āvi bhavissati.

Herein, one states: “Why, then, was this discourse on the Path of Purification begun with the subject matter as its precursor, and not with praise of the Teacher as its precursor?” It is answered: Because of its nature of not being a separate commentary, and so on. For this is not a separate commentary on the Dīghanikāya and others, like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others, nor is it another treatise like the Abhidhammāvatāra, Sumatāvatāra, and so on. Rather, it is a special work among those very Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. Therefore, he said, “In the middle is the Visuddhimagga,” and so on. Alternatively, it should be understood that this discourse also has praise as its precursor; it is not that it only has the subject matter as its precursor. For in the Dispensation, the stating of the subject matter is not merely as it is in the world; rather, because it states the accomplishment of the Dispensation, by revealing the Teacher's nature of having taught the Dhamma without error, it proceeds only by indicating the praise of the Teacher's qualities. Thus indeed, he will say, “By this much, the three trainings,” and so on. And here, in “the cause for the state of a Stream-enterer, etc.,” by the word 'etc.', just as all Once-returners and Non-returners are included, so too are all Arahants included, because a division has not been specified. Therefore, it should be understood that the virtue and other factors which are part of the penetration for all three kinds of Bodhisattas are included here by the phrase, “Having been established in virtue,” and so on. For, for all three of them, in their final existence, there is in particular the seeing of the danger of saṃsāra, and having been established in their respective virtue and having exerted themselves in serenity and insight, the practice of disentangling the tangle of craving is the same. Alternatively, by the general statement, “He would disentangle this tangle,” both the disentangling of the tangle of craving that is with remainder and that which is without remainder are taken. Therein, that which is without remainder is due to the abandoning of defilements together with their latent tendencies. By that, the Teacher's accomplishment in abandoning is praised, and as its cause, the accomplishment in knowledge. And through both of these, due to their inseparability, the accomplishment in power and so on are also praised. In this way also, it should be known that this discourse has praise as its precursor. Alternatively, it should be understood that this discourse indeed has praise as its precursor, because the commentary was begun by placing first the praise of the Teacher with phrases such as, “whose knowledge moves unhindered through all dhammas.” But this praise was set forth by way of clarifying the ability to answer in accordance with the questioner's disposition, and this is the teacher's custom: that is, the praise of the Teacher at the beginning of a commentary, in conformity with the Dhamma to be commented upon. Therefore, for this reason, the praise was set forth here in this way. While pointing out the reason for the manner of praise being spoken, having first set down the verse of reply, and having shown the verse of questioning—by way of its prompting cause—both in its form and in its meaning, the commentary on the intended Dhamma was made by placing first the praise of the Blessed One, which illuminates the ability to give an unerring answer to that question. Therefore, he said, “Having been established in virtue,” and so on. Therein, the meaning of the verse will become clear later.

Itītiādīsu itīti ayaṃ iti-saddo hetu parisamāpanādipadatthavipariyāyapakārāvadhāraṇanidassanādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa “ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā ‘rūpa’nti vuccatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.79) hetumhi āgato. “Tasmātiha me, bhikkhave, dhammadāyādā bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā. Atthi me tumhesu anukampā ‘kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.29) parisamāpane. “Iti vā iti evarūpā naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā paṭivirato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.197) ādiatthe. “Māgaṇḍiyoti tassa brāhmaṇassa saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro nāmaṃ [M 1.0004] nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ nirutti byañjanaṃ abhilāpo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 73, 75) padatthavipariyāye. “Iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito. Saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito. Saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.124) pakāre. “Atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ, kiṃpaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti ce vadeyya, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīya”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.96) avadhāraṇe, sanniṭṭhāneti attho. “Atthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto, natthīti kho, kaccāna, ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) nidassane. Idhāpi nidassane daṭṭhabbo, pakāretipi vattuṃ vaṭṭateva. Paṭhamo pana iti-saddo parisamāpane daṭṭhabbo. Hīti avadhāraṇe. Idanti āsannapaccakkhavacanaṃ yathādhigatassa suttapadassa abhimukhīkaraṇato.

In such terms as “iti,” this word “iti” has many different meanings, such as: reason, conclusion, 'and so on', inversion of the word's meaning, manner, determination, and illustration. For instance, it occurs in the sense of reason in such passages as, “It is subject to alteration, monks, therefore it is called ‘form.’” In the sense of conclusion, as in, “Therefore, monks, be my heirs in Dhamma, not heirs in material things. I have compassion for you, thinking, ‘How might my disciples become heirs in Dhamma, not heirs in material things?’” In the sense of 'and so on', as in, “Or thus, and so on, he abstains from such things as dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows.” In the sense of inversion of the word's meaning, as in, “‘Māgaṇḍiya’ is that brahmin’s designation, term, concept, expression, name, appellation, designation, utterance, phrasing, and speech.” In the sense of manner, as in, “In this manner, monks, the fool is with peril, the wise one is without peril. The fool is with affliction, the wise one is without affliction. The fool is with danger, the wise one is without danger.” In the sense of determination, the meaning is 'decision', as in, “When asked, ‘Ānanda, does aging-and-death exist dependent on a condition?’ one should say, ‘It exists.’ If one were to say, ‘Dependent on what condition is aging-and-death?’ one should say, ‘Aging-and-death is dependent on the condition of birth.’” In the sense of illustration, as in, “‘It exists,’ Kaccāna, this is one extreme. ‘It does not exist,’ Kaccāna, this is the second extreme.” Here also, it should be understood in the sense of illustration, though it is also fitting to say it is in the sense of manner. But the first 'iti'-word should be understood in the sense of conclusion. 'Hi' is in the sense of determination. 'Idaṃ' is a word indicating what is near and directly perceived, because of bringing face to face the sutta passage that has been taken up.

Vuttanti ayaṃ vutta-saddo saupasaggo, anupasaggo ca vappanavāpasamīkaraṇakesohāraṇajīvitavuttipamuttabhāvapāvacanapavattitaajjhesanakathanādīsu dissati. Tathā hi ayaṃ –

In the word “vuttaṃ,” this word “vutta,” both with and without a prefix, is seen in the meanings of: sowing, smoothing what has been sown, removing hair, livelihood, the state of being free, causing to proceed as noble speech, requesting, speaking, and so on. For instance, this—

“Gāvo [V 1.0005] tassa pajāyanti, khette vuttaṃ virūhati;

Vuttānaṃ phalamasnāti, yo mittānaṃ na dubbhatī”ti. –

“His cows are born, what is sown in the field sprouts, and he enjoys the fruit of what is sown—he who does not betray friends.”

Ādīsu (jā. 2.22.19) vappane āgato. “No ca kho paṭivutta”ntiādīsu (pārā. 289) aṭṭhadantakādīhi vāpasamīkaraṇe. “Kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.426) kesohāraṇe. “Pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharatī”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 332) jīvitavuttiyaṃ. “Seyyathāpi nāma paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto abhabbo haritatthāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.59; pārā. 92; pāci. 666; mahāva. 129) bandhanato pamuttabhāve. “Yesamidaṃ etarahi porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihita”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.285; ma. ni. 2.427; mahāva. 300) pāvacanabhāvena pavattite. Loke pana “vutto guṇo vutto pārāyano”tiādīsu ajjhesane. “Vuttaṃ kho [M 1.0005] panetaṃ bhagavatā ‘dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā’ti”ādīsu (ma. ni. 1.30) kathane. Idhāpi kathane eva daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā “iti hi evameva idaṃ suttaṃ desita”nti yathānikkhittaṃ gāthaṃ desitabhāvena nidasseti. Tassā vā desitākāraṃ avadhāreti.

It occurs in the sense of sowing in such passages as (Jā 2.22.19). In the sense of levelling a field for cultivation with an eight-toothed harrow and so forth, as in ‘but not yet harrowed’ (Pārā 289). In the sense of removing hair, as in ‘the young brahmin Kāpaṭika with shaven head’ (MN 2.426). In the sense of livelihood, as in ‘his hair of pride fallen, living on what is given by others, he dwells with a mind like a wild animal’ (Cv 332). In the sense of having fallen from its stalk, as in ‘Just as a withered leaf fallen from its stalk is incapable of returning to greenness’ (MN 3.59; Pārā 92; Pāci 666; Mv 129). In the sense of being promulgated by way of a noble utterance, as in ‘This ancient mantrapada sung, uttered, and well-established by them at present’ (DN 1.285; MN 2.427; Mv 300). In the world, however, it occurs in the sense of requesting, as in ‘Guṇa was requested, Pārāyana was requested’. In the sense of speaking, as in ‘This has been spoken by the Blessed One: “Be heirs to my Dhamma, monks, not heirs to material things”’ (MN 1.30). Here too it should be understood in the sense of speaking alone. Therefore, the phrase ‘thus indeed, in this way, this sutta was taught’ indicates the verse as it was laid down, by way of its having been taught. Or, it ascertains the manner in which it was taught.

Kasmāti hetumhi nissakkaṃ. Panāti vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ. Ubhayenāpi kāraṇaṃ pucchati. Etanti yathāvuttaṃ suttapadaṃ paccāmasati. Vuttanti pucchānimittaṃ. Tadatthassa attano buddhiyaṃ viparivattamānataṃ upādāya “ida”nti vatvā puna bhagavatā bhāsitākāraṃ sandhāya “eta”nti vuttaṃ. Sakalena panānena vacanena desanāya nidānaṃ jotitaṃ hoti. Parato tassā desakadesakālapaṭiggāhake vibhāvetuṃ “bhagavantaṃ kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kirāti anussavanatthe nipāto. Tena vuccamānassatthassa anu anu suyyamānataṃ dīpeti. Rattibhāgeti rattiyā ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse, majjhimayāmeti adhippāyo. Vessavaṇādayo viya apākaṭanāmadheyyattā aññataro. Devo eva devaputto. Saṃsayasamugghāṭatthanti vicikicchāsallasamuddharaṇatthaṃ pucchīti yojanā. “Saṃsayasamugghāṭattha”nti ca iminā pañcasu pucchāsu ayaṃ vimaticchedanāpucchāti dasseti. Yena atthena taṇhā “jaṭā”ti vuttā, tameva atthaṃ dassetuṃ “jāliniyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sā hi aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritappabhedo attano avayavabhūto eva jālo etissā atthīti “jālinī”ti vuccati.

The word “kasmā” (why?) is in the ablative case, in the sense of cause. The particle “pana” is merely a verbal embellishment. By both, it asks for the reason. The word “etaṃ” (this) refers back to the discourse passage mentioned as such. The word “vuttaṃ” (spoken) is the indicator of the question. Having said “idaṃ” (this) with reference to the meaning of that question as it is being revolved in one’s own understanding, it is then said “etaṃ” (that), referring to the manner in which it was spoken by the Blessed One. By this entire statement, moreover, the prelude of the teaching is illuminated. Further on, in order to clarify the teacher, the place, the time, and the recipients of that teaching, it is said “the Blessed One, it is said,” and so forth. Therein, the particle “kira” is in the sense of hearsay. By it, the state of the meaning being spoken of as having been heard successively is indicated. “In a part of the night” (rattibhāge) means in one portion of the night; the intention is the middle watch. Like Vessavaṇa and others, he is called “a certain one” due to his unmanifest name. A deva is indeed a devaputta. “For the sake of dispelling doubt” (saṃsayasamugghāṭatthaṃ) means for the purpose of extracting the dart of uncertainty; the construction is that he asked. And by this phrase “for the sake of dispelling doubt,” it is shown that among the five questions, this is a question for cutting off doubt. In order to show the very meaning by which craving is called “tangle” (jaṭā), “net-like” (jālinī) and so forth is said. For that craving indeed has a net, which is its own constituent part, consisting of the differentiation of the one hundred and eight kinds of craving’s proliferation; hence it is called “net-like” (jālinī).

Idānissā [V 1.0006] jaṭākārena pavattiṃ dassetuṃ “sā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rūpādīsu ārammaṇesūti tassā pavattiṭṭhānamāha, rūpādichaḷārammaṇavinimuttassa taṇhāvisayassa abhāvato. Heṭṭhupariyavasenāti kadāci rūpārammaṇe kadāci yāva dhammārammaṇe kadāci dhammārammaṇe kadāci yāva rūpārammaṇeti evaṃ heṭṭhā, upari ca pavattivasena. Desanākkamena cettha heṭṭhupariyatā daṭṭhabbā. Kadāci kāmabhave kadāci rūpabhave kadāci arūpabhave kadāci vā arūpabhave…pe… kadāci kāmabhaveti evamettha heṭṭhupariyavasena pavatti veditabbā. Sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanasabhāvattā aparāparuppatti ettha saṃsibbananti āha “punappunaṃ uppajjanato”ti. “Saṃsibbanaṭṭhenā”ti idaṃ yena sambandhena jaṭā viyāti jaṭāti [M 1.0006] jaṭātaṇhānaṃ upamūpameyyatā, taṃdassanaṃ. Ayaṃ hettha attho – yathā jālino veḷugumbassa sākhā, kosasañcayādayo ca attanā attano avayavehi saṃsibbitā vinaddhā “jaṭā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ taṇhāpi saṃsibbanasabhāvenāti, “saṃsibbitaṭṭhenā”ti vā pāṭho, attanāva attano saṃsibbitabhāvenāti attho. Ayaṃ hi taṇhā kosakārakimi viya attanāva attānampi saṃsibbantī pavattati. Tenāha bhagavā “rūpataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.86; vibha. 203). Ime sattā “mama ida”nti pariggahitaṃ vatthuṃ attanibbisesaṃ maññamānā abbhantarimaṃ karonti. Abbhantarattho ca antosaddoti sakaparikkhāre uppajjamānāpi taṇhā “antojaṭā”ti vuttā. Pabbajitassa pattādi, gahaṭṭhassa hatthiādi sakaparikkhāro.

Now, to illustrate its occurrence in the manner of a tangle, it is said, “For she...” Therein, by the phrase “regarding objects such as form, etc.,” it states her basis of occurrence, because there is no domain of craving devoid of the six objects beginning with form. “By way of below and above” means sometimes with form as object, sometimes up to mental phenomena as object; sometimes with mental phenomena as object, sometimes up to form as object—thus, by way of occurrence below and above. Here, the 'below-and-above' aspect should be understood according to the order of the teaching. Sometimes in the sensual realm, sometimes in the form realm, sometimes in the formless realm; or sometimes in the formless realm... and so on... sometimes in the sensual realm—thus here the occurrence should be understood by way of below and above. Because all conditioned things have the nature of perishing moment by moment, their successive arising is here the 'stitching together'; hence it is said, “because of arising again and again.” The phrase ‘in the sense of stitching together’ is that which shows the analogy between 'tangle' and 'craving': by which connection it is like a tangle, and is thus called a 'tangle'. The meaning here is this: Just as the branches of a netted bamboo thicket, and accumulations of cocoons and the like, being stitched together and interwoven by their own parts, are called a ‘tangle’, so too craving, by its nature of stitching together, is called a 'tangle'. Alternatively, the reading is ‘in the sense of being stitched together’, meaning by the state of being stitched together by itself. For this craving proceeds by stitching together even itself, like a silkworm making a cocoon. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Craving for forms in the world is a dear and agreeable form; wherein this craving, when arising, arises; wherein, when settling, it settles,” etc. These beings, regarding an object taken possession of with the thought, “This is mine,” as no different from themselves, make it internal. And the word “anta” has the meaning of “internal,” so craving, even when arising regarding one’s own requisites, is called an “internal tangle.” For one who has gone forth, the bowl, etc., and for a householder, the elephant, etc., are one’s own requisites.

“Attā”ti bhavati ettha abhimānoti attabhāvo, upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Sarīranti keci. Mama attabhāvo sundaro, asukassa viya mama attabhāvo bhaveyyāti vā ādinā sakaattabhāvādīsu taṇhāya uppajjamānākāro veditabbo. Attano cakkhādīni ajjhattikāyatanāni. Attano, paresañca rūpādīni bāhirāyatanāni. Paresaṃ sabbāni vā, saparasantatipariyāpannāni vā cakkhādīni ajjhattikāyatanāni. Tathā rūpādīni bāhirāyatanāni. Parittamahaggatabhavesu pavattiyāpi taṇhāya antojaṭābahijaṭābhāvo veditabbo. Kāmabhavo hi kassacipi kilesassa avikkhambhitattā kathañcipi avimutto ajjhattaggahaṇassa visesapaccayoti “ajjhattaṃ, anto”ti ca vuccati. Tabbipariyāyato rūpārūpabhavo “bahiddhā, bahī”ti ca. Tenāha bhagavā “ajjhattasaṃyojano puggalo, bahiddhāsaṃyojano puggalo”ti (a. ni. 2.37). Visayabhedena, pavattiākārabhedena ca anekabhedabhinnampi taṇhaṃ [V 1.0007] jaṭābhāvasāmaññena ekanti gahetvā “tāya evaṃ uppajjamānāya jaṭāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā pana “pajā”ti vuttasattasantānapariyāpannā eva hutvā punappunaṃ taṃ jaṭentī vinandhantī pavattatīti āha “jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā”ti. Tathā hi paramatthato yadipi avayavabyatirekena samudāyo natthi, ekadeso pana samudāyo nāma na hotīti avayavato samudāyaṃ bhinnaṃ katvā upamūpameyyaṃ dassento “yathā nāma [M 1.0007] veḷujaṭādīhi…pe… saṃsibbitā”ti āha. Imaṃ jaṭanti sambandho. Tīsu dhātūsu ekampi asesetvā saṃsibbanena tedhātukaṃ jaṭetvā ṭhitaṃ. Tenassā mahāvisayataṃ, vijaṭanassa ca sudukkarabhāvamāha. “Vijaṭetuṃ ko samattho”ti iminā “vijaṭaye”ti padaṃ sattiatthaṃ, na vidhiādiatthanti dasseti.

Herein, conceit as 'self' arises; therefore, it is called 'self-existence' (attabhāva), which is the five aggregates of clinging. Some say 'body.' The mode of craving's arising in regard to one's own self-existence and so forth should be understood thus: 'My self-existence is beautiful,' or 'May my self-existence be like so-and-so's,' and so on. One’s own eye and so forth are the internal sense bases. One’s own and others’ forms and so forth are the external sense bases. Alternatively, all of others’ sense bases, or the eye and so forth included in one’s own and others’ continuums, are internal sense bases. Similarly, forms and so forth are external sense bases. Even by its occurrence in the limited and exalted realms, the state of craving as an internal tangle and an external tangle should be understood. For the sensual realm, being one where no defilement whatsoever is suppressed, and where one is in no way freed, is a special condition for being taken as 'internal'; hence it is called 'internal' and 'within.' Conversely, the form and formless realms are called 'external' and 'outside.' Therefore the Blessed One said: 'A person with internal fetters, a person with external fetters' (AN 4.10). Though craving is distinguished into many varieties by differences in object and differences in mode of occurrence, it is taken as one by the common characteristic of being a tangle; thus it is said: 'by that tangle arising in this way.' But that craving, being included within the continuum of beings called 'progeny' (pajā), operates by repeatedly entangling and binding them; thus it is said: 'Progeny are entangled by the tangle.' For thus indeed, though in the ultimate sense there is no aggregate apart from its parts—and a part is not called an aggregate—yet, distinguishing the aggregate from its parts, he illustrates the comparison and the object of comparison, saying: 'Just as bamboo thickets and so forth... are interwoven.' The connection is with 'this tangle.' Leaving not even one of the three realms unentangled, it stands having entangled the triple realm by interweaving. By this, he speaks of its vast range and the extreme difficulty of disentangling it. By this phrase, 'Who is capable of disentangling it?', he shows that the word 'vijaṭaye' has the meaning of potentiality, not of injunction or the like.

Evaṃ “antojaṭā”tiādinā puṭṭho pana assa devaputtassa imaṃ gāthamāhāti sambandho. “Edisova imaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjeyyā”ti satthāraṃ guṇato dassento “sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇacāro”tiādimāha. Tattha sabbadhammesūti atītādibhedabhinnesu sabbesu ñeyyadhammesu. Appaṭihatañāṇacāroti anavasesañeyyāvaraṇappahānena nissaṅgacārattā navihatañāṇapavattiko. Etena tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇatāvibhāvanena ādito tiṇṇaṃ āveṇikadhammānaṃ gahaṇeneva tadekalakkhaṇatāya tadavinābhāvato ca bhagavato sesāveṇikadhammānampi gahitabhāvo veditabbo. Dibbanti kāmaguṇādīhi kīḷanti laḷanti, tesu vā viharanti, vijayasamatthatāyogena paccatthike vijetuṃ icchanti, issariyadhanādisakkāradānaggahaṇaṃ, taṃtaṃatthānusāsanañca karontā voharanti, puññātisayayogānubhāvappattāya jutiyā jotanti, yathādhippetañca visayaṃ appaṭighātena gacchanti, yathicchitanipphādane ca sakkontīti devā. Atha vā devanīyā taṃtaṃbyasananittharaṇatthikehi saraṇaṃ parāyaṇanti gamanīyā, abhitthavanīyā vā, sobhāvisesayogena kamanīyāti vā devā. Te tividhā – sammutidevā upapattidevā visuddhidevāti. Bhagavā pana niratisayāya abhiññākīḷāya uttamehi dibbabrahmaariyavihārehi saparasantānagatapañcavidhamāravijayicchānipphattiyā cittissariyasattadhanādisammāpaṭipatti aveccapasādasakkāradānaggahaṇasaṅkhātena, dhammasabhāvapuggalajjhāsayānurūpānusāsanīsaṅkhātena ca vohārātisayena paramāya paññāsarīrappabhāsaṅkhātāya jutiyā, anaññasādhāraṇāya ñāṇasarīragatiyā, māravijayasabbasabbaññuguṇaparahitanipphādanesu appaṭihatāya sattiyā ca samannāgatattā sadevakena lokena “saraṇa”nti gamanīyato, abhitthavanīyato, bhattivasena kamanīyato ca sabbe [V 1.0008] te deve tehi guṇehi abhibhuyya ṭhitattā tesaṃ devānaṃ seṭṭho uttamo devoti devadevo. Sabbadevehi [M 1.0008] pūjanīyataro devoti vā, visuddhidevabhāvassa vā sabbaññuguṇālaṅkārassa vā adhigatattā aññesaṃ devānaṃ atisayena devoti devadevo.

Furthermore, having been questioned thus with 'inner tangle,' and so on, the Blessed One spoke this verse to that devaputta; this is the connection. To show the Teacher's qualities, the commentator says, 'Only such a one could answer this question,' and then states, 'Unobstructed is his knowledge and conduct among all phenomena,' and so on. Therein, 'among all phenomena' means among all knowable phenomena, distinguished by the divisions of past, and so on. 'Unobstructed is his knowledge and conduct' means that the proceeding of his knowledge is unhindered because he proceeds without attachment, through the abandoning of all obstructions to the knowable without remainder. By this revelation of his unobstructed knowledge in the three times, it should be understood that through the inclusion of the first three unique qualities, the Blessed One's remaining unique qualities are also included, because they share the same characteristic and are inseparable from them. They are called 'devas' because they sport (dibbanti), that is, they play and delight in sensual pleasures, or they dwell in them; or because they wish to conquer their enemies, being endowed with the capacity for victory; or because they transact affairs by giving and receiving honor, such as sovereignty and wealth, and by instructing in various matters of welfare; or because they shine with a radiance attained through the power of an abundance of merit; or because they go without obstruction to whatever destination they desire; or because they are capable of accomplishing whatever they wish. Or alternatively, they are called 'devas' because they are to be approached (devanīyā) as a refuge and resort by those who wish to escape from various misfortunes; or they are to be praised; or they are desirable due to their special beauty. They are of three kinds: devas by convention, devas by birth, and devas by purity. But the Blessed One, because he is endowed with the unsurpassed sport of higher knowledge; with the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abidings; with the fulfillment of the wish to conquer the five kinds of Māra concerning his own and others' continuums; with the excellence in transaction designated as sovereignty over mind, the giving of right practice such as the seven noble treasures, and the receiving of unwavering confidence and honor; with the excellence in instruction designated as teaching that is in accordance with the nature of the Dhamma and the disposition of individuals; with the supreme radiance designated as the lustre of the wisdom-body and the physical body; with the unique movement of his knowledge-body and physical body; and with unobstructed power in conquering Māra, accomplishing all the qualities of omniscience, and fulfilling the welfare of others; and because he is to be approached as a 'refuge' by the world with its devas, is to be praised, and is beloved on account of his devotion; and because he stands having surpassed all those devas by these qualities, he is the best, the highest deva of those devas; thus, he is 'devadevo', the Deva of devas. Or, he is a deva more worthy of veneration than all devas; thus, he is 'devadevo'. Or, because he has attained the state of a deva by purity and the adornment of the qualities of omniscience, he is a deva who surpasses other devas; thus, he is 'devadevo'.

Aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sakkānaṃ, mahābrahmānañca guṇābhibhavanato adhiko atisayo atirekataro vā sakko brahmā cāti sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā. Ñāṇappahānadesanāvisesesu sadevake loke kenaci avikkhambhanīyaṭṭhānatāya kutocipi utrastābhāvato catūhi vesārajjehi visāradoti catuvesārajjavisārado. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhāti tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā…pe… vesārajjappatto viharāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.150; a. ni. 4.8). Ṭhānāṭhānañāṇādīhi dasahi ñāṇabalehi samannāgatattā dasabaladharo. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “idha tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato, aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādi (a. ni. 10.21; vibha. 809). Yaṃ kiñci ñeyyaṃ nāma, tattha sabbattheva anāvaṭañāṇatāya anāvaraṇañāṇo. Tañca sabbaṃ samantato sabbākārato hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya paccakkhato dassanasamatthena ñāṇacakkhunā samannāgatattā samantacakkhu, sabbaññūti attho. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi pacchimāni dve asādhāraṇañāṇāni gahitāni. Bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato buddhānussatiniddese (visuddhi. 1.123 ādayo) vitthārato āgamissati.

In countless world systems, by surpassing in qualities the countless Sakkas and the great Brahmās, he is a Sakka and a Brahmā who is superior, surpassing, and more excellent; thus, he is the Sakka of Sakkas and the Brahmā of Brahmās. Regarding the special qualities of his knowledge, abandoning, and teaching, in the world with its devas, due to his unassailable standing by anyone and his freedom from fear from any quarter, he is confident with the four kinds of fearlessness; thus, he is endowed with the four kinds of fearlessness. In reference to this, it is said: “For you, who declare yourself a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things are not fully understood’—in such a case, surely no ascetic or brahmin…pe… I dwell having attained fearlessness.” Endowed with the ten powers of knowledge, such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible, he is the possessor of the ten powers. In reference to this, it is said: “Here, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible, and what is impossible as impossible,” and so on. Whatever is to be known, his knowledge is unobstructed in every respect; thus, he has unobstructed knowledge. And because he is endowed with the eye of knowledge that is able to see all of that directly, completely, and in every aspect, like a myrobalan fruit on the palm of the hand, he is the All-Seeing One; the meaning is, the All-Knowing One. Now, by these two terms, the latter two unique kinds of knowledge are included. Due to reasons such as being fortunate, he is the Blessed One. What should be said here will come in detail later in the exposition on the recollection of the Buddha.

Ettha ca “sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇacāro”ti iminā tiyaddhāruḷhānaṃ pucchānaṃ bhagavato byākaraṇasamatthatāya dassitāya kiṃ devatānampi pucchaṃ byākātuṃ samattho bhagavāti āsaṅkāya tannivattanatthaṃ “devadevo”ti vuttaṃ. Devānaṃ atidevo sakko devānamindo devatānaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjeti, “tato imassa ko viseso”ti cintentānaṃ tannivattanatthaṃ “sakkānaṃ atisakko”ti vuttaṃ. Sakkenapi pucchitamatthaṃ sanaṅkumārādayo brahmāno vissajjenti, “tato imassa ko atisayo”ti cintentānaṃ tannivattanatthaṃ “brahmānaṃ atibrahmā”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ cassa viseso catuvesārajjadasabalañāṇehi pākaṭo jātoti dassanatthaṃ “catu…pe… [M 1.0009] dharo”ti vuttaṃ. Imāni ca ñāṇāni imassa ñāṇadvayassa adhigamena saheva siddhānīti dassanatthaṃ “anāvaraṇañāṇo samantacakkhū”ti vuttaṃ. Tayidaṃ ñāṇadvayaṃ puññañāṇasambhārūpacayasiddhāya bhaggadosatāya siddhanti dassento “bhagavā”ti avocāti. Evametesaṃ [V 1.0009] padānaṃ gahaṇe payojanaṃ, anupubbi ca veditabbā. Yaṃ panetaṃ pacchimaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇanti ñāṇadvayaṃ, taṃ atthato abhinnaṃ. Ekameva hi taṃ ñāṇaṃ visayapavattimukhena aññehi asādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ dvidhā katvā vuttaṃ. Anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutidhammārammaṇatāya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tatthāvaraṇābhāvato nissaṅgacāramupādāya “anāvaraṇañāṇa”ntipi vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato buddhānussatiniddese (visuddhi. 1.123 ādayo) vakkhāma.

And here, by the phrase “the movement of knowledge is unobstructed in all phenomena,” since the Blessed One's ability to answer questions pertaining to the three periods of time was demonstrated, lest the doubt arise, “Is the Blessed One capable of answering even the questions of devas?,” it is said, “God of gods.” Sakka, the lord of devas, who is the supreme deva of devas, answers the questions of deities. To ward off the thought of those who might think, “What is his distinction compared to him?,” it is said, “Sakka of Sakkas.” Even a matter questioned by Sakka, Brahmās such as Sanaṅkumāra answer. To ward off the thought of those who might think, “What is his pre-eminence compared to him?,” it is said, “Brahmā of Brahmās.” And to show that this distinction of his has become evident through the four fearlessnesses and the ten powers of knowledge, it is said, “endowed with the four…pe…possessor.” And to show that these knowledges are accomplished simultaneously with the attainment of this twofold knowledge, it is said, “he has unobstructed knowledge and is the All-Seeing One.” And showing that this twofold knowledge is accomplished by virtue of the destruction of defilements, which was perfected through the accumulation of the requisites of merit and knowledge, he said, “Bhagavā.” Thus, the purpose for the inclusion of these terms, and their sequence, should be understood. Now, this latter twofold knowledge—unobstructed knowledge and omniscient knowledge—is essentially one. For that single knowledge is spoken of as twofold to show its unique nature in relation to others by way of its operation regarding its object. It is called omniscient knowledge by virtue of its having all conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional phenomena without remainder as its object; and on account of its unimpeded movement due to the absence of obstruction therein, it is also called “unobstructed knowledge.” As for what should be said here, that we will state later in the exposition on the recollection of the Buddha.

2. Mahante sīlakkhandhādike esī gavesīti mahesi, bhagavā. Tena mahesinā. Vaṇṇayantoti vivaranto vitthārento. Yathābhūtanti aviparītaṃ. Sīlādibhedananti sīlasamādhipaññādivibhāgaṃ. Sudullabhanti aṭṭhakkhaṇavajjitena navamena khaṇena laddhabbattā suṭṭhu dullabhaṃ. Sīlādisaṅgahanti sīlādikkhandhattayasaṅgahaṃ. Ariyamaggo hi tīhi khandhehi saṅgahito sappadesattā nagaraṃ viya rajjena, na tayo khandhā ariyamaggena nippadesattā. Vuttañhetaṃ “na kho, āvuso visākha, ariyena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena tayo khandhā saṅgahitā; tīhi ca kho, āvuso visākha, khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito”ti (ma. ni. 1.462). Kilesacorehi aparipanthanīyatāya khemaṃ. Antadvayaparivajjanato, māyādikāyavaṅkādippahānato ca ujuṃ. Sabbesaṃ saṃkilesadhammānaṃ māraṇavasena gamanato pavattanato, nibbānassa magganato, nibbānatthikehi maggitabbato ca maggaṃ. Visuddhiyāti nibbānāya, visuddhibhāvāya vā, arahattāyāti attho.

2. Because he sought (esī) great (mahante) qualities such as the aggregates of virtue, he is a great seeker (mahesi); the Blessed One. By that great seeker. 'Explaining' means revealing and elaborating. 'As it truly is' means without distortion. 'The divisions of virtue and so forth' refers to the classifications of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and so on. 'Exceedingly rare' means very difficult to obtain, as it is to be attained with the ninth moment, which excludes the eight unfavorable moments. 'The inclusion of virtue and so on' refers to the inclusion of the three aggregates beginning with virtue. For the Noble Path is encompassed by the three aggregates because it is a component part, like a city by a kingdom; the three aggregates are not encompassed by the Noble Path because they are not a component part. And this was said: “Indeed, friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not encompassed by the Noble Eightfold Path; rather, the Noble Eightfold Path is encompassed by the three aggregates.” 'Safe' because it cannot be assailed by the thieves that are the defilements. 'Straight' because it avoids the two extremes and abandons deceit, bodily crookedness, and so forth. 'The path' (magga) because it proceeds (gacchati) by way of destroying (mārayati) all defiling states, because it seeks (maggati) Nibbāna, and because it is to be sought (maggitabba) by those who desire Nibbāna. 'For purity' means for Nibbāna, or for the state of purity, or for Arahantship—this is the meaning.

Yathābhūtaṃ ajānantāti evaṃ sīlavisuddhiādivisuddhiparamparāya adhigantabbo evarūpo evaṃkiccako evamatthoti yāthāvato anavabujjhantā. Sakalasaṃkilesato, saṃsārato ca suddhiṃ vimuttiṃ kāmenti patthentīti suddhikāmā. Api-saddo sambhāvane. Tena na kevalaṃ sīlamattena parituṭṭhā, atha kho visuddhikāmāpi samānāti dasseti. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Bhāvanāya yuttapayuttatāya yogino vāyamantāpi visuddhiṃ [M 1.0010] uddissa payogaṃ parakkamaṃ karontāpi upāyassa anadhigatattā visuddhiṃ nādhigacchantīti yojanā. Tesanti yogīnaṃ. Kāmañcāyaṃ visuddhimaggo samantabhaddakattā savanadhāraṇaparicayādipasutānaṃ sabbesampi pāmojjakaro, yogīnaṃ pana sātisayaṃ pamodahetūti āha “tesaṃ pāmojjakaraṇa”nti. Bāhirakanikāyantaraladdhīhi asammissatāya suṭṭhu visuddhavinicchayattā suvisuddhavinicchayaṃ. Mahāvihāravāsīnanti attano apassayabhūtaṃ nikāyaṃ dasseti[V 1.0010]. Desanānayanissitanti dhammasaṃvaṇṇanānayasannissitaṃ. Ettha ca “tesaṃ pāmojjakaraṇa”ntiādinā sabbasaṃkilesamalavisuddhatāya visuddhiṃ nibbānaṃ patthentānaṃ yogīnaṃ ekaṃsena tadāvahattā pāmojjakaro ñāṇuttarehi sammāpaṭipannehi adhiṭṭhitattā suṭṭhu sammā visuddhavinicchayo mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ kathāmaggoti dasseti. Sakkaccaṃ me bhāsato sakkaccaṃ nisāmayathāti yojetabbaṃ.

"Not knowing as it truly is": Not comprehending accurately that this path is to be attained through the sequence of purities beginning with the purity of virtue, that it has such a nature, such a function, and such a meaning. "Desiring purity": Because they desire and long for purity and liberation from all defilements and from saṃsāra, they are called 'those who desire purity'. The particle api is in the sense of affirmation. By this, it is shown that they are not merely content with virtue alone, but rather, they are also those who desire purity. "Here" means in this Dispensation. The connection is as follows: Yogis, due to being constantly engaged in development, though striving and making effort and exertion for the sake of purity, do not attain purity because the means has not been attained. "For them" means for the yogis. Although this Path of Purity, being entirely auspicious, brings joy to all who are diligent in listening, retaining, and familiarizing themselves with it, for the yogis it is a cause of surpassing delight; thus it is said, "bringing joy to them." "A perfectly purified discernment": because it is unmixed with the tenets of external schools and other sects, and because its discernment is thoroughly purified. "Of the dwellers of the Great Monastery": this indicates the school that is their own support. "Dependent on the method of teaching": dependent on the method of expounding the Dhamma. And here, by the phrase beginning with "bringing joy to them," it is shown that the path of discourse of the dwellers of the Great Monastery brings delight to yogis who long for purity, that is, Nibbāna, which is purity from all stains of defilements, because it unequivocally brings that [Nibbāna]; and that it is a perfectly and rightly purified discernment because it is established by those with supreme knowledge and right practice. "Listen carefully to me as I speak attentively"—this is how it should be connected.

Ettha ca “imissā dāni gāthāyā”ti iminā visuddhimaggabhāsanassa nissayaṃ, “kathitāya mahesinā”ti iminā tassa pamāṇabhāvaṃ, “yathābhūtaṃ atthaṃ sīlādibhedana”nti iminā aviparītapiṇḍatthaṃ, “sudullabhaṃ…pe… yogino”ti iminā nimittaṃ, “tesaṃ pāmojjakaraṇa”nti iminā payojanaṃ, “vaṇṇayanto atthaṃ, suvisuddhavinicchayaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ desanānayanissitaṃ, sakkacca”nti ca iminā karaṇappakāraṃ dassetvā “visuddhikāmā sabbepi, nisāmayatha sādhavo”ti iminā tattha sakkaccasavane sādhujane niyojeti. Sādhukaṃ savanapaṭibaddhā hi sāsanasampatti.

And here, by the phrase "of this stanza," he shows the basis of the exposition of the Visuddhimagga; by the phrase "spoken by the Great Sage," its authoritativeness; by the phrase "the meaning as it really is, with its divisions of virtue, etc.," the undistorted summary meaning; by the phrase "rare... a yogī," the cause; by the phrase "bringing joy to them," the purpose; and by the phrases "explaining the meaning," "a perfectly purified discernment of the dwellers of the Great Monastery," "dependent on the method of teaching," and "attentively," he shows the manner of composition. Then, having shown this, by the phrase "all you good people who desire purity, listen," he urges good people to listen attentively to it. For the accomplishment of the Dispensation is bound up with careful listening.

3. Vacanatthavibhāvanena paveditavisuddhimaggasāmaññatthassa visuddhimaggakathā vuccamānā abhiruciṃ uppādetīti padatthato visuddhimaggaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “tattha visuddhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti yadidaṃ “visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissa”nti ettha visuddhimaggapadaṃ vuttaṃ, tattha. Sabbamalavirahitanti sabbehi rāgādimalehi, sabbehi saṃkilesamalehi ca virahitaṃ vivittaṃ. Tato eva accantaparisuddhaṃ, sabbadā sabbathā ca visuddhanti attho. Yathāvuttaṃ visuddhiṃ maggati gavesati adhigacchati etenāti visuddhimaggo. Tenāha “maggoti adhigamūpāyo vuccatī”ti. Visuddhimaggoti ca nippariyāyena lokuttaramaggo veditabbo, tadupāyattā pana pubbabhāgamaggo, tannissayo kathāpabandho ca tathā vuccati.

3. For one for whom the general meaning of 'Visuddhimagga' has been made known by the explanation of the meaning of its words, the discourse on the Visuddhimagga, when spoken, produces delight. Therefore, in order to explain the Visuddhimagga according to the meaning of its terms, the passage beginning "Therein, purity..." was started. Therein, "tattha" refers to the term "Visuddhimagga" where it was stated, "I will speak on the Visuddhimagga." "Free from all stains" means devoid of and separated from all stains of lust and so on, and from all stains of defilement. For that very reason, it is utterly pure; the meaning is that it is purified always and in every way. The purification spoken of is sought (maggati), searched for, and attained by means of this; therefore, it is the Path of Purity (Visuddhimagga). For this reason, he said, "'Path' is called the means of attainment." And "Path of Purity" should be understood, in the direct sense, as the supramundane path. However, because it is a means to that, the preliminary path, and the treatise that is its basis, are also called thus.

Svāyaṃ [M 1.0011] visuddhimaggo satthārā desanāvilāsato, veneyyajjhāsayato ca nānānayehi desito, tesu ayameko nayo gahitoti dassetuṃ “so panāya”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha katthacīti kismiñci sutte. Vipassanāmattavasenevāti avadhāraṇena samathaṃ nivatteti. So hi tassā paṭiyogī, na sīlādi. Matta-saddena ca visesanivattiatthena savisesaṃ samādhiṃ nivatteti. So upacārappanābhedo vipassanāyānikassa desanāti katvā na samādhimattaṃ. Na hi [V 1.0011] khaṇikasamādhiṃ vinā vipassanā sambhavati. Vipassanāti ca tividhāpi anupassanā veditabbā, na aniccānupassanāva. Na hi aniccadassanamattena saccābhisamayo sambhavati. Yaṃ pana gāthāyaṃ aniccalakkhaṇasseva gahaṇaṃ kataṃ, taṃ yassa tadeva suṭṭhutaraṃ pākaṭaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, tādisassa vasena. Sopi hi itaraṃ lakkhaṇadvayaṃ vibhūtataraṃ katvā sammasitvā visesaṃ adhigacchati, na aniccalakkhaṇameva.

This Path of Purity was taught by the Teacher in various ways, according to the elegance of his teaching and the inclinations of those to be trained. To show that one method among these has been adopted, the passage beginning with “But this...” was started. Therein, "in some place" means in some discourse. By the phrase "merely by insight," with the emphasizing particle, he excludes serenity. For that is its counterpart, not virtue and so on. And by the word "matta," which has the meaning of excluding a specific quality, he excludes distinguished concentration. That is the concentration differentiated as access and absorption. Because this is a teaching for one whose vehicle is insight, it does not exclude mere concentration. For insight cannot occur without momentary concentration. And by "insight," the threefold contemplation should be understood, not merely the contemplation of impermanence. For the realization of the truths does not occur merely by seeing impermanence. As for the fact that in the verse only the characteristic of impermanence is mentioned, that is with reference to a person for whom that very characteristic appears very clearly and distinctly. For even such a person, having made the other two characteristics more manifest and having comprehended them, attains distinction, not by comprehending the characteristic of impermanence alone.

Sabbe saṅkhārāti sabbe tebhūmakasaṅkhārā, te hi sammasanīyā. Aniccāti na niccā addhuvā ittarā khaṇabhaṅgurāti. Paññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya. Passati sammasati. Atha pacchā udayabbayañāṇādīnaṃ uppattiyā uttarakālaṃ. Nibbindati dukkheti tasmiṃyeva aniccākārato diṭṭhe “sabbe saṅkhārā”ti vutte tebhūmake khandhapañcakasaṅkhāte dukkhe nibbindati nibbidāñāṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Esa maggo visuddhiyāti esa nibbidānupassanāsaṅkhāto virāgādīnaṃ kāraṇabhūto nibbānassa adhigamūpāyo.

"All conditioned phenomena": all conditioned phenomena of the three realms, for they are to be comprehended. "Impermanent": not permanent, unstable, transient, momentarily perishing. "With wisdom": with insight-wisdom. One sees, one comprehends. Then afterwards, at a time subsequent to the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away and so on. "One becomes disenchanted with suffering": one becomes disenchanted with, and attains the knowledge of disenchantment towards, that very suffering—designated as the five aggregates in the three realms and spoken of as 'all conditioned phenomena'—which has been seen in the mode of impermanence. "This is the path to purification": this, which is designated as the contemplation of disenchantment, being the cause of dispassion and so on, is the means for the attainment of Nibbāna.

Jhānapaññāvasenāti samathavipassanāvasena. Jhānanti cettha vipassanāya pādakabhūtaṃ jhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Yamhīti yasmiṃ puggale. Jhānañca paññā cāti etthāyamattho – yo puggalo jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā taṃ ussukkāpeti. Sa ve nibbānasantiketi so byattaṃ nibbānassa samīpe ekantato nibbānaṃ adhigacchatīti.

"Through jhāna and wisdom" means through serenity and insight. Herein, by "jhāna" is meant the jhāna that serves as the foundation for insight. "In whom" means in which person. In "jhāna and wisdom," this is the meaning: the person who, having made jhāna a foundation, establishes insight and then strives for it. By "he is indeed close to Nibbāna" is meant that he is clearly near Nibbāna; he certainly attains Nibbāna.

Kammanti maggacetanā. Sā hi apacayagāmitāya sattānaṃ suddhiṃ āvahati. Vijjāti sammādiṭṭhi. Sīlanti sammāvācākammantā. Jīvitamuttamanti sammāājīvo. Dhammoti avasesā cattāro ariyamaggadhammā. Atha vā kammanti sammākammantassa gahaṇaṃ. “Yā cāvuso visākha, sammādiṭṭhi, yo ca [M 1.0012] sammāsaṅkappo, ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) vacanato. Vijjāti sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Dhammoti samādhi “evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesu”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.378) viya. Taggahaṇeneva “yo cāvuso visākha, sammāvāyāmo, yā ca sammāsati, yo ca sammāsamādhi, ime dhammā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti vacanato sammāvāyāmasatīnampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīlanti sammāvācājīvānaṃ. Jīvitamuttamanti evarūpassa ariyapuggalassa jīvitaṃ uttamaṃ jīvitanti evamettha aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo vuttoti veditabbo.

"Action" is path-volition. For it indeed brings purity to beings by its nature of leading to Nibbāna. "Knowledge" is right view. "Virtue" is right speech and right action. "The highest life" is right livelihood. "Dhamma" is the remaining four noble path factors. Or alternatively: by "action" is meant the taking up of right action. As it is said: "Friend Visākha, right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom." By "knowledge" is meant the taking up of right view and right intention. By "Dhamma" is meant concentration, as in phrases such as: "Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature." By its inclusion, right effort and right mindfulness should also be understood as included, as it is said: "Friend Visākha, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration." By "virtue" is meant right speech and right livelihood. "The highest life" means that the life of such a noble person is the highest life. Thus, it should be understood that the Noble Eightfold Path is stated here.

Sīlādivasenāti [V 1.0012] sīlasamādhipaññāvīriyavasena. Sabbadāti samādānato pabhuti sabbakālaṃ. Sīlasampannoti catupārisuddhisīlasampadāya sampanno samannāgato. Paññavāti lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya samannāgato. Susamāhitoti taṃsampayuttena samādhinā suṭṭhu samāhito. Āraddhavīriyoti akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya paggahitavīriyo. Pahitattoti nibbānaṃ patipesitattatāya kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhacitto. Oghanti kāmoghādicatubbidhampi oghaṃ, saṃsāramahoghameva vā.

"Through virtue, etc." means through virtue, concentration, wisdom, and energy. "Always" means at all times, from the time of undertaking onwards. "Endowed with virtue" means endowed with the accomplishment of virtue consisting of the fourfold purity. "Wise" means endowed with mundane and supramundane wisdom. "Well-concentrated" means well-concentrated by means of the concentration associated therewith. "With energy aroused" means with energy exerted for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the undertaking of wholesome states. "Resolute" means having a mind sent forth towards Nibbāna, unconcerned with body and life. "The flood" means the fourfold flood beginning with the flood of sensuality, or indeed, the great flood of saṃsāra.

Ekāyanoti ekamaggo. Maggapariyāyo hi idha ayana-saddo, tasmā ekapathabhūto ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo, na dvedhāpathabhūtoti attho. Ekaṃ vā nibbānaṃ ayati gacchatīti ekāyano, ekena vā gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya vivekaṭṭhena ayitabbo paṭipajjitabboti ekāyano, ayanti tenāti vā ayano, ekassa seṭṭhassa bhagavato ayanoti ekāyano, tena uppāditattā, ekasmiṃ vā imasmiṃyeva dhammavinaye ayanoti ekāyano. Sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti rāgādimalehi, abhijjhāvisamalobhādiupakkilesehi ca sattānaṃ visuddhatthāya visujjhanatthāya. Yadidanti nipāto, ye imeti attho. Pubbe saraṇalakkhaṇena maggaṭṭhena ca maggoti vuttasseva kāyādivisayabhedena catubbidhattā “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti vuttaṃ. Sammappadhānādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena appamādābhiratiādīnaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo[M 1.0013]. Appamādābhiratiādivasenāpi hi katthaci visuddhimaggo desito. Yathāha –

"The one-way path" (ekāyano) means the single path (ekamaggo). For here the word 'ayana' is a synonym for 'path.' Therefore, this path, O bhikkhus, is a single track, not a path with two tracks—this is the meaning. Or, it is 'ekāyana' because it goes (ayati) to the one Nibbāna. Or, it is 'ekāyana' because it is to be travelled (ayitabbo) by one alone, in seclusion, having abandoned association with a group. Or, 'ayana' is that by which one goes, and 'ekāyana' is the path of the one, the supreme Blessed One, because it was established by him. Or, it is 'ekāyana' because it is the path found only in this one Dhamma and Discipline. "For the purification of beings" means for the sake of the purification and cleansing of beings from stains such as lust, and from defilements such as covetousness and unrighteous greed. "Namely" (yadidaṃ) is a particle, meaning "which are these." What was previously called "path" in the singular—due to its characteristic of mindfulness and its meaning as a path—is now called "the four foundations of mindfulness" in the plural because of its fourfold nature with respect to the domains of body, etc. In "in the right efforts, etc.," by the word "etc." the inclusion of qualities such as delight in heedfulness should be understood. For in some places, the path of purification is also taught by way of delight in heedfulness and so on. As it is said:

“Appamādarato bhikkhu, pamāde bhayadassi vā;

Abhabbo parihānāya, nibbānasseva santike”ti. (dha. pa. 32);

"The bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness, or who sees danger in heedlessness, is incapable of falling away; he is indeed in the vicinity of Nibbāna."

4. Tatrāti tassaṃ gāthāyaṃ. Upari vuccamānā gāthāya vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanā niddesapaṭiniddesaṭṭhāniyā, tato saṃkhittatarā atthavaṇṇanā uddesaṭṭhāniyāti āha “ayaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā”ti. Yathāuddiṭṭhassa hi atthassa niddesapaṭiniddesā sukarā, subodhā ca hontīti. Sīle patiṭṭhāyāti ettha sīleti kusalasīle. Yadipi “katame ca, thapati, akusalā sīlā”tiādīsu akusalā dhammāpi sīlanti āgatā. Vuccamānāya pana cittapaññābhāvanāya adhiṭṭhānāyogyatāya kiriyasīlānampi asambhavo, kuto itaresanti kusalasīlamevettha adhippetaṃ. Sīlaṃ paripūrayamānotiādīsu paripūrayamānoti paripālento, parivaḍḍhento vā, sabbabhāgehi saṃvaranto[V 1.0013], avītikkamanto cāti attho. Tathābhūto hi taṃ avijahanto tattha patiṭṭhito nāma hoti. “Sīle”ti hi idaṃ ādhāre bhummaṃ. Patiṭṭhāyāti duvidhā patiṭṭhā nissayūpanissayabhedato. Tattha upanissayapatiṭṭhā lokiyā, itarā lokuttarā abhinditvā gahaṇe. Bhinditvā pana gahaṇe yathā lokiyacittuppādesu sahajātānaṃ, purimapacchimānañca vasena nissayūpanissayapatiṭṭhā sambhavati, evaṃ lokuttaresu heṭṭhimamaggaphalasīlavasena upanissayapatiṭṭhāpi sambhavati. “Patiṭṭhāyā”ti ca padassa yadā upanissayapatiṭṭhā adhippetā, tadā “saddhaṃ upanissāyā”tiādīsu (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423) viya purimakālakiriyāvasena attho veditabbo. Tenāha “pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.431). Yadā pana nissayapatiṭṭhā adhippetā, tadā “cakkhuñca paṭiccā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.204; 3.421; saṃ. ni. 4.60) viya samānakālakiriyāvasena attho veditabbo. Sammāvācādayo hi attanā sampayuttānaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ sahajātavaseneva nissayapaccayā hontīti.

4. In `Tatrāti`, `tatra` means `tassaṃ gāthāyaṃ` (in that verse). The detailed explanation of the verse mentioned above serves as the exposition and re-exposition, while the more concise explanation of the meaning serves as the summary statement. Hence it is said, “This is a brief explanation.” For the exposition and re-exposition of a meaning that has been outlined are easy to do and readily comprehensible.

In `Sīle patiṭṭhāya` (Established in virtue), `sīle` means in wholesome virtue. Although in passages such as, “And what, carpenter, are unwholesome virtues?” and so forth, unwholesome states are also called 'virtue', nevertheless, because they are unsuitable as a foundation for the cultivation of concentration and wisdom being spoken of, even functional virtues are impossible, how much more so the others? Thus, only wholesome virtue is intended here.

In phrases such as `sīlaṃ paripūrayamāno` (fulfilling virtue), `paripūrayamāno` means protecting, developing, restraining in all aspects, and not transgressing; this is the meaning. For one who is such, not abandoning it, is said to be established therein. For the word `sīle` is in the locative case, indicating the basis.

Regarding `Patiṭṭhāya` (having been established): establishment is twofold, distinguished as dependence (nissaya) and strong dependence (upanissaya). Of these, when taken without distinction, the establishment as strong dependence is mundane, and the other is supramundane. But when taken with distinction, just as in mundane thought-processes establishment as dependence and strong dependence is possible by way of co-arisen states and preceding-and-succeeding states, so too in supramundane states, establishment as strong dependence is also possible by way of the virtue of the lower paths and fruitions.

And when for the word `patiṭṭhāya` the establishment as strong dependence is intended, then the meaning should be understood by way of a prior action, as in passages such as `saddhaṃ upanissāya` (relying on faith) and so forth. Hence it is said: “But previously, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are thoroughly purified.” When, however, the establishment as dependence is intended, then the meaning should be understood by way of a simultaneous action, as in passages such as `cakkhuñca paṭicca` (dependent on the eye) and so forth. For right speech and the like are conditions of dependence for right view and other states associated with them only by way of their co-arising nature.

Narati [M 1.0014] netīti naro, puriso. Yathā hi paṭhamapakatibhūto satto, itarāya pakatiyā seṭṭhaṭṭhena puri ucce ṭhāne seti pavattatīti “puriso”ti vuccati, evaṃ nayanaṭṭhena “naro”ti vuccati. Puttabhātubhūtopi hi puggalo mātujeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ netuṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, pageva itaro itarāsaṃ. Narena yogato, narassa ayanti vā nārī, itthī. Sāpi cettha kāmaṃ taṇhājaṭāvijaṭanasamatthatā atthi, padhānameva pana sattaṃ dassento “naro”ti āha yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.157, 255). Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana avibhāgena puggalapariyāyo ayanti dassetuṃ “naroti satto”ti vuttaṃ. Sapaññoti vipākabhūtāya saha paññāya pavattatīti sapañño. Tāya hi ādito paṭṭhāya santānavasena bahulaṃ pavattamānāya ayaṃ satto savisesaṃ “sapañño”ti vattabbataṃ arahati. Vipākapaññāpi hi santānavisesanena bhāvanāpaññuppattiyā upanissayo hoti ahetukadvihetukānaṃ tadabhāvato. Sampajaññasaṅkhātāya ca taṃtaṃkiccakārikāya paññāya vasena “sapañño”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana nipaka-saddena pārihārikapaññā gayhatīti vipākapaññāvasenevettha attho vutto. Kammajatihetukapaṭisandhipaññāyāti kammajāya tihetukapaṭisandhiyaṃ paññāyāti evaṃ tihetuka-saddo paṭisandhi-saddena sambandhitabbo, na paññā-saddena. Na hi paññā tihetukā atthi. Paṭisandhito pabhuti pavattamānā paññā “paṭisandhiyaṃ paññā”ti vuttā taṃmūlakattā, na paṭisandhikkhaṇe pavattā eva.

He is called 'nara' because he guides (neti); that is, a man (purisa). For just as the primary, natural being, by virtue of being superior to other kinds of beings, is called 'purisa' because he dwells or moves within a high place, so too he is called 'nara' due to his guiding role (nayana). For indeed, a person, even if he is a son or brother, stands in the position of guiding his mother and elder sisters—how much more so another man with respect to other women. A woman (nārī), that is, a female (itthī), is so called because she is associated with a man (nara), or because she belongs to a man. Although she too indeed has the capacity to disentangle the tangle of craving, the text indicates the primary being by saying 'nara', just as it says 'teacher of gods and humans'. In the commentary, however, to show that this is a synonym for a person without distinction, it is said: 'nara means a being'.

“Endowed with wisdom (sapañño)” means he proceeds accompanied by wisdom that is kamma-resultant. For from the very beginning, by virtue of that wisdom proceeding abundantly by way of continuity, this being deserves to be called 'endowed with wisdom' in a special sense. For even kamma-resultant wisdom, through the distinction of mental continuity, serves as a strong support for the arising of cultivation wisdom, which is absent in those without roots or with only two roots. It is also fitting to call him 'endowed with wisdom' by virtue of the wisdom termed 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña), which performs its respective functions. In the commentary, however, since protective wisdom is taken by the word 'discerning' (nipaka), the meaning here is stated solely in terms of kamma-resultant wisdom.

The phrase 'by wisdom in a triple-rooted rebirth-linking born of kamma' means: by wisdom in a rebirth-linking that is born of kamma and is triple-rooted. Thus, the term 'triple-rooted' should be connected with the word 'rebirth-linking', not with the word 'wisdom,' for wisdom is not triple-rooted. The wisdom that proceeds from rebirth-linking onward is called 'wisdom in rebirth-linking' because that is its root, not only the wisdom that proceeds at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Cinteti [V 1.0014] ārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyatīti cittaṃ, samādhi. So hi sātisayaṃ upanijjhānakicco. Na hi vitakkādayo vinā samādhinā tamatthaṃ sādhenti, samādhi pana tehi vināpi sādhetīti. Paguṇabalavabhāvāpādanena paccayehi citaṃ, tathā santānaṃ cinotītipi cittaṃ, samādhi. Paṭhamajjhānādivasena cittavicittatāya, iddhividhādicittakaraṇena ca samādhi cittanti vināpi paropadesenassa cittapariyāyo labbhateva. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana citta-saddo viññāṇe niruḷhoti katvā vuttaṃ “cittasīsena hettha samādhi niddiṭṭho”ti. Yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi jānātīti paññā. Sā yadipi kusalādibhedato bahuvidhā. “Bhāvaya”nti pana vacanato bhāvetabbā idhādhippetāti taṃ dassetuṃ “vipassana”nti vuttaṃ. “Bhāvaya”nti ca idaṃ paccekaṃ [M 1.0015] yojetabbaṃ “cittañca bhāvayaṃ, paññañca bhāvaya”nti. Tayidaṃ dvayaṃ kiṃ lokiyaṃ, udāhu lokuttaranti? Lokuttaranti daṭṭhabbaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesato. Taṃ hi bhāvayamāno ariyamaggakkhaṇe taṇhājaṭaṃ samucchedavasena vijaṭetīti vuccati, na lokiyaṃ. Nānantariyabhāvena panettha lokiyāpi gahitāva honti lokiyasamathavipassanāya vinā tadabhāvato. Samathayānikassa hi upacārappanāppabhedaṃ samādhiṃ itarassa khaṇikasamādhiṃ, ubhayesampi vimokkhamukhattayaṃ vinā na kadācipi lokuttarādhigamo sambhavati. Tenāha “samādhiñceva vipassanañca bhāvayamāno”ti. Tattha yadā lokiyā samathavipassanā adhippetā, tadā “bhāvaya”nti idaṃ bhāvanākiriyāya hetubhāvakathanaṃ, bhāvanāhetūti attho. Taṃbhāvanāhetukā hi vijaṭanakiriyāti. Yadā pana lokuttarā adhippetā, tadā kevalaṃ vattamānabhāvaniddeso. Tadubhayabhāvanāsamakālameva hi taṇhājaṭāvijaṭanaṃ.

Because it thinks of an object and closely contemplates it, it is called 'citta'; this is concentration (samādhi). For it has the function of contemplating with pre-eminence. Indeed, initial application and so forth cannot accomplish that purpose without concentration, but concentration can accomplish it even without them. Because it is accumulated by conditions that bring it to a state of proficiency and strength, or because it accumulates the continuity of concentration, it is also called 'citta'; this is concentration. Due to the great diversity by way of the first jhāna and so on, and due to performing wondrous acts such as the kinds of psychic power, the term 'citta' as a synonym for this concentration can indeed be obtained even without instruction from others. In the Commentary, however, considering that the word 'citta' is well-known in the sense of 'consciousness' (viññāṇa), it is said: 'Here, concentration is indicated under the heading of citta.' It knows things in their various aspects according to their intrinsic nature, so it is called wisdom (paññā). Although that wisdom is of many kinds, distinguished as wholesome and so on, yet because of the word 'developing', what is intended here is that which is to be developed. To show this, it is called 'insight' (vipassanā). And this word 'developing' should be applied to each individually, as 'developing concentration and developing wisdom'. This pair—is it mundane or is it supramundane? It should be understood as supramundane, because it is a supreme instruction. For it is said that one who is developing it untangles the tangle of craving by way of eradication at the moment of the noble path; this is not said of one developing the mundane. However, the mundane factors are also included here as indispensable conditions, because without mundane serenity and insight, that supramundane path does not arise. Indeed, for one whose vehicle is serenity, without concentration distinguished as access and absorption; for the other, without momentary concentration; and for both, without the three gateways to liberation, the attainment of the supramundane is never possible. Therefore, he said, 'developing both concentration and insight'. In this context, when mundane serenity and insight are intended, then this word 'developing' is a statement of the causal nature of the act of development; the meaning is 'because of developing'. For the act of untangling has that development as its cause. But when the supramundane factors are intended, it is merely an indication of the present development. For the untangling of the tangle of craving occurs at the very same time as the development of both.

“Ātāpī nipako”ti idaṃ yathāvuttabhāvanāya upakārakadhammakittanaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjantassa hi vīriyaṃ sati sampajaññanti ime tayo dhammā bahūpakārā. Vīriyūpatthaddhañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ satisampajaññānupālitaṃ na paripatati, upari ca visesaṃ āvahati. Patiṭṭhāsiddhiyā cettha saddhāsiddhi, saddhūpanissayattā sīlassa, vīriyādisiddhiyā ca. Na hi saddheyyavatthuṃ asaddahantassa yathāvuttavīriyādayo sambhavanti, tathā samādhipi. Yathā hi hetubhāvato vīriyādīhi saddhāsiddhi, evaṃ phalabhāvato tehi samādhisiddhi. Vīriyādīsu hi sampajjamānesu samādhi sampannova hoti asamāhitassa tadabhāvato. Kathaṃ panettha satisiddhi? Nipakaggahaṇato. Tikkhavisadabhāvappattā hi sati “nepakka”nti vuccati. Yathāha “paramena satinepakkena samannāgato”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “nepakkaṃ paññā”ti ayamattho dassito. Taggahaṇeneva [V 1.0015] satipi gahitāva hoti. Na hi sativirahitā paññā atthīti. Apare pana “sapañño”ti imināva pārihārikapaññāpi gayhatīti “nipako”ti padassa “sato”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Yadipi kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ ātāpanaṃ, taṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnampi attheva. Ātappasaddo viya pana ātāpasaddo vīriyeyeva [M 1.0016] niruḷhoti āha “ātāpīti vīriyavā”ti. Atha vā paṭipakkhappahāne sampayuttadhammānaṃ abbhussahanavasena pavattamānassa vīriyassa sātisayaṃ tadātāpananti vīriyameva tathā vuccati, na aññe dhammā. Ātāpīti cāyamīkāro pasaṃsāya, atisayassa vā dīpako. Vīriyavāti vā-saddopi tadattho eva daṭṭhabbo. Tena sammappadhānasamaṅgitā vuttā hoti. Tenāha “kilesānaṃ ātāpanaparitāpanaṭṭhenā”ti. Ātāpanaggahaṇena cettha ārambha dhātumāha ādito vīriyārambhoti katvā, paritāpanaggahaṇena nikkamaparakkamadhātuyo sabbaso paṭipakkhato nikkhantataṃ, uparūpari visesappattiñca upādāya. Nipayati visoseti paṭipakkhaṃ, tato vā attānaṃ nipāti rakkhatīti nipako, sampajāno. Kammaṭṭhānassa pariharaṇe niyuttāti pārihārikā.

The words 'ardent' and 'prudent' are a declaration of the qualities helpful to the development as described. Indeed, for a person practicing a meditation subject, these three qualities—energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—are very helpful. A meditation subject that is supported by energy and protected by mindfulness and clear comprehension does not fail, and it brings about further distinction. And here, the accomplishment of faith occurs through the accomplishment of its foundation (virtue)—for virtue has faith as its decisive support—and also through the accomplishment of energy and so forth. For in one who does not have faith in an object worthy of faith, the aforementioned energy and so forth do not arise, and neither does concentration. For just as the accomplishment of faith comes from energy and so forth in their role as cause, so the accomplishment of concentration comes from them in their role as fruit. Indeed, when energy and so forth are being accomplished, concentration is also accomplished, because for an unconcentrated person, they are absent. How is the accomplishment of mindfulness included here? Through the inclusion of 'prudent' (nipaka). For mindfulness that has reached a state of sharpness and clarity is called 'prudence' (nepakka), as it is said: 'endowed with supreme mindfulness and prudence'. In the Commentary, however, this meaning is shown: 'Prudence is wisdom.' By the inclusion of that wisdom, mindfulness is also included, for there is no wisdom devoid of mindfulness. Others, however, say that by the word 'wise' (sapañño) itself, administrative wisdom is also included, and therefore they state the meaning of the word 'prudent' (nipako) as 'mindful' (sato). Although 'ardor' (ātāpana) is the abandoning of defilements, and that exists for right view and so on as well, yet the word 'ardent' (ātāpī), like the word 'exertion' (ātappa), is well-known in the sense of energy alone. Therefore he said, '“ardent” means energetic'. Alternatively, the 'ardor' of energy—which proceeds by way of inciting the associated states in abandoning the opposing states—is pre-eminent. Therefore, energy alone is called thus, not the other states. And in the word 'ātāpī', this '-ī' suffix indicates either praise or pre-eminence. In the word 'vīriyavā', the '-vā' suffix should also be understood as having that same meaning. By that, endowment with the right strivings is expressed. Therefore he said, 'in the sense of burning and thoroughly burning the defilements'. And here, by the inclusion of 'burning' (ātāpana), considering it as the initial undertaking of energy, he speaks of the element of initiative. By the inclusion of 'thoroughly burning' (paritāpana), referring to the complete escape from opposing states and the progressive attainment of higher distinctions, he speaks of the elements of exertion and striving. One who makes the opposition wither and dry up, or one who protects and guards oneself from it, is 'prudent' (nipako); that is, clearly comprehending. Engaged in the administration of the meditation subject, thus it is 'administrative' (pārihārikā).

Abhikkamādīni sabbakiccāni sātthakasampajaññādivasena paricchijja netīti sabbakiccapariṇāyikā. Kammaṭṭhānassa vā uggaho paripucchā bhāvanārambho manasikāravidhi, tattha ca sakkaccakāritā sātaccakāritā sappāyakāritā nimittakusalatā pahitattatā antarāasaṅkoco indriyasamattapaṭipādanā vīriyasamatāpādanaṃ vīriyasamatāyojananti evamādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ kiccānaṃ pariṇāyikā sabbakiccapariṇāyikā. Bhayaṃ ikkhatīti bhikkhūti sādhāraṇato bhikkhulakkhaṇakathanena paṭipattiyāva bhikkhubhāvo, na bhikkhakabhinnapaṭadharādibhāvenāti dasseti. Evaṃ hi katakiccānaṃ sāmaṇerādīnaṃ, paṭipannānañca apabbajitānampi saṅgaho kato hoti. Idha pana paṭipajjanakavasena attho veditabbo. Bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti vā bhikkhu. So imaṃ vijaṭayeti yo naro sappañño sīle patiṭṭhāya ātāpī nipako cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayanti vutto, so bhikkhu imaṃ taṇhājaṭaṃ vijaṭayeti sambandho. Idāni tampi vijaṭanaṃ veḷugumbavijaṭanena upametvā dassetuṃ gāthāya yathāvutte sīlādidhamme “iminā ca sīlenā”tiādinā paccāmasati. Tattha yasmā yogāvacarasantānagatā nānākkhaṇikā missakā sīlādidhammā gāthāya gahitā, tasmā te ekaccaṃ gaṇhanto “chahi dhammehi samannāgato”ti āha. Na hi te cha dhammā ekasmiṃ santāne ekasmiṃ khaṇe [M 1.0017] labbhanti. Yasmā ca puggalādhiṭṭhānena gāthā bhāsitā, tasmā puggalādhiṭṭhānameva upamaṃ dassento “seyyathāpi nāma puriso”tiādimāha[V 1.0016]. Tattha sunisitanti suṭṭhu nisitaṃ, ativiya tikhiṇanti attho. Satthassa nisānasilāyaṃ nisitatarabhāvakaraṇaṃ, bāhubalena cassa ukkhipananti ubhayampetaṃ atthāpannaṃ katvā upamā vuttāti tadubhayaṃ upameyye dassento “samādhisilāyaṃ sunisitaṃ…pe… paññāhatthena ukkhipitvā”ti āha. Samādhiguṇena hi paññāya tikkhabhāvo. Tenāha bhagavā “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071; netti. 40; mi. pa. 2.1.14). Vīriyañcassā upatthambhakaṃ paggaṇhanato. Vijaṭeyyāti vijaṭetuṃ sakkuṇeyya. Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya hi vattamānāya yogāvacaro taṇhājaṭaṃ vijaṭetuṃ samattho nāma. Vijaṭanaṃ cettha samucchedavasena pahānanti āha “sañchindeyya sampadāleyyā”ti. Dakkhiṇaṃ arahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo, aggo ca so dakkhiṇeyyo cāti aggadakkhiṇeyyo, aggā vā dakkhiṇā aggadakkhiṇā, taṃ arahatīti aggadakkhiṇeyyo.

The guide of all duties (sabbakiccapariṇāyikā) is that which leads by distinguishing all tasks, such as going forward, by means of sampajañña with purpose, etc. Or, the undertaking of the meditation subject, inquiry, the beginning of cultivation, the method of attention, and therein acting carefully, persistently, and suitably, skillfulness in the sign, being resolute, not shrinking back in the interval, accomplishing the balance of the faculties, bringing energy to a state of balance, and yoking to balanced energy—the guide of all such duties is the 'guide of all duties'. 'One who sees danger (bhayaṃ ikkhati) is a bhikkhu'—by this statement of the characteristic of a bhikkhu in a general way, it is shown that the state of being a bhikkhu is through practice alone, not by being a beggar, a wearer of torn robes, and so on. For in this way, inclusion is made of novices and others who have done what is to be done, and even of those not gone forth who are practicing. Here, however, the meaning should be understood by way of one who is practicing. Or, a bhikkhu is one who breaks apart (bhindati) evil, unwholesome states. 'He would unravel this'—the connection is: the person who is wise, established in virtue, ardent, and discerning, who is said to cultivate the mind and wisdom, that bhikkhu would unravel this tangle of craving. Now, to show that unraveling by comparing it with the untangling of a bamboo thicket, he refers back to the qualities of virtue and so on, as stated in the verse, with 'by this virtue,' etc. Therein, because the qualities of virtue and so on—which are of various moments, mixed, and have gone to the continuum of the meditator—are taken up in the verse, taking them as a single whole, he said, 'endowed with six qualities.' For those six qualities are not obtained in a single continuum at a single moment. And because the verse was spoken with a person as its basis, showing a simile also with a person as its basis, he said, 'just as a man,' etc. Therein, 'well-sharpened' means well sharpened; the meaning is 'exceedingly keen.' The making of the sword sharper on the whetstone and its lifting by the strength of the arm—the simile is stated with both of these being implied. To show both of these in the subject of comparison, he said, 'well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration… having lifted it with the hand of wisdom.' For by the quality of concentration, there is sharpness of wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'One who is concentrated understands things as they really are.' And energy is its supporter because it exerts. 'Would unravel' means one would be able to unravel. For when insight leading to emergence is occurring, the meditator is indeed capable of unraveling the tangle of craving. And here, unraveling is the abandoning by way of eradication, so he said, 'would cut off, would demolish.' One is 'worthy of offerings' (dakkhiṇeyyo) because one is worthy of an offering (dakkhiṇa). He is the foremost (aggo) and he is worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyyo), thus he is 'foremost worthy of offerings' (aggadakkhiṇeyyo). Or, the foremost (aggā) offering (dakkhiṇā) is the 'foremost offering' (aggadakkhiṇā); he is worthy of that, thus he is 'foremost worthy of offerings' (aggadakkhiṇeyyo).
