5. Tatrāti tassaṃ gāthāyaṃ. Ayanti “naro”ti ca “bhikkhū”ti ca vutto yogāvacaro. Puna tatrāti tassaṃ paññāyaṃ. Assāti bhikkhuno. Kattari cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, anenāti attho. Karaṇīyaṃ natthi visesādhānassa tihetukapaṭisandhipaññāya abhāvato. Tenāha “purimakammānubhāveneva hissa sā siddhā”ti. Tenāti yoginā. Bhāvanāyaṃ satatapavattitavīriyatāya sātaccakārinā. Paññāvasenāti yathāvuttanepakkasaṅkhātapaññāvasena. Yaṃ kiñci kattabbaṃ, tassa sabbassa sampajānavaseneva karaṇasīlo, tattha vā sampajānakāro etassa atthi, sampajānassa vā asammohassa kārako uppādakoti sampajānakārī, tena sampajānakārinā. Atrāti assaṃ gāthāyaṃ. Sīlādisampādane vīriyassa tesaṃ aṅgabhāvato taṃ visuṃ aggahetvā “sīlasamādhipaññāmukhenā”ti vuttaṃ.

5. Therein (tatrā) refers to that verse. This one (ayaṃ) refers to the meditator, who is called both 'man' and 'bhikkhu.' Again, therein (tatrā) refers to that wisdom. Of him (assā) means of the bhikkhu. And this is the genitive case with an agentive sense; the meaning is 'by this one' (anena). There is nothing to be done to add a special quality, because for the wisdom of a triple-rooted rebirth-linking, the adding of a special quality does not exist. Therefore, it is said, 'For him, that (wisdom) is accomplished solely by the power of past kamma.' By that one (tena) means by the yogi. By the persistent one (sātaccakārinā) means one who acts persistently due to the constant exertion of energy in cultivation. By means of wisdom (paññāvasena) refers to the wisdom designated as prudence as stated. By the one who acts with full awareness (sampajānakārinā) means one whose habit is to do whatever is to be done solely by means of full awareness; or, for this person there is the characteristic of acting with full awareness in that regard; or, one who is a producer, a generator of the non-delusion of full awareness, thus being one who acts with full awareness. Herein (atra) refers to this verse. In accomplishing virtue, etc., because energy is a factor of those, it is not taken up separately; therefore, it is said 'through the means of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.'

“Visuddhimaggaṃ dassetī”ti avibhāgato desanāya piṇḍatthaṃ vatvā puna taṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “ettāvatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ettāvatāti ettakāya desanāya. Sikkhāti sikkhitabbaṭṭhena sikkhā. Sikkhanaṃ cettha āsevanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīlādidhammehi saṃvaraṇādivasena āsevanto te sikkhatīti [M 1.0018] vuccati. Sāsananti paṭipattisāsanaṃ. Upanissayo balavakāraṇaṃ. Vajjanaṃ anupagamanaṃ. Sevanā bhāvanā. Paṭipakkhoti pahāyakapaṭipakkho. Yadipi gāthāyaṃ “sīle”ti sāmaññato vuttaṃ, na “adhisīle”ti. Taṃ pana taṇhājaṭāvijaṭanassa patiṭṭhābhūtaṃ adhippetanti āha “sīlena adhisīlasikkhā pakāsitā”ti. Bhavagāmi hi sīlaṃ sīlameva, vibhavagāmi [V 1.0017] sīlaṃ adhisīlasikkhā. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti. Esa nayo sesasikkhāsupi.

"To show the Path of Purification"—having stated the condensed meaning of the teaching without differentiation, the section beginning "to this extent," etc., was then stated in order to show it in detail. Herein, "to this extent" means by this much of the teaching. "Training" (sikkhā) is so called in the sense of what is to be trained. And here, the act of training (sikkhana) should be understood as repeated practice (āsevana). One who repeatedly practices qualities beginning with virtue by way of restraint, etc., is said to 'train' in them. "The Dispensation" (sāsana) means the Dispensation of practice. Strong support (upanissayo) is a strong cause. Avoidance (vajjanaṃ) is not approaching. Pursuit (sevanā) is cultivation. Opponent (paṭipakkho) is the abandoning opponent. Although in the verse, "virtue" is spoken of generally, not as "higher virtue," it is nonetheless intended as the foundation for disentangling the tangle of craving. Hence it is said, "By 'virtue,' the training in higher virtue is shown." For virtue leading to existence is simply virtue, but virtue leading to non-existence is the training in higher virtue. Indeed, a general designation stands in the specific. This same method applies to the remaining trainings as well.

Sīlenāti adhisīlasikkhābhūtena sīlena. Taṃ hi anaññasādhāraṇatāya sāsanassa ādikalyāṇataṃ pakāseti, na yamaniyamādimattaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ, sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti ca. Kusalānanti maggakusalānaṃ. Kusalānanti vā anavajjānaṃ. Tena ariyaphaladhammānampi saṅgaho siddho hoti. Sabbapāpassa akaraṇanti sabbassāpi sāvajjassa akiriyā anajjhāpajjanaṃ. Etena cārittavārittabhedassa sabbassa sīlassa gahaṇaṃ kataṃ hoti. Kattabbākaraṇampi hi sāvajjamevāti. Ādivacanatoti gāthāyaṃ vuttasamādhipaññānaṃ ādimhi vacanato. Ādibhāvo cassa tammūlakattā uttarimanussadhammānaṃ. Ādīnaṃ vā vacanaṃ ādivacanaṃ. Ādisaddena cettha “sīlaṃ samādhi paññā ca, vimutti ca anuttarā”ti (dī. ni. 2.186) evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sīlassa visuddhattā vippaṭisārādihetūnaṃ dūrīkaraṇato avippaṭisārādiguṇāvahaṃ. “Avippaṭisārādiguṇāvahattā”ti etena na kevalaṃ sīlassa kalyāṇatāva vibhāvitā, atha kho ādibhāvopīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hissa sutte (pari. 366) avippaṭisārādīnaṃ vimuttiñāṇapariyosānānaṃ paramparapaccayatā vuttā. Samādhināti adhicittasikkhābhūtena samādhinā. Sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ saṅgahetvā pavattāya gāthāya ādipadena ādimhi paṭipajjitabbassa sīlassa, tatiyapadena pariyosāne paṭipajjitabbāya paññāya gahitattā majjhe paṭipajjitabbo samādhi pārisesato dutiyapadena gayhatīti “kusalassa upasampadātiādivacanato hi samādhi sāsanassa majjhe”ti vuttaṃ, na kusalasaddassa samādhipariyāyattā. Pubbūpanissayavato hi samāhitatādiaṭṭhaṅgasamannāgamena abhinīhārakkhamatā samādhissa iddhividhādiguṇāvahattaṃ, aggamaggapaññāya adhigatāya yadatthaṃ pabbajati, taṃ pariyositanti paññā sāsanassa [M 1.0019] pariyosānaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “sikkhānisaṃsamidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ vussati saddhādhipateyyaṃ paññuttaraṃ vimuttisāra”nti (a. ni. 4.245). Sakaṃ cittaṃ sacittaṃ, sacittassa sabbaso kilesānaṃ samucchindanena visodhanaṃ sacittapariyodāpanaṃ. Evaṃ pana paññākicce matthakappatte uttari karaṇīyābhāvato sāsanassa paññuttaratā veditabbā. Tādibhāvāvahanatoti yādiso iṭṭhesu, lābhādīsu ca anunayābhāvato, tādiso aniṭṭhesu, alābhādīsu ca paṭighābhāvato. Tato eva vā yādiso anāpāthagatesu iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu, tādiso āpāthagatesupīti tādī. Tassa bhāvo tādibhāvo, tassa āvahanato. Vātenāti [V 1.0018] vātahetu. Na samīratīti na calati. Na samiñjantīti na phandanti, kuto calananti adhippāyo.

“By morality” (Sīlena) means by the morality that constitutes the higher training in virtue. For, due to its uniqueness among teachings, it reveals the initial excellence of the Dispensation, not merely restraints and observances. Therefore it is said, “And morality well purified,” and “the non-doing of all evil.”

“Of skillful qualities” (Kusalānaṃ) refers to the skillful qualities of the path. Or, “of skillful qualities” means of the blameless. Thereby, the inclusion of the noble fruition states is also accomplished.

“The non-doing of all evil” (Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ) means the non-doing, the non-transgression, of anything blameworthy. By this, the taking of all morality, with its division into conduct to be performed and conduct to be avoided, is accomplished. For not doing what ought to be done is also blameworthy.

“Because of the initial statement” (Ādivacanato): this is because, of the concentration and wisdom mentioned in the verse, it is to be practiced at the beginning. And its nature as the beginning is because the supramundane states are rooted in it. Or, ādivacanaṃ is the statement of the beginnings. And here, by the word ādi (beginning), the inclusion of such statements as “Morality, concentration, and wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation” should be understood.

Because of the purity of morality, by removing the causes of remorse and so on, it brings the quality of non-remorse and so on. By this statement, “because it brings the quality of non-remorse and so on,” not only is the excellence of morality revealed, but also its nature as the beginning should be seen. For so, in the sutta, its sequential causality, starting with non-remorse and culminating in the knowledge of liberation, is stated.

“By concentration” (Samādhinā) means by the concentration that constitutes the higher training in mind. In the verse that proceeds by summarizing the entire Dispensation, since morality to be practiced at the beginning is taken by the first word, and wisdom to be practiced at the end is taken by the third word, the concentration to be practiced in the middle is taken by the second word by way of remainder. Therefore it is said, “From the statement ‘the undertaking of the skillful,’ concentration is in the middle of the Dispensation,” not because ‘skillful’ is a synonym for concentration.

For one with past supportive conditions, being endowed with the eight factors beginning with composure makes one capable of directing the mind; this is the quality of concentration bringing forth psychic powers and so on. When the wisdom of the highest path is attained, the purpose for which one goes forth is completed; thus, wisdom is the culmination of the Dispensation. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Monks, this holy life is lived having the trainings as its benefit, with faith as its sovereign, wisdom as supreme, and liberation as its essence.”

Sakaṃ cittaṃ (one's own mind) is sacittaṃ. The cleansing (visodhanaṃ) of one's own mind (sacittassa) by completely cutting off all defilements is sacittapariyodāpanaṃ (the purification of one's own mind). Furthermore, when the task of wisdom has reached its peak, because there is nothing further to be done, the supremacy of wisdom in the Dispensation should be understood.

“Because it brings about the state of being ‘such’” (Tādibhāvāvahanato): because, just as one is towards desirable things, gains, and so on, due to an absence of fondness, so one is towards undesirable things, losses, and so on, due to an absence of aversion. Or, for that very reason, just as one is towards desirable and undesirable things that have not come into range, so one is also towards those that have come into range—thus one is called tādī (one who is ‘such’). The state of that is tādibhāva, and this brings that about.

“By wind” (Vātena) means due to wind. “Does not stir” (na samīrati) means does not move. “They do not quiver” (na samiñjanti) means they do not tremble; the intention is, how could there be movement?

Tathāti yathā sīlādayo adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ pakāsakā, tathā tevijjatādīnaṃ upanissayassāti tesaṃ pakāsanākārūpasaṃhārattho tathā-saddo. Yasmā sīlaṃ visujjhamānaṃ satisampajaññabalena, kammassakatañāṇabalena ca saṃkilesamalato visujjhati pāripūriñca gacchati, tasmā sīlasampadā sijjhamānā upanissayasampattibhāvena satibalaṃ, ñāṇabalañca paccupaṭṭhapetīti tassā vijjattayūpanissayatā veditabbā sabhāgahetusampādanato. Satinepakkena hi pubbenivāsavijjāsiddhi, sampajaññena sabbakiccesu sudiṭṭhakāritāparicayena cutūpapātañāṇānubandhāya dutiyavijjāsiddhi, vītikkamābhāvena saṃkilesappahānasabbhāvato vivaṭṭūpanissayatāvasena ajjhāsayasuddhiyā tatiyavijjāsiddhi. Puretaraṃ siddhānaṃ samādhipaññānaṃ pāripūriṃ vinā sīlassa āsavakkhayañāṇūpanissayatā sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavehi dīpetabbā. Samādhipaññā viya abhiññāpaṭisambhidānaṃ sīlaṃ na sabhāgahetūti katvā vuttaṃ “na tato para”nti. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; netti. 40; mi. pa. 2.1.14) vacanato samādhisampadā chaḷabhiññatāya upanissayo. Paññā viya paṭisambhidānaṃ samādhi na sabhāgahetūti vuttaṃ “na tato para”nti. “Yogā ve jāyate bhūrī”ti (dha. pa. 282) vacanato pubbayogena, garuvāsadesabhāsākaosallauggahaparipucchādīhi ca paribhāvitā paññāsampatti paṭisambhidāpabhedassa upanissayo [M 1.0020] paccekabodhisammāsambodhiyopi paññāsampattisannissayāti paññāya anadhigantabbassa visesassa abhāvato, tassā ca paṭisambhidāpabhedassa ekantikakāraṇato heṭṭhā viya “na tato para”nti avatvā “na aññena kāraṇenā”ti vuttaṃ.

“Thus”: just as morality and so on are revealers of the higher training in virtue and so on, so too are they a supporting condition for the threefold knowledge and so on. The word “thus” has the meaning of summarizing the manner of their revealing.

Because morality, being purified by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension and by the power of the knowledge of ownership of actions, is purified from the stain of defilements and reaches fulfillment, therefore the accomplishment of morality, being achieved, through its nature as the accomplishment of a supporting condition, establishes the power of mindfulness and the power of knowledge. Therefore, its nature as a supporting condition for the three knowledges should be understood, because of its producing a congenial cause.

For, through mature mindfulness, the accomplishment of the knowledge of past lives occurs; through clear comprehension, by familiarity with acting from clear seeing in all activities, the accomplishment of the second knowledge, which is followed by the knowledge of passing away and reappearance, occurs; through the absence of transgression, due to the existence of the abandoning of defilements, by means of being a supporting condition for the Unbinding, through purity of intention, the accomplishment of the third knowledge occurs.

Without the prior fulfillment of concentration and wisdom, morality's role as a supporting condition for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints should be explained by the dry-insight arahants.

Unlike concentration and wisdom, morality is not a congenial cause for the direct knowledges and analytical knowledges; having considered this, it was said, “not beyond that.”

From the statement, “One who is concentrated knows things as they really are,” the accomplishment of concentration is a supporting condition for the state of having the six direct knowledges.

Unlike wisdom, concentration is not a congenial cause for the analytical knowledges; therefore it was said, “not beyond that.”

From the statement, “From application, indeed, wisdom is born,” the accomplishment of wisdom—developed through prior application, and through living with a teacher, skill in local languages, learning, questioning, and so on—is a supporting condition for the differentiation of the analytical knowledges. The enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha and perfect full enlightenment are also dependent on the accomplishment of wisdom. Therefore, because there is no superior quality that cannot be attained by wisdom, and because wisdom is the decisive cause for the differentiation of the analytical knowledges, unlike in the preceding sections, it was not said “not beyond that,” but rather “not by any other cause.”

Ettha ca “sīlasampattiñhi nissāyā”ti vuttattā yassa samādhivijambhanabhūtā anavasesā cha abhiññā na ijjhanti, tassa ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena na samādhisampadā atthīti. Satipi vijjānaṃ abhiññekadesabhāve sīlasampattisamudāgatā eva tisso vijjā gahitā. Yathā hi paññāsampattisamudāgatā catasso paṭisambhidā upanissayasampannassa maggeneva ijjhanti, maggakkhaṇe eva tāsaṃ paṭilabhitabbato, evaṃ sīlasampattisamudāgatā tisso vijjā samādhisampattisamudāgatā ca cha abhiññā upanissayasampannassa maggeneva ijjhantīti maggādhigameneva [V 1.0019] tāsaṃ adhigamo veditabbo. Paccekabuddhānaṃ, sammāsambuddhānañca paccekabodhisammāsambodhisamadhigamasadisā hi imesaṃ ariyānaṃ ime visesādhigamāti. Vinayasuttābhidhammesu sammāpaṭipattiyā tevijjatādīnaṃ upanissayatāpi yathāvuttavidhinā veditabbā.

And here, because it is said, 'relying on the accomplishment of virtue,' for whom the six supernormal knowledges, which are the flourishing of concentration, are not accomplished without remainder, for that person, by way of the highest determination, there is no accomplishment of concentration. Even though the knowledges are a part of the supernormal knowledges, the three knowledges are taken as arising only from the accomplishment of virtue. Just as the four analytical knowledges, which arise from the accomplishment of wisdom, are accomplished for one endowed with supporting conditions only through the path—because they are to be obtained only at the moment of the path—so too, the three knowledges arising from the accomplishment of virtue and the six supernormal knowledges arising from the accomplishment of concentration are accomplished for one endowed with supporting conditions only through the path. Therefore, their attainment should be understood as being only through the attainment of the path. Indeed, these special attainments of these noble ones are similar to the attainment of Paccekabodhi and Sammāsambodhi of the Paccekabuddhas and the Sammāsambuddhas. In the Vinaya, Suttas, and Abhidhamma, the nature of right practice being a supporting condition for the threefold knowledge and so on should also be understood in the manner described.

Sampannasīlassa kāmasevanābhāvato sīlena paṭhamantavivajjanaṃ vuttaṃ. Yebhuyyena hi sattā kāmahetu pāṇātipātādivasenāpi asuddhapayogā honti. Jhānasukhalābhino kāyakilamathassa sambhavo eva natthīti samādhinā dutiyantavivajjanaṃ vuttaṃ jhānasamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭakāyattā. Paññāyāti maggapaññāya. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena hi ekaṃsato ariyamaggova majjhimā paṭipatti nāma. Evaṃ santepi lokiyapaññāvasenapi antadvayavivajjanaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ.

For one possessed of accomplished virtue, due to the absence of indulging in sensual pleasures, the avoidance of the first extreme is said to be through virtue. Indeed, for the most part, beings, on account of sensual pleasures, have impure undertakings by way of killing living beings and so on. For one who obtains the bliss of jhāna, there is no possibility whatsoever of bodily fatigue; therefore, the avoidance of the second extreme is said to be through concentration, because of having a body pervaded by refined form arisen from jhāna. 'By wisdom' means by path-wisdom. Indeed, by way of the highest designation, it is exclusively the Noble Path that is named the Middle Practice. Even so, the avoidance of the two extremes should also be made clear by way of mundane wisdom.

Sīlaṃ taṃsamaṅgino kāmasugatīsuyeva nibbattāpanato catūhi apāyehi vimuttiyā kāraṇanti āha “sīlena apāyasamatikkamanupāyo pakāsito hotī”ti. Na hi pāṇātipātādipaṭivirati duggatiparikilesaṃ āvahati. Samādhi taṃsamaṅgino mahaggatabhūmiyaṃyeva nibbattāpanena sakalakāmabhavato vimocetīti vuttaṃ “samādhinā kāmadhātusamatikkamanupāyo pakāsito hotī”ti. Na hi kāmāvacarakammassa anubalappadāyīnaṃ kāmacchandādīnaṃ vikkhambhakaṃ jhānaṃ kāmadhātuparikilesāvahaṃ hoti. Na cettha upacārajjhānaṃ nidassetabbaṃ, appanāsamādhissa [M 1.0021] adhippetattā. Nāpi “sīleneva atikkamitabbassa apāyabhavassa samādhinā atikkamitabbatā”ti vacanokāso. Sugatibhavampi atikkamantassa duggatisamatikkamane kā kathāti. Sabbabhavasamatikkamanupāyoti kāmabhavādīnaṃ navannampi bhavānaṃ samatikkamanupāyo sīlasamādhīhi atikkantāpi bhavā anatikkantā eva, kāraṇassa apahīnattā. Paññāya panassa suppahīnattā te samatikkantā eva.

Virtue, because it causes one endowed with it to be reborn only in the blissful sense-sphere destinations, is the cause for deliverance from the four woeful states; thus it is said, 'By virtue, the means for transcending the woeful states is declared.' Indeed, abstinence from killing living beings and so on does not bring about the corruption of a bad destination. Concentration, by causing one endowed with it to be reborn only in the exalted planes, liberates from all sense-sphere existence; thus it is said, 'By concentration, the means for transcending the sense-sphere element is declared.' Indeed, jhāna, which suppresses sensual desire and so on that give supporting strength to sense-sphere kamma, does not bring about the corruption of the sense-sphere element. And here, access jhāna should not be indicated, because absorption concentration is intended. Nor is there an opportunity for the statement, 'The woeful state of existence, which is to be transcended by virtue alone, is to be transcended by concentration.' For one who transcends even the blissful state of existence, what is there to say about transcending the bad destination? 'The means of transcending all existence' is the means of transcending all nine states of existence, beginning with sense-sphere existence. Even states of existence transcended by virtue and concentration are in fact not transcended, because the cause has not been abandoned. But by wisdom, because its cause is well abandoned, they are indeed transcended.

Tadaṅgappahānavasenāti dīpālokeneva tamassa puññakiriyavatthugatena tena tena kusalaṅgena tassa tassa akusalaṅgassa pahānavasena. Samādhinā vikkhambhanappahānavasenāti upacārappanābhedena samādhinā pavattinivāraṇena ghaṭappahāreneva jalatale sevālassa tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ pahānavasena. Paññāyāti ariyamaggapaññāya. Samucchedappahānavasenāti catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato attano santāne “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 277) vuttassa [V 1.0020] samudayapakkhiyassa kilesagaṇassa accantaṃ appavattisaṅkhātasamucchindanappahānavasena.

By way of abandoning by substitution: like the dispelling of darkness by the light of a lamp, by way of abandoning each unwholesome factor by that respective wholesome factor comprised in the basis of meritorious action. By way of abandoning by suppression through concentration: like the removal of moss on the surface of water by a blow with a pot, by way of abandoning those various hindrances and other such states by preventing their occurrence through concentration, which is divided into access and absorption. 'By wisdom' means by the wisdom of the noble path. By way of abandoning by eradication: because the four noble paths have been developed, for one possessing each respective path, in one's own continuity, by way of abandoning by eradication—which is designated as utter non-occurrence—of the mass of defilements belonging to the origination-side, which is spoken of by the phrase beginning 'for the abandoning of wrong views' (Dhs 277).

Kilesānaṃ vītikkamapaṭipakkhoti saṃkilesadhammānaṃ, kammakilesānaṃ vā yo kāyavacīdvāresu vītikkamo ajjhācāro, tassa paṭipakkho sīlena pakāsito hoti, avītikkamasabhāvattā sīlassa. Okāsādānavasena kilesānaṃ citte kusalappavattiṃ pariyādiyitvā uṭṭhānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ samādhi vikkhambhetīti āha “samādhinā pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkho pakāsito hotī”ti, samādhissa pariyuṭṭhānappahāyakattā. Appahīnabhāvena santāne anu anu sayanato kāraṇalābhe uppattirahā anusayā, te pana anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ laddhā uppajjanārahā thāmagatā kāmarāgādayo satta kilesā veditabbā. Te ariyamaggapaññāya sabbaso pahīyantīti āha “paññāya anusayapaṭipakkho pakāsito hotī”ti.

'The counteragent to the transgression of defilements': whatever transgression or misconduct there is of defiling states or of kamma-defilements in the bodily and verbal doors, its counteragent is declared by virtue, because virtue has the nature of non-transgression. The uprising of defilements, having overpowered the occurrence of the wholesome in the mind, is obsession. Concentration suppresses that; thus it is said, 'By concentration, the counteragent to obsession is declared,' because concentration has the nature of abandoning obsession. Because they have not been abandoned, lying latent again and again in the continuity, fit to arise upon obtaining a condition, they are the underlying tendencies. But these, upon obtaining a suitable condition, are fit to arise and have gained strength; they should be understood as the seven defilements such as sensual desire. They are abandoned in every way by the wisdom of the noble path; thus it is said, 'By wisdom, the counteragent to the underlying tendencies is declared.'

Kāyaduccaritādi duṭṭhu caritaṃ, kilesehi vā dūsitaṃ caritanti duccaritaṃ, tameva yattha uppannaṃ, taṃ santānaṃ saṃkileseti vibādhati, upatāpeti cāti saṃkileso, tassa visodhanaṃ sīlena tadaṅgavasena pahānaṃ vītikkamapaṭipakkhattā sīlassa. Taṇhāsaṃkilesassa visodhanaṃ vikkhambhanavasena [M 1.0022] pahānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkhattā samādhissa, taṇhāya cassa ujuvipaccanikabhāvato. Diṭṭhisaṃkilesassa visodhanaṃ samucchedavasena pahānaṃ anusayapaṭipakkhattā paññāya, diṭṭhigatānañca ayāthāvagāhīnaṃ yāthāvagāhiniyā paññāya ujuvipaccanikabhāvato.

Bodily misconduct, etc., is bad conduct, or conduct corrupted by defilements, thus it is 'misconduct'. That very thing, wherever it has arisen, corrupts, afflicts, and torments that continuity, thus it is 'corruption'. Its purification is abandoning by substitution through virtue, because virtue is the counteragent to transgression. The purification of the corruption of craving is abandoning by way of suppression, because concentration is the counteragent to obsession, and because it is directly opposed to craving. The purification of the corruption of wrong view is abandoning by way of eradication, because wisdom is the counteragent to the underlying tendencies, and because wisdom, which grasps correctly, is directly opposed to wrong views, which grasp incorrectly.

Kāraṇanti upanissayapaccayo. Sīlesu paripūrakārīti maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtattā ādibrahmacariyakānaṃ pārājikasaṅghādisesasaṅkhātānaṃ mahāsīlasikkhāpadānaṃ avītikkamanato khuddānukhuddakānaṃ āpajjane sahasāva tehi vuṭṭhānena sīlesu yaṃ kattabbaṃ, taṃ paripūraṃ samatthaṃ karotīti sīlesu paripūrakārī. Tathā sakadāgāmīti “sīlesu paripūrakārī”ti etaṃ upasaṃharati tathā-saddena. Ete hi dve ariyā samādhipāripanthikānaṃ kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ paññāpāripanthikassa saccapaṭicchādakamohassa sabbaso asamūhatattā samādhiṃ, paññañca bhāventāpi samādhipaññāsu yaṃ kattabbaṃ, taṃ mattaso pamāṇena padesamattameva karontīti samādhismiṃ, paññāya ca mattaso kārino “sīlesu paripūrakārino”icceva vuccanti. Anāgāmī [V 1.0021] pana kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ samucchinnattā samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī. Arahā sabbaso sammohassa susamūhatattā paññāya paripūrakārī.

The reason is the decisive support condition. One who is a fulfiller in virtues: because it is the beginning of the holy life of the path, by not transgressing the major training rules fundamental to the holy life, known as the Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa, and by rising up at once from minor and very minor offenses, one completely and fully accomplishes what ought to be done in the virtues. Thus, one is called a 'fulfiller in virtues'. Regarding the once-returner, the word `tathā` (likewise) connects this with the designation 'one who is a fulfiller in virtues'. Indeed, these two noble ones, though they develop concentration and wisdom, because sensual desire and ill will (obstacles to concentration) and delusion that obscures the truth (an obstacle to wisdom) are not completely uprooted, only partially accomplish what needs to be done in concentration and wisdom. Thus, they are doers in measure regarding concentration and wisdom, but are called 'fulfillers in virtues'. The non-returner, having completely cut off sensual desire and ill will, is a fulfiller in concentration. The Arahant, having utterly destroyed all strong delusion, is a fulfiller in wisdom.

Vuttaṃ hetaṃ bhagavatā (a. ni. 3.87) –

Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One (AN 3.87):

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti, samādhismiṃ mattaso kārī, paññāya mattaso kārī. So yāni tāni khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni, tāni āpajjatipi vuṭṭhātipi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hi mettha, bhikkhave, abhabbatā vuttā. Yāni ca kho tāni sikkhāpadāni ādibrahmacariyakāni brahmacariyasāruppāni, tattha dhuvasīlo ca hoti ṭhitasīlo ca, samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. So tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo. Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu…pe… so tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī hoti. Sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu paripūrakārī [M 1.0023] hoti, samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī, paññāya mattaso kārī. So yāni tāni…pe… sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. So pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ…pe… anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti, samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī, paññāya paripūrakārī. So yāni tāni khuddānukhuddakāni…pe… sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. So āsavānaṃ khayā…pe… upasampajja viharatī”ti.

“Here, monks, a monk is a fulfiller in virtues, a doer in measure regarding concentration, and a doer in measure regarding wisdom. He may fall into and rise from whatever minor and very minor training rules there are. For what reason? Because, monks, I have not declared an incapacity herein. But as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life, that accord with the holy life, he is of steadfast virtue and established virtue, and trains in the training rules after having undertaken them. With the destruction of the three fetters, he is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, certain, and headed for enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, a monk… With the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner. Having returned to this world only once, he makes an end of suffering. Furthermore, monks, a monk is a fulfiller in virtues, a fulfiller in concentration, and a doer in measure regarding wisdom… trains in the training rules after having undertaken them. With the destruction of the five lower fetters… he is of a nature not to return from that world. Furthermore, monks, a monk is a fulfiller in virtues, a fulfiller in concentration, and a fulfiller in wisdom… trains in the training rules after having undertaken them. With the destruction of the taints… he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life.”

“Katha”nti pucchitvā sikkhādike vibhajitvā vuttamevatthaṃ nigametuṃ “eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha aññe cāti tayo vivekā, tīṇi kusalamūlāni, tīṇi vimokkhamukhāni, tīṇi indriyānīti evamādayo, sikkhattikādīhi aññe ca guṇattikā. Evarūpāti yādisakā sikkhattikādayo idha sīlādīhi pakāsitā honti, edisā.

Having asked, 'How?', and having analyzed the trainings and so on, in order to conclude the meaning already stated, the words 'Thus...' and so on were said. Therein, 'and others' refers to triads of qualities other than the triad of trainings and so on, such as: the three seclusions, the three wholesome roots, the three gateways to liberation, and the three faculties. 'Of such a nature' means: of the same kind as the triad of trainings and so on that are explained here by means of virtue and so on.

Ettha hi vivaṭṭasannissitassa sīlassa idhādhippetattā sīlena kāyaviveko pakāsito hoti, samādhinā cittaviveko, paññāya upadhiviveko. Tathā sīlena adoso kusalamūlaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti, titikkhappadhānatāya, aparūpaghātasabhāvatāya ca sīlassa. Samādhinā alobho [V 1.0022] kusalamūlaṃ, lobhapaṭipakkhato, alobhapadhānatāya ca samādhissa. Paññāya pana amohoyeva. Sīlena ca animittavimokkhamukhaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti. Adosappadhānaṃ hi sīlasampadaṃ nissāya dose ādīnavadassino aniccānupassanā sukheneva ijjhati, aniccānupassanā ca animittavimokkhamukhaṃ. Samādhinā appaṇihitavimokkhamukhaṃ. Paññāya suññatavimokkhamukhaṃ. Alobhappadhānaṃ hi kāmanissaraṇaṃ samādhisampadaṃ nissāya kāmesu ādīnavadassino dukkhānupassanā sukheneva ijjhati, dukkhānupassanā ca appaṇihitavimokkhamukhaṃ. Paññāsampadaṃ nissāya anattānupassanā sukheneva ijjhati, anattānupassanā ca suññatavimokkhamukhaṃ. Tathā sīlena anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti. Taṃ hi sīlesu paripūrakārino aṭṭhamakassa indriyaṃ. Samādhinā aññindriyaṃ. Taṃ hi ukkaṃsagataṃ samādhismiṃ paripūrakārino anāgāmino, aggamaggaṭṭhassa ca indriyaṃ. Paññāya aññātāvindriyaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti. Taduppattiyā hi arahā paññāya paripūrakārīti. Iminā nayena aññe ca evarūpā guṇattikā sīlādīhi pakāsetabbā.

Here, because virtue dependent on Nibbāna is intended, bodily seclusion is shown by virtue, mental seclusion by concentration, and seclusion from the substrata of existence by wisdom. Likewise, non-hatred as a wholesome root is shown by virtue, due to its emphasis on forbearance and its nature of non-harming. Non-greed as a wholesome root is shown by concentration, as it opposes greed and emphasizes non-greed. As for wisdom, it is simply non-delusion. And by virtue, the signless gateway to liberation is shown. For one who relies on the perfection of virtue, which emphasizes non-hatred, and who sees the danger in hatred, the contemplation of impermanence succeeds easily; and the contemplation of impermanence is the signless gateway to liberation. By concentration, the desireless gateway to liberation is shown. By wisdom, the emptiness gateway to liberation is shown. For one who relies on the perfection of concentration, which is the renunciation of sensual pleasures and emphasizes non-greed, and who sees the danger in sensual pleasures, the contemplation of suffering succeeds easily; and the contemplation of suffering is the desireless gateway to liberation. Relying on the perfection of wisdom, the contemplation of non-self succeeds easily; and the contemplation of non-self is the emptiness gateway to liberation. Likewise, by virtue, the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' is shown. For that is the faculty of the eighth person, the stream-enterer, who is a fulfiller in virtues. By concentration, the faculty of final knowledge is shown. For that, at its highest, is the faculty of the non-returner and of one standing in the highest path, who is a fulfiller in concentration. By wisdom, the faculty of one who has final knowledge is shown. For it is by the arising of this faculty that an Arahant is 'one who is a fulfiller in wisdom'. In this way, other such triads of qualities should be explained by means of virtue and so on.

1. Sīlaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition of Virtue

Sīlasarūpādikathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Nature of Virtue, etc.

6. Evanti [M 1.0024] vuttappakārena. Anekaguṇasaṅgāhakenāti adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ, aññesañca anekesaṃ guṇānaṃ saṅgāhakena. Sīlasamādhipaññāmukhenāti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 277; theragā. 676; netti. 5) viya vipassanāmattādimukhena saṅkhepato adesetvā sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena desitopi, sattatiṃsāyapi vā bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ visuddhimaggantogadhattā tattha sīlasamādhipaññā mukhaṃ pamukhaṃ katvā desitopi. Etena sīlasamādhipaññāsu avasesabodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ sabhāvato, upakārato ca antogadhabhāvo dīpitoti veditabbaṃ. Atisaṅkhepadesitoyeva hoti sabhāvavibhāgādito avibhāvitattā. Nālanti na pariyattaṃ na samatthaṃ. Sabbesanti nātisaṅkhepanātivitthārarucīnampi, vipañcitaññuneyyānampi vā. Saṅkhepadesanā hi saṃkhittarucīnaṃ, ugghaṭitaññūnaṃyeva ca upakārāya hoti, na panitaresaṃ. Assa visuddhimaggassa. Pucchanaṭṭhena pañhā, kiriyā karaṇaṃ kammaṃ, pañhāva kammaṃ pañhākammaṃ, pucchanapayogo.

6. Thus, in the manner stated. By “one who gathers many qualities” (anekaguṇasaṅgāhakena) is meant one who gathers the qualities of the higher training in virtue and so forth (adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ) and many other qualities (aññesañca anekesaṃ guṇānaṃ). By “through the doorway of virtue, concentration, and wisdom” (sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena) is meant that, not having taught concisely through the doorway of mere insight (vipassanāmattādimukhena) as in “All formations are impermanent” (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā) and so forth, it was taught through the doorway of virtue, concentration, and wisdom; or else, since the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (sattatiṃsāyapi bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ) are also included within the path of purification (visuddhimaggantogadhattā), it was taught there making virtue, concentration, and wisdom the principal doorway (mukhaṃ pamukhaṃ katvā). By this it should be understood that the inclusion of the remaining factors of enlightenment (avasesabodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ) within virtue, concentration, and wisdom is shown both in terms of their nature (sabhāvato) and their supportive function (upakārato). It is taught in an excessively concise manner (atisaṅkhepadesitoyeva) because its distinctions of nature (sabhāvavibhāgādito) and so forth are not elucidated (avibhāvitattā). By “not sufficient” (nālaṃ) is meant not complete (na pariyattaṃ), not adequate (na samatthaṃ). By “for all” (sabbesaṃ) is meant even for those who do not prefer excessive conciseness or excessive elaboration (nātisaṅkhepanātivitthārarucīnampi), or for those whose understanding requires detailed explanation and guidance (vipañcitaññuneyyānampi). For a concise teaching (saṅkhepadesanā) is helpful only for those who prefer conciseness (saṃkhittarucīnaṃ) and those who understand quickly (ugghaṭitaññūnaṃ), but not for others (na panitaresaṃ). Of this path of purification. Question (pañhā) in the sense of inquiring (pucchanaṭṭhena); action (kiriyā), performance (karaṇaṃ), deed (kammaṃ); the question itself is the action (pañhāva kammaṃ), question-action (pañhākammaṃ), the application of asking (pucchanapayogo).

Kiṃ sīlanti sarūpapucchā. Kenaṭṭhena sīlanti kena atthena sīlanti vuccati, “sīla”nti padaṃ kaṃ abhidheyyaṃ nissāya pavattanti attho. Tayidaṃ sīlaṃ sabhāvato, kiccato, upaṭṭhānākārato, āsannakāraṇato ca kathaṃ jānitabbanti āha “kānassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānī”ti. Paṭipatti nāma diṭṭhānisaṃse eva hotīti āha “kimānisaṃsa”nti. Katividhanti pabhedapucchā. Vibhāgavantānaṃ hi sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanamukheneva hotīti. Vodānaṃ visuddhi. Sā ca saṃkilesamalavimutti. Taṃ icchantena yasmā upāyakosallatthinā anupāyakosallaṃ viya saṃkileso jānitabboti āha “ko cassa saṃkileso”ti.

By “What is virtue?” (kiṃ sīlaṃ) is meant an inquiry into its intrinsic nature (sarūpapucchā). By “In what sense is it virtue?” (kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ) is meant: In what sense is it called virtue? What meaning does the word ‘virtue’ (sīlaṃ) convey, or upon what referent does it depend for its application? How should this virtue (tayidaṃ sīlaṃ) be understood in terms of its intrinsic nature (sabhāvato), its function (kiccato), its manifestation (upaṭṭhānākārato), and its proximate cause (āsannakāraṇato)? Thus it is said: “What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?” Practice (paṭipatti) indeed is for the sake of visible benefits (diṭṭhānisaṃse). Thus it is asked: “What is its benefit?” By “Of how many kinds is it?” (katividhaṃ) is meant an inquiry into its divisions (pabhedapucchā). For of things that have divisions, the elucidation of their nature (sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ) occurs precisely by way of showing their divisions (vibhāgadassanamukheneva). Purification (vodānaṃ) is purity (visuddhi). And that is freedom from the stain of defilements (saṃkilesamalavimutti). Since one who desires that purity (taṃ icchantena) and seeks skill in means (upāyakosallatthinā) should understand defilement (saṃkileso) as being like a lack of skill in means (anupāyakosallaṃ viya), it is asked: “And what is its defilement?”

Tatrāti [V 1.0024] tasmiṃ, tassa vā pañhākammassa. Vissajjananti vivaraṇaṃ. Pucchito hi attho avibhāvitattā nigūḷho muṭṭhiyaṃ kato viya tiṭṭhati. Tassa vivaraṇaṃ vissajjanaṃ vibhūtabhāvakāraṇato. Pāṇātipātādīhīti ettha [M 1.0025] pāṇoti vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tassa saraseneva patanasabhāvassa antare eva ativa pātanaṃ atipāto, saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghaṃ pātananti attho, atikkamma vā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātanaṃ atipāto, pāṇaghāto. Ādisaddena adinnādānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tehi pāṇātipātādīhi dussīlyakammehi. Viramantassāti samādānavirativasena, sampattavirativasena ca oramantassa. Vattapaṭipattinti upajjhāyavattādivattakaraṇaṃ. Cetanādayo dhammāti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ pāḷivasena vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cetayatīti cetanā, attanā sampayuttadhammehi saddhiṃ ārammaṇe abhisandahatīti attho. Cetanāya anukūlavaseneva hi taṃsampayuttā dhammā ārammaṇe pavattanti. Cetanā kāmaṃ kusalattikasādhāraṇā, idha pana sīlacetanā adhippetāti katvā “kusalā”ti veditabbā. Cetasi niyuttaṃ cetasikaṃ, cittasampayuttanti attho. Cetanāya satipi cetasikatte “cetanā sīla”nti visuṃ gahitattā tadaññameva viratianabhijjhādikaṃ cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ gobalībaddañāyena. Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro. Yathā akusalā dhammā citte na otaranti, tathā pidahanaṃ. Avītikkamo vītikkamassa paṭipakkhabhūtā avītikkamavasena pavattacittacetasikā. Tattha cetanā sīlaṃ nāmātiādi yathāvuttassa suttapadassa vivaraṇaṃ. Viramantassa cetanāti viratisampayuttaṃ padhānabhūtaṃ cetanamāha. Pūrentassa cetanāti vattapaṭipattiāyūhinī. Viramantassa viratīti viratiyā padhānabhāvaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ.

By “therein” (tatra) is meant in that (tasmiṃ), or of that question-action (tassa pañhākammassa). By “explanation” (vissajjanaṃ) is meant elucidation (vivaraṇaṃ). For the meaning that was asked (pucchito attho) remains unelucidated (avibhāvitattā) and hidden (nigūḷho), like something held in a clenched fist (muṭṭhiyaṃ kato viya). Its elucidation is the explanation (vissajjanaṃ) because it makes it manifest (vibhūtabhāvakāraṇato). In the phrase “from the destruction of life and so forth” (pāṇātipātādīhi), “life” (pāṇa) conventionally refers to a being (vohārato satto), but in the ultimate sense to the life faculty (paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ). The premature felling (ativa pātanaṃ) in the interim (antare eva) of that which by its own nature is bound to fall (saraseneva patanasabhāvassa) is “destruction” (atipāto); the meaning is not allowing it to fall slowly but making it fall quickly (saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghaṃ pātanaṃ). Or, having transgressed and overpowered with weapons and so forth (atikkamma vā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā), the felling (pātanaṃ) is “destruction” (atipāto), the killing of a living being (pāṇaghāto). By the word “and so forth” (ādisaddena), it includes taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and so on. By those immoral actions (tehi dussīlyakammehi), such as the destruction of life and so forth. By “of one who abstains” (viramantassa) is meant of one who refrains (oramantassa) by way of abstinence through undertaking (samādānavirativasena) and by way of abstinence upon encounter (sampattavirativasena). By “the practice of duties” (vattapaṭipatti) is meant the performance of duties such as those towards a preceptor (upajjhāyavattādivattakaraṇaṃ). In order to show the meaning stated concisely in “volition and other states” (cetanādayo dhammā) by analyzing it according to the Pāḷi text, the passage beginning with “For it has been said” (vuttañhetaṃ) was stated. Therein, “it wills” (cetayati), thus it is “volition” (cetanā); the meaning is that it directs (abhisandahati) the states associated with itself towards an object (attanā sampayuttadhammehi saddhiṃ ārammaṇe). For it is only in conformity with volition (cetanāya anukūlavaseneva) that its associated states (taṃsampayuttā dhammā) proceed towards an object (ārammaṇe). Although volition (cetanā) is common to the triad of wholesome states (kusalattikasādhāraṇā), here, however, since the volition of virtue (sīlacetanā) is intended, it should be understood as “wholesome” (kusalā). Connected to the mind (cetasi niyuttaṃ) is a mental factor (cetasikaṃ); the meaning is associated with consciousness (cittasampayuttaṃ). Although volition has the nature of a mental factor (cetanāya satipi cetasikatte), since “volition is virtue” (cetanā sīlaṃ) is taken separately (visuṃ gahitattā), it is just what is other than that (tadaññameva)—abstinence, non-covetousness, and so forth (viratianabhijjhādikaṃ)—that should be seen as mental virtue (cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ) by the analogy of the cow and the ox (gobalībaddañāyena). Restraint (saṃvaraṇaṃ) is the act of restraining (saṃvaro). It is the closing off (pidahanaṃ) so that unwholesome states (akusalā dhammā) do not descend into the mind (citte na otaranti). Non-transgression (avītikkamo) refers to the consciousness and mental factors (cittacetasikā) that proceed by way of non-transgression (avītikkamavasena) and are the opposite of transgression (vītikkamassa paṭipakkhabhūtā). Therein, the passage beginning with “volition is virtue” (cetanā sīlaṃ nāma) is an elucidation (vivaraṇaṃ) of the aforementioned sutta passage (yathāvuttassa suttapadassa). By “the volition of one who abstains” (viramantassa cetanā), it states the primary volition (padhānabhūtaṃ cetanaṃ) associated with abstinence (viratisampayuttaṃ). By “the volition of one who fulfills” (pūrentassa cetanā), it refers to the volition that strives in the practice of duties (vattapaṭipattiāyūhinī). The phrase “the abstinence of one who abstains” (viramantassa virati) is stated by taking the primacy of abstinence (viratiyā padhānabhāvaṃ) as the main point.

Ettha hi yadā “tividhā, bhikkhave, kāyasañcetanā kusalaṃ kāyakamma”ntiādi (kathā. 539) vacanato pāṇātipātādīnaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtā tabbirativisiṭṭhā cetanā tathāpavattā padhānabhāvena pāṇātipātādipaṭiviratisādhikā hoti, tadā taṃsampayuttā viratianabhijjhādayo ca cetanāpakkhikā vā, abbohārikā vāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya cetanāsīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Yadā pana pāṇātipātādīhi saṅkocaṃ āpajjantassa tato viramaṇākārena pavattamānā cetanāvisiṭṭhā virati, anabhijjhādayo ca tattha tattha padhānabhāvena kiccasādhikā honti, tadā taṃsampayuttā cetanā viratiādipakkhikā [M 1.0026] vā hoti, abbohārikā vāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya cetasikasīlaṃ vuttaṃ.

For herein, when, in accordance with the passage beginning, “Monks, threefold bodily volition is wholesome bodily kamma,” the volition (cetanā) that is the opposite of the destruction of life and so forth (pāṇātipātādīnaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtā) and is distinguished by abstinence from them (tabbirativisiṭṭhā), having arisen in such a way (tathāpavattā), becomes by its primacy (padhānabhāvena) the means of accomplishing abstinence from the destruction of life and so forth (pāṇātipātādipaṭiviratisādhikā), then “volitional virtue” (cetanāsīlaṃ) is stated with reference to this meaning (imamatthaṃ sandhāya): that the associated abstinence, non-covetousness, and so forth (taṃsampayuttā viratianabhijjhādayo) are either on the side of volition (cetanāpakkhikā) or are non-transactional (abbohārikā). But when, for one who is shrinking back (saṅkocaṃ āpajjantassa) from the destruction of life and so forth, the abstinence distinguished by volition (cetanāvisiṭṭhā virati) and non-covetousness and so forth (anabhijjhādayo), proceeding in the manner of abstaining from those things (tato viramaṇākārena pavattamānā), become in each case by their primacy (tattha tattha padhānabhāvena) the means of accomplishing the task (kiccasādhikā), then “mental virtue” (cetasikasīlaṃ) is stated with reference to this meaning (imamatthaṃ sandhāya): that the associated volition (taṃsampayuttā cetanā) is either on the side of abstinence and so forth (viratiādipakkhikā) or is non-transactional (abbohārikā).

Idāni [V 1.0025] sutte āgatanayena kusalakammapathavasena cetanācetasikasīlāni vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pajahantassāti samādānavasena “ito paṭṭhāya na karissāmī”ti sampattavatthukānipi anajjhācaraṇena pajahantassa. Satta kammapathacetanāti pāṇātipātādipahānasādhikā paṭipāṭiyā satta kusalakammapathacetanā. Abhijjhādivasena yaṃ paradāragamanādi karīyati, tassa pahāyakā anabhijjhādayo sīlanti āha “cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma anabhijjhā…pe… sammādiṭṭhidhammā”ti. Yathā hi abhijjhābyāpādavasena micchācārapāṇātipātādayo karīyanti, evaṃ micchādiṭṭhivasenāpi te puttamukhadassanādiatthaṃ karīyanti. Tesañca pajahanakā anabhijjhādayoti. Pātimokkhasaṃvaro cārittavārittavibhāgaṃ vinayapariyāpannaṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Satisaṃvaro manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ ārakkhā, sā ca tathāpavattā satiyeva. Ñāṇasaṃvaro paññā. Khantisaṃvaro adhivāsanā, sā ca tathāpavattā adosapadhānā khandhā, adoso eva vā. Vīriyasaṃvaro kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vinodanavasena pavattaṃ vīriyaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasatisaṃvarādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

Now, in accordance with the method that has come in the Sutta, the phrase 'Moreover,' etc., is stated in order to explain the virtues of volition and mental factors by dividing them according to the wholesome courses of action. By 'for one who abandons' is meant one who abandons by way of undertaking the resolve, 'From now on, I will not do it,' and by not transgressing even with regard to objects that have been encountered. By 'seven volitions of the courses of action' is meant the seven wholesome volitions of the courses of action in succession, which accomplish the abandoning of killing living beings and so forth. As for that which is done by way of covetousness and so forth, such as adultery, the abandoners of that, non-covetousness and so on, are virtue. Thus it is said: 'Mental virtue is non-covetousness... the states of right view.' For just as wrong conduct, killing living beings, and so forth, are done by way of covetousness and ill-will, so too they are done by way of wrong view, for the sake of seeing the face of a son and so forth. And the abandoners of these are non-covetousness and so on. The restraint of the Pātimokkha is the virtue of the training rules included in the Vinaya, comprising the division of conduct and avoidance. The restraint of mindfulness is the guarding of the sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth; and that, occurring in such a way, is mindfulness itself. The restraint of knowledge is wisdom. The restraint of patience is endurance; and that, occurring in such a way, is the aggregates with non-hatred as predominant, or it is simply non-hatred itself. The restraint of energy is the energy that arises by way of dispelling sensual thoughts and so forth. What is to be said concerning the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of mindfulness, and so forth, will become clear later.

Sotānīti taṇhādiṭṭhiavijjāduccaritaavasiṭṭhakilesasotāni. “Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmī”ti vatvā “paññāyete pidhiyyare”ti vacanena sotānaṃ saṃvaro pidahanaṃ samucchedanaṃ ñāṇanti viññāyati.

By 'the streams' are meant the streams of craving, wrong view, ignorance, misconduct, and the remaining defilements. Having said, 'I declare the restraint of the streams,' and by the statement, 'these are blocked by wisdom,' it is understood that the restraint of the streams is blocking, the knowledge that eradicates.

Idamatthikataṃ manasi katvā yena ñāṇena yoniso paccavekkhitvā paccayā paṭisevīyanti. Taṃ paccayapaṭisevanampi ñāṇasabhāvattā ettheva ñāṇasaṃvare eva samodhānaṃ saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Khamati adhivāsetīti khamo. Uppannanti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe jātaṃ nibbattaṃ. Kāmavitakkanti kāmūpasaṃhitaṃ vitakkaṃ. Nādhivāsetīti cittaṃ āropetvā abbhantare na vāseti. Ājīvapārisuddhipīti buddhapaṭikuṭṭhaṃ micchājīvaṃ pahāya anavajjena paccayapariyesanena sijjhanakaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīlampi ettheva vīriyasaṃvare eva samodhānaṃ gacchati vīriyasādhanattā. Ettha ca yathā ñāṇaṃ taṇhādisotānaṃ pavattinivāraṇato pidahanaṭṭhena saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro ca, parato pavattanakaguṇānaṃ ādhārādibhāvato sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ[M 1.0027], evaṃ khanti anadhivāsanena uppajjanakakilesānaṃ adhivāsanena saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro ca, khamanahetu uppajjanakaguṇānaṃ ādhārādibhāvato sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ, vīriyaṃ vinodetabbānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ vinodanena saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro ca, vinodanahetu uppajjanakaguṇānaṃ ādhārādibhāvato sīlanaṭṭhena sīlanti [V 1.0026] veditabbaṃ. Yathā pana pātimokkhasīlādi tassa tassa pāpadhammassa pavattituṃ appadānavasena saṃvaraṇaṃ pidahanaṃ, taṃ upādāya saṃvaro, evaṃ asamādinnasīlassa āgatavatthuto viramaṇampīti āha “yā ca pāpabhīrukānaṃ…pe… saṃvarasīlanti veditabba”nti. Na vītikkamati etenāti avītikkamo. Tathāpavatto kusalacittuppādo.

Having kept in mind this purpose, the requisites are used by wisely reflecting with that knowledge. That knowledge for using the requisites, being of the nature of knowledge, is included right here in the restraint by knowledge. 'One who endures' (khamo) is so called because one endures (khamati), one tolerates (adhivāseti). 'Arisen' (uppannaṃ) means born, produced, in regard to that particular object. 'Sensual thought' (kāmavitakkaṃ) means thought connected with sensuality. 'Does not tolerate' (nādhivāseti) means one does not let it dwell within after having let it ascend to the mind. The virtue of purity of livelihood, which is accomplished by abandoning wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddha and by seeking requisites in a blameless way, is also included right here in the restraint by energy, because it is accomplished by energy. And here, it should be understood that just as knowledge is restraint (saṃvara) because it restrains in the sense of blocking, by preventing the arising of the streams of craving and so on, and it is virtue (sīla) in the sense of being a foundation, because it is a basis for future qualities to arise; so too patience is restraint because it restrains by enduring the defilements that would arise from non-endurance, and it is virtue in the sense of being a foundation, because it is a basis for qualities that arise due to endurance; and energy is restraint because it restrains by dispelling evil states that should be dispelled, and it is virtue in the sense of being a foundation, because it is a basis for qualities that arise due to dispelling. Just as the virtue of the Pātimokkha and so on is restraint because it is a blocking, by way of not giving an opportunity for this or that evil state to arise, so too is the abstaining from an object that has presented itself for one who has not undertaken the virtue. Hence it is said: 'And for those who are fearful of evil... this should be known as the virtue of restraint.' 'Non-transgression' (avītikkamo) is so called because 'one does not transgress by means of this.' It is a wholesome arising of consciousness that occurs in such a way.

7. Avasesesu pana pañhesu. Samādhānaṃ saṇṭhapanaṃ. Dussīlyavasena hi pavattā kāyakammādayo sampati, āyatiñca ahitadukkhāvahā, na sammā ṭhapitāti asaṇṭhapitā vippakiṇṇā visaṭā ca nāma honti, susīlyavasena pana pavattā tabbipariyāyato saṇṭhapitā avippakiṇṇā avisaṭā ca nāma honti yathā taṃ okkhittacakkhutā abāhuppacālanādi. Tenāha “kāyakammādīnaṃ susīlyavasena avippakiṇṇatāti attho”ti. Etena samādhikiccato sīlanaṃ viseseti. Tassa hi samādhānaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ avikkhepahetutā. Idaṃ kāyakammādīnaṃ saṇṭhapanaṃ saṃyamanaṃ. Upadhāraṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ mūlabhāvo. Tathā hissa ādicaraṇādibhāvo vutto. Tena pathavīdhātukiccato sīlanaṃ visesitaṃ hoti. Sā hi sahajātarūpadhammānaṃ sandhāraṇavasena pavattati. Idaṃ pana anavajjadhammānaṃ mūlādhiṭṭhānabhāvena. Tenāha “kusalānaṃ dhammāna”ntiādi. Tattha kusaladhammā nāma sapubbabhāgā mahaggatānuttarā dhammā. Aññe pana ācariyā. Siraṭṭhoti yathā sirasi chinne sabbo attabhāvo vinassati, evaṃ sīle bhinne sabbaṃ guṇasarīraṃ vinassati. Tasmā tassa uttamaṅgaṭṭho sīlaṭṭho. “Siro sīsa”nti vā vattabbe niruttinayena “sīla”nti vuttanti adhippāyo. Sītalaṭṭho pariḷāhavūpasamanaṭṭho. Tena ta-kārassa lopaṃ katvā niruttinayeneva “sīla”nti vuttanti dasseti. Tathā hidaṃ payogasampāditaṃ sabbakilesapariḷāhavūpasamakaraṃ hoti. Evamādināti [M 1.0028] ādi-saddena sayanti akusalā etasmiṃ sati apaviṭṭhā hontīti sīlaṃ, supanti vā tena vihatussāhāni sabbaduccaritānīti sīlaṃ, sabbesaṃ vā kusaladhammānaṃ pavesārahasālāti sīlanti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

7. As for the remaining points. 'Composing' (samādhāna) means 'placing well' (saṇṭhapana). Indeed, bodily actions and so on that proceed by way of immorality bring harm and suffering both now and in the future; not being well-placed, they are called 'unestablished,' 'scattered,' and 'dispersed.' But those that proceed by way of good morality, being the opposite of that, are called 'established,' 'unscattered,' and 'undispersed'—such as having downcast eyes, not swinging the arms, and so on. Therefore, he said: 'The meaning is the unscattered state of bodily actions and so on through good morality.' By this, he distinguishes the meaning of 'sīlana' from the function of concentration. For the 'composing' of the latter is the cause of non-distraction for its associated states. This (sīla) is the establishing and restraining of bodily actions and so on. 'Supporting' (upadhāraṇa) means 'foundation' (adhiṭṭhāna), 'root-state' (mūlabhāvo). Thus, its nature as being the beginning of the practice and so on is stated. By this, the meaning of 'sīlana' is distinguished from the function of the earth element. For that (earth element) functions by way of supporting co-arisen material phenomena, whereas this (virtue) functions by way of being a root-foundation for blameless states. Therefore, he said: 'Of wholesome states,' etc. Therein, 'wholesome states' means the exalted and supramundane states, together with their preliminary stages. Other teachers, however, say: The meaning of 'head' (siraṭṭho) is that just as when the head is cut off, the entire person perishes, so when virtue is broken, the entire body of qualities perishes. Therefore, the meaning of 'highest limb' is the meaning of 'sīla'. The intention is that when 'siro' or 'sīsa' (head) should be said, 'sīla' is said by way of etymological derivation. The meaning of 'coolness' (sītalaṭṭho) is the meaning of calming feverishness. By this, he shows that from the word 'sītala', by eliding the letter 't', 'sīla' is said by way of etymological derivation. For this (virtue), when accomplished through practice, brings about the calming of the feverishness of all defilements. By 'and so on' (evamādinā), the inclusion of the following should be seen: it is called 'sīla' because when it is present, unwholesome states 'lie down' (sayanti), having been cast away; or it is called 'sīla' because all evil conducts, their effort destroyed by it, 'sleep' (supanti); or it is called 'sīla' because it is a hall worthy for the entrance of all wholesome states.

8. “Sīlanaṭṭhena sīla”nti pubbe saddatthuddhārena pakāsitopi bhāvattho evāti āha “sīlanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ tassā”ti. Na hi tassa cetanādibhedabhinnassa anavasesato saṅgāhako tato añño attho atthi, yo lakkhaṇabhāvena vucceyya. Nanu ca anekabhedasaṅgāhakaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ nāma siyā, na visesalakkhaṇanti anuyogaṃ manasi katvā āha “sanidassanattaṃ rūpassa, yathā bhinnassanekadhā”ti.

8. Although 'Virtue (sīla) in the sense of composing (sīlana)' was previously explained by way of etymological derivation, he states that it is indeed the essential meaning, saying: 'Composing (sīlana) is its characteristic.' For indeed, there is no other meaning than that which could be stated as a characteristic that comprehensively includes that virtue, which is differentiated by divisions such as volition. But is it not so that what comprehends many divisions would be called a general characteristic, not a specific characteristic? Having taken this inquiry to mind, he said: 'The visibility of form, just as it is differentiated in many ways.'

Yathā [V 1.0027] hi nīlādivasena anekabhedabhinnassāpi rūpāyatanassa sanidassanattaṃ visesalakkhaṇaṃ tadaññadhammāsādhāraṇato. Na aniccatādi viya, ruppanaṃ viya vā sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ, evamidhāpi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiṃ panetaṃ sanidassanattaṃ nāma? Daṭṭhabbatā cakkhuviññāṇassa gocarabhāvo. Tassa pana rūpāyatanato anaññattepi aññehi dhammehi rūpāyatanaṃ visesetuṃ aññaṃ viya katvā saha nidassanena sanidassananti vuccati. Dhammasabhāvasāmaññena hi ekībhūtesu dhammesu yo nānattakaro sabhāvo, so aññaṃ viya katvā upacarituṃ yutto. Evaṃ hi atthavisesāvabodho hotīti. Atha vā “saha nidassanenā”ti ettha tabbhāvattho saha-saddo yathā nandirāgasahagatāti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 14; paṭi. ma. 2.30).

For just as the visibility of the form-base—though differentiated into many divisions by way of blue, etc.—is a specific characteristic because it is not common to other dhammas, and not a general characteristic like impermanence, etc., or like affliction, so too should it be understood here. But what is this so-called 'visibility'? It is seeability, the state of being a domain for eye-consciousness. And although that visibility is not other than the form-base, it is called 'visible' (sanidassana) as 'with visibility' (saha nidassanena)—having treated it as if it were something else in order to specify the form-base from other dhammas. For among dhammas that are unified by a commonality of intrinsic nature, whatever intrinsic nature is a maker of diversity is fit to be spoken of figuratively, having treated it as if it were something else. For in this way, there is understanding of the specific meaning. Alternatively, in 'with visibility' (saha nidassanena), the word 'saha' has the meaning of 'its state' (tabbhāva), as in 'accompanied by delight and lust.'

Dussīlyaviddhaṃsanarasanti kāyikaasaṃvarādibhedassa dussīlyassa vidhamanakiccaṃ. Anavajjarasanti agārayhasampattikaṃ agarahitabbabhāvena sampajjanakaṃ, avajjapaṭipakkhabhāvena vā sampajjanakaṃ. Lakkhaṇādīsūti lakkhaṇarasādīsu vuccamānesu kiccameva, sampatti vā rasoti vuccati, na rasāyatanarasādīti adhippāyo. Keci pana “kiccamevā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ tassa itararasato balavabhāvadassanatthanti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ, kiccameva, sampatti eva vā rasoti imassa atthassa adhippetattā.

'Having the essence of destroying immorality' means it has the function of destroying immorality, which is divided into such things as bodily non-restraint. 'Having a faultless essence' means it has the accomplishment of being unblameworthy; it is accomplished by way of being unreproachable, or it is accomplished by way of being the opposite of what is faulty. In 'characteristics, etc.,' when characteristics, essences, and so on are being spoken of, it is function alone, or accomplishment, that is called 'essence'; the essence of the taste-base, etc., is not meant—this is the intention. But some say that the emphasis in 'function alone' is for the purpose of showing its state of being more powerful than other essences. That is merely their opinion, because this meaning is intended: 'function alone, or accomplishment alone, is essence.'

Soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānanti [M 1.0029] kāyādīhi sucibhāvena paccupaṭṭhāti. Gahaṇabhāvanti gahetabbabhāvaṃ. Tena upaṭṭhānākāraṭṭhena paccupaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ, phalaṭṭhena pana avippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, samādhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Sīlaṃ hi sampatiyeva avippaṭisāraṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti, paramparāya samādhiṃ. Imassa pana ānisaṃsaphalassa ānisaṃsakathāyaṃ vakkhamānattā idha aggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci pana phalassa anicchitattā idha aggahaṇanti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ phalassa anekavidhattā, lokiyādisīlassāpi vibhajiyamānattā. Tathā hi vakkhati “nissitānissitavasenā”tiādi (visuddhi. 1.10). Yathā pathavīdhātuyā kammādi dūrakāraṇaṃ, sesabhūtattayaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ, yathā ca vatthassa tantavāyaturivemasalākādi dūrakāraṇaṃ, tantavo āsannakāraṇaṃ, evaṃ sīlassa saddhammassavanādi dūrakāraṇaṃ, hiriottappamassa āsannakāraṇanti dassento āha “hirottappañca panā”tiādi. Hirottappe hītiādi tassa āsannakāraṇabhāvasādhanaṃ. Tattha uppajjati samādānavasena, tiṭṭhati avītikkamavasenāti veditabbaṃ.

'Having purity as its manifestation' means it manifests as a state of purity by means of body, etc. 'The state of being graspable' means the state of being fit to be taken up. By that, manifestation is stated in the sense of the mode of appearance; but in the sense of result, it has the manifestation of non-remorse, or the manifestation of concentration. For virtue causes non-remorse to manifest right in the present, and concentration in sequence. However, because this beneficial result will be spoken of in the discourse on benefits, its non-inclusion here should be understood. But some say its non-inclusion here is because the result is not intended; that is unsuitable, because the result is of many kinds, and because mundane virtue, etc., is also going to be analyzed. For so it will be said: 'By way of being dependent and independent,' and so on. Just as for the earth element, kamma, etc., are a distant cause, and the remaining three primary elements are a proximate cause; and just as for cloth, the weaver, shuttle, reed, etc., are a distant cause, and the threads are a proximate cause; so too for virtue, listening to the good Dhamma, etc., is a distant cause, and moral shame and moral dread are its proximate cause. Showing this, he said: 'And moral shame and moral dread...' and so on. The words 'In moral shame and moral dread...' etc., establish its state of being a proximate cause. Therein, it should be known that virtue arises by way of undertaking, and it persists by way of non-transgression.

Sīlānisaṃsakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on the Benefits of Virtue

9. Avippaṭisārādīti [V 1.0028] ettha vippaṭisārapaṭipakkho kusalacittuppādo avippaṭisāro. So pana visesato “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me, yassa me suparisuddhaṃ sīla”nti attano sīlassa paccavekkhaṇavasena pavattoti veditabbo. Ādi-saddena pāmojjabhogasampattikittisaddādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Avippaṭisāratthānīti avippaṭisārappayojanāni. Kusalānīti anavajjāni. Avippaṭisārānisaṃsānīti avippaṭisāruddayāni. Etena avippaṭisāro nāma sīlassa uddayamattaṃ, saṃvaḍḍhitassa rukkhassa chāyāpupphasadisaṃ. Añño eva panānena nipphādetabbo samādhiādiguṇoti dasseti.

9. 'Without remorse' and so forth: Here, 'without remorse' is the arising of a wholesome mind, which is the opposite of remorse. It should be understood that this arises specifically by way of reflecting on one's own virtue thus: 'It is truly a gain for me, it is truly well-gained by me, that my virtue is thoroughly pure.' By the word 'and so forth,' it includes delight, attainment of wealth, fame, and the like. 'Having non-remorse as their ground' means having non-remorse as their purpose. 'Wholesome' means faultless. 'Having non-remorse as their benefit' means having non-remorse as their result. By this it is shown that non-remorse is merely a result of virtue, like the shade and flowers of a grown tree, and that another quality, such as concentration, must be produced by this.

Sīlavato sīlasampadāyāti parisuddhaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā sīlassa sampādanena sīlavato, tāya eva sīlasampadāya. Appamādādhikaraṇanti appamādakāraṇā. Bhogakkhandhanti bhogarāsiṃ. Kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchatīti “itipi sīlavā, itipi kalyāṇadhammo”ti sundaro thutighoso uṭṭhahati, lokaṃ pattharati. Visāradoti attani kiñci garahitabbaṃ [M 1.0030] upavaditabbaṃ apassanto vigatasārajjo nibbhayo. Amaṅkubhūtoti avilakkho. Asammūḷhoti “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.248) vippaṭisārābhāvato, kusalakammādīnaṃyeva ca tadā upaṭṭhānato amūḷho pasannamānaso eva kālaṃkaroti. Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā, jīvitindriyassa upacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cutito uddhaṃ. Sugatinti sundaraṃ gatiṃ. Tena manussagatipi saṅgayhati. Sagganti devagatiṃ. Sā hi rūpādīhi visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo, lokiyati ettha uḷāraṃ puññaphalanti lokoti ca vuccati.

'For one endowed with virtue, through the perfection of virtue': This means, for one who is endowed with virtue by having purified and fully accomplished virtue, and by that very perfection of virtue. 'Due to heedfulness': Because of the cause of heedfulness. 'A mass of wealth': A heap of riches. 'A beautiful sound of praise arises': The lovely sound of acclaim arises, spreading throughout the world, saying, 'Indeed virtuous! Indeed, of good qualities!' 'Confident': Seeing nothing blameworthy or reproachful in oneself, free from timidity and fear. 'Unembarrassed': Not disgraced. 'Unbewildered': Due to the absence of remorse, such as "Alas, I have not done good," and because only wholesome actions and so forth present themselves at that time, one passes away with a clear and serene mind. 'Upon the breakup of the body': Through the relinquishing of the clung-to aggregates and the cessation of the life faculty. 'After death': Beyond deceasing. 'A good destination': A beautiful destination. This also includes the human destination. 'Heaven': The divine destination. For it is called 'heaven' (sagga) because it is supremely (suṭṭhu agga) excellent with respect to sense-objects like form, etc., and it is called 'the world' (loka) because a great fruit of merit is seen (lokiyati) here.

Ākaṅkheyya ceti yadi iccheyya. Piyo ca assanti piyāyitabbo piyacakkhūhi passitabbo pemaniyo bhaveyyanti attho. Manāpoti sabrahmacārīnaṃ manavaḍḍhanako, tesaṃ vā manena pattabbo, mettacittena pharitabboti vuttaṃ hoti. Garūti garuṭṭhāniyo pāsāṇachattasadiso. Bhāvanīyoti “addhā ayamāyasmā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passatī”ti sambhāvanīyo. Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti catupārisuddhisīlesu eva paripūrakārī assa, anūnakārī paripūraṇākārena samannāgato bhaveyya. “Ādinā nayenā”ti etena “ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto [V 1.0029] anirākatajjhāno vipassanāya samannāgato brūhetā suññāgārāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.65) evamādike sīlathomanasuttāgate sattarasa sīlānisaṃse saṅgaṇhāti.

'If he should wish': if he desires. 'And beloved': he should be dear, to be seen with eyes of affection, and lovable—this is the meaning. 'Agreeable': one who increases the minds of his fellow practitioners, or to be attained by their minds, to be pervaded with a mind of loving-kindness—this is what is said. 'Respected': one who stands in the place of a teacher, like a stone umbrella. 'Worthy of honor': to be esteemed thus: 'Surely this venerable one, knowing, knows; seeing, sees.' 'He should be a fulfiller of the virtues': he should be one who fulfills the fourfold purification virtues, one who practices without deficiency, he would be endowed with the characteristic of fulfilling them completely. By the phrase 'by this method, etc.': by this, it includes the seventeen benefits of virtue that come in the discourse praising virtue, such as, 'devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglecting jhāna, endowed with insight, a frequenter of empty dwellings.'

Idāni na kevalamime eva avippaṭisārādayo, atha kho aññepi bahū sīlānisaṃsā vijjantīti te dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sāsaneti imasmiṃ sakalalokiyalokuttaraguṇāvahe satthusāsane. Ācārakulaputtānaṃ yaṃ sīlaṃ vinā patiṭṭhā avaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, tassa evaṃ mahānubhāvassa sīlassa ānisaṃsānaṃ paricchedaṃ parimāṇaṃ ko vade ko vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyāti attho. Etena sabbesaṃyeva lokiyalokuttarānaṃ guṇānaṃ sīlameva mūlabhūtanti dassetvā tato parampi malavisodhanena, pariḷāhavūpasamanena, sucigandhavāyanena, sagganibbānādhigamūpāyabhāvena, sobhālaṅkārasādhanatāya bhayavidhamanena, kittipāmojjajanena ca sīlasadisaṃ aññaṃ sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ natthīti dassento “na gaṅgā”tiādikā gāthā abhāsi.

Now, not only these benefits such as freedom from remorse, but many other benefits of virtue also exist. To show them, the passage beginning with "and moreover" was started. Therein, "in the Dispensation" refers to this Teacher's Dispensation, which brings forth all worldly and supramundane qualities. For sons of good family with good conduct, without which virtue there is no foundation, no standing place. Of such a virtue of great power, who could state the limit, the measure of its benefits? This is the meaning. Having thus shown that virtue itself is the root of all worldly and supramundane qualities, and after that, wishing to show that there is nothing else like virtue that brings welfare and happiness to beings—by purifying defilements, by calming torment, by the spreading of a pure fragrance, by being a means for attaining heaven and Nibbāna, by accomplishing the state of being a beautiful ornament, by dispelling fear, and by generating fame and joy—he spoke the verses beginning with "Not the Ganges."

Tattha [M 1.0031] sarabhūti ekā nadī, “yaṃ loke sarabhū”ti vadanti. Ninnagā vāciravatīti “aciravatī”ti evaṃnāmikā nadī, vāti sabbattha vā-saddo aniyamattho. Tena avuttā godhāvarīcandabhāgādikā saṅgaṇhāti. Pāṇanaṭṭhena pāṇīnaṃ sattānaṃ yaṃ malaṃ sīlajalaṃ visodhayati, taṃ malaṃ visodhetuṃ na sakkuṇanti gaṅgādayo nadiyoti paṭhamagāthāya na-kāraṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Hārāti muttāhārā. Maṇayoti veḷuriyādimaṇayo. Ariyanti visuddhaṃ. Sīlasamuṭṭhāno kittisaddo gandho manoharabhāvato, disāsu abhibyāpanato ca “sīlagandho”ti vutto. So hi paṭivātepi pavattati. Tenāha bhagavā “satañca gandho paṭivātametī”ti (dha. pa. 54; a. ni. 3.80; mi. pa. 5.4.1). Dosānaṃ balaṃ nāma vatthujjhācāro, taṃ tesaṃ kātuṃ adentaṃ sīlaṃ dosānaṃ balaṃ ghātetīti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, Sarabhū is a river, which in the world they call Sarayū. The river named Aciravatī—the word 'vā' (or) in all instances has an unrestricted meaning. By that, it includes unmentioned rivers such as the Godhāvarī and the Candabhāgā. The defilement of beings—who are called 'pāṇī' because they breathe—which the water of virtue purifies, that defilement rivers such as the Ganges are not able to purify. Thus, the negative particle 'na' should be brought from the first verse and connected. 'Hārā' means pearl necklaces. 'Maṇayo' means gems such as beryl. 'Ariyaṃ' means pure. The sound of fame that arises from virtue is called 'the fragrance of virtue' because it is captivating to the mind and because it pervades the directions. Indeed, it travels even against the wind. Therefore the Blessed One said: "The fragrance of the good travels against the wind." The strength of defilements is the transgression of the object; it should be understood that virtue, by not allowing them to do that, destroys the strength of the defilements.

Sīlappabhedakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Varieties of Virtue

10. “Katividha”nti ettha vidha-saddo koṭṭhāsapariyāyo “ekavidhena rūpasaṅgaho”tiādīsu viya, pakārattho vā, katippakāraṃ kittakā sīlassa pakārabhedāti attho. Sīlanalakkhaṇenāti sīlanasaṅkhātena sabhāvena.

10. Herein, in the phrase 'Of how many kinds?' (katividhaṃ), the word 'vidha' is a synonym for 'division' (koṭṭhāsa), as in such phrases as 'the collection of form is of one division' (ekavidhena rūpasaṅgaho); or it has the meaning of 'kind' (pakāra). The meaning is: 'Of how many kinds? How many varieties of virtue are there?' 'By the characteristic of virtue' (sīlanalakkhaṇena) means: by the intrinsic nature designated as 'virtue'.

Caranti [V 1.0030] tena sīlesu paripūrakāritaṃ upagacchantīti carittaṃ, carittameva cārittaṃ. Vāritato tena attānaṃ tāyanti rakkhantīti vārittaṃ. Adhiko samācāro abhisamācāro, tattha niyuttaṃ, so vā payojanaṃ etassāti ābhisamācārikaṃ. Ādi brahmacariyassāti ādibrahmacariyaṃ, tadeva ādibrahmacariyakaṃ. Viramati etāya, sayaṃ vā viramati, viramaṇaṃ vā virati, na viratīti avirati. Nissayatīti nissitaṃ, na nissitanti anissitaṃ. Pariyanto etassa atthīti pariyantaṃ, kālena pariyantaṃ kālapariyantaṃ, yathāparicchinno vā kālo pariyanto etassāti kālapariyantaṃ. Yāva pāṇanaṃ jīvanaṃ koṭi etassāti āpāṇakoṭikaṃ. Attano paccayehi loke niyuttaṃ, tattha vā viditanti lokiyaṃ. Lokaṃ uttaratīti lokuttaraṃ.

They conduct themselves by means of it, attaining the state of being one who perfectly fulfills the duties in virtues; thus, it is 'caritta'. 'Caritta' itself is 'cāritta'. From what is prohibited, they protect themselves by means of it; thus, it is 'vāritta'. Superior conduct is 'abhisamācāra'. That which is engaged therein, or that for which this has that as its purpose, is 'ābhisamācārika'. The beginning of the holy life is 'ādibrahmacariya'. That itself is 'ādibrahmacariyaka'. One abstains by means of this, or it itself abstains, or abstention is 'virati'. Not 'virati' is 'avirati'. One depends on it; thus, it is 'nissita'. Not 'nissita' is 'anissita'. It has a limit; thus, it is 'pariyanta'. Limited by time is 'kālapariyanta'; or, that for which a precisely defined time is its limit is 'kālapariyanta'. That for which the limit is as long as there is life and breath is 'āpāṇakoṭika'. It is engaged in the world by its own conditions, or it is known therein; thus, it is 'lokiya' (worldly). It transcends the world; thus, it is 'lokuttara' (supramundane).

Paccayato, phalato ca majjhimapaṇītehi nihīnaṃ, tesaṃ vā guṇehi parihīnanti hīnaṃ. Attano paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nītanti paṇītaṃ. Ubhinnameva vemajjhe [M 1.0032] bhavaṃ majjhimaṃ. Attādhipatito āgataṃ attādhipateyyaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Taṇhāya, diṭṭhiyā vā parāmaṭṭhaṃ padhaṃsitanti parāmaṭṭhaṃ. Tappaṭikkhepato aparāmaṭṭhaṃ. Paṭippassaddhakilesaṃ paṭippassaddhaṃ. Sikkhāsu jātaṃ, sekkhassa idanti vā sekkhaṃ. Pariniṭṭhitasikkhākiccatāya asekkhadhammapariyāpannaṃ asekkhaṃ. Tadubhayapaṭikkhepena nevasekkhanāsekkhaṃ. Hānaṃ bhajati, hānabhāgo vā etassa atthīti hānabhāgiyaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Appaparimāṇattā pariyantavantaṃ, pārisuddhivantañca sīlaṃ pariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Anappaparimāṇattā apariyantaṃ, pārisuddhivantañca sīlaṃ apariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Sabbaso puṇṇaṃ, pārisuddhivantañca sīlaṃ paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīlaṃ.

That which is inferior to the middling and superior virtues by way of condition and by way of result, or is devoid of their qualities, is 'hīna' (inferior). That which is led to a state of pre-eminence by its own conditions is 'paṇīta' (superior). That which is in the middle of both is 'majjhima' (middling). That which comes from self-mastery is 'attādhipateyya'. This same method applies to the remaining two terms. That which is grasped or defiled by craving or by view is 'parāmaṭṭha' (grasped). By the rejection of that, it is 'aparāmaṭṭha' (ungrasped). Having its defilements calmed is 'paṭippassaddha' (calmed). Born in the trainings, or belonging to a trainee, is 'sekkha' (of a trainee). Because the task of training is completed, that which is included in the qualities of one beyond training is 'asekkha' (of one beyond training). By the rejection of both of those, it is 'nevasekkhanāsekkha' (of neither a trainee nor one beyond training). It partakes of decline, or it has a share in decline; thus, it is 'hānabhāgiya' (partaking of decline). This same method applies to the remaining terms. Because of being of small measure, the virtue that is limited and pure is 'pariyantapārisuddhisīla' (virtue of limited purity). Because of being of great measure, the virtue that is unlimited and pure is 'apariyantapārisuddhisīla' (virtue of unlimited purity). The virtue that is completely full and pure is 'paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīla' (virtue of complete purity).

11. Vuttanayenāti “sīlanaṭṭhena sīla”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.7) heṭṭhā vuttena nayena. Idaṃ kattabbanti paññattasikkhāpadapūraṇanti idaṃ ābhisamācārikaṃ kattabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti evaṃ paññattassa sikkhāpadasīlassa pūraṇaṃ. Sikkhāpadasīlaṃ hi pūrento sikkhāpadampi pūreti pāleti nāma. Sikkhā eva vā sikkhitabbato, paṭipajjitabbato ca sikkhāpadaṃ. Tassa pūraṇantipi yojetabbaṃ. Idaṃ na kattabbanti paṭikkhittassa akaraṇanti idaṃ duccaritaṃ na kattabbanti bhagavatā paṭikkhittassa akaraṇaṃ viramaṇaṃ. Caranti tasminti tasmiṃ sīle taṃsamaṅgino carantīti sīlassa adhikaraṇataṃ vibhāvento tesaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “sīlesu paripūrakāritāya pavattantī”ti. Vāritanti idaṃ na kattabbanti paṭikkhittaṃ akappiyaṃ[V 1.0031]. Tāyantīti akaraṇeneva tāyanti. Tenāti vārittasīlamāha. Vāreti vā satthā ettha, etena vāti vāritaṃ, sikkhāpadaṃ. Taṃ avikopento tāyanti tenāti vārittaṃ. Saddhāvīriyasādhananti saddhāya, uṭṭhānavīriyena ca sādhetabbaṃ. Na hi asaddho, kusīto ca vattapaṭipattiṃ paripūreti, saddho eva satthārā paṭikkhitte aṇumattepi vajje bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti āha “saddhāsādhanaṃ vāritta”nti.

11. “By the stated method” means by the method stated below, beginning with “virtue in the sense of its characteristic of composing.” “The fulfillment of the training rule laid down as ‘this should be done’” means the fulfillment of the virtue of the training rule laid down thus: “This superior conduct should be done, should be practiced.” For one who fulfills the virtue of the training rule is indeed called one who fulfills and protects the training rule itself. Or, the training itself is called a “training rule” because it is to be trained in and to be practiced. Its fulfillment should also be connected in this way. “The non-doing of what is prohibited as ‘this should not be done’” means the non-doing, the abstention, from misconduct prohibited by the Blessed One as “this should not be done.” “They conduct themselves in that”: clarifying that virtue is the basis, he shows it to be the place of their activity, meaning “those endowed with that virtue conduct themselves in that virtue.” Therefore, he said, “they proceed with the quality of being a fulfiller in regard to virtues.” “Prohibited” means the improper act prohibited as “this should not be done.” “They protect” means they protect simply by not doing.
