By this, he refers to the virtue of restraint. Or, the Teacher prohibits herein, or by means of this; thus, it is “vārita” (prohibited), which refers to the training rule. Not violating that, they protect by means of it; thus, it is “vāritta” (restraint). “To be accomplished through faith and energy” means it is to be accomplished through faith and through arising energy. For one who is without faith and is lazy does not fulfill the practice of the observances. Only one with faith, seeing danger even in the slightest fault prohibited by the Teacher, undertakes and trains in the training rules. Therefore, he said, “Restraint is accomplished through faith.”

Adhisīlasikkhāpariyāpannattā abhivisiṭṭho samācāroti abhisamācāroti āha “uttamasamācāro”ti. Abhisamācārova ābhisamācārikaṃ, yathā venayikoti (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8) adhippāyo. Abhisamācāro ukkaṭṭhaniddesato [M 1.0033] maggasīlaṃ, phalasīlañca, taṃ ārabbha uddissa tadatthaṃ tappayojanaṃ paññattaṃ ābhisamācārikaṃ. Suparisuddhāni tīṇi kāyakammāni, cattāri vacīkammāni, suparisuddho ājīvoti idaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakaṃ. Tattha kāmaṃ ājīvahetukato sattavidhaduccaritato virati sammāājīvoti sopi sattavidho hoti, sammājīvatāsāmaññena pana taṃ ekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Atha vā tividhakuhanavatthusannissayato micchājīvato viratiṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā vutto “ājīvo suparisuddho”ti. Seṭṭhacariyabhāvato maggo eva brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ, tassa. Ādibhāvabhūtanti ādimhi bhāvetabbataṃ nipphādetabbataṃ bhūtaṃ pattaṃ ādibhāvabhūtaṃ. Kiñcāpi desanānukkamena sammādiṭṭhi ādi, paṭipattikkamena pana ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ ādīti. Tassa sampattiyāti ābhisamācārikassa sampajjanena paripūraṇena ādibrahmacariyakaṃ sampajjati. Yo hi lahukānipi appasāvajjāni parivajjeti, so garukāni mahāsāvajjāni bahvādīnavāni parivajjessatīti vattabbameva natthīti. Suttaṃ pana etamatthaṃ byatirekavasena vibhāveti. Tattha dhammanti sīlaṃ. Taṃ hi upariguṇavisesānaṃ dhāraṇaṭṭhena dhammoti vuccati.

Because it is included in the training in higher virtue, excellent conduct is called ‘abhisamācāra’; thus it is said, ‘the highest conduct.’ ‘Abhisamācāra’ itself is ‘ābhisamācārika,’ as with the term ‘venayiko’—this is the intention. By way of the highest explanation, ‘abhisamācāra’ is path virtue and fruit virtue. ‘Ābhisamācārika’ is that which is prescribed relating to that, aiming at it, for its purpose, and for its benefit. The three perfectly pure bodily actions, the four verbal actions, and a perfectly pure livelihood—this is the eightfold virtue with livelihood as the eighth. Here, it is true that abstinence from the seven kinds of misconduct that have livelihood as their cause is right livelihood, and so it is of seven kinds; but due to the commonality of being right livelihood, it is spoken of as one. Alternatively, abstinence from wrong livelihood based on the three grounds of deceit is included and spoken of as ‘livelihood is perfectly pure.’ Because of being the noblest conduct, the path itself is the holy life, hence ‘path-holy-life.’ ‘Being in an initial state’ means having reached, at the beginning, the state of being what should be developed and what should be accomplished. Although right view is first in the order of the teaching, in the order of practice, the virtue with livelihood as the eighth is first. ‘Through its accomplishment’ means that through the completion and fulfillment of the ābhisamācārika, the beginning of the holy life is accomplished. For one who avoids even light and minor faults, it goes without saying that they will avoid heavy, major faults with great danger. The sutta, however, clarifies this meaning by way of the contrary method. Here, ‘dhamma’ is virtue. For it is called ‘dhamma’ in the sense of upholding the higher special qualities.

Viratisīlassa itarasīlena satipi sampayogādike asammissakatādassanatthaṃ “veramaṇimatta”nti vuttaṃ.

For the purpose of showing the unmixed nature of the virtue of abstinence with other virtue, even though there is association and so on, it is said, ‘mere abstinence’.

“Nissitānissitavasenā”ti ettha labbhamānanissayaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “nissayo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha taṇhācaritena nissayitabbato taṇhāva taṇhānissayo. Tathā diṭṭhinissayo. Diṭṭhicarito hi asatipi diṭṭhiyā taṇhāvirahe diṭṭhinissitova pavattati. Devoti catumahārājasakkasuyāmādipākaṭadevamāha[V 1.0032]. Devaññataroti apākaṭaṃ. Taṇhaṃ eva nissitanti taṇhānissitaṃ. Taṇhāya nissitanti ca keci vadanti. Tesaṃ “dve nissayā”tiādinā virujjhati. Suddhidiṭṭhiyāti “iti saṃsārasuddhi bhavissatī”ti evaṃ pavattadiṭṭhiyā, lokuttaraṃ sīlanti adhippāyo. Tassevāti lokuttarasseva sambhārabhūtaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ, vivaṭṭūpanissayanti attho.

In the phrase ‘By way of the dependent and the non-dependent,’ to first show the dependence that is obtained, the words ‘dependence,’ etc., are stated. Therein, because it is to be depended upon by one of a craving-temperament, craving itself is the ‘dependence on craving.’ Similarly for ‘dependence on view.’ For one of a view-temperament, even when there is no absence of craving in their view, proceeds as one who is dependent on view. ‘Deva’ refers to a manifest deva such as the Four Great Kings, Sakka, and Suyāma. ‘A certain deva’ refers to an unmanifest one. ‘Dependent on craving itself’ is `taṇhānissitaṃ`. Some say it means ‘depended upon by craving,’ but their statement is contradicted by the commentary beginning ‘two dependencies.’ ‘By the view of purity’ means by the view that occurs thus: ‘By this, there will be purity from saṃsāra.’ The intention is supramundane virtue. ‘Of that very one’ means being a requisite for, and a cause for, the supramundane itself; the meaning is having the turning away from the round of existence as its decisive support.

Kālaparicchedaṃ katvāti “imañca rattiṃ, imañca diva”ntiādinā (a. ni. 8.41) viya kālavasena paricchedaṃ katvā. Kālaparicchedaṃ akatvā samādinnampi antarāvicchinnaṃ [M 1.0034] sampattavirativasena yāvajīvaṃ pavattitampi āpāṇakoṭikaṃ na hotīti dassetuṃ “yāvajīvaṃ samādiyitvā tatheva pavattita”nti vuttaṃ.

‘Having made a time-limitation’ means having made a limitation by way of time, as in ‘for this night and for this day,’ and so on. To show that even if undertaken without making a time-limitation, virtue that is interrupted in the interval, or that which occurs for a lifetime merely by way of abstinence on occasion, is not ‘for the duration of one’s life,’ it is said, ‘having undertaken it for life and it proceeds thus.’

Lābhayasañātiaṅgajīvitavasenāti lābhayasānaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppādanavasena, uppannānaṃ rakkhaṇavasena ceva vaḍḍhanavasena ca ñātiaṅgajīvitānaṃ avināsanavasena. Kiṃ so vītikkamissatīti yo vītikkamāya cittampi na uppādeti, so kāyavācāhi vītikkamissatīti kiṃ idaṃ, natthetanti attho. Paṭikkhepe hi ayaṃ kiṃ-saddo.

‘By way of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, and life’ means: by way of producing gain and fame that have not yet arisen; by way of both protecting and increasing those that have arisen; and by way of not causing the loss of one's relatives, limbs, and life. As for ‘How could he transgress?’: one who does not even give rise to a thought to transgress—how could such a person transgress with body and speech? This does not happen; that is the meaning. For this word ‘kiṃ’ is used in the sense of negation.

Ārammaṇabhāvena vaṇo viya āsave kāmāsavādike paggharatīti sampayogabhāvābhāvepi sahāsavehīti sāsavaṃ. Tebhūmakadhammajātanti sīlaṃ tappariyāpannanti āha “sāsavaṃ sīlaṃ lokiya”nti. Bhavavisesā sampattibhavā. Vinayoti vinayapariyatti, tattha vā āgatasikkhāpadāni. Pāmojjaṃ taruṇapīti. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ sapaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ, tadadhiṭṭhānā vā taruṇavipassanā. Nibbidāti nibbidāñāṇaṃ. Tena balavavipassanamāha. Virāgo maggo. Vimutti arahattaphalaṃ. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ paccavekkhaṇā. Kathāti vinayakathā. Mantanāti vinayavicāraṇā. Upanisāti yathāvuttakāraṇaparamparāsaṅkhāto upanissayo. Lokuttaraṃ maggaphalacittasampayuttaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ. Tattha maggasīlaṃ bhavanissaraṇāvahaṃ hoti, paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa ca bhūmi, phalasīlaṃ pana paccavekkhaṇāñāṇasseva bhūmi.

Because, by being their object, it causes the taints—such as the taint of sensual pleasure—to flow out, just as a wound causes discharge to flow out, it is called ‘with taints’ (sāsava), even when there is no association, because it occurs together with the taints. The collection of phenomena of the three planes; since worldly virtue is included in that, it is said, ‘Worldly virtue is with taints.’ Special states of existence are prosperous states of existence. ‘Discipline’ (vinaya) is the study of the Vinaya, or the training rules found therein. ‘Joy’ (pāmojja) is tender joy. ‘Knowledge and vision of things as they are’ (yathābhūtañāṇadassana) is the vision of name-and-form with its conditions, or tender insight based on that. ‘Disenchantment’ (nibbidā) is the knowledge of disenchantment. By this is meant powerful insight. ‘Dispassion’ (virāga) is the path. ‘Liberation’ (vimutti) is the fruit of Arahantship. ‘Knowledge and vision of liberation’ (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge. ‘Talk’ (kathā) is a talk on the Vinaya. ‘Deliberation’ (mantanā) is investigation of the Vinaya. ‘Supporting condition’ (upanisā) is the supporting condition (upanissaya), which is designated as the aforementioned causal sequence. Supramundane virtue is the virtue with livelihood as the eighth associated with path and fruit consciousness. Therein, path-virtue both leads to escape from existence and is a ground for reviewing knowledge; but fruit-virtue is only a ground for reviewing knowledge.

12. Hīnādhimuttivasena chandādīnampi hīnatā. Paṇītādhimuttivasena paṇītatā. Tadubhayavemajjhatāvasena majjhimatā. Yatheva hi kammaṃ āyūhanavasena hīnādibhedabhinnaṃ hoti, evaṃ [V 1.0033] chandādayopi pavattiākāravasena. So ca nesaṃ pavattiākāro adhimuttibhedenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasakāmatāyāti kittisilokābhiratiyā, parivāricchāya vā. “Kathaṃ nāma mādiso īdisaṃ kareyyā”ti pāpajigucchāya ariyabhāvaṃ nissāya. Anupakkiliṭṭhanti attukkaṃsanaparavambhanāhi, aññehi ca upakkilesehi anupakkiliṭṭhaṃ. Bhavabhogatthāyāti bhavasampattiatthañceva bhogasampattiatthañca. Attano vimokkhatthāya pavattitanti sāvakapaccekabodhisattasīlamāha. Sabbasattānaṃ vimokkhatthāyāti sabbasattānaṃ saṃsārabandhanato [M 1.0035] vimocanatthāya. Pāramitāsīlaṃ mahābodhisattasīlaṃ. Yā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā mahābodhiṃ ārabbha pavattā paramukkaṃsagatasoceyyasallekhā desakālasattādivikapparahitā sīlapāramitā.

12. By the power of an inferior inclination, there is inferiority of aspiration (chanda) and other factors. By the power of a sublime inclination, there is superiority. By the power of being intermediate between those two, there is a middling state. For just as kamma is differentiated by the distinctions of inferior and so forth by the power of exertion, so too are aspiration and the other factors by the power of their mode of occurrence. And it should be understood that their mode of occurrence differs due to the difference in inclination. 'Due to desire for fame' (yasakāmatāya) means due to delight in fame and reputation, or due to the desire for a retinue. Relying on the noble state, with disgust for evil, one thinks, “How indeed could a person like me do such a thing?” 'Uncorrupted' (anupakkiliṭṭha) means uncorrupted by self-exaltation, disparaging others, and by other defilements. 'For the sake of existence and enjoyment' (bhavabhogatthāya) means for the sake of attainment in existence and for the sake of attainment in enjoyment. 'Undertaken for one’s own liberation' (attano vimokkhatthāya pavattitaṃ) refers to the virtue of disciple-bodhisattas and paccekabodhisattas. 'For the liberation of all beings' (sabbasattānaṃ vimokkhatthāya) means for the purpose of liberating all beings from the bondage of saṃsāra. The virtue of the perfections (pāramitāsīla) is the virtue of the Mahābodhisattas. That which is embraced by compassion and skill in means, which arises in connection with great enlightenment, which possesses the purity and austerity that has reached the utmost summit, and is free from distinctions of place, time, beings, and so forth, is the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramitā).

Ananurūpanti asāruppaṃ. Attā eva garu adhipati etassāti attagaru, lajjādhiko. Attādhipatito āgataṃ attādhipateyyaṃ. Loko adhipati garu etassāti lokādhipati, ottappādhiko. Dhammo nāmāyaṃ mahānubhāvo ekantaniyyāniko, so ca paṭipattiyāva pūjetabbo. Tasmā “naṃ sīlasampadāya pūjessāmī”ti evaṃ dhammamahattaṃ pūjetukāmena.

'Unsuitable' (ananurūpa) means unbefitting (asāruppa). For this person, the self alone is the revered one, the master; therefore, they are called 'self-revering' (attagaru), which refers to one who abounds in moral shame (lajjādhika). The virtue that comes from self-mastery (attādhipati) is called 'self-sovereignty' (attādhipateyya). For this person, the world is the master, the revered one; therefore, they are called 'world-revering' (lokādhipati), which refers to one who abounds in moral dread (ottappādhika). This Dhamma is indeed of great power, it certainly leads out, and it should be honored only through practice. Therefore, by one who wishes to honor the greatness of the Dhamma, it is thought, “I will honor it with the accomplishment of virtue.”

Parāmaṭṭhattāti parābhavavasena āmaṭṭhattā. Taṇhādiṭṭhiyo hi “imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā, iminā me sīlena saṃsārasuddhi bhavissatī”ti pavattassa sīlaṃ parāmasantiyo taṃ parābhavaṃ pāpenti maggassa anupanissayabhāvakaraṇato. Puthujjanakalyāṇakassāti puthujjanesu kalyāṇakassa. So hi puthujjanova hutvā kalyāṇehi sīlādīhi samannāgato. Parāmasanakilesānaṃ vikkhambhanato, samucchindanato ca tehi na parāmaṭṭhanti aparāmaṭṭhaṃ. Tassa tassa kilesadarathassa paṭippassambhanato vūpasamanato paṭippassaddhaṃ.

'Because of being wrongly grasped' (parāmaṭṭhattā) means because of being grasped in a way that leads to downfall. Indeed, craving (taṇhā) and wrong views (diṭṭhi), by wrongly grasping the virtue of one who thinks, “By this virtue I will become a deva or some other kind of deva,” or “By this virtue, there will be purification from saṃsāra for me,” lead that virtue to downfall because they make it not a supporting condition for the path. 'Of a virtuous worldling' (puthujjanakalyāṇakassa) means of a virtuous one among worldlings. For that person, though being a worldling, is endowed with good qualities such as virtue. Because of suppressing and eradicating the defilements of wrong grasping, it is not wrongly grasped by them; therefore, it is called 'ungrasped' (aparāmaṭṭha). Because of the calming and allaying of this and that fever of defilement, it is called 'calmed' (paṭippassaddha).

Katapaṭikammanti vuṭṭhānadesanāhi yathādhammaṃ katapaṭikāraṃ. Evaṃ hi taṃ sīlaṃ paṭipākatikameva hoti. Tenāha “taṃ visuddha”nti. “Katapaṭikamma”nti iminā ca “na punevaṃ karissa”nti adhiṭṭhānampi saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Acchamaṃsaṃ nu kho, sūkaramaṃsaṃ nu kho”tiādinā vatthumhi vā, “pācittiyaṃ nu kho, dukkaṭaṃ nu kho”tiādinā āpattiyā vā, “mayā taṃ vatthu vītikkantaṃ nu kho, na nu kho vītikkanta”ntiādinā ajjhācāre vā vematikassa saṃsayāpannassa. Visodhetabbaṃ yathādhammaṃ paṭikammena. Vimati eva vematikaṃ, tasmiṃ vematike sati, vimatiyā uppannāyāti attho. Vimati paṭivinetabbāti sayaṃ vā taṃ vatthuṃ [V 1.0034] vicāretvā, vinayadhare vā pucchitvā kaṅkhā vinodetabbā. Nikkaṅkhena pana kappiyaṃ ce kātabbaṃ, akappiyaṃ ce chaḍḍetabbaṃ. Tenāha “iccassa phāsu bhavissatī”ti.

'Having had the remedy applied' (katapaṭikammaṃ) means having had the remedy applied according to the Dhamma by means of rising from a grave offense and confession of a light offense. For, having been remedied thus, that virtue becomes restored to its natural state. Therefore, it is said, “it is purified.” And it should be understood that by this term 'having had the remedy applied,' the resolution “I will not do so again” is also included. For one who is doubtful and has fallen into uncertainty regarding the object, such as, “Is it bear’s flesh or pig’s flesh?”; or regarding the offense, such as, “Is it a pācittiya or a dukkaṭa?”; or regarding the transgression, such as, “Did I transgress that rule or did I not?”—it should be purified by a remedy in accordance with the Dhamma. Doubt (vimati) itself is 'doubtfulness' (vematikaṃ); when that doubtfulness is present, it means “when doubt has arisen.” 'Doubt should be dispelled' (vimati paṭivinetabbā) means the uncertainty should be removed either by investigating the matter oneself or by asking Vinaya experts. But by one who is free from doubt, if it is allowable, it should be done; if it is not allowable, it should be abandoned. Therefore, it is said, “thus there will be ease for him.”

“Catūhi [M 1.0036] ariyamaggehī”tiādinā maggaphalapariyāpannaṃ sīlaṃ maggaphalasampayuttaṃ vuttaṃ. Samudāyesu pavattavohārā avayavesupi pavattantīti. Sesanti sabbaṃ lokiyasīlaṃ.

By the text beginning with, “By the four noble paths,” the virtue included in the path and fruit is said to be associated with the path and fruit. It should be understood that conventional expressions used for a whole are also used for its parts. 'The rest' (sesa) means all mundane virtue.

Pakatipīti sabhāvopi. Sukhasīlo sakhilo sukhasaṃvāso. Tena pariyāyenāti pakatiatthavācakatthena. Ekaccaṃ abyākataṃ sīlaṃ idhādhippetasīlena ekasaṅgahanti akusalassevāyujjamānataṃ dassetuṃ “tattha akusala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi sekkhattikaṃ idha gahitaṃ, idha na upanītaṃ kusalattikanti adhippāyo. Vuttanayenevāti vutteneva nayena kusalattikaṃ aggahetvā hīnattikādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ tikānaṃ vasena assa sīlassa tividhatā veditabbā.

'Natural' (pakati) also means the natural disposition. One of pleasant character (sukhasīla) is amiable (sakhila) and easy to associate with (sukhasaṃvāsa). 'By that method' (tena pariyāyena) means in the sense of expressing the natural meaning. A certain indeterminate (abyākata) virtue is included together with the virtue intended here; thus, to show its non-connection only with the unwholesome, the passage beginning “therein, the unwholesome” was stated. Indeed, the triad of the trainee (sekkhattika) is taken here, while the wholesome triad (kusalattika) is not brought in here—this is the intention. 'By the method already stated' means that, by the method already stated, without taking the wholesome triad, the threefold nature of this virtue should be understood by way of the five triads beginning with the inferior triad.

13. Yodhāti yo idha. Vatthuvītikkameti āpattiyā vatthuno vītikkamane ajjhācāre. Kāmasaṅkappādayo nava mahāvitakkā micchāsaṅkappā. Evarūpassāti edisassa. Tassa hi sīlavante anupasaṅkamitvā dussīle sevantassa tato eva tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanena paṇṇattivītikkame adosadassāvino micchāsaṅkappabahulatāya manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni arakkhato sīlaṃ ekaṃseneva hānabhāgiyaṃ hoti, na ṭhitibhāgiyaṃ, kuto visesādibhāgiyatā. Sīlasampattiyāti sīlapāripūriyā catupārisuddhisīlena. Aghaṭantassa uttarīti uttari visesādhigamāya avāyamantassa. Ṭhitibhāgiyaṃ sīlaṃ bhavati asamādhisaṃvattaniyattā. Sampādite hi samādhismiṃ sīlassa samādhisaṃvattaniyatā nicchiyati. Samādhatthāyāti samathavasena samādhānatthāya. Nibbidanti vipassanaṃ. Balavavipassanādassanatthaṃ nibbidāgahaṇaṃ tāvatāpi sīlassa nibbedhabhāgiyabhāvasiddhito.

13. ‘Yodhā’ is the word division ‘yo idha’ (who here). ‘In the transgression of the basis’ (vatthuvītikkame) means in the transgression, the misconduct regarding the basis of an offense. The nine great thoughts beginning with sensual thought are wrong thoughts. For one who, not approaching the virtuous but associating with the unvirtuous, and for that very reason falling into imitation of their conduct, not seeing the fault in transgressing the precepts, due to an abundance of wrong thoughts and not guarding the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth—for such a one, virtue is exclusively of the part of decline. It is not of the part of stability; whence could there be the part of distinction? ‘By the accomplishment of virtue’ (sīlasampattiyā) means by the complete fulfillment of virtue, by the fourfold purification virtue. ‘Of one not striving for the higher’ (aghaṭantassa uttarī) means of one not striving for a higher, special attainment. The virtue of such a person is of the part of stability because it is not conducive to concentration. For when concentration is accomplished, the virtue's nature of leading to concentration is determined. ‘For the sake of concentration’ (samādhatthāya) means for the sake of concentration by way of tranquility (samatha). ‘Disenchantment’ (nibbidā) means insight (vipassanā). The taking up of disenchantment is to show powerful insight, because even by that much, virtue's nature as being of the part of penetration is accomplished.

Yāni ca sikkhāpadāni nesaṃ rakkhitabbānīti sambandho, tāni pana asādhāraṇapaññattito aññāni. Nesanti “rakkhitabbānī”ti padaṃ apekkhitvā kattari sāmivacanaṃ, tehi bhikkhūhīti attho. Sati vā ussāheti ussakkitvā sīlāni rakkhituṃ ussāhe sati. Dasāti sāmaṇerehi rakkhitabbasīlamāha ghaṭikārādīnaṃ viya. Aṭṭhāti naccādimālādiveramaṇiṃ ekaṃ katvā sabbapacchimavajjāni aṭṭha.

The connection is: “and which training rules are to be protected by them.” Moreover, these are other training rules. The word “nesaṃ” is a genitive noun used in the sense of the agent in relation to the word “rakkhitabbāni”; the meaning is “tehi bhikkhūhi” (by those bhikkhus). Or, regarding “sati vā ussāhe,” it means: when there is the ability, having striven further, to protect the virtues. By “dasa” (ten), it states the virtue to be protected by novices, like that of Ghaṭikāra and others. By “aṭṭha” (eight), it means the eight precepts which result from making the abstention from dancing, etc., and from garlands, etc., into one, and which exclude the very last one.

Avītikkamoti [M 1.0037][V 1.0035] pañcannaṃ sīlānaṃ avītikkamo. Pakatisīlanti sabhāvasīlaṃ. Tatrūpapattiniyataṃ hi sīlaṃ uttarakurukānaṃ. Mariyādācārittanti tassa tassa sāvajjassa akaraṇe mariyādabhūtaṃ, tattha tattha kulādīsu pubbapurisehi ṭhapitaṃ cārittaṃ. Kuladesapāsaṇḍadhammo hi “ācārasīla”nti adhippetaṃ. Tattha kuladhammo tāva brāhmaṇādīnaṃ amajjapānādi, desadhammo ekaccajanapadavāsīnaṃ ahiṃsanādi, pāsaṇḍadhammo titthiyānaṃ yamaniyamādi. Titthiyamataṃ hi diṭṭhipāsena, taṇhāpāsena ca ḍeti pavattati, pāsaṃ vā bādhaṃ ariyavinayassa ḍetīti “pāsaṇḍa”nti vuccati. “Pakatiyā sīlavatī hotī”ti (dī. ni. 2.20) vacanato bodhisattamātu pañcasikkhāpadasīlaṃ paripuṇṇameva. Idaṃ pana ukkaṃsagataṃ bodhisattapitaripi cittuppādamattenapi asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ “dhammatāsīla”nti vuttaṃ. Kāmaguṇūpasaṃhitanti kāmakoṭṭhāsesu assādūpasaṃhitaṃ kāmassādagadhitaṃ. Dhammatāsīlanti dhammatāya kāraṇaniyāmena āgataṃ sīlaṃ. Sīlapāramiṃ hi paramukkaṃsaṃ pāpetvā kucchigatassa mahābodhisattassa sīlatejena guṇānubhāvena bodhisattamātu saraseneva paramasallekhappattaṃ sīlaṃ hoti. Mahākassapādīnanti ādi-saddena bhaddādike saṅgaṇhāti. Te kira suciraṃ kālaṃ suparisuddhasīlā eva hutvā āgatā. Tenāha “suddhasattāna”nti. Tāsu tāsu jātīsūti sīlavarājamahiṃsarājādijātīsu. Pubbe purimajātiyaṃ siddho hetu etassāti pubbahetukasīlaṃ. Idaṃ pana pakatisīlādisamādānena vinā avītikkamalakkhaṇaṃ sampattaviratisaṅgahaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Non-transgression” is the non-transgression of the five precepts. “Natural virtue” is inherent virtue. Indeed, for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, virtue is fixed by rebirth there. “Boundary conduct” is conduct that has become a boundary in the non-doing of this or that blameworthy act; it is the custom established by ancestors in various clans and so on. The custom of the clan, the region, and the sectarians is intended by “customary virtue.” Among these, clan custom is, for Brahmins and others, abstaining from intoxicants and the like; regional custom is, for inhabitants of certain districts, non-violence and the like; sectarian custom is, for sectarians, restraints and observances and the like. A sectarian view is called “pāsaṇḍa” because it sets up and causes to proceed by the snare of views and the snare of craving, or because it causes a snare or an affliction for the Noble Discipline. In accordance with the statement, “By nature, she is virtuous,” the Bodhisatta’s mother’s virtue of the five precepts was indeed complete. Moreover, this virtue, having reached the supreme state and being unsullied even by the mere arising of a thought in the Bodhisatta’s father as well, is called “virtue as an inherent quality.” “Associated with sensual qualities” means associated with enjoyment in the portions of sensuality, or greedy for the taste of sensuality. “Virtue as an inherent quality” is virtue that has come about by its inherent nature, by causal necessity. Indeed, having brought the perfection of virtue to the supreme summit, through the spiritual power of the virtue and the majesty of the qualities of the great Bodhisatta who was in her womb, the Bodhisatta's mother's virtue becomes one that has reached the highest austerity, just by its own nature. Regarding “Mahākassapa and others,” by the word “etc.” it includes Bhaddā and the like. It is said that they came having been of completely pure virtue for a very long time. Therefore, it says “of pure beings.” “In those various births” means in births such as that of King Sīlava and King Mahiṃsa. “Virtue with a past cause” is so called because for this virtue, there is a cause accomplished in a previous life. Moreover, this natural virtue and so on should be understood as included in “abstinence by attainment,” which is characterized by non-transgression and is without formal undertaking.

Yaṃ bhagavatā evaṃ vuttaṃ sīlanti sambandho. Idhāti vakkhamānasīlaparipūrakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpanaṃ, aññasāsanassa ca tathābhāvapaṭisedhanaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214; ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241). Bhikkhūti tassa sīlassa paripūrakapuggalaparidīpanaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti idamassa pātimokkhasīle patiṭṭhitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Viharatīti idamassa tadanurūpavihārasamaṅgibhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Ācāragocarasampannoti idaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarassa, upariadhigantabbaguṇānañca upakārakadhammaparidīpanaṃ. Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti idaṃ pātimokkhato acavanabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Samādāyāti sikkhāpadānaṃ anavasesato ādānaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhatīti sikkhāya samaṅgibhāvaparidīpanaṃ[M 1.0038]. Sikkhāpadesūti sikkhitabbadhammaparidīpanaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvi bhavissati.

The connection is to that virtue which was spoken of thus by the Blessed One. “Here” indicates the Teaching which is the foundation for the person who will fulfill the virtue to be described, and it refutes that other teachings are of such a nature. For this was said: “Here alone, O bhikkhus, is the ascetic… empty are the doctrines of others of true ascetics.” “Bhikkhu” indicates the person who fulfills that virtue. “Restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint” indicates his state of being established in the Pātimokkha virtue. “He dwells” indicates his state of possessing a way of living suitable to that virtue. “Endowed with proper conduct and resort” indicates the qualities that are helpful to the Pātimokkha restraint and to the qualities to be attained further on. “Seeing danger in the slightest faults” indicates the state of not falling away from the Pātimokkha. “Having undertaken” indicates the undertaking of the training rules without remainder. “He trains” indicates the state of being endowed with the training. “In the training rules” indicates the qualities that are to be trained in. Whatever should be said in this matter will become clear later.

Soti [V 1.0036] pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle patiṭṭhitabhikkhu. Tena yādisassa indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ icchitabbaṃ, taṃ dasseti. Cakkhunāti yato so saṃvaro, taṃ dasseti. Rūpanti yattha so saṃvaro, taṃ dasseti. Disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhīti saṃvarassa upāyaṃ dasseti. Yatvādhikaraṇa…pe… anvāssaveyyunti saṃvarassa paṭipakkhaṃ tattha ādīnavaṃ dasseti. Saṃvarāya paṭipajjatīti pageva satiyā upaṭṭhapetabbataṃ dasseti. Rakkhati cakkhundriyanti satiyā upaṭṭhāpanameva cakkhundriyassa ārakkhāti dasseti. Cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatīti tathābhūtā satiyevettha saṃvaroti dasseti. Vītikkamassa vasenāti sambandho. Channaṃ sikkhāpadānanti “ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapatī”tiādinā āgatānaṃ channaṃ pārājikādipaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ. Sāmantajappanādinā tividhena kuhanavatthunā vimhāpanaṃ kuhanā. Attānaṃ, dāyakaṃ vā ukkhipitvā yathā so kiñci dadāti, evaṃ kathanaṃ lapanā. Nimittaṃ vuccati paccayadānasaññuppādakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ, tena nimittena carati, nimittaṃ vā karotīti nemittiko, tassa bhāvo nemittikatā. Gandhādayo viya lābhāya paresaṃ akkosanādinā nipisatīti nippeso, nippesova nippesiko, tassa bhāvo nippesikatā. Mahicchatāya attanā laddhalābhena parato lābhapariyesanā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā. Evamādīnanti ādi-saddena anuppiyabhāṇitācāṭukamyatādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Paṭisaṅkhānena paccavekkhaṇāya parisuddho asaṃkiliṭṭho paṭisaṅkhānaparisuddho. Cattāro paccayā paribhuñjīyanti etenāti catupaccayaparibhogo, tathāpavattā anavajjacetanā.

That is, a monk established in the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. By this, it is shown for what kind of monk the virtue of sense-restraint is to be desired. By 'eye,' it shows the sense-faculty from which that restraint arises. By 'forms,' it shows the object wherein that restraint occurs. By 'Having seen, he is not one who grasps the sign or the details,' it shows the means for restraint. By 'On account of which... evil, unwholesome states might flow in,' it shows the opposite of restraint and the danger therein. By 'He undertakes the practice for restraint,' it shows that mindfulness should be established beforehand. By 'He guards the eye-faculty,' it shows that the very establishment of mindfulness is the guarding of the eye-faculty. By 'He undertakes restraint in the eye-faculty,' it shows that in this context, restraint is just such mindfulness. The connection is by way of transgression. 'Of the six training rules' refers to the six training rules connected with the Pārājikas and so on, which are found in passages such as, 'For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, he claims a superhuman state that is non-existent and untrue.' Deception (kuhanā) is causing astonishment by three kinds of fraudulent means, such as speaking nearby. Flattery (lapanā) is speaking in such a way, having exalted oneself or the donor, so that he gives something. A sign (nimitta) is said to be a bodily or verbal action that produces the perception of giving requisites; one who acts by that sign or makes a sign is a schemer (nemittiko), and the state of being so is scheming (nemittikatā). Just as one grinds perfumes and the like for the sake of gain, one crushes others by reviling and so on; this is oppression (nippeso). 'Nippeso' itself is an oppressor (nippesiko), and the state of being so is oppressing (nippesikatā). The desire to surpass another's gain with one's own gain (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā) is seeking gain from another out of great desire, even after having received gain oneself. In 'and so on' (evamādīnaṃ), the word 'and so on' (ādi) includes endearing speech, ingratiating behavior, and the like. 'Purified by reflection' (paṭisaṅkhānaparisuddho) means being pure and undefiled through reviewing with reflection. 'Use of the four requisites' (catupaccayaparibhogo) is so called because by this reflection the four requisites are used; it is the blameless volition that has so occurred.

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Virtue of Pātimokkha Restraint

14. Tatrāti tesu pātimokkhasaṃvarādīsu. Ādito paṭṭhāyāti “idha bhikkhū”tiādinā (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 1.194) āgatadesanāya ādito pabhuti. Vinicchayakathāti tattha saṃsayavidhamanena vinicchayāvahā kathā. Paṭhamassa atthassa [M 1.0039] sabbasādhāraṇattā asādhāraṇaṃ pabbajitāveṇikaṃ pariyāyaṃ dassento “chinnabhinnapaṭadharāditāya vā”ti āha. Evaṃ hissa paripuṇṇapātimokkhasaṃvarayogyatā dassitā hoti. Bhinnapaṭadharādibhāvo ca nāma daliddassāpi niggahitassa hotīti tato visesetuṃ “saddhāpabbajito”ti vatvā paṭipattiyā yogyabhāvadassanatthaṃ “kulaputto”ti vuttaṃ. Ācārakulaputto vā hi paṭipajjituṃ sakkoti jātikulaputto vā. Sikkhāpadasīlanti cārittavārittappabhedaṃ sikkhāpadavasena paññattaṃ sīlaṃ. Yoti [V 1.0037] aniyamaniddeso yo koci puggalo. Nanti vinayapariyāpannaṃ sīlaṃ. Tanti puggalaṃ. Mokkheti sahakārikāraṇabhāvato. Apāye bhavāni āpāyikāni. Ādi-saddena tadaññaṃ sabbasaṃsāradukkhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Saṃvaraṇaṃ kāyavacīdvārānaṃ pidahanaṃ. Yena te saṃvutā pihitā honti, so saṃvaro. Yasmā pana so sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ avītikkamo vītikkamapaṭipakkhoti katvā, tasmā vuttaṃ “kāyikavācasikassa avītikkamassetaṃ nāma”nti. Pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarena pihitakāyavacīdvāro. Tathābhūto ca yasmā taṃ upeto tena ca samaṅgī nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “upagato samannāgatoti attho”ti.

14. 'Tatra' refers to those things such as Pātimokkha restraint. 'Ādito paṭṭhāya' means from the beginning of the discourse that begins, 'Here, a monk...' 'Vinicchayakathā' is a discourse that brings resolution by dispelling doubt concerning them. Because the first meaning is common to all, wishing to show the uncommon exposition, which is the specific property of the renunciant, he said, 'or due to being one who wears torn and tattered robes, etc.' For in this way, his suitability for the complete Pātimokkha restraint is shown. And the state of wearing torn robes and so on can also belong to a poor person who is destitute; therefore, to distinguish from that one, having said 'one gone forth in faith,' 'a son of good family' is said in order to show suitability for the practice. Indeed, either a son of good family by conduct or a son of good family by birth is able to practice. 'The virtue of the training rules' is the virtue prescribed by way of training rules, which is divided into what should be performed and what should be avoided. 'Yo' is an indefinite designation: any person whatsoever. 'Naṃ' refers to the virtue included in the Vinaya. 'Taṃ' refers to the person. 'It liberates' because of being a cooperative cause. 'Āpāyikāni' means things that exist in the states of deprivation. By the word 'ādi,' it includes all other suffering of saṃsāra. 'Saṃvaraṇa' is the closing of the doors of body and speech. That by which they are restrained and closed is 'saṃvaro.' Furthermore, because that restraint is the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses, being the opposite of transgression, therefore it is said, 'This is a name for the non-transgression of bodily and verbal acts.' 'Restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint' means one whose doors of body and speech are closed by the Pātimokkha restraint. And because one who is such is called one who has approached it and is endowed with it, therefore it is said, 'the meaning is "possessed and endowed".'

Aparo nayo – kilesānaṃ balavabhāvato, pāpakiriyāya sukarabhāvato, puññakiriyāya ca dukkarabhāvato bahukkhattuṃ apāyesu patanasīloti pātī, puthujjano. Aniccatāya vā bhavādīsu kammavegakkhitto ghaṭiyantaṃ viya anavaṭṭhānena paribbhamanato gamanasīloti pātī, maraṇavasena vā tamhi tamhi sattanikāye attabhāvassa pātanasīloti pātī, sattasantāno, cittameva vā. Taṃ pātinaṃ saṃsāradukkhato mokkhetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Cittassa hi vimokkhena satto “vimutto”ti vuccati. Vuttaṃ hi “cittavodānā visujjhantī”ti, “anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti (mahāva. 28) ca. Atha vā avijjādinā hetunā saṃsāre patati gacchati pavattatīti pātī, “avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarata”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.124) hi vuttaṃ. Tassa pātino sattassa taṇhādisaṃkilesattayato mokkho etenāti pātimokkhaṃ[M 1.0040]. “Kaṇṭhekāḷo”tiādīnaṃ viyassa samāsasiddhi veditabbā. Atha vā pāteti vinipāteti dukkheti pāti, cittaṃ. Vuttaṃ hi “cittena nīyati loko, cittena parikassatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.62). Tassa pātino mokkho etenāti pātimokkhaṃ, patati vā etena apāyadukkhe, saṃsāradukkhe cāti pātī, taṇhādisaṃkileso. Vuttaṃ hi “taṇhā janeti purisaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.55-57), taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti (itivu. 15, 105; a. ni. 4.9; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa) ca ādi. Tato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkhaṃ. Atha vā patati etthāti pātīni, cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Vuttaṃ hi “chasu loko samuppanno, chasu kubbati santhava”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.70; su. ni. 171). Tato chaajjhattikabāhirāyatanasaṅkhātato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkhaṃ. Atha vā pāto vinipāto assa [V 1.0038] atthīti pātī, saṃsāro. Tato mokkhoti pātimokkhaṃ, atha vā sabbalokādhipatibhāvato dhammissaro bhagavā “patī”ti vuccati. Muccati etenāti mokkho, patino mokkho tena paññattattāti patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkhaṃ. Sabbaguṇānaṃ vā mūlabhāvato uttamaṭṭhena pati ca so yathāvuttenatthena mokkho cāti patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkhaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “pātimokkhanti mukhametaṃ pamukhameta”nti (mahāva. 135) vitthāro.

Another explanation: Because of the strength of defilements, the ease of doing evil, and the difficulty of doing good, the worldling is by nature one who repeatedly falls into the states of deprivation; thus he is called pātī (one who falls). Or, hurled by the force of kamma into the states of existence and so on, he wanders on restlessly like a water-drawing machine due to impermanence; thus, because he is by nature one who goes, he is called pātī. Or, by way of death, individual existence is made to fall among this or that class of beings; thus the continuity of a being, or the mind itself, is called pātī. That which liberates this pātī from the suffering of saṃsāra is the Pātimokkha. For a being is said to be 'liberated' (vimutto) through the liberation of the mind. As it is said: 'Through the cleansing of the mind they are purified,' and 'Without clinging, the mind is liberated from the cankers.' Or alternatively, due to such causes as ignorance one falls, goes, and continues in saṃsāra; thus one is called pātī. For it has been said: 'For beings obstructed by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving, who are running on and wandering in saṃsāra.' Liberation by means of this [discipline] from the three defilements headed by craving for that being who falls is the Pātimokkha. The formation of this compound should be understood in the same way as 'Kaṇṭhekāḷo' (black-throated) and so on. Or, it causes to fall, causes downfall, and causes suffering; thus the mind is pāti. As it is said: 'By the mind the world is led, by the mind it is dragged around.' Liberation from that pāti [the mind] by means of this [discipline] is the Pātimokkha. Or, by this one falls into the suffering of the states of deprivation and the suffering of saṃsāra; thus defilement such as craving is pātī. For it has been said: 'Craving generates a person,' and 'A person has craving as his companion,' and so on. Liberation from that which causes falling is the Pātimokkha. Or, one falls herein; thus the six internal and external sense bases are pātīni (the places of falling). As it is said: 'In the six the world has arisen, in the six it forms intimacy.' Liberation from that which is called pātī, namely the six internal and external sense bases, is the Pātimokkha. Or, it has falling and downfall; thus saṃsāra is pātī. Liberation from that is the Pātimokkha. Or alternatively, due to his sovereignty over all the world, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, is called pati (lord). One is freed by means of this; thus it is mokkho (liberation). Because it is the liberation-discipline designated by the Lord, it is patimokkho; patimokkho is simply Pātimokkha. Or, because it is the root of all virtues and is chief (pati) in the supreme sense, and it is also liberation (mokkho) in the aforementioned sense, it is patimokkho; patimokkho is simply Pātimokkha. For thus it has been said in detail: 'This Pātimokkha is the entrance, it is the foremost.'

Atha vā pa-iti pakāre, atī-ti accantatthe nipāto, tasmā pakārehi accantaṃ mokkhetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Idaṃ hi sīlaṃ sayaṃ tadaṅgavasena, samādhisahitaṃ paññāsahitañca vikkhambhanavasena, samucchedavasena ca accantaṃ mokkheti mocetīti pātimokkhaṃ, pati pati mokkhoti vā patimokkho, tamhā tamhā vītikkamadosato paccekaṃ mokkhoti attho, patimokkho eva pātimokkhaṃ. Mokkhoti vā nibbānaṃ, tassa mokkhassa paṭibimbabhūtoti patimokkho. Sīlasaṃvaro hi sūriyassa aruṇuggamanaṃ viya nibbānassa udayabhūto tappaṭibhāgo viya yathārahaṃ kilesanibbāpanato, patimokkhoyeva pātimokkhaṃ. Atha vā mokkhaṃ pati vattati, mokkhābhimukhanti vā patimokkhaṃ, patimokkhameva pātimokkhanti evamettha pātimokkha-saddassa attho veditabbo. Iriyatīti attabhāvaṃ pavatteti. “Viharatī”ti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhitassa [M 1.0041] bhikkhuno iriyāpathavihāro dassito. Pāḷiyanti jhānavibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 508 ādayo).

Or, the particle 'pa-' is in the sense of 'various,' and 'ati-' is in the sense of 'completely'; therefore, because it completely liberates in various ways, it is called Pātimokkha. Indeed, this discipline—by itself through momentary liberation, and when accompanied by concentration and wisdom through liberation by suppression and liberation by eradication—completely liberates and frees; thus it is Pātimokkha. Or, 'liberation from each and every' (pati pati mokkho) is patimokkho; the meaning is liberation from each and every fault of transgression. Patimokkho is simply Pātimokkha. Or, mokkha is Nibbāna; because it is a counterpart (paṭibimba) of that liberation (mokkha), it is patimokkho. For moral restraint, being the precursor and counterpart of Nibbāna—just as the dawn is for the sun—is so because it appropriately quenches the defilements. Patimokkho is simply Pātimokkha. Or, it proceeds towards liberation (mokkhaṃ pati vattati), or it is directed towards liberation (mokkhābhimukhaṃ); hence it is patimokkho. Patimokkho is simply Pātimokkha. In this way, the meaning of the word Pātimokkha should be understood here. 'He conducts himself' (iriyati) means he maintains his individual existence. By 'he dwells' (viharati), the dwelling in the postures of a monk established in the Pātimokkha restraint is shown. 'In the Pāḷi' (Pāḷiyaṃ) refers to the Jhānavibhaṅga Pāḷi.

Tattha kāmaṃ samaṇacāraṃ, samaṇagocarañca dassetuṃ “ācāragocarasampanno”ti vuttaṃ, yathā pana maggaṃ ācikkhanto “vāmaṃ muñca, dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhā”ti vajjetabbapubbakaṃ gahetabbaṃ vadeyya, yathā vā sasīsanhānena pahīnasedamalajallikassa mālāgandhavilepanādivibhūsanasaṃvidhānaṃ yuttarūpaṃ, evaṃ pahīnapāpadhammassa kalyāṇadhammasamāyogo yuttarūpoti “atthi ācāro, atthi anācāro”ti dvayaṃ uddisitvā anācāraṃ tāva vibhajituṃ “tattha katamo anācāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kāyiko vītikkamoti tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ. Vācasiko vītikkamoti catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ. Kāyikavācasikoti tadubhayaṃ.

Therein, although it is said, 'endowed with proper conduct and resort,' in order to show the conduct and resort of a recluse, the following is stated. Just as one explaining the path might speak of what should be adopted, preceded by what should be avoided, saying, 'Leave the left, take the right'; or just as arranging adornments such as garlands, perfumes, and ointments is fitting for one who has rid himself of sweat, dirt, and grime through a head-bath; so too, for one who has abandoned unwholesome qualities, the association with wholesome qualities is fitting. Thus, having pointed out the pair, 'there is proper conduct, there is improper conduct,' in order to first analyze improper conduct, it is said, 'Therein, what is improper conduct?' and so on. Therein, 'bodily transgression' is the threefold bodily misconduct. 'Verbal transgression' is the fourfold verbal misconduct. 'Bodily and verbal' means both of these.

Evaṃ ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlassa vītikkamo dassito. Idāni mānasaṃ anācāraṃ dassetuṃ “sabbampi [V 1.0039] dussīlyaṃ anācāro”ti vatvā tattha ekacciyaṃ dassento “idhekacco veḷudānena vā”tiādimāha. Tattha veḷudānenāti paccayuppādanatthena veḷudānena. Pattadānādīsupi eseva nayo. Veḷūti manussānaṃ payojanāvaho yo koci veḷudaṇḍo. Pattaṃ gandhikādīnaṃ gandhapaliveṭhanādiatthaṃ vā, tālanāḷikerādipattaṃ vā. Pupphaṃ yaṃ kiñci manussānaṃ payojanāvahaṃ. Tathā phalaṃ. Sinānaṃ sirīsacuṇṇādinhāniyacuṇṇaṃ. Mattikāpi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Dantakaṭṭhaṃ yaṃ kiñci mukhasodhanatthaṃ dantaponaṃ. Cāṭukamyatā attānaṃ dāsaṃ viya nīcaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā parassa khalitavacanaṃ saṇṭhapetvā piyakāmatāya paggayhavacanaṃ. Muggasūpyatāti muggasūpasamatā saccālikena jīvitakappanaṃ. Yathā hi muggasūpe paccante bahū muggā paccanti, katipayā na paccanti, evaṃ saccālikena jīvitakappane bahu alikaṃ hoti, appakaṃ saccanti. Paribhaṭatīti paribhaṭo, paresaṃ dārake pariharanto. Paribhaṭassa kammaṃ pāribhaṭyaṃ, sā eva pāribhaṭyatā, alaṅkaraṇādinā kuladārakapariharaṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tesaṃ tesaṃ gihīnaṃ gāmantaradesantarādīsu sāsanapaṭisāsanaharaṇaṃ jaṅghapesanikaṃ. Aññataraññatarenāti etesaṃ vā veḷudānādīnaṃ vejjakammabhaṇḍāgārikakammapiṇḍapaṭipiṇḍakammasaṅghuppādacetiyuppādapaṭṭhapanādīnaṃ vā micchājīvena jīvitakappanakakammānaṃ yena kenaci[M 1.0042]. Buddhapaṭikuṭṭhenāti buddhehi garahitena paṭisiddhena. Micchājīvenāti na sammāājīvena. Ayaṃ vuccati anācāroti ayaṃ sabbopi “anācāro”ti kathīyati. Ācāraniddeso vuttapaṭipakkhanayeneva veditabbo.

Thus, the transgression of the Ājīvaṭṭhamakasīla (the virtue with right livelihood as the eighth) has been shown. Now, in order to show mental misconduct, having said, 'All immorality is misconduct,' and therein, wishing to show a certain type, he said the words beginning with, 'Here, a certain one, by giving bamboo…' Herein, 'by giving bamboo' means by giving bamboo for the purpose of producing requisites. In the giving of bowls and so on, this is the same method. 'Bamboo' is any bamboo stick that is useful for human beings. 'Leaf' is either a leaf for the purpose of wrapping perfumes and the like for perfumers, or a leaf of a palmyra palm, coconut palm, or the like. 'Flower' is any flower that is useful for human beings. Likewise, 'fruit.' 'Bathing powder' is bathing powder such as sirīsa powder. Clay is also included herein. 'Tooth-stick' is any tooth-cleaner for the purpose of cleansing the mouth. 'Flattery' is speaking in an ingratiating manner out of a desire to be liked, placing oneself in a low position like a servant, and smoothing over another's faulty speech. 'Bean-soup-like-ness' is making a living by means of truth and falsehood. For just as when bean soup is cooked, many beans are cooked and some are not cooked, so too, in making a living by means of truth and falsehood, much is false and little is true. 'He attends,' thus he is an 'attendant'; one who looks after the children of others. The work of an attendant is 'attendantship'; that itself is 'pāribhaṭyatā'. This is the name for looking after the children of householders by means of adorning them and so on. 'Carrying messages' is the carrying of messages and return-messages for those various householders to other villages, other regions, and so on. 'By one or another' means by any of these livelihood-making actions by means of wrong livelihood, such as the aforementioned giving of bamboo, etc., or medical practice, acting as a storekeeper, giving alms in return for alms, or improperly administering what is produced for the Sangha or for a cetiya. 'Condemned by the Buddhas' means censured and forbidden by the Buddhas. 'By wrong livelihood' means by that which is not right livelihood. 'This is called misconduct' means all this is called 'misconduct.' The exposition of proper conduct should be understood by the method opposite to what has been said.

Gocaraniddesepi paṭhamaṃ agocarassa vacane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Gocaroti piṇḍapātādīnaṃ atthāya upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ. Ayuttaṭṭhānaṃ agocaro. Vesiyā gocaro assāti vesiyāgocaro, mittasanthavavasena upasaṅkamitabbaṭṭhānanti attho. Vesiyā nāma rūpūpajīviniyo, tā mittasanthavavasena na upasaṅkamitabbā, samaṇabhāvassa antarāyakarattā, parisuddhāsayassāpi garahahetuto, tasmā dakkhiṇādānavasena satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva upasaṅkamitabbā. Vidhavā vuccanti matapatikā, pavutthapatikā vā. Thullakumārikāti mahallikā aniviṭṭhakumāriyo, paṇḍakāti napuṃsakā. Te hi ussannakilesā avūpasantapariḷāhā lokāmisasannissitakathābahulā, tasmā na upasaṅkamitabbā. Bhikkhuniyo nāma ussannabrahmacariyā. Tathā bhikkhūpi. Tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ visabhāgavatthubhāvato santhavavasena upasaṅkamane katipāheneva brahmacariyantarāyo siyā, tasmā na upasaṅkamitabbā. Gilānapucchanādivasena upasaṅkamane satokārinā bhavitabbaṃ. Pānāgāranti surāpānagharaṃ. Taṃ soṇḍajanehi [V 1.0040] avivittaṃ hoti. Tattha tehi soṇḍatādivasena na upasaṅkamitabbaṃ brahmacariyantarāyakarattā. Saṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhītiādīsu rājāno nāma ye rajjamanusāsanti. Rājamahāmattā rājissariyasadisāya issariyamattāya samannāgatā. Titthiyāti viparītadassanā bāhirakaparibbājakā. Titthiyasāvakāti tesu daḷhabhattā paccayadāyakā. Ananulomikena saṃsaggenāti tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ ananulomikena paccanīkabhūtena saṃsaggena saṃsaṭṭho viharati, yena brahmacariyantarāyaṃ vā sallekhaparihāniṃ vā pāpuṇāti.

In the exposition of resort, the reason for first stating what is not a resort should be understood by the method already stated. 'Resort' is a suitable place to approach for the sake of alms-food and so on. An unsuitable place is a non-resort. 'One whose resort is a courtesan' means a courtesan is his resort; the meaning is a place to be approached in the manner of friendship and familiarity. 'Courtesans' are those who make a living by means of their physical form. They are not to be approached in the manner of friendship and familiarity, because it is an obstacle to the state of a recluse, and because it is a cause for censure even for one of pure intention. Therefore, they are to be approached only after establishing mindfulness, for the purpose of giving a worthy donation. 'Widows' are said to be those whose husbands have died or whose husbands are away. 'Mature, unmarried women' are mature, grown-up young women who have not yet been established in a household. 'Eunuchs' are neuter persons. For they have abundant defilements, their fever is unallayed, and they are full of talk connected with the baits of the world; therefore, they are not to be approached. Nuns are of abundant holy life. Likewise, monks too. For them, due to being of dissimilar nature to one another, if they approach each other in the manner of familiarity, an obstacle to the holy life could arise in just a few days. Therefore, they are not to be approached. When approaching for reasons such as inquiring about the sick, one should be one who acts mindfully. 'A tavern' is a house for drinking liquor. It is not secluded from drunkards. There, one should not approach them in the manner of drunkards, because it is an obstacle to the holy life. In 'He lives associated with kings,' and so on, 'kings' are those who rule a kingdom. 'Royal chief ministers' are those endowed with a measure of authority similar to the sovereignty of a king. 'Sectarians' are outside wanderers with wrong view. 'Disciples of sectarians' are donors of requisites who have firm devotion to them. 'By an unsuitable association' means: he lives associated by an association that is unsuitable for and contrary to the three trainings, through which he may come to an obstacle to the holy life or a decline in the practice of effacement.

Idāni aparenapi pariyāyena agocaraṃ dassetuṃ “yāni vā pana tānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha assaddhānīti buddhādīsu saddhāvirahitāni. Tato eva appasannāni, kammakammaphalasaddhāya vā abhāvena assaddhāni. Ratanattayappasādābhāvena appasannāni. Akkosakaparibhāsakānīti akkosavatthūhi [M 1.0043] akkosakāni ceva bhayadassanena santajjanakāni ca. Atthaṃ na icchanti anatthameva icchantīti anatthakāmāni. Hitaṃ na icchanti ahitameva icchantīti ahitakāmāni. Phāsu na icchanti aphāsuṃyeva icchantīti aphāsukakāmāni. Yogakkhemaṃ nibbhayaṃ na icchanti, ayogakkhemameva icchantīti ayogakkhemakāmāni. Bhikkhūnanti ettha sāmaṇerānampi saṅgaho. Bhikkhunīnanti ettha sikkhamānasāmaṇerīnaṃ. Sabbesaṃ hi sāsanikānaṃ anatthakāmatādīpanapadamidaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathārūpāni kulānīti tādisāni khattiyakulādīni. Sevatīti nissāya jīvati. Bhajatīti upasaṅkamati. Payirupāsatīti punappunaṃ upagacchati. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ vesiyādiko, rājādiko, assaddhakulādiko ca taṃ taṃ sevantassa tippakāropi ayutto gocaroti agocaro. Ettha hi vesiyādiko pañcakāmaguṇanissayato agocaro. Yathāha “ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo? Yadidaṃ pañca kāmaguṇā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.372). Rājādiko samaṇadhammassa anupanissayato, lābhasakkārāsanivicakkanippothanadiṭṭhivipattihetuto ca. Assaddhakulādiko saddhāhānicittasantāsāvahato agocaro.

Now, to show the unsuitable resort in another way, the passage beginning, “Or whatever those families are…” is stated. Therein, “faithless” means devoid of faith in the Buddha and so forth. For that very reason, they are “displeased”; or, they are “faithless” due to the absence of faith in kamma and the fruit of kamma. They are “displeased” due to an absence of confidence in the Triple Gem. “Abusive and scornful” means they are abusive with grounds for abuse and also intimidating by showing danger. “They do not desire welfare but desire only what is not for one's welfare” means they are “those who desire what is not for one's welfare.” “They do not desire benefit but desire only what is not for one's benefit” means they are “those who desire what is not for one's benefit.” “They do not desire comfort but desire only discomfort” means they are “those who desire discomfort.” “They do not desire security from bondage, which is fearlessness, but desire only the absence of security from bondage” means they are “those who desire the absence of security from bondage.” In the word “monks,” novices are also included. In the word “nuns,” female probationers and female novices are included. For this statement is a term indicating the state of desiring what is not for one's welfare for all who are in the Dispensation. “Such families” means those kinds of families, such as those of the warrior caste and so on. “One associates with” means one lives in dependence upon. “One frequents” means one approaches. “One attends upon” means one goes again and again. This is said: This resort of courtesans and so on, royalty and so on, and faithless families and so on—for one who associates with them, even these three types are an improper resort; therefore, it is called an unsuitable resort (`agocaro`). Herein, the resort of courtesans and so on is an unsuitable resort because it is a basis for the five strands of sensual pleasure. As it is said: “And what, monks, is the unsuitable resort, the foreign territory for a monk? It is these five strands of sensual pleasure.” The resort of royalty and so on is an unsuitable resort because it is not a supporting condition for the recluse's practice, and because it is a cause for gain, honor, the thunderbolt of fame, crushing, and the corruption of views. The resort of faithless families and so on is an unsuitable resort because it brings about a decline of faith and terror of mind.

Gocaraniddese “na vesiyāgocaro”tiādīni vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbāni. Opānabhūtānīti udapānabhūtāni bhikkhusaṅghassa, bhikkhunīsaṅghassa ca catumahāpathe khatapokkharaṇī viya yathāsukhaṃ ogāhanakkhamāni. Kāsāvapajjotānīti bhikkhūnaṃ, bhikkhunīnañca nivatthapārutakāsāvānaṃyeva pabhāhi ekobhāsāni. Isivātapaṭivātānīti gehaṃ pavisantānaṃ[V 1.0041], nikkhamantānañca bhikkhubhikkhunīsaṅkhātānaṃ isīnaṃ cīvaravātena ceva samiñjanapasāraṇādijanitasarīravātena ca paṭivātāni pavāyitāni viniddhutakibbisāni vā.

In the exposition on the resort, the passages beginning with “is not the resort of a courtesan” should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated. “Being like watering places” means they are like wells for the Sangha of monks and the Sangha of nuns, like a dug pond at a crossroads, suitable for entering as one pleases. “Illuminated by saffron robes” means they are of a single radiance from the light of the saffron robes worn and draped by the monks and nuns. “Against the wind of the sages” means that for the sages—that is, monks and nuns—who are entering and leaving a house, there is a contrary wind from the wind of their robes and from the wind of their bodies generated by bending, stretching, and so on; or, it means they are places where defilements have been shaken off.

Idāni niddese āgatanayenāpi ācāragocare dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ pātimokkhasīlaniddese. Imināpi nayenāti idāni vuccamānavidhināpi. Saṅghagatoti saṅghasannipātaṃ gato. Acittīkārakatoti akatacittīkāro, akatagāravoti attho. Ghaṭṭayantoti sarīrena, cīvarena vā ghaṃsanto. Puratopi tiṭṭhati acittīkārakatoti [M 1.0044] sambandhitabbaṃ. Ṭhitakopīti upari tiṭṭhanto viya āsannataraṭṭhāne ṭhitakopi bhaṇati. Bāhāvikkhepakoti bāhuṃ vikkhipanto. Anupāhanānanti anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Saupāhanoti upāhanāruḷho. There bhikkhū anupakhajjāti therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ anupavisitvā tesaṃ āsannataraṭṭhānaṃ upagantvā. Kaṭṭhaṃ pakkhipati aggikuṇḍe. Vokkammāti passato atikkamitvā. Gūḷhāni sabhāvato paṭicchannāni sāṇipākārādinā paṭicchāditāni. Anāpucchāti anāpucchitvā. Assāti anācārassa.

Now, to show the proper conduct and resort also by the method that has come down in the exposition, the passage beginning “Furthermore…” is commenced. “Herein” means in this exposition of the Pātimokkha morality. “By this method too” means also by the procedure now being explained. “Gone to the Sangha” means having gone to the assembly of the Sangha. “Without showing respect” (`acittīkārakato`) means not having shown respect, not having shown reverence. “Jostling” means rubbing with the body or with the robe. It should be connected thus: “and stands in front without showing respect.” “Even one standing” means even one standing in a very close place speaks as if standing above. “Waving the arms” means swinging the arms. “`Anupāhanānaṃ`” (of those without footwear): this is a genitive case used in the sense of disrespect. “`Saupāhano`” (with footwear) means wearing footwear. “Encroaching on the elder monks” means having entered the place where the elder monks are standing and having approached a place very near to them. “He throws wood into the fire-pit.” “Passing by” means having gone past from the side. “Concealed” means hidden by nature, or covered by a hempen screen, a curtain, and so on. “`Anāpucchā`” means without having asked. “`Assa`” means of improper conduct.

Apica bhikkhūtiādi sabbasseva bhikkhuno ācāradassanavasena pavattaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ, na niddesapāḷi. Saddhāsīlasutacāgādiguṇahetuko garubhāvo garukaraṇaṃ vā gāravo, saha gāravenāti sagāravo. Garuṭṭhāniyesu gāravasārajjādivasena paṭissāyanā patissā, sappatissavapaṭipatti. Saha patissāyāti sappatisso. Savisesaṃ hirimanatāya, ottappibhāvena ca hirottappasampanno. Sekhiyadhammapāripūrivasena sunivattho supāruto. Pāsādikenāti pasādāvahena, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Eseva nayo ito paresupi chasu padesu. Abhikkantenāti abhikkamena. Iriyāpathasampannoti sampannairiyāpatho. Tena sesairiyāpathānampi pāsādikatamāha. Indriyesu guttadvāroti cakkhundriyādīsu chasu dvāresu susaṃvihitārakkho. Bhojane mattaññūti paribhuñjitabbato bhojanasaññite catubbidhepi paccaye pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogādivasena sabbaso pamāṇaññū. Jāgariyamanuyuttoti pubbarattāpararattaṃ bhāvanāmanasikārasaṅkhātaṃ jāgariyaṃ sātaccakāritāvasena anu anu yutto tattha yuttapayutto. Satisampajaññena samannāgatotiādi yathāvuttassa ācārassa sambhāradassanaṃ. Tattha appicchoti niiccho. Santuṭṭhoti yathālābhādivasena santosena tuṭṭho. Sakkaccakārīti ādarakārī. Garucittīkārabahuloti [V 1.0042] garuṭṭhāniyesu garukaraṇabahulo. Ayaṃ vuccati ācāroti ayaṃ sagāravatādi atthakāmehi ācaritabbato ācāro.

The passage beginning “Furthermore, a monk…” is a commentary statement that proceeds by way of showing the conduct of every monk; it is not the Pāḷi of the Niddesa. Respect (`gāravo`) is the state of being weighty or the act of respecting, caused by qualities such as faith, virtue, learning, and generosity. `Sagāravo` means with respect, hence respectful. Reverence (`patissā`) is deference towards those worthy of respect, shown through respect, humility, and so on. `Sappatisso` means with reverence, hence reverent. “Endowed with shame and moral dread” means especially due to having a mind with shame and a state of moral dread. “Well-dressed and well-robed” is by way of fulfilling the training rules. “Inspiring confidence” (`pāsādikena`) means bringing confidence; this is an instrumental case in the sense of indicating a characteristic. This same method applies also to the six terms that follow. “In advancing” means by advancing. “Perfect in deportment” means possessing perfect deportment. By that, he indicates the inspiring nature of the remaining postures as well. “With doors guarded in the faculties” means having a well-arranged guard at the six doors beginning with the eye faculty. “Knowing moderation in food” means knowing the measure in every way—by way of seeking, receiving, consuming, and so on—in regard to all four kinds of requisites, which are designated as “food” (`bhojana`) because they are to be consumed. “Devoted to wakefulness” means again and again devoted, constantly engaged therein, by way of continuous practice, to the wakefulness known as meditation and attention in the first and last watches of the night. The passage beginning “Endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension…” shows the supporting conditions for the aforesaid conduct. Therein, “of few wishes” means without wishes. “Contented” means satisfied with contentment according to what has been received, and so on. “Acting respectfully” means acting with respect. “Abounding in reverence” means abounding in showing respect towards those worthy of respect. “This is called conduct” means this practice, beginning with respectfulness, is called ‘conduct’ (`ācāra`) because it ought to be practiced (`ācaritabba`) by those who desire their own welfare.

Sīlādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ upanissayabhūto upanissayagocaro. Satisaṅkhāto cittassa ārakkhabhūto eva gocaro ārakkhagocaro. Kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhāto cittassa upanibandhanaṭṭhānabhūto gocaro upanibandhagocaro. Appicchatādīhi [M 1.0045] dasahi vivaṭṭanissitāya kathāya vatthubhūtehi guṇehi samannāgato dasakathāvatthuguṇasamannāgato. Tato eva kalyāṇo sundaro mittoti kalyāṇamitto. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ parato āgamissati. Assutaṃ suttageyyādiṃ. Suṇātīti sutamayaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppādeti. Sutaṃ pariyodāpetīti tameva yathāsutaṃ avisadatāya apariyodātaṃ punappunaṃ paripucchanādinā visodheti nijjaṭaṃ nigumbaṃ karoti. Tattha ca ye kaṅkhaṭṭhāniyā dhammā, tesu saṃsayaṃ chindanto kaṅkhaṃ vitarati. Kammakammaphalesu, ratanattaye ca sammādiṭṭhiyā ujukaraṇena diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karoti. Tato eva ca duvidhāyapi saddhāsampadāya cittaṃ pasādeti. Atha vā yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ pariyodapetvā tatthāgate rūpārūpadhamme pariggahetvā sapaccayaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggaṇhanto sattadiṭṭhivaṅkavidhamanena diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karoti. Dhammānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannatāmattadassanena tīsupi addhāsu kaṅkhaṃ vitarati. Tato paraṃ ca udayabbayañāṇādivasena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyabhūmiṃ okkamanto aveccapasādena ratanattaye cittaṃ pasādeti. Tathābhūtova tassa kalyāṇamittassa anusikkhanena saddhādīhi guṇehi na hāyati, aññadatthu vaḍḍhateva. Tenāha “yassa vā”tiādi.

The resort that is a supporting condition for virtues such as moral virtue is the resort of support. The resort that is a guard for the mind, known as mindfulness, is the resort of protection. The resort that is a place for binding the mind, known as a meditation subject, is the resort of binding. Endowed with the ten qualities beginning with fewness of wishes, which are the basis for discourse connected with emancipation, one is endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of talk. From this very fact, one becomes a good, excellent friend—a good friend. His characteristics will come later. Hearing what has not been heard, such as the Sutta and Geyya, one generates knowledge based on learning. Purifying what has been heard means that one repeatedly clarifies through questioning and so on what was learned, which was not yet pure due to a lack of clarity, making it free from tangles and thickets. And therein, regarding matters that are grounds for doubt, by cutting off uncertainty one overcomes doubt. Regarding actions and their results, and the Triple Gem, by making one’s view straight with right view, one makes one’s view straight. And from this very fact, one also clarifies the mind through the twofold accomplishment of faith. Alternatively, having purified the Dhamma as heard, having comprehended the material and immaterial phenomena that have arisen therein, and while comprehending name-and-form together with its causes, one makes one's view straight by dispelling the crookedness of the view of a self. By seeing merely the state of phenomena as cause and effect, one overcomes doubt regarding the three periods of time. Then, further developing insight through knowledge of arising and passing away and so on, one enters the noble plane and clarifies the mind with confidence based on penetration in the Triple Gem. Being such, by training in emulation of such a good friend, one does not decline in virtues like faith but only grows. Hence it is said: 'For whom...' and so on.

Antaragharanti antare antare gharāni ettha, taṃ etassāti vā “antaraghara”nti laddhanāmaṃ gocaragāmaṃ paviṭṭho. Tattha ghare ghare bhikkhāpariyesanāya vīthiṃ paṭipanno. Okkhittacakkhūti heṭṭhākhittacakkhu. Kittakena pana okkhittacakkhu hotīti āha “yugamattadassāvī”ti. Susaṃvutoti saṃyato. Yathā panettha susaṃvuto nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “na hatthiṃ olokento”tiādi vuttaṃ.

He entered the alms-village that had received the name 'Antaraghara' because 'herein are houses in the spaces between' or 'this village has them'. There, he proceeded along the street from house to house in search of alms. 'With downcast eyes' means with eyes cast downwards. To what extent is one 'with downcast eyes'? He said, 'seeing a yoke's length.' 'Well-restrained' means restrained. To show how one is called 'well-restrained' in this context, it was said, 'Not looking at an elephant,' and so on.

Yatthāti yesu satipaṭṭhānesu. Cittaṃ bhāvanācittaṃ. Upanibandhatīti upanetvā nibandhati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘Where’ means: in which foundations of mindfulness. ‘Mind’ means the mind of meditation. ‘Binds closely’ means brings near and binds. For it has been said:

“Yathā [V 1.0043] thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ damaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha”nti. (visuddhi. 1.217; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.374; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.107; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163);

“Just as a person here, taming a calf, would bind it to a post; even so, here a person taming their own mind should bind it firmly with mindfulness to the object.”

Satipaṭṭhānānaṃ upanibandhagocarabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sako pettiko visayoti attano pitu sammāsambuddhassa santako, tena diṭṭho dassito ca visayo.

To show that the foundations of mindfulness are the resort of binding, the passage beginning with 'For it has been said' was stated. Here, 'one's own paternal domain' means the domain belonging to one's father, the Perfectly Enlightened One, seen and shown by him.

Aṇuppamāṇesūti [M 1.0046] paramāṇuppamāṇesu. Asañciccaāpannasekhiyaakusalacittuppādādibhedesūti asañcicca āpannasekhiyesu akusalacittuppādādibhedesūti evaṃ asañciccaggahaṇaṃ sekhiyavisesanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sekhiyaggahaṇena cettha vattakkhandhakādīsu (cūḷava. 356 ādayo) āgatavattādīnampi gahaṇaṃ. Tepi hi sikkhitabbaṭṭhena “sekhiyā”ti icchitā. Tathā hi mātikāyaṃ pārājikādīnaṃ viya sekhiyānaṃ paricchedo na kato. Evañca katvā “asañcicca āpannasekhiyā”ti asañciccaggahaṇaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Na hi mātikāyaṃ āgatesu pañcasattatiyā sekhiyesu nosaññāvimokkho nāma atthi, asañciccaggahaṇeneva cettha asatiajānanānampi saṅgaho kato. Keci panettha asiñcicca āpannaggahaṇena acittakāpattiyo gahitāti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ, garukāpattīsupi kāsañci acittakabhāvasabbhāvato, adhiṭṭhānāvikammassa, desanāvikammasseva vā sabbalahukassa vajjassa idhādhippetattā. Tenāha “yāni tāni vajjāni appamattakāni oramattakāni lahukāni lahusammatānī”tiādi. Ādisaddena pātimokkhasaṃvaravisuddhatthaṃ anatikkamanīyānaṃ anāpattigamanīyānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Bhayadassanasīloti paramāṇumattaṃ vajjaṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanasatasahassubbedhasinerupabbatasadisaṃ katvā dassanasabhāvo, sabbalahukaṃ vā dubbhāsitamattaṃ pārājikasadisaṃ katvā dassanasabhāvo. Yaṃ kiñcīti mūlapaññattianupaññattisabbatthapaññattipadesapaññattiādibhedaṃ yaṃ kiñci sikkhitabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ pūretabbaṃ sīlaṃ. Sammā ādāyāti sammadeva sakkaccaṃ, sabbaso ca ādiyitvā. Ayaṃ pana ācāragocarasampadā kiṃ pātimokkhasīle pariyāpannā, udāhu apariyāpannāti? Pariyāpannā. Yadi evaṃ kasmā puna vuttāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “ettha cā”tiādi.

‘In things of minute measure’ means: in things the size of a fine atom. ‘In the divisions such as unintentionally incurred training rules and the arising of unwholesome thoughts’: thus, the term 'unintentional' should be seen as qualifying 'training rules'. Here, the inclusion of 'training rules' also covers the disciplinary procedures mentioned in the Khandhakas (such as in Cūḷavagga 356, etc.), for they too are called 'training rules' in the sense of what should be trained in. Indeed, in the matrix, the training rules are not delineated like the pārājika offenses, etc. And thus, the inclusion of the term 'unintentional' in 'unintentionally incurred training rules' is established. For among the seventy-five training rules mentioned in the matrix, there is no rule called 'non-release through perception'; and here, by the very term 'unintentional', the inclusion of acting without mindfulness or knowledge is made. Some, however, say that the term 'unintentionally incurred' here refers to offenses committed without thought, but that is merely their opinion, since even grave offenses can sometimes occur without thought, and because what is intended here is the very lightest fault, whether requiring an act of determination or an act of confession. Hence it is said, 'whatever offenses are minor, trivial, light, or considered light,' etc. The word 'etc.' should be understood to include those that must not be transgressed for the sake of purity in the Pātimokkha restraint and those that lead to no offense. 'Being disposed to see danger' means perceiving even a fault the size of a fine atom as if it were a massive Mount Meru one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high, or perceiving even the slightest wrong speech as if it were a pārājika offense. 'Whatever' refers to any precept that should be trained in, practiced, and fulfilled, whether root, derived, universally applicable, or specific. 'Having undertaken rightly' means doing so properly, respectfully, and completely. Now, is this accomplishment in conduct and resort included within the Pātimokkha discipline or not? It is included. If so, why was it stated again? With reference to this objection, it is said, 'And here...' etc.

Indriyasaṃvarasīlavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Morality of Sense Restraint

15. Indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ [V 1.0044] pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlassa sambhārabhūtaṃ, tasmiṃ satiyeva icchitabbanti vuttaṃ “soti pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhito bhikkhū”ti. Sampādite hi etasmiṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ suguttaṃ surakkhitameva hoti, susaṃvihitakaṇṭakavati viya sassanti. Kāraṇavasenāti asādhāraṇakāraṇassa vasena. Asādhāraṇakāraṇavasena [M 1.0047] hi phalaṃ apadisīyati, yathā yavaṅkuro bherisaddoti. Nissayavohārena vā etaṃ nissitavacanaṃ, yathā mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontīti. Rūpanti rūpāyatanaṃ. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti ettha yadi cakkhu rūpaṃ passeyya, aññaviññāṇasamaṅginopi passeyyuṃ, na cetaṃ atthi, kasmā? Acetanattā cakkhussa. Tenāha “cakkhu rūpaṃ na passati acittakattā”ti. Atha viññāṇaṃ rūpaṃ passeyya, tirokuṭṭādigatampi naṃ passeyya appaṭighabhāvato, idampi natthi sabbassa viññāṇassa dassanābhāvato. Tenāha “cittaṃ na passati acakkhukattā”ti. Tattha yathā cakkhusannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ passati, na yaṃ kiñci. Tañca kenaci kuṭṭādinā antarite na uppajjati, yattha ālokassa vibandho. Yattha pana na vibandho phalikagabbhapaṭalādike, tattha antaritepi uppajjateva. Evaṃ viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ cakkhu passati, na yaṃ kiñcīti viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ cakkhuṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”ti.

15. The morality of sense restraint is a support for the morality of Pātimokkha restraint; it is said that only when the latter is present is the former to be desired, as in the statement, “a monk stands firm in the morality of Pātimokkha restraint.” For when this morality of sense restraint is accomplished, the morality of Pātimokkha restraint is well-guarded and well-protected, just like grain with a well-arranged thorn fence. “By reason” means by way of an uncommon cause. For a result is designated by an uncommon cause, as in “barley sprout” or “sound of a drum.” Or this is a statement about the dependent by way of the terminology of the support, like “the benches are shouting.” “Form” means the form-base. In “having seen a form with the eye,” if the eye were to see a form, even those endowed with other consciousness would see it. But this is not the case. Why? Because the eye is non-sentient. Therefore, it is said, “The eye does not see a form because it is without mind.” Then, if consciousness were to see a form, it would see it even when behind a wall, etc., because of its non-impingement. But this also is not so, because of the absence of seeing for consciousness in general. Therefore, it is said, “The mind does not see because it is without an eye.” Here, just as the consciousness dependent on the eye sees, not just any consciousness sees. And that consciousness does not arise when obstructed by something like a wall, where there is an obstruction to light. But where there is no obstruction, such as in crystal chambers or sheets, it arises even when obstructed. Thus, the eye, supported by consciousness, sees; not just any eye sees. This statement, “having seen a form with the eye,” is said with reference to the eye supported by consciousness.

Dvārārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭeti dvārassa ārammaṇena saṅghaṭṭe sati, cakkhussa rūpārammaṇe āpāthagateti adhippāyo. Pasādavatthukena cittenāti cakkhupasādavatthukena tannissāya pavattena viññāṇena, yaṃ “cakkhuviññāṇa”nti vuccati. Passatīti oloketi. Cakkhupasādasannissaye hi viññāṇe ālokānuggahitaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ sannissayaguṇena obhāsente taṃsamaṅgipuggalo “rūpaṃ passatī”ti vuccati. Obhāsanañcettha ārammaṇassa yathāsabhāvato vibhāvanaṃ, yaṃ “paccakkhato gahaṇa”nti vuccati. Usunā lakkhassa vedhe sijjhante tassa sambhārabhūtena dhanunā vijjhatīti vacanaṃ viya viññāṇena rūpadassane sijjhante cakkhunā rūpaṃ passatīti īdisī sasambhārakathā nāmesā hoti. Sasambhārā kathā sasambhārakathā, dassanassa kāraṇasahitāti attho. Sasambhārassa vā dassanassa kathā sasambhārakathā. Tasmāti yasmā kevalena cakkhunā, kevalena vā viññāṇena rūpadassanaṃ natthi, tasmā.

“When the door and object collide” means that when the door collides with the object, the form-object comes into the range of the eye. “With consciousness having the sensitive-matter as its base” means by consciousness that has the eye-sensitivity as its base and arises in dependence on it, which is called “eye-consciousness.” “Sees” means “looks at.” For when consciousness, which has the eye-sensitivity as its support, illuminates the form-object, which is assisted by light, by the quality of its support, the person endowed with that consciousness is said to “see a form.” And illumination here is the clear showing of the object according to its true nature, which is called “grasping directly.” Just as when the piercing of a target by an arrow is being accomplished, there is the saying “one shoots with the bow,” which is the support for it, similarly, when the seeing of a form by consciousness is being accomplished, the saying “one sees a form with the eye” is such a statement that includes its support. A statement with its support is a “means-inclusive statement”; the meaning is a statement together with the cause of seeing. Or, a statement about seeing that has its support is a “means-inclusive statement.” Therefore—because seeing a form does not occur by the eye alone, nor by consciousness alone—therefore.

Itthipurisanimittaṃ vāti ettha itthisantānanissitarūpamukhena gayhamānaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ thanamaṃsāvisadatā [V 1.0045] nimmassumukhatā kesabandhanavatthaggahaṇaṃ avisadaṭṭhānagamanādi ca sabbaṃ “itthī”ti sañjānanassa kāraṇabhāvato itthinimittaṃ. Vuttavipariyāyato purisanimittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Subhanimittādikaṃ vāti ettha rāguppattihetubhūto iṭṭhākāro subhanimittaṃ. Ādi-saddena paṭighanimittādīnaṃ [M 1.0048] saṅgaho. So pana dosuppattiādihetubhūto aniṭṭhādiākāro veditabbo. Kāmañcettha pāḷiyaṃ abhijjhādomanassāva sarūpato āgatā, upekkhānimittassāpi pana saṅgaho icchitabbo, asamapekkhanena uppajjanakamohassāpi asaṃvarabhāvato. Tathā hi vakkhati “muṭṭhasaccaṃ vā aññāṇaṃ vā”ti. Upekkhānimittanti cettha aññāṇupekkhāya vatthubhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, tañcassa asamapekkhanavasena veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ saṅkhepato rāgadosamohānaṃ kāraṇaṃ “subhanimittādika”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimitta”nti. Diṭṭhamatteyeva saṇṭhātīti “diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissatī”ti (udā. 10) sutte vuttanayena vaṇṇāyatane cakkhuviññāṇena, vīthicittehi ca gahitamatteyeva tiṭṭhati, na tato paraṃ kiñci subhādiākāraṃ parikappeti. Pākaṭabhāvakaraṇatoti paribyattabhāvakaraṇato vibhūtabhāvakaraṇato. Visabhāgavatthuno hi hatthādiavayavesu subhādito parikappentassa aparāparaṃ tattha uppajjamānā kilesā paribyattā hontīti te tesaṃ anubyañjanā nāma. Te pana yasmā tathā tathā sanniviṭṭhānaṃ bhūtupādāyarūpānaṃ sannivesākāro. Na hi taṃ muñcitvā paramatthato hatthādi nāma koci atthi. Tasmā vuttaṃ “hatthapāda…pe… ākāraṃ na gaṇhātī”ti. Kiṃ pana gaṇhātīti āha “yaṃ tattha bhūtaṃ, tadeva gaṇhātī”ti. Yaṃ tasmiṃ sarīre vijjamānaṃ kesalomādi bhūtupādāyamattaṃ vā, tadeva yāthāvato gaṇhāti. Tattha asubhākāragahaṇassa nidassanaṃ dassento “cetiyapabbatavāsī”tiādinā mahātissattheravatthuṃ āhari.

Regarding “the sign of a woman or a man”: Here, the “sign of a woman” is anything that causes the perception “woman,” because it is a cause for such recognition. This includes the shape grasped with the form dependent on a woman's continuity as the principal feature, the indistinctness of the flesh of the breasts, a face without a beard, the manner of tying the hair and wearing clothes, and going to secluded places, etc. The “sign of a man” should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated. Regarding “a beautiful sign, etc.”: Here, a “beautiful sign” is a desirable aspect that is a cause for the arising of lust. By the word “etc.”, the sign of aversion and so on are included. That, however, should be understood as an undesirable aspect, etc., that is a cause for the arising of hatred, etc. And although in the Pāḷi only covetousness and dejection are mentioned in their own form, the inclusion of the “sign of equanimity” should also be intended, because delusion that arises through improper examination is also a state of non-restraint. For so it will be said: “forgetfulness or ignorance.” Here, the “sign of equanimity” is the object that is the basis for ignorant equanimity, and that should be understood by way of one's improper examination. Thus, in brief, the cause of lust, hatred, and delusion is called “the beautiful sign, etc.” Therefore, it is said: “the sign that is the basis for the defilements.” “One stands only in the seen” means that, in the way stated in the sutta, “In the seen, there will be only the seen,” one stands only in the mere grasping of the color-base by eye-consciousness and by the process-thoughts, and beyond that, one does not imagine any aspect of beauty, etc. “Because of making it manifest” means because of making it evident, because of making it distinct.
