For one who imagines beauty, etc., in the parts of a dissimilar object, like hands, the defilements that arise there again and again become manifest; therefore, those parts are called their “secondary characteristics.” But since those parts are the mode of arrangement of primary elements and derived matter that are arranged in such and such a way, apart from that, in an ultimate sense, there is nothing called “hand,” etc. Therefore, it is said: “one does not grasp the aspect of a hand, a foot…” What, then, does one grasp? It is said: “One grasps only what is actually there.” That is, whatever exists in that body, such as head-hair, body-hair, etc., or just the primary elements and derived matter, that alone one grasps as it really is. There, showing an illustration of grasping the aspect of unattractiveness, he brought forth the story of the Elder Mahātissa, the resident of Cetiyapabbata, with the words “the resident of Cetiyapabbata,” etc.

Tattha sumaṇḍitapasādhitāti suṭṭhu maṇḍitā pasādhitā ca. Ābharaṇādīhi āhārimehi maṇḍanaṃ. Sarīrassa ucchādanādivasena paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ pasādhananti vadanti, ābharaṇehi, pana vatthālaṅkārādīhi ca alaṅkaraṇaṃ pasādhanaṃ. Ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇaṃ maṇḍanaṃ. Vipallatthacittāti rāgavasena viparītacittā. Olokentoti thero kammaṭṭhānamanasikāreneva gacchanto saddakaṇṭakattā pubbabhāgamanasikārassa hasitasaddānusārena “kimeta”nti olokento. Asubhasaññanti aṭṭhikasaññaṃ. Aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhānaṃ hi thero tadā pariharati. Arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti thero [M 1.0049] kira tassā hasantiyā dantaṭṭhidassaneneva pubbabhāgabhāvanāya subhāvitattā paṭibhāganimittaṃ, sātisayañca upacārajjhānaṃ labhitvā yathāṭhitova tattha paṭhamajjhānaṃ adhigantvā taṃ pādakaṃ katvā [V 1.0046] vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggaparamparāya āsavakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Pubbasaññaṃ anussarīti pubbakaṃ yathāraddhaṃ kālena kālaṃ anuyuñjiyamānaṃ aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhānaṃ anussari samannāhari. Anumagganti anupathaṃ tassā padānupadaṃ. Therassa kira bhāvanāya paguṇabhāvato dantaṭṭhidassaneneva tassā sakalasarīraṃ aṭṭhikasaṅghātabhāvena upaṭṭhāsi. Na taṃ “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā sañjāni. Tenāha “nābhijānāmi…pe… mahāpathe”ti.

Therein, 'well-adorned and well-beautified' means thoroughly adorned and beautified. Adornment is with removable ornaments and the like. They say that the restoration of the body by means of anointing and so forth is 'beautifying'; however, decoration with ornaments, garments, and other embellishments is 'beautifying'. Filling in deficient places is 'adorning'. 'With a perverted mind' means with a mind distorted by lust. 'Looking': The elder, while walking with attention only to his meditation subject, looked, following the sound of laughter, because sound is a thorn to the preliminary stage of attention, thinking, 'What is this?' 'Perception of the foul' means the perception of the skeleton. Indeed, at that time the elder was practicing the meditation subject of the skeleton. 'He attained Arahantship': It is said that the elder, by the mere sight of the bones of her teeth, due to his preliminary meditation being well-developed, obtained the counterpart sign and, along with it, superior access concentration. Then, just as he stood, he attained the first jhāna therein. Making that the basis, he developed insight and, through the succession of paths, reached the destruction of the taints. 'He recalled his former perception' means he recollected and brought to mind the meditation subject of the skeleton, which he had previously undertaken and was practicing from time to time. 'Along the path' means along her path, step by step. It is said that due to the elder’s proficiency in meditation, by the mere sight of the bones of her teeth, her entire body appeared to him as a mass of bones. He did not perceive her as 'a woman' or 'a man'. Therefore he said, 'I do not recognize... on the great road.'

“Yassa cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetū”ti vatvā puna “tassa cakkhundriyassa satikavāṭena pidahanatthāyā”ti vuttaṃ, na asaṃvarassāti. Yadidaṃ yaṃ cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetu abhijjhādianvāssavanaṃ dassitaṃ, taṃ asaṃvutacakkhundriyasseva hetu pavattaṃ dassitanti katvā vuttaṃ. Cakkhudvārikassa hi abhijjhādianvāssavanassa taṃdvārikaviññāṇassa viya cakkhundriyaṃ padhānakāraṇaṃ. Cakkhundriyassa asaṃvutatte sati te anvāssavantīti asaṃvariyamānacakkhundriyahetuko so asaṃvaro tathā vuttoti. Yatvādhikaraṇanti hi yassa cakkhundriyassa kāraṇāti attho. Kīdisassa ca kāraṇāti? Asaṃvutassa, kiñca asaṃvutaṃ? Yassa cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetu abhijjhādayo anvāssavanti, tassa saṃvarāyāti ayamettha yojanā.

Having stated, 'Due to the cause which is the non-restraint of the eye faculty,' it is further said, 'for the sake of closing that eye faculty with the door of mindfulness,' not 'of non-restraint.' This was said because: that which was shown, namely the influx of covetousness and so forth due to the cause that is non-restraint of the eye faculty, is shown to have occurred due to the cause that is precisely the unrestrained eye faculty. For the eye faculty is the primary cause of the influx of covetousness and so forth at the eye-door, just as it is of the consciousness at that door. When the eye faculty is unrestrained, those defilements flow in. Thus that non-restraint, which has the unrestrained eye faculty as its cause, is spoken of in that way. Indeed, 'yatvādhikaraṇaṃ' means 'because of which eye faculty as a cause.' And of what kind of [faculty]? Of an unrestrained one. And what is 'unrestrained'? It is the eye faculty characterized by that influx, for which, due to the cause that is non-restraint of the eye faculty, covetousness and so forth flow in. 'For the restraint of that'—this is the connection here.

Javanakkhaṇe pana sace dussīlyaṃ vātiādi puna avacanatthaṃ idheva sabbaṃ vuttanti chasu dvāresu yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi pañcadvāre kāyavacīduccaritasaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ atthi, tasmā dussīlyāsaṃvaro manodvāravasena, sesāsaṃvaro chadvāravasena yojetabbo. Muṭṭhasaccādīnaṃ hi satipaṭipakkhākusaladhammādibhāvato siyā pañcadvāre uppatti, na tveva kāyikavācasikavītikkamabhūtassa dussīlyassa tattha uppatti, pañcadvārikajavanānaṃ aviññattijanakattā. Dussīlyādayo cettha pañca asaṃvarā sīlasaṃvarādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ saṃvarānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvena vuttā. Tasmiṃ satīti tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati.

However, regarding 'if at the moment of impulsion there is misconduct,' and so forth, all has been stated right here for the purpose of not repeating it. Therefore, it should be understood as applicable in the six doors as is possible. For in the five doors there is no misconduct consisting of bodily or verbal wrong conduct. Therefore, non-restraint in misconduct is to be connected with the mind-door, and the remaining non-restraints with the six doors. Indeed, forgetfulness and so forth may arise in the five doors, as they are unwholesome states, etc., opposed to mindfulness; but misconduct, which is a bodily or verbal transgression, cannot possibly arise there, because the impulsions of the five doors do not generate intimation. And here, the five non-restraints—misconduct and so forth—are stated as being the opposites of the five restraints: moral restraint and so forth. 'When that is present' means when that non-restraint is present in that impulsion.

Yathā [M 1.0050] kinti yena pakārena javane uppajjamāno asaṃvaro “cakkhundriye asaṃvaro”ti vuccati, taṃ nidassanaṃ kinti attho. Yathātiādinā nagaradvāre asaṃvare sati taṃsambandhānaṃ gharādīnaṃ asaṃvutatā viya javane asaṃvare sati taṃsambandhānaṃ dvārādīnaṃ asaṃvutatāti evaṃ aññāsaṃvare aññāsaṃvutatā sāmaññameva nidasseti, na pubbāparasāmaññaṃ, antobahisāmaññaṃ vā. Sati vā dvārabhavaṅgādike puna uppajjamānaṃ javanaṃ bāhiraṃ viya katvā nagaradvārasamānaṃ vuttaṃ[V 1.0047], itarañca antonagare gharādisamānaṃ. Paccayabhāvena hi purimanipphannaṃ javanakāle asantampi bhavaṅgādi cakkhādi viya phalanipphattiyā santaṃyeva nāma hoti. Na hi dharamānaṃyeva “santa”nti vuccati. “Bāhiraṃ viya katvā”ti ca paramatthato javanassa bāhirabhāve, itarassa ca abbhantarabhāve asatipi “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca kho āgantukehi upakkiliṭṭha”ntiādi (a. ni. 1.49) vacanato āgantukabhūtassa kadāci kadāci uppajjamānassa javanassa bāhirabhāvo, tabbidhurasabhāvassa itarassa abbhantarabhāvo ekena pariyāyena hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Javane vā asaṃvare uppanne tato paraṃ dvārabhavaṅgādīnaṃ asaṃvarahetubhāvāpattito. Asaṃvarassa hi uppattiyā dvārabhavaṅgādīnaṃ tassa hetubhāvo paññāyatīti. Nagaradvārasadisena javanena pavisitvā dussīlyādicorānaṃ dvārabhavaṅgādīsu musanaṃ kusalabhaṇḍavināsanaṃ kathitaṃ. Yasmiṃ hi dvāre asaṃvaro uppajjati, so tattha dvārādīnaṃ saṃvarūpanissayabhāvaṃ upacchindantoyeva pavattatīti. Dvārabhavaṅgādīnaṃ javanena saha sambandho ekasantatipariyāpannato daṭṭhabbo.

'How is it like?' means: in what way is non-restraint arising in the impulsion called 'non-restraint in the eye faculty'? What is the illustration for that? By 'just as' and so forth, it illustrates only a general correspondence: just as when there is non-restraint at the city gate, there is non-restraint of the houses and so forth connected with it, so too, when there is non-restraint in the impulsion, there is non-restraint of the doors and so forth connected with it. It does not show a general correspondence of before and after, nor of inside and outside. Or, when there are the door, life-continuum, and so forth, the impulsion that arises again, having been treated as if it were external, is said to be like the city gate, and the other is said to be like the houses inside the city. For by way of conditionality, even though the life-continuum and so forth, having previously arisen, are not present at the time of the impulsion, they are indeed called 'present' due to the accomplishment of their result, like the eye and so forth. For it is not only what is currently existing that is called 'present'. And the phrase 'having been treated as if it were external' is stated because, although in the ultimate sense there is no externality of the impulsion nor internality of the other, based on the saying, 'Monks, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements' (AN 1.49), it follows in one way that the impulsion, which is adventitious and arises only from time to time, has an external aspect, while the other, having a different nature, has an internal aspect. Or, it is said because when non-restraint has arisen in the impulsion, thereafter the door, life-continuum, and so forth attain the state of being a cause for non-restraint. For by the arising of non-restraint, their state as its cause is discerned. It is said that the thieves of misconduct and so forth, having entered through the impulsion which is like the city gate, plunder at the door, life-continuum, and so forth, destroying the goods of wholesomeness. For at whichever door non-restraint arises, it proceeds only by cutting off the state of the door and so forth as a supporting condition for restraint. The connection of the door, life-continuum, and so forth with the impulsion should be seen from their inclusion in a single mental continuum.

Ettha ca cakkhudvāre rūpārammaṇe āpāthagate niyamitādivasena kusalākusalajavane sattakkhattuṃ uppajjitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇe tadanurūpameva manodvārikajavane tasmiṃyevārammaṇe sattakkhattuṃyeva uppajjitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇe puna tasmiṃyeva dvāre tadevārammaṇaṃ nissāya “itthī puriso”tiādinā vavatthapentaṃ pasādarajjanādivasena sattakkhattuṃ javanaṃ javati. Evaṃ pavattamānaṃ javanaṃ sandhāya “javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi agutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

And here, at the eye-door, when a form-object has come into range, and after wholesome or unwholesome impulsion has arisen seven times by way of the fixed [series], etc., and descended into the life-continuum; and when, just in accordance with that, the mind-door impulsion has arisen just seven times on that very same object and descended into the life-continuum; then again, at that very same door, relying on that very same object, while determining it by way of “a woman,” “a man,” etc., the impulsion runs for seven times by way of clear confidence, lust, and so forth. With reference to an impulsion that occurs thus, it is said: “When misconduct and so forth arise in the impulsion, if there is non-restraint in it, the door is also unguarded,” and so forth.

Tasmiṃ pana javane. Sīlādīsūti sīlasaṃvarasatisaṃvarañāṇasaṃvarakhantisaṃvaravīriyasaṃvaresu uppannesu. Yathā hi pageva satiārakkhaṃ anupaṭṭhapentassa [M 1.0051] dussīlyādīnaṃ uppatti, evaṃ pageva satiārakkhaṃ upaṭṭhapentassa sīlādīnaṃ uppatti veditabbā. Saddādīsupi yathārahaṃ nimittānubyañjanāni veditabbāni. Sotaviññāṇena hi saddaṃ sutvā “itthisaddo”ti vā “purisasaddo”ti vā iṭṭhāniṭṭhādikaṃ vā kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ na gaṇhāti, sutamatte eva saṇṭhāti. Yo ca gītasaddādikassa kilesānaṃ anu anu byañjanato “anubyañjana”nti laddhavohāro mandatārādivasena vavatthito chajjādibhedabhinno ākāro, tampi na gaṇhātīti. Evaṃ gandhādīsupi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ. Manodvāre pana sāvajjanabhavaṅgaṃ manodvāraṃ tasmiṃ dvāre dhammārammaṇe [V 1.0048] āpāthagate taṃ javanamanasāva viññāya vijānitvātiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Kileso anubandho etassāti kilesānubandho, so eva nimittādigāho, tato parivajjanalakkhaṇaṃ kilesānubandhanimittādiggāhaparivajjanalakkhaṇaṃ. Ādi-saddena anubyañjanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

However, in that impulsion. ‘In morality, etc.’ means when restraint of morality, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, restraint of patience, and restraint of energy have arisen. For just as the arising of immorality, etc., is to be understood for one who does not establish the guard of mindfulness beforehand, so the arising of morality, etc., is to be understood for one who does establish the guard of mindfulness beforehand. In sounds, etc., also, the signs and details are to be understood as appropriate. For, having heard a sound with ear-consciousness, one does not grasp the sign—be it the sound of a woman, the sound of a man, or a sign that is pleasant, unpleasant, etc., and a basis for defilements; one stands fast in the mere hearing. And that feature which, because it makes the defilements manifest again and again (`anu anu byañjanato`), has received the designation ‘detail’ (`anubyañjana`)—a feature of sounds like singing, etc., established by way of being low, high, etc., and distinguished by the divisions of the note chajja, etc.—that too one does not grasp. Thus it should be stated as appropriate in the case of smells, etc., also. At the mind-door, however, the mind-door is the life-continuum together with advertence. When a mind-object has come into range at that door, it should be connected with: ‘having known and understood it with the impulsion-mind itself,’ etc. Defilement is the follower of this (`kileso anubandho etassa`), hence `kilesānubandho` (that which has a following of defilement). That itself is the grasping of signs, etc. The characteristic of avoidance of that is the characteristic of avoidance of the grasping of signs, etc., which has a following of defilement. By the word `ādi` (etc.), it includes `anubyañjana` (detail).

Ājīvapārisuddhisīlavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Morality of Purity of Livelihood

16. Vutteti idheva uddesavasena pubbe vutte. Tathā hi “ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadāna”nti paduddhāraṃ katvā tāni pāḷivaseneva dassetuṃ “yāni tānī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yāni tāni evaṃ paññattāni cha sikkhāpadānīti sambandho. Ājīvahetūti jīvikanimittaṃ, “evāhaṃ paccayehi akilamanto jīvissāmī”ti adhippāyena. Ājīvakāraṇāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Pāpicchoti pāpikāya asantaguṇasambhāvanicchāya samannāgato. Icchāpakatoti icchāya apakato upadduto, abhibhūto vā. Asantanti avijjamānaṃ. Abhūtanti anuppannaṃ. Anuppannattā hi tassa taṃ asantanti purimassa pacchimaṃ kāraṇavacanaṃ. Uttarimanussadhammanti uttarimanussānaṃ ukkaṭṭhapurisānaṃ dhammaṃ, manussadhammato vā uttari ukkaṭṭhaṃ. Ullapatīti uggatāyuko lapati. Sīlaṃ hi bhikkhuno āyu, taṃ tassa tathālapanasamakālameva vigacchati. Tenāha “āpatti pārājikassā”ti pārājikasaṅkhātā āpatti assa, pārājikasaññitassa vā vītikkamassa āpajjanaṃ ullapananti attho. Sañcarittaṃ samāpajjatīti sañcaraṇabhāvaṃ āpajjati, itthiyā vā purisamatiṃ, purisassa vā itthimatiṃ ārocetīti adhippāyo. “Imesaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vītikkamassa vasenā”ti sambandho heṭṭhā dassito eva.

16. ‘Stated’ (`vutte`): In what was stated previously in this very text by way of summary. Indeed, having made an extraction of the passage, ‘the six training rules prescribed for the sake of livelihood,’ it was begun with ‘Which are those,’ etc., in order to show them by way of the Pāḷi itself. Therein, the connection is: ‘Which are those six training rules that were thus prescribed.’ ‘For the sake of livelihood’ (`ājīvahetu`) means for the sake of subsistence, with the intention: ‘Thus I shall live without fatigue from the requisites.’ ‘For the reason of livelihood’ (`ājīvakāraṇā`) is a synonym for that very word. ‘Of evil wishes’ (`pāpiccho`) means one who is endowed with the evil desire for having non-existent virtues praised. ‘Overcome by desire’ (`icchāpakato`) means removed or afflicted by desire, or overwhelmed. ‘Non-existent’ (`asantaṃ`) means not present. ‘Not arisen’ (`abhūtaṃ`) means not produced. Indeed, because it has not been produced, it is non-existent for him; thus the latter word is an explanation of the reason for the former. ‘A state of superior humans’ (`uttarimanussadhammaṃ`) means the state of superior humans, i.e., excellent persons; or a state that is superior and excellent to the human state. ‘He claims’ (`ullapati`): he speaks with his life-force having departed (`uggatāyuko lapati`). Indeed, morality is a bhikkhu’s life (`āyu`), and that life of his departs at the very same time as he speaks thus. Therefore, it is said, ‘an offense of `pārājika` [is incurred] by him,’ meaning an offense called `pārājika` would be his; or, the claiming (`ullapanaṃ`) is the falling into a transgression designated as `pārājika`. ‘He engages in matchmaking’ (`sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati`): he reaches the state of being a go-between; the intention is that he reports a man’s intention to a woman, or a woman’s intention to a man. The connection, ‘by way of the transgression of these six training rules,’ has already been shown below.

Kuhanātiādīsūti [M 1.0052] heṭṭhā uddiṭṭhapāḷiyāva paduddhāro. Ayaṃ pāḷīti ayaṃ vibhaṅge (vibha. 861) āgatā niddesapāḷi.

‘In deception, etc.’: The extraction of the passage is from the Pāḷi indicated below. ‘This Pāḷi’: This is the Pāḷi of exposition that comes in the Vibhaṅga.

17. Cīvarādipaccayā labbhantīti lābhā. Te eva sakkaccaṃ ādaravasena diyyamānā sakkārā. Patthaṭayasatā kittisaddo. Taṃ lābhañca sakkārañca kittisaddañca. Sannissitassāti ettha taṇhānissayo adhippetoti āha “patthayantassā”ti. Asantaguṇadīpanakāmassāti asante attani avijjamāne saddhādiguṇe sambhāvetukāmassa. Asantaguṇasambhāvanatālakkhaṇā, paṭiggahaṇe [V 1.0049] ca amattaññutālakkhaṇā hi pāpicchatā. Icchāya apakatassāti pāpikāya icchāya sammāājīvato apeto katoti apakato. Tathābhūto ca ājīvūpaddavena upaddutoti katvā āha “upaddutassāti attho”ti.

17. Because requisites such as robes are obtained (`labbhanti`), they are called gains (`lābhā`). Those very things, when given carefully and by way of respect, are called honors (`sakkārā`). The state of having a widespread reputation is the word for fame (`kittisaddo`). That is, that gain, that honor, and that word of fame. In the word `sannissitassa` (for one dependent on), because dependence on craving is intended, he said `patthayantassa` (for one who desires). ‘For one with the desire to display non-existent virtues’ means for one who desires to have praised the qualities of faith, etc., which are non-existent in oneself. For evil desire (`pāpicchatā`) has the characteristic of having non-existent virtues praised and the characteristic of not knowing the measure in accepting. ‘For one overcome by desire’ (`icchāya apakatassa`): `apakato` means one who is made to be separated from right livelihood by evil desire. And because one who has become thus is afflicted by the calamity of livelihood, he said, ‘“for one who is afflicted” is the meaning.’

Kuhanameva paccayuppādanassa vatthūti kuhanavatthu. Tividhampetaṃ tattha āgataṃ tassa nissayabhūtāya imāya pāḷiyā dassetunti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Tadatthikassevāti tehi cīvarādīhi atthikasseva. Paṭikkhipanenāti cīvarādīnaṃ paṭikkhipanahetu. Assāti bhaveyya. Paṭiggahaṇena cāti ca-saddena pubbe vuttaṃ paṭikkhipanaṃ samuccinoti.

Deception itself is the basis (`vatthu`) for producing requisites, thus it is the ‘basis of deception’ (`kuhanavatthu`). The meaning should be understood thus: this threefold [basis of deception] that is found there is to be shown by this Pāḷi, which has become its support. ‘For one who has need of them’ (`tadatthikassa eva`) means for one who has need of those robes, etc. ‘By rejection’ (`paṭikkhipanena`) means because of the rejection of robes, etc. ‘It would be’ (`assā`) means `bhaveyya`. ‘And by acceptance’ (`paṭiggahaṇena ca`): with the word `ca` (and), it includes the rejection stated previously.

Bhiyyokamyatanti bahukāmataṃ. Yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ, tasmā “dhāreyyā”ti ettha yadetaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhāraṇaṃ, etaṃ samaṇassa sāruppanti yojanā. Pāpaṇikānīti āpaṇato chaḍḍitāni. Nantakānīti antarahitāni coḷakhaṇḍāni. Uccinitvāti uñchanena cinitvā saṅgahetvā. Uñchācariyāyāti uñchācariyāya laddhena. Gilānassa paccayabhūtā bhesajjasaṅkhātā jīvitaparikkhārā gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā. Pūtimuttanti purāṇassa, apurāṇassa ca sabbassa gomuttassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Pūtimuttenāti pūtibhāvena muttena parehi chaḍḍitena, pūtibhūtena vā gomuttena. Dhutavādoti paresampi dhutaguṇavādī. Sammukhībhāvāti sammukhato vijjamānattā, labbhamānatāyāti attho.

Bhiyyokamyatā means the state of desiring much. The word yanti refers to action; therefore, in the phrase ‘dhāreyya,’ the connection should be made thus: that wearing which is done by making a saṅghāṭi robe, this is suitable for an ascetic. Pāpaṇikāni means things discarded from a shop. Nantakāni means pieces of cloth without borders. Uccinitvā means having collected and gathered by gleaning. Uñchācariyāya means by that which is obtained through the practice of gleaning. The life-requisites which are supportive for the sick and are designated as medicine are the requisites of medicine as support for the sick. Pūtimutta is the name for all cow's urine, both old and new. Pūtimuttena means by that which is discarded by others due to its putrid state, or by cow's urine that has become putrid. Dhutavādo means one who speaks of the virtues of ascetic practices even to others. Sammukhībhāvā means due to being present face-to-face, due to being obtainable; this is the meaning.

Attānaṃ uttarimanussadhammādhigamassa sāmante katvā jappanaṃ sāmantajappanaṃ. Mahesakkhoti mahānubhāvo, uttarimanussadhammādhigamenāti adhippāyo. “Mitto”ti sāmaññato vatvā puna taṃ viseseti “sandiṭṭho sambhatto”ti[M 1.0053]. Diṭṭhamatto hi mitto sandiṭṭho. Daḷhabhattiko sambhatto. Sahāyoti saha āyanako, sakhāti attho. Sattapadino hi “sakhā”ti vuccanti. Vihāro pākāraparicchinno sakalo āvāso. Aḍḍhayogo dīghapāsādo, garuḷasaṇṭhānapāsādotipi vadanti. Pāsādo caturassapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Kūṭāgāraṃ dvīhi kaṇṇikāhi kattabbapāsādo. Aṭṭo paṭirājūnampi paṭibāhanayogyo catupañcabhūmako paṭissayaviseso. Māḷo ekakūṭasaṅgahito anekakoṇavanto paṭissayaviseso. Uddaṇḍo agabbhikā ekadvārā dīghasālāti vadanti. Apare pana bhaṇanti – vihāro nāma dīghamukhapāsādo. Aḍḍhayogo ekapassena chadanakasenāsanaṃ. Tassa kira ekapasse bhitti uccatarā hoti, itarapasse nīcā, tena taṃ ekapassachadanakaṃ [V 1.0050] hoti. Pāsādo āyatacaturassapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanaṃ candikaṅgaṇayuttaṃ. Guhā kevalā pabbataguhā. Leṇaṃ dvārabaddhaṃ. Kūṭāgāraṃ yo koci kaṇṇikābaddhapāsādo. Aṭṭo bahalabhittigehaṃ. Yassa gopānasiyo aggahetvā iṭṭhakāhi eva chadanaṃ hoti. Aṭṭālakākārena karīyatītipi vadanti. Māḷo vaṭṭākārena katasenāsanaṃ. Uddaṇḍo eko paṭissayaviseso. Yo “bhaṇḍasālā, udosita”ntipi vuccati. Upaṭṭhānasālā sannipatanaṭṭhānaṃ.

Speaking after having placed oneself in the vicinity of attaining superior human states is sāmantajappanaṃ. Mahesakkho means one of great power by means of attaining superior human states; this is the intention. Having spoken generally of ‘mitto’ (friend), he then specifies it as ‘sandiṭṭho’ and ‘sambhatto.’ Indeed, a friend who is merely seen is a sandiṭṭho. One of firm devotion is a sambhatto. Sahāyo means one who goes together; the meaning is sakhā (friend). Indeed, those who have gone seven steps together are called ‘sakhā.’ A vihāra is an entire monastery enclosed by a wall. An aḍḍhayoga is a long mansion; some also say it is a mansion shaped like a garuḍa. A pāsāda is a four-sided mansion. A hammiya is a mansion with a flat-topped roof. A kūṭāgāra is a mansion to be made with two pinnacles. An aṭṭa is a special building of four or five stories, suitable for repelling even enemy kings. A māḷa is a special building with many corners, its roof gathered into a single pinnacle. An uddaṇḍa is a long hall without an inner chamber and with a single door, so they say. But others say: a vihāra is a mansion with a long facade. An aḍḍhayoga is a dwelling with a roof on one side. It is said that of this dwelling, the wall on one side is higher and on the other side is lower; therefore, it has a roof on one side only. A pāsāda is a long, four-sided mansion. A hammiya is a building with a flat-topped roof, furnished with a moonlit terrace. A guhā is simply a mountain cave. A leṇa is a cave fitted with a door. A kūṭāgāra is any mansion fitted with a pinnacle. An aṭṭa is a house with thick walls. Its roof is made only of bricks, without using rafters. Some also say it is made in the shape of a watchtower. A māḷa is a dwelling made in a circular shape. An uddaṇḍa is a certain special building, which is also called a ‘bhaṇḍasālā’ (storehouse) or ‘udosita’ (warehouse). An upaṭṭhānasālā is a place for assembly.

Kucchitarajabhūtāya pāpicchatāya niratthakaṃ kāyavacīvipphandaniggaṇhanaṃ korajaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti korajiko, kohaññena saṃyatakāyo, ativiya, abhiṇhaṃ vā korajiko korajikakorajiko. Atiparisaṅkitoti keci. Ativiya kuho kuhakakuhako, sātisayavimhāpakoti attho. Ativiya lapo lapanako lapakalapako. Mukhasambhāvikoti korajikakorajikādibhāvena pavattavacanehi attano mukhamattena aññehi sambhāviko. So evarūpo evarūpatāya eva attānaṃ paraṃ viya katvā “ayaṃ samaṇo”tiādīni katheti. Gambhīrantiādi tassā kathāya uttarimanussadhammapaṭibaddhatāya vuttaṃ.

Due to a despicable stain, which is evil desire, the fruitless suppression of bodily and verbal activity is korajaṃ. He who has this is a korajiko; one whose body is restrained through hypocrisy. One who is excessively or constantly a korajiko is a korajikakorajiko. Some say this means 'one who is excessively scrupulous.' One who is an excessive hypocrite is a kuhakakuhako; the meaning is one who causes extreme astonishment. One who is an excessive flatterer is a lapakalapako. Mukhasambhāviko means one who is esteemed by others merely by his own mouth, through words proceeding from the state of being a korajikakorajiko, etc. Such a one, precisely because of being of such a nature, making himself out to be like another, says things like, 'This ascetic...' The phrase 'is profound,' etc., is said because that speech is connected with superior human states.

Sambhāvanādhippāyakatenāti “kathaṃ nu kho maṃ jano ‘ariyo’ti vā ‘visesalābhī’ti vā sambhāveyyā”ti iminā adhippāyena katena. Gamanaṃ saṇṭhapetīti visesalābhīnaṃ gamanaṃ viya attano gamanaṃ sakkaccaṃ ṭhapeti[M 1.0054], sato sampajānova gacchanto viya hoti. Paṇidhāyāti “arahāti maṃ jānantū”ti cittaṃ saṇṭhapetvā, patthetvā vā. Samāhito viyāti jhānasamādhinā samāhito viya. Āpāthakajjhāyīti manussānaṃ āpāthaṭṭhāne samādhisamāpanno viya nisīdanto āpāthake janassa pākaṭaṭṭhāne jhāyī. Iriyāpathasaṅkhātanti iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanasaṅkhātaṃ.

Sambhāvanādhippāyakatena means done with this intention: 'How indeed might people esteem me as a noble one or as one who has attained a special state?' Gamanaṃ saṇṭhapeti means he establishes his going carefully, like the going of those who have attained a special state; he is as if going mindfully and with clear comprehension. Paṇidhāya means having well established the mind, or having aspired, thus: 'May they know me as an Arahant.' Samāhito viya means as if concentrated with the concentration of jhāna. Āpāthakajjhāyī means sitting as if having attained concentration in a place visible to people; one who meditates in a place apparent to the public. Iriyāpathasaṅkhātaṃ means designated as the establishing of deportment.

Paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātenāti ayoniso uppāditānaṃ paccayānaṃ paṭisevananti evaṃ kathitena, tena vā paccayapaṭisevanena saṅkhātabbena kathitabbena. Aññaṃ viya katvā attano samīpe bhaṇanaṃ sāmantajappitaṃ. Ā-kārassa rassattaṃ katvā “aṭṭhapanā”ti vuttaṃ. Kuhanaṃ kuho, tassa ayanā pavatti kuhāyanā, kuhassa vā puggalassa ayanā gati kiriyā kuhāyanā. Kuheti, kuhena vā itoti kuhito, kuhako.

Paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātena means by that which is described as 'the partaking of requisites produced improperly'; or by that partaking of requisites which is to be designated or described. Making it as if to another, speaking near oneself is sāmantajappitaṃ. Having shortened the 'ā' vowel, it is said as 'aṭṭhapanā.' Hypocrisy is kuho; its process or occurrence is kuhāyanā. Or, the course, the action of a hypocritical person is kuhāyanā. He practices hypocrisy, or he proceeds by means of hypocrisy, therefore he is a kuhito or kuhako.

Puṭṭhassāti [V 1.0051] “ko tisso, ko rājapūjito”ti puṭṭhassa. Uddhaṃ katvāti ukkhipitvā vibhavasampattiādinā paggahetvā.

Puṭṭhassa means of one who was asked thus: 'Who is Tissa? Who is the one honored by the king?' Uddhaṃ katvā means having raised up, having extolled by means of abundance of wealth and so on.

Unnahanāti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ bandhanā paliveṭhanā. Dve kira bhikkhū ekaṃ gāmaṃ pavisitvā āsanasālāya nisīditvā ekaṃ kumārikaṃ pakkosiṃsu. Tāya āgatāya tatreko ekaṃ pucchi “ayaṃ, bhante, kassa kumārikā”ti? “Amhākaṃ upaṭṭhāyikāya telakandarikāya dhītā, imissā mātā mayi gehaṃ gate sappiṃ dadamānā ghaṭeneva deti, ayampi mātā viya ghaṭena detī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 862) ukkācesi. Imaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “telakandarikavatthu cettha vattabba”nti.

Unnahana means binding higher and higher; wrapping around. It is said that two monks, having entered a village and sat down in a rest-house, called a young girl. When she had come, one of them asked the other: 'Venerable sir, whose young girl is this?' He boasted thus: 'She is the daughter of our supporter, Telakandarikā. When I go to the house, her mother, when giving ghee, gives it by the potful. This one too, like her mother, gives by the potful.' With reference to this story, it was said: 'Here the story of Telakandarikā should be told.'

Dhammānurūpā vāti mattāvacanānurūpaṃ vā. Mattāvacanaṃ hi “dhammo”ti vuccati. Yathāha “subhāsitaṃ uttamamāhu santo, dhammaṃ bhaṇe nādhammaṃ taṃ dutiya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.213; su. ni. 452). Tena bahuṃ vippalapanamāha, saccato vā aññā subhāsitā vācā “dhammo”ti veditabbo. Muggasūpasadisakammo puggalo muggasūpyo. Tenāha “ayaṃ puggalo muggasūpyoti vuccatī”ti. Paribhaṭassa kammaṃ pāribhaṭyaṃ, tadeva pāribhaṭyatā.

“Dhammānurūpā” means in accordance with measured speech. For measured speech is called “Dhamma.” As it is said: “The good declare well-spoken words as the highest; one should speak the Dhamma, not what is contrary to the Dhamma; that is the second” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.213; Su. Ni. 452). By this, he indicates much frivolous talk. Alternatively, speech that is true or otherwise well-spoken should be understood as “Dhamma.” A person whose actions are like lentil soup is a muggasūpyo. Therefore, he said: “This person is called a muggasūpyo.” The work of a retainer is pāribhaṭyaṃ; that very state is pāribhaṭyatā.

Nimittena caranto, jīvanto vā nimittako, tassa bhāvo nemittikatā. Attano icchāya pakāsanaṃ obhāso. Ko pana soti[M 1.0055]? “Ajja bhikkhūnaṃ paccayā dullabhā jātā”tiādikā paccayapaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Icchitavatthussa samīpe kathanaṃ sāmantajappā.

One who goes about, or makes a living, by means of hinting is a nemittiko; the state of that is nemittikatā. Making one's own desire plain is obhāso. And what is that? It is talk connected with requisites, such as: “Today, requisites for the monks have become scarce.” Speaking in the vicinity of a desired object is sāmantajappā.

Akkosanabhayenāpi dadeyyāti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanaṃ. Tathā vambhanādayo. Upekkhanā upāsakānaṃ dāyakādibhāvato bahi chaḍḍanā. Khipanāti khepavacanaṃ. Taṃ pana avahasitvā vacanaṃ hotīti āha “uppaṇḍanā”ti. Pāpanāti adāyakattassa, avaṇṇassa vā patiṭṭhāpanaṃ. Paresaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsakhādanasīlo parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko, tassa bhāvo parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā. Abbhaṅganti abbhañjanaṃ. Nipisitvā gandhamagganā viyāti anippisite alabbhamānassa gandhassa nipisane lābho viya paraguṇe anippisite alabbhamānānaṃ paccayānaṃ nipisanena lābho daṭṭhabboti.

[Thinking,] “They might give even out of fear of being reviled,” is reviling with the ten grounds for reviling. Similarly for contempt and so on. Upekkhanā is the exclusion of lay supporters, casting them out from their status as donors and so forth. Khipanā is a word of rejection. But that, being a word spoken in derision, is called uppaṇḍanā. Pāpanā is the establishing of someone as a non-donor, or of their blame. One who has the habit of eating the flesh from the backs of others is a parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko; the state of that is parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā. Abbhaṅga is anointing. Just as fragrance, which is unobtainable when unpressed, is obtained by pressing, so too should the gain of requisites, which are unobtainable when the qualities of others are unpressed, be understood as being obtained by pressing them.

Nikattuṃ [V 1.0052] appena lābhena bahukaṃ vañcetvā gahetuṃ icchanaṃ nijigīsanaṃ, tassa bhāvo nijigīsanatā. Tasseva icchanassa pavattiākāro, taṃsahajātaṃ vā gavesanakammaṃ.

The desire to defraud, to take much with a small gain by deceiving, is nijigīsanaṃ; the state thereof is nijigīsanatā. It is the mode of operation of that very desire, or the activity of searching that arises together with it.

Aṅganti hatthapādādiaṅgāni uddissa pavattaṃ vijjaṃ. Nimittanti nimittasatthaṃ. Uppātanti ukkāpātadisāḍāha-bhūmicālādiuppātapaṭibaddhavijjaṃ. Supinanti supinasatthaṃ. Lakkhaṇanti itthipurisānaṃ lakkhaṇajānanasatthaṃ. Mūsikacchinnanti vatthādīnaṃ asukabhāge mūsikacchede sati idaṃ nāma phalaṃ hotīti jānanakasatthaṃ. Palāsaggiādīsu iminā nāma agginā hute idaṃ nāma hotīti aggivasena homavidhānaṃ aggihomaṃ. Iminā nayena dabbihomaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ādi-saddena thusahomādīnaṃ, aññesañca sutte āgatānaṃ micchājīvānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Vīriyasādhanattā ājīvapārisuddhisīlassa “paccayapariyesanavāyāmo”ti vuttaṃ. Tassa pārisuddhi anavajjabhāvo, yena dhammena samena paccayalābho hoti. Na hi alaso ñāyena paccaye pariyesituṃ sakkotīti.

“Aṅga” is the knowledge concerning limbs such as hands and feet. “Nimitta” is the science of omens. “Uppāta” is the knowledge connected with portents such as falling meteors, conflagration of the quarters, and earthquakes. “Supina” is the science of dreams. “Lakkhaṇa” is the science of knowing the marks on men and women. “Mūsikacchinna” is the science of knowing that ‘when a mouse gnaws on such-and-such a part of a cloth, etc., such-and-such a result will occur’. “Aggihoma” is the ritual of offering by means of fire, based on the principle that when an offering is made with a certain fire, such as from Palāsa wood, a certain result occurs. By this method, dabbihoma (ladle-offering) should be understood. By the word “ādi,” the inclusion of husk-offerings and other wrong livelihoods mentioned in the Sutta should be understood. Because the Purity of Livelihood Sīla is accomplished by effort, it is called ‘effort in searching for requisites’. Its purity is the state of being blameless, by which requisites are gained righteously and properly. Indeed, a lazy person cannot search for requisites in the right way.

Paccayasannissitasīlavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Virtue Dependent on Requisites

18. Paṭisaṅkhāti ayaṃ “sayaṃ abhiññā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 11) viya ya-kāralopena niddeso. Yonisoti cettha upāyattho yoniso-saddoti dassento āha “upāyena pathenā”ti. “Paṭisaṅkhāya ñatvā”ti [M 1.0056] vatvā tayidaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaṃ paccavekkhaṇanti dassetuṃ “paccavekkhitvāti attho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā hi paccavekkhitvāti sītapaṭighātādikaṃ taṃ taṃ payojanaṃ pati pati avekkhitvā, ñāṇena passitvāti attho, evaṃ paṭisaṅkhāyāti tadeva payojanaṃ pati pati saṅkhāya, jānitvāti attho. Ñāṇapariyāyo hi idha saṅkhā-saddoti. Ettha ca “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso”tiādi kāmaṃ paccayaparibhogakālena vuccati, dhātuvasena pana paṭikūlavasena vā paccavekkhaṇāya paccayasannissitasīlaṃ sujjhatīti apare. Bhijjatīti keci. Eke pana paṭhamaṃ eva pariyattanti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. “Cīvara”nti ekavacanaṃ ekattamattaṃ vācakanti adhippāyena “antaravāsakādīsu yaṃ kiñcī”ti vuttaṃ, jātisaddatāya pana tassa pāḷiyaṃ ekavacananti yattakāni cīvarāni yoginā pariharitabbāni, tesaṃ sabbesaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahaṇanti sakkā viññātuṃ, yaṃ kiñcīti vā anavasesapariyādānametaṃ, na aniyamavacanaṃ. “Nivāseti vā pārupati vā”ti vikappanaṃ pana paṭisevanapariyāyassa paribhogassa [V 1.0053] vibhāgadassananti taṃ paññapetvā sayananisīdana-cīvarakuṭikaraṇādivasenāpi paribhogassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

18. This word paṭisaṅkhā is an indication with the elision of the letter ‘ya’, like in “sayaṃ abhiññā,” etc. Here, in yoniso, to show that the word yoniso has the meaning of ‘means’, he said, “upāyena pathenā” (by a means, by a path). Having said, “paṭisaṅkhāya ñatvā” (having reflected and known), in order to show that this reflection is reviewing, “paccavekkhitvāti attho” (the meaning is ‘having reviewed’), etc., is said. For just as paccavekkhitvā means having individually reviewed each and every purpose, such as the counteracting of cold—that is, having seen with knowledge—so too paṭisaṅkhāya means having individually considered that very purpose—that is, having known. Indeed, here the word saṅkhā is a synonym for knowledge. And here, while “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso,” etc., is spoken with reference to the time of using the requisites, others say that the virtue dependent on requisites is purified by reviewing by way of the elements or by way of repulsiveness. Some say it is broken. But some say it is already perfected from the very beginning—this should be investigated. Regarding “cīvara,” the singular number expresses only singularity; with this intention it is said, ‘whatever among the under-robe, etc.’ However, because it is a generic term, the singular is used in the Pāḷi; therefore, it can be known that it is a collective taking of all the robes, however many, that are to be used by a yogi. Alternatively, this “yaṃ kiñci” (whatever) is an expression of complete inclusion, not an indefinite expression. The alternative expression ‘either wears or drapes’ is an indication of the division of usage, which is a synonym for partaking; therefore, having laid it out, the inclusion of usage should also be seen by way of lying down, sitting, making a robe-hut, and so on.

Payojanānaṃ mariyādā payojanāvadhi, tassa paricchindanavasena yo niyamo, tassa vacanaṃ payojanā…pe… vacanaṃ. Idāni taṃ niyamaṃ vivaritvā dassetuṃ “ettakameva hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avadhāraṇena līḷāvibhūsāvilambanānaṭambarādivasena vatthaparibhogaṃ nisedheti. Tenāha “na ito bhiyyo”ti. Līḷāvasena hi ekacce sattā vatthāni paridahanti ceva upasaṃviyanti ca. Yathā taṃ yobbane ṭhitā nāgarikamanussā. Ekacce vibhūsanavasena, yathā taṃ rūpūpajīviniādayo. Vilambanavasena vilambakā. Naṭambaravasena bhojādayo. Ajjhattadhātukkhobho sītarogādiuppādako. Utupariṇāmanavasenāti utuno parivattanavasena visabhāgasītautusamuṭṭhānena. Vā-saddena hemantādīsu himapātādivasena pavattassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, na uppādeti sītanti adhippāyo. Yadatthaṃ pana taṃ vinodanaṃ, taṃ matthakappattaṃ dassetuṃ “sītabbhāhate”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbatthāti “uṇhassa paṭighātāyā”tiādīsu sabbesu sesapayojanesu. Yadipi sūriyasantāpopi uṇhova, tassa pana ātapaggahaṇena gahitattā “aggisantāpassā”ti [M 1.0057] vuttaṃ. Ekacco dāvaggisantāpo kāyaṃ cīvarena paṭicchādetvā sakkā vinodetunti āha “tassa vanadāhādīsu sambhavo veditabbo”ti. Ḍaṃsāti piṅgalamakkhikā. Te pana yasmā ḍaṃsanasīlā, tasmā vuttaṃ “ḍaṃsanamakkhikā”ti. Sappādayoti sappasatapadiuṇṇanābhisarabūvicchikādayo. Phuṭṭhasamphassoti phuṭṭhavisamāha. Tividhā hi sappā – daṭṭhavisā phuṭṭhavisā diṭṭhavisā. Tesu purimakā dve eva gahitā. Satapadiādīnampi tādisānaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ. Niyatapayojanaṃ ekantikaṃ, sabbakālikañca payojanaṃ. Hirī kuppati nillajjatā saṇṭhāti. Tenāha “vinassatī”ti. Kūpāvataraṇaṃ vā paṭicchādanaṃ arahatīti kopinaṃ. Hiriyitabbaṭṭhena hirī ca taṃ kopinañcāti hirikopinanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tassa cāti ca-saddo pubbe vuttapayojanānaṃ sampiṇḍanattho.

The boundary of purposes is `payojanāvadhi`; the statement of the restriction which exists by way of defining that is `payojanā…pe… vacanaṃ`. Now, to explain that restriction, `ettakameva hī`, etc., is said. Therein, by the word of determination (`eva`), it prohibits the use of cloth by way of elegance, adornment, wearing with dangling parts, ostentation, and so on. Therefore, it says, `na ito bhiyyo`. For some beings wear and put on clothes by way of elegance, such as city-dwellers in their youth. Some do so by way of adornment, such as courtesans and the like. Jesters, by way of wearing with dangling parts. The wealthy and rulers, by way of ostentation. An internal disturbance of the elements is a producer of diseases from cold, etc. `Utupariṇāmanavasena` means: by the arising of an unsuitable cold season due to the change of season. By the word `vā`, the inclusion of what occurs by way of snowfall, etc., in the winter season and so on should be understood; the intention is that it does not produce cold. And to show the ultimate purpose for which that dispelling is done, `sītabbhāhate`, etc., is said. `Sabbatthā` means: in all the remaining purposes, such as `uṇhassa paṭighātāya`, etc. Although the heat of the sun is also heat, since it is included by the word `ātapa` (sun-heat), `aggisantāpassa` (of the heat of fire) is said. Because a certain heat from a forest fire can be dispelled by covering the body with a robe, it is said, 'its occurrence in forest fires and the like should be understood'. `Ḍaṃsa` are `piṅgalamakkhikā` (flies with variegated eyes). And since they are accustomed to biting, they are called `ḍaṃsanamakkhikā` (biting flies). `Sappādayo` means snakes, centipedes, spiders, geckos, scorpions, and so on. `Phuṭṭhasamphassa` refers to that with contact-poison. For snakes are of three kinds: those with bite-poison, those with contact-poison, and those with sight-poison. Among them, only the first two are taken, in order to include other such creatures like centipedes. A fixed purpose is a purpose that is both absolute and constant. Shame is agitated, and shamelessness is established. Therefore, it says, `vinassatī` (it is destroyed). Alternatively, `kopīna` is so-called because it is worthy (`arahati`) of covering (`paṭicchādanaṃ`) what is to be concealed (`kupaṃ`). Because it is something to be ashamed of (`hiriyitabbaṭṭhena`), it is `hirī`, and that (`taṃ`) is also `kopīna`; therefore it is `hirikopīna`. In this way the meaning should be understood here. In `tassa ca`, the word `ca` has the meaning of summarizing the previously mentioned purposes.

Yaṃ kiñci āhāranti khādanīyabhojanīyādibhedaṃ yaṃ kiñci āharitabbavatthuṃ. Piṇḍāya bhikkhāya ulatīti piṇḍolo, tassa kammaṃ piṇḍolyaṃ. Tena piṇḍolyena bhikkhācariyāya. Patitattāti pakkhipitattā. Piṇḍapāto patte pakkhittabhikkhāhāro. Piṇḍānaṃ vā pātoti ghare ghare laddhabhikkhānaṃ sannipāto. “Natthi davā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305) sahasā kiriyāpi [V 1.0054] “davā”ti vuccati, tato visesanatthaṃ “davatthaṃ, kīḷānimittanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha. Muṭṭhikamallā muṭṭhiyuddhayujjhanakā. Ādi-saddena nibuddhayujjhanakādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Balamadanimittanti balaṃ nissāya uppajjanakamado balamado. Taṃ nimittaṃ, balassa uppādanatthanti attho. Porisamadanimittanti porisamado vuccati purisamāno “ahaṃ puriso”ti uppajjanakamāno. Asaddhammasevanāsamatthataṃ nissāya pavatto māno, rāgo eva vā porisamadoti keci. Taṃ nimittaṃ. Antepurikā rājorodhā. Sabbesaṃ sannivesayogyatāya vesiyo rūpūpajīviniyo. Maṇḍanaṃ nāma idhāvayavapāripūrīti āha “aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ pīṇabhāvanimitta”nti, paribrūhanahetūti attho. Naṭā nāma raṅganaṭā. Naccakā laṅghakādayo. Vibhūsanaṃ sobhāsamuppādananti āha “pasannacchavivaṇṇatānimitta”nti.

`Yaṃ kiñci āhāraṃ` means: any object whatsoever that is to be consumed, of the various kinds such as hard food and soft food. Because one wanders (`ulati`) for alms (`piṇḍāya`), one is called a `piṇḍola`; their action is `piṇḍolyaṃ`. `Tena piṇḍolyena` means by the practice of going for alms. `Patitattā` means because of being placed. `Piṇḍapāta` is alms-food placed in the bowl. Or, `piṇḍānaṃ pāto` is the collection of alms received from house to house. In phrases like 'There is no sport (`davā`),' even a hasty action is called `davā`; therefore, to specify, it is said that it is for the sake of sport, as a sign of play. `Muṭṭhikamallā` (fist-fighters) are those who fight with fists. By the word `ādi` (etc.), wrestlers and the like are included. `Balamadanimittaṃ` means as a sign of intoxication by strength: `balamado` (intoxication of strength) is the intoxication that arises relying on strength. That is the sign, meaning for the sake of producing strength. `Porisamadanimittaṃ` means as a sign of intoxication by manliness: `porisamado` (manly pride) is called `purisamāno` (manly conceit), the conceit that arises thinking, 'I am a man.' Or, it is the conceit that arises relying on the ability to engage in wrong practice (i.e., sexual intercourse); or some say manly pride is simply lust. That is the sign. `Antepurikā` (women of the inner palace) are the king's harem (`rājorodhā`). Because of their suitability for association with all, they are called `vesiyo` (courtesans), who are `rūpūpajīviniyo` (those who live by their beauty). `Maṇḍanaṃ` (adornment) here is the filling out of the body parts; thus it is said, 'as a sign of the limbs and minor limbs being plump,' meaning for the purpose of making them plump. `Naṭā` are stage-performers. `Naccakā` are acrobats and the like. `Vibhūsanaṃ` (embellishment) is the production of beauty; thus it is said, 'as a sign of a clear and bright complexion.'

Etaṃ padaṃ. Mohūpanissayappahānatthanti mohassa upanissayatāpahānāya. Davā hi mohena hoti, mohañca vaḍḍhetīti tassā vajjanena mohassa anupanissayatā. Dosūpanissayappahānatthanti idaṃ balamadassa, purisamadassa [M 1.0058] ca dosahetuno vasena vuttaṃ, itarassa pana vasena “rāgūpanissayappahānattha”nti vattabbaṃ. Maṇḍanavibhūsanapaṭikkhepo siyā mohūpanissayappahānāyapi, rāgūpanissayatāya pana ujupaṭipakkhoti vuttaṃ “rāgūpanissayappahānattha”nti. Yadipi ekaccassa davamade ārabbha parassa paṭighasaṃyojanādīnaṃ uppatti hotiyeva manopadosikadevādīnaṃ viya, attano pana davamade ārabbha yesaṃ savisesaṃ rāgamohamānādayo pāpadhammā uppajjanti. Te sandhāya “attano saṃyojanuppattipaṭisedhanattha”nti vatvā maṇḍanavibhūsanāni paṭicca savisesaṃ parassapi rāgamohādayo pavattantīti “parassapi saṃyojanuppattipaṭisedhanattha”nti vuttaṃ. Ayoniso paṭipattiyāti ettha kāmasukhallikānuyogaṃ muñcitvā sabbāpi micchāpaṭipatti ayoniso paṭipatti. Purimehi dvīhi padehi ayoniso paṭipattiyā, pacchimehi dvīhi kāmasukhallikānuyogassa pahānaṃ vuttanti vadanti. “Catūhipi cetehī”ti pana vacanato sabbehi ubhinnampi pahānaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Kāmakīḷāpi davantogadhā hotiyeva, purisamadopi kāmasukhallikānuyogassa hetuyevāti.

“For abandoning the supporting condition for delusion” means for the abandoning of the state of being a supporting condition for delusion. For sport (davā) arises from delusion and increases delusion; thus, by avoiding it, it becomes a non-supporting condition for delusion. The phrase “for abandoning the supporting condition for hatred” is said with reference to intoxication by strength and manly pride, which are causes of hatred. However, with reference to the other type of pride—that which is a cause of lust—it should be said, “for abandoning the supporting condition for lust.” The rejection of adornment and embellishment might also be for abandoning the supporting condition for delusion, but since it is the direct opposite of being a supporting condition for lust, it is said, “for abandoning the supporting condition for lust.” Although on account of one person's sport and intoxication the fetter of resentment and so on may arise in another—as in the case of the mind-corrupting devas—this is said with reference to those in whom, on account of their own sport and intoxication, evil states such as lust, delusion, and conceit arise with special intensity. With reference to them, it was said, “for the purpose of preventing the arising of one's own fetters.” And because, on account of adornments and embellishments, lust, delusion, and so on also arise with special intensity in another, it was said, “for the purpose of preventing the arising of another's fetters.” Here, in the phrase “through unwise practice,” having excluded indulgence in sensual pleasures, all other wrong practice is “unwise practice.” Some say that by the first two phrases the abandoning of unwise practice is stated, and by the last two the abandoning of indulgence in sensual pleasures. However, from the statement “By these four,” it should be understood that by all of them the abandoning of both is stated. Indeed, sensual play is also included in sport (davā), and manly pride is also a cause of indulgence in sensual pleasures.

Cātumahābhūtikassāti catumahābhūte sannissitassa. Rūpakāyassāti catusantatirūpasamūhassa. Ṭhitiyāti ṭhitatthaṃ. Sā panassa ṭhiti pabandhavasena icchitāti āha “pabandhaṭṭhitattha”nti. Pavattiyāti jīvitindriyappavattiyā. Tathā hi jīvitindriyaṃ “yāpanā vattanā”ti [V 1.0055] (dha. sa. 19, 634) ca niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tassā ca avicchedo āhārūpayogena hoti. Kāyassa cirataraṃ yāva āyukappo, tāva avatthānaṃ yāpanāti dassento “cirakālaṭṭhitatthaṃ vā”ti āha. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “gharūpatthambhamivā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ yojanā – yathā jiṇṇagharasāmiko gharassa upatthambhanaṃ karoti tassa apatanatthaṃ, yathā ca sākaṭiko akkhabbhañjanaṃ karoti tassa sampavattanatthaṃ, evamesa yogī kāyassa ṭhitatthaṃ, yāpanatthañca piṇḍapātaṃ paṭisevati paribhuñjatīti. Etena ṭhiti nāma apatanaṃ yāpanā pavattīti dasseti. Na davamadamaṇḍanavibhūsanatthanti idaṃ “yāvadevā”ti avadhāraṇena nivattitatthadassanaṃ. Tiṭṭhanti upādinnadhammā etāyāti ṭhiti, āyūti āha “ṭhitīti jīvitindriyassetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Tathā hi taṃ āyu “ṭhitī”ti niddiṭṭhaṃ, ṭhitiyā yāpanāyāti kāyassa [M 1.0059] ṭhitihetutāya “ṭhitī”ti laddhavohārassa jīvitindriyassa pavattanatthanti attho. Tenāha “jīvitindriyapavattāpanattha”nti. Ābādhaṭṭhenāti vibādhanaṭṭhena, rogaṭṭhena vā. Jighacchāparamā hi rogā. Uparamatthanti vūpasamatthaṃ. Vaṇālepanamiva vaṇiko. Uṇhasītādīsu abhibhavantesu tappaṭikāraṃ sītuṇhaṃ viya paṭisevatīti sambandho. Maggabrahmacariyaṃ ṭhapetvā sikkhattayasaṅgahā sāsanāvacaritabbā anusāsanī sāsanabrahmacariyanti āha “sakalasāsanabrahmacariyassa ca maggabrahmacariyassa cā”ti. Anuggahaṇatthanti anu anu gaṇhanatthaṃ sampādanatthaṃ. Kāyabalaṃ nissāyāti yathāsamāraddhaṃ guṇavisesapāripūrihetubhūtaṃ kāyabalamattaṃ nissāya. Tenāha “sikkhattayānuyogavasenā”tiādi. Kantāranittharaṇatthikā jāyampatikā, nadīsamuddanittharaṇatthikā ca puttamaṃsādīni yathā agiddhā amucchitā kevalaṃ taṃ taṃ atthasiddhimeva avekkhantā paṭisevanti tehi vinā asijjhanato, evamayampi kevalaṃ bhavakantāranittharaṇatthiko agiddho amucchito tena vinā asijjhanato piṇḍapātaṃ paṭisevatīti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ.

“Of that which is comprised of the four great elements” means of that which is dependent on the four great elements. “Of the physical body” means of the aggregate of form which is a continuity from the four origins. “For stability” means for the purpose of remaining. Furthermore, that stability is desired by way of continuity; therefore, it is said, “for the purpose of continuous stability.” “For continuation” means for the continuation of the life faculty. Indeed, the life faculty is pointed out as “sustenance” and “continuation.” And its non-interruption occurs through the partaking of food. Showing that “sustenance” (yāpanā) is the enduring of the body for a very long time—for as long as the lifespan lasts—he said, “or for the purpose of long-term stability.” Now, to make the meaning already stated clearer, “like supporting a house...” and so on was said. Herein, this is the construction: just as the owner of a dilapidated house provides a support for the house for the purpose of its not collapsing, and just as a cart-driver applies grease to the axle for the purpose of its smooth running, so too this yogī partakes of and consumes almsfood for the purpose of the body's stability and for the purpose of its sustenance. By this, it is shown that “stability” is non-collapsing, and “sustenance” is continuation. The phrase “Not for sport, pride, adornment, or beautification” shows the meaning that is excluded by the delimitation “only for....” “Appropriated phenomena subsist (tiṭṭhanti) by means of this”; thus, it is “stability” (ṭhiti). It is life (āyu); thus, he said: “Stability is a designation for this life faculty.” Indeed, that life is pointed out as “stability.” Regarding the phrase “for stability, for sustenance,” the meaning is: for the continuation of the life faculty, which has received the designation “stability” because it is the cause of the body's stability. Therefore, he said, “for the purpose of causing the life faculty to continue.” “In the sense of ‘affliction’” means in the sense of oppression, or in the sense of illness. For hunger is the greatest of illnesses. “For the purpose of ceasing” means for the purpose of appeasement. One partakes of it like a person with a sore applying ointment; and when overcome by heat, cold, and so on, one partakes of a remedy for that, such as cold or heat. This is the connection. Setting aside the noble path holy life, the instruction to be practiced in the Dispensation, which is comprised of the threefold training, is the “Dispensation holy life.” Therefore, he said, “of the entire Dispensation holy life and of the path holy life.” “For the purpose of assisting” means for the purpose of undertaking again and again and for accomplishing. “Relying on bodily strength” means relying on just enough bodily strength to be a cause for the fulfillment of the special qualities that have been undertaken. Therefore, he said, “by means of devotion to the threefold training,” etc. Just as a husband and wife desiring to cross a wilderness, or those desiring to cross a river or ocean, partake of their son's flesh and so on without greed, without delusion, looking only toward the accomplishment of their respective goals, because it cannot be accomplished without it; so too this yogī, desiring only to cross the wilderness of existence, without greed, without delusion, partakes of almsfood because it cannot be accomplished without it. This is the connection of the simile.

Itīti pakāratthe nipātapadaṃ. Tena paṭiseviyamānassa piṇḍapātassa paṭisevanākāro gayhatīti āha “evaṃ iminā piṇḍapātapaṭisevanenā”ti. Purāṇanti bhojanato purimakālikattā purātanaṃ. Paṭihaṅkhāmīti paṭihanissāmi. Navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti paṭisevatīti yojanā. Kīdisaṃ, kathañcāti āha “aparimita…pe… aññataro viyā”ti. Aparimitaṃ aparimāṇaṃ bhojanaṃ paccayo etissāti aparimitabhojanapaccayā, taṃ aparimitabhojanapaccayaṃ attano gahaṇītejapamāṇato atikkantapamāṇabhojanahetukanti attho. Yo bahuṃ bhuñjitvā attano [V 1.0056] dhammatāya uṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto “āhara hattha”nti vadati, ayaṃ āharahatthako. Yo bhuñjitvā accuddhumātakucchitāya uṭṭhitopi sāṭakaṃ nivāsetuṃ na sakkoti, ayaṃ alaṃsāṭako. Yo bhuñjitvā uṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto tattheva parivattati, ayaṃ tatravaṭṭako. Yo yathā kākehi āmasituṃ sakkā, evaṃ yāva mukhadvāraṃ āhāreti, ayaṃ kākamāsako. Yo bhuñjitvā mukhe sandhāretuṃ asakkonto tattheva vamati, ayaṃ bhuttavamitako. Etesaṃ aññataro viya. Atha vā purāṇavedanā nāma abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanā. Taṃ “paṭihanissāmī”ti [M 1.0060] paṭisevati. Navavedanā nāma atibhuttapaccayena uppajjanakavedanā. Taṃ “na uppādessāmī”ti paṭisevati. Atha vā navavedanā nāma abhuttapaccayena uppajjanakavedanā, tassā anuppannāya anuppajjanatthameva paṭisevati. Abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakāti cetaṃ khuddāya visesanaṃ. Yassā appavatti bhojanena kātabbā, tassā dassanatthaṃ. Abhuttapaccayena, bhuttapaccayena ca uppajjanakānuppajjanakavedanāsu purimā yathāpavattā jighacchānimittā vedanā. Sā hi abhuñjantassa bhiyyopavaḍḍhanavasena uppajjati. Pacchimāpi khuddānimittāva aṅgadāhasūlādivedanā pavattā. Sā hi bhuttapaccayā pubbe anuppannāva nuppajjissatīti ayametāsaṃ viseso. Vihiṃsānimittatā cetāsaṃ vihiṃsāya viseso.

‘Iti’ is a particle in the sense of ‘manner’. By it, the mode of partaking of the almsfood that is being partaken of is grasped. Therefore, it is said, ‘thus, by this partaking of almsfood...’ ‘Old’ means former, because of its being of a prior time than the meal. ‘I will ward off’ is the meaning of ‘paṭihaṅkhāmi’. The construction is: he partakes of food thinking, ‘And I will not produce a new feeling.’ What kind of feeling and how? Thus, it is said: ‘immoderate... like one of...’ ‘Immoderate,’ that is, measureless, eating is the condition for this feeling; thus, it is ‘conditioned by immoderate eating.’ The meaning of ‘that which is conditioned by immoderate eating’ is: caused by eating in a measure that exceeds the measure of one's own digestive fire. One who, having eaten much, is unable to get up by his own nature and says, ‘Bring your hand,’ this one is an ‘Āharahatthaka’ (Hand-bringer). One who, having eaten, even though he has stood up, is unable to put on his lower garment due to a very bloated belly, this one is an ‘Alaṃsāṭaka’ (Garment-enough). One who, having eaten, being unable to get up, just rolls about right there, this one is a ‘Tatravaṭṭaka’ (There-roller). One who eats in such a way that crows can peck at it, right up to the opening of his mouth, this one is a ‘Kākamāsaka’ (Crow-pecked). One who, having eaten, being unable to hold it in his mouth, vomits right there, this one is a ‘Bhuttavamitaka’ (Eaten-vomiter). Like one of these. Alternatively, ‘old feeling’ is the feeling that is liable to arise from the condition of not having eaten. He partakes of food thinking, ‘I will ward that off.’ ‘New feeling’ is the feeling that is liable to arise from the condition of overeating. He partakes of food thinking, ‘I will not produce that.’ Alternatively, ‘new feeling’ is the feeling that is liable to arise from the condition of not having eaten; he partakes of food for the very purpose of its non-arising, it not having yet arisen. And this phrase ‘liable to arise from the condition of not having eaten’ is a qualification of hunger. It is for the purpose of showing that feeling whose non-occurrence is to be brought about by eating. Among the feelings that are liable to arise and not liable to arise from the condition of not having eaten and the condition of having eaten, the former is the normally occurring feeling that has hunger as its cause. For it arises in one who is not eating by way of greatly increasing. The latter—the feeling of burning in the limbs, piercing, and so on, which also has hunger as its cause—has not yet occurred. For, due to the condition of eating, it, not having arisen before, will not arise. This is the difference between them. And their having affliction as their cause is what distinguishes them from the affliction itself.

Yā vedanā. Adhunāti etarahi. Asappāyāparimitabhojanaṃ nissāyāti asappāyāparimitassa āhārassa bhuñjanapayogaṃ āgamma uppajjatīti attho. Purāṇakammapaccayavasenāti pubbe purimajātiyaṃ katattā purāṇassa kammassa paccayatāvasena payogavipattiṃ āgamma uppajjanārahatāya taṃ vajjetvā payogasampattiyā upaṭṭhāpanaṃ dukkhavedanāpaccayaghāto, paṭihananañca hotīti āha “tassā paccayaṃ vināsento taṃ purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmī”ti. Ayuttaparibhogo paccaye apaccavekkhitvā paribhogo. So eva katūpacitakammatāya kammūpacayo. Taṃ nissāya paṭicca āyatiṃ anāgate kāle uppajjanato yā cāyaṃ “navavedanā”ti vuccatīti yojanā. Yuttaparibhogavasenāti paccavekkhitvā paccayānaṃ paribhogavasena, tassā navavedanāya mūlaṃ ayuttaparibhogakammaṃ anibbattento sabbena sabbaṃ anuppādento. Ettāvatāti “iti purāṇa”ntiādinā vuttena padadvayena. “Vihiṃsūparatiyā”tiādinā vā padacatukkena yuttaparibhogasaṅgaho pabbajitānucchavikassa paccayaparibhogassa vuttattā. Attakilamathānuyogappahānaṃ jighacchādidukkhapaṭighātassa bhāsitattā. Jhānasukhādīnaṃ [V 1.0057] paccayabhūtassa kāyasukhassa avissajjanato dhammikasukhāpariccāgo ca dīpito hoti.

Which feeling. ‘Adhunā’ means ‘at the present time’. ‘Relying on unsuitable and immoderate eating’ means: it arises depending on the practice of consuming unsuitable and immeasurable food. ‘By the power of the conditionality of old kamma’ means: because of its liability to arise depending on the failure of effort, by the power of the conditionality of old kamma, which was done in a previous, former life. By avoiding that failure of effort and establishing the success of effort, there is the destruction of the condition for painful feeling and the warding of it off. Therefore, he said, “Destroying its condition, I will ward off that old feeling.” Improper use is the use of requisites without reflecting upon them. That very improper use, due to its nature as kamma that has been done and accumulated, is an accumulation of kamma. Because a feeling arises in the future, in time to come, depending on and conditioned by that, it is called ‘new feeling’; this is the connection. ‘By the power of proper use’ means: by the power of using requisites after reflecting, not producing the kamma of improper use which is the root of that new feeling, not causing it to arise in any way at all. Thus far: by the two phrases spoken, beginning with ‘Thus, the old...’, or by the four phrases beginning with ‘By abstaining from harming...’, the summary of proper use is illuminated, because the use of requisites appropriate for one who has gone forth has been stated. The abandoning of the practice of self-mortification is also illuminated, because the warding off of suffering such as hunger has been spoken of. And because of not abandoning bodily comfort, which is a condition for jhāna-bliss and so on, the non-abandonment of righteous happiness is also illuminated.

Asappāyāparimitūpayogena jīvitindriyupacchedako, iriyāpathabhañjanako vā siyā parissayo, sappāyaparimitūpayogena pana so na hoti. Tathā sati cirakālappavattisaṅkhātā sarīrassa yātrā [M 1.0061] yāpanā bhavissatīti imamatthaṃ dassento “parimitaparibhogena…pe… bhavissatī”ti āha. Yo rogo sāddho asāddho ca na hoti, so yāpyarogo, so etassa atthīti yāpyarogī. So hi niccakālaṃ bhesajjaṃ upasevati, tathā ayampīti. Yadi yātrāpi yāpanā, pubbepi “yāpanāyā”ti vuttaṃ, ko ettha visesoti? Pubbe “yāpanāyā”ti jīvitindriyayāpanā adhippetā, idha pana catunnampi iriyāpathānaṃ avicchedasaṅkhātā yāpanā yātrāti ayamettha viseso. Buddhapaṭikuṭṭhena micchājīvena paccayapariyesanā ayuttapariyesanā. Dāyakadeyyadhammānaṃ, attano ca pamāṇaṃ ajānitvā paṭiggahaṇaṃ, saddhādeyyavinipātanatthaṃ vā paṭiggahaṇaṃ ayuttapaṭiggahaṇaṃ, yena vā āpattiṃ āpajjati. Apaccavekkhitvā paribhogo ayuttaparibhogo. Tesaṃ parivajjanaṃ dhammena samena paccayuppādanādivasena veditabbaṃ. Dhammena hi paccaye pariyesitvā dhammena paṭiggahetvā paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanaṃ anavajjatā nāma.

Due to the application of unsuitable and immeasurable food, a danger that cuts off the life-faculty or that breaks the bodily postures may arise. But on the other hand, due to the application of suitable and measured food, that danger does not occur. That being so, showing this meaning that ‘the body's sustenance and maintenance, termed as its continuation for a long time, will be,’ he said, ‘By moderate use... it will be.’ A disease that is neither curable nor incurable is called a ‘manageable disease’ (yāpyaroga); he who has this is a yāpyarogī. For he constantly resorts to medicine; likewise this one too resorts to almsfood. If ‘yātrā’ is also ‘yāpanā’, and previously ‘for yāpanā’ was said, what is the distinction here? Previously, by the word ‘yāpanā’, the maintenance of the life-faculty was intended. But here, ‘yātrā’ is intended as the maintenance termed as the non-interruption of all four bodily postures. This is the distinction here. The seeking of requisites by means of wrong livelihood, which is censured by the Buddha, is improper seeking. The acceptance of requisites without knowing the measure of the donors and the things to be given, and of oneself; or acceptance for the purpose of causing the ruin of faith-offerings; or that acceptance by which one falls into an offense, is improper acceptance. Use without reflecting is improper use. The avoidance of these should be known by way of producing requisites, etc., righteously and equitably. Indeed, seeking requisites righteously, accepting them righteously, reflecting, and then using them is called blamelessness.

Aratīti ukkaṇṭhā. Pantasenāsanesu, adhikusaladhammesu ca anabhirati. Tandīti pacalāyikā niddā. Vijambhitāti thinamiddhābhibhavena kāyassa vijambhanā. Viññūhi garahā viññūgarahā. Ekacco hi anavajjaṃyeva sāvajjaṃ karoti, “laddhaṃ me”ti pamāṇādhikaṃ bhuñjitvā taṃ jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi kilamati, sakalavihāre bhikkhū tassa sarīrapaṭijagganabhesajjapariyesanāpasutā honti. Aññe te “kiṃ ida”nti pucchitvā “asukassa udaraṃ uddhumāta”ntiādīni sutvā “niccakālamesa evaṃpakatiko attano kucchipamāṇaṃ nāma na jānātī”ti nindanti, evaṃ anavajjaṃyeva sāvajjaṃ karoti. Evaṃ akatvā “anavajjatā ca bhavissatī”ti paṭisevati. Attano hi pakatiaggibalādiṃ jānitvā “evaṃ me aratiādīnaṃ abhāvena kāyasukhatā, agarahitabbatā ca bhavissatī”ti pamāṇayuttameva paṭisevati. Yāvatako bhojanena attho, tassa sādhanena yāvadatthaṃ udarassa paripūraṇena udarāvadehakaṃ bhojanaṃ yāvadatthaudarāvadehakabhojanaṃ, tassa parivajjanena. Seyyāya sayanena laddhabbasukhaṃ seyyasukhaṃ, ubhohi passehi [M 1.0062] samparivattanakaṃ sayantassa uppajjanasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ[V 1.0058], middhena niddāyanena uppajjanasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ, tesaṃ seyya…pe… sukhānaṃ pahānato catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yogyabhāvassa paṭipādanaṃ kāyassa catuiriyāpathayogyabhāvapaṭipādanaṃ, tato. Sukho iriyāpathavihāro phāsuvihāro. Pacchime vikappe, sabbavikappesu vā vuttaṃ phāsuvihāralakkhaṇaṃ āgamena samatthetuṃ “vuttampi heta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tīsupi vikappesu āhārassa ūnaparibhogavaseneva hi phāsuvihāro vuttoti.

`Arati` is dissatisfaction; it is non-delight in secluded lodgings and in higher wholesome states. `Tandī` is nodding sleep. `Vijambhitā` is the listless drooping of the body due to being overcome by sloth and torpor. Censure by the wise is `viññūgarahā`. Indeed, a certain person makes what is blameless into something blameworthy. Thinking, 'I have received,' he eats more than the proper measure and, being unable to digest it, becomes afflicted by vomiting, purging, and so on. The monks in the entire monastery become occupied with attending to his body and searching for medicine. Others, asking, 'What is this?' and hearing such things as, 'So-and-so's stomach is bloated,' censure him, saying, 'He is always of such a nature; he does not know the measure of his own stomach.' Thus he makes what is blameless into something blameworthy. Not doing so, he partakes of food thinking, 'There will also be blamelessness.' Indeed, knowing one's own natural digestive fire, strength, and so on, one partakes only of what is moderate, thinking, 'Thus, for me, through the absence of dissatisfaction and the like, there will be bodily comfort and freedom from censure.' Eating that fills the belly as much as is needed for accomplishing whatever purpose there is for eating is 'belly-filling eating'; by avoiding that. The pleasure to be obtained by lying on a bed is bed-pleasure. The pleasure that arises for one who lies down turning over on both sides is side-pleasure. The pleasure that arises from sleeping through drowsiness is drowsiness-pleasure. By abandoning those pleasures—bed-pleasure, etc.—is the accomplishment of the body's suitability for the four postures. From that, a comfortable abiding in the postures is a pleasant abiding. In the last alternative, or in all alternatives, in order to support with scripture the characteristic of pleasant abiding that has been mentioned, 'It was also said...' etc., was stated. Indeed, in all three alternatives, pleasant abiding is spoken of only by way of the moderate use of food.

Ettāvatāti “yātrā”tiādinā vuttena padattayena. “Yātrā ca me bhavissatī”ti payojanapariggahadīpanā. Yātrā hi naṃ āhārūpayogaṃ payojetīti. Dhammikasukhāpariccāgahetuko phāsuvihāro majjhimā paṭipadā antadvayaparivajjanato. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne aṭṭha aṅgāni samodhānetabbāni – “neva davāyā”ti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, “na madāyā”ti ekaṃ, “na maṇḍanāyā”ti ekaṃ, “na vibhūsanāyā”ti ekaṃ, “yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāyā”ti ekaṃ, “vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāyā”ti ekaṃ, “iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmī”ti ekaṃ, “yātrā ca me bhavissatī”ti ekaṃ. “Anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā”ti ayamettha bhojanānisaṃso. Mahāsivatthero panāha “heṭṭhā cattāri aṅgāni paṭikkhepo nāma, upari pana aṭṭhaṅgāni samodhānetabbānī”ti. Tattha “yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā”ti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, “yāpanāyā”ti ekaṃ, “vihiṃsūparatiyā”ti ekaṃ, “brahmacariyānuggahāyā”ti ekaṃ, “iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmī”ti ekaṃ, “navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmī”ti ekaṃ, “yātrā ca me bhavissatī”ti ekaṃ, “anavajjatā cā”ti ekaṃ. Phāsuvihāro pana bhojanānisaṃsoti. Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhārento paṭisaṅkhā yoniso piṇḍapātaṃ paṭisevati nāma.

“Up to this point” refers to the three words beginning with “sustenance.” “And my sustenance will be” is a statement showing the grasping of the purpose. For sustenance indeed prompts one to the use of food. Pleasant abiding, which has as its cause the non-abandonment of righteous happiness, is the middle way because it avoids the two extremes. In this context, eight factors should be combined: 1. “Not for sport” is one factor. 2. “Not for intoxication” is one factor. 3. “Not for adornment” is one factor. 4. “Not for embellishment” is one factor. 5. “Only for the maintenance and continuation of this body” is one factor. 6. “For the cessation of harm and for the support of the holy life” is one factor. 7. “Thus, I will ward off old feelings and not arouse new feelings” is one factor. 8. “And my sustenance will be” is one factor. “Blamelessness and pleasant abiding”—this here is the benefit of food. However, the Elder Mahāsiva says: “The four factors below are called ‘rejection’; but the eight factors above should be combined.” Therein: 1. “Only for the maintenance of this body” is one factor. 2. “For its continuation” is one factor. 3. “For the cessation of harm” is one factor. 4. “For the support of the holy life” is one factor. 5. “Thus, I will ward off old feelings” is one factor. 6. “And not arouse new feelings” is one factor. 7. “And my sustenance will be” is one factor. 8. “And blamelessness” is one factor. Pleasant abiding, however, is the benefit of food. Thus, one who consumes food endowed with these eight factors, reflecting wisely, is said to use almsfood with reflection.

Yattha yatthāti bhummaniddesena sena-saddassa adhikaraṇatthavuttimāha. Tathā āsana-saddassāti. Aḍḍhayogādimhīti ādi-saddena pāsādādiṃ, mañcādiñca saṅgaṇhāti. Yattha yattha vihāre vā aḍḍhayogādimhi vā āsatīti vihāraaḍḍhayogādike ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Idha ādi-saddena pīṭhasanthatādīnampi saṅgaho veditabbo. Parisahanaṭṭhenāti abhibhavanaṭṭhena, vibādhanaṭṭhenāti attho. Utuyeva utuparissayoti sītuṇhādiutuyeva [M 1.0063] asappāyo vuttanayena utuparissayo. Tassa utuparissayassa vinodanatthaṃ, anuppannassa anuppādanatthaṃ, uppannassa vūpasamanatthañcāti attho. Nānārammaṇato [V 1.0059] paṭisaṃharitvā kammaṭṭhānabhūte ekasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe cittassa sammadeva layanaṃ paṭisallānaṃ, tattha ārāmo abhirati paṭisallānārāmo, tadatthaṃ. Senāsanaṃ hi vivittaṃ yogino bhāvanānukūlaṃ suññāgārabhāvato. Taṃ panetaṃ atthadvayaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “yo sarīrābādhacittavikkhepakaro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ekībhāvasukhatthanti ekībhāvahetukaṃ sukhaṃ ekībhāvasukhaṃ, tadatthaṃ. Gaṇasaṅgaṇikakilesasaṅgaṇikābhāvena uppajjanakasukhaṃ.

“Wherever, wherever”—by this locative indication, it states the occurrence of the word ‘sena’ in the sense of location. Likewise for the word ‘āsana’. In “in a gabled house, etc.,” by the word ‘etc.,’ it includes palaces and the like, and couches and the like. “Wherever, wherever in a monastery or in a gabled house, etc., one dwells”—thus it should be brought and connected with ‘monastery, gabled house, etc.’. Here, by the word ‘etc.,’ the inclusion of stools, mats, and the like should also be understood. “In the sense of enduring” means in the sense of overcoming, in the sense of oppressing. “The season itself is the seasonal affliction” means the unsuitable season of cold, heat, etc., itself is the seasonal affliction, by the method stated. “For the purpose of dispelling that seasonal affliction, for not causing the unarisen to arise, and for pacifying the arisen”—this is the meaning. Having withdrawn from various objects, the proper settling of the mind on a single object which is the meditation subject is ‘seclusion’. Therein, delight, fondness, is ‘delight in seclusion’, for that purpose. Indeed, a secluded dwelling, because of being an empty house, is suitable for a yogi for the development of meditation. But to make these two meanings clear, “that which causes bodily affliction and mental distraction,” etc., is said. Therein, “for the sake of the happiness of solitude”: happiness that has solitude as its cause is ‘happiness of solitude’; for that purpose. The happiness that arises from the absence of association with groups and association with defilements.

Yadi utuyeva utuparissayo, “utu ca sītuṇha”nti sītuṇhapaṭighātaṃ vatvā utuparissayavinodanaṃ kasmā vuttanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “kāmañcā”tiādi. Tattha “niyataṃ utuparissayavinodana”nti etena “sītassa paṭighātāya uṇhassa paṭighātāyā”ti ettha vuttaṃ sītuṇhaṃ aniyataṃ kadāci kadāci uppajjanakaṃ, utuparissayo pana sabbadābhāvī adhippetoti dasseti. Vuttappakāroti “sītādiko, asappāyo”ti ca evaṃ vuttappakāro vivaṭaṅgaṇarukkhamūlādīsu nisinnassa apariguttiyā asaṃvutadvārāditāya pākaṭaparissayā, asappāyarūpadassanādinā apākaṭaparissayā ca bhikkhussa kāyacittānaṃ ābādhaṃ kareyyuṃ. Yattha gutte senāsane ābādhaṃ na karonti. Evaṃ jānitvāti ubhayaparissayarahitanti evaṃ ñatvā paṭisevanto bhikkhu veditabboti sambandho.

If the season itself were the seasonal affliction, and since 'the season is cold and heat,' then having stated the warding off of cold and heat, why is the dispelling of seasonal affliction mentioned? Referring to this objection, he says, 'kāmañca,' etc. Therein, by this phrase, 'the dispelling of the fixed seasonal affliction,' it is shown that the cold and heat mentioned in 'for warding off cold, for warding off heat' is uncertain, arising only from time to time, whereas the seasonal affliction is intended as being always present. 'Of the kind stated': of the kind stated thus as 'cold, etc.' and 'unsuitable.' For one sitting in open spaces, at the foot of a tree, and so on, due to a lack of protection and unguarded doors, etc., there are manifest afflictions; and due to seeing unsuitable forms, etc., there are unmanifest afflictions, and these would cause affliction to the monk's body and mind. Where, in a protected dwelling, they do not cause affliction. 'Having thus known': knowing thus that it is 'free from both afflictions,' the monk who resorts to it should be understood. This is the connection.

Dhātukkhobhalakkhaṇassa, taṃhetukadukkhavedanālakkhaṇassa vā rogassa paṭipakkhabhāvo paṭiayanaṭṭho. Tenāha “paccanīkagamanaṭṭhenāti attho”ti, vūpasamanaṭṭhenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yassa kassacīti sappiādīsu yassa kassaci. Sappāyassāti hi tassa vikāravūpasamenāti adhippāyo. Bhisakkassa kammaṃ tena vidhātabbato. Tenāha “tena anuññātattā”ti. Nagaraparikkhārehīti nagaraṃ parivāretvā rakkhaṇakehi. Vivaṭaparikkhepo parikkhā uḍḍāpo pākāro esikā paligho pākārapatthaṇḍilanti satta “nagaraparikkhārā”ti vadanti. Sīlaparikkhāroti suvisuddhasīlālaṅkāro[M 1.0064]. Ariyamaggo hi idha “ratho”ti adhippeto. Tassa ca sammāvācādayo alaṅkāraṭṭhena “parikkhāro”ti vuttā. Jīvitaparikkhārāti jīvitassa pavattikāraṇāni. Samudānetabbāti sammā uddhaṃ uddhaṃ ānetabbā pariyesitabbā. Parivāropi hoti antarāyānaṃ parito vāraṇato. Tenāha “jīvita…pe… rakkhaṇato”ti.

The state of being opposite to disease—which has the characteristic of disturbance of the elements, or has the characteristic of painful feeling caused by that—is the meaning of 'requisite' (paccaya). Therefore, it is said, 'The meaning is in the sense of going against,' which is to say, in the sense of pacifying. 'Of whatever' means of whatever among ghee and so on. 'Of the suitable' means, by pacifying that disorder; this is the intention. It is the physician's task because it is to be administered by him. Therefore, it is said, 'because it is permitted by him.' By 'city requisites' is meant the protective barriers surrounding the city. They say that the seven 'city requisites' are: the open surrounding path, the moat, the rampart base, the city wall, the gate pillar, the crossbar, and the rough ground at the wall's base. 'The requisite of virtue' means the ornament of perfectly purified virtue. Indeed, here the Noble Path is intended as the 'chariot.' And its components, such as Right Speech, are called 'requisites' in the sense of being ornaments. 'Requisites of life' means the causes for the continuation of life. 'Should be procured' means they should be thoroughly sought and acquired. It is also a protection because of warding off dangers from all around. Therefore, it is said, 'life... etc... because of guarding.'

Tattha antaranti vivaraṃ, okāsoti attho. Verikānaṃ antaraṃ adatvā attano sāmikānaṃ [V 1.0060] parivāretvā ṭhitasevakā viya rakkhaṇato. Assāti jīvitassa. Kāraṇabhāvatoti cirappavattiyā kāraṇabhāvato. Rasāyanabhūtaṃ hi bhesajjaṃ sucirampi kālaṃ jīvitaṃ pavattetiyeva. Yadipi anuppannā eva dukkhavedanā bhesajjaparibhogena paṭihaññanti, na uppannā tāsaṃ saraseneva bhijjanato, uppannasadisā pana “uppannā”ti vuccanti. Bhavati hi taṃsadisesu tabbohāro, yathā sā eva tittiri, tāniyeva osadhānīti. Tasmā vuttaṃ “uppannānanti jātānaṃ bhūtānaṃ nibbattāna”nti. Sañcayato paṭṭhāya so dhātukkhobho samuṭṭhānaṃ etesanti taṃsamuṭṭhānā. “Dukkhavedanā”ti vatvā sā akusalasabhāvāpi atthīti tato visesetuṃ “akusalavipākavedanā”ti vuttaṃ. Byābādhanaṭṭhena byābādho, byābādhova byābajjhaṃ, dukkhanti attho. Natthi ettha byābajjhanti abyābajjhaṃ, niddukkhatā. Tenāha “abyābajjhaparamatāyā”ti niddukkhaparamatāyāti. Taṃ dukkhanti roganimittakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Herein, 'antara' means a gap, an opening; the meaning is 'opportunity.' It is because of guarding, like a royal attendant who, not giving an opening to enemies, stands having surrounded his own master. 'Assā' means 'of life.' 'Kāraṇabhāvato' means due to being a cause for long continuation. Indeed, medicine that is an elixir causes life to continue for a very long time. Although painful feelings that have not yet arisen are warded off by the use of medicine, those that have arisen are not, since they are destroyed by their own nature; however, feelings similar to those that have arisen are called 'arisen.' For in similar cases, such a designation occurs, as in 'that very partridge' and 'those very herbs.' Therefore, it is said: '"Uppannānaṃ" means those that have been born, come into being, or have been produced.'
