From the accumulation onwards, that disturbance of elements is their cause of arising—thus, they are called 'taṃsamuṭṭhānā' (arising from that). Having said 'painful feeling,' to specify from that, since there is also feeling that has an unwholesome nature, it is stated as 'unwholesome resultant feeling.' 'Byābādha' is so called in the sense of tormenting; 'byābādha' itself is 'byāpajjha,' meaning suffering. Herein, there is no 'byāpajjha'—thus, it is 'abyābajjha,' the state of being without suffering. Therefore, he said 'abyābajjhaparamatāya,' meaning 'for the highest state of being without suffering.' 'That suffering' means suffering that has illness as its cause.

Cīvarādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ nissayanaṃ paribhogo evāti dassetuṃ “te paṭicca nissāyā”ti vatvā “paribhuñjamānā”ti vuttaṃ. Pavattantīti jīvanti. Jīvanampi hi pavattanaṃ, yato jīvitindriyaṃ “pavattanarasa”nti vuccati.

To show that depending on requisites such as robes is indeed using them, having said 'te paṭicca nissāya' (depending on them, relying on them), it is then said 'paribhuñjamānā' (while using). 'Pavattanti' means they live. For living is indeed continuation, which is why the life faculty is called 'that which has the function of causing continuation' (pavattanarasa).

Catupārisuddhisampādanavidhivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Method for Accomplishing the Fourfold Purity

19. Evaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarādibhedena niddiṭṭhaṃ sīlaṃ puna sādhanavibhāgena dassetuṃ “evametasmi”ntiādimāraddhaṃ. Tattha sādhīyati sampādiyati etenāti sādhanaṃ, saddhā sādhanaṃ etassāti saddhāsādhano. Nanu ca vīriyasatipaññāhipi vinā pātimokkhasaṃvaro na sijjhatīti? Saccaṃ na sijjhati, saddhāya pana visesahetubhāvaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttanti dassento āha

19. Thus, to show again by way of analyzing the means of accomplishment the virtue which has been explained by way of the divisions of Pātimokkha restraint and so forth, the passage beginning 'evametasmiṃ' is introduced. Therein, 'sādhana' (means) is so called because by this it is accomplished or completed. 'Saddhāsādhano' (having faith as its means) is so called because faith is the means for this. But is it not so that without energy, mindfulness, and wisdom, the Pātimokkha restraint cannot be achieved? It is true, it cannot be achieved. However, showing that this was said with reference to faith's state of being a special cause, he says:

“Sāvakavisayātītattā [M 1.0065] sikkhāpadapaññattiyā”ti. Garukalahukādibhede otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ tassa tassa aparādhassa anurūpaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ nāma sāvakānaṃ avisayo, buddhānaṃ eva visayo. Sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ tāva tiṭṭhatu, tassa kālopi nāma sāvakānaṃ avisayo, buddhānaṃ eva visayoti dassento “sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanapaṭikkhepo cettha nidassana”nti āha. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “āgamehi tvaṃ sāriputta, āgamehi tvaṃ sāriputta, tathāgatova tattha kālaṃ [V 1.0061] jānissatī”ti (pārā. 21). Tattha ca-saddo samuccayattho. Tena “apaññattaṃ na paññapema, paññattaṃ na samucchindāma, yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vattāmā”ti (pārā. 565) evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Saddhāyāti saddahanena satthari, dhamme ca saddhāya paccupaṭṭhāpanena. Jīvitepi pageva jīvitaparikkhāreti adhippāyo.

'Because the establishment of training rules is beyond the domain of disciples.' When a transgression involving distinctions of serious, minor, and so forth has occurred, the establishing of a training rule appropriate to each and every offense is not the domain of disciples; it is the domain of Buddhas alone. Let the establishing of a training rule stand aside; even the timing of it is not the domain of disciples, but the domain of Buddhas alone. To show this, he said: 'The rejection of the request to establish a training rule serves as an example here.' For so it was said: 'Wait, Sāriputta, wait, Sāriputta. The Tathāgata alone will know the time for that.' Therein, the particle 'ca' has a collective sense. By it, the inclusion of such passages as 'We shall not establish what has not been established, we shall not abolish what has been established; having undertaken them, we shall train in the training rules as they have been established' should be understood. 'Saddhāya' (by faith) means by belief, or by making faith in the Teacher and in the Dhamma present. The intention is: even for the sake of life, what is there to say of the requisites that protect life?

Kikīva aṇḍanti kikīsakuṇikā viya attano aṇḍaṃ. Sā kira jīvitampi pariccajitvā aṇḍameva rakkhati. Camarīva vāladhinti camarīmigo viya attano vāladhiṃ. Camarīmigā kira byādhena paripātiyamānā jīvitampi pariccajitvā kaṇḍakagumbādīsu laggaṃ attano vālameva rakkhanti. Piyaṃva puttaṃ ekakanti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Yathā hi ekaputtako kuṭumbiko taṃ ekaputtaṃ, ekanayano ca taṃ ekanayanaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ rakkhati. Tatheva sīlaṃ anurakkhamānakāti anukampanavasena vuttaṃ. Supesalāti suṭṭhu piyasīlā. Sadā sabbakālaṃ daharamajjhimatherakālesu. Channampi gāravānaṃ vasena sagāravā, garukāravantoti attho.

'Like a kikī bird its egg' means like a kikī hen her own egg. It is said that she protects the egg alone, even abandoning her own life. 'Like a camarī its tail-hair' means like the camarī animal its own tail-hair. It is said that camarī animals, when pursued by a hunter, protect their tail-hair alone when it is caught in thorny bushes and so forth, even abandoning their own life. 'Like a beloved only son' should be brought and connected thus: For just as a householder with an only son, or a person with only one eye, protects that only son or that one eye exceedingly well, in that very same way, 'constantly protecting virtue' is said by way of compassion. 'Supesalā' means possessing very dear virtue. 'Sadā' means at all times: in the periods of being a junior, middle, and senior monk. By way of all six kinds of reverence, they are 'sagāravā' (respectful); the meaning is they possess great respect.

Evameva khoti yathā mahāsamuddo ṭhitadhammo velaṃ nātikkamati, evameva. Mama sāvakāti ariyasāvake sandhāyāha. Te hi dhuvasīlā. Imasmiṃ attheti jīvitahetupi sīlassa avītikkamane.

'Evameva kho' means: just as the great ocean, being of a fixed nature, does not transgress its shore, just so... He said 'mama sāvakā' (my disciples) with reference to the noble disciples. For they are of steadfast virtue. 'Imasmiṃ atthe' (in this meaning) refers to the non-transgression of virtue even for the sake of life.

Mahāvattaniaṭavī nāma viñjhāṭavī. Himavantapasse aṭavīti keci. Theranti nāmagottavasena apaññātaṃ ekaṃ theraṃ. Nipajjāpesuṃ gantvā kassaci mā āroceyyāti.

The forest named Mahāvattani is the Viñjhā forest. Some say it is a forest on the slope of the Himalayas. 'Thera' refers to an elder who was unknown by name and clan. They went and made him lie down, intending that he should not tell anyone.

Pūtilatāyāti [M 1.0066] gaḷocilatāya. Samasīsīti jīvitasamasīsī. Yassa hi kilesasīsaṃ avijjaṃ maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattamaggo pariyādiyati, tato ekūnavīsatime paccavekkhaṇañāṇe patiṭṭhāya bhavaṅgottaraṇe vaṭṭasīsaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ cuticittaṃ pariyādiyati, so imāya vārasamatāya “jīvitasamasīsī”ti vuccati. So ca thero tathā parinibbāyi. Tena vuttaṃ “samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyī”ti. Abhayatthero kira mahābhiñño. Tasmā cetiyaṃ kārāpesīti vadanti. Appevāti appeva nāma attano jīvitampi jaheyya, na bhindeti na bhindeyya, na vītikkameyya.

'Pūtilatāya' means by the gaḷocī creeper. 'Samasīsī' means one whose life and the head of defilements are simultaneous. For, in the case of a certain person, the path of Arahantship, through the sequence of the noble path, completely destroys the head of defilements, which is ignorance. After that, being established in the nineteenth reviewing knowledge, upon descending into bhavaṅga, the death-consciousness completely destroys the head of the round of existence, which is the life faculty. Due to this state of sequential equality, that person is called 'jīvitasamasīsī.' And that elder attained Parinibbāna in that manner. Therefore it was said, 'having become samasīsī, he attained Parinibbāna.' It is said that the elder Abhaya possessed great supernormal knowledge. Therefore, they say, he had a cetiya built. 'Appeva nāma' means that one might even give up one's own life, but one should not break, one should not transgress.

Satiyā [V 1.0062] adhiṭṭhitānanti pageva upaṭṭhitāya satiyā ārakkhavasena adhiṭṭhitānaṃ indriyānaṃ. Ananvāssavanīyatoti dvārabhāvena abhijjhādīhi ananubandhitabbato. Varanti seṭṭhaṃ. Tattāyāti uṇhāya. Ādittāyāti ādito paṭṭhāya dittāya. Sampajjalitāyāti samantato jalantiyā. Sajotibhūtāyāti ekajālībhūtāya. Sampalimaṭṭhanti sabbaso āmaṭṭhaṃ, añcitanti attho. Na tveva varanti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Rūpesūti rūpārammaṇesu. Anubyañjanaso nimittaggāhoti kilesānaṃ anu anu byañjanavasena uppādanena pākaṭīkaraṇavasena subhādinimittaggāho, atha vā anubyañjanasoti hatthapādādianubyañjanato, nimittaggāhoti itthipurisādisubhādinimittaggahaṇaṃ. Cakkhudvārādipavattassāti cakkhudvārādīhi pavattassa. Viññāṇassāti javanaviññāṇassa. Nimittādiggāhaṃ nisedhentena sampādetabboti sambandho. Asaṃvihitasākhāparivāranti sammā avihitavatiparikkhepaṃ. Parassahārīhīti parasantakāvahārakehi corehi. Samativijjhatīti sabbaso ativijjhati anupavisati.

‘Established by mindfulness’ means of the faculties established by the power of protection with mindfulness that has already arisen beforehand. ‘Not to be followed after’ means because of not being fit to be followed after by covetousness and so on, by way of the sense doors. ‘Excellent’ means best. ‘Heated’ means hot. ‘Aflame’ means blazing from the start. ‘Fully ablaze’ means burning all around. ‘Turned into a single flame’ means having become a single mass of flame. ‘Completely touched’ means thoroughly touched, anointed; this is the meaning. ‘But it is not at all excellent’—this should be brought forward and connected. ‘In forms’ means in objects of form. ‘Grasping the sign through its features’ means the grasping of the sign of beauty and so on, by way of making it manifest through the arising of defilements again and again in detail; or, ‘through its features’ means by way of the secondary characteristics such as hands and feet, and ‘grasping the sign’ means the grasping of the sign of woman, man, and so on, the sign of beauty, and so on. ‘Of that which has arisen through the eye-door, etc.’ means of that which has arisen through the eye-door and so on. ‘Of consciousness’ means of impulsion consciousness. The connection is: it should be accomplished by one who is preventing the grasping of signs, etc. ‘With an unsecured surrounding of branches’ means having a surrounding enclosure that is not well-made. ‘By those who carry away others’ property’ means by thieves who take what belongs to others. ‘Pierces through’ means completely pierces through and enters.

Rūpesūti rūpahetu rūpanimittaṃ. Uppajjanakaanatthato rakkha indriyanti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesu. Ete hi dvārāti ete cakkhādidvārā. Satikavāṭena asaṃvutattā vivaṭā. Tato eva arakkhitā. Kilesuppattiyā hetubhāvena taṃsamaṅginaṃ hanantīti kāraṇūpacāreneva vuttaṃ. Ete vā rūpādayo. Kilesānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā dvārā cakkhādidvārā. Te kīdisā vivaṭā arakkhitā asaṃvutacakkhādihetuṃ taṃsamaṅginaṃ hanantīti kāraṇūpacāreneva vuttaṃ. Agāranti gehaṃ. Ducchannanti na sammā chāditaṃ. Abhāvitanti lokuttarabhāvanārahitaṃ.

'In forms' means: because of the form as cause, there is the form-sign. The connection is: 'guard the faculty' from the unbeneficial which is liable to arise. Likewise in the remaining cases. For 'these doors' means these eye-doors, etc. Because they are not closed by the door-leaf of mindfulness, they are open. For that very reason, they are unguarded. They harm the one endowed with them by being a cause for the arising of defilements; this is said only as a metaphor of the cause. Or, these forms and so on, having become objects for the defilements, harm the one endowed with them through the doors—the eye-door and so on. What are these like? Open, unguarded. Because of the cause, which is the unclosed eye-door and so on, they harm the one endowed with them; this is said only as a metaphor of the cause. 'A house' means a home. 'Poorly roofed' means not well-covered. 'Undeveloped' means devoid of supramundane development.

Sampāditetiādissa [M 1.0067] vodānapakkhassa attho vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana sabbaso kilesānaṃ anuppādo atiukkaṭṭhadesanā maggenāgatasadisattā. Sampādetabboti “na punevaṃ karissa”nti adhiṭṭhānasuddhiyā sampādetabbo.

The meaning of the aspect of purification, beginning with ‘sampādita’ (accomplished), should be understood in the opposite way to what has been stated. But this complete non-arising of defilements is a most excellent teaching, because of its similarity to what is attained by the path. It should be accomplished: it should be accomplished with the purity of resolve, [thinking] ‘I will not do so again’.

Adhunāpabbajitenāti na cirapabbajitena, navapabbajitenāti attho. Kāmarāgena ḍayhāmīti kāmarāgagginā pariḍayhāmi. So ca pana dāho idāni cittagatoti dassento āha “cittaṃ me pariḍayhatī”ti. Sādhūti āyācanā. Nibbāpananti tassa nibbāpanupāyaṃ. Gotamāti theraṃ gottena ālapati.

‘Recently gone forth’ means not long gone forth, that is, newly gone forth. ‘I am burning with sensual desire’ means I am being burned all around by the fire of sensual desire. And showing that this burning is now located in the mind, he said, ‘My mind is burning.’ ‘Sādhu’ is a request. ‘Quenching’ means the method for quenching it. ‘Gotama’—he addresses the Elder by his clan name.

Saññāya [V 1.0063] vipariyesāti “asubhe subha”nti pavattasaññāvipariyesahetu viparītasaññānimittaṃ. Nimittaṃ parivajjehi kīdisaṃ? Rāgūpasañhitaṃ rāguppattihetubhūtaṃ subhanimittaṃ parivajjehi na manasi karohi. Na kevalaṃ subhanimittassāmanasikāro eva, atha kho asubhabhāvanāya attano cittaṃ bhāvehi. Kathaṃ? Ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ yathā taṃ asubhārammaṇe vikkhepābhāvena ekaggaṃ, suṭṭhu appitabhāvena susamāhitañca hoti, evaṃ bhāvehīti. Evaṃ samathabhāvanāya kāmarāgassa vikkhambhanaṃ dassetvā idāni samucchedanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “saṅkhāre”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saṅkhāre parato passāti sabbepi saṅkhāre avidheyyakatāya “pare”ti passa. Aniccatāya pana udayabbayapaṭipīḷitattā dukkhato, anattasabhāvattā, attavirahato ca no attato passa. Evaṃ lakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento maggapaṭipāṭiyā catutthamaggena sabbaso nibbāpehi mahārāgaṃ tebhūmakassa abhibhavanato mahāvisayatāya mahārāgaṃ vūpasamehi. Yathā etarahi, evaṃ mā ḍayhittho punappunanti daḷhataraṃ rāgavinodane niyojesi.

‘Perversion of perception’ means the sign of perverted perception, due to the cause of perverted perception, which is ‘perceiving the unattractive as attractive’. What kind of sign should you avoid? Avoid the sign of beauty, which is connected with lust and serves as a cause for the arising of lust; do not attend to it. Not only should you refrain from attending to the sign of beauty, but you should also develop your mind through the cultivation of the unattractive. How? Develop it so that it is one-pointed and well-concentrated. Just as, with regard to the object of the unattractive, through the absence of distraction it becomes one-pointed, and through the state of being well-applied, it becomes well-concentrated, so should you develop it. Having thus shown the suppression of sensual lust through serenity development, now, to explain the method of eradication, ‘formations’ and so on is stated. There, ‘see formations as other’ means see all formations as ‘other’ because they are not subject to one's will. Furthermore, due to impermanence and because of being oppressed by rise and fall, see them as suffering; and due to their not-self nature and because they are devoid of a self, see them as not-self. Thus applying the three characteristics and developing insight, through the sequence of paths, with the fourth path completely extinguish the great lust. Pacify the great lust, so-called because of its vast domain and its overpowering of the three realms. Just as you burn now, may you not burn again and again. Thus, he urged him more firmly toward the removal of lust.

Evaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlassa sampādane vidhiṃ dassetvā evaṃ taṃ susampāditaṃ hotīti nayaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādinā tattha paripūrakārino there nidasseti. Tattha “leṇaṃ na ullokitapubba”nti idaṃ sabbattheva therassa yugamattadassitāya vuttaṃ. Kiṃ pana thero senāsanaṃ na sodheti[M 1.0068]? “Ullokā paṭhamaṃ ohāretabba”nti hi vuttaṃ, antevāsikādayo eva kirassa senāsanaṃ sodhenti. Assa nāgarukkhassa.

Having thus shown the method for accomplishing the virtue of sense-restraint, to demonstrate the way in which it is well accomplished, the text proceeds with ‘apicā’ (moreover) and so on, pointing to the elders who are fulfillers of it as an example. Here, ‘he had never before looked up at a dwelling’ is said because of the elder's habit of looking only a yoke's length everywhere. But what, does the elder not clean his dwelling? For it is said, ‘First, what is on the ceiling should be removed.’ It seems that only his resident disciples and others clean his dwelling. Of this Nāga tree.

Tasmiṃ gāmeti mahāgāme. Taruṇā thaññapivanakā puttadhītaro yāsaṃ tā taruṇaputtā, tāsaṃ. Lañjāpesīti thanapaṭṭikāya thane bandhāpetvā rājamuddikāya lañjāpesi. Rājā theraṃ cirataraṃ daṭṭhuṃ kālavikkhepaṃ karonto “sve sīlāni gaṇhissāmī”ti āha. Thero rañño ca deviyā ca vandanakāle sattākāramattaṃ gaṇhāti. Itthī purisoti pana vivekaṃ na karoti. Tenāha “vavatthānaṃ na karomī”ti. “Aho suparisuddhasīlo vatāyaṃ ayyo”ti daṇḍadīpikaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Atiparisuddhaṃ pākaṭanti sappāyalābhena kammaṭṭhānaṃ ativiya parisuddhaṃ vibhūtaṃ ahosi. Sakalaṃ pabbataṃ unnādayantoti pathavikampanena sakalaṃ pabbataṃ ekaṃ ninnādaṃ karonto. Tannivāsidevatānaṃ sādhukāradānenāti keci. Bhantoti anavaṭṭhito. Bāloti taruṇadārako. Utrastoti ñātakehi vinābhāvena santrasto.

‘In that village’ means in the great village. ‘Those with young children’ refers to those women whose sons and daughters are young and milk-drinking. ‘He had them sealed’ means he had them sealed with a royal seal after having their breasts bound with breast-bands. The king, delaying in order to see the elder for a longer time, said, “Tomorrow I will undertake the precepts.” The elder, at the time of being venerated by the king and queen, perceives only the mere state of a being. He does not make the distinction “woman” or “man.” Therefore, he said, “I do not make a determination.” “Oh, how very pure in virtue is this venerable one!”—thinking thus, he took a torch-staff and stood. ‘Exceedingly pure and manifest’ means that through obtaining what was suitable, the meditation subject became exceedingly pure and manifest. ‘Making the entire mountain resound’ means making the whole mountain produce a single roar by the trembling of the earth. Some say this was by the giving of cries of approval by the deities dwelling there. ‘Unstable’ means unestablished. ‘A fool’ means a young boy. ‘Terrified’ means terrified due to separation from relatives.

Visagaṇḍakarogoti [V 1.0064] thanakandaḷarogamāha. Māsarogādikopi visagaṇḍakarogoti vadanti. Yato pabbajito, tato paṭṭhāya pabbajitakālato pabhutīti attho. Indriyānīti indriyasaṃvarasīlāni. Tesu hi bhinnesu indriyānipi bhinnānīti vuccanti ārakkhābhāvato, indriyāneva vā nimittānubyañjanaggāhassa dvārabhūtāni bhinnāni nāma taṃsamaṅgino anatthuppattito, vipariyāyato abhinnānīti veditabbāni. Indriyānaṃ vā ayoniso upasaṃhāro bhedanaṃ, yoniso upasaṃhāro abhedananti apare. Mittattherovāti mahāmittatthero viya. Vareti seṭṭhe.

‘The disease of a poisonous boil’ refers to the disease of a boil on the breast. They say that diseases such as māsaroga are also called ‘the disease of a poisonous boil’. ‘From when he went forth’ means from the time of ordination onwards. ‘Faculties’ refers to the virtues of sense-restraint. For when these are broken, the sense faculties are also said to be broken, because of the absence of protection. Or, the sense faculties themselves, being the doors for grasping signs and secondary characteristics, are called ‘broken’ because they cause the arising of what is unbeneficial for one endowed with them; conversely, they should be known as ‘unbroken’. Others say that the unwise application of the sense faculties is ‘breaking’, and the wise application is ‘unbreaking’. ‘Like the Elder Mitta’ means like the Elder Mahāmitta. ‘Excellent’ means on the best.

Tathā vīriyenāti tathā-saddena vīriyaṃ viseseti. Yathā sati anavajjalakkhaṇāva indriyasaṃvarasādhanaṃ, tathā vīriyaṃ anavajjalakkhaṇaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisādhananti. Vīriyāpekkhameva visesanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha “sammāāraddhavīriyassā”ti. Ayuttā esanā anesanā, yathāvuttamicchājīvasaṅgahā. Sā eva satthusāsanassa na patirūpāti appatirūpaṃ, taṃ anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ. Atha vā patirūpavirodhinī appatirūpā, pariggahitadhutaṅgassa [M 1.0069] dhutaṅganiyamavirodhinī yassa kassaci sallekhavikopinī paṭipatti. Imasmiṃ pakkhe ca-saddo luttaniddiṭṭho, anesanaṃ, appatirūpañca pahāyāti. Paṭisevamānena parivajjayatā sampādetabbāti sambandho. “Parisuddhuppāde”ti imināva dhammadesanādīnaṃ parisuddhāya samuṭṭhānatā dīpitā hotīti “dhammadesanādīhi cassa guṇehi pasannāna”nti vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena bāhusaccavattaparipūraṇairiyāpathasampattiādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Dhutaguṇe cassa pasannānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Piṇḍapātacariyādīhīti ādi-saddena mittasuhajjapaṃsukūlacariyādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Dhutaṅganiyamānulomenāti taṃtaṃdhutaṅganiyatāya paṭipattiyā anulomavasena, avikopanavasenāti attho. Mahicchasseva micchājīvena jīvikā, na appicchassa. Appicchatāya ukkaṃsagatāya micchājīvassa asambhavo evāti dassetuṃ “ekabyādhivūpasamattha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pūtiharitakīti pūtimuttaparibhāvitaṃ, pūtibhāvena vā chaḍḍitaṃ haritakaṃ. Ariyavaṃso etassa atthīti, ariyavaṃse vā niyuttoti ariyavaṃsiko, paccayagedhassa dūrasamussāritattā uttamo ca so ariyavaṃsiko cāti uttamaariyavaṃsiko. Yassa kassacīti pariggahitāpariggahitadhutaṅgesu yassa kassaci.

In 'Tathā vīriyena,' the word 'tathā' qualifies 'vīriya.' Just as mindfulness, characterized as blameless, is a means for accomplishing restraint of the sense faculties, so too is energy, characterized as blameless, a means for accomplishing the purification of livelihood. The qualification should be seen as referring only to energy. For that very reason, it is said, 'for one who has rightly aroused energy.' Improper seeking is 'anesanā,' which is included in wrong livelihood as described. That very seeking is not suitable for the Teacher's dispensation, thus it is 'appatirūpa'; that 'anesanā' is 'appatirūpa.' Alternatively, 'appatirūpā' is that which is contrary to what is suitable; for one who has undertaken the ascetic practices, it is the practice that is contrary to the rule of the ascetic practices, and for anyone, it is the practice that corrupts the practice of effacement. In this alternative, the particle 'ca' is indicated as elided, meaning 'having abandoned anesanā and appatirūpa.' The connection is that this should be accomplished by one who resorts to what is proper and avoids what is improper. By this very phrase 'with pure arising,' the fact of having a pure origin for things such as teaching the Dhamma is shown. Thus, it is said, 'and for those who have faith in his qualities such as teaching the Dhamma.' By the word 'ādi,' the inclusion of things such as great learning, fulfillment of observances, and accomplishment in deportment should be understood. And in 'for those who have faith in his ascetic qualities,' here too, the same method applies. In 'piṇḍapātacariyādīhi,' by the word 'ādi,' the inclusion of practices such as seeking rag-robes among friends and companions should be understood. 'Dhutaṅganiyamānulomena' means in accordance with the practice prescribed by the respective ascetic practice, that is, in a way that does not corrupt it. Livelihood by wrong means is only for one with great desire, not for one with few desires. To show that when fewness of desires has reached its peak, wrong livelihood is simply impossible, it is said, 'for the sake of calming a single affliction,' etc. Therein, 'pūtiharitakī' means a myrobalan fruit that is either infused with stale urine or discarded because of its putrid state. He is 'ariyavaṃsiko' because 'the noble lineage belongs to him' or because 'he is devoted to the noble lineage.' And because greed for requisites has been driven far away, he is supreme and is one of the noble lineage; thus, he is an 'uttama-ariyavaṃsiko.' 'Yassa kassaci' means for anyone among those who have undertaken or not undertaken the ascetic practices.

Nimittaṃ nāma paccaye uddissa yathā adhippāyo ñāyati evaṃ nimittakammaṃ. Obhāso nāma [V 1.0065] ujukameva akathetvā yathā adhippāyo vibhūto hoti, evaṃ obhāsanaṃ. Parikathā nāma pariyāyena kathanaṃ. Tathā uppannanti nimittādivasena uppannaṃ.

'Nimitta' is the act of making a sign in such a way that, with reference to requisites, one's intention is known. 'Obhāsa' is the act of hinting in such a way that, without speaking directly, the intention becomes clear. 'Parikathā' is speaking in a roundabout way. 'Tathā uppannaṃ' means that which has arisen by way of signs and so forth.

Dvāraṃ dinnanti rogasīsena paribhogassa dvāraṃ dinnaṃ. Tasmā arogakālepi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, āpatti na hotīti attho. Tenāha “kiñcāpi āpatti na hotī”tiādi. Na vaṭṭatīti sallekhapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa na vaṭṭati, sallekhaṃ kopetīti adhippāyo. “Ājīvaṃ pana kopetī”ti imināva senāsanapaṭisaṃyuttadhutaṅgadharassa nimittādayo na vaṭṭantīti vadanti. Tadaññadhutaṅgadharassāpi na vaṭṭantiyevāti apare. Akarontoti yathāsakaṃ anuññātavisayepi akaronto. Aññatrevāti ṭhapetvā eva.

'Dvāraṃ dinnaṃ' means the door for use has been given under the heading of sickness. Therefore, it is permissible to use it even in a time of no sickness; the meaning is that there is no offense. Hence it is said, 'Even though there is no offense,' etc. 'Na vaṭṭati' means it is not permissible for one established in the practice of effacement; the intent is that it corrupts the practice of effacement. By this statement, 'But it corrupts the livelihood,' they say that signs and so forth are not permissible for one who observes the ascetic practice connected with lodging. Others say that they are not permissible even for one who observes other ascetic practices. 'Akaronto' means not doing so even in matters permitted according to one's own allowance. 'Aññatreva' means only having set it aside.

Gaṇavāsaṃ [M 1.0070] pahāya araññāyatane paṭippassaddhivivekassa muddhabhūtāya aggaphalasamāpattiyā viharanto mahāthero “pavivekaṃ brūhayamāno”ti vutto. Udarasannissito vātābādho udaravātābādho. Asambhinnaṃ khīraṃ etassāti asambhinnakhīraṃ, tadeva pāyāsanti asambhinnakhīrapāyāsaṃ, udakena asammissakhīrena pakkapāyāsanti attho. Tassāti pāyāsassa. Uppattimūlanti “gihikāle me, āvuso, mātā sappimadhusakkarādīhi yojetvā asambhinnakhīrapāyāsaṃ adāsi, tena me phāsu ahosī”ti attano vacīnicchāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ uppattihetuṃ. “Aparibhogāraho piṇḍapāto”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu therassa obhāsanādicittuppattiyeva natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi, ajjhāsayaṃ pana ajānantā ekacce puthujjanā tathā maññeyyuṃ, anāgate ca sabrahmacārino evaṃ mama diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjeyyunti paṭikkhipi. Apica mahātherassa paramukkaṃsagatā sallekhapaṭipatti. Tathā hi daharabhikkhuno “kassa sampannaṃ na manāpa”nti (pāci. 209, 257, 612, 1228, 1234; cūḷava. 343) vacanaṃ nissāya yāva parinibbānā piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ na khādati.

Having abandoned communal living and dwelling in a forest place by means of the attainment of the supreme fruition, which is the pinnacle of seclusion through calming, the great elder is said to be 'one who causes seclusion to grow.' 'Udarasannissito vātābādho' is 'udaravātābādho': a wind-illness that is dependent on the belly. It has unmixed milk ('asambhinnaṃ khīraṃ etassa'), thus it is 'asambhinnakhīra'; that itself is milk-rice ('pāyāsa'), thus it is 'asambhinnakhīrapāyāsa.' The meaning is: milk-rice cooked with milk unmixed with water. 'Tassa' (of that) refers to the milk-rice. 'Uppattimūla' (root of arising) refers to the cause of its arising, which is called his own utterance: 'In my household life, friends, my mother gave me milk-rice with unmixed milk, prepared with ghee, honey, sugar, and so on, and by that I felt well.' Why was it said, 'Almsfood unfit for consumption'? Is it not so that for the elder there is no arising of thought such as hinting? It is true, there is none. However, some ordinary people, not knowing his intention, might think so, and in the future, fellow monastics might fall into following my seen example; thus he rejected it. Moreover, the great elder’s practice of effacement had reached the highest excellence. For indeed, based on the statement of a young monk, 'To whom is well-prepared food not pleasing?', until his final passing away, he did not eat food made of flour.

Vacīviññattivipphārāti vacīnicchāraṇahetu. Atthaviññāpanavasena pavattamāno hi saddo asatipi viññattiyā tassa kenaci paccayena paccayabhāve vacīviññattivaseneva pavattatīti “vacīviññattivipphāro”ti vuccati. Bhuttoti bhuttavā sace bhaveyyaṃ ahaṃ. Sāti assa. Akāralopena hi niddeso “evaṃsa te”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58; 8.7) viya. Antaguṇanti antabhogo. Bahi careti āsayato nikkhamitvā gocaraggahaṇavasena [V 1.0066] bahi yadi vicareyya. Paramappicchaṃ dassetuṃ lokavohārenevamāha. Loke hi ayuttabhojanaṃ odariyaṃ garahantā evaṃ vadanti “kiṃsu nāma tassa antāni bahi carantī”ti. Ārādhemīti ādito paṭṭhāya rādhemi, vase vattemīti attho.

'Vacīviññattivipphāra' is so called because of the cause which is the utterance of speech. For indeed, a sound that proceeds by way of making the meaning known, even when there is no state of being a condition for that sound by intimation through any specific conditionality, proceeds solely by the power of verbal intimation; therefore it is called 'vacīviññattivipphāra.' 'Bhutto' means: 'if I were one who has eaten.' 'Sā' means 'assa' (it would be). Indeed, the indication is by elision of the letter 'a', as in such cases as 'evaṃsa te.' 'Antaguṇa' means the coiled intestines. 'Bahi care' means: if it were to wander outside, having gone out from its receptacle by way of taking food. To show extreme fewness of wishes, he spoke thus in accordance with worldly convention. For in the world, those who are censuring a glutton who eats what is unsuitable say thus: 'Why indeed do his intestines wander outside?' 'Ārādhemi' means: I satisfy from the beginning, I bring under my control; this is the meaning.

Mahātissatthero kira dubbhikkhakāle maggaṃ gacchanto bhattacchedena, maggakilamathena ca kilantakāyo dubbalo aññatarassa phalitassa ambassa mūle nipajji, bahūni ambaphalāni tahaṃ tahaṃ patitāni honti. Tattheko vuḍḍhataro upāsako therassa santikaṃ upagantvā parissamaṃ ñatvā [M 1.0071] ambapānaṃ pāyetvā attano piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ neti. Thero –

It is said that the Elder Mahātissa, during a time of famine, while traveling along a road, with his body weary and weak from the cutting off of food and from the fatigue of the road, lay down at the foot of a certain fruit-bearing mango tree. Many mango fruits had fallen here and there. There, an older lay devotee, approaching the elder and recognizing his fatigue, gave him a mango drink, and placing him on his own back, brought him to his dwelling place. The elder—

“Na pitā napi te mātā, na ñāti napi bandhavo;

Karotetādisaṃ kiccaṃ, sīlavantassa kāraṇā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.20) –

‘He is not your father, nor your mother, not a relative, nor a kinsman; he does such a deed as this on account of one who is virtuous.’

Attānaṃ ovaditvā sammasanaṃ ārabhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tassa piṭṭhigato eva maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Imaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ambakhādakamahātissattheravatthupi cettha kathetabba”nti. Sabbathāpīti sabbappakārenapi anesanavasena, cittuppattivasenapi, pageva kāyavacīvipphanditavasenāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “anesanāyā”tiādi.

Having admonished himself, having initiated comprehension, and having developed insight, while still situated on his back, he realized arahantship through the sequence of the path. With reference to this it was said: 'The story of the Elder Mahātissa, the Mango-Eater, should also be related here.' Sabbathāpi means: in every way, that is, by way of improper seeking and by way of the arising of thought; how much more so by way of bodily and verbal activity. This is the intention. Therefore, he said: anesanāya, etc.

Apaccavekkhitaparibhoge iṇaparibhogaāpattiādīnavassa, tabbipariyāyato paccavekkhitaparibhoge ānisaṃsassa ca dassanaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsadassanaṃ. Tassa pana paccayādhikārattā vuttaṃ “paccayesū”ti. Kāraṇakāraṇampi hi kāraṇabhāvena vuccati yathā tiṇehi bhattaṃ siddhanti. Yena kāraṇena bhikkhuno apaccavekkhitaparibhogo nāma siyā, tasmiṃ vajjite paccayasannissitasīlaṃ sijjhati, visujjhati cāti dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paccayagedhanti gedhaggahaṇeneva sammohopi gahitoti daṭṭhabbo tena saha pavattanato, tadupanissayato ca. Dhammena samena uppanneti idaṃ paccayānaṃ āgamanasuddhidassanaṃ, na paccayasannissitasīlavisuddhidassanaṃ. Paccayānaṃ hi idamatthitaṃ upadhāretvā paribhuñjanaṃ paccayasannissitasīlaṃ. Yasmā pana te paccayā ñāyādhigatā eva bhikkhunā paribhuñjitabbā, tasmā vuttaṃ “dhammena samena uppanne paccaye”ti. Yathāvuttena vidhināti “sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58; mahāni. 206) vuttavidhinā.

The seeing of the danger—such as using things as a debt and incurring offenses—in unreflecting use, and conversely, the seeing of the benefit in reflecting use, is ādīnavānisaṃsadassana, the seeing of danger and benefit. But because this has requisites as its subject, it is said 'in requisites.' For indeed, even the cause of a cause is spoken of as a cause, just as 'rice is cooked by means of grass.' To show that when the cause by which a monk's unreflecting use might occur is avoided, the virtue dependent on requisites is accomplished and purified, it was said tasmā, etc. Therein, in 'greed for requisites,' it should be understood that by the taking up of greed, delusion is also taken up, because it arises together with it and has that as its support. The phrase 'arisen through righteousness and fairness' shows the purity of the acquisition of the requisites, not the purity of the virtue dependent on requisites. For the virtue dependent on requisites is the using of them after having considered their purpose. But since those requisites should be used by a monk only when they are obtained by the right method, it was said 'requisites arisen through righteousness and fairness.' By the method as stated means: by the method stated in the passage beginning 'for the warding off of cold.'

Dhātuvasena [V 1.0067] vāti “yathāpaccayaṃ vattamānaṃ dhātumattamevetaṃ, yadidaṃ cīvarādi, tadupabhuñjako ca puggalo”ti evaṃ dhātumanasikāravasena vā. Paṭikūlavasena vāti piṇḍapāte tāva āhāre paṭikūlasaññāvasena, “sabbāni pana imāni cīvarādīni ajigucchanīyāni, imaṃ pūtikāyaṃ patvā ativiya jigucchanīyāni jāyantī”ti evaṃ paṭikūlamanasikāravasena vā. Tato uttarīti paṭilābhakālato upari. Anavajjova paribhogo [M 1.0072] āditova paññāya parisodhitattā adhiṭṭhahitvā ṭhapitapattacīvarānaṃ viyāti. Paccavekkhaṇāya ādisuddhidassanaparametaṃ, na paribhogakāle paccavekkhaṇapaṭikkhepaparaṃ. Tenāha “paribhogakālepī”tiādi. Tatrāti tasmiṃ paribhogakāle paccavekkhaṇe. Sanniṭṭhānakaroti asandehakaro ekantiko.

Or by way of elements: 'This which is occurring according to conditions—namely, the requisites such as robes, and the person who uses them—is merely a collection of elements.' Thus, or by way of reflection on the elements. Or by way of repulsiveness: first, in the case of alms-food, by way of the perception of repulsiveness in food; and then, by way of reflection on repulsiveness, 'Furthermore, all these requisites such as robes are not repulsive; having come into contact with this foul body, they become exceedingly repulsive.' Tato uttari means after the time of acquisition. The use is blameless from the very beginning because it has been purified by wisdom, like bowls and robes that have been determined and set aside. This is primarily for showing the initial purity of the reflection, not for rejecting reflection at the time of use. Therefore, he said, 'Even at the time of use,' and so on. Tatra means in that reflection at the time of use. Sanniṭṭhānakaro means that which makes a firm conclusion, that which is without doubt, definitive.

Theyyaparibhogo nāma anarahassa paribhogo. Bhagavatāpi attano sāsane sīlavato paccayā anuññātā, na dussīlassa. Dāyakānampi sīlavato eva pariccāgo, na dussīlassa. Attano kārānaṃ mahapphalabhāvassa paccāsīsanato. Iti satthārā ananuññātattā, dāyakehi ca apariccattattā dussīlassa paribhogo theyyāya paribhogo theyyaparibhogo. Iṇavasena paribhogo iṇaparibhogo, paṭiggāhakato dakkhiṇāvisuddhiyā abhāvato iṇaṃ gahetvā paribhogo viyāti attho. Tasmāti “sīlavato”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Cīvaraṃ kāyato mocetvā paribhoge paribhoge purebhatta…pe… pacchimayāmesu paccavekkhitabbanti sambandho. Tathā asakkontena yathāvuttakālavisesavasena ekadivase catukkhattuṃ tikkhattuṃ dvikkhattuṃ sakiṃyeva vā paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Sace aruṇaṃ uggacchati, iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Hiyyo yaṃ mayā cīvaraṃ paribhuttaṃ, taṃ yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya…pe… hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthaṃ. Hiyyo yo mayā piṇḍapāto paribhutto, so “neva davāyā”tiādinā sace atītaparibhogapaccavekkhaṇaṃ na kareyyāti vadanti, taṃ vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Senāsanampi paribhoge paribhogeti pavese pavese. Satipaccayatāti satiyā paccayabhāvo paṭiggahaṇassa, paribhogassa ca paccavekkhaṇasatiyā paccayabhāvo yujjati, paccavekkhitvāva paṭiggahetabbaṃ, paribhuñjitabbañcāti attho. Tenevāha “satiṃ katvā”tiādi. Evaṃ santepīti yadipi dvīsupi ṭhānesu paccavekkhaṇā yuttā, evaṃ santepi. Apare panāhu – sati paccayatāti sati bhesajjaparibhogassa paccayabhāve, sati paccayeti attho. Evaṃ santepīti paccaye satipīti. Taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Tathā hi paccayasannissitasīlaṃ paccavekkhaṇāya visujjhati, na paccayassa bhāvamattena.

Use by theft (`theyyaparibhoga`) is the use by one who is unworthy. By the Blessed One, requisites are permitted for the virtuous in his dispensation, not for the immoral. The donors' offerings are also for the virtuous, not for the immoral, because they hope for the great fruitfulness of their actions. Thus, because it is not permitted by the Teacher and not given up by the donors, the use by the immoral is use by theft, hence `theyyaparibhoga`. Use by way of debt (`iṇaparibhoga`) is use as a debt; since the purity of the offering is lacking on the recipient's part, it is like using something by taking a debt—this is the meaning. Therefore, with 'for the virtuous,' etc., he re-examines the same meaning already stated as the reason. The connection is this: having removed the robe from the body, at each and every use, one should reflect—before the meal... up to... in the last watches of the night. If one is unable to do so, one should reflect four times, three times, twice, or even just once a day, according to the specified times as stated. If dawn breaks, one stands in the position of debt-use. They say that if one does not perform the reflection on past use—[thinking]: 'The robe I used yesterday was only for protection against cold... up to... for covering the private parts,' and 'The alms-food I used yesterday was not for amusement...' and so on—[it becomes debt-use]; that statement should be examined. The dwelling, too, 'at each and every use' means at each and every entry. `Satipaccayatā` means that mindfulness is a condition for receiving and for using; it is proper that the mindfulness of reflection is a condition. The meaning is that one should receive and use only after reflecting. Therefore, he said, 'having established mindfulness,' and so on. `Evaṃ santepi` means: although reflection is proper in both instances, even so. But others say: `satipaccayatā` means 'when there is a condition'; that is, when there is a condition for the use of medicine, this is the meaning. `Evaṃ santepi` means 'even when there is a condition.' That is merely their opinion. For, virtue dependent on requisites is purified by reflection, not merely by the existence of the requisite.

Evaṃ [V 1.0068] paccayasannissitasīlassa visuddhiṃ dassetvā teneva pasaṅgena sabbāpi visuddhiyo dassetuṃ “catubbidhā hi suddhī”tiādimāha. Tattha sujjhati [M 1.0073] etāyāti suddhi, yathādhammaṃ desanāva suddhi desanāsuddhi. Vuṭṭhānassāpi cettha desanāya eva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Chinnamūlāpattīnaṃ pana abhikkhutāpaṭiññāva desanā. Adhiṭṭhānavisiṭṭho saṃvarova suddhi saṃvarasuddhi. Dhammena samena paccayānaṃ pariyeṭṭhi eva suddhi pariyeṭṭhisuddhi. Catūsupi paccayesu vuttavidhinā paccavekkhaṇāva suddhi paccavekkhaṇasuddhi. Esa tāva suddhīsu samāsanayo. Suddhimantesu pana desanā suddhi etassāti desanāsuddhi. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Suddhi-saddo pana vuttanayova. Evanti saṃvarabhedaṃ sandhāyāha. Pahāyāti vajjetvā, akatvāti attho.

Having thus shown the purity of virtue dependent on requisites, and to indicate all purities by that very connection, he said, 'For purity is fourfold,' and so on. Herein, `suddhi` (purity) is that by which one is purified. Confession in accordance with the Dhamma is purity, namely, purity of confession (`desanāsuddhi`). Herein, emergence from an offense should also be understood as included in confession. For those with root-cutting offenses, the declaration of no longer being a bhikkhu is itself the confession. Restraint distinguished by determination is purity, namely, purity of restraint (`saṃvarasuddhi`). The search for requisites that is righteous and fair is purity, namely, purity of search (`pariyeṭṭhisuddhi`). This, for now, is the summary method concerning the purities. But concerning the virtues that possess purity, `desanāsuddhi` means 'confession is the purity of this virtue.' The same method applies to the rest. The word `suddhi`, however, is in the manner already stated. 'Thus' is said with reference to the division of restraint. `Pahāya` means having avoided, that is, not having done.

Dātabbaṭṭhena dāyaṃ, taṃ ādiyantīti dāyādā. Ananuññātesu sabbena sabbaṃ paribhogābhāvato, anuññātesu eva ca paribhogasambhavato bhikkhūhi paribhuñjitabbapaccayā bhagavato santakā. “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha mā āmisadāyādā. Atthi me tumhesu anukampā ‘kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ no āmisadāyādā’”ti (ma. ni. 1.29) evaṃ pavattaṃ dhammadāyādasuttañca ettha etasmiṃ atthe sādhakaṃ.

By the meaning of 'to be given,' it is `dāya` (inheritance); those who take it are `dāyādā` (heirs). Because there is no use whatsoever of what is not permitted, and because use is possible only of what is permitted, the requisites to be used by bhikkhus are the property of the Blessed One. The Dhammadāyāda Sutta, which proceeds thus, also serves as evidence for this meaning: 'Be my heirs in the Dhamma, bhikkhus, not heirs in material things. I have compassion for you, [thinking], “How might my disciples become heirs in the Dhamma and not heirs in material things?”' (MN 1.29).

Avītarāgānaṃ taṇhāparavasatāya paccayaparibhoge sāmibhāvo natthi, tadabhāvena vītarāgānaṃ tattha sāmibhāvo yathāruciparibhogasambhavato. Tathā hi te paṭikūlampi appaṭikūlākārena, appaṭikūlampi paṭikūlākārena, tadubhayampi vajjetvā ajjhupekkhanākārena paccaye paribhuñjanti, dāyakānañca manorathaṃ paripūrenti. Tenāha “te hi taṇhāya dāsabyaṃ atītattā sāmino hutvā paribhuñjantī”ti.

For those not free from passion, there is no ownership in the use of requisites due to being under the control of craving. Due to the absence of that, for those free from passion, there is ownership in that matter, since use according to their wish is possible. Indeed, they use requisites by perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive, the non-repulsive as repulsive, or, having avoided both, with equanimity; and they fulfill the heart's wish of the donors. Therefore, he said: 'For they, having transcended slavery to craving, use requisites having become masters.'

Sabbesanti ariyānaṃ, puthujjanānañca. Kathaṃ puthujjanānaṃ ime paribhogā sambhavanti? Upacāravasena. Yo hi puthujjanassāpi sallekhapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa paccayagedhaṃ pahāya tattha tattha anupalittena cittena paribhogo, so sāmiparibhogo viya hoti. Sīlavato pana paccavekkhitaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo viya hoti, dāyakānaṃ manorathassa avirādhanato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “dāyajjaparibhogeyeva vā saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”ti. Kalyāṇaputhujjanassa paribhoge vattabbameva natthi, tassa sekkhasaṅgahato. Sekkhasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.13) hetassatthassa sādhakaṃ. Tenāha “sīlavāpi [M 1.0074] hī”tiādi. Paccanīkattāti yathā iṇāyiko attano ruciyā icchitadesaṃ gantuṃ na [V 1.0069] labhati, evaṃ iṇaparibhogayutto lokato nissarituṃ na labhatīti tappaṭipakkhattā sīlavato paccavekkhitaparibhogo āṇaṇyaparibhogoti āha “āṇaṇyaparibhogo vā”ti. Etena nippariyāyato catuparibhogavinimutto visuṃyevāyaṃ paribhogoti dasseti. Imāya sikkhāyāti sīlasaṅkhātāya sikkhāya. Kiccakārīti paṭiññānurūpaṃ paṭipajjanato yuttapattakārī.

For all, that is, for noble ones and for ordinary people. How can these uses—namely, the use of an owner and the use of an heir—arise for ordinary people? By way of figurative speech. For even of an ordinary person who is established in the practice of effacement, having abandoned greed for requisites, whatever use there is with a mind unattached to this or that, that use is like the use of an owner. For a virtuous person, however, use with reflection is like the use of an heir, because of not frustrating the heart's wish of the donors. Thus indeed it is said: ‘It is included in the use of an heir.’ Regarding the use of a virtuous ordinary person, there is nothing at all to be said, because that person is counted as a trainee. The Sekkha Sutta serves as that which establishes this meaning. Therefore, He said, ‘Even a virtuous one…,’ and so on. By ‘being its opposite’: just as a debtor cannot go to a desired place according to his own wish, so one who engages in the use of debt cannot escape from the world. Because of being the opposite of that, the use with reflection of a virtuous person is the ‘use free from debt’; thus He said, ‘or the use free from debt.’ By this, it is shown that this use is absolutely free from the four kinds of use and is entirely distinct. By ‘this training’ is meant by the training designated as virtue. By ‘one who does what should be done’ is meant one who does what is suitable and proper, because of practicing in accordance with one's admission.

Idāni tameva kiccakāritaṃ suttapadena vibhāvetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vihāranti patissayaṃ. Sayanāsananti mañcādiṃ. Ubhayenapi senāsanameva vuttaṃ. Āpanti udakaṃ. Saṅghāṭirajūpavāhananti paṃsumalādino saṅghāṭigatarajassa dhovanaṃ. Sutvāna dhammaṃ sugatena desitanti cīvarādīsu “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevati sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58; mahāni. 206) nayena bhagavatā desitaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā. Saṅkhāya seve varapaññasāvakoti “piṇḍa”nti vuttaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ, vihārādipadehi vuttaṃ senāsanaṃ, “pipāsāgelaññassa vūpasamanato pānīyampi gilānapaccayo”ti āpamukhena dassitaṃ gilānapaccayaṃ, saṅghāṭiyādicīvaranti catubbidhaṃ paccayaṃ saṅkhāya “yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; 2.24; 3.75; saṃ. ni. 4.120; a. ni. 6.58; 8.9; dha. sa. 1355) nayena paccavekkhitvā. Seve sevituṃ sakkuṇeyya uttamapaññassa bhagavato sāvako sekho vā puthujjano vā.

Now, in order to clarify that very fact of doing what should be done by means of a sutta passage, it was said, “vuttampi cetaṃ,” and so on. Therein, by ‘vihāraṃ’ is meant a monastery building. By ‘sayanāsanaṃ’ is meant a couch, etc. By both terms, only lodging and seating are meant. By ‘āpaṃ’ is meant water. By ‘saṅghāṭirajūpavāhanaṃ’ is meant the washing of dust that has settled on the outer robe, such as dust, dirt, and so on. By ‘Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata’ is meant having heard the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One concerning robes and so on, in the manner of ‘Reflecting wisely, one uses the robe only for warding off cold,’ etc. By ‘The disciple of the one with supreme wisdom, having reflected, should use,’ is meant: having reflected upon the four kinds of requisites—namely, the almsfood spoken of as ‘piṇḍaṃ’; the lodging and seating spoken of by the words ‘vihāraṃ,’ etc.; the requisite for the sick, indicated principally by ‘āpaṃ’ (water), as “water is also a requisite for the sick for quenching the illness of thirst”; and the robe, etc., indicated by ‘saṅghāṭi’—having reflected in the manner of ‘only for the maintenance of this body,’ etc., a disciple of the Blessed One of supreme wisdom, whether a trainee or an ordinary person, should use them, would be able to use them.

Yasmā ca saṅkhāya sevī varapaññasāvako, tasmā hi piṇḍe…pe… pokkhare vāribindu, tathā hoti. Kālenāti ariyānaṃ bhojanakāle. Laddhāti labhitvā. Paratoti aññato dāyakato. Anuggahāti anukampāya bahumhi upanīte mattaṃ so jaññā jāneyya satataṃ sabbakālaṃ upaṭṭhito upaṭṭhitassati. Ālepanarūhane yathāti bhesajjalepanena vaṇassa ruhane viya, mattaṃ jāneyyāti yojanā. Āhareti āhareyya. “Āhareyyāhāra”nti vā pāṭho. Yāpanatthanti sarīrassa yāpanāya. Amucchitoti taṇhāmucchāya amucchito gedhaṃ taṇhaṃ anāpanno.

And because the disciple of the one with supreme wisdom is accustomed to using after reflection, therefore, in almsfood… and so on… just as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, so he is unattached. By ‘at the proper time’ is meant at the mealtime of the noble ones. By ‘having received’ is meant having obtained. By ‘from another’ is meant from another donor. By ‘with favor’ is meant: with compassion, when much is offered, that monk, with mindfulness established, should always, at all times, know the measure. By ‘as with anointing for healing’ is meant just as in causing a wound to heal by applying medicine; the connection ‘he should know the measure’ is to be understood. By ‘he should partake’ is meant he should consume. Or, the reading is ‘he should consume nourishment.’ By ‘for the sake of sustenance’ is meant for the maintenance of the body. By ‘not stupefied’ is meant not being stupefied by the stupefaction that is craving, not having fallen into the greed that is craving.

Attano [M 1.0075] mātulassa saṅgharakkhitattherasseva nāmassa gahitattā bhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhitasāmaṇero. Sālikūranti sālibhattaṃ. Sunibbutanti susītalaṃ. Asaññatoti apaccavekkhaṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇoti parikkhīṇasabbāsavo.

Because of having taken the very name of his own maternal uncle, the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, he was the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew. By ‘sālikūraṃ’ is meant rice from Sāli grain. By ‘sunibbutaṃ’ is meant well-cooled. He said ‘unrestrained’ (asaññato) with reference to non-reflection. By ‘one with all cankers completely destroyed’ is meant one who has all cankers completely destroyed.

Paṭhamasīlapañcakavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the First Pentad on Virtue

20. Pariyanto [V 1.0070] etesaṃ atthīti pariyantāni, pariyantāni sikkhāpadāni yesaṃ te pariyantasikkhāpadā, tesaṃ pariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ. Upasampannānanti ṭhapetvā kalyāṇaputhujjanasekkhāsekkhe tadaññesaṃ upasampannānaṃ. Sāmaññajotanāpi hi visese tiṭṭhati. Kusaladhamme yuttānanti vipassanācāre yuttapayuttānaṃ. Sekkhadhammā pariyantā paramā mariyādā etassāti sekkhapariyanto. Nāmarūpaparicchedato, kusaladhammasamādānato vā pana paṭṭhāya yāva gotrabhū, tāva pavattakusaladhammappabandho sekkhadhamme āhacca ṭhito sekkhapariyanto. Sekkhadhammānaṃ vā heṭṭhimantabhūtā sikkhitabbā lokiyā tisso sikkhā sekkhapariyanto, tasmiṃ sekkhapariyante. Paripūrakārīnanti kiñcipi sikkhaṃ ahāpetvā pūrentānaṃ. Uparivisesādhigamatthaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhānaṃ. Tato eva sīlapāripūriatthaṃ pariccattajīvitānaṃ. Diṭṭhisaṃkilesena aparāmasanīyato pārisuddhivantaṃ sīlaṃ aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Kilesānaṃ sabbaso paṭippassaddhiyā pārisuddhivantaṃ sīlaṃ paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīlaṃ.

20. ‘Pariyanto etesaṃ atthī’ti pariyantāni’: ‘For these there is a limit, therefore they are limited.’ ‘Pariyantāni sikkhāpadāni yesaṃ te pariyantasikkhāpadā, tesaṃ pariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ’: ‘Those for whom the training rules are limited are “those with limited training rules”; of those with limited training rules.’ ‘Upasampannānan’ti ṭhapetvā kalyāṇaputhujjanasekkhāsekkhe tadaññesaṃ upasampannānaṃ’: ‘Regarding the fully ordained,’ this means of the other fully ordained ones, excluding the virtuous worldlings, trainees, and non-trainees. ‘Sāmaññajotanāpi hi visese tiṭṭhati’: ‘Indeed, even a general indication stands in a specific sense.’ ‘Kusaladhamme yuttānan’ti vipassanācāre yuttappayuttānaṃ’: ‘Of those engaged in wholesome states’ means of those diligently engaged in the practice of insight. ‘Sekkhadhammā pariyantā paramā mariyādā etassā’ti sekkhapariyanto’: ‘The trainee’s qualities are the limit, the highest boundary of this; therefore, it is that which has the trainee’s qualities as its limit.’ ‘Nāmarūpaparicchedato, kusaladhammasamādānato vā pana paṭṭhāya yāva gotrabhū, tāva pavattakusaladhammappabandho sekkhadhamme āhacca ṭhito sekkhapariyanto’: ‘Starting from the discernment of name-and-form, or from the undertaking of wholesome states, up to the change-of-lineage, the occurring stream of wholesome states stands having reached the trainee’s qualities; this is that which has the trainee’s qualities as its limit.’ ‘Sekkhadhammānaṃ vā heṭṭhimantabhūtā sikkhitabbā lokiyā tisso sikkhā sekkhapariyanto, tasmiṃ sekkhapariyante’: ‘Or, the three mundane trainings to be trained in, which are the lower limit of the trainee’s qualities, are that which has the trainee’s qualities as its limit; in that which has the trainee’s qualities as its limit.’ ‘Paripūrakārīnan’ti kiñcipi sikkhaṃ ahāpetvā pūrentānaṃ’: ‘Of those who are fulfillers’ means of those who fulfill without omitting any training whatsoever. ‘Uparivisesādhigamatthaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhānaṃ’: ‘For the purpose of attaining higher distinction, of those who are unconcerned with body and life.’ ‘Tato eva sīlapāripūriatthaṃ pariccattajīvitānaṃ’: ‘For that very reason, for the sake of the complete fulfillment of virtue, of those who have given up their lives.’ ‘Diṭṭhisaṃkilesena aparāmasanīyato pārisuddhivantaṃ sīlaṃ aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīlaṃ’: ‘Virtue possessing purity because it is not to be misapprehended with the defilement of views is the virtue of untouched purity.’ ‘Kilesānaṃ sabbaso paṭippassaddhiyā pārisuddhivantaṃ sīlaṃ paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīlaṃ’: ‘Virtue possessing purity through the complete calming of defilements is the virtue of purity through calming.’

Anupasampannānaṃ asekkhānaṃ, sekkhānaṃ, kalyāṇaputhujjanānañca sīlaṃ mahānubhāvatāya ānubhāvato apariyantamevāti āha “gaṇanavasena sapariyantattā”ti. Kāyavācānaṃ saṃvaraṇato, vinayanato ca saṃvaravinayā. Peyyālamukhena niddiṭṭhāti tattha tattha satthārā desitavitthāranayena yathāvuttagaṇanato niddiṭṭhā. Sikkhāti sīlasaṅkhātā sikkhā. Vinayasaṃvareti vinayapiṭake. Gaṇanavasena sapariyantampi upasampannānaṃ sīlanti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci hi upasampannena sikkhitabbaṃ sīlaṃ nāma, tattha kassacipi anavasesato anavasesavasena[M 1.0076]. Samādānabhāvanti samādānasabbhāvaṃ. Lābha…pe… vasena adiṭṭhapariyantabhāvo lābhādihetu sīlassa avītikkamo.

The virtue of those not fully ordained, of the non-trainees, of the trainees, and of the noble worldlings is indeed limitless in its influence due to its great power. Thus, it is said, 'because of being limited by way of enumeration.' Because they restrain and discipline the body and speech, they are called ‘restraint and discipline.’ ‘Indicated by way of abbreviation’ means they are indicated in various places by the Teacher according to the detailed method taught and by way of the aforesaid enumeration. ‘Training’ is the training designated as virtue. ‘In the restraint of the discipline’ means in the Vinaya Piṭaka. The previously stated phrase, “the virtue of the fully ordained, although limited by way of enumeration,” should be brought forward and connected. Indeed, whatever virtue is to be trained in by one who is fully ordained, therein, of any whatsoever, it is without remainder; this is meant by 'by way of non-remainder.' ‘The state of undertaking’ means the actual existence of undertaking. The non-transgression of virtue on account of gain and other causes is the state of having an unseen limit by way of gain, retinue, relatives, limbs, and life.

Dhanaṃ caje aṅgavarassa hetu pāripanthikacorādīhi upadduto. Aṅgaṃ caje jīvitaṃ rakkhamāno sappadaṭṭhādikāle. Aṅgaṃ dhanaṃ jīvitañcāpi sabbaṃ, caje naro dhammamanussaranto sutasomamahābodhisattādayo viya. Tenāha “imaṃ sappurisānussatiṃ avijahanto”ti. Jighacchāparissamena jīvitasaṃsaye satipi. Sikkhāpadaṃ avītikkammāti assāmikesu ambaphalesu [V 1.0071] bhūmiyaṃ patitesu samīpeyeva santesupi paṭiggāhakābhāvena aparibhuñjanto paṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadaṃ avītikkamitvā.

One should give up wealth for the sake of a noble limb when oppressed by highway robbers, thieves, and so on. One should give up a limb while protecting one's life at a time of a snakebite and so on. A person, while repeatedly recollecting the Dhamma, like the great bodhisatta Sutasoma and others, should give up a limb, wealth, and even life—all of it. Therefore, he said, “not abandoning this recollection of noble persons.” Even when there is doubt about one's life due to hunger and fatigue. ‘Not transgressing the training rule’ means: regarding ownerless mangoes that have fallen on the ground, even though they are right nearby, not consuming them due to the absence of a giver, he did not transgress the training rule concerning receiving.

Sīlavantassāti sīlavantabhāvassa kāraṇā, sīlavantassa vā tuyhaṃ etādisaṃ aṃsena vāhaṇādikaṃ kiccaṃ karoti, kāraṇā sīlassāti adhippāyo. Sudhotajātimaṇi viyāti catūsu pāsāṇesu sammadeva dhotajātimaṇi viya. Mahāsaṅgharakkhitabhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhitattherānaṃ viyāti mahāsaṅgharakkhitattherassa, tasseva bhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhitattherassa viya ca. “Kimatthaṃ mayaṃ idhāgatā”ti mahājanassa vippaṭisāro bhavissatīti adhippāyo. Accharikāyāti aṅguliphoṭanena. Asatiyāti satisammosena. Aññāṇapakatanti aññāṇena aparajjhitvā kataṃ, ajānitvā katanti attho.

‘Of one who is virtuous’ means either ‘because of the state of being virtuous,’ or ‘for you who are virtuous, he does such a task as carrying on the shoulder, etc., for the sake of virtue’; this is the intention. ‘Like a well-cleansed, genuine gem’ means like a genuine, mine-extracted gem that has been well cleansed on the four types of stones. ‘Like the elders Mahāsaṅgharakkhita and his nephew Saṅgharakkhita’ means like the elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita and like the elder Saṅgharakkhita, his nephew. The intention is that the great crowd of people will have regret, thinking, “For what purpose have we come here?” ‘With a snap of the fingers’ means by the snapping of the fingers. ‘Through unmindfulness’ means through a lapse of mindfulness. ‘Done through ignorance’ means done, having transgressed through ignorance; the meaning is something done without knowing.

Appassutopi ce hotīti suttageyyādisutarahito hoti ce. Sīlesu asamāhitoti pātimokkhasaṃvarādisīlesupi na sammā patiṭṭhito hoti ce. Nāssa sampajjate sutanti assa sīlarahitassa puggalassa sutaṃ attano, paresañca katthaci bhavasampattiāvahaṃ na hoti. “Dussīloyaṃ purisapuggalo”ti hi sikkhākāmā na tassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamanti. Bahussutopi ceti ettha ce-ti nipātamattaṃ. Pasaṃsitoti pasaṃsito eva nāma.

‘Even if one is of little learning’ means if one is devoid of learning in the Sutta, Geyya, etc. ‘Not concentrated in virtues’ means if one is not well established even in virtues such as the Pātimokkha restraint. ‘His learning does not succeed’ means the learning of that person who is devoid of virtue does not bring about success in any sphere of existence for himself or for others. Indeed, thinking, “This person is of bad virtue,” those who desire the training do not approach him. In the phrase ‘bahussuto’pi ce’ (‘even if one is very learned’), ‘ce’ is merely a particle. ‘Praised’ means he is indeed called ‘praised.’

Rāgavasena aparāmaṭṭhagahaṇena taṇhāparāmāsābhāvamāha. Tathārūpanti rāgavasena aparāmaṭṭhaṃ. Bhinditvāti hanitvā. Saññapessāmīti saññattiṃ [M 1.0077] karissāmi, appakaṃ velaṃ maṃ vissejjetunti adhippāyo. Aṭṭiyāmīti jigucchāmi. Harāyāmīti lajjāmi.

By the phrase ‘not misapprehended by way of lust,’ he states the absence of the misapprehension of craving. ‘Of such a kind’ means not misapprehended by way of lust. ‘Having broken’ means having struck. ‘I will make him understand’ means I will make an intimation; the intention is, “Let him release me for a short time.” ‘I am troubled’ means I am disgusted. ‘I am ashamed’ means I am ashamed.

Palipannoti sīdanto, sammakkhito vā. Sīleneva saddhiṃ marissāmīti sīlaṃ avināsento tena saheva marissāmi, na idāni kadācipi taṃ pariccajissāmi. Sati hi bhavādāne sīlena viyogo siyā, bhavameva nādiyissāmīti adhippāyo. Rogaṃ sammasantoti rogabhūtaṃ vedanaṃ vedanāmukhena sesārūpadhamme, rūpadhamme ca pariggahetvā vipassanto.

‘Fallen into’ means sinking, or smeared. ‘I will die together with virtue itself’ means: not destroying virtue, I will die together with it; now, I will never abandon it. Indeed, if there is the taking up of a new existence, there would be separation from virtue; therefore, I will not take up existence itself—this is the intention. ‘Contemplating disease’ means: comprehending feeling which has become a disease, and through the avenue of feeling, the remaining immaterial states and material states, and practicing insight.

Ruppatoti vikāraṃ āpādiyamānasarīrassa. Parisussatīti samantato sussati. Yathā kiṃ? Pupphaṃ yathā paṃsuni ātape kataṃ sūriyātapasantatte paṃsuni ṭhapitaṃ sirīsādipupphaṃ viyāti [V 1.0072] attho. Ajaññanti amanuññaṃ jigucchanīyaṃ. Jaññasaṅkhātanti bālehi “jañña”nti evaṃ kittitaṃ. Jaññarūpaṃ apassatoti yathābhūtaṃ appassato aviddasuno “jañña”nti pasaṃsitaṃ. Dhiratthumanti dhi atthu imaṃ, dhi-saddayogena sabbattha upayogavacanaṃ, imassa pūtikāyassa dhikāro hotūti attho. Duggandhiyanti duggandhikaṃ duggandhavantaṃ. Yattha yathāvutte pūtikāye rāgahetu pamattā pamādaṃ āpannā. Pajāti sattā. Hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyāti sugatūpapattiyā maggaṃ, sīlampi hāpenti, pageva jhānādinti adhippāyo. Kevalaṃ “arahanto”ti vattabbā sāvakakhīṇāsavā, itare pana paccekabuddhā sammāsambuddhāti saha visesanenāti āha “arahantādīna”nti. Sabbadarathappaṭippassaddhiyāti sabbakilesadarathappaṭippassaddhiyā.

‘Ruppati’ means: of the body being brought to a state of alteration. ‘Parisussati’ means: it dries up all around. Like what? The meaning is: just as a sirīsa flower or the like, placed on dust heated by the sun's heat, dries up. ‘Ajaññaṃ’ means: disagreeable, disgusting. ‘Jaññasaṅkhātaṃ’ means: it is proclaimed as “delightful” by fools. ‘Jaññarūpaṃ apassato’ means: for one who does not see it as it truly is, for the ignorant one, it is praised as “delightful”. The term ‘dhiratthu'maṃ’ is parsed as ‘dhi atthu imaṃ’; due to the connection with the word ‘dhi’, the accusative case is used for all related words. The meaning is: Let there be contempt for this putrid body. ‘Duggandhiyaṃ’ means: having a bad smell, possessing a foul odor. Wherein, in the aforesaid putrid body, beings become heedless due to lust as the cause, they fall into heedlessness. ‘Pajā’ means: beings. ‘Hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyā’ means: they cause the loss of the path to rebirth in a good destination; they cause the loss of even virtue, to say nothing of jhāna and so on—this is the intention. The disciple-arahants are to be called simply “arahants”, but others, such as Paccekabuddhas and Sammāsambuddhas, are to be called with their special designation. Therefore, it is said ‘arahantādīnaṃ’. ‘Sabbadarathappaṭippassaddhiyā’ means: for the pacification of the fever of all defilements.

Dutiyasīlapañcakavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Second Pentad of Virtue

Pāṇātipātādīnanti ādi-saddena adinnādānādīnaṃ aggamaggavajjhakilesapariyosānānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Pahānādīti ādi-saddena veramaṇiādīnaṃ catunnaṃ. Kesuci potthakesu “pahānavasenā”ti likhanti, sā pamādalekhā. Pāṇātipātassa pahānaṃ sīlanti hirottappakaruṇālobhādipamukhena yena kusalacittuppādena pāṇātipāto pahīyati, taṃ pāṇātipātassa pahānaṃ sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Tathā pāṇātipātā [M 1.0078] virati veramaṇī sīlaṃ. Pāṇātipātassa paṭipakkhacetanā cetanā sīlaṃ. Pāṇātipātassa saṃvaraṇaṃ pavesadvārapidhānaṃ saṃvaro sīlaṃ. Pāṇātipātassa avītikkamanaṃ avītikkamo sīlaṃ. Adinnādānassātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Abhijjhādīnaṃ pana anabhijjhādivasena pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Veramaṇī cetanā taṃsampayuttā saṃvarāvītikkamā tappamukhā dhammā.

In the term `pāṇātipātādīnaṃ`, by the word `ādi`, the inclusion of taking what is not given and so on, ending with the defilements to be destroyed by the highest path, should be understood. In `pahānādi`, by the word `ādi`, the four beginning with abstinence are included. In some books, they write `pahānavasena`, but that is a careless writing. "The abandoning of the destruction of life is virtue": that wholesome arising of consciousness—led by moral shame, moral dread, compassion, non-greed, and so on—by which the destruction of life is abandoned, that is the abandoning of the destruction of life, and it is virtue (`sīla`) in the sense of being virtuous (`sīlanaṭṭhena`). Similarly, abstinence (`veramaṇī`) from the destruction of life is virtue. The volition (`cetanā`) opposing the destruction of life is virtue. The restraint (`saṃvaro`) of the destruction of life, which is the closing of the door of entry, is virtue. The non-transgression (`avītikkamo`) of the destruction of life is virtue. This same method applies to taking what is not given and so on. Furthermore, the abandoning of covetousness and so on should be understood by way of non-covetousness and so on. Abstinence and volition are states associated with these. Restraint and non-transgression are states led by these.

Evaṃ dasakusalakammapathavasena pahānasīlādīni dassetvā idāni saupāyānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ, aṭṭhārasannaṃ mahāvipassanānaṃ, ariyamaggānañca vasena tāni dassetuṃ “nekkhammenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha nekkhammenāti alobhappadhānena kusalacittuppādena. Kusalā hi dhammā kāmapaṭipakkhā idha “nekkhamma”nti adhippetā. Tenāha “kāmacchandassa pahānaṃ sīla”ntiādi. Tattha pahānasīlādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Visesameva vakkhāma. Abyāpādenāti mettāya. Ālokasaññāyāti vibhūtaṃ katvā manasikaraṇena upaṭṭhitaālokasañjānanena[V 1.0073]. Avikkhepenāti samādhinā. Dhammavavatthānenāti kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvanicchayena. Sapaccayanāmarūpavavatthānenātipi vadanti.

Thus, having shown the virtue of abandoning and so on by way of the ten wholesome courses of action, now, in order to show them by way of the eight attainments with their means, the eighteen great insights, and the noble paths, the passage beginning with `nekkhammena` is introduced. Therein, `nekkhammena` means: by the wholesome arising of consciousness in which non-greed is predominant. Indeed, wholesome states that are the opposite of sensual pleasure are intended here by `nekkhamma`. Therefore, it is said, “the abandoning of sensual desire is virtue,” and so on. Therein, the virtue of abandoning and so on should be understood in the same way as explained previously. We shall speak only of the specifics. `Abyāpādena` means: by loving-kindness. `Ālokasaññāya` means: by the perception of light that has arisen through attending to it after making it distinct. `Avikkhepena` means: by concentration. `Dhammavavatthānena` means: by the correct determination of wholesome states and so on. Some also say: by the determination of name-and-form together with its causes.

Evaṃ kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānena “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā (vibha. 538) vuttāya paṭhamajjhānādhigamassa upāyabhūtāya pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya vasena pahānasīlādīni dassetvā idāni saupāyānaṃ aṭṭhasamāpattiādīnaṃ vasena dassetuṃ “ñāṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nāmarūpapariggahakaṅkhāvitaraṇānaṃ hi vibandhabhūtassa mohassa dūrīkaraṇena ñātapariññāya ṭhitassa aniccasaññādayo sijjhanti. Tathā jhānasamāpattīsu abhiratinimittena pāmojjena. Tattha anabhiratiyā vinoditāya jhānādīnaṃ samadhigamoti samāpattivipassanānaṃ arativinodanaavijjāpadālanādinā upāyoti vuttaṃ “ñāṇena avijjāya, pāmojjena aratiyā”ti. Uppaṭipāṭiniddeso pana nīvaraṇasabhāvāya avijjāya heṭṭhānīvaraṇesupi saṅgahadassanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Thus, having shown the virtue of abandoning and so on by way of the preliminary practice—which is the means for attaining the first jhāna and which was spoken of with the words, “having abandoned covetousness in the world,” and so on (Vibh 538), through the abandoning of the hindrances beginning with sensual desire—now, in order to show them by way of the eight attainments and so on with their means, the passage beginning with `ñāṇena` is stated. Indeed, for one established in the full understanding of the known, through the removal of delusion which is an obstacle to the comprehension of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt, the perceptions of impermanence and so on are accomplished. Similarly, in the jhāna-attainments, when discontent with them has been dispelled by joy, which is a cause for delight, the attainment of jhāna and so on is accomplished. Therefore, the dispelling of discontent, the splitting of ignorance, and so on is the means for the attainments and insights. Thus it is said: “By knowledge against ignorance; by joy against discontent.” Furthermore, the exposition in reverse order should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the inclusion of ignorance, which has the nature of a hindrance, even among the lower hindrances.

“Paṭhamena [M 1.0079] jhānena nīvaraṇāna”ntiādīsu kathaṃ jhānānaṃ sīlabhāvo, kathaṃ vā tattha viratiyā sambhavo. Suvisuddhakāyakammādikassa hi cittasamādānavasena imāni jhānāni pavattanti, na parittakusalāni viya kāyakammādivisodhanavasena, nāpi maggaphaladhammā viya duccaritadurājīvasamucchedapaṭippassambhanavasenāti? Saccametaṃ. Mahaggatadhammesu nippariyāyena natthi sīlanaṭṭho, kuto viramaṇaṭṭho. Pariyāyena panetaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ko pana so pariyāyo? Yadaggena mahaggatā kusaladhammā paṭipakkhe pajahanti, tadaggena tato oratā. Te ca yathā cittaṃ nārohanti, evaṃ saṃvutā nāma honti. Pariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhāto manodvāre vītikkamo natthi etesūti avītikkamāti ca vuccanti, cetanā pana taṃsampayuttāti. Soyamattho parato āgamissati. Evañca katvā vitakkādipahānavacanampi samatthitaṃ hoti. Na hi nippariyāyato sīlaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ pahāyakaṃ yujjati, na cettha akusalavitakkādayo adhippetā. Kiñcāpi paṭhamajjhānūpacāreyeva dukkhassa, catutthajjhānūpacāre ca sukhassa pahānaṃ hoti, atisayapahānaṃ pana sandhāya vuttaṃ “catutthena jhānena sukhadukkhānaṃ pahāna”nti. “Ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ āruppakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 1.275 ādayo) āgamissati.

In such passages as, 'By the first jhāna, of the hindrances...,' how is there the nature of virtue in the jhānas? Or how is the arising of abstinence possible in them? For these jhānas arise for one whose bodily action and so on is thoroughly purified, by the power of composing the mind, not like sense-sphere wholesome states by the power of purifying bodily action and so on, nor like the states of path and fruition by the power of utterly cutting off and calming misconduct and wrong livelihood. Is this not an objection? This statement is true. In the exalted states, there is no literal meaning of virtue; how then could there be the meaning of abstaining? However, it should be understood that this was said figuratively. What, then, is that figure of speech? To the extent that exalted wholesome states abandon their opposites, to that extent they abstain from them. And in so far as those opposites do not ascend into the mind, in that way they are called 'restrained.' In these jhānas, there is no transgression at the mind-door, which is called obsession; therefore, they are also called 'non-transgressive,' and the volition is that which is associated with them. This meaning will come later. And for this reason, the statement about abandoning thought, etc., is also justified. For it is not fitting that virtue, in the literal sense, is an abandoner of wholesome states, nor are unwholesome thoughts and so on intended here. Although the abandoning of pain occurs in the very access concentration of the first jhāna, and the abandoning of pleasure in the access concentration of the fourth jhāna, it was said, 'by the fourth jhāna, the abandoning of pleasure and pain,' with reference to the superior abandoning. Whatever is to be said regarding 'the attainment of the base of infinite space,' etc., that will come in the discussion on the formless attainments.

Aniccassa, aniccanti vā anupassanā aniccānupassanā. Tebhūmikadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā [V 1.0074] pavattāya vipassanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññāyāti “saṅkhatadhammā niccā sassatā”ti evaṃ pavattāya micchāsaññāya, saññāggahaṇeneva diṭṭhicittānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito parāsupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbindanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nandiyāti sappītikataṇhāya. Virāgānupassanāyāti virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Rāgassāti saṅkhāresu rāgassa. Nirodhānupassanāyāti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya. Yathā vā saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ punabbhavavasena na uppajjanti, evaṃ anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Tenevāha “nirodhānupassanāya nirodheti no samudetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.83). Muñcitukāmatāya hi ayaṃ balappattā. Saṅkhārānaṃ paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā hi ayaṃ[M 1.0080]. Ādānassāti niccādivasena gahaṇassa. Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇavasena ekattagahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā, tassā ghanasaññāya. Āyūhanassāti abhisaṅkharaṇassa. Saṅkhārānaṃ avatthādivisesāpatti vipariṇāmo. Dhuvasaññāyāti thirabhāvagahaṇassa. Nimittassāti samūhādighanavasena sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ saviggahatāya. Paṇidhiyāti rāgādipaṇidhiyā, taṇhāvasena saṅkhāresu ninnatāyāti attho. Abhinivesassāti attānudiṭṭhiyā. Aniccadukkhādivasena sabbatebhūmakadhammatiraṇā adhipaññādhammavipassanā. Sārādānābhinivesassāti asāresu sāragahaṇavipallāsassa. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ thirabhāvapattā aniccādianupassanāva. Udayabbayañāṇanti keci. Sappaccayanāmarūpadassananti apare. “Issarakuttādivasena loko samuppanno”ti abhiniveso sammohābhiniveso. Ucchedasassatābhinivesoti keci. “Ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”ntiādinayappavattā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20; mahāni. 174) saṃsayāpatti sammohābhinivesoti apare. Saṅkhāresu tāṇaleṇabhāvagahaṇaṃ ālayābhiniveso. “Ālayaratā ālayasammuditā”ti (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7-8) vacanato ālayo taṇhā. Sā eva cakkhādīsu, rūpādīsu ca abhinivisanavasena pavattiyā ālayābhinivesoti apare. “Evaṃ ṭhitā te saṅkhārā paṭinissajjīyantī”ti pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā. Appaṭisaṅkhā paṭisaṅkhāya paṭipakkhabhūtā mohappadhānā akusaladhammā. Vaṭṭato vigatattā vivaṭṭaṃ nibbānaṃ, tattha ninnabhāvasaṅkhātena anupassanena pavatti vivaṭṭānupassanā, saṅkhārupekkhā ceva anulomañāṇañca. Saññogābhiniveso saṃyujjanavasena saṅkhāresu abhinivisanaṃ.

Contemplation of the impermanent, or contemplation as 'impermanent,' is the contemplation of impermanence. This is the name for the insight that arises by grasping the impermanence of phenomena of the three realms. 'Of the perception of permanence' refers to the wrong perception that arises as 'conditioned formations are permanent, eternal'; by the taking up of 'perception,' the taking up of view and mind should also be understood. This is the method in the subsequent contemplations as well. 'By the contemplation of disenchantment' means by the contemplation that arises in the mode of being disenchanted with conditioned formations. 'Of delight' refers to craving accompanied by joy. 'By the contemplation of dispassion' means by the contemplation that arises in the mode of dispassion. 'Of lust' refers to lust for conditioned formations. 'By the contemplation of cessation' means by the contemplation of the cessation of conditioned formations. Or, the contemplation in such a way that conditioned formations just cease, and do not arise again in the future by way of renewed existence, is the contemplation of cessation. For that very reason, it is said: 'By the contemplation of cessation, one causes cessation, one does not cause arising.' For this has attained strength through the desire for deliverance. The contemplation that arises in the mode of relinquishing conditioned formations is the contemplation of relinquishment. For this is indeed reflective abiding. 'Of grasping' refers to the grasping by way of 'permanent,' etc. The perception of compactness is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, mass, function, and object; 'of that perception of compactness.' 'Of accumulation' refers to volitional formation. Alteration is the reaching of a particular stage of conditioned formations. 'Of the perception of stability' refers to the grasping of a state of permanence. 'Of the sign' refers to the substantiality of conditioned formations by way of the compactness of aggregates, etc., and by the delimitation of their own function. 'Of longing' refers to longing such as lust; the meaning is the inclination towards conditioned formations by way of craving. 'Of adherence' refers to the view of self. The insight into phenomena of higher wisdom is the penetration and determination of all phenomena of the three realms by way of 'impermanent,' 'suffering,' etc. 'Of the adherence of grasping the essential' refers to the perversion of grasping as essential that which is unessential. The knowledge and vision of things as they really are is simply the contemplation of impermanence, etc., that has reached a state of firmness. Some say it is the knowledge of arising and passing away. Others say it is the seeing of name-and-form together with its conditions. The adherence that 'the world has arisen by way of a creator, etc.' is the adherence of delusion. Some say it is the adherence to annihilationism and eternalism. Others say the adherence of delusion is the falling into doubt that arises in such ways as, 'Did I exist in the past?' The adherence to clinging is the grasping of conditioned formations as a protection and a refuge. Because of the statement, 'delighting in clinging, rejoicing in clinging,' clinging is craving. Others say that very craving, because of its occurrence by way of adhering to the eye, etc., and to forms, etc., is called the adherence to clinging. The knowledge that arises as, 'Thus established, these conditioned formations are to be relinquished,' is the contemplation of reflection. Non-reflection refers to the unwholesome states, having delusion as their chief, which are the opposite of the knowledge of reflection. Because it is devoid of the round of existence, Nibbāna is called the Unbinding. The contemplation of turning away is the occurrence of contemplation characterized as an inclination towards it, which comprises equanimity towards formations and conformity knowledge. The adherence of connection is adhering to conditioned formations by way of being yoked to them.

Diṭṭhekaṭṭhānanti [V 1.0075] diṭṭhiyā sahajekaṭṭhānañca pahānekaṭṭhānañca. Oḷārikānanti uparimaggavajjhe kilese upādāya vuttaṃ. Aññathā dassanena pahātabbāpi dutiyamaggavajjhehi oḷārikā. Aṇusahagatānanti aṇubhūtānaṃ, idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe upādāya vuttaṃ. Sabbakilesānanti avasiṭṭhasabbakilesānaṃ. Na hi paṭhamamaggādīhi pahīnā kilesā puna pahīyanti.

'Having a single basis with view' means both having a single basis in co-nascence with view and having a single basis for abandoning. 'Gross' is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths. Otherwise, even those defilements to be abandoned by seeing are grosser than those to be abandoned by the second path. 'Accompanied by the subtle' means of those that are subtle; this is said with reference to those to be abandoned by the lower paths. 'Of all defilements' means of all the remaining defilements.
