For indeed, the defilements abandoned by the first path and so on are not abandoned again.

“Cittassa [M 1.0081] avippaṭisārāya saṃvattantī”tiādīsu saṃvaro avippaṭisāratthāya. “Avippaṭisāratthāni kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlānī”ti (a. ni. 10.1) vacanato cetaso avippaṭisāratthāya bhavanti. Avippaṭisāro pāmojjatthāya. “Yoniso manasi karoto pāmojjaṃ jāyatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.359) vacanato pāmojjāya saṃvattanti. Pāmojjaṃ pītiyā. “Pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466; 3.359; a. ni. 3.96; 6.10; 11.12) vacanato pītiyā saṃvattanti. Pīti passaddhatthāya. “Pītimanassa kāyo passambhatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466; 3.359; a. ni. 3.96; 6.10; 11.12) vacanato passaddhiyā saṃvattanti. Passaddhi sukhatthāya. “Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedetī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466; 3.359; a. ni. 3.96; 6.10; 11.12) vacanato somanassāya saṃvattantīti. “Sukhatthāya sukhaṃ vedetī”ti cettha somanassaṃ “sukha”nti vuttaṃ. Āsevanāyāti samādhissa āsevanāya. Nirāmise hi sukhe siddhe “sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466; 3.359; a. ni. 3.96; 6.10; 11.12) vacanato samādhi siddhoyeva hoti, tasmā samādhissa āsevanāya paguṇabalavabhāvāya saṃvattantīti attho. Bhāvanāyāti tasseva samādhissa vaḍḍhiyā. Bahulīkammāyāti punappunaṃ kiriyāya. Alaṅkārāyāti tasseva samādhissa pasādhanabhūtasaddhindriyādinipphattiyā alaṅkārāya saṃvattanti. Parikkhārāyāti avippaṭisārādikassa samādhisambhārassa siddhiyā tasseva samādhissa parikkhārāya saṃvattanti. Sambhārattho hi idha parikkhāra-saddo. “Ye ca kho ime pabbajitena jīvitaparikkhārā samudānetabbā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.191) viya sambhāroti ca paccayo veditabbo. Kāmañcāyaṃ parikkhāra-saddo “ratho sīlaparikkhāro”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.4) alaṅkārattho. “Sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhattaṃ hotī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.67) parivārattho vutto. Idha pana alaṅkāraparivārānaṃ visuṃ gahitattā “sambhārattho”ti vuttaṃ[V 1.0076]. Parivārāyāti mūlakāraṇabhāveneva samādhissa parivārabhūtasativīriyādidhammavisesasādhanena parivārasampattiyā saṃvattanti. Pāripūriyāti vasībhāvasampāpanena, vipassanāya padaṭṭhānabhāvāpādanena ca paripuṇṇabhāvasādhanato samādhissa pāripūriyā saṃvattanti.

“They conduce to non-remorse of mind,” and so on: restraint is for the purpose of non-remorse. Because it is said, “Indeed, Ānanda, wholesome virtues are for the purpose of non-remorse” (AN 10.1), they are for the purpose of non-remorse of mind. Non-remorse is for the purpose of joy. Because it is said, “For one who attends wisely, joy arises” (DN 3.359), they conduce to joy. Joy is for the purpose of rapture. Because it is said, “For one who is joyful, rapture arises” (DN 1.466; 3.359; AN 3.96; 6.10; 11.12), they conduce to rapture. Rapture is for the purpose of tranquility. Because it is said, “For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil” (DN 1.466; 3.359; AN 3.96; 6.10; 11.12), they conduce to tranquility. Tranquility is for the purpose of happiness. Because it is said, “One with a tranquil body feels happiness” (DN 1.466; 3.359; AN 3.96; 6.10; 11.12), they conduce to gladness. Here, in “for the purpose of happiness, one feels happiness,” gladness is called “happiness.” “For cultivation” means for the cultivation of concentration. For when unworldly happiness is accomplished, because it is said, “the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated” (DN 1.466; 3.359; AN 3.96; 6.10; 11.12), concentration is indeed accomplished. Therefore, the meaning is that they conduce to the cultivation of concentration, for its proficiency and strength. “For development” means for the growth of that very concentration. “For frequent practice” means for repeated action. “For adornment” means they conduce to adornment through the accomplishment of the faculties of faith and so forth, which are the embellishment of that very concentration. “For requisites” means they conduce to the requisites of that very concentration through the achievement of the accumulation for concentration, such as non-remorse. Here, the term “requisite” has the meaning of accumulation. As in, “And these are the requisites of life that should be acquired by one gone forth” (MN 1.191), “accumulation” should be understood as an ancillary condition. Although this term “requisite” can mean ornament, as in “a chariot with virtue as its adornment” (SN 5.4), or retinue, as in “well-guarded with seven city fortifications” (AN 7.67), here, since ornament and retinue are taken separately, it is said to mean “accumulation.” “For retinue” means they conduce to the accomplishment of a retinue by, as the very root cause, bringing about the special qualities such as mindfulness and energy that form the retinue of concentration. “For fulfillment” means they conduce to the fulfillment of concentration by achieving mastery and by providing the foundation for insight, thus accomplishing its complete perfection.

Evaṃ suparisuddhasīlamūlakaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ samādhiṃ dassetvā idāni “samāhito pajānāti passati, yathābhūtaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati[M 1.0082], virāgā vimuccatī”ti (a. ni. 10.2; sa. ni. 3.14) vacanato sīlamūlakāni samādhipadaṭṭhānāni payojanāni dassetuṃ “ekantanibbidāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nibbidāya hi dassitāya tassā padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ dassitameva hoti, tasmiṃ asati nibbidāya asijjhanato. Nibbidādayo atthato vibhattā eva. Yathābhūtañāṇadassananti panettha sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Evamettha amatamahānibbānapariyosānaṃ sīlassa payojanaṃ dassitanti veditabbaṃ.

Having thus shown the concentration rooted in perfectly purified virtue and complete in all aspects, now, in order to show the benefits which are rooted in virtue and have concentration as their foundation, as stated in the phrase: “One who is concentrated understands and sees; knowing and seeing things as they really are, one becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated” (AN 10.2; SN 3.14), the words “for utter disenchantment” and so on are said. For when disenchantment is shown, its basis, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, is also shown as a matter of course, since without that, disenchantment cannot be accomplished. Disenchantment and the rest are distinct in meaning. Here, “knowledge and vision of things as they really are” is intended to mean the seeing of name-and-form with their conditions. Thus, in this context, it should be understood that the benefit of virtue is shown to culminate in the deathless great Nibbāna.

Idāni pahānādīsu sīlatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha pajahanaṃ anuppādanirodho pahānanti tassa bhāvasādhanataṃ sandhāya “pahānanti koci dhammo nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā panassa dhammabhāvo sambhavati, tathā heṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇitameva. Evaṃ hissa sīlabhāvo suṭṭhu yujjati. Taṃ taṃ pahānanti “pāṇātipātassa pahānaṃ, adinnādānassa pahāna”nti evaṃ vuttaṃ taṃ taṃ pahānaṃ. Tassa tassa kusaladhammassāti pāṇātipātassa pahānaṃ mettādikusaladhammassa, adinnādānassa pahānaṃ cāgādikusaladhammassāti evaṃ tassa tassa kusaladhammassa. Patiṭṭhānaṭṭhenāti patiṭṭhānabhāvena. Pahānaṃ hi tasmiṃ sati hoti, asati na hoti, tassa “patiṭṭhāna”nti vattabbataṃ labhatīti katvā yasmiṃ santāne pāṇātipātādayo tassa pakampahetavoti tappahānaṃ vikampābhāvakaraṇena ca samādhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sesapahānesupi vattabbaṃ. Samādhānaṃ saṇṭhapanaṃ, saṃyamanaṃ vā. Itare cattāroti veramaṇiādayo cattāro dhammā na pahānaṃ viya vohāramattanti adhippāyo. Tato tatoti tamhā tamhā pāṇātipātādito. Tassa tassāti pāṇātipātādikassa saṃvaraṇavasena, tassa tassa vā saṃvarassa vasena. Tadubhayasampayuttacetanāvasenāti veramaṇīhi, saṃvaradhammehi ca sampayuttāya cetanāya vasena. Taṃ taṃ avītikkamantassāti taṃ taṃ pāṇātipātādiṃ avītikkamantassa puggalassa, dhammasamūhassa vā vasena cetaso pavattisabbhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Tasmā ekakkhaṇepi labbhantīti adhippāyo.

Now, to explain the meaning of virtue in terms of abandoning and so on, the passage beginning with “And here” is introduced. Therein, abandoning is cessation by non-arising, called `pahāna`; referring to its nature as an accomplishment, it is said, “There is no such thing as `pahāna` as a phenomenon.” However, how its nature as a phenomenon comes to be has already been explained previously. For in this way, its nature as virtue is very fitting. “This and that abandoning” means the abandoning of this and that which is spoken of thus: “the abandoning of killing living beings,” “the abandoning of taking what is not given,” and so on. “Of this and that wholesome quality” means thus: the abandoning of killing living beings pertains to the wholesome quality of loving-kindness, etc.; the abandoning of taking what is not given pertains to the wholesome quality of generosity, etc. “In the sense of a foundation” means by being a foundation. For when that abandoning exists, a wholesome quality comes to be; when it does not exist, it does not come to be. Therefore, abandoning obtains the state of being called a “foundation.” In whatever mental continuum killing and the like exist, they are causes of agitation for it; therefore, the abandoning of them is called “stabilization” by bringing about the absence of agitation. The same should be said for the remaining abandonings. Stabilization is settling, or restraining. “The other four” means the four qualities beginning with abstinence are not, like abandoning, mere convention; this is the intention. “From this and that” means from this and that killing, etc. “Of this and that” means by way of restraining that killing, etc., or by way of that very restraint. “By means of the volition associated with both” means by means of the volition associated with both abstinences and the qualities of restraint. “Of one who does not transgress this and that” means they are spoken of with reference to the actual occurrence of the mind by means of the person or group of qualities that does not transgress this and that killing, etc. Therefore, the intention is that they are obtained even in a single moment.

Sīlasaṃkilesavodānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Defilement and Cleansing of Virtue

21. Saṃkilissati [M 1.0083][V 1.0077] tenāti saṃkileso. Ko pana soti āha “khaṇḍādibhāvo sīlassa saṃkileso”ti. Vodāyati visujjhati etenāti vodānaṃ, akhaṇḍādibhāvo. Lābhayasādīti ādi-saddena ñātiaṅgajīvitādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Sattasu āpattikkhandhesu ādimhi vā ante vā vemajjheti ca idaṃ tesaṃ uddesādipāḷivasena vuttaṃ. Na hi añño koci āpattikkhandhānaṃ anukkamo atthi. Khaṇḍanti khaṇḍavantaṃ, khaṇḍitaṃ vā. Chiddanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pariyante chinnasāṭako viyāti vatthante, dasante vā chinnavatthaṃ viya.

21. By that, it is defiled; therefore, it is defilement. What is that? He said: 'The state of being broken and so forth is the defilement of virtue.' By this, one is purified, is cleansed; therefore, it is purification, meaning the state of being unbroken. In 'gain, fame, and so on,' the word 'and so on' includes relatives, limbs, life, and the like. Regarding the seven groups of offenses, 'at the beginning, at the end, or in the middle' is stated according to the Pāli texts' recitation sections and so on. For indeed, there is no other sequence for the groups of offenses. 'Broken' means having a break, or broken. For 'perforated' as well, this is the same method. It is like a garment cut at its border, or like a cloth cut at its hem.

Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena. Methunasaṃyogavasenāti rāgapariyuṭṭhānena sadisabhāvāpattiyā mithunānaṃ idanti methunaṃ, nibandhanaṃ. Methunavasena samāyogo methunasaṃyogo. Idha pana methunasaṃyogo viyāti methunasaṃyogo, tassa vasena. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Ekaccoti eko. Samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vāti pabbajjāmattena samaṇo vā jātimattena brāhmaṇo vā. Dvayaṃdvayasamāpattinti dvīhi dvīhi samāpajjitabbaṃ, methunanti attho. Na heva kho samāpajjatīti sambandho. Ucchādanaṃ ubbattanaṃ. Sambāhanaṃ parimaddanaṃ. Sādiyatīti adhivāseti. Tadassādetīti taṃ ucchādanādiṃ abhiramati. Nikāmetīti icchati. Vittinti tuṭṭhiṃ. Idampi khoti ettha idanti yathāvuttaṃ sādiyanādiṃ khaṇḍabhāvādivasena ekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Pi-saddo vakkhamānaṃ upādāya samuccayattho. Kho-saddo avadhāraṇattho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadetaṃ brahmacārīpaṭiññassa asatipi dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiyaṃ mātugāmassa ucchādananhāpanasambāhanasādiyanādi, idampi ekaṃsena tassa brahmacariyassa khaṇḍādibhāvāpādanato khaṇḍampi chiddampi sabalampi kammāsampīti. Evaṃ pana khaṇḍādibhāvāpattiyā so aparisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati, na parisuddhaṃ, saṃyutto methunasaṃyogena, na visaṃyutto. Tato cassa na jātiādīhi parimuttīti dassento “ayaṃ vuccatī”tiādimāha.

`Evaṃ` means: now, in the manner about to be stated. 'By means of sexual union': through the arising of passion, because of attaining a similar state, this act of a couple is called `methuna`, meaning sexual intercourse. Association by means of sexual intercourse is `methunasaṃyoga`. Here, however, it is like a sexual union, and therefore it is called `methunasaṃyoga`; by means of that. `Idha` means in this world. `Ekacco` means a certain one. `Samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā` means an ascetic by mere ordination or a brahmin by mere birth. `Dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti` means the act to be engaged in by two and two, that is, sexual intercourse. The connection is with 'he does not indeed engage.' `Ucchādana` is rubbing. `Sambāhana` is massaging. `Sādiyati` means he consents. `Tadassādeti` means he delights in that rubbing and so forth. `Nikāmeti` means he desires. `Vittiṃ` means satisfaction. Here in `idampi kho`, `idaṃ` is stated, having made into one—by way of the state of being broken, etc.—the aforementioned consenting and so forth. The particle `pi`, with reference to what will be said, has a collective meaning. The particle `kho` has the meaning of emphasis. This is what is said: For one who professes to be a celibate, even though there is no two-by-two attainment, whatever this consenting to a woman's rubbing, bathing, and massaging is, this too, by definitely bringing about the state of being broken, etc., for that holy life, is called broken, perforated, spotted, and stained. Thus, by attaining the state of being broken, etc., he practices an impure holy life, not a pure one; he is connected with sexual union, not disconnected. And showing that, because of that, there is no liberation from birth and so on for him, He said, 'This is called...' and so forth.

Sañjagghatīti kilesavasena mahāhasitaṃ hasati. Saṃkīḷatīti kāyasaṃsaggavasena kīḷati. Saṃkelāyatīti sabbaso mātugāmaṃ kelāyanto [M 1.0084] viharati. Cakkhunāti attano cakkhunā. Cakkhunti mātugāmassa cakkhuṃ. Upanijjhāyatīti upecca nijjhāyati oloketi. Tirokuṭṭāti kuṭṭassa [V 1.0078] parato. Tathā tiropākārā. Mattikāmayā bhitti kuṭṭaṃ, iṭṭhakāmayā pākāroti vadanti. Yā kāci vā bhitti porisato diyaḍḍharatanuccappamāṇā kuṭṭaṃ, kuṭṭato adhiko pākāro.

`Sañjagghati` means: due to defilements, he laughs a great laugh. `Saṃkīḷati` means: he plays by way of bodily contact. `Saṃkelāyati` means: he dwells cherishing a woman in every way. `Cakkhunā` means with one's own eye. `Cakkhuṃ` means a woman's eye. `Upanijjhāyati` means: having approached, he gazes intently, he looks. `Tirokuṭṭā` means from the other side of a wall. Likewise for `tiropākārā`. A wall made of clay is a `kuṭṭa`; one made of brick is a `pākāra`, so they say. Alternatively, any wall whatsoever that is a man's height plus one and a half cubits high is a `kuṭṭa`; an enclosure higher than a `kuṭṭa` is a `pākāra`.

Assāti brahmacārīpaṭiññassa. Pubbeti vatasamādānato pubbe. Kāmaguṇehīti kāmakoṭṭhāsehi. Samappitanti suṭṭhu appitaṃ sahitaṃ. Samaṅgībhūtanti samannāgataṃ. Paricārayamānanti kīḷantaṃ, upaṭṭhahiyamānaṃ vā. Paṇidhāyāti patthetvā. Sīlenātiādīsu yamaniyamādisamādānavasena sīlaṃ. Avītikkamavasena vataṃ. Ubhayampi sīlaṃ. Dukkaracariyavasena pavattitaṃ vataṃ. Taṃtaṃakiccasammatato vā nivattilakkhaṇaṃ sīlaṃ. Taṃtaṃsamādānavato vesabhojanakiccakaraṇādivisesapaṭipatti vataṃ. Sabbathāpi dukkaracariyā tapo. Methunavirati brahmacariyaṃ.

`Assa` means: of one who professes to be a celibate. `Pubbe` means: before the undertaking of the vow. `Kāmaguṇehi` means: by the portions of sensuality. `Samappitaṃ` means well applied, accompanied. `Samaṅgībhūtaṃ` means endowed. `Paricārayamānaṃ` means playing, or being attended to. `Paṇidhāya` means having yearned for. In 'by virtue,' etc., `sīla` is by way of undertaking restraints, observances, and so on. `Vata` is by way of non-transgression. Both are also `sīla`. `Vata` is a practice undertaken by way of difficult conduct. Alternatively, `sīla` has the characteristic of refraining from those various things considered to be improper actions. For one who has undertaken various observances, `vata` is a special practice concerning matters of dress, food, duties, and so on. In every way, difficult conduct is austerity. Abstinence from sexual intercourse is the holy life.

Sabbasoti anavasesato, sabbesaṃ vā. Abhedenāti avītikkamena. Aparāya ca pāpadhammānaṃ anuppattiyā, guṇānaṃ uppattiyā saṅgahitoti yojanā. Tattha kujjhanalakkhaṇo kodho. Upanandhanalakkhaṇo upanāho. Paresaṃ guṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho. Yugaggāhalakkhaṇo paḷāso. Parasampattiusūyanalakkhaṇā issā. Attasampattinigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ macchariyaṃ. Santadosapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā. Asantaguṇasambhāvanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ. Cittassa thaddhabhāvalakkhaṇo thambho. Karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho. Unnatilakkhaṇo māno. Abbhunnatilakkhaṇo atimāno. Majjanalakkhaṇo mado. Cittavosaggalakkhaṇo pamādo. Ādi-saddena lobhamohaviparītamanasikārādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

`Sabbaso` means without remainder, or of all. `Abhedena` means without transgression. The connection should be understood thus: it is included through the non-arising of other evil states and the arising of virtues. Therein, `kodha` (anger) has the characteristic of being angry. `Upanāha` (malice) has the characteristic of bearing a grudge. `Makkha` (contempt) has the characteristic of disparaging others' virtues. `Paḷāso` (rivalry) has the characteristic of competitiveness. `Issā` (envy) has the characteristic of being envious of others' success. `Macchariyaṃ` (stinginess) has the characteristic of concealing one's own success. `Māyā` (deceit) has the characteristic of concealing an existing fault. `Sāṭheyyaṃ` (fraud) has the characteristic of proclaiming a non-existent virtue. `Thambho` (obstinacy) has the characteristic of mental rigidity. `Sārambho` (contentiousness) has the characteristic of trying to outdo others. `Māno` (conceit) has the characteristic of exaltation. `Atimāno` (arrogance) has the characteristic of great exaltation. `Mado` (vanity) has the characteristic of mental intoxication. `Pamādo` (heedlessness) has the characteristic of mental negligence. By the word `ādi`, the inclusion of greed, delusion, perverse attention, and so on, is meant.

Idāni “akhaṇḍādibhāvo panā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “yāni hī”tiādimāha. Tattha anupahatānīti anupaddutāni. Vivaṭṭūpanissayatāya taṇhādāsabyato mocanena bhujissabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Aviññūnaṃ appamāṇattā vuttaṃ “viññūhi pasatthattā”ti. Samādhisaṃvattanaṃ vā etesaṃ payojanaṃ, samādhisaṃvattane vā niyuttānīti samādhisaṃvattanikāni. Niddānena sassasampatti viya paṭipakkhavigamena sīlasampadā, sā ca tattha [M 1.0085] sati dosadassaneti āha “sīlavipattiyā ca ādīnavadassanenā”ti. Nisammakārīnaṃ payojanagarukatāya diṭṭhaguṇeyeva sammāpaṭipattīti vuttaṃ “sīlasampattiyā ca ānisaṃsadassanenā”ti.

Now, to make the already stated meaning clearer, beginning with 'But the state of being unbroken, etc.,' He said, 'For whatever...' and so on. Therein, `anupahatāni` means unafflicted. Because it is a support for the rolling back of saṃsāra, it makes one a free person by liberating from slavery to craving. Because it is not a standard for the unwise, it is said: 'praised by the wise.' Or, their purpose is the production of concentration; or, they are employed in the production of concentration; therefore, they are called 'conducive to concentration.' Just as the perfection of crops comes from weeding, so the perfection of virtue comes from the removal of opposing factors. And that perfection occurs when there is the seeing of faults therein; therefore, He said, 'and by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue.' For those who act with consideration, because of their high regard for the benefit, right practice is only in what has a visible benefit; therefore, it is said, 'and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue.'

Tattha [V 1.0079] sīlavipattiyā ādīnavo sīlasampadāya heṭṭhā dassitaānisaṃsapaṭipakkhato veditabbo, taṃ suviññeyyanti avitthāretvā pakārantarehi dassetuṃ “apicā”ti āraddhaṃ. Tattha yathā sīlasampadā sattānaṃ manuññabhāvakāraṇaṃ, evaṃ sīlavipatti amanuññabhāvakāraṇanti āha “dussīlo…pe… devamanussāna”nti. Ananusāsanīyo jigucchitabbato. Dukkhitoti sañjātadukkho. Vippaṭisārīti “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇa”ntiādinā paccānutāpī. Dubbaṇṇoti guṇavaṇṇena, kāyavaṇṇena ca virahito. Assāti dussīlassa. Samphassitānaṃ dukkho dukkhāvaho samphasso etassāti dukkhasamphasso. Guṇānubhāvābhāvato appaṃ agghatīti appaggho. Anekavassagaṇikagūthakūpo viyāti anekavassasamūhe sañcitukkārāvāṭo viya. Dubbisodhano sodhetuṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Chavālātaṃ chavaḍāhe santajjanummukkaṃ. Ubhato paribāhiroti sāmaññato, gihibhogato ca parihīno. Sabbesaṃ verī, sabbe vā verī etassāti sabbaverī, so eva sabbaveriko, puriso. Saṃvāsaṃ nārahatīti asaṃvāsāraho. Saddhammeti paṭipattisaddhamme, paṭivedhasaddhamme ca.

Herein, the danger in the failure of virtue should be understood as the opposite of the benefits of the perfection of virtue shown below. Thinking, 'that is easily understood,' and not elaborating, it is begun with 'Moreover...' in order to show it by other aspects. Herein, just as the perfection of virtue is a cause for beings to be agreeable, so the failure of virtue is a cause for them to be disagreeable—thus it is said: 'The immoral one... among devas and humans.' He is not to be admonished because he is despicable. 'Miserable' means one for whom suffering has arisen. 'Regretful' means one who is later tormented by regret with thoughts such as, 'Alas, no good has been done by me.' 'Of bad appearance' means devoid of the appearance of virtue and the appearance of the body. As for 'assa' (of this one), it means 'of the immoral one.' For those who come into contact, his contact is painful and brings pain; therefore, he is one of 'painful contact.' Due to the absence of the influence of virtue, he is worth little; thus, he is 'of little worth.' Like a cesspit where filth has been collected over many years. 'Hard to purify' means unable to be cleansed. A 'chavālāta' is a firebrand from a corpse-burning place for poking the pyre. 'Excluded from both' means fallen from both the state of a recluse and the enjoyments of a householder. An enemy of all, or all are enemies to him; thus, he is a 'universal enemy' (sabbaverī), which is 'sabbaveriko,' a person. He is not worthy of association; thus, he is 'unfit for association.' 'In the true Dhamma' means in the true Dhamma of practice and in the true Dhamma of realization.

“Aggikkhandhapariyāye vuttadukkhabhāgitāyā”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “dussīlānañhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Pañcakāmaguṇaparibhogasukhe, parehi kayiramānavandanamānanādisukhe ca assādena gadhitacittā pañcakāma…pe… gadhitacittā, tesaṃ. Te yathāvuttasukhassādā paccayā etassāti tappaccayaṃ. Dukkhanti sambandho.

To show in detail the meaning spoken in brief as 'regarding the share of suffering spoken of in the Discourse on the Mass of Fire,' it is begun with 'For the immoral...' etc. Those whose minds are engrossed with relish in the happiness of enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure and in the happiness of homage, honor, and so on, done by others, are those whose minds are engrossed in the five strands of sensual pleasure... of them. Those aforementioned relishes of happiness are conditions for this suffering; hence, it is 'conditioned by that' (tappaccayaṃ). The connection is with 'suffering'.

Passatha noti passatha nu, api passatha. Mahantanti vipulaṃ. Aggikkhandhanti aggisamūhaṃ. Ādittanti padittaṃ. Sampajjalitanti samantato pajjalitaṃ acchivipphuliṅgāni muccantaṃ. Sajotibhūtanti sapabhaṃ samantato uṭṭhitāhi jālāhi ekappabhāsamudayabhūtaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāti taṃ idāni mayā vuccamānamatthaṃ kiṃ maññathāti anumatigahaṇatthaṃ pucchati. Āliṅgetvāti upagūhitvā. Upanisīdeyyāti teneva āliṅganena upecca nisīdeyya. Yadatthamettha satthā aggikkhandhāliṅganaṃ, kaññāliṅganañca ānesi, tamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ārocayāmī”tiādimāha[M 1.0086]. Tattha ārocayāmīti āmantemi. Voti tumhe. Paṭivedayāmīti pabodhemi. Dussīlassāti nissīlassa sīlavirahitassa. Pāpadhammassāti dussīlattā eva hīnajjhāsayatāya lāmakasabhāvassa. Asucisaṅkassarasamācārassāti aparisuddhakāyasamācārāditāya asucissa hutvā saṅkāya saritabbasamācārassa. Dussīlo hi kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ [V 1.0080] asukena kataṃ bhavissatī”ti paresaṃ āsaṅkanīyova hoti, kenacideva vā karaṇīyena mantayante bhikkhū disvā “kacci nu kho ime mayā kataṃ kammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti attanoyeva saṅkāya saritabbasamācāroti. Paṭicchannakammantassāti lajjitabbatāya paṭicchādetabbakammantassa. Assamaṇassāti na samaṇassa. Salākaggahaṇādīsu “ahampi samaṇo”ti micchāpaṭiññāya samaṇapaṭiññassa. Aseṭṭhacāritāya abrahmacārissa. Uposathādīsu “ahampi brahmacārī”ti micchāpaṭiññāya brahmacāripaṭiññassa. Pūtinā kammena sīlavipattiyā anto anupaviṭṭhattā antopūtikassa. Chahi dvārehi rāgādikilesānuvassanena tintattā avassutassa. Sañjātarāgādikacavarattā, sīlavantehi chaḍḍetabbattā ca kasambujātassa. Aggikkhandhūpamāya hīnūpamabhūtāyāti attho. Tenāha bhagavā – “etadeva tassa vara”nti. Bhagavā dukkhaṃ dassetvā dukkhaṃ dassetīti sambandho.

As for 'Passatha no,' it means 'Do you see?' (passatha nu), 'Do you see?' (api passatha). 'Great' means immense. 'A mass of fire' means a collection of fire. 'Aflame' means burning brightly. 'Fully ablaze' means blazing all around, emitting flames and sparks. 'Radiant' means with radiance, having become a single mass of light with flames arisen from all around. As for 'What do you think of that?,' he asks for the purpose of getting their consent, meaning, 'What do you think of that meaning now being spoken by me?' 'Having embraced' means having hugged. 'Would sit close' means would approach and sit down with that very embrace. To make clear the purpose for which the Teacher here brought forth the embracing of a mass of fire and the embracing of a maiden, he said, 'I announce,' etc. Therein, 'I announce' means I address. 'To you' (vo) means you (tumhe). 'I make known' means I cause to understand. 'Of an immoral one' means of one without virtue, devoid of virtue. 'Of evil nature' means of base nature due to having a low disposition because of immorality. 'Of impure and suspect behavior' means one whose behavior is to be remembered with suspicion, being impure due to impure bodily conduct, etc. For an immoral one, upon seeing something inappropriate, is indeed to be suspected by others, who think, 'This must have been done by so-and-so.' Or, upon seeing monks conferring on some matter, he has behavior that is remembered with his own suspicion, thinking, 'Could it be that these monks, having known the deed done by me, are conferring?' 'Of one with hidden deeds' means of one whose deeds should be concealed because they are shameful. 'Of one who is not a recluse' means not a recluse, but one who professes to be a recluse by falsely claiming 'I too am a recluse' in matters like receiving voting-tickets. 'Of one who does not lead the holy life' means one who does not practice the noble life, but one who professes to lead the holy life by falsely claiming 'I too lead the holy life' on Uposatha days, etc. 'Of one who is rotten within' because the failure of virtue, a rotten deed, has entered within. 'Of one who is oozing' because of being soaked by the constant downpour of defilements like lust through the six doors. 'Become like rubbish' because of having arisen rubbish such as lust, and because of being fit to be discarded by the virtuous. The meaning is: by the simile of the mass of fire, which has become an inferior simile. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'This indeed is better for him.' The connection is: The Blessed One, having shown suffering, shows suffering.

Vāḷarajjuyāti vāḷehi katarajjuyā. Sā hi kharatarā hoti. Ghaṃseyyāti padhaṃsanavasena ghaṃseyya. Teladhotāyāti telena nisitāya. Paccorasminti patiurasmiṃ urābhimukhaṃ, uramajjheti adhippāyo. Ayosaṅkunāti saṇḍāsena. Pheṇuddehakanti pheṇaṃ uddehetvā, anekavāraṃ pheṇaṃ uṭṭhapetvāti attho.

'With a horsehair rope' means with a rope made of horsehairs. For it is harsher. 'Would scour' means would scour by way of assaulting. 'Washed with oil' means sharpened with oil. 'Against the chest' means against the chest, facing the chest; the intention is in the middle of the chest. 'With an iron spike' means with tongs. 'Causing foam to come up' means having caused foam to come up; the meaning is having raised foam many times.

Aggikkhandhāliṅganadukkhatopi adhimattadukkhatāya kaṭukabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ phalaṃ etassāti aggikkhandhāliṅganadukkhādhikadukkhakaṭukaphalaṃ. Kāmasukhaṃ avijahato bhinnasīlassa dussīlassa kuto tassa sukhaṃ natthevāti adhippāyo. Sādaneti sādiyane. Yanti añjalikammasādanaṃ. Asīlinoti dussīlassa. Upahatanti sīlabyasanena upaddutaṃ. Khatanti kusalamūlānaṃ khaṇanena khataṃ, khaṇitaṃ vā guṇaṃ sarīreti adhippāyo. Sabbabhayehīti attānuvādādisabbabhayehi. Upacārajjhānaṃ upādāya sabbehi adhigamasukhehi.

This sensual pleasure has a painful and bitter result because its suffering is more intense than the suffering of embracing a mass of fire; thus, it is called 'having a painful and bitter result that is greater than the suffering of embracing a mass of fire.' For one who does not abandon sensual pleasure, whose virtue is broken, who is immoral, from where is there happiness for him? There is none at all—this is the intention. 'Sādana' is in the sense of 'sādiyana' (relishing). As for 'yaṃ' (which), it refers to the relishing of the act of reverential salutation. 'Asīlino' means of an immoral one. 'Upahata' means afflicted by the disaster of broken virtue. 'Khata' means destroyed by the digging up of wholesome roots, or the intention is 'a body whose virtue has been dug up.' 'From all fears' means from all fears such as self-reproach. From all the happinesses of attainment, beginning with access concentration.

Vuttappakāraviparītatoti [M 1.0087] sīlavipattiyaṃ vuttākārapaṭipakkhato “manāpo hoti devamanussāna”ntiādinā. Kāyagandhopi pāmojjaṃ, sīlavantassa bhikkhuno. Karoti api devānanti ettha “gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitāna”ntiādikā (jā. 2.17.55) gāthā vitthāretabbā. Avighātīti appaṭighātī. Vadhabandhādiparikilesā diṭṭhadhammikā āsavā upaddavā. Samparāyikadukkhānaṃ mūlaṃ nāma dussīlyaṃ. Antamatikkantaṃ accantaṃ, accantaṃ santā accantasantā [V 1.0081] kilesapariḷāhasaṅkhātadarathānaṃ abhāvena sabbadā santā. Ubbijjitvāti ñāṇutrāsena uttasitvā. Vodāpetabbanti visodhetabbaṃ.

By 'opposite to the manner stated' is meant: by the opposite of the manner described in the failure of virtue, with the text beginning, 'He is pleasing to devas and humans.' Regarding the text, 'Even the bodily fragrance of a virtuous monk brings delight, even to the devas,' here the verses beginning, 'The fragrance of the sages, long-dedicated...' should be elaborated upon. 'Unobstructed' (avighātīti) means unopposed (appaṭighātī). The torments such as killing and binding are the taints and dangers seen in this present life. Immorality is indeed the root of suffering in future lives. That which has transcended the end (antamatikkantaṃ) is accantaṃ. Accantaṃ santā is accantasantā (utterly peaceful), meaning always peaceful due to the absence of the anxiety called the burning of defilements. 'Having been agitated' (ubbijjitvāti) means having been terrified by the terror that is knowledge. 'Should be cleansed' (vodāpetabbanti) means should be purified (visodhetabbaṃ).

Sīlaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Virtue is concluded.

Iti paṭhamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus concludes the commentary on the first chapter.

2. Dhutaṅganiddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Ascetic Practices

22. Appā [M 1.0088][V 1.0082] icchā etassāti appiccho, paccayagedharahito. Tassa bhāvo appicchatā, alobhajjhāsayatāti attho. Samaṃ tuṭṭhi, santena, sakena vā tuṭṭhi santuṭṭhi, santuṭṭhi eva santuṭṭhitā, aññaṃ apatthetvā yathāladdhehi itarītarehi paccayehi paritussanā. Santuṭṭhitādīhīti ta-kāro vā padasandhikaro. “Santuṭṭhiādīhī”ti vā pāṭho. Te guṇeti te sīlavodānassa hetubhūte appicchatādiguṇe. Sampādetunti sampanne kātuṃ. Te hi sīlavisuddhiyā paṭiladdhamattā hutvā dhutadhammehi sampannatarā honti. Dhutaṅgasamādānanti kilesānaṃ dhunanakaaṅgānaṃ viddhaṃsanakāraṇānaṃ sammadeva ādānaṃ. Evanti evaṃ sante, dhutaṅgasamādāne kateti attho. Assa yogino. Sallekho kilesānaṃ sammadeva likhanā chedanā tanukaraṇaṃ. Paviveko cittavivekassa upāyabhūtā vivekaṭṭhakāyatā. Apacayo yathā paṭipajjanato kilesā naṃ apacinanti na ācinanti, tathā paṭipajjanā. Vīriyārambho anuppannānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ anuppādanādivasena āraddhavīriyatā. Subharatā yathāvuttaappicchabhāvādisiddhā upaṭṭhakānaṃ sukhabharaṇīyatā suposatā. Ādi-saddena appakiccatāsallahukavuttiādike saṅgaṇhāti. Sīlañceva yathāsamādinnaṃ paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ dūrībhāvena suparisuddhaṃ bhavissati. Vatāni ca dhutadhammā ca sampajjissanti sampannā bhavissanti, nipphajjissanti vā. Yā thirabhūtā itarītaracīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanasantuṭṭhi porāṇānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ paveṇibhāvena ṭhitā, tattha patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha “porāṇe ariyavaṃsattaye patiṭṭhāyā”ti. Bhāvanā āramitabbaṭṭhena ārāmo etassāti bhāvanārāmo, tabbhāvo bhāvanārāmatā, samathavipassanābhāvanāsu yuttappayuttatā. Yasmā adhigamāraho bhavissati, tasmāti sambandho.

22. 'His desires are few' (appā icchā etassā) thus he is 'one with few desires' (appiccho); this means one who is without greed for requisites. The state of such a person is 'fewness of desires' (appicchatā); the meaning is the state of having a disposition of non-greed. 'Equal satisfaction' (samaṃ tuṭṭhi), or 'satisfaction with what one has' (santena... tuṭṭhi), or 'satisfaction with one's own' (sakena vā tuṭṭhi) is santuṭṭhi (contentment). The very state of contentment is santuṭṭhitā; it is being perfectly content with whatever various requisites are obtained, without longing for anything else. In the phrase santuṭṭhitādīhi, the letter 'ta' is a word-connector. Or, the reading is santuṭṭhiādīhi. 'Those qualities' (te guṇe) means those qualities, such as fewness of desires, that are the cause for the purification of virtue. 'To bring to perfection' (sampādetunti) means to make them complete. For these qualities, having been merely obtained through purity of virtue, become even more complete through the ascetic practices (dhutadhammehi). 'The undertaking of the ascetic practices' (dhutaṅgasamādānanti) is the proper undertaking of the factors that shake off, the causes that destroy, defilements. 'Thus' (evanti) means 'this being so,' that is, when the undertaking of the ascetic practices is done. 'Of this yogi' (assa yogino). 'Effacement' (sallekho) is the thorough scraping, cutting, and thinning of defilements. 'Seclusion' (paviveko) is the state of having a body that abides in seclusion, which is a means for mental seclusion. 'Non-accumulation' (apacayo) is practicing in such a way that defilements diminish (apacinanti) and do not increase (na ācinanti). 'Arousing of energy' (vīriyārambho) is the state of having aroused energy for the sake of not allowing unarisen evil, unwholesome states to arise, and so on. 'Being easy to support' (subharatā) is the state of being easily supported, easy to nourish, by attendants, which is accomplished through the aforesaid state of fewness of desires, etc. By the word 'etc.' (ādi-saddena), he includes having few duties, a light way of living, and so on. And the virtue that has been undertaken will become thoroughly pure through the distancing of opposing states. And the observances (vatāni) and ascetic practices (dhutadhammā) will be accomplished, will become complete, or will be fulfilled. That steadfast contentment with the various kinds of robes, alms-food, and lodgings, which has stood as the traditional practice of the ancient noble ones, the Buddhas and others—referring to the state of being established therein, he said, 'having become established in the three ancient noble traditions' (porāṇe ariyavaṃsattaye patiṭṭhāyā'ti). 'For him, development (bhāvanā) is a delight (ārāma) in the sense that it is to be delighted in (āramitabbaṭṭhena), thus he is one who delights in development (bhāvanārāmo). The state of being such is bhāvanārāmatā; it is being diligently engaged in the development of serenity and insight. The connection is: 'Because he will be worthy of attainment, therefore...'

Lābhasakkārādi taṇhāya āmasitabbato, lokapariyāpannatāya ca lokāmisaṃ. Nibbānādhigamassa anulomato anulomapaṭipadā vipassanābhāvanā. Atthatoti vacanatthato. Pabhedatoti [V 1.0083] vibhāgato. Bhedatoti vināsato. Dhutādīnanti dhutadhutavādadhutadhammadhutaṅgānaṃ. Samāsabyāsatoti saṅkhepavitthārato.

Gain, honor, and so on, are called 'worldly bait' (lokāmisaṃ) because they are to be touched by craving and because they are included in the world. Because it is in conformity with the attainment of Nibbāna, insight development (vipassanābhāvanā) is the 'conformable practice' (anulomapaṭipadā). 'By way of meaning' (atthatoti) means by way of the word's meaning. 'By way of classification' (pabhedatoti) means by way of division. 'By way of breaking' (bhedatoti) means by way of destruction. 'Of the ascetic practices, etc.' (dhutādīnanti) refers to the person who has shaken off (dhuta), the person who advocates shaking off (dhutavāda), the quality of shaking off (dhutadhamma), and the factor of shaking off (dhutaṅga). 'Concisely and in detail' (samāsabyāsatoti) means summarily and extensively.

23. Rathikāti [M 1.0089] racchā. Saṅkārakūṭādīnanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Abbhuggataṭṭhenāti ussitaṭṭhena. “Nadiyā kūla”ntiādīsu viya samussayattho kūla-saddoti āha “paṃsukūlamiva paṃsukūla”nti. Ku-saddo kucchāyaṃ ula-saddo gatiatthoti āha “kucchitabhāvaṃ gacchatīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti, paṃsu viya kucchitaṃ ulati pavattatīti vā paṃsukūlaṃ. Paṃsukūlassa dhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ uttarapadalopena, taṃ sīlamassāti paṃsukūliko, yathā “āpūpiko”ti. Aṅgati attano phalaṃ paṭicca hetubhāvaṃ gacchatīti aṅgaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Yena puggalo “paṃsukūliko”ti vuccati, so samādānacetanāsaṅkhāto dhammo paṃsukūlikassa aṅganti paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ. Tenāha “paṃsukūlikassā”tiādi. Tassāti samādānassa. Samādiyati etenāti samādānaṃ, cetanā.

23. 'On the road' (rathikāti) means a street (racchā). The word saṅkārakūṭādīnaṃ is a genitive of specification. 'In the sense of being heaped up' (abbhuggataṭṭhenāti) means in the sense of being piled up (ussitaṭṭhena). Just as in phrases like 'the bank of a river' (nadiyā kūlaṃ), the word kūla has the meaning of a mound, so he said, 'paṃsukūla is like a dust-heap' (paṃsukūlamiva paṃsukūlanti). The sound ku is in the sense of 'despicable,' and the sound ula has the meaning of 'going,' thus he said, 'it is said to go to a despicable state.' Or, because it is despicable and arises like dust (paṃsu), it is paṃsukūla. The wearing of a dust-heap robe (paṃsukūlassa dhāraṇaṃ) is called paṃsukūla through the elision of the latter word. 'He has that as his practice' (taṃ sīlamassā), thus he is a paṃsukūliko (a wearer of dust-heap robes), just as in āpūpiko (a cake-eater). 'It goes' (aṅgati), meaning it goes to the state of being a cause in dependence on its own fruit, thus it is an aṅga (factor); it means a cause. That dhamma by which a person is called a paṃsukūliko—that dhamma, known as the volition of undertaking, is the factor (aṅga) of the paṃsukūlika; thus it is the paṃsukūlikaṅga (the factor of the dust-heap-robe wearer). Therefore, he said, 'of the paṃsukūlika,' etc. 'Of that' (tassāti) means of the undertaking. 'One undertakes by means of this' (samādiyati etena), thus it is samādāna (undertaking); it means volition (cetanā).

Eteneva nayenāti yathā paṃsukūladhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, taṃsīlo paṃsukūliko, tassa aṅgaṃ samādānacetanā “paṃsukūlikaṅga”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ eteneva vacanatthanayena ticīvaradhāraṇaṃ ticīvaraṃ, taṃsīlo tecīvariko, tassa aṅgaṃ samādānacetanā “tecīvarikaṅga”nti veditabbaṃ. Saṅghāṭiādīsu eva tīsu cīvaresu ticīvarasamaññā, na kaṇḍupaṭicchādivassikasāṭikādīsūti tāni sarūpato dassento “saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakasaṅkhāta”nti āha.

'By this same method' (eteneva nayenāti) means: just as it was said that the wearing of the dust-heap robe is paṃsukūla, one whose practice this is is a paṃsukūliko, and his factor (aṅga), the volition of undertaking, is the paṃsukūlikaṅga; so too, by this same verbal analysis, it should be understood that the wearing of the three robes is ticīvara, one whose practice this is is a tecīvariko, and his factor, the volition of undertaking, is the tecīvarikaṅga. The designation 'three robes' (ticīvara) applies only to the three robes beginning with the saṅghāṭi, not to things like an itch-covering cloth or a rains-cloth. Thus, showing them by their specific nature, he said, 'designated as the outer cloak, upper robe, and inner robe' (saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakasaṅkhāta).

Taṃ piṇḍapātanti parehi diyyamānānaṃ piṇḍānaṃ patte patanasaṅkhātaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ, taṃ uñchatīti piṇḍapātiko, yathā bādariko sāmākiko. Piṇḍapāti eva piṇḍapātiko, yathā bhaddo eva bhaddako. Avakhaṇḍanaṃ vicchindanaṃ nirantaramappavatti. Tappaṭikkhepato anavakhaṇḍanaṃ avicchindanaṃ nirantarappavatti. Saha apadānenāti saha anavakhaṇḍanena. Sapadānanti padassa kiriyāvisesanabhāvaṃ, yattha ca taṃ anavakhaṇḍanaṃ, tañca dassetuṃ “avakhaṇḍanarahitaṃ anugharanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Ekāsaneti iriyāpathantarena anantaritāya ekāyayeva nisajjāya. Patte piṇḍoti ettha vatthubhedo idhādhippeto, na sāmaññaṃ. Eva-kāro ca luttaniddiṭṭhoti dassento “kevalaṃ ekasmiṃyeva patte”ti āha. Uttarapadalopaṃ katvā ayaṃ niddesoti dassento “pattapiṇḍagahaṇe pattapiṇḍasaññaṃ katvā”ti āha. Esa nayo ito paresupi.

Regarding `piṇḍapāta`: it is the falling of alms into the bowl, so designated, when given by others. One who seeks that is a `piṇḍapātika`, just as there is a `bādarika` (jujube-seeker) or a `sāmākika` (millet-seeker). A `piṇḍapātī` is simply a `piṇḍapātika`, just as a `bhaddo` is a `bhaddaka`. `Avakhaṇḍana` is interruption, a discontinuous occurrence. By its rejection, `anavakhaṇḍana` is non-interruption, a continuous occurrence. `Saha apadānena` means 'together with non-interruption.' To show the adverbial nature of the word `sapadāna`, and where that non-interruption occurs, it is said: 'It means it is said they go from house to house without interruption.' `Ekāsane` means by a single sitting only, not interrupted by another posture. In `patte piṇḍo` (alms in the bowl), a specific object is intended here, not a general one. And to show that the particle `eva` is indicated by elision, he said, 'only in a single bowl.' To show that this exposition is made by eliding the latter word, he said, 'having made the perception of "alms in the bowl" when taking alms in the bowl.' This is the method in the subsequent cases as well.

Pacchābhattaṃ [M 1.0090][V 1.0084] nāma pavāraṇato pacchā laddhabhattaṃ eva. Khalu-saddassa paṭisedhatthavācakattā tena samānatthaṃ na-kāraṃ gahetvā āha “na pacchābhattiko”ti. Sikkhāpadassa visayo sikkhāpadeneva paṭikkhitto. Yo tassa avisayo, so eva samādānassa visayoti āha “samādānavasena paṭikkhittātirittabhojanassā”ti. Abbhokāse nivāso abbhokāso. Susāne nivāso susānaṃ, taṃ sīlaṃ assātiādinā sabbaṃ vattabbanti āha “eseva nayo”ti. Yathāsanthataṃ viya yathāsanthataṃ, ādito yathāuddiṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ hesa “idaṃ bahumaṅkuṇaṃ duggandhapavāta”ntiādivasena appaṭikkhipitvāva sampaṭicchati. Tenevāha “idaṃ tuyha”ntiādi. Sayananti nipajjanamāha. Tena tena samādānenāti tena tena paṃsukūlikaṅgādikassa samādānena dhutakilesattāti viddhaṃsitakilesattā, tadaṅgavasena pahīnataṇhupādānādipāpadhammattāti attho. Yehi taṃ kilesadhunanaṃ, tāniyeva idha dhutassa bhikkhuno aṅgānīti adhippetāni, na aññāni yāni kānici, aññena vā dhutassāti ayamattho atthato āpanno. “Ñāṇaṃ aṅgaṃ etesa”nti iminā ñāṇapubbakataṃ tesaṃ samādānassa vibhāveti. Paṭipattiyāti sīlādisammāpaṭipattiyā. Samādiyati etenāti samādānaṃ, samādānavasena pavattā cetanā, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etesanti samādānacetanālakkhaṇāni. Vuttampi cetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

`Pacchābhattaṃ` means simply the meal received after the refusal (pavāraṇā). Because the word `khalu` expresses prohibition, taking the negative particle `na` which has the same meaning, he says, `na pacchābhattiko` (not one who eats afterwards). The scope of the training rule is prohibited by the training rule itself. What is not its scope is precisely the scope for undertaking; hence it says, 'of the extra food prohibited by way of undertaking.' Dwelling in the open is the open-air practice. Dwelling in a charnel ground is the charnel-ground practice; he says, 'this is the method,' meaning all should be explained in this way, such as 'that is his practice.' `Yathāsanthataṃ` means 'as it is spread out,' that is, as originally designated. For this monk accepts it without rejecting it on grounds such as, 'this is full of bugs, has a foul-smelling wind,' and so on. Therefore he says, 'this is yours,' etc. `Sayanaṃ` means reclining. By 'by that very undertaking' is meant by the undertaking of the rag-robe practice and so forth. 'Because the defilements are shaken off' means because they are destroyed, and because unwholesome states such as craving and clinging are abandoned by way of that factor; this is the meaning. Those very things by which the defilements are shaken off are here intended as the factors of the monk who has shaken off defilements, not any other things whatsoever, nor of one who has shaken them off by other means—this is the meaning arrived at in essence. By 'knowledge is a factor of these,' he explains that their undertaking is preceded by knowledge. 'By practice' means by the right practice of virtue, etc. `Samādāna` is that by which one undertakes; it is the intention that proceeds by way of undertaking. These have that as their characteristic, thus they have the characteristic of the intention of undertaking. This has also been stated in the commentary—

“Samādānakiriyāya, sādhakatamabhāvato;

Sampayuttadhammā yenāti, karaṇabhāvena dassitā”ti.

Because they are most effective in the act of undertaking, the associated states are shown by the word 'yena' in the instrumental sense.

Samādānacetanāya gahaṇaṃ taṃmūlakattā pariharaṇacetanāpi dhutaṅgameva. Attanā, parammukhena ca kusalabhaṇḍassa bhusaṃ viluppanaṭṭhena loluppaṃ taṇhācāro, tassa viddhaṃsanakiccattā loluppaviddhaṃsanarasāni. Tato eva nilloluppabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhanti, taṃ vā paccupaṭṭhāpentīti nilloluppabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāni. Ariyadhammapadaṭṭhānānīti parisuddhasīlādisaddhammapadaṭṭhānāni.

The taking up [of the dhutaṅga] is by the intention of undertaking; because the intention of practicing is rooted in that, it too is a dhutaṅga. `Loluppa` is the conduct of craving, in the sense that it intensely plunders the treasure of the wholesome, by oneself and through others. Because their function is to destroy that, they have the characteristic of destroying greed. Therefore, they manifest as the state of being without greed, or they cause that state to manifest; thus, their manifestation is the state of being without greed. `Ariyadhammapadaṭṭhānāni` means they are the proximate cause for the true Dhamma, such as pure virtue.

Bhagavatova santike samādātabbānīti idaṃ antarā avicchedanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, rañño santike paṭiññātārahassa atthassa tadupajīvino ekaṃsato avisaṃvādanaṃ viya. Sesānaṃ santike samādānepi eseva nayo. Ekasaṅgītikassāti [M 1.0091] pañcasu dīghanikāyādīsu nikāyesu ekanikāyikassa. Aṭṭhakathācariyassāti yassa aṭṭhakathātantiyeva visesato paguṇā, tassa. Etthāti attanāpi samādānassa ruhane. Jeṭṭhakabhātu dhutaṅgappicchatāya vatthūti so kira thero nesajjiko[V 1.0085], tassa taṃ na koci jānāti. Athekadivasaṃ rattiyā sayanapiṭṭhe nisinnaṃ vijjulatobhāsena disvā itaro pucchi “kiṃ, bhante, tumhe nesajjikā”ti. Thero dhutaṅgappicchatāya tāvadeva nipajjitvā pacchā samādiyīti evamāgataṃ vatthu.

That they should be undertaken in the presence of the Blessed One is said to prevent interruption, just as there is unwavering adherence by a dependent to a matter promised in the presence of a king. The same method applies when undertaking them in the presence of others. `Ekasaṅgītikassa` means one who masters a single Nikāya among the five Nikāyas, such as the Dīgha Nikāya. `Aṭṭhakathācariyassa` means one for whom the textual tradition of the commentaries is especially proficient. `Etthā` means in the establishment of the undertaking even by oneself. The story of the elder brother's humility regarding the ascetic practices: It is said that this elder was a practitioner of the sitter's practice, but no one knew this. Then one night, seeing him seated on his sleeping board by a flash of lightning, another monk asked, 'Venerable sir, are you a practitioner of the sitter's practice?' The elder, due to his humility regarding the ascetic practice, lay down at that very moment and undertook it again later—this is the story that has come down.

1. Paṃsukūlikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Rag-Robe-Wearer's Ascetic Practice

24. Gahapatidānacīvaranti ettha dāyakabhāvena samaṇāpi ukkaṭṭhassa gahapatipakkhaṃyeva paviṭṭhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Pabbajito gaṇhissatī”ti ṭhapitakaṃ siyā gahapaticīvaraṃ, na pana gahapatidānacīvaranti tādisaṃ nivattetuṃ dānaggahaṇaṃ. Aññatarenāti ettha samādānavacanena tāva samādinnaṃ hotu, paṭikkhepavacanena pana kathanti? Atthato āpannattā. Yathā “devadatto divā na bhuñjatī”ti vutte “rattiyaṃ bhuñjatī”ti atthato āpannameva hoti, tassa āhārena vinā sarīraṭṭhiti natthīti, evamidhāpi bhikkhuno gahapatidānacīvare paṭikkhitte tadaññacīvarappaṭiggaho atthato āpanno eva hoti, cīvarena vinā sāsane ṭhiti natthīti.

24. Regarding 'a robe given by a householder' (`gahapatidānacīvara`), it should be understood that here, in the case of a strict practitioner, even monastics, by being donors, are included in the category of householders. A robe set aside with the thought, 'An ascetic will take it,' may be a householder's robe, but it would not be a robe given by a householder. Therefore, to preclude such a case, the word 'gift' (`dāna`) is included. Regarding 'by either' (`aññatarena`), let it be undertaken by the word of undertaking; but how is it undertaken by the word of rejection? Because it is implied by the meaning. Just as when it is said, 'Devadatta does not eat during the day,' it is indeed implied by the meaning that 'he eats at night,' because without food his body cannot be sustained; so too here, when a robe given by a householder is rejected by a monk, the acceptance of another robe is indeed implied by the meaning, because without a robe there is no continuance in the Dispensation.

Evaṃ samādinnadhutaṅgenātiādividhānaṃ paṃsukūlikaṅge paṭipajjanavidhi. Susāne laddhaṃ sosānikaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā tattha kenaci chaḍḍitattā patitaṃ hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “susāne patitaka”nti. Evaṃ pāpaṇikampi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tālaveḷimaggo nāma mahāgāme ekā vīthi. Anurādhapureti ca vadanti. Ḍaḍḍho padeso etassāti ḍaḍḍhappadesaṃ, vatthaṃ. Magge patitakaṃ bahudivasātikkantaṃ gahetabbanti vadanti. “Dvattidivasātikkanta”nti apare. Thokaṃ rakkhitvāti katipayaṃ kālaṃ āgametvā. Vātāhatampi sāmikānaṃ satisammosena patitasadisanti “sāmike apassantena gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā thokaṃ āgametvā gahetabbaṃ.

The method beginning with 'Thus, by one who has undertaken the ascetic practice...' is the procedure of practice in the rag-robe-wearer's ascetic practice. What is obtained in a charnel ground is a 'charnel-ground cloth' (`sosānika`). And since it has fallen there from being discarded by someone, it is called 'fallen in a charnel ground.' In the same way, what is from a shop (`pāpaṇika`) should be understood. Tālaveḷimagga is the name of a street in Mahāgāma. And they say it is in Anurādhapura. 'A part of it is burnt' (`ḍaḍḍho padeso etassa`), hence `ḍaḍḍhappadesaṃ`; this refers to a cloth. They say a cloth fallen on the road should be taken after many days have passed. Others say, 'after two or three days have passed.' 'Having waited a little' (`thokaṃ rakkhitvā`) means having waited for some time. Even a cloth carried by the wind is similar to a fallen one due to the owner's forgetfulness, thus it is said, 'It is allowable to take it when not seeing the owners.' Therefore, it should be taken after waiting a little.

“Saṅghassa demā”ti dinnaṃ, coḷakabhikkhāvasena laddhañca laddhakālato paṭṭhāya “samaṇacīvaraṃ siyā nu kho, no”ti āsaṅkaṃ nivattetuṃ “na taṃ paṃsukūla”nti vuttaṃ. Na hi taṃ tevīsatiyā uppattiṭṭhānesu katthaci pariyāpannaṃ. Idāni imināva pasaṅgena yaṃ bhikkhudattiye lakkhaṇapattaṃ [M 1.0092] paṃsukūlaṃ, tassa ca ukkaṭṭhānukkaṭṭhavibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “bhikkhudattiyepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha gāhetvā vā dīyatīti saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā dentehi yaṃ cīvaraṃ vassaggena pāpetvā bhikkhūnaṃ dīyati. Senāsanacīvaranti senāsanaṃ kāretvā “etasmiṃ senāsane vasantā paribhuñjantū”ti [V 1.0086] dinnacīvaraṃ. Na taṃ paṃsukūlanti apaṃsukūlabhāvo pubbe vuttakāraṇato, gāhetvā dinnattā ca. Tenāha “no gāhāpetvā dinnameva paṃsukūla”nti. Tatrapīti yaṃ gāhetvā na dinnaṃ bhikkhudattiyaṃ, tatrapi yena bhikkhunā cīvaraṃ dīyati, tassa lābhe, dāne ca visuṃ visuṃ ubhayattha ādaragāravānaṃ sabbhāvato, tadabhāvato ca bhikkhudattiyassa ekatosuddhi ubhatosuddhi anukkaṭṭhatā hontīti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ dāyakehī”tiādi vuttaṃ, pādamūle ṭhapetvā dinnakaṃ samaṇenāti adhippāyo. Yassa kassacīti ukkaṭṭhādīsu yassa kassaci. Ruciyāti chandena. Khantiyāti nijjhānakkhantiyā.

To dispel the doubt, 'From the time it is obtained, might a robe given with the thought, "We give to the Sangha," and one obtained by way of begging for cloth be a monastic's robe or not?', it is said, 'That is not a rag-robe.' For it is not included anywhere among the twenty-three sources of origin. Now, in this very connection, to show the rag-robe that has the characteristics of one in a gift from a monk, and its division into superior and non-superior, the words beginning with 'Even in a gift from a monk...' were said. Therein, 'is given after having it taken' refers to a robe that is given to monks by donors to the Sangha or a group after having it apportioned by seniority. 'A dwelling-place robe' is a robe given after having a dwelling built, with the thought, 'May those who reside in this dwelling use it.' 'That is not a rag-robe'—its not being a rag-robe is due to the reason stated before and because it was given after having it taken. Therefore, he said, 'Only what is given without having it taken is a rag-robe.' 'Even in that case' (`tatrāpi`): in the case of a gift from a monk that was not given after having it taken, there too, depending on the presence or absence of respect and reverence, separately in both the acquisition and the giving on the part of the monk who gives the robe, the gift from a monk has one-sided purity, two-sided purity, or is non-superior. To show this meaning, the words beginning with 'What by donors...' were said. The meaning is: a robe given by an ascetic after placing it at the feet. 'To whomever' (`yassa kassaci`) means to anyone among the superior practitioners, etc. 'By preference' (`ruciyā`) means by will (`chandena`). 'By approval' (`khantiyā`) means by approval after consideration (`nijjhānakkhantiyā`).

Nissayānurūpapaṭipattisabbhāvoti upasampannasamanantaraṃ ācariyena vuttesu catūsu nissayesu attanā yathāpaṭiññātadutiyanissayānurūpāya paṭipattiyā vijjamānatā. Ārakkhadukkhābhāvoti cīvarārakkhanadukkhassa abhāvo paṃsukūlacīvarassa alobhanīyattā. Paribhogataṇhāya abhāvo savisesalūkhasabhāvattā. Pāsādikatāti paresaṃ pasādāvahatā. Appicchatādīnaṃ phalanipphatti dhutaṅgapariharaṇassa appicchatādīhiyeva nipphādetabbato. Dhutadhamme samādāya vattanaṃ yāvadeva upari sammāpaṭipattisampādanāyāti vuttaṃ “sammāpaṭipattiyā anubrūhana”nti. Mārasenavighātāyāti mārassa, mārasenāya ca vihananāya viddhaṃsanāya. Kāyavācācittehi yato saṃyatoti yati, bhikkhu. Dhāritaṃ yaṃ lokagarunā paṃsukūlaṃ, taṃ ko na dhāraye, yasmā vā lokagarunā paṃsukūlaṃ dhāritaṃ, tasmā ko taṃ na dhārayeti yojanā yaṃtaṃsaddānaṃ ekantasambandhibhāvato. Paṭiññaṃ samanussaranti upasampadamāḷe “āma bhante”ti ācariyapamukhassa saṅghassa sammukhā dinnaṃ paṭiññaṃ samanussaranto.

'The existence of practice in accordance with the requisites' (`nissayānurūpapaṭipattisabbhāva`) means the existence of practice in accordance with the second requisite as one has personally professed it, among the four requisites taught by the teacher immediately after higher ordination. 'The absence of the suffering of guarding' (`ārakkhadukkhābhāva`) means the absence of the suffering of guarding the robe, because a rag-robe is not desirable. The absence of craving for its use is because it has an especially coarse nature. 'Being inspiring' (`pāsādikatā`) means being able to bring forth the confidence of others. The fruition of the benefits of having few wishes and so on is because the observance of the ascetic practice is to be accomplished precisely by having few wishes and so on. Undertaking and observing the ascetic qualities is solely for the purpose of fulfilling the higher right practice, hence it is said, 'for the strengthening of right practice.' 'For the destruction of Māra's army' (`mārasenavighātāya`) means for the striking down and destruction of Māra and Māra's army. Because he is restrained and controlled in body, speech, and mind (`kāyavācācittehi yato saṃyato`), he is a `yati` (ascetic); this refers to a monk. 'What rag-robe was worn by the Teacher of the World, who would not wear it?' Or, the construction is: 'Because the rag-robe was worn by the Teacher of the World, therefore who would not wear it?'—this is due to the invariable connection of the words `yaṃ` and `taṃ`. 'Recalling the promise' (`paṭiññaṃ samanussaranti`) means recalling the promise given in the presence of the Sangha headed by the preceptor in the ordination hall, saying, 'Yes, venerable sir.'

Iti paṃsukūlikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the rag-robe-wearer's ascetic practice.

2. Tecīvarikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ascetic Practice of the Three Robes

25. Catutthakacīvaranti [M 1.0093] nivāsanapārupanayogyaṃ catutthakacīvaranti adhippāyo, aṃsakāsāvassa appaṭikkhipitabbato. Aññataravacanenāti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Yāva na sakkoti, yāva na labhati, yāva na sampajjatīti paccekaṃ yāva-saddo sambandhitabbo. Na sampajjatīti na sijjhati. Nikkhittapaccayā doso natthīti nicayasannidhidhutaṅgasaṃkilesadoso [V 1.0087] natthi. Āsanneti cīvarassa āsanne ṭhāne. Rajanakkhaṇe paribhuñjanakāsāvaṃ rajanakāsāvaṃ. Tatraṭṭhakapaccattharaṇaṃ nāma attano, parassa vā santakaṃ senāsane paccattharaṇavasena adhiṭṭhitaṃ. “Aṃsakāsāvaṃ parikkhāracoḷaṃ hoti, iti paccattharaṇaṃ, aṃsakāsāvanti imāni dvepi atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne ṭhitānipi dhutaṅgabhedaṃ na karontī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanti vadanti. Pariharituṃ pana na vaṭṭatīti rajanakāle eva anuññātattā niccaparibhogavasena na vaṭṭati tecīvarikassa. Aṃsakāsāvanti khandhe ṭhapetabbakāsāvaṃ. Kāyaparihārikenāti vātātapādiparissayato kāyassa pariharaṇamattena. Samādāyevāti gahetvā eva. Appasamārambhatāti appakiccatā. Kappiye mattakāritāyāti nisīdanādivasena, parikkhāracoḷavasena ca bahūsu cīvaresu anuññātesupi ticīvaramatte ṭhitattā. Saha pattacaraṇāyāti sapattacaraṇo. Pakkhī sapakkhako.

25. The fourth robe: The meaning is a fourth robe suitable for wearing as a lower or upper garment, since a shoulder-robe should not be rejected. Regarding the phrase 'by a certain statement,' what should be said here is just in the manner explained below. The word 'as long as' should be connected separately to each phrase: 'as long as one is unable,' 'as long as one does not obtain,' 'as long as one does not succeed.' 'Does not succeed' means it is not accomplished. 'There is no fault regarding a requisite that has been set aside' means there is no fault of defilement of the ascetic practice regarding hoarding and storing. 'Near' means in a place near the robe. The 'robe for use at the time of dyeing' is the dyeing-robe. A 'ground-covering placed there' refers to a robe belonging to oneself or to another that has been determined as a ground-covering in a lodging. They say that it is said in the commentary: 'The shoulder-robe is an accessory cloth. Thus, these two—the ground-covering and the shoulder-robe—even though they are in the position of an extra robe, do not cause a breach of the ascetic practice.' However, it is not allowable to use it: because it is permitted only at the time of dyeing, it is not allowable for one who observes the three-robe practice by way of constant use. 'Shoulder-robe' is the ochre robe to be placed on the shoulder. 'By what protects the body' means by the mere protection of the body from dangers such as wind and sun. 'Having undertaken' means having taken it up. 'Having few undertakings' means having few duties. 'By being moderate in what is allowable' means that even though many robes are permitted by way of sitting cloths and accessory cloths, one remains with just the three robes. With bowl and wandering, one is like a bird with its own wings.

Iti tecīvarikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the ascetic practice of the three robes.

3. Piṇḍapātikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Ascetic Practice of an Alms-food Eater

26. Atirekalābhanti “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāyā”ti (mahāva. 73, 128) evaṃ vuttabhikkhāhāralābhato atirekalābhaṃ, saṅghabhattādinti attho. Sakalassa saṅghassa dātabbabhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ. Katipaye bhikkhū uddisitvā dātabbabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ. Ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekadivasaṃ dātabbabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ. Uposathe uposathe dātabbabhattaṃ uposathikaṃ. Paṭipadadivase dātabbabhattaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ. Vihāraṃ uddissa dātabbabhattaṃ vihārabhattaṃ. Dhuragehe eva ṭhapetvā dātabbabhattaṃ dhurabhattaṃ. Gāmavāsīādīhi vārena dātabbabhattaṃ [M 1.0094] vārakabhattaṃ. “Saṅghabhattaṃ gaṇhathātiādinā”ti ādi-saddena uddesabhattādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sādituṃ vaṭṭantīti bhikkhāpariyāyena vuttattā. Bhesajjādipaṭisaṃyuttā nirāmisasalākā. Yāvakālikavajjāti ca vadanti. Vihāre pakkabhattampīti upāsakā idheva bhattaṃ pacitvā “sabbesaṃ ayyānaṃ dassāmā”ti vihāreyeva bhattaṃ sampādenti, taṃ piṇḍapātikānampi vaṭṭati. Āharitvāti pattaṃ gahetvā gehato ānetvā. Taṃ divasaṃ nisīditvāti “mā, bhante, piṇḍāya carittha, vihāreyeva bhikkhā ānīyatī”ti vadantānaṃ sampaṭicchanena taṃ divasaṃ nisīditvā. Serivihārasukhanti aparāyattavihāritāsukhaṃ[V 1.0088]. Ariyavaṃsoti ariyavaṃsasuttapaṭisaṃyuttā (dī. ni. 3.309; a. ni. 4.28) dhammakathā. Dhammarasanti dhammūpasañhitaṃ pāmojjādirasaṃ.

26. 'Extra gain' means gain beyond the almsfood obtained by 'relying on the eating of lumps of almsfood,' as stated; that is, gains such as a meal for the Saṅgha. A meal to be given to the entire Saṅgha is a Saṅgha-meal. A meal to be given after designating a few bhikkhus is a designated-meal. A meal to be given on one day in a fortnight is a fortnightly meal. A meal to be given on each Uposatha day is an Uposatha-meal. A meal to be given on the first day of the lunar fortnight is a first-day meal. A meal to be given with a monastery as the object is a monastery-meal. A meal to be given by placing it at the head-house is a head-house-meal. A meal to be given by villagers and others in turn is a rotational-meal. By the word 'etc.' in 'accept the Saṅgha-meal, etc.,' it includes the designated-meal and so on. It is allowable to accept them because they are spoken of by the term 'almsfood.' A ticket connected with medicines and so on is a non-material ticket. And some say this excludes what is allowable for a limited time. 'Even a meal cooked in the monastery': lay devotees cook a meal right in the monastery saying, 'We will give to all the venerable sirs,' and they prepare the meal right in the monastery. That is allowable even for those who practice the alms-round observance. 'Having brought' means having taken the bowl and brought it from the house. 'Having sat for that day' means having sat for that day by accepting the word of those who say, 'Venerable sirs, do not wander for alms; the almsfood will be brought right to the monastery.' 'The happiness of living at liberty' refers to the happiness of living independently. 'The Noble Lineage' is the Dhamma talk connected with the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta. 'The taste of the Dhamma' is the taste of joy and so on, connected with the Dhamma.

Jaṅghabalaṃ nissāya piṇḍapariyesanato kosajjanimmaddanatā. “Yathāpi bhamaro puppha”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 49; netti. 123) vuttavidhinā āhārapariyesanato parisuddhājīvatā. Niccaṃ antaragharaṃ pavisantasseva suppaṭicchannagamanādayo sekhiyadhammā sampajjantīti sekhiyapaṭipattipūraṇaṃ. Paṭiggahaṇe mattaññutāya, saṃsaṭṭhavihārābhāvato ca aparapositā. Kule kule appakaappakapiṇḍagahaṇena parānuggahakiriyā. Antimāya jīvikāya avaṭṭhānena mānappahānaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ, yadidaṃ piṇḍolya”ntiādi (itivu. 91; saṃ. ni. 3.80). Missakabhattena yāpanato rasataṇhānivāraṇaṃ. Nimantanāsampaṭicchanato gaṇabhojanādisikkhāpadehi anāpattitā.

By relying on the strength of one's legs for seeking alms, laziness is crushed. By seeking food according to the method stated in 'Just as a bee from a flower...' and so on, there is purity of livelihood. For one who constantly enters within the village, the training rules such as going well-covered are accomplished; thus, there is the fulfillment of the Sekhiya practice. Through knowing moderation in receiving and through the absence of living in association, one is not supported by others. By taking a very small amount of almsfood from family to family, there is the act of helping others. By being established in the lowest livelihood, there is the abandoning of conceit. For this was said: 'This, bhikkhus, is the lowest of livelihoods, that is, wandering for alms,' and so on. By subsisting on mixed food, there is the prevention of craving for tastes. Through not accepting invitations, there is no offense in regard to the training rules on group meals and so on.

Appaṭihatavuttitāya catūsupi disāsu vattanaṭṭhena cātuddiso. Ājīvassa visujjhatīti ājīvo assa visujjhati. Attabharassāti appānavajjasulabharūpehi paccayehi attano bharaṇato attabharassa. Tato eva ekavihāritāya saddhivihārikādīnampi aññesaṃ aposanato anaññaposino. Padadvayenāpi kāyaparihārikena cīvarena kucchiparihārikena piṇḍapātena vicaraṇato sallahukavuttitaṃ, subharataṃ, paramaappicchataṃ, santuṭṭhiñca dasseti. Devāpi pihayanti tādinoti tādisassa bhusaṃ ativiya santakāyavacīmanokammatāya upasantassa paramena satinepakkena samannāgamato sabbakālaṃ satimato piṇḍapātikassa bhikkhussa sakkādayo [M 1.0095] devāpi pihayanti patthenti. Tassa sīlādiguṇesu bahumānaṃ uppādentā ādaraṃ janenti, pageva manussā. Sace so lābhasakkārasilokasannissito na hoti, tadabhikaṅkhī na hotīti attho.

Because of having an unhindered way of life and because of acting in all four directions, he is 'of the four directions.' 'His livelihood is purified' means his livelihood is purified. 'Of one who supports himself' means: because of supporting oneself with requisites that are of little value, blameless, and easy to obtain. For that very reason, because of living alone and not supporting others such as co-residents, he is 'not a supporter of others.' By means of two things—a robe for protecting the body and almsfood for maintaining the belly—he demonstrates a light way of life, being easy to support, extreme fewness of wishes, and contentment. 'Even the gods envy such a one': Sakka and other gods also envy and long for such a bhikkhu who practices the alms-round observance, who is ever mindful, who is greatly and exceedingly peaceful on account of his peaceful bodily, verbal, and mental actions, and because of being endowed with supreme mindfulness and prudence. Generating great esteem for his virtues such as morality, they produce reverence; how much more so humans. The meaning is: if he is not dependent on gain, honor, and fame, he is not one who longs for them.

Iti piṇḍapātikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the alms-food-eater's practice.

4. Sapadānacārikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Practice of Going for Alms from House to House Without Skipping

27. Imināti sapadānacārikena. Kālataranti kālasseva. Aphāsukaṭṭhānanti saparissayādivasena [V 1.0089] duppavesanaṭṭhānaṃ. Puratoti vīthiyaṃ gacchantassa purato gharaṃ apaviṭṭhasseva. Pattavissaṭṭhaṭṭhānanti pesakāravīthiyaṃ pesakārabhāvaṃ nimminitvā ṭhitassa sakkassa gharadvāre pattavissaṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātiko taṃ divasaṃ na bhikkhaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdati, tasmā taṃ anulometi. Katthacipi kule nibaddhaṃ upasaṅkamanābhāvato paricayābhāvena kulesu niccanavakatā. Sabbattha alaggamānasatāya ca sommabhāvena ca candūpamatā. Kulesu pariggahacittābhāvena tattha maccherappahānaṃ. Hitesitāya vibhāgābhāvato samānukampitā. Kulānaṃ saṅgaṇhanasaṃsaṭṭhatādayo kulūpakādīnavā. Avhānānabhinandanāti nimantanavasena avhānassa asampaṭicchanā. Abhihārenāti bhikkhābhihārena. Sericāranti yathāruci vicaraṇaṃ.

27. 'By this' means by one who goes for alms from house to house without skipping. 'Very early' means early on. 'An uncomfortable place' means a place that is difficult to enter on account of dangers and so on. 'In front' refers to the situation of one going along the street, before he has even entered a house in front of him. 'The place where the bowl was set down' refers to the doorway of the house of Sakka, who stood in the weavers' street having created the form of a weaver. The strict alms-round-goer does not sit on that day waiting for alms; therefore, this practice conforms to his. In any family, because he does not approach them constantly, there is a lack of familiarity, resulting in a constant newness in relation to them. Everywhere, due to having an unattached mind and a gentle nature, he is like the moon. Patronizing, mixing with families, and so on, are the dangers of a family-frequenter. 'Not delighting in an invitation' means not accepting a call in the form of an invitation. 'By the bringing' means by the bringing of alms-food. 'Wandering at will' means wandering according to one's wish.

Iti sapadānacārikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the explanation of the practice of going for alms from house to house without skipping.

5. Ekāsanikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the One-Sessioner's Practice

28. Nānāsanabhojananti anekasmiṃ āsane bhojanaṃ, ekanisajjāya eva abhuñjitvā visuṃ visuṃ nisajjāsu āhāraparibhoganti attho. Patirūpanti yuttarūpaṃ anuṭṭhāpanīyaṃ. Vattaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti vattaṃ kātuṃ yujjati. Vattaṃ nāma garuṭṭhānīye kattabbameva. Tattha pana paṭipajjanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ yaṃ theravādaṃ āha “āsanaṃ vā rakkheyya bhojanaṃ vā”tiādi. Tassattho – ekāsanikaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhuñjantaṃ āsanaṃ vā rakkheyya, dhutaṅgabhedato yāva bhojanapariyosānā na vuṭṭhātabbanti vuttaṃ hoti[M 1.0096]. Bhojanaṃ vā rakkheyya dhutaṅgabhedato, abhuñjiyamānaṃ yāva bhuñjituṃ nārabhati, tāva vuṭṭhātabbanti attho. Yasmā tayidaṃ dvayaṃ idha natthi, tasmā vattakaraṇaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na rakkhatīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “ayañcā”tiādi. “Bhesajjatthamevā”ti iminā bhesajjaparibhogavaseneva sappiādīnipi vaṭṭantīti dasseti. Appābādhatāti arogatā. Appātaṅkatāti akicchajīvitā sarīradukkhābhāvo. Lahuṭṭhānanti kāyassa lahuparivattitā. Balanti sarīrabalaṃ. Phāsuvihāroti sukhavihāro. Sabbametaṃ bahukkhattuṃ bhuñjanapaccayā uppajjanavikārapaṭikkhepapadaṃ. Rujāti rogā. Na kammamattanoti attano yogakammaṃ purebhattaṃ, pacchābhattañca na parihāpeti, bahuso bhojane abyāvaṭabhāvato, arogabhāvato cāti adhippāyo.

28. 'Eating at various seats' means eating food at many seats; the meaning is consuming food in separate sittings, not having eaten in just one sitting. 'Suitable' means fitting, a situation from which one should not be made to rise out of respect. 'It is allowable to perform a duty' means it is proper to perform a duty. A 'duty,' it should be noted, is what must be done in a situation where respect is owed. However, to show the method of practice in this regard, the Theravāda teaching was stated: 'One should guard either the seat or the meal,' and so on. Its meaning is this: a monk practicing the one-sessioner's practice, while eating, should guard the seat, lest the ascetic practice be broken, meaning he should not rise until the meal is finished. Or he should guard the meal, lest the ascetic practice be broken; the meaning is that as long as he has not yet begun to eat, he may rise. Because these two conditions are not present here, the intention is that performing the duty does not protect the ascetic practice. For that reason, it is said, 'And this...' and so on. By the phrase 'for the sake of medicine only,' it is shown that even ghee and so on are allowable only for medicinal use. 'Few ailments' means healthiness. 'Few afflictions' means living without hardship, the absence of bodily suffering. 'Lightness' means the body's ease of movement. 'Strength' means bodily strength. 'Comfortable abiding' means a pleasant abiding. All this is for the purpose of rejecting the ailments that arise from eating many times. 'Ailments' means diseases. 'He does not neglect his own practice' means he does not diminish his meditative practice before or after the meal, because he is not occupied with eating many times and because he is healthy; this is the intention.

Iti ekāsanikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the explanation of the one-sessioner's practice.

6. Pattapiṇḍikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Alms-bowl-Eater's Practice

29. Appaṭikūlaṃ [V 1.0090] katvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati paṭikūlassa bhuttassa agaṇhanampi siyāti adhippāyo. Pamāṇayuttameva gaṇhitabbanti “ekabhājanameva gaṇhāmī”ti bahuṃ gahetvā na chaḍḍetabbaṃ. Nānārasataṇhāvinodananti nānārasabhojane taṇhāya vinodanaṃ. Atra atra nānābhājane ṭhite nānārase icchā etassāti atriccho, tassa bhāvo atricchatā, tassā atricchatāya pahānaṃ. Āhāre payojanamattadassitāti asambhinnanānārase gedhaṃ akatvā āhāre satthārā anuññātapayojanamattadassitā. Visuṃ visuṃ bhājanesu ṭhitāni byañjanāni gaṇhato tattha tattha sābhogatāya siyā vikkhittabhojitā, na tathā imassa ekapattagatasaññinoti vuttaṃ “avikkhittabhojitā”ti. Okkhittalocanoti pattasaññitāya heṭṭhākhittacakkhu. Paribhuñjeyyāti paribhuñjituṃ sakkuṇeyya.

29. It is proper to eat, having made it non-repulsive. The meaning is that repulsive food, once eaten, might not be retained. 'One should take only what is appropriate in measure' means that one should not take a large amount and then discard it, thinking, 'I am taking from only one vessel.' 'Dispelling craving for various flavors' means the dispelling of craving for food with various flavors. For this person, there is desire for various flavors situated in various separate dishes here and there; thus, he is one with excessive desire (atriccho). His state is excessive desire (atricchatā). The abandoning of that excessive desire is meant. 'Seeing only the purpose in food' means, not creating greed for various unmixed flavors, but seeing in food only the purpose permitted by the Teacher. For one who takes curries placed in separate, individual dishes, there may be distracted eating due to engagement here and there. It is not so for this one who has the perception of it being in a single bowl; thus, it is said, 'undistracted eating.' 'With eyes cast down' means having the eyes cast downwards due to the perception of the bowl. 'Should partake' means one would be able to partake.

Iti pattapiṇḍikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the explanation of the alms-bowl-eater's practice.

7. Khalupacchābhattikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Refuser-of-Later-Food's Practice

30. Bhuñjantassa [M 1.0097] yaṃ upanītaṃ, tassa paṭikkhepena taṃ atirittaṃ bhojananti atirittabhojanaṃ. Puna bhojanaṃ kappiyaṃ kāretvā na bhuñjitabbaṃ, tabbisayattā imassa dhutaṅgassa. Tenāha “idamassa vidhāna”nti. Yasmiṃ bhojaneti yasmiṃ bhuñjiyamāne bhojane. Tadeva bhuñjati, na aññaṃ. Anatirittabhojanapaccayā āpatti anatirittabhojanāpatti, tato dūrībhāvo anāpajjanaṃ. Odarikattaṃ ghasmarabhāvo kucchipūrakatā, tassa abhāvo ekapiṇḍenāpi yāpanato. Nirāmisasannidhitā nihitassa abhuñjanato. Puna pariyesanavasena pariyesanāya khedaṃ na yāti. Abhisallekhakānaṃ santosaguṇādīnaṃ vuddhiyā sañjananaṃ santosaguṇādivuḍḍhisañjananaṃ. Idanti khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ.

30. For one who is eating, whatever food is brought, by the rejection of that, that food is 'extra food'; thus it is called extra food. One should not eat food again after having it made allowable, because that is the domain of this ascetic practice. Therefore, he said, 'This is its rule.' 'In whatever food' means in whatever food is being eaten. One eats only that, and not another. The offense on account of food that is not extra is the 'non-extra-food offense'; being far from that is non-incurring. Gluttony, voraciousness, and belly-filling—the absence of that is because one can be sustained even by a single lump of food. Non-hoarding of material things is because of not eating what has been set aside. He does not go to weariness in searching by way of searching again. For those who are austere, it is a generator of the growth of the qualities of contentment, etc.; thus, it is a 'generator of the growth of the qualities of contentment, etc.' This is the refuser-of-later-food's practice.

Iti khalupacchābhattikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the explanation of the refuser-of-later-food's practice.

8. Āraññikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Forest-Dweller's Practice

31. Gāmantasenāsanaṃ [V 1.0091] pahāya araññe aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbanti ettha gāmantaṃ, araññañca sarūpato dassetuṃ “tattha saddhiṃ upacārenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha gāmapariyāpannattā gāmantasenāsanassa “gāmoyeva gāmantasenāsana”nti vuttaṃ. Yo koci satthopi gāmo nāmāti sambandho. Indakhīlāti ummārā. Tassāti leḍḍupātassa. Vinayapariyāyena araññalakkhaṇaṃ adinnādānapārājike (pārā. 92) āgataṃ. Tattha hi “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti anavasesato avahāraṭṭhānapariggahe tadubhayaṃ asaṅkarato dassetuṃ “ṭhapetvā gāmañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gāmūpacāro hi loke gāmasaṅkhameva gacchatīti. Nippariyāyato pana gāmavinimuttaṃ ṭhānaṃ araññameva hotīti abhidhamme (vibha. 529) gāmā “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā, sabbametaṃ arañña”nti vuttaṃ. Suttantikapariyāyena āraññakasikkhāpade (pārā. 654) “pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti āgataṃ āraññikaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya. Na hi so vinayapariyāyike “araññe vasanato āraññiko pantasenāsano”ti sutte vutto. Ayañca suttasaṃvaṇṇanāti idha sabbattha suttantakathāva [M 1.0098] pamāṇaṃ. Tasmā tattha āgatameva lakkhaṇaṃ gahetabbanti dassento “taṃ āropitena ācariyadhanunā”tiādinā minanavidhiṃ āha. Teneva hi majjhimaṭṭhakathānayova (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.296) idamettha pamāṇanti ca vutto.

31. Here, regarding 'Having abandoned dwellings near a village, one should greet the dawn in the forest,' the passage beginning 'Therein, together with its vicinity...' is introduced to show the essential nature of 'village-vicinity' and 'forest.' Therein, because a dwelling near a village is included within the village, it is said, 'A dwelling near a village is the village itself.' The connection is that any caravan is also called a village. 'Indakhīla' means gate-posts. 'Of that' means of the clod-throwing distance. The characteristic of a forest according to the Vinaya method is found in the Pārājika offense on theft. For there, in order to show both categories without confusion when comprehending the place of theft without exception, the phrase 'from a village or from a forest' is stated, and also the passage beginning 'excluding the village...' is stated. For in the world, the vicinity of a village is indeed included in the designation of 'village.'
