In the direct sense, however, any place free from a village is simply a forest; thus in the Abhidhamma it is said: 'Having gone out from the village, outside the gate-posts, all of this is a forest.' According to the Suttanta method, in the training rule for a forest-dweller, the phrase 'five hundred bow-lengths at the minimum' is found, referring to a forest-dwelling monk. For that monk is not called in the Sutta a 'forest-dweller, one who frequents remote lodgings' simply for dwelling in a forest as defined by the Vinaya method. And this is a commentary on the Suttas, so herein the word of the Suttanta is the authority in all matters. Therefore, showing that the characteristic mentioned there should be taken, he explains the method of measurement with the phrase beginning 'By that teacher's bow when it is strung...' For that very reason, the method of the Majjhima Nikāya commentary is also said to be the authority in this matter.

Tato tato magganti tattha tattha khuddakamaggaṃ pidahati. Dhutaṅgasuddhikena dhutaṅgasodhanapasutena. Yathāparicchinne kāleti ukkaṭṭhassa tayopi utū, majjhimassa dve, mudukassa eko utu. Tatthapi dhutaṅgaṃ na bhijjati saussāhattā. Nipajjitvā gamissāmāti cittassa sithilabhāvena dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjatīti vuttaṃ. Araññasaññaṃ manasi karontoti “ahaṃ vivekavāsaṃ vasissāmi, yathāladdhova kāyaviveko sātthako kātabbo”ti manasikārasabbhāvato “bhabbo…pe… rakkhitu”nti vuttaṃ. Assa āraññikassa cittaṃ na vikkhipanti āpāthamanupagamanato. Vigatasantāso hoti vivekaparicayato. Jīvitanikantiṃ jahati bahuparissaye araññe nivāseneva maraṇabhayassa dūrīkaraṇato. Pavivekasukharasaṃ assādeti anubhavati janasaṃsaggābhāvato. Ārādhayantoti anunayanto. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattiyā vivekassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato āraññikaṅgayogino vāhanasadisanti katvā vuttaṃ “avasesadhutāyudho”ti, avasiṭṭhadhutadhammāyudhoti attho.

'From path to path' means he blocks the minor paths in various places. `Dhutaṅgasuddhikena` means being intent on the purification of the ascetic practice. 'In the defined time' means: for the strict practitioner, all three seasons; for the moderate, two; for the mild, one season. Even then, the ascetic practice is not broken, due to his energy. It is said that the ascetic practice is broken by the mind's slackness with the thought, 'I will lie down and then go.' 'Applying the mind to the perception of the forest' means that because of the presence of the mental application, 'I will live in seclusion; the bodily seclusion I have obtained should be made fruitful,' it is said, 'He is able... to protect.' The mind of this forest-dweller is not scattered, because sense objects do not come into range. He becomes free from terror through familiarity with seclusion. He abandons craving for life because dwelling in a forest full of many dangers removes the fear of death. He tastes and experiences the flavor of the bliss of seclusion due to the absence of association with people. `Ārādhayanto` means gratifying. Through practice as instructed, and because seclusion is the foundation, the forest-dweller's practice is like a vehicle for the yogī; thinking thus, it was said, 'armed with the remaining ascetic weapons.' The meaning is: he has the remaining ascetic qualities as his weapons.

Iti āraññikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus, the Explanation of the Discourse on the Forest-Dweller's Practice.

9. Rukkhamūlikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Practice of Dwelling at the Root of a Tree

32. Channanti [V 1.0092] iṭṭhakāchadanādīhi chāditaṃ, āvasathanti attho. Sīmantarikarukkhoti dvinnaṃ rājūnaṃ rajjasīmāya ṭhitarukkho. Tattha hi tesaṃ rājūnaṃ balakāyo upagantvā antarantarā yuddhaṃ kareyya, corāpi pāripanthikā samosarantā bhikkhussa sukhena nisīdituṃ na denti. Cetiyarukkho “devatādhiṭṭhito”ti manussehi sammatarukkho pūjetuṃ upagatehi manussehi avivitto hoti. Niyyāsarukkho sajjarukkhādi. Vaggulirukkho vaggulinisevito. Sīmantarikarukkhādayo saparissayā, dullabhavivekā cāti āha “ime rukkhe vivajjetvā”ti. Paṇṇasaṭanti [M 1.0099] rukkhato patitapaṇṇaṃ. Paṭicchanne ṭhāne nisīditabbaṃ rukkhamūlikabhāvassa paṭicchādanatthaṃ. Channe vāsakappanā dhammassavanādīnamatthāyapi hoti. Tasmā “jānitvā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpitamatte”ti vuttaṃ.

32. 'Channa' (covered) means covered with things such as tiles; it means a dwelling place (āvasatha). 'Sīmantarika-rukkha' is a tree standing on the border of two kingdoms. For there, the armies of those kings might approach and wage war intermittently; and dangerous thieves, gathering, would not allow a monk to sit in peace. A 'cetiya-rukkha' is a tree designated by people as 'inhabited by a deity,' and it is not secluded because of the people who come to worship. A 'niyyāsa-rukkha' is a resin-tree, such as a Sal tree. A 'vagguli-rukkha' is a tree frequented by bats. Trees such as the boundary tree are both dangerous and have solitude that is difficult to obtain; therefore, it is said, 'having avoided these trees.' 'Paṇṇasaṭa' means a leaf fallen from a tree. One should sit in a concealed place for the purpose of concealing one's state as a tree-root-dweller. Dwelling in a covered place is also for the purpose of listening to the Dhamma and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'as soon as dawn arises'.

Abhiṇhaṃ tarupaṇṇavikāradassanenāti abhikkhaṇaṃ tarūsu, tarūnaṃ vā paṇṇesu vikārassa khaṇabhaṅgassa dassanena. Senāsanamaccherakammārāmatānanti āvāsamacchariyanavakammaratabhāvānaṃ. Devatāhīti rukkhadevatāhi. Tāpi hi rukkhaṭṭhavimānesu vasantiyo rukkhesu vasanti. Ayampi rukkheti sahavāsitā. Vaṇṇitoti “appāni cevā”tiādinā pasaṃsito. “Rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ nissāya pabbajjā”ti (mahāva. 73, 128) evaṃ nissayoti ca bhāsito. Abhirattāni taruṇakāle, nīlāni majjhimakāle, paṇḍūni jiṇṇakāle. Patitāni milāyanavasena. Evaṃ passanto tarupaṇṇāni paccakkhato eva niccasaññaṃ panūdati pajahati, aniccasaññā evassa saṇṭhāti. Yasmā bhagavato jātibodhidhammacakkapavattanaparinibbānāni rukkhamūleyeva jātāni, tasmā vuttaṃ “buddhadāyajjaṃ rukkhamūla”nti.

'By constantly observing the changes in the leaves of trees' means by repeatedly seeing the change and momentary destruction of trees or their leaves. 'Stinginess regarding lodging places and fondness for new construction' refers to the states of being stingy with dwellings and delighting in new construction work. 'With deities' means with tree-deities. For they too, dwelling in mansions situated in trees, reside in trees. 'This one, too, in a tree' means there is co-residence. 'It has been praised' as stated in phrases like 'even if few' and so on. 'The going forth is dependent on a tree-root lodging' — thus it is spoken of as a 'dependence'. They are reddish when young, dark green in middle age, and pale yellow in old age, and have fallen by way of withering. Seeing the tree leaves in this way, one directly dispels and abandons the perception of permanence, and the perception of impermanence becomes firmly established in him. Because the Blessed One’s birth, enlightenment, turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and final Parinibbāna all occurred at the root of a tree, it is said: 'The root of a tree is the Buddha’s heritage'.

Iti rukkhamūlikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus concludes the explanation of the discourse on the practice of dwelling at the root of a tree.

10. Abbhokāsikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Open-Air Dweller's Practice

33. “Rukkhamūlaṃ paṭikkhipāmī”ti ettake vutte channaṃ appaṭikkhittameva hotīti “channañca [V 1.0093] rukkhamūlañca paṭikkhipāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Dhutaṅgassa sabbaso paṭiyogipaṭikkhepena hi samādānaṃ ijjhati, no aññathāti. “Dhammassavanāyā”ti imināva dhammaṃ kathentenāpi uposathadivasādīsu suṇantānaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthaṃ tehi yācitena channaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati, dhammaṃ pana kathetvā abbhokāsova gantabbo. Rukkhamūlikassāpi eseva nayo. Uposathatthāyāti uposathakammāya. Uddisantenāti paresaṃ uddesaṃ dentena. Uddisāpentenāti sayaṃ uddesaṃ gaṇhantena. Maggamajjhe ṭhitaṃ sālanti sīhaḷadīpe viya maggā anokkamma ujukameva pavisitabbasālaṃ. Vegena gantuṃ na vaṭṭati asāruppattā. Yāva vassūparamā ṭhatvā gantabbaṃ, na tāva dhutaṅgabhedo hotīti adhippāyo.

33. When 'I reject the root of a tree' is said, this much having been said, a roofed place is not yet rejected. Therefore, it is said, 'I reject both a roofed place and the root of a tree.' For the undertaking of the ascetic practice is accomplished only by completely rejecting its counterpart; otherwise, it is not accomplished. By the phrase 'For hearing the Dhamma': even one who is teaching the Dhamma, on Uposatha days and the like, for the sake of protecting the minds of the listeners, it is permissible to enter a roofed place if requested by them. However, after having taught the Dhamma, one must go only to the open air. For the tree-root dweller also, this is the same method. 'By one who recites' means by one who gives the recitation to others. 'By one who has it recited' means by one who himself receives the recitation. 'A hall standing in the middle of the road' means a hall that should be entered straight from the road without deviating, as on the island of Sīhaḷa. It is not proper to go quickly, due to its unsuitability. One should stay until the rain stops and then go; for that long, there is no breaking of the ascetic practice—this is the meaning.

Rukkhassa [M 1.0100] anto nāma rukkhamūlaṃ. Pabbatassa pana pabbhārasadiso pabbatapadeso. Acchannamariyādanti yathā vassodakaṃ anto na pavisati, evaṃ chadanasaṅkhepena upari akatamariyādaṃ. Anto pana pabbhārassa vassodakaṃ pavisati ce, abbhokāsasaṅkhepamevāti tattha pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. Sākhāmaṇḍapoti rukkhasākhāhi viraḷacchannamaṇḍapo. Pīṭhapaṭo khalitthaddhasāṭako.

The 'inside' of a tree is the root of the tree. But for a mountain, it is a mountain region similar to a mountain slope. 'An unroofed boundary' means a boundary not made above in the manner of a roof, so that rainwater does not enter within. However, if rainwater enters inside the mountain slope, it is counted simply as open air; therefore, it is permissible to enter there. A 'branch pavilion' is a pavilion sparsely roofed with tree branches. A `pīṭhapaṭa` is a cloth stiffened with rice-gruel.

Paviṭṭhakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati yathāvuttapabbhārādike ṭhapetvāti adhippāyo. Jānitvāti dhammassavanādiatthaṃ channaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pavisitvā nisinno “idāni aruṇo uṭṭhahatī”ti jānitvā. Rukkhamūlepi katthaci attheva nivāsaphāsukatāti siyā tattha āsaṅgapubbako āvāsapalibodho, na pana abbhokāseti idheva āvāsapalibodhupacchedo ānisaṃso vutto. Pasaṃsāyānurūpatāti aniketāti vuttapasaṃsāya anālayabhāvena anucchavikatā. Nissaṅgatāti āvāsapariggahābhāveneva tattha nissaṅgatā. Asukadisāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, tasmā tattha gantuṃ neva sakkāti edisassa parivitakkassa abhāvato cātuddiso. Migabhūtenāti pariggahābhāvena migassa viya bhūtena. Sitoti nissito. Vindatīti labhati.

The meaning is that the ascetic practice is broken at the moment of entering, except for the aforementioned mountain slopes and so on. 'Having known' means: having entered a roofed place or the root of a tree for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma and so on, and while seated, knowing, 'Now the dawn is rising.' Even at the root of some tree, there is indeed comfort in dwelling; therefore, there can be the obstruction of a dwelling, preceded by attachment. But in the open air, this cannot be. Therefore, right here, the benefit of cutting off the obstruction of a dwelling is stated. 'Suitability for praise' is the suitability, through having no abode, for the praise spoken as 'homeless.' 'Detachment' is detachment there precisely because of the non-appropriation of a dwelling. Because of the absence of such deliberation as, 'There is no dwelling place in such-and-such a direction, therefore it is not possible to go there,' one is of the four directions. 'Having become like a deer' means having become like a deer due to the absence of appropriation. `Sita` means `nissita` (dependent). `Vindati` means `labhati` (obtains).

Iti abbhokāsikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus, the Exposition on the Open-Air Dweller's Practice.

11. Sosānikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

11. The Exposition on the Charnel-Ground-Dweller's Practice

34. Na [V 1.0094] susānanti asusānaṃ. Aññattho na-kāro, susānalakkhaṇarahitaṃ vasanaṭṭhānanti adhippāyo. Na tatthāti “susāna”nti vavatthapitamatte ṭhāne na vasitabbaṃ. Na hi nāmamattena susānalakkhaṇaṃ sijjhati. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Jhāpitakālato pana paṭṭhāya…pe… susānameva chavena sayitamattāya susānalakkhaṇappattito. Chavasayanaṃ hi “susāna”nti vuccati.

34. “Not a charnel ground” means a non-charnel ground. The particle ‘na’ has another meaning; the intention is a dwelling place devoid of the characteristics of a charnel ground. “Not there” means one should not dwell in a place merely designated as a “charnel ground.” For the characteristic of a charnel ground is not accomplished by a mere name. For that reason, he said, “For not…” and so on. But from the time of cremation onwards… it is indeed a charnel ground because it attains the characteristic of a charnel ground by the mere lying of a corpse. For the lying place of a corpse is called a “charnel ground.”

Sosānikena nāma appakiccena sallahukavuttinā bhavitabbanti dassetuṃ “tasmiṃ pana vasantenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Garukanti dupparihāraṃ. Tameva hi dupparihārabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha uppannaparissayavighātatthāyāti [M 1.0101] “susānaṃ nāma manussarāhasseyyaka”nti corā katakammāpi akatakammāpi osaranti, tattha coresu bhaṇḍasāmike disvā bhikkhusamīpe bhaṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā palātesu manussā bhikkhuṃ “coro”ti gahetvā potheyyuṃ, tasmā vihāre saṅghattheraṃ vā gocaragāme raññā niyuttaṃ rājayuttakaṃ vā attano sosānikabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā yathā tādiso, añño vā parissayo na hoti, tathā appamattena vasitabbaṃ. Caṅkamantassa yadā āḷahanaṃ abhimukhaṃ na hoti, tadāpi saṃvegajananatthaṃ tattha diṭṭhi vissajjetabbāti dassetuṃ “addhakkhikena āḷahanaṃ olokentenā”ti vuttaṃ.

To show that a charnel-ground dweller should have few duties and a light livelihood, the passage beginning “While dwelling there…” was stated. “Difficult” means difficult to manage. To show this very state of being difficult to manage, the passage beginning “Therefore…” was stated. Therein, for the purpose of averting arisen dangers: “A charnel ground is a place for deeds done in seclusion from people,” and so thieves, whether they have already committed a crime or not, resort there. There, when the thieves, having seen the owners of the goods, abandon the goods near the monk and flee, people might seize the monk, thinking, “He is a thief,” and beat him. Therefore, having informed either the Elder of the Sangha in the monastery or a royal official appointed by the king in the alms-resort village of one’s state as a charnel-ground dweller, one should dwell with diligence so that such a danger, or another, does not arise. To show that even when the cremation ground is not in front of one who is practicing walking meditation, one’s gaze should be directed there for the purpose of generating a sense of spiritual urgency, the passage beginning “...by one looking at the cremation ground...” was stated.

Uppathamaggena gantabbaṃ attano sosānikabhāvassa apākaṭabhāvatthaṃ. Ārammaṇanti tasmiṃ susāne “ayaṃ vammiko, ayaṃ rukkho, ayaṃ khāṇuko”tiādinā divāyeva ārammaṇaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Bhayānakanti bhayajanakaṃ vammikādiṃ. Kenaci leḍḍupāsāṇādinā āsanne vicarantīti na paharitabbā. Tilapiṭṭhaṃ vuccati palalaṃ. Māsamissaṃ bhattaṃ māsabhattaṃ. Guḷādīti ādi-saddena tilasaṃguḷikādighanapūvañca saṅgaṇhāti. Kulagehaṃ na pavisitabbanti petadhūmena vāsitattā, pisācānubandhattā ca kulagehassa abbhantaraṃ na pavisitabbaṃ. Devasikaṃ chavaḍāho dhuvaḍāho. Matañātakānaṃ tattha gantvā devasikaṃ rodanaṃ dhuvarodanaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “jhāpitakālato pana paṭṭhāyā”ti vuttanayena. “Pacchimayāme paṭikkamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti icchitattā “susānaṃ agatadivase”ti aṅguttarabhāṇakā.

One should go by an unfrequented path so that one’s state as a charnel-ground dweller is not manifest. “Object” means that in that charnel ground, one should determine an object during the daytime itself, such as, “This is an anthill, this is a tree, this is a stump.” “Frightful” means a fear-inducing thing such as an anthill. Thinking, “They are wandering nearby,” they should not be struck with any clod, stone, or the like. Sesame paste is called sesame meal. Rice mixed with beans is `māsabhatta`. In `guḷādi`, by the word `ādi` (and so on), it also includes solid cakes such as sesame-jaggery balls. “One should not enter a family’s house” means one should not enter the interior of a supporter’s house because of being permeated by the smoke of corpses and because of being followed by demons. The daily burning of a corpse is called “constant burning.” The daily weeping of the relatives of the deceased who have gone there is called “constant weeping.” “By the stated method” means by the method stated as “from the time of cremation onwards…” Because it was intended that “it is allowable to depart in the last watch,” the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya state, “on a day one has not gone to the charnel ground…”

Susāne niccakālaṃ sivathikadassanena maraṇassatipaṭilābho. Tato eva appamādavihāritā[V 1.0095]. Tattha chaḍḍitassa matakaḷevarassa dassanena asubhanimittādhigamo. Tato eva kāmarāgavinodanaṃ. Bahulaṃ sarīrassa asuciduggandhajegucchabhāvasallakkhaṇato abhiṇhaṃ kāyasabhāvadassanaṃ. Tato maraṇassatipaṭilābhato ca saṃvegabahulatā. Byādhikānaṃ, jarājiṇṇānañca matānaṃ tattha dassanena ārogyayobbanajīvitamadappahānaṃ. Khuddakassa, mahato ca bhayassa abhibhavanato bhayabheravasahanatā. Saṃviggassa yoniso padahanaṃ sambhavatīti amanussānaṃ garubhāvanīyatā. Niddāgatampīti suttampi, supinantepīti adhippāyo.

In the charnel ground, by constantly seeing the cemetery, there is the attainment of mindfulness of death. From that very thing comes the state of dwelling with diligence. There, by seeing a discarded corpse, there is the attainment of the sign of foulness. From that very thing comes the dispelling of sensual lust. By frequently and thoroughly noting the body's state of being impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting, there is the constant seeing of the body's true nature. From that, and from the attainment of mindfulness of death, comes an abundance of spiritual urgency. By seeing there the dead who were sick and decrepit with old age, there is the abandoning of the intoxication with health, youth, and life. By overcoming fear both small and great, there is the ability to endure fear and dread. For one with spiritual urgency, wise exertion is possible, and thus one becomes worthy of reverence by non-human beings. “Even when asleep” means even when sleeping, that is, even in a dream; this is the intention.

Iti sosānikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus, the Exposition on the Charnel-Ground-Dweller's Practice.

12. Yathāsanthatikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

12. The Exposition on the Practice of Accepting Whatever Lodging is Allotted.

35. Senāsanagāhaṇe [M 1.0102] pare uṭṭhāpetvā gahaṇaṃ, “idaṃ sundaraṃ, idaṃ na sundara”nti paritulayitvā pucchanā, olokanā ca senāsanaloluppaṃ. Tuṭṭhabbanti tussitabbaṃ. Vihārassa pariyantabhāvena dūreti vā bahūnaṃ sannipātaṭṭhānādīnaṃ accāsanneti vā pucchituṃ na labhati, pucchanenapissa dhutaṅgassa saṃkilissanato. Oloketunti loluppavasena passituṃ. Sacassa taṃ na ruccatīti assa yathāsanthatikassa taṃ yathāgāhitaṃ senāsanaṃ aphāsukabhāvena sace na ruccati, mudukassa asati roge yathāgāhitaṃ pahāya aññassa senāsanassa gahaṇaṃ loluppaṃ, majjhimassa gantvā olokanā, ukkaṭṭhassa pucchanā. Sabbesampi uṭṭhāpetvā gahaṇe vattabbameva natthi.

35. Taking a lodging after making others get up; asking after weighing, “Is this beautiful? Is this not beautiful?”; and looking—this is called greed for lodgings. “Being content” means one should be satisfied. One is not allowed to ask whether it is far, being at the edge of the monastery, or too close to the gathering places of many people and so on, because even by asking, this ascetic practice is defiled. “To look” means to see with the power of fickle craving. If it is not agreeable to him—that is, if that lodging which has been accepted is not agreeable to him who practices accepting whatever lodging is allotted, due to being uncomfortable—then for the mild practitioner, in the absence of illness, abandoning the accepted lodging and taking another is greed. For the middling practitioner, going and looking is greed. For the strict practitioner, asking is greed. For all, in the case of taking a lodging after making others get up, there is nothing at all to be said.

Upaṭṭhāpanīyānampi anuṭṭhāpanena sabrahmacārīnaṃ hitesitā. Tāya karuṇāvihārānuguṇatā. Sundarāsundaravibhāgākaraṇato hīnapaṇītavikappapariccāgo. Tena tādilakkhaṇānuguṇatā. Tato eva anurodhavirodhappahānaṃ. Dvārapidahanaṃ okāsādānato. Yathāsanthatarāmatanti yathāgāhite yathāniddiṭṭhe senāsane abhiratabhāvaṃ.

By not causing even junior monks who could be made to get up, to get up, it is the state of desiring the welfare of one's fellows in the holy life. By that, it is the state of being in accordance with the dwelling in compassion. Because of not making a distinction of 'good' and 'not good,' it is the abandoning of the thought 'inferior' or 'superior.' By that, it is the state of being in accordance with the characteristic of equanimity. Precisely from that, it is the abandoning of attraction and aversion. It is the closing of the door by not giving an opportunity. Delighting in what is assigned means the state of delighting in the lodging as it has been accepted or as it has been pointed out.

Iti yathāsanthatikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the Explanation of the Ascetic Practice of Being Content with Whatever Lodging is Assigned.

13. Nesajjikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā

13. The Explanation of the Ascetic Practice of Sitting

36. Seyyanti [V 1.0096] iriyāpathalakkhaṇaṃ seyyaṃ. Tappaṭikkhepeneva hi tadatthā “mañco bhisī”ti evamādikā (cūḷava. 321, 322) seyyā paṭikkhittā eva honti. “Nesajjiko”ti ca sayanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā nisajjāya eva viharituṃ sīlamassāti imassa atthassa idha adhippetattā seyyā evettha paṭiyoginī, na itare tathā aniṭṭhattā, asambhavato ca. Kosajjapakkhiyo hi iriyāpatho idha paṭiyogibhāvena icchito, na itare. Na ca sakkā ṭhānagamanehi vinā nisajjāya eva yāpetuṃ tathā pavattetunti seyyāvettha paṭiyoginī. Tenāha “tena panā”tiādi. Caṅkamitabbaṃ na “nesajjiko aha”nti sabbarattiṃ nisīditabbaṃ. Iriyāpathantarānuggahito hi kāyo manasikārakkhamo hoti.

36. Lying down means the lying down which has the characteristic of a posture. Indeed, just by the rejection of that, beds for the purpose of lying down, such as couches, mattresses, and so forth, are certainly rejected. And since the meaning intended here by 'nesajjika' (a sitter) is that 'he has the habit of dwelling only by sitting, having rejected lying down,' lying down alone is the opposing factor here, not the other postures, because they are not undesired in that way, and because it is impossible. For the posture that is on the side of laziness is intended here as the opposing factor, not the others. And it is not possible to maintain oneself or to proceed only by sitting, without standing and walking; therefore, lying down alone is the opposing factor here. Therefore, he said, "By that, however..." and so on. One should walk; one should not sit the whole night through thinking, "I am a sitter." For the body, when supported by another posture, is fit for mental application.

Cattāro [M 1.0103] pādā, piṭṭhiapassayo cāti imehi pañcahi aṅgehi pañcaṅgo. Catūhi aṭṭanīhi, piṭṭhiapassayena ca pañcaṅgoti apare. Ubhosu passesu piṭṭhipasse ca yathāsukhaṃ apassāya viharato nesajjikassa “anesajjikato ko viseso”ti gāhaṃ nivāretuṃ abhayatthero nidassito “thero anāgāmī hutvā parinibbāyī”ti.

Four legs and a backrest—with these five parts, it is a five-limbed seat. Others say it is five-limbed with four arm-rests and a backrest. In order to prevent the view, 'What is the difference from one who is not a sitter?' for a nesajjika practitioner who dwells leaning comfortably on both sides and on the back, the Elder Abhaya was pointed out as an example: 'The elder, having become a non-returner, attained final Nibbāna.'

Upacchedīyati etenāti upacchedananti vinibandhupacchedassa sādhakatamabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Sabbakammaṭṭhānānuyogasappāyatā alīnānuddhaccapakkhikattā nisajjāya. Tato eva pāsādikairiyāpathatā. Vīriyārambhānukūlatā vīriyasamatāyojanassa anucchavikatā. Tato eva sammāpaṭipattiyā anubrūhanatā. Paṇidhāyāti ṭhapetvā. Tanunti uparimakāyaṃ. Vikampetīti cāleti, icchāvighātaṃ karotīti adhippāyo. Vatanti dhutaṅgaṃ.

It is called 'upacchedana' (cutting off) because 'it is cut off by this'; the state of being the most effective means for cutting off the bonds of the mind should be understood. There is suitability for the practice of all meditation subjects because sitting is not on the side of shrinkage or restlessness. Precisely from that, there is the state of having a posture that inspires confidence. The state of being conducive to the arousal of energy is the suitability for yoking to the balancing of energy. Precisely from that, there is the state of augmenting the right practice. 'Paṇidhāya' means 'having placed.' 'Tanuṃ' means 'the upper body.' 'Vikampeti' means 'shakes'; the meaning is that it causes the destruction of one's will. 'Vataṃ' means 'the ascetic practice.'

Iti nesajjikaṅgakathāvaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the Explanation of the Ascetic Practice of Sitting.

Dhutaṅgapakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Miscellaneous Matters Concerning the Dhutaṅga Practices

37. Sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ vasena siyā kusalāni, khīṇāsavānaṃ vasena siyā abyākatāni[V 1.0097]. Tattha sekkhaputhujjanā paṭipattipūraṇatthaṃ, khīṇāsavā phāsuvihāratthaṃ dhutaṅgāni pariharanti. Akusalampi dhutaṅganti akusalacittenāpi dhutaṅgasevanā atthīti adhippāyo. Taṃ na yuttaṃ, yena akusalacittena pabbajitassa āraññikattaṃ, taṃ dhutaṅgaṃ nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Lakkhaṇābhāvato. Yaṃ hidaṃ kilesānaṃ dhunanato dhutassa puggalassa, ñāṇassa, cetanāya vā aṅgattaṃ, na taṃ akusaladhammesu sambhavati. Tasmā araññavāsādimattena āraññikādayo tāva hontu, āraññikaṅgādīni pana na hontīti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “na maya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha imānīti dhutaṅgāni. Vuttaṃ heṭṭhā vacanatthaniddese. Na ca akusalena koci dhuto nāma hoti, kilesānaṃ dhunanaṭṭhenāti adhippāyo. Yassa bhikkhuno etāni samādānāni aṅgāni, etena paṭhamenāpi atthavikappena “natthi akusalaṃ dhutaṅga”nti dasseti. Na ca akusalaṃ kiñci dhunātīti akusalaṃ kiñci pāpaṃ na ca dhunāti eva appaṭipakkhato. Yesaṃ samādānānaṃ taṃ akusalaṃ ñāṇaṃ viya [M 1.0104] aṅganti katvā tāni dhutaṅgānīti vucceyyuṃ. Iminā dutiyenāpi atthavikappena “natthi akusalaṃ dhutaṅga”nti dasseti. Nāpi akusalantiādi tatiyaatthavikappavasena yojanā. Tasmātiādi vuttassevatthassa nigamanaṃ.

37. By way of trainees and ordinary people, they may be wholesome; by way of those whose cankers are destroyed, they may be indeterminate. Herein, trainees and ordinary people undertake the ascetic practices to fulfill the practice, while those whose cankers are destroyed undertake them for the sake of a comfortable abiding. 'Even unwholesome is an ascetic practice'—this implies that there is engagement in ascetic practices even with an unwholesome mind. This is not proper. For the state of being a forest-dweller for one gone forth with an unwholesome mind, that is not called a dhutaṅga. Why? Because it lacks the characteristic. That which is the quality of being a factor of the person who is 'shaken off,' or of knowledge, or of volition, due to the shaking off of defilements—that does not exist in unwholesome states. Therefore, merely by residing in the forest and so on, let them be forest-dwellers and the like, but they do not have the factors of forest-dwelling and so on. To show this meaning, it was said, 'Not by us,' and so forth. Herein, 'these' means the ascetic practices. This was stated below in the explanation of the meaning of the term. And no one is called 'shaken off' by means of the unwholesome; the intention is 'because of the meaning of shaking off defilements.' For whichever bhikkhu these undertakings are factors, by this first alternative meaning it is shown that 'there is no unwholesome ascetic practice.' 'And the unwholesome does not shake off anything' means: the unwholesome does not shake off any evil at all, because it is not an opponent. If, having considered that unwholesome state as a factor of those undertakings, like knowledge, they might be called dhutaṅgas—by this second alternative meaning also, it is shown that 'there is no unwholesome ascetic practice.' The connection of 'Nor the unwholesome,' and so forth, is by way of the third alternative meaning. 'Therefore,' and so forth, is the conclusion of the meaning already stated.

Yesanti abhayagirivāsike sandhāyāha. Te hi dhutaṅgaṃ nāma paññattīti vadanti. Tathā sati tassa paramatthato avijjamānattā kilesānaṃ dhunanaṭṭhopi na siyā, samādātabbatā cāti tesaṃ vacanaṃ pāḷiyā virujjhatīti dassetuṃ “kusalattikavinimutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā paññattipakkhe ete dosā dunnivārā, tasmā taṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ na gahetabbaṃ, vuttanayo cetanāpakkhoyeva gahetabboti attho. Yasmā ete dhutaguṇā kusalattike paṭhamatatiyapadasaṅgahitā, tasmā siyā sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, siyā adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, siyā vipākadhammadhammā, siyā nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammā, siyā anupādinnupādāniyā, siyā asaṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikāti evaṃ sesatikadukapadehipi nesaṃ yathārahaṃ saṅgaho vibhāvetabbo.

Saying 'Of which,' he spoke referring to the Abhayagirivāsins. For they say that the dhutaṅga is a concept. If that were so, then because of its non-existence in an ultimate sense, there would be no meaning of shaking off defilements, nor would it be something to be undertaken. To show that their statement contradicts the Pāḷi, it was said, 'Excluded from the wholesome triad,' and so forth. Therefore, because in the view that it is a concept these faults are hard to prevent, that statement of theirs should not be accepted. The meaning is that only the volition-based view, the method already stated, should be accepted. Because these dhuta qualities are included in the first and third terms of the wholesome triad, therefore they may be associated with pleasant feeling, or they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. They may be states that are kamma-results, or states that are neither kamma-results nor productive of kamma-results. They may be un-grasped but graspable, or undefiled but defiling. Thus, their inclusion in the remaining triad- and dyad-terms should be explained according to what is appropriate.

Kāmaṃ sabbopi arahā dhutakileso, idha pana dhutaṅgasevanāmukhena kilese vidhunitvā ṭhito khīṇāsavo “dhutakileso puggalo”ti adhippeto. Tathā sabbopi ariyamaggo nippariyāyena kilesadhunano dhammo, visesato aggamaggo. Pariyāyena pana vipassanāñāṇādi. Heṭṭhimaparicchedena dhutaṅgacetanāsampayuttañāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ dhutaṃ dassetvā dhutavāde dassetabbe yasmā dhutavādabhedena [V 1.0098] dhuto viya dhutabhedena dhutavādopi duvidho, tasmā tesaṃ, tadubhayapaṭikkhepassa ca vasena catukkamettha sambhavatīti taṃ dassetuṃ “atthi dhuto”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Indeed, every Arahant has shaken off defilements, but here it is one whose cankers are destroyed, who stands having shaken off defilements by means of practicing the dhutaṅgas, that is intended as 'a person with shaken-off defilements.' Likewise, every noble path is, in a definitive sense, a state that shakes off defilements, especially the highest path. In a figurative sense, it is insight-knowledge and so forth. By the lowest limit, the knowledge associated with the dhutaṅga-volition should be understood. Having thus explained the 'shaken-off,' when the 'advocate of the shaken-off practice' is to be explained: because, just as the shaken-off one is, as it were, twofold by the division of the advocate of the shaken-off practice, so too the advocate of the shaken-off practice is twofold by the division of the shaken-off one, therefore, by way of them and the rejection of both, a tetrad arises here. To show this, it was said, 'There is the shaken-off one,' and so forth.

Tayidanti nipāto, tassa “so aya”nti attho. Dhutadhammā nāmāti dhutaṅgasevanāya paṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ dhunanavasena pavattiyā “dhuto”ti laddhanāmāya dhutaṅgacetanāya upakārakā dhammāti katvā dhutadhammā nāma. Asampattasampattesu paccayesu alubbhanākārena pavattanato appicchatā santuṭṭhitā ca atthato alobho. Paccayagedhādihetukānaṃ lolatādīnaṃ saṃkilesānaṃ sammadeva likhanato [M 1.0105] chedanato gaṇasaṅgaṇikādibhedato saṃsaggato cittassa vivecanato sallekhatā pavivekatā ca alobho amohoti imesu dvīsu dhammesu anupatanti tadantogadhā tappariyāpannā honti, tadubhayasseva pavattivisesabhāvato. Imehi kusaladhammehi atthī idamatthī, yena ñāṇena pabbajitena nāma paṃsukūlikaṅgādīsu patiṭṭhitena bhavitabbanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ dhutaguṇe samādiyati ceva pariharati ca, taṃ ñāṇaṃ idamatthitā. Tenāha “idamatthitā ñāṇamevā”ti. Paṭikkhepavatthūsūti gahapaticīvarādīsu tehi tehi dhutaṅgehi paṭikkhipitabbavatthūsu. Lobhanti taṇhaṃ. Tesveva vāti paṭikkhepavatthūsu eva. Ādīnavapaṭicchādakanti ārakkhadukkhaparādhīnavutticorabhayādiādīnavapaṭicchādakaṃ. Anuññātānanti satthārā nicchandarāgaparibhogavasena anuññātānaṃ sukhasamphassaattharaṇapāvuraṇādīnaṃ. Paṭisevanamukhenāti paṭisevanadvārena, tena lesenāti attho. Atisallekhamukhenāti ativiya sallekhapaṭipattimukhena, ukkaṭṭhassa vattanakānampi paṭikkhipanavasenāti attho.

`Tayidaṃ` is a particle; its meaning is 'that this.' They are called 'dhutadhammas' because they are states that are helpful to the dhutaṅga-volition—which has received the name 'dhuta' (shaken off) due to its occurrence by way of shaking off evil states that are the opposition to the practice of dhutaṅgas. Because of occurring in the manner of non-greed towards requisites obtained and not yet obtained, fewness of wishes and contentment are, in essence, non-greed. Because of rightly scraping, cutting off, and secluding the mind from defilements such as fickleness, etc., caused by greed for requisites, etc., and from association with its divisions such as group-association, both effacement and seclusion fall into these two states, non-greed and non-delusion; they are included within them, comprised by them, because they are just specific modes of occurrence of those two. One who has need for these wholesome states is an `idamatthī`. `Idamatthitā` is the knowledge by which one who has gone forth, thinking, 'I should be established in practices such as wearing rag-robes,' undertakes and maintains the dhuta-qualities as instructed. That knowledge is `idamatthitā`. Therefore he said, '`Idamatthitā` is indeed knowledge.' 'In the objects of rejection' means: in the objects to be rejected by those respective dhutaṅgas, such as robes from householders. 'Greed' means craving. 'Or in those very things' means: precisely in the objects of rejection. 'Concealing the dangers' means: concealing the dangers such as the suffering of guarding, dependence on others for one's livelihood, and fear of thieves. 'Of the permitted things' means: of the things with pleasant contact such as floor-coverings and blankets, permitted by the Teacher for use without desire and lust. 'By means of using' means: through the door of using; the meaning is 'by that pretext.' 'By means of extreme effacement' means: by means of the practice of very extreme effacement; the meaning is 'by way of rejecting even the requisites allowable for an eminent practitioner.'

Sukhumakaraṇasannissayo rāgo dukkhāya paṭipattiyā patiṭṭhaṃ na labhatīti āha “dukkhāpaṭipadañca nissāya rāgo vūpasammatī”ti. Sallekho nāma sampajānassa hoti, satisampajaññe moho apatiṭṭhova appamādasambhavatoti vuttaṃ “sallekhaṃ nissāya appamattassa moho pahīyatī”ti. Etthāti etesu dhutaṅgesu. Tatthāti araññarukkhamūlesu.

Because lust, which is based on the requisites of comfort, does not gain a foothold in the difficult practice, he said: 'Relying on the difficult practice, lust is calmed.' Effacement is for one who is fully aware; and since heedfulness can arise when mindfulness and clear comprehension are present, delusion finds no footing. Therefore it was said: 'Relying on effacement, the delusion of one who is heedful is abandoned.' 'Herein' means 'among these dhutaṅgas.' 'Therein' means 'in the forest and at the roots of trees.'

Sīsaṅgānīti sīsabhūtāni aṅgāni, paresampi kesañci nānantarikatāya, sukaratāya ca saṅgaṇhanato uttamaṅgānīti attho. Asambhinnaṅgānīti kehici sambhedarahitāni, visuṃyeva aṅgānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhati rāgacaritassa mohacaritassa dosacaritassāpi, taṃ ekaccaṃ [V 1.0099] dhutaṅgaṃ sevantassāti adhippāyo. Hāyati kammaṭṭhānaṃ sukumārabhāvenalūkhapaṭipattiṃ asahantassa. Vaḍḍhateva mahāpurisajātikassāti adhippāyo. Na vaḍḍhati kammaṭṭhānaṃ upanissayarahitassa. Ekameva hi dhutaṅgaṃ yathā kilesadhunanaṭṭhena, evaṃ cetanāsabhāvattā. Tenāha “samādānacetanā”ti.

'Chief practices' (sīsaṅgāni) means practices that are like the head, that is, principal practices; because they gather in some other practices due to their inseparability and their being easy to do, they are the highest practices—this is the meaning. 'Unmixed practices' (asambhinnaṅgāni) means those free from mixture with any other practices; they are said to be just separate practices. The meditation subject increases for one of a greedy temperament, a deluded temperament, and also a hateful temperament, when that one practices a certain ascetic practice—this is the intention. The meditation subject declines for one who, due to being delicate, cannot endure the austere practice. It certainly increases for one of the nature of a great man—this is the intention. The meditation subject does not increase for one who is without a supporting condition. Indeed, just as an ascetic practice is one in the sense of shaking off defilements, so too it is one because of its nature as volition. Therefore, it is said: 'the volitions of undertaking.'

Terasāpi [M 1.0106] dhutaṅgāni samādāya pariharantānaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena “dvācattālīsa hontī”ti vatvā bhikkhūnaṃ terasannampi pariharaṇassa ekajjhaṃyeva sambhavaṃ dassetuṃ “sace hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “ekappahārena sabbadhutaṅgāni paribhuñjituṃ sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ abbhokāse viharantassa rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ? “Channaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti (visuddhi. 1.32) vacanato channe aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpitamatte dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati, na abbhokāse, tasmā bhedahetuno abhāvena tampi arogameva. Tathā senāsanaloluppassa abhāvena yathāsanthatikaṅganti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āraññikaṅgaṃ gaṇamhā ohīyanasikkhāpadena (pāci. 691-692) paṭikkhittaṃ, khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ anatirittabhojanasikkhāpadena (pāci. 238-240). Pavāritāya hi bhikkhuniyā atirittaṃ katvā bhuñjituṃ na labbhati. Kappiye ca vatthusmiṃ lolatāpahānāya dhutaṅgasamādānaṃ, na akappiye, sikkhāpadeneva paṭikkhittattā. Aṭṭheva honti bhikkhuniyā saṃkaccikacīvarādīhi saddhiṃ pañcapi ticīvarasaṅkhameva gacchantīti katvā. Yathāvuttesūti bhikkhūnaṃ vuttesu terasasu ticīvarādhiṭṭhānavinayakammābhāvato ṭhapetvā tecīvarikaṅgaṃ dvādasa sāmaṇerānaṃ. Sattāti bhikkhunīnaṃ vuttesu aṭṭhasu ekaṃ pahāya satta ticīvarādhiṭṭhānavinayakammābhāvato. “Ṭhapetvā tecīvarikaṅga”nti hi imaṃ anuvattamānameva katvā “satta sikkhamānasāmaṇerīna”nti vuttaṃ. Patirūpānīti upāsakabhāvassa anucchavikāni.

Having stated that 'there are forty-two' by way of the individuals who undertake and maintain the thirteen ascetic practices, the passage beginning 'if indeed' was spoken to show that it is possible for monks to maintain all thirteen simultaneously. Therein, it is said, 'One is able to practice all the ascetic practices at once.' How does the tree-root-dweller's practice apply to one dwelling in the open air? From the statement, 'I reject a roofed dwelling, I undertake the tree-root-dweller's practice,' the ascetic practice is broken at the mere rising of dawn under a roof, but not in the open air. Therefore, due to the absence of a cause for breaking, that practice too remains unbroken. Similarly, due to the absence of greed for lodgings, the any-lodging-user's practice should be understood to be unbroken. The forest-dweller's practice is rejected for nuns by the training rule on lagging behind the group, and the later-food-refuser's practice is rejected by the training rule on not eating leftover food. For a nun who has completed her meal, it is not allowed to eat food that has been made leftover. The undertaking of an ascetic practice is for abandoning greed in regard to an allowable object, not an unallowable one, as the latter is already rejected by a training rule itself. There are only eight for nuns, because even the five robes, together with the shoulder-cloth, etc., are included in the count of the 'three robes.' As for what was said: among the thirteen mentioned for monks, excluding the three-robe-wearer's practice due to the absence of the Vinaya act of determination of the three robes, there are twelve for male novices. Seven: among the eight mentioned for nuns, excluding one due to the absence of the Vinaya act of determination of the three robes, there are seven. For, having taken the phrase 'excluding the three-robe-wearer's practice' as continuing, it is said, 'seven for female probationers and female novices.' 'Suitable' means befitting the state of a male lay follower.

Dhutaṅganiddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the ascetic practices is concluded.

Iti dutiyaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the second chapter.

3. Kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Explanation of Taking Up Meditation Subjects

38. Appicchatādīhīti [M 1.0107][V 1.0100] appicchatāsantuṭṭhisallekhapavivekāpacayavīriyārambhādīhi. Pariyodāteti suvisuddhe nirupakkilese. Imasmiṃ sīleti yathāvutte catupārisuddhisīle. “Cittaṃ bhāvaya”nti imameva desanaṃ sandhāyāha “atisaṅkhepadesitattā”ti. Ko samādhīti sarūpapucchā. Kenaṭṭhena samādhīti kena atthena samādhīti vuccati, “samādhī”ti padaṃ kaṃ abhidheyyatthaṃ nissāya pavattanti attho. Katividhoti pabhedapucchā.

38. ‘With fewness of wishes, etc.’ means with fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, destroying of defilements, exertion of energy, and so on. ‘Purified’ means very pure, free from defilements. ‘In this virtue’ refers to the aforementioned fourfold purity of virtue. Referring to this very teaching, ‘Develop the mind,’ he said, ‘because it is taught too concisely.’ ‘What is concentration?’ is a question about its nature. ‘In what sense is it concentration?’ means: For what reason is it called ‘concentration’? Relying on what designative meaning does the word ‘concentration’ occur? This is the meaning. ‘How many kinds?’ is a question about its divisions.

“Ko samādhī”ti kāmañcāyaṃ sarūpapucchā, vibhāgavantānaṃ pana sarūpavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanamukheneva hotīti vibhāgo tāva anavasesato dassetabbo. Taṃdassane ca ayamādīnavoti dassetuṃ “samādhi bahuvidho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bahuvidhoti kusalādivasena anekavidho. Nānappakārakoti ālambanamanasikārachandapaṇidhiadhimokkhaabhinīhārasaññānānattādinānappakāro. Na sādheyyāti lokiyasamādhissa bhāvanā idha adhippetattho, tañca na sādheyya. Jhānavimokkhādīsu hi samādhiṃ uddharitvā tassa labbhamānehi vibhāgehi vissajjane kariyamāne jhānavibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 508 ādayo) āgato sabbo samādhipabhedo vissajjetabbo siyā. Tathā ca sati yvāyaṃ lokiyasamādhissa bhāvanāvidhi adhippeto, tassa vissajjanāya okāsova na bhaveyya. Kiñca yenassa tikacatukkajhānikena hīnādibhedabhinnena pavattivibhāgena brahmapārisajjādivasena navavidho, pañcamajjhānikena vehapphalādivasena dasavidho vā ekādasavidho vā bhavappabhedo nippajjati. Svāssa pavattivibhāgo ayaṃ soti niddhāretvā vuccamāno vikkhepāya siyā, yathā taṃ avisaye. Tenāha “uttari ca vikkhepāya saṃvatteyyā”ti. Kusalacittekaggatāti kusalā anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇā cittekaggatā.

‘What is concentration?’ Although this is a question about its nature, for things that have divisions, the explanation of their nature occurs only by means of showing the divisions. Therefore, the divisions should first be shown without remainder. And in showing them, to point out ‘this is the disadvantage,’ it was said, ‘Concentration is of many kinds,’ and so on. Therein, ‘of many kinds’ means of numerous kinds by way of the wholesome, etc. ‘Of various types’ means of various types due to the diversity of object, attention, wish, resolve, determination, aspiration, perception, and so on. ‘It would not accomplish’ means that the development of mundane concentration is the intended meaning here, and that would not be accomplished. For if, having extracted concentration from the absorptions, liberations, etc., an explanation were made with its available divisions, then the entire division of concentration that comes in the Jhānavibhaṅga and so on would have to be explained. And that being the case, there would be no opportunity at all for the explanation of the method for developing mundane concentration, which is what is intended. Furthermore, by its division of occurrence, which is differentiated by way of the threefold and fourfold absorptions, divided into inferior, etc., the ninefold division of existence by way of the Brahmā’s retinue, etc., is produced. By way of the fivefold absorption, the tenfold or elevenfold division of existence by way of the Vehapphala realm, etc., is produced. If that division of its occurrence were determined and stated as ‘this is it,’ it would be for distraction, just as something that is not the proper subject. Therefore, he said, ‘Moreover, it would lead to further distraction.’ ‘Wholesome one-pointedness of mind’ means one-pointedness of mind that is wholesome, characterized by being faultless and having a pleasant result.

Cittacetasikānaṃ samaṃ avisāravasena sampiṇḍentassa viya ādhānaṃ samādhānaṃ. Avisāralakkhaṇo [V 1.0101] hi samādhi, sampiṇḍanaraso ca. Sammā avikkhipanavasena ādhānaṃ samādhānaṃ. Avikkhepalakkhaṇo vā hi [M 1.0108] samādhi, vikkhepaviddhaṃsanaraso cāti. Svāyaṃ yasmā ekārammaṇe cittassa ṭhitihetu, tasmā “ṭhapananti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha. Tathā hesa “cittassa ṭhiti saṇṭhiti avaṭṭhitī”ti (dha. sa. 15) niddiṭṭho. Ekārammaṇaggahaṇañcettha samādhissa santānaṭṭhitibhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tathā hissa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dīpacciṭṭhiti nidassitā. Ānubhāvenāti balena, paccayabhāvenāti attho. Avikkhipamānāti na vikkhipamānā vūpasamamānā. Upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno hi samādhi. Etenassa vikkhepapaṭipakkhataṃ dasseti. Avippakiṇṇāti avisaṭā. Etena avisāralakkhaṇataṃ.

The placing, samādhāna, of mind and mental factors is the even placing, ādhāna, by way of non-scattering, like water binding soap powder. For concentration has the characteristic of non-scattering and the function of binding together. Or, the placing, samādhāna, is the correct placing, ādhāna, by way of non-distraction. For concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction and the function of destroying distraction. Because this concentration is the cause for the mind's stability on a single object, he therefore said, 'it is said to be establishing.' For this reason, it is expounded as 'stability, firm stability, and settled stability of mind.' And here, the taking up of 'single object' is for the purpose of showing the state of concentration's continuous stability. Thus, in its commentary, the stability of a lamp flame is given as an example. 'By power' means by strength; the meaning is by way of being a condition. 'Not being distracted' means not being distracted, being calmed. For concentration is manifest as tranquility. By this, he shows its state as the opponent of distraction. 'Unscattered' means not dispersed. By this, he shows its characteristic of non-scattering.

Sayaṃ na vikkhipati, sampayuttā vā na vikkhipanti etenāti avikkhepo, so lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti avikkhepalakkhaṇo. Vikkhepaṃ viddhaṃseti, tathā vā sampajjatīti vikkhepaviddhaṃsanaraso. Uddhacce avikampanavasena paccupatiṭṭhati, sampayuttānaṃ vā taṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti avikampanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Sukhanti nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It is not distracted itself, or associated states are not distracted by it; therefore, it is non-distraction. That is its characteristic; therefore, it has the characteristic of non-distraction. It destroys distraction, or it is accomplished in that way; therefore, its function is the destroying of distraction. It is manifest by way of non-agitation in the face of restlessness, or it causes that to be manifest for its associated states; therefore, its manifestation is non-agitation. 'Happiness' should be understood as happiness that is non-carnal.

39. Avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ nāma samādhissa āveṇiko sabhāvo, na tenassa koci vibhāgo labbhatīti āha “avikkhepalakkhaṇena tāva ekavidho”ti. Sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe appento viya pavattatīti vitakko appanā. Tathā hi so “appanā byappanā”ti (dha. sa. 7) niddiṭṭho. Tappamukhatāvasena pana sabbasmiṃ mahaggatānuttare jhānadhamme “appanā”ti aṭṭhakathāvohāro. Tathā tassa anuppattiṭṭhānabhūte parittajhāne upacāravohāro. Gāmādīnaṃ samīpaṭṭhāne gāmūpacārādisamaññā viyāti āha “upacārappanāvasena duvidho”ti. Idha pana samādhivasena veditabbaṃ. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti vuccati vaṭṭaṃ, tappariyāpannatāya loke niyutto, tattha vā viditoti lokiyo. Tattha apariyāpannatāya lokato uttaro uttiṇṇoti lokuttaro. Kāmañcettha lokiyasamādhi bhāvetabbabhāvena gayhati, ubhayaṃ pana ekajjhaṃ gahetvā tato itaraṃ niddhāretuṃ “lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidho”ti vuttaṃ. Sappītikanippītikavasenāti saha pītiyā vattatīti sappītiko, pītisampayutto. Natthi etassa pītīti nippītiko, pītivippayutto. Tesaṃ vasena. Sukhena saha ekuppādādibhāvaṃ gatoti sukhasahagato[M 1.0109], sukhasampayuttoti attho. Upekkhāsahagatepi eseva nayo. Upekkhāti cettha adukkhamasukhavedanā adhippetā. Sā hi sukhadukkhākārapavattiṃ upekkhati majjhattākārasaṇṭhitattā. Sukhasahagata-padena [V 1.0102] cettha sappītiko, nippītikekadeso ca saṅgahito, upekkhāsahagata-padena pana nippītikekadesovāti ayametesaṃ padānaṃ viseso.

39. The characteristic of non-distraction is the unique, intrinsic nature of concentration; by that characteristic, no division of it is obtained. Therefore, he said, 'Firstly, by the characteristic of non-distraction, it is of one kind.' Because it occurs as if applying the associated states to the object, applied thought (vitakka) is called application (appanā). For so it is expounded as 'application, thorough application.' But by way of that applied thought being primary, the term 'application' is the usage in the commentary for all sublime and supramundane absorption-states. Similarly, for the limited absorption which is not the place of its arising, the term 'access' is used, just like the term 'village-access' for the vicinity of a village. Therefore, he said, 'It is twofold by way of access and application.' Here, however, it should be understood by way of concentration. The round of existence (vaṭṭa) is called 'world' (loka) in the sense of crumbling and utterly crumbling. Because of being included in that, it is connected with the world, or it is known therein; therefore, it is mundane (lokiya). Because of not being included therein, it is superior to, has escaped from, the world; therefore, it is supramundane (lokuttara). And although here mundane concentration is taken as that which is to be developed, having taken both together, in order to distinguish the other from it, it was said, 'It is twofold by way of mundane and supramundane.' By way of with-joy and without-joy: that which occurs together with joy (pīti) is 'with-joy,' associated with joy. That which has no joy is 'without-joy,' dissociated from joy. By way of these. It has reached the state of co-arising, etc., with pleasure (sukha); therefore, it is 'accompanied by pleasure,' meaning associated with pleasure. The same method applies to 'accompanied by equanimity.' And here by 'equanimity,' neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is intended. For that feeling, because it is established in a neutral manner, regards with equanimity the occurrence in the manner of pleasure and pain. And here, by the term 'accompanied by pleasure,' both the with-joy type and a part of the without-joy type are included. But by the term 'accompanied by equanimity,' only a part of the without-joy type is included. This is the difference between these terms.

Sabhāvato, paccayato, phalato ca majjhimapaṇītehi nihīno, tesaṃ vā guṇehi parihīnoti hīno, attano paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nīto paṇīto, ubhinnaṃ majjhe bhavo majjhimo. Sampayogavasena pavattamānena saha vitakkena savitakko, saha vicārena savicāro, savitakko ca so savicāro cāti savitakkasavicāro. Ādi-saddena avitakkavicāramatto, avitakkāvicāro ca gahito. Tattha vicārato uttari vitakkena sampayogābhāvato avitakko ca so vicāramatto cāti avitakkavicāramatto. Visesanivattiattho vā matta-saddo. Savitakkasavicāro hi samādhi vitakkavisiṭṭhena vicārena savicāro, ayaṃ pana vicāramattena vitakkasaṅkhātavisesarahitena, tasmā avitakkavicāramatto. Atha vā bhāvanāya pahīnattā vitakkābhāvenāyaṃ vicāramatto, na vicārato aññassa attano sampayuttadhammassa kassaci abhāvāti dassetuṃ avitakka-vacanena vicāramatta-padaṃ visesetvā vuttaṃ. Ubhayarahito avitakkāvicāro. Pītisahagatādivasenāti pītisahagatasukhasahagataupekkhāsahagatavasena. Yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ sukhasahagataduke vuttanayameva. Paṭipakkhehi samantato khaṇḍitattā paritto. Parittanti vā appamattakaṃ vuccati, ayampi appānubhāvatāya paritto viyāti paritto. Kilesavikkhambhanato, vipulaphalato, dīghasantānato ca mahantabhāvaṃ gato, mahantehi vā uḷāracchandādīhi gato paṭipannoti mahaggato. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasenāpi natthi etassa pamāṇakaradhammā, tesaṃ vā paṭipakkhoti appamāṇo.

By its intrinsic nature, by its cause, and by its result, it is inferior to the middling and sublime; or, being devoid of their qualities, it is 'inferior' (hīna). Led to a state of prominence by its own causes, it is 'sublime' (paṇīta). Arising in the middle of both, it is 'middling' (majjhima). It is 'with thought' (savitakka) because it is together with thought that occurs by way of association. It is 'with examination' (savicāra) because it is together with examination. It is with thought and it is with examination, thus it is 'with thought and with examination' (savitakkasavicāra). By the word 'etc.' (ādi), 'merely with examination without thought' and 'without thought and without examination' are also included. Therein, because there is no association with thought beyond examination, it is without thought and is merely with examination; thus, it is 'merely with examination without thought' (avitakkavicāramatta). Alternatively, the word 'merely' (matta) has the meaning of excluding a distinction. Indeed, the concentration that is with thought and with examination is 'with examination' by means of examination distinguished by thought; this concentration, however, is so by means of mere examination, which is devoid of the distinction called thought. Therefore, it is 'merely with examination without thought'. Or, because thought has been abandoned through development, this is 'merely with examination' due to the absence of thought. To show that this is not because of the absence of any other associated state of its own apart from examination, the term 'merely with examination' is specified by the word 'without thought'. Devoid of both, it is 'without thought and without examination' (avitakkāvicāra). 'By way of being accompanied by joy, etc.' means by way of being accompanied by joy, accompanied by happiness, and accompanied by equanimity. Whatever should be said here follows the same method as was stated in the dyad on 'accompanied by happiness'. Because it is cut off on all sides by opposing factors, it is 'limited' (paritta). Or, 'limited' is said of what is minor; this concentration, too, due to having little power, is like something minor, thus it is 'limited'. Because it suppresses the defilements and has extensive fruit, it has reached a state of greatness. Or, because it is gone to and practiced by great ones with noble aspirations, etc., it is 'greatly attained' (mahaggata). Even by way of making an object, there are no limiting factors for it; or, it is the opposite of them, thus it is 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa).

Paṭipajjati jhānaṃ etāyāti paṭipadā, pubbabhāgabhāvanā. Dukkhā kicchā paṭipadā etassāti dukkhāpaṭipado. Pakatipaññāya abhivisiṭṭhattā abhiññā nāma appanāvahā bhāvanāpaññā, dandhā mandā abhiññā etassāti dandhābhiñño. Dukkhāpaṭipado ca so dandhābhiñño cāti dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiñño[M 1.0110], samādhi. Tadādivasena. Catujhānaṅgavasenāti catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ aṅgabhāvavasena, catukkanayavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Hānabhāgiyādivasenāti hānakoṭṭhāsikādivasena.

One reaches jhāna by this, thus it is the 'path' (paṭipadā); this refers to the preliminary-part development. The practice for this one is difficult and painful, thus he is 'one with difficult practice' (dukkhāpaṭipado). Because it is more distinguished than ordinary wisdom, the developmental wisdom that brings absorption is called 'higher knowledge' (abhiññā). The higher knowledge for this one is slow and dull, thus he is 'one with slow higher knowledge' (dandhābhiñño). He is one with difficult practice and he is one with slow higher knowledge, thus he is 'one with difficult practice and slow higher knowledge' (dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiñño); this refers to concentration. By way of that, etc. 'By way of the four jhāna factors' means by way of being factors of the four jhānas; and this is said by the method of the tetrad. 'By way of the portion of decline, etc.' means by way of the portion pertaining to decline, etc.

Samādhiekakadukavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Concentration in Singles and Dyads

Channaṃ [V 1.0103] anussatiṭṭhānānanti buddhānussatiādīnaṃ channaṃ anussatikammaṭṭhānānaṃ. Imesaṃ vasenāti imesaṃ dasannaṃ kammaṭṭhānānaṃ vasena. “Pubbabhāge ekaggatā”ti iminā appanāya upakārakanānāvajjanupacārassapi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, na ekāvajjanasseva. Appanāsamādhīnanti upakattabbaupakārakasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ “purisassa attho”tiādīsu viya. Parikammanti gotrabhu. Aparitto samādhīti dassetuṃ “paṭhamassa jhānassā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Of the six bases for recollection' means of the six meditation subjects of recollection beginning with the recollection of the Buddha. 'By means of these' means by means of these ten meditation subjects. By 'one-pointedness in the preliminary part', the inclusion of access concentration with varied advertence, which is helpful for absorption, should also be understood, not only that with a single advertence. The genitive case in 'of absorption concentrations' (appanāsamādhīnaṃ) is used in the sense of the relationship between that which is helped and that which helps, as in 'the man's purpose', etc. 'Preliminary work' (parikamma) means change-of-lineage (gotrabhu). To show that the concentration is not limited, 'of the first jhāna', etc., is said.

Tīsu bhūmīsūti kāmarūpārūpabhūmīsu. Kusalacittekaggatāya adhippetattā “ariyamaggasampayuttā”ti vuttaṃ. Siyā sappītiko, siyā nippītikoti aniyamavacanaṃ upacārasamādhisāmaññena sabbesampi vā jhānānaṃ nānāvajjanavīthiyaṃ upacārasamādhi siyā sappītiko, siyā nippītiko. Ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ pana ādito dukatikajjhānānaṃ upacārasamādhi sappītikova, itaresaṃ nippītikova, visabhāgavedanassa cittassa āsevanapaccayatābhāvato, ekavīthiyaṃ vedanāparivattanābhāvato ca. Siyā sukhasahagato, siyā upekkhāsahagatoti etthāpi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Tattha pana “dukatikajjhānāna”nti vuttaṃ, idha “tikacatukkajjhānāna”nti vattabbaṃ.

'In the three planes' means in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial planes. Because one-pointedness of wholesome consciousness is intended, it is said to be 'associated with the noble path'. 'It may be with joy, it may be without joy' is an indefinite statement, due to the generality of access concentration. Or, for all jhānas, in a cognitive process with varied advertence, the access concentration may be with joy or may be without joy. In a cognitive process with a single advertence, however, the access concentration of the first two or three jhānas is only with joy, while that of the others is only without joy. This is because a consciousness with a dissimilar feeling does not have the nature of a repetition condition, and because there is no change of feeling in a single cognitive process. In the case of 'It may be accompanied by happiness, it may be accompanied by equanimity', here too the meaning should be understood by the method already stated. However, there 'of the two or three jhānas' was said; here 'of the three or four jhānas' should be said.

Samādhitikavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Triad on Concentration.

Paṭiladdhamattoti adhigatamatto anāsevito abahulīkato. So hi paridubbalabhāvena hīno hoti. Nātisubhāvitoti ativiya paguṇabhāvaṃ apāpito. Subhāvitoti suṭṭhu bhāvito sammadeva paguṇataṃ upanīto. Tenāha “vasippatto”ti. Chandādīnaṃ hīnatādivasenāpi imesaṃ hīnāditā veditabbā. Tathā hi uḷārapuññaphalakāmatāvasena pavattito hīno, lokiyābhiññāsampādanāya pavattito majjhimo, vivekakāmatāya ariyabhāve ṭhitena pavattito paṇīto[M 1.0111]. Attahitāya bhavasampattiatthaṃ pavattito vā hīno, kevalaṃ alobhajjhāsayena pavattito majjhimo, parahitāya pavattito paṇīto. Vaṭṭajjhāsayena vā pavattito hīno, vivekajjhāsayena pavattito majjhimo, vivaṭṭajjhāsayena lokuttarapādakatthaṃ pavattito paṇīto.

“Just obtained” means merely attained, uncultivated, not made much of. For it is inferior due to its extreme feebleness. “Not well-developed” means not brought to a state of great proficiency. “Well-developed” means thoroughly cultivated, properly brought to a state of proficiency. Hence it is said, “mastery attained.” The inferiority, mediocrity, and excellence of these should also be understood in terms of the inferiority, etc., of zeal and other factors. For example: Inferior when it proceeds by way of the desire for the fruit of great merit; Middling when it proceeds for the accomplishment of mundane higher knowledges; Superior when it proceeds by one established in the noble state with a desire for seclusion. Or inferior when it proceeds for one's own welfare, for the attainment of existence; Middling when it proceeds solely with the disposition of non-greed; Superior when it proceeds for the welfare of others. Or inferior when it proceeds with the disposition towards the round of existence; Middling when it proceeds with the disposition towards seclusion; Superior when it proceeds with the disposition towards that which is free from the round, for the purpose of being a foundation for the supramundane.

Saddhiṃ upacārasamādhināti sabbesampi jhānānaṃ upacārasamādhinā saha. Vitakkamatteyeva ādīnavaṃ [V 1.0104] disvāti vitakkeyeva oḷārikato upaṭṭhahante “cittassa khobhakaradhammo aya”nti ādīnavaṃ disvā vicārañca santato manasi karitvā. Tenāha “vicāre adisvā”ti. Taṃ sandhāyāti taṃ evaṃ paṭiladdhaṃ samādhiṃ sandhāya. Etaṃ “avitakkavicāramatto samādhī”ti dutiyapadaṃ vuttaṃ. Tīsūti ādito tīsu.

“Together with access concentration” means together with the access concentration of all the jhānas. “Having seen the drawback in initial application alone” means that when initial application itself appears coarsely, seeing the drawback, “This is a factor that disturbs the mind,” and having attended to sustained application as tranquil. Therefore it is said, “not having seen [the drawback] in sustained application.” “Referring to that” means referring to that concentration thus obtained. It is with reference to this that the second term, “concentration with only sustained application and without initial application,” is stated. “Among the three” means among the first three.

Tesvevāti tesu eva catukkapañcakanayesu. Tatiye catuttheti catukkanaye tatiye, pañcakanaye catuttheti yojetabbaṃ. Avasāneti dvīsupi nayesu pariyosānajjhāne. Yathākkamaṃ catutthe, pañcame vā. Pītisukhasahagato vāti etthāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Ettha ca satipi pītisahagatassāpi samādhissa sukhasahagatatte tīṇipi padāni asaṅkarato dassetuṃ nippītikasukhato sappītikasukhassa visesadassanatthaṃ satthu pītitikadesanāti nippītikasseva sukhassa vasena sukhasahagato samādhi gahitoti daṭṭhabbo.

“In those very ones” means in those very fourfold and fivefold systems. “In the third, in the fourth” should be connected as: in the third in the fourfold system, and in the fourth in the fivefold system. “At the end” means in the final jhāna in both systems, respectively, the fourth or the fifth. “Or accompanied by joy and pleasure”—here too, the meaning should be understood in the way stated previously. And here, even though concentration accompanied by joy is also accompanied by pleasure, in order to show the three terms without confusion, and to show the distinction of pleasure accompanied by joy from pleasure without joy, the Teacher's teaching is the triad on joy; therefore, it should be understood that “concentration accompanied by pleasure” is taken by way of pleasure that is without joy.

Upacārabhūmiyanti upacārajjhānasampayuttacittuppāde. Cittuppādo hi sahajātadhammānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānatāya “bhūmī”ti vuccati “sukhabhūmiyaṃ kāmāvacare”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 988) viya. Paritto samādhi kāmāvacarabhāvato.

“In the access plane” means in the occurrence of consciousness associated with access jhāna. For an occurrence of consciousness is called a “plane” because it is the place of origin for co-arisen states, just as in instances such as “in the plane of pleasure, in the sense-sphere,” etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 988). Concentration is limited because of its sense-sphere nature.

Samādhicatukkavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Tetrad on Concentration.

Paṭhamasamannāhāro bhāvanaṃ ārabhantassa “pathavī pathavī”tiādinā kammaṭṭhāne paṭhamābhiniveso. Tassa tassa jhānassa upacāranti nīvaraṇavitakkavicāranikantiādīnaṃ vūpasame thirabhūtaṃ kāmāvacarajjhānaṃ. “Yāva appanā”ti iminā pubbabhāgapaññāya eva abhiññābhāvo vutto viya dissatīti vadanti[M 1.0112]. Appanāpaññā pana abhiññāva. Yadaggena hi pubbabhāgapaññāya dandhasīghatā, tadaggena appanāpaññāyapīti. Samudācāragahaṇatāyāti samudācārassa gahaṇabhāvena, pavattibāhullatoti attho. Asukhāsevanāti kasirabhāvanā.

The first application of mind for one beginning meditation with “earth, earth,” etc., is the first engagement with the meditation subject. The access concentration of that jhāna, with the calming of the hindrances, initial thought, sustained thought, delight, and so on, becomes stable as a sense-sphere jhāna. They say that by “as far as absorption,” it seems as if the state of higher knowledge is stated only for preliminary-stage wisdom. But absorption wisdom is indeed higher knowledge. For by whatever degree the preliminary-stage wisdom is slow or quick, by that degree is the absorption wisdom also. By 'because of the complexity of its occurrence' is meant due to the complex nature of its arising; the meaning is 'because of the abundance of its occurrence.' 'Not cultivating ease' means arduous development.

Palibodhupacchedādīnīti ādi-saddena bhāvanāvidhānāparihāpanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Asappāyasevīti upacārādhigamato pubbe asappāyasevitāya dukkhā paṭipadā. Pacchā asappāyasevitāya dandhā abhiññā hoti. Sappāyasevinoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pubbabhāgeti upacārajjhānādhigamato [V 1.0105] orabhāge. Aparabhāgeti tato uddhaṃ. Tassa vomissakatāti yo pubbabhāge asappāyaṃ sevitvā aparabhāge sappāyasevī, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā. Itarassa sukhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā hoti. Evaṃ paṭhamacatutthānaṃ vomissakatāya dutiyatatiyāti attho. Akatapalibodhupacchedassa saparipanthatāya paṭipadā dukkhā hoti, itarassa sukhā. Asampāditaappanākosallassa ñāṇassa avisadatāya dandhā abhiññā hoti, visadatāya khippā abhiññā.

“By cutting off obstacles, etc.”—by the word “etc.” is included not neglecting the method of development, and so on. For one who associates with the unsuitable: before the attainment of access concentration, due to associating with the unsuitable, the practice is difficult. Afterwards, due to associating with the unsuitable, the higher knowledge is slow. For one who associates with the suitable, this same method applies. By 'in the preliminary stage' is meant the stage before the attainment of access jhāna. By 'in the later stage' is meant the stage above that. Regarding the mixing of these: for one who, having associated with the unsuitable in the preliminary stage, associates with the suitable in the later stage, for him the practice is difficult and the higher knowledge is quick. For the other, the practice is pleasant and the higher knowledge is slow. Thus, the meaning is that by the mixing of the first and fourth, the second and third [types of practice] come to be. For one who has not cut off the obstacles, because of the presence of dangers, the practice is difficult; for the other, it is pleasant. For one who has not accomplished skill in absorption, due to the lack of clarity of the knowledge, the higher knowledge is slow; for the other, due to its clarity, the higher knowledge is quick.

Taṇhāavijjāvasenāti taṇhāavijjānaṃ abhibhavānabhibhavavasena. Samathavipassanādhikāravasenāti samathavipassanāsu asato, sato ca adhikārassa vasena. Taṇhāya samādhissa ujupaṭipakkhattā sā samathapaṭipadāya paripanthinīti āha “taṇhābhibhūtassa hi dukkhā paṭipadā hotī”ti. Abhibhavo cassā itarakilesehi adhikatāya anabhibhūtassa taṇhāyāti adhikārato veditabbaṃ. Tathā avijjā paññāya ujupaṭipakkhāti tadabhibhūtassa dandhābhiññatā vuttā. Akatādhikāroti bhavantare akataparicayo yathā paguṇaṃ katvā vissaṭṭhagantho appamattakena payogena suppavatti vācuggatova hoti, evaṃ pubbe kataparicayassa bhāvanā appakasireneva ijjhatīti āha “katādhikārassa sukhā”ti. Svāyaṃ akato, kato ca adhikāro samathanissito paṭipadāyaṃ vutto samādhippadhānattā paṭipadāya. Vipassanānissito abhiññāyaṃ ñāṇappadhānattā appanāya. Kilesindriyavasenāti tikkhātikkhānaṃ kilesindriyānaṃ vasena. Tenāha “tibbakilesassā”tiādi[M 1.0113]. Tattha kilesā kāmacchandādayo, indriyāni saddhādīni.

By 'by way of craving and ignorance' is meant by way of the overcoming or not overcoming of craving and ignorance. By 'by way of the foundation in serenity and insight' is meant by way of the absence or presence of a foundation in serenity and insight. Since craving is a direct opponent of concentration, it is an enemy to the path of serenity; thus it is said, 'For one overcome by craving, the practice is difficult.' And its overcoming is due to its being more excessive than other defilements; that for one not overcome by craving [the path is pleasant] should be understood from the context. Similarly, ignorance is a direct opponent of wisdom; thus, for one overcome by it, the state of having slow higher knowledge is stated. 'One who has not made the foundation' means one who has not cultivated familiarity in a previous existence. Just as a text that one had previously mastered and then set aside is easily made to proceed well and is recited from memory with little effort, so too for one who has previously cultivated familiarity, the development succeeds with little difficulty; thus it is said, 'For one who has made the foundation, it is pleasant.' This foundation, unmade and made, when based on serenity, is spoken of in relation to the path, because of the predominance of concentration for the path. When based on insight, it is spoken of in relation to higher knowledge, because of the predominance of wisdom for absorption. By 'by way of defilements and faculties' is meant by way of keen and unkeen defilements and faculties. Therefore it is said, 'For one with strong defilements,' etc. Therein, the defilements are sensual desire and so on; the faculties are faith and so on.

Yathāvuttā paṭipadābhiññā puggalādhiṭṭhānāti dhammaniddesampi puggalādhiṭṭhānamukhena dassetuṃ “yo puggalo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Appaguṇoti na subhāvito vasībhāvaṃ apāpito. Tenāha “uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkotī”ti. Ayaṃ parittoti ayaṃ samādhi appānubhāvatāya paritto. Avaḍḍhiteti ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi na vaḍḍhite yathāupaṭṭhite ārammaṇe. Ekaṅgulamattampi hi vaḍḍhitaṃ appamāṇamevāti vadanti. “Paguṇo subhāvito”ti vatvā “uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ sakkotī”ti iminā yathā paguṇopi uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ asakkonto samādhi parittoyeva hoti, na appamāṇo, evaṃ ñāṇuttarassa ekāsaneneva uparijhānanibbattanenāti subhāvitopi uparijhānassa paccayabhāvasaṅkhātāya subhāvitakiccasiddhiyā “appamāṇo”tveva vuccati. Apare pana sace subhāvito paguṇo vasībhāvaṃ patto [V 1.0106] uparijhānassa paccayo ahontopi appamāṇo eva, pamāṇakarānaṃ rāgādipaṭipakkhānaṃ suvidūrabhāvatoti vadanti. Vuttalakkhaṇavomissatāyāti yo appaguṇo uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, vaḍḍhite ārammaṇe pavatto, ayaṃ paritto appamāṇārammaṇo. Yo pana paguṇo uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ sakkoti, avaḍḍhite ārammaṇe pavatto, ayaṃ appamāṇo parittārammaṇoti evaṃ paṭhamacatutthasamādhīnaṃ vuttalakkhaṇassa vomissakabhāvena dutiyatatiyasamādhisaṅgāhako vomissakanayo veditabbo.

As has been stated, the path and higher knowledge are founded on the individual; therefore, to show the exposition of the Dhamma also by way of the individual as the main foundation, it is said, 'Which person,' etc. 'Not proficient' means not well-developed, not brought to a state of mastery. Therefore it is said, 'it is not able to become a condition for a higher jhāna.' 'This is limited' means this concentration is limited due to its small power. 'In an un-increased [object]' means in an object that has not been increased even by the measure of one or two finger-breadths, but remains as it appeared. For they say that an object increased even by the measure of one finger-breadth is indeed measureless. Having said, 'proficient, well-developed,' and by this, 'is able to become a condition for a higher jhāna,' [the meaning is this]: just as even a proficient concentration, when it is unable to become a condition for a higher jhāna, is indeed limited, not measureless, so too for one with superior knowledge, when a higher jhāna is produced in a single sitting, even a concentration that is not very well-developed is called 'measureless' due to the accomplishment of the function of being well-developed, which is reckoned as the state of being a condition for a higher jhāna. Others, however, say that if a concentration is well-developed, proficient, and has reached a state of mastery, even if it is not a condition for a higher jhāna, it is still measureless, because the limiting factors which are opponents, such as lust, are very far away. By 'due to the mixing of the stated characteristics': that concentration which is not proficient and is unable to become a condition for a higher jhāna, but which occurs in an increased object—this is 'limited with a measureless object'. But that concentration which is proficient and is able to become a condition for a higher jhāna, but which occurs in an un-increased object—this is 'measureless with a limited object'. In this way, the mixed method which includes the second and third concentrations should be understood by the mixing of the stated characteristics of the first and fourth concentrations.

Tatoti tato paṭhamajjhānato uddhaṃ. Virattapītikanti atikkantapītikaṃ vā jigucchitapītikaṃ vā. Avayavo samudāyassa aṅganti vuccati, “senaṅgaṃ rathaṅga”ntiādīsu viyāti āha “catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ aṅgabhūtā cattāro samādhī”ti.

From that, meaning from the first jhāna upwards. 'Having dispassion for joy' means either having transcended joy or being disgusted with joy. A part is called a limb of a whole, as in 'a limb of an army,' 'a part of a chariot,' and so on. Thus it is said, 'The four concentrations that are the limbs of the four jhānas.'

Hānaṃ bhajatīti hānabhāgiyo, hānabhāgo vā etassa atthīti hānabhāgiyo, parihānakoṭṭhāsikoti attho. Ālayassa apekkhāya apariccajanato ṭhitiṃ bhajatīti ṭhitibhāgiyo. Visesaṃ bhajatīti visesabhāgiyo. Paccanīkasamudācāravasenāti tassa tassa [M 1.0114] jhānassa paccanīkānaṃ nīvaraṇavitakkavicārādīnaṃ pavattivasena. Tadanudhammatāyāti tadanurūpabhūtāya satiyā. Saṇṭhānavasenāti saṇṭhahanavasena patiṭṭhānavasena. “Sā pana tadassādasaṅkhātā, tadassādasampayuttakkhandhasaṅkhātā vā micchāsatī”ti sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 799) vuttaṃ. Tattha sāpekkhassa upari visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā avigatanikantikā taṃtaṃpariharaṇasatītipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Evañca katvā “satiyā vā nikantiyā vā”ti vikappavacanañca yuttaṃ hoti. Visesādhigamavasenāti visesādhigamassa paccayabhāvavasena, visesaṃ vā adhigacchati etenāti visesādhigamo, tassa vasena. Nibbidāsahagatasaññāmanasikārasamudācāravasenāti ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamanibbindanañāṇasampayuttasaññāya ca ābhogassa ca pavattivasena. Nibbedhabhāgiyatāti saccānaṃ nibbijjhanapakkhikatā vipassanāya saṃvattatīti attho.

It resorts to decline, therefore it is of the portion of decline; or, a portion of decline exists for it, therefore it is of the portion of decline; the meaning is: having a share in deterioration. Due to not abandoning longing, which is attachment, it resorts to stability, therefore it is of the portion of stability. It resorts to distinction, therefore it is of the portion of distinction. 'By way of the occurrence of opposing factors': that is, by way of the arising of hindrances, initial thought, sustained thought, and so on, which are opposed to each respective jhāna. 'By way of its nature of conformity': that is, by mindfulness that has become conformable to that. 'By way of establishment': that is, by way of being well-established, by way of being founded. 'But that is wrong mindfulness, designated as delight in that, or designated as the aggregate associated with delight in that,' is stated in the Sammohavinodanī. In that context, because one with longing is unable to produce a higher distinction, it is also fit to say that it is the mindfulness that maintains that respective state, which has not abandoned craving. And having considered thus, the alternative expression 'by mindfulness or by craving' is also suitable. 'By way of the attainment of distinction': that is, by way of being a condition for the attainment of distinction; or, one attains distinction by this, therefore it is the attainment of distinction; by way of that. 'By way of the occurrence of perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment': that is, by way of the arising of perception associated with the knowledge of disenchantment which is preceded by seeing the danger, and of attention. 'The state of being of the portion of penetration': the meaning is, it is the state of being on the side of penetrating the truths; it leads to insight.

Kāmasahagatāti kāmārammaṇā, kāmasaññāhi vā vokiṇṇā. Avitakkasahagatāti “kathaṃ nu kho me avitakkaṃ jhānaṃ bhaveyyā”ti evaṃ avitakkārammaṇā avitakkavisayā. Kāmañcāyaṃ “paṭhamassa jhānassā”tiādiko pāṭho paññāvasena āgato, samādhissāpi panettha saṅgaho [V 1.0107] atthevāti udāharaṇassa sātthakataṃ dassetuṃ “tāya pana paññāya sampayuttā samādhīpi cattāro hontī”ti tesaṃ vasena evaṃ vuttanti attho.

‘Accompanied by the sensual sphere’: that is, having an object of the sensual sphere, or being mixed with perceptions of the sensual sphere. ‘Accompanied by that which is without initial thought’: that is, with the thought, 'How, indeed, might a jhāna without initial thought be for me?'; thus, having that which is without initial thought as its object, having it as its domain. And although this passage, 'of the first jhāna,' etc., comes by way of wisdom, the inclusion of concentration here also certainly exists. Therefore, to show that the example is meaningful, it is said, 'The concentrations associated with that wisdom also become four'; the meaning is that it was stated thus by way of them.

Bhāvanāmayassa samādhissa idhādhippetattā upacārekaggatā “kāmāvacaro samādhī”ti vuttaṃ. Adhipatiṃ karitvāti “chandavato ce samādhi hoti, mayhampi evaṃ hotī”ti chandaṃ adhipatiṃ, chandaṃ dhuraṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā. Labhati samādhinti evaṃ yaṃ samādhiṃ labhati, ayaṃ vuccati chandasamādhi, chandādhipatisamādhīti attho. Evaṃ vīriyasamādhiādayopi veditabbā.
