For here, the arising of access concentration is by the breaking of the boundary only, not by the arising of the sign. If so, how can the jhāna have a limited object, etc.? He said, 'The state of having a limited or immeasurable object here is also by way of grasping.' Having grasped a few beings, loving-kindness and so on, which proceed, have a limited object; having grasped many, they have an immeasurable object—this is the meaning. Space, being merely what is revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa, should not be developed—this is the connection. Or, it should be connected with what will be said. Only a conceptually constructed object can be developed, not another—thus he said, 'for it is not possible to develop a natural phenomenon.' The limited or immeasurable objectivity of the formless attainments should be understood by their proceeding in the space revealed by the removal of a limited kasiṇa or a vast kasiṇa. The remaining are the ten meditation subjects beginning with the recollection of the Buddha. 'Because they are without a sign' means because of the absence of a counterpart sign.

Paṭibhāganimittārammaṇānīti paṭibhāganimittabhūtāni ārammaṇāni. Sesāni aṭṭhārasa. Sesāni chāti cattāro brahmavihārā, ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, ākiñcaññāyatananti imāni sesāni cha. Vissandamānapubbatāya vipubbakaṃ. Paggharamānalohitatāya lohitakaṃ. Kimīnaṃ pacalanena puḷuvakaṃ, calitārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Vātapānavivarādīhi antopaviṭṭhassa sūriyālokādikassa calanākāro paññāyatīti obhāsamaṇḍalārammaṇampi calitārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Pubbabhāgeti paṭibhāganimittappavattiyā pubbabhāge. Sannisinnamevāti santaṃ niccalameva.

'Objects that are counterpart signs' means objects that have become counterpart signs. The remaining are eighteen. 'The remaining six' are: the four divine abodes, the base of infinite space, and the base of nothingness—these are the remaining six. Because of the state of having flowing pus, the festering corpse. Because of the state of having oozing blood, the bloody corpse. Because of the movement of worms, the worm-infested corpse is called a moving object. Because the manner of movement of sunlight and so on that has entered inside through openings such as a window is perceived, the object of the light-circle is also called a moving object. 'In the preliminary part' means in the preliminary part of the arising of the counterpart sign. 'Perfectly settled' means calm and indeed motionless.

Devesūti kāmāvacaradevesu, tattha asubhānaṃ paṭikūlassa ca āhārassa abhāvato. Assāsapassāsānaṃ brahmaloke abhāvato “ānāpānassati cā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Among the gods' means among the sense-sphere gods, because in that realm there is an absence of foul things and of repulsive food. Because of the absence of in-breaths and out-breaths in the Brahma world, it is said, 'and mindfulness of breathing'.

Diṭṭhenāti diṭṭhena vatthunā kāraṇabhūtena. Gahetabbānīti uggahetabbāni, uppādetabbauggahanimittānīti attho. Tenāha “pubbabhāge”tiādi. Tassāti kāyagatāsatiyā. Ucchusassādīnaṃ pattesu pacalamānavaṇṇaggahaṇamukhena vā tassa gahetabbattā vuttaṃ “vāyokasiṇaṃ diṭṭhaphuṭṭhenā”ti. Na ādikammikena gahetabbānīti ādikammikena na gahetabbāni, bhāvanārambhavasena na paṭṭhapetabbāni, heṭṭhime tayo brahmavihāre, kasiṇesu rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānañca anadhigantvā sampādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā.

'By what is seen' means by a seen object that has become an instrument. 'They are to be grasped' means they are to be taken up; the meaning is, they are learning signs to be produced. Therefore, he said, 'in the preliminary part,' and so on. 'Of that' means of mindfulness directed to the body. Or because it is to be grasped by means of apprehending the moving appearance in the leaves of sugarcane, crops, and so on, it is said, 'the wind kasiṇa by what is seen and touched.' 'Not to be grasped by a beginner' means they are not to be taken up by a beginner; they are not to be established by way of starting the development, because it is impossible to accomplish them without having attained the three lower divine abodes and the fourth form-sphere jhāna in the kasiṇas.

Imesu pana kammaṭṭhānesūti ettha kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇena yathārahaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ, jhānānañca gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sukhavihārassāti diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārassa.

'But in these meditation subjects': here, by the taking up of 'meditation subject', the taking up of the objects and of the jhānas, as is appropriate, should be understood. 'Of a pleasant abiding' means of a pleasant abiding in the here and now.

“Ekādasa kammaṭṭhānāni anukūlānī”ti ujuvipaccanīkavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Vakkhati hi “sabbañceta”ntiādi. Anukūlāni rāgavikkhambhanassa upāyabhāvato. Aṭṭha anukūlānīti yojanā. Evaṃ sesesu. Ekanti idaṃ anussatiapekkhaṃ anussatīsu ekanti, na mohacaritavitakkacaritāpekkhaṃ tesaṃ aññassāpi anukūlassa alabbhanato[V 1.0124]. “Saddhācaritassa [M 1.0133] purimā cha anussatiyo”ti idaṃ atisappāyavasena vuttaṃ. Imasseva ujuvipaccanīkaṃ imassa atisappāyanti gahetabbassa visesassa abhāvato sabbacaritānaṃ anukūlāni. Parittanti sarāvamattaṃ, appamāṇanti tato adhikapamāṇaṃ. Parittaṃ vā suppasarāvamattaṃ, appamāṇaṃ adhikapamāṇaṃ khalamaṇḍalādikasiṇabhāvena pariggahitaṃ.

'Eleven meditation subjects are suitable': this is said by way of direct opposition. Likewise in the remaining cases. Indeed, it will be said, 'And all this,' and so on. They are suitable because they are a means for the suppression of lust. The connection should be made as: 'eight are suitable.' Likewise in the remaining cases. This word 'one' refers to the recollections, as in 'one among the recollections'; it does not refer to a person of deluded temperament or speculative temperament, because for them another suitable meditation subject can also be obtained. The statement, 'For a person of faith-temperament, the first six recollections,' is said by way of being especially beneficial. Because there is no specific distinction to be grasped that 'this is a direct opposite only for this person' or 'this is especially beneficial for this person,' they are suitable for all temperaments. 'Limited' means the size of a pot-lid; 'immeasurable' means a measure greater than that. Or, 'limited' is the size of a winnowing basket or a pot-lid, while 'immeasurable' is a greater measure, taken up as a kasiṇa-disk of a threshing floor and so on.

Cattāro dhammāti cattāro manasikaraṇīyā dhammā. Uttarīti sīlasampadā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyadhammassavanaṃ, vīriyaṃ; paññāti imesu pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhānato upari. Asubhāti asubhabhāvanā ekādasasu asubhakammaṭṭhānesu bhāvanānuyogā. Mettāti anodhiso, odhiso vā pavattā mettābhāvanā. Ānāpānassatīti soḷasavatthukā ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā. Vitakkupacchedāyāti micchāvitakkānaṃ upacchindanatthāya. Aniccasaññāti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti (a. ni. 3.137; dha. pa. 277; mahāni. 27) evaṃ pavattā aniccānupassanā. Asmimānasamugghātāyāti “asmī”ti uppajjanakassa navavidhassāpi mānassa samucchindanāya. Ettha hi ekasseva cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā vuttā, na ekassa catucariyatāya. Tena viññāyati “sabbānipi kammaṭṭhānāni sabbākusalavikkhambhanāni sabbakusalaparibrūhanānī”ti.

'Four things' means four things to be attended to. 'Further' means further to being established in these five things: accomplishment in virtue, having good friends, hearing the suitable Dhamma, energy, and wisdom. 'The foul' means the development of the foul, that is, the application to development in the eleven meditation subjects of the foul. 'Loving-kindness' means the development of loving-kindness that proceeds either without limitation or with limitation. 'Mindfulness of breathing' means the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing, which has sixteen bases. 'For cutting off thoughts' means for the purpose of cutting off wrong thoughts. 'Perception of impermanence' means the insight into impermanence that proceeds thus: 'All formations are impermanent.' 'For the uprooting of the conceit "I am"' means for the complete cutting off of the ninefold conceit that arises as 'I am.' Indeed, here it is said that four things are to be developed by just one person; it is not said because one person has four temperaments. Therefore, it is understood: 'All meditation subjects suppress all unwholesome states and augment all wholesome states.'

Ekasseva satta kammaṭṭhānāni vuttāni, na cāyasmā rāhulo sabbacaritoti adhippāyo. Vacanamatteti “asukakammaṭṭhānaṃ asukacaritassa anukūla”nti evaṃ vuttavacanamatte. Adhippāyoti tathāvacanassa adhippāyo. So pana “sabbañceta”ntiādinā vibhāvito eva.

Seven meditation subjects were taught to just one person, and the Venerable Rāhula is not of all temperaments—this is the intention. 'Merely a statement' means in the mere statement that is said thus: 'Such-and-such a meditation subject is suitable for a person of such-and-such a temperament.' 'The intention' means the intention of such a statement. But that intention has already been clarified by 'And all this,' and so on.

48. “Piyo garū”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.37) vuttappakāraṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ. “Attano pattacīvaraṃ sayameva gahetvā”tiādinā vuttanayena upasaṅkamitvā. Somanassameva uppajjati “evaṃ bahuparissayoyaṃ attabhāvo ṭhāneyeva mayā niyyātito”ti. Tenāha “yathā hī”tiādi.

48. ‘A dear and venerable one,’ and so on, as mentioned (AN 7.37), refers to a good friend. Approaching in the manner described by ‘having taken one’s own bowl and robe,’ and so on, joy indeed arises, thinking: ‘Thus, this body, full of so many dangers, has indeed been rightly relinquished by me.’ Therefore it is said: ‘Just as...’ and so on.

Atajjanīyoti na tajjetabbo na niggahetabbo. Svāyaṃ atajjanīyabhāvo dovacassatāya vā siyā, ācariye aniviṭṭhapematāya vāti tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “dubbaco vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yo hi ācariyena tajjiyamāno kopañca dosañca apaccayañca pātukaroti, yo vā “kimassa [M 1.0134][V 1.0125] santike vāsenā”ti pakkamati, ayaṃ duvidhopi atajjanīyo. Dhammenāti ovādānusāsanidhammena. Gūḷhaṃ ganthanti kammaṭṭhānaganthaṃ, saccapaṭiccasamuppādādisahitaṃ gambhīraṃ suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttañca.

‘Not to be scolded’ means he should not be scolded or reprimanded. This state of being not liable to scolding may be due to disobedience or due to lack of established affection for the teacher; to show both of these, ‘disobedient,’ and so on, was said. For whoever, being scolded by the teacher, manifests anger, aversion, and disrespect, or whoever thinks, ‘What is the use of living near this one?’ and departs—both of these are not to be scolded. ‘By the Dhamma’ means by the Dhamma of instruction and advice. ‘The hidden knot’ means the knot of the meditation subject, which is profound, together with the truths, dependent origination, and so on, and connected with emptiness.

Tumhākamatthāyāti vutteti “sataporise papāte patanena tumhākaṃ koci attho hotī”ti kenaci vutte. Ghaṃsentoti “manussakakkena tumhākaṃ koci attho”ti vutte ghaṃsento niravasesaṃ attabhāvaṃ khepetuṃ ussaheyyaṃ. “Mama assāsapassāsanirundhanena tumhākaṃ koci rogavūpasamādiko attho atthī”ti kenaci vutte. Tīhipi bhikkhūhi ācariye bhattipavedanamukhena vīriyārambho eva pavedito.

As for the saying, "For your benefit": When it is said by someone, "By falling into a precipice one hundred men deep, is there any benefit to you?" As for "rubbing": When it is said, "Is there any benefit to you by means of human dust?"—"Rubbing, I would be able to exhaust my existence without remainder." When it is said by someone, "By the stopping of my in-breaths and out-breaths, is there any benefit to you, such as the pacification of disease?" By the three monks, through the means of declaring devotion to the teacher, the undertaking of energy itself was declared.

49. Aññattha pavattitvāpi cittaṃ āgamma yattha seti, so tassa āsayo “migāsayo” viya, āsayo eva ajjhāsayo. So duvidho vipanno, sampannoti. Tattha vipanno sassatādimicchābhinivesanissito. Sampanno duvidho vaṭṭanissito, vivaṭṭanissitoti. Tesu vivaṭṭanissito ajjhāsayo “sampannajjhāsayenā”ti idhādhippeto. Idāni naṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “alobhādīnaṃ vasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha chahākārehīti alubbhanādīhi chahi ākārehi. Sampannajjhāsayenāti pubbabhāgiyānaṃ sīlasampadādīnaṃ sādhanavasena, lokuttarānaṃ upanissayabhāvena ca sampanno ajjhāsayo etassāti sampannajjhāsayo, tena. Alobhādayo hi anekadosavidhamanato, anekaguṇāvahato ca sattānaṃ bahukārā visesato yogino. Tathā hi alobhādayo maccheramalādīnaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvena pavattanti. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 mūlarāsīvaṇṇanā) –

49. Even after having occurred elsewhere, the mind, having come, settles in a certain place; that is its abode (āsaya), like a "deer's resting place" (migāsayo). Abode itself is underlying tendency (ajjhāsaya). That is twofold: corrupted (vipanna) and perfected (sampanna). Therein, the corrupted is dependent on wrong adherence to views such as eternalism. The perfected is twofold: dependent on the round of existence (vaṭṭanissito) and dependent on the unwinding of the round (vivaṭṭanissito). Of these, the underlying tendency dependent on the unwinding of the round is intended here by "with a perfected underlying tendency." Now, to show it in detail, "by way of non-greed, etc." and so on was said. Therein, "by six modes" means by the six modes beginning with non-coveting. "With a perfected underlying tendency" means: because for this person the underlying tendency is perfected by way of accomplishing the preliminary virtues, etc., and by being a decisive support for the supramundane, he is one with a perfected underlying tendency; by that. For non-greed and so on, by dispelling many faults and by bringing many virtues, are of great help to beings, and especially to a yogī. Thus, non-greed and so on proceed by way of being the opposite of the stains of stinginess and so on. For this was said:

“Alobho maccheramalassa paṭipakkho, adoso dussīlyamalassa, amoho kusalesu dhammesu abhāvanāya. Alobho cettha dānahetu, adoso sīlahetu, amoho bhāvanāhetu. Tesu ca alobhena anadhikaṃ gaṇhāti luddhassa adhikaggahaṇato, adosena anūnaṃ duṭṭhassa ūnaggahaṇato, amohena aviparītaṃ mūḷhassa viparītaggahaṇato.

"Non-greed is the opposite of the stain of stinginess; non-hatred, of the stain of bad morality; non-delusion, of the non-cultivation of wholesome states. And herein, non-greed is the cause of giving, non-hatred is the cause of morality, and non-delusion is the cause of cultivation. And among them, through non-greed one takes without excess, because of the greedy person's taking in excess; through non-hatred one takes without deficiency, because of the hostile person's taking deficiently; through non-delusion one takes without distortion, because of the deluded person's taking in a distorted way.

“Alobhena [M 1.0135] cettha vijjamānaṃ dosaṃ dosato dhārento dose pavattati, luddho hi dosaṃ paṭicchādeti. Adosena vijjamānaṃ guṇaṃ guṇato dhārento guṇe pavattati, duṭṭho hi guṇaṃ makkheti. Amohena yāthāvasabhāvaṃ yāthāvasabhāvato dhārento yāthāvasabhāve pavattati[V 1.0126], mūḷho hi tacchaṃ ‘ataccha’nti, atacchañca ‘taccha’nti gaṇhāti. Alobhena ca piyavippayogadukkhaṃ na hoti luddhassa piyasabbhāvato, piyavippayogāsahanato ca, adosena appiyasampayogadukkhaṃ na hoti duṭṭhassa appiyasabbhāvato, appiyasampayogāsahanato ca, amohena icchitālābhadukkhaṃ na hoti, amūḷhassa hi ‘taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti evamādipaccavekkhaṇasabbhāvato.

"And herein, through non-greed, while regarding an existing fault as a fault, one persists in regard to the fault, for the greedy person conceals a fault. Through non-hatred, while regarding an existing virtue as a virtue, one persists in regard to the virtue, for the hostile person disparages virtue. Through non-delusion, while regarding the actual state as the actual state, one persists in regard to the actual state, for the deluded person takes the true as 'not true' and the not true as 'true.' And through non-greed, the suffering of separation from the beloved does not occur, because for the greedy person there is the existence of the beloved and the inability to endure separation from the beloved. Through non-hatred, the suffering of association with the unloved does not occur, because for the hostile person there is the existence of the unloved and the inability to endure association with the unloved. Through non-delusion, the suffering of not obtaining what is desired does not occur, for there is for the undeluded person the existence of reflection such as, 'How could that be obtained here?'"

“Alobhena cettha jātidukkhaṃ na hoti alobhassa taṇhāpaṭipakkhato, taṇhāmūlakattā ca jātidukkhassa, adosena jarādukkhaṃ na hoti tikkhadosassa khippaṃ jarāsambhavato, amohena maraṇadukkhaṃ na hoti, sammohamaraṇañhi dukkhaṃ, na ca taṃ amūḷhassa hoti. Alobhena ca gahaṭṭhānaṃ, amohena pabbajitānaṃ, adosena pana sabbesampi sukhasaṃvāsatā hoti.

And herein, through non-greed, the suffering of birth does not occur, because non-greed is the opposite of craving, and because the suffering of birth has craving as its root. Through non-hatred, the suffering of aging does not occur, because for one with sharp hatred, aging occurs quickly. Through non-delusion, the suffering of death does not occur, for death with delusion is suffering, and that does not occur for one who is undeluded. And through non-greed, there is pleasant cohabitation for householders; through non-delusion, for the ordained; but through non-hatred, there is pleasant cohabitation for all.

“Visesato cettha alobhena pettivisaye upapatti na hoti, yebhuyyena hi sattā taṇhāya pettivisayaṃ upapajjanti, taṇhāya ca paṭipakkho alobho. Adosena niraye upapatti na hoti, dosena hi caṇḍajātitāya dosasadisaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti, dosassa ca paṭipakkho adoso. Amohena tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbatti na hoti, mohena hi niccasammūḷhaṃ tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjanti, mohapaṭipakkho ca amoho. Etesu ca alobho rāgavasena upagamanassa abhāvakaro, adoso dosavasena apagamanassa, amoho mohavasena amajjhattabhāvassa.

Specifically, herein, through non-greed, rebirth in the sphere of spirits does not occur; for beings are, for the most part, reborn in the sphere of spirits through craving, and non-greed is the opposite of craving. Through non-hatred, rebirth in hell does not occur; for through hatred, because of a fierce nature, they are reborn in a hell similar to hatred, and non-hatred is the opposite of hatred. Through non-delusion, birth in the animal womb does not occur; for through delusion, they are reborn in the perpetually deluded animal womb, and non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. And among these, non-greed causes the absence of approaching by way of lust; non-hatred, of departing by way of hatred; non-delusion, of the state of not being neutral by way of delusion.

“Tīhipi [M 1.0136] cetehi yathāpaṭipāṭiyā nekkhammasaññā abyāpādasaññā avihiṃsāsaññāti imā tisso, asubhasaññā appamāṇasaññā dhātusaññāti imā ca tisso saññāyo honti. Alobhena pana kāmasukhallikānuyogaantassa, adosena attakilamathānuyogaantassa parivajjanaṃ hoti, amohena majjhimāya paṭipattiyā paṭipajjanaṃ. Tathā alobhena abhijjhākāyaganthassa pabhedanaṃ hoti, adosena byāpādakāyaganthassa, amohena sesaganthadvayassa. Purimāni ca dve satipaṭṭhānāni purimānaṃ dvinnaṃ ānubhāvena, pacchimāni pacchimasseva ānubhāvena ijjhanti.

And by these three, in respective order, these three perceptions arise: the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-harming; and also these three perceptions: the perception of unattractiveness, the perception of the boundless, and the perception of the elements. Furthermore, through non-greed there is the avoidance of the extreme of indulgence in sensual pleasures; through non-hatred, the avoidance of the extreme of self-mortification; through non-delusion, the practice of the middle path. Likewise, through non-greed there is the destruction of the bodily knot of covetousness; through non-hatred, of the bodily knot of ill will; through non-delusion, of the remaining two knots. And the first two foundations of mindfulness are accomplished through the power of the first two, while the latter two are accomplished through the power of the last one alone.

“Alobho [V 1.0127] cettha ārogyassa paccayo hoti, aluddho hi lobhanīyampi asappāyaṃ na sevati, tena arogo hoti. Adoso yobbanassa, aduṭṭho hi valitapalitāvahena dosagginā aḍayhamāno dīgharattaṃ yuvā hoti. Amoho dīghāyukatāya, amūḷho hi hitāhitaṃ ñatvā ahitaṃ parivajjento, hitañca paṭisevamāno dīghāyuko hoti.

Herein, non-greed is a condition for health; for one who is not greedy does not partake of what is unsuitable, even if it is desirable, and thereby is healthy. Non-hatred is a condition for youthfulness; for one who is not hostile, not being burned by the fire of hatred which brings wrinkles and grey hair, remains young for a long time. Non-delusion is a condition for longevity; for one who is not deluded, having known the beneficial and the harmful, while avoiding the harmful and partaking of the beneficial, becomes long-lived.

“Alobho cettha bhogasampattiyā paccayo cāgena bhogapaṭilābhato, adoso mittasampattiyā mettāya mittānaṃ paṭilābhato, aparihānato ca, amoho attasampattiyā, amūḷho hi attano hitameva karonto attānaṃ sampādeti. Alobho ca dibbavihārassa paccayo hoti, adoso brahmavihārassa, amoho ariyavihārassa.

Among these, non-greed is a condition for the accomplishment of wealth, because of obtaining wealth through generosity. Non-hatred is a condition for the accomplishment of friends, because of obtaining friends through loving-kindness and because of their non-decline. Non-delusion is a condition for self-accomplishment, for one who is not deluded, while doing only what is beneficial for oneself, brings oneself to accomplishment. And non-greed is a condition for the divine abiding, non-hatred for the Brahma-abiding, and non-delusion for the noble abiding.

“Alobhena cettha sakapakkhesu sattasaṅkhāresu nibbuto hoti tesaṃ vināsena abhisaṅgahetukassa dukkhassa abhāvā, adosena parapakkhesu, aduṭṭhassa hi verīsupi verisaññāya abhāvato, amohena udāsīnapakkhesu amūḷhassa sabbābhisaṅgatāya abhāvato.

And among these, through non-greed, one is at peace in regard to beings and formations of one's own faction, because upon their destruction, there is an absence of that suffering which is caused by attachment. Through non-hatred, one is at peace in regard to the other faction, for one who is not malicious lacks the perception of 'enemy' even towards enemies. Through non-delusion, one is at peace in regard to the neutral faction, because one who is not deluded lacks attachment to all things.

“Alobhena [M 1.0137] ca aniccadassanaṃ hoti, luddho hi upabhogāsāya aniccepi saṅkhāre aniccato na passati. Adosena dukkhadassanaṃ, adosajjhāsayo hi pariccattaāghātavatthupariggaho saṅkhāreyeva dukkhato passati. Amohena anattadassanaṃ, amūḷho hi yāthāvagahaṇakusalo apariṇāyakaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ apariṇāyakato bujjhati. Yathā ca etehi aniccadassanādīni, evaṃ etepi aniccadassanādīhi honti. Aniccadassanena hi alobho hoti, dukkhadassanena adoso, anattadassanena amoho. Ko hi nāma ‘aniccamida’nti sammā ñatvā tassatthāya pihaṃ uppādeyya, saṅkhāre vā ‘dukkha’nti jānanto aparampi accantatikhiṇaṃ kodhadukkhaṃ uppādeyya, attasuññatañca bujjhitvā puna sammohaṃ āpajjeyyā”ti.

And through non-greed, there is the seeing of impermanence; for a greedy person, with a desire for enjoyment, does not see even impermanent formations as impermanent. Through non-hatred, there is the seeing of suffering; for a person with a disposition of non-hatred, having relinquished the grasping of the bases of resentment, sees formations themselves as suffering. Through non-delusion, there is the seeing of not-self; for one who is not deluded, being skilled in correct comprehension, understands the five aggregates, which are without a director, as being without a director. And just as from these qualities the seeing of impermanence and so forth arise, so too do these qualities arise from the seeing of impermanence and so forth. For through the seeing of impermanence, non-greed arises; through the seeing of suffering, non-hatred arises; through the seeing of not-self, non-delusion arises. For who indeed, having rightly known, ‘This is impermanent,’ would generate longing for its sake? Or, knowing formations as ‘suffering,’ who would produce other, extremely sharp suffering of anger? Or, having understood the emptiness of self, who would again fall into delusion?

Tena vuttaṃ “pubbabhāgiyānaṃ sīlasampadādīnaṃ sādhanavasena lokuttarānaṃ, upanissayabhāvena ca sampanno ajjhāsayo etassāti sampannajjhāsayo”ti. Tenāha “evaṃ tissannaṃ bodhīnaṃ aññataraṃ pāpuṇātī”ti.

Therefore, it was said: 'One whose underlying inclination is perfected by means of accomplishing the preliminary virtues and so forth, and by way of being a supporting condition for the supramundane—such a one has a perfected underlying inclination.' For that reason, he said: 'Thus one attains one or another of the three enlightenments.'

Idāni [V 1.0128] te ajjhāsaye pāḷiyāva vibhāvetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha chāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Ajjhāsayāti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Ubhayaṃ pana ekajjhaṃ katvā chabbidhā ajjhāsayāti attho. Bodhisattāti bujjhanakasattā, bodhiyā vā niyatabhāvena sattā laggā, adhimuttā tanninnā tappoṇāti attho. Bodhiparipākāya saṃvattantīti yathābhinīhāraṃ attanā pattabbabodhiyā paripācanāya bhavanti. Alobhajjhāsayāti alubbhanākārena pavattaajjhāsayā, ādito “kathaṃ nu kho mayaṃ sabbattha, sabbadā ca aluddhā eva hessāmā”ti, majjhe ca alubbhanavaseneva, pacchā ca tasseva rocanavasena pavattaajjhāsayā. Lobhe dosadassāvinoti lubbhanalakkhaṇe lobhe sabbappakārena ādīnavadassāvino. Idaṃ tassa ajjhāsayassa ekadesato brūhanākāradassanaṃ. Lobhe hi ādīnavaṃ, alobhe ca ānisaṃsaṃ passantassa alobhajjhāsayo parivaḍḍhati, svāyaṃ tattha ādīnavānisaṃsadassanavidhi vibhāvitoyeva. Sesapadesupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ [M 1.0138] pana viseso – nekkhammanti idha pabbajjā. Paviveko tadaṅgaviveko, vikkhambhanaviveko, kāyaviveko, cittaviveko ca. Nissaraṇaṃ nibbānaṃ. Sabbabhavagatīsūti sabbesu bhavesu, sabbāsu ca gatīsu. Tadadhimuttatāyāti yadatthaṃ bhāvanānuyogo, yadatthā ca pabbajjā, tadadhimuttena. Tenevāha “samādhādhimuttenā”tiādi.

Now, to explain these underlying inclinations by means of the Pāḷi itself, the passage beginning “as follows” was stated. Therein, 'six' is a numerical classification. 'Underlying inclinations' is an indication of the qualities so classified. Combining both, the meaning is 'six kinds of underlying inclinations.' 'Bodhisattas' means beings who will awaken, or beings attached and fixed to enlightenment with certainty, meaning they are resolved on it, inclined toward it, and sloping toward it. 'They conduce to the maturing of enlightenment' means they are for the maturing of the enlightenment to be attained by oneself according to one's aspiration. 'The underlying inclination of non-greed' refers to an underlying inclination that operates in the manner of non-greed: at the beginning, thinking, 'How indeed shall we remain entirely free from greed in all things and at all times?'; in the middle, by way of non-greed itself; and at the end, by way of delighting in that very non-greed. 'Seeing the danger in greed' means seeing in every way the danger in greed, which is characterized by craving. This shows, in one aspect, the manner of augmenting that underlying inclination. For one who sees the danger in greed and the benefit in non-greed, the underlying inclination of non-greed grows; and the method of seeing that danger and benefit has already been explained. The meaning of the remaining passages should be understood in this way. This, however, is a specific point: here, 'renunciation' is the monastic life. 'Seclusion' is seclusion by substitution, seclusion by suppression, bodily seclusion, and mental seclusion. 'Escape' is Nibbāna. 'In all states of existence and destinies' means in all states of existence and in all destinies. 'By being resolved on that' means being resolved on that for the sake of which there is the practice of development and for the sake of which there is the monastic life. For that reason, he said, 'resolved on concentration,' and so on.

50. “Kiṃ caritosī”ti pucchito sace “na jānāmī”ti vadeyya, “ke vā te dhammā bahulaṃ samudācarantī”ti pucchitabbo. Kiṃ vāti kiṃ asubhaṃ vā anussatiṭṭhānaṃ vā aññaṃ vā. Kiṃ te manasi karoto phāsu hotīti cittassa ekaggabhāvena sukhaṃ hoti. Cittaṃ namatīti pakatiyāva abhirativasena namati. Evamādīhīti ādi-saddena iriyāpathādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tepi hi na sabbassa ekaṃsato byabhicārino eva. Tathā hi samudācāro pucchitabbo vutto. “Asukañca asukañca manasikāravidhiṃ katipayadivasaṃ anuyuñjāhī”ti ca vattabbo.

50. If, when asked, 'What is your temperament?' one should say, 'I do not know,' then one should be asked, 'Or what states frequently occur to you?' What is it—the unattractive, or a subject of recollection, or another? When applying your mind to what is there ease for you? This means there is happiness through the mind's one-pointedness. The mind inclines—this means it inclines naturally by way of delight. By 'and so on'—by this word 'ādi', the inclusion of postures and the like should be understood. For these too are not invariably inconsistent for everyone. Thus, it was said that the habitual occurrence should be asked about. And one should be told, 'Apply yourself to such-and-such a method of attention for some days.'

“Pakatiyā uggahitakammaṭṭhānassā”ti idaṃ yaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetukāmo, tattha sajjhāyavasena vā manasikāravasena vā kataparicayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ekaṃ dve nisajjānīti ekaṃ vā dve vā uṇhāsanāni. Sajjhāyaṃ kāretvā attano sammukhāva adhīyāpetvā dātabbaṃ, so ce aññattha gantukāmoti adhippāyo. Tenāha “santike vasantassā”ti. Āgatāgatakkhaṇe kathetabbaṃ, pavattiṃ sutvāti adhippāyo.

This phrase, 'for one who has by nature taken up a meditation subject,' was said in reference to one who, wishing to take up a meditation subject, has become familiar with it by way of recitation or by way of attention. 'One or two sittings' means one or two sessions. Having had him recite and learn it in one's own presence, it should be given; this is the meaning if he wishes to go elsewhere. Therefore, he said, 'for one living nearby.' The meaning is that one should speak to him on each occasion that he comes, after having heard of his progress.

Pathavīkasiṇanti [V 1.0129] pathavīkasiṇakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Katassāti katassa kasiṇassa. Taṃ taṃ ākāranti ācariyena kammaṭṭhāne vuccamāne padapadatthādhippāyaopammādikaṃ attano ñāṇassa paccupaṭṭhitaṃ taṃ taṃ ākāraṃ, yaṃ yaṃ nimittanti vuttaṃ. Upanibandhitvāti upanetvā nibaddhaṃ viya katvā, hadaye ṭhapetvā apamussantaṃ katvāti attho. Evaṃ suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitassatitāya nimittaṃ gahetvā tattha sampajānakāritāya sakkaccaṃ suṇantena. Tanti taṃ yathāvuttaṃ suggahitaṃ nissāya. Itarassāti tathā agaṇhantassa. Sabbākārenāti kassacipi pakārassa tattha asesitattā vuttaṃ.

As for 'Earth kasiṇa': it means the earth-kasiṇa meditation subject. As for 'of that which is made': it means of the kasiṇa that has been made. As for 'that very aspect': when the teacher explains the meditation subject, that very aspect which is presented to one's own knowledge—comprising the word, the meaning of the word, the intention, the simile, and so on—is what is called the 'sign'. As for 'having connected': having brought it near and made it as if firmly bound, placing it in the heart and making it unforgotten; this is the meaning. Thus, by one who listens respectfully, acting with clear comprehension therein, having grasped the sign through the state of well-established mindfulness. As for 'that': by relying on that which is well-grasped as has been stated. As for 'for another': for one who does not grasp it in that way. 'In every aspect' is said because no aspect whatsoever is left remaining therein.

Kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Taking Up a Meditation Subject is concluded.

Iti tatiyaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the Commentary on the Third Chapter.

4. Pathavīkasiṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Earth Kasiṇa

51. Phāsu [M 1.0139][V 1.0130] hotīti āvāsasappāyādilābhena manasikāraphāsutā bhāvanānukūlatā hoti. Parisodhentenāti tesaṃ tesaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānānaṃ chindanavasena visodhentena. Akilamantoyevāti akilantakāyo eva. Sati hi kāyakilamathe siyā kammaṭṭhānamanasikārassa antarāyoti adhippāyo. Gaṇṭhiṭṭhānanti atthato, adhippāyato ca dubbinivedhatāya gaṇṭhibhūtaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Chinditvāti yāthāvato atthassa, adhippāyassa ca vibhāvanena chinditvā, vibhūtaṃ supākaṭaṃ katvāti adhippāyo. Suvisuddhanti suṭṭhu visuddhaṃ, nigumbaṃ nijjaṭanti attho.

51. As for 'it is comfortable': by obtaining a suitable dwelling and other such things, there is comfort in attention, which is conduciveness to development. As for 'by one who purifies': by one who clarifies by way of cutting through those various knotty points. As for 'without fatigue': only with an unfatigued body. For if there is bodily fatigue, it would be an obstacle to the attention to the meditation subject; this is the intention. A 'knotty point' is a place that has become like a knot due to the difficulty of penetrating it in terms of meaning and intention. As for 'having cut through': having cut through by making the meaning and the intention clear as they truly are, having made them manifest and very clear; this is the intention. As for 'well-purified': thoroughly purified, without thickets, without tangles; this is the meaning.

Ananurūpavihāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on Unsuitable Monasteries

52. Aññatarenāti aññatarenāpi, pageva anekehīti adhippāyo. Mahantabhāvo mahattaṃ. Tathā sesesu. Soṇḍavā soṇḍī. Tathā paṇṇantiādīsu. Bodhiaṅgaṇādīsu kātabbaṃ idha “vatta”nti adhippetanti āha “pānīyaghaṭaṃ vā ritta”nti. Niṭṭhitāyāti paviṭṭhapaviṭṭhānaṃ dānena parikkhīṇāya. Jiṇṇavihārepi yatra bhikkhū evaṃ vadanti “āyasmā, yathāsukhaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karotu, mayaṃ paṭijaggissāmā”ti. Evarūpe vihātabbanti ayampi nayo labbhati, vuttanayattā pana na vutto.

52. As for 'by any': even by any one, how much more so by many; this is the intention. The state of being great is 'greatness'. Likewise in the remaining terms. A monastery with a stone reservoir is a 'soṇḍī'. Likewise in the terms beginning with 'paṇṇa'. Regarding the Bodhi-tree enclosure and so on, the duty to be done is here called 'vatta'. As for 'when it is finished': when it is exhausted by giving to those who have entered again and again. Even in an old monastery where the monks say thus: 'Venerable sir, practice the ascetic's duties as you please; we will maintain it.' In such a monastery, one should dwell. This method is also obtained, but because of the method already stated, it is not mentioned here.

Mahāpathavihāreti mahāpathasamīpe vihāre. Bhājanadārudoṇikādīnīti rajanabhājanāni, rajanatthāya dāru, dārumayadoṇikā, rajanapacanaṭṭhānaṃ, dhovanaphalakanti evamādīni. Sākahārikāti sākahāriniyo itthiyo. Visabhāgasaddo kāmaguṇūpasaṃhito gītasaddoti vadanti, kevalopi itthisaddo visabhāgasaddo eva. Tatrāti pupphavante vihāre. Tādisoyevāti “tatthassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā”tiādinā yādiso paṇṇavante vihāre upaddavo vutto, tādisoyeva. “Pupphahārikāyo pupphaṃ ocinantiyo”ti pana vattabbaṃ. Ayamidha viseso.

In a monastery on the great road means in a monastery near the great road. Pots, wood, troughs, and so on means dyeing pots, wood for dyeing, a wooden trough, a place for boiling dye, a board for washing robes, and so on. Vegetable-gatherers means women who habitually gather vegetables. They say that a discordant sound is the sound of singing connected with sensual pleasures; even the mere sound of a woman is itself a discordant sound. There means in a monastery with flowers. Just like that means just like the disturbance that was mentioned in the case of the monastery with vegetables, with the words beginning, 'having taken a meditation subject there...'. However, it should be stated as, 'women gathering flowers are picking flowers'. This is the difference here.

Patthanīyeti [V 1.0131] tattha vasantesu sambhāvanāvasena upasaṅkamanādinā patthetabbe. Tenāha “leṇasammate”ti. Dakkhiṇāgirīti magadhavisaye dakkhiṇāgirīti vadanti.

Desirable means it is to be desired by those dwelling there by way of approaching, etc., with esteem. Therefore, he said, 'esteemed as a lodging'. Dakkhiṇāgiri means Dakkhiṇāgiri in the country of Magadha, they say.

Visabhāgārammaṇāni [M 1.0140] iṭṭhāni, aniṭṭhāni ca. Aniṭṭhānaṃ hi dassanatthaṃ “ghaṭehi nighaṃsantiyo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dabbūpakaraṇayoggā rukkhā dabbūpakaraṇarukkhā.

Discordant objects are both desirable and undesirable. Indeed, to show the undesirable objects, that which begins with, 'pounding with pots,' was said. Trees suitable for being used as tools and implements are called tool-and-implement-trees.

Yo pana vihāro. Khalanti dhaññakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Gāvo rundhanti “sassaṃ khādiṃsū”ti. Udakavāranti kedāresu sassānaṃ dātabbaudakavāraṃ. Ayampīti mahāsaṅghabhogopi vihāro. Vāriyamānā kammaṭṭhānikena bhikkhunā.

Moreover, as for the monastery... Khala means a place for threshing grain. They confine cattle, thinking, 'They ate the crops.' Udakavāra means the turn for water to be given to the crops in the fields. This too means a monastery that is a great possession of the Sangha. Being prevented means being prevented by a monk practicing meditation.

Samuddasāmuddikanadīnissitaṃ udakapaṭṭanaṃ. Mahānagarānaṃ āyadvārabhūtaṃ aṭavimukhādinissitaṃ thalapaṭṭanaṃ. Appasannā honti. Tenassa tattha phāsuvihāro na hotīti adhippāyo. Maññamānā rājamanussā.

A water-port dependent on the ocean or a river connected to the ocean. A land-port that is an entrance for revenue for great cities, dependent on a forest entrance, and so on. They are displeased. Therefore, for that monk, there is no comfortable abiding there; this is the intention. Royal officials, thinking...

Samosaraṇenāti ito cito sañcaraṇena. Papāteti papātasīse ṭhatvā gāyi “gītasaddena idhāgataṃ papāte pātetvā khādissāmī”ti. Vegena gahetvāti vegenāgantvā “kuhiṃ yāsī”ti khandhe gahetvā.

By gathering means by wandering from here to there. He makes fall means: having stood on the edge of a precipice, he sang, thinking, 'I will make him who has come here due to the sound of my song fall into the precipice and I will eat him.' Having seized swiftly means: having come quickly and having seized him by the shoulder, saying, 'Where are you going?'

Yatthāti yasmiṃ vihāre, vihārasāmantā vā na sakkā hoti kalyāṇamittaṃ laddhuṃ, tattha vihāre so alābho mahādosoti yojanā.

Where means: in whichever monastery, or in the vicinity of a monastery, it is not possible to find a good friend, in that monastery that lack is a great fault. This is the connection.

Panthaninti panthe nīto pavattitoti panthanī, magganissito vihāro. Taṃ panthaniṃ. Soṇḍinti soṇḍisahito vihāro soṇḍī, taṃ soṇḍiṃ. Tathā paṇṇantiādīsu. Nagaranissitaṃ nagaranti vuttaṃ uttarapadalopena yathā “bhīmaseno bhīmo”ti. Dārunāti dārunissitena saha. Visabhāgenāti yo visabhāgehi vusīyati, visabhāgānaṃ vā nivāso, so vihāro visabhāgo. Tena visabhāgena saddhiṃ. Paccantanissitañca sīmānissitañca asappāyañca paccantasīmāsappāyaṃ. Yattha mitto na labbhati, tampīti sabbattha ṭhāna-saddāpekkhāya napuṃsakaniddeso. Iti viññāyāti “bhāvanāya ananurūpānī”ti evaṃ vijānitvā.

Panthanī means: because it is led or made to proceed on the path, it is called 'panthanī'; it means a monastery dependent on a road. That is panthaniṃ. Soṇḍī means: a monastery together with a stone reservoir is 'soṇḍī'; that is soṇḍiṃ. Likewise in the terms beginning with paṇṇa. A monastery dependent on a city is called nagara by eliding the latter word, just as 'Bhīmasena' is called 'Bhīma'. Dārunā means together with a monastery dependent on a forest of firewood or timber. Visabhāgena means: a monastery that is inhabited by incompatible persons, or is the residence of incompatible persons, that monastery is 'visabhāga'. Together with that 'visabhāga' monastery. And a monastery dependent on a border region, and one dependent on a boundary, and an unsuitable one. And also that place where a friend is not found. In all cases, the neuter designation is with reference to the word 'place'. Having thus known means: having known thus, 'These are unsuitable for development'.

Anurūpavihāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Suitable Dwellings

53. Ayaṃ [V 1.0132] anurūpo nāmāti ayaṃ vihāro bhāvanāya anurūpo nāma. Nātidūranti gocaraṭṭhānato aḍḍhagāvutato orabhāgatāya na [M 1.0141] atidūraṃ. Nāccāsannanti pacchimena pamāṇena gocaraṭṭhānato pañcadhanusatikatāya na atiāsannaṃ. Tāya ca pana nātidūranāccāsannatāya, gocaraṭṭhānaṃ parissayādirahitamaggatāya ca gamanassa ca āgamanassa ca yuttarūpattā gamanāgamanasampannaṃ. Divasabhāge mahājanasaṃkiṇṇatābhāvena divā appākiṇṇaṃ. Abhāvattho hi ayaṃ appa-saddo “appiccho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.336) viya. Rattiyaṃ janālāpasaddābhāvena rattiṃ appasaddaṃ. Sabbadāpi janasannipātanigghosābhāvena appanigghosaṃ. Appakasirenāti akasirena sukheneva. Sīlādiguṇānaṃ thirabhāvappattiyā therā. Suttageyyādi bahu sutaṃ etesanti bahussutā. Vācuggatakaraṇena, sammadeva garūnaṃ santike āgamitabhāvena ca āgato pariyattidhammasaṅkhāto āgamo etesanti āgatāgamā. Suttābhidhammasaṅkhātassa dhammassa dhāraṇena dhammadharā. Vinayassa dhāraṇena vinayadharā. Tesaṃyeva dhammavinayānaṃ mātikāya dhāraṇena mātikādharā. Tattha tattha dhammaparipucchāya paripucchati. Atthaparipucchāya paripañhati vīmaṃsati vicāreti. Idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ imassa ko atthoti paripucchanaparipañhākāradassanaṃ. Avivaṭañceva pāḷiyā atthaṃ padesantarapāḷidassanena āgamato vivaranti. Anuttānīkatañca yuttivibhāvanena uttānīkaronti. Kaṅkhaṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu saṃsayuppattiyā hetutāya gaṇṭhiṭṭhānabhūtesu pāḷipadesesu yāthāvato vinicchayadānena kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Ettha ca “nātidūraṃ, nāccāsannaṃ, gamanāgamanasampanna”nti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, “divā appākiṇṇaṃ, rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosa”nti ekaṃ, “appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassa”nti ekaṃ, “tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa…pe… parikkhārā”ti ekaṃ, “tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā…pe… kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodentī”ti ekaṃ. Evaṃ pañca aṅgāni veditabbāni.

53. This is called suitable means this dwelling is called suitable for development. Not too far means it is not too far, being within half a gāvuta from the alms-resort. Not too close means by the latter measure, it is not too close, being five hundred bow-lengths from the alms-resort. And furthermore, because of that state of being neither too far nor too close, and because the path to the alms-resort is free from dangers and so on, and because of its suitability for going and coming, it is endowed with ease of coming and going. In the daytime, due to the absence of being crowded with a great mass of people, it is uncrowded by day. For here the word 'appa' has the meaning of absence, as in 'appiccho' (of few wishes) and so on. At night, due to the absence of the sound of people’s talk, it is quiet at night. At all times, due to the absence of the clamor of a gathering of people, it has little clamor. With little difficulty means without difficulty, with ease. Elders (therā) are so called because they have attained a state of firmness in virtues such as morality. They are very learned (bahussutā) because they have heard much, such as the Suttas and Geyya. They are those who have received the tradition (āgatāgamā) because the tradition, known as the scriptural Dhamma, has come to them by means of learning by heart and by having been properly made to come to it in the presence of teachers. They are Dhamma-bearers (dhammadharā) because they bear the Dhamma, known as the Suttas and Abhidhamma. They are Vinaya-bearers (vinayadharā) because they bear the Vinaya. They are Mātikā-bearers (mātikādharā) because they bear the mātikā of that same Dhamma and Vinaya. Here and there, one questions with a question on the Dhamma. One investigates, examines, and analyzes with a question on the meaning. The words, 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' show the manner of questioning and investigating. They open up the meaning of the Pāli that has not been opened up by showing a Pāli passage from another place, by means of the scriptures. And they make plain what has not been made plain by demonstrating a suitable reason. In Dhamma points that are grounds for doubt, in Pāli passages that have become knotty places because of being a cause for the arising of doubt, they dispel doubt by giving a decision in accordance with reality. And herein, 'not too far, not too close, endowed with ease of coming and going' is one factor; 'uncrowded by day, quiet at night, with little clamor' is one factor; 'with few gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents' is one factor; 'for one dwelling in that lodging… requisites' is one factor; 'in that lodging, the elder bhikkhus… dispel doubt' is one factor. Thus, five factors should be understood.

Khuddakapalibodhavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Minor Impediments

54. Khuddakapalibodhupacchede payojanaṃ parato āgamissati. Aggaḷaanuvātaparibhaṇḍadānādinā daḷhīkammaṃ vā. Tantacchedādīsu tunnakammaṃ vā kātabbaṃ.

54. The benefit in cutting off minor impediments will come later. Or, strengthening should be done by means of applying patches, hems, borders, and so on. Or, in cases of broken threads and so on, sewing work should be done.

Bhāvanāvidhānavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Method of Development

55. Sabbakammaṭṭhānavasenāti [M 1.0142][V 1.0133] anukkamena niddisiyamānassa cattālīsavidhassa sabbassa kammaṭṭhānassa vasena. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantenāti piṇḍapātaparibhogato paṭinivattena, piṇḍapātabhuttāvinā onītapattapāṇināti attho. Bhattasammadaṃ paṭivinodetvāti bhojananimittaṃ parissamaṃ vinodetvā. Āhāre hi āsayaṃ paviṭṭhamatte tassa āgantukatāya yebhuyyena siyā sarīrassa koci parissamo, taṃ vūpasametvā. Tasmiṃ hi avūpasante sarīrakhedena cittaṃ ekaggataṃ na labheyyāti. Pavivitteti janavivitte. Sukhanisinnenāti pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya nisajjāya sukhanisinnena. Vuttañhetanti yaṃ “katāya vā”tiādinā pathaviyā nimittaggahaṇaṃ idha vuccati, vuttaṃ hetaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ.

55. “By way of all the meditation subjects” means by way of all forty kinds of meditation subjects that are being indicated in sequence. “Having returned from the alms-round” means having returned from consuming the alms-food; the meaning is: having eaten the alms-food and having put down one’s hand from the bowl. “Having dispelled the languor from the meal” means having dispelled the fatigue on account of the meal. For indeed, as soon as food has entered the stomach, due to its being a new arrival, there might mostly be some fatigue of the body; having calmed that. For if that is not calmed, the mind would not obtain one-pointedness due to bodily fatigue. “In a secluded place” means secluded from people. “Comfortably seated” means having sat down comfortably by folding the legs crosswise and setting the body upright. “For this was said” means that the taking up of the sign of the earth, which is spoken of here beginning with the words “or made,” was indeed spoken of in the ancient commentary.

Idāni taṃ aṭṭhakathāpāḷiṃ dassento “pathavīkasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto”tiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – pathavīkasiṇaṃ uggaṇhantoti uggahanimittabhāvena pathavīkasiṇaṃ gaṇhanto ādiyanto, uggahanimittabhūtaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ uppādentoti attho. Uppādanañcettha tathānimittassa upaṭṭhāpanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pathaviyanti vakkhamānavisese pathavīmaṇḍale. Nimittaṃ gaṇhātīti tattha cakkhunā ādāsatale mukhanimittaṃ viya bhāvanāñāṇena vakkhamānavisesaṃ pathavīnimittaṃ gaṇhāti. “Pathaviya”nti vatvāpi maṇḍalāpekkhāya napuṃsakaniddeso. Kateti vakkhamānavidhinā abhisaṅkhateti attho. Vā-saddo aniyamattho. Akateti pākatike khalamaṇḍalādike pathavīmaṇḍale. Sāntaketi saantake eva, saparicchede evāti attho. Sāvadhāraṇañhetaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathā hi tena nivattitaṃ dassetuṃ “no anantake”ti vuttaṃ. Sakoṭiyetiādīnipi tasseva vevacanāni. Suppamatte vātiādīsu suppasarāvāni samappamāṇāni icchitāni. Keci pana vadanti “sarāvamattaṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ hoti, suppamattaṃ tato adhikappamāṇanti. Kittimaṃ kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedena sarāvamattaṃ, uparimaparicchedena suppamattaṃ, na tato adho, uddhaṃ vāti parittappamāṇabhedasaṅgaṇhanatthaṃ ‘suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā’ti vutta”nti. Yathāupaṭṭhite ārammaṇe ekaṅgulamattampi vaḍḍhitaṃ appamāṇamevāti vuttovāyamattho. Keci pana “chattamattampi kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ kātabba”nti vadanti.

Now, showing that commentary text, he said, “Taking up the earth kasiṇa,” and so on. Therein, this is the summary meaning: “Taking up the earth kasiṇa” means taking or acquiring the earth kasiṇa as the learning sign; the meaning is producing the earth kasiṇa that has become the learning sign. And here, “producing” should be understood as the establishing of such a sign. “Of the earth” means in the earth-circle with the characteristics to be described. “He takes the sign” means that, just as one takes the sign of the face in the surface of a mirror with the eye, so he takes the earth sign with the characteristics to be described from that earth-circle with the knowledge of development. Although “pathaviyā” (of the earth) is said, the neuter gender is used in reference to the circle (maṇḍala). “Made” means prepared by the method to be described. The particle “vā” has the meaning of indefiniteness. “Unmade” means in a natural earth-circle, such as a threshing floor. “With a boundary” means with an end only, with a limit only. And this statement is emphatic. Thus, to show what is excluded by that, it is said, “not without a boundary.” The words “with a limit,” and so on, are synonyms for that very word. In the phrase “the size of a winnowing basket,” and so on, winnowing baskets and bowls of equal size are intended. Some, however, say: “A bowl-sized device is a span and four finger-breadths; a winnowing-basket-sized device is of a larger measure than that. An artificial kasiṇa-circle has a bowl-size as its lower limit and a winnowing-basket-size as its upper limit, not below or above that.” Thus, in order to include the distinction between the limited and the immeasurable, it was said, “the size of a winnowing basket or the size of a bowl.” This meaning has already been stated: in whatever object has appeared, even if it is increased by a mere finger-breadth, it is just immeasurable. Some, however, say: “A kasiṇa-circle should be made even as large as a parasol.”

So [M 1.0143] taṃ nimittaṃ suggahitaṃ karotīti so yogāvacaro taṃ pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ suggahitaṃ nimittaṃ [V 1.0134] karoti. Yadā cakkhuṃ ummīletvā oloketvā tattha nimittaṃ gahetvā nimmīletvā āvajjentassa ummīletvā olokitakkhaṇe viya upaṭṭhāti, tadā suggahitaṃ karoti nāma. Athettha satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā abahigatena mānasena punappunaṃ sallakkhento sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāreti nāma. Evaṃ upadhāritaṃ pana naṃ punappunaṃ āvajjento manasi karonto tamevārabbha āsevanaṃ bhāvanaṃ bahulaṃ pavattento suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapeti nāma. Tasmiṃ ārammaṇeti evaṃ suggahitakaraṇādinā sammadeva upaṭṭhite tasmiṃ pathavīkasiṇasaññite ārammaṇe. Cittaṃ upanibandhatīti attano cittaṃ upacārajjhānaṃ upanetvā nibandhati aññārammaṇato vinivattaṃ karoti. Addhā imāyātiādi ānisaṃsadassāvitādassanaṃ.

“He makes that sign well-grasped” means that the meditator makes that earth-circle a well-grasped sign. When, having opened the eyes and looked, having taken the sign there, he closes his eyes, and it appears to him who is adverting to it just as in the moment of opening the eyes and looking, then it is called “making it well-grasped.” Then, having made mindfulness well-established herein, marking it well again and again with a mind that has not gone outside, he is said to consider it well-considered. Having thus considered it, adverting to it and attending to it again and again, taking that very thing as the object, and causing much practice and development to occur, he is said to define it well-defined. “On that object” means on that object called the earth kasiṇa, which has appeared properly through making it well-grasped, and so on. “He binds the mind to it” means he leads his own mind to access concentration and binds it, making it turn back from other objects. The phrase beginning with “Assuredly, by this…” is a statement showing the benefits.

Idāni yathādassitassa aṭṭhakathāpāṭhassa atthappakāsanena saddhiṃ bhāvanāvidhiṃ vibhāvetukāmo akate tāva nimittaggahaṇaṃ dassento “tattha yena atītabhavepī”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ aṭṭhakathāpāṭhe. Catukkapañcakajjhānānīti catukkapañcakanayavasena vadati. Puññavatoti bhāvanāmayapuññavato. Upanissayasampannassāti tādiseneva upanissayena samannāgatassa. Khalamaṇḍaleti maṇḍalākāre dhaññakaraṇaṭṭhāne. Taṃṭhānappamāṇamevāti olokitaṭṭhānappamāṇameva.

Now, wishing to clarify the method of development together with the explanation of the meaning of the commentary passage as shown, first showing the taking of the sign in an unmade device, he said, “Therein, one who, even in a past existence…” and so on. Therein, “therein” means in that commentary passage. “The fourfold and fivefold jhānas” means he speaks by way of the fourfold and fivefold methods. “Of a meritorious one” means of one with merit consisting of development. “Of one endowed with a supportive condition” means of one who is endowed with such a supportive condition. “In a threshing floor” means in a place for threshing grain that has a circular shape. “Just the size of that place” means just the size of the place that was observed.

Avirādhetvāti avirajjhitvā vuttavidhinā eva. Nīlapītalohitaodātasambhedavasenāti nīlādivaṇṇāhi mattikāhi paccekaṃ, ekajjhañca saṃsaggavasena. Gaṅgāvaheti gaṅgāsote. Sīhaḷadīpe kira rāvaṇagaṅgā nāma nadī, tassā sotena chinnataṭaṭṭhāne mattikā aruṇavaṇṇā. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “gaṅgāvahe mattikāsadisāya aruṇavaṇṇāyā”ti. Aruṇavaṇṇāya aruṇanibhāya, aruṇappabhāvaṇṇāyāti attho.

“Without failing” means without erring, only by the method that has been stated. “By way of the combination of blue, yellow, red, and white” means with clays of blue and other colors, both each separately and by way of mixing them together. “In the Ganges’ current” means in the stream of the Ganges. It is said that in the island of Sri Lanka there is a river named Rāvaṇagaṅgā; in the place on the bank cut away by its current, the clay is the color of dawn. Referring to that, it was said, “…of the color of dawn, like the clay in the Ganges’ current.” “Of the color of dawn” means resembling the dawn, having the color of the radiance of dawn; this is the meaning.

Evaṃ kasiṇadose dassetvā idāni kasiṇakaraṇādike sesākāre dassetuṃ “tañca kho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṃhārimanti saṃharitabbaṃ gahetvā caraṇayoggaṃ. Tatraṭṭhakanti yatra kataṃ, tattheva tiṭṭhanakaṃ. Vuttappamāṇanti [M 1.0144] “suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā”ti vuttappamāṇaṃ. Vaṭṭanti maṇḍalasaṇṭhānaṃ. Parikammakāleti nimittuggahaṇāya bhāvanākāle. Etadevāti yaṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulavitthāraṃ, etadeva pamāṇaṃ sandhāya “suppamattaṃ vā sarāvamattaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Suppaṃ hi nātimahantaṃ, sarāvañca mahantaṃ cāṭipidhānappahonakanti samappamāṇaṃ hoti.

Having thus shown the faults of the kasiṇa, now, in order to show the remaining aspects such as the making of the kasiṇa, the passage beginning 'tañca kho' was stated. 'Saṃhārimam' means that which should be carried; having been taken, it is suitable for moving. 'Tatraṭṭhakam' means that where it is made, it remains stationary in that very place. 'Of the stated measure' means the measure stated as 'the size of a winnowing basket or the size of a bowl.' 'Circular' means having the shape of a circle. 'At the time of preliminary work' means at the time of development for the purpose of grasping the sign. 'This very one' means: referring to this very measure which is a span and four fingers wide, it was said, 'the size of a winnowing basket or the size of a bowl.' Indeed, a winnowing basket is not too large, and a bowl-lid large enough to cover a water pot are of equal measure.

56. Tasmāti [V 1.0135] paricchedatthāya vuttattā. Evaṃ vuttapamāṇaṃ paricchedanti yathāvuttappamāṇaṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulavitthāraṃ paricchedaṃ katvā, evaṃ vuttappamāṇaṃ vā kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ visabhāgavaṇṇena paricchedaṃ katvā. Rukkhapāṇikāti kucandanādirukkhapāṇikā aruṇavaṇṇassa visabhāgavaṇṇaṃ samuṭṭhapeti. Tasmā taṃ aggahetvāti vuttaṃ. Pakatirukkhapāṇikā pana pāsāṇapāṇikāgatikāva. Ninnunnataṭṭhānābhāvena bherītalasadisaṃ katvā. Tato dūrataretiādi yathāvuttato padesato, pīṭhato ca aññasmiṃ ādīnavadassanaṃ. Kasiṇadosāti hatthapāṇipadādayo idha kasiṇadosā.

56. 'Therefore' means because it was stated for the purpose of delimitation. 'Thus delimiting the stated measure' means having made a delimitation of the stated measure, which is a span and four fingers wide; or, having made a delimitation of the kasiṇa-circle of the stated measure with a contrasting color. 'A wooden trowel' means a wooden trowel of red sandalwood, etc., produces a color that contrasts with the dawn-colored kasiṇa. Therefore, it was said, 'not taking that.' An ordinary wooden trowel, however, is just like a stone trowel. Having made it like the surface of a drum, due to the absence of depressed and raised spots. The passage beginning 'further than that' is a statement showing the disadvantage in another place or seat than the one mentioned. 'Faults of the kasiṇa' means that here, marks of fingers, palms, feet, and so on, are faults of the kasiṇa.

Vuttanayenevāti “aḍḍhateyyahatthantare padese, vidatthicaturaṅgulapādake pīṭhe”ti ca vuttavidhināva. Kāmesu ādīnavanti “kāmā nāmete aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā nirassādaṭṭhena, tiṇukkūpamā anudahanaṭṭhena, aṅgārakāsūpamā mahābhitāpaṭṭhena, supinakūpamā ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, yācitakūpamā tāvakālikaṭṭhena, rukkhaphalūpamā sabbaṅgapaccaṅgapalibhañjanaṭṭhena, asisūnūpamā adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhena, sattisūlūpamā vinivijjhanaṭṭhena, sappasirūpamā sapaṭibhayaṭṭhenā”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 417; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.234) “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā”tiādinā (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.234; 2.42) “kāmasukhañca nāmetaṃ bahuparissayaṃ, sāsaṅkaṃ, sabhayaṃ, saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ, mīḷhaparibhogasadisaṃ, hīnaṃ, gammaṃ, pothujjanikaṃ, anariyaṃ, anatthasaṃhita”ntiādinā ca anekākāravokāraṃ vatthukāmakilesakāmesu ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ paccavekkhitvā. Kāmanissaraṇeti kāmānaṃ nissaraṇabhūte, tehi vā nissaṭe. Aggamaggassa pādakabhāvena sabbadukkhasamatikkamassa upāyabhūte. Nekkhammeti jhāne. Jātābhilāsena sañjātacchandena. “Sammāsambuddho vata bhagavā aviparītadhammadesanattā, svākkhāto [M 1.0145] dhammo ekantaniyyānikattā, suppaṭipanno saṅgho yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjanato”ti evaṃ buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇānussaraṇena ratanattayavisayaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ janayitvā. Nekkhammaṃ paṭipajjati etāyāti nekkhammapaṭipadā, saupacārassa jhānassa, vipassanāya, maggassa, nibbānassa ca adhigamakāraṇanti attho. Pubbe pana paṭhamajjhānameva nekkhammanti vuttattā vuttāvasesā sabbepi nekkhammadhammā. Yathāha –

'By the stated method' means by the method stated as: 'in a place at a distance of two and a half cubits,' and 'on a seat with a base of a span and four fingers.' 'The danger in sensual pleasures' means having reflected on the fault and danger in object-sensual pleasures and defilement-sensual pleasures, which are mixed with numerous aspects, in accordance with such passages as: 'These things called sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, in the sense of being without savor; like a grass torch, in the sense of sequential burning; like a pit of embers, in the sense of great torment; like a dream, in the sense of fleeting manifestation; like borrowed goods, in the sense of being temporary; like the fruit of a tree, in the sense of breaking all major and minor limbs; like a sword and a chopping block, in the sense of cutting and slicing; like a spear and a stake, in the sense of piercing; like a snake’s head, in the sense of being accompanied by peril'; and 'Sensual pleasures have little savor, much suffering, much distress'; and 'This so-called sensual pleasure is fraught with much trouble, is accompanied by anxiety, is accompanied by fear, is defiled, is like the partaking of filth, is inferior, is of the village, is of ordinary folk, is ignoble, is not connected with benefit.' 'The escape from sensual pleasures' means being the escape from sensual pleasures, or being liberated from them. Being the foundation for the supreme path. 'In renunciation' means in jhāna. With desire arisen, with zeal generated. Having generated joy and gladness that has the Triple Gem as its object, thus: 'Truly, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, due to his teaching of the unerring Dhamma! Truly, the Dhamma is well-expounded, as it is exclusively leading out! Truly, the Saṅgha is of good practice, as it practices in accordance with what was taught!' 'The path of renunciation' is so called because by this one attains renunciation; the meaning is that it is the cause for the attainment of jhāna together with its access, of insight, of the path, and of Nibbāna. However, since it was previously stated that only the first jhāna is 'renunciation,' all the remaining states mentioned are also states of renunciation. As was said:

“Pabbajjā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, nibbānaṃ ca vipassanā;

Sabbepi kusalā dhammā, ‘nekkhamma’nti pavuccare”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 109);

“Going forth, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and insight; all wholesome states, too, are called ‘renunciation.’”

Pavivekasukharasassāti [V 1.0136] cittavivekādivivekajassa sukharasassa. Evametehi pañcahi padehi “ānisaṃsadassāvī”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samena ākārenāti atiummīlanaatimandālocanāni vajjetvā nātiummīlananātimandālocanasaṅkhātena samena ālocanākārena. Nimittaṃ gaṇhantenāti pathavīkasiṇe cakkhunā gahitanimittaṃ manasā gaṇhantena. Bhāvetabbanti tathāpavattaṃ nimittaggahaṇaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ āsevitabbaṃ bahulīkātabbaṃ.

'Of the taste of the bliss of seclusion' means of the taste of bliss born of seclusion, such as mental seclusion. Thus, it should be understood that by these five terms, the meaning of the terms beginning with 'one who sees the benefit' is shown. 'In an even manner' means having avoided looking with the eyes excessively open and looking excessively dimly, by means of an even manner of looking, which is designated as neither looking too open nor looking too dimly. 'By one who is grasping the sign' means by one who is grasping with the mind the sign of the earth kasiṇa that has been apprehended by the eye. 'It should be developed' means that such grasping of the sign that has occurred should be increased, frequented, and made much of.

Cakkhu kilamati atisukhumaṃ, atibhāsurañca rūpagataṃ upanijjhāyato viya. Ativibhūtaṃ hoti attano sabhāvāvibhāvato. Tathā ca vaṇṇato vā lakkhaṇato vā upatiṭṭheyya. Tena vuttaṃ “tenassa nimittaṃ nuppajjatī”ti. Avibhūtaṃ hoti gajanimmīlanena pekkhantassa rūpagataṃ viya. Cittañca līnaṃ hoti dassane mandabyāpāratāya kosajjapātato. Tenāha “evampi nimittaṃ nuppajjatī”ti. Ādāsatale mukhanimittadassinā viyāti yathā ādāsatale mukhanimittadassī puriso na tattha atigāḷhaṃ ummīlati, nāpi atimandaṃ, na ādāsatalassa vaṇṇaṃ paccavekkhati, nāpi lakkhaṇaṃ manasi karoti. Atha kho samena ākārena olokento attano mukhanimittameva passati, evameva ayampi pathavīkasiṇaṃ samena ākārena olokento nimittaggahaṇappasutoyeva hoti, tena vuttaṃ “samena ākārenā”tiādi. Na vaṇṇo paccavekkhitabboti yo tattha pathavīkasiṇe aruṇavaṇṇo, so na cintetabbo. Cakkhuviññāṇena pana gahaṇaṃ na sakkā nivāretuṃ. Tenevettha “na oloketabbo”ti [M 1.0146] avatvā paccavekkhaṇaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Na lakkhaṇaṃ manasi kātabbanti yaṃ tattha pathavīdhātuyā thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ na manasi kātabbaṃ.

The eye becomes fatigued, like that of one who gazes intently at a collection of forms that is very subtle and very brilliant. It becomes excessively manifest due to the manifestation of its own nature. And so, it might appear by way of color or by way of characteristic. Therefore it is said: 'For him, the sign does not arise.' It becomes indistinct, like a collection of forms for one looking with an elephant's half-closed eyes. And the mind becomes sluggish due to weak activity in seeing and falling into laziness. Therefore, he said: 'In this way too, the sign does not arise.' This is like a person looking at their reflection in a mirror. Just as a person looking at their reflection on the surface of a mirror does not open their eyes too widely, nor too slightly, does not reflect on the color of the mirror's surface, nor bring its characteristic to mind, but rather, gazing with a balanced manner, sees only their own reflection; even so, this person, gazing at the earth-kasiṇa with a balanced manner, becomes intent on grasping the sign. Therefore, it is said, 'with a balanced manner,' and so on. 'The color should not be reflected upon' means that the dawn-like color in the earth-kasiṇa should not be contemplated. It is not possible, however, to prevent its apprehension by eye-consciousness. For that very reason, instead of saying here, 'it should not be looked at,' the word 'reflection' is used. 'The characteristic should not be brought to mind' means that the characteristic of hardness of the earth element there should not be brought to mind.

Disvā gahetabbattā “vaṇṇaṃ amuñcitvā”ti vatvāpi vaṇṇavasenettha ābhogo na kātabbo, so pana vaṇṇo nissayagatiko kātabboti dassento āha “nissayasavaṇṇaṃ katvā”ti. Nissayena samānākārasannissito so vaṇṇo tāya pathaviyā samānagatikaṃ katvā, vaṇṇena saheva “pathavī”ti manasi kātabbanti attho. Ussadavasena paṇṇattidhammeti pathavīdhātuyā ussannabhāvena sattito adhikabhāvena sasambhārapathaviyaṃ “pathavī”ti yo lokavohāro, tasmiṃ paṇṇattidhamme cittaṃ paṭṭhapetvā “pathavī, pathavī”ti manasi kātabbaṃ. Yadi lokavohārena paṇṇattimatte cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ, nāmantaravasenapi pathavī manasi kātabbā bhaveyyāti, hotu, ko dosoti dassento “mahī medinī”tiādimāha. Tattha yamicchatīti yaṃ nāmaṃ vattuṃ icchati, taṃ vattabbaṃ. Tañca kho yadassa saññānukūlaṃ [V 1.0137] hoti yaṃ nāmaṃ assa yogino pubbe tattha gahitasaññāvasena anukūlaṃ pacuratāya, paguṇatāya vā āgacchati, taṃ vattabbaṃ. Vattabbanti ca paṭhamasamannāhāre kassaci vacībhedopi hotīti katvā vuttaṃ, ācariyena vā vattabbataṃ sandhāya. Kiṃ vā bahunā, pākaṭabhāvoyevettha pamāṇanti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kālena ummīletvā kālena nimmīletvāti kiñci kālaṃ cakkhuṃ ummīletvā nimittaggahaṇavasena pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ oloketvā puna kiñci kālaṃ cakkhuṃ nimmīletvā āvajjitabbaṃ. Yenākārena oloketvā gahitaṃ, tenākārena puna taṃ samannāharitabbaṃ.

Because it is to be grasped after having been seen, even though it was said, 'without abandoning the color,' attention should not be given here by way of the color. Rather, showing that 'that color should be made to have the same nature as its support,' he said, 'having made the color the same as the support.' The meaning is: that color is well-supported by and has a similar form to its support; having made it have the same nature as that earth, one should, together with the color itself, bring to mind 'earth.' 'A conceptual phenomenon by way of predominance' means: one should establish the mind on that conceptual phenomenon which is the worldly convention 'earth'—a convention used for the earth with its components due to the abundance, power, and predominance of the earth element—and bring to mind, 'earth, earth.' If the mind is to be established on a mere concept by worldly convention, then 'earth' could be brought to mind by way of another name as well. To show, 'So be it, what is the fault in that?', he said, 'Mahī, Medinī,' and so on. Therein, 'whatever one wishes' means: whatever name one wishes to say, that should be said. And that should be a name that is agreeable to his perception. Whatever name comes to that yogī—being agreeable by way of a perception previously grasped there, either through frequency or proficiency—that name should be said. And 'should be said' is stated because for some, in the initial application of mind, there is also verbal utterance; or it is said in reference to it being something that should be spoken by the teacher. Or what is the use of saying much? To show that 'here, manifestness itself is the measure,' it is said, 'Moreover,' and so on. 'Opening the eyes at times, closing them at times' means: having opened the eyes for some time and looked at the earth-disk by way of grasping the sign, one should then, having closed the eyes for some time, advert to it. In whatever manner it was grasped by looking, in that same manner it should be brought to mind again.

57. Āpāthamāgacchatīti manodvārikajavanānaṃ gocarabhāvaṃ upagacchati. Tassa uggahanimittassa. Na tasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīditabbaṃ. Kasmā? Yadi uggahanimitte jātepi pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ oloketvā bhāveti, paṭibhāganimittuppatti na siyā. Samīpaṭṭhena ca na oloketuṃ na sakkā. Tena vuttaṃ “attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā”tiādi. Nissaddabhāvāya ekapaṭalikūpāhanāgahaṇaṃ, parissayavinodanatthaṃ kattaradaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ. Sace nassati, athānena bhāvetabbanti sambandho. Vakkhamānesu asappāyesu kenacideva asappāyena kāraṇabhūtena. Nimittaṃ ādāyāti yathājātaṃ uggahanimittaṃ gahetvā. Samannāharitabbanti āvajjitabbaṃ nimittanti adhippāyo, sammā vā anu [M 1.0147] anu āharitabbaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti attho. Takkāhataṃ vitakkāhatanti takkanato, savisesaṃ takkanato ca “takko, vitakko”ti ca evaṃ laddhanāmena bhāvanācittasampayuttena sammāsaṅkappena āhananapariyāhananakiccena aparāparaṃ vattamānena kammaṭṭhānaṃ āhataṃ, pariyāhatañca kātabbaṃ, balappattavitakko manasikāro bahulaṃ pavattetabboti attho. Evaṃ karontassāti evaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karontassa. Yathā bhāvanā pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ āvahati, evaṃ anuyuñjantassa. Anukkamenāti bhāvanānukkamena. Yadā saddhādīni indriyāni suvisadāni tikkhāni pavattanti, tadā assaddhiyādīnaṃ dūrībhāvena sātisayathāmappattehi sattahi balehi laddhūpatthambhāni vitakkādīni kāmāvacarāneva jhānaṅgāni bahūni hutvā pātubhavanti. Tato eva tesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhūtā kāmacchandādayo saddhiṃ tadekaṭṭhehi pāpadhammehi vidūrī bhavanti, paṭibhāganimittuppattiyā saddhiṃ taṃ ārabbha upacārajjhānaṃ uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhantī”tiādi. Tattha sannisīdantīti sammadeva sīdanti, upasamantīti attho.

57. 'It comes into range' means it enters the sphere of the mind-door impulsion-cognitions. This pertains to the learning sign. One should not sit in that place. Why? If, even when the learning sign has arisen, one develops it by looking at the earth-disk, the counterpart sign would not arise. And one who is nearby cannot help but look at it. Therefore it is said, 'having entered one's own dwelling place,' and so on. The taking of single-soled sandals is for the sake of silence; the taking of a staff is for dispelling danger. The connection is: If it is lost, then it should be developed by this person. This is due to some unsuitable thing that has become a cause among the unsuitable things that will be mentioned. 'Having taken up the sign' means having taken up the learning sign as it has arisen. 'One should bring it to mind'—the intention is that the sign should be adverted to; or, the meaning is that the meditation subject should be properly brought to mind again and again. 'Struck by thought, struck by applied thought' means that the meditation subject should be struck and thoroughly struck by right thought. This right thought is associated with the meditation mind, occurs successively with the function of striking and thoroughly striking, and has obtained the names 'thought' (takka) and 'applied thought' (vitakka) from 'thinking' and 'thinking with distinction,' respectively. The meaning is that attention with applied thought that has reached strength should be made to occur frequently. 'For one doing so' means for one who makes the meditation subject thus struck by thought and applied thought. For one who practices thus, it is just as development brings about a later distinction from what came before. 'By sequence' means by the sequence of development. When the faculties of faith and so on proceed, being very clear and sharp, then, because of the removal of lack of faith and so on, the jhāna factors such as applied thought—which are still of the sense-sphere and have obtained support from the seven powers that have reached a state of excessive strength—arise in abundance. For that very reason, their direct opposites, sensual desire and so on, together with the evil states that share the same basis, become far removed. Together with the arising of the counterpart sign, access concentration arises taking that as its object. Therefore it is said, 'The hindrances are suppressed,' and so on. Therein, 'they settle down' means they sink down properly, they are calmed; this is the meaning.

Imassāti paṭibhāganimittassa. Aṅgulipadapāṇipadādiko kasiṇadoso. Ādāsamaṇḍalūpamādīhi [V 1.0138] uggahanimittato paṭibhāganimittassa suparisuddhataṃ, saṇhasukhumatañca dasseti. Tañca kho paṭibhāganimittaṃ neva vaṇṇavantaṃ na saṇṭhānavantaṃ aparamatthasabhāvattā. Īdisanti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavantaṃ. Tilakkhaṇabbhāhatanti uppādādilakkhaṇattayānupaviṭṭhaṃ, aniccatādilakkhaṇattayaṅkitaṃ vā. Yadi na panetaṃ tādisaṃ vaṇṇādivantaṃ, kathaṃ jhānassa ārammaṇabhāvoti āha “kevalañhī”tiādi. Saññajanti bhāvanāsaññājanitaṃ, bhāvanāsaññāya sañjātamattaṃ. Na hi asabhāvassa kutoci samuṭṭhānaṃ atthi. Tenāha “upaṭṭhānākāramatta”nti.

'Of this' means 'of the counterpart sign.' A kasiṇa defect is, for example, a fingerprint or a palm print. By means of examples such as a mirror-disc, it shows the thorough purity and the subtlety and refinement of the counterpart sign over the learning sign. And that counterpart sign is neither possessed of color nor possessed of shape, because it does not have an ultimate nature. 'Such' means 'possessed of color and shape.' 'Struck by the three characteristics' means 'penetrated by the three characteristics beginning with arising,' or 'marked by the three characteristics of impermanence, etc.' If this counterpart sign were not such, possessed of color and so on, how could it be the object of jhāna? Because of this question, he said, 'For it is merely...' and so on. 'Produced by perception' means 'generated by the perception of development,' or 'merely arisen from the perception of development.' Indeed, for that which has no intrinsic nature, there is no arising from any cause whatsoever. Therefore, he said, 'merely the mode of presentation.'

58. Vikkhambhitāneva sannisinnāva, na pana tadatthaṃ ussāho kātabboti adhippāyo. “Upacārasamādhinā”ti vutte itaropi samādhi atthīti atthato āpannanti tampi dassetuṃ “duvidho hi samādhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Dvīhākārehīti jhānadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhadūrībhāvo, thirabhāvappatti cāti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi. Idāni tāni kāraṇāni avatthāmukhena dassetuṃ “upacārabhūmiyaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upacārabhūmiyanti upacārāvatthāyaṃ. Yadipi tadā jhānaṅgāni paṭutarāni mahaggatabhāvappattāni na uppajjanti, tesaṃ [M 1.0148] pana paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanena cittaṃ samādhiyati. Tenāha “nīvaraṇappahānena cittaṃ samāhitaṃ hotī”ti. Paṭilābhabhūmiyanti jhānassa adhigamāvatthāyaṃ. Tadā hi appanāpattānaṃ jhānadhammānaṃ uppattiyā cittaṃ samādhiyati. Tenāha “aṅgapātubhāvenā”ti. Cittaṃ samāhitaṃ hotīti sambandho.

58. The meaning is that they are suppressed and settled down, and one should no longer make an effort for that purpose. When 'by access concentration' is said, it is implied in meaning that there is also another concentration. Therefore, to show that other concentration as well, 'For concentration is twofold...' and so on was begun. 'By two modes' means by these two reasons: the state of the opponents of the jhāna factors being far away, and the attainment of a state of stability. Now, to show those reasons primarily through the aspect of the stage, it is said, 'either on the access level...' and so on. 'On the access level' means at the stage of access. Although at that time the jhāna factors do not arise having become especially sharp and having attained the exalted state, yet the mind becomes concentrated through the suppression of their opposing states. Hence it is said, 'the mind becomes concentrated through the abandonment of hindrances.' 'On the attainment level' means at the stage of attaining jhāna. For then, the mind becomes concentrated through the arising of the jhāna factors that have attained absorption. Hence it is said, 'through the manifestation of the factors.' The connection is: 'the mind becomes concentrated.'

Na thāmajātānīti na jātathāmāni, na bhāvanābalaṃ pattānīti attho. Cittanti jhānacittaṃ. Kevalampi rattiṃ kevalampi divasaṃ tiṭṭhatīti samāpattivelaṃ sandhāyāha. Upacārabhūmiyaṃ nimittavaḍḍhanaṃ yuttanti katvā vuttaṃ “nimittaṃ vaḍḍhetvā”ti. Laddhaparihānīti laddhaupacārajjhānaparihāni. Nimitte avinassante tadārammaṇajhānampi aparihīnameva hoti, nimitte pana ārakkhābhāvena vinaṭṭhe laddhaṃ laddhaṃ jhānampi vinassati tadāyattavuttito. Tenāha “ārakkhamhī”tiādi.

'Not having developed their strength' means they do not have developed strength; the meaning is that they have not attained the power of development. 'Mind' means the jhāna-mind. The phrase 'lasting the entire night or the entire day' is said with reference to the time of attainment. Having considered that increasing the sign is suitable on the access level, it was said, 'having increased the sign.' 'Loss of what is gained' means the loss of the attained access jhāna. When the sign does not perish, the jhāna that has it as its object also does not decline; but when the sign is lost due to a lack of protection, whatever jhāna has been attained also perishes, since its existence depends on it. Therefore, he said, 'One should protect...' and so on.

Sattasappāyavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Seven Kinds of Suitability

59. “Thāvarañca hotī”ti vatvā yathā thāvaraṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “sati upaṭṭhāti, cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathāladdhañhi nimittaṃ tattha satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ekaggataṃ vindantassa [V 1.0139] thiraṃ nāma hoti, surakkhitañca. Sati-ggahaṇena cettha sampajaññaṃ, samādhiggahaṇena vīriyañca saṅgahitaṃ hoti nānantariyabhāvato. Tatthāti tesu āvāsesu. Tīṇi tīṇīti ekekasmiṃ āvāse avutthaavutthaṭṭhāne vasananiyāmena tayo tayo divase vasitvā.

59. Having said, 'and it becomes stable,' in order to show how it becomes stable, it was said, 'mindfulness is established, the mind becomes concentrated.' Indeed, for one who, having made mindfulness well-established on the sign as it was obtained, finds one-pointedness, it is called 'stable' and 'well-guarded.' And here, by the taking up of mindfulness, clear comprehension is also included; and by the taking up of concentration, energy is also included, because of their state of being inseparable. 'There' means 'in those dwellings.' 'Three by three' means: having resided for three days each in each dwelling, in a place not previously dwelt in, according to the rule of residence.

Uttarena vā dakkhiṇena vāti vuttaṃ gamanāgamane sūriyābhimukhabhāvanivāraṇatthanti. Sahassadhanuppamāṇaṃ diyaḍḍhakosaṃ.

'To the north or to the south' was said for the purpose of preventing facing the sun when coming and going. A thousand bow-lengths is one and a half kosas.

Dvattiṃsa tiracchānakathāti rājakathādike (dī. ni. 1.17; ma. ni. 2.223; saṃ. ni. 5.1080; a. ni. 10.69; pāci. 508) sandhāyāha. Tā hi pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato anāgatāpi araññapabbatanadīdīpakathā iti-saddena saṅgahetvā saggamokkhānaṃ tiracchānabhāvato “dvattiṃsa tiracchānakathā”ti vuttā. Dasakathāvatthunissitanti “appicchatā, santuṭṭhi, paviveko, asaṃsaggo, vīriyārambho, sīla, samādhi, paññā, vimutti, vimuttiñāṇadassana”nti imāni appicchakathādīnaṃ vatthūni, tannissitaṃ bhassaṃ sappāyaṃ.

'The thirty-two kinds of animal talk' is said with reference to topics such as talk about kings. Indeed, although those topics are not found explicitly in the Pāḷi, they are included by the particle 'iti' along with talk of forests, mountains, rivers, and islands. Because they are 'animal-like' with respect to heaven and liberation, they are called the 'thirty-two kinds of animal talk.'
