'Based on the ten topics of conversation': 'fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, non-association, arousal of energy, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation'—these are the bases for talk on fewness of wishes and so on. Talk based on these is suitable.

Atiracchānakathikoti [M 1.0149] natiracchānakathiko, tiracchānakathā vidhuraṃ dhammikaṃ kammaṭṭhānapaṭisaṃyuttameva kathaṃ kathetīti adhippāyo. Sīlādiguṇasampannoti sīlasamādhiādiguṇasampanno. Yo hi samādhikammaṭṭhāniko, samādhikammaṭṭhānassa vā pāraṃ patto, so imassa yogino sappāyo. Tenāha “yaṃ nissāyā”tiādi. Kāyadaḷhībahuloti kāyassa santappanaposanappasuto. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.320; ma. ni. 1.186; a. ni. 5.206).

'One who does not engage in animal talk' means one who is not a speaker of animal talk; the meaning is that he speaks talk that is different from animal talk, is in accordance with the Dhamma, and is connected only with the meditation subject. 'Endowed with virtues such as morality' means endowed with virtues such as morality and concentration. Indeed, one who is devoted to the meditation subject of concentration, or has reached the far shore of the meditation subject of concentration, is suitable for this yogī. Therefore, he said, 'depending on whom...' and so on. 'Given to bodily strengthening' means one who is devoted to satisfying and nourishing the body. It is with reference to such a person that it was said: 'Having eaten his fill, as much as he needs, he dwells dedicated to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of lying on his side, and the pleasure of torpor.'

Bhojanaṃ yebhuyyena madhurambilarasavasena sattānaṃ upayogaṃ gacchati dadhiādīsu tathā dassanato. Kaṭukādirasā pana kevalaṃ abhisaṅkhārakā evāti āha “kassaci madhuraṃ, kassaci ambilaṃ sappāyaṃ hotī”ti.

Food, for the most part, becomes useful to beings by way of sweet or sour tastes, as this is seen in the case of curd and so on. But pungent and other tastes are merely conditioners. Therefore, it is said: 'For some, sweetness is agreeable; for others, sourness is agreeable.'

Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe ādhārabhūte, vattamāne vā, yasmiṃ vā iriyāpathe pavattamānassa. Nimittāsevanabahulassāti nimitte āsevanābahulassa paṭibhāganimitte visayabhūte bhāvanāmanasikāraṃ [V 1.0140] bahulaṃ āsevantassa, nimittassa vā gocarāsevanavasena āsevanābahulassa. Yena hi bhāventassa bhāvanāsevanā, tena gocarāsevanāpi icchitabbāti.

'In which posture': this refers to the posture that serves as a basis, or the posture in which one is engaged. 'Of one who frequently cultivates the sign' means: of one who frequently applies development-attention to the counterpart sign as his object; or of one who frequently cultivates the sign by way of taking it as his resort. Indeed, in whatever way the cultivation of the development is desirable for him, in that same way the cultivation of its object-domain should also be desired.

Dasavidhaappanākosallavaṇṇanā

Description of the Ten Kinds of Skill in Absorption

60. Na hoti appanā. Yena vidhinā appanāyaṃ kusalo hoti, so dasavidho vidhi appanākosallaṃ, tannibbattaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ. Vatthuvisadakiriyatoti vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇato appanākosallaṃ icchitabbanti sambandho. Evaṃ sesesupi.

60. Absorption does not occur. The tenfold method by which one becomes skilled in absorption is called 'skill in absorption,' or the knowledge produced by that method is so called. As for the phrase 'by the act of making the objects clear,' the connection is thus: skill in absorption should be desired because it is the act of making the objects clear. Thus it is also for the remaining terms.

61. Cittacetasikānaṃ hi pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato sarīraṃ, tappaṭibaddhāni cīvarādīni ca idha “vatthūnī”ti adhippetāni. Tāni yathā cittassa sukhāvahāni honti, tathā karaṇaṃ tesaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “ajjhattikabāhirāna”ntiādi. Sarīraṃ vāti vā-saddo aṭṭhānappayutto, sarīraṃ sedamalaggahitaṃ vā aññena vā avassutakiccena vibādhitanti adhippāyo. Senāsanaṃ vāti vā-saddena pattādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nanu cāyaṃ nayo [M 1.0150] khuddakapalibodhupacchedena saṅgahito, puna kasmā vuttoti? Saccaṃ saṅgahito, so ca kho bhāvanāya ārambhakāle. Idha pana āraddhakammaṭṭhānassa upacārajjhāne ṭhatvā appanāparivāsaṃ vasantassa kālantare jāte tathāpaṭipatti appanākosallāya vuttā. Avisade sati, visayabhūte vā. Kathaṃ bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa tāni visayo? Antarantarā pavattanakacittuppādavasenevaṃ vuttaṃ. Te hi cittuppādā cittekaggatāya aparisuddhabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Cittacetasikesu nissayādipaccayabhūtesu. Ñāṇampīti pi-saddo sampiṇḍane. Tena “na kevalaṃ taṃ vatthuyeva, atha kho tasmiṃ aparisuddhe ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ hotī”ti dassitaṃ. Taṃsampayuttānaṃ pana aparisuddhatā avuttasiddhā, ñāṇassa ca visuṃ gahaṇaṃ appanāya bahukārattā. Tathā hi jhānaṃ “dandhābhiññaṃ, khippābhiñña”nti ñāṇamukhena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Nissayanissayopi nissayotveva vuccatīti āha “dīpakapallikavaṭṭitelāni nissāyā”ti. Ñāṇe avisade vipassanābhāvanā viya samādhibhāvanāpi paridubbalā hotīti dassetuṃ “aparisuddhena ñāṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kammaṭṭhānanti samathakammaṭṭhānaṃ āha. Vuḍḍhiṃ aṅgapātubhāvena, virūḷhiṃ guṇabhāvena, vepullaṃ sabbaso vasibhāvappattiyā veditabbaṃ. Visade panāti sukkapakkho, tassa vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo.

61. Indeed, because they are the place of occurrence for mind and mental factors, the body, and the robes and other things connected to it, are here intended by the term 'bases.' Making them in such a way that they bring comfort to the mind is the act of making them clear. Therefore, it was said, 'internal and external,' and so on. In the phrase 'the body or,' the particle 'or' (vā) is used in an inappropriate place; the intention is that the body is afflicted by being soiled with sweat and dirt or by some other moist affair. In the phrase 'the lodging or,' by the particle 'or,' the inclusion of the bowl and other requisites should also be understood. But is not this method included in the cutting off of minor obstacles? Why is it stated again? Truly, it is included, but that is at the time of beginning the development. Here, however, for one who has undertaken the meditation subject, is abiding in access concentration, and is dwelling in the preliminary stage of absorption, when a later time arises, such practice is stated for the sake of skill in absorption. When the basis is unclear, or when it has become an object of thought. How do those things become an object for one practicing the development? It is said thus because of the power of intermittently arising thoughts. For those arising thoughts lead to the impurity of one-pointedness of mind. In mind and mental factors, which are the basis and other conditions. In the word 'knowledge too' (ñāṇampi), the particle 'pi' is for aggregation. By this it is shown: 'Not only is that basis impure, but rather, when that is impure, the knowledge also becomes impure.' The impurity of the states associated with it, however, is understood without being stated. And the separate mention of knowledge is because it is of great help to absorption. Thus indeed, jhāna is described through the aspect of knowledge as 'slow direct-knowledge' and 'swift direct-knowledge.' The support of a support is also called a support, thus it is said, 'relying on a lamp, wick, and oil.' To show that when knowledge is unclear, the development of concentration also becomes very weak, like the development of insight, it was said, 'with impure knowledge,' and so on. Therein, by 'meditation subject,' it refers to the serenity meditation subject. Growth (vuḍḍhi) should be known by the manifestation of the factors, development (virūḷhi) by proficiency, and expansion (vepullaṃ) by the attainment of mastery in all respects. As for 'when it is clear,' this is the bright side; its meaning should be known as the opposite of what has been said.

62. Samabhāvakaraṇanti [V 1.0141] kiccato anūnādhikabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yathāpaccayaṃ saddheyyavatthusmiṃ adhimokkhakiccassa paṭutarabhāvena, paññāya avisadatāya, vīriyādīnaṃ ca sithilatādinā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Tenāha “itarāni mandānī”ti. Tatoti tasmā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvato, itaresañca mandattā. Kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggaṇhanaṃ anubalappadānaṃ paggaho, paggahova kiccaṃ, paggahakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti sambandhitabbaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, anissajjanaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ, vikkhepapaṭipakkho. Yena vā sampayuttā avikkhittā honti, so avikkhepo. Rūpagataṃ viya cakkhunā yena yāthāvato visayasabhāvaṃ passati, taṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti balavatā saddhindriyena abhibhūtattā. Sahajātadhammesu hi indaṭṭhaṃ kārentānaṃ sahapavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekarasatāvaseneva atthasiddhi, na aññathā. Tasmāti vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati[M 1.0151]. Tanti saddhindriyaṃ. Dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇenāti yassa saddheyyavatthuno uḷāratādiguṇe adhimuccanassa sātisayappavattiyā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tassa paccayapaccayuppannādivibhāgato yāthāvato vīmaṃsanena. Evañhi evaṃdhammatānayena sabhāvarasato pariggayhamāne savipphāro adhimokkho na hoti, “ayaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvo”ti parijānanavasena paññābyāpārassa sātisayattā. Dhuriyadhammesu hi yathā saddhāya balavabhāve paññāya mandabhāvo hoti, evaṃ paññāya balavabhāve saddhāya mandabhāvo hotīti. Tena vuttaṃ “taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena hāpetabba”nti.

62. 'Making them balanced' means making them neither deficient nor excessive in function. When, according to conditions, the faculty of faith becomes strong due to the greater prominence of its function of resolving on a credible object, the non-clarity of wisdom, and the slackness of energy and other faculties. Therefore, it is said, 'the others are weak.' 'Therefore' means: because of the strength of the faculty of faith and the weakness of the others. Not allowing the mind to fall into the side of laziness, the uplifting of associated states, the giving of support, is called exertion (paggaha). Exertion itself is the function. The connection should be made thus: 'it is not able to perform the function of exertion.' Approaching and staying on the object, or not abandoning it, is establishment (upaṭṭhāna), the opponent of distraction. Or, that by which associated states are not distracted is non-distraction. Just as one sees a collection of forms with the eye, that by which one sees the nature of the object as it really is—it is unable to perform that function of seeing, because it is overpowered by the strong faculty of faith. Indeed, among co-arisen states that are performing the role of a chief, the accomplishment of the goal occurs only through the power of their single function, not otherwise. By 'therefore,' it refers back to the stated meaning as the cause. 'That' refers to the faculty of faith. 'By reviewing the nature of phenomena' means: by investigating as it really is, through analysis of cause, effect, and so on, that credible object in whose excellent qualities the faculty of faith has become strong due to the excessive operation of its resolving function. For when the object is being grasped according to its nature and function by the principle of 'things being thus,' a vibrant confidence does not occur, due to the abundance of wisdom's activity through fully understanding, 'This is the nature of these phenomena.' Indeed, among the leading factors, just as when faith is strong, wisdom becomes weak, so when wisdom is strong, faith becomes weak. Therefore, it was said, 'That should be diminished by reviewing the nature of phenomena.'

Tathā amanasikārenāti yenākārena bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, tenākārena bhāvanāya ananuyuñjanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha duvidhena saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo, attano vā paccayavisesato kiccuttariyena, vīriyādīnaṃ vā mandakiccatāya. Tattha paṭhamavikappe hāpanavidhi dassito, dutiyavikappe pana yathā manasi karoto vīriyādīnaṃ mandakiccatāya saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena vīriyādīnaṃ paṭukiccabhāvāvahena manasikārena saddhindriyaṃ tehi samarasaṃ karontena hāpetabbaṃ. Iminā nayena sesindriyesupi hāpanavidhi veditabbo.

'Likewise by not attending' means this: by not engaging in the development in that manner which makes the faculty of faith strong for the practitioner. Here, the strength of the faculty of faith occurs in two ways: either through its own particular conditions due to superiority of function, or through the weak functioning of energy and other faculties. Therein, in the first alternative, the method of diminishing has been shown. In the second alternative, however, just as the faculty of faith became strong for one attending due to the weak functioning of energy and other faculties, so it should be diminished by not attending in that manner, and instead attending in a way that brings about the sharp functioning of energy and the others, thereby making the faculty of faith equal in function to them. By this method, the way of diminishing should be understood for the remaining faculties as well.

Vakkalittheravatthūti so hi āyasmā saddhādhimuttatāya katādhikāro satthu rūpakāyadassanappasuto eva hutvā viharanto satthārā “kiṃ te, vakkali, iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena? Yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.87) ovaditvā [V 1.0142] kammaṭṭhāne niyojitopi taṃ ananuyuñjanto paṇāmito attānaṃ vinipātetuṃ papātaṭṭhānaṃ abhiruhi. Atha naṃ satthā yathānisinnova obhāsaṃ visajjento attānaṃ dassetvā –

The story of the Elder Vakkali: Indeed, that venerable one, having made a supreme aspiration and being one with faith as his dominant faculty, dwelt solely intent on seeing the Teacher's physical form. The Teacher admonished him, saying, "What is there for you, Vakkali, in seeing this foul body? Indeed, Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, sees me," and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 3.87). Though he was enjoined to a meditation subject, he did not apply himself to it and climbed to a precipice to throw himself down. Then the Teacher, just as he was seated, emitting a radiance, revealed himself, saying—

“Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane;

Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 381) –

A monk full of joy, serene in the Buddha's teaching, may attain the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of conditioned formations.

Gāthaṃ vatvā “ehi vakkalī”ti āha. So tena amateneva abhisitto haṭṭhatuṭṭho hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Saddhāya pana balavabhāvato [M 1.0152] vipassanāvīthiṃ na otari. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā indriyasamataṃ paṭipādento kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā adāsi. So satthārā dinnanayena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ “vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassana”nti.

Having recited the verse, he said, "Come, Vakkali." Then, as if anointed with that deathless nectar, he became joyful and delighted, and established insight. However, due to the strength of his faith, he did not enter upon the path of insight. Knowing this, the Blessed One, bringing about the balance of the faculties, purified the meditation subject and gave it to him. Following the method given by the Teacher, he made an effort in insight and, in due order of the path, attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said, "Here, the story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration."

Itarakiccabhedanti upaṭṭhānādikiccavisesaṃ. Passaddhādīti ādi-saddena samādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Hāpetabbanti yathā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena hāyati, evaṃ vīriyindriyassa adhimattatā passaddhiādibhāvanāya hāyati, samādhipakkhiyattā tassā. Tathā hi sā samādhindriyassa adhimattataṃ kosajjapātato rakkhantī vīriyādibhāvanā viya vīriyindriyassa adhimattataṃ uddhaccapātato rakkhantī ekaṃsato hāpeti. Tena vuttaṃ “passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabba”nti.

`Itarakiccabheda` means the distinction of other duties, the specific duties such as establishing mindfulness and so forth. In `passaddhādi`, by the word `ādi`, the inclusion of the enlightenment factors of concentration and equanimity should be understood. As for `hāpetabba` (should be diminished): just as the strength of the faculty of faith is diminished by reflecting on the nature of phenomena, so too the excessiveness of the faculty of energy is diminished by the development of serenity and so on, because that belongs to the side of concentration. For indeed, that development of serenity and so on diminishes the excessiveness of the faculty of energy by guarding against the fall into restlessness, just as the development of energy and so on protects the faculty of concentration from falling into sloth. Therefore, it is said, 'it should be diminished through the development of serenity and so on.'

Soṇattherassa vatthūti (mahāva. 243) sukumārassa soṇattherassa vatthu. So hi āyasmā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sītavane viharanto “mama sarīraṃ sukhumālaṃ, na ca sakkā sukheneva sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ, kāyaṃ kilametvāpi samaṇadhammo kātabbo”ti ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāya padhānamanuyuñjanto pādatalesu phoṭesu uṭṭhitesupi vedanaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā daḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ karonto accāraddhavīriyatāya visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Satthā tattha gantvā vīṇovādena ovaditvā vīriyasamatāyojanavidhiṃ dassento kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā gijjhakūṭaṃ gato. Theropi satthārā dinnanayena vīriyasamataṃ yojento vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabba”nti.

The story of the Elder Soṇa (Mahāvagga 243): The story of the refined Elder Soṇa. Indeed, that venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, while dwelling in the Cool Grove, thought, "My body is refined, and it is not possible to attain happiness with ease; the ascetic's duty must be done even by exhausting the body." Resolving on standing and walking meditation alone and applying himself to striving, even when blisters arose on the soles of his feet, he disregarded the pain and made strong effort, yet he was unable to produce any special attainment due to his excessively aroused energy. The Teacher went there and advised him with the simile of the lute, showing the method of applying the balance of energy. He then purified the meditation subject and went to Vulture Peak. The elder, following the method given by the Teacher, applying the balance of his energy, made an effort in insight and was established in Arahantship. Therefore, it is said, "The story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown."

Sesesupīti [V 1.0143] satisamādhipaññindriyesupi. Ekassāti ekekassa. Sāmaññaniddesovāyaṃ daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ paccekaṃ adhimattatāya pana hāpanavasena samataṃ dassetvā idāni tattha yesaṃ visesato asādhāraṇato, sādhāraṇato ca samatā icchitabbā, taṃ dassetuṃ “visesato panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Etthāti etesu pañcasu indriyesu. Samatanti saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ anūnānadhikabhāvaṃ. Tathā samādhivīriyānaṃ[M 1.0153]. Yathā hi saddhāpaññānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ dhuriyadhammabhūtānaṃ kiccato aññamaññānativattanaṃ visesato icchitabbameva, yato nesaṃ samadhuratāya appanā sampajjatīti, evaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ kosajjauddhaccapakkhikānaṃ samarasatāya sati aññamaññūpatthambhanato sampayuttadhammānaṃ antadvayapātābhāvena sammadeva appanā ijjhati.

In the remaining ones also—that is, in the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. `Ekassa` means of each one. This should be understood as a general indication. Having thus shown the balance of the five faculties by way of diminishing the excessiveness of each one, now, to show of which of them balance is to be desired especially, both in a non-common and common way, the words "But especially..." and so on were said. Here means among these five faculties. Balance means the state of faith and wisdom not being deficient or excessive in relation to each other. Similarly for concentration and energy. For just as it is especially desired that faith and wisdom, which are distinct burden-bearing states, do not surpass each other in function—since through their balanced yoking, absorption is accomplished—so too, when concentration and energy, which belong to the side of sloth and restlessness, are of a harmonious function, then due to their mutual support, absorption is rightly accomplished by the associated states because of their not falling into the two extremes.

“Balavasaddho hī”tiādi nidassanavasena vuttaṃ. Tassattho – yo balavatiyā saddhāya samannāgato avisadañāṇo, so muddhappasanno hoti, na aveccappasanno. Tathā hi so avatthusmiṃ pasīdati seyyathāpi titthiyasāvakā. Kerāṭikapakkhanti sāṭheyyapakkhaṃ bhajati. Saddhāhīnāya paññāya atidhāvanto “deyyavatthupariccāgena vinā cittuppādamattenapi dānamayaṃ puññaṃ hotī”tiādīni parikappeti hetupaṭirūpakehi vañcito. Evaṃbhūto pana sukkhatakkaviluttacitto paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ nādiyati, saññattiṃ na gacchati. Tenāha “bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hotī”ti. Yathā cettha saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaviraho na atthāvaho anatthāvaho ca, evamidhāpi samādhivīriyānaṃ aññamaññaviraho na avikkhepāvaho vikkhepāvaho cāti veditabbaṃ. Kosajjaṃ abhibhavati, tena appanaṃ na pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo. Uddhaccaṃ abhibhavatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tadubhayanti taṃ saddhāpaññādvayaṃ, samādhivīriyadvayañca. Samaṃ kātabbanti samarasaṃ kātabbaṃ.

"One who has strong faith," and so on, is said by way of illustration. Its meaning is: one who is endowed with strong faith but has unclear knowledge becomes blindly devoted, not devoted with verified confidence. For indeed, such a person is pleased with what is baseless, like the disciples of sectarians. `Kerāṭikapakkhanti` means he resorts to the side of deceit. One who overruns with wisdom that is deficient in faith, being deceived by semblances of reason, speculates such things as, "Merit consisting of giving arises even by a mere arising of thought, without the giving up of things to be given." Such a person, with a mind plundered by dry logic, does not accept the word of the wise and does not come to understanding. Therefore, it was said, "Like a disease arising from medicine, it becomes incurable." And just as here the absence of one from the other of faith and wisdom is not beneficial but is harmful, so too here it should be known that the absence of one from the other of concentration and energy does not lead to non-distraction but leads to distraction. Sloth overcomes, therefore he does not attain absorption—this is the meaning. In "restlessness overcomes" also, this is the same method. `Tadubhayaṃ` means that pair of faith and wisdom, and that pair of concentration and energy. `Samaṃ kātabbaṃ` means they should be made of harmonious function.

Samādhikammikassāti samathakammaṭṭhānikassa. Evanti evaṃ sante, saddhāya tesaṃ balavabhāve satīti attho. Saddahantoti “pathavī pathavī”ti manasikaraṇamattena kathaṃ jhānuppattīti acintetvā “addhā sammāsambuddhena vuttavidhi ijjhissatī”ti saddahanto saddhaṃ janento. Okappentoti ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā viya adhimuccanavasena okappento pakkhandanto. Ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati samādhipadhānattā jhānassa. Ubhinnanti samādhipaññānaṃ, samādhikammikassa samādhino adhimattatāpi icchitabbāti āha “samatāyapī”ti, samabhāvenāpīti attho. Appanāti idhādhippetaappanā. Tathā hi “hotiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati[V 1.0144], lokuttarappanā pana tesaṃ samabhāveneva icchitā. Yathāha – “samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.1, 5).

For the practitioner of concentration means: for one whose meditation subject is serenity. Thus means: when this is so, the meaning is that faith among them is strong. Believing means: not thinking, 'How could the arising of jhāna occur merely by the mental application "earth, earth"?', but generating faith with the thought, 'Surely, the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One will succeed.' Placing trust means: placing trust and plunging in by way of resolve, as if entering into the object. It is proper for one-pointedness to be strong, because concentration is the primary factor of jhāna. Of both refers to concentration and wisdom. For the practitioner of concentration, an excess of concentration is also desirable—hence, it is said 'by balance also,' meaning 'also by evenness.' Absorption means the absorption intended here. Indeed, the statement 'it surely arises' is spoken with doubt, but supramundane absorption, on the other hand, is desired only with their evenness. As it is said: 'He develops serenity and insight yoked together' (Paṭi. ma. 2.1, 5).

Yadi [M 1.0154] visesato saddhāpaññānaṃ, samādhivīriyānañca samatā icchitā, kathaṃ satīti āha “sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭatī”ti. Sabbatthāti līnuddhaccapakkhesu pañcasu indriyesu. Uddhaccapakkhiye gaṇhanto “saddhāvīriyapaññāna”nti āha. Aññathāpīti ca gahetabbā siyā. Tathā hi “kosajjapakkhena samādhinā” icceva vuttaṃ, na “passaddhisamādhiupekkhāhī”ti. Sā sati. Sabbesu rājakammesu niyutto sabbakammiko. Tena kāraṇena sabbattha icchitabbatthena. Āha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Sabbattha niyuttā sabbatthikā, sabbena vā līnuddhaccapakkhiyena bojjhaṅgaggahaṇena atthetabbā sabbatthiyā, sabbatthiyāva sabbatthikā. Cittanti kusalacittaṃ. Tassa hi sati paṭisaraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya. Tenāha “ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”tiādi.

If balance is particularly desired between faith and wisdom, and between concentration and energy, what about mindfulness? To this, it is said: 'But as for mindfulness, it is proper for it to be strong everywhere.' 'Everywhere' means: in the five faculties, in the aspects of sloth and restlessness. Taking those on the side of restlessness, he said, 'faith, energy, and wisdom.' Otherwise, joy should also be taken. For indeed, it is said only 'with concentration on the side of sloth,' not 'with tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.' That mindfulness is like an 'all-doer' appointed to all royal duties. For that reason, because it is to be desired everywhere, the commentary says: 'Engaged everywhere, it is 'all-pervading' (sabbatthikā). Or, because it is needed by the entire group of enlightenment factors on the sides of both sloth and restlessness, it is 'needed everywhere' (sabbatthiyā); 'needed everywhere' is indeed 'all-pervading.' 'Mind' means the wholesome mind. For that mind, mindfulness is indeed the refuge, the final resort for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized. Therefore, it is said, 'Its manifestation is protection,' and so on.

63. Cittekaggatānimittassāti cittekaggatāya nimittassa, cittekaggatāsaṅkhātassa ca nimittassa. Cittassa hi samāhitākāraṃ sallakkhetvā samathanimittaṃ rakkhantoyeva kasiṇanimittaṃ rakkhati. Tasmā pathavīkasiṇādikassāti ādi-saddena na kevalaṃ paṭibhāganimittasseva, atha kho samathanimittassāpi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tanti rakkhaṇakosallaṃ. Idha appanākosallakathāyaṃ “nimittakosalla”nti adhippetaṃ, karaṇabhāvanākosallānaṃ pageva siddhattāti adhippāyo.

63. The sign of one-pointedness of mind means: the sign for one-pointedness of mind, and also the sign designated as one-pointedness of mind. For, having discerned the composed aspect of the mind, only one who protects the sign of serenity thereby protects the kasiṇa sign. Therefore, in the case of 'the earth kasiṇa and so forth,' the term 'and so forth' should be understood to include not only the counterpart sign, but also the sign of serenity. That is skill in maintaining. Here, in this discussion of skill in absorption, 'skill in the sign' is intended, since the skills in preparation and development are already established—this is the meaning.

64. Atisithilavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena pamodanasaṃvejanavipariyāye saṅgaṇhāti. Līnanti saṅkucitaṃ kosajjapakkhapatitaṃ. Cittanti bhāvanācittaṃ. Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo bhāvetīti ettha “tayo”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Yathā pana te bhāvetabbā, taṃ sayameva vakkhati.

64. With excessive slackness of energy, etc.—here, 'etc.' includes the opposite of gladdening and rousing. 'Slothful' means contracted, fallen to the side of sloth. 'Mind' refers to the mind of development. 'One develops the enlightenment factors, such as investigation of phenomena'—here, the word 'three' should be supplied and connected. As for how they should be developed, that will be explained by himself.

Parittanti appakaṃ. Ujjāletukāmoti padīpetukāmo. Udakavātaṃ dadeyyāti udakamissaṃ vātaṃ upaneyya. Akāloti nakālo, ayuttakālo vā. Satiādidhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā bujjhati etāyāti katvā, taṃsamaṅgino vā bujjhatīti bodhino yogino aṅganti bojjhaṅgo[V 1.0145], pasattho, sundaro vā bojjhaṅgo sambojjhaṅgo[M 1.0155]. Kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā passaddhiyeva sambojjhaṅgo passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, tassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa. Samādhisambojjhaṅgādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – samādhissa tāva padatthalakkhaṇāni heṭṭhā āgatāneva. Upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā. Sā panāyaṃ atthato tatramajjhattupekkhāva idha bojjhaṅgupekkhā veditabbā. Dusamuṭṭhāpayanti samuṭṭhāpetuṃ uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ. Dhammānaṃ, dhammesu vā vicayo dhammavicayo, paññāti attho. Vīrassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā, vidhinā vā īretabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vīriyaṃ, ussāho. Pīṇeti kāyaṃ, cittaṃ ca santappetīti pīti.

“Limited” means little. “Desiring to illuminate” means desiring to light up. “Would give water and wind” means would bring wind mixed with water. “At the wrong time” means not the time, or an inappropriate time. One awakens by this awakening, which is designated as the harmony of mindfulness and other states; or, it is an 'awakening factor' (bojjhaṅga) because it is a factor of an awakened one (bodhino), i.e., a yogi who awakens (bujjhati). An excellent or beautiful awakening factor is a 'factor of full awakening' (sambojjhaṅga). Tranquility, which has the characteristic of calming bodily and mental distress, is itself the 'awakening factor of tranquility' (passaddhisambojjhaṅga); of this awakening factor of tranquility. The same method applies to the awakening factor of concentration and the others. This, however, is a special point: for concentration, its word-meanings and characteristics have already been given below. 'Equanimity' (upekkhā) is so called because one looks on (ikkhati) fittingly. Here, however, this should be understood as the equanimity that is an awakening factor, which in essence is specific neutrality. 'They cannot arouse' means they would be unable to arouse, to produce. 'Investigation of phenomena' (dhammavicayo) means investigation of phenomena, or in phenomena; the meaning is wisdom. 'Energy' (vīriyaṃ) is the state of an energetic person, or their action, or that which should be stirred up and set in motion according to a method; it means exertion. 'Joy' (pīti) is so called because it gladdens the body and satisfies the mind.

Yaṃ yaṃ sakaṃ yathāsakaṃ, attano attanoti attho. Āhāravasenāti paccayavasena. Bhāvanāti uppādanā, vaḍḍhanā ca. Kusalākusalāti kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalā, tappaṭipakkhato akusalā. Ye akusalā, te sāvajjā. Ye kusalā, te anavajjā. Akusalā hīnā, itare paṇītā. Kusalāpi vā hīnehi chandādīhi āraddhā hīnā, itare paṇītā. Kaṇhāti kāḷakā cittassa apabhassarabhāvakaraṇā, sukkāti odātā cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Kaṇhābhijātihetuto vā kaṇhā, sukkābhijātihetuto sukkā. Te eva sappaṭibhāgā. Kaṇhā hi ujuvipaccanīkatāya sukkehi sappaṭibhāgā. Tathā sukkāpi itarehi. Atha vā kaṇhā ca sukkā ca sappaṭibhāgā ca kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā. Sukhā hi vedanā dukkhāya vedanāya sappaṭibhāgā, dukkhā ca vedanā sukhāya sappaṭibhāgāti. Anuppannassāti anibbattassa. Uppādāyāti uppādanatthāya. Uppannassāti nibbattassa. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunabhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Bhāvanāyāti vaḍḍhiyā. Pāripūriyāti paripūraṇatthāya.

“Whatever one's own, as one's own” means belonging to oneself. “By way of nutriment” means by way of condition. “Development” means production and growth. “Wholesome and unwholesome”: wholesome (kusalā) is so called in the sense of being born of skill; unwholesome (akusalā) is the opposite of that. Those that are unwholesome are blameworthy. Those that are wholesome are blameless. The unwholesome are inferior; the others are superior. Or even wholesome states, when undertaken with inferior desire and so on, are inferior; the others are superior. “Dark” means black, because it makes the mind non-luminous. “Bright” means white, because it makes the mind luminous. Or, they are dark because they are of a dark birth, and bright because they are of a bright birth. These very things are counterparts. For the dark are counterparts to the bright because they are directly contrary. Similarly, the bright are also counterparts to the others. Or, 'dark-bright-with-counterpart' (kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā) means dark and bright and with a counterpart. For pleasant feeling is a counterpart to painful feeling, and painful feeling is a counterpart to pleasant feeling. “Of the unarisen” means of what has not been generated. “For the arising” means for the purpose of production. “Of the arisen” means of what has been generated. “For increase” means for its repeated occurrence. “For abundance” means for its state of vastness. “For development” means for its growth. “For fulfillment” means for the purpose of completion.

Tatthāti “atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā dassitapāṭhe. Sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasenāti ekajjhaṃ katvā gahaṇe anavajjasukhavipākādikassa visuṃ visuṃ pana phusanādikassa sabhāvalakkhaṇassa, aniccādikassa sāmaññalakkhaṇassa ca paṭivijjhanavasena. Pavattamanasikāroti kusalādīnaṃ taṃtaṃsabhāvalakkhaṇādikassa yāthāvato avabujjhanavasena uppannajavanacittuppādo. So hi aviparītamanasikāratāya “yonisomanasikāro”ti vutto. Tadābhogatāya āvajjanāpi taggatikāva. Ruppanalakkhaṇādikampi [M 1.0156] idha sāmaññalakkhaṇeneva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kusalakiriyāya ādiārambhavasena pavattavīriyaṃ dhitisabhāvatāya “dhātū”ti vuttanti āha “ārambhadhātūti paṭhamavīriyaṃ vuccatī”ti. Laddhāsevanaṃ vīriyaṃ balappattaṃ [V 1.0146] hutvā paṭipakkhaṃ vidhamatīti āha “kosajjato nikkhantattā tato balavatara”nti. Adhimattādhimattatarānaṃ paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ vidhamanasamatthaṃ paṭupaṭutarādibhāvappattaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavatara”nti. Tiṭṭhati pavattati etthāti ṭhāniyā, pītisambojjhaṅgassa ṭhāniyā pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā. Ṭhātabbo vā ṭhāniyo, pītisambojjhaṅgo ṭhāniyo etesūti pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā, aparāparaṃ vattamānā pītisambojjhaṅgasampayuttā dhammā. Yasmā pana tesu pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgassa visesakāraṇaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “pītiyā eva etaṃ nāma”nti. Uppādakamanasikāroti yathā manasi karoto anuppanno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati, uppanno ca vaḍḍhati, tathā pavattamanasikāro.

“Therein” refers to the text indicated by “There is, O monks,” etc. “By way of penetrating the individual and general characteristics”: this means, when grasping collectively that which is blameless, has pleasant results, and so on, it is by way of penetrating the individual characteristics of such things as contact, one by one, and the general characteristics of such things as impermanence. “Occurring attention” is the arising of an impulsion-consciousness by way of correctly understanding the respective individual characteristics and so on of wholesome states and so on. Since this is non-perverse attention, it is called “wise attention.” Because of its inclination, even the adverting consciousness has the same nature. The characteristic of “being afflicted,” etc., should be understood as included here under the general characteristic. The energy that proceeds by way of the initial undertaking of a wholesome action, because of its nature as steadfastness, is called an “element”; thus it is said: “The element of arousal is called the initial energy.” Energy that has been cultivated becomes strong and shatters the opposition; thus it is said: “Because it has departed from laziness, it is stronger than that.” It becomes capable of shattering opposing states that are intense and more intense, attaining a state of being more and more sharp; thus it is said: “Because it surmounts successive stages, it is even stronger than that.” It stands and proceeds in this, thus it is a “basis” (ṭhāniyā); the basis for the awakening factor of joy is “the basis for the awakening factor of joy” (pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā). Or, that which should be established is a basis (ṭhāniyo). The awakening factor of joy is to be established in these states, thus they are called 'bases for the awakening factor of joy'; these are the successively occurring states associated with the awakening factor of joy. But since joy itself is the specific cause for the awakening factor of joy among them, it is said: “This name is because of joy.” “Generative attention” is attention that occurs in such a way that, for one attending to it, the unarisen awakening factor of joy arises and the arisen one grows.

Paripucchakatāti pariyogāhetvā pucchakabhāvo. Pañcapi hi nikāye uggahetvā ācariye pariyupāsitvā tassa tassa atthaṃ paripucchantassa, te vā saha aṭṭhakathāya pariyogāhetvā yaṃ yaṃ tattha gaṇṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ taṃ “idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ, imassa ko attho”ti pucchantassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo uppajjatīti. Vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā saṅkhepato, vitthārato ca pakāsitā eva. Tattha pana samādhisaṃvattaniyabhāvena āgatā, idha paññāsaṃvattaniyabhāvena. Yadaggena hi samādhisaṃvattanikā, tadaggena paññāsaṃvattanikā samādhissa ñāṇapaccupaṭṭhānato. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.99; 5.1071) vuttaṃ. Duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā nāma duppaññānaṃ mandabuddhīnaṃ bhattanikkhittakākamaṃsanikkhittasunakhasadisānaṃ momūhapuggalānaṃ dūrato pariccajanā. Paññavantapuggalasevanā nāma paññāya katādhikārānaṃ saccapaṭiccasamuppādādīsu kusalānaṃ ariyānaṃ, vipassanākammikānaṃ vā mahāpaññānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ. Gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇāti gambhīrañāṇehi caritabbānaṃ khandhāyatanadhātādīnaṃ, saccapaccayākārādidīpanānaṃ vā suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ suttantānaṃ paccavekkhaṇā. Tadadhimuttatāti paññādhimuttatā, paññāya ninnapoṇapabbhāratāti attho.

“Thorough questioning” means the state of being a questioner after having thoroughly investigated. For one who, having learned the five Nikāyas and attended on a teacher, questions the meaning of this and that; or for one who, having thoroughly investigated them together with the commentaries, asks about any knotty points therein, saying, “Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?”—for such a one the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena arises. “Making the basis pure” and “bringing the faculties to a state of balance” have been explained in brief and in detail. There, however, they were presented as being conducive to concentration; here, as being conducive to wisdom. For in as much as they are conducive to concentration, to that extent they are also conducive to wisdom, because concentration has knowledge as its proximate cause. For it is said: “One who is concentrated understands things as they really are.” “Avoiding persons of deficient wisdom” means keeping at a distance those of deficient wisdom, the dull-witted, utterly deluded persons who are like crows for which a meal has been put down or dogs for which meat has been put down. “Associating with wise persons” means from time to time approaching noble ones who have made a foundation in wisdom and are skilled in the truths, dependent origination, and so on, or those of great wisdom who are practitioners of insight meditation. “Reflecting on the domain of profound knowledge” means reflecting on the aggregates, sense bases, elements, etc., which are to be traversed by profound knowledge, or on the suttas connected with emptiness that illuminate the truths, conditions, modes, and so on. “Being resolved on that” means being resolved on wisdom; the meaning is having a bent, tendency, and inclination towards wisdom.

Apāyādīti [M 1.0157] ādi-saddena jātiādiṃ atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakañca dukkhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vīriyāyattassa lokiyalokuttaravisesassa adhigamo eva ānisaṃso, tassa dassanasīlatā vīriyāyatta…pe… dassitā. Sapubbabhāgo nibbānagāmimaggo gamanavīthi gantabbā paṭipajjitabbā paṭipadāti katvā[V 1.0147]. Dāyakānaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena piṇḍāpacāyanatāti paccayadāyakānaṃ attani kārassa attano sammāpaṭipattiyā mahapphalakārabhāvassa karaṇena piṇḍassa bhikkhāya paṭipūjanā. Itarathāti āmisapūjāya. Kusītapuggalaparivajjanatāti alasānaṃ bhāvanāya nāmamattampi ajānantānaṃ kāyadaḷhībahulānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhādianuyuñjanakānaṃ tiracchānakathikānaṃ puggalānaṃ dūrato pariccajanā. Āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatāti “divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāyā”tiādinā (vibha. 519; a. ni. 3.16) bhāvanārambhavasena āraddhavīriyānaṃ daḷhaparakkamānaṃ puggalānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanā. Sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatāti catubbidhasammappadhānānubhāvassa paccavekkhaṇatā. Tadadhimuttatāti tasmiṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅge adhimutti sabbiriyāpathesu ninnapoṇapabbhāratā. Ettha ca thinamiddhavinodanakusītapuggalaparivajjanaāraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatadadhimuttatā paṭipakkhavidhamanapaccayūpasaṃhāravasena, apāyādibhayapaccavekkhaṇādayo samuttejanavasena vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādakā daṭṭhabbā.

“States of woe, etc.”: by the word “etc.” it includes suffering rooted in the round in the past, such as birth, etc.; suffering rooted in the round in the future; and suffering rooted in the search for sustenance in the present. The benefit is the very attainment of the mundane and supramundane distinction, which is dependent on energy; the habit of seeing this is dependent on energy… as shown. The path leading to Nibbāna, which has a preliminary part, is a 'road to be travelled' (gamanavīthi), since it is a course (paṭipadā) to be travelled (gantabbā) and to be practiced (paṭipajjitabbā). “Venerating the almsfood by making it of great fruit for the donors”: this means venerating in return the almsfood received on almsround by making the donors' gift to oneself become of great fruit through one's own right practice. “Otherwise” means by a material offering. “Avoiding lazy persons” means keeping at a distance lazy persons who do not know even the name of development, who are much given to physical strengthening, who eat as much as they want and are devoted to the pleasure of lying down, etc., and who engage in animal talk. “Associating with persons of aroused energy” means from time to time approaching persons of aroused energy and firm striving, who have undertaken development as stated: “by walking and sitting during the day,” etc. “Reflecting on the right strivings” means reflecting on the power of the fourfold right striving. “Being resolved on that” means being resolved on the awakening factor of energy, having a bent, tendency, and inclination towards it in all postures. And here, the removal of sloth and torpor, avoiding lazy persons, associating with persons of aroused energy, and being resolved on that should be seen as producers of the awakening factor of energy by way of adducing conditions that shatter the opposition; while reflecting on the fear of the states of woe, etc., should be seen as producers by way of stimulation.

Buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena thusakharahadayā lūkhapuggalā, tabbipariyāyena siniddhapuggalā veditabbā. Buddhādīnaṃ guṇaparidīpanā sampasādanīyasuttādayo (dī. ni. 3.141 ādayo) pasādanīyasuttantā. Imehi ākārehīti yathāvuttehi kusalādīnaṃ sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭivijjhanādiākārehi ceva paripucchakatādiākārehi ca. Ete dhammeti ete kusalādīsu yonisomanasikārādike ceva dhammatthaññutādike ca.

Persons with hearts as rough as coarse chaff, due to an absence of the affection of faith towards the Buddha and others, are coarse persons; by way of the opposite, refined persons are to be known. Discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Buddha and others, such as the Sampasādanīya Sutta, are inspiring suttantas. 'By these modes' means by the aforementioned modes of penetrating the intrinsic nature and general characteristic of wholesome states and so on, and by the modes of questioning and so on. 'These dhammas' means these dhammas such as wise attention in regard to wholesome states and so on, and the state of knowing the meaning of the Dhamma and so on.

65. Accāraddhavīriyatādīhīti ativiya paggahitavīriyatādīhi. Ādi-saddena saṃvejanapamodanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Uddhatanti samādhiādīnaṃ mandatāya avūpasantaṃ. Duvūpasamayanti vūpasametuṃ samādhātuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ.

65. 'Due to the state of overly aroused energy, etc.' means due to the state of having exceedingly exerted energy and so on. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it includes causing spiritual urgency, causing joy, and so on. 'Restless' means unpacified due to the weakness of concentration and so on. 'Hard to pacify' means unable to be pacified or well-composed.

Taṃ [M 1.0158] ākāraṃ sallakkhetvāti yenākārena assa yogino passaddhi samādhi upekkhāti ime passaddhiādayo dhammā pubbe yathārahaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle uppannapubbā, taṃ cittataṃsampayuttadhammānaṃ passaddhākāraṃ, samāhitākāraṃ, ajjhupekkhitākārañca upalakkhetvā upadhāretvā. Tīsupi padesūti “atthi, bhikkhave, kāyappassaddhī”tiādinā āgatesu tīsupi vākyesu, tehi vā pakāsitesu tīsu dhammakoṭṭhāsesu. Yathāsamāhitākāraṃ sallakkhetvā gayhamāno [V 1.0148] samatho eva samathanimittanti āha “samathanimittanti ca samathassevetamadhivacana”nti. Nānārammaṇe paribbhamanena vividhaṃ aggaṃ etassāti byaggo, vikkhepo. Tathā hi so anavaṭṭhānaraso, bhantatāpaccupaṭṭhāno ca vutto. Ekaggatābhāvato byaggapaṭipakkhoti abyaggo, samādhi. So eva nimittanti pubbe viya vattabbaṃ. Tenāha “avikkhepaṭṭhena ca tasseva abyagganimittanti adhivacana”nti.

'Having marked that mode' means: having marked and ascertained the tranquil mode, the composed mode, and the equanimous mode of the mind and its associated states, by which mode for this yogī these dhammas—tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—have arisen before at such and such a time, as appropriate. 'In the three passages' means in the three statements that have come down, beginning with "There is, bhikkhus, bodily tranquility," or in the three sections of the Dhamma explained by them. He said, "The sign of serenity is a designation for serenity itself," because serenity, being grasped by marking the composed mode as it is, is itself the sign of serenity. Because it wanders among various objects, it has various ends (agga); thus it is 'byagga,' which means distraction. Indeed, it is said to have the function of instability and the manifestation of agitation. Because it is the state of one-pointedness, the opposite of 'byagga' is 'abyagga,' which means concentration. That itself is the sign; this should be stated as before. Therefore, he said, "And by the meaning of non-distraction, that itself is a designation for the sign of non-agitation (abyagga)."

Sarīrāvatthaṃ ñatvā mattaso paribhutto paṇītāhāro kāyalahutādīnaṃ samuṭṭhāpanena passaddhiyā paccayo hoti, tathā utusappāyaṃ, iriyāpathasappāyañca sevitaṃ, payogo ca kāyiko pavattitoti āha “paṇītabhojanasevanatā”tiādi. Payogasamatādīnaṃ abhāvena sadarathakāyacittā puggalā sāraddhapuggalā. Vuttavipariyāyena passaddhakāyā puggalā veditabbā.

Having known the body's condition, excellent food consumed in moderation becomes a condition for tranquility by causing the arising of bodily lightness and so on; similarly, when a suitable climate and a suitable posture are resorted to, and bodily exertion is undertaken, thus he said, 'the partaking of excellent food,' and so on. Persons with agitated body and mind due to the absence of balance in exertion and so on are agitated persons. By way of the opposite of what was said, persons with tranquil bodies are to be known.

Nirassādassāti bhāvanassādarahitassa. Bhāvanā hi vīthipaṭipannā pubbenāparaṃ visesavatī pavattamānā cittassa assādaṃ upasamasukhaṃ āvahati, tadabhāvato nirassādaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Saddhāsaṃvegavasenāti saddhāvasena, saṃvegavasena ca. Sampahaṃsanatāti sammadeva pahaṃsanatā saṃvejanapubbakapasāduppādanena bhāvanā cittassa tosanā. Sammāpavattassāti līnuddhaccavirahena, samathavīthipaṭipattiyā ca samaṃ, savisesañca pavattiyā sammadeva pavattassa bhāvanācittassa. Ajjhupekkhanatāti paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāvaṭatā. Jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatāti paṭhamādīni jhānāni paccanīkadhammehi suṭṭhu vimuttatādinā teyeva vimokkhā tesaṃ “evaṃ bhāvanā, evaṃ samāpajjanā, evaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ saṃkileso, evaṃ vodāna”nti pati pati avekkhaṇā.

'Of one without delight' means of one devoid of delight in meditation. For meditation, having entered the right path and proceeding from a former time to a later time with distinction, brings the mind's delight, which is the happiness of tranquility; due to the absence of that, the mind is without delight. 'By the power of faith and spiritual urgency' means by the power of faith and by the power of spiritual urgency. 'Gladdening' is the state of gladdening rightly; it is the satisfying of the meditation-mind by producing clarity preceded by spiritual urgency. 'Of that which proceeds rightly' means of the meditation-mind that proceeds rightly, by proceeding evenly and with distinction, being free from sloth and restlessness, and by following the right path of serenity. 'Equanimity' is the state of not being occupied with exerting, restraining, and gladdening. 'Reviewing the jhānas and liberations' means that the first jhāna and so on are jhānas; they themselves are liberations due to being well-liberated from opposing states, and so on. It is the reviewing of them again and again: "Thus is the meditation, thus the attainment, thus the determination, thus the emergence, thus the defilement, thus the purification."

Sattamajjhattatāti [M 1.0159] sattesu piyaṭṭhāniyesupi gahaṭṭhapabbajitesu majjhattākāro ajjhupekkhanā. Saṅkhāramajjhattatāti ajjhattikesu cakkhādīsu, bāhiresu pattacīvarādīsu majjhattākāro ajjhupekkhanā. Sattasaṅkhārānaṃ mamāyanaṃ sattasaṅkhārakelāyanaṃ. Imehākārehīti imehi yathāvuttehi kāyacittānaṃ passaddhākārasallakkhaṇādiākārehi ceva sappāyāhārasevanādiākārehi ca. Ete dhammeti ete passaddhiādidhamme.

'Neutrality towards beings' is the mode of neutrality, equanimity, towards beings, whether they be householders or renunciates, even those in the position of loved ones. 'Neutrality towards formations' is the mode of neutrality, equanimity, towards internal formations such as the eye and so on, and external ones such as the bowl and robe and so on. Cherishing beings and formations as 'mine' is attachment to beings and formations. 'By these modes' means by these aforementioned modes such as marking the tranquil mode of body and mind, and by modes such as partaking of suitable food. 'These dhammas' means these dhammas such as tranquility.

66. Paññāpayogamandatāyāti paññābyāpārassa appabhāvena. Yathā hi dānasīlāni alobhādosappadhānāni[V 1.0149], evaṃ bhāvanā amohappadhānā visesato appanāvahā. Tattha yadā paññā na balavatī hoti, tadā bhāvanācittassa anabhisaṅkhato viya āhāro purisassa abhiruciṃ na janeti, tena taṃ nirassādaṃ hoti. Yadā ca bhāvanā pubbenāparaṃ visesāvahā na hoti sammadeva avīthipaṭipattiyā, tadā upasamasukhassa alābhena cittaṃ nirassādaṃ hoti. Tadubhayaṃ sandhāyāha “paññāpayogamandatāyā”tiādi. Nanti cittaṃ. Jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni yathārahaṃ sugatiyaṃ, duggatiyañca hontīti tadaññameva pañcavidhabandhanādikhuppipāsādiaññamaññavibādhanādihetukaṃ apāyadukkhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ paccuppannabhavanissitaṃ gahitanti atīte, anāgate ca kāle vaṭṭamūlakadukkhāni visuṃ gahitāni. Ye pana sattā āhārūpajīvino, tattha ca uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino, tesaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ jīvitadukkhaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ saṃvegavatthu vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

66. 'Due to weakness in the application of wisdom' means due to the weakness of the activity of wisdom. For just as giving and virtue are predominated by non-greed and non-hatred, so meditation is predominated by non-delusion and especially brings absorption. In this context, when wisdom is not strong, then meditation, like unprepared food for a person, does not produce delight for the mind; because of that, it is without delight. And when meditation does not bring distinction from a former time to a later time because of not following the right path, then due to not obtaining the happiness of tranquility, the mind is without delight. Referring to both of these, he said, 'due to weakness in the application of wisdom,' and so on. 'That' means the mind. Since birth, aging, sickness, and death occur appropriately in good and bad destinations, the suffering of the plane of misery, caused by other factors such as the five kinds of bondage, hunger and thirst, and mutual affliction, should be seen as distinct from that. All this is taken as being based on the present existence of those respective beings; thus, the root sufferings of the cycle in the past and future are taken separately. Furthermore, for those beings who live by food, and among them, those who live by the fruit of their exertion, their suffering of livelihood, which is not shared with others, is said to be the eighth ground for spiritual urgency; thus it should be seen.

Assāti cittassa. Alīnantiādīsu kosajjapakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ anadhimattatāya alīnaṃ. Uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ dhammānaṃ anadhimattatāya anuddhataṃ. Paññāpayogasampattiyā, upasamasukhādhigamena ca anirassādaṃ. Pubbenāparaṃ savisesaṃ tato eva ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ, samathavīthipaṭipannañca. Tattha alīnatāya paggahe, anuddhatatāya niggahe, anirassādatāya sampahaṃsane na byāpāraṃ āpajjati. Alīnānuddhatatāya hi ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ anirassādatāya samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ. Samappavattiyā vā alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ, samathavīthipaṭipattiyā anirassādanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

`Assa` means 'of the mind'. In `alīna`, etc.: due to the non-excessiveness of states belonging to the faction of laziness, it is not sluggish (`alīna`). Due to the non-excessiveness of states belonging to the faction of restlessness, it is not agitated (`anuddhata`). And by the accomplishment of the application of wisdom and by the attainment of the happiness of tranquility, it is not without savor (`anirassāda`). The later mind, compared to the earlier, is with distinction; for that very reason, it proceeds evenly in the object and has entered upon the path of serenity. Therein, due to non-sluggishness, it does not engage in the effort of exertion; due to non-agitation, in restraint; and due to being not without savor, in gladdening. Indeed, by being non-sluggish and non-agitated, it proceeds evenly in the object; by being not without savor, it has entered upon the path of serenity. Or, it should be understood that, through even progression, it is not sluggish and not agitated; and through having entered upon the path of serenity, it is not without savor.

Nekkhammapaṭipadanti jhānapaṭipattiṃ. Samādhiadhimuttatāti samādhinibbattane jhānādhigame yuttappayuttatā. Sā pana yasmā samādhiṃ garuṃ katvā tattha ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena [M 1.0160] pavattiyā hoti, tasmā “samādhigarū”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The path of renunciation (`nekkhammapaṭipadā`) means the practice of jhāna. Being resolved on concentration (`samādhiadhimuttatā`) means the state of being unceasingly engaged in bringing about concentration and in attaining jhāna. Furthermore, since that occurs by making concentration weighty, with a state of leaning, sloping, and inclining towards it, therefore it is said, 'respectful of concentration (`samādhigaru`),' and so on.

67. Paṭiladdhe nimittasmiṃ evaṃ hi sampādayato appanākosallaṃ imaṃ appanā sampavattatīti sambandho. Sāti appanā. Hitvā hīti hi-saddo hetuattho. Yasmā ṭhānametaṃ na vijjati, tasmā cittappavattiākāraṃ bhāvanācittassa līnuddhatādivasena pavattiākāraṃ sallakkhayaṃ upadhārento. Samataṃ vīriyasseva vīriyassa samādhinā samarasataṃyeva yojayetha. Kathaṃ pana yojayethāti āha “īsakampī”tiādi. Tattha layanti līnabhāvaṃ, saṅkocanti attho. Yantanti gacchantaṃ[V 1.0150], paggaṇhetheva samabhāvāyāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “accāraddhaṃ nisedhetvā samameva pavattaye”ti. Kathaṃ pana samameva pavattayeti āha “reṇumhī”tiādi. Yathāti reṇuādīsu yathā madhukarādīnaṃ pavatti upamābhāvena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sammavaṇṇitā, evaṃ līnuddhatabhāvehi mocayitvā vīriyasamatāyojanena nimittābhimukhaṃ mānasaṃ paṭipādaye paṭibhāganimittābhimukhaṃ bhāvanācittaṃ sampādeyyāti attho.

67. The connection is thus: Indeed, for the yogi who, when the counterpart sign has been obtained, accomplishes this skill in absorption, absorption proceeds well. `Sā` means absorption. In `hitvā hi`, the word `hi` has the meaning of 'cause'. Since this condition does not exist, therefore, while marking and considering the mode of the mind's occurrence—the mode of occurrence of the meditation mind by way of sluggishness, agitation, and so on—one should yoke only the evenness of energy with concentration. 'But how should one yoke it?' Since this question arises, He said, 'Even slightly,' and so on. Therein, `laya` means the state of being sluggish, contraction. `Yantaṃ` means going; the intention is that one should indeed exert it for the sake of a state of balance. Therefore, He said, 'Having restrained over-exertion... one should proceed evenly.' 'But how does one proceed evenly?' Since this question arises, He said, 'In the pollen,' and so on. The meaning is: Just as the activity of bees and so on in relation to pollen and so on is well described in the commentary by way of simile, so too, having freed it from the states of sluggishness and agitation, by yoking it with the evenness of energy, one should direct the mind, the meditation mind, towards the sign, the counterpart sign.

Nimittābhimukhapaṭipādanavaṇṇanā

Exposition on Accomplishing the Facing of the Sign

68. Tatrāti tasmiṃ “reṇumhī”tiādinā vuttagāthādvaye. Atthadīpanā upamūpameyyatthavibhāvanā. Achekoti akusalo. Pakkhandoti dhāvituṃ āraddho. Vikasanakkhaṇeyeva sarasaṃ kusumaparāgaṃ hoti, pacchā vātādīhi paripatati, virasaṃ vā hoti. Tasmā nivattane reṇu khīyatīti āha “khīṇe reṇumhi sampāpuṇātī”ti. Puppharāsinti rukkhasākhāsu nissitaṃ pupphasañcayaṃ.

68. Herein (`tatra`), in those two verses spoken beginning with 'in the pollen' (`reṇumhi`), is the elucidation of meaning, the explanation of the meaning of the simile and the subject of the simile. `Acheko` means unskilled. `Pakkhando` means having started to run. At the very moment of blooming, the flower pollen is savory, but afterwards it is scattered by wind and so on, or it becomes without savor. Therefore, upon returning, the pollen is exhausted; thus, He said, 'When the pollen is exhausted, he attains.' `Puppharāsiṃ` means a collection of flowers resting on tree branches.

Sallakattaantevāsikesūti sallakattaācariyassa antevāsikesu. Udakathālagateti udakathāliyaṃ ṭhapite. Satthakammanti sirāvedhanādisatthakammaṃ. Phusitumpi uppalapattanti sambandho. Samenāti purimakā viya garuṃ, mandañca payogaṃ akatvā samappamāṇena payogena. Tatthāti uppalapatte. Pariyodātasippoti suvisuddhasippo nipphannasippo.

`Sallakattaantevāsikesu` means among the pupils of the surgeon-teacher. `Udakathālagate` means placed in a water bowl. `Satthakammaṃ` means a knife-deed such as vein-lancing. The connection is to 'to touch even a lotus petal.' `Samena` means: not making the effort heavy or sluggish like the previous pupils, but with an effort of balanced measure. `Tattha` means on the lotus petal. `Pariyodātasippo` means one whose craft is well-purified, one whose craft is perfected.

Makkaṭakasuttanti [M 1.0161] lūtasuttaṃ. Niyāmako nāvāsārathī. Laṅkāranti kilañjādimayaṃ nāvākaṭasārakaṃ. Telena achaḍḍento nāḷiṃ pūretīti sarāvādigatena telena achaḍḍento sukhumacchiddakaṃ telanāḷiṃ pūreti. Evamevāti yathā te ādito vuttamadhukarasallakattaantevāsisuttākaḍḍhakaniyāmakatelapūrakā vegena payogaṃ karonti, evameva yo bhikkhu “sīghaṃ appanaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti gāḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ karoti, yo majjhe vuttamadhukarādayo viya vīriyaṃ na karoti, ime dvepi vīriyasamatābhāvena appanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkonti. Yo pana avasāne vuttamadhukarādayo viya samappayogo, ayaṃ appanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ sakkoti vīriyasamatāyogatoti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “eko bhikkhū”tiādi. Līnaṃ bhāvanācittanti adhippāyo.

`Makkaṭakasuttaṃ` means a spider's thread. A `niyāmako` is a helmsman. `Laṅkāraṃ` means a boat's sail-mat made of woven rushes and so on. 'He fills a tube with oil without spilling' means: he fills a fine-holed oil tube with oil from a small bowl or the like without spilling it. The application of the simile should be understood thus: Just as those mentioned at the beginning—the bee, the surgeon's pupil, the thread-puller, the helmsman, and the oil-filler—apply effort with speed, so too, the bhikkhu who makes strong effort, thinking, 'I will quickly attain absorption,' and the one who, in the middle, like the aforementioned bee and others, does not make effort—both of these are not able to attain absorption due to the absence of evenness of energy. But the one who, at the end, like the aforementioned bee and others, has balanced application, this one is able to attain absorption due to the yoking of evenness of energy. Therefore, it was said, 'one bhikkhu,' and so on. The intention is: a sluggish meditation mind.

Paṭhamajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on the First Jhāna

69. Evanti [V 1.0151] vuttappakārena. Vīriyasamatāyojanavasena vīthipaṭipannaṃ bhāvanāmānasaṃ paṭibhāganimitteyeva ṭhapanavasena nimittābhimukhaṃ paṭipādayato assa yogino. Ijjhissatīti samijjhissati, uppajjissatīti attho. Anuyogavasenāti bhāvanāvasena. Sesānīti sesāni tīṇi, cattāri vā. Pakaticittehīti pākatikehi kāmāvacaracittehi. Balava…pe… cittekaggatāni bhāvanābalena paṭutarasabhāvappattiyā. Parikammattāti paṭisaṅkhārakattā. Yadi āsannattā upacāratā, gotrabhuno eva upacārasamaññā siyāti āha “samīpacārittā vā”ti. Anaccāsannopi hi nātidūrapavattī samīpacārī nāma hoti. Appanaṃ upecca carantīti upacārāni. Ito pubbe parikammānanti nānāvajjanavīthiyaṃ parikammānaṃ. Etthāti etesu parikammupacārānulomasaññitesu. Sabbantimanti tatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ vā. Parittagottābhibhavanatoti parittassa gottassa abhibhavanato. Gaṃtāyatīti hi gottaṃ, “paritta”nti pavattamānaṃ abhidhānaṃ, buddhiñca ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti parittagottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena atthena vinā na pavattati, evaṃ abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena. Tasmā so tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. Taṃ pana mahaggatānuttaravidhuraṃ kāmataṇhāya gocarabhūtaṃ kāmāvacaradhammānaṃ āveṇikarūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahaggatagottepi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Bhāvanatoti uppādanato.

69. Thus, in the manner spoken of: for this yogi who, by means of applying balanced energy, causes the meditation mind that has entered upon the path to face the counterpart sign by the power of establishing it on the counterpart sign itself. 'It will succeed' means it will be accomplished, it will arise. 'By means of application' means by means of meditation. 'The remaining' means the remaining three or four. 'With natural consciousnesses' means with natural sense-sphere consciousnesses. 'Strong... one-pointedness of mind' is because of attaining a sharper state by the power of meditation. 'Because of being a preliminary' means because of being a preparation. If access were due to proximity, the designation 'access' would apply only to the change-of-lineage; therefore, he said, 'or because of proceeding near.' Indeed, even if not extremely near, that which occurs not too far away is called 'one that proceeds near.' Because they proceed having approached absorption, they are called 'access' moments. 'The preliminaries before this' means the preliminaries in the cognitive process with various advertings. 'Herein' means among these impulsions designated as preliminary, access, and adaptation. 'The very last' means the third or the fourth. 'Because of overcoming the limited lineage' means because of overcoming the lineage that is limited. For because it protects (`tāyati`) the designation and knowledge (`gaṃ`), it is called 'lineage' (`gotta`). Because it protects the designation and knowledge that occurs as 'limited' by means of having a definite object, it is 'limited lineage' (`parittagotta`). Indeed, just as knowledge does not proceed without its object, so too, designation does not proceed without what is designated. Therefore, it is said that it protects them. Furthermore, that lineage should be seen as distinct from the exalted and the supramundane, as the resort of sensual craving, and as the unique nature of sense-sphere phenomena. In the exalted lineage also, the meaning should be understood by this method. 'Because of meditation' means because of producing.

Avisesena [M 1.0162] sabbesaṃ sabbā samaññāti paṭhamanayo gahitaggahaṇaṃ hotīti āha “aggahitaggahaṇenā”tiādi. Nānāvajjanaparikammameva parikammanti adhippāyena “paṭhamaṃ vā upacāra”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Catutthaṃ appanācittaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā appanācittaṃ pubbe vuttanayena sace catutthaṃ gotrabhu hotīti attho. Pañcamaṃ vāti vā-saddo aniyame. Svāyaṃ aniyamo iminā kāraṇenāti dassetuṃ “tañca kho khippābhiññadandhābhiññavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha khippābhiññassa catutthaṃ appeti, dandhābhiññassa pañcamaṃ. Kasmā pana catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā appeti, na tato paranti āha “tato paraṃ javanaṃ patatī”ti. Tato pañcamato paraṃ chaṭṭhaṃ, sattamañca javanaṃ patantaṃ viya hoti parikkhīṇajavattāti adhippāyo.

Without distinction, every designation applies to all impulsions; because this first method becomes a 'grasping of what has been grasped,' he said, 'by grasping what has not been grasped,' etc. With the intention that only the preliminary with various advertings is the preliminary, 'the first or access,' etc., was said. The fourth is the absorption consciousness, or the fifth is the absorption consciousness; the meaning is that if, by the method previously stated, the fourth is the change-of-lineage, then the fifth is the absorption consciousness. In 'or the fifth,' the word 'or' (`vā`) is in the sense of non-determination. To show that this non-determination is for this reason, it was said: 'and that is by way of one with quick direct knowledge and one with slow direct knowledge.' Therein, for one with quick direct knowledge, the fourth attains absorption; for one with slow direct knowledge, the fifth does. But why does the fourth or the fifth attain absorption, and not beyond that? Therefore, he said, 'beyond that, the impulsion falls.' The intention is that beyond that fifth impulsion, the sixth and seventh impulsions are as if falling, due to the exhaustion of the impulsion-force.

Yathā aladdhāsevanaṃ paṭhamajavanaṃ dubbalattā gotrabhuṃ na uppādeti, laddhāsevanaṃ pana balavabhāvato [V 1.0152] dutiyaṃ, tatiyaṃ vā gotrabhuṃ uppādeti, evaṃ laddhāsevanatāya balavabhāvato chaṭṭhaṃ, sattamampi appetīti therassa adhippāyo. Tenāha “tasmā chaṭṭhepi sattamepi appanā hotī”ti. Tanti therassa vacanaṃ. Suttasuttānulomaācariyavādehi anupatthambhitattā vuttaṃ “attanomatimatta”nti. “Purimā purimā kusalā dhammā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.12) pana suttapadamakāraṇaṃ āsevanapaccayalābhassa balavabhāve anekantikattā. Tathā hi aladdhāsevanāpi paṭhamacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā hoti, laddhāsevanā dutiyacetanā yāva chaṭṭhacetanā aparāpariyavedanīyā. Catutthapañcamesuyevātiādi vuttassevatthassa yuttidassanamukhena nigamanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yadi chaṭṭhasattamaṃ javanaṃ patitaṃ nāma hoti parikkhīṇajavattā, kathaṃ sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyā, ānantariyā ca hotīti? Nāyaṃ viseso āsevanapaccayalābhena balappattiyā. Kiñcarahi kiriyāvatthāvisesato. Kiriyāvatthā hi ārambhamajjhapariyosānavasena tividhā. Tattha ca pariyosānāvatthāya sanniṭṭhāpakacetanābhāvena upapajjavedanīyāditā hoti, na balavabhāvenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭisandhiyā anantarapaccayabhāvino vipākasantānassa anantarapaccayabhāvena tathā abhisaṅkhatattāti ca vadanti. Tasmā chaṭṭhasattamānaṃ papātābhimukhatāya parikkhīṇajavatā na sakkā nivāretuṃ. Tathā hi “yathā hi puriso”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Just as the first impulsion, not having obtained repetition and being weak, cannot produce the change-of-lineage, whereas the second or third, having obtained repetition and being strong, produces the change-of-lineage; so too, due to having obtained repetition and being strong, the sixth and seventh also attain absorption—this is the Elder’s intention. Therefore he said, 'Thus, absorption occurs even in the sixth or seventh.' That is the Elder’s word. Because it is unsupported by the Suttas, the Suttānuloma, and the teachings of the masters, it was said to be 'merely one's own opinion.' However, the Sutta phrase 'the preceding wholesome states...' is not a valid reason, because the strength in gaining the repetition condition is not conclusive. For indeed, even the first volition, though not having obtained repetition, is experienceable in the present life, while the second volition up to the sixth, having obtained repetition, are experienceable in a subsequent life. The statement beginning 'only in the fourth and fifth...' was said for the purpose of concluding the meaning already stated, primarily by showing the reasoning. Therein, if the sixth and seventh impulsions are called 'fallen' due to the exhaustion of their impulsion-force, how is it that the seventh impulsion-volition is experienceable in the next life and is an immediately effective kamma? This distinction is not due to gaining strength by obtaining the repetition condition. Why then? It is due to the distinction in the stage of the action. Indeed, the stage of the action is threefold by way of beginning, middle, and end. And therein, due to being the volition that brings the process to completion in the concluding stage, it becomes experienceable in the next life, etc.; it is not due to its strength. Thus it should be understood. And they also say it is because it has been conditioned in such a way as to be the immediate condition for the resultant continuum, which is the immediate condition for future rebirth-linking. Therefore, the exhaustion of the impulsion-force of the sixth and seventh, due to their facing a precipice, cannot be prevented. For that very reason, 'just as a person,' etc., was said.

Sā [M 1.0163] ca pana appanā. Addhānaparicchedoti kālaparicchedo. So panettha sattasu ṭhānesu katthaci aparimāṇacittakkhaṇatāya, katthaci atiittarakhaṇatāya natthīti vutto. Na hettha sampuṇṇajavanavīthi addhā labbhati. Tenevāha “ettha maggānantaraphala”ntiādi. Sesaṭṭhānesūti paṭhamappanā, lokiyābhiññā, maggakkhaṇo, nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa phalakkhaṇoti etesu catūsu ṭhānesu.

And that absorption also. 'The delimitation of duration' means the delimitation of time. That, it is said, does not exist here in seven instances, sometimes due to having an immeasurable number of mind-moments, and sometimes due to having an extremely brief moment. Indeed, here a duration of a complete impulsion process is not obtained. For that very reason, he said, 'here, the fruit immediately following the path,' etc. 'In the remaining instances' means in these four instances: the first absorption, mundane direct knowledge, the path-moment, and the fruition-moment for one emerging from cessation.

Ettāvatāti ettakena bhāvanākkamena esa yogāvacaro paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evaṃ viharatā ca anena tadeva paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇanti sambandho.

'With this much' means: with this much of a sequence of meditation, this yogi dwells having attained the first jhāna. And while dwelling thus, that very first jhāna which has the earth kasiṇa as its object has been attained by him. Thus is the connection.

70. Tatthāti tasmiṃ jhānapāṭhe. Viviccitvāti visuṃ hutvā. Tenāha “vinā hutvā apakkamitvā”ti, pajahanavasena apasakkitvāti attho. Vivicceva kāmehīti ettha “viviccā”ti iminā vivecanaṃ jhānakkhaṇe kāmānaṃ abhāvamattaṃ vuttaṃ. “Viviccevā”ti pana iminā ekaṃsato kāmānaṃ vivecetabbatādīpanena tappaṭipakkhatā jhānassa, kāmavivekassa ca jhānādhigamūpāyatā [V 1.0153] dassitā hotīti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭhamaṃ jhāna”ntiādiṃ vatvā tamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Andhakāre sati padīpobhāso viyā”ti etena yathā padīpobhāsābhāvena rattiyaṃ andhakārābhibhavo, evaṃ jhānābhāvena sattasantatiyaṃ kāmābhibhavoti dasseti.

70. Tatthā means in that section on jhāna. Viviccitvā means having become separate. Therefore, it is said, “having become without, having withdrawn,” meaning having moved away by way of abandoning. In “quite secluded from sensual pleasures” (vivicceva kāmehīti), by “secluded” (viviccā), the mere absence of sensual pleasures at the moment of jhāna is stated. But by “quite secluded” (viviccevā), by indicating that sensual pleasures must be secluded from entirely, it is shown that jhāna is their opposite, and that seclusion from sensual pleasures is the means for attaining jhāna. To show this meaning, after saying “the first jhāna,” etc., and to make that very meaning clearer, “how,” etc., is said. By this phrase, “like the light of a lamp when there is darkness,” it is shown that just as by the absence of lamplight at night there is an overwhelming by darkness, so too by the absence of jhāna in the continuity of a being there is an overwhelming by sensual pleasures.

Etanti pubbapadeyeva avadhāraṇavacanaṃ. Na kho pana evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “kāmehi evā”ti avadhāraṇassa akatattā. Nissaranti niggacchanti etena, ettha vāti nissaraṇaṃ. Ke niggacchanti? Kāmā, tesaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ pahānaṃ tannissaraṇaṃ, tato. Kathaṃ pana samāne vikkhambhane kāmānamevetaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, na byāpādādīnanti codanaṃ yuttito, āgamato ca sodhetuṃ “kāmadhātū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kāmadhātusamatikkamanatoti sakalassapi kāmabhavassa samatikkamapaṭipadābhāvato. Tena imassa jhānassa kāmapariññābhāvamāha. Kāmarāgapaṭipakkhatoti vakkhamānavibhāgassa kilesakāmassa paccatthikabhāvato. Tena yathā mettā byāpādassa, karuṇā vihiṃsāya, evamidaṃ jhānaṃ kāmarāgassa ujuvipaccanīkabhūtanti dasseti. Evamattano pavattiyā, vipākappavattiyā ca kāmarāgato, kāmadhātuto [M 1.0164] ca vinivattasabhāvattā idaṃ jhānaṃ visesato kāmānameva nissaraṇaṃ. Svāyamattho pāṭhagato evāti āha “yathāhā”tiādi. Kāmañcetamatthaṃ dīpetuṃ purimapadeyeva avadhāraṇaṃ gahitaṃ, uttarapadepi pana taṃ gahetabbameva tathā atthasambhavatoti dassetuṃ “uttarapadepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Itoti kāmacchandato. Esa niyamo. Sādhāraṇavacanenāti avisesavacanena. Tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappaṭipassaddhinissaraṇavivekā tadaṅgavivekādayo. Cittakāyaupadhivivekā cittavivekādayo. Tayo eva idha jhānakathāyaṃ daṭṭhabbā samucchedavivekādīnaṃ asambhavato.

Etaṃ is an emphatic statement in the earlier phrase itself. However, it should not be understood as “only from sensual pleasures,” because the emphasis is not made. They escape, they depart by this, or in this; hence, it is “escape” (nissaraṇa). Who departs? Sensual pleasures. The escape from them, the abandonment of those sensual pleasures, is that escape (tannissaraṇa); hence, “from that.” But how, when the suppression is the same, is this an escape only from sensual pleasures and not from ill-will and so forth? To clarify this objection by way of reason and scripture, “from the sense-sphere element,” etc., is said. Therein, 'by transcending the sense-sphere element' means because it is the opposite of transcending the entire sensual existence. And because it is the opponent of sensual lust, it is shown that just as loving-kindness is the direct opponent of ill-will and compassion of cruelty, so this jhāna is the direct opponent of sensual lust. Thus, by its own arising and by the arising of its result, and because of its nature of turning away from sensual lust and from the sense-sphere element, this jhāna is specifically an escape from sensual pleasures alone. This meaning is present in the text itself; therefore, it says, “as it is said,” etc. Although to clarify this meaning, the emphasis is taken in the earlier phrase, it must also be taken in the later phrase, as the meaning is possible in that way; to show this, “in the later phrase also,” etc., is said. Ito means from sensual desire. This is the rule. “By a general statement” means by an undifferentiated expression. The seclusions by substitution, suppression, cutting off, tranquillization, and escape are the seclusion by substitution and so on. The seclusions of mind, body, and substrata are the seclusion of mind and so on. Only three should be understood here in the discussion of jhāna, because of the impossibility of the seclusion of cutting off and so on.

Niddeseti mahāniddese (mahāni. 1, 7). Tattha hi “uddānato dve kāmā – vatthukāmā kilesakāmā cā”ti uddisitvā “tattha katame vatthukāmā? Manāpiyā rūpā…pe… manāpiyā phoṭṭhabbā”tiādinā vatthukāmā niddiṭṭhā. Te pana kāmīyantīti kāmāti veditabbā. Tatthevāti niddese eva. Vibhaṅgeti jhānavibhaṅge (vibha. 564). Patthanākārena pavatto dubbalo lobho chandanaṭṭhena chando, tato balavā rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo, tatopi balavataro bahalarāgo chandarāgo. Nimittānubyañjanāni saṅkappeti etenāti saṅkappo, tathāpavatto lobho, tato balavā rañjanaṭṭhena rāgo, saṅkappanavaseneva pavatto tatopi balavataro saṅkapparāgoti. Svāyaṃ [V 1.0154] pabhedo ekasseva lobhassa pavattiākāravasena, avatthābhedavasena ca veditabbo yathā “vaccho dammo balībaddo”ti. Ime kilesakāmā. Kāmentīti kāmā, kāmenti etehīti vā.

In the Niddesa means in the Mahāniddesa. For there, having pointed out in summary, “In summary, there are two sensual pleasures: object-sensual pleasures and defilement-sensual pleasures,” the object-sensual pleasures are explained in detail by way of “Therein, what are object-sensual pleasures? Agreeable forms… agreeable tangible objects,” and so on. But these should be understood as “sensual pleasures” (kāmā) because they are desired (kāmīyanti). Tattheva means in the Niddesa itself. In the Vibhaṅga means in the Jhānavibhaṅga. Weak greed that has arisen in the manner of longing is chanda (desire) in the sense of wishing. Stronger than that is rāga (lust) in the sense of delighting. Even stronger than that, intense lust, is chandarāga (sensual lust). Saṅkappa (conception) is that by which one conceives the sign and its details; it is greed that has arisen in that way. Stronger than that is rāga (lust) in the sense of delighting. Even stronger, having arisen by way of conception itself, is saṅkapparāga (lust of conception). This distinction of one and the same greed should be understood by way of its manner of arising and by way of its different stages, just as with “a calf, a steer, a bull.” These are defilement-sensual pleasures. They are called kāmā because they desire, or because one desires through them.

Evañhi satīti evaṃ ubhayesampi kāmānaṃ saṅgahe sati. Vatthukāmehipīti “vatthukāmehi viviccevā”tipi attho yujjatīti evaṃ yujjamānatthantarasamuccayattho pi-saddo, na kilesakāmasamuccayattho. Kasmā? Imasmiṃ atthe kilesakāmehi vivekassa dutiyapadena vuttattā. Tenāti vatthukāmavivekena. Kāyaviveko vutto hoti puttadārādipariggahavivekadīpanato. Purimenāti kāyavivekena. Etthāti “vivicceva kāmehi, vivicca akusalehi dhammehī”ti etasmiṃ padadvaye, ito vā niddhārite vivekadvaye. Akusala-saddena yadipi [M 1.0165] kilesakāmā, sabbākusalāpi vā gahitā, sabbathā pana kilesakāmehi viveko vuttoti āha “dutiyena kilesakāmehi vivekavacanato”ti. Dutiyenāti ca cittavivekenāti attho. Etesanti yathāvuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ, niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Taṇhādisaṃkilesānaṃ vatthuno pahānaṃ saṃkilesavatthuppahānaṃ. Lolabhāvo nāma tattha tattha rūpādīsu taṇhuppādo, tassa hetu vatthukāmā eva veditabbā. Bālabhāvo avijjā, duccintitacintitādi vā, tassa ayonisomanasikāro, sabbepi vā akusalā dhammā hetu. Kāmaguṇādhigamahetupi pāṇātipātādiasuddhapayogo hotīti tabbivekena payogasuddhi vibhāvitā. Taṇhāsaṃkilesasodhanena, vivaṭṭūpanissayasaṃvaḍḍhanena ca ajjhāsayavisodhanaṃ āsayaposanaṃ. Kāmesūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ.

Evañhi sati means: when there is thus the inclusion of both kinds of sensual pleasures. Vatthukāmehipi means that the meaning “secluded even from object-sensual pleasures” is also suitable; thus, the particle pi has the meaning of including another suitable meaning, not the meaning of including defilement-sensual pleasures. Why? Because in this meaning, seclusion from defilement-sensual pleasures is stated by the second phrase. Tena means by seclusion from object-sensual pleasures. Physical seclusion is stated.
