Purimena means by physical seclusion. Ettha refers to this pair of phrases: “quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,” or to the two seclusions specified from this. Although by the word “unwholesome,” defilement-sensual pleasures or all unwholesome states are taken, in every way seclusion from defilement-sensual pleasures is stated; hence it is said: “because of the statement of seclusion from defilement-sensual pleasures by the second phrase.” And dutiyena means by mental seclusion. Etesaṃ refers to the two phrases as stated, and this is a genitive in the sense of specification. The abandoning of the basis of defilements such as craving is the abandoning of the basis of defilements. Lolabhāvo (fickleness) is the arising of craving for forms and so forth here and there; its cause should be known as object-sensual pleasures. Bālabhāvo (foolishness) is ignorance, or thinking ill-thoughts and so on; its cause is unwise attention, or all unwholesome states. Also, as a cause for attaining sensual qualities, there is impure conduct such as killing living beings; thus, by seclusion from that, purity of conduct is shown. By the purification of the defilement of craving and by the development of the support for turning away from the round of rebirth, the purification of disposition is the nurturing of inclination. Kāmesu is a locative in the sense of specification.

Anekabhedoti kāmāsavakāmarāgasaṃyojanādivasena, rūpataṇhādivasena ca anekappabhedo. Kāmacchandoyevāti kāmasabhāvoyeva chando, na kattukamyatāchando, nāpi kusalacchandoti adhippāyo. Jhānapaṭipakkhatoti jhānassa paṭipakkhabhāvato taṃhetu tannimittaṃ visuṃ vutto. Akusalabhāvasāmaññena aggahetvā visuṃ sarūpena gahito. Yadi kilesakāmova purimapade vutto, kathaṃ bahuvacananti āha “anekabhedato”tiādi.

'Manifold' means having many distinctions, by way of the influx of sensuality, the fetter of sensual lust, etc., and by way of craving for forms, etc. 'It is only sensual desire' means that it is desire whose nature is sensual, not the desire-to-do, nor wholesome desire—this is the intention. 'Because it is an opponent of jhāna' means that due to its being an opponent of jhāna, for that reason and on that account, it is mentioned separately. It is not taken generally as an unwholesome state but is grasped distinctly by its own nature. If only defilement-sensuality were mentioned in the preceding phrase, how could the plural be used? Hence, it is said, 'due to being manifold,' etc.

Aññesampi diṭṭhimānaahirikānottappādīnaṃ, taṃsahitaphassādīnañca. Upari vuccamānāni jhānaṅgāni uparijhānaṅgāni, tesaṃ attano paccanīkānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvadassanato tappaccanīkanīvaraṇavacanaṃ. Nīvaraṇāni hi jhānaṅgapaccanīkāni tesaṃ pavattinivāraṇato. Samādhi kāmacchandassa [V 1.0155] paṭipakkho rāgappaṇidhiyā ujuvipaccanīkabhāvato, nānārammaṇehi palobhitassa paribbhamantassa cittassa samādhānato ca. Pīti byāpādassa paṭipakkhā pāmojjena samānayogakkhemattā. Vitakko thinamiddhassa paṭipakkho yoniso saṅkappanavasena savipphārapavattito. Sukhaṃ avūpasamānutāpasabhāvassa uddhaccakukkuccassa paṭipakkhaṃ vūpasantasītalasabhāvattā. Vicāro vicikicchāya paṭipakkho ārammaṇe anumajjanavasena paññāpaṭirūpasabhāvattā. Mahākaccānattherena desitaṃ piṭakānaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā peṭakaṃ, tasmiṃ peṭake.

Also of others, such as views, conceit, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, etc., and of contact, etc., associated with them. The jhāna factors to be mentioned hereafter are the higher jhāna factors. Because it shows their nature as opponents to their own adversaries, there is this statement about the hindrances that are their opponents. Indeed, the hindrances are the opponents of the jhāna factors because they prevent their arising. Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire because it is in direct opposition to the aspiration that is lust, and because it steadies the mind that, having been lured by various objects, wanders about. Rapture is the opponent of ill will because of its similarity to gladness and its state of security. Applied thought is the opponent of sloth and torpor because it proceeds expansively by way of wise reflection. Happiness is the opponent of restlessness and remorse, which have the nature of non-pacification and subsequent torment, because happiness has a peaceful and cool nature. Sustained thought is the opponent of doubt because, by way of repeatedly examining the object, it has a nature resembling wisdom. The explanation of the Piṭakas taught by the Elder Mahākaccāna is the Peṭaka; in that Peṭaka.

Pañcakāmaguṇabhedavisayassāti [M 1.0166] rūpādipañcakāmaguṇavisesavisayassa. Āghātavatthubhedādivisayānanti byāpādavivekavacanena “anatthaṃ me acarī”ti (dī. ni. 3.340; a. ni. 9.29; vibha. 960) ādiāghātavatthubhedavisayassa dosassa, mohādhikehi thinamiddhādīhi vivekavacanena paṭicchādanavasena dukkhādipubbantādibhedavisayassa mohassa vikkhambhanaviveko vutto. Kāmarāgabyāpādatadekaṭṭhathinamiddhādivikkhambhakañcetaṃ sabbākusalapaṭipakkhasabhāvattā. Sabbakusalānaṃ tena sabhāvena sabbākusalappahāyakaṃ hoti, hontampi kāmarāgādivikkhambhanasabhāvameva hoti taṃsabhāvattāti avisesetvā nīvaraṇākusalamūlādīnaṃ “vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hotī”ti āha.

'Of that which has as its object the distinctions of the five strands of sensual pleasure' means of that which has as its object the specific five strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms. 'Of that which has as its object the distinctions of the grounds for resentment, etc.': by the statement of seclusion from ill will, the suppression-seclusion of hatred is stated, which has as its object the distinctions of the grounds for resentment, such as 'he has done me harm,' etc. By the statement of seclusion from sloth and torpor, etc., which are dominated by delusion, the suppression-seclusion of delusion is stated, which has as its object the distinctions of suffering, the past, etc., by way of concealment. And this jhāna suppresses sensual lust, ill will, and sloth and torpor, etc., which share a common basis with them, because it has the nature of being an opponent to all unwholesome states. By that nature, it becomes the abandoner of all unwholesome states for all wholesome states. Even while being so, it is essentially of the nature of suppressing sensual lust, etc. Because it has that nature, he says that, without specifying, 'the suppression-seclusion of the hindrances, unwholesome roots, etc., is stated.'

71. Yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ natthi kāci vasavattitāti vasavattibhāvanivāraṇatthaṃ “vitakkanaṃ vitakko”ti vuttaṃ. Tayidaṃ “vitakkanaṃ īdisamida”nti ārammaṇassa parikappananti āha “ūhananti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Yasmā cittaṃ vitakkabalena ārammaṇaṃ abhiniruḷhaṃ viya hoti, tasmā so ārammaṇābhiniropanalakkhaṇo vutto. Yathā hi koci rājavallabhaṃ, taṃsambandhinaṃ mittaṃ vā nissāya rājagehaṃ ārohati anupavisati, evaṃ vitakkaṃ nissāya cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohati. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ avitakkaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohatīti? Vitakkabaleneva. Yathā hi so puriso paricayena tena vināpi nirāsaṅko rājagehaṃ pavisati, evaṃ paricayena vitakkena vināpi avitakkaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ārohati. Paricayenāti ca santāne pavattavitakkabhāvanāsaṅkhātena paricayena. Vitakkassa hi santāne abhiṇhaṃ pavattassa vasena cittassa ārammaṇābhiruhaṇaṃ ciraparicitaṃ. Tena taṃ kadāci vitakkena vināpi tattha pavattateva. Yathā taṃ ñāṇasahitaṃ hutvā sammasanavasena ciraparicitaṃ kadāci ñāṇavirahitampi sammasanavasena pavattati, yathā vā kilesasahitaṃ hutvā pavattaṃ sabbaso [V 1.0156] kilesarahitampi paricayena kilesavāsanāvasena pavattati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ādito, abhimukhaṃ vā hananaṃ āhananaṃ. Parito, parivattetvā vā āhananaṃ pariyāhananaṃ. “Rūpaṃ rūpaṃ, pathavī pathavī”ti ākoṭentassa viya pavatti “āhananaṃ, pariyāhanana”nti ca veditabbaṃ. Ānayanaṃ cittassa ārammaṇe upanayanaṃ, ākaḍḍhanaṃ vā.

71. Of natural phenomena that proceed according to conditions, there is no mastery whatsoever. To prevent the idea of a state of mastery, it is said, 'Thinking is applied thought.' That thinking is the conceiving of the object as 'this is of such a nature'; hence, he says, 'it is called "reasoning" (ūhana).' Because the mind, by the power of applied thought, seems to have ascended to the object, it is therefore said to have the characteristic of placing the mind onto the object. Just as someone, relying on a royal favorite or a friend connected to him, ascends to and enters the king's palace, so too the mind, relying on applied thought, ascends to the object. If so, how does a mind without applied thought ascend to the object? By the power of applied thought itself. For just as that person, through familiarity, enters the king's palace without hesitation even without that connection, so too the mind without applied thought, through familiarity, ascends to the object even without applied thought. And 'by familiarity' means by the familiarity known as the cultivation of applied thought that occurs in the mental continuum. Indeed, through the power of applied thought occurring frequently in the continuum, the mind's ascending to the object becomes long-practiced. Therefore, that mind sometimes arises there even without applied thought. Just as that mind, having become long-practiced in investigation by being associated with knowledge, sometimes proceeds by way of investigation even when devoid of knowledge; or just as that mind, having proceeded while associated with defilements, proceeds through the latent tendencies of defilements due to habituation even when entirely free of defilements—this matter should be understood as being accomplished in this way. Initially, or striking towards, is 'striking' (āhanana). Striking all around, or striking repeatedly, is 'repeated striking' (pariyāhanana). The process should be understood as 'striking' and 'repeated striking,' like one hammering away, saying, 'Form, form; earth, earth.' 'Bringing' (ānayana) is the leading of the mind to the object, or the drawing of it.

Anusañcaraṇaṃ [M 1.0167] anuparibbhamanaṃ. Svāyaṃ viseso santānamhi labbhamāno eva santāne pākaṭo hotīti daṭṭhabbo. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Anumajjanaṃ ārammaṇe cittassa anumasanaṃ, parimajjananti attho. Tathā hi vicāro “parimajjanahattho viya, sañcaraṇahattho viyā”ti ca vutto. Tatthāti ārammaṇe. Sahajātānaṃ anuyojanaṃ ārammaṇe anuvicāraṇasaṅkhātaanumajjanavaseneva veditabbaṃ. Anuppabandhanaṃ ārammaṇe cittassa avicchinnassa viya pavatti. Tathā hi so “anusandhānatā”ti (dha. sa. 8) niddiṭṭho. Teneva ca “ghaṇḍānuravo viya, paribbhamanaṃ viyā”ti ca vutto.

'Following after' (anusañcaraṇa) is wandering about repeatedly. This distinction, being found in the continuum, becomes manifest in the continuum; this should be understood. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. 'Touching upon' (anumajjana) is the mind's stroking of the object; the meaning is 'rubbing over' (parimajjana). Indeed, sustained thought is described as 'like a rubbing hand, like a moving hand.' 'There' (tattha) means in the object. The yoking of co-nascent states should be understood by way of this 'touching upon,' which is known as 'investigating' the object. 'Sustaining' (anuppabandhana) is the proceeding of the mind on the object as if uninterrupted. Indeed, it is pointed out as 'connectedness' (anusandhānatā) (Dhs §8). And for that reason, it is also said to be 'like the reverberation of a bell, like a revolving.'

Katthacīti paṭhamajjhāne, parittacittuppādesu ca. Vicārato oḷārikaṭṭhena, vicārasseva ca pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena anuravato oḷāriko, tassa ca pubbaṅgamo ghaṇḍābhighāto viya vitakko. Yathā hi ghaṇḍābhighāto paṭhamābhinipāto hoti, evaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhaniropanaṭṭhena vitakko cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto hoti. Abhighāta-ggahaṇena cettha abhighātajo saddo gahitoti veditabbo. Vipphāravāti vicalanayutto saparipphando. Paribbhamanaṃ viya parissayābhāvavīmaṃsanatthaṃ. Anuppabandhena pavattiyanti upacāre vā appanāyaṃ vā santānena pavattiyaṃ. Tattha hi vitakko niccalo hutvā ārammaṇaṃ anupavisitvā viya pavattati, na paṭhamābhinipāte. Pākaṭo hotīti vitakkassa viseso abhiniropanākāro oḷārikattā paṭhamajjhāne pākaṭo hoti, tadabhāvato pañcakanaye dutiyajjhāne vicārassa viseso anumajjanākāro pākaṭo hoti.

'Somewhere' means in the first jhāna, and in the arising of sense-sphere consciousness. Initial application is grosser than sustained application due to its coarse nature and because it is the precursor of sustained application itself, just as the striking of a bell is grosser than the subsequent reverberating sound and is its precursor. Just as the striking of a bell is the first impact, so too is initial application the first impact of the mind in directing it toward the object. Here, by the taking of the term 'strike' (abhighāta), the sound produced by the strike should be understood as being taken. 'Vipphāravāti' means endowed with movement, with vibration. Like wandering around, for the purpose of investigating the absence of danger. 'Anuppabandhena pavattiyanti' means occurring as a continuum in access or absorption. For there, initial application, having become motionless, proceeds as if entering the object, not in the first impact. 'Pākaṭo hoti' means: the special characteristic of initial application—its mode of directing towards—is manifest in the first jhāna due to its coarseness. Due to its absence, in the second jhāna of the five-fold system, the special characteristic of sustained application—its mode of sustained examination—becomes manifest.

Vālaṇḍupakaṃ eḷakalomādīhi katacumbaṭakaṃ. Uppīḷanahatthoti piṇḍassa uppīḷanahattho. Tasseva ito cito ca sañcaraṇahattho. Maṇḍalanti kaṃsabhājanādīsu kiñci maṇḍalaṃ vaṭṭalekhaṃ karontassa. Yathā pupphaphalasākhādiavayavavinimutto avijjamānopi rukkho “sapuppho saphalo”ti voharīyati, evaṃ vitakkādiaṅgavinimuttaṃ avijjamānampi jhānaṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti voharīyatīti dassetuṃ “rukkho viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Jhānabhāvanāya puggalavasena desetabbattā [V 1.0157] “idha bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī”tiādinā puggalādhiṭṭhānena jhānāni uddiṭṭhānīti. Yadipi vibhaṅge puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā katā, attho pana tatrāpi vibhaṅgepi yathā idha “iminā [M 1.0168] ca vitakkenā”tiādinā dhammavasena vutto, evameva daṭṭhabbo, paramatthato puggalasseva abhāvatoti adhippāyo. Attho…pe… daṭṭhabbo jhānasamaṅgino vitakkavicārasamaṅgitādassanena, jhānasseva ca savitakkasavicāratāya vuttattāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

A `vālaṇḍupaka` is a coil-pad made of sheep's wool and so on. 'The pressing hand' means the hand that presses the lump. The hand that moves it from here to there. 'Circle' means of one who is making some circle, a round line, on a bronze vessel, etc. Just as a tree, even when it is devoid of its parts such as flowers, fruits, and branches, and these are non-existent, is still referred to as 'with flowers' or 'with fruit,' so too, to show that jhāna, even when it is devoid of factors such as initial application, and these are non-existent, is referred to as 'with initial application' and 'with sustained application,' the passage beginning 'like a tree' was stated. Because the development of jhāna is to be taught in terms of a person, the jhānas are pointed out with a person as the basis in the passage beginning, 'Here, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures...' Although in the Vibhaṅga the teaching is made with a person as the basis, the meaning there, in the Vibhaṅga, should be understood in the very same way as it is stated here in terms of phenomena in the passage beginning, 'by this initial application,' for in the ultimate sense, a person does not exist. This is the intention. Or, the meaning here should be understood thus: because it is stated that the jhāna itself is with initial and sustained application, thereby showing that one endowed with jhāna is endowed with initial and sustained application.

Vivekāti vivekā hetubhūtāti viveka-saddassa bhāvasādhanataṃ sandhāyāha. Viveketi kattusādhanataṃ, kammasādhanataṃ vā. “Vivitto”ti hi iminā nīvaraṇehi vinābhūto tehi vivecitoti ca sādhanadvayampi saṅgahitamevāti.

'From seclusion' (`vivekā`): because seclusion is the cause. This is said with reference to the word 'viveka' being a noun of state (`bhāvasādhana`). Regarding 'in seclusion' (`viveke`): this is said with reference to it being an agent noun (`kattusādhana`) or an object noun (`kammasādhana`). For by this word 'secluded' (`vivitto`), both derivations are included: 'being without the hindrances' and 'having been separated from them.'

72. Pīṇayatīti tappeti, vaḍḍheti vā. Sampiyāyanalakkhaṇāti paritussanalakkhaṇā. Pīṇanarasāti paribrūhanarasā. Pharaṇarasāti paṇītarūpehi kāyassa byāpanarasā. Udaggabhāvo odagyaṃ. Khuddikā lahuṃ lomahaṃsanamattaṃ katvā bhinnā na puna uppajjati. Khaṇikā bahulaṃ uppajjati. Ubbegato pharaṇā niccalattā, ciraṭṭhitikattā ca paṇītatarā. Cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvāti puṇṇavallikavihāre cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā. Pakatiyā diṭṭhārammaṇavasenāti pubbe mahācetiyaṃ gahitārammaṇavasena. Citrageṇḍuko vicitrākārena katageṇḍuko. Upanissayeti samīpe, tassa vā vihārassa nissayabhūte, gocaraṭṭhānabhūteti attho.

72. 'Pīṇayati' means it gladdens, or it increases. 'Characteristic of gladdening' means having the characteristic of being fully satisfied. 'Function of gladdening' means having the function of augmenting. 'Function of pervading' means having the function of pervading the body with excellent forms. The state of being uplifted is `odagya` (elation). Minor joy (`khuddikā`), having quickly caused mere horripilation, breaks and does not arise again. Momentary joy (`khaṇikā`) arises frequently. Pervading joy is more sublime than uplifting joy due to its motionlessness and long-lasting nature. 'Going to the cetiya courtyard' means going to the cetiya courtyard at the Puṇṇavallika monastery. 'By the power of an object seen by nature' means by the power of the great cetiya taken as an object previously. A `citrageṇḍuka` is a ball made in a variegated manner. `Upanissaye` means nearby, or being a support for that monastery, meaning being a place of resort for alms. This is the meaning.

Gharājireti gehaṅgaṇe. Pabbatasikhare katacetiyaṃ “ākāsacetiya”nti vuttaṃ. Gahitanimittenevāti cetiyavandanaṃ, dhammassavanañca uddissa “dhaññā vatime”tiādinā gahitakusalanimitteneva kāraṇabhūtena. Gahitaṃ vā nimittaṃ etenāti gahitanimittaṃ, vuttākārena pavattacittaṃ, tena gahitanimitteneva cittena saha. Pakkhandanti anupaviṭṭhaṃ. Anuparipphuṭanti anu anu samantato phuṭaṃ, sabbaso anuvisaṭanti attho.

'In the house-yard' (`gharājire`) means in the house-enclosure (`gehaṅgaṇe`). A cetiya made on a mountain peak is called an 'ākāsa-cetiya' (sky-shrine). 'By the taken sign itself' means: by the wholesome sign which is the cause, taken with the thought 'Oh, how fortunate are they!' and so on, directed towards venerating the cetiya and listening to the Dhamma. Or, `gahitanimitta` ('taken sign') is that by which a sign is taken, meaning the mind proceeding in the manner described; [the phrase is to be understood as] 'together with that mind which has thus taken a sign.' 'They leap forth' (`pakkhandanti`) means it is entered (`anupaviṭṭhaṃ`). 'They pervade along' (`anuparipphuṭanti`) means pervaded again and again from all around; spread along in every way. This is the meaning.

Passaddhiyā nimittabhāvena gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī. Paripācanavasena paripākaṃ gacchantī. Appanāsampayuttāva pīti appanāsamādhipūrikā. Khaṇikasamādhipūrikā ca upacārasamādhipūrikā ca appanāsamādhissa vidūratarāti tadubhayaṃ anāmasanto “tāsu yā appanāsamādhissā”tiādimāha[V 1.0158]. Samādhisampayogaṃ gatāti pubbe upacārasamādhinā sampayuttā hutvā anukkamena vaḍḍhitvā appanāsamādhinā sampayogaṃ gatā.

Taking up the embryo, as it were, by being a sign for tranquility. It reaches maturity by way of ripening. Only the joy associated with absorption is the fulfiller of absorption-concentration. Because the joy that fulfills momentary concentration and that which fulfills access concentration are very far from absorption-concentration, not mentioning those two, he said, 'Among those, that which is the fulfiller of absorption-concentration...' and so on. 'Having come into association with concentration' means: having first been associated with access concentration, and having grown in sequence, it has come into association with absorption concentration.

73. Sukhayatīti [M 1.0169] sukhaṃ, attanā sampayuttadhamme laddhassāde karotīti attho. Svāyaṃ kattuniddeso pariyāyaladdho dhammato aññassa kattu nivattanattho, nippariyāyena pana bhāvasādhanameva labbhatīti “sukhanaṃ sukha”nti vuttaṃ. Iṭṭhasabhāvattā taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ, sampayuttadhamme vā attani sādayatīti sātaṃ da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Sātaṃ “madhura”nti vadanti. Sātaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti sātalakkhaṇaṃ. Upabrūhanaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ saṃvaḍḍhanaṃ. Dukkhaṃ viya avissajjetvā adukkhamasukhā viya anajjhupekkhitvā anu anu gaṇhanaṃ, upakāritā vā anuggaho. Katthaci paṭhamajjhānādike. Paṭilābhatuṭṭhīti paṭilābhavasena uppajjanakatuṭṭhi. Paṭiladdharasānubhavananti paṭiladdhassa ārammaṇarasassa anubhavananti sabhāvato pītisukhāni vibhajitvā dasseti. Yattha pīti, tattha sukhanti vitakkassa viya itarena pītiyā sukhena accantasaṃyogamāha. “Yattha sukhaṃ, tattha na niyamato pītī”ti vicārassa viya vitakkena sukhassa pītiyā anaccantasaṃyogaṃ. Tena accantānaccantasaṃyogitāya pītisukhānaṃ visesaṃ dasseti. Kaṃ tārenti etthāti kantāraṃ, nirudakamaruṭṭhānaṃ. Vanameva vanantaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samayeti iṭṭhārammaṇassa paṭilābhasamaye, paṭiladdhassa rasānubhavanasamaye, vanacchāyādīnaṃ savanadassanasamaye, pavesaparibhogasamaye ca. Pākaṭabhāvatoti yathākkamaṃ pītisukhānaṃ vibhūtabhāvato.

73. It makes happy, therefore it is happiness (sukha); the meaning is that it causes the states associated with itself to acquire a savored taste. This designation of an agent is obtained indirectly for the purpose of excluding an agent other than the ultimate reality (dhamma). Directly, however, only the derivation in the sense of state (bhāvasādhana) is obtained; therefore, it is said, 'The state of being happy is happiness (sukhanaṃ sukhaṃ).' Because of its agreeable nature, it causes the person endowed with it, or its associated states, to delight in itself; therefore, it is called 'sātaṃ', by changing the letter 'da' to 'ta'. They call 'sātaṃ' 'sweet' (madhura). It has the characteristic of being pleasant (sātaṃ), therefore it is 'sātalakkhaṇaṃ'. Enhancement (upabrūhanaṃ) is the augmentation of associated states. Not abandoning it like suffering, and not being indifferent to it like the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, but repeatedly taking it up—or helpfulness—is support (anuggaho). In some cases, such as in the first jhāna. 'Delight in attainment' (paṭilābhatuṭṭhi) is the contentment that arises by way of attainment. 'Experiencing the taste of what has been attained' (paṭiladdharasānubhavanaṃ) means experiencing the taste of the object that has been attained. Thus, he shows the distinction between joy (pīti) and happiness (sukha) according to their intrinsic nature. With the phrase, 'Where there is joy, there is happiness,' he speaks of the absolute connection of joy with happiness, just as with initial thought (vitakka) and the other (i.e., sustained thought). With the phrase, 'Where there is happiness, there is not necessarily joy,' he speaks of the non-absolute connection of happiness with joy, just as with sustained thought (vicāra) and initial thought (vitakka). Thereby, he shows the distinction between joy and happiness through their state of being absolutely and non-absolutely connected. 'They cross water (kaṃ) here (ettha),' therefore it is a wilderness (kantāraṃ); a waterless desert place is meant. The forest itself is 'vanantaṃ'. 'At that very time' (tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye) means: at the time of attaining a desirable object, at the time of experiencing the taste of what has been attained, at the time of hearing and seeing forest shades and so on, and at the time of entering and making use of them. 'Because of their manifest nature' (pākaṭabhāvato) means because of the manifest nature of joy and happiness, respectively.

Vivekajaṃ pītisukhanti ettha purimasmiṃ atthe vivekajanti jhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Pītisukhasaddato ca atthiatthavisesato “assa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne”ti ettha a-kāro daṭṭhabbo. Dutiye pītisukhameva vivekajaṃ. “Vivekajaṃpītisukha”nti ca aññapadatthasamāso, paccattaniddesassa ca alopo kato. Lope vā sati “vivekajapītisukha”nti pāṭhoti ayaṃ viseso.

Here, in the phrase 'the joy and happiness born of seclusion' (vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ), in the first meaning, by the word 'born of seclusion' (vivekajaṃ), jhāna is meant. And from the word 'pītisukha', because of the specific meaning of 'possessing', the suffix 'a' should be understood here in the sense of 'of this jhāna' or 'in this jhāna'. In the second meaning, joy and happiness themselves are 'born of seclusion'. And 'vivekajaṃpītisukhaṃ' is a Bahubbīhi compound (a compound whose meaning refers to something other than its constituents), and the non-elision of the individual designation has been made. Or, if there is elision, the reading is 'vivekajapītisukhaṃ'. This is the distinction.

Upasampajjāti ettha upa-saṃ-saddā “upalabbhati, saṃbhuñjatī”tiādīsu viya niratthakāti dassetuṃ “upagantvā”tiādiṃ vatvā puna tesaṃ sātthakabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “upasampādayitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ, tasmā patvā, sādhetvāti vā attho. Iriyanti kiriyaṃ. Vuttiādīni tasseva vevacanāni. Pālanāti hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ iriyāpathantarehi rakkhaṇā.

Here, in the word 'upasampajjā', having said 'upagantvā' (having approached), etc., to show that the prefixes 'upa-' and 'saṃ-' are meaningless, as in words like 'upalabbhati' and 'saṃbhuñjati', again, 'upasampādayitvā' (having caused to attain), etc., is said to show their meaningfulness. Therefore, the meaning is 'having attained' (patvā) or 'having accomplished' (sādhetvā). 'Iriyaṃ' means action (kiriyaṃ). 'Vutti' and so on are its synonyms. Indeed, 'maintenance' (pālanā) is protecting from the affliction of one posture by means of other postures.

Pañcaṅgavippahīnādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of 'Abandoned in Five Factors', etc.

74. Pañca [M 1.0170][V 1.0159] aṅgāni vikkhambhanavasena pahīnāni etassāti pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ. “Agyāhito”ti ettha āhita-saddassa viya vippahīna-saddassettha paravacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, pañcahi aṅgehi vippahīnanti vā pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ. Nanu aññepi akusalā dhammā iminā jhānena pahīyanti, atha kasmā pañcaṅgavippahīnatāva vuccatīti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Jhānalābhinopi ajhānasamaṅgikāle jhānapaṭipakkhalobhacittādīnaṃ pavattisabbhāvato “jhānakkhaṇe”ti vuttaṃ. Pahīyantīti vigacchanti, nappavattantīti attho. Ekattārammaṇeti pathavīkasiṇādivasena ekasabhāve, ekaggatāsaṅkhāte ekattāvahe vā ārammaṇe. Tanti taṃ nānāvisayapalobhitaṃ cittaṃ. Kāmadhātuppahānāyāti nānāvisayasamūpabyūḷhāya kāmadhātuyā pahānāya samatikkamāya paṭipadaṃ jhānaṃ nappaṭipajjati. Nirantaranti vikkhepena anantaritaṃ, sahitanti attho. Akammaññanti akammanīyaṃ, bhāvanākammassa ayogyanti attho. Uddhaccakukkuccaparetanti uddhaccakukkuccena abhibhūtaṃ. Paribbhamati anavaṭṭhānato, avaṭṭhānassa samādhānassa abhāvatoti attho. Vicikicchāya upahatanti sātisayassa vicārassa abhāvato “sammāsambuddho nu kho bhagavā, na nu kho”ti, “pathavī pathavī”tiādinā manasikārena, “jhānaṃ siyā nu kho, na nu kho”tiādinā ca pavattāya vicikicchāya upahataṃ. Nārohati appaṭipattinimittattā. Visesena jhānantarāyakarattāti samādhiādīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhāvena jhānādhigamassa antarāyakaraṇato.

74. Five factors are abandoned for it by way of suppression; therefore, it is 'that which has five factors abandoned' (pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ). Here, as in the word 'agyāhito' the word 'āhita' is placed after, so too here the word 'vippahīna' should be understood as being placed after. Or, it is 'abandoned by five factors' (pañcahi aṅgehi vippahīnaṃ), therefore it is 'pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ'. 'Are not other unwholesome states also abandoned by this jhāna? Why, then, is only the state of having abandoned five factors mentioned?' To this, he replies with 'Although' (kiñcāpi), etc. Even for one who has attained jhāna, at a time when one is not endowed with jhāna, because of the existence of the arising of states not hostile to jhāna, such as thoughts of greed, the phrase 'at the moment of jhāna' is said. 'They are abandoned' (pahīyanti) means they depart (vigacchanti), they do not arise; this is the meaning. 'On a single object' (ekattārammaṇe) means: on an object that has a single nature, by way of the earth kasiṇa, etc., or on an object that brings about singularity, which is designated as one-pointedness (ekaggatā). 'It' (taṃ) refers to that mind which is enticed by various sense objects. 'For the abandoning of the sense-sphere' (kāmadhātuppahānāya) means: it does not enter upon the jhāna which is the practice for abandoning and transcending the sense-sphere, which is a conglomeration of various sense objects. 'Uninterrupted' (nirantaraṃ) means not interrupted by distraction; the meaning is 'connected' (sahitaṃ). 'Unwieldy' (akammaññaṃ) means unworkable, unsuitable for the task of meditation; this is the meaning. 'Overcome by restlessness and remorse' (uddhaccakukkuccaparetaṃ) means overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse. It wanders due to instability, that is, due to the absence of stability; this is the meaning. 'Afflicted by doubt' (vicikicchāya upahataṃ) means: due to the absence of profound investigation, it is afflicted by the doubt that arises, such as, 'Is the Blessed One a Perfectly Enlightened One, or is he not?' and, through attention such as 'earth, earth,' 'Might this be jhāna, or might it not?' It does not ascend (nārohati) because it is a cause for non-practice. 'Because it is especially an obstacle to jhāna' (visesena jhānantarāyakarattā) means: because it creates an obstacle to the attainment of jhāna by being directly opposed to concentration and other such factors.

Tehīti jhānādhigamassa paccayabhūtehi vitakkavicārehi. Avikkhepāya sampāditappayogassāti tato evaṃ samādhānāya nipphāditabhāvanāpayogassa. Cetaso payogasampattisambhavāti yathāvuttabhāvanāpayogasampattisamuṭṭhānā. Pīti pīṇanaṃ bhāvanāvasena tappanaṃ. Upabrūhanaṃ bhāvanāvasena parivuddhiṃ cetaso karotīti sambandho. Nanti cittaṃ. Sasesasampayuttadhammanti avasiṭṭhaphassādidhammasahitaṃ, samaṃ sammā ca ādhiyatīti sambandho. Indriyasamatāvasena samaṃ, paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ. Dūrībhāve līnuddhaccābhāvena sammā ca ṭhapetīti attho. Ekaggatā hi samādhānakiccena cittaṃ, sampayuttadhamme ca attānaṃ anuvattāpentī jhānakkhaṇe sātisayaṃ samāhite karotīti. Uppattivasenāti yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjanavasena[M 1.0171]. Etesu [V 1.0160] vitakkādīsu jhānaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti tattheva jhānavohārato. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. “Yathā panā”tiādināpi upamāvasena tamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ karoti.

'By these' means by initial and sustained thought, which are the conditions for the attainment of jhāna. 'For one whose effort has been applied for non-distraction' means for one whose cultivation-effort has been accomplished for the sake of concentration. 'Arising from the attainment of the mind's effort' means arisen from the accomplishment of the aforesaid cultivation-effort. Joy is delighting and refreshing by way of cultivation. The connection is: 'It causes the mind's increase and expansion by way of cultivation.' 'It' refers to the mind. 'With the remaining associated states' means together with the remaining states such as contact. The connection is: 'It is placed equally and rightly.' It is placed 'equally' by way of the balance of the faculties, and 'rightly' by the absence of sloth and restlessness in the distancing of opposing states; this is the meaning. Indeed, one-pointedness, by its function of concentration, making the mind and its associated states conform to itself, renders them exceedingly concentrated at the moment of jhāna. 'By way of arising' means by way of arising according to conditions. Jhāna is said to have arisen in these factors, such as initial thought, because of the designation 'jhāna' in regard to them. Therefore, he said, 'Therefore,' etc. Also, by the phrase 'Just as,' etc., he makes that very meaning clearer by way of a simile.

Pakaticittatoti pākatikakāmāvacaracittato. Suvisadenāti suṭṭhu visadena, paṭutarenāti attho. Sabbāvantanti sabbāvayavavantaṃ, anavasesanti attho. Apphuṭanti asamphuṭṭhaṃ. Ārammaṇesu phusitāti appanāvasena pavattamānā cittekaggatā samantato ārammaṇaṃ pharantī viya hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Kasmā panettha jhānapāṭhe aggahitā cittekaggatā gahitāti anuyogaṃ sandhāya “tattha cittekaggatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu jhānaṅgesu. Na niddiṭṭhāti sarūpato na niddiṭṭhā, sāmaññato pana jhānaggahaṇena gahitā. Evaṃ vuttattāti sarūpeneva vuttattā, aṅgameva cittekaggatāti sambandho. Yena adhippāyenāti yena vitakkādīhi saha vattantaṃ dhammaṃ dīpetuṃ tassa pakāsanādhippāyena “savitakkaṃ savicāra”ntiādinā uddeso kato. So eva adhippāyo tena bhagavatā vibhaṅge “cittekaggatā”ti niddisantena pakāsito. Tasmā sā jhānapāṭhe aggahitāti na cintetabbaṃ.

'Than the natural mind' means than the ordinary sense-sphere mind. 'With a very clear one' means with one that is exceedingly clear, that is, sharper; this is the meaning. 'The whole' means possessing all parts, without remainder; this is the meaning. 'Unpervaded' means untouched. 'Touched on the objects' was said because the one-pointedness of mind occurring by way of absorption is as if pervading the object all around. With reference to the question, 'Why is one-pointedness of mind, which is not included in the jhāna recitation, included here?', the passage beginning 'Therein, one-pointedness of mind...' was stated. 'Therein' means among those jhāna factors. 'Not pointed out' means not pointed out in its own form, but it is included generally by the taking up of 'jhāna.' 'Because it was said thus' means because it was stated in its own form; the connection is that one-pointedness of mind is indeed a factor. 'With which intention': The recitation 'with initial thought, with sustained thought,' etc., was made with the intention of explaining the state that occurs together with initial thought and so on. That very intention was clarified by the Blessed One in the Vibhaṅga when he pointed it out as 'one-pointedness of mind.' Therefore, it should not be thought that it is not included in the jhāna recitation.

Tividhakalyāṇavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Threefold Goodness

75. Ādimajjhapariyosānavasenāti jhānassa ādimajjhapariyosānavasena. Lakkhaṇavasenāti tesaṃyeva appanāyaṃ lakkhitabbabhāvavasena.

75. 'By way of beginning, middle, and end' means by way of the beginning, middle, and end of the jhāna. 'By way of characteristic' means by way of the nature of those very things being what is to be marked in absorption.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ kalyāṇatālakkhaṇānaṃ vibhāvane. Paṭipadāvisuddhīti paṭipajjati jhānaṃ etāyāti paṭipadā, gotrabhupariyosāno pubbabhāgiyo bhāvanānayo. Paripanthato visujjhanaṃ visuddhi, paṭipadāya visuddhi paṭipadāvisuddhi. Sā panāyaṃ yasmā jhānassa uppādakkhaṇe labbhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “paṭipadāvisuddhi ādī”ti. Upekkhānubrūhanāti visodhetabbatādīnaṃ abhāvato jhānapariyāpannāya tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccanipphattiyā anubrūhanā. Sā panāyaṃ visesato jhānassa ṭhitikkhaṇe labbhati. Tena vuttaṃ “upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe”ti. Sampahaṃsanāti tattha dhammānaṃ anativattanādisādhakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena pariyodapanā. Sā pana yasmā jhānassa osānakkhaṇe pākaṭā hoti[M 1.0172], tasmā vuttaṃ “sampahaṃsanā pariyosāna”nti. Imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇānīti paripanthato cittassa visujjhanākāro[V 1.0161], majjhimassa samathanimittassa paṭipajjanākāro, tattha pakkhandanākāroti imāni tīṇi jhānassa ādito uppādakkhaṇe appanāpattilakkhaṇāni tehi ākārehi vinā appanāpattiyā abhāvato, asati ca appanāya tadabhāvato. Ādikalyāṇañceva visuddhipaṭipadattā. Yathāvuttehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgatattā, sampannalakkhaṇattā ca tilakkhaṇasampannañca. Iminā nayena majjhapariyosānalakkhaṇānañca yojanā veditabbā.

'Therein' means in that clarification of the goodness and the characteristics. 'Purity of the path': 'Path' is so called because by it one attains jhāna; it is the preliminary method of cultivation that culminates in change-of-lineage. Purity is the being purified from obstacles. The purity of the path is 'purity of the path.' And since this is obtained at the arising-moment of the jhāna, it was therefore said, 'Purity of the path is the beginning.' 'Strengthening of equanimity' is the strengthening, through the accomplishment of its function, of the specific neutrality which is included in the jhāna, due to the absence of things to be purified. And this, especially, is obtained at the static-moment of the jhāna. Therefore it was said, 'Strengthening of equanimity is in the middle.' 'Gladdening' is the cleansing by way of the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that brings about the non-transgression of the states therein. And since this becomes manifest at the concluding-moment of the jhāna, it was therefore said, 'Gladdening is the conclusion.' These three characteristics—the mode of the mind's purification from obstacles, the mode of attaining the intermediate sign of calm, and the mode of plunging into it—these three are the characteristics of attaining absorption at the arising-moment, which is the beginning of the jhāna. For without these modes, there is no attainment of absorption, and when there is no absorption, they are absent. It is good in the beginning because it is the pure path. And because it is endowed with the aforesaid characteristics and possesses accomplished characteristics, it is endowed with the three characteristics. By this method, the application of the characteristics of the middle and the end should also be understood.

Sambharīyati jhānaṃ etenāti sambhāro, nānāvajjanaparikammaṃ. Saha sambhārenāti sasambhāro, so eva sasambhāriko. Upacāroti ekāvajjanūpacāramāha. Paggahādikiccassa pubbabhāge bhāvanāya eva sādhitattā yā tattha ekāvajjanūpacāre siddhā ajjhupekkhanā, sā jhānakkhaṇe paribrūhitā nāma hotīti vuttaṃ “upekkhānubrūhanā nāma appanā”ti. Yathādhigataṃ jhānaṃ nissāya yo pahaṭṭhākāro cittassa paritoso, taṃ paccavekkhaṇāvasena pavattaṃ sandhāyāha “sampahaṃsanā nāma paccavekkhaṇā”ti. Eketi abhayagirivāsino. Te hi evaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhiādike vaṇṇayanti, tadayuttaṃ. Tathā hi sati ajjhānadhammehi jhānassa guṇasaṃkittanaṃ nāma kataṃ hoti. Na hi bhūmantaraṃ bhūmantarapariyāpannaṃ hoti. Pāḷiyā cetaṃ viruddhanti dassetuṃ “yasmā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ekattagataṃ cittanti indriyānaṃ ekarasabhāvena, ekaggatāya ca sikhāppattiyā tadanuguṇaṃ ekattaṃ gatanti ekattagataṃ, sasampayuttaṃ appanāpattacittaṃ. Tasseva paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandatādi anantarameva vuccati. Tasmāti yasmā ekasmiṃyeva appanācittakkhaṇe paṭipadāvisuddhiādi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā āgamanavasenāti parikammāgamanavasena. Anativattanādīti ādi-saddena indriyekarasatātadupagavīriyavāhanāsevanāni saṅgaṇhāti. Pariyodāpakassāti parisodhakassa pabhassarabhāvakarassa. Anativattanādibhāvasādhanameva cettha ñāṇassa kiccanipphatti veditabbā.

Jhāna is well cultivated by this, thus it is 'sambhāra' (cultivation); this refers to the preliminary work of varied attention. With cultivation, it is 'sasambhāra'; that very thing is 'sasambhāriko'. 'Upacāra' (approach) refers to the approach of single attention. Because the function of exertion and so forth is accomplished in the preliminary stage by the development itself, the equanimity established there in the approach of single attention is said to be augmented at the moment of jhāna. Thus it is said, 'Absorption is called the augmentation of equanimity.' Referring to that gladdened state and satisfaction of mind which occurs by way of reviewing, based on the jhāna as attained, he says, 'Rejoicing is called reviewing.' 'Some' refers to the dwellers of Abhayagiri. For they describe the purity of practice and so forth in this way, which is unfitting. For if that were so, it would be a proclamation of the virtues of jhāna by means of non-jhāna states. For one plane is not included within another plane. To show that this is contrary to the Pāḷi, the passage beginning 'But because...' is stated. There, 'the mind that has gone to oneness' means the mind that has reached absorption, together with its associated states, having gone to oneness through the single function of the faculties and the attainment of the peak of one-pointedness, in conformity with that. Of that very mind, the purity of practice, plunging in, and so forth are spoken of immediately after. 'Therefore': because in the Pāḷi the purity of practice and so forth are spoken of in a single moment of absorption-consciousness, 'by way of its origin' means by way of the origin which is the preliminary work. 'Not transgressing, etc.': by the word 'etc.,' it includes the single function of the faculties, the application of energy conforming to that, and the cultivation thereof. 'Of the one who cleanses' means of the one who purifies, who makes luminous. Here, the completion of the function of knowledge should be understood as the very accomplishment of the state of not transgressing, etc.

Tasminti tasmiṃ vāre, catupañcacittaparimāṇāya appanāvīthiyanti attho. Tato paripanthato. Cittaṃ visujjhatīti yadipi āgamanaṃ gahetuṃ avisesena viya vuttaṃ, parikammavisuddhito pana appanāvisuddhi sātisayāva. Tenāha “visuddhattā”tiādi. Āvaraṇavirahitaṃ hutvāti yenāvaraṇena [M 1.0173] āvaṭattā cittaṃ tato pubbe majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjituṃ na sakkoti, tena vivittaṃ hutvā, taṃ vikkhambhetvāti attho. Līnuddhaccasaṅkhātānaṃ ubhinnaṃ antānaṃ anupagamanena majjhimo, savisesaṃ paccanīkadhammānaṃ vūpasamanato [V 1.0162] samatho, yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato nimittañcāti majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ. Tenāha “samappavatto appanāsamādhiyevā”ti. Tadanantaraṃ pana purimacittanti tassa appanācittassa anantarapaccayabhūtaṃ purimaṃ cittaṃ, gotrabhucittanti attho. Ekasantatipariṇāmanayenāti yathā “tadeva khīraṃ dadhisampanna”nti, evaṃ satipi parittamahaggatabhāvabhede, paccayapaccayuppannabhāvabhede ca ekissā eva santatiyā pariṇāmūpagamananayena ekattanayavasena. Tathattanti tathabhāvaṃ appanāsamādhivasena samāhitabhāvaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipannattāti vuttākārena paṭipajjamānattā. Yasmiñhi khaṇe tathattaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe tathattupagamanena appanāsamādhinā samāhitabhāvūpagamanena tattha pakkhandati nāma. Purimacitteti appanācittassa purimasmiṃ citte gotrabhucitte. Vijjamānākāranipphādikāti tasmiṃ citte vijjamānānaṃ paripanthavisuddhimajjhimasamathapaṭipattipakkhandanākārānaṃ nipphādikā, tenākārena nipphajjamānāti attho. Teyeva hi ākārā paccayavisesato jhānakkhaṇe nipphajjamānā “paṭipadāvisuddhī”ti laddhasamaññā jhānassa taṃ visesaṃ nipphādentā viya vuttā. Uppādakkhaṇeyevāti attalābhavelāyameva. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ te ākārā nipphajjantīti āha “āgamanavasenā”ti.

'In that' means: in that impulsion-series, in the absorption process lasting four or five mind-moments; this is the meaning. From that obstacle. Although 'the mind is purified' is stated as if generally, to refer to its source, the preliminary work, yet the purification of absorption is indeed superior to the purification of preliminary work. Therefore he says, 'due to being purified,' etc. 'Having become free from hindrances' means: having become secluded from and having suppressed that hindrance by which the mind, being enveloped, was previously unable to enter upon the intermediate sign of serenity; this is the meaning. It is 'middle' (majjhima) because it does not approach the two extremes of sloth and agitation; it is 'serenity' (samatha) because it distinctively pacifies opposing states; and it is a 'sign' (nimitta) because it is the cause of the yogi's special kinds of happiness. Thus it is the 'intermediate sign of serenity.' Therefore he says, 'It is the absorption-concentration that proceeds evenly.' 'But the preceding mind immediately after that' means the preceding mind which is the proximate condition for that absorption-mind, that is, the change-of-lineage mind. 'By the method of the transformation of a single continuity': just as it is said, 'that very milk has become curd,' so too, even though there is a difference in being of the sense-sphere and the sublime, and a difference in being condition and conditioned, it is by way of the principle of oneness, through the method of undergoing transformation within a single continuity. 'Suchness' (tathatta) means that state, the state of being concentrated by way of absorption-concentration. 'Because of having practiced thus' means because of practicing in the manner stated. For in the moment one enters upon 'suchness,' the intermediate sign of serenity, in that very moment, by approaching that 'suchness,' by approaching the state of concentration through absorption-concentration, one is said to plunge into that. 'In the preceding mind' means in the change-of-lineage mind, which is the mind preceding the absorption-mind. 'Producer of the existing modes' means producer of the modes existing in that mind, namely: purification from obstacles, entering upon the intermediate sign of serenity, and plunging in; that is, being produced in that manner. For those very modes, arising at the moment of jhāna due to a special condition and having received the designation 'purity of practice,' are spoken of as if they produce that distinction of the jhāna. 'At the very moment of arising' means at the very time of acquiring its own nature. If so, how do those modes arise? He says, 'by way of its origin.'

Tassāti cittassa. “Visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhatī”ti pāḷiyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.158) puggalādhiṭṭhānena āgatāti “byāpāraṃ akaronto”ti āha. Samathapaṭipattitathattupagamanañca idha samathabhāvāpattiyevāti āha “samathabhāvūpagamanenā”ti. Kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya ekattena upaṭṭhitassāti pubbe “kathaṃ nu kho kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pajaheyya”nti paṭipannassa idāni samathapaṭipattiyā tassa pahīnattā kilesasaṅgaṇikābhāvena ekattena upaṭṭhitassa jhānacittassa. Paripanthavisuddhimajjhimasamathapaṭipattipakkhandanehi vuddhippattiyā anubrūhite jhānacitte laddhokāsā tatramajjhattupekkhā sampayuttesu samavāhitabhāvena pavattamānā te anubrūhentī viya hotīti āha “tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā veditabbā”ti.

'Of that' means of the mind. Since 'one observes the purified mind' (Paṭis.M. i. 158) comes in the Pāḷi with the individual as the basis, he says, 'without making an effort.' And the approaching of 'suchness' through the practice of serenity here is simply the attainment of a state of serenity; hence he says, 'by approaching a state of serenity.' 'Of the one who stands in oneness, having abandoned association with defilements' refers to the jhāna-mind of one who, having previously practiced thinking, 'How indeed might I abandon association with defilements?', now, through the practice of serenity, has abandoned it and stands in oneness, without association with defilements. The equanimity of neutrality, having found its opportunity in the jhāna-mind that has been augmented by the attainment of growth through purification from obstacles, entering upon the intermediate sign of serenity, and plunging in, proceeds in a balanced way among the associated states and is as if it augments them. Thus he says, 'The augmentation of equanimity should be understood by way of the function of the equanimity of neutrality therein.'

Ye [M 1.0174] panete yuganaddhadhammāti sambandho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ jhānacitte. Aññamaññānativattanavasena kiccakaraṇato yuge naddhā baddhā viya yuganaddhā. Vimuttirasenāti vimuccanakiccena, vimuccanasampattiyā vā. Esa yogī. Vāhayatīti pavatteti. Assāti jhānacittassa. Tasmiṃ khaṇeti bhaṅgakkhaṇe. Uppādakkhaṇe atīte hi ṭhitikkhaṇato paṭṭhāya āsevanā [V 1.0163] pavattati nāma. Te ākārāti aññamaññānativattanādayo tattha dhammānaṃ pavattiākārā. Āsevanāpi hi āsevanapaccayabhāvīnaṃ dhammānaṃ pavattiākāroyeva. Saṃkilesavodānesūti samādhipaññānaṃ samarasatāya akaraṇaṃ bhāvanāya saṃkileso, karaṇaṃ vodānaṃ. Tathā sesesupi. Evametesu saṃkilesavodānesu taṃ taṃ ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ guṇaṃ puretaraṃ pāṭihāriyañāṇena disvā yathā aññamaññānativattanādayo honti, tathā bhāvanāya sampahaṃsitattā teneva ñāṇena visodhitattā. Visodhanaṃ hettha sampahaṃsanaṃ. Te ākārā yasmā nipphannā, tasmā “dhammānaṃ…pe… veditabbāti vutta”nti lakkhaṇasaṃvaṇṇanāya ādimhi vuttaṃ nigamanavasena dasseti.

Another point. 'These yoked-together dharmas'—thus is the connection. Therein: in that jhānic mind. They are 'yoked-together' because they perform their function by way of not transgressing one another, like being tied or bound to a yoke. 'By the taste of liberation' means by the function of liberation, or by the accomplishment of liberation. This yogī. 'Drives' means causes to proceed. 'Of it' refers to the jhānic mind. 'At that moment' means at the moment of dissolution. Indeed, when the moment of arising has passed, repetition is said to occur beginning from the moment of presence. 'Those modes' are the modes of occurrence of the dharmas therein, such as not transgressing one another. Indeed, repetition is itself the mode of occurrence for dharmas that are wont to arise due to the repetition condition. In 'defilements and purifications': for the development, the non-making of concentration and wisdom to have an equal function is a defilement; the making of them to have an equal function is purification. Likewise for the remaining dharmas. Thus, in these defilements and purifications, having first seen with the preparatory knowledge the respective danger and fault, and the respective benefit and virtue, in such a way that the modes such as not transgressing one another occur, so it is because the development has been gladdened and purified by that very knowledge. Herein, purification is gladdening. Because those modes are produced, therefore it was said, 'Of the dharmas... should be understood.' By this, he shows by way of conclusion what was said at the beginning of the exposition of the characteristic.

“Yasmā upekkhāvasena ñāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti ko sambandho. Kasmā sampahaṃsanāva pariyosānanti vuttā, na upekkhānubrūhanāti codanaṃ sandhāya “tattha yasmā upekkhāvasena ñāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ bhāvanācitte. Upekkhāvasena ñāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti appanākāle bhāvanāya samappavattiyā, paṭipakkhassa ca pahānato paggahādīsu byāpārassa akātabbato ajjhupekkhanāva hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “samaye cittassa ajjhupekkhanā, visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhatī”ti ca ādi. Sā panāyaṃ ajjhupekkhanā ñāṇassa kiccasiddhiyā hoti, visesato ñāṇasādhanattā appanābyāpārassāti phalena kāraṇānumānañāyena. Yasmā upekkhāvasena ñāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā ñāṇakiccabhūtā sampahaṃsanā pariyosānanti vuttāti sambandho.

What is the connection with the passage, 'Because knowledge becomes manifest by way of equanimity'? Why is gladdening alone said to be the conclusion, and not the fostering of equanimity? In reference to this objection, it was said: 'Therein, because knowledge becomes manifest by way of equanimity.' 'Therein' means in that mind of development. 'Knowledge becomes manifest by way of equanimity' means that at the time of absorption, because of the balanced proceeding of the development and the abandonment of opposing factors, and because exertion and other activities are not to be done, there is only looking on with equanimity. It is in reference to this that it was said, 'at the right time, looking on the mind with equanimity,' and 'one looks on the purified mind with equanimity,' and so on. Furthermore, this looking on with equanimity occurs through the accomplishment of the function of knowledge, especially because the activity of absorption is accomplished by knowledge; this is by the method of inferring the cause from the effect. Because knowledge becomes manifest by way of equanimity, therefore gladdening, which is the function of knowledge, is said to be the conclusion. Thus is the connection.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā samatthetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathāpaggahitaṃ cittanti yathā bhāvanācittaṃ kosajjapakkhe na patati, tathā vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyānaṃ dhammānaṃ bahulīkāravasena paggahitaṃ. Sādhukaṃ ajjhupekkhatīti paggaṇhantenāpi samādhissa vīriyasamatāyojanavasena paggahitattā sakkaccaṃ ajjhupekkhati, tatramajjhattupekkhā okāsaṃ [M 1.0175] labhati. Taṃ pana ajjhupekkhanaṃ upekkhāvasena pubbe pavattapārihāriyapaññāvasena appanāpaññāya kiccādhikatāti āha “paññāvasena paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hotī”ti. Tassa adhimattattā eva ajjhupekkhantasseva nānāsabhāvehi nīvaraṇapamukhehi kilesehi appanācittaṃ vimuccati. Vimokkhavasena vimuccanavasena. Paññāvasenāti pubbe pavattapārihāriyapaññāvasena. Vimuttattāti nānākilesehi vimuttattā eva. Te dhammā saddhādayo, visesato saddhāpaññāvīriyasamādhayo [V 1.0164] ca ekarasā samānakiccā honti. Evamayaṃ indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhena bhāvanā nipphajjamānā ñāṇabyāpāroti āha “ñāṇakiccabhūtā sampahaṃsanā pariyosāna”nti. Evaṃ tividhāya paṭipadāvisuddhiyā laddhavisesāya tividhāya upekkhānubrūhanāya sātisayaṃ paññindriyassa adhimuttabhāvena catubbidhāpi sampahaṃsanā sijjhatīti āgamanupekkhā ñāṇakiccavasena dasapi ākārā jhāne eva veditabbā.

Now, in order to establish with the Pāḷi the meaning as it has been stated, 'as he said,' etc., was said. 'A mind so exerted' means: exerted by way of frequently practicing the dharmas that are the basis for the energy enlightenment-factor, in such a way that the mind of development does not fall into the side of laziness. 'He looks on well with equanimity' means: even while exerting, because of having exerted concentration by way of yoking it with balanced energy, one looks on carefully with equanimity; therein, equanimity as neutrality finds its opportunity. Furthermore, that looking on with equanimity, by way of equanimity and by way of the preparatory wisdom that occurred previously, is the superior function of the absorption-wisdom. Therefore, he said, 'by way of wisdom, the wisdom faculty becomes predominant.' Just because of its predominance, even while one is looking on with equanimity, the absorption-mind is liberated from the defilements of various natures, headed by the hindrances. By way of deliverance, by way of liberation. 'By way of wisdom' means by way of the preparatory wisdom that occurred previously. 'Because of being liberated' means just because of being liberated from the various defilements. Those dharmas, faith and so on, and especially faith and wisdom, energy and concentration, become of one taste, of equal function. Thus, this development, being accomplished through the faculties having a single taste, is the activity of knowledge. Therefore, he said, 'gladdening, which is the function of knowledge, is the conclusion.' Thus, by the threefold purity of practice by which distinction is obtained, by the threefold fostering of equanimity, through the pre-eminent state of the wisdom faculty being exceedingly great, the fourfold gladdening is also accomplished. Therefore, the ten modes, by way of the source, equanimity, and the function of knowledge, should be understood in the jhāna alone.

Gaṇanānupubbatāti gaṇanānupubbatāya, gaṇanānupubbatāmattaṃ vā paṭhamanti idanti attho. Tena desanākkamaṃ ulliṅgeti. “Paṭhamaṃ uppannanti paṭhama”nti iminā paṭipattikkamaṃ, uppannanti hi adhigatanti attho. “Paṭhamaṃ samāpajjitabbanti paṭhama”nti idaṃ pana na ekantalakkhaṇanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 160) paṭisiddhattā idha na gahitaṃ. Ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṃ lakkhaṇūpanijjhānanti duvidhe jhāne idhādhippetajjhānameva dassetuṃ “ārammaṇūpanijjhānato”ti vuttaṃ. Pathavīkasiṇasaṅkhātassa attano attano ārammaṇassa rūpaṃ viya cakkhunā upanijjhāyanato. Paccanīkajhāpanatoti nīvaraṇādīnaṃ paccanīkadhammānaṃ dahanato vikkhambhanavasena pajahanato. Sakalaṭṭhenāti heṭṭhā vuttanayena kate vā akate vā paricchijja gahite pathavībhāge pathavīmaṇḍale sakalārammaṇakaraṇaṭṭhena. Na hi tassa ekadesamārammaṇaṃ karīyati. Pathavīkasiṇasannissayatāya nimittaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Taṃsahacaraṇato jhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti.

'First' means being first in the sequence of counting, or this term 'first' is merely being first in the sequence of counting; this is the meaning. By that, he indicates the order of the teaching. By this, '"First" means first arisen,' he indicates the order of practice; for 'arisen' here has the meaning 'attained.' However, this etymology, '"First" means first to be entered upon,' is not taken here because it is rejected in the commentary (Dhs.A. 160) as not being a definite characteristic. Among the two kinds of jhāna, namely absorption into the object and absorption into the characteristics, in order to show that only the jhāna intended here is meant, it was said 'from absorption into the object.' This is because of closely contemplating one's own object, designated as the earth kasiṇa, just as one contemplates a form with the eye. 'From burning the adversaries' means because of burning the opposing dharmas such as the hindrances, because of abandoning them by way of suppression. 'In the sense of the whole' means in the sense of making the whole thing the object, with regard to the earth-portion or earth-disk, whether prepared or not prepared according to the method stated below, having been taken up by delimiting it. Indeed, not just a part of it is made the object. Because it is dependent on the earth kasiṇa, the sign is called 'earth kasiṇa', just as in the expression 'the beds are shouting.' Because it occurs together with that sign, the jhāna is called 'earth kasiṇa', just as in the expression 'the spears are moving about.'

Ciraṭṭhitisampādanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Attainment of Long-lasting Stability

76. Lakkhaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ sarena vālaṃ vijjhatīti vālavedhī. Idha pana anekadhā bhinnassa vālassa aṃsuṃ vijjhanto “vālavedhī”ti adhippeto. Tena [M 1.0176] vālavedhinā. Sūdenāti bhattakārena. “Ākārā pariggahetabbā”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sukusaloti suṭṭhu cheko. Dhanuggahoti issāso. Kammanti yogyaṃ. Akkantapadānanti vijjhanakāle akkamanavasena pavattapadānaṃ. Ākāranti dhanujiyāsarānaṃ gahitākāraṃ. Pariggaṇheyyāti upadhāreyya. Bhojanasappāyādayoti ādi-saddo avuttākārānampi saṅgāhako daṭṭhabbo. Tena utubhāvanānimittādīnampi pariggaṇhanaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Tasminti tasmiṃ taruṇasamādhimhi.

76. He pierces a hair placed at the target with an arrow; thus he is a 'hair-piercer'. Here, however, one who pierces a fiber of a hair that has been split into many parts is intended by 'hair-piercer'. By that hair-piercer. By 'cook' is meant a food-preparer. To elaborate on the meaning briefly stated as 'the manners should be grasped', the phrase 'just as...' and so forth is stated. Therein, 'highly skilled' means thoroughly expert. 'An archer' means a bowman. 'Work' means suitable work. By 'of the steps taken' is meant of the feet that move by way of treading at the time of shooting. By 'the manner' is meant the manner of grasping the bow, string, and arrows. 'He should grasp' means he should observe. In 'suitable for food and so forth', the word 'and so forth' should be understood as inclusive of even unmentioned manners. By that, the grasping of season, development, signs, and so forth is also said to be. By 'in that' is meant in that tender concentration.

Bhattāranti [V 1.0165] sāminaṃ, bhattavetanādīhi posakanti attho. Parivisantoti bhojento. Tassa ruccitvā bhuñjanākāraṃ sallakkhetvā tassa upanāmentoti yojanā. Ayampi yogī. Adhigatakkhaṇe bhojanādayo ākāreti pubbe jhānassa adhigatakkhaṇe kiccasādhake bhojanādigate ākāre. Gahetvāti pariggahetvā sallakkhetvā. Naṭṭhe naṭṭhe samādhimhi punappunaṃ appanāya.

By 'provider' is meant the master; the meaning is one who nourishes with food, wages, and so forth. By 'serving' is meant feeding. 'Having noted the manner of eating that he enjoys, he presents it to him'—this is the connection. This yogī also. '[He grasps] the manners related to food and so forth at the moment of attainment' means: the manners related to food, etc., which accomplish the task at the moment of previously attaining jhāna. By 'having taken' is meant having grasped and noted. For attaining absorption again and again whenever the concentration is lost.

Mahānasavijjāparicayena paṇḍito. Tattha visadañāṇatāya byatto. Ṭhānuppattikakaosallayogena kusalo. Nānaccayehīti nānaccayehi nānāsabhāvehi, nānārasehīti attho. Tenāha “ambilaggehī”tiādi. Sūpehīti byañjanehi. Ambilaggehīti ambilakoṭṭhāsehi, ye vā ambilarasā hutvā aggabhūtā, tehi caturambilādimissehi. Esa nayo tittakaggādīsupi. Khārikehīti vātiṅgaṇakaḷīrādimissehi. Nimittanti ākāraṃ ruccanavasena bhuñjanākāraṃ. Uggaṇhātīti uparūpari gaṇhāti upadhāreti. Imassa vā sūpeyyassa atthāya hatthaṃ abhiharati. Abhihārānanti abhimukhena haritabbānaṃ paṇṇākārānaṃ, pūjābhihārānaṃ vā. Nimittaṃ uggaṇhātīti “evaṃ me cittaṃ samāhitaṃ ahosī”ti nimittaṃ gaṇhāti sallakkheti.

Wise due to familiarity with the art of the kitchen. Therein, discerning due to clarity of knowledge. Skillful due to the application of skill appropriate to the occasion. By 'with various assortments' is meant with various collections, with various natures, or with various tastes. Therefore, he said 'with excellent sour things', etc. By 'with soups' is meant with curries. By 'with excellent sour things' is meant with portions of sour taste, or those which, being of sour taste, are excellent, mixed with the four sour fruits, etc. This is the method also in 'with excellent bitter things', etc. By 'with salty dishes' is meant mixed with eggplant, bamboo shoots, etc. By 'sign' is meant the manner, the manner of eating according to what is pleasing. 'He grasps' means he takes up and observes again and again. Or, 'for the sake of this curry, he extends his hand'. By 'of offerings' is meant of gifts to be brought forward, or of offerings of veneration. 'He grasps the sign' means he takes up and notes the sign, thinking, 'Thus my mind was concentrated.'

Samādhiparipanthānanti samādhissa paripanthabhūtānaṃ. Dhammānanti kāmacchandādinīvaraṇadhammānaṃ. Suvisodhitattāti suṭṭhu visodhitattā, vikkhambhanavaseneva sammadeva pahīnattāti attho. Kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādīhīti ādi-saddena asubhamanasikāranekkhammānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Nekkhammaguṇadassanenāpi [M 1.0177] hi tassa vibandhabhūte kāmacchande ādīnavo visesato pākaṭo hotīti. Kāyaduṭṭhullanti kāyadarathaṃ sāraddhakāyataṃ. Tena kāyacittānaṃ sārambhanimittassa byāpādanīvaraṇassa na visodhanamāha. Ārambhadhātumanasikārādīti ādi-saddena vīriyasambojjhaṅganimittānaṃ, ālokasaññādīnañca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Samathanimittamanasikārādīti ādi-saddena samādhisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyānaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Aññepi samādhiparipantheti vicikicchāṭṭhāniye, madamānādike ca sandhāyāha. Āsayanti vasanakasusiraṃ. Suparisuddhanti āsaṅkanīyattābhāvena suṭṭhu parisuddhaṃ. Etthāha – nanu cāyaṃ pageva kāmādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā samathapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno upacārakkhaṇeyeva jhānena nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāni, atha kasmā puna kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādi gahitanti? Saccametaṃ. Taṃ pana pahānamattanti jhānassa ciraṭṭhitiyā atisayapahānatthaṃ puna gahitaṃ.

By 'of obstacles to concentration' is meant of those things that have become obstacles to concentration. By 'of dhammas' is meant of the hindrance-dhammas such as sensual desire. By 'because of being well-purified' is meant because of being well purified, because of being rightly abandoned just by way of suppression; this is the meaning. In 'by reflecting on the danger of sensual pleasures, etc.', by the word 'etc.' he includes attention to the foul, reflection on the benefit of renunciation, and so on. For by seeing the virtue of renunciation, the danger in sensual desire, which is an obstruction to it, becomes especially evident. By 'bodily coarseness' is meant bodily agitation, the state of having an agitated body. By that, he speaks of the non-purification of the hindrance of ill will, which is the cause of agitation for body and mind. In 'attention to the element of exertion, etc.', by the word 'etc.', the inclusion of the causes of the energy enlightenment-factor, and of the perception of light, etc., should be understood. In 'attention to the sign of serenity, etc.', by the word 'etc.', the inclusion of the dhammas that are the basis for the concentration enlightenment-factor should be understood. When it says 'other obstacles to concentration', it is said referring to things that are the basis for doubt, and to conceit, arrogance, and so on. By 'residence' is meant the hollow place of dwelling. By 'well-purified' is meant thoroughly pure due to the absence of being suspect. Here, one says: 'Is it not so that this person, having already reflected on the danger of sensual pleasures, entered upon the path of serenity? And were not the hindrances suppressed at the very moment of access? Then why is reflecting on the danger of sensual pleasures, etc., taken up again?' This is true. However, that is mere abandonment. It is taken up again for the sake of superior abandonment for the long-lasting stability of the jhāna.

Uddhacca [V 1.0166] middhanti kukkuccaṃ, thinañca tadekaṭṭhatāya gahitamevāti katvā vuttaṃ. Suddhantagatoti suparisuddhapariyantaṃ sabbaso visodhitakoṇapariyantaṃ uyyānaṃ gato. Tahiṃ rameti tasmiṃ jhāne rameyya divasabhāgampi jhānasamaṅgī eva bhaveyya.

By 'restlessness and torpor', it is said having included worry and sloth, as they are taken together due to having the same basis. By 'gone to a pure end' is meant gone to a garden with a well-purified boundary, with its corners and boundaries completely cleansed in every way. By 'delights therein' is meant one should delight in that jhāna; one should be endowed with jhāna for even a part of the day.

Cittabhāvanāvepullatthanti samādhibhāvanāya vipulabhāvāya. Yathā hi bhāvanāvasena nimittassa uppatti, evamassa bhāvanāvaseneva vaḍḍhanampi. Tasmā ekaṅgulādivasena nimittaṃ vaḍḍhentassa punappunaṃ bahulīkārena jhānaṃ bhāvanāpi vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “cittabhāvanāvepullatthañca yathāladdhaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ vaḍḍhetabba”nti. Tassāti paṭibhāganimittassa.

By 'for the sake of the amplitude of the development of mind' is meant for the ample state of the development of concentration. For just as the sign arises by the power of development, so too its growth is only by the power of development. Therefore, for one who expands the sign by way of one finger-breadth, etc., the development of jhāna also, through frequent practice again and again, attains growth, increase, and amplitude. Therefore it was said: 'And for the sake of the mind's development reaching amplitude, the counterpart sign, as it has been obtained, should be expanded.' By 'its' is meant of the counterpart sign.

Nimittavaḍḍhananayavaṇṇanā

The Elaboration on the Method of Increasing the Sign.

77. Tatrāti sāmiatthe bhummavacanaṃ, tassāti attho. Avaḍḍhetvāti yathā kumbhakāro mattikāya pattaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ aparicchinditvāva pattaṃ vaḍḍheti, evaṃ pattavaḍḍhanayogena pattavaḍḍhanayuttiyā avaḍḍhetvā pūvikassa pūvavaḍḍhanaṃ. Bhattassa upari bhattapakkhipanaṃ bhattavaḍḍhanaṃ. Vatthassa tintassa añchanādi dussavaḍḍhanaṃ. Paccekaṃ yoga-saddo yojetabbo. Aparicchinditvā [M 1.0178] na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ saparicchede eva bhāvanāpavattito. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sāntake no anantake”ti (visuddhi. 1.55).

77. The word `tatra` is a locative term in the sense of the genitive; the meaning is 'of that [counterpart sign]'. Regarding `avaḍḍhetvā` (not having increased): Just as a potter, when making a bowl from clay, first increases the bowl without defining its limits, one should not increase [the sign] in that way, by the method of increasing a bowl. Nor should one increase it like the increasing of a cake by a baker, the increasing of food by putting more food on top of it, or the increasing of cloth by stretching the wet cloth, and so on. The word `yoga` (method) should be connected with each of these. It should not be increased without defining its limits, because the development proceeds only within a defined limit. For so it has been said: 'With a limit, not without a limit.'

Haṃsapotakāti javanahaṃsapotakā. Ukkūlaṃ unnataṭṭhānaṃ. Vikūlaṃ ninnaṭṭhānaṃ. Nadīsotena kataṃ viduggaṃ nadīviduggaṃ. Visamākārena ṭhito pabbatapadeso pabbatavisamo.

By `haṃsapotakā` (young swans) is meant young swans of a swift species. `Ukkūlaṃ` is an elevated place. `Vikūlaṃ` is a low-lying place. `Nadīviduggaṃ` is a place difficult to traverse made by the river's current. `Pabbatavisamo` is a mountain region that stands in an uneven manner.

Thūlāni hutvā upaṭṭhahanti paccavekkhaṇābāhullena vibhūtabhāvato. Dubbalāni hutvā upaṭṭhahanti paguṇabalavabhāvassa anāpādikattā. Upari ussukkanāyāti bhāvanāya upari ārohanāya, dutiyajjhānādhigamāyāti attho.

They appear, having become coarse, due to the abundance of reflection and because of their manifest nature. They appear, having become weak, because a state of proficiency and strength has not been brought about. `Upari ussukkanāya` (for striving upwards) means for ascending higher in the development; the meaning is for the attainment of the second jhāna.

Pabbateyyāti pabbate bahulacārinī. Akhettaññūti agocaraññū. Samādhiparipanthānaṃ visodhanānabhiññātāya bālo. Jhānassa paguṇabhāvāpādanaveyyattiyassa abhāvena abyatto. Uparijhānassa [V 1.0167] padaṭṭhānabhāvānavabodhena akhettaññū. Sabbathāpi samāpattikosallābhāvena akusalo. Samādhinimittassa vā anāsevanāya bālo. Abhāvanāya abyatto. Abahulīkārena akhettaññū. Sammadeva anadhiṭṭhānato akusaloti yojetabbaṃ. Ubhato bhaṭṭhoti ubhayato jhānato bhaṭṭho. So hi appaguṇatāya na suppatiṭṭhitatāya saussāhopi vināsato, asāmatthiyato ca jhānadvayato parihīno. Ciṇṇavasināti āsevitavasinā.

`Pabbateyyā` means one who wanders frequently in the mountains. `Akhettaññū` (not knowing the field) means one who does not know the proper range. One is a fool (`bālo`) because of not fully knowing the purification of the obstacles to concentration. One is inexpert (`abyatto`) due to the absence of skill in bringing about a state of proficiency in jhāna. One is `akhettaññū` because of not understanding the state of being a basis for the higher jhāna. In every way, one is unskillful (`akusalo`) due to the absence of skill in attainment. Alternatively, one is a fool (`bālo`) because of not cultivating the sign of concentration; inexpert (`abyatto`) because of not developing it; `akhettaññū` because of not practicing it frequently. It should be construed that one is unskillful (`akusalo`) because of not properly resolving upon it. `Ubhato bhaṭṭho` (fallen from both) means fallen from both jhānas. For that person, although making an effort, due to lack of proficiency and not being well-established, has fallen away from the two jhānas: through the destruction [of the first] and through the inability [to attain the second]. `Ciṇṇavasinā` (by one who has practiced mastery) means by one who has cultivated mastery.

Pañcavasīkathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Five Masteries

78. Vasanaṃ vasīti dhātuniddesatāya kiriyāniddesoti adhippāyenāha “vasiyo”ti, yathāruci pavattiyoti attho. Āvajjanāya vasī, āvajjanāvasena vā vasī āvajjanavasī. Jhānaṃ āvajjituṃ yattha yattha padese icchā yatthicchakaṃ. Yadā yadā, yasmiṃ yasmiṃ vā jhānaṅge icchā yadicchakaṃ. Yāva yāva icchā yāvadicchakaṃ, da-kāro padasandhikaro. “Yāvā”ti ca idaṃ bahūnaṃ javanavārānaṃ nirantaraṃ viya tathāpavattanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na ekameva. So hi paricchinnacittakkhaṇoti. Āvajjanāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti vuttanayena yattha katthaci ṭhāne yadā yadā [M 1.0179] yaṃ kiñci jhānaṅgaṃ āvajjentassa yathicchitaṃ kālaṃ āvajjanāya āvajjanappavattiyā dandhāyitattaṃ vitthāyitattaṃ, cirāyitattaṃ vā natthi. Evaṃ āvajjanavasī siddhā nāma hotīti attho. Sesāti vuṭṭhānaadhiṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇāvasiyo.

78. With the intention that this is an indication of action by way of indicating the root—`vasī` meaning 'to desire' or 'to have power'—he said `vasiyo`; the meaning is 'occurrences as one wishes'. Mastery in adverting, or mastery by way of adverting, is `āvajjanavasī` (adverting-mastery). The wish to advert to the jhāna in whatever place is `yatthicchakaṃ`. The wish to advert at whatever time, or to whatever jhāna factor, is `yadicchakaṃ`. The wish to advert for whatever duration is `yāvadicchakaṃ`; the letter `d` is a euphonic consonant. And this `yāvā` is said with reference to the occurrence of many series of impulsions as if uninterrupted, not with reference to just one. For that single cognitive process has a limited number of mind-moments. 'There is no slowness in adverting' means that, in the way stated, for one adverting to any jhāna factor at any place, at any time, for as long as desired, there is no slowness, diffuseness, or delay in the adverting or in the process of adverting. Thus, the meaning is that adverting-mastery is accomplished. `Sesā` (the rest) refers to the masteries of emerging, resolving, and reviewing.

Aṅgasamudāyabhāvato jhānassa jhāne āvajjanavasiṃ nipphādetukāmena paṭipāṭiyā jhānaṅgāni āvajjetabbānīti āha “paṭhamaṃ vitakkaṃ āvajjayato”ti. Yadipi āvajjanamevettha icchitaṃ āvajjanavasiyā adhippetattā, āvajjanāya pana uppannāya javanehi bhavitabbaṃ. Tāni ca kho āvajjanatapparatāya cittābhinīhārassa yathāvajjitajhānaṅgārammaṇāni katipayāneva honti, na paripuṇṇānīti vuttaṃ “vitakkārammaṇāneva cattāri pañca vā javanāni javantī”ti. Cattāri tikkhindriyassa. Pañca nātitikkhindriyassāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nirantaranti visabhāgehi nirantaraṃ. Ayaṃ panāti bhavaṅgadvayantaritā catujavanacittā yathāvuttā āvajjanavasī. Aññesaṃ vā dhammasenāpatiādīnaṃ. Evarūpe kāleti uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya lahutaraṃ āvajjanavasīnibbattanakāle. Sā ca kho ittarā parittakālā, na satthu yamakamahāpāṭihāriye viya [V 1.0168] ciratarappabandhavatī. Tathā hi taṃ sāvakehi asādhāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Adhigamena samaṃ sasampayuttassa jhānassa sammā āpajjanaṃ paṭipajjanaṃ samāpajjanaṃ, jhānasamaṅgitā.

Because jhāna is a collection of factors, one who wishes to accomplish adverting-mastery in jhāna should advert to the jhāna factors in sequence; therefore it is said, 'first adverting to initial application.' Although adverting itself is intended here, being the aim of adverting-mastery, when adverting has arisen, there must be impulsions. And those impulsions, because the mind's application is devoted to adverting, have the adverted jhāna factor as their object and are only a few, not the full amount; thus it is said, 'only four or five impulsions run with initial application as their object.' It should be understood that there are four for one with sharp faculties, and five for one with not-so-sharp faculties. `Nirantaraṃ` (uninterrupted) means uninterrupted by dissimilar cognitive processes. This adverting-mastery as described is with four impulsion-moments, separated by two bhavaṅga moments. Or this may apply to others, such as the General of the Dhamma, and so on. 'At such a time' means at the time of producing the adverting-mastery very quickly, having arisen and exerted oneself. And that mastery of others is brief, of short duration; it is not of very long duration like the Buddha's Twin Miracle. For that miracle is said to be uncommon to the disciples. `Samāpajjanaṃ` is the proper entering and attaining of the jhāna together with its associated factors and together with its realization; this is being endowed with jhāna (`jhānasamaṅgitā`).

Sīghanti ettha samāpajjitukāmatānantaraṃ dvīsu bhavaṅgesu uppannesu bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ samāpajjanaṃ sīghaṃ samāpajjanasamatthatā. Ayañca matthakappattā samāpajjanavasī satthu dhammadesanāyaṃ labbhati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “so kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tassā eva kathāya pariyosāne tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi yenassudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.387). Ito sīghatarā hi samāpajjanavasī nāma natthi. Juṇhāya rattiyā navoropitehi kesehi kapotakandarāyaṃ viharantassa āyasmato sāriputtassa yakkhena mahantampi pabbatakūṭaṃ padāletuṃ samatthe pahāre sīse dinne samāpajjanampettha nidassetabbaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “tadā thero tassa paharaṇasamaye samāpattiṃ appesī”ti (visuddhi. 2.374). Pāḷiyaṃ pana “aññataraṃ samādhiṃ samāpajjitvā nisinno”ti (udā. 34) vuttaṃ. Ime pana therā [M 1.0180] “samāpattito vuṭṭhānasamakālaṃ tena pahāro dinno”ti vadanti.

Here, 'swiftly' (`sīghaṃ`) refers to the ability to swiftly enter absorption, which occurs immediately after the desire to enter arises, after two bhavaṅga moments have arisen, the bhavaṅga has been cut off, and immediately after the adverting has arisen. And this mastery in entering absorption, having reached its pinnacle, is found in the Teacher's discourse. This is what is meant by the statement: 'At the end of that very talk, Aggivessana, I internally steadied my mind on that very same former sign of concentration, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it, by which I dwell, as it were, constantly.' (MN 36). Indeed, there is no mastery in entering absorption swifter than this. For example, when the venerable Sāriputta was dwelling in the Pigeon’s Grotto during a moonlit night with freshly shaven hair, a yakkha struck his head with a blow powerful enough to split even a great mountain peak; the entering of absorption should be shown as an example here. For it will be said: 'At that time, at the moment of the blow, the elder entered into attainment.' (Vism. XII.74). In the Pāḷi Canon, however, it is stated: 'Having entered a certain concentration, he was seated.' (Ud. 4.4). But these elders say: 'The blow was delivered at the very moment of his emerging from the attainment.'

Accharāmattanti aṅguliphoṭamattaṃ khaṇaṃ. Ṭhapetunti setu viya sīghasotāya nadiyā oghaṃ vegena pavattituṃ adatvā yathāvuttakkhaṇaṃ jhānaṃ ṭhapetuṃ samatthatā. Abhibhuyya ṭhapanaṃ, adhiṭṭhānaṃ viyāti vā adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha vasī adhiṭṭhānavasī. Tatheva lahuṃ vuṭṭhātunti accharāmattaṃ vā dasaccharāmattaṃ vā lahuṃ khaṇaṃ jhānasamaṅgī hutvā jhānato vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthatā. Bhavaṅgacittuppattiyeva hettha jhānato vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Ettha ca yathā “ettakameva khaṇaṃ jhānaṃ ṭhapessāmī”ti pubbaparikammavasena adhiṭṭhānasamatthatā adhiṭṭhānavasī, evaṃ “ettakameva khaṇaṃ jhānasamaṅgī hutvā jhānato vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti pubbaparikammavasena vuṭṭhānasamatthatā vuṭṭhānavasī veditabbā, yā samāpatti “vuṭṭhānakusalatā”ti vuccati. Tadubhayadassanatthanti adhiṭṭhānavuṭṭhānavasīdassanatthaṃ.

'A finger-snap's duration' (accharāmattaṃ) means a moment the length of a finger-snap. 'To establish' (ṭhapetuṃ) means the ability to establish the jhāna for the aforementioned duration, like a dam not allowing the current of a swift-flowing river to flow with speed. Or, it is establishing by overpowering, which is determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Mastery in that is mastery of determination (adhiṭṭhānavasī). Similarly, 'to emerge swiftly' (lahuṃ vuṭṭhātuṃ) means the ability to emerge from jhāna after being endowed with jhāna for a short duration, for a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps. Here, the arising of a bhavaṅga-consciousness itself is what is called emerging from jhāna. And here, just as the ability, by the power of preliminary preparation, to determine, 'I will establish the jhāna for just this long,' is mastery of determination (adhiṭṭhānavasī), so too, the ability, by the power of preliminary preparation, to determine, 'Having been endowed with jhāna for just this long, I will emerge from jhāna,' should be known as mastery of emergence (vuṭṭhānavasī), which is called 'skill in emergence from attainment'. 'For the purpose of showing both' means for the purpose of showing mastery of determination and mastery of emergence.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ nimmitapabbate tassa vivare. Kiñcāpi ekaṃyeva taṃ abhiññācittaṃ yena pabbataṃ nimmineyya, abhiññāpādakassa pana jhānassa lahutaraṃ ṭhapanaṃ, vuṭṭhānañca idha nidassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Ettakā iddhimantā ekaṃ upaṭṭhākaṃ garuḷato rakkhituṃ na sakkhiṃsū”ti gārayhā assāma.

'There' (tattha) means in that created mountain, in its hollow.
