Although it is one and the same supernormal consciousness by which one might create the mountain, it should be understood that the swifter establishing of and emerging from the jhāna that is the basis for supernormal power is shown here. 'So many powerful ones were not able to protect one attendant from a garuḍa'; thus we would be blameworthy.

Āvajjanānantarānīti [V 1.0169] āvajjanavasībhāvāya yathākkamaṃ vitakkādīnaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ āvajjanāya parato yāni javanāni pavattāni, tāni tesaṃ paccavekkhaṇāni. Yadaggena āvajjanavasīsiddhi, tadaggena paccavekkhaṇāvasīsiddhi veditabbā.

'Immediately after adverting' (āvajjanānantarāni): For the sake of achieving mastery of adverting, the impulsions that occur subsequent to adverting to the jhāna factors—initial application and so on—in sequence, are the reviewings of them. To the extent that mastery of adverting is accomplished, to that extent mastery of reviewing should be understood to be accomplished.

Dutiyajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Second Jhāna

79. Nīvaraṇappahānassa tappaṭhamatāya āsannanīvaraṇapaccatthikā. Thūlaṃ nāma vipulampi pheggu viya sukhabhañjanīyanti āha “oḷārikattā aṅgadubbalā”ti. Santato manasi karitvāti paṭhamajjhānaṃ viya anoḷārikaṅgattā, santadhammasamaṅgitāya ca “santa”nti manasi katvā. Ye hi dhammā dutiyajjhāne pītisukhādayo, kāmaṃ te paṭhamajjhānepi santi, tehi pana te santatarā ceva paṇītatarā ca bhavantīti. Nikantinti nikāmanaṃ, apekkhanti [M 1.0181] attho. Pariyādāyāti khepetvā. Cattāri pañcāti vā-saddo luttaniddiṭṭho. Dutiyajjhānaṃ etassa atthīti dutiyajjhānikaṃ. Vuttappakārānevāti paṭhamajjhāne vuttappakārāniyeva, parikammādināmakānīti attho.

79. Because the first jhāna is the first step in abandoning the hindrances, it has the hindrances as near adversaries. What is called 'gross', although extensive, is easily broken like pith; therefore, it is said, 'because of coarseness, the factors are weak.' As for 'having attended in mind to serenity': having attended in mind to 'serene' because it does not have coarse factors, and because, like the first jhāna, it is endowed with tranquil qualities. For indeed, whatever qualities such as rapture and happiness are in the second jhāna, they are certainly present in the first jhāna as well; however, compared to those in the first jhāna, these in the second jhāna are more serene and more sublime. As for `nikanti`, it means fondness; the meaning is attachment. As for `pariyādāya`, it means having exhausted. In 'four, five,' the word `vā` (or) is indicated by elision. Because 'the second jhāna exists for this one,' one is called a `dutiyajjhānika` (one of the second jhāna). As for 'of the kind already described,' the meaning is: of the very kind described in the first jhāna, those named 'preliminary work' and so on.

80. Vūpasamāti vūpasamahetu, vūpasamoti cettha pahānaṃ adhippetaṃ, tañca vitakkavicārānaṃ. Atikkamo atthato dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe anuppādoti āha “samatikkamā”tiādi. Katamesaṃ panettha vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo adhippeto, kiṃ paṭhamajjhānikānaṃ, udāhu dutiyajjhānikānanti. Kiñcettha yadi paṭhamajjhānikānaṃ, natthi tesaṃ vūpasamo. Na hi kadāci paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārarahitaṃ atthi. Atha dutiyajjhānikānaṃ, evampi nattheva vūpasamo, sabbena sabbaṃ tesaṃ tattha abhāvatoti? Vuccate – yehi vitakkavicārehi paṭhamajjhānassa oḷārikatā, tesaṃ samatikkamā dutiyassa jhānassa samadhigamo, na sabhāvato anoḷārikānaṃ phassādīnaṃ samatikkamāti ayamattho “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti etena dīpito. Tasmā “kiṃ paṭhamajjhānikānaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo idhādhippeto, udāhu dutiyajjhānikāna”nti edisī codanā anokāsāva. Yasmā diṭṭhādīnavassa taṃtaṃjhānakkhaṇe anuppattidhammatāpādanaṃ vūpasamanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Vitakkādayo eva jhānaṅgabhūtā tathā karīyanti, na taṃsampayuttā phassādayo, tasmā vitakkādīnaṃyeva vūpasamādivacanaṃ ñāyāgataṃ. Yasmā pana vitakkādīnaṃ viya taṃsampayuttadhammānampi etena “etaṃ oḷārika”nti ādīnavadassanaṃ sutte āgataṃ, tasmā avisesena [V 1.0170] vitakkādīnaṃ, taṃsahagatānañca vūpasamādike vattabbe vitakkādīnaṃyeva vūpasamo vuccamāno adhikavacanaṃ aññaṃ atthaṃ bodhetīti katvā kiñci visesaṃ dīpetīti dassetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “oḷārikassa panā”tiādi gahitanti idha “yehi vitakkavicārehī”tiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Pītiyā ca virāgā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tasmā vitakkavicārapītisukhasamatikkamavacanāni oḷārikoḷārikaṅgasamatikkamā dutiyādiadhigamadīpakānīti tesaṃ ekadesabhūtaṃ vitakkavicārasamatikkamavacanaṃ taṃdīpakaṃ vuttaṃ. Visuṃ visuṃ ṭhitepi hi vitakkavicārasamatikkamavacanādike paheyyaṅganiddesatāsāmaññena cittena samūhato gahite vitakkavicāravūpasamavacanassa tadekadesatā daṭṭhabbā. Ayañca attho [M 1.0182] avayavena samudāyopalakkhaṇanayena vutto. Atha vā vitakkavicāravūpasamavacaneneva taṃsamatikkamā dutiyādhigamadīpakena pītivirāgādivacanānaṃ pītiādisamatikkamā tatiyādiadhigamadīpakatā dīpitā hotīti tassa taṃdīpakatā vuttā.

80. As for `vūpasama` (calming): it is because of the cause which is calming, or because of the cause which brings about calming. And here, by `vūpasama` is meant abandoning, and that is of applied and sustained thought. The transcending is, in meaning, their non-arising at the moment of the second jhāna; therefore, he said `samatikkama` (transcending), etc. Here, the calming of which applied and sustained thought is intended? Is it that of the first jhāna, or that of the second jhāna? In this regard, if it is that of the first jhāna, there is no calming of them, for the first jhāna is never without applied and sustained thought. If it is that of the second jhāna, in that case also there is no calming, because of their complete and utter absence there. It is said: The attainment of the second jhāna is through the transcending of that applied and sustained thought by which the first jhāna is coarse, not through the transcending of contact and so on, which are not coarse by nature. This meaning is shown by the phrase 'the calming of applied and sustained thought.' Therefore, such an objection as, 'Is the calming of the applied and sustained thought of the first jhāna intended here, or that of the second jhāna?' has no opportunity to arise. This is because by 'calming' is intended the causing of that which has its fault seen to have the nature of not arising at the moment of that respective jhāna. Only applied thought and so on, which are jhāna factors, are treated in this way, not contact and so on, which are associated with them. Therefore, the statement of 'calming,' etc., of only applied thought and so on is logically arrived at. However, since in the Sutta it is stated that the fault of the states associated with them is also seen, with the words 'by this, this is coarse,' therefore, when the calming, etc., of applied thought and so on and their co-arisen states should be spoken of without distinction, the fact that the calming of only applied thought and so on is mentioned is an additional statement that makes known another meaning. To show that it indicates some distinction, in the commentary, the passage beginning 'But of the coarse...' was taken. Therefore, it should be seen that here the passage beginning 'by which applied and sustained thought...' was stated. This same method applies also to 'with the fading away of rapture,' etc. Therefore, the statements about transcending applied and sustained thought, rapture, and happiness indicate the attainment of the second jhāna and so on through the transcending of the progressively coarser factors. Thus, the statement about transcending applied and sustained thought, being a part of these, is said to be indicative of that. For when the statements about transcending applied and sustained thought, etc., even when they stand separately, are taken collectively by the mind through the commonality of indicating the factors to be abandoned, the statement about the calming of applied and sustained thought should be seen as one part of that. And this meaning is stated by the method of indicating a whole by a part. Alternatively, by the very statement of the calming of applied and sustained thought, which indicates the attainment of the second jhāna through their transcending, the fact that the statements about the fading of rapture, etc., indicate the attainment of the third jhāna and so on through the transcending of rapture, etc., is shown. Thus, its function as an indicator of that is stated.

Niyakajjhattamadhippetaṃ na ajjhattajjhattādi. Tattha kāraṇamāha “vibhaṅge panā”tiādi. Nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viyāti nīlayogato vatthaṃ nīlaṃ viyāti adhippāyo. Yena sampasādanena yogā jhānaṃ sampasādanaṃ. Tasmiṃ dassite “sampasādanaṃ jhāna”nti samānādhikaraṇaniddeseneva taṃyogā jhāne taṃsaddappavatti dassitāti avirodho yutto. Ekodibhāve kathanti ekodimhi dassite ekodibhāvaṃ jhānanti samānādhikaraṇaniddeseneva jhānassa ekodivaḍḍhanatā vuttā hotīti ce? “Ekodibhāva”nti padaṃ uddharitvā ekodissa niddeso na kātabbo siyāti ekodibhāvasaddo eva samādhimhi pavatto sampasādanasaddo viya jhāne pavattatīti yuttaṃ. Imasmiñca atthavikappeti “cetaso sampasādayatī”ti etasmiṃ pakkhe “cetaso”ti ca upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Purimasminti “sampasādanayogato jhānaṃ sampasādana”nti vuttapakkhe. Cetasoti sambandhe sāmivacanaṃ.

One's own internal state is intended, not 'internal of the internal,' and so on. There, he states the reason: 'But in the Vibhaṅga...,' etc. Just as a cloth is blue from connection with the color blue—this is the intention. The jhāna is 'sampasādana' (serene) because of its connection with sampasādana (serene faith). When that is shown, simply by the co-referential expression 'serene jhāna,' it is shown that the term's usage in relation to the jhāna is due to its connection with that faith; thus, the lack of contradiction is proper. How is it in the case of 'ekodibhāva' (unification)? If it is said that when 'ekodi' (one-pointedness) is shown, by the co-referential expression 'unification jhāna,' the jhāna's function of developing one-pointedness is stated, then the word 'ekodibhāva' should not be extracted and a separate description of 'ekodi' given. Rather, it is proper that the very word 'ekodibhāva', which applies to concentration, applies to the jhāna, just like the word 'sampasādana'. And in this alternative meaning, in the case of 'it clarifies the mind' (cetaso sampasādayati), the word 'cetaso' is a genitive in the sense of application (accusative). In the former case, stated as 'the jhāna is sampasādana due to its connection with sampasādana,' the word 'cetaso' is a genitive in the sense of relation.

Seṭṭhopi loke “eko”ti vuccati “yāva pare ekāhaṃ te karomī”tiādīsu. Eko adutiyo “ekākībhi khuddakehi jita”ntiādīsu asahāyatthopi eka-saddo diṭṭhoti āha “eko asahāyo hutvā”ti. Saddhādayopi kāmaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ sādhāraṇato, asādhāraṇato ca paccayā hontiyeva, samādhi pana jhānakkhaṇe sampayuttadhammānaṃ avikkhepalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhakaraṇena sātisayaṃ paccayo hotīti dassento “sampayuttadhamme…pe… adhivacana”nti āha.

Even the best in the world is called 'one' in such phrases as, 'I alone will do it for you before others.' In such phrases as 'conquered by small, solitary ones,' the word 'eka' is also seen in the sense of 'without a companion'; therefore, he said, 'being one, without a companion.' Faith and so on are indeed conditions for their associated states, both in a general and a specific way; concentration, however, at the moment of jhāna, becomes an especially powerful condition for its associated states by performing the function of sovereignty in the characteristic of non-distraction. To show this, he said, '...a designation for the associated states...'

“Sampasādanaṃ[V 1.0171], cetaso ekodibhāva”nti visesanadvayaṃ jhānassa atisayavacanicchāvasena gahitaṃ. Svāyamatisayo yathā imasmiṃ jhāne labbhati, na tathā paṭhamajjhāneti imaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ “nanu cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ārammaṇe āhananapariyāhananavasena, anumajjanaanuyojanavasena ca pavattamānā dhammā satipi nīvaraṇappahānena kilesakālussiyāpagame [M 1.0183] sampayuttānaṃ kañci khobhaṃ karontā viya tehi ca te na sannisinnā hontīti vuttaṃ “vitakkavicārakkhobhena na suppasanna”nti. Khuddikā ūmiyo vīciyo. Mahatiyo taraṅgā. Satipi indriyasamatte, vīriyasamatāya ca teneva khobhena, sampasādābhāvena ca samādhipi na suṭṭhu pākaṭo bahale viya jale maccho. Yathāvuttakkhobho eva palibodho. Evaṃ vuttenāti yassā saddhāya vasena sampasādanaṃ, yassā ca cittekaggatāya vasena ekodibhāvanti ca jhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tāsaṃ eva “saddahanā”tiādinā pavattiākārassa visesavibhāvanāvasena vuttena. Tena vibhaṅgapāṭhena. “Sampasādanayogato, sampasādanato vā sampasādanaṃ, ekodiṃ bhāvetīti ekodibhāvanti jhānaṃ vutta”nti evaṃ pavattā ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā na virujjhati. Yathā pana avirodho, so vutto eva.

‘Serenity, unification of mind’—this pair of special qualities is mentioned out of a desire to express the excellence of the jhāna. To show this distinction—that this excellence is obtained in this jhāna in a way that it is not in the first jhāna—the passage beginning ‘Is it not so…’ was stated. Even with the abandonment of the hindrances and the removal of the defilements' turbidity, the mental states of initial and sustained thought, which proceed by way of striking and striking all around the object, and by way of repeatedly touching and applying, are as if causing some disturbance to their associated states. Because of them, those states are not well settled. Thus it is said, ‘not fully serene due to the disturbance of initial and sustained thought.’ Small waves are ripples (vīciyo); large ones are billows (taraṅgā). Even with the balance of the faculties and the balance of energy, due to that very disturbance and the absence of serenity, concentration is not very clear, like a fish in thick water. The aforementioned disturbance is itself the obstacle. Regarding 'thus it was said': the jhāna is described as 'serenity' by way of confidence, and as 'unification' by way of one-pointedness of mind. This explanation, proceeding in line with that Vibhaṅga passage spoken to clarify the special mode of occurrence of just those two with 'believing' and so on—'The jhāna is described as “serenity” from its connection with serenity or from serenity itself, and as “unification” because it develops what is unified'—does not conflict. And the manner in which there is no contradiction has indeed been stated.

81. Santāti samaṃ nirodhaṃ gatā. Samitāti bhāvanāya samaṃ gamitā nirodhitā. Vūpasantāti tato eva suṭṭhu upasantā. Atthaṅgatāti atthaṃ vināsaṃ gatā. Abbhatthaṅgatāti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vuttaṃ. Appitāti vināsaṃ gamitā. Sositāti pavattisaṅkhātassa santānassa abhāvena sosaṃ sukkhabhāvaṃ itā. Byantikatāti vigatantakatā.

81. ‘Santā’ means they have gone to peace, to cessation. ‘Samitā’ means by means of development, they are brought to peace, made to cease. ‘Vūpasantā’ means because of that very pacification, they are well pacified. ‘Atthaṅgatā’ means they have gone to setting, to destruction. ‘Abbhatthaṅgatā’ is said by augmenting the word with a prefix. ‘Appitā’ means they are brought to destruction. ‘Sositā’ means due to the absence of the continuity called 'occurrence', they have gone to a dried up state, a state of being parched. ‘Byantīkatā’ means they are made to have their end removed.

Ayamatthoti bhāvanāya pahīnattā vitakkavicārānaṃ abhāvo. Codakena vuttamatthaṃ sampaṭicchitvā pariharituṃ “evametaṃ siddhovāyamattho”ti vatvā “na paneta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha etanti “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ. Tadatthadīpakanti tassa vitakkavicārābhāvamattasaṅkhātassa atthassa dīpakaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – dutiyajjhānādiadhigamūpāyadīpakena ajjhattasampasādanatāya, cetaso ekodibhāvatāya ca hetudīpakena, avitakkaavicārabhāvahetudīpakena ca vitakkavicāravūpasamavacaneneva vitakkavicārābhāvo dīpitoti kiṃ puna avitakkaavicāravacanena katenāti? Na, adīpitattā. Na hi vitakkavicāravūpasamavacanena vitakkavicārānaṃ appavatti vuttā hoti. Vitakkavicāresu hi taṇhāppahānaṃ etesaṃ vūpasamanaṃ, ye ca saṅkhāresu taṇhāppahānaṃ karonti, tesu maggesu, pahīnataṇhesu [V 1.0172] ca phalesu saṅkhārapavatti hoti eva[M 1.0184], evamevidhāpi vikkhambhitavitakkavicārataṇhassa dutiyajjhānassa vitakkavicārasampayogo purimena na nivārito siyāti taṃnivāraṇatthaṃ, āvajjitukāmatādiatikkamova tesaṃ vūpasamoti dassanatthañca “avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭhamampīti paṭhamaṃ jhānampi.

This is the meaning: the absence of initial and sustained thought is due to their abandonment through development. Having accepted the meaning stated by the objector in order to resolve it, after saying, ‘Thus, this meaning is established,’ the passage beginning ‘But not this…’ was stated. Therein, 'this' refers to the statement, ‘the stilling of initial and sustained thought.’ 'Illuminator of that meaning' means it illuminates the meaning which is simply the absence of initial and sustained thought. Herein, this is the meaning of the objection: Since the absence of initial and sustained thought is already illuminated by the very statement 'the stilling of initial and sustained thought'—which illuminates the means for attaining the second jhāna and so on, illuminates the cause through inner serenity and unification of mind, and illuminates the cause of the state of being without initial and sustained thought—what, then, is the purpose of again making the statement 'without initial thought, without sustained thought'? The reply is: No, because it was not yet illuminated. For the non-occurrence of initial and sustained thought is not stated by the words 'the stilling of initial and sustained thought.' Indeed, the abandoning of craving for initial and sustained thought is their 'stilling.' And in those paths that bring about the abandoning of craving for formations, and in the fruits where craving is abandoned, the occurrence of formations still exists. Similarly here, for one in the second jhāna who has only suppressed craving for initial and sustained thought, the association with initial and sustained thought might not be prevented by the preceding phrase ('the stilling of...'). Therefore, to prevent that, and to show that their 'stilling' is precisely the overcoming of the desire to advert and so on, it was said, ‘without initial thought, without sustained thought.’ 'Even the first' means even the first jhāna.

“Dutiyaṃ uppannantipi dutiya”nti vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Na tathā imassa vitakkavicārāti yathā paṭhamajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇe nīvaraṇāni pahīyanti, tathā imassa dutiyajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇe vitakkavicārā na pahīyanti asaṃkiliṭṭhasabhāvattā, upacārabhāvanāya ca te pahātuṃ asamatthabhāvato. Yadipi tāya tesu taṇhā pahīyati, na pana savisesaṃ. Savisesañhi tattha taṇhāppahānaṃ appanāya eva hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “appanākkhaṇeyevā”tiādi. Pahānaṅgatāpi atisayappahānavaseneva veditabbā yathā nīvaraṇānaṃ paṭhamajjhānassa. Tasmāti yasmā tivaṅgamevetaṃ jhānaṃ, tasmā. Tanti vibhaṅge vacanaṃ. Rathassa paṇḍukambalaṃ viya sampasādo jhānassa parikkhāro, na jhānaṅganti āha “saparikkhāraṃ jhānaṃ dassetu”nti.

It is indeed proper to say: 'Because it has arisen for a second time, it is called the second.' Just as the hindrances are abandoned at the access moment of the first jhāna, initial and sustained thought are not abandoned in the same way at the access moment of this second jhāna. This is because of their undefiled nature, and because the access-development is incapable of abandoning them. Although craving for them is abandoned by that development, it is not abandoned with distinction. For the abandoning of craving with distinction occurs there only by means of absorption. For that reason it was said, “only at the moment of absorption,” and so on. The status of being an abandoned factor should also be understood by way of a surpassing abandonment, just as for the hindrances in the first jhāna. Regarding 'Therefore': because this jhāna has only three factors, 'therefore' [was said]. That statement is in the Vibhaṅga. Just as a pale blanket is an accessory of a chariot, serenity is an accessory of the jhāna, not a jhāna factor; thus, he said, 'to show the jhāna with its accessories.'

Tatiyajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Third Jhāna

82. Uppilāvitanti kāmañcāyaṃ pariggahesu apariccattapemassa anādīnavadassino taṇhāsahagatāya pītiyā pavattiākāro, idha pana dutiyajjhānapīti adhippetā. Tathāpi sabbaso pītiyaṃ avirattaṃ, sāpi anubandheyyāti vuttaṃ. Uppilāvitaṃ viyāti vā uppilāvitaṃ. Ādīnavaṃ hi tattha pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

82. Regarding 'buoyancy' (uppilāvita): Indeed, this is the mode of occurrence of joy accompanied by craving for a person who has not abandoned affection for possessions and who does not see the danger. Here, however, the joy of the second jhāna is intended. Nevertheless, for one not entirely detached from joy, that craving-accompanied joy might also follow along; thus, it is stated. Alternatively, it is 'buoyancy' because it is like being buoyant (uppilāvitaṃ viya). It should be understood that it is stated thus in order to show the danger therein more clearly.

83. Virajjanaṃ virāgo. Taṃ pana virajjanaṃ nibbindanamukhena hīḷanaṃ vā tappaṭibaddharāgappahānaṃ vāti tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “vuttappakārāya pītiyā jigucchanaṃ vā samatikkamo vā”ti āha. Vuttappakārāyāti “yadeva tattha pītī”tiādinā vuttappakārāya. Sampiṇḍanaṃ samuccayo.

83. Fading away (virajjana) is dispassion (virāga). That fading away, in turn, is either scorning, primarily through disenchantment, or it is the abandonment of the lust connected with it. To show both these aspects, he said: 'disgust for the joy of the aforementioned kind, or the transcending of it.' 'Of the aforementioned kind' means of the kind stated in the passage beginning with 'whatever joy there is...' Compilation (sampiṇḍanaṃ) is accumulation (samuccayo).

Maggoti upāyo. Tadadhigamāyāti tatiyamaggādhigamāya.

'Path' means the means. 'For the attainment of that' means for the attainment of the third path.

84. Upapattitoti [V 1.0173] samavāhitabhāvena patirūpato. Jhānupekkhāpi samavāhitameva antonītaṃ katvā pavattatīti āha “samaṃ passatī”ti. Visadāyāti [M 1.0185] paribyattāya saṃkilesavigamena. Vipulāyāti mahatiyā sātisayaṃ mahaggatabhāvappattiyā. Thāmagatāyāti pītivigamena thirabhāvappattāya.

84. 'Upapattito' means by way of being evenly borne and appropriately. The equanimity of jhāna also proceeds having brought that very evenness within; thus, he said, 'he sees evenly.' 'Visadāya' means by being manifest through the departure of defilements. 'Vipulāya' means by being great, through attaining an exceedingly sublime state. 'Thāmagatāya' means having attained a state of firmness through the departure of joy.

Parisuddhapakati khīṇāsavapakati nikkilesatā. Sattesu kammassakatādassanahetuko samabhāvadassanākāro majjhattākāro brahmavihārupekkhā.

The inherently pure nature is the inherent nature of one whose taints are destroyed, the state of being without defilements. The mode of being neutral towards beings, which is the mode of seeing with evenness caused by seeing that kamma is one's own property, is the equanimity of the divine abidings.

Sahajātadhammānanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Samappavattiyā bhāvanāya vīthipaṭipannāya alīnānuddhatā nirassādatāya paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu byāpārābhāvato sampayuttadhammesu majjhattākārabhūtā bojjhaṅgupekkhā.

The word 'sahajātadhammānaṃ' is the genitive case in the sense of specification. When the development has proceeded evenly on the right path, due to the state of being not sluggish, not agitated, and without savoring, and because of the absence of exertion in encouraging, restraining, and gladdening, that which has become the mode of neutrality towards associated states is the equanimity enlightenment factor.

Upekkhānimittanti ettha līnuddhaccapakkhapātarahitaṃ majjhattaṃ vīriyaṃ upekkhā. Tadeva taṃ ākāraṃ gahetvā pavattetabbassa tādisassa vīriyassa nimittabhāvato upekkhānimittaṃ bhāvanāya samappavattikāle upekkhīyatīti upekkhā, vīriyameva upekkhā vīriyupekkhā.

Here, in the phrase 'the sign of equanimity,' the neutral energy that is devoid of falling into the side of sluggishness or agitation is called equanimity. That very energy is the 'sign of equanimity' because it is the cause for subsequent energy of such a kind that should be made to proceed by taking on that mode. At the time of the even proceeding of development, it is regarded with equanimity (upekkhīyati), thus it is called equanimity (upekkhā). Energy itself is equanimity; hence, energy-equanimity.

“Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ paṭilābhatthāya nīvaraṇe…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ paṭilābhatthāya ākiñcaññāyatanasaññaṃ paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.57) evamāgatā imā aṭṭha samādhivasena uppajjanti. “Sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭilābhatthāya uppādaṃ pavattaṃ nimittaṃ āyūhanaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gatiṃ nibbattiṃ upapattiṃ jātiṃ jaraṃ byādhiṃ maraṇaṃ sokaṃ paridevaṃ upāyāsaṃ. Sotāpattiphalasamāpattatthāya uppādaṃ pavattaṃ…pe… arahattamaggaṃ paṭilābhatthāya uppādaṃ…pe… upāyāsaṃ…pe… arahattaphalasamāpattatthāya suññatāvihārasamāpattatthāya animittavihārasamāpattatthāya uppādaṃ pavattaṃ nimittaṃ āyūhanaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gatiṃ nibbattiṃ upapattiṃ jātiṃ jaraṃ byādhiṃ maraṇaṃ sokaṃ paridevaṃ upāyāsaṃ paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇa”nti evamāgatā imā dasa vipassanāvasena uppajjanti. Ettha ca paṭhamajjhānādīhi vikkhambhitāni nīvaraṇavitakkavicārādīni paṭisaṅkhāya sabhāvato upaparikkhitvā sanniṭṭhānavasena tiṭṭhamānā nīvaraṇādipaṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā diṭṭhādīnavattā tesaṃ gahaṇe uppādane ajjhupekkhantī vipassanāpaññā gahaṇe majjhattabhūtā upekkhā.

'For the sake of attaining the first jhāna, the wisdom that is the well-established reflection upon the hindrances… for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, upon the perception of the base of nothingness, is knowledge in equanimity towards formations.' Thus, these eight that are mentioned arise by way of concentration. 'For the sake of attaining the stream-entry path, the wisdom that is the well-established reflection upon arising, proceeding, the sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, destination, production, rebirth, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and despair… for the sake of attaining the fruition-attainment of stream-entry… for the sake of attaining the fruition-attainment of arahantship… for the sake of attaining the attainment of the dwelling in emptiness… for the sake of attaining the attainment of the signless dwelling… upon arising… despair, is knowledge in equanimity towards formations.' Thus, these ten that are mentioned arise by way of insight. And here, the wisdom that is well-established by reflecting on the hindrances, initial and sustained thought, etc.—which have been suppressed by the first jhāna and so on—having examined them according to their intrinsic nature and standing firm by way of determination; and the insight-wisdom that, because the danger in them has been seen, looks on with equanimity at the grasping and producing of them, and has become neutral in that grasping, is equanimity.

Tattha [M 1.0186][V 1.0174] uppādanti purimakammapaccayā khandhānaṃ idha uppattimāha. Pavattanti tathāuppannassa pavattiṃ. Nimittanti sabbampi tebhūmakasaṅkhāragataṃ nimittabhāvena upaṭṭhānato. Āyūhananti āyatiṃ paṭisandhihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ. Paṭisandhinti āyatiṃ uppattiṃ. Gatinti yāya gatiyā sā paṭisandhi hoti. Nibbattinti khandhānaṃ nibbattanaṃ. Upapattinti “samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.72) ettha “upapannassā”ti vuttavipākappavattiṃ. Jātinti jarādīnaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ bhavapaccayā jātiṃ. Jarābyādhimaraṇādayo pākaṭā eva. Ettha ca uppādādayo pañceva saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇassa visayavasena vuttā, sesā tesaṃ vevacanavasena. “Nibbatti, jātī”ti idañhi dvayaṃ uppādassa ceva paṭisandhiyā ca vevacanaṃ, “gati, upapatti cā”ti idaṃ dvayaṃ pavattassa, jarādayo nimittassāti veditabbaṃ. Appaṇihitavimokkhavasena magguppattihetubhūtā catasso, tathā phalasamāpattiyā catasso, suññatavihāraanimittavihāravasena dveti dasa saṅkhārupekkhā.

Therein, by 'arising' he speaks of the arising of the aggregates in this life due to the condition of kamma in a previous life. By 'proceeding,' the continuous proceeding of the aggregates thus arisen. By 'sign,' all conditioned things of the three planes, because of their appearing as a sign. By 'accumulation,' the kamma that is the cause for rebirth-linking in the future. By 'rebirth-linking,' arising in a future life. By 'destination,' the destination in which that rebirth-linking occurs. By 'production,' the production of the aggregates. By 'rebirth,' the proceeding of the resultant spoken of as 'of one who has arisen' in the passage 'of one who has attained or of one who has arisen.' By 'birth,' the birth conditioned by becoming, which is the condition for aging, etc. Aging, sickness, death, and so on are self-evident. And here, only the five beginning with 'arising' are stated by way of being the object of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations; the remaining are stated by way of being their synonyms. Indeed, the two, 'production' and 'birth,' are synonyms for both 'arising' and 'rebirth-linking.' The two, 'destination' and 'rebirth,' are synonyms for 'proceeding.' Aging and so on are synonyms for 'sign'; thus it should be known. There are ten kinds of equanimity towards formations: four that are the cause for the arising of the path by way of the desireless liberation; similarly, four for the attainment of fruition; and two by way of the dwelling in emptiness and the dwelling in the signless.

Yāti vipassanāpaññā. Yadatthīti yaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇattayaṃ upalabbhati. Yaṃ bhūtanti yaṃ paccayanibbattattā bhūtaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Taṃ pajahatīti aniccānupassanādīhi niccasaññādayo pajahanto sammadeva diṭṭhādīnavattā tappaṭibaddhacchandarāgappahānena pajahati, yathā āyatiṃ ādānaṃ na hoti, tathā paṭipattiyā pajahati. Tathābhūto ca tattha upekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Vicinaneti aniccādivasena sammasanepi.

'Proceeds' (yāti) means insight-wisdom. 'What exists' (yadatthi) means the three characteristics, such as impermanence, that are found. 'What has come to be' (yaṃ bhūtaṃ) means the five aggregates which have come to be because they are produced by conditions. 'He abandons that' (taṃ pajahati) means: while abandoning perceptions of permanence and so on by means of the contemplation of impermanence and so on, he abandons rightly, because the danger has been seen; he abandons by abandoning the desire and lust connected with those five aggregates; he abandons by means of a practice whereby there is no grasping in the future. And one who has become thus attains equanimity towards that. 'Investigating' (vicinane) means even in comprehending by way of impermanence and so on.

Sampayuttadhammānaṃ samappavattihetutāya samavāhitabhūtā. Nīvaraṇavitakkavicārādisabbapaccanīkehi vimuttattā sabbapaccanīkaparisuddhā. Tesaṃ vūpasantattā paccanīkavūpasamanepi abyāpārabhūtā abyāpārabhāvena pavattā, abyāpārataṃ vā pattā.

It brings about harmony among associated states by being the cause of their simultaneous occurrence. Because it is free from all opposing states, such as the hindrances, initial thought, and sustained thought, it is completely purified of all opposing states. Because those opposing states are stilled, even in the stilling of opposing states, it is without exertion and proceeds in a state of non-exertion, or has attained non-exertion.

Yadi atthato ekā, kathamayaṃ bhedoti āha “tena tenā”tiādi. Tasmāti yasmā satipi sabhāvato abhede yehi pana paccayavisesehi svāyamimāsaṃ avatthābhedo, tesaṃ ekajjhaṃ appavattito na tāsaṃ abhedo, ekajjhaṃ vā pavatti, tasmā. Tenāha “yattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā”tiādi.

If it is one in essence, how is there this division? He said, “by this and that,” etc. As for ‘Therefore’: since, although there is no difference in intrinsic nature, this division of their states arises from specific conditions, and because those conditions do not occur together, they are not identical—or rather, there is no simultaneous occurrence—therefore. For this reason, he said, “where there is six-factored equanimity,” etc.

Ekībhāvoti [M 1.0187] ekatā. Satipi majjhattābhāvasāmaññe visayabhedena panassā bhedo. Yamatthaṃ [V 1.0175] sandhāya “kiccavasena dvidhā bhinnā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ vitthārato dassento “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Ayaṃ vipassanupekkhā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ, taṃ pajahati, upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.71; a. ni. 7.55). Tattha yadatthi yaṃ bhūtanti khandhapañcakaṃ, taṃ muñcitukamyatāñāṇena pajahati. Diṭṭhasovattikattayassa sabbalakkhaṇavicinane viya diṭṭhalakkhaṇattayassa bhūtassa saṅkhāralakkhaṇavicinane upekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Saṅkhārānaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇassa sudiṭṭhattā tesaṃ vicinane majjhattabhūtāya vipassanupekkhāya siddhāya tathā diṭṭhādīnavānaṃ tesaṃ gahaṇepi ajjhupekkhanā siddhāva hoti, sabbaso visaṅkhāraninnattā ajjhāsayassa.

‘Oneness’ (ekībhāva) means unity. Although there is a commonality in being of a neutral nature, there is a distinction in it due to the difference in the object. To elaborate on the meaning for which it was said, “divided into two by way of function,” he stated, “just as,” and so forth. This is the equanimity of insight (vipassanūpekkhā). It is with reference to this that it is said in the Pāli: “Whatever exists, whatever has come to be, one abandons it and attains equanimity.” Here, “whatever exists, whatever has come to be” refers to the five aggregates; one abandons them with the knowledge of the desire for release. Just as in the investigation of the characteristics of a snake with three coils that has been seen, so too in the investigation of the characteristics of formations—of that which has come to be and has the three characteristics that have been seen—one attains equanimity. Because the characteristics of formations, such as impermanence, have been well seen, when the equanimity of insight, which is neutral, is established in the investigation of them, then even in grasping those formations whose danger has been seen, indifference is indeed established, because the disposition is entirely inclined towards the unconditioned.

Anābhogarasāti paṇītasukhepi tasmiṃ avanatipaṭipakkhakiccāti attho. Abyāpārapaccupaṭṭhānāti satipi sukhapāramippattiyaṃ tasmiṃ sukhe abyāvaṭā hutvā paccupatiṭṭhati, sampayuttānaṃ vā tattha abyāpāraṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti attho. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ khobhaṃ, uppilavañca āvahantehi vitakkādīhi abhibhūtattā aparibyattaṃ. Tattha tatramajjhattatāya kiccaṃ. Tadabhāvato idha paribyattaṃ.

Its function is non-inclination, meaning that even in sublime happiness, its role is to oppose inclination. Its manifestation is non-exertion, meaning that even when the peak of happiness is attained, it manifests as being unengaged in that happiness, or it causes the associated states to be without exertion therein. Because of being overwhelmed by initial thought and so on, which bring about agitation and elation for the associated states, the function of neutrality there was not distinct. Due to their absence, here it is distinct.

Niṭṭhitā “upekkhako ca viharatī”ti etassa

The explanation of “and he dwells equanimous” is concluded.

Sabbaso atthavaṇṇanā.

The complete explanation of the meaning.

85. “Saratīti sato”ti padassa kattusādhanatamāha. Sampajānātīti sammadeva pajānāti. Saraṇaṃ cintanaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ lakkhaṇametissāti saraṇalakkhaṇā. Sammussanapaṭipakkho asammussanaṃ, taṃ kiccaṃ etissāti asammussanarasā. Kilesehi ārakkhā hutvā paccupatiṭṭhati, tato vā ārakkhaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā. Asammuyhanaṃ sammadeva pajānanaṃ, sammohapaṭipakkho vā asammoho. Tīraṇaṃ kiccassa pāragamanaṃ. Pavicayo vīmaṃsā.

85. He states the agent-noun derivation of the word ‘sato’ as ‘saratīti sato’ (one remembers, therefore one is mindful). ‘Sampajānāti’ means one knows rightly. Recollection, thought, and presence is its characteristic; thus it is defined by the characteristic of recollection. Non-forgetfulness is the opposite of forgetfulness; that is its function, thus its function is non-forgetfulness. It manifests as protection from defilements, or it causes protection from them to arise; thus its manifestation is protection. Non-confusion is knowing rightly, or non-delusion, which is the opposite of delusion. Discernment (tīraṇa) is bringing a task to completion. Discrimination (pavicayo) is investigation (vīmaṃsā).

Kāmaṃ upacārajjhānādīni upādāya paṭhamadutiyajjhānānipi sukhumāneva, imaṃ pana uparijhānaṃ upādāya “oḷārikattā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā ca oḷārikatā vitakkādithūlaṅgatāya veditabbā. Keci “bahucetasikatāyā”ti ca vadanti[M 1.0188]. Gati sukhā hoti tattha jhānesūti adhippāyo. Abyattaṃ tattha satisampajaññakiccaṃ “idaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ karīyatī”ti vattabbassa abhāvato. Oḷārikaṅgappahānena sukhumattāti ayamattho kāmaṃ dutiyajjhānepi sambhavati, tathāpi yebhuyyena [V 1.0176] avippayogībhāvena vattamānesu pītisukhesu pītisaṅkhātassa oḷārikaṅgassa pahānena sukhumatāya idha sātisayo satisampajaññabyāpāroti vuttaṃ “purisassā”tiādi. Punadeva pītiṃ upagaccheyyāti hānabhāgiyaṃ jhānaṃ siyā dutiyajjhānameva sampajjeyyāti attho. Tenāha “pītisampayuttameva siyā”ti. “Idañca atimadhuraṃ sukha”nti tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ sandhāyāha. Atimadhuratā cassa pahāsodagyasabhāvāya pītiyā abhāveneva veditabbā. Idanti “sato, sampajāno”ti padadvayaṃ.

Indeed, in relation to access concentration and the like, the first and second jhānas are also subtle; however, in relation to this higher jhāna, they are said to be ‘gross.’ And that grossness should be understood as due to having coarse factors such as initial thought. Some also say it is due to ‘having many mental factors.’ The meaning is that progress in those jhānas is easy. The function of mindfulness and clear comprehension there is not distinct, because there is nothing to be said like, ‘This difficult task is being done.’ Although this meaning—that subtlety arises from abandoning gross factors—may also apply to the second jhāna, nevertheless, because joy and happiness mostly occur inseparably, it is said here, in ‘for a man,’ etc., that the activity of mindfulness and clear comprehension is exceptional due to the subtlety gained by abandoning the gross factor called joy. If one were to revert to joy again, the jhāna would be one pertaining to decline, meaning it would become merely the second jhāna. Therefore, he says, ‘it would be associated with joy.’ He says, ‘And this happiness is exceedingly sweet,’ with reference to the happiness of the third jhāna. And its extreme sweetness should be understood precisely by the absence of joy, which has a nature of great elation and buoyancy. By ‘this’ is meant the pair of words ‘mindful’ and ‘clearly comprehending’.

Tasmā etamatthaṃ dassentoti yasmā tassa jhānasamaṅgino yaṃ nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, taṃ so paṭisaṃvedeyya. Yaṃ vā tanti atha vā yaṃ taṃ yathāvuttaṃ nāmakāyasampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ. Taṃsamuṭṭhānena tato samuṭṭhitena atipaṇītena rūpena assa jhānasamaṅgino rūpakāyo yasmā phuṭo. Yassa rūpakāyassa phuṭattā jhānā vuṭṭhitopi jhānasamaṅgī kāyikaṃ sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya. Tasmā etaṃ cetasikakāyikasukhapaṭisaṃvedanasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ dassento “sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti āhā”ti yojanā. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – nāmakāyena cetasikasukhaṃ, kāyikasukhaheturūpasamuṭṭhāpanena kāyikasukhañca jhānasamaṅgī paṭisaṃvedetīti vuccati. Phuṭattāti byāpitattāti attho. Yathā hi udakena phuṭasarīrassa tādise nātipaccanīke vātādiphoṭṭhabbe phuṭe sukhaṃ uppajjati, evametehi phuṭasarīrassāti. Aparo nayo – sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti ettha kathamābhogena vinā sukhapaṭisaṃvedanāti codanāyaṃ “kiñcāpi…pe… evaṃ santepī”ti. Yasmā tassa nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, tasmā sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti yojanā. Idāni sahāpi ābhogena sukhapaṭisaṃvedanaṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ vā ta”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Therefore, to show this meaning: because that person endowed with jhāna would experience the pleasure that is associated with the mental body. Or, alternatively: because the physical body of that person endowed with jhāna is suffused by the extremely refined material form arisen from that pleasure which was previously mentioned as being associated with the mental body. Due to the suffusion of that physical body, even after having emerged from jhāna, the person endowed with jhāna would experience bodily pleasure. Therefore, showing this meaning, which is designated as the experience of mental and bodily pleasure, He said, ‘and he experiences pleasure with the body’—thus is the connection. Herein, this is the brief meaning: it is said that the person endowed with jhāna experiences mental pleasure by way of the mental body, and bodily pleasure through the production of material form that is the cause of bodily pleasure. ‘Due to being suffused’ means due to being pervaded. For just as pleasure arises for one whose body is suffused with water when it is touched by a non-opposing tangible object such as wind, so it is for one whose body is suffused by these. Another method: regarding the phrase ‘and he experiences pleasure with the body,’ in response to the objection, ‘How is there an experience of pleasure without application of mind?’, it is said, ‘Although… and so on… even so…’ Because for him there is pleasure associated with the mental body, therefore the connection is: ‘and he experiences pleasure with the body.’ Now, to show the experience of pleasure even with application of mind, ‘Or whatever that is,’ and so on, was stated.

86. Yanti hetuatthe nipāto, yasmāti attho. Tenāha “yaṃjhānahetū”ti. “Ācikkhantī”tiādīni padāni kittanatthānīti adhippāyenāha “pasaṃsantīti adhippāyo”ti. Kintīti pasaṃsanākārapucchā. Edisesu [M 1.0189] ṭhānesu satiggahaṇeneva sampajaññampi gahitaṃ hotīti idha pāḷiyaṃ satiyā eva gahitattā evaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitāya “satimā” icceva vuttaṃ, “sampajāno”ti heṭṭhā vuttattā vā.

86. The word ‘yaṃ’ is a particle in the sense of cause; the meaning is ‘because.’ Therefore, He said, ‘because of the jhāna.’ With the intention that the words beginning with ‘ācikkhanti’ have the meaning of proclaiming, He said, ‘the intention is “they praise.”’ The word ‘kinti’ is a question about the mode of praise. In such instances, by the grasping of mindfulness alone, clear comprehension is also grasped. Therefore, because here in the Pāḷi only mindfulness is taken up, and because mindfulness is thus established, only ‘mindful’ was said; or, alternatively, because ‘clearly comprehending’ was stated previously.

Jhānakkhaṇe cetasikasukhameva labbhatīti “sukhaṃ nāmakāyena paṭisaṃvedetī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Tatiyanti [V 1.0177] gaṇanānupubbatāti ito paṭṭhāya dutiyatatiyajjhānakathāhi aviseso, viseso ca vuttoti.

Because at the moment of jhāna only mental pleasure is obtained, it was also said, ‘he experiences pleasure with the mental body.’ As for ‘the third,’ this refers to the sequential enumeration. From this point onward, both the non-difference from and the difference to the discussions of the second and third jhānas have been stated.

Catutthajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna

87. Idāni nibbattitavisesaṃ dassento “ayaṃ pana viseso”ti vatvā “yasmā”tiādimāha. Āsevanapaccayena paccayo na hoti, aniṭṭhe ṭhāne padantarasaṅgahitassa āsevanapaccayattābhāvato. Adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya uppajjitabbaṃ sātisayaṃ sukhavirāgabhāvanābhāvato. Tānīti appanāvīthiyaṃ javanāni sandhāyāha.

87. Now, showing the distinction that has been produced, having said, ‘But this is the distinction,’ He began with ‘Because…’ It is not a condition by way of the repetition condition, because in an undesirable instance, there is an absence of the nature of a repetition condition for that which is comprised in another factor. The neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is to be arisen because of the existence of the exceptional development of dispassion towards pleasure. Regarding ‘Those,’ He said this referring to the impulsion moments in the absorption process.

88. “Pubbevā”ti vuttattā kadā pana tesaṃ pahānaṃ hotīti codanāyaṃ āha “catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe”ti. Evaṃ veditabbanti sambandho. Pahānakkamo nāma pahāyakadhammānaṃ uppattipaṭipāṭi. Tena pana vuccamāne “dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ sukhaṃ somanassa”nti vattabbaṃ siyā. Kasmā ito aññathā vacananti āha “indriyavibhaṅge”tiādi. Atha kasmā jhānesveva nirodho vuttoti sambandho.

88. Because ‘previously’ was stated, in response to the objection, ‘But when does their abandonment occur?’, He said, ‘At the access moment of the four jhānas.’ This is how it should be understood; thus is the connection. The order of abandonment is the sequence of the arising of the abandoning states. But when being stated according to that order, it should be said: ‘pain, displeasure, pleasure, and joy.’ ‘Why is the statement otherwise than this?’—in response, He said, ‘In the Analysis of the Faculties,’ and so on. Then, ‘Why is cessation stated only in the jhānas?’—thus is the connection.

Kattha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyanti attano paccayehi uppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ. Kattha ca aparisesaṃ nirujjhatīti nirodhaṭṭhānaṃ pucchati. Tena “katthā”ti pucchāyaṃ, “etthā”ti vissajjanepi hetumhi bhummavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jhānānubhāvanimittaṃ hi anuppajjantaṃ “dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Atisayanirodho suṭṭhu pahānaṃ ujupaṭipakkhena vūpasamo.

‘Where does the pain faculty arise?’ means the pain faculty that has arisen from its own conditions. ‘And where does it cease without remainder?’—thus he asks the place of cessation. Therefore, in the question ‘Where?’ and in the answer ‘Here,’ the locative case should be understood as being in the sense of cause. For, on account of the jhāna’s power as the cause, the non-arising pain faculty is said to ‘cease without remainder.’ Complete cessation is thorough abandonment, a calming by way of the direct opposite.

Nānāvajjaneti yena āvajjanena appanāvīthi, tato bhinnāvajjane, anekāvajjane vā. Appanāvīthiyañhi upacāro ekāvajjano, itaro anekāvajjano anekakkhattuṃ pavattanato. Visamanisajjāya uppannakilamatho visamāsanupatāpo. Pītipharaṇenāti pītiyā pharaṇarasattā, pītisamuṭṭhānānaṃ vā paṇītarūpānaṃ kāyassa byāpanato vuttaṃ. Tenāha “sabbo kāyo sukhokkanto hotī”ti. Vitakkavicārapaccayepīti pi-saddo [M 1.0190] aṭṭhānappayutto, so “pahīnassā”ti ettha ānetvā sambandhitabbo “pahīnassāpi domanassindriyassā”ti. Etaṃ domanassindriyaṃ uppajjatīti sambandho. “Tassa mayhaṃ aticiraṃ vitakkayato vicārayato kāyopi kilamicittampi uhaññī”ti vacanato kāyacittakhedānaṃ vitakkavicārappaccayatā veditabbā[V 1.0178]. “Vitakkavicārabhāve uppajjati domanassindriya”nti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tatthassa siyā uppattīti tattha dutiyajjhānūpacāre assa domanassassa uppatti bhaveyya.

'By various advertings' means: the adverting by which there is an absorption process, and an adverting different from that, or multiple advertings. For in the absorption process, access is of a single adverting, while the other is of multiple advertings because it occurs many times. Fatigue arisen from uneven sitting is distress from an improper seat. 'By the suffusion of rapture' is said because of rapture's nature of pervading, or because of the pervading of the body by refined material forms originated from rapture. Therefore He said, 'The entire body is steeped in pleasure.' In the phrase 'even with thought and examination as a condition,' the particle 'pi' is applied in the wrong place; it should be brought to 'pahīnassa' and connected thus: 'of the displeasure faculty, even though abandoned.' The connection is: 'This displeasure faculty arises.' From the statement, 'For me, when thinking and pondering for too long, the body became tired and the mind was agitated,' the fact that bodily and mental fatigue are conditioned by thought and examination should be understood. It should be brought in and connected as: 'In the presence of thought and examination, the displeasure faculty arises.' 'There its arising might occur' means: there, in the access to the second jhāna, the arising of that displeasure could occur.

Ettha ca yadeke “tatthassa siyā uppattī”ti vadantena jhānalābhīnampi domanussuppatti atthīti dassitaṃ hoti. Tena ca anīvaraṇasabhāvo lobho viya dosopi atthīti dīpeti. Na hi dosena vinā domanassaṃ pavattati. Na cettha paṭṭhānapāḷiyā virodho cintetabbo. Yasmā tattha parihīnaṃ jhānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānaṃ domanassaṃ dassitaṃ, aparihīnajjhānamārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānassa domanassassa asambhavato. Jhānalābhīnaṃ sabbaso domanassaṃ nuppajjatīti ca na sakkā vattuṃ, aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino api tassa uppannattā. Na heva kho so pahīnajjhāno ahosīti vadanti, taṃ ayuttaṃ anīvaraṇasabhāvassa dosassa abhāvato. Yadi siyā, rūpārūpāvacarasattānampi uppajjeyya, na ca uppajjati. Tathā hi “arūpe kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ uddhaccanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇa”ntiādīsu byāpādakukkuccanīvaraṇāni anuddhaṭāni. Na cettha nīvaraṇattā parihāro, kāmacchandādīnampi anīvaraṇānaṃyeva nīvaraṇasadisatāya nīvaraṇapariyāyassa vuttattā. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino api tassa uppannattā”ti, tampi akāraṇaṃ uppajjamānena ca domanassena jhānato parihāyanato. Lahukena pana paccayena parihīnaṃ tādisā appakasireneva paṭipākatikaṃ karontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Tatthassa siyā uppattī”ti idaṃ pana parikappavacanaṃ upacārakkhaṇe domanassassa appahīnabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “na tveva antoappanāya”nti. Yadi pana tadā domanassaṃ uppajjeyya, paṭhamajjhānampissa parihīnamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pahīnampi somanassindriyaṃ pīti viya na dūreti katvā [M 1.0191] “āsannattā”ti vuttaṃ. Nānāvajjanūpacāre pahīnampi pahānaṅgaṃ paṭipakkhena avihatattā antarantarā uppajjeyya vāti imamatthaṃ dassento “appanāppattāyā”tiādimāha. Tādisāya āsevanāya icchitabbattā yathā maggavīthito pubbe dve tayo javanavārā sadisānupassanāva pavattanti, evamidhāpi appanāvārato pubbe dve tayo javanavārā upekkhāsahagatāva pavattantīti vadanti.

Herein, by some who say, 'Therein might be its arising,' it is shown that even for those who have attained jhāna, the arising of displeasure exists. And by that, it is indicated that hatred, having a nature that is not a hindrance, exists, like greed. For displeasure does not occur without hatred. And herein, a contradiction with the Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi should not be considered. Because therein, displeasure is shown as occurring having taken a declined jhāna as its object, due to the impossibility of displeasure arising having taken an undeclined jhāna as its object. And it cannot be said that for those who have attained jhāna, displeasure does not arise at all, because it arose even for Asita, the attainer of the eight attainments. They say, 'Indeed, he was not one whose jhāna had declined.' That is incorrect, due to the absence of hatred that has a non-hindrance nature. If there were such a thing, it would arise even for beings of the form and formless spheres, but it does not arise. For so it is: in texts such as 'In the formless, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire...', the hindrances of ill will and remorse are not mentioned. And herein, there is no refutation by way of it not being a hindrance, because even for sensual desire and so on, which are indeed not hindrances there, the category of 'hindrance' is spoken of due to their similarity to a hindrance. But as for what was said, 'because it arose even for Asita, the attainer of the eight attainments,' that too is not a valid reason, because with the arising of displeasure, he declined from jhāna. However, it should be understood that when their jhāna has declined due to a slight cause, such persons restore it to its natural state with very little difficulty. But this statement, 'Therein might be its arising,' is a speculative statement for the purpose of showing the state of displeasure not being well abandoned at the moment of access. For so it was said: 'But not within absorption.' But if displeasure were to arise then, it should be understood that for him even the first jhāna has declined. It was said 'due to its nearness' because, although abandoned, the faculty of gladness is not far away like rapture. Showing this meaning—'In access with various advertings, an abandoned factor, though abandoned, might arise from time to time because it is not destroyed by its opposite'—he said, 'due to the attainment of absorption,' etc. Because such a practice is desirable, they say: 'Just as before the path process, two or three javana-courses occur as uniform insight, so too here, before the absorption-course, two or three javana-courses occur accompanied only by equanimity.'

Samāhaṭāti samānītā, saṅgahetvā vuttāti attho. Sukhadukkhāni viya anoḷārikattā avibhūtatāya sukhumā. Tato eva anuminitabbasabhāvattā duviññeyyā. Duṭṭhassāti duṭṭhapayogassa, duddammassāti attho. Sakkā hoti esā gāhayituṃ aññāpohananayenāti adhippāyo.

'Samāhaṭā' means brought together, spoken of comprehensively; this is the meaning. Unlike pleasure and pain, it is subtle due to its non-grossness and its unmanifest nature. For that very reason, it is difficult to discern because its nature must be inferred. 'Duṭṭhassa' means of one with corrupt practice, or of one who is difficult to tame; this is the meaning. The intention is that it is possible to grasp this by the method of excluding the others.

Adukkhamasukhāya [V 1.0179] cetovimuttiyāti idameva catutthajjhānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paccayadassanatthanti adhigamassa upāyabhūtapaccayadassanatthaṃ. Tenāha “dukkhappahānādayo hi tassā paccayā”ti. Dukkhappahānādayoti ca sopacārā paṭhamajjhānādayovettha adhippetā.

'The neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind' should be understood as this very fourth jhāna. 'For the purpose of showing the conditions' means for the purpose of showing the conditions that are the means for its attainment. Therefore, he said, 'For the abandoning of pain and so on are its conditions.' And herein, by 'the abandoning of pain and so on,' the first jhāna and so on, together with their access concentrations, are intended.

Pahīnāti vuttā “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā”ti. Etāti sukhādayo vedanā.

They are said to be abandoned by the phrase 'through the utter destruction of the five lower fetters.' 'These' refers to feelings such as pleasure and so on.

Somanassaṃ rāgassa paccayo. Vuttañhi “sukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya rāgānusayo anusetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.465). Domanassaṃ dosassa paccayo. Vuttampi cetaṃ “dukkhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti. Sukhādighātenāti sukhādīnaṃ pahānena. Assa jhānassa.

Gladness is a condition for lust. For it has been said: 'In pleasant feeling, friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust lies latent.' Displeasure is a condition for hatred. And this too has been said: 'In painful feeling, friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent.' 'By the striking down of pleasure and so on' means by the abandoning of pleasure and so on. Of this jhāna.

Na dukkhanti adukkhaṃ, dukkhavidhuraṃ. Yasmā tattha dukkhaṃ natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “dukkhābhāvenā”ti. Asukhanti etthapi eseva nayo. Etenāti dukkhasukhapaṭikkhepavacanena. “Paṭipakkhabhūta”nti idaṃ idha tatiyavedanāya dukkhādīnaṃ samatikkamavasena pattabbattā vuttaṃ, na kusalākusalānaṃ viya ujuvipaccanīkatāya. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītassa majjhattārammaṇassa, iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītaṃ vā majjhattākārena anubhavanalakkhaṇā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā. Tato eva majjhattarasā. Avibhūtapaccupaṭṭhānāti sukhadukkhāni viya na vibhūtākārā[M 1.0192], piṭṭhipāsāṇe migagatamaggo viya tehi anumātabbā avibhūtākāropaṭṭhānā. Sukhanirodho nāma idha catutthajjhānūpacāro, so padaṭṭhānaṃ etissāti sukhanirodhapadaṭṭhānā.

‘Not painful,’ thus ‘neither-painful-nor-pleasant’; it is devoid of pain. Because there is no pain therein, it is therefore said, ‘due to the absence of pain.’ Regarding ‘not pleasant,’ this is the same method. ‘By this’ means by the statement rejecting pain and pleasure. This term ‘being the opposite’ is said here because of the attainability of the third feeling by way of transcending pain and so on, not because of direct opposition like that of wholesome and unwholesome states. It has the characteristic of experiencing a neutral object, which is the opposite of the desirable and undesirable; or, it has the characteristic of experiencing what is the opposite of the desirable and undesirable in a neutral mode. For that very reason, its function is neutrality. ‘Its manifestation is unmanifest’ means that unlike pleasure and pain, its mode is not manifest; like the track of a deer on a stone slab, it is to be inferred from them, manifesting with an unmanifest mode. Herein, ‘the cessation of pleasure’ is the access to the fourth jhāna; that is its proximate cause, thus its proximate cause is the cessation of pleasure.

89. “Upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti purimapade uttarapadalopenetaṃ samāsapadanti āha “upekkhāya janitasatipārisuddhi”nti. Sabbapaccanīkadhammaparisuddhāya paccanīkasamanepi abyāvaṭāya pārisuddhiupekkhāya vattamānāya catutthajjhāne sati sampahaṃsanapaññā viya suparisuddhā, suvisadā ca hotīti āha “yā ca tassā satiyā pārisuddhi, sā upekkhāya katā, na aññenā”ti. Yadi tatramajjhattatā idha “upekkhā”ti adhippetā, kathaṃ satiyeva “parisuddhā”ti vuttāti āha “na kevala”ntiādi.

89. Regarding ‘purity of mindfulness through equanimity,’ he says that this is a compound word with the elision of a latter word in the former term, meaning ‘purity of mindfulness generated by equanimity.’ Because in the fourth jhāna, mindfulness—being purified of all opposing states, being untroubled even in the calming of opposing states, and proceeding with pure equanimity—becomes exceedingly pure and very clear, like wisdom that greatly gladdens, he therefore says: ‘And whatever purity of that mindfulness there is, that is made by equanimity, not by anything else.’ If specific neutrality is intended here by ‘equanimity,’ how is it that mindfulness alone is said to be ‘purified’? To this, he says, ‘Not only…’ and so on.

Evampi [V 1.0180] kasmā ayameva sati “upekkhāsatipārisuddhī”ti vuttāti anuyogaṃ sandhāya “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha heṭṭhā tīsu jhānesu vijjamānāyapi tatramajjhattatāya paccanīkābhibhavato, sahāyapaccayavekallato ca apārisuddhi, tathā taṃsampayuttānaṃ. Tadabhāvato idha pārisuddhīti imamatthaṃ rūpakavasena dassetuṃ “yathā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sūriyappabhābhibhavāti sūriyappabhāya abhibhuyyamānattā. Atikkhatāya candalekhā viya rattipi sommasabhāvā sabhāgāya rattiyameva ca candalekhā samujjalatīti sā tassā sabhāgāti dassento “sommabhāvena ca attano upakārakattena vā sabhāgāya rattiyā”ti āha.

With reference to the question, ‘Even so, why is this very mindfulness called “purity of mindfulness due to equanimity”?,’ the passage beginning ‘Therein, although…’ was stated. Therein, although specific neutrality is present in the lower three jhānas, it is impure due to being overcome by opposing factors and the deficiency of supporting conditions, and so too are the states associated with it. Because of the absence of these, there is purity here. To show this meaning by way of a simile, the passage beginning ‘Just as…’ was stated. ‘Overcome by the sun’s radiance’ means because of being overcome by the sun’s radiance. Just as the crescent of the moon, not being bright, shines brightly only in the night, which is of a gentle and similar nature; thus, showing that it, the night, is of a similar nature to it, the moon’s crescent, he says, ‘…by its gentle nature and by being helpful to it, or, in the night which is of a similar nature…’

“Ekavīthiya”nti idaṃ tattha somanassassa ekaṃsena abhāvato vuttaṃ, na tato purimataresu ekaṃsena bhāvato. Yathā pana vitakkādayo dutiyādijjhānakkhaṇeyeva pahīyanti, na tesaṃ ekavīthiyaṃ purimajavanesu, na evametanti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Catukkajjhāneti catukkanayavasena nibbattitajjhānacatukke.

‘In a single process’ is said because of the complete absence of joy therein, not because of its complete presence in the preceding ones. It is said to show that this is not like how initial thought and so on are abandoned only at the very moment of the second and subsequent jhānas, and not in the preceding javanas of that single process. ‘In the fourfold jhāna’ means in the set of four jhānas produced by way of the fourfold method.

Pañcakajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discussion on the Fivefold Jhāna

90. Tatthāti paṭhamajjhāne. Catukkanayassa dutiyajjhāne viyāti catukkanayasambandhini dutiyajjhāne viya. Taṃ dvidhā bhinditvāti catukkanaye dutiyaṃ [M 1.0193] “avitakkaṃ vicāramattaṃ, avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti ca evaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā pañcakanaye dutiyañceva tatiyañca hoti abhidhammeti (dha. sa. 168) adhippāyo. Suttantesu pana sarūpato pañcakanayo na gahito.

90. ‘Therein’ means in the first jhāna. ‘Like in the second jhāna of the fourfold method’ means like in the second jhāna related to the fourfold method. ‘Having divided it into two’ means: having divided the second jhāna in the fourfold method into two, as ‘without initial thought, with only sustained thought’ and ‘without initial thought and without sustained thought,’ it thus becomes the second and the third jhāna in the fivefold method in the Abhidhamma; this is the meaning. In the Suttas, however, the fivefold method is not adopted in its own form.

Kasmā panettha nayadvayavibhāgo gahitoti? Abhidhamme nayadvayavasena jhānānaṃ desitattā. Kasmā ca tattha tathā tāni desitāni? Puggalajjhāsayato, desanāvilāsato ca. Sannipatitadevaparisāya kira yesaṃ yathādesite paṭhamajjhāne vitakko eva oḷārikato upaṭṭhāsi, itare santato. Tesaṃ ajjhāsayavasena ca caturaṅgikaṃ avitakkaṃ vicāramattaṃ jhānaṃ desitaṃ. Yesaṃ vicāro, yesaṃ pīti, yesaṃ sukhaṃ oḷārikato upaṭṭhāsi, itare santato. Tesaṃ tesaṃ ajjhāsayavasena tatiyādīni jhānāni desitāni. Ayaṃ tāva puggalajjhāsayo.

Why is the division into two methods adopted here? Because in the Abhidhamma, the jhānas are taught by way of two methods. And why are they taught that way there? Due to the dispositions of individuals and the grace of the teaching. It is said that for those in the assembled congregation of devas for whom, in the first jhāna as taught, only initial thought appeared as gross and the other factors as subtle, the four-factored jhāna without initial thought and with only sustained thought was taught according to their disposition. For those for whom sustained thought, or for whom rapture, or for whom happiness appeared as gross and the other factors as subtle, the third and subsequent jhānas were taught according to their respective dispositions. This, for a start, is the disposition of individuals.

Yassā pana dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā bhagavā yasmā desanāvilāsappatto, tasmā ñāṇamahantatāya [V 1.0181] desanāya sukusalo yaṃ yaṃ aṅgaṃ labbhati, tassa tassa vasena yathāruciṃ desanaṃ niyāmento catukkanayavasena, pañcakanayavasena ca. Tattha ca pañcaṅgikaṃ paṭhamaṃ, caturaṅgikaṃ dutiyaṃ, tivaṅgikaṃ tatiyaṃ, duvaṅgikaṃ catutthaṃ, duvaṅgikameva pañcamaṃ jhānaṃ desesīti ayaṃ desanāvilāso. Ettha ca pañcakanaye dutiyajjhānaṃ catukkanaye dutiyajjhānapakkhikaṃ katvā vibhattaṃ “yasmiṃ samaye rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti avitakkaṃ vicāramattaṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (dha. sa. 168). Kasmā? Ekattakāyanānattasaññīsattāvāsaphalatāya dutiyajjhānena samānaphalattā, paṭhamajjhānasamādhito jātattā ca. Paṭhamajjhānameva hi “kāmehi akusalehi ca vivitta”nti tadabhāvā na idha “vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehī”ti sakkā vattuṃ, nāpi “vivekaja”nti. Suttantadesanāsu ca pañcakanaye dutiyatatiyajjhānāni dutiyajjhānameva bhajanti vitakkavūpasamā vicāravūpasamā avitakkattā, avicārattā ca. Evañca katvā suttantadesanāyapi pañcakanayo labbhatevāti siddhaṃ hoti. Nanu suttante cattāriyeva jhānāni vibhattānīti pañcakanayo na labbhatīti? Na, “savitakkasavicāro samādhī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.305) samādhittayāpadesena pañcakanayassa [M 1.0194] labbhamānattā. Catukkanayanissito pana katvā pañcakanayo vibhattoti suttantadesanāyapi pañcakanayo niddhāretabbo. “Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti hi vitakkassa, vicārassa, vitakkavicārānañca “vitakkavicārāna”nti sakkā vattuṃ. Tathā “avitakkaṃ, avicāra”nti ca vinā, saha ca vicārena vitakkappahānena avitakkaṃ, saha, vinā ca vitakkena vicārappahānena avicāranti avitakkaṃ, avicāraṃ, avitakkañca avicārañcāti vā tividhampi sakkā saṅgahetuṃ.

Furthermore, because the Blessed One attained the grace of teaching from having thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma-element, he was, due to the greatness of his knowledge, highly skilled in teaching. Setting forth the teaching as he pleased by way of whichever factor was available, he taught by way of the fourfold method and the fivefold method. And therein he taught the first jhāna with five factors, the second with four, the third with three, the fourth with two, and the fifth jhāna also with just two factors. This is the grace of the teaching. Here, in the fivefold method, the second jhāna is analyzed by treating it as included in the second jhāna of the fourfold method, as in: 'At the time when one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, one enters and abides in the second jhāna, which is without initial thought, with only sustained thought, born of concentration, with rapture and happiness.' Why? Because it has the same result as the second jhāna of the fourfold method, namely, the fruit of the plane of beings with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, and because it is born from the concentration of the first jhāna. For only the first jhāna is described as 'secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states.' Due to the absence of that seclusion, it is not possible to say here, 'secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,' nor 'born of seclusion.' And in the Suttanta teachings, the second and third jhānas of the fivefold method are included in the second jhāna of the fourfold method because of the stilling of initial thought, the stilling of sustained thought, and because they are without initial thought and without sustained thought. And so it is established that the fivefold method is indeed found in the Suttanta teachings as well. Is it not so that since only four jhānas are analyzed in the Suttanta, the fivefold method is not found? No, because the fivefold method is obtainable through the indication of the three concentrations by the passage beginning 'concentration with initial thought and with sustained thought.' However, the fivefold method is analyzed by making it dependent on the fourfold method, and thus the fivefold method should also be extracted from the Suttanta teachings. For in the phrase 'with the stilling of initial and sustained thought,' it is possible to say 'of initial and sustained thought' to refer to the stilling of initial thought, of sustained thought, or of both initial and sustained thought. Similarly, regarding the phrase 'without initial thought, without sustained thought,' it is possible to include all three types of jhāna: either by understanding 'without initial thought' as the abandonment of initial thought with or without sustained thought, and 'without sustained thought' as the abandonment of sustained thought with or without initial thought; or by understanding it as 'without initial thought,' 'without sustained thought,' and 'both without initial thought and without sustained thought.'

Dutiyanti ca vitakkarahite, vitakkavicāradvayarahite ca ñāyāgatā desanā dutiyaṃ adhigantabbattā, vicāramattarahitepi dvayappahānādhigatasamānadhammattā. Evañca katvā pañcakanayaniddese dutiye vūpasantopi vitakko sahāyabhūtavicārāvūpasamena na sammā vūpasantoti vitakkavicāradvayarahite viya vicāravūpasameneva tadupasamaṃ, sesadhammānaṃ samānatañca dassentena “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti tatiyaṃ catukkanaye dutiyena nibbisesaṃ vibhattaṃ. Duvidhassāpi sahāyavirahena, aññathā ca vitakkappahānena avitakkattaṃ, samādhijaṃ pītisukhattañca samānanti samānadhammattāpi dutiyanti niddeso[V 1.0182]. Vicāramattampi hi vitakkavicāradvayarahitaṃ viya “yasmiṃ samaye rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti avitakkaṃ vicāramattaṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (dha. sa. 168) avitakkaṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhanti vibhattaṃ. Paṭhamajjhāne vā sahacārīsu vitakkavicāresu ekaṃ atikkamitvā dutiyampi tatraṭṭhameva dosato disvā ubhayampi sahātikkamantassa pañcakanaye tatiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tatiyaṃ adhigantabbattā. Paṭhamato anantarabhāvena panassa dutiyabhāvo ca uppajjatīti. Kasmā panevaṃ sarūpato pañcakanayo na vibhattoti? Vineyyajjhāsayato. Yathānulomadesanā hi suttantadesanāti.

And the teaching 'the second' is arrived at by way of reason. In the case of that which is devoid of initial thought (the second jhāna of the fivefold method), it is so called because it is to be attained second. And even in the case of that which is devoid only of sustained thought (the third jhāna of the fivefold method), it is so called because of having similar qualities to that attained by the abandoning of the pair (i.e., the second jhāna of the fourfold method). And so, in the exposition of the fivefold method, although initial thought is stilled in the second jhāna, it is not properly stilled because its companion, sustained thought, is not stilled. Thus, to show that its stilling and the similarity of the remaining states are achieved by the stilling of sustained thought alone—just as in the case of that which is devoid of the pair, initial thought and sustained thought—the third jhāna is analyzed as undifferentiated from the second of the fourfold method with the words: 'With the stilling of initial and sustained thought, with internal confidence and unification of mind, without initial thought, without sustained thought, born of concentration, with rapture and happiness, one enters and abides in the third jhāna.' For both kinds of jhāna, the state of being without initial thought (due to the absence of its companion and otherwise by the abandoning of initial thought) and the state of having joy and bliss born of concentration are similar. Therefore, also because of the similarity of qualities, the exposition is as 'the second'. For indeed, that which has only sustained thought is analyzed, just like that which is devoid of the pair, initial thought and sustained thought, as being 'without initial thought' and having 'joy and bliss born of concentration' in the passage: 'At the time when one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, one enters and abides in the second jhāna, which is without initial thought, has only sustained thought, and has joy and bliss born of concentration.' Alternatively, among the co-arisen initial thought and sustained thought in the first jhāna, for one who, having overcome one, and having seen the second, which still remains there, as a fault, overcomes both together, the third jhāna is stated in the fivefold method, because it is to be attained third. Moreover, due to its immediacy after the first, its nature as the second also arises. But why is the fivefold method not analyzed thus in its own form? Because of the disposition of those to be trained. For the Suttanta teaching is a teaching that conforms to the listeners' disposition.

Pathavīkasiṇaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the earth kasiṇa is concluded.

Iti catutthaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the fourth chapter.

5. Sesakasiṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Remaining Kasiṇas

Āpokasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Water Kasiṇa

91. Yathāvitthāritassa [M 1.0195][V 1.0183] atthassa atidesopi vitthāraṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhatīti āha “vitthārakathā hotī”ti. Āpokasiṇanti āpokasiṇajjhānaṃ, āpokasiṇakammaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Sabbaṃ vitthāretabbanti pathavīkasiṇakammaṭṭhāne vuttanayena vitthāretabbaṃ. Ettakampīti “kate vā akate vāti sabbaṃ vitthāretabba”nti ettakampi avatvā. Sāmuddikena loṇudakena bharito jalāsayo loṇī. Nīlādivaṇṇasaṅkarapariharaṇatthaṃ “suddhavatthena gahita”nti vuttaṃ. Aññanti bhūmiṃ sampattaṃ. Tathārūpanti yādisaṃ ākāsajaṃ udakaṃ, tādisaṃ. Tenāha “vippasannaṃ anāvila”nti, yaṃ pana udakanti sambandho. “Na vaṇṇo paccavekkhitabbo”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ pathavīkasiṇakathāyaṃ vuttameva. Lakkhaṇaṃ pana idha paggharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

91. Because the extension of a meaning that has already been explained in detail itself stands in the place of a detailed explanation, he said, 'it becomes a detailed discussion.' 'Āpokasiṇa' refers to the water-kasiṇa jhāna or, alternatively, the water-kasiṇa meditation subject. 'All should be elaborated' means it should be detailed in the manner stated for the earth-kasiṇa meditation subject. Regarding 'even this much': this means without saying even the phrase 'whether it is a prepared or unprepared device, all should be elaborated.' A reservoir filled with saltwater from the sea is a loṇī. 'Taken with a clean cloth' is said for the purpose of avoiding the mixing of colors like blue, etc. 'Other' refers to water that has reached the ground. 'Such' means like the water originating from the sky, that is, of such a kind. Hence he said, 'clear and unclouded'; the connection is to 'what water.' What needs to be said regarding 'The color should not be reviewed,' etc., has already been stated in the discussion of the earth-kasiṇa. Here, however, the characteristic should be understood as the characteristic of flowing.

Vuttanayenevāti pathavīkasiṇabhāvanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva. Taraṅguṭṭhānādi, pheṇamissatādi ca idha kasiṇadoso. Soti yogāvacaro. Tassāti paṭibhāganimittassa.

'In the manner stated' means in the manner stated in the development of the earth-kasiṇa. The arising of waves, etc., and being mixed with foam, etc., are faults of the kasiṇa here. 'He' refers to the meditator. 'Of it' refers to the counterpart sign.

Tejokasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Fire Kasiṇa

92. Siniddhāni sinehavantāni. Sāradārūni na pheggudārūni. Jālāya ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ siniddhasāradāruggahaṇaṃ. Ghaṭikaṃ ghaṭikaṃ katvāti khandhaso karitvā. Ālimpetvāti jāletvā. Ghanajālāyāti aviraḷavasena pavattaaggijālāyaṃ.

92. Oily means resinous. Heartwood means not sapwood. The taking of oily heartwood is for the long endurance of the flame. 'Having made it piece by piece' means having made it in sections. 'Having kindled it' means having set it ablaze. 'In a dense flame' means in a flame of fire that proceeds without gaps.

Patanasadisanti patamānasadisaṃ. Akate gaṇhantassāti vuttanayena yathā kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ paññāyati, evaṃ anabhisaṅkhate kevale tejasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhantassa.

'Like something falling' means similar to what is falling. 'For one who apprehends it without it being made' means: for one who apprehends the sign in mere, unfabricated fire, just as the kasiṇa-disk becomes apparent by the method stated.

Vāyokasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Wind Kasiṇa

93. Vuttañhetanti [V 1.0184] ettha hi-saddo hetuattho, yasmāti attho. Tassa “tasmā”ti iminā sambandho. Ucchagganti ucchukhette yathāṭhitānaṃ aggaṃ. Eritanti [M 1.0196] vātena calitaṃ. Sameritanti sabbaso calitaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā “vāyokasiṇaṃ…pe… upalakkhetī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, tasmā. Samasīsaṭṭhitanti upari pattānaṃ vasena samasīsaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ. Veḷuṃ vā rukkhaṃ vāti etthāpi “samasīsaṃ ṭhitaṃ ghanapattaveḷuṃ vā ghanapattarukkhaṃ vā”ti ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Ekaṅgulādippamāṇesu kesesu rassabhāvato, dīghataresu olambanato, viraḷesu anuppavesato vātappahāro na paññāyatīti caturaṅgulappamāṇaggahaṇaṃ, ghanaggahaṇañca kataṃ. Etasmiṃ ṭhāne paharatīti satiṃ ṭhapetvāti ucchaggādīnaṃ pacalanākāraggahaṇamukhena tesaṃ pahārake vātasaṅghāte satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. Tattha satiṃ ṭhapetvāti tasmiṃ kāyapadesassa saṅghaṭṭanavasena pavatte vāyupiṇḍe saṅghaṭṭanākāraggahaṇamukhena satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. “Usumavaṭṭisadisa”nti etena purimakasiṇassa viya imassāpi nimittassa saṃviggahataṃ dasseti. “Niccala”nti iminā niccalabhāvoyeva uggahanimittato imassa visesoti paṭibhāganimittassāpi usumavaṭṭisadisatāva vibhāvitā hoti.

93. In the phrase 'For it has been said' (vuttañhetaṃ), the particle 'hi' has the meaning of cause, that is, 'because' (yasmā). It is connected with the word 'therefore' (tasmā). 'The tip of a sugarcane' (ucchaggaṃ) means the tip of sugarcanes as they stand in a field. 'Stirred' (eritaṃ) means moved by the wind. 'Thoroughly stirred' (sameritaṃ) means completely moved. 'Therefore' (tasmā): since it was said in the commentary, 'One should observe the wind kasiṇa… etc.', therefore... 'Standing with level tops' (samasīsaṭṭhitaṃ) means standing with level tops by way of the leaves above. In the phrase 'a bamboo or a tree', one should also supply and connect the following: 'a bamboo with dense leaves standing with a level top, or a tree with dense leaves'. In hairs that are about a finger-breadth long, the wind’s impact is not apparent due to their shortness; in longer hairs, due to their hanging down; and in sparse hairs, due to the wind entering in between. Thus, the taking of a four finger-breadth measure and the taking of 'dense' are mentioned. 'Having established mindfulness that "it strikes in this place"' means establishing mindfulness on the striking masses of wind by way of apprehending the manner of movement of the sugarcane tips and so on. 'There, establishing mindfulness' means establishing mindfulness on the mass of wind that arises through contact with a part of the body, by way of apprehending the manner of contact. With the phrase 'like a ball of steam', he shows the corporeal nature of this sign, just as with the previous kasiṇa. With the word 'motionless', it is shown that the very state of being motionless is the distinction of this counterpart sign from the learning sign; thus, the counterpart sign's nature of being like a ball of steam is also made clear.

Nīlakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Blue Kasiṇa

94. Añjanarājivaṭṭādi vaṇṇadhātuyā vā. Tathārūpaṃ mālāgacchanti aviraḷavikasitanīlavaṇṇapupphasañchannaṃ pupphagacchaṃ. Itarenāti akatādhikārena. Girikaṇṇikaggahanena nīlaṃ girikaṇṇikamāha. Karaṇḍapaṭalaṃ samuggapidhānaṃ. Pattehiyevāti nīluppalādīnaṃ kesaravaṇṭāni apanetvā kevalehi pattehiyeva. Pūretabbanti nīlavaṇṇaṃ vatthaṃ gahetvā bhaṇḍikaṃ viya bandhitvā yathā nīlamaṇḍalaṃ hutvā paññāyati, tathā caṅkoṭakaṃ vā karaṇḍapaṭalaṃ vā pūretabbaṃ. Mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ vā assāti assa caṅkoṭakassa, karaṇḍapaṭalassa vā mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ bandhitabbaṃ. Maṇitālavaṇṭaṃ indanīlamaṇimayaṃ tālavaṇṭaṃ.

94. Or in the mineral element of blue color, such as dark kohl, rājivaṭṭa, and so on. 'Such a flower bush' means a flower bush covered with densely blooming blue-colored flowers. As for 'by another', it means by a person who has not made the requisite preparations. By the term 'girikaṇṇikā', he speaks of the blue girikaṇṇikā. 'A karaṇḍapaṭala' means a casket lid. As for 'with petals only', it means, having removed the filaments and stalks of blue water lilies and so on, with petals only. As for 'it should be filled', it means: taking a blue cloth and tying it like a bundle, a flower basket or a casket cover should be filled in such a way that a blue circle becomes apparent. As for 'or at its mouth-rim', it means it should be bound at the mouth-rim of that flower basket or that casket cover. 'A jeweled fan' means a fan made of the sapphire gem.

Pītakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Yellow Kasiṇa

95. Pītakasiṇe mālāgacchanti ikkaṭādimālāgacchaṃ. Haritālaṃ, manosilā vā dhātu. Pattaṅgapupphehīti [V 1.0185] pattaṅganāmikā pītavaṇṇapupphā ekā gacchajāti, tassa pupphehi. Āsanapūjanti cetiyaṅgaṇe kataṃ āsanapūjaṃ[M 1.0197]. Kaṇikārapupphādināti ādi-saddena ākulikiṅkirātapupphādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

95. In the yellow kasiṇa, 'a flower bush' means a flower bush such as the ikkaṭa and others. The mineral element is orpiment or realgar. 'With pattaṅga flowers' means with the flowers of a species of bush named pattaṅga, which has yellow-colored flowers. 'A seat offering' means a seat offering made in the courtyard of a cetiya. By 'with kaṇikāra flowers and so on,' the inclusion of flowers like the ākulī, kiṅkirāta, and others should be understood through the word 'and so on'.

Lohitakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā
