The Exposition of the Red Kasiṇa

96. Lohitamaṇi lohitaṅgamaṇiādi. Lohitadhātu gerukajātihiṅgulikādi.

96. 'A red gem' means a ruby and so on. 'A red mineral element' means red ochre, vermilion, and so on.

Odātakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the White Kasiṇa

97. Odātakasiṇe mālāgacchanti nandiyāvattādimālāgacchaṃ. Dhātu kakkaṭimuttasetikādi.

97. In the white kasiṇa, 'a flower bush' means a flower bush such as the nandiyāvatta and others. 'A mineral element' means crab shell, pearl, limestone, and so on.

Ālokakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Light Kasiṇa

98. Tathā asakkontenāti yathā sūriyālokādivasena obhāsanimittuppādanaṃ vuttaṃ, tassa obhāsamaṇḍalassa na ciraṭṭhititāya tathā nimittuppādanaṃ kātuṃ asakkontena. Ghaṭamukhena niggacchanakaobhāsassa mahantabhāvato “ghaṭamukhaṃ pidahitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Bhittimukhanti bhittiabhimukhaṃ. Uṭṭhitamaṇḍalasadisanti bhittiādīsu uṭṭhitapākatikaālokamaṇḍalasadisaṃ. Ghanavippasannaṃ ālokapuñjasadisanti bhagavato byāmappabhā viya bahalo, vippasanno ca hutvā puñjabhūto āloko atthi ce, taṃsadisoti attho.

98. As for 'by one unable to do so': just as the production of the light-sign by means of sunlight and so on was stated, it means by one who is unable to produce the sign in that way because that circle of light is not long-lasting. Because the light emerging from the mouth of a pot is extensive, it was said, 'having covered the mouth of the pot.' 'Facing the wall' means towards the wall. 'Like a circle that has arisen' means like a natural circle of light that has arisen on a wall and so on. As for 'dense, very clear, and like a mass of light', the meaning is this: if there is light that, like the Blessed One's fathom-wide aura, is thick and very clear, having become a mass, it is like that.

Paricchinnākāsakasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Limited-Space Kasiṇa

99. Chiddasadisameva hotīti yehi bhittipariyantādīhi paricchinnaṃ, taṃ chiddaṃ, taṃsadisaṃ, tenavākārena uggahanimittaṃ upaṭṭhātīti attho. “Vaḍḍhiyamānampi na vaḍḍhatī”ti uggahanimittassa avaḍḍhanīyataṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbampi hi uggahanimittaṃ vaḍḍhiyamānaṃ na vaḍḍhatiyeva. Satipi ca vaḍḍhetukāmatāyaṃ vaḍḍhanā na sambhavati bhāvanāya paridubbalattā. Bhāvanāvasena hi nimittavaḍḍhanā[V 1.0186]. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana tasmiṃ uppanne bhāvanā thirāti katvā “vaḍḍhiyamānaṃ vaḍḍhatī”ti vuttaṃ.

99. 'It is just like a hole': that which is demarcated by wall-edges and so on is a hole; it is like that. By that very manner, the learning sign appears. This is the meaning. The statement, 'Though being developed, it does not grow,' was said to show the non-developable nature of the learning sign. Indeed, any learning sign, though being developed, does not grow at all. And even when there is a desire to develop it, development does not occur because of the extreme weakness of the cultivation. For the development of the sign is by means of cultivation. As for the counterpart sign, however, because the cultivation becomes firm when that sign has arisen, it was said, 'being developed, it grows.'

Kiñcāpi [M 1.0198] pāḷiyaṃ “pathavīkasiṇādīni rūpajhānārammaṇāni aṭṭheva kasiṇāni sarūpato āgatāni, odātakasiṇe pana ālokakasiṇaṃ, ākāsakasiṇe ca paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ antogadhaṃ katvā desanā katā”ti adhippāyenāha “iti kasiṇāni dasabalo, dasa yāni avocā”ti. Pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyāti pubbe viya asādhāraṇaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kasiṇe paṭiniyatameva atthaṃ aggahetvā asādhāraṇato, sādhāraṇato ca tattha tattha pakiṇṇakaṃ visaṭaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā pavattā pakiṇṇakakathāpi vijānitabbā.

Although in the Pāḷi the eight kasiṇas which are objects of the form-sphere jhānas—namely, the earth kasiṇa and so on—are given in their own form, the teaching was given by including the light kasiṇa in the white kasiṇa, and the limited-space kasiṇa in the space kasiṇa. With this intention, he said: 'Thus the Ten-Powered One spoke of the ten kasiṇas.' As for the statement, 'The miscellaneous discourse should also be known,' this means: the miscellaneous discourse which proceeds by not taking only the specific, uncommon meaning fixed in each respective kasiṇa, as was done before, but by taking the scattered and widespread meaning found here and there, both in its uncommon and common aspects, should also be known.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discourse

100. Ādibhāvoti ettha ādi-saddena yassa kassaci pathavīpakkhiyassa vatthuno nimmānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ṭhānanisajjādikappanaṃ vāti etthāpi “ākāse vā udake vā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Parittaappamāṇanayenāti nīlādivaṇṇaṃ anāmasitvā parittaappamāṇanayeneva. Evamādīnīti ādi-saddena sarīrato udakadhārānimmānādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

100. In the phrase `Ādibhāvoti` (beginning, etc.), the word `ādi` (etc.) includes the creation, etc., of any object whatsoever belonging to the earth-group. Also in the phrase `ṭhānanisajjādikappanaṃ vā` (or the arranging of standing, sitting, etc.), it should be connected by bringing in the words 'in the sky or in the water.' As for `parittaappamāṇanayena` (by the method of the limited and the immeasurable), this is without touching upon the colors blue, etc., but only by the method of the limited and the immeasurable. In `evamādīni` (and so on), the word `ādi` (etc.) includes the creation of a stream of water from the body, and so on.

Yadeva so icchati tassa ḍahanasamatthatāti bahūsu kappāsapicusāradāruādīsu ekajjhaṃ rāsibhūtesu ṭhitesu yaṃ yadeva icchati, tassa tasseva ḍahanasamatthatā. Idha ādi-saddena andhakāravidhamanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

As for the statement, 'Whatever one desires, there is the capability to burn that': when many things like cotton, pith, heartwood, etc., are standing in a single heap, whatever one desires, there is the capability of burning just that very thing. Here, the word `ādi` (etc.) includes the dispelling of darkness and so on.

Vāyugatiyā gamanaṃ vāyugatigamanaṃ, atisīghagamanaṃ. Idha ādi-saddena yadicchitadesantaraṃ pāpuṇanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Going by the motion of wind is `vāyugatigamana`; it means very swift going. Here, the word `ādi` (etc.) includes reaching another desired place, and so on.

Suvaṇṇanti adhimuccanā suvaṇṇabhāvādhiṭṭhānaṃ seyyathāpi āyasmā pilindavaccho (pārā. 619-620) tiṇaṇḍupagapāsādādīnaṃ. Vuttanayenāti suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇanayena.

Resolving 'as gold' is the determination of the state of gold, just as the venerable Pilindavaccha did for grass huts, palaces, and so on. 'By the method stated' means by the method of 'good color' and 'bad color'.

Vaṇṇakasiṇesu [V 1.0187] tattha tattha ādi-saddena nīlobhāsanimmānādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Pathavīpabbatādīti ādi-saddena samuddādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

Among the color kasiṇas, here and there the word `ādi` (etc.) should be seen as including the creation of a blue radiance, and so on. In the phrase `pathavīpabbatādi` (earth, mountains, etc.), the word `ādi` (etc.) should be seen as including oceans and so on.

Sabbāneva [M 1.0199] dasapi kasiṇāni. Imaṃ pabhedaṃ labhantīti imaṃ vaḍḍhanādivisesaṃ pāpuṇanti. Ekoti ekacco. Sañjānātīti bhāvanāpaññāya sañjānāti. Ādi-saddena “āpokasiṇa”ntiādipāḷiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

All ten kasiṇas indeed. 'They obtain this distinction' means they reach this distinction of development, and so on. `Eko` (one) means a certain person. `Sañjānāti` (perceives) means one perceives with the wisdom of cultivation. The word `ādi` (etc.) includes the Pāḷi text beginning with 'water kasiṇa'.

Uparigaganatalābhimukhaṃ “pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānātī”ti pāḷipadāni ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tañca kho vaḍḍhanavasena. Tenāha “ekacco hi uddhameva kasiṇaṃ vaḍḍhetī”ti. Heṭṭhābhūmitalābhimukhantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Pubbe vaḍḍhanakāle payojanaṃ anapekkhitvā vaḍḍhentānaṃ vasena vuttattā idāni “tena tena vā kāraṇena evaṃ pasāretī”ti āha, kasiṇaṃ vaḍḍhetīti attho. Yathā kinti āha “ālokamiva dibbacakkhunā rūpadassanakāmo”ti. Uddhañce rūpaṃ daṭṭhukāmo uddhaṃ ālokaṃ pasāreti, adho ce rūpaṃ daṭṭhukāmo adho ālokaṃ pasāreti, samantato ce rūpaṃ daṭṭhukāmo samantato ālokaṃ pasāreti, evamayaṃ kasiṇanti attho.

The Pāḷi words, 'a certain person perceives the earth kasiṇa,' should be brought and connected with the phrase 'facing the surface of the sky above.' And this is by way of development. Therefore, he said, 'For a certain person develops the kasiṇa only upwards.' This same method applies also to the phrases beginning with 'facing the surface of the ground below.' Because it was spoken previously by way of those who develop it at the time of development without regard for the purpose, it is now said, 'For this or that reason, one spreads it thus,' the meaning of which is, 'one develops the kasiṇa.' As to 'How so?' he said, 'Like one who desires to see forms with the divine eye, like light.' If one desires to see a form above, one spreads the light upwards. If one desires to see a form below, one spreads the light below. If one desires to see a form all around, one spreads the light all around. In this way, this person spreads the kasiṇa; this is the meaning.

Ekassāti pathavīkasiṇādīsu ekekassa. Aññabhāvānupagamanatthanti aññakasiṇabhāvānupagamanadīpanatthaṃ, na aññaṃ pathavīādi. Na hi udakena ṭhitaṭṭhāne sasambhārapathavī atthi. Añño kasiṇasambhedoti āpokasiṇādinā saṅkaro. Sabbatthāti sabbesu āpokasiṇādīsu sesakasiṇesu. Ekadese aṭṭhatvā anavasesena pharaṇappamāṇassa aggahaṇato pharaṇaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Teneva hi nesaṃ kasiṇasamaññā. Tathā cāha “tañhī”tiādi. Tattha cetasā pharantoti bhāvanācittena ālambanaṃ karonto. Bhāvanācittañhi kasiṇaṃ parittaṃ vā vipulaṃ vā ekakkhaṇe sakalameva manasi karoti, na ekadesanti.

`Ekassa` (of one) means of each one among the earth kasiṇa and so on. `Aññabhāvānupagamanatthanti` (for the purpose of not arriving at the state of another) means for the purpose of showing the non-arrival at the state of another kasiṇa; the earth kasiṇa, etc., does not become another kasiṇa. Indeed, in a place where water stands, there is no earth with its components. `Añño kasiṇasambhedoti` (mixture with another kasiṇa) means mixture with the water kasiṇa, etc. `Sabbattha` (everywhere) means in all the remaining kasiṇas, such as the water kasiṇa, etc. Because of not standing in one part, and because of not grasping a measure of the pervasion that is without remainder, the pervasion is immeasurable. For that very reason, their designation is 'kasiṇa' (whole, entire). And so he said, 'For that...' and so on. There, `cetasā pharanto` (pervading with the mind) means making it an object with the mind of cultivation. For the mind of cultivation, in a single moment, attends to the entire kasiṇa, whether it is small or vast, and not to just a part.

101. Ānantariyakammasamaṅginoti pañcasu ānantariyakammesu yena kenaci samannāgatā. Niyatamicchādiṭṭhikāti ahetukadiṭṭhi akiriyadiṭṭhi natthikadiṭṭhīti tīsu micchādiṭṭhīsu yāya kāyaci niyatāya micchādiṭṭhiyā samannāgatā. Ubhatobyañjanakapaṇḍakāti ubhatobyañjanakā, paṇḍakā ca. Kāmañcete ahetukapaṭisandhikattā vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatā honti, tathāpi tibbakilesattā kilesāvaraṇena samannāgatā vuttā. Ahetukadvihetukapaṭisandhikāti ahetukapaṭisandhikā[V 1.0188], dvihetukapaṭisandhikā ca. Duhetukapaṭisandhikānampi hi ariyamaggapaṭivedho, jhānapaṭilābho [M 1.0200] ca natthi, tasmā tepi vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatā eva.

101. `Ānantariyakammasamaṅginoti` (those endowed with an act of immediate result) means those endowed with any one of the five acts of immediate result. `Niyatamicchādiṭṭhikāti` (those with a fixed wrong view) means those endowed with any fixed wrong view among the three wrong views, namely, the rootless view, the inefficacy-of-action view, and the nihilistic view. `Ubhatobyañjanakapaṇḍakāti` means both those with the characteristics of both sexes and eunuchs. And although they are endowed with the obstruction of result because of having a rootless rebirth-linking, nevertheless, because of having intense defilements, they are said to be endowed with the obstruction of defilements. `Ahetukadvihetukapaṭisandhikāti` (those with rootless or two-rooted rebirth-linking) means those with rootless rebirth-linking and those with two-rooted rebirth-linking. For even for those with two-rooted rebirth-linking, there is no penetration of the noble path and no attainment of jhāna; therefore, they too are indeed endowed with the obstruction of result.

Apaccanīkapaṭipadāyanti maggassa anulomapaṭipadāyaṃ saccānulomikāyaṃ vipassanāyaṃ. Acchandikāti “kattukamyatāchandarahitā”ti sammohavinodaniyaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi nibbānādhigamatthameva kattukamyatāchandaṃ sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uttarakurukāpi manussā mārādayo viya acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā nibbutichandarahitattā. Duppaññāti bhavaṅgapaññāya parihīnā. “Bhavaṅgapaññāya paripuṇṇāyapi yassa bhavaṅgaṃ lokuttarassa pādakaṃ na hoti, sopi duppaññoyevā”ti sammohavinodaniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmiṃ hi bhavaṅge vattamāne taṃsantatiyaṃ lokuttaraṃ nibbattati, taṃ tassa pādakaṃ nāma hoti.

`Apaccanīkapaṭipadāyanti` (in the practice that is not contrary) means: in the practice that is in conformity with the path, in insight that is in conformity with the truths. `Acchandikāti` (those without desire) means: “those who are devoid of the desire which is the wish to act,” so it is said in the Sammohavinodanī. That too should be understood as stated with reference to the desire to act for the sake of attaining Nibbāna alone. The humans of Uttarakuru also, like Māra and others, have entered the state of those without wholesome desire, because they are devoid of the desire for Nibbāna. `Duppaññāti` (one of little wisdom) means: those who are deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum. “Even if one is fully endowed with the wisdom of the life-continuum, if that person's life-continuum is not a foundation for the supramundane, that person too is indeed one of little wisdom,” so it is said in the Sammohavinodanī. For, when the supramundane arises in the continuity of that life-continuum which is occurring, that life-continuum is called its foundation.

Kusalesu dhammesūti anavajjadhammesu, sukhavipākadhammesu vā. Okkamitunti adhigantuṃ. Kasiṇeyevāti kasiṇakammaṭṭhāneyeva. Etesanti kammāvaraṇasamannāgatādīnaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā ete vipākantarāyādayo evaṃ atthajānikarā, anatthahetubhūtā ca, tasmā. Tiṇṇameva cettha antarāyānaṃ gahaṇaṃ itarassa sappaṭikārattā, kammantarāyapakkhikattā vāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sappurisūpanissayādīhīti ādi-saddena tajjaṃ yonisomanasikārādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Saddhanti kammaphalasaddhaṃ, ratanattayasaddhañca. Chandanti bhāvanānuyoge tibbakattukamyatāsaṅkhātaṃ kusalacchandaṃ. Paññanti pārihāriyapaññaṃ. Vaḍḍhetvāti yathā bhāvanā ijjhati, tathā paribrūhetvā. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyattā, heṭṭhā vuttanayattā ca na vibhattaṃ.

“In wholesome qualities” means: in blameless qualities, or in qualities that have a happy result. “To enter upon” means: to attain. “Only in the kasiṇa” means: only in the kasiṇa meditation subject. “Of these” means: of those endowed with kamma-obstruction and so on. “Therefore” means: because these obstructions to the result and so on are thus destructive of benefit and are a cause of harm, therefore. And here, the inclusion of only three obstructions should be understood as being because the other is remediable, or because it is included within the kamma-obstruction. “By reliance on a good person, etc.”: by the word “etc.” it includes wise attention and so on, which is suitable to that. “Faith” means: faith in kamma and its result, and faith in the Three Jewels. “Desire” means: wholesome desire, termed intense wish-to-do, in the application to development. “Wisdom” means: the wisdom that manages. “Having developed” means: having cultivated in such a way that the development succeeds. Whatever herein is not analyzed in terms of meaning, that is not analyzed because it is easily understood and because of the method stated below.

Sesakasiṇaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the remaining kasiṇas is concluded.

Iti pañcamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the fifth chapter.

6. Asubhakammaṭṭhānaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Foulness Meditation Subject

Uddhumātakādipadatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of Terms Beginning with 'The Bloated'

102. “Aviññāṇakāsubhesū”ti [M 1.0201][V 1.0189] idaṃ uddhumātakādīnaṃ sabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Tasmā bhūtakathanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na saviññāṇakaasubhassa akammaṭṭhānabhāvato. Tathā hi vakkhati “na kevalaṃ matasarīra”ntiādi (visuddhi. 1.122). Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānāti jīvitakkhayato upari maraṇato paraṃ. Samuggatenāti uṭṭhitena. Uddhumātattāti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ dhumātattā sūnattā. Uddhumātameva uddhumātakanti ka-kārena padavaḍḍhanamāha anatthantarato yathā “pītakaṃ lohitaka”nti. Paṭikkūlattāti jigucchanīyattā. Kucchitaṃ uddhumātaṃ uddhumātakanti kucchanatthe vā ayaṃ ka-kāroti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ yathā “pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti (mahāva. 285; pari. 325; dī. ni. 2.149; a. ni. 5.213). Tathārūpassāti “bhastā viya vāyunā”tiādinā yathārūpaṃ vuttaṃ, tathārūpassa.

102. “In the foul objects that are without consciousness”: this is said by way of showing the intrinsic nature of the bloated corpse and so on. Therefore, it should be seen as a mere statement of fact, and not as something stated because a foul object with consciousness is an unsuitable meditation subject. For so it will be said: “not only a dead body,” and so on. “Beyond the end of life” means: after the destruction of life, subsequent to death. “Emerged” means: risen. “Because of being bloated” means: because of being inflated, swollen up. “A bloated thing itself is a bloated corpse”: by the suffix 'ka' it indicates an extension of the word without a difference in meaning, as in 'yellowish' (pītakaṃ), 'reddish' (lohitakaṃ). “Because of its repulsiveness” means: because of its loathsomeness. “A contemptible bloated thing is a bloated corpse”: this is said to show that this suffix 'ka' is alternatively in the sense of contempt, as in “an evil reputation (pāpako kittisaddo) arises”. “Of such a form” means: of such a form as was stated, beginning with “like a bellows with wind.”

Setarattehi paribhinnaṃ vimissitaṃ nīlaṃ vinīlaṃ, purimavaṇṇavipariṇāmabhūtaṃ vā nīlaṃ vinīlaṃ.

The blue, discolored by and mixed with white and red, is 'livid'; or, the blue that has become a change from its former color is 'livid'.

Paribhinnaṭṭhānesu kākakaṅkādīhi. Vissandamānapubbanti vissavantapubbaṃ, tahaṃ tahaṃ paggharantapubbanti attho.

In places destroyed by crows, vultures, and so on. “Oozing with pus” means: having pus flowing out, that is, having pus trickling out here and there.

Apadhāritanti vivaṭaṃ ugghāṭitaṃ. Khittanti chaḍḍitaṃ, soṇasiṅgālādīhi visuṃ katvā khādanena sarīrasaṅghātato luñcitvā tahaṃ tahaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Vividhaṃ khittanti vikkhittaṃ.

“Uncovered” means: opened, laid bare. “Thrown away” means: discarded; having been torn from the bodily frame by dogs, jackals, and so on, by their eating after having separated the parts, and discarded here and there. “Thrown about variously” is 'scattered'.

Purimanayenāti “vividhaṃ khitta”ntiādinā pubbe vuttanayena. Satthena hanitvāti verīhi khaggakaravālādinā [V 1.0190] satthena paharitvā. Vuttanayenāti “aññena hattha”ntiādinā pubbe vuttanayena.

“By the former method” means: by the method stated before, beginning with “thrown about variously.” “Having been struck with a weapon” means: having been struck by enemies with a weapon such as a sword, a dagger, and so on. “By the stated method” means: by the method stated before, beginning with “a hand in another place.”

Abbhantarato nikkhamantehi kimīhi paggharantakimikulaṃ puḷavakanti āha “kimiparipuṇṇassā”ti.

A corpse with a teeming colony of worms oozing out due to the worms emerging from within is called 'worm-infested'; therefore, it is said: “of one full of worms.”

Uddhumātakādīni [M 1.0202] āmakasusānādīsu chaḍḍitāsubhāni. Nissāyāti paṭicca tānipi ārabbha. Nimittānanti uggahapaṭibhāganimittānaṃ. Etāneva uddhumātakādīneva nāmāni.

The bloated corpse and so on are foul objects discarded in a charnel ground for uncremated bodies and the like. “Relying on” means: depending on, having taken them as an object. “Of the signs” means: of the learning sign and the counterpart sign. These very things—the bloated corpse and so on—are the names.

Uddhumātakakammaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meditation Subject of the Bloated Corpse

103. Bhāvetukāmenāti uppādetukāmena. Tenāti ācariyena. Assāti yogino. Asubhanimittatthāyāti asubhanimittassa uggaṇhanatthāya, asubhe vā uggahanimittassa atthāya. Gamanavidhānanti gamanavidhi. Yena vidhinā gantabbaṃ, so vidhi. Uggahanimittassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya pathavīkasiṇe vuttaṃ paṭipajjanavidhiṃ sandhāyāha “appanāvidhānapariyosāna”nti.

103. “By one who wishes to develop” (`Bhāvetukāmena`): means by one who wishes to produce. “By him” (`Tena`): by the teacher. “For him” (`Assa`): for the yogi. “For the sake of the sign of the foul” (`Asubhanimittatthāya`): for the sake of grasping the sign of the foul, or for the sake of the learning sign in the foul. “The procedure for going” (`Gamanavidhānaṃ`): the method of going. The method by which one should go, that is the method. Referring to the method of practice stated in the section on the earth kasiṇa, beginning from the time the learning sign has arisen, he says: “ending with the procedure for absorption” (`appanāvidhānapariyosānaṃ`).

104. Tāvadevāti sutakkhaṇeyeva. Atitthena puṇṇanadīādiṃ pakkhandantena viya anupavisantena viya. Kedārakoṭiyāti kedāramariyādāya. Visabhāgarūpanti khettarakkhikādivisabhāgavatthurūpaṃ. Sarīranti uddhumātakakaḷevaraṃ. Adhunāmatanti aciramataṃ uddhumātakabhāvaṃ appattaṃ. Takkayatīti sambhāveti bhāriyaṃ katvā na maññati.

104. “Just then” (`Tāvadeva`): at the very moment of hearing. Like one rushing into or plunging into a full river, etc., at a place that is not a ford. “By the edge of the field” (`Kedārakoṭiyā`): by the boundary of the rice-paddy. “A dissimilar form” (`Visabhāgarūpaṃ`): an object of a dissimilar nature, such as a female field-guardian or the like. “The body” (`Sarīraṃ`): the bloated corpse. “Recently dead” (`Adhunāmataṃ`): not long dead, not yet having reached the state of being bloated. “He reflects” (`Takkayati`): he esteems it; he does not regard it as a heavy matter.

105. Rūpasaddādīti ettha amanussānaṃ rūpehi, sīhabyagghādīnaṃ saddādīhi, amanussānampi vā rūpasaddādīhi. Tathā sīhabyagghādīnanti yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Aniṭṭhārammaṇābhibhūtassāti bheravādibhāvena aniṭṭhehi ārammaṇehi abhibhūtassa ajjhotthaṭassa. Na paṭisaṇṭhātīti vidāhavasena āsaye na tiṭṭhati, ucchaḍḍetabbaṃ hotīti attho. Aññoti amanussādīnaṃ vasena vā aññathā vā vuttappakārato añño ābādho hoti. Soti saṅghatthero, abhiññātabhikkhu vā. Yassānena ārocitaṃ, so. Katakammāti katatheyyakammā. Akatakammāti theyyakammaṃ kātukāmā. Katakammā pana idhādhippetā. Tasmā teti katakammā corā. Saha oḍḍhenāti sahoḍḍhaṃ, thenetvā gahiyamānabhaṇḍena saddhinti attho. Yajamānoti yaññaṃ yajanto [V 1.0191] yaññasāmiko. “Addhā imāya paṭipattiyā jarāmaraṇato muccissāmī”ti pītisomanassaṃ uppādetvā.

105. “Forms, sounds, etc.” (`Rūpasaddādi`): here, this refers to the forms of non-human beings, the sounds, etc., of lions, tigers, and the like, or the forms, sounds, etc., of non-human beings as well. Similarly, “lions, tigers, and the like” should be connected as is appropriate. “Of one overcome by a disagreeable object” (`Aniṭṭhārammaṇābhibhūtassa`): of one overwhelmed and oppressed by disagreeable objects that are terrifying and so on. “It does not stay down” (`Na paṭisaṇṭhāti`): it does not remain in his stomach due to agitation; the meaning is that it has to be thrown up. “Another” (`Añño`): another affliction arises, either due to non-human beings and so on, or otherwise, different from the kind already described. “He” (`So`): the elder of the Sangha, or a well-known monk. He is the one to whom this was reported by him. “Those who have committed the act” (`Katakammā`): those who have committed theft. “Those who have not committed the act” (`Akatakammā`): those who wish to commit theft. Here, however, those who have committed the act are intended. Therefore, “they” (`te`) are the thieves who have committed the act. “With the stolen goods” (`Saha oḍḍhenāti`): `sahoḍḍhaṃ`, meaning together with the goods that are seized after being stolen. “The one sacrificing” (`Yajamāno`): the master of the sacrifice who is performing the sacrifice. Having generated joy and gladness thus: 'Surely, by this practice I will be freed from aging and death!'

Evaṃ [M 1.0203] gamanavidhānaṃ ekadesena vatvā idāni aṭṭhakathāsu āgatanayena taṃ dassetuṃ “aṭṭhakathāsu vuttena vidhinā”tiādimāha. Tattha uggaṇhantoti uggaṇhanahetu. Ekoti ayaṃ eka-saddo asahāyattho, na aññādiatthoti “adutiyo”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā vaṇṇādito vavatthānaṃ ekaṃsato samuditameva icchitabbaṃ sabbatthakabhāvato, na tathā sandhiāditoti dassanatthaṃ “vaṇṇatopī”tiādinā chasu ṭhānesu sampiṇḍanattho pi-saddo gahito. Puna eko adutiyotiādi gahitanimittassa yogino nivattitvā vasanaṭṭhānagamanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tabbhāgiyaññevāti tappakkhiyaṃyeva asubhanimittamanasikārasahitameva. Āsanaṃ paññapetīti nisajjaṃ kappeti. Yaṃ pana “asubhanimittadisābhimukhe bhūmippadese”ti (visuddhi. 1.113) vakkhati, tampi imamevatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi kevalena disābhimukhabhāvena kiñci ijjhati.

Having thus explained the procedure for going in part, now, to show it according to the method that has come down in the commentaries, he says: “by the method stated in the commentaries,” etc. Therein, “one who is grasping” (`uggaṇhanto`): for the sake of grasping. “Alone” (`eko`): this word `eka` has the meaning 'without a companion,' not the meaning 'another,' etc.; thus it is said “without a second” (`adutiyo`). To show that just as the determination of color, etc., should be desired as definitely consolidated because it is desired in all circumstances, it is not so with the junction, etc., the particle `pi` is taken in six places, such as “from color too” (`vaṇṇato pi`), with a collective meaning. Again, the words “alone, without a second,” etc., are said with reference to the yogi who, having grasped the sign, turns back and goes to his dwelling place. “Only what is conducive to that” (`tabbhāgiyaññeva`): only what is allied to that, that is, accompanied by attention to the sign of the foul. “He prepares a seat” (`āsanaṃ paññapeti`): he arranges a sitting place. And as to what will be said, “on a plot of ground facing the direction of the sign of the foul,” that too is said with reference to this very meaning. For nothing is accomplished by merely facing in that direction.

Samantā nimittupalakkhaṇāti uddhumātakassa samantā pāsāṇādinimittasallakkhaṇā. Asammohatthāti uggahanimitte upaṭṭhite uppajjanakasammohavigamatthā. Ekādasavidhenāti vaṇṇādivasena ekādasavidhena. Upanibandhanatthoti asubhārammaṇe cittaṃ upanetvā nibandhanattho. Vīthisampaṭipādanatthāti kammaṭṭhānavīthiyā sammadeva paṭipādanatthā. Puññakiriyavatthu adhigataṃ hotīti sambandho.

“Discerning the signs all around” (`samantā nimittupalakkhaṇā`): discerning the signs of stones, etc., all around the bloated corpse. “For the sake of non-delusion” (`asammohatthā`): for the purpose of dispelling the delusion that is liable to arise when the learning sign has appeared. “In eleven ways” (`ekādasavidhena`): in eleven ways, by way of color, etc. “For the purpose of binding” (`upanibandhanattho`): for the purpose of leading the mind to the foul object and binding it there. “For the purpose of setting the course aright” (`vīthisampaṭipādanatthā`): for the purpose of setting the course of the meditation subject aright. “A basis for meritorious action has been acquired” (`puññakiriyavatthu adhigataṃ hoti`): this is the connection.

106. Tasmāti yasmā asubhanimittassa uggaṇhanaṃ ariyamaggapadaṭṭhānassa paṭhamajjhānassa adhigamupāyo, yasmā vā “asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhanto eko adutiyo gacchatī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā. Cittasaññattatthāyāti sarīrasabhāvasallakkhaṇena, saṃvegajananena ca attano cittassa saññattiatthaṃ saññāpanatthaṃ. “Cittasaññatatthāyā”ti vā pāṭho, kilesavasena asaṃyatassa cittassa saṃyamanatthaṃ damanatthaṃ, na kammaṭṭhānatthanti attho. Kammaṭṭhānasīsenāti kammaṭṭhānena sīsabhūtena, taṃ uttamaṅgaṃ padhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ katvā. Mūlakammaṭṭhānanti pakatiyā attanā kālena kālaṃ parihariyamānaṃ buddhānussatiādisabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ. “Kammaṭṭhānasīsena gacchāmī”ti taṃ avissajjetvā. Tenāha “taṃ manasikarontenevā”ti. Sūpaṭṭhitabhāvasampādanenāti mūlakammaṭṭhāne suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitabhāvassa sampādanena. Evaṃ [M 1.0204] hi sati asammuṭṭhā nāma hoti. Bahiddhā [V 1.0192] puthuttārammaṇe appavattitvā kammaṭṭhāneyeva pavattamānaṃ mānasaṃ abahigataṃ nāma. Tathābhūtena cānena rūpindriyāni appavattakiccāni katāni hontīti āha “manacchaṭṭhānaṃ…pe… gantabba”nti.

106. “Therefore” (`tasmā`): because grasping the sign of the foul is the means for attaining the first jhāna, which is the proximate cause of the noble path, or because it is said, 'one who grasps the sign of the foul goes alone, without a second,' therefore. “For the sake of persuading the mind” (`cittasaññattatthāya`): for the purpose of persuading one's own mind by discerning the intrinsic nature of the body and by generating spiritual urgency. Or the reading is “for the sake of restraining the mind” (`cittasaññatatthāya`), meaning for the purpose of restraining and taming the mind that is unrestrained by the defilements, not for the sake of the meditation subject. “With the meditation subject as the head” (`kammaṭṭhānasīsena`): with the meditation subject as the head, making that the chief, primary cause. “The root meditation subject” (`mūlakammaṭṭhāna`): a universally applicable meditation subject, such as the recollection of the Buddha, which one naturally maintains from time to time. “I go with the meditation subject as the head”: means without abandoning it. Hence it is said: “by attending to that very thing.” “By accomplishing a state of being well established” (`sūpaṭṭhitabhāvasampādanena`): by accomplishing a state of being well established in the root meditation subject. For when this is so, mindfulness is called 'unmuddled.' The mind, not proceeding externally towards a variety of objects but proceeding only on the meditation subject, is called 'not gone abroad.' And by such a one, the physical sense faculties are made to have non-operation as their function; thus it is said: “one should go... with the mind as the sixth.”

Dvāraṃ sallakkhetabbanti vihāre puratthimādīsu disāsu asukadisāya idaṃ dvāraṃ, tato eva tāya disāya sallakkhitena asukadvārena nikkhantomhīti dvāraṃ upadhāretabbaṃ. Tatoti dvārasallakkhaṇato pacchā. Yena maggena gacchati sayaṃ. Nimittaṭṭhānanti asubhanimittassa gaṇhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Āhāraṃ chaḍḍāpeyyāti vamanaṃ kārāpeyya. Kaṇṭakaṭṭhānanti kaṇṭakavantaṃ ṭhānaṃ.

“The door should be marked” (`dvāraṃ sallakkhetabbaṃ`): in the monastery, in the eastern and other directions, the door should be determined thus: 'In such-and-such a direction is this door; from there, by that direction, by the marked door of such-and-such a name, I have gone out.' “From there” (`tato`): after marking the door. The path by which he himself goes. “The place of the sign” (`nimittaṭṭhānaṃ`): the place for grasping the sign of the foul. “He should make himself discard the food” (`āhāraṃ chaḍḍāpeyya`): he should make himself vomit. “A place of thorns” (`kaṇṭakaṭṭhānaṃ`): a place that has thorns.

107. Disā vavatthapetabbāti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “ekasmiṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Khāyatīti upaṭṭhāti. Kammaniyanti bhāvanāya kammakkhamaṃ. Ubbāḷhassāti bādhitassa. Vidhāvatīti nānārammaṇe visarati. Ukkammāti ujukaṃ anuvātato apakkamma. Matakaḷevaraṃ puthujjanassa yebhuyyena bhayato upaṭṭhātīti āha “accāsanne bhayamuppajjatī”ti. Anupādanti pādasamīpaṃ. Yattha ṭhitassa sukhena oloketuṃ sakkā, taṃ olokentassa phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ.

107. The directions should be determined—to elaborate on this meaning stated in brief, the passage beginning 'in one' was stated. 'It appears' means it presents itself. 'Workable' means suitable for the work of cultivation (bhāvanā). 'Of one oppressed' means of one afflicted. 'It runs about' means it scatters among various objects. 'Having stepped aside' means having stepped away directly from the downwind side. Since a corpse generally presents itself as fearsome to an ordinary person, it is said, 'fear arises when very near.' 'Not far from the feet' means near the foot. A place where one can stand and observe with ease is a comfortable place for one who is observing.

108. Samantāti samantato. Puna samantāti sāmantā samīpe. Kacchakoti kāḷakacchako, “pilakkho”tipi vadanti. Kapītanoti pippalirukkho. Sindīti khuddakakhajjurī. Karamandādayo pākaṭā eva. Sāmāti sāmalatā. Kāḷavallīti kāḷavaṇṇā apattikā ekā latājāti. Pūtilatāti jīvanavalli, yā “galocī”ti vuccati.

108. “All around” (`samantā`) means from all around. Again, “all around” (`samantā`) means in the vicinity, nearby. “Kacchaka” is the black kacchaka; they also call it “pilakkha.” “Kapītana” is the pippali tree. “Sindī” is the small date palm. Karamanda and so on are well known. “Sāmā” is the sāmā creeper. “Kāḷavallī” is a species of leafless, black-colored creeper. “Pūtilatā” is the jīvanavalli, which is called “galocī.”

109. Taṃ nimittakaraṇādi idheva yathāvutte pāsāṇādinimittakaraṇe eva antogadhaṃ pariyāpannaṃ. Sanimittaṃ karotīti saha nimittaṃ karoti, asubhaṃ pāsāṇādinimittena saha karoti vavatthapeti. Atha vā asubhanimittaṃ, pāsāṇādinimittañca saha ekajjhaṃ karonto vavatthapento “sanimittaṃ karotī”ti vutto. Samānakālatādīpakena hi saha-saddena ayaṃ samāso yathā “sacakkaṃ dehī”ti. Tayidaṃ nimittakaraṇaṃ aparāparaṃ sallakkhaṇena [M 1.0205] hoti, na ekavāramevāti āha “punappunaṃ vavatthapento hi sanimittaṃ karotī”ti. Dveti pāsāṇāsubhanimittāni. Samāsetvā saṅgahetvā ekajjhaṃ katvā. Sārammaṇanti asubhārammaṇena saddhiṃ pāsāṇādiṃ samānārammaṇaṃ karoti, saha vā ārammaṇaṃ karoti, ekārammaṇaṃ viya ubhayaṃ [V 1.0193] ārammaṇaṃ karoti, ekajjhaṃ viya ca aparāparaṃ sallakkhento pāsāṇādiṃ, asubhanimittañcāti dvayaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti attho.

109. That making of a sign and so forth is included and comprised right here in the aforesaid making of a sign with a stone and so forth. 'He makes it with a sign' means he makes it together with a sign; he defines the foulness together with the sign of a stone and so forth. Or else, one who makes and defines the sign of foulness and the sign of a stone and so forth together as one is said to 'make it with a sign.' For this compound with the word saha, which indicates simultaneity, is like 'Give it with the wheel.' This making of a sign occurs through repeated contemplation, not just once—hence it is said: 'For by repeatedly defining, he makes it with a sign.' 'The two' are the signs of the stone and of foulness. Having combined them, collected them, and made them one. 'With an object' means he makes the stone and so forth have the same object as the object of foulness; or he takes them as an object together; he makes both objects as if they were a single object. And by alternately contemplating the stone and so forth and the sign of foulness as if they were one, he makes the pair his object—this is the meaning.

Attaniyoti sako. Vaṇitanti sūnaṃ. Sabhāvena sarasenāti uddhumātakabhāvasaṅkhātena attano lakkhaṇena, paresaṃ jigucchuppādanasaṅkhātena attano kiccena ca, sabhāvo eva vā tathā nipphajjanato “raso”ti vutto.

'One's own' means his own. 'Afflicted' means swollen. 'By its own nature, with its own essence' means: by its own characteristic, designated as the state of bloatedness, and by its own function, designated as the production of disgust in others. Or else, its own nature itself, because it is produced in such a way, is called 'essence.'

110. Chabbidhena nimittaṃ gahetabbanti vaṇṇādinā chappakārena tāva uddhumātakaasubhanimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Keci “kaḷevarassa dīgharassādippamāṇena saddhiṃ sattavidhenā”ti vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi. Liṅgatoti ettha liṅgaṃ nāma vayo liṅgaṃ, na thanamassuādi itthipurisaliṅganti dassentena “itthiliṅgaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ṭhitassa sattassa idaṃ sarīranti sambandho. Uddhumātakasaṇṭhānavaseneva, na pākatikasaṇṭhānavasena. Etena yadi tattha koci anuddhumātakabhāvappatto padeso siyā, so na gahetabboti dasseti. Oḷārikāvayavavasena idaṃ saṇṭhānavavatthānaṃ, na sukhumāvayavavasenāti sīsasaṇṭhānādikaṃ navavidhameva saṇṭhānaṃ gahitaṃ.

110. 'The sign should be grasped in six ways' means: first, the sign of the bloated foulness should be grasped in six ways, by way of color and so forth. Some say, 'in seven ways, including the measurements of the corpse such as long and short,' but that is not found in the commentary. 'By the characteristic': here 'characteristic' means the characteristic of age, not the male or female characteristic such as breasts, beard, and so forth. To show this, the passage beginning 'whether the female characteristic...' was stated. The connection is: 'This is the body of a being that was established.' It is by way of the bloated form only, not by way of the natural form. By this it is shown that if there is any part there that has not reached the state of bloatedness, it should not be grasped. This definition of the form is by way of the gross members, not by way of the subtle members; thus, only the ninefold form, such as the form of the head, was taken.

Imissā disāyāti imissā puratthimāya, dakkhiṇapacchimauttarāya disāya, anudisāya vā ṭhitoti yojanā. Imasmiṃ nāma okāse hatthāti imasmiṃ nāma bhūmippadese imassa kaḷevarassa hatthā ṭhitāti vavatthapetabbanti yojanā.

'In this direction' means: the construction is that it is situated in this eastern, southern, western, or northern direction, or in an intermediate direction. 'The hands in such and such a place' means: the construction is that one should define, 'In such and such a region of the ground, the hands of this corpse are situated.'

Adho pādatalenātiādi nābhiyā heṭṭhā adho, tato uddhaṃ uparīti imassa vavatthānassa vasena vuttaṃ. Hatthaparicchedo heṭṭhā aṅguliaggena upari aṃsakūṭasandhinā tiriyaṃ tacapariyantena gahetabbo. Esa nayo pādaparicchedādīsupi. Yattakaṃ vā pana ṭhānaṃ gaṇhatīti sace sabbaṃ sarīraṃ paricchinditvā gahetuṃ na sakkoti, padeso tassa uddhumāto, so [M 1.0206] yattakaṃ sarīrappadesaṃ uddhumātakavasena ñāṇena pariggaṇhāti, tattakameva yathāpariggahitameva. Idaṃ īdisanti idaṃ hatthādikaṃ īdisaṃ evamākāraṃ. Uddhumātakanti yathāsabhāvato paricchinditabbaṃ. Visabhāge sarīre ārammaṇanti kammaṭṭhānaṃ paṭikkūlākāro na upaṭṭhāti na khāyati, subhato upaṭṭhaheyya. Tenāha “vipphandanasseva paccayo hotī”ti, kilesaparipphandanasseva nimittaṃ hotīti attho. Ugghāṭitāpīti [V 1.0194] uddhumātabhāvappattāpi, sabbaso kuthitasarīrāpīti vā attho. Svāyamattho paṭhamapārājike (pārā. 67 ādayo) vinītavatthūhi dīpetabbo.

'Below by the sole of the foot,' and so forth: this was stated by way of the definition: 'below is beneath the navel, above is from there upwards.' The delimitation of the hand should be taken as: below, by the tips of the fingers; above, by the shoulder joint; and across, by the boundary of the skin. This is the method for the delimitation of the feet and so forth as well. 'Or whatever part one takes' means: if one is unable to grasp the entire body by delimiting it, and a part of it is bloated, then just that much of the bodily region as one comprehends with knowledge by way of its bloatedness should be delimited. 'This is such' means: this hand and so forth is of such a nature, of such a form. 'Bloated' means: it should be delimited according to its actual state. When the body as object is dissimilar, the repulsive aspect of the meditation subject does not present itself, does not appear; it might present itself as beautiful. Therefore he said: 'It becomes a condition for agitation,' meaning, it becomes a cause for the agitation of the defilements only. 'Even if opened up' means: even if it has reached the state of bloatedness, or the meaning is, even if the body is entirely putrid. This meaning should be illustrated with the resolved cases from the first Pārājika (Pārā. 67ff).

111. Āsevitakammaṭṭhānoti asubhakammaṭṭhāne kataparicayo. Sosānikaṅgādīnaṃ vasena parihatadhutaṅgo. Catudhātuvavatthānavasena parimadditamahābhūto. Salakkhaṇato ñāṇena pariggahitasaṅkhāro. Paccayapariggahavasena vavatthāpitanāmarūpo. Salakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya ukkaṃsanena suññatānupassanābalena ugghāṭitasattasañño. Vipassanāya paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhisampāpanena katasamaṇadhammo. Tato eva sabbaso kusalavāsanāya, kusalabhāvanāya ca pūraṇena vāsitavāsano bhāvitabhāvano. Vivaṭṭūpanissayakusalabījena sabījo. Ñāṇassa paripakkabhāvena ñāṇuttaro. Yathāvuttāya paṭipattiyā kilesānaṃ tanukaraṇena appakileso. Olokitolokitaṭṭhāneyevāti uddhumātakādiasubhassa yattha yattha olokitolokitaṭṭhāne eva, tādisassa kālaviseso, asubhassa padesaviseso vā apekkhitabbo natthīti attho. No ce evaṃ upaṭṭhātīti evaṃ yathāvuttapurisavisesassa viya paṭibhāganimittaṃ no ce upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ chabbidhenāti evaṃ vuttākārena vaṇṇādivasena chabbidhena. Punapīti pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena nimittaggahaṇavidhiṃ sampiṇḍeti, na pañcavidhataṃ. Chabbidhena hi pubbe nimittaggahaṇaṃ vihitaṃ.

111. ‘One whose meditation subject is cultivated’ means: one who is familiar with the meditation subject of foulness. One who has undertaken the ascetic practices, such as the charnel-ground dweller’s practice. One who has thoroughly handled the great elements by way of defining the four elements. One who has comprehended formations with knowledge by way of their specific characteristics. One who has defined name-and-form by way of comprehending their conditions. One who, by intensifying insight that has specific characteristics as its object, has removed the perception of a being with the power of the contemplation of emptiness. One who has fulfilled the ascetic’s duties by accomplishing the purification by knowledge and vision of the way of practice through insight. Hence, one whose tendencies are perfumed and whose being is developed by the complete fulfillment of wholesome perfuming and wholesome development. One with the seed, through the wholesome seed that is a supporting condition for the turning away from the round of existence. One who is superior in knowledge through the maturity of his knowledge. One of few defilements through the attenuation of the defilements by the aforesaid practice. ‘Just in the place looked at’ means: for such a one, there is no need to look for a special time or a special region of the foul object, such as the bloated one, in any place whatsoever that is looked at. This is the meaning. ‘If it does not present itself thus’ means: if the counterpart sign does not present itself as it does for the aforementioned special person. ‘Thus in six ways’ means: in the manner stated, by way of color and so forth, in six ways. ‘Again’: the word pi is for the purpose of summarizing. By it, he summarizes the method of grasping the sign, not a fivefoldness. For the grasping of the sign was previously prescribed in six ways.

112. Asītisatasandhitoti sabbepi sandhayo tadāpi atthevāti dassanatthaṃ vatvā uddhumātabhāvena yebhuyyena na paññāyanti. Ye pana paññāyanti, te vavatthapetabbāti dassetuṃ “uddhumātake panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tayo dakkhiṇahatthasandhīti aṃsakapparamaṇibandhānaṃ vasena [M 1.0207] tayo dakkhiṇahatthasandhayo. Tathā vāmahatthasandhayo. Kaṭijaṇṇugopphakānaṃ vasena tayo dakkhiṇapādasandhayo. Tathā vāmapādasandhayo. Eko kaṭisandhīti kaṭiyā saddhiṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakasandhiṃ sandhāya vadati. Hatthantaranti dakkhiṇahatthadakkhiṇapassānaṃ, vāmahatthavāmapassānañca antaraṃ vivaraṃ. Pādantaranti ubhinnaṃ pādānaṃ vemajjhaṃ. Udarantaranti nābhiṭṭhānasaññitaṃ kucchivemajjhaṃ, udarassa vā abbhantaraṃ. Kaṇṇantaranti kaṇṇachiddaṃ. Iti-saddo ādiattho, tena nāsacchiddādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Akkhīnaṃ, mukhassa ca vasenāpi vivaraṃ labbhatevāti dassetuṃ “akkhīnampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samantatoti evaṃ sandhiādito uddhumātakaṃ vavatthapentassa ce nimittaṃ upatiṭṭhati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce, samantato vavatthapetabbanti vavatthāpanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “sakalasarīre”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ñāṇaṃ cāretvāti sabbatthakameva sarīraṃ [V 1.0195] āvajjetvā tattha paṭikkūlākārasahitaṃ uddhumātakabhāvaṃ ārabbha nirantaraṃ bhāvanāñāṇaṃ pavattetvā. Yaṃ ṭhānanti evaṃ pana ñāṇaṃ cārentassa tasmiṃ sarīre yo padeso vibhūto hutvā uddhumātakākārena vibhūtabhāvena upaṭṭhāti. Udarapariyosānaṃ uparimasarīraṃ.

112. ‘One hundred and eighty joints’: this was said to show that all the joints are still there even then, but they are mostly not apparent because of the bloatedness. But to show that those that are apparent should be defined, the passage beginning ‘But in the bloated one’ was stated. Herein, ‘three right hand joints’ means the three joints of the right hand by way of the shoulder, elbow, and wrist. Similarly for the left hand joints. ‘Three right foot joints’ means the three joints of the right foot by way of the hip, knee, and ankle. Similarly for the left foot joints. ‘One hip joint’: this refers to the joint of the spine with the hip. ‘The space between the hands’ is the opening between the right hand and the right side, and between the left hand and the left side. ‘The space between the feet’ is the middle of both feet. ‘The space within the belly’ is the middle of the abdomen, identified as the navel region, or the interior of the belly. ‘The space within the ears’ is the ear-hole. The word ‘iti’ has the meaning ‘and so on’; by this, the inclusion of the nostrils, etc., should be seen. To show that an opening is also found by way of the eyes and mouth, the passage beginning ‘of the eyes’ was stated. ‘From all around’: if the sign presents itself to one who is thus defining the bloated one starting from the joints, etc., that is good. If not, one should define it from all around. To show this method of defining, the passage beginning ‘in the entire body’ was stated. Herein, ‘having made knowledge roam’ means having adverted to the entire body everywhere and having continuously set in motion the knowledge of development concerning the state of bloatedness together with its repulsive aspect. ‘Whatever place’: for one who is thus making knowledge roam, whatever region in that body becomes manifest and presents itself with the form of bloatedness, with its manifest nature. The upper body ending at the belly.

Vinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse of Ascertainment

113. Vinicchayakathāti vinicchayasahitā atthavaṇṇanā. Yathāvuttanimittaggāhavasenāti vaṇṇādito, sandhiādito ca vuttappakārauddhumātakanimittaggahaṇavasena. Suṭṭhu nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbanti yathā uggahanimittaṃ upaṭṭhahati, evaṃ sammadeva asubhanimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Idāni tameva nimittassa suṭṭhu gahaṇākāraṃ upadisanto “satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā”tiādimāha. Tattha evaṃ punappunaṃ karontenāti yathā “imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇato muccissāmī”ti sañjātādarena satisampajaññañca suṭṭhu upaṭṭhapetvā uddhumātakaasubhaṃ paṭhamaṃ āvajjitaṃ, evaṃ punappunaṃ tattha āvajjanaṃ karontena. Sādhukaṃ upadhāretabbañceva vavatthapetabbañcāti sakkaccaṃ satiyā sallakkhetabbañceva paññāya nicchetabbañca. Sati hi “dhāraṇā”ti niddiṭṭhā, dhāraṇañcettha sallakkhaṇaṃ. Paññā “pavicayo”ti (dha. sa. 16) niddiṭṭhā, pavicayo cettha nicchayoti. Atha vā upadhāretabbanti satipubbaṅgamāya paññāya upalakkhetabbaṃ[M 1.0208]. Na hi kadāci satirahitā paññā atthi. Vavatthapetabbanti paññāpubbaṅgamāya satiyā nicchinitabbaṃ. Paññāsahitā eva hi sati idhādhippetā, na tabbirahitā. Addhakkhiapaṅgādivasenāpi olokanaṃ atthīti “ummīletvā oloketvā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena paribyattameva olokanaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ punappunaṃ karontassāti vuttappakārena cakkhuṃ ummīletvā olokanaṃ, nimmīletvā āvajjanañca aparāparaṃ anekavāraṃ karontassa. Uggahanimittanti uddhumātake uggaṇhananimittaṃ. Suggahitanti suṭṭhu gahitaṃ. Yathā na vinassati na pamuṭṭhaṃ hoti, evaṃ gahitaṃ. Ekasadisanti samānasadisaṃ. Samānattho hi ayaṃ eka-saddo, yathā “ariyavinayeti vā, sappurisavinayeti vā, esese eke ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge tajjāte taññe vā”ti.

113. The Discourse on Ascertainment (vinicchayakathā) is an explanation of meaning conjoined with ascertainment. By means of grasping the sign as previously stated: by means of grasping the sign of a bloated corpse in the manner described, from color and so forth, and from the joints and so forth. The sign should be well grasped: just as the learning sign appears, so the sign of foulness should be properly grasped. Now, to instruct on that very manner of well grasping the sign, he said, “Having established mindfulness well…” and so on. Therein, by one doing so again and again: just as, with respect born from the thought, “By this practice, I will be freed from aging and death,” having well established mindfulness and clear comprehension, the bloated corpse as a foul object was first adverted to, so by one who repeatedly adverts to it in this way. It should be well noted and determined: it should be diligently observed with mindfulness and ascertained with wisdom. For mindfulness is pointed out as “retention,” and here retention is observation. Wisdom is pointed out as “investigation,” and here investigation is decision. Alternatively, it should be noted means it should be examined with wisdom preceded by mindfulness, for wisdom never exists without mindfulness. It should be determined means it should be decided with mindfulness preceded by wisdom, for here, only mindfulness accompanied by wisdom is intended, not that which is devoid of it. Since there is also looking by means of a half-closed eye, the corner of the eye, and so on, it is said, “having opened the eyes, having looked.” By that, it shows a distinct looking. Of one who does so again and again: of one who, in the manner described, opens the eyes and looks, and closes the eyes and adverts, successively, many times. The learning sign: the sign to be apprehended in the bloated corpse. Well grasped: thoroughly grasped. Grasped in such a way that it does not perish and is not forgotten. Uniform: of the same likeness. For this word ‘eka’ has the meaning of ‘sameness,’ as in: “in the noble discipline or in the discipline of good people, this is the same, it is one, of one meaning, the same, of equal share, of that same nature, or that very same thing.”

Āgamanakāleti vihārato susānaṃ uddissa āgamanakāle. Vuttanayenevāti atidesavasena dīpitampi atthaṃ “ekakenā”tiādinā sarūpato dasseti. Tattha tadeva kammaṭṭhānanti uddhumātakakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Mūlakammaṭṭhānanti eke, tadayuttaṃ. Upaṭṭhitanimittaṃ hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā [V 1.0196] kammaṭṭhānantaramanasikāro rañño rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā videsagamanaṃ viyāti. Āgatenāti attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgatena.

At the time of coming: at the time of coming from the monastery, having aimed for the charnel ground. By the method stated: the meaning that was also explained by way of extension, he shows in its own form by “alone,” and so on. Therein, that very meditation subject: the meditation subject of the bloated corpse. Some say it is the root meditation subject; that is unsuitable. For, having abandoned the meditation subject for which the sign has arisen, to attend to another meditation subject is like a king abandoning his kingdom and going to a foreign country. By one who has come: by one who has come to his own dwelling place.

114. Avelāyanti sañjhāvelādiayuttavelāyaṃ. Bībhacchanti virūpaṃ. Bheravārammaṇanti vetāḷasadisaṃ bhayānakaṃ visayaṃ. Vikkhittacittoti bhīrukapuriso viya pisācādiṃ disvā cittavikkhepaṃ patto. Ummattako viyāti yakkhummattako viya ekacco hoti. Jhānavibbhantakoti jhānato viccutako sīlavibbhantakamantavibbhantakā viya. Santhambhetvāti uppannaparittāsavūpasamanena vigatakampatāya niccalo hutvā. Satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitantiādi santhambhanassa upāyadassanaṃ. Matasarīraṃ uṭṭhahitvā anubandhanakaṃ nāma natthi asati tādise mantappayoge. Sopi uddhumātakādibhāvamappatte avinaṭṭharūpe eva ijjhati, tathā devatādhiggaho, na evarūpeti adhippāyo. Saññajoti bhāvanāparikappasaññāya jāto. Tato eva saññāsambhavo saññāmattasamuṭṭhāno. Tāsaṃ vinodetvāti nimittupaṭṭhānanimittaṃ uppannacittasantāsaṃ vuttappakārena vinodetvā vūpasametvā[M 1.0209]. “Idāni tava parissamo sapphalo jāto”ti hāsaṃ pītiṃ pamodanaṃ uppādetvā. Cittaṃ sañcarāpetabbanti bhāvanācittaṃ pavattetabbaṃ manasikātabbaṃ.

114. At an unsuitable time: at an unsuitable time, such as dusk. Loathsome: deformed. A terrifying object: a frightening object similar to a ghoul. With a distracted mind: like a timid person who, having seen a ghost or the like, has become distracted in mind. Like one who is mad: like one who is mad from being seized by a yakkha, so a certain one becomes. Fallen away from jhāna: fallen from jhāna, like those who have lapsed from virtue or lapsed from mantras. Having become steadfast: having become motionless due to the absence of trembling, by the pacification of arisen terror. The words “Having established mindfulness well,” and so on, are for showing the method for becoming steadfast. There is no such thing as a dead body rising up and pursuing, in the absence of such a use of mantras. And that use of mantras succeeds only in a body whose form is not yet destroyed, which has not yet reached the state of being bloated, and so on; likewise the possession by a deity. It does not succeed in a corpse of this sort—this is the intention. Born of perception: born from the perception of meditative conceptualization. From that very thing, it arises from perception; its origin is mere perception. Having dispelled them: having dispelled and pacified, in the manner described, the terror of mind that has arisen on account of the appearance of the sign. Having aroused gladness, joy, and delight, thinking, “Now your effort has become fruitful.” The mind should be made to proceed: the meditation mind should be made to proceed, should be attended to.

Nimittaggāhanti nimittassa uggaṇhanaṃ, uggahanimittaṃ. Sampādentoti sādhento nipphādento. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ upanibandhatīti bhāvanaṃ yathāvutte nimitte upanento nibandhati. Yogakammaṃ hi yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato “kammaṭṭhāna”nti adhippetaṃ, yogakammassa vā pavattiṭṭhānatāya yathāupaṭṭhitanimittaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ bhāvanācitte upanibandhati. Taṃ panassa upanibandhanaṃ sandhāya cittaṃ sañcarāpetabbaṃ. Evaṃ “visesamadhigacchatī”ti vuttanti dassento “tassa hī”tiādimāha. Tattha tassāti yogino, tassa vā uddhumātakāsubhassa. Mānasaṃ cārentassāti bhāvanācittaṃ aparāparaṃ pavattentassa, uggahanimittaṃ punappunaṃ manasi karontassāti attho.

‘The grasping of the sign’ means the apprehending of the sign, the learning sign. ‘Accomplishing’ means one who accomplishes, one who brings to completion. ‘He binds the meditation subject to it’ means bringing the meditation near to the sign as described, he binds it. For the yogi's work is intended as the “meditation subject” because it is a cause of special kinds of happiness for the yogi; or, because it is the place where the yogi's work occurs, the sign as it has appeared is the meditation subject; that he binds to the meditation-mind. And with reference to that binding of his, it was said, “The mind should be made to proceed.” Thus, showing that it is said, “he attains distinction,” he stated the passage beginning with “For him…” and so on. Therein, ‘of him’ means of the yogi, or of that bloated foul object. ‘Of one directing the mind’ means of one who successively causes the meditation-mind to proceed, that is, of one who again and again attends to the learning sign.

115. “Vīthisampaṭipādanatthā”ti padassa “kammaṭṭhānavīthiyā sampaṭipādanatthā”ti atthaṃ vatvā taṃ pana kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ, tassā ca sampaṭipādanavidhiṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “sace hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha katimīti pakkhassa katamī, kiṃ dutiyā, tatiyādīsu vā aññatarāti attho. Tuṇhībhūtena gantuṃ na vaṭṭati pucchantānaṃ cittassa aññathattapariharaṇatthaṃ. Appasannānañhi pasādāya, pasannānañca bhiyyobhāvāya sāsanasampaṭipatti. Nassatīti na dissati[V 1.0197], na upaṭṭhātīti attho. “Āgantukapaṭisanthāro kātabbo”ti iminā āgantukavattaṃ ekadesena dassitanti “avasesānipī”ti vatvā āgantukavattaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ gahetuṃ puna āgantukaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Gamikavattādīnīti ādi-saddena āvāsikaanumodanapiṇḍacārikaanumodanapiṇḍacārikaāraññikasenāsanavaccakuṭivattādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Vattakkhandhake (cūḷava. 356) hi āgatāni mahāvattāni idha “khandhakavattānī”ti vuttāni. Tajjanīyakammakatādikāle pana pārivāsikādikāle ca caritabbāni imassa bhikkhuno asambhavato idha nādhippetāni. Nimittaṃ vā antaradhāyatīti susāne ṭhitaṃ asubhanimittaṃ uddhumātakabhāvāpagamena antaradhāyati. Tenāha “uddhumātaka”ntiādi. Tasmāti tena [M 1.0210] kāraṇena, imassa kammaṭṭhānassa dullabhattāti attho. Nisīditvā paccavekkhitabboti sambandho.

115. Of the phrase, “for the purpose of establishing the path,” having stated the meaning as “for the purpose of establishing the path of the meditation subject,” the passage beginning with “if indeed” was stated in order to then show in detail that path of the meditation subject and the method for establishing it. Therein, “which one” means: which one of the lunar fortnight? Is it the second, or any other among the third and so on? This is the meaning. It is not proper to go silently, for the purpose of preventing the minds of those who ask from becoming otherwise. For indeed, the proper practice of the Dispensation is for the confidence of the unconvinced and for the increase of confidence in the convinced. “It is lost” means it is not seen, it does not appear. This is the meaning. By the phrase, “Hospitality towards a newcomer should be shown,” the duties towards a newcomer are shown in part. In order to grasp the duties towards a newcomer in their entirety, the word “newcomer” is mentioned again. Regarding “duties for departing monks, etc.,” by the word “etc.,” the inclusion of the duties for resident monks, for giving thanks, for alms-goers, for forest-dwellers, for lodging, for the latrine, and so on, should be understood. For, the great duties that are found in the Chapter on Duties (Cūḷavagga 356) are here called the “duties of the Khandhaka.” However, the duties to be practiced at the time of having an act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) performed, etc., and at the time of being on probation (pārivāsika), etc., are not intended here, since they are impossible for this monk. “Or the sign disappears” means: the sign of the foul, which is in the charnel ground, disappears with the passing away of the state of being bloated. For that reason, he said the passage beginning with “a bloated corpse.” “Therefore” means: for that reason, because this meditation subject is difficult to obtain. This is the meaning. The connection is: “having sat down, it should be reviewed.”

Nimittaṃ gahetuṃ gamane viya nimittaṃ gahetvā nivattanepi yathāsallakkhitadisādipaccavekkhaṇaṃ yāva nimittavināsā pavattitakiriyāya avicchedena upadhāraṇatthaṃ. Sati hi tassa nirantarūpadhāraṇe vihāraṃ pavisitvā nisinnakāle kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhitākāro samathanimittassa gahaṇe cittassa samāhitākāro viya pākaṭo hutvā upatiṭṭheyyāti. Tenāha “tassevaṃ…pe… vīthiṃ paṭipajjatī”ti. Purimākārena nimittassa pākaṭabhāvena upaṭṭhitattā purimākāreneva kammaṭṭhānamanasikāro bhāvanāvīthiṃ paṭipajjati.

Just as when going to grasp the sign, so also when returning after having grasped it, the reviewing of the direction and so on, as it was marked, is for the purpose of uninterruptedly retaining the activity that was performed, up until the disappearance of the sign. For, when there is continuous retention of it, then at the time of sitting down after having entered the monastery, the mode of appearance of the meditation subject would appear, having become manifest, like the mode of concentration of the mind in the grasping of the sign of calm. For that reason, he said, “Thus for him… he enters upon the path.” Because the sign has appeared with a manifest nature in its former mode, the attention to the meditation subject enters upon the path of development in that very same former mode.

116. Uddhumātakaṃ nāma ativiya asuciduggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlaṃ bībhacchaṃ bhayānakañca, evarūpe ārammaṇe bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa evaṃ ābaddhaparikammassa thirībhūtasseva yogino adhippāyo samijjhatīti dassetuṃ “ānisaṃsadassāvī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evanti evameva vuttappakāreneva ānisaṃsadassāvinā. Taṃ rakkheyyāti “addhā iminā sukhaṃ jīvissāmī”ti attano jīvitaṃ viya taṃ maṇiratanaṃ rakkheyya. Catudhātukammaṭṭhānikotiādi nesaṃ kammaṭṭhānānaṃ sulabhatādassanaṃ. Tattha catudhātukammaṭṭhānikoti catudhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ vā tattha vā niyutto, catudhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ vā pariharanto. Itarānīti vuttāvasiṭṭhāni anussatibrahmavihārādīni. Taṃ nimittanti taṃ yathāladdhaṃ uggahanimittaṃ. “Rakkhitabba”nti vatvā rakkhaṇavidhiṃ puna dassetuṃ “rattiṭṭhāne”tiādi vuttaṃ.

116. A bloated corpse is by nature extremely impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, repulsive, hideous, and frightening. In order to show that the intention of a yogī who applies himself to development on such an object, who has thus undertaken the preliminary work, succeeds only when he has become steadfast, the passage beginning with “one who sees the benefit” was stated. “Thus” means: in this very way as was described, by one who sees the benefit. “He should guard it” means: he should guard that jewel of a sign like his own life, thinking, “Surely with this I will live happily.” The passage beginning with “one practicing the four elements meditation” shows the ease of obtaining these meditation subjects. Therein, “one practicing the four elements meditation” means: one who has the four elements meditation, or one who is engaged in it, or one who maintains the four elements meditation. “The others” means the remaining ones that have been mentioned: the recollections, the divine abidings, and so on. “That sign” means that learning-sign as it was obtained. Having said, “it should be guarded,” the passage beginning with “at the night-time lodging” was stated in order to show again the method of guarding it.

117. Nānā karīyati etenāti nānākaraṇaṃ, bhedo. Bībhacchaṃ bheravadassanaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti manasikārassa [V 1.0198] anuḷāratāya, anupasantatāya ca ārammaṇassa. Tabbipariyāyato “paṭibhāganimittaṃ thūlaṅgapaccaṅgapuriso viya upaṭṭhātī”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Bahiddhāti gocarajjhattato bahiddhā. Kāmānaṃ amanasikārāti asubhabhāvanānubhāvena kāmasaññāya dūrasamussāritattā kāmaguṇe ārabbha manasikārasseva abhāvā. Amanasikārāti vā manasikārapaṭipakkhahetu. Yāya hi kāmasaññāya vasena sattā kāme manasi karonti, tassā paṭipakkhabhūtā asubhasaññā kāmānaṃ amanasikāro, tannimittanti attho. Tenāha [M 1.0211] “vikkhambhanavasena kāmacchando pahīyatī”ti. Paṭibhāganimittārammaṇāya hi asubhasaññāya saddhiṃ balappatto samādhi uppajjamānova kāmacchandaṃ vikkhambheti, anurodhamūlako āghāto mūlakāraṇe vikkhambhite vikkhambhitoyeva hotīti āha “anunaya…pe… pahīyatī”ti. Na hi kadāci pahīnānunayassa byāpādo sambhavati. Yathāvuttaasubhasaññāsahagatā hi pīti sātisayā pavattamānāva byāpādaṃ vikkhambhentī pavattati. Tathā āraddhavīriyatāyāti yathā upacārajjhānaṃ uppajjati, tathā kammaṭṭhānamanasikāravasena paggahitavīriyatāya. Vīriyañhi paggaṇhantassa sammāsaṅkappo micchāsaṅkappaṃ viya savipphāratāya thinamiddhaṃ vikkhambhentameva uppajjati.

117. “It is made various by this,” thus it is “diversification” (nānākaraṇa); it is a difference. It appears as something hideous, with a terrifying appearance, due to the non-exalted nature of the attention and the non-tranquil nature of the object. Conversely, the connection should be made by supplying the words: “the counterpart-sign appears like a person with stout major and minor limbs.” “External” means: external to the internal resort. “Non-attention to sensual pleasures” is due to the very absence of attention concerning sensual qualities, because the perception of sensuality has been driven far away by the power of the development of the foul. Or, “non-attention” is the cause that is the counterpart to attention. For, that perception of the foul, which is the counterpart to the perception of sensuality by means of which beings attend to sensual pleasures, is the non-attention to sensual pleasures; that is its cause. This is the meaning. For that reason, he said, “By way of suppression, sensual desire is abandoned.” For, concentration that has attained strength, together with the perception of the foul which has the counterpart-sign as its object, suppresses sensual desire at the very moment of its arising. Aversion, which is rooted in compliance, is itself suppressed when its root cause is suppressed. Thus he said, “Compliance… is abandoned.” For ill will never arises for one who has abandoned compliance. For, rapture accompanied by the perception of the foul as described, when it proceeds with excellence, proceeds while suppressing ill will. Likewise, “due to having aroused energy” means: due to the energy that has been exerted by means of attention to the meditation subject in such a way that access concentration arises. For, for one who is exerting energy, right thought arises while suppressing sloth and torpor with its pervasiveness, just as it suppresses wrong thought.

Vippaṭisāro pacchānutāpo, tappaṭipakkhato avippaṭisāro darathapariḷāhābhāvena cittassa nibbutatā. Tassa avippaṭisārassa paccayabhūtaṃ sīlaṃ, taṃsahagatā tadupanissayā ca pītipassaddhisukhādayo sabhāvato, hetuto ca santasabhāvā, tesaṃ anuyuñjanena avūpasantasabhāvaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyatīti āha “avippaṭisārakarasantadhammānuyogavasena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyatī”ti. Bhāvanāya hi pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ āvahantiyā yaṃ sātisayaṃ sukhaṃ labbhati, taṃ anupasantasabhāvaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ vikkhambhentameva uppajjati. Adhigatavisesassāti yathādhigatassa bhāvanāvisesassa. Paccakkhatāyāti paṭipajjantassa yogino paccakkhabhāvato “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā, yo evarūpiṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ desetī”ti paṭipattidesake satthari. Paṭipattiyanti paṭipajjamānajjhānapaṭipattiyaṃ. Paṭipattiphaleti tāya sādhetabbe lokiyalokuttaraphale. Vicikicchā pahīyati dhammanvayavicārāhitabalena vicārabalena. Iti pañca nīvaraṇāni pahīyantīti evaṃ paṭibhāganimittapaṭilābhasamakālameva heṭṭhā pavattabhāvanānubhāvanipphannehi samādhiādīhi kāmacchandādīni pañca nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanavasena pahīyanti. Na hi paṭipakkhena vinā pahātabbassa pahānaṃ sambhavati, paṭipakkhā [V 1.0199] ca samādhiādayo kāmacchandādīnaṃ. Yathāha peṭake “samādhi kāmacchandassa paṭipakkho”tiādi.

Remorse is subsequent regret. Its opposite, non-remorse, is the mind's peaceful state due to the absence of anxiety and feverishness. Virtue is the cause of that non-remorse; and joy, tranquility, happiness, and so on, which are associated with it and have it as their decisive support, are peaceful by their intrinsic nature and by their cause. By engaging with these, restlessness and remorse, which have an unpacified nature, are abandoned. Thus, he said: 'Through the practice of peaceful qualities that cause non-remorse, restlessness and remorse are abandoned.' For, by the meditation that brings about a distinction from a former to a later time, the excellent happiness that is obtained arises only while suppressing restlessness and remorse, which have an unpacified nature. 'Of the attained distinction' means of the distinction in meditation as it has been attained. 'By its direct visibility' means that for the practicing yogī, due to its being directly visible, [faith arises] in the Teacher who teaches the practice: 'Truly, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who teaches such a right practice!' 'In the practice' means in the practice of the jhānic path that is being undertaken. 'In the fruit of the practice' means in the mundane and supramundane fruit to be accomplished by that practice. Doubt is abandoned by the power of investigation, with strength produced by the analytical examination that follows the course of the Dhamma. Thus, 'the five hindrances are abandoned' means that in this way, at the very same time as attaining the counterpart sign, the five hindrances—sensual desire and so on—are abandoned by way of suppression through concentration and other factors produced by the power of the meditation that has occurred before. Indeed, without an opposite, the abandonment of that which is to be abandoned is not possible. And the opposites of sensual desire and so on are concentration and so forth. As it is said in the Peṭaka: 'Concentration is the opposite of sensual desire,' and so on.

Teneva [M 1.0212] ca “imehi tesaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ pahāna”nti pahānaparidīpanamukhena jhānaṅgāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “tasmiññeva cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tasmiññeva cāti yaṃ taṃ yathāupaṭṭhitaṃ uggahanimittaṃ bhinditvā viya upaṭṭhitaṃ, tassa paṭicchannabhūtaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ, tasmiññeva nimitte. Cetasoti attanā sampayuttacittassa. Abhiniropanalakkhaṇoti āropanalakkhaṇo, appanāsabhāvoti attho. Nimittānumajjanaṃ paṭibhāganimitte anuvicaraṇaṃ. Ārammaṇe hi bhamarassa padumassūpari anuparibbhamanaṃ viya vicārassa anuvicāraṇākārena pavatti anumajjanakiccaṃ. Viseso eva adhigantabbato visesādhigamo, paṭiladdho ca so visesādhigamo cāti paṭi…pe… gamo, tappaccayā taṃhetukā paṭiladdhavisesādhigamapaccayā pīti. Pītimanassa pītisahitacittassa. Passaddhisambhavatoti kāyacittapassaddhīnaṃ saṃsijjhanato. “Pītimanassa kāyo passambhatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Passaddhinimittaṃ passaddhihetukaṃ sukhaṃ “passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vediyatī”ti vacanato. Sukhanimittā sukhapaccayā ekaggatā. “Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.466; a. ni. 3.96; 11.12) hi vuttaṃ. Iti jhānaṅgāni pātubhavantīti evaṃ etāni vitakkādīni jhānaṅgāni tasmiṃyeva nimitte uppajjanti. Paṭhamajjhānapaṭibimbabhūtanti paṭhamajjhānassa paṭicchannabhūtaṃ. Taṅkhaṇaññeva paṭibhāganimittapaṭilābhasamakālameva upacārajjhānampi nibbattati, na nīvaraṇappahānamevāti adhippāyo.

For that very reason, in order to show the jhāna factors in their own nature by way of elucidating the abandonment of the hindrances, the passage beginning with 'And in that very...' was stated. Therein, 'in that very...' refers to the counterpart sign, which appears as if breaking through the learning sign that has appeared as it is, and which is a counterpart of that learning sign; it means in that very sign. 'Of the mind' means of the mind associated with oneself. 'The characteristic of directing onto' means having the characteristic of applying to the object; the meaning is that it has the nature of absorption. 'Polishing the sign' is sustained application upon the counterpart sign. Indeed, just as a bee hovers over a lotus, the proceeding of sustained thought in the manner of repeatedly moving over the object is the function of polishing. Distinction itself, because it is to be attained, is the 'attainment of distinction'; and that attainment of distinction is attained...; joy has that attained distinction as its cause. 'Of one with a joyful mind' means of one whose mind is accompanied by joy. 'From the arising of tranquility' means due to the accomplishment of bodily and mental tranquility. For it is said: 'For one with a joyful mind, the body becomes tranquil.' Happiness is caused by tranquility, according to the saying: 'One with a tranquil body experiences happiness.' One-pointedness is conditioned by happiness. For it is said: 'The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.' Thus, 'the jhāna factors appear' means that in this way these jhāna factors, beginning with applied thought, arise in that very sign. 'Being an image of the first jhāna' means being a counterpart of the first jhāna. At that very moment, at the same time as attaining the counterpart sign, access concentration also arises—it is not merely the abandonment of the hindrances. This is the intended meaning.

Vinīlakādikammaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meditation Subjects Beginning with the Bluish Corpse

118. Vinīlakādīsupi kammaṭṭhānesu. Lakkhaṇaṃ vuttanti yaṃ taṃ nimittaggahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttanayenevāti uddhumātake vuttanayeneva. Saha vinicchayena, adhippāyena cāti savinicchayādhippāyaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ veditabbanti sambandho.

118. Also in the meditation subjects beginning with the bluish corpse. 'The characteristic is stated' means: that characteristic of grasping the sign which was stated. 'In the same way as stated' means: in the very same way as was stated in the section on the bloated corpse. 'With ascertainment and intention' is the meaning of `savinicchayādhippāyaṃ`. The connection is: 'that entire characteristic should be understood'.

Kabarakabaravaṇṇanti yebhuyyena sabalavaṇṇaṃ. Ussadavasenāti rattasetanīlavaṇṇesu ussadassa vaṇṇassa vasena.

'Of variegated color' means for the most part having a mottled color. 'By way of the predominant' means by way of the predominant color among the red, white, and blue colors.

Sannisinnanti [V 1.0200] niccalabhāveneva sabbaso thirataṃ.

'Settled' means completely stable, precisely because of its state of being motionless.

Corāṭaviyanti corehi pariyuṭṭhitaaraññe. Yatthāti yasmiṃ āghātane. Chinnapurisaṭṭhāneti chinnapurisavante ṭhāne. Nānādisāyaṃ patitampīti [M 1.0213] chinnaṃ hutvā sarīrassa khaṇḍadvayaṃ visuṃ disāsu patitampi. Ekāvajjanenāti ekasamannāhārena. Āpāthamāgacchatīti ekajjhaṃ āpāthaṃ āgacchati. Vissāsaṃ āpajjatīti ajegucchitaṃ upagaccheyya seyyathāpi chavaḍāhako. Sahatthā aparāmasane jigucchā saṇṭhātiyevāti āha “kattarayaṭṭhiyā vā daṇḍakena vā…pe… upanāmetabba”nti. Vicchiddakabhāvapaññāyanatthaṃ ekaṅgulantarakaraṇaṃ. Upanāmetabbanti upanetabbaṃ.

'In a thieves' forest' means in a forest beset by thieves. 'Where' means in which place of slaughter. 'In a place of cut-up men' means in a place with men who have been cut up. 'Even if fallen in various directions' means even if the two parts of the body, having been cut, have fallen in separate directions. 'With a single advertence' means with a single act of attention. 'It comes into range' means it comes into the perceptual field as one. 'He becomes familiar' means he should attain a state of non-disgust, just like a corpse-burner. Because disgust indeed remains when not touching it with one's own hand, he said: 'with a pointed stick or a staff... it should be brought near.' The making of a one-finger-width gap is for the purpose of making clear the state of being cut apart. 'It should be brought near' means it should be brought close.

Khāyitasadisamevāti khāyitāsubhasadisameva. Aṅgulaṅgulantaranti vividhaṃ khittaṃ sarīrāvayavaṃ aṅgulantaraṃ aṅgulantaraṃ. Katvā vāti kattarayaṭṭhiyā vā daṇḍakena vā sayaṃ katvā vā.

'Just like one that has been gnawed' means just like a foul corpse that has been gnawed. 'A finger-width gap' means making a finger-width gap between the various scattered limbs of the body. 'Or having done it' means having done it oneself, either with a pointed stick or a staff.

Laddhappahārānanti laddhāvudhappahārānaṃ mukhatoti sambandho. Mukhatoti pahārādimukhato. Paggharamānakāleti lohitaṃ paggharamānakāle. Lohitakaṃ labbhatīti yojanā.

'Of those who have received blows': the connection is with 'from the opening' (`mukhato`), meaning 'from the opening of the wounds of those who have received weapon-blows.' 'From the opening' means from the opening of the wound and so on. 'At the time of flowing' means at the time when blood is flowing. The syntactical construction is: 'the blood meditation subject is obtained'.

Tanti puḷavakaṃ. Tesūti soṇādisarīresu. Aṭṭhikanti aṭṭhikaasubhaṃ nānappakārato vuttanti sambandho. Purimanayenevāti pubbe uddhumātake vuttanayeneva.

`Tanti` means the foul object full of worms. `Tesūti` means in the bodies of dogs and so forth. The connection is that `aṭṭhikanti` means the foulness of the bone is described in various ways. `Purimanayenevāti` means in the same way as was stated previously in the meditation subject of the bloated corpse.

119. Tanti aṭṭhikaṃ. Na upaṭṭhātīti sabhāvato na upaṭṭhāti, paṭikkūlavasena na upaṭṭhātīti attho. Tenāha “odātakasiṇasambhedo hotī”ti. Aṭṭhike paṭhamavayādisaṃlakkhaṇaṃ na sakkāti “liṅganti idha hatthādīnaṃ nāma”nti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā pana “ayaṃ daharassa, ayaṃ yobbane ṭhitassa, ayaṃ avayavehi vuddhipattissā”ti evaṃ vayavasena vavatthapetuṃ sakkuṇeyyāva, abyāpitāya pana na gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Yadipi aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāyaṃ sandhito vavatthāpanaṃ labbhati, aṭṭhike pana na labbhatīti tassa aniyatabhāvadīpanatthaṃ kamavilaṅghanaṃ katvā “tassa tassa aṭṭhino ninnaṭṭhānathalaṭṭhānavasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ninnaṭṭhānaṃ nāma aṭṭhino vinatappadeso. Thalaṭṭhānaṃ unnatappadeso. Ghaṭitaghaṭitaṭṭhānavasenāti anupagatanhārubandhānaṃ, itaresañca aññamaññaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkiliṭṭhaṭṭhānavasena. Antaravasenāti aññamaññassa antaravasena, susiravasena ca. Sabbatthevāti sakalāya aṭṭhisaṅkhalikāya, sabbasmiṃ vā aṭṭhike.

119. `Tanti` means the bone. `Na upaṭṭhāti` means it does not appear by its nature; the meaning is that it does not appear by way of repulsiveness. Therefore, it is said, “It becomes mixed with the white kasiṇa.” In a disconnected bone, it is not possible to distinguish the first stage of life and so forth; therefore, it is said, “`liṅgaṃ` here means the name of the hands, etc.” A skeleton, however, could indeed be determined by way of age, thus: “This is of a young person, this is of one in their youth, this is of one who has reached growth in their limbs.” But it should be known that it is not taken up because it is not pervasive. Although in a skeleton a determination can be made by way of the joints, in a disconnected bone it cannot be obtained. Therefore, to show its uncertain nature, having skipped the sequence, it is said, “by way of the low place and the high place of each bone,” and so on. Therein, `ninnaṭṭhānaṃ` (low place) means the concave part of the bone. `Thalaṭṭhānaṃ` (high place) means the convex part. `Ghaṭitaghaṭitaṭṭhānavasenāti` means by way of the places where those bones with remaining sinew-connections and the others without them are mutually attached. `Antaravasenāti` means by way of the interval between one another and by way of the hollows. `Sabbatthevāti` means in the entire skeleton or in every single bone.

120. Etthāti [M 1.0214][V 1.0201] etasmiṃ aṭṭhikāsubhe. Yujjamānavasena sallakkhetabbanti yaṃ nimittaggahaṇaṃ yattha yujjati, taṃ tattha uggaṇhanatthaṃ nimittaggahaṇavasena upalakkhetabbaṃ. Sakalāyāti anavasesabhāgāya paripuṇṇāvayavāya. Sampajjati nimittupaṭṭhānavasena. Tesūti aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṭṭhikesu. Vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Tanti “ekasadisamevā”ti vacanaṃ. Ekasmiṃ aṭṭhike yuttanti idaṃ yathā vinīlakādīsu ubhinnaṃ nimittānaṃ yathārahaṃ vaṇṇavisesato, paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇato, savivarāvivarato, calācalato ca viseso labbhati, na evametassāti katvā vuttaṃ, na pana sabbena sabbaṃ visesābhāvato. Tenevāha “ekaṭṭhikepi cā”tiādi. Tattha bībhacchenāti suvibhūtaaṭṭhirūpattā aṭṭhibhāveneva virūpena. Bhayānakenāti teneva pākatikasattānaṃ bhayāvahena. Pītisomanassajanakenāti saṇhamaṭṭhabhāvena upaṭṭhānato, bhāvanāya ca savisesattā pītiyā, somanassassa ca uppādakena. Tenevāha “upacārāvahattā”ti.

120. `Etthāti` means in this foul object of the bone. `Yujjamānavasena sallakkhetabbaṃ` means that whichever grasping of the sign is suitable in a particular foul object, that should be marked for the purpose of learning it by way of grasping the sign in that foul object. `Sakalāyāti` means with no part remaining, with complete limbs. It is accomplished by way of the appearance of the sign. `Tesūti` means in skeletons and disconnected bones. It is stated in the commentary. `Tanti` refers to the statement, “It is just of one likeness.” This is said because, unlike in the case of the bluish corpse and so on, where a distinction between the two signs is obtained according to the difference in color, completeness or incompleteness, presence or absence of openings, and movement or stillness, such a distinction is not obtained for this sign. It is not, however, said due to a complete and total absence of distinction. For that very reason, it is said, “Even in a single bone,” and so on.
