Therein, `bībhacchenāti` means by being deformed by its very nature as a bone, due to its form as a bone being very distinct. `Bhayānakenāti` means by bringing fear to ordinary beings due to that very deformity. `Pītisomanassajanakenāti` means by being a producer of joy and gladness due to its appearing with a smooth and polished nature, and due to the meditation possessing a special quality. For that very reason, it is said, “because it brings access concentration.”

Imasmiṃ okāseti uggahapaṭibhāganimittānaṃ vuttaṭṭhāne. Dvāraṃ datvā vāti “paṭikkūlabhāveyeva diṭṭhe nimittaṃ nāma hotī”ti ettake eva aṭṭhatvā anantarameva “duvidhaṃ idha nimitta”ntiādinā uggahapaṭibhāganimittāni vibhajitvā vacanena yathāvuttassa nimittavibhāgassa dvāraṃ datvāva vuttaṃ. Nibbikappanti “subha”nti vikappena nibbikappaṃ, asubhantvevāti attho. Vicāretvāti “ekasmiṃ aṭṭhike yutta”ntiādinā vicāretvā.

`Imasmiṃ okāseti` means in the place where the learning and counterpart signs are mentioned. `Dvāraṃ datvā vāti` means that it is stated having given an opening to the aforementioned division of signs, not by stopping at just this much—“The sign comes to be only when it is seen in its repulsive aspect”—but immediately after, by distinguishing the learning and counterpart signs with the statement beginning, “Here, the sign is twofold.” `Nibbikappanti` means without the conceptualization “beautiful”; the meaning is, just as “foul.” `Vicāretvāti` means having investigated with the passage beginning, “it is suitable in a single bone.”

Mahātissattherassāti cetiyapabbatavāsīmahātissattherassa. Nidassanānīti dantaṭṭhikamattadassanena sakalassāpi tassā itthiyā sarīrassa aṭṭhisaṅghātabhāvena upaṭṭhānādīni ettha aṭṭhikakammaṭṭhāne uggahapaṭibhāganimittānaṃ visesavibhāvanāni udāharaṇāni.

`Mahātissattherassāti` means of the Great Elder Tissa, a resident of Cetiyapabbata. `Nidassanānīti` means that the appearance, etc., of the entire body of that woman as a mass of bones through the mere sight of a tooth-bone are examples that clarify the distinction between the learning and counterpart signs here in the meditation subject of the bone.

Subhaguṇoti savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahīnattā suparisuddhaguṇo. Dasasatalocanenāti sahassakkhena devānamindena. So hi ekāsaneneva sahassaatthānaṃ vicāraṇasamatthena paññācakkhunā samannāgatattā “sahassakkho”ti vuccati. Thutakittīti “yo dhīro sabbadhi danto”tiādinā (mahāva. 58) abhitthutakittisaddo.

`Subhaguṇoti` means one with completely pure qualities because the defilements with their latent tendencies have been abandoned. `Dasasatalocanenāti` means by Sahassakkha (Thousand-Eyed), the lord of the devas. For he is called “Sahassakkha” because he is endowed with the eye of wisdom, which is capable of investigating a thousand matters in a single sitting. `Thutakittīti` means the sound of praised fame, by the passage beginning, “The wise one, restrained in all things…” (Mahāvagga 58).

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of Miscellaneous Topics

121. Ujupaṭipakkhena [M 1.0215][V 1.0202] pahīnabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha “suvikkhambhitarāgattā”ti. Asubhappabhedoti uddhumātakādiasubhavibhāgo. Sarīrasabhāvappattivasenāti sarīrassa attano sabhāvūpagamanavasena. Sarīrañhi vinassamānaṃ aññarūpena ṭhitassa rakkhasassa viya sabhāvappattivaseneva vinassati. Rāgacaritabhedavasenāti rāgacaritavibhāgavasena. Yadi sarīrasabhāvappattivasena ayamasubhappabhedo vutto, mahāsatipaṭṭhānādīsu (dī. ni. 2.372 ādayo; ma. ni. 1.105 ādayo) kathaṃ navappabhedoti? So sarasato eva sabhāvappattivasena vutto, ayaṃ pana parūpakkamenāpi. Tattha ca idhāgatesu dasasu asubhesu ekaccāneva gahitāni, aṭṭhikañca pañcavidhā vibhattaṃ. Tāni ca vipassanāvasena, imāni samathavasenāti pākaṭoyaṃ bhedoti.

121. He said, 'because lust is thoroughly suppressed,' referring to the state of abandonment by means of its direct opposite. The classification of the unattractive is the division of the unattractive, such as the bloated and so on. 'By way of the body attaining its own nature' means by way of the body approaching its own natural state. For the body, when perishing, perishes only by way of attaining its natural state, like a demon standing in another form. 'By way of the division of lustful temperament' means by way of the classification of those with a lustful temperament. If this classification of the unattractive is stated by way of the body attaining its own nature, how then is the ninefold classification stated in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness and other texts (e.g., DN 22; MN 10)? That [ninefold classification] was stated purely by its own nature, by way of attaining its natural state; but this [tenfold classification] is also by the intervention of others. And there [in those suttas], among the ten unattractive objects that have come here [in this text], only some are taken, and the skeleton is divided in five ways. And those are by way of insight, while these are by way of serenity—thus, this distinction is clear.

Imesaṃ pana dassanampi asubhabhāvasāmaññena satipi avisesato rāgacaritānaṃ sappāyabhāve yaṃ vuttaṃ “rāgacaritabhedavasena cā”ti, taṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “visesato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sūnabhāvena susaṇṭhitampi sarīraṃ dussaṇṭhitameva hotīti uddhumātakasarīre saṇṭhānavipattiṃ dīpetīti āha “sarīrasaṇṭhānavipattippakāsanato”ti. Saṇṭhānasampattiyaṃ ratto saṇṭhānarāgī, tassa sappāyaṃ saṇṭhānarāgassa vikkhambhanupāyabhāvato. Kāyo eva kāyavaṇo, tattha paṭibaddhassa nissitassa. Susirabhāvappakāsanatoti susirassa vivarassa atthibhāvappakāsanato. Sarīre ghanabhāvarāginoti sarīre aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ thirabhāvaṃ paṭicca uppajjanakarāgavato. Vikkhepappakāsanatoti soṇasiṅgālādīhi ito cito ca vikkhepassa pakāsanato aṅgapaccaṅgalīlārāgino sappāyaṃ. Īdisānaṃ kira anavaṭṭhitarūpānaṃ avayavānaṃ ko līḷāvilāsoti virāgasambhavato. Saṅghātabhedavikārappakāsanatoti saṅghātassa aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ saṃhatabhāvassa susambandhatāya bhedo eva vikāro saṅghātabhedavikāro, tassa pakāsanato. Lohitaṃ makkhitaṃ hutvā paṭikkūlabhāvo lohitamakkhitapaṭikkūlabhāvo, tassa pakāsanato. Mamattarāginoti “mama aya”nti uppajjanakarāgavato. Dantasampattirāginoti dantasampattiyaṃ rajjanasīlassa.

Furthermore, to explain in detail what was stated as 'and by way of the division of lustful temperament'—that is, although the sight of these [unattractive objects] is generally suitable for those of a lustful temperament due to the common characteristic of unattractiveness—the words 'especially,' etc., were stated. Because even a well-formed body becomes ill-formed through bloating, the bloated corpse shows the distortion of form in the body; therefore, he said, 'because it shows the distortion of the body's form.' One attached to the perfection of form is 'one with lust for form'; this is suitable for such a person because it is a means for suppressing lust for form. The body itself is a bodily wound, for one who is attached to and dependent on it. 'Because it shows the state of being hollow' means because it shows the existence of hollowness and openings. 'For one with lust for solidity in the body' means for one who has lust that arises in dependence on the firmness of the major and minor limbs. 'Because it shows the scattering'—that is, because it shows the scattering here and there by dogs, jackals, and so on—it is suitable for one with lust for the graceful movements of the major and minor limbs. For what graceful charm can there be for such unstable parts? Thus, dispassion can arise. 'Because it shows the breaking and distortion of the aggregate': the breaking of the aggregate—the well-connected state of the major and minor limbs—is itself a distortion; because it shows this breaking and distortion of the aggregate. The state of being repulsive from being smeared with blood is 'the repulsiveness of being smeared with blood'; because it shows this. 'For one with lust for ownership' means for one who has lust that arises from the thought, 'This is mine.' 'For one with lust for the perfection of the teeth' means for one whose nature is to be attached to the perfection of the teeth.

Kasmā [M 1.0216] panettha uddhumātakādike paṭhamajjhānameva uppajjati, na dutiyādīnīti anuyogaṃ [V 1.0203] manasi katvā āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Aparisaṇṭhitajalāyāti sotavasena pavattiyā samantato aṭṭhitajalāya asannisinnasalilāya. Arittabalenāti pājanadaṇḍabalena. Dubbalattā ārammaṇassāti paṭikkūlabhāvena attani cittaṃ ṭhapetuṃ asamatthabhāvo ārammaṇassa dubbalatā. Paṭikkūle hi ārammaṇe sarasato cittaṃ pavattituṃ na sakkoti, abhiniropanalakkhaṇena pana vitakkena abhiniropiyamānameva cittaṃ ekaggataṃ labhati. Na vinā vitakkenāti vitakkarahitāni dutiyādijjhānāni tattha patiṭṭhaṃ na labhanti. Tenāha “vitakkabalenevā”tiādi.

Why is it that in this case, regarding the bloated corpse and so on, only the first jhāna arises, and not the second and so forth? Having taken this question to mind, he said, 'Because,' and so on. 'Of water that is not still' means of water that is not stationary all around due to the force of the current, of water that has not settled. 'By the force of an oar' means by the force of a driving stick. 'Because of the weakness of the object': the weakness of the object is the inability, due to its repulsive nature, to keep the mind placed upon it. Indeed, in a repulsive object, the mind is not able to proceed on its own accord; but only when being directed by initial application, which has the characteristic of directing, does the mind attain one-pointedness. 'Not without initial application' means that the second jhāna and so forth, which are devoid of initial application, do not find a footing there. Therefore, he said, 'Only by the power of initial application,' and so on.

Yadi paṭikkūlabhāvato uddhumātādiārammaṇe dutiyādijjhānāni na pavattanti, evaṃ sante paṭhamajjhānenāpi tattha na uppajjitabbaṃ. Na hi tattha pītisomanassānaṃ sambhavo yuttoti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “paṭikkūlepi ca etasmi”ntiādi. Tattha ānisaṃsadassāvitānīvaraṇasantāparogavūpasamānaṃ yathākkamaṃ pupphacchaḍḍaka, vamanavirecanaupamā yojetabbā.

If, due to its repulsive nature, the second jhāna and so forth do not proceed with regard to objects such as a bloated corpse, then, that being the case, even the first jhāna should not arise there. For it is not suitable that the arising of joy and happiness should occur there. Referring to this objection, he said, 'Even in this repulsive object,' and so on. There, the analogies of the flower-discarder, vomiting, and purging should be connected respectively to seeing the benefit, the torment of the hindrances, and the pacification of the disease.

122. Yathāvuttakāraṇena dasadhā vavatthitampi sabhāvato ekavidhamevāti dassetuṃ “dasavidhampi ceta”ntiādiṃ vatvā svāyaṃ sabhāvo yathā aviññāṇakesu, evaṃ saviññāṇakesupi labbhateva. Tasmā tatthāpi yonisomanasikāravato bhāvanā ijjhatevāti dassento “tadetaṃ iminā lakkhaṇenā”tiādimāha. Etthāti etasmiṃ jīvamānakasarīre. Alaṅkārenāti paṭijagganapubbakena alaṅkaraṇena. Na paññāyati pacurajanassāti adhippāyo. Atirekatisataaṭṭhikasamussayaṃ dantaṭṭhikehi saddhiṃ, tehi pana vinā “timattāni aṭṭhisatānī”ti (visuddhi. 1.190) kāyagatāsatiyaṃ vakkhati. Chiddāvachiddanti khuddānukhuddachiddavantaṃ. Medakathālikā medabharitabhājanaṃ. Niccuggharitapaggharitanti niccakālaṃ upari, heṭṭhā ca vissavantaṃ. Vemattanti nānattaṃ. Nānāvatthehīti nānāvaṇṇehi vatthehi. Hiriyā lajjāya kopanato vināsanato hirikopinaṃ, uccārapassāvamaggaṃ. Yāthāvasarasanti yathābhūtaṃ sabhāvaṃ. Yāthāvato rasīyati ñāyatīti hi raso, sabhāvo. Ratinti abhiratiṃ abhiruciṃ. Attasinehasaṅkhātena [M 1.0217] rāgena rattā attasineharāgarattā. Vihaññamānenāti icchitālābhena vighātaṃ āpajjantena.

122. To show that although it is established as tenfold for the reason already stated, by nature it is of one kind only, he said, 'Even though this is tenfold,' and so on. And just as this nature is found in inanimate things, so too it is indeed found in animate beings. Therefore, to show that for one who applies wise attention, the development of meditation indeed succeeds even in that case, he said, 'This is so by this characteristic,' and so on. 'Here' means in this living body. 'By adornment' means by decoration that is preceded by cleansing. The meaning is, 'it is not apparent to the great mass of people.' 'A collection of over three hundred bones' is together with the teeth-bones; but without them, it will be said in the section on mindfulness of the body, 'three hundred bones.' 'With holes throughout' means having small and very small holes. A 'pot of fat' is a vessel filled with fat. 'Constantly oozing up and trickling down' means constantly seeping from above and below. 'Difference' means variety. 'With various cloths' means with cloths of various colors. Because it destroys (`kopana`) shame (`hiri`), it is called a `hirikopīna` (loincloth that covers shame); this refers to the passage for feces and urine. 'The nature as it really is' means the true nature. Indeed, because it is known (`rasīyati`) as it truly is (`yāthāvato`), it is called `rasa` (essence); this refers to its nature. 'Delight' means great pleasure, great satisfaction. 'Those attached by the lust of self-love' are those attached by the lust called love for oneself. 'Being tormented' means experiencing frustration due to not obtaining what is desired.

Kiṃsukanti pālibhaddakaṃ, palāsoti keci, simbalīti apare. Atilolupoti ativiya lolasabhāvo[V 1.0204]. Adunti etaṃ. Nanti kesādisarīrakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Mucchitāti mohitā, mucchāpāpikāya vā taṇhāya vasena mucchaṃ pattā. Sabhāvanti paṭikkūlabhāvaṃ.

A 'kiṃsuka' is a pālibhaddaka tree; some say it is a palāsa tree, others a simbali tree. 'Extremely fickle' (`atilolupo`) means having a very fickle nature. 'That' (`aduṃ`) means this. 'It' (`naṃ`) means a part of the body such as hair. 'Infatuated' (`mucchitā`) means deluded; or alternatively, having reached delusion by the power of craving which leads to delusion. 'Nature' (`sabhāvaṃ`) means the state of being repulsive.

Ukkarūpamoti uccārapassāvaṭṭhānasamo, vaccakūpasamo vā. Cakkhubhūtehīti cakkhuṃ pattehi paṭiladdhapaññācakkhukehi, lokassa vā cakkhubhūtehi. Allacammapaṭicchannoti allacammapariyonaddho.

'Like a rubbish heap' (`ukkarūpamo`) means similar to a place for excrement and urine, or alternatively, similar to a cesspool. 'By those who have become the eye' (`cakkhubhūtehi`) means by those who have attained the eye, who have obtained the eye of wisdom; or alternatively, by those who have become the eye of the world. 'Covered with moist skin' (`allacammapaṭicchanno`) means enveloped by moist skin.

Dabbajātikenāti uttarimanussadhamme paṭiladdhuṃ bhabbarūpena. Yattha yattha sarīre, sarīrassa vā yattha yattha koṭṭhāse. Nimittaṃ gahetvāti asubhākārassa suṭṭhu sallakkhaṇavasena yathā uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati, evaṃ uggaṇhanavasena nimittaṃ gahetvā, uggahanimittaṃ uppādetvāti attho. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ appanaṃ pāpetabbanti yathāladdhe uggahanimitte kammaṃ karontena paṭibhāganimittaṃ uppādetvā upacārajjhāne ṭhitena tameva bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpentena asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ appanaṃ pāpetabbaṃ. Adhigatappano hi paṭhamajjhāne ṭhito tameva jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā saṅkhāre sammasanto nacirasseva sabbāsave khepetīti.

'By one of good stuff' (`dabbajātikenāti`) means by one of a nature suitable for attaining the higher human states. In whatever body, or alternatively, in whatever part of the body. 'Having grasped the sign' means: having grasped the sign by way of learning in such a manner that the learning sign arises through thoroughly marking the aspect of foulness; that is, having produced the learning sign. 'The meditation subject should be brought to absorption' means: the meditation subject of foulness should be brought to absorption by one who, while practicing the meditation on the learning sign as it has been obtained, produces the counterpart sign, and being established in access concentration, makes effort in that very meditation. For a person who has attained absorption and is established in the first jhāna, having made that very jhāna the basis, having begun insight, and while comprehending the formations, will in no long time destroy all the cankers.

Asubhakammaṭṭhānaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the meditation subject of foulness is finished.

Iti chaṭṭhaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the sixth chapter.

7. Chaanussatiniddesavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Six Recollections

1. Buddhānussatikathāvaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Recollection of the Buddha

123. Asubhānantaranti [M 1.0218][V 1.0205] asubhakammaṭṭhānānantaraṃ. Anussatīsūti anussatikammaṭṭhānesu. “Anu anu sati anussatī”ti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “punappunaṃ uppajjanato”ti vatvā na ettha anu-saddayogena sati-saddo atthantaravācakoti dassetuṃ “satiyeva anussatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tena nāyamanu-saddo “upalabbhatī”tiādīsu upa-saddo viya anatthako, nāpi “sañjānanaṃ pajānana”ntiādīsu saṃ-saddādayo viya atthantaradīpakoti dasseti. “Pavattitabbaṭṭhānamhiyeva vā pavattattā”ti iminā ca anussatiyā anussaritabbānurūpatā vuttā hotīti pavattakasseva anurūpataṃ dassetuṃ “kulaputtassa anurūpā”ti vuttaṃ, saddhāpabbajitassa vā kulaputtassa. Anurūpatā nāma pavattitabbaṭṭhānassa anurūpatāya eva hotīti pavattakasseva anurūpatā vuttā, na ubhayassa. Anurūpāti ca yuttāti attho. Buddhanti ye guṇe upādāya bhagavati “buddho”ti paññatti, te guṇe ekajjhaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Tenāha “buddhaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacana”nti. Ārabbhāti ālambitvā. Dhammanti pariyattidhammena saddhiṃ navavidhampi lokuttaradhammaṃ. Nanu ca nibbānaṃ visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvena vakkhati? Kiñcāpi vakkhati, dhammabhāvasāmaññena pana maggaphalehi saddhiṃ idha pāḷiyā saṅgahitattā tassāpi dhammānussatikammaṭṭhāne gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, asaṅkhatāmatādibhāvena pana maggaphalehi visiṭṭhatāya tassa visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvena gahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Sīlānussatiādīnaṃ pana tissannaṃ anussatīnaṃ visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvena gahaṇaṃ yogāvacarassa attano eva sīlassa cāgassa saddhādīnañca anussatiṭṭhānabhāvena gahetabbattā. Rūpakāyaṃ gatāti attano karajakāyaṃ ārabbha ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pavattā. Kāyeti kāye visayabhūte. Koṭṭhāsanimittārammaṇāyāti kesādikoṭṭhāsesu paṭikkūlanimittārammaṇāya. Ito purimāsu sattasu anussatīsu natthi nimittuppatti[V 1.0206], idha atthīti dassanatthaṃ nimitta-ggahaṇaṃ. Tathā assāsapassāsanimittārammaṇāyāti etthāpi. Upasamanti sabbasaṅkhārūpasamaṃ, nibbānanti attho.

123. Asubhānantaraṃ means immediately after the meditation subject of unattractiveness. Anussatīsu means among the meditation subjects of recollection. To show the meaning of 'anu anu sati anussati' (mindfulness again and again is recollection), and to show that here the word 'sati', through its connection with the prefix 'anu', does not denote a different meaning, it is said, 'satiyeva anussati' (mindfulness itself is recollection). By this it is shown that this prefix 'anu' is not meaningless like the prefix 'upa' in words such as 'upalabbhati', nor does it indicate a different meaning like the prefixes 'saṃ' and so on in words such as 'sañjānanaṃ pajānanaṃ'. And by this phrase, 'or because it occurs only in a place where it should occur,' the suitability of the recollection to that which is to be recollected is stated. Therefore, to show the suitability for the one who causes it to arise, it is said, 'suitable for a clansman,' or for a clansman who has gone forth in faith. Suitability, it is said, arises only from the suitability of the place where recollection should occur; therefore, the suitability for the one who causes it to arise is stated, not for both. And 'anurūpā' means 'suitable.' This is the meaning. Buddhaṃ: this is said having taken together those qualities on account of which there is the designation 'Buddha' for the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, 'this is a designation for the mindfulness that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object.' Ārabbha means having taken as an object. Dhammaṃ means the ninefold supramundane Dhamma together with the Dhamma of the scriptures. But will not Nibbāna be spoken of separately as a meditation subject? Although it will be spoken of, it should be understood that its inclusion in the meditation subject of recollection of the Dhamma is because it is included here in the Pāḷi together with the paths and fruits under the general state of 'Dhamma'. However, because of its distinction from the paths and fruits by way of being unconditioned, deathless, etc., it is taken up separately as a meditation subject. The three recollections beginning with the recollection of virtue, however, are taken up as separate meditation subjects because the yogāvacara's own virtue, generosity, faith, and so on are to be taken as the basis for recollection. Rūpakāyaṃ gatā means occurred with reference to one's own physical body by way of making it an object. Kāye means in the body, which has become the object-domain. Koṭṭhāsanimittārammaṇāya means having the repulsive sign in the parts beginning with the hair of the head as its object. The word 'sign' is included to show that whereas in the preceding seven recollections there is no arising of a sign, here there is. Likewise also in the case of assāsapassāsanimittārammaṇāya. Upasamaṃ means the stilling of all formations; that is, Nibbāna. This is the meaning.

124. Avecca [M 1.0219] buddhaguṇe yāthāvato ñatvā uppanno pasādo aveccappasādo, ariyamaggena āgatappasādo, taṃsadisopi vā yo diṭṭhigatavātehi acalo asampakampiyo, tena samannāgatena. Tādisassa buddhānussatibhāvanā ijjhati, na itarassa. Patirūpasenāsaneti yathāvuttaaṭṭhārasadosavajjite pañcaṅgasamannāgate senāsane. Rahogatenāti rahasi gatena. Tena kāyavivekaṃ dasseti. Paṭisallīnenāti nānārammaṇato paṭisallīnena, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato paṭikkamāpetvā kammaṭṭhāne sallīnena, susiliṭṭhacittenāti attho. Evanti imāya pāḷiyā āgatanayena.

124. Aveccappasāda is the confidence that has arisen after having known the qualities of the Buddha as they really are with penetration; it is the confidence that comes by way of the noble path, or one that is similar to it, which is unshaken and unshakeable by the winds of wrong views. For one endowed with that, the development of the recollection of the Buddha succeeds, not for another. Patirūpasenāsane means in a dwelling that is devoid of the eighteen faults as described and is endowed with the five factors. Rahogatena means gone to a secluded place. Paṭisallīnena means withdrawn from various objects, having made the mind turn back from external, manifold objects and become absorbed in the meditation subject; with a well-composed mind. This is the meaning. Evaṃ means according to the method that has come down in this Pāḷi text.

So bhagavāti ettha soti yo so samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho devānaṃ atidevo brahmānaṃ atibrahmā lokanātho bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi sadevake loke “bhagavā”ti patthaṭakittisaddo, so. Bhagavāti idaṃ satthu nāmakittanaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kata”ntiādi (mahāni. 198, 210; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2). Parato pana bhagavāti guṇakittanaṃ. Arahantiādīsu navasu ṭhānesu paccekaṃ itipi-saddaṃ yojetvā buddhaguṇā anussaritabbāti dassento “itipi arahaṃ…pe… itipi bhagavāti anussaratī”ti āha. “Itipetaṃ bhūtaṃ itipetaṃ taccha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.6) viya iti-saddo āsannapaccakkhakaraṇattho, pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena nesaṃ bahubhāvo dīpito, tāni ca guṇasallakkhaṇakāraṇāni bhāventena cittassa sammukhībhūtāni kātabbānīti dassento “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha.

Herein, regarding So bhagavā (He, the Blessed One): So refers to He who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having destroyed all defilements, has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; who is the god beyond gods, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the protector of the world; and for reasons such as possessing fortune, has the renowned fame 'Bhagavā' spread throughout the world with its gods. Bhagavā—this is the proclamation of the Teacher's name. For so it is said: 'Bhagavā—this name was not given by his mother,' and so on (Mahāni. 198, 210; Cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2). Further on, however, bhagavā is a proclamation of his qualities. To show that the qualities of the Buddha should be recollected by applying the particle itipi to each of the nine instances beginning with Arahant, he said, 'He recollects thus: itipi arahaṃ... itipi bhagavā.' The particle iti, as in such phrases as 'Itipetaṃ bhūtaṃ itipetaṃ tacchaṃ' (Thus this is real, thus this is true) (Dī. Ni. 1.6), has the meaning of making something immediately present. The particle pi has the meaning of aggregation. By this, their multiplicity is shown. And to show that those causes for discerning the qualities should be made mentally present by one who is developing them, he said, 'It is said to mean: by this reason and by that reason.'

125. Dūratā nāma āsannatā viya upādāyupādāya vuccatīti paramukkaṃsagataṃ dūrabhāvaṃ dassento “suvidūravidūre”ti āha, suṭṭhu vidūrabhāveneva vidūreti attho. Sā panassa kilesato dūratā tesaṃ sabbaso pahīnattāti dassento āha “maggena kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattā”ti. Nanu aññesampi khīṇāsavānaṃ te pahīnā evāti anuyogaṃ manasi katvā vuttaṃ “savāsanāna”nti. Na hi bhagavantaṃ ṭhapetvā aññe saha vāsanāya kilese pahātuṃ sakkonti[V 1.0207], etena aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ [M 1.0220] bhagavato arahattanti dassitaṃ hoti. Kā panāyaṃ vāsanā nāma? Pahīnakilesassāpi appahīnakilesassa payogasadisapayogahetubhūto kilesanihito sāmatthiyaviseso āyasmato pilindavacchassa (pārā. 621) vasalasamudācāranimittaṃ viya. Kathaṃ pana “ārakā”ti vutte “kilesehī”ti ayamattho labbhatīti? Sāmaññajotanāya visese avaṭṭhānato, visesatthinā ca visesassa anupayojetabbato, “ārakāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā”tiādīni (ma. ni. 1.434) suttapadānettha udāharitabbāni. Ārakāti cettha ā-kārassa rassattaṃ, ka-kārassa ca ha-kāraṃ, sānusāraṃ katvā niruttinayena “araha”nti padasiddhi veditabbā. Vuttamevatthaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ “so tato ārakā nāmā”ti gāthābandhamāha. Tattha samañjanasīlo samaṅgī, na samaṅgitā asamaṅgitā asamannāgamo asahavuttitā.

125. The term 'distance' is spoken of relatively, like 'proximity.' Therefore, to show the state of distance that has reached the highest excellence, he said, 'suvidūravidūre' (very, very far). The meaning is: far by being thoroughly far. To show that this distance of his is from the defilements, due to their being completely abandoned, he said, 'because the defilements have been destroyed by the path.' 'But surely, for other destroyers of the taints too, those defilements are abandoned?' Keeping this objection in mind, it was said, 'with their latent tendencies.' Indeed, apart from the Blessed One, others are not able to abandon the defilements together with their latent tendencies. By this, it is shown that the Arahantship of the Blessed One is not shared with others. What, then, is this so-called 'latent tendency'? It is a special capacity deposited by the defilements which, even in one whose defilements are abandoned, is the cause for conduct similar to the conduct of one whose defilements are not abandoned, like the cause for the Venerable Pilindavaccha's habit of addressing others as 'outcaste.' But how, when 'ārakā' (far) is said, is this meaning 'from the defilements' obtained? Because a particular meaning is established from a general expression, and because a particular need not be supplied by one who seeks a particular meaning. Here, scriptural passages such as, 'Evil, unwholesome states are far (ārakā) from him,' should be cited. And here, in the word ārakā, by shortening the vowel ā, changing the consonant ka to ha, and making it nasalized, the formation of the word arahaṃ should be understood according to the method of etymology. To make the meaning already stated easy to grasp, he stated the verse beginning, 'So tato ārakā nāma.' Therein, one who has the nature of being associated with is samaṅgī (endowed). Not being endowed (asamaṅgitā) is non-possession, non-coexistence.

126. Anatthacaraṇena kilesā eva arayoti kilesārayo. “Arīnaṃ hatattā arihā”ti vattabbe niruttinayena “araha”nti vuttaṃ.

126. Because they practice what is harmful, the defilements themselves are enemies (arayo); hence, they are 'defilement-enemies' (kilesārayo). When it should be said 'arihā' because of having slain the enemies (arīnaṃ), it is instead said 'arahaṃ' according to the method of etymology.

127. Yañcetaṃ saṃsāracakkanti sambandho. Rathacakkassa nābhi viya mūlāvayavabhūtaṃ anto, bahi ca samavaṭṭhitaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayaṃ dvayanti vuttaṃ “avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhī”ti. Nābhiyā, nemiyā ca sambandhā arasadisā paccayaphalabhūtehi avijjātaṇhājarāmaraṇehi sambandhā puññādisaṅkhārāti vuttaṃ “puññādiabhisaṅkhārāra”nti. Tattha tattha bhave pariyantabhāvena pākaṭaṃ jarāmaraṇanti taṃ nemiṭṭhāniyaṃ katvā āha “jarāmaraṇanemī”ti. Yathā ca rathacakkapavattiyā padhānakāraṇaṃ akkho, evaṃ saṃsāracakkapavattiyā āsavasamudayoti āha “āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā”ti. Āsavā eva avijjādīnaṃ kāraṇattā āsavasamudayo. Yathāha “āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103). Vipākakaṭattārūpappabhedo kāmabhavādiko tibhavo eva ratho, tasmiṃ tibhavarathe. Attano paccayehi samaṃ, sabbaso vā ādito paṭṭhāya yojitanti samāyojitaṃ. Ādirahitaṃ kālaṃ pavattatīti katvā anādikālappavattaṃ.

127. The connection is to the phrase 'and this wheel of saṃsāra.' Like the hub of a chariot wheel, the twofold group consisting of ignorance and craving for existence, which is the root component established both internally and externally, is called 'the hub made of ignorance and craving for existence.' The meritorious and other formations, connected with ignorance, craving, aging, and death, which are cause and effect, are like the spokes connected to the hub and rim; thus it is called 'the spokes of meritorious and other volitional formations.' Since aging and death are manifest as the final end in each and every existence, treating them as the rim, he said, 'the rim of aging and death.' And just as the axle is the primary cause for the turning of a chariot wheel, so the origin of the taints is the primary cause for the turning of the wheel of saṃsāra; thus he said, 'having pierced it with the axle made of the origin of the taints.' The taints themselves, being the cause of ignorance and so on, are the 'origin of the taints.' As it is said: 'From the origin of the taints comes the origin of ignorance.' The threefold existence itself—such as the desire-realm existence, which is differentiated by resultant kaṭattā-form—is the chariot. On that chariot of threefold existence, it is 'completely yoked' (samāyojitaṃ) because it is yoked together with its own causes, or yoked completely from the beginning. Because it turns throughout beginningless time, it is 'that which has been turning from beginningless time' (anādikālappavattaṃ).

“Khandhānañca [M 1.0221] paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, ‘saṃsāro’ti pavuccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95 apasādanāvaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.60; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.199) –

The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense bases, proceeding without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra’.

Evaṃ [V 1.0208] vuttasaṃsārova saṃsāracakkaṃ. Anenāti bhagavatā. Bodhimaṇḍeti bodhisaṅkhātassa ñāṇassa maṇḍabhāvappatte ṭhāne, kāle vā. Vīriyapādehīti saṃkilesavodānapakkhiyesu sannirumbhanasannikkhipanakiccatāya dvidhā pavattehi attano vīriyasaṅkhātehi pādehi. Sīlapathaviyanti patiṭṭhaṭṭhena sīlameva pathavī, tassaṃ. Patiṭṭhāyāti sampādanavasena patiṭṭhahitvā. Saddhāhatthenāti anavajjadhammādānasādhanato saddhāva hattho, tena. Kammakkhayakaranti kāyakammādibhedassa sabbassapi kammassa khayakaraṇato kammakkhayakaraṃ. Ñāṇapharasunti samādhisilāyaṃ sunisitamaggañāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā.

The saṃsāra thus spoken of is itself the wheel of saṃsāra. Anena (by him) means: by the Blessed One. At the Bodhi-maṇḍa means: at the place, or time, that had reached the state of being the essence of the knowledge called Bodhi (enlightenment). With the feet of energy means: with his own feet, known as energy, which proceed in two ways with the function of suppressing (the defilement-side) and applying (the purification-side) in matters concerning defilement and purity. On the ground of virtue means: virtue itself is the ground, in the sense of being a foundation; on that ground. Having stood firm means: having become firmly established by way of accomplishment. With the hand of faith means: faith itself is the hand, as it is the instrument for taking up blameless states; with that hand. That which makes an end of kamma means: it brings about the end of kamma because it causes the destruction of all kamma, differentiated as bodily kamma and so on. The axe of knowledge means: having taken the axe of path-knowledge, well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration.

128. Evaṃ “arānaṃ hatattā”ti ettha vuttaaraghāte saṃsāraṃ cakkaṃ viya cakkanti gahetvā atthayojanaṃ katvā idāni paṭiccasamuppādadesanākkamenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha anamataggaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭanti anu anu amataggaṃ aviññātakoṭikaṃ saṃsāramaṇḍalaṃ. Sesā dasa dhammā saṅkhārādayo jātipariyosānā arā. Kathaṃ? Nābhiyā avijjāya mūlato, nemiyā jarāmaraṇena antato sambandhattāti dassento āha “avijjāmūlakattā jarāmaraṇapariyantattā cā”ti. Dukkhādīsūti dukkhasamudayanirodhamaggesu. Tattha dukkhe aññāṇaṃ tadantogadhattā, tappaṭicchādanato ca, sesesu paṭicchādanatova. Dukkhanti cettha dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ adhippetanti taṃ kāmabhavādivasena tidhā bhinditvā tathā tappaṭicchādikaṃ avijjaṃ, avijjādipaccaye tīsu bhavesu saṅkhārādike ca paṭipāṭiyā dassento “kāmabhave ca avijjā”tiādimāha. Tattha kāmabhave avijjāti kāmabhave ādīnavappaṭicchādikā avijjā. Rūpabhave arūpabhave avijjāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kāmabhave saṅkhārānanti kāmabhūmipariyāpannānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ, kāmabhave vā nipphādetabbā ye saṅkhārā, tesaṃ kāmabhavūpapattinibbattakasaṅkhārānanti attho. Paccayo hotīti puññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ tāva ārammaṇapaccayena ceva upanissayapaccayena cāti dvidhā paccayo hoti. Apuññābhisaṅkhāresu sahajātassa sahajātādivasena[M 1.0222], asahajātassa anantarasamanantarādivasena, nānantarassa pana ārammaṇavasena ceva upanissayavasena ca paccayo hoti. Arūpabhave saṅkhārānanti āneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ[V 1.0209]. Paccayo hoti upanissayavaseneva. Imasmiṃ panatthe ettha vitthāriyamāne atippapañco hoti, sayameva ca parato āgamissatīti na naṃ vitthārayāma.

128. Thus, in the text 'because the spokes are struck,' having taken saṃsāra to be a wheel, made the connection of meaning, and now, in order to show it also by the sequence of the teaching on dependent origination, the passage beginning with 'Or else...' was stated. Therein, 'the saṃsāric cycle with an unconceived beginning' means the round of saṃsāra with an unknown end. The remaining ten factors, beginning with formations and ending with birth, are the spokes. How so? Showing that it is because of the connection at the root with ignorance as the hub, and at the end with aging-and-death as the rim, he said: 'because it is rooted in ignorance and ends in aging-and-death.' 'In suffering, etc.' means in the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Therein, ignorance regarding suffering is due to being included within it and due to its concealing nature; regarding the remaining truths, it is only due to its concealing nature. And here, since by 'suffering' the noble truth of suffering is intended, he stated the passage beginning with 'And ignorance in sensual existence...' in order to show in sequence that truth divided threefold by way of sensual existence and so on, and likewise the ignorance that conceals it, and the formations and so on in the three existences which are conditioned by ignorance and so on. Therein, 'ignorance in sensual existence' means the ignorance that conceals the danger in sensual existence. This same method applies also to 'ignorance in the form existence and in the formless existence.' 'Formations in sensual existence' means formations included in the sensual plane, or those formations that are to be produced in sensual existence; the meaning is: for the formations that bring about rebirth in sensual existence. 'It is a condition' means: for meritorious formations, it is a condition in two ways, namely by way of object condition and decisive support condition. Among demeritorious formations, for a co-nascent one, it is a condition by way of co-nascence, etc.; for a non-co-nascent one, by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, etc.; but for a non-contiguous one, it is a condition by way of object and by way of decisive support. 'Formations in the formless existence' means for the imperturbable formations. It is a condition solely by way of decisive support. However, were this meaning to be elaborated upon here, it would become an excessive proliferation; and since it will come later of its own accord, we do not elaborate upon it.

Tiṇṇaṃ āyatanānanti cakkhusotamanāyatanānaṃ. Ekassāyatanassāti manāyatanassa. Iminā nayena phassādīnampi vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha tattha sā sā taṇhāti rūpataṇhādibhedā tattha tattha kāmabhavādīsu uppajjanakā taṇhā.

'Of the three sense bases' means of the eye, ear, and mind bases. 'Of one sense base' means of the mind base. By this method, the division of contact and so on should also be known. 'That very craving in each respective case' means the craving, differentiated as craving for forms and so on, that arises in each respective sensual existence, etc.

Taṇhādimūlikā kathā atisaṃkhittāti taṃ, upādānabhave ca vibhajitvā vitthāretvā dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “kāme paribhuñjissāmī”ti iminā kāmataṇhāpavattimāha. Tathā “saggasampattiṃ anubhavissāmī”tiādīhi. Sā pana taṇhā yasmā bhusamādānavasena pavattamānā kāmupādānaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “kāmupādānapaccayā”ti. Tathevāti kāmupādānapaccayā eva.

The discourse rooted in craving and so on is exceedingly concise; therefore, in order to analyze and elaborate upon it, along with clinging and becoming, and to show it, the passage beginning with 'How...?' was stated. Therein, by the statement 'I will enjoy sensual pleasures,' he indicates the occurrence of craving for sensual pleasures. Likewise with the statements beginning 'I will experience the bliss of heaven.' But since that craving, when it occurs by way of intense grasping, is called 'clinging to sensual pleasures,' it was therefore stated 'conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures.' 'Just so' means: solely conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures.

Brahmalokasampattinti rūpībrahmaloke sampattiṃ. “Sabbepi tebhūmakā dhammā kāmanīyaṭṭhena kāmā”ti (mahāni. 1; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 8 thoka visadisaṃ) vacanato bhavarāgopi kāmupādānamevāti katvā “kāmupādānapaccayā eva mettaṃ bhāvetī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesupādānamūlikāsupīti etthāyaṃ yojanā – idhekacco “natthi paro loko”ti natthikadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti, so diṭṭhupādānapaccayā kāyena duccaritaṃ caratītiādi vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ. Aparo “asukasmiṃ sampattibhave attā ucchijjatī”ti ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti, so tatrūpapattiyā kāyena sucaritaṃ caratītiādi vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Aparo “rūpī manomayo hutvā attā ucchijjatī”ti rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti. Bhāvanāpāripūriyāti sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Aparo “arūpabhave uppajjitvā attā ucchijjatī”ti arūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāveti. Bhāvanāpāripūriyāti sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Etāhiyeva attavādupādānamūlikāpi yojanā saṃvaṇṇitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādavasenāpi [M 1.0223] yojanā veditabbā. Aparo “sīlena suddhī”ti “asuddhimaggaṃ suddhimaggo”ti parāmasanto sīlabbatupādānapaccayā kāyena duccaritaṃ caratītiādinā sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

'Attainment of the Brahma world' means attainment in the form-Brahma-world. In accordance with the text, 'All phenomena of the three realms are "sensual" in the sense of being desirable,' having considered that even the lust for existence is indeed clinging to sensual pleasures, the passage beginning with 'Conditioned solely by clinging to sensual pleasures, he develops loving-kindness...' was stated. Herein, regarding actions rooted in the remaining kinds of clinging, this is the application: Here, someone holds the nihilistic view, thinking, 'There is no other world.' Conditioned by clinging to views, they engage in bodily misconduct, and so on; this should be applied in the manner stated. Another holds the annihilationist view, thinking, 'The self is annihilated in such-and-such a prosperous existence.' For the sake of rebirth there, they practice bodily good conduct, and so on; this should be applied in the very same manner stated. Another, thinking, 'The self, having become possessed of form and mind-made, is annihilated,' develops the path for rebirth in the form realm. Upon the fulfillment of the development, and so on, all should be known in the very same manner stated. Another, thinking, 'The self, having arisen in the formless existence, is annihilated,' develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm. Upon the fulfillment of the development, and so on, all should be known in the very same manner stated. It should be seen that by these very applications, the application rooted in clinging to the doctrine of self has also been explained. Thus, the application should also be known by way of the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life. Another, misapprehending 'Purity comes through virtue' and 'The path of impurity is the path of purity,' and conditioned by clinging to rules and observances, engages in bodily misconduct, and so on; all this should be applied in the very same manner stated.

Idāni yvāyaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ dassentena “kāmabhave avijjā kāmabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hotī”tiādinā [V 1.0210] avijjādīnaṃ paccayabhāvo, saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayuppannabhāvo ca dassito, tameva paṭisambhidāmaggapāḷiṃ ānetvā nigamanavasena dassento “evaṃ aya”ntiādimāha. Tattha yathā saṅkhārā hetunibbattā, evaṃ avijjāpi kāmāsavādinā sahetukā evāti āha “ubhopete hetusamuppannā”ti. Paccayapariggaheti nāmarūpassa paccayānaṃ avijjādīnaṃ paricchijja gahaṇe, nipphādetabbe bhummaṃ. Paññāti kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhisaṅkhātā pakārato jānanā. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti paṭiccasamuppādāvabodho. Idañca dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ yasmā addhāttaye kaṅkhāmalavitaraṇavasena pavattati, tasmā “atītampi addhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Eteneva nayenāti etena “avijjā hetū”tiādinā avijjāyaṃ vuttena nayena. “Saṅkhārā hetu, viññāṇaṃ hetusamuppanna”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.46) sabbapadāni vitthāretabbāni.

Now, as the commentator was showing the cycle of existence, the fact that ignorance and so on are conditions, and the fact that formations and so on are conditionally arisen, was demonstrated with the passage beginning, 'In the sensual existence, ignorance is a condition for formations.' Citing that very passage from the Paṭisambhidāmagga and presenting it by way of a conclusion, he said, 'Thus, this...' and so on. Therein, just as formations are produced from a cause, so too ignorance has a cause through the influx of sensuality and so on; thus he said, 'Both of these are causally arisen.' The phrase `Paccayapariggahe` (in the comprehension of conditions) means in the grasping, having delimited, the conditions of name-and-form, namely ignorance and so on; the locative case here signifies that which is to be accomplished. Wisdom is the knowing in its various aspects, which is designated as the Purification by Overcoming Doubt. Knowledge of the stability of phenomena is the penetrative understanding of dependent origination. And because this knowledge of the stability of phenomena proceeds by way of overcoming the stain of doubt throughout the three periods of time, it is therefore said, 'the past period as well,' and so on. 'By this very method' means by this method stated regarding ignorance, beginning with 'Ignorance is a cause.' All the terms are to be elaborated, beginning with 'Formations are a cause, consciousness is causally arisen' (Paṭi. Ma. 1.46).

Saṃkhippanti ettha avijjādayo, viññāṇādayo cāti saṅkhepo, hetu, vipāko ca. Hetu vipākoti vā saṃkhippatīti saṅkhepo, avijjādayo viññāṇādayo ca. Saṅkhepabhāvasāmaññena pana ekavacanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Te pana saṅkhepā atīte hetu, etarahi vipāko, etarahi hetu, āyatiṃ vipākoti evaṃ kālavibhāgena cattāro jātā. Tenāha “purimasaṅkhepo cettha atīto addhā”tiādi. Saṅkhepa-saddo vā bhāgādhivacananti atīto hetubhāgo paṭhamo saṅkhepo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Taṇhupādānabhavā gahitāva honti kilesakammabhāvasāmaññato, tehi vinā avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ sakiccākaraṇato ca. Kammaṃ taṇhā ca tassa sahakārīkāraṇaṃ hutvā vaṭṭanatthena kammavaṭṭaṃ.

Ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on, are summarized herein; thus, it is a `saṅkhepa` (summary), which comprises cause and result. Or, because it is summarized as 'cause' and 'result', it is a `saṅkhepa`, comprising ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on. It should be understood that the singular form is used due to the common characteristic of being a summary. These summaries, however, become four when divided by time: cause in the past, result in the present, cause in the present, and result in the future. Therefore, it is said, 'The first summary here is the past period,' and so on. Or, the word `saṅkhepa` is a term for a portion; thus, the past cause-portion is the first summary. This is the method for the remaining ones as well. Craving, clinging, and becoming are indeed included, due to their commonality of being defilements and kamma, and because without them, ignorance and formations cannot perform their own function. Kamma, and craving as its cooperative cause, constitute the cycle of kamma (`kammavaṭṭaṃ`) in the sense of revolving.

Viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanānaṃ jātijarābhaṅgāvatthā “jātijarāmaraṇa”nti vuttāti āha “jātijarāmaraṇāpadesena viññāṇādīnaṃ [M 1.0224] niddiṭṭhattā”ti. Imeti viññāṇādayo. Āyatiṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ paccuppannahetuto bhāvīnaṃ anāgatānaṃ gahitattā. Teti avijjādayo. Ākāratoti sarūpato avuttāpi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ saṅgahe ākirīyanti avijjāsaṅkhārādiggahaṇehi pakāsīyantīti ākārā, atītahetuādīnaṃ vā pakārā ākārā, tato ākārato. Vīsatividhā honti atītehetupañcakādibhedato.

Because the states of birth, aging, and breaking up of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are called 'birth, aging, and death,' he said, 'because consciousness and so on are indicated by the designation of birth, aging, and death.' 'These' refers to consciousness and so on. The cycle of result in the future (`āyatiṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ`) is so called because future states that are bound to occur are included on account of the present cause. 'Those' refers to ignorance and so on. As for `ākārato` (by way of modes): although not stated in their own form, they are included in each respective grouping and are revealed by the inclusion of ignorance, formations, and so on; thus they are called 'modes' (`ākārā`). Or, the varieties (`pakārā`) of past causes and so on are 'modes' (`ākārā`); hence `ākārato`. They become twentyfold due to the division into the pentad of past causes and so on.

Saṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ antarā eko sandhīti hetuto phalassa avicchedappavattibhāvato hetuphalasambandhabhūto eko sandhi. Tathā bhavajātīnamantarā. Vedanātaṇhānamantarā pana phalato hetuno [V 1.0211] avicchedappavattibhāvato phalahetusambandhabhūto eko sandhi. Phalabhūtopi hi dhammo aññassa hetusabhāvassa dhammassa paccayo hotīti.

Between formations and consciousness there is one link, which has become the connection between cause and result due to the uninterrupted proceeding of the result from the cause. Similarly, between becoming and birth. Between feeling and craving, however, there is one link, which has become the connection between result and cause due to the uninterrupted proceeding of the cause from the result. For a phenomenon that has become a result is indeed a condition for another phenomenon that has the nature of a cause.

Itīti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Tenāha “catusaṅkhepa”ntiādi. Sabbākāratoti idha vuttehi, avuttehi ca paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅge (vibha. 225 ādayo), anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānādīsu ca āgatehi sabbehi ākārehi. Jānātīti avabujjhati. Passatīti dassanabhūtena ñāṇacakkhunā paccakkhato passati. Aññāti paṭivijjhatīti tesaṃyeva vevacanaṃ. Tanti taṃ jānanaṃ. Ñātaṭṭhenāti yathāsabhāvato jānanaṭṭhena. Pajānanaṭṭhenāti aniccādīhi pakārehi paṭivijjhanaṭṭhena.

`Iti` is a reference to the manner already stated. Therefore, he said, 'the fourfold summary,' and so on. `Sabbākārato` (in all modes) means: with all modes, both those stated and unstated here, and those that have come in the Analysis of Dependent Origination (Vibhaṅga 225 ff.), and in the All-embracing Paṭṭhāna of Infinite Methods, and so on. `Jānāti` (he knows) means he understands. `Passati` (he sees) means he sees directly with the eye of knowledge, which has become vision. `Aññā` (he finally knows) and `paṭivijjhati` (he penetrates) are synonyms for those very terms. `Taṃ` (that) refers to that knowing. `Ñātaṭṭhena` (in the sense of what is known) means in the sense of knowing according to true nature. `Pajānanaṭṭhena` (in the sense of discerning) means in the sense of penetrating through the modes of impermanence and so on.

Idāni yadatthamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ idhānītaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “iminā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha te dhammeti te avijjādike dhamme. Yathābhūtaṃ ñatvāti mahāvajirañāṇena yāthāvato jānitvā. Nibbindanto balavavipassanāya virajjanto vimuccanto ariyamaggehi are hanīti yojanā. Tattha yadā bhagavā virajjati vimuccati, tadā are hanati nāma. Tato paraṃ pana abhisambuddhakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ “hani vihani viddhaṃsesī”ti.

Now, to show for what purpose this wheel of becoming has been brought here, the passage beginning 'By this...' was stated. Therein, 'those states' means those states beginning with ignorance. 'Having known as it really is' means having known accurately with the great diamond-like wisdom. The connection of the words is as follows: becoming disenchanted through powerful insight, becoming dispassionate and liberated through the noble paths, he destroyed the spokes (`are hani`). Therein, when the Blessed One becomes dispassionate and is liberated, then he is said to destroy the spokes. Furthermore, taking the moment of full enlightenment, it was said: 'He destroyed, he utterly destroyed, he demolished.'

129. Cakkavattino acetane cakkaratane uppanne tattheva loko pūjaṃ karoti, aññattha pūjāvisesā pacchijjanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana sammāsambuddhe uppanneti dassento “uppanne tathāgate”tiādimāha. Ko pana vādo aññesaṃ pūjāvisesānanti yathāvuttato aññesaṃ amahesakkhehi devamanussehi kariyamānānaṃ nātiuḷārānaṃ pūjāvisesānaṃ arahabhāve [M 1.0225] kā nāma kathā. Atthānurūpanti arahattatthassa anurūpaṃ anvatthaṃ.

129. When the inanimate wheel-treasure appears for a wheel-turning monarch, the world makes offerings to it right there, and special offerings elsewhere cease. How much more so when a Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen? To show this, he said, 'When the Tathāgata has arisen...' and so on. 'What then is to be said of other special offerings?' This means: apart from the offerings already mentioned, what is there to say about the worthiness of other special offerings, which are not very magnificent and are made by gods and humans of no great power? `Atthānurūpaṃ` (suitable to the meaning) means it is a name suitable for and corresponding to the meaning of Arahantship.

130. Asilokabhayenāti akittibhayena. Raho pāpaṃ karonti “mā naṃ koci jaññā”ti esa bhagavā na kadāci karoti pāpahetūnaṃ bodhimaṇḍe eva suppahīnattā. Aparo nayo – ārakāti arahaṃ, suvidūrabhāvatoicceva attho. Kuto pana suvidūrabhāvatoti? Ye abhāvitakāyā abhāvitasīlā abhāvitacittā abhāvitapaññā, tato eva appahīnarāgadosamohā ariyadhammassa akovidā ariyadhamme avinītā ariyadhammassa adassāvino appaṭipannā micchāpaṭipannā ca, tato suvidūrabhāvato. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

130. `Asilokabhayena` (out of fear of disgrace) means out of fear of ill repute. Just as fools commit evil in secret, thinking, 'Let no one know of it,' this Blessed One never does so, because the causes of evil were thoroughly abandoned by him at the very seat of enlightenment. Another method: because he is 'distant' (`ārakā`), he is an `arahaṃ`; the meaning is simply 'due to being very far removed.' From what is he very far removed? From those whose bodies are undeveloped, whose virtue is undeveloped, whose minds are undeveloped, and whose wisdom is undeveloped; who for that very reason have not abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion; who are unskilled in the Noble Dhamma, untrained in the Noble Dhamma, who do not see the Noble Dhamma, and who are either not practicing or are practicing wrongly—from such persons he is very far removed. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Saṅghāṭikaṇṇecepi [V 1.0212] me, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gahetvā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandho assa pāde pādaṃ nikkhipanto, so ca hoti abhijjhālu kāmesu tibbasārāgo byāpannacitto paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo muṭṭhassati asampajāno asamāhito vibbhantacitto pākatindriyo. Atha kho so ārakāva mayhaṃ, ahañca tassa. Taṃ kissa hetu? Dhammaṃ hi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu na passati, dhammaṃ apassanto maṃ na passatī”ti (itivu. 92).

“Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu, grasping the corner of my outer robe, were to follow along right behind me, placing his foot in my footprint, if he is covetous, with intense passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt mental resolves, with lapsed mindfulness, without clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties, then he is indeed far from me, and I am far from him. For what reason? Because, Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu does not see the Dhamma. Not seeing the Dhamma, he does not see me.”

Yathāvuttapuggalā hi sacepi sāyaṃ pātaṃ satthu santikāvacarāva siyuṃ, na te tāvatā “satthu santikā”ti vattabbā, tathā satthāpi nesaṃ. Iti asappurisānaṃ ārakā dūreti arahaṃ.

Indeed, even if such persons as were described were to frequent the Teacher’s presence morning and evening, they are not, on that account, to be called ‘near the Teacher,’ nor is the Teacher near to them. Thus, because He is far (`ārakā`) from the unvirtuous, He is an `Arahaṃ`.

“Sammā na paṭipajjanti, ye nihīnāsayā narā;

Ārakā tehi bhagavā, dūre tenārahaṃ mato”ti.

“Those people with base intentions who do not practice rightly; the Blessed One is far from them. For that reason, He is considered an ‘Arahaṃ’.”

Tathā ārakāti arahaṃ, āsannabhāvatoti attho. Kuto pana āsannabhāvatoti? Ye bhāvitakāyā bhāvitasīlā bhāvitacittā bhāvitapaññā, tato eva pahīnarāgadosamohā ariyadhammassa kovidā ariyadhamme suvinītā ariyadhammassa dassāvino sammāpaṭipannā, tato āsannabhāvato. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

Similarly, ‘because He is far’ (`ārakā`) He is an `Arahaṃ`; the meaning is ‘because of being near.’ From what, then, is He near? From those whose physical comportment is developed, whose virtue is developed, whose mind is developed, and whose wisdom is developed; who, for that very reason, have abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion; who are skilled in the Noble Dhamma, well-trained in the Noble Dhamma, and who see the Noble Dhamma; who practice rightly—because of being near to them. For this was also said by the Blessed One:

“Yojanasate [M 1.0226] cepi me, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya, so ca hoti anabhijjhālu kāmesu na tibbasārāgo abyāpannacitto appaduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo upaṭṭhitassati sampajāno samāhito ekaggacitto saṃvutindriyo. Atha kho so santikeva mayhaṃ, ahañca tassa. Taṃ kissa hetu? Dhammaṃ hi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu passati, dhammaṃ passanto maṃ passatī”ti (itivu. 92).

“Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to live a hundred yojanas away, if he is not covetous, without intense passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind free of ill will, with uncorrupted mental resolves, with established mindfulness, with clear comprehension, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, and with restrained faculties, then he is indeed near to me, and I am near to him. For what reason? Because, Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu sees the Dhamma. Seeing the Dhamma, he sees me.”

Tathārūpā hi puggalā satthu yojanasahassantarikāpi honti, na tāvatā te “satthu dūracārino”ti vattabbā, tathā satthāpi nesaṃ. Iti sappurisānaṃ ārakā āsanneti arahaṃ.

Indeed, such persons may be a thousand yojanas distant from the Teacher, but they are not, on that account, to be called ‘those who dwell far from the Teacher,’ nor is the Teacher far from them. Thus, because He is near to the virtuous, He is an `Arahaṃ`.

Ye [V 1.0213] sammā paṭipajjanti, suppaṇītādhimuttikā;

Ārakā tehi āsanne, tenāpi arahaṃ jino.

“Those with most excellent resolve who practice rightly; He is near to them. For that reason also, the Victor is an ‘Arahaṃ’.”

Ye ime rāgādayo pāpadhammā yasmiṃ santāne uppajjanti, tassa diṭṭhadhammikampi samparāyikampi anatthaṃ āvahanti. Nibbānagāminiyā paṭipadāya ekaṃseneva ujuvipaccanīkabhūtā ca, te attahitaṃ, parahitañca paripūretuṃ sammā paṭipajjantehi sādhūhi dūrato rahitabbā pariccajitabbā pahātabbāti rahā nāma, te ca yasmā bhagavato bodhimūleyeva ariyamaggena sabbaso pahīnā samucchinnā. Yathāha –

These evil states, such as greed, that arise in one’s continuity bring harm in the present life and in the future life. They are also absolutely and directly opposed to the path leading to Nibbāna. They are to be kept far from, abandoned, and relinquished by the virtuous who practice rightly to fulfill their own welfare and the welfare of others. Therefore, they are called `rahā` (things to be abandoned). And since these were, for the Blessed One, completely abandoned and eradicated by the Noble Path at the very root of the Bodhi tree, as it is said:

“Tathāgatassa kho, brāhmaṇa, rāgo pahīno doso moho, sabbepi pāpakā akusalā dhammā pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā”ti (pārā. 9-10 atthato samānaṃ).

“Brahmin, for the Tathāgata, greed is abandoned, hatred is abandoned, delusion is abandoned. All evil, unwholesome states are abandoned, uprooted, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future.”

Tasmā sabbaso na santi etassa rahāti arahoti vattabbe okārassa sānusāraṃ a-kārādesaṃ katvā “araha”nti vuttaṃ.

Therefore, since for him these `rahā` are entirely absent, when `araho` should be said, having substituted the letter ‘a’ with an anusāra for the letter ‘o’, it is said as `arahaṃ`.

Pāpadhammā rahā nāma, sādhūhi rahitabbato;

Tesaṃ suṭṭhu pahīnattā, bhagavā arahaṃ mato.

“Evil states are called `rahā`, because they are to be abandoned by the virtuous. Because of His thorough abandonment of them, the Blessed One is considered an `Arahaṃ`.”

Ye te sabbaso pariññātakkhandhā pahīnakilesā bhāvitamaggā sacchikatanirodhā arahanto khīṇāsavā, ye ca sekkhā appattamānasā anuttaraṃ [M 1.0227] yogakkhemaṃ patthayamānā viharanti, ye ca parisuddhapayogā kalyāṇajjhāsayā saddhāsīlasutādiguṇasampannā puggalā, tehi na rahitabbo na pariccajitabbo, te ca bhagavatāti arahaṃ. Tathā hi ariyapuggalā satthārā diṭṭhadhammassa paccakkhakaraṇato satthu dhammasarīrena avirahitā eva honti. Yathāha āyasmā piṅgiyo –

Those Arahants with taints destroyed who have completely understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, and realized cessation; and those trainees who have not yet reached their goal and dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage; and those persons of purified application and noble disposition, endowed with the qualities of faith, virtue, learning, and so on—He is not to be abandoned by them, nor are they to be abandoned by the Blessed One; therefore, He is an `Arahaṃ`. For indeed, the noble individuals are not separated from the Teacher's Dhamma-body, due to their direct realization of the Dhamma that has been seen. As the Venerable Piṅgiya said:

“Passāmi naṃ manasā cakkhunāva,

Rattindivaṃ brāhmaṇa appamatto;

Namassamāno [V 1.0214] vivasemi rattiṃ,

Teneva maññāmi avippavāsaṃ.

“I see him with my mind as if with my eye; day and night, O Brahmin, I am heedful. Paying homage, I pass the night; for that reason, I consider myself not separated from him.”

“Saddhā ca pīti ca mano sati ca,

Nāpentime gotamasāsanamhā;

Yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ vajati bhūripañño,

Sa tena teneva natohamasmī”ti. (su. ni. 1148-1149);

“Faith, joy, mind, and mindfulness—these do not depart from Gotama’s Dispensation. To whatever direction the One of Broad Wisdom goes, toward that very direction am I inclined.”

Teneva ca te aññaṃ satthāraṃ na uddisanti. Yathāha –

And for that very reason, they do not designate another as their teacher. As it is said:

“Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.128; a. ni. 1.276).

“Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is not possible, that a person accomplished in view would designate another as his teacher. Such a thing cannot be found.”

Kalyāṇaputhujjanāpi yebhuyyena satthari niccalasaddhā eva honti. Iti suppaṭipannehi purisavisesehi avirahitabbato, tesañca avirahanato na santi etassa rahā pariccajanakā, natthi vā etassa raho sādhūhi pariccajitabbatāti arahaṃ.

Virtuous worldlings, too, for the most part have unshakable faith in the Teacher. Thus, because He is not to be abandoned by these excellent individuals of good practice, and because of their non-abandonment of Him, there are no persons who would abandon Him. Or, there is no abandonment (`raho`) of Him that is to be done by the virtuous. Therefore, He is an `Arahaṃ`.

“Ye sacchikatasaddhammā, ariyā suddhagocarā;

Na tehi rahito hoti, nātho tenārahaṃ mato”ti.

“Those noble ones who have realized the true Dhamma, whose resort is pure; the Protector is not abandoned by them. For that reason, He is considered an `Arahaṃ`.”

Rahoti ca gamanaṃ vuccati, bhagavato ca nānāgatīsu paribbhamanasaṅkhātaṃ saṃsāre gamanaṃ natthi kammakkhayakarena ariyamaggena bodhimūleyeva sabbaso sasambhārassa kammavaṭṭassa viddhaṃsitattā. Yathāha –

`Raho` is also said to mean ‘going.’ For the Blessed One, there is no going in saṃsāra, which is described as wandering through various destinies, because the cycle of kamma, together with its supporting conditions, was completely destroyed by the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of kamma at the very root of the Bodhi tree. As it is said:

“Yena [V 1.0215] devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36);

“That by which there would be rebirth as a deva, or as a gandhabba, or a being that moves through the air; that by which I might reach the state of a yakkha, or return to the human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, annihilated, and made stalk-less.”

Evaṃ [M 1.0228] natthi etassa rahogamanaṃ gatīsu paccājātītipi arahaṃ.

Thus, for him there is no `raho`-going, which is rebirth in the destinies; for this reason also, He is an `Arahaṃ`.

Raho vā gamanaṃ yassa, saṃsāre natthi sabbaso;

Pahīnajātimaraṇo, arahaṃ sugato mato.

Or, for whom there is no secret going in saṃsāra whatsoever, that Well-gone One, having abandoned birth and death, is considered an Arahant.

Pāsaṃsattā vā bhagavā arahaṃ. Akkharacintakā hi pasaṃsāyaṃ araha-saddaṃ vaṇṇenti. Pāsaṃsabhāvo ca bhagavato anaññasādhāraṇo yathābhuccaguṇādhigato sadevake loke suppatiṭṭhito. Tathā hesa anuttarena sīlena anuttarena samādhinā anuttarāya paññāya anuttarāya vimuttiyā asamo asamasamo appaṭimo appaṭibhāgo appaṭipuggaloti evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ guṇe vibhajitvā vuccamāne paṇḍitapurisehi devehi brahmehi bhagavatā vā pana pariyosāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyarūpo. Iti pāsaṃsattāpi bhagavā arahaṃ.

Or, the Blessed One is an Arahant because of being worthy of praise. Indeed, grammarians explain the word 'araha' in the sense of praise. And the state of being worthy of praise of the Blessed One is not shared with other individuals, is attained through genuine qualities, and is well-established in the world with its devas. For He is incomparable, equal only to the unequaled, without peer, without counterpart, and without rival through unsurpassed virtue, unsurpassed concentration, unsurpassed wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation. Thus, when each of these qualities is analyzed and spoken of by wise men, devas, brahmās, or even by the Blessed One himself, it is of such a nature that it cannot be brought to a conclusion. Therefore, the Blessed One is also an Arahant because of being worthy of praise.

Guṇehi sadiso natthi, yasmā loke sadevake;

Tasmā pāsaṃsiyattāpi, arahaṃ dvipaduttamo.

Because there is no one equal in virtues in the world with its devas, therefore, also because of being worthy of praise, the Supreme among two-legged beings is an Arahant.

Evaṃ sabbathāpi –

Thus, in all respects—

“Ārakā mandabuddhīnaṃ, ārakā ca vijānataṃ;

Rahānaṃ suppahīnattā, vidūnamaraheyyato;

Bhavesu ca rahābhāvā, pāsaṃsā arahaṃ jino”ti.

“Far from those of dull intellect, and near to the wise; because the ‘rahas’ (unwholesome states) are well abandoned, and because He is not to be abandoned by the wise; and because there is no ‘raha’ (going) in states of existence, and because He is worthy of praise, the Conqueror is an Arahant.”

131. Sammāti aviparītaṃ. Sāmanti sayameva. Sambuddhoti hi ettha saṃ-saddo “saya”nti etassa atthassa bodhako daṭṭhabbo. Sabbadhammānanti anavasesānaṃ ñeyyadhammānaṃ. Kathaṃ panettha sabbadhammāvabodho [V 1.0216] labbhatīti? Ekadesassa aggahaṇato. Padesaggahaṇe hi asati gahetabbassa nippadesatāva viññāyati yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti. Evañca katvā atthavisesānapekkhā kattari eva buddhasaddasiddhi veditabbā kammavacanicchāya abhāvato. “Sammā sāmaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddho”ti ettakameva hi idha saddato labbhati, “sabbadhammāna”nti pana atthato labbhamānaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Na hi bujjhanakiriyā avisayā yujjati.

131. ‘Sammā’ means correctly. ‘Sāmaṃ’ means by oneself. Indeed, here in ‘Sambuddho’, the prefix ‘saṃ-’ should be understood as indicating the meaning of ‘sayaṃ’ (by oneself). ‘Sabbadhammānaṃ’ refers to all knowable phenomena without remainder. How, then, is the understanding of all phenomena obtained here? By not taking a part. For when there is no taking of a part, the partlessness of what is to be taken is understood, just as in the phrase, ‘The consecrated one does not give.’ For this reason, the derivation of the word ‘buddha’ should be understood as being in the agent sense only, without regard to a specific object, because of the absence of the desire to express the object. Indeed, ‘Because He has awakened correctly and by Himself, He is Sammāsambuddho’—only this much is obtained from the word itself. However, ‘sabbadhammānaṃ’ is stated by taking what is obtained from the meaning. For the act of awakening is not suitable without an object.

Idāni [M 1.0229] tassā visayaṃ “sabbadhamme”ti sāmaññato vuttaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “abhiññeyye dhamme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha abhiññeyyeti abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena jānitabbe. Ke pana teti? Catusaccadhamme. Abhiññeyyato buddhoti abhiññeyyabhāvato bujjhi. Pubbabhāge vipassanāpaññāya, adhigamakkhaṇe maggapaññāya, aparabhāge sabbaññutaññāṇādīhi aññāsīti attho. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Pariññeyye dhammeti dukkhaṃ ariyasaccamāha. Pahātabbeti samudayapakkhiye. Sacchikātabbeti nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Bahuvacananiddeso pana sopādisesādikaṃ pariyāyasiddhaṃ bhedaṃ gahetvā kato, uddeso vā ayaṃ catusaccadhammānanti. Tathā hi vakkhati “cakkhuṃ dukkhasacca”ntiādi. Uddeso ca avinicchitatthaparicchedassa dhammassa vasena karīyati. Uddesena hi uddisiyamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthitāmattaṃ vuccati, na paricchedoti aparicchedena bahuvacanena vuttaṃ yathā “appaccayā dhammā, asaṅkhatā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 7-8). Sacchikātabbeti vā phalavimuttīnampi gahaṇaṃ, na nibbānassevāti bahuvacananiddeso kato. Evañca bhāvetabbeti ettha jhānānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Now, to show in detail its object, which was stated generally as ‘all phenomena’, the passage beginning ‘the phenomena to be directly known’ is stated. Therein, ‘to be directly known’ means to be known with distinguished knowledge. What are they? The phenomena of the Four Truths. ‘He awakened from what is to be directly known’ means He awakened because of the state of being what is to be directly known. The meaning is: in the preliminary stage, He knew through insight-wisdom; at the moment of attainment, through path-wisdom; in the subsequent stage, through the knowledge of omniscience and so forth. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. ‘Phenomena to be fully understood’ refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering. ‘To be abandoned’ refers to those things on the side of the origin. ‘To be realized’ is said in reference to Nibbāna. The plural designation, however, is made by taking the distinctions established by way of synonyms, such as ‘with residue remaining,’ etc.; or this is a summary statement of the phenomena of the Four Truths. For it will be said later, ‘The eye is the truth of suffering,’ and so forth. A summary statement is made with respect to a phenomenon whose meaning and scope have not been determined. For by a summary statement, only the existence of the summarized phenomena is stated, not their scope; therefore, it is stated in the plural without specification, as in ‘unconditioned phenomena, uncompounded phenomena.’ Or, the plural designation is made because ‘to be realized’ includes the fruitions and liberations, not just Nibbāna. And thus, in ‘to be developed’, the inclusion of the jhānas should be understood.

Gāthāyaṃ bhāvetabbañcāti ettha ca-saddo avuttasamuccayattho, tena sacchikātabbassa gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tasmā buddhosmīti yasmā cattāri saccāni mayā buddhāni, saccavinimuttañca kiñci ñeyyaṃ natthi, tasmā sabbampi ñeyyaṃ buddhosmi, abbhaññāsinti attho.

In the verse, in the word ‘bhāvetabbañca’, the particle ‘ca’ has the meaning of collecting what has not been stated; by it, the inclusion of what is ‘to be realized’ should be understood. Therefore, ‘buddhosmi’ (I am awakened) has this meaning: ‘Because the four truths have been awakened to by me, and there is nothing knowable apart from the truths, therefore I am one who has awakened to all that is knowable; I have directly known.’

132. Evaṃ saccavasena sāmaññato vuttamatthaṃ dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattadhammehi, khandhādīhi ca saccavaseneva vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “api cā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha mūlakāraṇabhāvenāti santesupi avijjādīsu aññesu kāraṇesu tesampi mūlabhūtakāraṇabhāvena. Taṇhā hi kammassa vicittabhāvahetuto, sahāyabhāvūpagamanato ca dukkhavicittatāya padhānakāraṇaṃ. Samuṭṭhāpikāti uppādikā. Purimataṇhāti purimabhavasiddhā taṇhā. Ubhinnanti cakkhussa[V 1.0217], taṃsamudayassa ca. Appavattīti appavattinimittaṃ. Nirodhapajānanāti sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena nirodhassa paṭivijjhanā. Ekekapaduddhārenāti “cakkhuṃ cakkhusamudayo”tiādinā ekekakoṭṭhāsaniddhāraṇena[M 1.0230]. Taṇhāyapi pariññeyyabhāvasabbhāvato, upādānakkhandhantogadhattā ca dukkhasaccasaṅgahaṃ dassetuṃ “rūpataṇhādayo cha taṇhākāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

132. Thus, to show in detail—by way of the truths themselves—the meaning stated generally by way of the truths, in terms of the doors and objects, the phenomena occurring at the doors, and the aggregates, etc., the passage beginning ‘api ca’ is commenced. Therein, ‘by way of being the root cause’ means: even though there are other causes such as ignorance, etc., it is the root cause of even those. For craving, being the cause for the diversity of kamma, is the principal cause for the diversity of suffering. ‘Samuṭṭhāpikā’ means that which gives rise. ‘Purimataṇhā’ refers to craving established in a previous existence. ‘Ubhinnanti’ refers to both the eye and its origin. ‘Appavattīti’ means the cause for non-arising. ‘Nirodhapajānanā’ means the penetration of cessation by way of the act of realization and direct understanding. ‘Ekekapaduddhārenāti’ means by the specification of each single part, such as ‘the eye, the origin of the eye,’ and so forth. To show the inclusion of craving in the truth of suffering—because it has the nature of being something to be fully understood and because it is included within the aggregates of clinging—it is said, ‘the six bodies of craving, beginning with craving for forms.’

Kasiṇānīti kasiṇajjhānāni. Dvattiṃsākārāti dvattiṃsa koṭṭhāsā, tadārammaṇajjhānāni ca. Nava bhavāti kāmabhavādayo tayo, saññībhavādayo tayo, ekavokārabhavādayo tayoti nava bhavā. Cattāri jhānānīti aggahitārammaṇavisesāni cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni, vipākajjhānānaṃ vā etaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Ettha ca kusaladhammānaṃ upanissayabhūtā taṇhā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhāti veditabbā. Kiriyadhammānaṃ pana yattha te tassa attabhāvassa kāraṇabhūtā.

‘Kasiṇānīti’ refers to the kasiṇa jhānas. ‘Dvattiṃsākārāti’ means the thirty-two parts and the jhānas that have them as their object. ‘Nava bhavāti’ refers to the nine states of existence: the three beginning with the sense-sphere existence, the three beginning with the existence with perception, and the three beginning with the one-constituent existence. ‘Cattāri jhānānīti’ refers to the four form-sphere jhānas with their specific, unapprehended objects, or this is the inclusion of the resultant jhānas. And here, for wholesome states, the craving that is their decisive support condition should be understood as ‘samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā’. As for functional states, however, the craving that is the cause of the individual existence wherein they arise is to be understood as such.

Anubuddhoti bujjhitabbadhammassa anurūpato buddho. Tenāti tasmā. Yasmā sāmaññato, visesato ca ekekapaduddhārena sabbadhamme buddho, tasmā vuttaṃ. Kinti āha “sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā”ti, sabbassapi ñeyyassa sabbākārato aviparītaṃ sayameva abhisambuddhattāti attho. Imināssa paropadesarahitassa sabbākārena sabbadhammāvabodhanasamatthassa ākaṅkhappaṭibaddhavuttino anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa adhigamo dassito.

‘Anubuddha’ means one who has awakened suitably to the dhamma that should be known. ‘Tena’ means therefore. Because he has awakened to all dhammas both generally and specifically through the elucidation of each single term, therefore it is said. What is it? He said, ‘due to having been rightly and by himself awakened to all dhammas,’ the meaning of which is: due to having fully awakened by himself without error to all that is knowable in every aspect. By this is shown the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience—designated as unobstructed knowledge—which is without the instruction of another, is capable of comprehending all dhammas in every way, and whose operation is dependent on his will.

Nanu ca sabbaññutaññāṇato aññaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ, aññathā “cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni buddhañāṇānī”ti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.73) vacanaṃ virujjheyyāti? Na virujjhati, visayapavattibhedavasena aññehi asādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ ekasseva ñāṇassa dvidhā vuttattā. Ekameva hi taṃ ñāṇaṃ anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutidhammavisayatāya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha ca āvaraṇābhāvato nissaṅgacāramupādāya “anāvaraṇañāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Yathāha paṭisambhidāyaṃ “sabbaṃ saṅkhatamasaṅkhataṃ anavasesaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇa”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.119). Tasmā natthi nesaṃ atthato bhedo, ekantena cetaṃ evamicchitabbaṃ. Aññathā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇānaṃ sādhāraṇatā, asabbadhammārammaṇatā ca āpajjeyya. Na hi bhagavato ñāṇassa aṇumattampi āvaraṇaṃ atthi, anāvaraṇañāṇassa ca asabbadhammārammaṇabhāve yattha taṃ na pavattati, tatthāvaraṇasabbhāvato anāvaraṇabhāvoyeva na siyā. Atha vā pana hotu [M 1.0231] aññameva anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇato, idha pana sabbattha appaṭihatavuttitāya [V 1.0218] anāvaraṇañāṇanti sabbaññutaññāṇameva adhippetaṃ. Tassa cādhigamena bhagavā “sabbaññū, sabbavidū, sammāsambuddho”ti ca vuccati na sakiṃyeva sabbadhammāvabodhato. Tathā ca vuttaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.162) “vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ “buddho”ti. Sabbadhammāvabodhanasamatthañāṇasamadhigamena hi bhagavato santāne anavasesadhamme paṭivijjhituṃ samatthatā ahosīti.

Is it not that unobstructed knowledge is different from the knowledge of omniscience? Otherwise, the statement, ‘The six unshared knowledges are the Buddha’s knowledges,’ would be contradicted. It is not contradicted, because one and the same knowledge is spoken of in two ways for the purpose of showing its unshared nature with others, by way of the difference in its operation regarding its objects. For that one and the same knowledge is called the ‘knowledge of omniscience’ because its object is all conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional dhammas without remainder; and it is called ‘unobstructed knowledge’ on account of its unimpeded functioning, due to the absence of obstruction therein. As it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘He knows all that is conditioned and unconditioned without remainder, thus it is the knowledge of omniscience. Therein there is no obstruction, thus it is unobstructed knowledge,’ and so on. Therefore, there is no difference between them in terms of their intrinsic nature, and this should be accepted definitively in this way. Otherwise, it would follow that the knowledge of omniscience would have obstructions and the unobstructed knowledge would not have all dhammas as its object. For there is not even an atom's worth of obstruction to the Blessed One’s knowledge; and if unobstructed knowledge did not have all dhammas as its object, then wherever it does not operate, due to the presence of an obstruction there, its very nature of being unobstructed would not exist. Or, alternatively, let unobstructed knowledge indeed be different from the knowledge of omniscience. But here, ‘unobstructed knowledge’ is intended to mean precisely the knowledge of omniscience, because of its unimpeded operation everywhere. And it is through the attainment of this that the Blessed One is called ‘Omniscient,’ ‘All-knowing,’ and ‘Perfectly Self-Awakened,’ and not because of comprehending all dhammas all at once. And so it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘This designation, “Buddha,” is the culmination of liberation for the Blessed Buddhas, a designation made manifest at the root of the Bodhi tree simultaneously with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience.’ For through the attainment of knowledge capable of comprehending all dhammas, the capability to penetrate all dhammas without remainder arose in the Blessed One’s mental continuum.

Etthāha – kiṃ panidaṃ ñāṇaṃ pavattamānaṃ sakiṃyeva sabbasmiṃ visaye pavattati, udāhu kamenāti? Kiñcettha – yadi tāva sakiṃyeva sabbasmiṃ visaye pavattati, atītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhādibhedabhinnānaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ, asaṅkhatasammutidhammānañca ekajjhaṃ upaṭṭhāne dūrato cittapaṭaṃ pekkhantassa viya paṭivibhāgenāvabodho na siyā, tathā ca sati “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti vipassantānaṃ anattākārena viya sabbadhammā anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇassa visayā hontīti āpajjati. Yepi “sabbañeyyadhammānaṃ ṭhitalakkhaṇavisayaṃ vikapparahitaṃ sabbakālaṃ buddhānaṃ ñāṇaṃ pavattati, tena te ‘sabbavidū’ti vuccanti, evañca katvā ‘caraṃ samāhito nāgo, tiṭṭhantopi samāhito’ti idampi vacanaṃ suvuttaṃ hotī”ti vadanti, tesampi vuttadosānātivatti, ṭhitalakkhaṇārammaṇatāya ca atītānāgatasammutidhammānaṃ tadabhāvato ekadesavisayameva bhagavato ñāṇaṃ siyā. Tasmā sakiṃyeva ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti na yujjati.

Here it is asked: Does this knowledge, when it arises, operate on every object all at once, or does it operate sequentially? In this regard, if it operates on every object all at once, then when conditioned dhammas—divided into past, future, present, internal, external, and so on—and unconditioned and conventional dhammas are present all together, there would be no comprehension with detailed distinction, like one looking at a colorful cloth from afar. And if that were so, it would follow that, just as for those practicing insight meditation that ‘all dhammas are non-self’ all dhammas appear with the characteristic of non-self, so too all dhammas would be objects for the Blessed One's knowledge in an undifferentiated form.
