Even for those who say, ‘The knowledge of the Buddhas operates at all times, without conceptualization, having as its object the static characteristic of all knowable dhammas; therefore, they are called “all-knowing.” And for this reason, this statement, “The Nāga is composed while walking, composed also while standing,” is well-spoken’—their view also does not overcome the aforesaid fault. And because its object is the static characteristic, and since past, future, and conventional dhammas lack that, the Blessed One's knowledge would have only a partial object. Therefore, the view that the knowledge operates all at once is not tenable.

Atha kamena sabbasmiṃ visaye ñāṇaṃ pavattati? Evampi na yujjati. Na hi jātibhūmisabhāvādivasena, disādesakālādivasena ca anekabhedabhinne ñeyye kamena gayhamāne tassa anavasesapaṭivedho sambhavati, apariyantabhāvato ñeyyassa. Ye pana “atthassa avisaṃvādanato ñeyyassa ekadesaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā ‘sesepi eva’nti adhimuccitvā vavatthāpanena sabbaññū bhagavā, tañca ñāṇaṃ na anumānikaṃ saṃsayābhāvato. Saṃsayānubaddhaṃ hi loke anumānañāṇa”nti vadanti, tesampi taṃ na yuttaṃ. Sabbassa hi appaccakkhabhāve atthāvisaṃvādanena ñeyyassa ekadesaṃ paccakkhaṃ [M 1.0232] katvā “sesepi eva”nti adhimuccitvā vavatthāpanassa asambhavato. Yañhi taṃ sesaṃ, taṃ appaccakkhanti.

Then does the knowledge operate sequentially on every object? This too is not tenable. For when the knowable—which is divided into numerous distinctions by way of birth, plane, intrinsic nature, etc., and by way of direction, location, time, etc.—is being grasped sequentially, a complete penetration of it is not possible, because of the limitless nature of the knowable. As for those who say, ‘The Blessed One is omniscient by way of determination, having directly perceived a part of the knowable and, due to the infallibility regarding the meaning, resolving, “The rest is also thus.” And that knowledge is not inferential, due to the absence of doubt. For in the world, inferential knowledge is accompanied by doubt’—their view is also not correct. For when the whole is not directly perceived, it is impossible to make a determination by directly perceiving a part of the knowable through infallibility regarding the meaning and resolving, ‘The rest is also thus.’ For that which is the rest is not directly perceived.

Atha tampi paccakkhaṃ, tassa sesabhāvo eva na siyāti? Sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Kasmā[V 1.0219]? Avisayavicāraṇabhāvato. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ bhagavatā “buddhavisayo, bhikkhave, acinteyyo na cintetabbo. Yo cinteyya, ummādassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti (a. ni. 4.77). Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – yaṃkiñci bhagavatā ñātuṃ icchitaṃ sakalaṃ, ekadeso vā, tattha appaṭihatavuttitāya paccakkhato ñāṇaṃ pavattati, niccasamādhānañca vikkhepābhāvato. Ñātuṃ icchitassa ca sakalassa avisayabhāve tassa ākaṅkhappaṭibaddhavuttitā na siyā, ekanteneva sā icchitabbā “sabbe dhammā buddhassa bhagavato āvajjanappaṭibaddhā ākaṅkhappaṭibaddhā manasikārappaṭibaddhā cittuppādappaṭibaddhā”ti vacanato. Atītānāgatavisayampi bhagavato ñāṇaṃ anumānāgamatakkaggahaṇavirahitattā paccakkhameva.

Alternatively, if that remainder were also directly perceived, would its very state as a remainder not cease to be? All this is not a valid reason. Why? Because it is a deliberation on what is not the proper domain. For this was said by the Blessed One: “The domain of a Buddha, monks, is inconceivable, not to be deliberated upon. Whoever should deliberate upon it would partake of madness and vexation.” Herein, this is the firm conclusion: Whatever the Blessed One wished to know, whether in whole or in part, therein his knowledge operates by direct perception due to its unobstructed functioning, and there is constant concentration due to the absence of distraction. And if the entirety of what is wished to be known were not its domain, its functioning would not be bound to aspiration. That functioning is certainly to be accepted, according to the saying: “All phenomena are bound to the adverting, bound to the aspiration, bound to the attention, bound to the arising of thought of the Buddha, the Blessed One.” Even the Blessed One's knowledge concerning past and future objects is indeed direct perception, because it is devoid of being grasped through inference, scripture, or reasoning.

Nanu ca etasmiṃ pakkhe yadā sakalaṃ ñātuṃ icchitaṃ, tadā sakiṃyeva sakalavisayatāya anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavatteyyāti vuttadosānātivattiyevāti? Na, tassa visodhitattā. Visodhito hi so buddhavisayo acinteyyoti. Aññathā pacurajanañāṇasamānavuttitāya buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ ñāṇassa acinteyyatā na siyā. Tasmā sakaladhammārammaṇampi taṃ ekadhammārammaṇaṃ viya suvavatthāpiteyeva te dhamme katvā pavattatīti idamettha acinteyyaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Ñeyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇapariyantikaṃ ñeyya”nti (mahāni. 69; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5). Evamekajjhaṃ, visuṃ, sakiṃ, kamena vā icchānurūpaṃ sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddho.

Is it not that in this position, when it is wished to know the whole, the Blessed One's knowledge would then operate at once in an undefined manner due to having the whole as its object, and thus the aforesaid fault would not be overcome? No, because that fault has been cleared away. Indeed, that fault has been cleared away by the statement, 'The domain of a Buddha is inconceivable.' Otherwise, due to its functioning being similar to the knowledge of the multitude, the inconceivability of the knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would not be. Therefore, even though it has all phenomena as its object, that knowledge operates by having well-defined those phenomena, as if it had a single phenomenon as its object. This is what is inconceivable herein. And this was said: “As far as the knowable extends, so far does knowledge extend. As far as knowledge extends, so far does the knowable extend. Knowledge is limited by the knowable; the knowable is limited by knowledge.” Thus, because of having rightly and by himself known all phenomena—whether all together, separately, at once, or sequentially, in accordance with his wish—he is a Sammāsambuddha.

133. Vijjāhīti ettha vindiyaṃ vindatīti vijjā, yāthāvato upalabbhatīti attho. Attano vā paṭipakkhassa vijjhanaṭṭhena vijjā, tamokkhandhādikassa padālanaṭṭhenāti attho. Tato eva attano visayassa viditakaraṇaṭṭhenapi vijjā. Sampannattāti samannāgatattā, paripuṇṇattā vā, avikalattāti attho. Tissannaṃ, aṭṭhannaṃ ca vijjānaṃ tattha tattha sutte gahaṇaṃ vineyyajjhāsayavasenāti [M 1.0233] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Satta saddhammā nāma saddhā hirī ottappaṃ bāhusaccaṃ vīriyaṃ sati paññā ca. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ “idha bhikkhu saddho hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 10.11). Cattāri jhānānīti yāni kānici cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni.

133. Herein, regarding `vijjāhi`: because it finds what is to be found (`vindiyaṃ`), it is `vijjā` (knowledge); the meaning is, it is obtained as it really is. Or, it is `vijjā` in the sense of piercing its own opposite; the meaning is, in the sense of splitting the mass of darkness, etc. For that very reason, it is also `vijjā` in the sense of making its own object known. ‘Because of being endowed’ (`sampannattā`) means because of being possessed of (`samannāgatattā`), or complete (`paripuṇṇattā`), and without deficiency (`avikalattā`); this is the meaning. It should be understood that the taking up of the three and eight knowledges in various suttas is according to the disposition of those to be trained. The seven qualities of a good person (`saddhammā`) are faith, moral shame, moral dread, great learning, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom. With reference to these it was said: “Here, a bhikkhu is faithful,” and so on. 'The four jhānas' means whichever four form-sphere jhānas.

Kasmā panettha sīlādayo pannaraseva “caraṇa”nti vuttāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “imeyeva hī”tiādi[V 1.0220]. Tena tesaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahato nibbānupagamane ekaṃsato sādhanabhāvamāha. Idāni tadatthasādhanāya āgamaṃ dassento “yathāhā”tiādimāha. Bhagavātiādi vuttassevatthassa nigamanavasena vuttaṃ.

With reference to the objection, 'Why are only the fifteen factors beginning with virtue called “conduct” herein?', he says, 'Because these very ones…' and so on. By this, he states their nature as a certain means for the attainment of Nibbāna, due to their inclusion in the threefold training. Now, to demonstrate the scriptural authority for that meaning, he says, 'As it is said…' and so on. The phrase 'The Blessed One…' and so on is stated by way of a conclusion for the meaning that has already been stated.

Nanu cāyaṃ vijjācaraṇasampadā sāvakesupi labbhatīti? Kiñcāpi labbhati, na pana tathā, yathā bhagavatoti dassetuṃ “tattha vijjāsampadā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Caraṇadhammapariyāpannattā karuṇābrahmavihārassa, so cettha mahaggatabhāvappattā sādhāraṇabhāvoti āha “caraṇasampadā mahākāruṇikataṃ pūretvā ṭhitā”ti. Yathā sattānaṃ anatthaṃ parivajjetvā atthe niyojanaṃ paññāya vinā na hoti, evaṃ nesaṃ atthānatthajānanaṃ satthu karuṇāya vinā na hotīti ubhayampi ubhayattha sakiccakameva siyā. Yattha pana yassā padhānabhāvo, taṃ dassetuṃ “so sabbaññutāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā taṃ vijjācaraṇasampannoti yathā aññopi vijjācaraṇasampanno, tena vijjācaraṇasampannassevāyaṃ āveṇikā paṭipattīti dasseti. Sā panāyaṃ satthu vijjācaraṇasampadā sāsanassa niyyānikatāya sāvakānaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā ekantakāraṇanti dassetuṃ “tenassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

Is it not that this accomplishment in knowledge and conduct is found in disciples too? Although it is found, it is not in the same way as it is in the Blessed One. To show this, it is said, 'Herein, the accomplishment in knowledge…' and so on. Because the divine abiding of compassion is included in the qualities of conduct, and because it here has the unique nature of having reached the sublime state, he says, 'The accomplishment in conduct stands, having fulfilled great compassion.' Just as engaging beings in their welfare, having avoided what is not their welfare, does not happen without wisdom, so too their knowing of welfare and non-welfare does not happen without the Teacher's compassion. Thus, both have their own function in both respects. But to show which is predominant where, it is said, 'He, through omniscience…' and so on. Therein, 'as one accomplished in knowledge and conduct' means 'just as another is accomplished in knowledge and conduct'; by this he shows that this is the unique practice of one accomplished in knowledge and conduct alone. Furthermore, to show that this accomplishment in knowledge and conduct of the Teacher is the sole cause for the disciples' right practice, due to the teaching's quality of leading out, it is said, 'Therefore, for him…' and so on. That is easy to understand.

Ettha ca vijjāsampadāya satthu paññāmahattaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti, caraṇasampadāya karuṇāmahattaṃ. Tesu paññāya bhagavato dhammarajjappatti, karuṇāya dhammasaṃvibhāgo. Paññāya saṃsāradukkhanibbidā, karuṇāya saṃsāradukkhasahanaṃ. Paññāya paradukkhaparijānanaṃ, karuṇāya paradukkhapatikārārambho. Paññāya parinibbānābhimukhabhāvo, karuṇāya tadadhigamo. Paññāya sayaṃ taraṇaṃ, karuṇāya paresaṃ tāraṇaṃ. Paññāya buddhabhāvasiddhi, karuṇāya buddhakiccasiddhi. Karuṇāya vā bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ saṃsārābhimukhabhāvo, paññāya tattha anabhirati. Tathā karuṇāya paresaṃ abhiṃsāpanaṃ[M 1.0234], paññāya sayaṃ parehi abhāyanaṃ. Karuṇāya paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati, paññāya attānaṃ rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati. Tathā karuṇāya aparantapo, paññāya anattantapo. Tena attahitāya paṭipannādīsu catūsu puggalesu catutthapuggalabhāvo siddho hoti. Tathā karuṇāya lokanāthatā, paññāya attanāthatā. Karuṇāya cassa ninnatābhāvo, paññāya unnamābhāvo. Tathā karuṇāya sabbasattesu janitānuggaho paññānugatattā na ca na sabbattha virattacitto, paññāya sabbadhammesu virattacitto karuṇānugatattā na ca na sabbasattānuggahāya pavatto. Yathā hi karuṇā bhagavato sinehasokavirahitā, evaṃ paññā ahaṃkāramamaṃkāravinimuttāti [V 1.0221] aññamaññavisodhitā paramavisuddhā guṇavisesā vijjācaraṇasampadāhi pakāsitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And here, by the accomplishment of knowledge, the Teacher's greatness of wisdom is revealed; by the accomplishment of conduct, the greatness of compassion. Among them, by wisdom, the Blessed One's attainment of the sovereignty of the Dhamma is revealed; by compassion, the distribution of the Dhamma. By wisdom, there is disenchantment with the suffering of saṃsāra; by compassion, endurance of the suffering of saṃsāra. By wisdom, there is full understanding of the suffering of others; by compassion, the undertaking to remedy the suffering of others. By wisdom, there is the state of facing towards Parinibbāna; by compassion, its attainment. By wisdom, he crosses over himself; by compassion, he causes others to cross over. By wisdom, the accomplishment of Buddhahood is achieved; by compassion, the accomplishment of a Buddha's duties. Or, by compassion, in the stage of a bodhisatta, there is the state of facing towards saṃsāra; by wisdom, there is no delight in it. Likewise, by compassion, he does not cause harm to others; by wisdom, he himself does not fear others. By compassion, while protecting others he protects himself; by wisdom, while protecting himself he protects others. Thus, by compassion, he does not torment others; by wisdom, he does not torment himself. Thereby, among the four types of individuals, such as the one practicing for his own welfare, the state of being the fourth type of individual is accomplished. Likewise, by compassion, there is the state of being a refuge for the world; by wisdom, the state of being one's own refuge. By compassion, there is no lowliness in him; by wisdom, no haughtiness. Thus, by compassion, helpfulness is generated towards all beings, and because it is accompanied by wisdom, his mind is indeed detached everywhere. By wisdom, his mind is detached from all phenomena, and because it is accompanied by compassion, he is indeed engaged for the welfare of all beings. For just as the Blessed One’s compassion is devoid of affection and sorrow, so his wisdom is freed from 'I-making' and 'mine-making.' Thus, it should be understood that these special qualities, purified by each other and exceedingly pure, are revealed by the accomplishments of knowledge and conduct.

134. Gamanampi hi gatanti vuccati “gate ṭhite”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.214; 2.376). Sobhananti subhaṃ. Subhabhāvo visuddhatāya, visuddhatā dosavigamenāti āha “parisuddhamanavajja”nti. Gamanañca nāma bahuvidhanti idhādhippetaṃ gamanaṃ dassento “ariyamaggo”ti āha. So hi nibbānassa gati adhigamoti katvā “gataṃ, gamana”nti ca vuccati. Idāni tasseva gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “tena hesā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Khemaṃ disanti nibbānaṃ. Asajjamānoti paripanthābhāvena sugatigamanepi asajjanto saṅgaṃ akaronto, pageva itarattha. Atha vā ekāsane nisīditvā khippabhiññāvaseneva catunnampi maggānaṃ paṭiladdhabhāvato asajjamāno asajjanto gato. Yaṃ gamanaṃ gacchanto sabbamanatthaṃ apaharati, sabbañca anuttaraṃ sampattiṃ āvahati, tadeva sobhanaṃ nāma. Tena ca bhagavā gatoti āha “iti sobhanagamanattā sugato”ti sobhanattho su-saddoti katvā.

134. For 'going' (gamana) is also called 'gone' (gata), as in such phrases as 'when gone, when standing.' 'Beautiful' (sobhana) means auspicious (subha). The state of being auspicious is due to purity, and purity is due to the removal of faults; therefore, it is said to be 'utterly pure and blameless.' And since 'going' is of many kinds, showing the 'going' intended here, he said, 'the Noble Path.' For that path is the way to Nibbāna, the attainment of it; therefore, it is called 'gone' and 'going.' Now, to show the reason for taking this very meaning, 'Therefore, this...' and so on was said. 'The secure direction' means Nibbāna. 'Not clinging' means, due to the absence of obstacles, not becoming attached even when going to a good destination, making no attachment; how much more so in other cases. Or alternatively, having sat down in one sitting, by the power of swift direct knowledge alone, he went without clinging, without getting stuck, because of having attained all four paths. That very going, by which one who goes removes all that is unbeneficial and brings all unsurpassed attainment, is what is called 'beautiful.' And the Blessed One has gone by that going; therefore, because the word 'su' has the meaning 'beautiful', it is said: 'Thus, because of his beautiful going, he is Sugata'.

Asundarānaṃ dukkhānaṃ saṅkhārappavattīnaṃ abhāvato accantasukhattā ekantato sundaraṃ nāma asaṅkhatā dhātūti āha “sundarañcesa ṭhānaṃ gato amataṃ nibbāna”nti. Tenāha bhagavā “nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (ma. ni. 2.215; dha. pa. 203-204). Sammāti suṭṭhu. Suṭṭhu gamanañca nāma paṭipakkhena anabhibhūtassa gamananti āha “pahīne kilese puna apaccāgacchanto”ti. Idañca sikhāppattaṃ sammāgamanaṃ, yāya āgamanīyapaṭipadāya siddhaṃ, sāpi sammāgamanamevāti evampi [M 1.0235] bhagavā sugatoti dassetuṃ “sammā vā gato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sammāpaṭipattiyāti sammāsambodhiyā sampāpane aviparītapaṭipattiyā. “Sabbalokassa hitasukhameva karonto”ti etena mahābodhiyā paṭipadā avibhāgena sabbasattānaṃ sabbadā hitasukhāvahabhāveneva pavattatīti dasseti. “Sassataṃ ucchedanti ime ante anupagacchanto gato”ti etena paṭiccasamuppādagatiṃ dasseti. “Kāmasukhaṃ attakilamathanti ime anupagacchanto gato”ti etena ariyamaggagatiṃ dasseti.

Because of the absence of un-beautiful, painful, conditioned processes, and because of its nature as ultimate bliss, the unconditioned element is called 'absolutely beautiful.' Therefore, it is said: 'He has gone to this beautiful place, the deathless, Nibbāna.' For that reason, the Blessed One said: 'Nibbāna is the highest bliss.' 'Rightly' (sammā) means 'perfectly' (suṭṭhu). And 'perfect going' is the going of one who is not overcome by opposition; therefore, it is said: 'Having abandoned the defilements, not returning again.' And this perfect going has reached the peak; the path of approach by which it is accomplished is also perfect going itself. Thus, to show that in this way also the Blessed One is 'Sugata' (Well-Gone), 'or rightly gone,' etc., was said. 'By right practice' means by the non-deviating practice in attaining perfect full enlightenment. By this phrase, 'doing only what is for the welfare and happiness of the whole world,' it shows that the path to great enlightenment operates without distinction for all beings, always, only in a way that brings welfare and happiness. By this, 'He has gone without approaching these extremes of eternalism and annihilationism,' it shows the going of dependent origination. By this, 'He has gone without approaching these extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification,' it shows the going of the Noble Path.

Tatrāti yuttaṭṭhāne yuttasseva bhāsane nipphādetabbe, sādhetabbe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Abhūtanti abhūtatthaṃ. Atthamukhena hi vācāya abhūtatā, bhūtatā vā. Atacchanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Abhūtanti [V 1.0222] vā asantaṃ avijjamānaṃ. Atacchanti atathākāraṃ aññathāsantaṃ. Anatthasañhitanti diṭṭhadhammikena, samparāyikena vā anatthena sañhitaṃ, anatthāvahaṃ. Na atthoti anattho, atthassa paṭipakkho, abhāvo ca, tena sañhitaṃ, pisuṇavācaṃ, samphappalāpañcāti attho. Evamettha catubbidhassāpi vacīduccaritassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Ettha ca paṭhamā vācā sīlavantaṃ “dussīlo”ti, acaṇḍālādimeva “caṇḍālo”tiādinā bhāsamānassa daṭṭhabbā. Dutiyā dussīlaṃ “dussīlo”ti, caṇḍālādimeva “caṇḍālo”tiādinā avinayena bhāsamānassa. Tatiyā nerayikādikassa nerayikādibhāvavibhāvanīkathā yathā “āpāyiko devadatto nerayiko”tiādikā (cūḷava. 348). Catutthī “vedavihitena yaññavidhinā pāṇātipātādikataṃ sugatiṃ āvahatī”ti lokassa byāmohanakathā. Pañcamī bhūtena pesuññūpasaṃhārādikathā. Chaṭṭhā yuttappattaṭṭhāne pavattitā dānasīlādikathā veditabbā. Evaṃ sammā gadattāti yathāvuttaṃ abhūtādiṃ vajjetvā bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasañhitaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ tato eva sammā suṭṭhu gadanato sugato da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Āpāthagamanamattena kassaci appiyampi hi bhagavato vacanaṃ piyaṃ manāpameva atthasiddhiyā lokassa hitasukhāvahattā.

Regarding `Tatrāti`: this is a word in the locative case, in the sense of 'to be accomplished' in a suitable place and in speaking only what is suitable. `Abhūtanti` means having an untrue meaning. For by means of its meaning, speech is untruthful or truthful. `Atacchanti` is a synonym for that. Alternatively, `abhūtanti` means non-existent, not present. `Atacchanti` means having a nature that is not so, existing in another way. `Anatthasañhitanti` means connected with what is not beneficial, either in the present life or in the future life; it brings what is not beneficial. `Na attho` means 'not beneficial'; it is the opposite of benefit and its absence. Connected with that, it means slanderous speech and frivolous chatter. Thus, the inclusion of all four kinds of verbal misconduct should be understood here. And herein, the first speech should be seen as that of one who speaks, calling a virtuous person 'immoral,' or one who is not an outcaste 'an outcaste,' and so on. The second is of one who speaks without discipline, calling an immoral person 'immoral,' or one who is an outcaste 'an outcaste,' and so on. The third is speech that reveals the hell-bound state of one who is destined for hell, such as 'Devadatta is bound for a state of loss, bound for hell,' and so on. The fourth is speech that deludes the world, such as 'The act of killing living beings, etc., done according to the sacrificial method prescribed in the Vedas, brings a good destination.' The fifth is speech that brings about slander, etc., based on what is true. The sixth should be known as talk about generosity, virtue, etc., that occurs in a suitable and appropriate place. Thus, regarding `sammā gadattā`: having avoided the untrue, etc., as stated, and because of speaking rightly and well what is true, factual, connected with benefit, pleasant, and agreeable, he is `Sugato`, the 'da' being changed to 'ta'. Indeed, even if the Blessed One's speech is unpleasant to someone merely upon reaching the ear, it is still pleasant and agreeable because it accomplishes the goal and brings welfare and happiness to the world.

Apica sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato. Bhagavato hi veneyyajanupasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato sobhanaṃ bhaddakaṃ[M 1.0236]. Tathā lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya dutavilambitakhalitānukaḍḍhananippīḷanukkuṭikakuṭilākulatādidosarahitavilāsitarājahaṃsavasabhavāraṇamigarājagamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ, ñāṇagamanañca vipulanimmalakaruṇāsativīriyādiguṇavisesasahitaṃ abhinīhārato yāva mahābodhi anavajjatāya, sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahatāya ca sobhanameva. Atha vā sayambhūñāṇena sakalampi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanto sammā gato avagatoti sugato. Tathā lokasamudayaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammataṃ āpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato. Lokanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā gato adhigatoti sugato. Lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā gato paṭipannoti sugato. Tathā yaṃ imassa sadevakassa lokassa diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, sabbaṃ taṃ hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya sammā paccakkhato gato abbhaññāsīti sugato.

Furthermore, because his going (`gamanaṃ`) is beautiful (`sobhanaṃ`), he is `Sugato`. Indeed, the Blessed One’s approaching of people to be trained is beautiful and excellent because it certainly accomplishes their welfare and happiness. Likewise, because of having a physical body adorned with the major and minor characteristics, his physical going is graceful like that of a king of swans, a bull, a king of elephants, and a king of beasts, and is free from faults such as being too fast, too slow, stumbling, dragging, pressing down, squatting, crookedness, and agitation. And his going of knowledge, accompanied by special qualities such as vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, and energy, from the initial aspiration up to great enlightenment, is also beautiful because it is faultless and because it brings welfare and happiness to beings. Alternatively, because, with self-arisen knowledge, he rightly went, that is, understood, fully comprehending the entire world by means of the realization of full understanding, he is `Sugato`. Likewise, having abandoned the origin of the world by means of the realization of abandonment, bringing it to a state of non-arising, he has rightly gone beyond; thus he is `Sugato`. Having realized the cessation of the world, Nibbāna, by means of the realization of direct experience, he has rightly gone to, that is, attained it; thus he is `Sugato`. Having followed the path leading to the cessation of the world by means of the realization of development, he has rightly gone, that is, practiced; thus he is `Sugato`. Furthermore, whatever in this world with its devas has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or mentally explored—all that he rightly went to, that is, directly knew, as if it were a myrobalan fruit on the palm of his hand; therefore, he is `Sugato`.

135. Sabbathāti sabbappakārena. Yo yo loko yathā yathā veditabbo, tathā tathā. Te [V 1.0223] pana pakāre dassetuṃ “sabhāvato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabhāvatoti dukkhasabhāvato. Sabbo hi loko dukkhasabhāvo. Yathāha “saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (mahāva. 14; dī. ni. 2.387). Samudayatoti yato so samudeti, tato taṇhādito. Nirodhatoti yattha so nirujjhati, tato visaṅkhārato. Nirodhūpāyatoti yena vidhinā so nirodho pattabbo, tato ariyamaggato, ito aññassa pakārassa abhāvā.

135. 'In every way' (`sabbathā`) means by all means (`sabbappakārena`). Whatever world is to be known in whatever way, he knows it in that way. But to show those aspects, 'by its nature' (`sabhāvato`), etc., is said. Therein, 'by its nature' means by its nature of suffering. Indeed, the entire world has the nature of suffering. As it is said: 'In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.' 'By its origin' (`samudayato`) means from which it arises, that is, from craving, etc. 'By its cessation' (`nirodhato`) means wherein it ceases, that is, from the unconditioned. 'By the means to its cessation' (`nirodhūpāyato`) means by which method that cessation is to be attained, that is, from the noble path, because there is no other aspect than these.

Iti “sabbathā lokaṃ avedī”ti vatvā tadatthasādhakaṃ suttaṃ dassento “yattha kho āvuso”tiādimāha. Tattha “na jāyatī”tiādinā ujukaṃ jātiādīni paṭikkhipitvā “na cavati na upapajjatī”ti padadvayena aparāparaṃ cavanupapajjanāni paṭikkhipati. Keci pana “na jāyatītiādi gabbhaseyyakavasena vuttaṃ, itaraṃ opapātikavasenā”ti vadanti. Tanti jātiādirahitaṃ. Gamanenāti padasā gamanena. Ñāteyyanti jānitabbaṃ. “Ñātāya”nti vā pāṭho, ñātā ayaṃ nibbānatthikoti adhippāyo.

Thus, having said 'he knew the world in every way,' and showing a sutta that establishes that meaning, he said 'Where, friend...' and so on. Therein, with 'is not born,' etc., having directly rejected birth and the like, with the two words 'does not pass away, is not reborn,' he rejects successive passing away and rebirth. But some say that 'is not born,' etc., is said with reference to womb-born beings, and the other part with reference to spontaneously arisen beings. `Tanti` means devoid of birth, etc. `Gamanenāti` means by going on foot. `Ñāteyyanti` means to be known. Alternatively, the reading is `ñātāya'nti`; the meaning is: this person, who has Nibbāna as their goal, is a knower.

Kāmaṃ [M 1.0237] pādagamanena gantvā lokassantaṃ ñātuṃ, daṭṭhuṃ, pattuṃ vā na sakkā, apica parimitaparicchinnaṭṭhāne taṃ paññāpetvā dassemīti dassento “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha sasaññimhīti saññāsahite. Tato eva samanake saviññāṇake. Aviññāṇake pana utusamuṭṭhānarūpasamudāyamatte paññāpetuṃ na sakkāti adhippāyo. Lokanti khandhādilokaṃ. Lokanirodhanti tassa lokassa nirujjhanaṃ, nibbānameva vā. Adesampi hi taṃ yesaṃ nirodho, tesaṃ vasena upacārato, desatopi niddisīyati yathā “cakkhuṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.401; ma. ni. 1.134; vibha. 204).

Although it is not possible to know, see, or reach the end of the world by going on foot, nevertheless, showing 'I will declare it in a limited and defined place,' he said 'Moreover...' and so on. Therein, `sasaññimhi` means accompanied by perception; for that very reason, with mind and with consciousness. The meaning is that it is not possible to declare it in what is without consciousness, in a mere aggregate of matter arisen from temperature. `Lokanti` means the world of aggregates, etc. `Lokanirodhanti` means the cessation of that world, or Nibbāna itself. For indeed, though it is without a location, it is pointed out also as a location by way of convention, with reference to those whose cessation it is, as in: 'The eye in the world is a pleasing form, an agreeable form. Here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; here, when ceasing, it ceases.'

Gamanenāti pākatikagamanena. Lokassantoti saṅkhāralokassa anto antakiriyāhetubhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ. Kudācananti kadācipi. Apatvāti aggamaggena anadhigantvā. Pamocananti pamutti nissaraṇaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā lokassantaṃ apatvā vaṭṭadukkhato mutti natthi, tasmā. Haveti nipātamattaṃ. Lokavidūti sabhāvādito sabbaṃ lokaṃ jānanto. Sumedhoti sundarapañño. Lokantagūti pariññābhisamayena lokaṃ viditvā pahānābhisamayena lokantagū. Maggabrahmacariyavāsassa pariniṭṭhitattā vusitabrahmacariyo. Sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ samitattā, catusaccadhammānaṃ [V 1.0224] vā abhisamitattā samitāvī. Nāsīsati na pattheti. Yathā imaṃ lokaṃ, evaṃ parañca lokaṃ appaṭisandhikattā.

'By going' means by ordinary going. 'The end of the world' refers to Nibbāna, which is the end of the world of formations, being the cause for making an end. 'Never' means at any time at all. 'Without reaching' means without attaining by the supreme path. 'Liberation' means release, escape. 'Therefore' means because without reaching the end of the world there is no release from the suffering of the round, therefore. 'Have' is merely a particle. 'Knower of the world' means one who knows the entire world by way of its nature and so on. 'Wise' means one possessing beautiful wisdom. 'One who has gone to the end of the world' means one who, having known the world through the realization of full understanding, has gone to the end of the world through the realization of abandonment. 'One who has lived the holy life' is so called because the dwelling in the holy life of the path is completed. 'One who is pacified' is so called because all defilements have been pacified, or because the dhammas of the Four Truths have been realized. 'He does not long for' means he does not aspire. Just as he does not long for this world, so too he does not long for the next world, due to having no re-linking.

136. Evaṃ yadipi lokavidutā anavasesato dassitā sabhāvato dassitattā, loko pana ekadeseneva vuttoti taṃ anavasesato dassetuṃ “apica tayo lokā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha indriyabaddhānaṃ khandhānaṃ samūho, santāno ca sattaloko. Rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya satto, lokīyanti ettha kusalākusalaṃ, tabbipāko cāti lokoti. Anindriyabaddhānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ samūho, santāno ca okāsaloko lokiyanti ettha tasā, thāvarā ca, tesañca okāsabhūtoti. Tadādhāratāya hesa “bhājanaloko”tipi vuccati. Ubhayepi khandhā saṅkhāraloko paccayehi saṅkharīyanti, lujjanti palujjanti cāti. Āhāraṭṭhitikāti paccayaṭṭhitikā, paccayāyattavuttikāti [M 1.0238] attho. Paccayattho hettha āhāra-saddo “ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāyā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.232) viya. Evaṃ hi “sabbe sattā”ti iminā asaññasattāpi pariggahitā honti. Sā panāyaṃ āhāraṭṭhitikatā nippariyāyato saṅkhāradhammo, na sattadhammoti āha “āhāraṭṭhitikāti āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhāraloko veditabbo”ti.

136. Thus, although the knowledge of the world has been shown completely because it was shown in terms of its nature, the world was spoken of only in part; to show it completely, it is said: 'Moreover, there are three worlds.' Therein, the collection and continuity of aggregates connected with the sense faculties is the world of beings. Because of being attached and exceedingly attached to forms and so on, one is a 'being' (satta); and because the wholesome, the unwholesome, and their results are seen (lokīyanti) herein, it is a 'world' (loka). The collection and continuity of forms and so on not connected with the sense faculties is the spatial world; herein moving and non-moving beings are seen (lokiyanti), and it is their location. Because it is their support, it is also called the 'container world.' Both these aggregates are the world of formations, because they are conditioned by causes, and they perish and utterly perish. 'Sustained by nutriment' means subsisting by conditions, having an existence dependent on conditions—this is the meaning. Herein, the word 'nutriment' has the meaning of 'cause,' as in passages such as: 'This nutriment is for the arising of unarisen sensual desire...' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232). For in this way, by the phrase 'all beings,' even non-percipient beings are included. But this state of being sustained by nutriment is, in the primary sense, a conditioned phenomenon, not a phenomenon of a being. Thus, he said: 'In the passage where "sustained by nutriment" occurs, the world of formations should be understood.'

Yadi evaṃ “sabbe sattā”ti idaṃ kathanti? Puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanāti nāyaṃ doso. Yathā aññatthāpi “ekadhamme, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamasmiṃ ekadhamme? Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti (a. ni. 10.27). Diṭṭhigatikānaṃ sassatādivasena “attā, loko”ti ca parikappanā yebhuyyena sattavisayā, na saṅkhāravisayāti āha “sassato lokoti vā asassato lokoti vā āgataṭṭhāne sattaloko veditabbo”ti.

If so, how is this [phrase] 'all beings' [to be understood]? The teaching is founded on the individual, so this is not a fault. Just as elsewhere it is said: 'Monks, when a monk rightly becomes disenchanted with one thing, rightly becomes dispassionate, rightly becomes liberated, rightly sees the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In what one thing? All beings are sustained by nutriment.' (A.N. 10.27). For those holding wrong views, the speculation of 'self' and 'world' by way of eternalism, etc., mostly has beings as its object, not formations. Therefore, he said: 'In the passage where "the world is eternal" or "the world is not eternal" occurs, the world of beings should be understood.'

Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharantīti yattake ṭhāne candimasūriyā parivattanti paribbhamanti. Disā bhanti virocamānāti tesaṃ paribbhamaneneva tā disā pabhassarā hutvā virocanti. Tāva sahassadhā lokoti tattakaṃ sahassappakāro okāsaloko, sahassalokadhātuyoti attho. “Tāva sahassavā”ti vā pāṭho.

'As far as the moon and sun revolve' means in whatever space the moon and sun revolve and wander. 'The directions shine brightly' means by their very wandering, those directions, having become radiant, shine. 'So far a thousandfold world' means that much is a thousand-type spatial world, meaning a thousand world-elements. Alternatively, the reading is 'so far a thousandfold.'

Tampīti [V 1.0225] taṃ tividhampi lokaṃ. Tathā hissa sabbathāpi viditoti sambandho. Eko lokoti “sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti yāya puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya sabbesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paccayāyattavuttitā vuttā, tāya sabbo saṅkhāraloko eko ekavidho pakārantarassa abhāvato. Dve lokātiādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Nāma-ggahaṇena cettha nibbānassa aggahaṇaṃ, tassa alokasabhāvattā. Nanu ca “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti ettha paccayāyattavuttitāya maggaphaladhammānampi lokatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, pariññeyyānaṃ dukkhasaccadhammānaṃ idha “loko”ti adhippetattā. Atha vā “na lujjati na palujjatī”ti [M 1.0239] yo gahito tathā na hoti, so lokoti taṃgahaṇarahitānaṃ lokuttarānaṃ natthi lokatā. Upādānānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Dasāyatanānīti dasa rūpāyatanāni.

'That too' means that threefold world. 'For in every way it is known to him'—this is the connection. 'One world': by the discourse founded on the individual, 'All beings are sustained by nutriment,' the dependent nature of all formations is stated. By this, the entire world of formations is one, of a single kind, due to the absence of another kind. In 'two worlds,' etc., also, the meaning should be understood by this method. And here, by the term 'name,' Nibbāna is not included, because of its nature of not being a world. But does it not follow that, in the phrase 'sustained by nutriment,' because of dependent existence, the path and fruition dhammas also become 'world'? It does not follow, because here 'world' is intended to mean the dhammas of the truth of suffering which are to be fully understood. Alternatively, that which is grasped as 'it does not perish, it does not utterly perish,' but is not in fact so, is 'world.' Therefore, for the supramundane states, which are devoid of such grasping, there is no 'world-ness.' The aggregates that are the objects for clinging are the aggregates of clinging. 'The ten sense bases' means the ten material sense bases.

Ettha ca “āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti paccayāyattavuttitāvacanena saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatā. Tāya ca “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) vacanato dukkhānattatā ca pakāsitā hontīti tīṇipi sāmaññalakkhaṇāni gahitāni. Nāmanti cattāro arūpino khandhā, te ca atthato phassādayo. Rūpanti bhūtupādāyarūpāni, tāni ca atthato pathavīādayoti aviseseneva salakkhaṇato saṅkhārā gahitā. Taggahaṇeneva ye tesaṃ visesā kusalādayo, hetuādayo ca, tepi gahitā eva hontīti āha “iti ayaṃ saṅkhāralokopi sabbathā vidito”ti.

And here, by the statement of dependent existence, 'sustained by nutriment,' the impermanence of formations is shown. And by that, according to the maxim, 'What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15), suffering and non-self are also shown. Thus, all three general characteristics are included. 'Name' means the four immaterial aggregates, and they, in essence, are contact and so on. 'Form' means primary and derived matter, and they, in essence, are the earth element and so on. Thus, formations are included generally by their specific characteristics. By their very inclusion, those specific aspects of theirs—such as wholesome, etc., and cause, etc.—are also included. Therefore, he said: 'Thus, this world of formations is also known in every way.'

Āgamma cittaṃ seti etthāti āsayo migāsayo viya. Yathā migo gocarāya gantvā paccāgantvā tattheva vanagahane sayatīti so tassa āsayo, evaṃ aññathā pavattitvāpi cittaṃ āgamma yattha seti, so tassa āsayoti vuccati. So pana sassatadiṭṭhiādivasena catubbidho. Vuttañca –

'The mind, having come, lies down herein'; thus, it is an 'abode' (āsayo), like a deer's resting place. Just as a deer, having gone for pasture and returned, lies down in that very forest thicket, so that is its abode; similarly, even after having arisen elsewhere, where the mind comes and lies down, that is called its 'abode'. And that is fourfold, by way of eternalist view and so on. And it is said:

“Sassatucchedadiṭṭhi ca, khanti cevānulomikā;

Yathābhūtañca yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, etaṃ āsayasaddita”nti.

The view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism, the insight-knowledge that is in conformity with the truths, and the knowledge of things as they truly are—these are called 'disposition' (āsaya).

Tattha sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ sassatucchedadiṭṭhīhi saṅgahitattā sabbepi diṭṭhigatikā sattā imā eva dve diṭṭhiyo sannissitā. Yathāha “dvayanissito khvāyaṃ, kaccāna, loko yebhuyyena atthitañca natthitañcā”ti [V 1.0226] (saṃ. ni. 2.15). Atthitāti hi sassataggāho adhippeto, natthitāti ucchedaggāho. Ayaṃ tāva vaṭṭanissitānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ āsayo. Vivaṭṭanissitānaṃ pana suddhasattānaṃ anulomikā khanti, yathābhūtañāṇanti duvidho āsayo.

Therein, because all views are included by the views of eternalism and annihilationism, all beings who hold views rely only on these two views. As was said: 'This world, Kaccāna, for the most part, relies on the duality of "it is" and "it is not"' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.15). By 'it is', the grasping at eternalism is meant; by 'it is not', the grasping at annihilationism is meant. This, firstly, is the disposition of worldlings who rely on the round of existence. But for purified beings who rely on that which is free from the round, there are two kinds of disposition: the insight-knowledge that is in conformity and the knowledge of things as they truly are.

Āsayaṃ jānātīti catubbidhampi sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānāti. Jānanto ca tesaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ, tesañca ñāṇānaṃ appavattikkhaṇepi jānāti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'He knows disposition' means he knows the fourfold disposition of beings. And in knowing, he knows of those with wrong views and of those knowledges even at the moment when they are not occurring. For this was said:

“Kāmaṃ [M 1.0240] sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo kāmagaruko kāmāsayo kāmādhimutto’ti, kāmaṃ sevantaññeva jānāti ‘ayaṃ puggalo nekkhammagaruko nekkhammāsayo nekkhammādhimutto’ti”ādi (paṭi. ma. 1.113).

'Even while a person is indulging in sensual pleasure, he knows: "This person esteems sensual pleasure, has sensual pleasure as his disposition, and is intent on sensual pleasure." Even while a person is indulging in sensual pleasure, he knows: "This person esteems renunciation, has renunciation as his disposition, and is intent on and inclined toward renunciation,"' and so on (Paṭi. Ma. 1.113).

Appahīnabhāvena santāne anu anu sayantīti anusayā, anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantīti attho. Etena nesaṃ kāraṇalābhe uppajjanārahataṃ dasseti. Appahīnā hi kilesā kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjanti. Ke pana te? Rāgādayo satta anāgatā kilesā, atītā, paccuppannā ca taṃsabhāvattā tathā vuccanti. Na hi dhammānaṃ kālabhedena sabhāvabhedo atthi. Taṃ sattavidhaṃ anusayaṃ tassa tassa sattassa santāne paroparabhāvena pavattamānaṃ jānāti.

Because they have not been abandoned, they lie dormant again and again in the mental continuum; therefore, they are 'latent tendencies' (anusayā). The meaning is that they arise upon obtaining a suitable cause. By this, it shows their potential to arise when a cause is obtained. Indeed, unabandoned defilements arise when a cause is present. What are they? The seven defilements beginning with sensual passion, which are of the future; those of the past and present are also called thus because they have that same nature. Indeed, there is no difference in the nature of phenomena due to a difference in time. He knows that sevenfold latent tendency as it occurs in the mental continuum of each and every being with varying degrees of coarseness and subtlety.

Caritanti sucaritaduccaritaṃ. Taṃ hi vibhaṅge (vibha. 814, 817) caritaniddese niddiṭṭhaṃ. Atha vā caritanti cariyā veditabbā. Tā pana rāgadosamohasaddhābuddhivitakkavasena cha mūlacariyā, tāsaṃ apariyanto antarabhedo, saṃsaggabhedo pana tesaṭṭhividho. Taṃ caritaṃ sabhāvato saṃkilesavodānato samuṭṭhānato phalato nissandatoti evamādinā pakārena jānāti.

'Conduct' (carita) means good conduct and bad conduct. This is explained in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 814, 817) in the section on the definition of conduct. Alternatively, 'conduct' should be known as temperament (cariyā). There are six root temperaments, by way of lust, hatred, delusion, faith, wisdom, and discursive thought. Their internal divisions are endless, but their mixed divisions are of sixty-three kinds. He knows that conduct by way of its nature, its cause of defilement and purity, its origin, its fruit, its outflow, and so on.

Adhimutti ajjhāsayadhātu. Sā duvidhā hīnādhimutti paṇītādhimuttīti. Yāya hīnādhimuttikā sattā hīnādhimuttikeyeva sevanti, paṇītādhimuttikā ca paṇītādhimuttikeyeva. Sā ajjhāsayadhātu ajjhāsayasabhāvo adhimutti. Taṃ adhimuttiṃ jānāti “imassa adhimutti hīnā, imassa paṇītā”ti, tatthāpi “imassa mudu, imassa mudutarā, imassa mudutamā”tiādinā. Indriyānaṃ hi tikkhamudubhāvādinā yathārahaṃ adhimuttiyā tikkhamudubhāvādiko veditabbo. Tathā hi vuttaṃ sammohavinodanīyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 818, 820) “heṭṭhā [V 1.0227] gahitāpi adhimutti idha sattānaṃ tikkhindriyamudindriyabhāvadassanatthaṃ puna gahitā”ti.

'Inclination' (adhimutti) is the element of disposition (ajjhāsayadhātu). It is twofold: inferior inclination and superior inclination. By which beings with inferior inclination associate only with those of inferior inclination, and those with superior inclination associate only with those of superior inclination. That element of disposition, the nature of disposition, is 'inclination'. He knows that inclination thus: 'This one's inclination is inferior, this one's is superior.' And therein also: 'This one's is soft, this one's is softer, this one's is softest,' and so on. Indeed, according to the sharpness, softness, etc., of the faculties, the sharpness, softness, etc., of the inclination should be known. Thus it is said in the Sammohavinodanī: 'Although inclination was taken up below, it is taken up again here for the purpose of showing the state of beings as having sharp or soft faculties.'

Apparajaṃ akkhaṃ etesanti apparajakkhā, appaṃ vā rajaṃ paññāmaye akkhimhi etesanti apparajakkhā, anussadarāgādirajā sattā, te apparajakkhe. Mahārajakkheti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ussadarāgādirajā mahārajakkhā.

'They have little dust in the faculty (eye)'; therefore, they are 'those with little dust' (apparajakkhā). Or, 'they have little dust in the eye of wisdom'; therefore, they are 'those with little dust'. They are beings with little dust of passion, and so on. In 'those with much dust' (mahārajakkhā) also, this is the method. Those with much dust of passion, and so on, are 'those with much dust'.

Tikkhindriyeti [M 1.0241] tikhiṇehi saddhādīhi indriyehi samannāgate. Mudindriyeti mudukehi saddhādīhi indriyehi samannāgate. Upanissayaindriyāni nāma idhādhippetāni. Svākāreti sundarākāre kalyāṇapakatike, vivaṭṭajjhāsayeti attho. Suviññāpayeti sammattaniyāmaṃ viññāpetuṃ sukare saddhe, paññavante ca. Bhabbe abhabbeti ettha bhabbeti kammāvaraṇakilesāvaraṇavipākāvaraṇarahite. Vuttavipariyāyena dvākāraduviññāpayābhabbā veditabbā. Ettha ca “imassa rāgarajo appo, imassa dosarajo appo”tiādinā apparajakkhesu jānanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tasmāti yasmā bhagavā aparimāṇe satte āsayādito anavasesetvā jānāti, tasmā assa bhagavato sattalokopi sabbathā vidito.

'Sharp-facultied' means endowed with sharp faculties such as faith. 'Soft-facultied' means endowed with soft faculties such as faith. Here, the faculties that are a supporting condition are meant. 'Of good form' means of beautiful appearance, of good nature; the meaning is having a disposition for that which is free from the round. 'Easy to instruct' means easy to make known the right path to Nibbāna; those with faith and those with wisdom. Regarding 'capable' and 'incapable', 'capable' means free from the obstructions of kamma, defilements, and results. By way of the reverse of what was said, those of bad form, difficult to instruct, and incapable should be known. And here, regarding 'those with little dust', the knowing should be understood as: 'This one has little dust of passion, this one has little dust of hatred,' and so on. In the remaining cases also, this is the method. Therefore, because the Blessed One knows immeasurable beings without remainder by way of their disposition, etc., for that Blessed One the world of beings is also known in every way.

Nanu ca sattesu pamāṇādipi jānitabbo atthīti? Atthi. Tassa pana jānanaṃ na nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāyāti idha na gahitaṃ, bhagavato pana tampi suviditaṃ suvavatthāpitameva, payojanābhāvā desanaṃ nāruḷhaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

Is it not so that there is also the measure, etc., of beings to be known? There is. But the knowing of that is not for disenchantment, for dispassion, for cessation; therefore, it is not taken up here. But for the Blessed One, that too is well-known and well-determined. Because of the lack of benefit, it was not included in the teaching. By that, it was said:

“Atha kho bhagavā parittaṃ nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsuṃ āropetvā bhikkhū āmantesi ‘taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ – yo vāyaṃ mayā paritto nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsu āropito, ayaṃ vā mahāpathavī’”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1121).

Then the Blessed One, having placed a little dust on his fingernail, addressed the monks: 'What do you think of this, monks? Which, indeed, is more—this little dust placed by me on my fingernail, or this great earth?' and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1121).

137. Okāsalokopi sabbathā viditoti sambandho. Cakkavāḷanti lokadhātu. Sā hi nemimaṇḍalasadisena cakkavāḷapabbatena samantato parikkhittattā “cakkavāḷa”nti vuccati. Catutiṃsasatāni cāti catuadhikāni tiṃsasatāni, tīṇisahassāni, cattārisatāni cāti attho[V 1.0228]. Aḍḍhuḍḍhānīti upaḍḍhacatutthāni, tīṇisatāni, paññāsañcāti attho. Nahutānīti dasasahassāni. Saṅkhātāti kathitā. Saṇṭhitīti heṭṭhā, uparito cāti sabbaso ṭhiti.

137. The connection is: 'The world of space is also known in every way.' 'Cakkavāḷa' is a world-system. Indeed, because it is surrounded on all sides by the Cakkavāḷa mountain, which is like the rim of a wheel, it is called 'Cakkavāḷa'. 'Thirty-four hundred' means three thousand and four hundred. 'The fourth with a half' (aḍḍhuḍḍhāni) means three hundred and fifty. 'A nahuta' is ten thousand. 'Counted' (saṅkhātā) means spoken. 'Position' (saṇṭhiti) means its station in every way, below and above.

Evaṃ saṇṭhiteti evamavaṭṭhite. Etthāti cakkavāḷe. Accuggato tāvadevāti tattakameva caturāsīti yojanasahassāniyeva ubbedho[M 1.0242]. Na kevalaṃ cettha ubbedhova, atha kho āyāmavitthārāpissa tattakāyeva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘Thus established’ means thus fixed. ‘Here’ means in this world-system. ‘Just that high’ means exactly eighty-four thousand yojanas in height. Not only is the height just that, but its length and breadth are also exactly that. For it has been said:

“Sineru, bhikkhave, pabbatarājā caturāsīti yojanasahassāni āyāmena, caturāsīti yojanasahassāni vitthārenā”ti (a. ni. 7.66).

“Bhikkhus, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and eighty-four thousand yojanas in breadth” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.66).

Tatoti sinerussa heṭṭhā, upari ca vuttappamāṇato. Upaḍḍhupaḍḍhenāti upaḍḍhena upaḍḍhena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – dvācattālīsa yojanasahassāni samudde ajjhogāḷho tattakameva ca upari uggato yugandharapabbato, ekavīsa yojanasahassāni samudde ajjhogāḷho tattakameva ca upari uggato īsadharo pabbatoti iminā nayena sesesupi upaḍḍhupaḍḍhapamāṇatā veditabbā. Yathā mahāsamuddo yāva cakkavāḷapādamūlā anupubbaninno, evaṃ yāva sinerupādamūlāti heṭṭhā sinerupamāṇato upaḍḍhapamāṇopi yugandharapabbato pathaviyaṃ suppatiṭṭhito, evaṃ īsadharādayopīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “mahāsamuddo, bhikkhave, anupubbaninno anupubbapoṇo anupubbapabbhāro”ti (udā. 45; cūḷava. 384; a. ni. 8.19). Sineruyugandharādīnaṃ antare sīdantarasamuddā nāma. Te vitthārato yathākkamaṃ sineruādīnaṃ accuggatasamānaparimāṇāti vadanti. Brahāti mahanto.

‘From that’ means from the stated measure of Sineru, both below and above it. ‘By half and half’ means by half, by half. This is what is said: The Yugandhara mountain is submerged in the ocean to a depth of forty-two thousand yojanas and rises to the same height above it; the Isadhara mountain is submerged to a depth of twenty-one thousand yojanas and rises to the same height above it. In this way, the remaining mountains should also be understood as having half-and-half proportions. Just as the great ocean slopes gradually down to the base of the Cakkavāḷa mountain, so too, down to the base of Sineru. Thus, it should be understood that the Yugandhara mountain, being half the measure of Sineru below, is firmly established on the earth; and so too are Isadhara and the others. For it has been said: “Bhikkhus, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually” (Udāna 5.5; Vinaya, Cūḷavagga 9.1.4; Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.19). Between Sineru, Yugandhara, and so forth, are the seas named Sīdantara. They say that their breadth corresponds respectively to the heights of Sineru and the other mountains. ‘Brahā’ means great.

Sinerussa samantatoti parikkhipanavasena sinerussa samantato ṭhitā. Sineruṃ tāva parikkhipitvā ṭhito yugandharo, taṃ parikkhipitvā īsadharo. Evaṃ taṃ taṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitā “sinerussa samantato”ti vuttā.

‘Surrounding Sineru’ means they are situated all around Sineru by way of encircling it. First, Yugandhara stands encircling Sineru; encircling that stands Isadhara. In this way, those mountains that stand encircling each preceding one are said to be ‘surrounding Sineru.’

Yojanānaṃ satānucco, himavā pañca pabbatoti himavā pabbato pañca yojanānaṃ satāni ucco ubbedho. Nagavhayāti naga-saddena avhātabbā rukkhābhidhānā. Paññāsayojanakkhandhasākhāyāmāti’ ubbedhato paññāsayojanakkhandhāyāmā, ubbedhato, samantato ca paññāsayojanasākhāyāmā [V 1.0229] ca. Tato eva satayojanavitthiṇṇā, tāvadeva ca uggatā. Yassānubhāvenāti yassā mahantatā kappaṭṭhāyitādippakārena pabhāvena.

‘Five hundred yojanas high is Himavā, the mountain’: the Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high in elevation. ‘Nagavhayā’ means appellations of trees that are to be called by the word ‘naga’. ‘Fifty yojanas in trunk and branch length’ means: the length of its trunk is fifty yojanas in height, and the length of its branches is fifty yojanas both in height and all around. Therefore, it is one hundred yojanas wide and just as high. ‘By whose power’ means by the power of its various aspects, such as its greatness and its lasting for an entire eon.

Garuḷānaṃ simbalirukkho sinerussa dutiyaparibhaṇḍe patiṭṭhito.

The Simbali tree of the Garuḷas is established on the second terrace of Sineru.

Sirīsenāti [M 1.0243] paccatte karaṇavacanaṃ. Sattamanti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ, sirīso bhavati sattamoti attho.

The word ‘Sirīsenā’ is an instrumental case form used in the sense of the nominative. The word ‘Sattamaṃ’ is stated with a change of gender; the meaning is, ‘the Sirīsa tree is the seventh.’

Tattha caṇḍamaṇḍalaṃ heṭṭhā, sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ upari. Tassa āsannabhāvena candamaṇḍalaṃ attano chāyāya vikalabhāvena upaṭṭhāti. Tāni yojanantarikāni yugandharaggapamāṇe ākāse vicaranti. Asurabhavanaṃ sinerussa heṭṭhā. Avīci jambudīpassa. Jambudīpo sakaṭasaṇṭhāno. Aparagoyānaṃ ādāsasaṇṭhāno. Pubbavideho addhacandasaṇṭhāno. Uttarakuru pīṭhasaṇṭhāno. Taṃtaṃnivāsīnaṃ, taṃtaṃparivāradīpavāsīnañca manussānaṃ mukhampi taṃtaṃsaṇṭhānanti vadanti. Tadantaresūti tesaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ antaresu. Tiṇṇaṃ hi pattānaṃ aññamaññaāsannabhāvena ṭhapitānaṃ antarasadise tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ antare ekeko lokantaranirayo.

There, the moon’s disc is below, and the sun’s disc is above. Due to its proximity to the sun, the moon’s disc appears with a deficient phase because of its own shadow. These travel in the sky, one yojana apart, at the level of the Yugandhara peak. The Asura realm is below Sineru. Avīci is below Jambudīpa. Jambudīpa is shaped like a cart. Pubbavideha is shaped like a half-moon. Uttarakuru is shaped like a dais. They say that the faces of the humans dwelling in each of these continents, as well as those living in the surrounding attendant islands, also have the shape of their respective continents. ‘Between them’ means between those world-systems. For in the space between three world-systems, similar to the space between three bowls placed close to one another, there is a single Lokantarika hell.

Anantānīti aparimāṇāni, “ettakānī”ti aññehi minituṃ asakkuṇeyyāni. Bhagavā anantena buddhañāṇena avedi “ananto ākāso, ananto sattanikāyo, anantāni cakkavāḷānī”ti tividhampi anantaṃ buddhañāṇaṃ paricchindati sayampi anantattā. Yāvatakaṃ hi ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Ñeyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇapariyantikaṃ ñeyyanti. Tena vuttaṃ “anantena buddhañāṇena avedī”ti. Anantatā cassa anantañeyyapaṭivijjhaneneva veditabbā tattha appaṭihatacārattā. Nanu cettha vivaṭṭādīnampi viditatā vattabbāti? Saccaṃ vattabbaṃ, sā pana parato abhiññākathāyaṃ āgamissatīti idha na gahitā.

‘Boundless’ means immeasurable, unable to be measured by others as ‘this many.’ The Blessed One comprehended with boundless Buddha-knowledge. ‘Boundless is space, boundless is the host of beings, boundless are the world-systems’—the Buddha-knowledge delimits this threefold boundless because it itself is boundless. For as far as the knowable extends, so far extends the knowledge. As far as the knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Therefore it is said, ‘He comprehended with boundless Buddha-knowledge.’ And its boundlessness should be understood precisely through the penetration of the boundless knowable, because of its unimpeded movement therein. ‘But should not the knowledge of the cycles of cosmic evolution and so on also be mentioned here?’ Truly, it should be mentioned, but since that will come later in the discussion on direct knowledge, it is not included here.

138. Attanāti nissakkavacanametaṃ. Guṇehi attanā visiṭṭhatarassāti sambandho. Tara-ggahaṇaṃ cettha “anuttaro”ti padassa atthaniddesatāya kataṃ, na visiṭṭhassa kassaci atthitāya. Sadevake hi loke sadisakappopi nāma koci tathāgatassa natthi, kuto sadiso. Visiṭṭhe pana kā [V 1.0230] kathā. Kassacīti kassacipi. Abhibhavatīti sīlasampadāya upanissayabhūtānaṃ hirottappamettākaruṇānaṃ, visesapaccayānaṃ saddhāsativīriyapaññānañca ukkaṃsappattiyā samudāgamato paṭṭhāya anaññasādhāraṇo savāsanapaṭipakkhassa pahīnattā ukkaṃsapāramippatto satthu sīlaguṇo. Tena bhagavā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ aññadatthu abhibhuyya [M 1.0244] pavattati, na sayaṃ kenaci abhibhuyyatīti adhippāyo. Evaṃ samādhiguṇādīsupi yathārahaṃ vattabbaṃ. Sīlādayo cete lokiyalokuttaramissakā veditabbā. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ pana lokiyaṃ kāmāvacarameva.

138. ‘By oneself’ (attanā)—this is an ablative term (nissakka-vacana). The connection is: ‘of one more distinguished than oneself by means of qualities.’ The inclusion of the comparative suffix ‘-tara’ (more) here is done to explain the meaning of the word ‘unsurpassed’ (anuttaro), not because there exists anyone who is merely distinguished. For in the world with its gods, there is no one even comparable to the Tathāgata, let alone one who is similar. What, then, can be said of one who is superior? ‘Of anyone’ means of anyone whatsoever. ‘He surpasses’: from its very arising, due to the attainment of excellence in the virtues of conscience, shame, loving-kindness, and compassion, which are the supporting conditions for the perfection of morality, and in the special conditions of faith, mindfulness, energy, and wisdom, the Teacher’s quality of morality is unique and has reached the highest perfection, because the opposing states together with their latent tendencies have been abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One proceeds, having truly overcome the world with its gods, and is not himself overcome by anyone—this is the intention. Similarly, this should be stated as appropriate regarding the qualities of concentration and so on. And these qualities of morality and so forth should be understood as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. The knowledge and vision of liberation, however, is purely mundane, belonging only to the sense-sphere.

Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ tena sadevakaṃ lokaṃ abhibhavatīti? Tassāpi ānubhāvato asadisattā. Tampi hi visayato, pavattito, pavatti ākārato ca uttaritarameva. Taṃ hi anaññasādhāraṇaṃ satthu vimuttiguṇaṃ ārabbha pavattati, pavattamānañca atakkāvacaraṃ paramagambhīraṃ saṇhasukhumaṃ savisayaṃ paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ suppahīnattā suṭṭhu pākaṭaṃ vibhūtataraṃ katvā pavattati, sammadeva ca vasībhāvassa pāpitattā, bhavaṅgaparivāsassa ca atiparittakattā lahuṃ lahuṃ pavattatīti.

If it is so, how does it overwhelm the world with its devas by that [knowledge and vision of liberation]? Because of the power of that [knowledge and vision of liberation] also being incomparable. For indeed, that [knowledge and vision of liberation] is also more excellent by way of its object, by way of its arising, and by way of the mode of its arising. For it arises taking as its object the Teacher's quality of liberation, which is not shared with others; and while arising, being beyond the range of conjecture, extremely profound, subtle and fine, it arises having made its own object very clear and exceedingly manifest due to the opposing states having been well abandoned. And because of having been brought perfectly to a state of mastery, and because of the extreme brevity of the dwelling in bhavaṅga, it arises very quickly.

Evaṃ sīlādiguṇehi bhagavato uttaritarassa abhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni sadisassāpi abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “asamo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha asamoti ekasmiṃ kāle natthi etassa sīlādiguṇena samā sadisāti asamo. Tathā asamehi atītānāgatabuddhehi samo, asamā vā samā etassāti asamasamo. Sīlādiguṇena natthi etassa paṭimāti appaṭimo. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tattha upamāmattaṃ paṭimā, sadisūpamā paṭibhāgo, yugaggāhavasena ṭhito paṭipuggalo veditabbo.

Having thus shown the absence of one superior to the Blessed One in qualities such as virtue, now, to show the absence of even an equal, 'unequaled' (asamo), and so forth, is said. Therein, 'unequaled' (asamo) means: at any one time, there are none equal or similar to him in qualities such as virtue. Likewise, 'equal to the unequaled' (asamasamo) means: he is equal to the past and future Buddhas who are unequaled; or, the unequaled ones are his equals. 'Without likeness' (appaṭimo) means: there is no likeness to him in qualities such as virtue. In the remaining two terms as well, this is the method. Therein, a mere simile is a 'likeness' (paṭimā); a similar simile is a 'counterpart' (paṭibhāgo); one who stands by way of taking up a yoke-pair should be known as a 'rival' (paṭipuggalo).

Na kho panāhaṃ samanupassāmīti mama samantacakkhunā hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya sabbalokaṃ passantopi tattha sadevake…pe… pajāya attanā attato sīlasampannataraṃ sampannatarasīlaṃ kañci puggalaṃ na kho pana passāmi, tādisassa abhāvatoti adhippāyo. Aggappasādasuttādīnīti ettha –

As for 'But I certainly do not see': Even while seeing the entire world with my all-around eye like a myrobalan fruit on the palm of my hand, I certainly do not see any person there in the world with its devas... among that populace of beings who is more accomplished in virtue than myself. The intended meaning is: because of the absence of such a one. Herein, in 'the Aggappasāda Sutta and others'—

“Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā catuppadā vā bahuppadā vā rūpino vā arūpino vā saññino vā asaññino vā nevasaññināsaññino vā, tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Ye, bhikkhave, buddhe pasannā, agge [V 1.0231] te pasannā. Agge kho pana pasannānaṃ aggo vipāko hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; 5.32; 10.15; itivu90) –

‘Monks, inasmuch as there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is declared the foremost of them. Monks, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost. And for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is, indeed, foremost.’

Idaṃ [M 1.0245] aggappasādasuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena –

This is the Aggappasāda Sutta. By the word 'ādi' (and others)—

“Sadevake…pe… sadevamanussāya tathāgato abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavattī, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.24; dī. ni. 3.188) –

‘In the world with its devas... among the populace with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the vanquisher, the unvanquished, one who sees for certain, a master of his will. Therefore, he is called “Tathāgata”.’

Evamādīni suttapadāni veditabbāni. Ādikā gāthāyoti ettha –

Such Sutta passages as these should be known. Herein, in 'the initial verses'—

“Ahaṃ hi arahā loke, ahaṃ satthā anuttaro;

Ekomhi sammāsambuddho, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto. (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341);

‘I am indeed the Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed Teacher; I am the one Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, I have become cool, am extinguished.’

“Danto damayataṃ seṭṭho, santo samayataṃ isi;

Mutto mocayataṃ aggo, tiṇṇo tārayataṃ varo. (itivu. 112);

‘Being tamed, he is the best among those who tame; being peaceful, the sage is the best among those who pacify; being liberated, he is the foremost among those who liberate; having crossed over, he is the most excellent among those who help others cross over.’

“Nayimasmiṃ loke parasmiṃ vā pana,

Buddhena seṭṭho sadiso ca vijjati;

Yamāhu dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ aggataṃ gato,

Puññatthikānaṃ vipulaphalesina”nti. (vi. va. 1047; kathā. 799) –

‘Not in this world, nor in another, is there found one superior or equal to the Buddha; whom they call the one who has reached the foremost place among those worthy of offerings for seekers of merit who wish for abundant fruit.’

Evamādikā gāthā vitthāretabbā.

Such verses as these should be elaborated upon.

139. Dametīti sameti, kāyasamādīhi yojetīti attho. Taṃ pana kāyasamādīhi yojanaṃ yathārahaṃ tadaṅgavinayādīsu patiṭṭhāpanaṃ hotīti āha “vinetīti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Dametuṃ yuttāti [V 1.0232] damanārahā. Amanussapurisāti ettha na manussāti amanussā. Taṃsadisatā ettha jotīyati, tena manussattamattaṃ natthi, aññaṃ samānanti yakkhādayo “amanussā”ti adhippetā, na ye keci manussehi aññe. Tathā hi tiracchānapurisānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ kataṃ, yakkhādayo eva ca niddiṭṭhā. Apalālo himavantavāsī. Cūḷodaramahodarā nāgadīpavāsino. Aggisikhadhūmasikhā sīhaḷadīpavāsino. Nibbisā katā dosavisassa vinodanena. Tenāha “saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpitā”ti. Kūṭadantādayoti ādi-saddena ghoṭamukhaupāligahapatiādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sakkadevarājādayoti ādi-saddena ajakalāpayakkhabakabrahmādīnaṃ [M 1.0246] saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Idaṃ cettha suttanti idaṃ kesisuttaṃ. Vinītā vicitrehi vinayanūpāyehīti etasmiṃ atthe vitthāretabbaṃ yathārahaṃ saṇhādīhi upāyehi vinayassa dīpanato.

139. 'Dameti' means 'pacifies'; the meaning is, it yokes one with bodily tranquility and so on. But that yoking with bodily tranquility and so on is the establishing in temporary disciplines, etc., as is appropriate; therefore, he says, 'it comes to be said as “vineti” (it disciplines)'. 'Fit to be tamed' means worthy of being tamed. Herein, in 'non-human men' (amanussapurisā), 'not human' means 'non-human' (amanussā). Herein, similarity to them is revealed; by that, there is not the mere state of being human, but other things are similar. Thus, yakkhas and others are intended by 'non-humans', not just any who are other than humans. For so it is that animal-men are taken up separately, and only yakkhas and others are indicated. Apalāla was a resident of the Himālaya. Cūḷodara and Mahodara were residents of Nāgadīpa. Aggisikha and Dhūmasikha were residents of the island of Sīhaḷa. They were made poisonless by the removal of the poison of hatred. Therefore, he said, 'they were established in the refuges and in the moral precepts'. In 'Kūṭadanta and others', by the word 'ādi' (and others), the inclusion of Ghoṭamukha, the householder Upāli, and others should be seen. In 'Sakka, king of the devas, and others', by the word 'ādi', the inclusion of the yakkha Ajakalāpa, Baka Brahmā, and others should be seen. 'And this sutta here' means this Kesi Sutta. 'Tamed by various means of discipline' should be elaborated upon in this sense, because it shows the discipline by gentle and other means, as is appropriate.

Visuddhasīlādīnaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīnīti “visuddhasīlassa paṭhamajjhānaṃ, paṭhamajjhānalābhino dutiyajjhāna”ntiādinā tassa tassa uparūpari visesaṃ ācikkhantoti sambandho. Sotāpannādīnanti etthāpi eseva nayo. “Dantepi dametiyevā”ti idaṃ pubbe “sabbena sabbaṃ damathaṃ anupagatā purisadammā”ti vuttāti katvā vuttaṃ. Ye pana vippakatadammabhāvā sabbathā dametabbataṃ nātivattā, te satte sandhāya “dantepi dametiyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tepi hi purisadammā evāti, yato ne satthā dameti.

As for 'for those of purified virtue, etc., the first jhānas, etc.': the connection is that he is explaining the successively higher distinction for each one, in the manner of 'for one of purified virtue, the first jhāna; for one who has obtained the first jhāna, the second jhāna,' and so on. Herein also, in 'for the stream-enterers, etc.', this is the method. This phrase, 'Even the tamed are to be tamed,' was said having considered that it was previously said, 'Those to be tamed are persons who have not in every way attained taming.' But with reference to those beings who, being in a state of incomplete tameness, have not in every way gone beyond the state of needing to be tamed, it was said, 'Even the tamed are to be tamed.' For they too are indeed persons to be tamed, since the Teacher tames them.

Atthapadanti atthābhibyañjakapadaṃ, vākyanti attho. Vākyena hi atthābhibyatti, na nāmādipadamattena. Ekapadabhāvena ca anaññasādhāraṇo satthu purisadammasārathibhāvo dassito hoti. Tenāha “bhagavā hī”tiādi. Aṭṭha disāti aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Tā hi aññamaññasambandhāpi asaṃkiṇṇabhāvena dissanti apadissantīti disā, disā viyāti vā disā. Asajjamānāti na sajjamānā vasībhāvappattiyā nissaṅgacārā. Dhāvanti javanavuttiyogato. Ekaṃyeva disaṃ dhāvati, attano kāyaṃ aparivattentoti adhippāyo. Satthārā pana damitā purisadammā ekiriyāpatheneva aṭṭha disā dhāvanti. Tenāha “ekapallaṅkeneva nisinnā”ti. Aṭṭha disāti ca nidassanamattametaṃ, lokiyehi agatapubbaṃ nirodhasamāpattidisaṃ, amatadisañca pakkhandanato.

The term `atthapada` is a word that reveals the meaning; `vākya` is the meaning. Indeed, the meaning is expressed through a sentence, not merely by a word such as a noun. And by the nature of a single word, the Teacher's quality as the incomparable tamer of men to be tamed is shown. Therefore, he said, “The Blessed One, indeed,” and so on. The eight directions are the eight attainments. Indeed, though they are interconnected, they are seen as unmixed, hence they are called `disā` (directions); or, because they are like directions, they are called `disā`. `Asajjamānā` means not clinging; due to the attainment of mastery, they move without attachment. They run because of their connection with swift occurrence. The intended meaning is that one can run in only one direction without turning one's body. But the men to be tamed, who have been tamed by the Teacher, run to the eight directions with just a single posture. Therefore, he said, “seated in a single cross-legged posture.” And this phrase “the eight directions” is merely an illustration, because of their leaping towards the direction of the attainment of cessation, where worldly beings have not gone before, and towards the deathless direction.

140. Diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkho attabhāvo, tattha niyuttoti diṭṭhadhammiko, idhalokattho[V 1.0233]. Kammakilesavasena samparetabbato sammā gantabbato samparāyo, paraloko, tattha niyuttoti samparāyiko, paralokattho. Paramo uttamo attho paramattho, nibbānaṃ. Tehi diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi. Yathārahanti yathānurūpaṃ. Tesu atthesu yo yo puggalo yaṃ yaṃ arahati, tadanurūpaṃ. Anusāsatīti vineti tasmiṃ atthe patiṭṭhapeti, saha atthena vattatīti sattho, bhaṇḍamūlena vāṇijjāya desantaraṃ gacchanto janasamūho. Hitupadesādivasena paripāletabbo sāsitabbo so etassa [M 1.0247] atthīti satthā, satthavāho. So viya bhagavāti āha “satthā viyāti satthā, bhagavā satthavāho”ti.

140. The present existence is called `diṭṭhadhamma`. One engaged therein is called `diṭṭhadhammika`; one who has benefit in this present world. Because one must fare on or go properly due to kamma and defilements, it is called `samparāya`, the next world. One engaged therein is called `samparāyika`; one who has benefit in the next world. The supreme, highest benefit is `paramattha`, which is Nibbāna. By means of these benefits—that of the present, that of the future, and the supreme benefit. `Yathārahaṃ` means according to suitability. Among those benefits, whichever person is worthy of whichever benefit, it is accordingly. `Anusāsati` means he trains, he establishes one in that benefit. Because it proceeds together with goods, it is called `sattha`, a group of people traveling to another country for trade with merchandise capital. Because he has this group which is to be protected and instructed by means of beneficial advice and so on, he is called a `satthā`, a caravan leader. Because the Blessed One is like him, it is said: “Like a caravan leader, he is a `satthā`; the Blessed One is a `satthavāho` (caravan leader).”

Idāni tamatthaṃ niddesapāḷinayena dassetuṃ “yathā satthavāho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sattheti satthike jane. Kaṃ tārenti etthāti kantāro, nirudako araññappadeso. Ruḷhīvasena pana itaropi araññappadeso tathā vuccati. Corakantāranti corehi adhiṭṭhitakantāraṃ. Tathā vāḷakantāraṃ. Dubbhikkhakantāranti dullabhabhikkhaṃ kantāraṃ. Tāretīti akhemantaṭṭhānaṃ atikkāmeti. Uttāretītiādi upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vuttaṃ. Atha vā uttāretīti khemantabhūmiṃ upanento tāreti. Nittāretīti akhemantaṭṭhānato nikkhāmento tāreti. Patāretīti pariggahetvā tāreti, hatthena pariggahetvā viya tāretīti attho. Sabbampetaṃ tāraṇuttāraṇādikhemaṭṭhāne ṭhapanamevāti āha “khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpetī”ti. Satteti veneyyasatte. Mahāgahanatāya, mahānatthatāya, dunnittharaṇatāya ca jātiyeva kantāro jātikantāro, taṃ jātikantāraṃ.

Now, to show that meaning in the manner of the Niddesa Pāḷi, it was said, “Just as a caravan leader,” and so on. Therein, `satthe` means the people belonging to the caravan. Because one crosses it for water (`kaṃ`), it is called `kantāra`; it means a waterless forest region. However, by way of convention, another forest region is also called thus. `Corakantāra` means a wilderness controlled by robbers. `Vāḷakantāra` should be understood similarly. `Dubbhikkhakantāra` means a wilderness where almsfood is difficult to obtain. `Tāreti` means he makes them cross beyond a place of insecurity. `Uttāreti`, and so on, is said by augmenting the word with a prefix. Alternatively, `uttāreti` means he makes them cross over while leading them to a place of safety. `Nittāreti` means he makes them cross over while leading them out from a place of insecurity. `Patāreti` means he makes them cross over, having taken hold of them; the meaning is that he makes them cross over as if having taken hold of them by the hand. Because all this—`tāraṇa`, `uttāraṇa`, and so on—is simply establishing them in a place of safety, he said, “he brings them to a place of safety.” `Satte` means beings to be trained. Due to being a great thicket, a great danger, and difficult to escape from, birth itself is a wilderness—the wilderness of birth.

Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasenāti ukkaṭṭhasattaparicchedavasena. Devamanussā eva hi ukkaṭṭhasattā, na tiracchānādayo. Bhabbapuggalaparicchedavasenāti sammattaniyāmokkamanassa yogyapuggalassa paricchindanavasena. Etanti “devamanussāna”nti etaṃ vacanaṃ. Bhagavatoti nissakkavacanaṃ yathā “upajjhāyato ajjhetī”ti, bhagavato santiketi vā attho. Upanissayasampattinti tihetukapaṭisandhiādikaṃ maggaphalādhigamassa balavakāraṇaṃ.

By way of distinguishing superior beings (`ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena`) means by way of distinguishing superior beings (`ukkaṭṭhasattaparicchedavasena`). Indeed, only gods and humans are superior beings, not animals and the like. By way of distinguishing capable individuals (`bhabbapuggalaparicchedavasena`) means by way of distinguishing a person suitable for entering the fixed course of rightness. `Etaṃ` refers to this statement “of gods and humans.” The word `bhagavato` is an ablative expression, as in “he learns from the preceptor”; or, the meaning is “in the presence of the Blessed One.” Accomplishment of supporting conditions (`upanissayasampatti`) means the strong cause for the attainment of the path and fruit, such as rebirth with three root-conditions and so on.

Gaggarāyāti gaggarāya nāma rañño deviyā, tāya vā kāritattā “gaggarā”ti laddhanāmāya. Sare nimittaṃ aggahesīti “dhammo eso vuccatī”ti dhammasaññāya sare nimittaṃ gaṇhi, gaṇhanto ca pasannacitto parisapariyante nipajji. Sannirumbhitvā aṭṭhāsīti tassa sīse daṇḍassa ṭhapitabhāvaṃ apassanto tattha daṇḍaṃ uppīḷetvā aṭṭhāsi. Maṇḍūkopi daṇḍe ṭhapitepi [V 1.0234] uppīḷitepi dhammagatena pasādena vissaramakarontova kālamakāsi. Devaloke nibbattasattānaṃ ayaṃ dhammatā, yā “kutohaṃ idha nibbatto, tattha kiṃ nu kho kammamakāsi”nti āvajjanā. Tasmā attano purimabhavassa diṭṭhattā āha “are ahampi nāma idha nibbatto”ti[M 1.0248]. Bhagavato pāde vandi kataññutāsaṃvaḍḍhitena pemagāravabahumānena.

`Gaggarāya` refers to the lotus pond of the queen of a king named Gaggarā; or, because it was caused to be made by her, it received the name “Gaggarā.” “He grasped the sign in the sound” means he took the sign in the sound with the perception, “This is the Dhamma being spoken.” And while grasping it, with a confident mind, he lay down at the edge of the assembly. “He stood, pressing down” means, not seeing that the staff had been placed on its head, he stood pressing the staff down on it there. The frog, too, though the staff was placed and pressed down upon it, died without making a discordant sound, due to its confidence directed towards the Dhamma. This is the nature of beings reborn in the deva world: the reflection, “From where have I been reborn here? What kamma, indeed, did I do there?” Therefore, because he had seen his previous existence, he said, “Oh, I too have been reborn here!” He paid homage to the Blessed One's feet with love, reverence, and great esteem, which were augmented by gratitude.

Bhagavā jānantova mahājanassa kammaphalaṃ, buddhānubhāvañca paccakkhaṃ kātukāmo “ko me vandatī”ti gāthāya pucchi. Tattha koti devanāgayakkhagandhabbādīsu ko, katamoti attho. Meti mama. Pādānīti pāde. Iddhiyāti imāya evarūpāya deviddhiyā. “Yasasā”ti iminā edisena parivārena, paricchedena ca. Jalanti vijjotamāno. Abhikkantenāti ativiya kantena kamanīyena sundarena. Vaṇṇenāti chavivaṇṇena sarīravaṇṇanibhāya. Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disāti sabbā dasapi disā pabhāsento, cando viya, sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekālokaṃ karontoti attho.

The Blessed One, knowing full well, yet wishing to make the fruit of kamma and the power of a Buddha directly perceptible to the great assembly, asked with the verse, “Who pays homage to me?” Therein, `ko` means: among the devas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on, who? Which one? This is the meaning. `Me` means my. `Pādāni` means the feet. `Iddhiyā` means by this very kind of divine psychic power. `Yasasā` means by this kind of retinue and distinction. `Jalaṃ` means shining. `Abhikkantena` means exceedingly pleasing, desirable, and beautiful. `Vaṇṇena` means by the color of the skin, by the radiance of the body's complexion. `Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā` means illuminating all ten directions, like the moon and like the sun, making a single radiance, a single light; this is the meaning.

Evaṃ pana bhagavatā pucchito devaputto attānaṃ pavedento “maṇḍūkohaṃ pure āsi”nti gāthamāha. Tattha pureti purimajātiyaṃ. “Udake”ti idaṃ tadā attano uppattiṭṭhānadassanaṃ. “Udake maṇḍūko”ti etena uddhamāyikādikassa thale maṇḍūkassa nivattanaṃ kataṃ hoti. Gāvo caranti etthāti gocaro, gunnaṃ ghāsesanaṭṭhānaṃ. Idha pana gocaro viyāti gocaro, vāri udakaṃ gocaro etassāti vārigocaro. Udakacārīpi hi koci kacchapādi avārigocaropi hotīti “vārigocaro”ti visesetvā vuttaṃ. Tava dhammaṃ suṇantassāti brahmassarena karavīkarutamañjunā desentassa tava dhammaṃ “dhammo eso vuccatī”ti sare nimittaggāhavasena suṇantassa. Anādare cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Avadhi vacchapālakoti vacche rakkhanto gopāladārako mama samīpaṃ āgantvā daṇḍamolubbha tiṭṭhanto mama sīse daṇḍaṃ sannirumbhitvā maṃ māresīti attho.

Then, when questioned thus by the Blessed One, the deity, revealing himself, spoke this verse: 'I was a frog in a former time.' Therein, 'in a former time' (pure) means in a previous birth.
