The phrase 'in the water' (udake) indicates his place of birth at that time. By 'a frog in the water,' the exclusion of a land-frog, such as an uddhumāyika frog, is made. 'Cows roam here' (gāvo caranti ettha), therefore it is a 'pasture' (gocaro); it is a place for cattle to seek food. Here, however, it is called 'gocara' because it is like a pasture; for this one, water (vāri) is the pasture (gocara), hence 'one whose pasture is water' (vārigocaro). For indeed, some creature that moves in water, such as a turtle, may not have water as its pasture; therefore, to specify, it is said 'one whose pasture is water.' 'While listening to your Dhamma' means: while listening—by way of grasping the sign in the sound, thinking, 'This is called the Dhamma'—to your Dhamma, as you were teaching with a voice like that of Brahmā. And this genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. 'The cowherd struck me' means: a cowherd boy, while tending calves, came near me, and standing leaning on his staff, he pressed the staff down on my head and killed me. This is the meaning.

Sitaṃ katvāti “tathā parittatarenāpi puññānubhāvena evaṃ ativiya uḷārā lokiyalokuttarā sampattiyo labbhantī”ti pītisomanassajāto bhāsurataradhavalavipphurantadassanakiraṇāvalīhi bhiyyoso mattāya taṃ padesaṃ obhāsento sitaṃ katvā. Pītisomanassavasena hi so –

‘Having smiled’ means: reflecting, ‘Even by the power of such a very small merit, such exceedingly sublime worldly and supramundane attainments are obtained,’ he, with joy and gladness having arisen, smiled, illuminating that place all the more with rows of tooth-rays that were very brilliant, white, and sparkling. For it was by the power of joy and gladness that he –

“Muhuttaṃ [M 1.0249] cittapasādassa, iddhiṃ passa yasañca me;

Ānubhāvañca me passa, vaṇṇaṃ passa jutiñca me.

“Behold my psychic power and retinue, born of a moment of mental clarity; behold my might, behold my complexion and my radiance.

“Ye [V 1.0235] ca te dīghamaddhānaṃ, dhammaṃ assosuṃ gotama;

Pattā te acalaṭṭhānaṃ, yattha gantvā na socare”ti. (vi. va. 859-860);

“And those, O Gotama, who for a long time have heard your Dhamma, they have reached the unshakable state, where, having gone, they do not grieve.”

Imā dve gāthā vatvā pakkāmi.

Having spoken these two verses, he departed.

141. Yaṃ pana kiñcīti ettha yanti aniyamitavacanaṃ. Tathā kiñcīti. Panāti vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ kiñcīti ñeyyassa anavasesapariyādānaṃ kataṃ hoti. Panāti vā visesatthadīpako nipāto. Tena “sammāsambuddho”ti iminā saṅkhepato, vitthārato ca satthu catusaccābhisambodho vutto. “Buddho”ti pana iminā tadaññassapi ñeyyassāvabodho. Purimena vā satthu paṭivedhañāṇānubhāvo, pacchimena desanāñāṇānubhāvo. Pīti upari vuccamāno viseso jotīyati. Sabbaso paṭipakkhehi vimuccatīti vimokkho, aggamaggo. Tassa anto aggaphalaṃ, tattha bhavaṃ tasmiṃ laddhe laddhabbato vimokkhantikañāṇaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ sabbampi buddhañāṇaṃ. Evaṃ pavattoti ettha –

141. Herein, in 'yaṃ pana kiñci,' 'yaṃ' is an indefinite word. Likewise for 'kiñci.' 'Pana' is merely an embellishment of speech. Therefore, by 'yaṃ kiñci,' the complete inclusion of what is to be known is made. Or, 'pana' is a particle that illuminates a special meaning. By it, through this word 'sammāsambuddho,' the Teacher's full awakening to the Four Truths is stated both concisely and in detail. But by this word 'Buddho,' the understanding of other knowable things as well is stated. Or, by the former, the power of the Teacher's penetration-knowledge is stated; by the latter, the power of his teaching-knowledge. Thus, the distinction to be mentioned later is illuminated. 'Because one is liberated from all opposing factors, it is liberation (vimokkho)'; this is the supreme path (aggamaggo). Its end (anta) is the supreme fruit (aggaphalaṃ). The knowledge that arises therein—since it is to be obtained when that fruit is obtained—is the 'knowledge at the end of liberation' (vimokkhantikañāṇaṃ), which, together with the knowledge of omniscience, is all the Buddha-knowledge. Herein, in 'thus it proceeds' –

“Sabbaññutāya buddho, sabbadassāvitāya buddho, anaññaneyyatāya buddho, visavitāya buddho, khīṇāsavasaṅkhātena buddho, nirupalepasaṅkhātena buddho, ekantavītarāgoti buddho, ekantavītadosoti buddho, ekantavītamohoti buddho, ekantanikkilesoti buddho, ekāyanamaggaṃ gatoti buddho, eko anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti buddho, abuddhivihatattā buddhipaṭilābhā buddho. Buddhoti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ, na pitarā kataṃ, na bhātarā kataṃ, na bhaginiyā kataṃ, na mittāmaccehikataṃ, na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ, na devatāhi kataṃ. Vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ buddho”ti (mahāni. 192) –

“‘He is Buddha because of omniscience; he is Buddha because of all-seeingness; he is Buddha because he is not led by others; he is Buddha because of his pervasiveness; he is Buddha because he is reckoned as one whose cankers are destroyed; he is Buddha because he is reckoned as stainless; he is Buddha because he is entirely free of passion; he is Buddha because he is entirely free of aversion; he is Buddha because he is entirely free of delusion; he is Buddha because he is entirely without defilements; he is Buddha because he has gone on the one-way path; he is Buddha because he alone has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect awakening; he is Buddha because of having dispelled non-wisdom and having acquired wisdom. This name, “Buddha,” is not given by his mother, nor given by his father, nor given by his brother, nor given by his sister, nor given by his friends and ministers, nor given by his relatives and kin, nor given by ascetics and brahmins, nor given by deities. This—the name “Buddha”—is a designation at the culmination of liberation, a concept born of direct realization for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, simultaneous with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience.’”

Ayaṃ [M 1.0250] niddesapāḷinayo. Yasmā cettha tassā paṭisambhidāpāḷiyā bhedo natthi, tasmā dvīsu ekenāpi atthasiddhīti dassanatthaṃ “paṭisambhidānayo vā”ti aniyamattho vā-saddo vutto.

This is the method of the Niddesa-pāḷi. And since there is no difference herein between it and the Paṭisambhidā-pāḷi, therefore, to show that the purpose is accomplished by even one of the two, the word 'vā'—which has an indefinite meaning—is used in the phrase 'or the method of the Paṭisambhidā'.

Tattha [V 1.0236] yathā loke avagantā “avagato”ti vuccati, evaṃ bujjhitā saccānīti buddho suddhakattuvasena. Yathā paṇṇasosā vātā “paṇṇasusā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ bodhetā pajāyāti buddho hetukattuvasena, hetuattho cettha antonīto.

Therein, just as in the world one who understands (avagantā) is called 'one who has understood' (avagato), so 'one who has understood the truths' (bujjhitā saccāni), hence 'Buddha'; this is an agent derivation. Just as winds that dry leaves (paṇṇasosā) are called 'leaf-dryers' (paṇṇasusā), so 'one who causes the populace to understand' (bodhetā pajāya), hence 'Buddha'; this is a causal agent derivation, and the causal meaning is included herein.

Sabbaññutāya buddhoti sabbadhammabujjhanasamatthāya buddhiyā buddhoti attho. Sabbadassāvitāya buddhoti sabbadhammānaṃ ñāṇacakkhunā diṭṭhattā buddhoti attho. Anaññaneyyatāya buddhoti aññena abodhanīto sayameva buddhattā buddhoti attho. Visavitāya buddhoti nānāguṇavisavanato padumamiva vikasanaṭṭhena buddhoti attho. Khīṇāsavasaṅkhātena buddhoti evamādīhi chahi pariyāyehi niddakkhayavibuddho puriso viya sabbakilesaniddakkhayavibuddhattā buddhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekāyanamaggaṃ gatoti buddhoti gamanatthānaṃ buddhiatthatāya buddhiatthānampi gamanatthatā labbhatīti ekāyanamaggaṃ gatattā buddhoti vuccatīti attho. Eko anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti buddhoti na parehi buddhattā buddho, atha kho sayameva anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhattā buddhoti attho. Abuddhivihatattā buddhipaṭilābhā buddhoti buddhi buddhaṃ bodhoti anatthantaraṃ. Tattha yathā rattaguṇayogato ratto paṭo, evaṃ buddhaguṇayogato buddhoti ñāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ buddhoti netaṃ nāmantiādi atthānugatāyaṃ paññattīti bodhanatthaṃ vuttanti evamettha imināpi kāraṇena bhagavā buddhoti veditabbaṃ.

‘Buddha because of omniscience’ means: He is called Buddha because of the wisdom capable of understanding all phenomena. ‘Buddha because of all-seeingness’ means: He is called Buddha because all phenomena have been seen with the eye of wisdom. ‘Buddha because of not being dependent on another for knowledge’ means: He is called Buddha because of not being made to understand by another, but having awakened by Himself. ‘Buddha because of blossoming’ means: He is called Buddha because of causing various virtues to arise and in the sense of blooming like a lotus. By six ways, such as ‘Buddha by the designation of one whose taints are destroyed,’ it is said that He is called Buddha because He is awakened through the destruction of the sleep of all defilements, just like a person who is awakened by the destruction of sleep. ‘Buddha because of having gone to the one and only path’ means: Because roots meaning ‘to go’ have the meaning of ‘to know,’ and roots meaning ‘to know’ can also have the meaning of ‘to go,’ He is called Buddha because of having gone to the one and only path. ‘The one who has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect self-awakening is Buddha’ means: He is not called Buddha because of being made to understand by others, but rather, He is called Buddha because He Himself has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect self-awakening. ‘Buddha because of the attainment of wisdom by dispelling non-wisdom’ means: The terms ‘buddhi’ (wisdom), ‘buddhaṃ’ (the awakened), and ‘bodho’ (awakening) are not different in meaning. Therein, just as a cloth is called red (ratto) due to its connection with the quality of redness, so too is He called Buddha due to His connection with the quality of awakening; this is stated to make this known. Thereafter, the statement beginning with ‘Buddha is not a name…’ is said to make it understood that this is a designation that follows the meaning. Thus, it should be understood that for this reason also, the Blessed One is called Buddha.

142. Assāti bhagavato. Guṇavisiṭṭhasabbasattuttamagarugāravādhivacananti sabbehi sīlādiguṇehi visiṭṭhassa tato eva sabbasattehi uttamassa garuno gāravavasena vuttavacanamidaṃ bhagavāti. Tathā hi lokanātho aparimitanirupamappabhāvasīlādiguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya sabbānatthaparihārapubbaṅgamāya [M 1.0251] niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya, accantupakāritāya ca aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamagāravaṭṭhānanti.

142. ‘Assa’ means ‘of the Blessed One.’ ‘An appellation of reverence for the Venerable One who is distinguished by qualities and supreme among all beings’ means: This word ‘Bhagavā’ is an appellation spoken out of reverence for the Venerable One, who is distinguished by all virtues such as morality and is for that very reason supreme among all beings. For it is true that the Lord of the World—because He is endowed with special qualities such as immeasurable, incomparable power and morality, and because of His utmost helpfulness to the populace of gods and humans through an unsurpassed accomplishment of effort which has the removal of all harm as its forerunner and is intent on arranging complete welfare and happiness—is the supreme object of reverence for innumerable beings in innumerable world-systems.

Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhanti seṭṭhavācakaṃ vacanaṃ seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato “seṭṭha”nti vuttaṃ. Atha vā vuccatīti vacanaṃ, attho. Tasmā yo “bhagavā”ti vacanena vacanīyo attho, so seṭṭhoti attho. Bhagavāti vacanamuttamanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogato, garukaraṇaṃ vā sātisayaṃ arahatīti gāravayutto, gāravārahoti attho.

‘The word “Bhagavā” is supreme (seṭṭha)’ means: A word that denotes the supreme is called ‘supreme’ because it is accompanied by supreme qualities. Alternatively, that which is spoken (vuccati) is a word (vacana); this is the meaning. Therefore, the meaning to be expressed by the word ‘Bhagavā’ is supreme; this is the meaning. For ‘The word “Bhagavā” is the highest (uttama),’ the method is the same. ‘Worthy of reverence (gāravayutta)’ means: He is endowed with gravity (garubhāva) due to His connection with weighty qualities; or, He is worthy of exceptional veneration, therefore He is called ‘gāravayutta.’ The meaning is ‘worthy of reverence (gāravāraha).’

Guṇavisesahetukaṃ [V 1.0237] “bhagavā”ti idaṃ bhagavato nāmanti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato vibhajitukāmo nāmaṃyeva tāva atthuddhāravasena dassento “catubbidhaṃ vā nāma”ntiādimāha. Tattha āvatthikanti avatthāya viditaṃ taṃ taṃ avatthaṃ upādāya paññattaṃ voharitaṃ. Tathā liṅgikaṃ tena tena liṅgena voharitaṃ. Nemittikanti nimittato āgataṃ. Adhiccasamuppannanti yadicchāya pavattaṃ, yadicchāya āgataṃ yadicchakaṃ. Paṭhamena ādi-saddena bālo, yuvā, vuḍḍhoti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, dutiyena muṇḍī, jaṭīti evamādiṃ, tatiyena bahussuto, dhammakathiko, jhāyīti evamādiṃ, catutthena aghamarisanaṃ pāvacananti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Nemittika”nti vuttamatthaṃ byatirekavasena patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “na mahāmāyāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Vimokkhantika”nti iminā idaṃ nāmaṃ ariyāya jātiyā jātakkhaṇeyeva jātanti dasseti. Yadi vimokkhantikaṃ, atha kasmā aññehi khīṇāsavehi asādhāraṇanti āha “saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā”ti. Buddhānañhi arahattaphalaṃ nipphajjamānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇādīhi sabbehi buddhaguṇehi saddhiṃyeva nipphajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “vimokkhantika”nti. Sacchikā paññattīti sabbadhammānaṃ sacchikiriyānimittā paññatti. Atha vā sacchikā paññattīti paccakkhasiddhā paññatti. Yaṃguṇanimittā hi sā, te satthu paccakkhabhūtāti guṇā viya sāpi sacchikatā eva nāma hoti, na paresaṃ vohāramattenāti adhippāyo.

Wishing to analyze in detail the meaning stated concisely as, ‘This name of the Blessed One, “Bhagavā,” is caused by special qualities,’ he first demonstrates by way of extracting the meaning of ‘name’ itself, saying, ‘Or, a name is fourfold,’ and so on. Therein, ‘circumstantial’ (āvatthika) is that which is known by a circumstance, a term designated and used in dependence on that particular circumstance. Likewise, ‘characteristic’ (liṅgika) is a term used in relation to a particular characteristic. ‘Causal’ (nemittika) is that which comes from a cause. ‘Accidental’ (adhiccasamuppanna) is that which arises by chance; what comes by chance is ‘random’ (yādicchaka). With the first ‘and so on’ (ādi), he includes such terms as ‘child,’ ‘youth,’ and ‘elder.’ With the second, such terms as ‘one with a shaven head’ and ‘one with matted hair.’ With the third, such terms as ‘one of great learning,’ ‘a preacher of the Dhamma,’ and ‘one who practices jhāna.’ With the fourth, such terms as ‘the sacred utterance that endures or dispels evil.’ To establish the meaning of ‘causal’ by way of exclusion, the passage beginning ‘not from Mahāmāyā’ is stated. By the term ‘culminating in liberation’ (vimokkhantika), he shows that this name arose at the very moment of His birth into the noble lineage. If it culminates in liberation, then why is it not common to other destroyers of the taints? To this, he says, ‘because of the attainment of omniscient knowledge together with it.’ For in Buddhas, the fruit of Arahantship, when it is produced, is produced only together with all the Buddha-qualities, such as omniscient knowledge. Therefore, it is called ‘culminating in liberation.’ ‘A designation by direct realization’ (sacchikā paññatti) means a designation whose cause is the direct realization of all phenomena. Alternatively, ‘a designation by direct realization’ means a designation established by direct perception. For the qualities that are its cause were directly perceived by the Teacher; therefore, like the qualities, that designation itself is also indeed directly realized, and is not merely a term used by others—this is the intention.

143. Vadantīti [M 1.0252] mahātherassa garubhāvato bahuvacanenāha, saṅgītikārehi vā katamanuvādaṃ sandhāya. Issariyādibhedo bhago assa atthīti bhagī. Akāsi bhagganti rāgādipāpadhammaṃ bhaggaṃ akāsi, bhaggavāti attho. Bahūhi ñāyehīti kāyabhāvanādikehi anekehi bhāvanākkamehi. Subhāvitattanoti sammadeva bhāvitasabhāvassa. Paccatte cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ.

143. Regarding ‘vadanti’ (they say), he (the commentator) says this was spoken in the plural out of respect for the great elder, or with reference to the recitation made by the compilers of the canon. ‘He who possesses fortune (bhaga), of the kinds such as sovereignty, is “bhagī.”’ ‘He made a breaking (akāsi bhaggaṃ)’ means: He caused the breaking of evil states such as lust; the meaning is ‘bhaggavā’ (one who has broken). ‘By many ways’ means: by numerous stages of development, such as the development of the body. ‘Of one whose self is well-developed (subhāvitattano)’ means: of one whose nature is truly well-developed. And this is a word in the genitive case used in the sense of the nominative.

Niddese vuttanayenāti etthāyaṃ niddesanayo –

In the phrase ‘according to the method stated in the Niddesa,’ the method of the Niddesa is as follows:

“Bhagavāti gāravādhivacanametaṃ. Apica bhaggarāgoti bhagavā, bhaggadosoti bhagavā, bhaggamohoti bhagavā, bhaggamānoti bhagavā, bhaggadiṭṭhīti bhagavā, bhaggataṇhoti bhagavā, bhaggakilesoti bhagavā, bhaji vibhaji pavibhaji dhammaratananti bhagavā, bhavānaṃ antakaroti bhagavā, bhāvitakāyo bhāvitasīlo bhāvitacitto bhāvitapaññoti bhagavā, bhaji [V 1.0238] vā bhagavā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni appasaddāni appanigghosāni vijanavātāni manussarāhasseyyakāni paṭisallānasāruppānīti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānanti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā attharasassa dhammarasassa vimuttirasassa adhisīlassa adhicittassa adhipaññāyāti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ catunnaṃ appamaññānaṃ catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnanti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ abhibhāyatanānaṃ navannaṃ anupubbavihārasamāpattīnanti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā dasannaṃ saññābhāvanānaṃ dasannaṃ kasiṇasamāpattīnaṃ ānāpānassatisamādhissa asubhasamāpattiyāti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ pañcannaṃ balānaṃ sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassāti bhagavā, bhāgī vā bhagavā dasannaṃ tathāgatabalānaṃ catunnaṃ vesārajjānaṃ catunnaṃ paṭisambhidānaṃ channaṃ abhiññānaṃ channaṃ buddhadhammānanti bhagavā, bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ…pe… sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ bhagavā”ti (mahāni. 83).

“‘Bhagavā’ is a term of reverence. Furthermore, one is called ‘Bhagavā’ because he has destroyed lust (bhaggarāgo), destroyed hatred (bhaggadoso), destroyed delusion (bhaggamoho), destroyed conceit (bhaggamāno), destroyed wrong view (bhaggadiṭṭhi), destroyed craving (bhaggataṇho), and destroyed defilements (bhaggakileso). He has analyzed concisely, analyzed in detail, and thoroughly analyzed the jewel of the Dhamma (dhammaratana); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. He is the ender of existences (bhavānaṃ antakaro); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. He has a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom (bhāvitakāyo bhāvitasīlo bhāvitacitto bhāvitapañño); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā resorted to forest and woodland thickets, remote dwellings with little sound, little clamor, secluded from people, suitable for people’s privacy, and fit for seclusion (bhaji vā bhagavā araññavanapatthāni… paṭisallānasāruppāni); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick (bhāgī vā bhagavā cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma, the flavor of liberation, of higher virtue, of higher mind, and of higher wisdom (bhāgī vā bhagavā attharasassa… adhipaññāya); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments (bhāgī vā bhagavā catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ… arūpasamāpattīnaṃ); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of the eight liberations, the eight spheres of mastery, and the nine successive dwelling attainments (bhāgī vā bhagavā aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ… anupubbavihārasamāpattīnaṃ); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of the ten developments of perception, the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the attainment of foulness (bhāgī vā bhagavā dasannaṃ saññābhāvanānaṃ… asubhasamāpattiyā); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path (bhāgī vā bhagavā catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ… ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. Or, the Bhagavā is a partaker of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four confidences, the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the six qualities of a Buddha (bhāgī vā bhagavā dasannaṃ tathāgatabalānaṃ… channaṃ buddhadhammānaṃ); therefore, he is called ‘Bhagavā’. This name ‘Bhagavā’ is not… and so on… it is a realized designation, that is, ‘Bhagavā’.”

Ettha [M 1.0253] ca “gāravādhivacana”ntiādīni yadipi gāthāyaṃ āgatapadānukkamena na niddiṭṭhāni, yathārahaṃ pana tesaṃ sabbesampi niddesabhāvena veditabbāni. Tattha gāravādhivacananti garūnaṃ garubhāvavācakaṃ vacanaṃ. Bhajīti bhāgaso kathesi. Tenāha “vibhajī”ti. Dhammaratananti maggaphalādiariyadhammaratanaṃ. Puna bhajīti sevi. Bhāgīti bhāgadheyyavā. Puna bhāgīti bhajanasīlo. Attharasassāti atthasannissayassa rasassa. Vimuttāyatanasīse hi ṭhatvā dhammaṃ kathentassa, suṇantassa ca tadatthaṃ ārabbha uppajjanakapītisomanassaṃ attharaso. Dhammaṃ ārabbha dhammaraso. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammaveda”nti (a. ni. 6.10). Vimuttirasassāti vimuttibhūtassa, vimuttisannissayassa vā rasassa. Saññābhāvanānanti aniccasaññādīnaṃ dasannaṃ saññābhāvanānaṃ. Channaṃ buddhadhammānanti cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha tattha “bhagavā”ti saddasiddhi niruttinayena veditabbā.

And here, although terms such as ‘term of reverence’ are not explained in the order of the words as they appear in the verse, they should nevertheless be understood as explanations of all of them, as is suitable. Therein, ‘term of reverence’ means a word that expresses the venerable state of the venerable ones. ‘Bhaji’ means he taught in parts. For that reason, it is said, ‘vibhaji’ (he analyzed in detail). ‘The jewel of the Dhamma’ means the noble Dhamma-jewel of the path, fruit, and so on. Again, ‘bhaji’ means he resorted to. ‘Bhāgī’ means one who possesses great merit. Again, ‘bhāgī’ means one who is accustomed to frequenting. ‘Of the flavor of meaning’ means of the flavor that is dependent on the meaning. Indeed, for one who stands at the head of the sphere of liberation and teaches the Dhamma, and for the listener, the joy and mental pleasure that arises concerning that meaning is the flavor of meaning. The flavor of the Dhamma arises concerning the Dhamma. It was in reference to this that it was said: “He obtains the joy of meaning, he obtains the joy of the Dhamma” (AN 6.10). ‘Of the flavor of liberation’ means of the flavor that has become liberation, or of the flavor that is dependent on liberation. ‘Of the developments of perception’ means of the ten developments of perception beginning with the perception of impermanence. ‘Of the six qualities of a Buddha’ was said in reference to the six unshared knowledges. In each case, the derivation of the word ‘Bhagavā’ should be understood according to the method of etymology.

144. Yadipi “bhāgyavā”tiādīhi padehi vuccamāno attho “bhagī bhajī”ti niddesagāthāya saṅgahito eva, tathāpi padasiddhi atthavibhāgaatthayojanādisahito saṃvaṇṇanānayo tato aññākāroti vuttaṃ “ayaṃ pana aparo nayo”ti. Ādikanti ādi-saddena vaṇṇavikāro[V 1.0239], vaṇṇalopo, dhātuatthena niyojanañcāti imaṃ tividhaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Saddanayenāti byākaraṇanayena. Pisodarādīnaṃ saddānaṃ ākatigaṇabhāvato vuttaṃ “pisodarādipakkhepalakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā”ti. Pakkhipanameva lakkhaṇaṃ. Tappariyāpannatākaraṇaṃ hi pakkhipanaṃ. Pārappattanti paramukkaṃsagataṃ pāramibhāvappattaṃ. Bhāgyanti kusalaṃ. Tattha maggakusalaṃ lokuttarasukhanibbattakaṃ, itaraṃ lokiyasukhanibbattakaṃ, itarampi vā vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ pariyāyato lokuttarasukhanibbattakaṃ siyā.

144. Although the meaning expressed by words such as ‘bhāgyavā’ is indeed included in the explanatory verse ‘bhagī bhajī,’ nevertheless, the commentarial method—which includes word derivation, analysis of meaning, application of meaning, and so on—has a different character from that; hence it was said, “But this is another method.” In the word ‘ādi,’ the term ‘ādi’ includes these three characteristics: modification of a letter, elision of a letter, and connection with the meaning of a root. ‘By the method of grammar’ means by the grammatical method. Because words like ‘pisodara’ and so on belong to an irregular group, it was said, “having taken the characteristic of inclusion in the pisodara group.” Inclusion itself is the characteristic. For making something included in that group is called inclusion. ‘Pārappatta’ means gone to the highest excellence, attained the state of a perfection. ‘Bhāgya’ means wholesome merit. Therein, the wholesome merit of the path produces supramundane happiness; the other, mundane wholesome merit, produces mundane happiness. Alternatively, even that other mundane wholesome merit, having Nibbāna as its support, may indirectly be a producer of supramundane happiness.

Lobhādayo ekakavasena gahitā. Tathā viparītamanasikāro vipallāsabhāvasāmaññena, ahirikādayo dukavasena. Lobhādayo ca puna “tividhākusalamūla”nti tikavasena gahitā. Kāyaduccaritādi-taṇhāsaṃkilesādirāgamalādirāgavisamādikāmasaññādikāmavitakkāditaṇhāpapañcādayo tividhaduccaritādayo. Subhasaññādikā catubbidhavipariyesā. “Cīvarahetu vā bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, piṇḍapāta[M 1.0254], senāsana, itibhavābhavahetu vā”ti (a. ni. 4.9) evamāgatā cattāro taṇhuppādā. “Buddhe kaṅkhati, dhamme, saṅghe, sikkhāya, sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khīlajāto”ti (dī. ni. 3.319; ma. ni. 1.185; a. ni. 5.205; 9.71; vibha. 941) evamāgatāni pañca cetokhīlāni. “Kāme avītarāgo hoti, kāye avītarāgo, rūpe avītarāgo, yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati, aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ caratī”ti (dī. ni. 3.320; ma. ni. 1.186) āgatā pañca vinibandhā. Rūpābhinandanādayo pañcābhinandanā. Kodho, makkho, issā, sāṭheyyaṃ, pāpicchatā, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsoti imāni cha vivādamūlāni. Rūpataṇhādayo cha taṇhākāyā.

Greed and so forth are taken as a single unit. Similarly, wrong attention is taken by way of the commonality of being a perversion, while shamelessness and so forth are taken as a pair. Greed and so forth are also taken as a triad by way of the 'threefold unwholesome roots.' Bodily misconduct and so forth, the defilements of craving and so forth, the stains of lust and so forth, the unevenness of lust and so forth, the perceptions of sensuality and so forth, the thoughts of sensuality and so forth, and the proliferations of craving and so forth are the threefold misconducts and so forth. Perceptions of beauty and so forth are the four perversions. “For a monk, when craving arises, it arises on account of robes, or on account of almsfood, or on account of lodging, or for the sake of this or that state of existence” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.9)—thus are the four origins of craving. “He doubts the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training; he is angry and displeased with his fellow practitioners, his mind smitten, and has become mentally rigid” (Dīgha Nikāya 3.319; Majjhima Nikāya 1.185; Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.205; 9.71; Vibhaṅga 941)—thus are the five mental barrennesses. “He is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, for the body, for forms; having eaten his fill, he dwells dedicated to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of turning on his side, and the pleasure of drowsiness; he lives the holy life with the aspiration for some group of deities” (Dīgha Nikāya 3.320; Majjhima Nikāya 1.186)—thus are the five bonds. Delight in forms and so forth are the five delights. Anger, denigration, envy, deceit, evil desires, and adherence to one's own views—these are the six roots of contention. Craving for forms and so forth are the six groups of craving.

Kāmarāgapaṭighadiṭṭhivicikicchābhavarāgamānāvijjā sattānusayā. Micchādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha micchattā. “Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo, chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ, ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho, pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ, macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkhā, ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānādayo”ti (dī. ni. 2.103; 3.359) ete nava taṇhāmūlakā. Cattāro sassatavādā, cattāro ekaccasassatavādā, cattāro antānantikā, cattāro amarāvikkhepikā, dve adhiccasamuppannikā, soḷasa saññīvādā, aṭṭha asaññīvādā, aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā[V 1.0240], satta ucchedavādā, pañca paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti etāni dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni. Ajjhattikassa upādāya “asmī”ti hoti, “itthasmī”ti, “evasmī”ti, “aññathāsmī”ti, “bhavissa”nti, “itthaṃ bhavissa”nti, “evaṃ bhavissa”nti, “aññathā bhavissa”nti, “asasmī”ti, “sātasmī”ti, “siya”nti, “itthaṃ siya”nti, “evaṃ siya”nti, “aññathā siya”nti, “apāhaṃ siya”nti, “apāhaṃ itthaṃ siya”nti, “apāhaṃ evaṃ siya”nti, “apāhaṃ aññathā siya”nti hotīti aṭṭhārasa, bāhirassupādāya “iminā asmī”ti hoti, “iminā itthasmī”ti, “iminā evasmī”ti, “iminā aññathāsmī”tiādikā (vibha. 975-976) vuttanayā aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa, atītā chattiṃsa, anāgatā chattiṃsa, paccuppannā chattiṃsāti aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni.

Sensual lust, aversion, views, doubt, craving for existence, conceit, and ignorance are the seven underlying tendencies. The eight wrongnesses begin with wrong view. “Conditioned by craving is seeking; conditioned by seeking is acquisition; conditioned by acquisition is decision; conditioned by decision is lustful desire; conditioned by lustful desire is attachment; conditioned by attachment is possession; conditioned by possession is stinginess; conditioned by stinginess is guarding; and because of guarding, the taking up of rods and weapons, and so forth, come to be” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.103; 3.359). These nine are rooted in craving. The four eternalist views, four partial-eternalist views, four views on finitude and infinitude, four evasive views, two views of accidental origination, sixteen views of a conscious post-mortem existence, eight views of an unconscious post-mortem existence, eight views of a neither-conscious-nor-unconscious post-mortem existence, seven annihilationist views, and five views of Nibbāna in this very life—these are the sixty-two speculative views. With regard to the internal, it occurs: “I am,” “I am thus,” “I am so,” “I am otherwise,” “I will be,” “I will be thus,” “I will be so,” “I will be otherwise,” “I am eternal,” “I am not eternal,” “May I be,” “May I be thus,” “May I be so,” “May I be otherwise,” “May I not be,” “May I not be thus,” “May I not be so,” “May I not be otherwise”—these are eighteen. With regard to the external, it occurs: “By this I am,” “By this I am thus,” “By this I am so,” “By this I am otherwise,” and so forth, in the manner stated, are another eighteen. Thus there are thirty-six. Thirty-six for the past, thirty-six for the future, and thirty-six for the present make one hundred and eight roamings of craving.

Pabheda-saddo [M 1.0255] paccekaṃ sambandhitabbo. Tatthāyaṃ yojanā – lobhappabhedā dosappabhedā yāva aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritappabhedāti. Sabbāni sattānaṃ darathapariḷāhakarāni kilesānaṃ anekāni satasahassāni abhañjīti yojanā. Ārammaṇādivibhāgato hi pavattiākāravibhāgato ca anantappabhedā kilesāti. Saṅkhepatoti ettha samucchedappahānavasena sabbaso appavattikaraṇena kilesamāraṃ, samudayappahānapariññāvasena khandhamāraṃ, sahāyavekallakaraṇavasena sabbathā appavattikaraṇena abhisaṅkhāramāraṃ, balavidhamanavisayātikkamanavasena devaputtamaccumārañca abhañji bhagge akāsi. Parissayānanti upaddavānaṃ. Sampati, āyatiñca sattānaṃ anatthāvahattā māraṇaṭṭhena vibādhanaṭṭhena kilesāva māroti kilesamāro. Vadhakaṭṭhena khandhāva māroti khandhamāro. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “vadhakaṃ rūpaṃ ‘vadhakaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.85). Jātijarādimahābyasananibbattanena abhisaṅkhārova māroti abhisaṅkhāramāro. Saṃkilesanimittaṃ hutvā guṇamāraṇaṭṭhena devaputtova māroti devaputtamāro. Sattānaṃ jīvitassa, jīvitaparikkhārānañca jānikaraṇena mahābādharūpattā maccu eva māroti maccumāro.

The word ‘variety’ (pabheda) should be connected to each item. Here is the application: the varieties of greed, the varieties of hatred, up to the varieties of the one hundred and eight roamings of craving. The application is: He destroyed all the countless hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause anxiety and burning for beings. For by way of the division of their objects, the division of their modes of occurrence, and so forth, the defilements are of infinite variety. In the passage beginning with ‘in brief,’ he broke and shattered: the Defilement-Māra by completely preventing its arising through abandonment by eradication; the Aggregate-Māra through abandoning its origin and through full understanding; the Formation-Māra by rendering it completely inactive by removing its support; and the God-Māra and the Death-Māra by repelling his forces and transcending his domain. ‘Dangers’ means calamities. In the present and in the future, because they bring harm to beings, and due to their nature of killing and oppressing, the defilements themselves are Māra; thus, the Defilement-Māra. Due to their nature of being a killer, the aggregates themselves are Māra; thus, the Aggregate-Māra. For so it is said: “One does not understand as it really is that form, the killer, is ‘a killer,’” and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.85). Because they produce the great disasters of birth, aging, and so forth, the formations themselves are Māra; thus, the Formation-Māra. By being a cause for defilement and due to his nature of killing virtue, the god himself is Māra; thus, the God-Māra. By causing the loss of the life of beings and of the requisites of life, and because it has the nature of great affliction, death itself is Māra; thus, the Death-Māra.

Satapuññalakkhaṇadharassāti anekasatapuññanibbattamahāpurisalakkhaṇavahato rūpakāyasampatti dīpitā hoti, itarāsaṃ phalasampadānaṃ mūlabhāvato, adhiṭṭhānabhāvato ca. Dhammakāyasampatti dīpitā hoti, pahānasampadāpubbakattā ñāṇasampadādīnaṃ. Bhāgyavatāya lokiyānaṃ bahumatabhāvo. Bhaggadosatāya parikkhakānaṃ bahumatabhāvoti yojanā. Evaṃ ito paresupi yathāsaṅkhyaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Puññavantaṃ hi gahaṭṭhā khattiyādayo abhigacchanti, pahīnadosaṃ pabbajitatāpasaparibbājakādayo [V 1.0241] “dosavinayāya dhammaṃ desetī”ti. Abhigatānañca nesaṃ kāyacittadukkhāpanayane paṭibalabhāvo, āmisadānadhammadānehi upakārasabbhāvato. Rūpakāyaṃ tassa pasādacakkhunā, dhammakāyaṃ paññācakkhunā disvā dukkhadvayassa paṭippassambhanato upagatānañca tesaṃ āmisadānadhammadānehi upakāritā, “pubbe āmisadānadhammadānehi mayā ayaṃ [M 1.0256] lokaggabhāvo adhigato, tasmā tumhehipi evameva paṭipajjitabba”nti evaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ niyojanena abhigatānaṃ lokiyalokuttarasukhehi saṃyojanasamatthatā ca dīpitā hoti.

By [the phrase] 'one who bears the marks of a hundred merits'—meaning, one who bears the characteristics of a great man produced by innumerable hundreds of merits—the perfection of the form-body is shown, because it is the root and foundation of the other perfections of fruition. The perfection of the Dhamma-body is shown, because the perfections of knowledge and so on are preceded by the perfection of abandonment. By 'fortunate,' the state of being highly esteemed by worldly people [is shown]. By 'having destroyed the corruptions,' the state of being highly esteemed by discerning people [is shown]—thus is the connection. In this way, in the subsequent phrases as well, it should be connected according to the numerical order. Indeed, householders such as khattiyas and so on approach one who is meritorious; and those who have gone forth, such as ascetics and wanderers, approach one who has abandoned faults, [thinking,] 'He teaches the Dhamma for the removal of faults.' And for those who have approached, the capability to dispel their bodily and mental suffering [is shown], because of the existence of help through the gift of material things and the gift of the Dhamma. Having seen his form-body with the eye of faith and his Dhamma-body with the eye of wisdom, and due to the calming of the twofold suffering, for those who have approached there is also helpfulness through the gift of material things and the gift of the Dhamma. [This is shown by his teaching:] 'In the past, this supreme state in the world was attained by me through the gift of material things and the gift of the Dhamma; therefore, you too should practice in this very way.' Thus, by urging those who have approached towards right practice, the capability of connecting them with worldly and supramundane happiness is also shown.

Sakacitte issariyaṃ attano cittassa vasībhāvāpādanaṃ, yena paṭikkūlādīsu appaṭikkūlasaññitādivihārasiddhi, adhiṭṭhāniddhiādiko iddhividhopi cittissariyameva cittabhāvanāya vasībhāvappattiyā ijjhanato. Aṇimālaghimādikanti ādi-saddena mahimā patti pākammaṃ īsitā vasitā yatthakāmāvasāyitāti ime chapi saṅgahitā. Tattha kāyassa aṇubhāvakaraṇaṃ aṇimā. Lahubhāvo laghimā ākāse padasā gamanādinā. Mahattaṃ mahimā kāyassa mahantatāpādanaṃ. Iṭṭhadesappatti patti. Adhiṭṭhānādivasena icchitanipphādanaṃ pākammaṃ. Sayaṃvasitā issarabhāvo īsitā. Iddhividhe vasībhāvo vasitā. Ākāsena vā gacchato, aññaṃ vā kiñci karoto yattha katthaci vosānappatti yatthakāmāvasāyitā. “Kumārakarūpādidassana”ntipi vadanti. Evamidaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ lokiyasammataṃ issariyaṃ. Taṃ pana bhagavato iddhividhantogadhaṃ, anaññasādhāraṇañcāti āha “sabbākāraparipūraṃ atthī”ti.

Sovereignty over one's own mind is bringing one's own mind to a state of mastery, by which is achieved the accomplishment of dwelling with the perception of the non-repulsive in the repulsive, and so on. The kinds of psychic power, such as the psychic power of determination and so on, are also just sovereignty of mind, because they are accomplished when a state of mastery is attained through mental development. In the phrase '`aṇimā`, `laghimā`, and so on,' by the word 'and so on,' these six are also included: `mahimā`, `patti`, `pākamma`, `īsitā`, `vasitā`, and `yatthakāmāvasāyitā`. Therein, `aṇimā` is making the body minute. `Laghimā` is lightness, such as by walking in the sky on foot. `Mahimā` is greatness, bringing the body to a state of greatness. `Patti` is reaching a desired place. `Pākamma` is accomplishing a desired thing by means of determination and so on. `Īsitā` is self-mastery, the state of a lord. `Vasitā` is mastery in the kinds of psychic power. `Yatthakāmāvasāyitā` is reaching the final point anywhere at all, whether for one going through the sky or for one doing something else. They also say it is 'the showing of forms such as that of a young boy.' Thus, this eightfold sovereignty is that which is esteemed as worldly. But for the Blessed One, it is included within the kinds of psychic power and is not shared with others; thus it is said, 'it is complete in all aspects.'

Kesañci padesavutti, ayathābhūtaguṇasannissayattā aparisuddho ca yaso hoti, na evaṃ tathāgatassāti dassetuṃ “lokattayabyāpako”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha idha adhigatasatthuguṇānaṃ āruppe uppannānaṃ “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā bhagavato guṇe anussarantānaṃ yaso pākaṭo hotīti āha “lokattayabyāpako”ti. Yathābhuccaguṇādhigatattā eva ativiya parisuddho. Anavasesalakkhaṇānubyañjanādisampattiyā sabbākāraparipūrā. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgasirī sabbesaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ sobhā. “Tiṇṇo tāreyya”ntiādinā yaṃ yaṃ etena lokanāthena icchitaṃ manovacīpaṇidhānavasena, patthitaṃ kāyapaṇidhānavasena. Tathevāti paṇidhānānurūpameva. Vīriyapāramibhāvappatto, ariyamaggapariyāpanno ca sammāvāyāmasaṅkhāto payatto.

For some, fame is regional and, because it is based on unreal qualities, is impure. To show that it is not so for the Tathāgata, 'pervading the three worlds,' etc., was said. Therein, for those who have here attained the Teacher's qualities and are reborn in the formless realm, when they recollect the Blessed One's qualities with 'Thus is the Blessed One...' etc., his fame becomes manifest; therefore, it is said 'pervading the three worlds.' Because it is attained through qualities that are true, it is exceedingly pure. Due to the perfection of all major and minor characteristics without exception, it is complete in all aspects. 'Splendor of all major and minor limbs' is the beauty of all major and minor limbs. By [the phrase] 'Having crossed, may I lead others across,' etc., [is meant] whatever was wished for by this Lord of the World by means of mental and verbal resolution, and what was aspired to by means of bodily resolution. 'Just so' means 'in accordance with the resolution.' The effort that has reached the state of the perfection of energy and is included in the noble path is the effort designated as 'right effort'.

Bhedehīti sabbattikadukapadasaṃhitehi pabhedehi. Paṭiccasamuppādādīhīti ādi-saddena na kevalaṃ [V 1.0242] vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ āgatā satipaṭṭhānādayova saṅgahitā, atha kho saṅgahādayo, samayavimuttādayo, ṭhapanādayo[M 1.0257], tikapaṭṭhānādayo ca saṅgahitāti veditabbaṃ. Dukkhasaccassa pīḷanaṭṭho taṃsamaṅgino sattassa hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ. Saṅkhataṭṭho sameccasambhūyapaccayehi katabhāvo. Santāpaṭṭho dukkhadukkhatādīhi santappanaṃ paridahanaṃ. Vipariṇāmaṭṭho jarāya, maraṇena cāti dvidhā vipariṇāmetabbatā. Samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho dukkhassa nibbattanavasena sampiṇḍanaṃ. Nidānaṭṭho “idaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti nidadantassa viya samuṭṭhāpanaṃ. Saṃyogaṭṭho saṃsāradukkhena saṃyojanaṃ. Palibodhaṭṭho maggādhigamassa nivāraṇaṃ. Nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho sabbūpadhīnaṃ paṭinissaggasabhāvattā tato vinissaṭatā, tannissaraṇanimittatā vā. Vivekaṭṭho sabbasaṅkhāravisaṃyuttatā. Asaṅkhataṭṭho kenacipi paccayena anabhisaṅkhatatā. Amataṭṭho niccasabhāvattā maraṇābhāvo, sattānaṃ maraṇābhāvahetutā vā. Maggassa niyyānaṭṭho vaṭṭadukkhato niggamanaṭṭho. Hetuattho nibbānassa sampāpakabhāvo. Dassanaṭṭho accantasukhumassa nibbānassa sacchikaraṇaṃ. Ādhipateyyaṭṭho catusaccadassane sampayuttānaṃ ādhipaccakaraṇaṃ, ārammaṇādhipatibhāvo vā visesato maggādhipativacanato. Satipi hi jhānādīnaṃ ārammaṇādhipatibhāve “jhānādhipatino dhammā”ti evamādiṃ avatvā “maggādhipatino dhammā” icceva vuttaṃ, tasmā viññāyati “atthi maggassa ārammaṇādhipatibhāve viseso”ti. Ete ca pīḷanādayo soḷasākārā nāma. Kasmā panettha aññesu rogagaṇṭhādiākāresu vijjamānesu eteva pariggayhantīti? Salakkhaṇato ca saccantaradassanato ca āvibhāvato. Svāyamattho parato saccakathāyameva āvi bhavissati.

“By divisions” means by the divisions counted by all the triad-terms and dyad-terms. “By dependent origination and so forth”: By the word “and so forth” it should be understood that not only the foundations of mindfulness and others that appear in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi are included, but also the Saṅgaha, Samayavimutta, Ṭhapana, and Tikapaṭṭhāna, and so on. The meaning of “oppression” in the truth of suffering is the harming of a being endowed with it, the making of it unexpansive. The meaning of “conditioned” is the state of having been made by causes that have assembled and arisen together. The meaning of “torment” is the tormenting and burning by suffering as suffering and so on. The meaning of “change” is the state of being subject to alteration in two ways: by aging and by death. The meaning of “accumulation” in the origin of suffering is the amassing by way of producing suffering. The meaning of “source” is the cause of arising, as if one were assigning, “This is that suffering.” The meaning of “bondage” is the yoking with the suffering of saṃsāra. The meaning of “hindrance” is the obstruction of the attainment of the path. The meaning of “escape” in the cessation of suffering is the state of being released from all substrata of existence due to its nature of relinquishment, or its being the cause for escape from them. The meaning of “seclusion” is the state of being disjoined from all conditioned things. The meaning of “unconditioned” is the state of not being formed by any cause whatsoever. The meaning of “deathless” is the absence of death due to its permanent nature, or its being the cause for the absence of death for beings. The meaning of “leading out” in the path is the meaning of departure from the suffering of the round. The meaning of “cause” is the state of leading to Nibbāna. The meaning of “seeing” is the realization of the extremely subtle Nibbāna. The meaning of “dominance” is the exercising of sovereignty over things associated with the seeing of the four truths, or its state of being a dominant object, especially due to the statement “path as dominant.” For although there is the state of being a dominant object for jhāna and so on, without saying “states with jhāna as dominant” and so on, it is said only “states with the path as dominant.” Therefore, it is understood: “There is a distinction in the path's state of being a dominant object.” And these, beginning with oppression, are called the sixteen aspects. Why, when other aspects such as disease, boils, etc., exist here, are only these comprehended? Because they become manifest through their own characteristic and through the seeing of the other truths. This meaning will become manifest later in the discussion on the truths itself.

Dibbavihāro kasiṇādiārammaṇāni rūpāvacarajjhānāni. Mettādijjhānāni brahmavihāro. Phalasamāpatti ariyavihāro. Kāmehi vivekaṭṭhakāyatāvasena ekībhāvo kāyaviveko. Paṭhamajjhānādinā nīvaraṇādīhi vivittacittatā cittaviveko. Upadhiviveko nibbānaṃ. Aññeti lokiyābhiññādike.

The divine abiding refers to the fine-material sphere jhānas whose objects are kasiṇas and so forth. The sublime abidings are the jhānas of loving-kindness and so forth. The attainment of fruition is the noble abiding. Bodily seclusion is the state of being alone by way of having a body situated in seclusion from sensual pleasures. Mental seclusion is the state of a mind secluded from the hindrances and so on, by means of the first jhāna and so on. Nibbāna is the seclusion from the substrata of existence. “Others” refers to mundane supernormal knowledges and the like.

Kilesābhisaṅkhāravasena bhavesu paribbhamanaṃ, so ca taṇhāppadhānoti vuttaṃ “taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamana”nti. Vantanti ariyamaggamukhena uggiritaṃ puna apaccāvamanavasena chaḍḍitaṃ. Bhagavāti vuccati niruttinayenāti dassento āha “yathā…pe… mekhalā”ti.

Wandering in existences occurs by the power of defilement-formations; and that wandering has craving as its chief. Therefore, it is said, “the going designated as craving.” “Vanta” (vomited) means: vomited out by the mouth of the noble path, discarded by way of not swallowing again. Showing that “Bhagavā” is said according to the etymological method, he said: “just as...pe... a girdle.”

Aparo [M 1.0258][V 1.0243] nayo – bhāgavāti bhagavā, bhatavāti bhagavā, bhāge vanīti bhagavā, bhage vanīti bhagavā, bhattavāti bhagavā, bhage vamīti bhagavā. Bhāge vamīti bhagavā.

Another method: Bhagavā because he possesses cultivated qualities (bhāgavā); Bhagavā because he has cultivated (bhatavā); Bhagavā because he resorted to the portions such as daily attainments (bhāge vani); Bhagavā because he resorted to worldly and supramundane fortunes (bhage vani); Bhagavā because he has many devotees (bhattavā); Bhagavā because he relinquished worldly glories (bhage vami); Bhagavā because he relinquished the portions of phenomena such as the aggregates (bhāge vami).

Bhāgavā bhatavā bhāge, bhage ca vani bhattavā;

Bhage vami tathā bhāge, vamīti bhagavā jino.

He has a share of good qualities (bhāgavā), he has cultivated perfections (bhatavā), and to portions (bhāge) he resorted (vani); he has many devotees (bhattavā); glories (bhage) he relinquished (vami), and likewise portions (bhāge) he relinquished (vami); thus the Conqueror is Bhagavā.

Tattha kathaṃ bhāgavāti bhagavā? Ye te sīlādayo dhammakkhandhā guṇakoṭṭhāsā, te anaññasādhāraṇā niratisayā tathāgatassa atthi upalabbhanti. Tathā hissa sīlaṃ samādhi paññā vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ, hirī ottappaṃ, saddhā vīriyaṃ, sati sampajaññaṃ, sīlavisuddhi diṭṭhivisuddhi, samatho vipassanā, tīṇi kusalamūlāni, tīṇi sucaritāni, tayo sammāvitakkā, tisso anavajjasaññā, tisso dhātuyo, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, cattāro ariyamaggā, cattāri ariyaphalāni, catasso paṭisambhidā, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇāni, cattāro ariyavaṃsā, cattāri vesārajjañāṇāni, pañca padhāniyaṅgāni, pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi, pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhi, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, pañca nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, pañca vimuttāyatanañāṇāni, pañca vimuttiparipācanīyā saññā, cha anussatiṭṭhānāni, cha gāravā, cha nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, cha satatavihārā, cha anuttariyāni, cha nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā, cha abhiññā, cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni, satta aparihāniyā dhammā, satta ariyadhammā, satta ariyadhanāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, satta sappurisadhammā, satta nijjaravatthūni, satta saññā, sattadakkhiṇeyyapuggaladesanā, sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitidesanā, sattakhīṇāsavabaladesanā, aṭṭhapaññāpaṭilābhahetudesanā, aṭṭha sammattāni, aṭṭhalokadhammātikkamā, aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni, aṭṭhaakkhaṇadesanā, aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā, aṭṭhaabhibhāyatanadesanā, aṭṭha vimokkhā, nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni, navasattāvāsadesanā, nava āghātapaṭivinayā, nava saññā, nava nānattā, nava anupubbavihārā, dasa nāthakāraṇā dhammā, dasa kasiṇāyatanāni, dasa kusalakammapathā, dasa sammattāni, dasa ariyavāsā, dasa asekkhadhammā, dasa tathāgatabalāni, ekādasa mettānisaṃsā, dvādasa [M 1.0259] dhammacakkākārā, terasa dhutaguṇā, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, pañcadasa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā, soḷasavidhā ānāpānassati, soḷasa aparantapanīyā dhammā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni[V 1.0244], paññāsa udayabbayañāṇāni, paropaññāsa kusaladhammā, sattasattatiñāṇavatthūni, catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasamāpattisañcārimahāvajirañāṇaṃ, anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānapavicayapaccavekkhaṇadesanāñāṇāni, tathā anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantānaṃ sattānaṃ āsayādivibhāvanañāṇāni cāti evamādayo anantāparimāṇabhedā anaññasādhāraṇā niratisayā guṇabhāgā guṇakoṭṭhāsā saṃvijjanti upalabbhanti. Tasmā yathāvuttavibhāgā guṇabhāgā assa atthīti bhāgavāti vattabbe ā-kārassa rassattaṃ katvā “bhagavā”ti vutto. Evaṃ tāva bhāgavāti bhagavā.

Herein, how is it that from possessing portions of qualities (bhāgavā), he is called Bhagavā? Those aggregates of Dhamma, portions of qualities such as virtue and so forth, which are unique and unsurpassed, exist in the Tathāgata and are found in him. For indeed, his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation; his moral shame and moral dread; his faith, energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension; his purification of virtue and purification of view; his serenity and insight; the three wholesome roots, the three kinds of good conduct, the three right thoughts, the three blameless perceptions, the three elements; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the four noble paths, the four noble fruits, the four analytical knowledges, the knowledges for discerning the four kinds of birth, the four noble lineages, the four knowledges of intrepidity; the five factors of exertion, the five-factored right concentration, the right concentration endowed with five knowledges, the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements conducive to escape, the five knowledges of the spheres of liberation, the five perceptions ripening into liberation; the six bases of recollection, the six objects of reverence, the six elements conducive to escape, the six continuous abidings, the six unsurpassable qualities, the six perceptions partaking of penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six uncommon knowledges; the seven conditions of non-decline, the seven noble qualities, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of awakening, the seven qualities of a true person, the seven grounds for wearing away, the seven perceptions, the teaching on the seven persons worthy of offerings, the teaching on the seven stations of consciousness, the teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed; the teaching on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom, the eight rightnesses, the eight transcendences of worldly states, the eight grounds for exertion, the teaching on the eight inopportune moments, the eight thoughts of a great person, the teaching on the eight bases of mastery, the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention, the nine factors of exertion for purity, the teaching on the nine abodes of beings, the nine ways of dispelling resentment, the nine perceptions, the nine diversities, the nine progressive abidings; the ten qualities that are a refuge, the ten kasiṇa bases, the ten courses of wholesome action, the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abidings, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the ten powers of the Tathāgata; the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; the twelve aspects of the wheel of Dhamma; the thirteen ascetic qualities; the fourteen Buddha-knowledges; the fifteen qualities ripening into liberation; the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing; the sixteen qualities that do not cause subsequent remorse; the eighteen Buddha-qualities; the nineteen knowledges of review; the forty-four bases of knowledge; the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away; the more than fifty wholesome states; the seventy-seven bases of knowledge; the great diamond knowledge that traverses 240 million attainments; the knowledges for teaching, investigating, and reviewing the Paṭṭhāna with its infinite methods; and likewise the knowledges for making plain the dispositions and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—and so on—these infinite, immeasurable, unique, and unsurpassed portions of qualities, divisions of qualities, exist and are found in him. Therefore, because he possesses these portions of qualities with their divisions as described, when `bhāgavā` should be said, having shortened the `ā` vowel, he is called `Bhagavā`. Thus, indeed, he is Bhagavā because he possesses portions of qualities.

Yasmā sīlādayo sabbe, guṇabhāgā asesato;

Vijjanti sugate tasmā, “bhagavā”ti pavuccati.

Because all portions of qualities, beginning with virtue, are found without remainder in the Well-Farer, therefore he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Kathaṃ bhatavāti bhagavā? Ye te sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpannehi manussattādike aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā sammāsambodhiyā katamahābhinīhārehi mahābodhisattehi paripūretabbā dānapāramī, sīlanekkhammapaññāvīriyakhantisaccaadhiṭṭhānamettāupekkhāpāramīti dasa pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsa pāramiyo, dānādīni cattāri saṅgahavatthūni, saccādīni cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni, attapariccāgo, nayana, dhana, rajja, puttadārapariccāgoti pañca mahāpariccāgā, pubbayogo, pubbacariyā, dhammakkhānaṃ, ñātatthacariyā, lokatthacariyā, buddhatthacariyāti evamādayo, saṅkhepato vā sabbe puññasambhārañāṇasambhārabuddhakārakadhammā, te mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya kappānaṃ satasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyāni yathā hānabhāgiyā, saṃkilesabhāgiyā, ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na honti, atha kho uttaruttari visesabhāgiyāva honti, evaṃ sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ anavasesato bhatā sambhatā assa atthīti bhatavāti vattabbe “bhagavā”ti vutto niruttinayena ta-kārassa ga-kāraṃ katvā. Atha vā bhatavāti teyeva yathāvutte buddhakārakadhamme vuttanayena bhari sambhari, paripūresīti attho. Evampi bhatavāti bhagavā.

How is it that from having cultivated (bhatavā), he is called Bhagavā? Those qualities that make one a Buddha—which are to be fulfilled by Great Bodhisattvas who, having combined the eight qualities beginning with human existence, have undertaken the endeavor for the welfare of all the world and made the great aspiration for perfect self-awakening—namely: the ten perfections of giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity; the ten subsidiary perfections; and the ten ultimate perfections, thus thirty perfections in total; the four bases of beneficence beginning with giving; the four resolutions beginning with truth; the five great relinquishments, namely, the relinquishment of self, of eyes, of wealth, of kingdom, and of children and spouse; former practice, former conduct, teaching the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of relatives, conduct for the welfare of the world, and conduct for the purpose of Buddhahood; and so on—in brief, all these Buddha-making qualities, which are the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom, starting from the great aspiration, for four incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons, were cultivated in such a way that they did not partake of decline, of defilement, or of stagnation, but on the contrary, partook only of ever-higher distinction. Thus, because these were thoroughly, ceaselessly, and completely borne and accumulated by him, when `bhatavā` should be said, he is called `Bhagavā`, the letter `t` having been changed to `g` according to the method of etymology. Alternatively, `bhatavā` means: he bore, accumulated, and fulfilled those very Buddha-making qualities in the way described. In this way too, from having cultivated (bhatavā), he is Bhagavā.

Sammāsambodhiyā [M 1.0260] sabbe, dānapāramiādike;

Sambhāre bhatavā nātho, tasmāpi bhagavā mato.

Because the Lord has cultivated all the requisites for perfect self-awakening, beginning with the perfection of giving, for that reason too he is considered 'Bhagavā'.

Kathaṃ [V 1.0245] bhāge vanīti bhagavā? Ye te catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā devasikaṃ vaḷañjanakasamāpattibhāgā, te anavasesato lokahitatthaṃ, attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ niccakappaṃ niccakappaṃ vani bhaji sevi bahulamakāsīti bhāge vanīti bhagavā. Atha vā abhiññeyyadhammesu, kusalādīsu, khandhādīsu ca ye te pariññeyyādivasena saṅkhepato vā catubbidhā abhisamayabhāgā, vitthārato pana “cakkhuṃ pariññeyyaṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ pariññeyya”ntiādinā anekapariññeyyabhāgā, “cakkhussa samudayo pahātabbo…pe… jarāmaraṇassa samudayo pahātabbo”tiādinā pahātabbabhāgā, “cakkhussa nirodho…pe… jarāmaraṇassa nirodho sacchikātabbo”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.21) sacchikātabbabhāgā, “cakkhussa nirodhagāminī paṭipadā”tiādinā, “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā ca anekabhedā bhāvetabbabhāgā ca dhammā, te sabbe vani bhaji yathārahaṃ gocarabhāvanāsevanānaṃ vasena sevi. Evampi bhāge vanīti bhagavā. Atha vā ye ime sīlādayo dhammakkhandhā sāvakehi sādhāraṇā guṇakoṭṭhāsā guṇabhāgā, “kinti nu kho te veneyyasantānesu patiṭṭhapeyya”nti mahākaruṇāya vani abhipatthayi, sā cassa abhipatthanā yathādhippetaphalāvahā ahosi. Evampi bhāge vanīti bhagavā.

How is he 'Bhagavā' because he partook of (`vani`) portions (`bhāge`)? Because he constantly and ceaselessly partook of, resorted to, cultivated, and abundantly practiced the portions of attainment for daily use, numbering twenty-four hundred thousand crores, for the welfare of the world and for his own happy abiding in the present life; thus, he is 'Bhagavā' because he partook of portions. Alternatively, with regard to things to be directly known, such as wholesome states, the aggregates, and so on, there are the fourfold portions of realization by way of what is to be fully understood, etc. In brief, these are the portions of realization; but in detail, there are the many portions to be fully understood, beginning with “the eye is to be fully understood… aging and death are to be fully understood”; the portions to be abandoned, beginning with “the origin of the eye is to be abandoned… the origin of aging and death is to be abandoned”; the portions to be realized, beginning with “the cessation of the eye… the cessation of aging and death is to be realized”; and the many kinds of portions to be developed, beginning with “the path leading to the cessation of the eye” and “the four establishments of mindfulness,” etc. He partook of, resorted to, and cultivated all these by means of suitable range, development, and cultivation. In this way, too, he is 'Bhagavā' because he partook of portions. Alternatively, there are these aggregates of the Dhamma, such as virtue and so on, which are portions of virtue, collections of virtue common to the disciples. With great compassion, he desired and aspired, “How might I establish these in the mental continuities of trainable beings?” And that aspiration of his brought the desired fruit. In this way, too, he is 'Bhagavā' because he partook of portions.

Yasmā ñeyyasamāpatti-guṇabhāge tathāgato;

Bhaji patthayi sattānaṃ, hitāya bhagavā tato.

Because the Tathāgata resorted to the portions of things to be known, of attainments, and of virtues, and aspired to them for the welfare of beings, therefore he is Bhagavā.

Kathaṃ bhage vanīti bhagavā? Samāsato tāva katapuññehi payogasampannehi yathāvibhavaṃ bhajīyantīti bhagā, lokiyalokuttarasampattiyo. Tattha lokiye tāva tathāgato sambodhito pubbe bodhisattabhūto paramukkaṃsagate vani bhaji sevi, yattha patiṭṭhāya niravasesato buddhakārakadhamme samannānento buddhadhamme paripācesi. Buddhabhūto [M 1.0261] pana te niravajjasukhūpasaṃhite anaññasādhāraṇe lokuttarepi vani bhaji sevi. Vitthārato pana padesarajjaissariyacakkavattisampattidevarajjasampattiādivasena, jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattiñāṇadassanamaggabhāvanāphalasacchikiriyādiuttarimanussadhammavasena ca anekavihite anaññasādhāraṇe bhage vani bhaji sevi. Evampi bhage vanīti bhagavā.

How is he 'Bhagavā' because he partook of (`vani`) fortunes (`bhage`)? In brief, 'bhaga' are worldly and supramundane accomplishments, so called because they are partaken of (`bhajīyanti`) by those who have made merit and are endowed with effort, according to their capacity. Among these, with regard to worldly fortunes, the Tathāgata, before his enlightenment while he was a bodhisatta, partook of and cultivated those that had reached the highest excellence. Established in these, while thoroughly undertaking the qualities that make a Buddha, he brought the Buddha-dharmas to maturity. And having become a Buddha, he partook of and cultivated those worldly fortunes connected with faultless happiness, as well as the incomparable supramundane fortunes. In detail, by way of regional sovereignty, the accomplishment of universal sovereignty, the accomplishment of divine kingship, and so on, and by way of superhuman states such as jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, path development, and fruition-realization, he partook of and cultivated various incomparable fortunes. In this way, too, he is 'Bhagavā' because he partook of fortunes.

Yā [V 1.0246] tā sampattiyo loke, yā ca lokuttarā puthū;

Sabbā tā bhaji sambuddho, tasmāpi bhagavā mato.

Whatever accomplishments exist in the world, and whatever many supramundane ones there are; all these the Perfectly Enlightened One partook of. Therefore, he is also known as 'Bhagavā'.

Kathaṃ bhattavāti bhagavā? Bhattā daḷhabhattikā assa bahū atthīti bhattavā. Tathāgato hi mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgi bhāvato sabbasattuttamo sabbānatthaparihārapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantupakāritāya dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanabyāmappabhādianaññasādhāraṇaguṇavisesapaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya yathābhuccaguṇādhigatena “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinayappavattena lokattayabyāpināsuvipulena, suvisuddhena ca thutighosena samannāgatattā, ukkaṃsapāramippattāsu appicchatāsantuṭṭhiādīsu supatiṭṭhitabhāvato, dasabalacatuvesārajjādiniratisayaguṇavisesasamaṅgibhāvato ca “rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno, ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno, lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno, dhammappamāṇo dhammappasanno”ti evaṃ catuppamāṇike lokasannivāse sabbathāpi pasādāvahabhāvena samantapāsādikattā aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ sadevamanussānaṃ ādarabahumānagāravāyatanatāya paramapemasambhattiṭṭhānaṃ. Ye tassa ovāde patiṭṭhitā aveccappasādena samannāgatā honti, kenaci asaṃhāriyā tesaṃ sambhatti samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vāti. Tathā hi te attano jīvitapariccāgepi tattha pasādaṃ na pariccajanti, tassa vā āṇaṃ daḷhabhattibhāvato. Tenevāha –

How is he 'Bhagavā' from `bhattavā` (one who has devotees)? Because he has many firm devotees, he is `bhattavā`. Indeed, the Tathāgata, because he is endowed with special qualities of immeasurable, incomparable, and mighty power, such as great compassion, the knowledge of omniscience, and so on, is the most excellent of all beings. Because of his extreme helpfulness to the populace of gods and humans through his unsurpassed accomplishment in effort, which is preceded by the removal of all that is unbeneficial and is intent on arranging welfare and happiness without remainder; because he has a physical form adorned with special qualities not shared with others, such as the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura; because he is endowed with a very vast and very pure sound of praise that pervades the three worlds, which proceeds in the manner of “Thus indeed is the Bhagavā…” and is obtained through qualities that are true to fact; because he is well-established in qualities that have reached the pinnacle of perfection, such as fewness of wishes, contentment, and so on; and because he is endowed with unsurpassed special qualities such as the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, and so on; he is inspiring of confidence all around. In the abode of beings of four measures—where some are measured by form and are pleased by form, some are measured by fame and are pleased by fame, some are measured by a frugal life and are pleased by a frugal life, and some are measured by the Dhamma and are pleased by the Dhamma—he is in every way one who brings forth confidence. Thus, for countless beings, gods and humans, he is the basis for reverence, great esteem, and respect, the ground for supreme love and firm devotion. The devotion of those who are established in his instruction and are endowed with unshakable confidence cannot be carried away by any ascetic or brahmin, by a deva, by Māra, or by a Brahmā. Indeed, even at the cost of their own lives, they do not abandon their confidence in him or his command, because of their firm devotion. Therefore, he said:

“Yo ve kataññū katavedi dhīro,

Kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hotī”ti. (jā. 2.17.78);

“Whoever is indeed grateful, acknowledges what has been done, is wise, has good friends, and is of firm devotion.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 1.0262], bhikkhave, mahāsamuddo ṭhitadhammo velaṃ nātivattati, evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (udā. 45; cūḷava. 385) ca.

“Just as, bhikkhus, the great ocean has a stable nature and does not transgress its shore, even so, bhikkhus, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.”

Evaṃ bhattavāti bhagavā niruttinayena ekassa ta-kārassa lopaṃ katvā itarassa ga-kāraṃ katvā.

Thus, `bhattavā` becomes 'Bhagavā' by the method of etymology, by eliding one `ta`-sound and making the other into a `ga`-sound.

Guṇātisayayuttassa[V 1.0247], yasmā lokahitesino;

Sambhattā bahavo satthu, bhagavā tena vuccati.

Because the Teacher, who seeks the welfare of the world, is endowed with surpassing qualities, he has many devotees; therefore, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Kathaṃ bhage vamīti bhagavā? Yasmā tathāgato bodhisattabhūtopi purimāsu jātīsu pāramiyo pūrento bhagasaṅkhātaṃ siriṃ, issariyaṃ, yasañca vami uggiri kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍayi. Tathā hissa somanassakumārakāle (jā. 1.15.211 ādayo) hatthipālakumārakāle (jā. 1.15.337 ādayo) ayogharapaṇḍitakāle (jā. 1.15.363 ādayo) mūgapakkhapaṇḍitakāle (jā. 2.22.1 ādayo) cūḷasutasomakāleti (jā. 2.17.195 ādayo) evamādīsu nekkhammapāramipūraṇavasena devarajjasadisāya rajjasiriyā pariccattaattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ natthi. Carimattabhāvepi hatthagataṃ cakkavattisiriṃ devalokādhipaccasadisaṃ catudīpissariyaṃ, cakkavattisampattisannissayaṃ sattaratanasamujjalaṃ yasañca tiṇāyapi amaññamāno nirapekkho pahāya abhinikkhamitvā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tasmā ime siriādike bhage vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā, sineruyugandharauttarakuruhimavantādibhājanalokavisesasannissayā sobhā kappaṭṭhiyabhāvato. Tepi bhagavā vami tannivāsasattāvāsasamatikkamanato tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahīti. Evampi bhage vamīti bhagavā.

How is he ‘Bhagavā’ because “he vomited forth (vami) splendors (bhage)”? Because the Tathāgata, even when he was a bodhisatta in former lives, while fulfilling the perfections, vomited forth and disgorged splendor, sovereignty, and retinue—which are called ‘bhaga’—like a gob of spittle, abandoning them without attachment. Indeed, for him, in the times of Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, the wise Ayoghara, the wise Mūgapakkha, and King Cūḷasutasoma, and so on, by means of fulfilling the perfection of renunciation, there is no measure of the existences in which he renounced royal splendor comparable to the state of a deva king. Even in his final existence, not considering the splendor of a wheel-turning monarch that was about to come into his hand—sovereignty over the four great continents, which is like sovereignty over the deva world, and the retinue, blazing with the seven treasures, which is dependent on the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch—to be even as much as a blade of grass, he, without attachment, abandoned it, went forth in the great renunciation, and fully awakened to perfect enlightenment. Therefore, because he vomited forth these bhaga, namely splendor and so on, he is ‘Bhagavā’. Alternatively, bhāni are the constellations. Because they proceed or exist uniformly with them, they are called bhagā—these are the splendors dependent on special locations in the receptacle world such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavanta, due to their nature of lasting for a whole eon. The Blessed One also vomited forth those splendors, because of transcending the abodes of beings which are the location of those splendors and by abandoning the desire and lust connected with them. Thus also, because he vomited forth the splendors called bhaga, he is ‘Bhagavā’.

Cakkavattisiriṃ yasmā, yasaṃ issariyaṃ sukhaṃ;

Pahāsi lokacittañca, sugato bhagavā tato.

Because the Sugata abandoned the splendor of a wheel-turning monarch, the retinue, sovereignty, happiness, and the variegated splendor of the world, therefore he is called Bhagavā.

Kathaṃ bhāge vamīti bhagavā? Bhāgā nāma sabhāvadhammakoṭṭhāsā, te khandhāyatanadhātādivasena, tatthāpi rūpavedanādivasena, atītādivasena ca anekavidhā, te ca bhagavā “sabbaṃ papañcaṃ, sabbaṃ yogaṃ, sabbaṃ [M 1.0263] ganthaṃ, sabbaṃ saṃyojanaṃ samucchinditvā amataṃ dhātuṃ samadhigacchanto vami uggiri anapekkho chaḍḍayi na paccāvami. Tathā hesa sabbatthakameva pathaviṃ āpaṃ tejaṃ vāyaṃ, cakkhuṃ sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhaṃ kāyaṃ manaṃ, rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe dhamme, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ, cakkhusamphassaṃ…pe… manosamphassaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ vedanaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ saññaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ saññaṃ, cakkhusamphassajaṃ cetanaṃ…pe… manosamphassajaṃ cetanaṃ, rūpataṇhaṃ [V 1.0248] …pe… dhammataṇhaṃ, rūpavitakkaṃ…pe… dhammavitakkaṃ, rūpavicāraṃ…pe… dhammavicāra”ntiādinā anupadadhammavibhāgavasenapi sabbeva dhammakoṭṭhāse anavasesato vami uggiri anapekkhapariccāgena chaḍḍayi. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

How is he ‘Bhagavā’ because “he vomited forth (vami) portions (bhāge)”? Portions of intrinsic phenomena are called bhāgā. They are of many kinds by way of aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so on; and among those, by way of form, feeling, and so on; and by way of past, and so on. And the Blessed One, having cut off all proliferation... and all fetters without remainder and attaining the deathless element, vomited and disgorged those portions of phenomena, abandoning them without attachment; he did not swallow them again. Indeed, by means of analyzing the dhammas term by term—“the earth element which exists everywhere... reflections on mental objects”—he vomited and disgorged all portions of the Dhamma without remainder, abandoning them with a relinquishment free from attachment. For this was said:

“Yaṃ taṃ, ānanda, cattaṃ vantaṃ muttaṃ pahīnaṃ paṭinissaṭṭhaṃ, taṃ tathāgato puna paccāvamissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.183).

“Ānanda, that the Tathāgata would swallow again that which has been given up, vomited, released, abandoned, and relinquished—this circumstance does not exist.”

Evampi bhāge vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāge vamīti sabbepi kusalākusale sāvajjānavajje hīnapaṇīte kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme ariyamaggañāṇamukhena vami uggiri anapekkho pariccaji pajahi, paresañca tathattāya dhammaṃ desesi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Thus also, because he vomited forth portions, he is ‘Bhagavā’. Alternatively, as for “he vomited forth portions”: through the mouth that is the knowledge of the noble path, he vomited and disgorged, and without attachment, relinquished and abandoned all dhammas—wholesome and unwholesome; blameworthy and blameless; inferior and superior; those with dark and bright counterparts. And he taught the Dhamma to others for the sake of their becoming likewise. And this was said:

“Dhammāpi vo, bhikkhave, pahātabbā, pageva adhammā (ma. ni. 1.240). Kullūpamaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāyā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.240).

“Bhikkhus, even dhammas are to be abandoned by you, how much more so non-dhammas. Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma with the simile of the raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping.”

Evampi bhāge vamīti bhagavā.

Thus also, because he vomited forth portions of the Dhamma, such as wholesome and unwholesome states, he is called ‘Bhagavā’.

Khandhāyatanadhātādi-dhammabhedā mahesinā;

Kaṇhā sukkā yato vantā, tatopi bhagavā mato.

Because the portions of the Dhamma with distinctions such as aggregates, sense bases, and elements, as well as the dark and the bright dhammas, were vomited forth by the Great Sage, for that reason also he is known as ‘Bhagavā’.

Tena vuttaṃ –

Therefore, it was said:

“Bhāgavā bhatavā bhāge, bhage ca vani bhattavā;

Bhage vami tathā bhāge, vamīti bhagavā jino”ti.

“The Possessor of Portions (bhāgavā) has analyzed (bhattavā) the portions (bhāge); and having destroyed (bhattavā) craving (vani) for the portions (bhage), he vomited (vami) the portions (bhage); thus, because he vomited, the Victor is bhagavā.”

Ettha ca yasmā saṅkhepato attahitasampattiparahitapaṭipattivasena duvidhā buddhaguṇā, tāsu attahitasampatti pahānasampadāñāṇasampadābhedato duvidhā, ānubhāvasampadādīnaṃ tadavinābhāvena tadantogadhattā. Parahitapaṭipatti payogāsayabhedato [M 1.0264] duvidhā. Tattha payogato lābhasakkārādinirapekkhacittassa sabbadukkhaniyyānikadhammūpadeso, āsayato paṭiviruddhesupi niccaṃ hitesitā, ñāṇaparipākakālāgamanādiparahitapaṭipatti ca, āmisapaṭiggahaṇādināpi atthacariyā [V 1.0249] parahitapaṭipatti hotiyeva. Tasmā tesaṃ vibhāvanavasena pāḷiyaṃ “araha”ntiādīnaṃ padānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, because, in brief, the qualities of a Buddha are twofold—by way of the accomplishment of one's own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others. Among these, the accomplishment of one's own welfare is twofold, distinguished as the accomplishment of abandonment and the accomplishment of knowledge, because the accomplishment of power, etc., being inseparable from them, is included within them. The practice for the welfare of others is twofold, distinguished by application and intention. Therein, from the perspective of application, it is the teaching of the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering, with a mind unconcerned with gain, honor, and so on. From the perspective of intention, it is the constant wish for the welfare even of those who are hostile, and the practice for the welfare of others includes awaiting the arrival of the time for the maturity of their knowledge, etc. Even acting for their benefit by accepting material requisites, etc., is indeed the practice for the welfare of others. Therefore, the usage of terms such as ‘arahant’ in the Pāli should be understood as an exposition of these qualities.

Tattha “araha”nti iminā padena pahānasampadāvasena bhagavato attahitasampatti vibhāvitā. “Sammāsambuddho, lokavidū”ti ca imehi padehi ñāṇasampadāvasena. Nanu ca “lokavidū”ti imināpi sammāsambuddhatā vibhāvīyatīti? Saccaṃ vibhāvīyati, atthi pana viseso, “sammāsambuddho”ti iminā sabbaññutaññāṇānubhāvo vibhāvito, “lokavidū”ti pana iminā āsayānusayañāṇādīnampi ānubhāvo vibhāvitoti. “Vijjācaraṇasampanno”ti iminā sabbāpi bhagavato attahitasampatti vibhāvitā. “Sugato”ti pana iminā samudāgamato paṭṭhāya bhagavato attahitasampatti, parahitapaṭipatti ca vibhāvitā. “Anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussāna”nti imehi padehi bhagavato parahitapaṭipatti vibhāvitā. “Buddho”ti iminā bhagavato attahitasampatti, parahitapaṭipatti ca vibhāvitā. Evañca katvā “sammāsambuddho”ti vatvā “buddho”ti vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Tenevāha “attanāpi bujjhi aññepi satte bodhesī”tiādi. “Bhagavā”ti ca imināpi samudāgamato paṭṭhāya bhagavato sabbā attahitasampatti, parahitapaṭipatti ca vibhāvitā.

Herein, by the term ‘Arahaṃ,’ the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare is revealed by way of the accomplishment of abandonment. And by the terms ‘Sammāsambuddho’ and ‘Lokavidū,’ it is revealed by way of the accomplishment of knowledge. But is it not so that by the term ‘Lokavidū’ the state of being a Sammāsambuddha is also revealed? Truly, it is revealed, but there is a distinction: by the term ‘Sammāsambuddho,’ the power of omniscient knowledge is revealed, whereas by the term ‘Lokavidū,’ the power of the knowledges of dispositions and underlying tendencies, and so on, is also revealed. By the term ‘Vijjācaraṇasampanno,’ all of the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare is revealed. By the term ‘Sugato,’ however, the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the welfare of others, starting from his arising, are revealed. By the terms ‘Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi, Satthā Devamanussānaṃ,’ the Blessed One’s practice for the welfare of others is revealed. By the term ‘Buddho,’ the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the welfare of others are revealed. And for this reason, having said ‘Sammāsambuddho,’ the utterance ‘Buddho’ is justified. Therefore he said, ‘Having understood by himself, he awakens other beings,’ and so on. And also by the term ‘Bhagavā,’ starting from his arising, all the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare and his practice for the welfare of others are revealed.

Aparo nayo – hetuphalasattūpakāravasena saṅkhepato tividhā buddhaguṇā.
