'And it is seen in one Buddha-interval' means it is seen when one interval between Buddhas has passed. By the word 'ca,' it shows that sometimes it is seen when even an incalculable aeon has passed. 'Unmixed' means unmingled with opposing factors; and this is an adverbial modifier. The qualities that make one dear and beloved are morality and so on; these are well-established in the noble Saṅgha. Herein, this is the intention: separated relatives and friends meet again only after a long time, and the state of being dear and beloved in them is not firmly established; the noble Saṅgha is not like that. Therefore, the Saṅgha alone is worthy of hospitality. 'A prior act' means a foremost action. 'In every way' means with reverence, respect, great esteem, and so on, and by carefully preparing the gift, and so on—in every way. That word 'pāhavanīya' is called 'pāhuneyya' by way of being a synonym.

Dakkhanti etāya sattā yathādhippetāhi sampattīhi vaḍḍhantīti dakkhiṇā. Tathābhāvakaraṇena dakkhiṇaṃ arahati. Yathā uḷārātivipuludrayalābhena visodhitaṃ nāma hoti, evaṃ dakkhiṇā vipulaphalatāyāti vuttaṃ “mahapphalakaraṇatāya visodhetī”ti.

Beings prosper or grow by means of this with the attainments they desire; therefore, it is called a 'donation.' Because it causes such a state, one is worthy of a donation. Just as a worldly matter, such as debt, is said to be cleared by gaining a vast and great profit, so too a donation, due to its great fruitfulness, is said to be purified. Therefore, it was said: 'it purifies by producing great fruit.'

Puññatthikehi añjali karaṇīyā etthāti añjalikaraṇīyo.

An 'añjali' should be made here by those who desire merit; therefore, he is 'one to whom an añjali should be made'.

Yadipi pāḷiyaṃ “anuttara”nti vuttaṃ. Natthi ito uttaraṃ visiṭṭhanti hi anuttaraṃ. Samampissa pana natthīti dassento “asadisa”nti āha. Khittaṃ vuttaṃ bījaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena tāyati rakkhati, khipanti vapanti ettha bījānīti vā khettaṃ, kedārādi, khettaṃ viya khettaṃ, puññānaṃ khettaṃ puññakkhettaṃ. Sesaṃ buddhānussatiyaṃ vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

Although in the Pāḷi it is said 'unsurpassed'—for indeed, there is no other more excellent than this, therefore it is 'unsurpassed'—yet, to show that there is not even an equal to it, He said 'unequalled.' It protects a seed that has been cast and sown by causing it to become greatly fruitful, therefore it is a 'field.' Or, they cast and sow seeds here, therefore it is a 'field,' like a paddy field and so on. It is like a field, hence a 'field'; a field of merit is a 'field of merit.' The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha.

4. Sīlānussatikathāvaṇṇanā

4. An Explanation of the Discourse on the Recollection of Virtue

158. Aho vata sīlāni akhaṇḍāni, aho vata acchiddānīti evaṃ sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Aho vatāti ca sambhāvane nipāto. Tenāha “akhaṇḍatādiguṇavasenā”ti. Akhaṇḍabhāvādisampattivasenāti attho. Parassa sīlāni anussariyamānāni piyamanāpabhāvāvahanena kevalaṃ mettāya padaṭṭhānaṃ honti, na visuṃ kammaṭṭhānanti āha “attano sīlāni anussaritabbānī”ti. Cāgādīsupi eseva nayo.

158. “Oh, indeed, my virtues are unbroken! Oh, indeed, they are without holes!”—thus it should be applied everywhere. The particle 'Aho vata' is used in the sense of praise. Therefore, he said, “by the power of the qualities of unbrokenness, etc.” The meaning is: by the power of the accomplishment of such states as being unbroken. When the virtues of another are recollected, by bringing about a state that is dear and pleasant, they become merely a proximate cause for loving-kindness, not a separate meditation subject. Therefore, he said, “one’s own virtues are to be recollected.” This same method applies also to generosity and so on.

Yesanti [V 1.0266] sīlādīnaṃ. Paṭipāṭiyā samādāne samādānakkamena, ekajjhaṃ samādāne uddesakkamena sīlānaṃ ādiantaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pariyante chinnasāṭako viyāti vatthante, dasante vā chinnavatthaṃ viya, visadisūdāharaṇaṃ cetaṃ. Evaṃ sesānipi udāharaṇāni. Vinivedhavasena chinnasāṭako vinividdhasāṭako. Visabhāgavaṇṇena gāvī viyāti sambandho. Sabalarahitāni vā asabalāni. Tathā akammāsāni. Sattavidhamethunasaṃyogo heṭṭhā sīlakathāyaṃ vutto eva. Kodhūpanāhādīhīti ādi-saddena makkhapaḷāsaissāmacchariyamāyāsāṭheyyamānātimānādayo gahitā. Tāniyeva akhaṇḍādiguṇāni sīlāni. Sīlassa taṇhādāsabyato [M 1.0282] mocanaṃ vivaṭṭūpanissayabhāvāpādanaṃ. Tato eva taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo serī sayaṃvasī bhujisso nāma hoti. Tenāha “bhujissabhāvakaraṇena bhujissānī”ti. “Imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhaveyyaṃ devaññataro vā, tattha nicco dhuvo sassato”ti, “sīlena suddhī”ti ca evamādinā taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattā ayaṃ te sīlesu dosoti catūsu vipattīsu yāya kāyaci vipattiyā dassanena parāmaṭṭhuṃ anuddhaṃsetuṃ. Samādhisaṃvattanappayojanāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni.

The word `yesaṃ` refers to `sīlādīnaṃ`, of virtue and so on. When undertaking them sequentially, the beginning and end of the virtues should be known by the order of undertaking; when undertaking them all at once, by the order of recitation. 'Like a garment torn at the edge' means like a cloth torn at its border or at its fringe; and this is a dissimilar example. Thus should the remaining examples also be understood. By way of being pierced through, a torn garment is a pierced-through garment. The connection is 'like a cow of dissimilar color.' Or, virtues free from variegation are 'unvariegated.' Similarly, they are 'unblotched.' The sevenfold sexual intercourse has already been stated below in the discourse on virtue. In the phrase 'by anger, hostility, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes contempt, malice, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, conceit, arrogance, and so on. Those very virtues possess the qualities of being unbroken, and so on. The liberation of virtue from slavery to craving is the bringing about of the state of having the Unwinding as its support. Precisely from that, a person endowed with such virtue, being independent and self-mastered, is called a `bhujissa` (freedman). Therefore, it is said: 'Because they bring about the state of a freedman, they are called `bhujissāni` (liberating).' Because they are not grasped by craving and views—such as, 'By this virtue, may I become a god or some other divine being, and there be constant, stable, eternal,' or, 'There is purification through virtue,' and so on—it is not possible to grasp them or to impute a stain by pointing to any of the four failures, saying, 'This is a fault in your virtues.' Virtues that have the purpose of leading to concentration are called 'conducive to concentration.'

159. Sikkhāya sagāravoti sīladhanaṃ nissāya paṭiladdhasamādānattā sātisayaṃ sikkhāya sagāravo sappatisso hoti. Sabhāgavuttīti sampannasīlehi sabhāgavuttiko, tāya eva vā sikkhāya sabhāgavutti. Yo hi sikkhāgāravarahito, so tāya visabhāgavutti nāma hoti vilomanato. Yathā parehi saddhiṃ attano chiddaṃ na hoti, evaṃ dhammāmisehi paṭisantharaṇaṃ paṭisanthāro. Sikkhāya sagāravattā eva tattha appamatto hoti. Attānuvādabhayaṃ parānuvādabhayaṃ daṇḍabhayaṃ duggatibhayanti evamādīni bhayāni imassa dūrasamussāritānīti āha “attānuvādādibhayavirahito”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

159. ‘Respectful towards the training’: because of having obtained the firm undertaking by relying on the wealth of virtue, one is exceedingly respectful and reverential towards the training. ‘Living in harmony’: one has a way of life in harmony with those accomplished in virtue, or one’s way of life is in harmony with that very training. For one who is devoid of respect for the training is said to have a way of life in disharmony with it, because of acting contrary to it. Just as one has no rift with others, so `paṭisanthāra` (reconciliation) is the mending of relationships with both the Dhamma and material things. Precisely because of being respectful towards the training, one is heedful in regard to it. Fears such as the fear of self-reproach, the fear of others’ reproach, the fear of punishment, and the fear of a bad destination—these and similar fears are far removed from this person. Therefore, it is said: ‘free from the fear of self-reproach, etc.’ The rest is easily understood.

5. Cāgānussatikathāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Recollection of Generosity

160. Pakatiyāti sabhāvena. Cāgādhimuttenāti deyyadhammapariccāge yuttappayuttena tanninnena tappoṇena. Niccaṃ sadā pavattā dānasaṃvibhāgā yassa so niccapavattadānasaṃvibhāgo, tena. Idhāpi “pakatiyā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Yaṃ parassa paṭiyattaṃ diyyati, taṃ dānaṃ. Yaṃ attanā paribhuñjitabbato saṃvibhajati, so saṃvibhāgo. Ito dāni pabhutīti ito paṭṭhāya dāni ajjatagge ajjadivasaṃ ādiṃ katvā. Adatvā na bhuñjissāmīti dānasamādānaṃ katvā[V 1.0267]. Taṃdivasanti tasmiṃ bhāvanārambhadivase. Tattha nimittaṃ gaṇhitvāti tasmiṃ dāne pariccāgacetanāya pavattiākārassa sallakkhaṇavasena nimittaṃ gahetvā. Vigatamalamaccheratādiguṇavasenāti vigatāni malamaccherāni etasmāti vigatamalamacchero, cāgo, tassa bhāvo vigatamalamaccheratā. Tadādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ, sampattīnaṃ, ānisaṃsānaṃ vā vasena.

160. 'By nature' (`pakatiyā`) means by intrinsic quality. 'Inclined to generosity' (`cāgādhimuttena`) means constantly engaged in the relinquishing of things to be given, inclined towards it, sloping towards it. One whose giving and sharing are constantly ongoing is 'one whose giving and sharing are constantly ongoing' (`niccapavattadānasaṃvibhāgo`); by that. Here too, 'by nature' should be brought in and connected. What is prepared for another and given is giving (`dāna`). What one shares from what is to be used by oneself is sharing (`saṃvibhāga`). 'From now on' (`ito dāni pabhuti`) means from this point forward, now, from today onwards, making this very day the beginning. Having undertaken the resolution of giving, thinking, 'I will not eat without having given.' 'On that day' (`taṃdivasaṃ`) means on that day of commencing the meditation. 'There, having grasped the sign' (`tattha nimittaṃ gaṇhitvā`) means having grasped the sign by way of discerning the mode of occurrence of the volition of relinquishing in that act of giving. 'By means of the qualities of being free from stain and stinginess, etc.' (`vigatamalamaccheratādiguṇavasenāti`) means: stains and stinginess have departed from this, thus one is 'free from stain and stinginess' (`vigatamalamacchero`), which is generosity (`cāgo`); its state is 'being free from stain and stinginess' (`vigatamalamaccheratā`). By means of those qualities, or attainments, or benefits.

Sataṃ [M 1.0283] dhammaṃ anukkamanti sādhūnaṃ bodhisattānaṃ dhammaṃ paveṇiṃ anu anu kamanto okkamanto, avokkamanto vā. Ye ime dāyakassa lābhā āyuvaṇṇasukhabalapaṭibhānādayo, piyabhāvādayo ca bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇitā pakittitā. Manussattaṃ vāti vā-saddo avuttavikappattho, tena indriyapāṭavabhāvakammassakatāñāṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

'They follow the Dhamma of the good' (`sataṃ dhammaṃ anukkamanti`) means repeatedly treading upon and entering into the tradition, the practice of good bodhisattas, or not transgressing it. These gains for a donor—longevity, beauty, happiness, strength, ready wit, and so on, and states of being beloved, and so on—have been praised and proclaimed by the Blessed One. Regarding 'or the human state' (`manussattaṃ vā`), the word `vā` has the meaning of an unstated alternative; by that, the inclusion of keenness of the faculties, knowledge of ownership of kamma, and so on, should be understood.

Maccheramalenāti maccherasaṅkhātena malena. Atha vā maccherañca malañca maccheramalaṃ, tena maccherena ceva lobhādimalena cāti attho. Pajāyanavasenāti yathāsakaṃ kammanibbattanavasena. Kaṇhadhammānanti lobhādiekantakāḷakānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ. Vigatattāti pahīnattā. Vigatamalamaccherena cetasāti itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ. Sotāpannassa satoti gehaṃ āvasantassa sotāpannassa samānassa. Nissayavihāranti nissāya viharitabbavihāraṃ, devasikaṃ vaḷañjanakakammaṭṭhānanti attho. Abhibhavitvāti agāraṃ āvasantānaṃ aññesaṃ uppajjanakarāgādiupakkilese abhibhuyya.

'By the stain of stinginess' (`maccheramalena`) means by the stain designated as stinginess. Or alternatively, stinginess and stain is 'stinginess-stain'; the meaning is by that stinginess and by stains such as greed. 'By way of generation' (`pajāyanavasena`) means by way of production through one's own respective kamma. 'Of dark qualities' (`kaṇhadhammānaṃ`) means of evil qualities that are entirely black, such as greed. 'Because of being rid of' (`vigatattā`) means because of being abandoned. 'With a mind free from the stain of stinginess' (`vigatamalamaccherena cetasā`) is an instrumental word in the sense of indicating a state. 'Of a stream-enterer, being...' (`sotāpannassa sato`) means of a stream-enterer who is dwelling at home. 'A supportive dwelling' (`nissayavihāraṃ`) means a dwelling that should be dwelt in with support; the meaning is a daily practice-subject. 'Having overcome' (`abhibhavitvā`) means having mastered the defilements such as lust that are apt to arise in others who dwell in a house.

Yo kiñci dentopi sāpekkhova deti, so muttacāgo na hoti, ayaṃ pana na evanti “muttacāgo”ti vuttaṃ. Vissaṭṭhacāgoti nirapekkhapariccāgoti attho. Yathā pāṇātipātabahulo puggalo “lohitapāṇī”ti vuccati, evaṃ dānabahulo puggalo “payatapāṇī”ti vuttoti dassento “dātuṃ sadā dhotahatthoyevā”ti āha. Tattha sadāti niccaṃ, abhiṇhanti attho. Pariccāgoti deyyadhammapariccāgoti adhikārato viññāyati. Yaṃ yaṃ deyyadhammaṃ pare yācanakā. Yācane yogo yācanayogo, parehi yācituṃ yuttoti attho. Yājena yuttoti dānena yutto sadā pariccajanato. Ubhayeti yathāvutte dāne, saṃvibhāge ca rato abhirato.

Whoever, though giving something, gives with attachment, is not one of open-handed generosity (`muttacāgo`). But this person is not so, thus it is said 'open-handed generosity.' 'Released generosity' (`vissaṭṭhacāgo`) means relinquishment without attachment. Just as a person much given to killing is called 'bloody-handed' (`lohitapāṇī`), so a person much given to giving is called 'pure-handed' (`payatapāṇī`). To show this, it says, 'always with hands washed for giving.' Therein, 'always' (`sadā`) means constantly, repeatedly. 'Relinquishment' (`pariccāgo`) is understood from the context as the relinquishment of things to be given. 'Fit for asking' (`yācanayogo`) means there is suitability in asking; the meaning is that it is suitable for others to ask. 'Endowed with sacrifice' (`yājena yutto`) means endowed with giving, because of always relinquishing. 'In both' (`ubhaye`) means one delights and takes delight in both giving and sharing, as was stated.

161. Yathā parisuddhasīlassa puggalassa akhaṇḍatādiguṇavasena attano sīlassa anussarantassa sīlānussatibhāvanā ijjhati, evaṃ parisuddhauḷārapariccāgassa puggalassa anupakkiliṭṭhameva [V 1.0268] attano pariccāgaṃ anussarantassa bhāvanā ijjhatīti dassetuṃ “vigatamalamaccheratādiguṇavasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ vuttatthameva.

161. Just as for a person of pure virtue, the cultivation of the recollection of virtue succeeds when they recollect their own virtue by way of qualities such as its unbrokenness, so too, to show that for a person of pure and noble relinquishment, the cultivation succeeds when they recollect their own unblemished relinquishment, it was said, 'by means of qualities such as being free from the stain of stinginess,' and so on. That has the meaning already stated.

Bhiyyosoti [M 1.0284] uparipi. Mattāya pamāṇassa mahatiyā mattāya, vipulena pamāṇenāti attho. Cāgādhimuttoti pariccāge adhimutto ninnapoṇapabbhāro. Tato eva alobhajjhāsayo katthacipi anabhisaṅgacitto. Paṭiggāhakesu mettāyanavasena pariccāgo hotīti mettāya mettābhāvanāya anulomakārī anurūpapaṭipatti. Visāradoti visado attanova guṇena katthacipi amaṅkubhūto abhibhuyya vihārī. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Exceedingly' (bhiyyoso) means even further. 'By a measure' (mattāya) means by a great measure of magnitude, by a vast measure; this is the meaning. 'Intent on generosity' (cāgādhimutto) means one who is intent on relinquishment, inclined, sloping, and tending towards it. From that very thing, one has a disposition of non-greed, a mind unattached to anything anywhere. The phrase 'relinquishment towards recipients occurs by way of extending loving-kindness' means it is a suitable practice conforming to loving-kindness, to the development of loving-kindness. 'Confident' (visārado) means clear; by one's own virtue, one is not downcast anywhere, dwelling as a master. The rest is easily understood.

6. Devatānussatikathāvaṇṇanā

6. Elucidation of the Discourse on the Recollection of Deities

162. Ariyamaggavasenāti ariyamaggassa adhigamavasena. Samudāgatehīti sammadeva taduppattito uddhaṃ āgatehi. Yādisā hi ariyānaṃ santāne lokiyāpi saddhādayo, na tādisā kadācipi pothujjanikā saddhādayo. Dibbantīti devā. Cattāro mahārājāno etesanti catumahārājā, te eva cātumahārājikā. Tettiṃsa sahapuññakārino tatthūpapannāti taṃsahacaritaṃ ṭhānaṃ tāvatiṃsaṃ, tannivāsinopi devā taṃsahacaraṇato eva tāvatiṃsā. Dukkhato yātā apayātāti yāmā. Tusāya pītiyā itā upagatāti tusitā. Bhogānaṃ nimmāne rati etesanti nimmānaratino. Paranimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattentīti paranimmitavasavattino. Brahmānaṃ kāyo samūho brahmakāyo, tappariyāpannatāya tattha bhavāti brahmakāyikā. Tatuttarīti tato brahmakāyikehi uttari, upari parittābhādike sandhāya vadati. Devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvāti “yathārūpāya maggenāgatāya saddhāya samannāgatā, sīlena sutena cāgena paññāya samannāgatā ito cutā tattha upapannā tā devatā, mayhampi tathārūpā saddhā sīlaṃ sutaṃ cāgo paññā ca saṃvijjatī”ti devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā sakkhiṃ otārentena viya attano saddhādiguṇā anussaritabbā.

162. “By way of the Noble Path” means by way of the attainment of the Noble Path. “Have arisen” (samudāgatehi) means having truly come forth after that arising. For whatever faith and other qualities, even if mundane, are in the mental continuum of the noble ones, such faith and other qualities of an ordinary person never exist. “They sport” (dibbanti), thus they are deities (devā). There are four great kings for them, thus they are the Catumahārājā; those very ones are the Cātumahārājikā. “Thirty-three who performed meritorious deeds together were reborn there,” thus the place associated with them is Tāvatiṃsa, and the deities dwelling there are also Tāvatiṃsa because of their association with that place. “They have gone away from suffering” (dukkhato yātā apayātā), thus they are Yāmā. “They have gone to, attained, satisfaction and joy” (tusāya pītiyā itā upagatā), thus they are Tusitā. “They have delight in creating pleasures” (bhogānaṃ nimmāne rati etesaṃ), thus they are Nimmānaratino. “They wield power over pleasures created by others” (paranimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattenti), thus they are Paranimmitavasavattino. The body, the group, of Brahmās is the Brahmakāya; those who exist there by being included in it are Brahmakāyikā. “Higher than that” means higher than the Brahmakāyikā, referring to the Parittābhā and others above them. “Having placed the deities in the position of a witness” means that one should recollect one’s own qualities of faith and so on, as if presenting a witness, by placing the deities in the position of a witness, thinking: “Those deities were endowed with such faith that has come by way of the path, and endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Having passed away from here, they were reborn there. For me too, such faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom exist.”

Yadi evaṃ sutte (a. ni. 6.10) ubhayaguṇānussaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ kathanti anuyogaṃ manasi katvā āha “sutte panā”tiādi. Tattha kiñcāpi vuttanti “attano ca, tāsañca devatāna”nti ubhayaṃ samadhuraṃ viya sutte (a. ni. 6.10) kiñcāpi vuttaṃ. Atha [M 1.0285] kho taṃ “devatānaṃ saddhañca sīlañcā”tiādivacanaṃ. Sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbanti “vutta”nti parato padaṃ [V 1.0269] ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Kimatthaṃ pana sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapananti āha “devatānaṃ attano saddhādīhi samānaguṇadīpanatthanti veditabba”nti. Kasmā pana sutte yathārutavasena atthaṃ aggahetvā evaṃ attho gayhatīti āha “aṭṭhakathāyañhī”tiādi.

If it is asked thus: “If in the Sutta (AN 6.10) the recollection of the qualities of both is mentioned, how is that?”—considering this question, he says, “But in the Sutta,” and so on. There, although it is said in the Sutta (AN 6.10), “of oneself and of those deities,” as if both were equally important, nevertheless that statement, “the faith and virtue of the deities,” and so on, should be connected by bringing the word “said” from further on, to mean that it is said for the purpose of placing them in the position of a witness. But for what purpose is this placing in the position of a witness? He says, “It should be understood as for the purpose of showing the qualities common to oneself and the deities, such as faith and so on.” Why then, in the Sutta, is the meaning grasped in this way, without taking the meaning according to the literal wording? He says, “For in the commentary,” and so on.

163. Tasmāti yasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā attano guṇānussaraṇaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, sīlacāgānussatīsu viya idhāpi attano guṇānussaraṇaṃ jhānuppattinimittaṃ yuttaṃ, tasmā. Pubbabhāge bhāvanārambhe. Aparabhāgeti yathā bhāventassa upacārajjhānaṃ ijjhati, tathā bhāvanākāle. Yadi attano eva idha guṇā anussaritabbā, kathamayaṃ devatānussatīti āha “devatānaṃ guṇasadisasaddhādiguṇānussaraṇavasenā”ti. Tena sadisakappanāya ayaṃ bhāvanā “devatānussatī”ti vuttā, na devatānaṃ, tāsaṃ guṇānaṃ vā anussaraṇenāti dasseti. Pubbabhāge vā pavattaṃ devatāguṇānussaraṇaṃ upādāya “devatānussatī”ti imissā samaññā veditabbā. Tathā hi vakkhati “pubbabhāge devatā ārabbha pavattacittavasenā”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

163. Therefore: because in the commentary it is stated that one should place the deities in the position of a witness and firmly establish the recollection of one’s own qualities; and because here too, just as in the recollections of virtue and generosity, the recollection of one’s own qualities is a suitable cause for the arising of jhāna—for these reasons. In the preliminary stage means at the beginning of the development of meditation. In the later stage means during the time of developing meditation, in such a way that the meditator succeeds in attaining access concentration. If only one’s own qualities should be recollected here, how can this be called the recollection of deities? He says, “Through the recollection of qualities such as faith, etc., that are similar to the qualities of the deities.” By this he shows that this meditation is called “recollection of deities” by way of conceiving similarity, not by way of recollecting the deities themselves or their qualities. Alternatively, the designation “recollection of deities” should be understood by reason of the recollection of the qualities of deities that occurs in the preliminary stage. For thus it will be said: “in the preliminary stage, by way of the mind that has arisen with deities as its object.” The rest is easily understood.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Miscellaneous Discourse

164. Etāsanti etāsaṃ buddhānussatiādīnaṃ channaṃ anussatīnaṃ. Vitthāradesanāyanti vitthāravasena pavattadesanāyaṃ, mahānāmasuttaṃ (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11) sandhāya vadati. Bhagavātiādīnaṃ atthanti bhagavātiādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ. Atthavedanti vā hetuphalaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ tuṭṭhimāha. Dhammavedanti hetuṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ. “Ārakattā araha”nti anussarantassa hi yaṃ taṃ bhagavato kilesehi ārakattaṃ, so hetu. Ñāpako cettha hetu adhippeto, na kārako, sampāpako vā. Yonena ñāyamāno arahattattho, taṃ phalaṃ. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi hetuphalavibhāgo veditabbo. Dhammānussatiādīsupi “ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇattā”tiādinā, “yasmā pana sā sammāpaṭipadā”tiādinā ca tattha tattha hetuapadeso katoyevāti. Dhammūpasaṃhitanti yathāvuttahetuhetuphalasaṅkhātaguṇūpasaṃhitaṃ. Guṇeti attano guṇe.

164. ‘Of these’ (etāsaṃ) means of these six recollections, beginning with the recollection of the Buddha. ‘In a detailed teaching’ (vitthāradesanāyaṃ) means in a teaching that has proceeded by way of detail; he speaks referring to the Mahānāma Sutta. ‘The meaning of “Bhagavā,” etc.’ (bhagavātiādīnaṃ atthaṃ) means the meaning of the words such as “Bhagavā.” Or, by ‘one who experiences the meaning’ (atthaveda), he speaks of the delight that has arisen in dependence on the effect of the cause. By ‘one who experiences the Dhamma’ (dhammaveda), he speaks of the delight that has arisen in dependence on the cause. For one who recollects, “Because of being far, he is an Arahant,” indeed, that farness of the Blessed One from the defilements is the cause. And here, an indicating cause is intended, not a creative cause or a completing cause. That meaning of Arahantship which is being known by this one is the effect. By this method, the distinction of cause and effect should be understood in the remaining terms as well. In the recollection of the Dhamma and so on, by such phrases as “because it is good in the beginning, middle, and end,” and “because that is the right practice,” in each respective case, the indication of the cause has indeed been made. ‘Connected with the Dhamma’ (dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ) means connected with the qualities described as the aforesaid cause and effect-of-the-cause. ‘Qualities’ (guṇe) means one's own qualities.

165. Ariyasāvakānaññeva [M 1.0286] ijjhantīti ariyasāvakānaṃ ijjhantiyevāti uttarapadāvadhāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, avadhāraṇañca tesaṃ sukhasiddhidassanatthaṃ. Tenāha “tesaṃ hī”tiādi. Na puthujjanānaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ ijjhantīti. Tathā hi vakkhati “evaṃ santepī”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ[V 1.0270], kasmā mahānāmasuttādīsu (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11) bahūsu suttesu ariyasāvakaggahaṇaṃ katanti? Tesaṃ bahulavihāratāyāti ācariyā.

165. ‘They are accomplished only for noble disciples’ (ariyasāvakānaññeva ijjhanti) should be understood as an exclusive emphasis on the latter term, meaning, “they are accomplished for noble disciples only.” And the exclusive emphasis is for the purpose of showing their easy accomplishment. Therefore, he said, “For them, indeed…” and so on. This is not to show that for worldlings they are not accomplished in any way at all. For thus he will say, “Even so…” and so on. If so, why in many suttas, such as the Mahānāma Sutta, is the term ‘noble disciples’ employed? The teachers say it is because of their frequent abiding.

Nikkhantanti niggataṃ nissaṭaṃ. Muttanti vissaṭṭhaṃ. Vuṭṭhitanti apetaṃ. Sabbametaṃ vikkhambhanameva sandhāya vadati. Gedhamhāti palibodhato. Idampīti buddhānussativasena laddhaṃ upacārajjhānamāha. Ārammaṇaṃ karitvāti paccayaṃ katvā, pādakaṃ katvāti attho. Visujjhantīti paramatthavisuddhiṃ pāpuṇanti.

‘Gone out’ (nikkhantaṃ) means departed, escaped. ‘Released’ (muttaṃ) means relinquished. ‘Risen from’ (vuṭṭhitaṃ) means departed. He says all this referring only to suppression. ‘From greed’ (gedhamhā) means from the obstruction. By ‘this too’ (idampi), he speaks of the access concentration attained by way of the recollection of the Buddha. ‘Having made it an object’ (ārammaṇaṃ karitvā) means having made it a condition, having made it a foundation. ‘They are purified’ (visujjhanti) means they reach ultimate purity.

Sambādheti taṇhāsaṃkilesādinā sampīḷe saṃkaṭe gharāvāse. Okāsādhigamo lokuttaradhammassa adhigamāya adhigantabbaokāso. Anussatiyo eva anussatiṭṭhānāni. Visuddhidhammāti visujjhanasabhāvā, visujjhituṃ vā bhabbā. Paramatthavisuddhidhammatāyāti paramatthavisuddhiyā nibbānassa bhabbabhāvena. Upakkamenāti payogena. Pariyodapanāti visodhanā.

‘In the confinement’ (sambādhe) means in the household life, which is cramped and confined, oppressed by craving, defilements, and so on. ‘The attainment of opportunity’ (okāsādhigamo) is the opportunity to be attained for the attainment of the supramundane Dhamma. The recollections (anussatiyo) themselves are the stations of recollection. ‘States of purity’ (visuddhidhammā) means they have the nature of purification, or are fit to be purified. ‘Because of being states of ultimate purity’ (paramatthavisuddhidhammatāya) means because of the fitness for Nibbāna, which is ultimate purity. ‘By endeavor’ (upakkamena) means by exertion. ‘Cleansing’ (pariyodapanā) means purification.

166. Evaṃ santepīti evaṃ mahānāmasuttādīsu anekesu suttesu ariyasāvakasseva vasena chasu anussatīsu desitāsupi. Yassānubhāvenāti yassa cittappasādassa balena. Pītiṃ paṭilabhitvāti anussavavasena buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā.

166. ‘Even so’ (evaṃ santepi) means: even though in many suttas, such as the Mahānāma Sutta, the six recollections are taught only with reference to a noble disciple. ‘By whose power’ (yassānubhāvena) means by the power of which mental confidence. ‘Having obtained joy’ (pītiṃ paṭilabhitvā) means having generated joy with the Buddha as its object by way of hearsay.

Chaanussatiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Exposition of the Six Recollections is finished.

Iti sattamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus is the Elucidation of the Seventh Chapter.

8. Anussatikammaṭṭhānaniddesavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Recollection Meditation Subjects

Maraṇassatikathāvaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

167. Itoti [M 1.0287][V 1.0271] devatānussatiyā. Sā hi chasu anussatīsu sabbapacchā niddiṭṭhattā āsannā, paccakkhā ca. Anantarāyāti tadanantaraṃ uddiṭṭhattā vuttaṃ. Maraṇassa sati maraṇassatīti maraṇaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “tattha maraṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Kāmañcettha khandhānaṃ bhedo “jarāmaraṇaṃ dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahita”nti (dhātu. 71) vacanato cutikhandhānaṃ vināso maraṇanti vattabbaṃ, visesato pana taṃ jīvitindriyassa vināsabhāvena kammaṭṭhānikānaṃ paccupatiṭṭhatīti “jīvitindriyassa upacchedo”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha niddese “kaḷevarassa nikkhepo jīvitindriyassupacchedo”ti (vibha. 236; dī. ni. 2.390; ma. ni. 1.92, 123). Tattha ekabhavapariyāpannassāti ekena bhavena paricchinnassa. Jīvitindriyassa upacchedoti jīvitindriyappabandhassa vicchedo āyukkhayādivasena antaradhānaṃ. Samucchedamaraṇanti arahato santānassa sabbaso ucchedabhūtaṃ maraṇaṃ. Saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgasaṅkhātanti saṅkhatadhammānaṃ udayavayaparicchinnassa pavattikhaṇassa bhaṅgo nirodhoti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Khaṇikamaraṇanti yathāvuttakhaṇavantaṃ tasmiṃyeva khaṇe labbhamānaṃ maraṇaṃ. Yaṃ khandhappabandhaṃ upādāya rukkhādisamaññā, tasmiṃ anupacchinnepi allatādivigamanaṃ nissāya matavohāro sammutimaraṇaṃ. Na taṃ idha adhippetanti taṃ samucchedakhaṇikasammutimaraṇaṃ idha maraṇānussatiyaṃ nādhippetaṃ abāhullato, anupaṭṭhahanato, asaṃvegavatthuto cāti adhippāyo.

167. Thus, after the recollection of deities. For that recollection, being mentioned last among the six recollections, is proximate and evident. 'Immediately following' is said because it is mentioned immediately after that. Mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) is mindfulness (sati) of death (maraṇassa). First, to show what death is, it is said, 'Therein, death,' and so on. Although here the breaking up of the aggregates should be called death, as stated in the phrase, 'aging and death are included in two aggregates,' and specifically, the destruction of the passing-away aggregates, nevertheless, for meditators, it appears more precisely as the cutting off of the life faculty. Hence, it is said, 'the cutting off of the life faculty.' Therefore, in the exposition, it is said, 'the casting off of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty.' Therein, 'of that which is included in a single existence' means of that which is confined to one existence. 'The cutting off of the life faculty' means the interruption of the continuity of the life faculty, its disappearance due to the exhaustion of life, and so on. 'Death by cutting off' refers to the death of an arahant, which is the complete cutting off of their continuum. 'Known as the momentary dissolution of formations' means what is known as the dissolution and cessation of the moment of occurrence of conditioned phenomena, which are defined by arising and passing away. 'Momentary death' is the death that is obtainable in that very moment, possessing the aforementioned moment. While the continuity of aggregates, on which the designation 'tree,' etc., is based, remains unbroken, the conventional expression 'dead' is used based on the departure of moisture, etc.; this is called 'conventional death.' That is not intended here—meaning, death by cutting off, momentary death, and conventional death are not intended here in the recollection of death, due to not being common, not being readily manifest, and not being a basis for spiritual urgency. This is the intended meaning.

Adhippetaṃ satiyā ārammaṇabhāvena. Āyuādīnaṃ khayakāle maraṇaṃ kālamaraṇaṃ. Tesaṃ aparikkhīṇakāle maraṇaṃ akālamaraṇaṃ. “Kālamaraṇaṃ puññakkhayenā”ti idaṃ yathādhikāraṃ sampattibhavavasena vuttaṃ, vipattibhavavasena pana “pāpakkhayenā”ti vattabbaṃ.

It is intended as an object of mindfulness. Death at the time of the exhaustion of lifespan, etc., is timely death. Death when these are not exhausted is untimely death. The statement, 'Timely death is due to the exhaustion of merit,' is said according to the context by way of a state of accomplishment. But by way of a state of failure, it should be said, 'due to the exhaustion of demerit.'

Āyusantānajanakapaccayasampattiyāti [V 1.0272] āyuppabandhassa pavattāpanakānaṃ āhārādipaccayānaṃ sampattiyaṃ. Vipakkavipākattāti attano phalānurūpaṃ dātabbavipākassa dinnattā. Gatikālāhārādisampattiyā abhāvenāti [M 1.0288] devānaṃ viya gatisampattiyā, paṭhamakappiyānaṃ viya kālasampattiyā, uttarakurukādīnaṃ viya āhārasampattiyā ca abhāvena. Ādi-saddena utusukkasoṇitādiṃ pariggayhati. Ajjatanakālapurisānaṃ viyāti viya-saddo aṭṭhāne paṭṭhapito, ajjatanakālapurisānaṃ vassasatamattaparimāṇassa viya āyuno khayavasenāti yojanā. Evaṃ hi anāgatepi paramāyuno saṅgaho kato hoti, atīte pana gatisampattiyā viya kālāhārādisampattiyā bhāvena anekavassasahassa parimāṇopi āyu ahosi. Ayañca vibhāgo vattamānassa antarakappassa vasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kalāburājādīnanti ādi-saddena nandayakkhanandamāṇavakādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Taṃ sabbampīti yaṃ “kālamaraṇaṃ akālamaraṇaṃ, tatthāpi puññakkhayamaraṇaṃ āyukkhayamaraṇaṃ ubhayakkhayamaraṇaṃ upakkamamaraṇa”nti vuttappabhedaṃ maraṇaṃ, taṃ sabbampi.

‘The accomplishment of conditions that generate the continuity of life’ means the accomplishment of conditions such as food that sustain the continuity of life. ‘Due to the ripened result’ means because the result to be given has been given in accordance with its own power. ‘Due to the absence of the accomplishment of destination, time, food, etc.’ means due to the absence of the accomplishment of destination, as in the case of devas; the accomplishment of time, as in the case of beings of the first aeon; and the accomplishment of food, as in the case of those in Uttarakuru, and so on. By the word ‘etc.,’ it includes climate, semen, and blood. The word ‘like’ in ‘like the people of today’ is misplaced; the construction is: ‘by way of the exhaustion of the lifespan of the people of the present time, a lifespan measuring about a hundred years.’ For in this way, the inclusion of the maximum lifespan in the future is also made. But in the past, due to the existence of the accomplishment of time, food, etc., like the accomplishment of destination, the lifespan was of the measure of many thousands of years. And this distinction should be understood as having been stated by way of the present intermediate aeon. By ‘such as King Kalābu,’ the inclusion of the yakkha Nanda, the youth Nandamāṇava, and others should be understood. ‘All of that’ refers to all the distinctions of death mentioned, namely, ‘timely death, untimely death, and therein also, death due to the exhaustion of merit, death due to the exhaustion of lifespan, death due to the exhaustion of both, and death due to an overriding cause.’

168. Yonisoti upāyena. Manasikāroti maraṇārammaṇo manasikāro. Yena pana upāyena manasikāro pavattetabbo, taṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “ayoniso pavattayato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ayoniso pavattayatoti anupāyena satiṃ, saṃvegaṃ, ñāṇañca anupaṭṭhapetvā maraṇaṃ anussarato. Tadetaṃ sabbampīti sokapāmojjānaṃ uppajjanaṃ, saṃvegassa anuppajjanaṃ, santāsassa uppajjanañca yathākkamaṃ satisaṃvegañāṇaviharato hoti. Yo hi “maraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ jātassa ekantika”nti paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ sarati, tattha saṃvegajāto hoti sampajāno ca, tassa iṭṭhajanamaraṇādinimittaṃ sokādayo anokāsāva. Tasmāti yasmā ayoniso manasikāraṃ pavattayato ete dosā, tasmā. Tattha tatthāti araññasusānādīsu. Hatamatasatteti corādīhi hate, sarasena mate ca satte. Diṭṭhapubbā sampatti yesaṃ te diṭṭhapubbasampattī, tesaṃ diṭṭhapubbasampattīnaṃ. Yojetvāti upaṭṭhapetvā. Ekaccassāti tikkhindriyassa ñāṇuttarassa.

168. ‘Systematically’ means by a suitable means. ‘Attention’ means attention that has death as its object. But to show, by way of contrast, the means by which attention should be aroused, it is said, ‘for one who arouses it unsystematically,’ and so on. Therein, ‘for one who arouses it unsystematically’ means for one who recollects death by an unsuitable means, without establishing mindfulness, spiritual urgency, and knowledge. ‘All of this’ refers to the arising of sorrow and joy, the non-arising of spiritual urgency, and the arising of terror, which occur in sequence due to the absence of mindfulness, spiritual urgency, and knowledge. For one who remembers the saying of the wise, ‘This thing called death is certain for one who is born,’ spiritual urgency arises, and they are possessed of clear comprehension. For such a person, there is no opportunity for sorrow and the like to arise on account of a sign such as the death of a loved one. ‘Therefore’ means because these faults arise for one who arouses unsystematic attention, therefore. ‘Here and there’ means in places such as forests and charnel grounds. ‘Beings killed or dead’ means beings killed by thieves, etc., and beings dead from natural causes. ‘Those whose previous prosperity has been seen’ refers to those whose former prosperity has been observed. ‘Having applied’ means having established in mind. ‘For a certain one’ means for one with keen faculties, who is supreme in knowledge.

169. Vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānatoti ghātakassa viya pati pati upaṭṭhānato āsannabhāvato. Sampattivipattitoti ārogyādisampattīnaṃ viya jīvitasampattiyā vipajjanato. Upasaṃharaṇatoti paresaṃ maraṇaṃ dassetvā attano [M 1.0289] maraṇassa upanayanato. Kāyabahusādhāraṇatoti sarīrassa bahūnaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvato. Āyudubbalatoti jīvitassa dubbalabhāvato. Animittatoti maraṇassa vavatthitanimittābhāvato[V 1.0273]. Addhānaparicchedatoti kālassa paricchannabhāvato. Khaṇaparittatoti jīvitakkhaṇassa ittarabhāvato.

169. ‘Due to appearing like a murderer’ means due to its appearing constantly like a murderer, due to its being near. ‘Due to the failure of accomplishment’ refers to the perishing of the accomplishment of life, just as the accomplishments of health, etc., perish. ‘Due to applying to oneself’ means due to bringing one’s own death near by pointing to the death of others. ‘Due to the body being common to many’ refers to the body being common to many beings. ‘Due to the weakness of life’ means due to the weakness of life. ‘Due to being without a sign’ means due to the absence of a fixed sign for death. ‘Due to the limitation of the life-span’ means due to the limited nature of the time of life. ‘Due to the brevity of the moment’ means due to the briefness of the life-moment.

Vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānatoti ettha viya-saddo luttaniddiṭṭhoti dassento “vadhakassa viya paccupaṭṭhānato”ti vatvā tamevatthaṃ vivaranto “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Tattha cārayamānoti āgurento paharaṇākāraṃ karonto. Paccupaṭṭhitova upagantvā ṭhito samīpe eva. Jarāmaraṇaṃ gahetvāva nibbattanti “yathā hi ahicchattakamakuḷaṃ uggacchantaṃ paṃsuvirahitaṃ na hoti, evaṃ sattā nibbattantā jarāmaraṇavirahitā na hontī”ti ettakena upamā. Ahicchattakamakuḷaṃ kadāci katthaci paṃsuvirahitampi bhaveyya, sattā pana kathañcipi jarāmaraṇavirahitā na hontīti khaṇikamaraṇaṃ tāva upamābhāvena dassetvā idhādhippetaṃ maraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “tathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā yadime sattā jarāmaraṇaṃ gahetvāva nibbattanti, nibbattisamanantarameva maritabbanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tathā hī”tiādi. Avassaṃ maraṇatoti avassaṃ maritabbato, ekantena maraṇasabbhāvato vā. Pabbateyyāti pabbatato āgatā. Hārahārinīti pavāhe patitassa tiṇapaṇṇādikassa ativiya haraṇasīlā. Sandatevāti savati eva. Vattatevāti pavāhavasena vattati eva na tiṭṭhati.

In the phrase ‘due to appearing like a murderer,’ to show that the word ‘like’ is indicated as elided, having said, ‘because of appearing like a murderer,’ and then, wishing to explain that very meaning, the author said, ‘For just as…’ and so on. Therein, ‘menacing’ means threatening, making a gesture of striking. ‘Appeared’ means having approached and standing right nearby. ‘They are born taking along old age and death’: The simile is to this extent: ‘For just as a snake's hood mushroom sprout, when rising up, is not devoid of dust, so beings, when being born, are not devoid of old age and death.’ A snake's hood mushroom sprout might sometimes, somewhere, be without dust, but beings are in no way without old age and death. Thus, having first shown momentary death by way of a simile, to show the death intended here, it is said, ‘so too…’ and so on. Alternatively, with reference to the objection, ‘If these beings are born taking along old age and death, they must die immediately after birth,’ the author said, ‘so too…’ and so on. ‘Due to the inevitability of death’ means because one must inevitably die, or because of the certain existence of death. ‘Of a mountain stream’ means come from a mountain. ‘Sweeping all before it’ means having the nature of carrying away very much the grass, leaves, etc., that have fallen into the current. ‘It just flows’ means it just flows. ‘It just moves on’ means it just moves on by the force of the current; it does not stand still.

Yamekarattinti yassaṃ ekarattiyaṃ, bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, accantasaṃyoge vā. Paṭhamanti sabbapaṭhamaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe. Gabbheti mātukucchiyaṃ. Māṇavoti satto. Yebhuyyena sattā rattiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantīti rattiggahaṇaṃ. Abbhuṭṭhitovāti uṭṭhitaabbho viya, abhimukhabhāvena vā uṭṭhitova maraṇassāti adhippāyo. So yātīti so māṇavo yāti, paṭhamakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya gacchateva. Sa gacchaṃ na nivattatīti so evaṃ gacchanto khaṇamattampi na nivattati, aññadatthu maraṇaṃyeva upagacchati.

In ‘for one night,’ which means ‘in which one night,’ the accusative case should be understood in the sense of the locative, or in the sense of continuous connection. ‘First’ means the very first, at the moment of rebirth-linking. ‘In the womb’ means in the mother's womb. ‘A young man’ means a being. The term ‘night’ is used because beings mostly take rebirth-linking at night. ‘Having arisen’ means like a risen cloud, or the meaning is that he has risen up facing death. ‘He goes’ means that being goes; starting from the first moment, he just goes. ‘Going, he does not return’ means that being, going thus, does not turn back even for a moment; on the contrary, he just approaches death.

Kunnadīnanti pabbatato patitānaṃ khuddakanadīnaṃ. Pāto āporasānugatabandhanānanti purimadivase divā sūriyasantāpena anto anupavisitvā puna rattiyaṃ bandhanamūlaṃ upagatena āporasena tintasithilabandhanatāya pāto āporasānugatabandhanānaṃ.

‘Of small rivers’ means of the small rivers, or streams, falling from the mountain. ‘Of those whose bonds are pervaded by the water element in the morning’ means ‘of those whose bonds are pervaded by the water element in the morning,’ because on the previous day, during the day, having been penetrated within by the sun's heat, and again at night, the water element having reached the root of the bond, the bond becomes moist and slackened.

Accayantīti [M 1.0290] atikkamanti. Uparujjhatīti nirujjhati. Udakameva odakaṃ, udakoghaṃ vā[V 1.0274]. Yasmā accayanti ahorattā, tasmā jīvitaṃ uparujjhati. Yasmā jīvitaṃ uparujjhati, tasmā āyu khīyati maccānaṃ. Papatatoti papatanato bhayaṃ sāmikānaṃ rukkhe ṭhatvā kamme viniyuñjitukāmānaṃ, heṭṭhā paviṭṭhānaṃ vā. Uggamanaṃ pati uggamananimittaṃ. Mā maṃ amma nivāraya pabbajjāyāti adhippāyo.

‘Pass away’ means they pass beyond. ‘Is cut short’ means it ceases. ‘Water’ is just water, or a flood of water. Because days and nights pass away, life is cut short. Because life is cut short, the lifespan of mortals wastes away. ‘From falling’ means the danger of falling for the owners who, standing on a tree, wish to engage in work, or for those who have entered below. ‘On account of the rising’ means on account of the rising of the sun. The intended meaning is: ‘Oh mother, do not prevent me from the going forth.’

Koci mittamukhasatturandhagavesī saha vattamānopi na haneyya, ayaṃ pana ekaṃsena hanatiyevāti dassetuṃ “sahajātiyā āgatato”ti vatvā “jīvitaharaṇato cā”ti vuttaṃ.

Some enemy with a friend's face, seeking an opportunity, might not kill even while living together; this one, death, however, certainly kills. To show this, having said ‘from coming along with birth,’ it is also said ‘and from taking life.’

170. Nanti sampattiṃ. Sukhīti dibbasadisehi bhogehi, ādhipateyyena ca sukhasamaṅgī. Dehabandhenāti sarīrena. Asokoti asokamahārājā. Sokamāgatoti socitabbataṃ gato.

170. ‘It’ means accomplishment. ‘Happy’ means endowed with happiness through possessions like those of the gods and through sovereignty. ‘By the bond of the body’ means by the body. ‘Asoka’ means the great king Asoka. ‘Came to sorrow’ means gone to a state to be sorrowed for.

Ārogyaṃ yobbanānaṃ. Byādhijarāpariyosānatā jīvitassa maraṇapariyosānatāya udāharaṇavasena ānītā, paccayabhāgavasena vā. Lokoyeva lokasannivāso yathā sattāvāsāti, sannivasitabbatāya vā sattanikāyo lokasannivāso. Anugatoti anubandho paccatthikena viya. Anusaṭoti anupaviṭṭho upavisena viya. Abhibhūtoti ajjhotthaṭo maddahatthīhi viya. Abbhāhatoti pahaṭo bhūtehi viya.

The fact that health and youth end in sickness and old age is adduced as an example for the fact that life ends in death, or by way of being a condition. The world of beings itself is the `lokasannivāso` (world-assemblage), just as in the word `sattāvāsa` (abode of beings); or, because it is to be co-habited, the host of beings is the `lokasannivāso`. `Anugato` means pursued, as if by an enemy. `Anusaṭo` means penetrated, as if by smeared-on poison. `Abhibhūto` means overwhelmed, as if by elephants in rut. `Abbhāhato` means struck, as if by non-human beings.

Selāti silāmayā, na paṃsuādimayā. Vipulāti mahantā anekayojanāyāmavitthārā. Nabhaṃ āhaccāti vipulattā eva ākāsaṃ abhivihacca sabbadisāsu pharitvā. Anupariyeyyunti anuvicareyyuṃ. Nippothentāti attanā āghātitaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karontā. Adhivattantīti adhibhavanti. Kulena vā rūpena vā sīlena vā sutena vā saddhādīhi vā seṭṭhoti sambhāvanāya khattiyādīsu na kañci parivajjeti. Tehi eva nihīnoti avamaññamānāya suddādīsu na kañci parivajjeti. Aññadatthu sabbameva abhimaddati nimmathati. Daṇḍādiupāyā ca tattha avisayā evāti dassetuṃ “na tattha hatthīnaṃ bhūmī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha mantayuddhenāti [M 1.0291] āthabbaṇavedavihitena mantasaṅgāmappayogena. Dhanenāti dhanadānena. Vā-saddo avuttavikappanattho. Tena sāmaṃ, bhedañca saṅgaṇhāti.

`Selā` means made of stone, not of dust and so on. `Vipulā` means great, many yojanas in length and breadth. `Nabhaṃ āhacca` means, because of their vastness, having struck the sky and pervading all directions. `Anupariyeyyuṃ` means they would roam about. `Nippothentā` means making what they have struck into powder and fragments. `Adhivattanti` means they overpower. It spares no one among khattiyas and others esteemed as superior on account of clan, appearance, virtue, learning, faith, and so on. It spares no one among suddas and others who are despised as inferior on account of these same things. On the contrary, it crushes and grinds down everything. To show that means such as punishment are ineffective there, it is said, “there is no ground for elephants,” and so on. Therein, `mantayuddhena` means by the application of mantra-combat prescribed in the Athabbana Veda. `Dhanena` means by giving wealth. The word `vā` (or) has the meaning of including unstated alternatives. Thereby it includes conciliation (`sāma`) and sowing dissension (`bheda`).

171. Parehi saddhiṃ attano upasaṃharaṇatoti parehi matehi saddhiṃ “tepi nāma matā, kimaṅgaṃ [V 1.0275] pana mādisā”ti attano maraṇassa upanayanato. Yasamahattatoti parivāramahattato, vibhavamahattato ca. Puññamahattatoti mahāpuññabhāvato. Thāmamahattatoti vīriyabalamahattato. Yudhiṭṭhilo dhammaputto. Cānuro yo baladevena nibbuddhaṃ katvā mārito.

171. “By comparison of oneself with others” means by applying it to one's own death in comparison with others who have died, thinking: “Even they have died, so what then of one like me?” “Greatness of fame” means greatness of retinue and greatness of wealth. “Greatness of merit” means the state of having great merit. “Greatness of strength” means greatness of energy and power. Yudhiṭṭhila is the son of the god Dhamma. Cānura is the one who was killed by Baladeva in a wrestling match.

Saha iddhīhīti vejayantakampananandopanandadamanādīsu diṭṭhānubhāvāhi attano iddhīhi saddhiṃ maccumukhaṃ paviṭṭho.

“With his psychic powers” means he entered the mouth of death together with his own psychic powers, whose might had been seen in such acts as the shaking of the Vejayanta palace, the subduing of the nāga-king Nandopananda, and so on.

Kalaṃ nagghanti soḷasinti soḷasannaṃ pūraṇabhāgaṃ na agghanti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āyasmato therassa sāriputtassa paññaṃ soḷasabhāge katvā tato ekaṃ bhāgaṃ soḷasadhā gahetvā laddhaṃ ekabhāgasaṅkhātaṃ kalaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ sattānaṃ paññā na agghantīti.

“They are not worth a sixteenth part” means they are not worth the sixteenth part. This is what is said: If one were to divide the wisdom of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta into sixteen parts, and then take one of those parts and divide it by sixteen, the wisdom of all other beings—setting aside the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—is not worth that single resulting fraction.

Sabbassāpi saṃkilesapakkhassa samugghāto ñāyena āraddhavīriyassa hotīti āha “ñāṇavīriyabalenā”ti. Sammādiṭṭhisammāvāyāmesu hi siddhesu aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo siddhova hotīti. Ekākībhāvena khaggavisāṇakappā. Paratoghosena vinā sayameva bhūtā paṭividdhākuppāti sayambhuno.

To show that the eradication of the entire side of defilement occurs for one who has aroused energy in accordance with the method, he said: “by the power of knowledge and energy.” For when right view and right effort are accomplished, the Noble Eightfold Path is itself accomplished. Because of being solitary, they are “like a rhinoceros horn.” “Self-become” (sayambhuno) means those who have become realized by themselves without a declaration from another, having penetrated the unshakable fruit of Arahantship.

Hatthagatasuvaṇṇavalayānaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanaṃ vaṃsakaḷīrassa katthaci asattatāti evamādikaṃ taṃ taṃ nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ āgamma. Vīmaṃsantāti pavattinivattiyo upaparikkhantā. Mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ esanaṭṭhena mahesayo. Ekacariyanivāsenāti ekacariyanivāsamattena, na sīlādinā. Khaggamigasiṅgasamā upamā yesaṃ, khaggamigasiṅgaṃ vā samūpamā yesaṃ te khaggasiṅgasamūpamā.

Having taken up this or that sign and cause, such as the clashing against one another of golden bracelets on the arm, or the non-adherence of a bamboo shoot somewhere… “Investigating” means examining occurrence (dukkha and samudaya) and cessation (nirodha and magga). “Great seers” (mahesayo) because of seeking for the great aggregates of virtue, etc. “By dwelling in solitude” means merely by dwelling and practicing in solitude, not on account of virtue and so on. Those whose simile is like the horn of a rhinoceros, or for whom the horn of a rhinoceros is a simile, are “those with a simile like a rhinoceros horn.”

Tambanakhatuṅganakhatādiasītianubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitehi suppatiṭṭhitapādatādīhi dvattiṃsāya mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi vicitro acchariyabbhuto rūpakāyo etassāti asīti…pe… rūpakāyo. Saha vāsanāya sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ [M 1.0292] pahīnattā sabbākāraparisuddhasīlakkhandhādiguṇaratanehi samiddho dhammakāyo etassāti sabbākāra…pe… dhammakāyo. Ṭhānasoti taṅkhaṇeyeva.

His form-body (rūpakāya) is wonderful and marvelous, variegated by the thirty-two marks of a great man beginning with the well-placed feet, and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics beginning with copper-colored nails and high-arched nails. Thus he is “one with a form-body adorned with the eighty…” His Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) is endowed with the gems of the qualities of the aggregates of virtue, etc., completely purified in all aspects because of the abandonment of all defilements together with their latent dispositions. Thus he is “one with a Dhamma-body completely purified in all aspects…” “Instantly” means at that very moment.

Evaṃ [V 1.0276] mahānubhāvassāti evaṃ yathāvuttarūpakāyasampattiyā, dhammakāyasampattiyā ca viññāyamānavipulāparimeyyabuddhānubhāvassa, vasaṃ nāgataṃ anupagamanavasenāti adhippāyo.

“Of one with such great power” means of one whose vast and immeasurable Buddha-power is known through the aforesaid accomplishment of the form-body and accomplishment of the Dhamma-body. The meaning is: “did not come under his control,” in the sense of not approaching or submitting to it.

Maraṇaṃ sāmaññaṃ etassāti maraṇasāmañño, tassa bhāvo maraṇasāmaññatā, tāya.

One for whom death is common is “one with death in common” (maraṇasāmañño). The state of that is “the commonality of death” (maraṇasāmaññatā); by that [commonality of death].

172. Kimikulānanti kimisamūhānaṃ, kimijātīnaṃ vā. Jīyantīti jaraṃ pāpuṇanti.

172. “Of families of worms” means of multitudes of worms, or of species of worms. “They decay” means they reach old age.

Nikkhanteti vītivatte. Paṭihitāyāti paccānugatāya. So mamassa antarāyoti sā yathāvuttā na kevalaṃ kālakiriyāva, atha kho mama atidullabhaṃ khaṇaṃ labhitvā ṭhitassa satthusāsanamanasikārassa antarāyo assa bhaveyya. Byāpajjeyyāti vipattiṃ gaccheyya. Satthakena viya aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kantanakā maraṇakāle sandhibandhanacchedanakavātā satthakavātā.

“Departed” means passed beyond. “Set against” means followed after. “That would be an obstacle for me” means: that aforesaid death would not only be my demise, but it would be an obstacle to my attention to the Teacher's instruction, which I am undertaking having gained this extremely rare opportunity. “One would perish” means one would meet with disaster. The “dagger-like winds” are the winds at the time of death that sever the ligaments of the joints, cutting the limbs and members like a small knife.

173. Abalanti balahīnaṃ. Dubbalanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Abhāvattho hi ayaṃ du-saddo “dussīlo (a. ni. 5.213; a. ni. 10.75) duppañño”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.449) viya. Tadetaṃ āyu. Assāsapassāsānaṃ samavuttitā aparāparaṃ pavesanikkhamova. Bahi nikkhantanāsikavāte anto apavisante, paviṭṭhe vā anikkhamanteti ekasseva pavesanikkhamo viya vuttaṃ, taṃ nāsikavātabhāvasāmaññenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Adhimattatāya accāsannaadhiṭṭhānādinā. Tadabhāvo hi iriyāpathānaṃ samavuttitā. Atisītena abhibhūtassa kāyassa vipajjanaṃ mahiṃsaraṭṭhādīsu himapātakālena dīpetabbaṃ. Tattha hi sattā sītena bhinnasarīrā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇanti. Atiuṇhena abhibhūtassa vipajjanaṃ marukantāre uṇhābhitattāya pacchiṃ, tattha ṭhapitaṃ upari sāṭakaṃ, puttañca akkamitvā matāya itthiyā dīpetabbaṃ. Mahābhūtānaṃ samavuttitā pakopābhāvo[M 1.0293]. Pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ pakopena sarīrassa vikārāpatti parato dhātukammaṭṭhānakathāyaṃ āgamissati. Yuttakāleti bhuñjituṃ yuttakāle khuddābhibhūtakāle.

173. 'Weak' (abalaṃ) means deficient in strength. 'Feeble' (dubbalaṃ) is a synonym for that. For this prefix 'du-' has the sense of absence, as in 'immoral' (dussīlo), 'unwise' (duppañño), and so on. This life-faculty is the even occurrence of the in-breaths and out-breaths, their successive entering and exiting. When the nasal breath that has gone out does not enter in, or when what has entered does not go out, it is spoken of as if it were the entering and exiting of a single breath; this should be understood from the commonality of its being nasal breath. Due to excessiveness in matters such as sitting or standing for too long. The even occurrence of the postures is indeed the absence of that. The perishing of a body overwhelmed by extreme cold should be illustrated by the time of snowfall in regions like Mahiṃsaraṭṭha. There, beings whose bodies are shattered by cold meet the end of their lives. The perishing of one overwhelmed by extreme heat should be illustrated by the woman who died in the Maru desert, scorched by heat, after sitting upon a basket, an upper garment placed in it, and her son. The even occurrence of the great elements is the absence of their disturbance. The body's falling into disorder through the disturbance of the earth element, etc., will be discussed later in the section on the meditation subject of the elements. 'At the proper time' means at the time suitable for eating, when one is overcome by hunger.

174. Avavatthānatoti kālādivasena vavatthānābhāvato. Vavatthānanti cettha paricchedo adhippeto, na asaṅkarato vavatthānaṃ, nicchayo cāti āha “paricchedābhāvato”ti. Na nāyareti na ñāyanti.

174. 'Because of being undetermined' means because of the absence of determination by way of time, etc. Here, by 'determination' (vavatthāna), delimitation (pariccheda) is intended, not determination in the sense of non-confusion (asaṅkarato vavatthāna), nor certainty (nicchayo). Thus he says, 'because of the absence of delimitation.' 'Are not known' (na nāyare) means they are not known (na ñāyanti).

Ito [V 1.0277] paranti ettha paranti paraṃ aññaṃ kālanti attho. Tena orakālassāpi saṅgaho siddho hoti. Paramāyuto orakālaṃ eva cettha “para”nti adhippetaṃ. Tato paraṃ sattānaṃ jīvanassa abhāvato “vavatthānābhāvato”ti vattuṃ na sakkāti. Abbudapesītiādīsu “abbudakāle pesikāle”tiādinā kāla-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo. Kāloti idha pubbaṇhādivelā adhippetā. Tenāha “pubbaṇhepi hī”tiādi. Idheva dehena patitabbanti sambandho. Anekappakāratoti nagare jātānaṃ gāme, gāme jātānaṃ nagare, vane jātānaṃ janapade, janapade jātānaṃ vanetiādinā anekappakārato. Ito cutenāti ito gatito cutena. Idha imissaṃ gatiyaṃ. Yantayuttagoṇo viyāti yathā yante yuttagoṇo yantaṃ nātivattati, evaṃ loko gatipañcakanti ettakena upamā.

Regarding 'hereafter' (ito paraṃ): here 'hereafter' (paraṃ) means a future, other time. Thereby the inclusion of a nearer time is also established. Here, by 'hereafter,' a time within the maximum lifespan is intended. Because beyond that there is no life for beings, it is not possible to say 'because of the absence of determination.' In 'in the 'abbuda' and 'pesi' stages,' etc., the word 'time' should be connected with each, as 'at the time of the abbuda,' 'at the time of the pesi,' etc. Here 'time' (kālo) means a time of day such as morning. Hence he says, 'even in the morning,' etc. The connection is 'falling with this very body.' 'In many ways' means in various ways, such as: those born in a city die in a village, those born in a village die in a city, those born in a forest die in the country, those born in the country die in a forest. 'Fallen from here' means fallen from this destination. 'Here' means in this destination. 'Like an ox yoked to a machine': just as an ox yoked to a machine does not go beyond the machine, so the world of beings does not go beyond the five destinations. This is the extent of the simile.

175. Appaṃ vā bhiyyoti vassasatato upari “dasa vā vassāni, vīsati vā”tiādinā dutiyaṃ vassasataṃ apāpuṇanto appakaṃ vā jīvatīti attho. Gamanīyoti gandhabbo upapajjanavasena. Samparāyoti paraloko.

175. 'A little or more' means that living beyond one hundred years for 'ten years or twenty,' and so on, yet not reaching a second hundred years, one lives for only a short additional time. 'To be gone to' (gamanīyo) means 'to be gone to' (gantabbo) by way of taking rebirth. 'The next world' (samparāyo) means the world beyond.

Hīḷeyyāti paribhaveyya na sambhāveyya. Nanti āyuṃ. Suporisoti sādhupuriso paññavā. Careyyāti sucaritaṃ careyya. Tenāha “ādittasīsovā”ti.

'One should disdain' (hīḷeyya) means one should despise, not honor. 'It' (naṃ) means life. 'A good person' (suporiso) means a virtuous, wise person. 'One should practice' (careyya) means one should practice good conduct. Therefore, he said, 'like one whose head is on fire'.

Sattahi upamāhīti –

By seven similes:

“Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, tiṇagge ussāvabindu sūriye uggacchante khippaṃyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikaṃ hoti. Udake udakapubbuḷaṃ. Udake [M 1.0294] daṇḍarāji. Nadī pabbateyyā dūraṅgamā sīghasotā hārahārinī. Balavā puriso jivhagge kheḷapiṇḍaṃ saṃyūhitvā akasireneva vameyya. Divasaṃ santatte ayokaṭāhe maṃsapesi pakkhittā khippaṃyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikā hoti. Gāvī vajjhā āghātanaṃ nīyamānā yaṃ yadeva pādaṃ uddharati, santikeva hoti vadhassa, santikeva maraṇassa, evamevaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, govajjhūpamaṃ jīvitaṃ manussānaṃ parittaṃ lahukaṃ bahudukkhaṃ bahupāyāsaṃ mantāyaṃ boddhabbaṃ, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ, caritabbaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, natthi jātassa amaraṇa”nti (a. ni. 7.74) –

"Just as, brahmin, a dewdrop on a blade of grass quickly vanishes when the sun rises, not lasting long; like a bubble in water; like a line drawn in water; like a mountain river, far-reaching, swift-flowing, sweeping all before it; just as a strong man, having gathered a ball of spittle on the tip of his tongue, might spit it out with ease; just as a piece of meat thrown into an iron pan heated all day quickly perishes, not lasting long; just as a cow to be slaughtered, being led to the slaughterhouse, with every single step she takes, is ever nearer to the slaughter, ever nearer to death; even so, brahmin, the life of human beings is like a cow to be slaughtered—it is short, swift, with much suffering and much distress. It should be understood with wisdom, the wholesome should be done, the holy life should be lived; for one who has been born, there is no immortality."

Evamāgatāhi [V 1.0278] imāhi sattahi upamāhi alaṅkataṃ.

Adorned with these seven similes thus presented.

Rattindivanti ekaṃ rattindivaṃ. Bhagavato sāsananti ariyamaggapaṭivedhāvahaṃ satthu ovādaṃ. Bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti bahuṃ vata mayā attahitaṃ pabbajitakiccaṃ kataṃ bhaveyya. Tadantaranti taṃ khaṇaṃ tattakaṃ velaṃ. Ekaṃ piṇḍapātanti ekaṃ divasaṃ yāpanappahonakaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ. Dandhanti mandaṃ cirāya. Avissāsiyo avissāsanīyo.

'A day and night' means one day and night. 'The Blessed One's teaching' means the Teacher's instruction which brings about the penetration of the noble path. 'Much indeed would have been done by me' means: 'Much indeed of the renunciate's duty, which is for my own welfare, would have been done by me.' 'In that interval' means that moment, that much time. 'A single alms-bowlful' means an alms-bowlful sufficient to sustain one for a day. 'Slowly' means sluggishly, for a long time. 'Untrustworthy' means not to be trusted.

176. Citte dharanteyeva sattānaṃ jīvitavohāro, cittassa ca atiittaro khaṇo lahuparivattibhāvato. Yathāha bhagavā “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, yathayidaṃ citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48; kathā. 335). Tasmā sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikattā lahusaṃ ittaranti dassento “paramatthato”tiādimāha. Tattha “paramatthato”ti iminā yāyaṃ “yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasata”ntiādinā sattānaṃ (dī. ni. 2.7; saṃ. ni. 1.145; a. ni. 7.74) jīvitappavatti vuttā, sā pabandhavisayattā vohāravasenāti taṃ paṭikkhipati. “Atiparitto”ti iminā –

176. The conventional designation of 'life' for beings exists only while the mind is present; and a moment of mind is exceedingly brief because of its nature of changing swiftly. As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, I do not see even one other thing that changes so swiftly as this mind.' Therefore, to show that the life of beings is swift and brief because it lasts for only a single mind-moment, he said, 'in the ultimate sense,' and so on. Therein, by this phrase 'in the ultimate sense,' he rejects that continuity of life of beings which is spoken of in such passages as 'one who lives long lives for a hundred years,' because it pertains to a series and is by way of conventional usage. By 'exceedingly brief'—

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, cattāro daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā susikkhitā katahatthā katūpāsanā catuddisā ṭhitā assu, atha puriso āgaccheyya ‘ahaṃ imesaṃ…pe… katūpāsanānaṃ catuddisā kaṇḍe khitte appatiṭṭhite pathaviyaṃ gahetvā āharissāmī’ti. Yathā [M 1.0295] ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo, yathā ca candimasūriyānaṃ javo, tato sīghataro. Yathā ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo, yathā ca candimasūriyānaṃ javo, yathā ca yā devatā candimasūriyānaṃ purato dhāvanti, tāsaṃ devatānaṃ javo, tato sīghataraṃ āyusaṅkhārā khīyantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.228) –

Just as, monks, there might be four strong-bowed archers—well-trained, skillful-handed, and practiced—standing in the four directions. Then a man might come and say, 'I will catch and bring back the arrows shot in the four directions by these... practiced archers before they have struck the ground.' And, monks, swifter than the speed of that man is the speed of the sun and moon. And, monks, swifter than the speed of that man, and swifter than the speed of the sun and moon, is the speed of those deities who run before the sun and moon. The life-formations decay even more swiftly than that.

Evaṃ vuttaṃ parittampi paṭikkhipati. Tatra hi gamanassādānaṃ devaputtānaṃ heṭṭhupariyena paṭimukhaṃ dhāvantānaṃ sirasi, pāde ca baddhakhuradhārāsannipātatopi parittako rūpajīvitindriyassa so khaṇo vutto, cittassa pana ativiya parittataro, yassa upamāpi natthi. Tenevāha “yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, upamāpi na sukarā, yāva lahuparivattaṃ citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48). Jīvitakkhaṇoti jīvanakkhaṇo. Ekacittappavattimattoyeva ekassa cittassa pavattimatteneva [V 1.0279] sattānaṃ paramatthato jīvanakkhaṇassa paricchinnattā. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya pakāsento “yathā nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha pavattamānanti pavattantaṃ. Ekacittakkhaṇikanti ekacittakkhaṇamattavantaṃ. Tasmiṃ citte niruddhamatteti yena vattamānacittakkhaṇena “jīvatī”ti vuccati, tasmiṃ citte nirodhaṃ bhaṅgaṃ pattamatte taṃsamaṅgī satto niruddho matoti vuccati. Vuttamevatthaṃ pāḷiyā vibhāvetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena tīsupi kālesu sattānaṃ paramatthato jīvanaṃ nāma cittakkhaṇavasenevāti dasseti.

Even the brevity spoken of is rejected. For in that teaching, the moment of the physical life-faculty is said to be briefer than the moment of impact of razor blades bound to the heads and feet of celestial youths who delight in running and who rush towards each other from above and below. But the moment of the mind is exceedingly briefer still, for which there is not even a simile. Therefore, He said: 'So much so, monks, that it is not easy to give a simile for how swiftly the mind changes.' 'Life-moment' means the moment of living. Because the living-moment of beings, in the ultimate sense, is defined by merely the occurrence of a single mind-moment, it is just the occurrence of a single mind-moment. Now, to illuminate that meaning with a simile, he says, 'Just as...' and so on. Therein, 'occurring' means 'in process.' 'Lasting for a single mind-moment' means possessing only the duration of one mind-moment. 'At the very cessation of that mind' means: by whichever present mind-moment one is said to 'live,' just as that mind attains cessation and dissolution, the being endowed with it is said to have 'ceased' or 'died.' To clarify this very meaning with the Pāḷi text, the passage beginning 'As he said...' was stated. By this, he shows that in all three periods of time, the 'living' of beings, in the ultimate sense, is solely by way of the mind-moment.

Jīvitanti jīvitindriyaṃ. Sukhadukkhāti sukhadukkhavedanā. Upekkhāpi hi sukhadukkhāsu eva antogadhā iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvato. Attabhāvoti jīvitavedanāviññāṇāni ṭhapetvā avasiṭṭhadhammā vuttā. Kevalāti attanā, niccabhāvena vā avomissā. Ekacittasamāyuttāti ekekena cittena sahitā. Lahuso vattati khaṇoti vuttanayena ekacittakkhaṇikatāya lahuko atiittaro jīvitādīnaṃ khaṇo vattati.

'Life' means the life faculty. 'Pleasure and pain' means pleasant and painful feeling. Indeed, even equanimity is included within pleasant and painful feelings because of its nature of being desirable or undesirable. By 'individual existence' are meant the remaining phenomena, setting aside life, feeling, and consciousness. 'Pure' means unmixed with a self or with a state of permanence. 'Associated with a single mind' means arisen together with each single mind. 'A moment occurs swiftly' means that, in the way described, because it lasts for only a single mind-moment, the moment of life and so on occurs, being swift and exceedingly brief.

Ye niruddhā marantassāti cavantassa sattassa cutito uddhaṃ “niruddhā”ti vattabbā ye khandhā. Tiṭṭhamānassa vā idhāti ye vā idha pavattiyaṃ tiṭṭhantassa dharantassa bhaṅgappattiyā niruddhā khandhā. Sabbepi sadisā te sabbepi ekasadisā. Kathaṃ? Gatā appaṭisandhikā puna āgantvā paṭisandhānābhāvena vigatā. Yathā [M 1.0296] hi cutikhandhā na nivattanti, evaṃ tato pubbepi khandhā, tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitanti adhippāyo.

Those aggregates that are said to have 'ceased' for a being who is passing away, from the moment of decease onwards. Or, those aggregates that, for one who is existing and enduring here in this course of existence, have ceased upon reaching dissolution. All of them are similar; all are of one and the same nature. How so? They are gone, without relinking, vanished due to the absence of relinking. For just as the aggregates at death do not return, so too the aggregates before that do not return. Therefore, the meaning is that the life of beings lasts for a single mind-moment.

Anibbattena na jātoti anuppannena cittena jāto na hoti ajāto nāma hoti. Paccuppannena vattamānena cittena jīvati jīvamāno nāma hoti. Cittabhaṅgā mato lokoti cuticittassa viya sabbassapi tassa tassa cittassa bhaṅgappattiyā ayaṃ loko paramatthato mato nāma hoti niruddhassa appaṭisandhikattā. Evaṃ santepi paññatti paramatthiyā yā taṃ taṃ dharantaṃ cittaṃ upādāya “tisso jīvati, phusso jīvatī”ti vacanappavattiyā visayabhūtā santānapaññatti, sā ettha paramatthiyā paramatthabhūtā. Tathā hi vadanti “nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.76).

One is not born by a mind that has not arisen; one is called 'unborn.' One lives by the presently occurring mind; one is called 'living.' At the dissolution of the mind, the world is dead: just as with the death-consciousness, so too with the reaching of dissolution of each and every mind, this world is, in the ultimate sense, called 'dead,' because of the non-relinking of that which has ceased. Even so, there is a designation that is ultimately real. That continuity-designation which, depending on each enduring mind, becomes the object for the occurrence of speech such as 'Tissa lives, Phussa lives'—that designation is here ultimately real, having become the ultimate reality. For so they say: 'Name and clan do not decay.'

177. Aññataraññatarena ākārena. Cittanti kammaṭṭhānārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ. Āsevanaṃ labhatīti bhāvanāsevanaṃ [V 1.0280] labhati, bahiddhā vikkhepaṃ pahāya ekattavasena maraṇārammaṇameva hotīti. Tenāha “maraṇārammaṇā sati santiṭṭhatī”ti. Sabhāvadhammānaṃ bhedo sabhāvadhammagatiko evāti āha “sabhāvadhammattā pana ārammaṇassā”ti. Tenāha bhagavā “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.20). Saṃvejanīyattāti saṃvegajananato mahābhūtesu mahāvikāratā viya gayhamānā maraṇaṃ anussariyamānaṃ uparūpari ubbegameva āvahatīti tattha na bhāvanācittaṃ appetuṃ sakkoti. Yadi sabhāvadhammattā appanaṃ na pāpuṇāti, lokuttarajjhānaṃ ekaccāni arūpajjhānāni ca kathanti āha “lokuttarajjhānaṃ panā”tiādi. Visuddhibhāvanānukkamavasenāti heṭṭhimavisuddhiyā ānubhāvena adhigatātisayāya paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhibhāvanāya, sabbasaṅkhārehi nibbindanavirajjanādivisaṃyogādhimuttiappanāya ca paṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ vigamoti evaṃbhūtassa visuddhibhāvanānukkamassa vasena lokuttarajjhānaṃ appanāppattameva hoti. Ārammaṇasamatikkamanamattaṃ tattha hotīti aññesaṃ sabhāvadhammārammaṇakammaṭṭhānānaṃ viya cittassa samādhāne byāpāro natthi. Yathāsamāhitena pana cittena ārammaṇasamatikkamanamattameva bhāvanāya kātabbaṃ, tasmā sabhāvadhammepi āruppajjhānaṃ appetīti.

177. In one way or another. The mind: the mind that has the meditation subject as its object. It gains practice: it gains the practice of development; having abandoned external distraction, by way of unification, it becomes solely the object of death. Therefore He said: 'Mindfulness with death as its object is established.' The dissolution of natural phenomena is of the nature of natural phenomena; thus He said: 'but because of the object's being a natural phenomenon.' Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Aging and death, bhikkhus, are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen,' and so forth. Because it is stirring: because it generates spiritual urgency. Just as a great disturbance in the great elements, when grasped, brings agitation, so too death, when recollected again and again, brings only agitation, and thus the meditation mind is not able to be applied there. If, due to its being a natural phenomenon, it does not reach absorption, how then do supramundane jhāna and certain formless jhānas reach it? Thus He said: 'But the supramundane jhāna...' and so forth. By the power of the gradual development of purification: by the power of the lower purifications, by the development of the purification of knowledge and vision of the way, which has attained excellence; and by the resolve towards disjunction from all formations through disenchantment, dispassion, and so forth, and by the removal of evil states that are opposed to absorption—by the power of such a gradual development of purification, the supramundane jhāna indeed reaches absorption. There, it is merely the transcending of the object: unlike other meditation subjects that have natural phenomena as their object, there is no exertion in the concentration of the mind. But with a mind that is well-concentrated as it is, only the mere transcending of the object is to be done by the development. Therefore, even when the object is a natural phenomenon, the formless jhāna is applied.

Satataṃ [M 1.0297] appamatto hoti saṃvegabahulattā, tato evassa sabbabhavesu anabhiratisaññāpaṭilābho. Jīvitanikantiṃ jahāti maraṇassa avassaṃbhāvitādassanato. Pāpagarahī hoti aniccasaññāpaṭilābhato, tato eva asannidhibahulatā, vigatamalamaccheratā ca. Tadanusārenāti aniccasaññāparicayānusārena. Abhāvitamaraṇāti abhāvitamaraṇānussaraṇā. Abhayo asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti pageva maraṇasaññāya sūpaṭṭhitattā.

Because of being full of spiritual urgency, one is constantly heedful, and for that very reason, one obtains the perception of non-delight in all forms of existence. One abandons craving for life because of seeing the inevitability of death. From obtaining the perception of impermanence, one becomes a reprover of evil, and for that very reason, there is an absence of much hoarding and the state of being without the stain of stinginess. Following that: in accordance with the cultivation of the perception of impermanence. Those for whom death is undeveloped: those for whom the recollection of death is undeveloped. Because the perception of death is well-established from the very beginning, one dies fearless and unconfused.

Kāyagatāsatikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body

178. Buddhā uppajjanti etthāti buddhuppādo, buddhānaṃ uppajjanakālo, tasmā. Aññatra taṃ ṭhapetvā, aññasmiṃ kāleti attho. Na pavattapubbanti apavattapubbaṃ. Tato eva sabbatitthiyānaṃ avisayabhūtaṃ. Nanu ca sunettasatthārādayo (a. ni. 6.54; 7.66, 73), aññe ca tāpasaparibbājakā sarīraṃ “asubha”nti jāniṃsu. Tathā hi sumedhatāpasena sarīraṃ jigucchantena vuttaṃ –

178. Buddhas arise in this, thus it is a 'Buddha-arising,' the time of the arising of Buddhas; therefore. 'Except for that' means having set that aside, at another time is the meaning. 'Not having occurred before' means it is what has not occurred before. For that very reason, it is beyond the scope of all sectarians. Now, did not teachers like Sunetta and others, and other ascetics and wanderers, know the body as 'unattractive'? For so it was said by the ascetic Sumedha, who was disgusted with the body—

“Yannūnimaṃ [V 1.0281] pūtikāyaṃ, nānākuṇapapūritaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gaccheyyaṃ, anapekkho anatthiko”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.8) –

‘How good it would be if I, having abandoned this foul body filled with various kinds of corpses, were to go forth, without concern and without need.’

Ādi. Kāmaṃ bodhisattā, aññe ca tāpasādayo sarīraṃ “asubha”nti jānanti, kammaṭṭhānabhāvena pana na jānanti. Tena vuttaṃ “aññatra buddhuppādā”tiādi. Saṃvegāya saṃvattati yāthāvato kāyasabhāvappavedanato. Atthāyāti diṭṭhadhammikādiatthāya. Yogakkhemāyāti catūhi yogehi khemabhāvāya. Satisampajaññāyāti sabbattha satiavippavāsāya ca sattaṭṭhāniyasampajaññāya ca. Ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāyāti vipassanāñāṇādhigamāya. Vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāyāti tisso vijjā, cittassa adhimutti nibbānaṃ, cattāri sāmaññaphalānīti etesaṃ paccakkhakaraṇāya. Amatassa nibbānassa adhigamahetutāya, amatasadisātappakasukhasahitatāya ca kāyagatāsati “amata”nti vuttā. Paribhuñjantīti jhānasamāpajjanena vaḷañjanti. Parihīnanti jinaṃ. Viraddhanti anadhigamena virajjhitaṃ. Āraddhanti sādhitaṃ nipphāditaṃ. Anekehi ākārehi tesu tesu suttantesu pasaṃsitvā yaṃ taṃ kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhanti sambandho[M 1.0298]. Kattha pana niddiṭṭhanti? Kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.153 ādayo). Tattha hi “kathaṃ bhāvitā ca bhikkhave”tiādinā ayaṃ desanā āgatā. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, kena pakārena kāyagatāsatibhāvanā bhāvitā, kena ca pakārena punappunaṃ katā ānāpānajjhānādīnaṃ nipphattiyā mahapphalā, tesaṃ tesaṃ vijjābhāgiyānaṃ, abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyānañca dhammānaṃ, aratiratisahanatādīnañca saṃsiddhiyā mahānisaṃsā ca hotīti? Ānāpānapabbanti ānāpānakammaṭṭhānāvadhi. Esa nayo sesesupi.

And so forth. Indeed, Bodhisattas and other ascetics and the like know the body as 'unattractive,' but they do not know it as a meditation subject. Therefore it is said: 'except when a Buddha arises,' and so forth. It leads to a sense of urgency by revealing the true nature of the body. 'For the sake of benefit' means for the sake of benefit in this life and so forth. 'For the sake of security from bondage' means for the sake of security from the four bonds. 'For the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension' means for the sake of the non-abandonment of mindfulness everywhere and for the sake of clear comprehension in the seven instances. 'For the attainment of knowledge and vision' means for the attainment of insight knowledge. 'For the realization of the fruits of knowledge and liberation' means for the direct experience of the three knowledges, the mind’s liberation (Nibbāna), and the four fruits of recluseship. Because it is the cause for attaining the deathless Nibbāna, and because it is accompanied by non-afflictive bliss similar to the deathless, mindfulness directed to the body is called 'the deathless.' 'They partake of it' means they make use of it by attaining jhāna. 'It is missed' means it is lost. 'It is failed' means it is missed through non-attainment. 'It is undertaken' means it is accomplished, brought to completion. Having praised that meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body in various ways in various discourses, the connection is that it is pointed out. But where is it pointed out? In the Kāyagatāsati Sutta. For there, this teaching is given with the words, 'And how, bhikkhus, is it developed?' and so forth.
