Here is the summary meaning: Bhikkhus, in what way is the development of mindfulness directed to the body developed, and in what way, when repeatedly done, does it become of great fruit for the attainment of jhānas like mindfulness of breathing, and of great benefit for the realization of those states pertaining to knowledge, and of things to be directly known by higher knowledge, and for the accomplishment of enduring discontent and delight, and so forth? 'The section on mindfulness of breathing' means up to the limit of the mindfulness of breathing meditation subject. The same method applies to the rest.

Dhātumanasikārakammaṭṭhānena yadipi upacārasamādhi ijjhati, sammasanavāro pana tattha sātisayoti dhātumanasikārapabbampi “vipassanāvasena vutta”nti vuttaṃ. “Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto”ti (dī. ni. 2.379; ma. ni. 1.112) tattha tattha asubhāniccatādīhi saddhiṃ kāye ādīnavassa vibhāvanavasena desanāya āgatattā “navasivathika…pe… vuttānī”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha uddhumātakādīsūti etesu sivathikapabbesu āgatauddhumātakādīsu. Ānāpānassativasenāti ānāpānassatibhāvanāvasena. Yo upari “karīsaṃ matthaluṅga”nti matthaluṅgakoṭṭhāso gayhati, taṃ idha pāḷiyaṃ (ma. ni. 3.154) aṭṭhimiñjeneva saṅgaṇhitvā desanā āgatāti dassento “matthaluṅgaṃ aṭṭhimiñjena saṅgahetvā”ti āha[V 1.0282]. Idhāti imasmiṃ anussatiniddese. Kāyaṃ gatā, kāye vā gatā sati kāyagatāsatīti satisīsena idaṃ dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ adhippetanti yojanā.

Even if access concentration is achieved by the meditation subject of attention to the elements, the sphere of comprehension there is exceptional; therefore, the section on attention to the elements is also said to be 'taught by way of insight.' Because the teaching has come in various places by way of demonstrating the danger in the body along with unattractiveness, impermanence, and so forth, with the words, “This body too is of such a nature, it will become so, it cannot go beyond becoming so,” it is said, “the nine charnel ground sections... are spoken of.” Here, 'in the case of the bloated, etc.' means in the case of the bloated, etc., that have come in these sections on the charnel grounds. 'By way of mindfulness of breathing' means by way of the development of mindfulness of breathing. The brain-portion which is taken above as “excrement, brain,” is here in the Pāḷi included with just the bone marrow when the teaching is given; showing this, he said, “taking the brain together with the bone marrow.” 'Here' means in this exposition on recollection. Mindfulness gone to the body, or mindfulness that has occurred in the body, is 'mindfulness directed to the body' (kāyagatāsati); thus, with mindfulness as the main heading, this meditation subject of the thirty-two parts is intended—this is the construing.

179. Catumahābhūtikanti catumahābhūtasannissayaṃ. Pūtikāyanti pūtibhūtaṃ paramaduggandhakāyaṃ. Ṭhānagamanāvatthaṃ sarīraṃ sandhāya, tassa vā avayavesu sabbaheṭṭhimaṃ pādatalanti vuttaṃ “uddhaṃ pādatalā”ti. Tiriyaṃ tacaparicchinnanti ettha nanu kesalomanakhānaṃ, tacassa ca atacaparicchinnatā atthīti? Kiñcāpi atthi, tacaparicchinnabahulatāya pana kāyassa tacaparicchinnatā hotīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Taco pariyanto assāti tacapariyantoti etena pana vacanena kāyekadesabhūto taco gahito eva, tappaṭibaddhā ca kesādayo tadanupaviṭṭhamūlā tacapariyantāva hontīti [M 1.0299] dvattiṃsākārasamūho sabbopi kāyo tacapariyanto vuttoti veditabbo.

179. 'Composed of the four great elements' means dependent on the four great elements. 'Foul body' means a putrid and extremely foul-smelling body. Referring to the body in its states of standing and going, or because among its parts the sole of the foot is the very lowest, it is said, 'above the soles of the feet.' In the phrase 'horizontally, bounded by skin,' is it not so that the head hair, body hair, nails, and the skin itself are not bounded by skin? Although that is so, because the greater part of the body is bounded by skin, it is said to be bounded by skin. Alternatively, 'the skin is its boundary' (tacapariyanto): by this statement, the skin, which is a part of the body, is indeed taken. And the hairs, etc., attached to it and with roots entered into it, are themselves bounded by the skin. Thus, the entire collection of the thirty-two constituents, the whole body, is said to be bounded by the skin; this should be understood.

Atthīti vacanavipallāsena vuttaṃ, nipātapadaṃ vā etaṃ. Tasmā tīsupi saṅkhāsu tadevassa rūpaṃ. Tenāha “saṃvijjantī”ti. Akkharacintakehi sarīre kāya-saddaṃ vaṇṇantehipi asucisamudāyabhāveneva icchitabboti dassento “asucisañcayato”ti vatvā puna naṃ niruttinayena dassetuṃ “kucchitāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āyabhūtatoti uppattiṭṭhānabhūtattā. “Pūraṃ nānappakārassā”ti vuttaṃ. “Ke pana te pakārā? Yehi nānappakāraṃ asuci vutta”nti te kesādike dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “kesā lomā”tiādi vuttanti imamatthaṃ dīpento āha “ete kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā”ti. Ākārā pakārāti hi eko atthoti. Evaṃ sambandhoti “atthi imasmiṃ kāye nakhā”tiādinā sabbakoṭṭhāsesu “atthi imasmiṃ kāye”ti padattayena sambandho veditabbo.

The word Atthi ('there is') is said with an inversion of number, or it is an indeclinable particle. Therefore, in all three numbers, its form is just that. For that reason, he said, 'they exist' (saṃvijjanti). Even by grammarians explaining the word kāya in the context of the body, it should be accepted only as an accumulation of the impure. To show this, having said, 'from the collection of impurities,' then to show it again by way of etymology, 'of the disgusting,' etc., was said. Therein, āyabhūtato means 'because it is the place of origin.' 'Full of various kinds' was said. 'But what are those kinds? By which the impure is said to be of various kinds?'—to show those kinds beginning with hair, in the Pāḷi, 'hair, body hair,' etc., was said. Explaining this meaning, he said, 'these, beginning with hair, are the thirty-two aspects.' For ākārā (aspects) and pakārā (kinds) have one meaning. Thus is the connection: by 'there are nails in this body,' etc., the connection with the triad of words 'there are in this body' should be understood in all the parts.

Paritoti tiriyaṃ, samantato vā pādatalakesamūlesu ca tacassa labbhanato. Sucibhāvanti sucino sabbhāvaṃ, sucimeva vā.

'All around' (parito) means horizontally, or on all sides, because the skin is found on the soles of the feet and at the roots of the hair. 'State of purity' (sucibhāvaṃ) means the existence of what is pure, or simply what is pure itself.

180. Yena vidhinā uggahe kusalo hoti, so sattavidho vidhi “uggahakosalla”nti vuccati, tannibbattaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ. Manasikārakosallepi eseva nayo.

180. The sevenfold method by which one becomes skilled in learning is called 'skill in learning' (uggahakosalla), or the knowledge produced by that method is so called. In the case of skill in attention (manasikārakosalla), this is the same principle.

Sajjhāyantā vāti sajjhāyaṃ karontā eva. Tesaṃ kira cattāro māse sajjhāyantānaṃ sajjhāyamaggeneva [V 1.0283] koṭṭhāse upadhārentānaṃ paṭipāṭiyā dvattiṃsākārā vibhūtatarā hutvā khāyiṃsu, paṭikkūlasaññā saṇṭhāsi, te tasmiṃ nimitte jhānaṃ appetvā jhānapādakaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dassanamaggaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “sajjhāyantā va sotāpannā ahesu”nti.

Sajjhāyantā vā means 'just while reciting.' It is said that for those two elders who were reciting for four months, as they were contemplating the parts in sequence by way of recitation itself, the thirty-two aspects, having become exceedingly clear, appeared. The perception of repulsiveness was well established. They, having applied jhāna to that sign and having developed insight which has jhāna as its basis, penetrated the path of vision. For that reason it was said, 'Just while reciting, they became stream-enterers.'

Paricchinditvāti tacapañcakādivaseneva paricchedaṃ katvā. Pathavīdhātubahulabhāvato matthaluṅgassa karīsāvasāne tantiāropanamāha. Ettha ca maṃsaṃ, nhāru, aṭṭhi, aṭṭhimiñjaṃ vakkaṃ, vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ, aṭṭhi, nhāru, maṃsaṃ, taco, dantā, nakhā, lomā, kesāti evaṃ vakkapañcakādīsu anulomasajjhāyaṃ vatvā paṭilomasajjhāyo purimehi sambandho vutto. Svāyaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ [M 1.0300] (vibha. aṭṭha. 356) visuṃ tipañcāhaṃ, purimehi ekato tipañcāhanti chapañcāhaṃ sajjhāyo vutto, tattha ādiantadassanavasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Anulomapaṭilomasajjhāyepi hi paṭilomasajjhāyo antimo hoti, sajjhāyappakārantaraṃ vā etampīti veditabbaṃ.

'Having delineated' (paricchinditvā) means having made a delimitation by way of the pentad beginning with skin, and so on. Due to the abundance of the earth element in the brain, he speaks of placing it in the Pāḷi text at the end of the feces part. And here, having stated the forward recitation in the pentads beginning with the kidneys, and so on—'flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys... hair'—the reverse recitation is said to be connected with the preceding ones. This recitation is spoken of in the Sammohavinodanī as for three five-day periods separately, and for three five-day periods together with the preceding ones—thus for six five-day periods. There, it should be understood as spoken by way of showing the beginning and the end. For in forward and reverse recitation, the reverse recitation is the final one; or this too should be known as another type of recitation.

Hatthasaṅkhalikāti aṅgulipantimāha.

By 'hand-chain' (hatthasaṅkhalikā), he speaks of a row of fingers.

Manasā sajjhāyoti cittena cintanamāha, yaṃ mānasaṃ “jappana”nti vuccati, sammadeva ajjhāyoti vā sajjhāyo, cintananti attho. Cirataraṃ suṭṭhu pavattanena paguṇabhūtā kammaṭṭhānatanti samāvajjitvā manasi karontassa ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā katthaci asajjamānā nirantarameva upaṭṭhāti, tadanusārena tadatthopi vibhūtataro hutvā khāyatīti āha “vacasā sajjhāyo hi…pe… paṭivedhassa paccayo hotī”ti. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhassāti asubhalakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa.

'Recitation with the mind' (manasā sajjhāyo) means he speaks of thinking with the mind, which, being mental, is called 'muttering' (jappana); or, because it is 'thinking rightly towards' (sammadeva ajjhāyo), it is sajjhāyo. The meaning is 'thinking.' For one who, having reflected well, brings to mind the Pāḷi of the meditation subject that has become proficient through proceeding well for a very long time, it appears continuously without interval from the beginning up to the very end, not getting stuck anywhere. In accordance with that, its meaning also, having become exceedingly clear, appears. Thus he said, 'Recitation by speech... is a condition for penetration.' 'Of penetration of the characteristic' means of penetration of the characteristic of foulness.

Paṭikkūlasabhāvasallakkhaṇassa kassaci vaṇṇaggahaṇamukhena koṭṭhāsā vavatthānaṃ gacchanti, kassaci saṇṭhānaggahaṇamukhena, kassaci disāvibhāgaggahaṇamukhena, kassaci patiṭṭhitokāsaggahaṇamukhena, kassaci sabbaso paricchijjaggahaṇamukhenāti vaṇṇādito sallakkhaṇaṃ uggahakosallāvahaṃ vuttanti taṃ dassento “kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇo vavatthapetabbo”tiādimāha.

For a certain person who is marking well the repulsive nature, the parts become determined by means of apprehending color; for another, by means of apprehending shape; for another, by means of apprehending the division of direction; for another, by means of apprehending the established location; for another, by means of apprehending through complete delimitation. Thus, because the marking well of characteristics beginning with color is said to bring skill in learning, showing that, he said, "the color of the hair, etc., should be determined," and so on.

Attano bhāgo sabhāgo, sabhāgena paricchedo sabhāgaparicchedo, heṭṭhuparitiriyapariyantehi, sakoṭṭhāsikakesantarādīhi [V 1.0284] ca paricchedoti attho. Amissakatāvasenāti koṭṭhāsantarehi avomissakatāvasena. Asabhāgo hi idha “visabhāgo”ti adhippeto, na viruddhasabhāgo. Svāyamattho kesādisaddato eva labbhati. Saddantaratthāpohanavasena saddo atthaṃ vadatīti “kesā”ti vutte “akesā na hontī”ti ayamattho viññāyati. Ke pana te akesā? Lomādayo, na ca ghaṭādīsu pasaṅgopakaraṇeneva tesaṃ nivattitattā.

One's own part is sabhāga. Delimitation by one's own part is sabhāgapariccheda. The meaning is delimitation by the lower, upper, and transverse boundaries, and by one's own individual parts, such as a single hair, etc. "By way of non-mixture" means by way of not being mixed with other parts. For here asabhāga (not one's own part) is intended as visabhāga (dissimilar part), not viruddhasabhāga (a contrary part). This meaning is obtained from the very word kesa (hair), etc. A word speaks its meaning by way of excluding the meaning of another word. Thus, when kesā (hair) is said, this meaning, "what is not hair does not exist [here]," is understood. But what are those 'not-hairs'? Body hair, etc. And there is no application to pots and so on, because they are excluded by the context itself.

Paṭikkūlavaseneva kathitaṃ dhātuvibhāgassa sāmaññatopi agahitattā. Tattheva visuṃ dhātukammaṭṭhānassa kathitattā ca dhātuvibhaṅgo pakkusātisuttaṃ [M 1.0301] (ma. ni. 3.342) vibhaṅgappakaraṇe dhātuvibhaṅgapāḷi (vibha. 172 ādayo) ca. Yassa vaṇṇato upaṭṭhāti kesādi, taṃ puggalaṃ sandhāya jhānāni kesādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇārammaṇāni vibhattāni. Ñatvā ācikkhitabbanti yadatthaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “tattha dhātuvasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ paṭikkūlamanasikārapabbe. Kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.153 ādayo) hi paṭikkūlamanasikārapabbaṃ gahetvā idha kāyagatāsatibhāvanā niddisīyati.

It is taught only by way of the repulsive, because the analysis of elements is not taken up even in a general way, and because the meditation subject of the elements is taught separately in that very [Sutta]. The "analysis of elements" (dhātuvibhaṅga) is the Pukkusāti Sutta and the Pāḷi on the analysis of elements in the book of the Vibhaṅga. With reference to the person for whom hair, etc., appears by way of color, the jhānas, having the color kasiṇas in hair, etc., as their object, are analyzed. To show the purpose for which it was said, "Having known, one should explain," the passage beginning "there, by way of elements" was stated. "Here" means in this section on attention to the repulsive. For in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, having taken the section on attention to the repulsive, here the development of mindfulness directed to the body is indicated.

181. Na ekantarikāyāti ekantarikāyapi na manasi kātabbaṃ, pageva dvantarikādināti adhippāyo. Na bhāvanaṃ sampādeti, lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ na pāpuṇāti ekantarikāya manasi karontoti sambandho.

181. "Not with one in between" (na ekantarikāya): The intention is that it should not be brought to mind even with one [part] in between, how much more so with two in between, etc. The connection is: one who brings [the parts] to mind with one in between does not accomplish the development and does not attain the penetration of the characteristic.

Okkamanavissajjananti paṭipajjitabbavissajjetabbe magge. Pucchitvāva gantabbaṃ hoti gahetabbavissajjetabbaṭṭhānassa asallakkhaṇato. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ pāpuṇātīti ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā manasikāramattaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Avibhūtaṃ pana hoti paṭikkūlākārassa suṭṭhu asallakkhaṇato. Tato eva na visesaṃ āvahati.

"Okkamanavissajjana" (entering and letting go) means the path of what should be entered upon and what should be let go of. One must go only after asking, due to not discerning the place of what should be taken up and what should be let go of. "The meditation subject reaches completion"—the intention is that from the beginning up to the end, it is mere attention. However, it is indistinct due to not properly discerning the repulsive aspect. For that very reason, it does not bring about any distinction.

Kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ na gacchatīti paṭipāṭiyā sabbakoṭṭhāse manasi karotoyeva vibhūtā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Te sātisayaṃ pāṭikkūlato manasi karontassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ gaccheyya, imassa pana ativiya dandhaṃ manasi karoto vibhūtato upaṭṭhānameva natthi, kuto paṭikkūlatāya saṇṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “visesādhigamassa paccayo na hotī”ti.

The meditation subject does not reach completion. For only when one attends to all the sections in sequence do they become distinct and appear. For one who attends to them with extreme repulsiveness, the meditation subject might reach completion; but for this one who attends to it too slowly, a distinct appearance does not even arise—how much less the establishment of repulsiveness. Therefore, it is said, 'It is not a condition for the attainment of distinction.'

Bahiddhā [V 1.0285] puthuttārammaṇeti “asuci paṭikkūla”nti kesādīsu pavattetabbaṃ asubhānupassanaṃ hitvā subhādivasena gayhamānā kesādayopi idha “bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇamevā”ti veditabbā. Rūpādayo hi nīlādivasena puthusabhāvatāya puthuttārammaṇaṃ nāma, nānārammaṇanti attho. Asamādhānaṃ cetaso virūpo khepoti vikkhepo. So satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā sakkaccaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karontena paṭibāhitabbo. Parihāyatīti hāyati. Paridhaṃsatīti vinassati.

Regarding "bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇa" (external diverse objects): abandoning the contemplation of the foul (asubhānupassanā) that should be applied to hair, etc., as "impure, repulsive," even hair and the like, which are grasped by way of the beautiful, etc., should be known here as "nothing but external diverse objects." Indeed, forms, etc., because of their diverse nature by way of blue, etc., are called "diverse objects" (puthuttārammaṇa); the meaning is "various objects" (nānārammaṇa). Distraction (vikkhepo) is the un-composedness (asamādhāna), the distorted (virūpo) scattering (khepo) of the mind. That should be prevented by one who, having well-established mindfulness, earnestly attends to the meditation subject. "Parihāyati" means it declines. "Paridhaṃsati" means it perishes.

Yā [M 1.0302] ayaṃ kesā lomātiādikā lokasaṅketānugatā. Paṇṇattīti aṭṭha dhamme upādāya paṇṇatti. Taṃ kesādipaṇṇattiṃ. Atikkamitvāti paṭikkūlabhāvanāya atikkamitvā ugghāṭetvā. Tassā ugghāṭitattā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ koṭṭhāse paṭikkūlato upaṭṭhahante “paṭikkūla”nti cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvento “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Tatridaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ – manussā viya yogāvacaro. Udapānaṃ viya koṭṭhāsā. Tālapaṇṇādisaññāṇaṃ viya kesādipaññatti. Tena manussānaṃ udapāne nhānapivanādi viya yogāvacarassa pubbabhāge kesā lomāti paṇṇattivasena manasikāro. Abhiṇhasañcārena manussānaṃ saññāṇena vinā udapāne kiccakaraṇaṃ viya yogāvacarassa manasikārabalena paṇṇattiṃ atikkamitvā paṭikkūlabhāveyeva cittaṃ ṭhapetvā bhāvanānuyogo. Pubbabhāge…pe… pākaṭo hotīti “kesā lomā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.154) bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa kesādipaññattiyā saddhiṃyeva koṭṭhāsānaṃ paṭikkūlabhāvo pubbabhāge pākaṭo hoti. Athāti pacchā bhāvanāya vīthipaṭipannakāle. Paṭikkūlabhāveyeva cittaṃ ṭhapetabbanti koṭṭhāsānaṃ paṭikkūlākāreyeva bhāvanācittaṃ pavattetabbaṃ.

That which is the designation (paṇṇatti) "hair, body hair," etc., follows worldly convention. A designation is a designation made by depending on eight things. Regarding that designation of hair, etc. "Having overcome" means having overcome by means of the cultivation of repulsiveness, having stripped it away. Because that designation has been stripped away, when in each and every part repulsiveness appears, the mind should be established on "repulsive." Now, explaining that meaning with a simile, he says, "Just as..." Here is the application of the simile: the yogī is like the people; the parts are like the well; the designation of hair, etc., is like the sign of palm leaves, etc. Just as for people there is bathing, drinking, etc., in the well by means of that sign, so for the yogī in the preliminary stage there is attention by way of the designation "hair, body hair." Just as for people, due to frequent coming and going, there is the doing of tasks at the well without the sign, so for the yogī, by the power of attention, having overcome the designation and established the mind only on the state of repulsiveness, there is the application to the cultivation. "In the preliminary stage... it becomes clear" means that for one applying oneself to the cultivation with "hair, body hair," etc., the repulsiveness of the parts together with the designation of hair, etc., becomes clear in the preliminary stage. "Then" means later, at the time when the cultivation has entered its course. "The mind should be established only on the state of repulsiveness" means the mind of cultivation should be made to proceed only in the aspect of repulsiveness of the parts.

Anupubbena muñcanaṃ anupubbamuñcanaṃ, anupaṭṭhahantassa anupaṭṭhahantassa muñcananti attho. Kathaṃ pana anupaṭṭhānaṃ hotīti āha “ādikammikassā”tiādi. Pariyosānakoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhatīti idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ tantianusārena ādito kammaṭṭhānamanasikāro pavattatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Tathā hissa manasā sajjhāyo viya manasikāro te te koṭṭhāse āmaṭṭhamatte katvā gacchati, na lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena. Yadā pana ne lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena suṭṭhu upadhārento manasi karoti, tadā keci upaṭṭhahanti, keci na upaṭṭhahanti. Tattha paṭipajjanavidhiṃ dassento “athassā”tiādimāha. Tattha kammanti manasikārakammaṃ tāva kātabbaṃ. Kīva ciranti? Yāva dvīsu upaṭṭhitesu, tesampi dvinnaṃ eko suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhahati tāva.

Releasing in sequence is `anupubbamuñcana`; the meaning is the releasing of each part that does not appear. But how does non-appearance occur? He said, 'For a beginner,' and so on. 'It stands striking only the final section'—this was said on the grounds that the attention to the meditation subject proceeds from the beginning according to the meditation text. Indeed, for this person, the attention, like a mental recitation, proceeds by merely touching upon those various parts, not by way of properly discerning the characteristic. But when one attends well, investigating them by way of properly discerning the characteristic, then some parts appear, and some do not appear. There, showing the method of practice, he said, 'Then for him,' and so on. There, `kamma` (work) means the work of attention is to be done. For how long? For as long as it takes until, when two parts have appeared, of those two, one appears even more clearly.

Ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhiṭṭhāneyeva [V 1.0286] uṭṭhahitvāti pubbe viya ekatthakatāya ukkuṭṭhiyā kamena sabbatālesu patitvā uṭṭhahitvā uṭṭhahitvā pariyantatālaṃ[M 1.0303], āditālañca āgantvā tato tato tattha tattheva katāya ukkuṭṭhiyā uṭṭhahitvāti attho.

Regarding 'having risen from the very place of the cry': the meaning is this. It is not as before—where, by a cry made in one place, it would jump down to all the palm trees in sequence, rise up again and again, and go to the last palm tree and the first—but rather, it is having risen from each respective place by the cry made at that very palm tree.

Dve bhikkhāti dvīsu gehesu laddhabhikkhā.

‘Two alms’ means almsfood obtained from two houses.

Appanātoti appanākārato dvattiṃsākāre appanā honti. Kiṃ paccekaṃ koṭṭhāsesu hoti udāhu aññathāti vicāraṇāyaṃ āha “appanākoṭṭhāsato”ti, koṭṭhāsato koṭṭhāsatoti attho. Tenāha “kesādīsū”tiādi.

Regarding `appanāto`: this means by way of the aspect of `appanā`. When `appanā` occurs in the thirty-two-fold aspect, in the investigation 'Does it occur in each part individually, or otherwise?' he said, `appanākoṭṭhāsato`. The meaning is 'from part to part.' Therefore, he said, 'in hair, etc.'

Adhicittanti samathavipassanācittaṃ.

`Adhicitta` (the higher mind) is the mind of serenity (`samatha`) and insight (`vipassanā`).

Anuyuttenāti yuttappayuttena, bhāventenāti attho. Kālenakālanti kāle kāle. Samādhinimittaṃ upalakkhitasamādhānākāro samādhi eva. Manasi kātabbanti citte kātabbaṃ, uppādetabbanti attho. Samādhikāraṇaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ samādhinimittaṃ, taṃ āvajjitabbanti attho. Paggahanimittaupekkhānimittesupi eseva nayo. Ṭhānaṃ atthīti vacanaseso. Taṃ bhāvanā cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya, etassa saṃvattanassa ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthīti attho. Taṃ vā manasikaraṇacittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya, etassa ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthīti attho. Mudunti subhāvitabhāvena mudubhūtaṃ, vasībhāvappattanti attho. Muduttā eva kammaññaṃ kammakkhamaṃ kammayoggaṃ. Pabhassaranti upakkilesavigamena parisuddhaṃ, pariyodātanti attho. Na ca pabhaṅgūti kammaniyabhāvūpagamanena na ca pabhijjanasabhāvaṃ suddhantaṃ viya suvaṇṇaṃ viniyogakkhamaṃ. Tenāha “sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāyā”ti.

`Anuyuttena` means diligently engaged or greatly striving, that is, developing. `Kālena kālaṃ` means from time to time. The sign of concentration is concentration itself, which has the characteristic of previously marked collectedness. `Manasi kātabbaṃ` means it should be done in the mind, that is, it should be aroused. Or, the cause or object of concentration is the sign of concentration; the meaning is it should be attended to. This same principle applies also to the signs of exertion and equanimity. `Ṭhānaṃ atthi` (there is a ground) is the remainder of the statement. The meaning is: that mind of development might turn towards laziness; there is a ground, a cause, for this turning. Or, that mind of application might turn towards laziness; there is a ground, a cause, for this. `Mudu` (soft) means it has become soft through being well-developed; the meaning is it has attained mastery. Because of its softness, it is workable, fit for work, and suitable for work. `Pabhassara` (luminous) means it is purified through the departure of defilements; the meaning is it is thoroughly cleansed. `Na ca pabhaṅgu` (and not brittle) means, due to having reached a state of workability, it does not have a nature of breaking, like well-smelted gold that is fit for various applications. Therefore, He said, 'one is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.'

Ukkaṃ bandhatīti mūsaṃ sampādeti. Ālimpetīti ādīpeti jāleti. Tañcāti taṃ piḷandhanavikatisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ assa suvaṇṇakārassa anubhoti pahoti sādheti. Assa vā suvaṇṇassa atthaṃ suvaṇṇakāro anubhoti pāpuṇāti.

`Ukkaṃ bandhati` (he prepares the furnace) means he gets the crucible ready. `Ālimpeti` (he heats it) means he lights it and makes it blaze. `Tañca` (and that): that purpose, designated as a special ornament, that goldsmith is able to accomplish. Or, the goldsmith attains the purpose of that gold.

Abhiññāya iddhividhādiñāṇena sacchikaraṇīyassa iddhividhapaccanubhavanādikassa abhiññā sacchikaraṇīyassa[V 1.0287]. Yassa paccakkhaṃ atthi, so sakkhi. Sakkhino bhabbatā sakkhibhabbatā, sakkhibhavananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakkhi ca so [M 1.0304] bhabbo cāti vā sakkhibhabbo. Ayañhi iddhividhādīnaṃ bhabbo, tattha ca sakkhīti sakkhibhabbo, tassa bhāvo sakkhibhabbatā, taṃ pāpuṇāti. Sati sati āyataneti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pubbahetuādike kāraṇe sati.

`Abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassa` means: of that which is to be realized (`sacchikaraṇīyassa`)—such as the experiencing of supernormal powers and the like—by direct knowledge (`abhiññāya`), that is, by the knowledge of supernormal powers and the like. One who has direct perception is a witness (`sakkhi`). The capability of a witness is `sakkhibhabbatā`; this is said to be the state of being a witness (`sakkhibhavana`). Or, because he is both a witness (`sakkhi`) and capable (`bhabba`), he is a `sakkhibhabbo` (capable witness). Indeed, this person is capable of supernormal powers and the like, and is a witness thereof; therefore, he is a `sakkhibhabbo`. The state of such a one is `sakkhibhabbatā`; he attains it. `Sati sati āyatane` (when there is a basis) means: when there is this or that condition, such as a past cause.

Sītibhāvanti nibbānaṃ, kilesadarathavūpasamaṃ vā. Niggaṇhātīti uddhaṭaṃ cittaṃ uddhaccapātato rakkhaṇavasena niggaṇhāti. Paggaṇhātīti līnaṃ cittaṃ kosajjapātato rakkhaṇavasena paggaṇhāti. Sampahaṃsetīti samappavattaṃ cittaṃ tathāpavattiyaṃ paññāya toseti, uttejeti vā. Yadā vā nirassādaṃ cittaṃ bhāvanāya na pakkhandati, tadā jātiādīni saṃvegavatthūni (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.418; itivu. aṭṭha. 37) paccavekkhitvā sampahaṃseti samuttejeti. Ajjhupekkhatīti yadā pana cittaṃ alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ sammadeva bhāvanāvīthiṃ otiṇṇaṃ hoti, tadā paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu kañci byāpāraṃ akatvā samappavattesu yugesu sārathi viya ajjhupekkhati upekkhakova hoti. Paṇītādhimuttikoti paṇīte uttame maggaphale adhimutto ninnapoṇapabbhāro.

`Sītibhāva` (the state of coolness) means Nibbāna, or the calming of the torment of the defilements. `Niggaṇhāti` (he restrains) means he restrains the agitated mind by way of protecting it from falling into restlessness. `Paggaṇhāti` (he exerts) means he uplifts the sluggish mind by way of protecting it from falling into laziness. `Sampahaṃseti` (he gladdens) means he delights or inspires the evenly proceeding mind with wisdom in that state of proceeding. Or, when the mind is joyless and does not enter into development, then, having reflected upon grounds for urgency such as birth and so on, he gladdens and greatly inspires it. `Ajjhupekkhati` (he looks on with equanimity) means when the mind is neither sluggish nor agitated and has rightly entered the path of development, then, without making any effort in exerting, restraining, or gladdening, like a charioteer with an evenly-running pair of horses, he looks on with equanimity and becomes equanimous. `Paṇītādhimuttiko` (one resolved on the sublime) means one who is resolved on the sublime, supreme path and fruit, inclined, bent, and sloping towards it.

Suggahitaṃ katvāti yathāvuttaṃ uggahakosallasaṅkhātaṃ vidhiṃ suṭṭhu uggahitaṃ pariyāpuṇanādinā supariggahitaṃ katvā. Suṭṭhu vavatthapetvāti manasikārakosallasaṅkhātaṃ vidhiṃ sammadeva sallakkhaṇavasena upadhāretvā. Visesanti pubbenāparaṃ bhāvanāya visesaṃ. Punappunaṃ parivattetvāti kammaṭṭhānatantiṃ paguṇabhāvaṃ pāpento bhiyyo bhiyyo vācāya, manasā ca parivattetvā. Gaṇṭhiṭṭhānanti yathā rukkhassa dubbinibhedo araññassa vā gahanabhūto padeso “gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna”nti vuccati, evaṃ kammaṭṭhānatantiyā atthato dubbinibhedo gahanabhūto ca padeso “gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Taṃ paripucchanādiladdhena ñāṇapharasunā chinditvā.

Having well grasped it: means having well learned and well comprehended, through study and so on, the method called the skill in learning. Having well determined it: means properly considering the method known as the skill in attention by way of careful marking. The distinction: means the distinction in development from an earlier to a later time. Turning it over repeatedly: means causing the text of the meditation subject to become proficient by reviewing it again and again, both verbally and mentally. A knotty point: just as a part of a tree that is difficult to split or a dense region of a forest is called a 'knotty place,' so too, in the text of the meditation subject, a passage that is difficult to penetrate in meaning and is obscure is called a 'knotty place.' This is cut with the axe of knowledge obtained through questioning and so on.

Nimittanti kammaṭṭhānanimittaṃ, asubhākāro. Edisena payojanena luñcanampi anavajjanti dassetuṃ “luñcitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Chinnaṭṭhāneti muṇḍitaṭṭhāne. Vaṭṭatiyeva nissaraṇajjhāsayena olokanato. Ussadavasenāti aphalitānaṃ, phalitānaṃ vā bahulatāvasena. Disvāva nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ dassanayogyatāya tacapañcakassa, itaresu sutvā ca ñatvā ca nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

The sign: means the sign of the meditation subject, the aspect of foulness. To show that with such a purpose even plucking is blameless, it was said, "having plucked." At the cut place: means at the shaven place. It is indeed proper, because it is viewed with the intention of escape. By way of abundance: means by way of the abundance of either non-grey or grey hairs. For the five parts ending in skin, because they are suitable for seeing, the sign should be grasped only after seeing; for the others, the sign should be grasped after hearing and knowing.

Koṭṭhāsavavatthāpanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Delineation of the Constituents

182. Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇāti [M 1.0305][V 1.0288] abhinavāriṭṭhaphalavaṇṇā. Kaṇṇacūḷikāti uparikaṇṇasakkhalikāya parabhāgaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā, kathaṃ? Dve kesā ekato natthīti.

182. Having the color of a fresh soapberry: means having the color of a fresh ariṭṭha fruit. The tip of the ear: refers to the outer part of the upper ear cartilage. They are transversely separated from each other. How so? Two hairs are not together.

Āsayoti nissayo, paccayoti attho.

Āsaya: means support (nissayo), condition (paccayo); this is the meaning.

184. Asambhinnakāḷakā aññena vaṇṇena asammissakāḷakā.

184. Unmixed black: means black that is not mixed with another color.

185. Pattasadisattā nakhā eva nakhapattāni. Nakhā tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnāti visuṃ vavatthitataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “dve nakhā ekato natthī”ti āha.

185. Because of their similarity to leaves, the nails themselves are called 'nail-leaves.' The nails are transversely separated from each other: this is said with reference to their being established separately. Indeed, to show that very meaning, he said, "Two nails are not together."

186. Dantapāḷiyāti dantāvaliyā. Yānakaupatthambhinīti sakaṭassa dhuraṭṭhāne upatthambhakadaṇḍo. Dantānaṃ ādhārabhūtā aṭṭhi hanukaṭṭhi.

186. A row of teeth: means a line of teeth. A support for a vehicle: is a supporting pole at the yoke-position of a cart. The bone that is the support for the teeth is the jawbone.

187. Saṅkaḍḍhiyamānāti sampiṇḍiyamānā. Kosakārakakoso upalliṇḍupoṭṭalakaṃ, yaṃ “koseyyaphala”ntipi vuccati. Puṭabandhaupāhano sakalapiṭṭhipādacchādanaupāhano. Ānisadaṃ āsanapadeso. Tūṇiro sarāvāso. Galakañcukaṃ kaṇṭhattāṇaṃ. Kīṭakulāvakaṃ kharamukhakuṭi.

187. Being drawn together: means being gathered into a ball. A silkworm's cocoon: is the case of the upalliṇḍu insect, which is also called the 'silk-fruit.' A layered shoe: is a shoe that covers the entire top of the foot. The buttocks: is the seat-region. A quiver: is a container for arrows. A throat-guard: is a throat protector. An insect's nest: is the nest of a rough-mouthed creature.

Anulomena paṭilomena cāti ettha aṃsapadesato paṭṭhāya bāhuno piṭṭhipadesena otaraṇaṃ anulomo, maṇibandhato paṭṭhāya bāhuno purimabhāgena ārohanaṃ paṭilomo. Teneva nayenāti dakkhiṇahatthe vuttena nayena anulomena paṭilomena cāti attho. Sukhumampīti yathāvuttaoḷārikacammato sukhumaṃ. Antomukhacammādikoṭṭhāsesu vā tacena paricchinnattā yaṃ durupalakkhaṇīyaṃ, taṃ “sukhuma”nti vuttaṃ. Tañhi vuttanayena ñāṇena tacaṃ vivaritvā passantassa pākaṭaṃ hoti. Idha chavipi tacagatikā evāti “taco upari ākāsena paricchinno”ti vutto.

Regarding 'in the forward order and in the reverse order': here, starting from the shoulder region and descending along the back of the arm is the forward order; starting from the wrist and ascending along the front of the arm is the reverse order. By that very method: means by the method explained for the right hand, that is, both in the forward order and in the reverse order. Even the subtle: means that which is more subtle than the aforementioned gross skin. Or, among the parts, such as the inner skin of the mouth, that which is difficult to discern because it is covered by the skin, is called 'subtle.' Indeed, that subtle part becomes manifest to one who sees after having opened the skin with knowledge by the aforementioned method. Here, the epidermis too is of the nature of the dermis; thus it is said, 'the dermis is bounded above by space.'

188. Nisadapoto [M 1.0306][V 1.0289] silāputtako. Uddhanakoṭīti mattikāpiṇḍena katauddhanassa koṭi. Tālaguḷapaṭalaṃ nāma pakkatālaphalalasikaṃ tālapaṭṭikādīsu limpitvā sukkhāpetvā uddharitvā gahitapaṭalaṃ. Sukhumanti yathāvuttamaṃsato sukhumaṃ. Paṇhikamaṃsādithūlānaṃ sakalasarīrassa kisānaṃ yebhuyyena maṃsena paṭicchāditattā vuttaṃ “tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinna”nti.

188. A nisadapota: is a small grinding stone. The edge of an oven: is the edge of an oven made from a lump of clay. What is called a 'sheet of palm sugar': is a sheet obtained by smearing the juice of ripe palm fruit on palm-leaf mats and so on, drying it, and peeling it off. Subtle: means more subtle than the aforementioned flesh, such as the flesh of the heel. Because the entire body of the stout, and for the most part that of the thin, is covered by flesh, it is said, 'transversely separated from each other.'

189. Jālākāro kañcuko jālakañcuko. Visuṃ vavatthitabhāveneva nhārū tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā.

189. A tunic that has the appearance of a net is a 'net-tunic.' It is precisely because of their state of being separately established that the sinews are transversely separated from each other.

190. Dantānaṃ visuṃ gahitattā “ṭhapetvā dvattiṃsa dantaṭṭhīnī”ti vuttaṃ. Ekaṃ jaṇṇukaṭṭhi, ekaṃ ūruṭṭhīti eka-ggahaṇaṃ “ekekasmiṃ pāde”ti adhikatattā. Evaṃ timattānīti evaṃ mattasaddehi ānisadaṭṭhiādīni idha avuttānipi dassetīti veditabbaṃ. Evañca katvā “atirekatisataaṭṭhikasamussaya”nti (visuddhi. 1.122) idañca vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti.

190. Because the teeth are taken separately, it is said, 'excluding the thirty-two teeth-bones.' In 'one knee bone, one thigh bone,' the use of 'one' is because it is connected with the additional phrase 'in each leg.' Regarding 'thus only three,' it should be understood that by such words as 'only,' even bones not mentioned here, such as the hip bone, are indicated. And by this reasoning, the statement 'a collection of more than three hundred bones' is justified.

Kīḷāgoḷakāni suttena bandhitvā aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭetvā kīḷanagoḷakāni. Dhanukadaṇḍo dārakānaṃ kīḷanakakhuddakadhanukaṃ. Tattha jaṅghaṭṭhikassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānanti jaṇṇukaṭṭhimhi pavisitvā ṭhitaṭṭhānanti adhippāyo. Tena ūruṭṭhinā patiṭṭhitaṃ ṭhānaṃ yaṃ kaṭiṭṭhino, taṃ aggacchinnamahāpunnāgaphalasadisaṃ.

Playing balls: are balls for playing with by tying them with a string and striking them against each other. A bow-stick: is a small toy bow for children. Therein, 'the place where the shin bone is established' means the place where it stands, having entered into the knee bone. The place in the hip bone where the thigh bone is established is similar to a large punnāga fruit with its top cut off.

Kumbhakārena nipphāditaṃ uddhanaṃ kumbhakārikauddhanaṃ. Sīsakapaṭṭaveṭhakaṃ veṭhetvā ṭhapitaṃ sīsamayaṃ paṭṭakaṃ. Yena suttaṃ kantanti, tasmiṃ takkamhi vijjhitvā ṭhapitagoḷakā vaṭṭanā nāma, vaṭṭanānaṃ āvaḷi vaṭṭanāvaḷi.

An oven made by a potter is a 'potter's oven.' A coil of lead sheeting: is a leaden sheet placed after being coiled. The balls placed, having been pierced onto that spindle with which they spin thread, are called 'spindle-whorls'; a row of spindle-whorls is a 'row of spindle-whorls.'

Maṇḍalākārena chinnavaṃsakaḷīrakhaṇḍāni vaṃsakaḷīracakkalakāni. Avalekhanasatthakaṃ ucchutacāvalekhanasatthakaṃ.

Pieces of bamboo shoot cut in a circular shape are 'bamboo-shoot wheels.' A peeling knife: is a knife for peeling sugarcane bark.

192. Vakkabhāgena paricchinnanti vakkapariyantena bhāgena paricchinnaṃ. Ito paresupi evarūpesu eseva nayo.

192. Delimited by the kidney-part: means delimited by the part that is the boundary of the kidney. In similar cases after this, this is the same method.

193. Yaṃ [V 1.0290] nissāyāti yaṃ lohitaṃ nissāya, nissayanissayopi “nissayo”tveva vuccati. Bhavati hi kāraṇakāraṇepi kāraṇavohāro yathā “corehi gāmo daḍḍho”ti. Atha vā yasmiṃ rūpakalāpe hadayavatthu[M 1.0307], tampi lohitagatikameva hutvā tiṭṭhatīti “yaṃ nissāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

193. “Depending on which” means depending on the blood; even the support of a support is called a “support.” Indeed, the designation “cause” occurs even for the cause of a cause, as in “the village was burned by thieves.” Alternatively, the material group in which the heart-base is, that too exists by being of the nature of blood; therefore it is said, “depending on which.”

194. Paṇḍukadhātukanti paṇḍusabhāvaṃ.

194. “Having a pale element” means having a pale nature.

195. Pariyonahanamaṃsanti paṭicchādakamaṃsaṃ.

195. “Enveloping flesh” means covering flesh.

196. Udarajivhāmaṃsanti jivhāsaṇṭhānaṃ udarassa matthakapasse tiṭṭhanakamaṃsaṃ. “Nīla”nti vatvā nīlaṃ nāma bahudhātukanti āha “nigguṇḍipupphavaṇṇa”nti.

196. “Stomach-tongue flesh” is the tongue-shaped flesh that is situated on the upper side of the stomach. Having said “blue,” because “blue” has many aspects, he said “the color of the nigguṇḍi flower.”

197. Papphāsamaṃsanti yathāṭhāne eva lambitvā thokaṃ parivattakamaṃsaṃ. Nirasanti nihīnarasaṃ. Nirojanti nippabhaṃ, ojārahitaṃ vā.

197. “Lung-flesh” is the flesh that, hanging in its own place, is slightly turned. “Tasteless” means having a deficient taste. “Without nutritive essence” means without luster, or devoid of nutritive essence.

198. Obhaggāti avabhujitvā ṭhitā. Sakkharasudhāvaṇṇanti marumbehi katasudhāvaṇṇaṃ. “Setasakkharasudhāvaṇṇa”ntipi pāṭho, setasakkharavaṇṇaṃ, sudhāvaṇṇañcāti attho.

198. “Bent” means standing bent down. “Having the color of gravel-plaster” means having the color of plaster made with gravel. There is also the reading “having the color of white-gravel-plaster,” and the meaning is the color of white gravel and the color of plaster.

199. Antassa ābhujitvā ābhujitvā ṭhitappadesā antabhogaṭṭhānāni. Tesaṃ bandhanabhūtaṃ antaguṇaṃ nāmāti dassento āha “antaguṇanti antabhogaṭṭhānesu bandhana”nti. Kuddālapharasukammādīni karontānaṃ antabhoge agaḷante ekato ābandhitvā, kiṃ viya? Yantasuttakamiva yantaphalakānīti. Kimiva tattha ṭhitanti āha “pādapuñchana…pe… ṭhita”nti. Purimañcettha ābandhanassa, dutiyaṃ ṭhānākārassa nidassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

199. The places where the intestine, having coiled and coiled, remains are the “places of the intestinal coils” (antabhogaṭṭhānāni). Showing that what is called the “intestinal mesentery” (antaguṇa) is a binding for these, he said: “The intestinal mesentery is a binding in the places of the intestinal coils.” For those doing work like hoeing or using an adze, it binds the intestinal coils together so they do not loosen. What is it like? Like the thread of a machine binds the planks of the machine. As to what it is like staying there, he said: “Like a foot-wiping cloth… it stays.” And here, it should be understood that the first is an illustration of the binding, and the second is an illustration of the manner of its placement.

200. Asitaṃ nāma bhuttaṃ odanādi. Pītaṃ nāma pivanavasena ajjhohaṭapānakādi. Khāyitaṃ nāma saṃkhāditaṃ piṭṭhamūlaphalakhajjādi. Sāyitaṃ nāma assāditaṃ ambapakkamadhuphāṇitādi.

200. What is called “asita” is what has been eaten, such as rice. What is called “pīta” is what has been swallowed by way of drinking, such as beverages. What is called “khāyita” is what has been chewed, such as flour-based edibles, roots, and fruits. What is called “sāyita” is what has been savored, such as ripe mangoes, honey, and molasses.

Yatthāti [V 1.0291] yasmiṃ udare. Yanti ca udarameva paccāmasati. Yattha pānabhojanādīni patitvā tiṭṭhatīti sambandho. Suvānavamathu sārameyyavantaṃ. Vivekanti vibhāgaṃ.

“Yattha” means “in which stomach.” And “yaṃ” refers only to the stomach. The connection is: “where drinks, food, and so on, having fallen, remain.” “Suvānavamathu” is a dog’s vomit (sārameyyavanta). “Viveka” means “separation” (vibhāga).

201. Heṭṭhānābhipiṭṭhikaṇṭakamūlānaṃ [M 1.0308] antareti purimabhāgavasena nābhiyā heṭṭhāpadesassa pacchimabhāgavasena heṭṭhimapiṭṭhikaṇṭakānaṃ vemajjhe. Veḷunāḷikasadiso padesoti adhippāyo.

201. “Between the lower navel and the root of the spine” means, by way of the front part, the area below the navel, and by way of the rear part, the middle of the lower spinal vertebrae. The meaning is a place similar to a bamboo tube.

202. Samohitanti nicitaṃ.

202. “Samohita” means “collected” (nicita).

204. Pūtibhāvaṃ āpannaṃ kukkuṭaṇḍaṃ pūtikukkuṭaṇḍaṃ. Uddeko pittādīhi vinā kevalo uddhaṅgamavāto.

204. A hen’s egg that has reached a state of rottenness is a “rotten hen’s egg” (pūtikukkuṭaṇḍa). “Uddeka” is merely upward-moving wind, without bile and so on.

205. Ācāmo avassāvanakañjikaṃ.

205. “Ācāma” is strained rice-gruel (avassāvanakañjika).

206. Vakkahadayayakanapapphāse temayamānanti ettha yakanaṃ heṭṭhābhāgapūraṇeneva temeti, itarāni tesaṃ upari thokaṃ thokaṃ paggharaṇenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

206. Regarding “moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs,” it should be understood that here it moistens the liver only by filling its lower part, while it moistens the others by trickling little by little onto them.

207. Utuvikāro uṇhavalāhakādihetuko. Visamacchinno bhisādikalāpo visamaṃ udakaṃ paggharati, evamevaṃ sarīraṃ kesakūpādivivarehi upari, heṭṭhā, tiriyañca sedaṃ visamaṃ paggharatīti dassetuṃ visamacchinna-ggahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

207. A disturbance of the seasons is caused by things like heat and clouds. Just as a bundle of lotus roots cut unevenly makes water trickle unevenly, so too, to show that the body makes sweat trickle unevenly from openings such as hair follicles—above, below, and across—the term “unevenly cut” is used.

208. Visamāhāranti tadāpavattamānasarīrāvatthāya asappāyāhāraṃ, atikaṭukaaccuṇhādivisabhāgāhāraṃ vā. Sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 356) pana “visabhāgāhāra”ntveva vuttaṃ tadā pavattamānānaṃ dhātūnaṃ visabhāgattā.

208. “Visamāhāra” means unsuitable food for the body’s currently existing state, or food of an incompatible nature, such as that which is excessively pungent or excessively hot. In the Sammohavinodanī, however, it is simply called “food of an incompatible nature” because of its incompatibility with the elements currently existing.

209. “Nhānakāle”ti idaṃ udakassa upari sinehassa sambhavadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Paribbhamantasinehabinduvisaṭasaṇṭhānāti visaṭaṃ hutvā paribbhamantasinehabindusaṇṭhānā. Utuvisabhāgo bahiddhāsamuṭṭhāno. Dhātuvisabhāgo antosamuṭṭhāno. Te padesāti te hatthatalādipadesā.

209. The phrase “at the time of bathing” is said to show the appearance of oil on top of water. “Having the shape of spreading, swirling oil drops” means that, having spread, they have the shape of swirling oil drops. An imbalance of the seasons is of external origin. An imbalance of the elements is of internal origin. “Those places” means those places such as the palms of the hands.

210. Kiñcīti [V 1.0292] uṇhādirasānaṃ aññataraṃ āhāravatthu. Nesanti sattānaṃ. Hadayaṃ āgilāyatīti visabhāgāhārādiṃ paṭicca hadayappadeso vivattati.

210. “Kiñci” means a certain food item among those with tastes such as heat. “Nesaṃ” means “of beings.” “The heart is afflicted” means that on account of incompatible food and so on, the region of the heart is disturbed.

211. Dadhino [M 1.0309] vissandanaaccharaso dadhimuttaṃ. Gaḷitvāti sanditvā. Tālumatthakavivarena otaritvāti matthakavivarato āgantvā tālumatthakena otaritvā.

211. The clear liquid that flows out from curds is “dadhimutta.” “Gaḷitvā” means “having flowed” (sanditvā). “Having descended through the opening at the top of the palate” means having come from the opening of the head and descended by way of the top of the palate.

212. Telaṃ viya sakaṭassa nābhiakkhasīsānaṃ aṭṭhisandhīnaṃ abbhañjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā. Kaṭakaṭāyantīti “kaṭa kaṭā”ti saddaṃ karonti. Anuravadassanaṃ hetaṃ. Dukkhantīti dukkhitāni sañjātadukkhāni honti.

212. It performs the function of anointing the bone joints, just as grease does for the hub and axle-heads of a cart. “Kaṭakaṭāyanti” means they make a “kaṭa kaṭā” sound. This, indeed, is to show an onomatopoeia. “Dukkhanti” means they are afflicted; they have suffering that has arisen.

213. Samūlakūlamāsaṃ jhāpetvā chārikaṃ avassāvetvā gahitayūso māsakhāro. Ucchiṭṭhodakagabbhamalādīnaṃ chaḍḍanaṭṭhānaṃ candanikā. Ravaṇaghaṭaṃ nāma pakatiyā sammukhameva hoti. Yassa pana āraggamattampi udakassa pavisanamukhaṃ natthi, taṃ dassetuṃ “amukhe ravaṇaghaṭe”ti vuttaṃ. Āyūhananti samīhanaṃ.

213. Having burned a large bean plant together with its root, the liquid obtained by filtering the ash is called “bean-alkali” (māsakhāro). The place for discarding things like dishwater and impurities from pregnancy is called a “cesspool” (candanikā). A “yavana-pot” by nature is without a mouth. However, to indicate one that does not have an opening for water to enter even the size of an awl’s tip, it is said, “in a mouthless yavana-pot.” “Āyūhana” means “striving” (samīhana).

214. Evañhītiādi yathāvuttāya uggahakosallapaṭipattiyā nigamanaṃ. Idāni yathāvuttaṃ manasikārakosallapaṭipattimpi nigamanavasena gahetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassetuṃ “anupubbato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha paṇṇattisamatikkamāvasāneti kesādipaṇṇattisamatikkamavasena pavattāya bhāvanāya avasāne. Apubbāpariyamivāti ekajjhamiva. Kesāti iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, evamādinā iminā pakārena vāti attho. Te dhammāti vaṇṇādivasena vavatthāpitā paṭikkūlākārato upaṭṭhitā koṭṭhāsadhammā.

214. The words “Thus, indeed,” etc., are the conclusion for the practice of skill in learning as described. Now, also taking up the practice of skill in attention as described by way of conclusion, in order to show the meditation subject brought to its culmination, the passage beginning “anupubbato” is started. Therein, “at the end of transcending concepts” means at the end of the development that proceeds by way of transcending the concepts of hair, etc. “As if without prior or subsequent” means as if at once. In “kesāti,” the word “iti” has the meaning of “beginning” or the meaning of “kind”; that is, “beginning with this” or “in this manner.” “Those phenomena” are the phenomena of the bodily parts, established by way of color, etc., and appearing in a repulsive manner.

Bahiddhāpīti sasantānato bahipi, parasantānakāyepīti attho. Manasikāraṃ upasaṃharatīti yathāvuttaṃ paṭikkūlamanasikāraṃ upaneti. Yathā idaṃ, tathā etanti. Evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsesu pākaṭībhūtesūti yathā attano kāye, evaṃ paresampi kāye sabbesu kesādikoṭṭhāsesu paṭikkūlavasena vibhūtabhāvena upaṭṭhitesūti attho. Ayamettha kasiṇesu vaḍḍhanasadiso yogino bhāvanāviseso dassito.

'Also externally' means also external to one's own continuum, that is, in the body of another's continuum. 'Applies attention' means one applies the attention to repulsiveness as described, thinking: 'As this is, so is that.' 'Thus, when all parts have become manifest' means: when all the parts beginning with hair, in the bodies of others just as in one's own body, have appeared with distinctness by way of their repulsiveness. Herein, a special development for the yogi, similar to the expansion in the kasiṇas, is shown.

Anupubbamuñcanādīti [V 1.0293] ādi-saddena suttantanayena vibhāvitaṃ vīriyasamatāyojanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Punappunaṃ manasi karototi vuttanayena attano [M 1.0310] kāye kesādike “paṭikkūlā paṭikkūlā”ti abhiṇhaso manasikāraṃ pavattentassa yadā saddhādīni indriyāni laddhasamathāni visadāni pavattanti, tadā assaddhiyādīnaṃ dūrībhāvena sātisayaṃ balappattehi sattahi saddhammehi laddhūpatthambhāni vitakkādīni jhānaṅgāni paṭutarāni hutvā pātubhavanti. Tesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāneva honti saddhiṃ tadekaṭṭhehi pāpadhammehi. Upacārasamādhinā cittaṃ samādhiyati, so taṃyeva nimittaṃ āsevanto bhāvento bahulīkaronto appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tena vuttaṃ “anukkamena appanā uppajjatī”ti. Sabbākāratoti vaṇṇādivasena pañcadhāpi. Sāti appanā.

In the phrase `Anupubbamuñcanādi`, by the word `ādi` (etc.), the application of the balancing of energy, which has been made clear by the Suttanta method, is included. As for `Punappunaṃ manasi karoti` (repeatedly brings to mind), by the stated method, for the yogi who constantly causes attention to arise regarding the hair and other parts in one's own body as 'repulsive, repulsive,' when the faculties of faith and so on, having obtained calm and become pure, proceed, then, due to the remoteness of faithlessness and so on, the jhāna factors such as initial application, having obtained support from the seven good qualities that have exceedingly reached strength, arise, having become especially sharp. Due to being their direct opposite, the hindrances, together with the unwholesome states that have a similar basis, are indeed suppressed. By means of access concentration, the mind becomes well concentrated. That yogi, by frequenting, developing, and making much of that very sign, reaches absorption. Therefore, it was said, 'absorption arises in sequence.' As for `sabbākārato` (in all aspects), it means in five ways by means of color, etc. That is absorption.

Yadi panetaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ aviññāṇakāsubhakammaṭṭhānāni viya paṭhamajjhānavasena sijjhati, atha kasmā “kāyagatāsatī”ti vuttanti āha “evaṃ paṭhamajjhānavasenā”tiādi. Nānāvaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīsu dvattiṃsāya koṭṭhāsesu pavattamānāya satiyā kiccamettha sātisayanti āha “satibalena ijjhanato”ti.

Now, if this meditation subject is accomplished by means of the first jhāna, like the meditation subjects on foulness in inanimate things, then why is it called `kāyagatāsati` (mindfulness directed to the body)? To this objection, he said, `evaṃ paṭhamajjhānavasena` (thus by means of the first jhāna), etc. Because the function of mindfulness that is proceeding in the thirty-two parts having various colors, shapes, and so on, is exceedingly great here, he said, 'because it is accomplished through the power of mindfulness.'

Pantasenāsanesu, adhikusalesu ca aratiṃ, kāmaguṇesu ca ratiṃ sahati abhibhavatīti aratiratisaho sarīrasabhāvacintanena anabhiratiyā pahīnattā. Tathā koṭṭhāsabhāvanāya attasinehassa parikkhīṇattā bhayabheravaṃ sahati, sītādīnañca adhivāsakajātiko hoti. Attasinehavasena hi purisassa bhayabheravaṃ hoti, dukkhassa ca anadhivāsanaṃ. Imaṃ pana koṭṭhāsabhāvanamanuyuttassa na kevalaṃ paṭhamajjhānamattameva, uttaripi paṭivedho atthīti dassetuṃ “kesādīna”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

One endures and overcomes discontent in remote lodgings and in higher wholesome states, and delight in sensual pleasures; therefore, one is called `aratiratisaho` (the endurer of discontent and delight). This is because non-delight is abandoned by contemplating the true nature of the body. Similarly, because affection for the self has been exhausted through the development of the parts of the body, one endures fear and terror, and one becomes of a nature to endure cold and so on. Indeed, it is through the power of affection for the self that fear and terror arise for a person, as well as an inability to endure suffering. However, in order to show that for one devoted to this development of the parts, not only the first jhāna is accomplished, but there is also higher penetration, `kesādīna` (of hair, etc.), and so on was said.

Ānāpānassatikathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing

215. Yaṃ taṃ evaṃ pasaṃsitvā ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhanti sambandho. Tattha yasmā “kathaṃ bhāvito”tiādikāya pucchāpāḷiyā atthe vibhāvite thomanāpāḷiyāpi attho vibhāvitoyeva hoti bhedābhāvato, tasmā taṃ laṅghitvā “kathaṃ bhāvito cā”tiādinā ārabhati. Tattha hi ito pasaṃsābhāvo “ayampi kho”ti vacanañca viseso. Tesu pasaṃsābhāvaṃ [V 1.0294] dassetuṃ “evaṃ pasaṃsitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Pasaṃsā ca tattha abhirucijananena ussāhanatthā. Tañhi sutvā bhikkhū “bhagavā imaṃ samādhiṃ anekehi ākārehi pasaṃsati, santo [M 1.0311] kirāyaṃ samādhi paṇīto ca asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro pāpadhamme ca ṭhānaso antaradhāpetī”ti sañjātābhirucayo ussāhajātā sakkaccaṃ anuyuñjitabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ maññanti. “Ayampi kho”ti padassa ye ime mayā nibbānamahāsarassa otaraṇatitthabhūtā kasiṇajjhānaasubhajjhānādayo desitā, na kevalaṃ te eva, ayampi khoti bhagavā attano paccakkhabhūtaṃ samādhiṃ desanānubhāvena tesampi bhikkhūnaṃ āsannaṃ, paccakkhañca karonto sampiṇḍanavasena evamāhāti sambandhamukhena attho veditabbo.

215. The connection is: 'Having praised thus, that meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing was pointed out.' Therein, because when the meaning of the question-Pāḷi beginning with 'How is it developed?' is explained, the meaning of the praise-Pāḷi is also indeed explained due to the absence of difference, therefore, having skipped that, he begins with 'How is it developed?', etc. Indeed, the points of distinction therein are the praise itself and the phrase 'this too.' Among these, to show the fact of praise, 'having praised thus' was said. And the praise there is for the purpose of encouraging effort by generating delight. Indeed, having heard that, the monks think, 'The Blessed One praises this concentration in many ways; it is said this concentration is peaceful, sublime, satisfying in itself, and a pleasant abiding, and it makes unwholesome states disappear instantly.' Thus, with delight arisen and effort generated, they think it should be diligently practiced and undertaken. As for the phrase 'this too,' the meaning should be understood by way of the connection as follows: The Blessed One said thus by way of summary, 'Not only those kasiṇa-jhānas, asubha-jhānas, and so on, which were taught by me and are the landing-places for entering the great ocean of Nibbāna, but this too,' thereby, through the power of his teaching, making the concentration that was directly experienced by himself near and directly perceptible also for those monks.

Soḷasavatthukanti catūsu anupassanāsu catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena soḷasaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbākāraparipūroti kammaṭṭhānapāḷiyā padattho piṇḍattho upamā codanā parihāro payojananti evamādīhi sabbehi ākārehi paripuṇṇo. Niddesoti kammaṭṭhānassa nissesato vitthāro.

`Soḷasavatthukaṃ` (having sixteen bases) means having sixteen instances by way of the four tetrads in the four contemplations. `Sabbākāraparipūro` (complete in all aspects) means complete in all aspects of the Pāḷi on the meditation subject, such as the meaning of the words, the collective meaning, simile, objection, refutation, purpose, and so on. `Niddeso` (exposition) means the exhaustive elaboration of the meditation subject.

216. Kathanti idaṃ pucchanākāravibhāvanapadaṃ. Pucchā cettha kathetukamyatāvasena aññāsaṃ asambhavato. Sā ca upari desanaṃ āruḷhānaṃ sabbesaṃ pakāravisesānaṃ āmasanavasenāti imamatthaṃ dassento “kathanti…pe… kamyatāpucchā”ti āha. Kathaṃ bahulīkatoti etthāpi “ānāpānassatisamādhī”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tattha kathanti ānāpānassatisamādhibahulīkāraṃ nānappakārato vitthāretukamyatāpucchā. Bahulīkato ānāpānassatisamādhīti tathāpuṭṭhadhammanidassananti imamatthaṃ “eseva nayo”ti iminā atidisati. Tathā santabhāvādayopi tassa yehi bhāvanābahulīkārehi siddhā, taggahaṇeneva gahitā hontīti dassetuṃ “kathaṃ bahulīkato…pe… vūpasametīti etthāpi eseva nayo”ti vuttaṃ.

216. This word `kathaṃ` (how) is a word that clarifies the mode of questioning. And here the question is by way of the desire to explain, because other questions are not possible. And that question is by way of touching upon all the particular kinds that have come up in the teaching above. Showing this meaning, he said, '`kathaṃ`... is a question of desire to explain.' Also here in `kathaṃ bahulīkato` (how is it made much of?), the phrase `ānāpānassatisamādhi` (the concentration of mindfulness of breathing) should be brought in and connected. Therein, `kathaṃ` is a question from the desire to elaborate in various ways on the making much of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing. The phrase `bahulīkato ānāpānassatisamādhi` (the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, having been made much of) is a demonstration of the teaching thus asked about. He indicates this meaning with 'this is the same method.' Similarly, in order to show that the state of peace and so on, which are accomplished for that concentration by means of development and making much of it, are included by the very taking up of that, it was said, 'also here in "how is it made much of... and is pacified," this is the same method.'

“Puna ca paraṃ, udāyi, akkhātā mayā sāvakānaṃ paṭipadā, yathāpaṭipannā me sāvakā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāventī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.247) uppādanavaḍḍhanaṭṭhena bhāvanā vuccatīti tadubhayavasena atthaṃ dassento “bhāvitoti uppādito vaḍḍhito vā”ti āha. Tattha bhāvaṃ vijjamānataṃ ito gatoti bhāvito, uppādito paṭiladdhamattoti attho. Uppanno pana laddhāsevano, bhāvito paguṇabhāvaṃ āpādito, vaḍḍhitoti attho[M 1.0312]. Ānāpānapariggāhikāyāti dīgharassādivisesehi saddhiṃ assāsapassāse paricchijjagāhikāya, te ārabbha pavattāya, satiyaṃ [V 1.0295] paccayabhūtāyanti attho. Purimasmiñhi atthe samādhissa satiyā sahajātādipaccayabhāvo vutto sampayuttavacanato, dutiyasmiṃ pana upanissayabhāvopi. Upacārajjhānasahagatā hi sati appanāsamādhissa upanissayo hotīti. Bahulīkatoti bahulaṃ pavattito, tena āvajjanādivasībhāvappattimāha. Yo hi vasībhāvaṃ āpādito, so icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjitabbato punappunaṃ pavattīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “punappunaṃ kato”ti. Yathā “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241), “vivicceva kāmehī”ti (dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123) ca evamādīsu paṭhamapade vutto eva-saddo dutiyādīsupi vutto eva hoti, evamidhāpīti āha “ubhayattha evasaddena niyamo veditabbo”ti. Ubhayapadaniyamena laddhaguṇaṃ dassetuṃ “ayañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“‘Furthermore, Udayi, the path has been declared by me to the disciples, practicing in which way my disciples develop the four foundations of mindfulness.’ In such passages, ‘development’ (bhāvanā) is said in the sense of causing to arise and increasing. Thus, showing the meaning in both these ways, he said, ‘“developed” (bhāvito) means caused to arise or increased.’ Therein, ‘developed’ (bhāvito) means ‘gone from here to a state of being, to existence’; the meaning is ‘caused to arise,’ ‘just having been attained.’ But that which has arisen and has been cultivated is ‘developed,’ brought to a state of proficiency; the meaning is ‘increased.’ ‘By that which grasps the in-and-out-breaths’ means: in mindfulness that grasps by discerning the in-and-out-breaths together with their distinctions of long, short, etc., which proceeds taking them as object, and which has become a condition. Indeed, in the former meaning, the state of mindfulness being a co-nascent condition, etc., for concentration was stated because of the word ‘associated’; but in the second, also its state of being a support condition. For mindfulness accompanied by access concentration is a support condition for absorption concentration. ‘Made much of’ means frequently made to occur; by that, he indicates the attainment of mastery in adverting, etc. For that which has been brought to a state of mastery is made to occur again and again because it is to be attained at any desired moment. Therefore it is said, ‘done again and again.’ Just as in such passages as ‘Here, monks, a mendicant…’ and ‘secluded from sensual pleasures…,’ the word ‘eva’ stated in the first phrase is also stated in the second and following phrases, so too here. Thus he said, ‘the restriction by the word “eva” should be understood in both instances.’ To show the quality obtained by the restriction of both terms, what begins with ‘For this…’ was said.

Asubhakammaṭṭhānanti asubhārammaṇajhānamāha. Taṃ hi asubhesu yogakammabhāvato, yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato ca “asubhakammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. “Kevala”nti iminā ārammaṇaṃ nivatteti. Paṭivedhavasenāti jhānapaṭivedhavasena. Jhānañhi bhāvanāvisesena ijjhantaṃ attano visayaṃ paṭivijjhantameva pavattati, yathāsabhāvato paṭivijjhīyati cāti “paṭivedho”ti vuccati. Oḷārikārammaṇattāti bībhacchārammaṇattā. Paṭikkūlārammaṇattāti jigucchitabbārammaṇattā. Pariyāyenāti kāraṇena, lesantarena vā. Ārammaṇasantatāyāti anukkamena vicetabbataṃ pattaṃ ārammaṇassa paramasukhumataṃ sandhāyāha. Sante hi sannisinne ārammaṇe pavattamāno dhammo sayampi sannisinnova hoti. Tenāha “santo vūpasanto nibbuto”ti, nibbutasabbapariḷāhoti attho. Ārammaṇasantatāya tadārammaṇadhammānaṃ santatā lokuttaradhammārammaṇāhi paccavekkhaṇāhi dīpetabbā.

By ‘the meditation subject of foulness,’ he indicates the jhāna with a foul object. For it is called ‘the meditation subject of foulness’ because it is the work of a yogi in regard to foul things, and because it is a cause of special happiness for the yogi. By this word ‘only,’ he excludes the object. ‘By way of penetration’ means by way of the penetration of jhāna. For jhāna, when it succeeds through a special development, proceeds by penetrating its own object, and it is penetrated according to its true nature; therefore it is called ‘penetration.’ ‘Because of having a gross object’ means because of having a repulsive object. ‘Because of having a disagreeable object’ means because of having an object to be loathed. ‘Indirectly’ means by a reason, or by another implication. By ‘due to the peacefulness of the object,’ he refers to the extreme subtlety of the object, which is attained by gradual investigation. For when a mental state occurs in relation to a peaceful and settled object, it itself is also settled. Therefore he said, ‘peaceful, tranquil, extinguished’; the meaning is ‘with all fevers extinguished.’ The peacefulness of the mental states having that object, due to the peacefulness of the object, should be illustrated by the reviews that have supramundane dhammas as their object.

Nāssa santapaṇītabhāvāvahaṃ kiñci secananti asecanako. Asecanakattā anāsittako. Anāsittakattā eva abbokiṇṇo asammisso parikammādinā. Tato eva pāṭiyekko visuṃyeveko. Āveṇiko asādhāraṇo. Sabbametaṃ sarasato eva santabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ [M 1.0313] vuttaṃ. Parikammaṃ vā santabhāvanimittaṃ, parikammanti ca kasiṇakaraṇādīni nimittuppādapariyosānaṃ, tādisaṃ idha natthīti adhippāyo. Tadā hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ nirassādattā asantamappaṇītaṃ siyā. Upacārena vā natthi ettha santatāti yojanā. Yathā upacārakkhaṇe nīvaraṇavigamena, aṅgapātubhāvena [V 1.0296] ca paresaṃ santatā hoti, na evamimassa. Ayaṃ pana ādisamannā…pe… paṇīto cāti yojanā. Kecīti uttaravihāravāsike sandhāyāha. Anāsittakoti upasecanena na āsittako. Tenāha “ojavanto”ti, ojavantasadisoti attho. Madhūroti iṭṭho, cetasikasukhapaṭilābhasaṃvattanaṃ tikacatukkajjhānavasena, upekkhāya vā santabhāvena sukhagatikattā sabbesampi vasena veditabbaṃ. Jhānasamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭṭhasarīratāvasena pana kāyikasukhapaṭilābhasaṃvattanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tañca kho jhānato vuṭṭhitakāle. Imasmiṃ pakkhe “appitappitakkhaṇe”ti idaṃ hetumhi bhummavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avikkhambhiteti jhānena sakasantānato anīhaṭe appahīne. Akosallasambhūteti akosallaṃ vuccati avijjā, tato sambhūte. Avijjāpubbaṅgamā hi sabbe pāpadhammā. Khaṇenevāti attano pavattikkhaṇeneva. Antaradhāpetīti ettha antaradhāpanaṃ vināsanaṃ, taṃ pana jhānakattukassa idhādhippetattā pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ hotīti āha “vikkhambhetī”ti. Vūpasametīti visesena upasameti. Visesena upasamanaṃ pana sammadeva upasamanaṃ hotīti āha “suṭṭhu upasametī”ti.

Because there is no sprinkling whatsoever for it that brings about a state of peace and sublimity, it is ‘asecanaka’ (not needing sprinkling). Because of not needing sprinkling, it is ‘anāsittaka’ (not infused). Just because of not being infused, it is ‘abbokiṇṇa’ (unmixed), unmingled with preliminary work and so on. For that very reason, it is ‘pāṭiyekka’ (individual), distinctly one, ‘āveṇika’ (unique), ‘asādhāraṇa’ (uncommon). All this is said to show its peaceful nature from its own essence. Or, preliminary work is a cause of the peaceful state; and ‘preliminary work’ refers to the actions beginning with making a kasiṇa and ending with the arising of the counterpart sign—the intention is that such is not present here. For at that time, the meditation subject, being without savor, might be unpeaceful and unsublime. Or, the construction is: ‘there is no peacefulness here by way of access concentration.’ Just as for others there is peacefulness at the moment of access through the removal of hindrances and the manifestation of the factors, it is not so for this one. But the construction for this one is: ‘from the very first application of mind… it is sublime.’ By ‘some,’ he refers to the residents of the Northern Monastery. ‘Anāsittaka’ means not infused by sprinkling. Therefore he said ‘savory’ (ojavanta); the meaning is ‘like something savory.’ ‘Sweet’ (madhuro) means desirable; its being conducive to the attainment of mental happiness should be understood by way of the triad and tetrad of jhānas, or, because of the peaceful nature of equanimity being in the category of happiness, it should be understood by way of all of them. But its being conducive to the attainment of bodily happiness should be seen by way of the body being pervaded by the sublime form born of jhāna, and that too, at the time of emerging from jhāna. In this view, this phrase ‘at the moment of absorption’ should be seen as a locative expressing cause. ‘Unsuppressed’ means not removed from one’s own continuity by jhāna, not abandoned. ‘Arisen from non-skill’: ‘non-skill’ is a name for ignorance; ‘arisen from that.’ For all evil states are preceded by ignorance. ‘In a moment’ means in the very moment of its occurrence. In ‘causes to disappear,’ the causing to disappear is destruction; but since the agent of jhāna is intended here, it is the abandoning of the obsessions. Therefore he said, ‘suppresses.’ ‘Thoroughly pacifies’ means pacifies in a special way. But since pacifying in a special way is indeed proper pacification, he said, ‘pacifies well.’

Nanu ca aññopi samādhi attano pavattikkhaṇeneva paṭipakkhadhamme antaradhāpeti vūpasameti, atha kasmā ayameva samādhi evaṃ visesetvā vuttoti? Pubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya nānāvitakkavūpasamasabbhāvato. Vuttañhetaṃ – “ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāyā”ti (a. ni. 9.1; udā. 31). Apica tikkhapaññassa ñāṇuttarassetaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, ñāṇuttarassa ca kilesappahānaṃ itarehi sātisayaṃ, yathā saddhādhimuttehi diṭṭhippattassa. Tasmā imaṃ visesaṃ sandhāya “ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasametī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā nimittapātubhāve sati khaṇeneva aṅgapātubhāvasabbhāvato ayameva samādhi “ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasametī”ti vutto. Yathā taṃ mahato akālameghassa uṭṭhitassa dhārānipāte khaṇeneva pathaviyaṃ [M 1.0314] rajojallassa vūpasamo. Tenāha – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāakālamegho uṭṭhito”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.985; pārā. 165). Sāsanikassa jhānabhāvanā yebhuyyena nibbedhabhāgiyāva hotīti āha “nibbedhabhāgiyattā”ti. Buddhānaṃ pana ekaṃsena nibbedhabhāgiyāva hoti. Imameva hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā sabbepi sammāsambuddhā sammāsambodhiṃ adhigacchanti. Ariyamaggassa pādakabhūto ayaṃ samādhi anukkamena vaḍḍhitvā ariyamaggabhāvaṃ upagato viya hotīti āha “anupubbena ariyamaggavuddhippatto”ti.

But does not any other concentration also suppress and pacify opposing states at the very moment of its occurrence? So why is this concentration alone distinguished in this way? Because, from the preliminary part onwards, it has the nature of pacifying various thoughts. For it was said: 'Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of thoughts.' Moreover, this meditation subject is for one with keen wisdom and superior knowledge; and the abandoning of defilements by one with superior knowledge surpasses that of others, just as that of one who has attained the view surpasses that of those released by faith. Therefore, with this distinction in mind, it is said, 'it suppresses and pacifies on the spot.' Or, when the sign appears, this concentration alone, due to the existence of the manifestation of its factors, is said to 'suppress and pacify on the spot.' Just as when a great unseasonal cloud arises, the dust and grime on the ground are instantly pacified by the downpour of rain. Hence He said: 'Just as, monks, when a great unseasonal cloud arises,' and so on. For a follower of the Dispensation, the development of jhāna is for the most part conducive to penetration, hence it is said, 'because it is conducive to penetration.' For the Buddhas, however, it is exclusively conducive to penetration. For it is by developing this very meditation subject that all the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones attain perfect self-enlightenment. This concentration, being the basis for the noble path, gradually develops and is as if it has attained the state of the noble path. Hence it is said, 'having progressively attained the growth of the noble path'.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0297] panattho virāganirodhapaṭinissaggānupassanānaṃ vasena sammadeva yujjati. Heṭṭhā papañcavasena vuttamatthaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ saṅgahetvā dassento “ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho”ti āha, piṇḍatthoti vuttaṃ hoti.

This meaning, however, is indeed fitting by way of the contemplation of dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment. Summarizing the meaning previously stated by way of proliferation to make it easy to grasp, He presents it, saying, 'Here this is the condensed meaning'; which is to say, the summary meaning is stated.

217. Tamatthanti taṃ “kathaṃ bhāvito”tiādinā pucchāvasena saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ. “Idha tathāgato loke uppajjatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.190; ma. ni. 1.291; a. ni. 3.61) idha-saddo lokaṃ upādāya vutto, “idheva tiṭṭhamānassā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.369) okāsaṃ, “idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhuttāvī assaṃ pavārito”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.30) padapūraṇamattaṃ, “idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇātī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.73) pana sāsanaṃ, “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhū”ti idhāpi sāsanamevāti dassento “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti vatvā tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “ayañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbappakāraānāpānassatisamādhinibbattakassāti sabbappakāraggahaṇaṃ soḷasa pakāre sandhāya. Te hi imasmiṃyeva sāsane. Bāhirakā hi jānantā ādito catuppakārameva jānanti. Tenāha “aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano”ti, yathāvuttassa puggalassa nissayabhāvapaṭisedhanoti attho. Etena “idha bhikkhave”ti idaṃ antogadhevasaddanti dasseti. Santi hi ekapadānipi sāvadhāraṇāni yathā “vāyubhakkho”ti. Tenevāha “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo”tiādi. Paripuṇṇasamaṇakaraṇadhammo hi so, yo sabbappakāraānāpānassatisamādhinibbattako. Parappavādāti paresaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ nānappakārā vādā titthāyatanāni.

217. By 'that meaning' is meant the meaning briefly stated in the form of a question, 'How is it developed?' and so on. In phrases like 'Here the Tathāgata arises in the world,' the word 'here' (idha) is used with reference to the world. In phrases like 'right here while standing,' it refers to a place. In phrases like 'Here, monks, I would have eaten and been satisfied,' it is merely a particle to fill out the line. But in phrases like 'Here a monk learns the Dhamma,' it refers to the Dispensation. And in 'Here, monks, a monk,' it also refers to the Dispensation. To show this, having said 'Monks, in this Dispensation a monk,' and in order to show that meaning by making it clear, the passage beginning 'For this one...' was stated. Therein, the taking up of 'all kinds' is with reference to the sixteen aspects. For they are found only in this Dispensation. For outsiders, if they know them, know only four aspects from the beginning. Therefore, He said, 'it is a denial of such a state for another dispensation,' the meaning being that it is a denial of the state of being a resort for the aforementioned person. By this, it is shown that the phrase 'Here, monks' has the particle 'eva' (alone/only) included within it. For there are even single words that are emphatic, such as 'wind-eater' (vāyubhakkho). For that very reason, He said, 'Here alone, monks, is the ascetic,' and so on. For he who is a producer of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in all its aspects possesses the qualities that make one a complete ascetic. 'Others' doctrines' (parappavādā) are the various doctrines and sectarian tenets of other sectarians.

Araññādikasseva [M 1.0315] bhāvanānurūpasenāsanataṃ dassetuṃ “imassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Duddamo damathaṃ anupagato goṇo kūṭagoṇo. Yathā thanehi sabbaso khīraṃ na paggharati, evaṃ dohapaṭibandhinī kūṭadhenu. Rūpasaddādike paṭicca uppajjanako assādo rūpārammaṇādiraso. Pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇanti pabbajjato pubbe, anādimati vā saṃsāre paricitārammaṇaṃ.

To show that only such places as a forest are dwellings suitable for meditation, the passage beginning 'For this one...' was stated. A bull that is hard to tame and has not undergone taming is a `kūṭagoṇa` (a treacherous bull). Just as milk does not flow at all from the udders, so a cow that obstructs milking is a `kūṭadhenu` (a treacherous cow). The pleasure that arises in dependence on forms, sounds, and so on, is the savour of objects such as form. 'An object previously practiced' means an object familiarized either before going forth or in beginningless saṃsāra.

Nibandheyyāti bandheyya. Satiyāti sammadeva kammaṭṭhānasallakkhaṇasampavattāya satiyā. Ārammaṇeti kammaṭṭhānārammaṇe. Daḷhanti thiraṃ, yathā satokārissa upacārappanābhedo samādhi ijjhati, tathā thāmagataṃ katvāti attho.

'He should bind' (`nibandheyya`) means he should bind (`bandheyya`). 'With mindfulness' (`satiyā`) means with mindfulness that proceeds by way of correctly marking the characteristics of the meditation subject. 'On the object' (`ārammaṇe`) means on the meditation subject as object. 'Firmly' (`daḷhaṃ`) means steadily; the meaning is: having made it powerful, in such a way that the concentration of one who acts mindfully, distinguished as access and absorption, succeeds.

Visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānanti [V 1.0298] sabbesaṃ buddhānaṃ, ekaccānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ, buddhasāvakānañca visesādhigamassa ceva aññakammaṭṭhānena adhigatavisesānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārassa ca padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ.

'The basis for the attainment of distinction and for pleasant abiding in the present life' means being the proximate cause for both the attainment of distinction for all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha's disciples, and for the pleasant abiding in the present life for those who have attained distinction through another meditation subject.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya bhagavā yogīnaṃ anurūpanivāsaṭṭhānupadisanato.

The Blessed One is like a master of the science of sites (`vatthuvijjācariyo`) because of his pointing out suitable dwelling places for yogis.

Bhikkhu dīpisadiso araññe ekiko viharitvā paṭipakkhanimmathanena icchitatthasādhanato. Phalamuttamanti sāmaññaphalamāha. Parakkamajavayoggabhūminti bhāvanussāhajavassa yoggakaraṇabhūmibhūtaṃ.

A bhikkhu is like a leopard (`dīpi`) because, dwelling alone in the forest, he achieves his desired goal by crushing the opposing defilements. By 'the highest fruit' (`phalamuttamaṃ`), He speaks of the fruits of recluseship. 'A ground for striving and swiftness' (`parakkamajavayoggabhūmi`) means being a ground that makes one fit for the energy and swiftness of the effort in cultivation.

218. Evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇesūti abhidhammapariyāyena (vibha. 530), suttantapariyāyena ca vuttalakkhaṇesu. Rukkhasamīpanti “yāvatā majjhanhike kāle samantā chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūlanti vuccatī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ rukkhassa samīpaṭṭhānaṃ. Avasesasattavidhasenāsananti pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjanti evaṃ vuttaṃ.

218. Regarding 'the characteristics thus stated' means the characteristics stated by way of the Abhidhamma exposition and by way of the Suttanta exposition. 'Near a tree' (`rukkhasamīpaṃ`) refers to the location near a tree, which is defined thus: 'To the extent that the shadow extends all around at midday, and where leaves fall when there is no wind, to that extent it is called “the root of a tree.”' 'The remaining seven kinds of dwellings' refers to the dwellings stated thus: a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest thicket, the open air, and a heap of straw.

Ututtayānukūlaṃ dhātucariyānukūlanti gimhādiututtayassa, semhādidhātuttayassa, mohādicariyattayassa ca anukūlaṃ. Tathā hi gimhakāle ca araññaṃ anukūlaṃ, hemante rukkhamūlaṃ, vassakāle suññāgāraṃ, semhadhātukassa semhapakatikassa araññaṃ, pittadhātukassa rukkhamūlaṃ[M 1.0316], vātadhātukassa suññāgāraṃ anukūlaṃ, mohacaritassa araññaṃ, dosacaritassa rukkhamūlaṃ, rāgacaritassa suññāgāraṃ anukūlaṃ. Alīnānuddhaccapakkhikanti asaṅkocāvikkhepapakkhikaṃ. Sayanañhi kosajjapakkhikaṃ, ṭhānacaṅkamanāni uddhaccapakkhikāni, na evaṃ nisajjā. Tato evassa santatā. Nisajjāya daḷhabhāvaṃ pallaṅkābhujanena, assāsapassāsānaṃ pavattanasukhataṃ uparimakāyassa ujukaṭṭhapanena, ārammaṇapariggahūpāyaṃ parimukhaṃ satiyā ṭhapanena dassento. Ūrubaddhāsananti ūrūnamadhobandhanavasena nisajjā. Heṭṭhimakāyassa anujukaṃ ṭhapanaṃ nisajjā-vacaneneva bodhitanti “ujuṃ kāya”nti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayoti āha “uparimasarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti.
