Taṃ pana ujukaṭṭhapanaṃ sarūpato, payojanato ca dassetuṃ “aṭṭhārasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na paṇamantīti na onamanti. Na paripatatīti [V 1.0299] na vigacchati vīthiṃ na vilaṅghati, tato eva pubbenāparaṃ visesuppattiyā vuddhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati. Idha pari-saddo abhi-saddena samānatthoti āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purakkhitvāti attho. Parīti pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 16) viya. Niyyānaṭṭho paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho. Tasmā pariggahitaniyyānanti sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ pariccattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā, paramaṃ satinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho.

“Favorable to the three seasons, favorable to the three elements, and favorable to the three temperaments”—thus, it is suitable for the three seasons of summer, etc., the three elements of phlegm, etc., and the three temperaments of delusion, etc. For instance, in the summer season, the forest is suitable; in the winter, the foot of a tree; in the rainy season, a secluded dwelling. For one with a phlegmatic element, the forest is suitable; for one with a bilious element, the foot of a tree; for one with a windy element, a secluded dwelling is suitable. For one with a deluded temperament, the forest is suitable; for one with a hateful temperament, the foot of a tree; for one with a greedy temperament, a secluded dwelling is suitable. “On the side of non-lethargy and non-restlessness” (alīnānuddhaccapakkhikaṃ) means on the side of non-contraction and non-distraction. For lying down is on the side of lethargy, while standing and walking are on the side of restlessness, but not so sitting. Hence, its continuity. He shows the firmness of sitting through the cross-legged posture, the ease in the flow of in-and-out breaths by straightening the upper body, and the means of grasping the object by establishing mindfulness in front. The “thigh-bound posture” (ūrubaddhāsana) means sitting with the thighs bound to each other. The placing of the lower body not straight is made known by the very word ‘sitting’. Therefore, in the phrase ‘the body straight’ (ujuṃ kāyaṃ), the word ‘body’ (kāya) refers to the upper body; thus he said, ‘having straightened the upper body’ (uparimasarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā). To show that straightening of the body in terms of its nature and its purpose, the passage beginning ‘eighteen’ (aṭṭhārasā) was stated. ‘They do not bend down’ (na paṇamanti) means they do not stoop. ‘It does not fall away’ (na paripatatīti) means it does not depart, it does not transgress the path; for that very reason, by the arising of a special quality from the former to the latter, it attains growth and increase. Here, the prefix ‘pari-’ has the same meaning as ‘abhi-’; thus he said, ‘facing the meditation object’ (kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ). The meaning is: having prevented the mind from various external objects and having placed only the meditation object in front. ‘Pari-’ has the meaning of grasping, as in ‘leading’ (pariṇāyikā) and so on. ‘Niyyāna’ has the meaning of departure, of going out from the opposing side. Therefore, ‘grasped departure’ (pariggahitaniyyānaṃ) means: having made mindfulness in every way grasped without forgetfulness, with forgetfulness abandoned; having established supreme maturity of mindfulness. This is the meaning.

219. Satovāti satiyā samannāgato eva saranto eva assasati nāssa kāci sativirahitā assāsappavatti hotīti attho. Sato passasatīti etthāpi satova passasatīti eva-saddo ānetvā vattabbo. Satokārīti sato eva hutvā, satiyā eva vā kātabbassa kattā, karaṇasīlo vā. Yadi “satova assasati sato passasatī”ti etassa vibhaṅge (ma. ni. 3.148; saṃ. ni. 5.986; pārā. 165) vuttaṃ, atha kasmā “assasati passasati”cceva avatvā “satokārī”ti vuttaṃ? Ekarasaṃ desanaṃ kātukāmatāya. Paṭhamacatukke padadvayameva hi vattamānakālavasena āgataṃ, itarāni anāgatakālavasena. Tasmā ekarasaṃ desanaṃ kātukāmatāya sabbattha (paṭi. ma. 1.165 ādayo) “satokāri”cceva vuttaṃ.

219. “Mindful” (sato) means: being endowed with mindfulness, being mindful, he breathes in; for him there is no occurrence of in-breathing devoid of mindfulness—this is the meaning. In the phrase “mindfully he breathes out” (sato passasati) as well, the word “eva” (indeed) should be brought in and connected thus: “mindfully indeed he breathes out.” “One who acts mindfully” (satokārī) means: being mindful indeed, or one who does what should be done with mindfulness indeed, or one who is in the habit of so doing. If it was stated in the analysis of “mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out,” then why was it not said as “he breathes in, he breathes out,” but as “one who acts mindfully”? Because of the desire to make the teaching of a single essence. For in the first tetrad, only two terms came by way of the present tense; the others by way of the future tense. Therefore, because of the desire to make the teaching of a single essence, everywhere it was said only as “one who acts mindfully.”

Dīghaṃ [M 1.0317] assāsavasenāti dīghaassāsavasena vibhattialopaṃ katvā niddeso. Dīghanti vā bhagavatā vuttaassāsavasena. Cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepanti vikkhepassa paṭipakkhabhāvato “avikkhepo”ti laddhanāmacittassa ekaggabhāvaṃ pajānato. Sati upaṭṭhitā hotīti ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇenāti yathāvuttāya satiyā, yathāvuttena ca ñāṇena. Idaṃ vutta hoti – dīghaṃ assāsaṃ ārammaṇabhūtaṃ avikkhittacittassa, asammohato vā pajānantassa tattha sati upaṭṭhitā eva hoti, taṃ sampajānantassa ārammaṇakaraṇavasena, asammohavasena vā sampajaññaṃ, tadadhīnasatisampajaññena taṃsamaṅgī yogāvacaro satokārī nāma hotīti. Paṭinissaggānupassī assāsavasenāti paṭinissaggānupassī hutvā assasanassa vasena. “Paṭinissaggānupassīassāsavasenā”ti vā pāṭho. Tassa paṭinissaggānupassino assāsā paṭinissaggānupassīassāsā, tesaṃ vasenāti attho. Vinayanayena anto uṭṭhitasasanaṃ assāso, bahi uṭṭhitasasanaṃ passāso. Suttantanayena pana bahi uṭṭhahitvāpi anto sasanato assāso, anto uṭṭhahitvāpi bahi sasanato passāso. Ayameva ca nayo –

“By way of a long in-breath” (dīghaṃ assāsavasena): this is an exposition made by not eliding the case ending in “long-in-breath” (dīghaassāsavasena). Or, “long” (dīghaṃ) is said by the Blessed One by way of the in-breath. “The mind’s one-pointedness, which is non-distraction” (cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ): he understands the one-pointedness of the mind, which has obtained the name ‘non-distraction’ because it is the opposite of distraction. “Mindfulness is established” (sati upaṭṭhitā hoti) means that having approached the object, it remains established. “By that mindfulness, by that knowledge” (tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena) means by the aforesaid mindfulness and by the aforesaid knowledge. This is what is said: for one whose mind is undistracted, or for one who understands without delusion, mindfulness is indeed established there, with the long in-breath as its object. For one who clearly comprehends that, clear comprehension arises either by way of making it an object or by way of non-delusion. The meditator, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension dependent on that, is called ‘one who acts mindfully’ (satokārī). “Observing relinquishment by way of in-breath” (paṭinissaggānupassī assāsavasena) means by way of inhaling while being one who observes relinquishment. Alternatively, the reading is “by way of the in-breaths of one observing relinquishment” (paṭinissaggānupassīassāsavasena). The meaning of that is: the in-breaths of one who observes relinquishment are ‘in-breaths of one observing relinquishment’; by way of them. According to the Vinaya method, breathing that has arisen inside is the in-breath (assāsa); breathing that has arisen outside is the out-breath (passāsa). But according to the Suttanta method, because of breathing in what has arisen outside, it is the in-breath; and because of breathing out what has arisen inside, it is the out-breath. And this very method:

“Assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ [V 1.0300] satiyā anugacchato ajjhattaṃ vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti, “passāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato bahiddhā vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.157) –

“For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath with mindfulness, with a mind that has gone to distraction internally, both body and mind become agitated, unsteady, and tremulous.” “For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath with mindfulness, with a mind that has gone to distraction externally, both body and mind become agitated, unsteady, and tremulous.” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.157) –

Imāya pāḷiyā sameti.

accords with this Pāḷi text.

Paṭhamaṃ abbhantaravāto bahi nikkhamati, tasmā pavattikkamena assāso paṭhamaṃ vuttoti vadanti. Tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyatīti tāluṃ āhacca nirujjhati. Tena kira sampatijāto bāladārako khipitaṃ karoti. Evaṃ tāvātiādi yathāvuttassa atthassa nigamanaṃ. Keci “evaṃ tāvāti anena pavattikkamena assāso bahinikkhamanavātoti gahetabbanti adhippāyo”ti vadanti.

First, the internal wind goes out; therefore, they say that in the order of occurrence, assāsa is mentioned first. “Striking the palate, it ceases” (tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyati) means striking the palate, it ceases. For that reason, it is said, a newly born infant sneezes. The passage beginning “Thus far” (evaṃ tāva) is the conclusion of the meaning as stated. Some say, “The intention is that by this phrase ‘thus far,’ it should be understood that, in the order of occurrence, assāsa is the wind exiting outward.”

Addhānavasenāti [M 1.0318] kāladdhānavasena. Ayaṃ hi addhāna-saddo kālassa, desassa ca vācako. Tattha desaddhānaṃ udāharaṇabhāvena dassetvā kāladdhānavasena assāsapassāsānaṃ dīgharassataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha okāsaddhānanti okāsabhūtaṃ addhānaṃ. Pharitvāti byāpetvā. Cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi anekakalāpabhāvena. Dīghaṃ addhānanti dīghaṃ padesaṃ. Tasmāti saṇikaṃ pavattiyā dīghasantānatāya “dīghā”ti vuccanti. Ettha ca hatthiādisarīre, sunakhādisarīre ca assāsapassāsānaṃ desaddhānavisiṭṭhena kāladdhānavaseneva dīgharassatā vuttāti veditabbā. “Saṇikaṃ pūretvā saṇikameva nikkhamanti”, “sīghaṃ pūretvā sīghameva nikkhamantī”ti ca vacanato. Manussesūti samānappamāṇesupi manussasarīresu. Dīghaṃ assasantīti dīghaṃ assāsappabandhaṃ pavattentīti attho. Passasantīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sunakhasasādayo viya rassaṃ assasanti ca passasanti cāti yojanā. Idaṃ pana dīghaṃ, rassañca assasanaṃ, passasanañca tesaṃ sattānaṃ sarīrasabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesanti sattānaṃ. Teti assāsapassāsā. Ittaramaddhānanti appakaṃ kālaṃ.

`Addhānavasena` means by way of temporal duration. For this word `addhāna` indeed signifies both time and space. Among these, having shown spatial duration by way of an example, the passage beginning with `yathā hi` is stated in order to clarify the longness and shortness of the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of temporal duration. Therein, `okāsaddhāna` means the duration that is space. `Pharitvā` means having pervaded. `Cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi` means by being of many groups. `Dīghaṃ addhāna` means a long region. Therefore, because of the slow occurrence and long continuity, they are called `dīghā` (long). And here, in the bodies of elephants and so on, and in the bodies of dogs and so on, it should be understood that the longness and shortness of the in-breaths and out-breaths are stated only by way of temporal duration, which is distinguished by spatial duration. This is because of the statement, 'Having filled slowly, they exit slowly,' and 'Having filled quickly, they exit quickly.' `Manussesu` means even in human bodies of similar size. `Dīghaṃ assasanti` means they cause a long continuum of in-breath to occur; this is the meaning. The same method applies to `passasanti`. The connection is: like dogs, hares, and so on, they inhale shortly and exhale shortly. However, this long and short inhaling and exhaling should be seen as the bodily nature of those beings. `Tesaṃ` means of beings. `Te` means the in-breaths and out-breaths. `Ittaramaddhānaṃ` means for a short time.

Navahākārehīti bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa pubbenāparaṃ aladdhavisesassa kevalaṃ addhānavasena ādito [V 1.0301] vuttā tayo ākārā, te ca kho ekacco assāsaṃ suṭṭhu sallakkheti, ekacco passāsaṃ, ekacco tadubhayanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena. Keci pana “assasatipi passasatipīti ekajjhaṃ vacanaṃ bhāvanāya nirantaraṃ pavattidassanattha”nti vadanti. Chandavasena pubbe viya tayo, tathā pāmojjavasenāti imehi navahākārehi.

`Navahākārehi` (By nine aspects): For a yogi practicing meditation who has not yet attained a special distinction from a previous time to a later time, there are the three aspects stated at the beginning merely by way of duration. And these are by way of these three persons: one person marks the in-breath well, another the out-breath, and another both. Some, however, say that the single utterance `assasatipi passasatipīti` is for the purpose of showing the uninterrupted occurrence of the meditation. By way of desire, there are three aspects as before; similarly, by way of joy, three. Thus, by these nine aspects.

Kāmaṃ cettha ekassa puggalassa tayo eva ākārā labbhanti, tantivasena pana sabbesaṃ pāḷiāruḷhattā, tesaṃ vasena parikammassa kātabbattā ca “tatrāyaṃ bhikkhu navahākārehī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pajānatoti evaṃ yathāvuttehi ākārehi assāsapassāse pajānato, tattha manasikāraṃ pavattentassa. Ekenākārenāti dīghaṃ assāsādīsu catūsu ākāresu ekena ākārena, navasu tīsu vā ekena. Tathā hi vakkhati –

Although here for a single person only three aspects are obtainable, it is nevertheless said, `tatrāyaṃ bhikkhu navahākārehi` (Therein, this monk by nine aspects), because by way of the textual tradition all of them are included in the Pāḷi, and because the preliminary work must be done by way of them. `Evaṃ pajānato` (Thus understanding) means: for one who understands the in-breaths and out-breaths by the aspects thus stated, causing attention to arise therein. `Ekena ākārena` (By one aspect) means: by one aspect among the four aspects beginning with the long in-breath, or by one among the nine, or among the three. For so it will be said:

“Dīgho rasso ca assāso, passāsopi ca tādiso;

Cattāro vaṇṇā vattanti, nāsikagge va bhikkhuno”ti.

“Long and short is the in-breath, and the out-breath is also similar; four modes occur at the tip of the monk’s nose.”

Ayaṃ [M 1.0319] bhāvanā assāsapassāsakāyānupassanāti katvā vuttaṃ “kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā sampajjatī”ti.

Because this meditation is the contemplation of the body which is the in-breaths and out-breaths, it is said: 'The development of the establishment of mindfulness as contemplation of the body is accomplished.'

Idāni pāḷivaseneva te nava ākāre, bhāvanāvidhiñca dassetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kathaṃ pajānātīti pajānanavidhiṃ kathetukamyatāya pucchati. Dīghaṃ assāsanti vuttalakkhaṇaṃ dīghaṃ assāsaṃ. Addhānasaṅkhāteti “addhāna”nti saṅkhaṃ gate dīghe kāle, dīghaṃ khaṇanti attho. Koṭṭhāsapariyāyo vā saṅkhāta-saddo “theyyasaṅkhāta”ntiādīsu (pārā. 91) viya, tasmā addhānasaṅkhāteti addhānakoṭṭhāse, desabhāgeti attho. Chando uppajjatīti bhāvanāya pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ āvahantiyā laddhassādattā tattha sātisayo kattukāmatālakkhaṇo kusalacchando uppajjati. Chandavasenāti tathāpavattachandassa vasena savisesaṃ bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuddhiṃ phātiṃ gamentassa. Tato sukhumataranti yathāvuttachandappavattiyā purimato sukhumataraṃ. Bhāvanābalena hi paṭippassaddhadarathapariḷāhatāya kāyassa assāsapassāsā sukhumatarā hutvā pavattanti. Pāmojjaṃ uppajjatīti assāsapassāsānaṃ sukhumatarabhāvena ārammaṇassa santataratāya, kammaṭṭhānassa ca vīthipaṭipannatāya bhāvanācittasahagato pamodo khuddikādibhedā [V 1.0302] taruṇapīti uppajjati. Cittaṃ vivattatīti anukkamena assāsapassāsānaṃ ativiya sukhumatarabhāvappattiyā anupaṭṭhahane vicetabbākārappattehi cittaṃ vinivattatīti keci. Bhāvanābalena pana sukhumatarabhāvappattesu assāsapassāsesu tattha paṭibhāganimitte uppanne pakatiassāsapassāsato cittaṃ nivattati. Upekkhā saṇṭhātīti tasmiṃ paṭibhāganimitte upacārappanābhede samādhimhi uppanne puna jhānanibbattanatthaṃ byāpārābhāvato ajjhupekkhanaṃ hotīti. Sā panāyaṃ upekkhā tatramajjhattupekkhāti veditabbā.

Now, to show those nine aspects and the method of development by means of the Pāḷi itself, the section beginning with `yathāhā` is commenced. Therein, the question `kathaṃ pajānāti` (How does he know?) is asked with the desire to explain the method of knowing. `Dīghaṃ assasanti` (He breathes in long) means the long in-breath with the characteristic already stated. `Addhānasaṅkhāte` (reckoned as duration) means in a long time that is reckoned as 'duration', that is, for a long moment. Alternatively, the word `saṅkhāta` is a synonym for 'portion,' as in `theyyasaṅkhāta` (reckoned as theft). Therefore, `addhānasaṅkhāte` means in the portion of duration, or in the part of space. `Chando uppajjati` (Desire arises) means: because delight is obtained from the meditation bringing successive distinction, an excessive wholesome desire, characterized by the wish to act, arises therein. `Chandavasena` (By way of desire) means for one who applies himself to meditation with special distinction due to such desire, causing the meditation subject to grow and expand. `Tato sukhumataraṃ` (Then more subtle) means subtler than before due to the aforementioned arising of desire. For, through the power of meditation, as the body's distress and fever are calmed, the in-breaths and out-breaths become more subtle and continue. `Pāmojjaṃ uppajjati` (Joy arises) means: due to the in-breaths and out-breaths becoming more subtle, the object becoming more tranquil, and the meditation subject proceeding on the right path, joy (pamoda) accompanied by the meditation-mind arises—which is nascent zest (taruṇapīti) of the kinds beginning with minor zest. `Cittaṃ vivattatīti` (The mind turns away) means: some say that as the in-breaths and out-breaths gradually become extremely subtle and no longer appear, the mind turns away from them, which have reached a state requiring investigation. In truth, however, through the power of meditation, when the in-breaths and out-breaths have become more subtle and the counterpart sign arises in relation to them, the mind turns away from the normal in-breaths and out-breaths. `Upekkhā saṇṭhāti` (Equanimity is established) means: when concentration, distinguished as access and absorption, arises in that counterpart sign, then due to the absence of exertion for producing jhāna again, there is overlooking. This equanimity should be understood as equanimity as neutrality towards that (tatramajjhattatā).

Imehi navahi ākārehīti imehi yathāvuttehi navahi pakārehi pavattā. Dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā kāyoti dīghākārā assāsapassāsā cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi samūhaṭṭhena kāyo. Assāsapassāse nissāya uppannanimittampettha assāsapassāsasamaññameva vuttaṃ. Upaṭṭhānaṃ satīti ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhatīti sati upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Anupassanā [M 1.0320] ñāṇanti samathavasena nimittassa anupassanā, vipassanāvasena assāsapassāse, tannissayañca kāyaṃ “rūpa”nti, cittaṃ taṃsampayuttadhamme ca “arūpa”nti vavatthapetvā nāmarūpassa anupassanā ca ñāṇaṃ, tattha yathābhūtāvabodho. Kāyo upaṭṭhānanti so kāyo ārammaṇakaraṇavasena upagantvā sati ettha tiṭṭhatīti upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Ettha ca “kāyo upaṭṭhāna”nti iminā itarakāyassāpi saṅgaho hoti yathāvuttasammasanacārassāpi idha icchitattā. No satīti so kāyo sati nāma na hoti. Sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati ca saraṇaṭṭhena, upatiṭṭhanaṭṭhena ca. Tāya satiyāti yathāvuttāya satiyā. Tena ñāṇenāti yathāvutteneva ñāṇena. Taṃ kāyanti taṃ assāsapassāsakāyañceva tannissayarūpakāyañca. Anupassatīti jhānasampayuttañāṇena ceva vipassanāñāṇena ca anu anu passati. Tena vuccati kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti tena anupassanena yathāvutte kāye ayaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti vuccati.

‘By these nine aspects’ means by these nine modes as stated, it proceeds. ‘Long in-breaths and out-breaths are the body’ means in-breaths and out-breaths having a long characteristic, even if they are minute and scattered, are called ‘body’ because of the meaning of ‘aggregate’. The counterpart sign that has arisen dependent on the in-breaths and out-breaths is also, here in this teaching, called by the very name ‘in-breath and out-breath’. ‘Establishment is mindfulness’ means: because it approaches an object and stands there, mindfulness is called ‘establishment’. ‘Contemplation is knowledge’ means: by way of serenity, the contemplation of the sign; and by way of insight, having defined the in-breaths and out-breaths and the body dependent on them as ‘form’, and the mind and its associated states as ‘non-form’, the contemplation of name-and-form is also knowledge; therein, it is the thorough understanding of things as they really are. ‘The body is the establishment’ means: that body, by way of being made an object, is where mindfulness approaches and stands; because it is a place for standing, it is called ‘establishment’. And here, by this phrase ‘the body is the establishment’, the inclusion of the other body also occurs, because the physical body, which is the domain of the aforementioned examination, is also desired here. ‘Not mindfulness’ means that body is not called mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness, due to the meaning of recollecting and the meaning of being present. ‘With that mindfulness’ means with the mindfulness as stated. ‘With that knowledge’ means with the very knowledge as stated. ‘That body’ means that body of in-breaths and out-breaths and the physical body dependent on it. ‘He contemplates’ means he sees again and again with knowledge associated with jhāna and with insight knowledge. Therefore it is said, ‘the development of the establishment of mindfulness as contemplation of the body in the body’: because of that contemplation in the body as stated, this is called ‘the development of the establishment of mindfulness as contemplation of the body in the body’.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā ayaṃ yathāvutte assāsapassāsakāye, tassa nissayabhūte karajakāye ca kāyasseva anupassanā anudakabhūtāya marīciyā udakānupassanā viya na aniccādisabhāve kāye niccādibhāvānupassanā, atha kho yathārahaṃ aniccadukkhānattāsubhabhāvassevānupassanā. Atha vā kāye “aha”nti vā “mama”nti vā “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā gahetabbassa kassaci abhāvato tādisaṃ ananupassitvā kāyamattasseva anupassanā [V 1.0303] kāyānupassanā, tāya kāyānupassanāya sampayuttā satiyeva upaṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, tassa bhāvanā vaḍḍhanā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāti.

This is what is meant: This contemplation of the body itself, in the body of in-breaths and out-breaths as stated and in the physical body which is its support, is not the contemplation of the nature of permanence and so on in a body whose nature is impermanence and so on, like the contemplation of water in a mirage where there is no water. But rather, it is indeed the contemplation of the state of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and unattractiveness, as is appropriate. Alternatively, because in the body there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped as ‘I,’ or ‘mine,’ or ‘a woman,’ or ‘a man,’ not contemplating it in such a way, the contemplation of the mere body itself is the contemplation of the body. The mindfulness associated with that contemplation of the body is itself the establishment, the establishment of mindfulness. The development and cultivation of that is the development of the establishment of mindfulness as contemplation of the body.

Esa nayoti “navahi ākārehī”tiādinā vuttavidhiṃ rassa-pade atidisati. Etthāti etasmiṃ yathādassite “kathaṃ dīghaṃ assasanto”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.148; saṃ. ni. 5.986; pārā. 165) āgate pāḷinaye. Idhāti imasmiṃ rassapadavasena āgate pāḷinaye.

‘This is the method’ extends the method stated beginning with ‘by nine aspects’ to the section on the short breath. ‘Here’ means in this Pāli method which has come down as shown, beginning with ‘How, when breathing in long…’. ‘In this context’ means in this Pāli method which has come down by way of the section on the short breath.

Ayanti yogāvacaro. Addhānavasenāti dīghakālavasena. Ittaravasenāti parittakālavasena. Imehi ākārehīti imehi navahi ākārehi.

‘This’ means the yogī. ‘By way of a long time’ means by way of a long period of time. ‘By way of a short time’ means by way of a brief period of time. ‘By these aspects’ means by these nine aspects.

Tādisoti [M 1.0321] dīgho, rasso ca. Cattāro vaṇṇāti cattāro ākārā, te ca dīghādayo eva. Nāsikagge va bhikkhunoti gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vuttaṃ “nāsikagge vā”ti, vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena uttaroṭṭhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

‘Of such a kind’ means both long and short. ‘Four descriptions’ means four aspects, and they are just the long, etc. The phrase ‘nāsikagge va bhikkhu’ (at the tip of the nose, a monk) is stated, having been shortened for the sake of ease in composing the verse, as ‘nāsikagge vā’ (at the tip of the nose, or). The word ‘vā’ has the meaning of non-fixity. By that, it includes the upper lip.

220. Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedīti sabbassa kāyassa paṭi paṭi paccekaṃ sammadeva vedanasīlo jānanasīlo, tassa vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedo etassa atthi, taṃ vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedamānoti attho. Tattha tattha sabba-ggahaṇena assāsādikāyassa anavasesapariyādāne siddhepi anekakalāpasamudāyabhāvato tassa sabbesampi bhāgānaṃ saṃvedanadassanatthaṃ paṭi-saddaggahaṇaṃ. Tattha sakkaccakārībhāvadassanatthaṃ saṃ-saddaggahaṇanti imamatthaṃ dassento “sakalassā”tiādimāha. Tattha yathā samānepi assāsapassāsesu yogino paṭipattividhāne paccekaṃ sakkaccaṃyeva paṭipajjitabbanti dassetuṃ visuṃ desanā katā, evaṃ tamevatthaṃ dīpetuṃ satipi atthassa samānatāya “sakalassā”tiādinā padadvayassa visuṃ visuṃ atthavaṇṇanā katāti veditabbaṃ. Pākaṭaṃ karontoti vibhūtaṃ karonto, sabbaso vibhāventoti attho. Pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ vibhāvanaṃ tattha asammuyhanaṃ ñāṇeneva nesaṃ pavattanena hotīti dassento “evaṃ viditaṃ karonto”tiādimāha. Tattha tasmāti yasmā ñāṇasampayuttacitteneva assāsapassāse pavatteti, na vippayuttacittena, tasmā evaṃbhūto sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatīti vuccati buddhādīhīti yojanā. Cuṇṇavicuṇṇavisaṭeti anekakalāpatāya cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhāvena [V 1.0304] visaṭe. Ādi pākaṭo hoti satiyā, ñāṇassa ca vasena tathā pubbābhisaṅkhārassa pavattattā. Tādisena bhavitabbanti catutthapuggalasadisena bhavitabbaṃ, pageva satiṃ, ñāṇañca paccupaṭṭhapetvā tīsupi ṭhānesu ñāṇasampayuttameva cittaṃ pavattetabbanti adhippāyo.

220. ‘Experiencing the whole body’ means: one who is by nature properly and individually experiencing and knowing the entire body; or, for whom there is a proper and individual experience of it; or, one who is properly and individually experiencing it. This is the meaning. Therein, although the complete inclusion of the body of breath, etc., is established by the taking of the word ‘whole,’ the word ‘paṭi’ (each, individually) is used to show the experiencing of all its parts, because it is an aggregate of many groups of material qualities. Therein, the word ‘saṃ’ (well, thoroughly) is used to show the state of being one who acts carefully. Showing this meaning, the text states ‘of the entire body,’ etc. Therein, just as, although the method of practice for the yogī regarding the in-breaths and out-breaths is the same, a separate teaching was given to show that one should practice each one carefully, so too, to illuminate that very meaning, it should be known that although there is a similarity of meaning, a separate explanation of the meaning for the two phrases was made. ‘Making it clear’ means making it evident, thoroughly clarifying it. This making clear, this clarification, which is non-bewilderment regarding them, happens by directing them with knowledge alone, as stated in the text beginning ‘thus making it known.’ Therein, ‘therefore’ means: since one produces the in-breaths and out-breaths only with a mind associated with knowledge, not with a mind dissociated from it, therefore such a person is said by the Buddhas and others to be one who trains thus: ‘I will breathe in, I will breathe out, experiencing the whole body.’ This is the connection. ‘Scattered as if ground to powder’ refers to being scattered in a state of being ground to powder due to being a multitude of many groups of material qualities. The beginning becomes manifest by means of mindfulness and knowledge, and because of the operation of previous formations in that way. ‘One must become like that’ means one must become like the fourth type of person; having established mindfulness and knowledge from the very beginning, one should produce a mind associated with knowledge in all three instances. This is the intention.

Evanti vuttappakārena sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedanavaseneva. Ghaṭatīti ussahati. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti, manasikāraṃ pavattetīti attho. Tathābhūtassāti ānāpānassatiṃ bhāventassa. Saṃvaroti sati[M 1.0322], vīriyampi vā. Tāya satiyāti yā ānāpāne ārabbha pavattā sati, tāya. Tena manasikārenāti yo so tattha satipubbaṅgamo bhāvanāmanasikāro, tena saddhinti adhippāyo. Āsevatīti “tisso sikkhāyo”ti vutte adhikusaladhamme āsevati. Tadāsevanañhettha sikkhananti adhippetaṃ.

Thus, in the manner stated, it is solely by way of distinctly knowing the entire body of in-breaths and out-breaths. ‘He strives’ (ghaṭati) means he makes an effort (ussahati). ‘He exerts himself’ (vāyamati) means he makes an exertion, that is, he causes attention to arise; this is the meaning. ‘For one who is thus’ (tathābhūtassa) means for one who develops mindfulness of breathing. ‘Restraint’ (saṃvaro) means mindfulness, or also energy. ‘With that mindfulness’ (tāya satiyā) means with that mindfulness that has arisen taking the in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. ‘With that attention’ (tena manasikārena) means with that attention for development which is preceded by mindfulness there; this is the intended meaning. ‘He cultivates’ (āsevati) means he cultivates the highly wholesome qualities mentioned as ‘the three trainings.’ Indeed, here that cultivation is intended as training.

Purimanayeti purimasmiṃ bhāvanānaye, paṭhamavatthudvayeti adhippāyo. Tatthāpi kāmaṃ ñāṇuppādanaṃ labbhateva assāsapassāsānaṃ yāthāvato dīgharassabhāvāvabodhasabbhāvato, tathāpi taṃ na dukkaraṃ yathāpavattānaṃ tesaṃ gahaṇamattabhāvatoti tattha vattamānakālappayogo kato. Idaṃ pana dukkaraṃ purisassa khuradhārāyaṃ gamanasadisaṃ, tasmā sātisayenettha pubbābhisaṅkhārena bhavitabbanti dīpetuṃ anāgatakālappayogo katoti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha yasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ñāṇuppādanādīsūti ādi-saddena kāyasaṅkhārapassambhanapītipaṭisaṃvedanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Keci panettha “saṃvarasamādānānaṃ saṅgaho”ti vadanti.

‘In the previous method’ (purimanaye) means in the previous method of development, in the first pair of objects; this is the intended meaning. Even there, the arising of knowledge can indeed be obtained, due to the existence of understanding the long and short nature of the in-breaths and out-breaths as they really are; yet, that is not difficult, because it is merely a matter of grasping them as they occur. Therefore, the use of the present tense is made there. But this is difficult, like a man walking on a razor’s edge. Therefore, to show that here one must act with exceeding prior preparation, the future tense is used; to show this meaning, the passage beginning ‘because there’ (tattha yasmā) was stated. There, in ‘the arising of knowledge, etc.’ (ñāṇuppādanādīsu), by the word ‘etc.’, he includes the calming of bodily formations, the experiencing of rapture, and so on. Some, however, say here that it is an inclusion of restraint and undertaking.

Kāyasaṅkhāranti assāsapassāsaṃ. So hi cittasamuṭṭhānopi samāno karajakāyappaṭibaddhavuttitāya tena saṅkharīyatīti kāyasaṅkhāroti vuccati. Yo pana “kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.102) evamāgato kāyasaṅkhāro cetanālakkhaṇo satipi dvārantaruppattiyaṃ yebhuyyavuttiyā, tabbahulavuttiyā ca kāyadvārena lakkhito, so idha nādhippeto. Passambhentotiādīsu pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ padaṃ purimassa purimassa atthavacanaṃ, tasmā passambhanaṃ nāma vūpasamanaṃ, tañca tathāpayoge asati uppajjanārahassa oḷārikassa kāyasaṅkhārassa payogasampattiyā anuppādananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tatrāti “oḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento”ti ettha. Apariggahitakāleti kammaṭṭhānassa anāraddhakāle, tato eva kāyacittānampi apariggahitakāle. “Nisīdati [V 1.0305] pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā”ti hi iminā kāyapariggaho, “parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti iminā cittapariggaho vutto. Tenevāha “kāyopi cittampi pariggahitā hontī”ti. Kāyoti karajakāyo. Sadarathāti sapariḷāhā, sā [M 1.0323] ca nesaṃ sadarathatā garubhāvena viya oḷārikatāya avinābhāvinīti āha “oḷārikā”ti. Balavatarāti sabalā thūlā. Santā hontīti cittaṃ tāvaṃ bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvena ekaggaṃ hutvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā pavattamānaṃ santaṃ hoti vūpasantaṃ, tato eva taṃsamuṭṭhānā rūpadhammā lahumudukammaññabhāvappattā, tadanuguṇatāya sesaṃ tisantatirūpanti evaṃ citte, kāye ca vūpasante pavattamāne tannissitā assāsapassāsā santasabhāvā anukkamena sukhumatarasukhumatamā hutvā pavattanti. Tena vuttaṃ “yadā panassa kāyopī”tiādi.

‘Bodily formation’ (kāyasaṅkhāra) means in-breaths and out-breaths. Indeed, although it arises from the mind, because its occurrence is bound up with the physical body, it is conditioned by it; thus it is called ‘bodily formation.’ However, the bodily formation mentioned in the phrase ‘bodily formation and verbal formation,’ which has the characteristic of volition—although it arises at another door, it is characterized by the body-door due to its general occurrence and its frequent occurrence there—is not intended here. In the phrase ‘calming’ (passambhento) and so on, each subsequent word explains the meaning of the preceding one. Therefore, ‘calming’ means pacification, and it should be understood as the non-arising—due to the accomplishment of the practice—of the gross bodily formation that is liable to arise when there is no such practice. ‘There’ (tatra) refers to the phrase ‘calming the gross bodily formation.’ ‘At the time when it is not taken up’ (apariggahitakāle) means at the time when the meditation subject has not been begun, and therefore at the time when body and mind are also not taken up. Indeed, by this phrase ‘sitting down, folding the legs, holding the body straight,’ the taking up of the body is stated, and by this phrase ‘establishing mindfulness at the forefront,’ the taking up of the mind is stated. Therefore he said, ‘both body and mind are taken up.’ ‘Body’ (kāya) refers to the physical body. ‘Afflicted’ (sadarathā) means with burning. And their state of being afflicted is inseparable from grossness, just as it is from heaviness; hence he said ‘gross’ (oḷārikā). ‘Stronger’ (balavatarā) means powerful, coarse. ‘They become tranquil’ (santā honti) means that first, the mind, due to the absence of external distraction, becomes unified, and having taken up the meditation subject, it proceeds tranquil and pacified. For that very reason, the material phenomena arising from it attain a state of lightness, softness, and workability. In accordance with that, the remaining three continuities of form also become tranquil and pacified. Thus, when the mind and body proceed in a pacified state, the in-breaths and out-breaths dependent on them, having a tranquil nature, proceed having become successively subtler and most subtle. Therefore, it is said, ‘but when his body too…’ and so on.

Ābhujanaṃ ābhogo, “passambhemī”ti paṭhamāvajjanā. Sammā anu anu āharaṇaṃ samannāhāro, tasmiṃyeva atthe aparāparaṃ pavattaāvajjanā. Tasseva atthassa manasi karaṇaṃ citte ṭhapanaṃ manasikāro. Vīmaṃsā paccavekkhaṇā.

Bending (ābhujana) is initial application of mind (ābhoga). ‘I will calm’ (passambhemi) is the first advertence. Properly and repeatedly bringing near is sustained application (samannāhāra), that is, the successively arising advertence to that very matter. The placing in the mind, the setting in the consciousness, of that very object is attention (manasikāra). Investigation (vīmaṃsā) is reflection (paccavekkhaṇā).

Sāraddheti sadarathe sapariḷāhe. Adhimattanti balavaṃ oḷārikaṃ. Liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. Kāyasaṅkhāroti hi adhippeto. “Adhimattaṃ hutvā pavattatī”ti kiriyāvisesanaṃ vā etaṃ. Sukhumanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kāyamhīti ettha “citte cā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

‘Agitated’ (sāraddhe) means with affliction, with burning. ‘Excessive’ (adhimattaṃ) means strong, coarse. This is stated with a change of gender. Indeed, ‘bodily formation’ (kāyasaṅkhāro) is intended. Or, this is an adverb: ‘it occurs excessively’ (adhimattaṃ hutvā pavattati). The same method applies here to ‘subtle’ (sukhumam). In ‘in the body’ (kāyamhi), it should be connected by bringing in ‘and in the mind’ (citte ca).

221. Paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya kariyamānaṃ dutiyajjhānassa nānāvajjanaṃ parikammaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ viya dūrasamussāritapaṭipakkhanti katvā taṃsamuṭṭhāno kāyasaṅkhāro paṭhamajjhāne ca dutiyajjhānūpacāre ca oḷārikoti sadiso vutto. Esa nayo sesūpacāradvayepi. Atha vā dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamāya paṭipajjato dukkhāpaṭipadādivasena kilamato yogino kāyakilamathacittūpaghātādivasena, vitakkādisaṅkhobhena ca sapariphandatāya cittappavattiyā dutiyajjhānādiupacāresu kāyasaṅkhārassa oḷārikatā veditabbā. Atisukhumoti aññattha labbhamāno kāyasaṅkhāro catutthajjhāne atikkantasukhumo. Sukhumabhāvopissa tattha natthi, kuto oḷārikatā appavattanato. Tenāha “appavattimeva pāpuṇātī”ti.

221. Having considered that the preliminary work for the second jhāna—which is the varied advertence performed after emerging from the first jhāna—has its opposing factors far removed like the first jhāna, the bodily formation arising from it is said to be coarse and similar in the first jhāna and in the access to the second jhāna. This is the method in the remaining two access states as well. Or alternatively, for a yogi who is practicing for the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, who becomes exhausted by way of difficult practice, etc., the coarseness of the bodily formation in the access to the second jhāna, etc., should be understood as due to the oscillation in the mind's occurrence, which is caused by way of bodily fatigue, mental affliction, etc., and by the agitation of thought, etc. ‘Exceedingly subtle’ (atisukhumo) means that the bodily formation, which is obtainable elsewhere, in the fourth jhāna transcends subtlety. Even its state of subtlety does not exist there; how then could there be coarseness? Because of its non-occurrence. Therefore, he said, ‘It reaches non-occurrence.’

Lābhissa [M 1.0324] sato anupubbasamāpattisamāpajjanavelaṃ, ekāsaneneva vā sabbesaṃ jhānānaṃ paṭilābhaṃ [V 1.0306] sandhāya majjhimabhāṇakā heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato uparūparijhānūpacārepi sukhumataraṃ icchanti. Tattha hi sopacārānaṃ jhānānaṃ uparūpari visesavantatā, santatā ca sambhaveyya, ekāvajjanūpacāraṃ vā sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Evañhi heṭṭhā vuttavādena imassa vādassa avirodho siddho bhinnavisayattā. Sabbesaññevāti ubhayesampi. Yasmā te sabbepi vuccamānena vidhinā passaddhimicchantiyeva. “Apariggahitakāle pavattakāyasaṅkhāro pariggahitakāle paṭippassambhatī”ti idaṃ sadisasantānatāya vuttaṃ. Na hi te eva oḷārikā assāsādayo sukhumā honti. Passambhanākāro pana nesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

The Middle Reciters, referring to the time of entering the successive attainments for one who has attained them, or to the attainment of all jhānas in a single sitting, desire what is subtler even in the access concentration of the higher and higher jhānas than in the lower and lower jhānas. For there, for those jhānas with their access concentration, the state of having distinction and the state of being tranquil would be possible in the higher and higher states. Or, this is said with reference to the access with a single advertence. Indeed, thus, by the doctrine previously stated, the non-contradiction of this doctrine is established because of having different objects. ‘All indeed’ refers to both teachers. Because all of them indeed desire tranquility by the method that will be described. This statement, ‘The bodily formation that occurs at the unapprehended time subsides at the apprehended time,’ is said because of having a similar continuity. For indeed, those same coarse in-breaths and so on do not become subtle. However, the manner of their subsiding has already been stated below.

Mahābhūtapariggahe sukhumoti catudhātumukhena vipassanābhinivesaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sakalarūpapariggahe sukhumo bhāvanāya uparūpari paṇītabhāvato. Tenevāha “rūpārūpapariggahe sukhumo”ti. Lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāti kalāpasammasanamāha. Nibbidānupassanato paṭṭhāya balavavipassanā. Tato oraṃ dubbalavipassanā. Pubbe vuttanayenāti “apariggahitakāle”tiādinā samathanaye vuttena nayena “apariggahe pavatto kāyasaṅkhāro mahābhūtapariggahe paṭippassambhatī”tiādinā vipassanānayepi paṭippassaddhi yojetabbāti vuttaṃ hoti.

The statement ‘subtle in the grasping of the great elements’ is said with reference to the initial application of insight by way of the four elements. It is subtle in the grasping of all material form because of the progressively sublime nature of the development. Therefore, he said, ‘subtle in the grasping of material and immaterial forms.’ By ‘insight that has characteristics as its object,’ he speaks of the comprehension of groups. Beginning from the contemplation of disenchantment, it is strong insight. Below that, it is weak insight. ‘By the method previously stated’ means that, by the method stated in the section on serenity beginning with ‘at the unapprehended time,’ calming should also be applied in the section on insight, beginning with ‘the bodily formation that occurs in the unapprehended state subsides in the grasping of the great elements.’ Thus it is said.

Assāti imassa “passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāra”nti padassa. Codanāsodhanāhīti anuyogaparihārehi. Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena.

‘Of this’ refers to this phrase: ‘calming the bodily formation.’ ‘With reproof and correction’ means with questioning and answering. ‘Thus’ means in the manner that is now about to be described.

Kathanti yaṃ idaṃ “passambhayaṃ…pe… sikkhatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.171) vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ kena pakārena kāyasaṅkhārassa passambhanaṃ, yogino ca sikkhanaṃ hotīti kathetukamyatāya pucchitvā kāyasaṅkhāre sarūpato, oḷārikasukhumato, vūpasamato, anuyogaparihārato ca dassetuṃ “katame kāyasaṅkhārā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha kāyikāti rūpakāye bhavā. Kāyapaṭibaddhāti kāyasannissitā. Kāye sati honti, asati na honti, tato eva te akāyasamuṭṭhānāpi kāyena saṅkharīyantīti kāyasaṅkhārā. Passambhentoti oḷārikoḷārikaṃ passambhento. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Oḷārikañhi kāyasaṅkhāraṃ avūpasantasabhāvaṃ sannisīdāpento [M 1.0325] “passambhento”ti vuccati, anuppādanirodhaṃ pāpento “nirodhento”ti, suṭṭhu santasabhāvaṃ nayanto “vūpasamento”ti.

‘How?’: Having asked out of a desire to explain how, in what manner, the calming of the bodily formation and the training of the yogī occurs—as stated in the passage ‘calming… one trains’—and in order to show the bodily formations in terms of their nature, their grossness and subtlety, their pacification, and in terms of questioning and answering, the passage beginning ‘What are the bodily formations?’ is commenced. Therein, ‘bodily’ means existing in the form-body. ‘Bound to the body’ means dependent on the body. They exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not. Therefore, even though they do not originate from the body, they are conditioned by the body, and thus are called ‘bodily formations.’ ‘Calming’ means calming the grosser and grosser bodily formation. The remaining two terms are synonyms of that very word. Indeed, one who causes a gross bodily formation, which has an unpacified nature, to settle down is called ‘one who calms’; one who brings it to the cessation that is non-arising is called ‘one who stops’; one who leads it to a thoroughly tranquil state is called ‘one who pacifies.’

Yathārūpehīti [V 1.0307] yādisehi. Kāyasaṅkhārehīti oḷārikehi kāyasaṅkhārehi. Ānamanāti abhimukhabhāvena kāyassa namanā. Vinamanāti visuṃ visuṃ passato namanā. Sannamanāti sabbato, suṭṭhu vā namanā. Paṇamanāti pacchato namanā. Iñjanādīni ānamanādīnaṃ vevacanāni, adhimattāni vā abhimukhaṃ calanādīni ānamanādayo, mandāni iñjanādayo. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti tathārūpaṃ ānamanādīnaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ oḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento. Tasmiṃ hi passambhite ānamanādayopi passambhitā eva honti.

‘Of such a kind’ means ‘of whatever sort.’ ‘With bodily formations’ means with gross bodily formations. ‘Bending forward’ is the bending of the body in a forward-facing manner. ‘Bending aside’ is bending to various sides separately. ‘Bending all around’ is bending everywhere, or bending thoroughly. ‘Bending back’ is bending backward. ‘Shaking’ and so forth are synonyms for ‘bending forward’ and so forth. Or, excessive movements such as moving forward are ‘bending forward’ and so forth, while slight movements are ‘shaking’ and so forth. ‘Calming the bodily formation’ means calming such a gross bodily formation that is the cause of bending forward and so forth. For when that is calmed, bending forward and so forth are also calmed.

Santaṃ sukhumanti yathārūpehi kāyasaṅkhārehi kāyassa aparipphandanahetūhi ānamanādayo na honti, tathārūpaṃ darathābhāvato santaṃ, anoḷārikatāya sukhumaṃ. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāranti sāmaññato ekaṃ katvā vadati. Atha vā pubbe oḷārikoḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambhento anukkamena kāyassa aparipphandanahetubhūte sukhumasukhumatare uppādetvā tepi paṭippassambhetvā paramasukhumatāya koṭippattaṃ yaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ paṭippassambheti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “santaṃ sukhumaṃ passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāra”nti.

‘Peaceful and subtle’: It refers to a bodily formation of such a kind that, being a cause for the body’s non-agitation, bending forward and so forth do not occur. Such a formation is peaceful due to the absence of distress, and subtle due to its non-coarseness. He speaks of ‘calming the bodily formation’ generally, making it one thing. Alternatively, one first calms the grosser and grosser bodily formation; then, having gradually generated subtler and subtler formations that have become the cause for the body’s non-agitation, and having calmed even those, one calms the bodily formation that has reached the peak on account of its extreme subtlety. It is with reference to that that it is said: ‘calming the peaceful, subtle bodily formation.’

Itītiādi codakavacanaṃ. Tattha itīti pakāratthe nipāto. Kirāti arucisūcane, evaṃ ceti attho. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – vuttappakārena yadi atisukhumampi kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhetīti. Evaṃ santeti evaṃ sati tayā vuttākāre labbhamāne. Vātūpaladdhiyāti vātassa upaladdhiyā. Ca-saddo samuccayattho, assāsādivātārammaṇassa cittassa pabhāvanā uppādanā pavattanā na hoti, te ca tena passambhetabbāti adhippāyo. Assāsapassāsānañca bhāvanāti oḷārike assāsapassāse bhāvanāya paṭippassambhetvā sukhumānaṃ tesaṃ pabhāvanā ca na hoti, ubhayesaṃ tesaṃ tena paṭippassambhetabbato. Ānāpānassatiyāti ānāpānārammaṇāya satiyā ca pavattanaṃ na hoti, ānāpānānaṃ abhāvato. Tato eva taṃsampayuttassa ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā uppādanāpi na hoti. Na hi kadāci ārammaṇena vinā sārammaṇadhammā sambhavanti. Na ca naṃ tanti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ[M 1.0326]. Taṃ vuttavidhānaṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā paññavanto na ceva samāpajjantipi tato na vuṭṭhahantipīti yojanā. Evaṃ codako sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvūpanayanaṃ passambhananti adhippāyena codeti.

‘Thus’ (iti) and so forth is the objector’s statement. Therein, ‘thus’ (iti) is a particle in the sense of manner. ‘Indeed’ (kira) indicates displeasure, meaning ‘if it were thus’. Indeed, this is the intention herein: ‘If, in the manner described, one calms even the very subtle bodily formation...’ ‘When it is thus’ (evaṃ sante) means ‘when it is so, when the state described by you is obtained.’ ‘By the obtaining of wind’ (vātūpaladdhiyā) means by the obtaining of wind. The word ‘and’ (ca) has the sense of conjunction; the arising, production, and continuation of the mind that has the wind of in-breaths and so forth as its object does not occur, and those are to be calmed by him—this is the intention. ‘And the development of in-breaths and out-breaths’ (assāsapassāsānañca bhāvanā) means that having calmed the gross in-breaths and out-breaths through development, the development of the subtle ones also does not occur, because both of them are to be calmed by him. ‘By mindfulness of breathing’ (ānāpānassatiyā) means that the continuation of mindfulness that has in-breaths and out-breaths as its object also does not occur, due to the absence of the in-breaths and out-breaths. For that very reason, the arising and production of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing associated with that mindfulness also does not occur. For phenomena that have an object never arise without an object. In ‘Nor that’ (na ca naṃ taṃ), herein ‘naṃ’ is merely a particle. The connection is thus: ‘Wise and discerning individuals neither enter that attainment with the described method, nor do they emerge from it.’ Thus, the objector objects with the intention that calming means bringing to a state of non-existence in every single way.

Puna iti kirātiādi yathāvuttāya codanāya vissajjanā. Tattha kirāti “yadī”ti etassa [V 1.0308] atthe nipāto. Iti kira sikkhati, mayā vuttākārena yadi sikkhatīti attho. Evaṃ santeti evaṃ passambhane sati. Pabhāvanā hotīti yadipi oḷārikā kāyasaṅkhārā paṭippassambhanti, sukhumā pana atthevāti anukkamena paramasukhumabhāvappattassa vasena nimittuppattiyā ānāpānassatiyā, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā ijjhatevāti adhippāyo.

Again, ‘thus, indeed’ (iti kira) and so forth is the reply to the aforesaid objection. Therein, ‘indeed’ (kira) is a particle in the sense of ‘if’ (yadi). ‘Thus, indeed, one trains’ (iti kira sikkhati) means ‘if one trains in the manner described by me.’ ‘When it is thus’ (evaṃ sante) means ‘when there is such calming.’ ‘Development occurs’ (pabhāvanā hoti) means that even though the gross bodily formations subside, the subtle ones, however, still exist. Therefore, by means of the bodily formations having gradually attained a state of extreme subtlety, and due to the arising of the counterpart sign, the development of mindfulness of breathing and of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing certainly succeeds—this is the intention.

Yathā kathaṃ viyāti yathāvuttavidhānaṃ taṃ kathaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ, atthi kiñci tadatthasampaṭipādane opammanti adhippāyo. Idāni opammaṃ dassetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha seyyathāpīti opammatthe nipāto. Kaṃseti kaṃsabhājane. Nimittanti nimittassa, tesaṃ saddānaṃ pavattākārassāti attho. Sāmiatthe hi idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Suggahitattāti suṭṭhu gahitattā. Sumanasikatattāti suṭṭhu citte ṭhapitattā. Sūpadhāritattāti sammadeva upadhāritattā sallakkhitattā. Sukhumakā saddāti anurave āha, ye appakā. Appattho hi ayaṃ ka-saddo. Sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpīti sukhumo saddova nimittaṃ sukhumasaddanimittaṃ, tadārammaṇatāyapi. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Kāmaṃ tadāsukhumāpi saddā niruddhā, saddanimittassa pana suggahitattā sukhumatarasaddanimittārammaṇabhāvenāpi cittaṃ pavattati. Ādito paṭṭhāya hi tassa tassa niruddhassa saddassa nimittaṃ avikkhittena cittena upadhārentassa anukkamena pariyosāne atisukhumasaddanimittampi ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittaṃ pavattateva. Cittaṃ na vikkhepaṃ gacchati tasmiṃ yathāupaṭṭhite nimitte samādhānasabbhāvato.

‘How is it like?’ (yathā kathaṃ viya) means ‘How is the aforesaid method to be seen? Is there any simile to accomplish that meaning?’—this is the intention. Now, to show a simile, ‘just as’ (seyyathāpi) and so forth is stated. Therein, ‘just as’ (seyyathāpi) is a particle in the sense of a simile. ‘In a bronze vessel’ (kaṃse) means in a bronze vessel. ‘The sign’ (nimittaṃ) means of the sign, that is, of the manner of occurrence of those sounds. Indeed, this is a term in the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive. ‘Because it is well-grasped’ (suggahitattā) means because it is thoroughly grasped. ‘Because it is well-attended to’ (sumanasikatattā) means because it is well-placed in the mind. ‘Because it is well-discerned’ (sūpadhāritattā) means because it is rightly discerned and marked. ‘Subtle sounds’ (sukhumakā saddā): he speaks of the reverberations, which are slight. Indeed, this suffix ‘ka’ has the meaning of ‘slight’. ‘Even by the state of having a subtle-sound-sign as object’ (sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpi) means: a subtle sound itself is the sign, a subtle-sound-sign; and even by the state of having that as an object. What is meant? Although at that time the subtle sounds have ceased, yet because the sign of the sound is well-grasped, the mind continues even through the state of having an even subtler sound-sign as its object. Indeed, for one who, from the beginning, discerns with an undistracted mind the sign of each sound that has ceased, the mind, having taken even the extremely subtle sound-sign as its object at the end, certainly continues. The mind does not go to distraction because of the presence of concentration on that counterpart sign as it has appeared.

Evaṃ santetiādi vuttassevatthassa nigamanavasena vuttaṃ. Tattha yassa suttapadassa saddhiṃ codanāsodhanāhi attho vutto, taṃ uddharitvā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānāni vibhāgato dassetuṃ “passambhaya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ vuttanayattā uttānameva.

‘When it is thus’ (evaṃ sante) and so forth is stated by way of concluding the meaning that has already been stated. Therein, having extracted that sutta passage whose meaning was stated together with the objection and clarification, ‘calming’ (passambhayaṃ) and so forth is stated in order to show the body, contemplation, and the foundations of mindfulness by way of their divisions. All of that is plain indeed, because the method has been stated.

222. Ādikammikassa [M 1.0327] kammaṭṭhānavasenāti samathakammaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vipassanaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pana itaracatukkesupi labbhateva. Etthāti paṭhamacatukke. Pañcasandhikanti pañcapabbaṃ, pañcabhāganti attho.

222. ‘By way of the meditation subject for a beginner’ (ādikammikassa kammaṭṭhānavasena) is stated with reference to the tranquility meditation subject. The insight meditation subject, however, is indeed obtainable also in the other tetrads. ‘Herein’ (ettha) means in the first tetrad. ‘Having five sections’ (pañcasandhikaṃ) means having five sections, having five parts.

Kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhananti kammaṭṭhānaganthassa uggaṇhanaṃ. Tadatthaparipucchā kammaṭṭhānassa paripucchanā[V 1.0309]. Atha vā ganthato, atthato ca kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanaṃ uggaho. Tattha saṃsayaparipucchanā paripucchā. Kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhānanti nimittupaṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa “evamidha nimittaṃ upaṭṭhātī”ti upadhāraṇaṃ, tathā kammaṭṭhānappanā “evaṃ jhānamappetī”ti. Kammaṭṭhānassa lakkhaṇanti gaṇanānubandhanāphusanānaṃ vasena bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ṭhapanāya sampatti, tato parampi vā sallakkhaṇādivasena matthakappattīti kammaṭṭhānasabhāvassa sallakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha “kammaṭṭhānasabhāvūpadhāraṇanti vuttaṃ hotī”ti.

‘Learning of the meditation subject’ (kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanaṃ) is the learning of the treatise on the meditation subject. Inquiring into its meaning is the ‘inquiry’ (paripucchā) concerning the meditation subject. Alternatively, the learning of the meditation subject both by way of the text and by way of the meaning is ‘learning’ (uggaho). Therein, inquiring about points of doubt is ‘inquiry’ (paripucchā). ‘Appearance of the meditation subject’ (kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhānaṃ) is the appearance of the sign; for one practicing the development thus, it is the discerning, ‘Thus the sign appears here.’ Similarly, ‘absorption in the meditation subject’ (kammaṭṭhānappanā) is discerning, ‘Thus one attains jhāna.’ ‘Characteristic of the meditation subject’ (kammaṭṭhānassa lakkhaṇaṃ) is the accomplishment of establishment or absorption by having made an effort in the development by means of counting, following, and touching; or, beyond that, the attainment of the culmination by means of discernment and so forth. Thus it is the proper marking of the nature of the meditation subject. Therefore, he said, ‘It is called the discerning of the nature of the meditation subject.’

Attanāpi na kilamati odhiso kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanato. Tato eva ācariyampi na viheseti dhammādhikaraṇampi bhāvanāya matthakaṃ pāpanato. Tasmāti taṃ nimittaṃ attano akilamanaācariyāvihesanahetu. Thokanti thokaṃ thokaṃ. Uggahetabbato uggaho, sabbopi kammaṭṭhānavidhi, na pubbe vuttauggahamattaṃ. Ācariyato uggaho ācariyuggaho, tato. Ekapadampīti ekakoṭṭhāsampi.

Because of learning the meditation subject in sections, one does not tire oneself. For that very reason, one does not trouble the teacher. Alternatively, on account of the teaching, one does not trouble the teacher, because one brings the development to its culmination. ‘Therefore’ (tasmā) means for that reason, for the reason of not tiring oneself and not troubling the teacher. ‘A little’ (thokaṃ) means little by little. Because it is to be learned, it is called ‘learning’ (uggaho); it is the entire method of the meditation subject, not merely the learning mentioned before. Learning from a teacher is ‘learning from a teacher’ (ācariyuggaho); from that. ‘Even one part’ (ekapadampi) means even one portion.

223. Anuvahanāti assāsapassāsānaṃ anugamanavasena satiyā nirantaraṃ anupavattanā. Phusanāti assāsapassāse gaṇentassa gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā te satiyā anubandhantassa yathā appanā hoti, tathā cittaṃ ṭhapentassa ca nāsikaggādiṭṭhānassa nesaṃ phusanā. Yasmā pana gaṇanādivasena viya phusanāvasena visuṃ manasikāro natthi, phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva gaṇanādi kātabbanti dassetuṃ idha phusanāgahaṇanti dīpento “phusanāti phuṭṭhaṭṭhāna”nti āha. Ṭhapanāti samādhānaṃ. Taṃ hi sammadeva ārammaṇe cittassa ādhānaṃ ṭhapanaṃ hoti. Tathā hi samādhi “cittassa ṭhiti saṇṭhitī”ti (dha. sa. 11.15) niddiṭṭho. Samādhippadhānā pana appanāti āha “ṭhapanāti appanā”ti. Aniccatādīnaṃ sallakkhaṇato sallakkhaṇā vipassanā. Pavattato, nimittato ca vinivaṭṭanato vivaṭṭanā nāma maggo. Sakalasaṃkilesapaṭippassaddhibhāvato [M 1.0328] sabbaso suddhīti pārisuddhi phalaṃ. Tesanti vivaṭṭanāpārisuddhīnaṃ. Paṭipassanāti paṭi paṭi dassanaṃ pekkhanaṃ. Tenāha “paccavekkhaṇā”ti.

223. ‘Following’ (anuvahanā) is the uninterrupted continuation of mindfulness by way of tracking the in-breaths and out-breaths. ‘Touching’ (phusanā) is the touching of the in-breaths and out-breaths at the location of the nose-tip and so forth, for one who, while counting the in-breaths and out-breaths, withdraws from counting and follows them with mindfulness, and for one who establishes the mind in such a way that absorption occurs. However, since there is no separate attention by way of touching, as there is by way of counting and so forth, in order to show that counting and so forth should be done only at the very place that is touched, he illuminates this by saying: ‘Touching’ (phusanā) means ‘the place touched’ (phuṭṭhaṭṭhāna). ‘Establishing’ (ṭhapanā) is proper placement (samādhāna). For that placing of the mind properly on an object is ‘establishing’ (ṭhapana). Indeed, concentration (samādhi) is pointed out as ‘the steadiness of the mind, its stability’ (Dhs 11, 15). However, since absorption (appanā) has concentration as its chief component, he says: ‘Establishing’ (ṭhapanā) means ‘absorption’ (appanā). By reason of discerning impermanence and so forth, insight (vipassanā) is ‘discerning’ (sallakkhaṇā). By reason of turning away from occurrence and from the sign, the path (maggo) is named ‘turning away’ (vivaṭṭanā). By reason of being the state of complete pacification of all defilements, the fruit (phala) is ‘complete purity’ (pārisuddhi). ‘Of these’ (tesaṃ) refers to ‘turning away’ and ‘complete purity’. ‘Reviewing’ (paṭipassanā) is seeing again and again, observing. Therefore, he says: ‘reviewing’ (paccavekkhaṇā).

Khaṇḍanti ekaṃ tīṇi pañcāti evaṃ gaṇanāya khaṇḍanaṃ. Okāseti gaṇanavidhiṃ sandhāyāha. Gaṇananissitova na kammaṭṭhānanissito. “Sikhāppattaṃ nu kho”ti idaṃ cirataraṃ gaṇanāya manasi karontassa vasena vuttaṃ. So hi tathā laddhaṃ avikkhepamattaṃ nissāya evaṃ maññeyya[V 1.0310]. “Assāsapassāsesu yo upaṭṭhāti, taṃ gahetvā”ti idaṃ assāsapassāsesu yassa ekova paṭhamaṃ upaṭṭhāti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, yassa pana ubhopi upaṭṭhahanti, tena ubhayampi gahetvā gaṇetabbaṃ. “Yo upaṭṭhātī”ti iminā ca dvīsu nāsāpuṭavātesu yo pākaṭataro upaṭṭhāti, so gahetabboti ayampi attho dīpitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pavattamānaṃ pavattamānanti āmeḍitavacanena nirantaraṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ upalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Evanti vuttappakārena upalakkhetvā vāti attho. Pākaṭā honti gaṇanāvasena bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato.

‘Breaking’ (khaṇḍa) is the breaking of the counting, thus: ‘one, three, five’. He says ‘gives an opportunity’ (okāseti) with reference to the method of counting. One is dependent on counting, not dependent on the meditation subject. This statement, “Has it reached the peak?” is said by way of one who attends with counting for a very long time. For, relying on the mere non-distraction thus obtained, one might think in this way. This statement, “Among the in-breaths and out-breaths, taking up whichever appears,” is said with reference to one for whom only one appears first among the in-breaths and out-breaths. But for one for whom both appear, both should be taken up and counted. And by this phrase, “whichever appears,” it should be understood that this meaning is also explained: whichever of the two nostril-winds appears more evident, that one should be taken up. With the repetitive phrase, “occurring, occurring,” he shows the uninterrupted observation of the in-breaths and out-breaths. ‘Thus’ (evaṃ) means ‘having observed in the manner described’. They become evident by way of counting, due to the absence of external distraction.

Palighassa parivattanaṃ, taṃ yattha nikkhipanti, so palighatthambho. Tiyāmarattinti accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Purimanayenāti sīghagaṇanāya, gopālakagaṇanāyāti attho. Eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañcāti gaṇanāvidhidassanaṃ. Tasmā aṭṭhātiādīsupi ekato paṭṭhāyeva paccekaṃ aṭṭhādīni pāpetabbāni. Sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gaṇetabbameva. Kasmāti tattha kāraṇaṃ, nidassanañca dasseti “gaṇanapaṭibaddhe hī”tiādinā. Tattha arīyati tena nāvāti arittaṃ, pājanadaṇḍo. Arittena upatthambhanaṃ arittupatthambhanaṃ, tassa vasena.

The ring for the bar (paligha); the post in which they place it is the bar-post (palighatthambha). The phrase ‘for the three watches of the night’ (tiyāmarattiṃ) is a usage in the sense of continuous connection. ‘By the former method’ means by quick counting, by the cowherd’s counting. ‘One, two, three, four, five’ is a demonstration of the counting method. Therefore, also in the cases of ‘eight’ and so on, starting from one itself, each should be made to reach eight and so on respectively. One should indeed count very quickly. Why? There, he shows the reason and an illustration with the words beginning, ‘For it is connected with counting’ (gaṇanapaṭibaddhe hī). There, ‘the boat is propelled by that’ (arīyati tena nāvā), therefore it is an ‘oar’ (arittaṃ), a propelling pole (pājanadaṇḍo). Supporting with the oar is ‘support of the oar’ (arittupatthambhanaṃ); by means of that.

Nippariyāyato nirantarappavatti nāma ṭhapanāyamevāti āha “nirantaraṃ pavattaṃ viyā”ti. Anto pavisantaṃ vātaṃ manasi karonto anto cittaṃ paveseti nāma. Bahi cittanīharaṇepi eseva nayo. Vātabbhāhatanti abbhantaragataṃ vātaṃ bahulaṃ manasi karontassa vātena taṃ ṭhānaṃ abbhāhataṃ viya, medena pūritaṃ viya ca hoti, tathā upaṭṭhāti. Nīharato phuṭṭhokāsaṃ [M 1.0329] muñcitvā, tathā pana nīharato vātassa gatisamannesanamukhena nānārammaṇesu cittaṃ vidhāvatīti āha “puthuttārammaṇe cittaṃ vikkhipatī”ti.

Because what is called uninterrupted occurrence, in the direct sense, is only in ‘establishing’ (ṭhapanā), he said, “as if occurring uninterruptedly.” One who attends to the wind entering inside is said to make the mind enter inside. This same method applies also to leading the mind outside. ‘Struck by wind’ (vātabbhāhata) means that for one who frequently attends to the wind that has gone inside, that place is as if struck by the wind and as if filled with fat; it appears in that way. However, for one who leads the mind out by abandoning the touched spot and seeking the path of the wind, the mind runs about among various objects. Therefore, he said, “it scatters the mind among various objects.”

Etanti etaṃ assāsapassāsajātaṃ.

‘This’ (etaṃ) means this collection of in-breaths and out-breaths.

224. Anugamananti pavattapavattānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena satiyā anu anu pavattanaṃ anugacchanaṃ. Tenevāha “tañca kho na ādimajjhapariyosānānugamanavasenā”ti. Nābhi ādi tattha paṭhamaṃ uppajjanato. Paṭhamuppattivasena hi idha ādicintā, na uppattimattavasena. Tathā hi te nābhito paṭṭhāya yāva nāsikaggā sabbattha uppajjanteva. Yattha yattha ca uppajjanti, tattha tattheva bhijjanti dhammānaṃ gamanābhāvato. Yathāpaccayaṃ pana desantaruppattiyaṃ [V 1.0311] gatisamaññā. Hadayaṃ majjhanti hadayasamīpaṃ tassa uparibhāgo majjhaṃ. Nāsikaggaṃ pariyosānanti nāsikaṭṭhānaṃ tassa pariyosānaṃ assāsapassāsasamaññāya tadavadhibhāvato. Tathā hete “cittasamuṭṭhānā”ti vuttā, na ca bahiddhā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ sambhavo atthi. Tenāha “abbhantaraṃ pavisanavātassa nāsikaggaṃ ādī”ti. Pavisananikkhamanapariyāyo pana taṃsadisavasena vuttoti veditabbo. Vikkhepagatanti vikkhepaṃ upagataṃ, vikkhittaṃ asamāhitanti attho. Sāraddhāyāti sadarathabhāvāya. Iñjanāyāti kammaṭṭhānamanasikārassa calanāya.

224. ‘Following’ (anugamana) is the following in sequence, the repeated occurrence of mindfulness, by way of making the in-breaths and out-breaths that occur again and again an object. For that reason, he said, “And that, indeed, is not by way of following the beginning, middle, and end.” The navel is the beginning, because of its first arising there. For here, the thought of ‘beginning’ is by way of the first arising, not by way of mere arising. Indeed, they arise everywhere from the navel up to the tip of the nose. And wherever they arise, right there they cease, because of the non-traveling of phenomena. However, according to conditions, in their arising in another place, there is the designation ‘going’. The heart is the middle. The tip of the nose is the end, meaning the location of the nose is its end, because that is the boundary for the designation ‘in-breath and out-breath’. Thus indeed, these are said to be ‘mind-originated’, and there is no arising of mind-originated matter externally. Therefore, he said, “For the wind entering inside, the nose-tip is the beginning.” However, the term ‘entering and exiting’ should be understood as being spoken by way of similarity to that. ‘Gone to distraction’ (vikkhepagata) means gone to distraction, scattered, unconcentrated. ‘For agitation’ (sāraddhāya) means for the state of distress. ‘For stirring’ (iñjanāya) means for the shaking of the attention to the meditation subject.

Vikkhepagatena cittenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe vā. Sāraddhāti sadarathā. Iñjitāti iñjanakā calanakā. Tathā phanditā.

The phrase ‘with a mind gone to distraction’ (vikkhepagatena cittena) is an instrumental in the sense of cause, or in the sense of describing a state. ‘Agitated’ (sāraddhā) means distressed. ‘Stirred’ (iñjitā) means shaking, moving. Similarly, ‘throbbing’ (phanditā).

Ādimajjhapariyosānavasenāti ādimajjhapariyosānānugamanavasena na manasi kātabbanti sambandho. “Anubandhanāya manasi karontena phusanāvasena ca ṭhapanāvasena ca manasi kātabba”nti yenādhippāyena vuttaṃ, taṃ vivarituṃ “gaṇanānubandhanāvasena viyā”tiādimāha. Tattha visuṃ manasikāro natthīti gaṇanāya, anubandhanāya ca vinā yathākkamaṃ kevalaṃ phusanāvasena, ṭhapanāvasena ca kammaṭṭhānamanasikāro natthi. Nanu phusanāya vinā ṭhapanāya viya, phusanāya vinā gaṇanāyapi manasikāro natthiyeva? Yadipi natthi, gaṇanā pana yathā kammaṭṭhānamanasikārassa mūlabhāvato padhānabhāvena [M 1.0330] gahetabbā, evaṃ anubandhanā ṭhapanāya, tāya vinā ṭhapanāya asambhavato. Tasmā satipi phusanāya nānantarikabhāve gaṇanānubandhanā eva mūlabhāvato padhānabhāvena gahetvā itarāsaṃ tadabhāvaṃ dassento āha “gaṇanānubandhanāvasena viya hi phusanāṭhapanāvasena visuṃ manasikāro natthī”ti. Yadi evaṃ tā kasmā uddese visuṃ gahitāti āha “phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyevā”tiādi. Tattha “phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva gaṇento”ti iminā gaṇanāya phusanā aṅganti dasseti. Tenāha “gaṇanāya ca phusanāya ca manasi karotī”ti. Tatthevāti phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva. Teti assāsapassāse. Satiyā anubandhantoti gaṇanāvīthiṃ anugantvā satiyā nibandhanto, phuṭṭhokāseyeva te nirantaraṃ upadhārentoti attho. Appanāvasena cittaṃ ṭhapentoti yathā appanā hoti, evaṃ yathāupaṭṭhite nimitte cittaṃ ṭhapento samādahanto. Anubandhanāya cātiādīsu anubandhanāya ca phusanāya ca ṭhapanāya ca manasi karotīti vuccatīti yojanā. Svāyamatthoti yvāyaṃ “phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva gaṇento, tattheva gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā [V 1.0312] te satiyā anubandhanto”ti ca vutto, so ayamattho. Yā accantāya na minoti na vinicchināti, sā mānassa samīpeti upamā yathā “goṇo viya gavayo”ti.

“By way of beginning, middle, and end”: the connection is that one should not attend by way of following the beginning, middle, and end. To explain the intended meaning of the statement, “When attending by way of connecting, one should attend by way of touching and by way of fixing,” he said, “as by way of counting and connecting,” and so on. Therein, “there is no separate attention” means that without counting and connecting, there is no attention to the meditation subject merely by way of touching and by way of fixing, respectively. Is it not so that just as there is no attention by fixing without touching, there is also no attention by counting without touching? Although there is not, counting, however, should be taken as primary because it is the root of attention to the meditation subject; similarly, connecting is for fixing, because without it, fixing is impossible. Therefore, even though touching has the nature of immediacy, taking only counting and connecting as primary because they are the root, and showing the absence of that root-nature in the others, he said, “For there is no separate attention by way of touching and fixing as there is by way of counting and connecting.” If so, why are they taken separately in the summary exposition? He said, “Only at the place where it is touched,” and so on. Therein, by “counting only at the place where it is touched,” it is shown that touching is a component of counting. Therefore, he said, “one attends by way of counting and by way of touching.” “There itself” means only at the place where it is touched. “Them” refers to the in-breaths and out-breaths. “Connecting with mindfulness” means: having followed the path of counting, one binds with mindfulness, continuously paying attention to them only at the place of contact; this is the meaning. “Fixing the mind by way of absorption” means: placing and composing the mind on the counterpart sign as it has appeared, in such a way that absorption occurs. In “by way of connecting,” etc., the construction is that it is said one attends by way of connecting, by way of touching, and by way of fixing. “This is that meaning”: this is the meaning of what was said: “Counting only at the place where it is touched, and having withdrawn the counting there itself, connecting them with mindfulness.” That which does not completely measure or decide is near that which measures; this is a simile, just as in “a gavaya is like an ox.”

225. Paṅguḷoti pīṭhasappī. Dolā pekholo. Kīḷatanti kīḷantānaṃ. Mātāputtānanti attano bhariyāya, puttassa ca. Ubho koṭiyoti āgacchantassa purimakoṭiṃ, gacchantassa pacchimakoṭinti dvepi koṭiyo. Majjhanti dolāphalakasseva majjhaṃ. Upanibandhanathambho viyāti upanibandhanathambho, nāsikaggaṃ, mukhanimittaṃ vā, tassa mūle samīpe ṭhatvā. Kathaṃ ṭhatvā? Satiyā vasena. Satiñhi tattha sūpaṭṭhitaṃ karonto yogāvacaro tattha ṭhito nāma hoti, avayavadhammena samudāyassa apadisitabbato. Nimitteti nāsikaggādinimitte. Satiyā nisīdantoti sativasena nisīdanto. “Satiñhi tatthā”tiādinā ṭhāne viya vattabbaṃ. Tatthāti phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāne.

225. “Paṅguḷo” means a cripple, one who moves by means of a stool. “Dolā” is a swing (pekholo). “Kīḷataṃ” means of those who are playing. “Mātāputtānaṃ” means of one's own wife and son. “Ubho koṭiyo” (both ends) means both ends: the front end of the approaching swing and the back end of the departing swing. “Majjhaṃ” (the middle) means the very middle of the swing-plank. “Upanibandhanathambho viya” (like a tying-post) means it is a tying-post, or the tip of the nose, or the sign of the upper lip; standing near its base. How standing? By way of mindfulness. For a yogi who makes mindfulness well-established there is said to be ‘standing’ there, because the whole (the person) is to be indicated by a part (the quality). “Nimitte” (in the sign) means in the sign such as the tip of the nose. “Satiyā nisīdanto” (sitting with mindfulness) means sitting by way of mindfulness. It should be stated as in the case of ‘standing’, beginning with “For mindfulness there…”. “Tattha” (there) means at the place where it is touched.

226. Teti [M 1.0331] nagarassa antobahigatā manussā, tesaṃ saṅgahā ca hatthagatā.

226. “Te” (they) means: the people who are inside and outside the city, and their possessions that are in their hands.

227. Ādito paṭṭhāyāti upameyyatthadassanato paṭṭhāya. Gāthāyaṃ nimittanti upanibandhanānimittaṃ. Anārammaṇamekacittassāti ekassa cittassa na ārammaṇaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ na hontīti attho. Ajānato ca tayo dhammeti nimittaṃ assāso passāsoti ime tayo dhamme ārammaṇakaraṇavasena avindantassa. Ca-saddo byatireke. Bhāvanāti ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā. Nupalabbhatīti na upalabbhati na sijjhatīti ayaṃ codanāgāthāya attho, dutiyā pana parihāragāthā suviññeyyāva.

227. “Ādito paṭṭhāya” (from the beginning) means starting from the statement that shows the meaning of the object of comparison. In the verse, “nimittaṃ” (sign) means the sign for mindfulness which is the cause for binding the mind to the object. “Anārammaṇam ekacittassa” (not an object for a single mind) means: they are not the object of a single mind; they do not become objects, this is the meaning. “Ajānato ca tayo dhamme” (and for one not knowing the three things) means for one who does not get these three things—the sign, the in-breath, and the out-breath—by way of making them an object. The word “ca” is in the sense of contrast. “Bhāvanā” (development) means the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. “Na upalabbhati” (is not obtained) means it is not obtained, it is not accomplished. This is the meaning of the verse of objection. The second verse, however, the verse of reply, is very easy to understand.

Kathanti tāsaṃ atthaṃ vivarituṃ kathetukamyatāpucchā. Ime tayo dhammātiādīsu padayojanāya saddhiṃ ayamatthaniddeso – ime nimittādayo tayo dhammā ekacittassa kathaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na honti, tathāpi na cime na ca ime tayo dhammā aviditā honti, kathaṃ na ca honti aviditā? Tesañhi aviditatte cittañca kathaṃ vikkhepaṃ na gacchati, padhānañca bhāvanāya nipphādakaṃ vīriyañca kathaṃ paññāyati, nīvaraṇānaṃ vikkhambhakaṃ sammadeva samādhānāvahaṃ bhāvanānuyogasaṅkhātaṃ payogañca yogī kathaṃ sādheti, uparūpari lokiyalokuttarañca visesaṃ kathamadhigacchatīti.

“Kathaṃ” (How?) is a question expressing the desire to speak in order to explain their meaning. In “these three things,” etc., together with the syntactical connection of the words, this is the detailed explanation of the meaning: How are these three things, beginning with the sign, not the objects of a single mind? Even so, it is not that these three things are unknown. How are they not unknown? For if they were unknown, how would the mind not go to distraction? And how would the striving, the effort that accomplishes the development, be known? And how does the yogi accomplish the application—called devotion to development—which suppresses the hindrances and rightly brings about concentration? And how would one attain, higher and higher, the mundane and supramundane distinction?

Idāni [V 1.0313] tamatthaṃ kakacūpamāya sādhetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhūmibhāgassa visamatāya cañcale rukkhe chedanakiriyā na sukarā siyā, tathā ca sati kakacadantagati dubbiññeyyāti āha “same bhūmibhāge”ti. Kakacenāti khuddakena kharapattena. Tenāha “puriso”ti. Phuṭṭhakakacadantānanti phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhakakacadantānaṃ vasena. Tena kakacadantehi phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva purisassa satiyā upaṭṭhānaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “na āgate vā gate vā kakacadante manasi karotī”ti. Kakacassa ākaḍḍhanakāle purisābhimukhaṃ pavattā āgatā. Pellanakāle tato vigatā “gatā”ti vuttā. Na ca āgatā vā gatā vā kakacadantā aviditā honti sabbattha satiyā upaṭṭhitattā chinditabbaṭṭhānaṃ aphusitvā gacchantānaṃ, āgacchantānañca kakacadantānaṃ abhāvato. Padhānanti rukkhassa chedanavīriyaṃ[M 1.0332]. Payoganti tasseva chedanakiriyaṃ. Visesanti anekabhāvāpādanaṃ, tena ca sādhetabbaṃ payojanavisesaṃ.

Now, to establish that meaning with the saw simile, the passage beginning ‘Just as…’ was stated. Because of the unevenness of the ground, when the log is unstable, the act of cutting would not be easy, and thus the movement of the saw’s teeth would be difficult to discern. Hence, it is said, ‘on level ground.’ ‘With a saw’ means with a small, rough-bladed saw. Therefore, He says, ‘a person.’ ‘Of the touched saw teeth’ is by way of the saw teeth that have repeatedly touched. Thus, it shows the establishment of the person’s mindfulness precisely at the place repeatedly touched by the saw’s teeth. Therefore, He says, ‘he does not attend to the saw teeth that are coming or going.’ When the saw is pulled, the teeth moving toward the person are ‘coming.’ When pushed, the teeth moving away from him are called ‘going.’ And the coming or going saw teeth are not unknown, both because mindfulness is established at every point of contact and because there are no saw teeth that go and come without touching the spot to be cut. ‘Striving’ is the energy for cutting the log. ‘Application’ is the very act of cutting it. ‘Distinction’ is the bringing into being of many pieces, and the special purpose to be accomplished thereby.

Yathā rukkhotiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Upanibandhati ārammaṇe cittaṃ etāyāti sati upanibandhanā nāma, tassā assāsapassāsānaṃ sallakkhaṇassa nimittanti upanibandhanānimittaṃ, nāsikaggaṃ, mukhanimittaṃ vā. Evamevāti yathāpi so puriso kakacena rukkhaṃ chindanto āgatagate kakacadante amanasikarontopi phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva satiyā upaṭṭhapanena āgatagate kakacadante jānāti, suttapadañca avirajjhanto atthakiccaṃ sādheti, evameva. Nāsikagge mukhanimitteti dīghanāsiko nāsikagge itaro mukhaṃ dasanaṃ nimīyati chādīyati etenāti mukhanimittanti laddhanāme uttaroṭṭhe.

The passage beginning ‘As with a log…’ is the connection with the simile. ‘By this, the mind is bound to the object’; thus, mindfulness is called ‘binding’. The sign for marking the in-breaths and out-breaths of that mindfulness is the ‘binding-sign,’ namely, the tip of the nose or the mouth-sign. ‘Just so’ means: just as that person, while cutting a log with a saw, though not attending to the coming and going saw-teeth, knows the coming and going saw-teeth by establishing mindfulness precisely at the place of repeated contact, and accomplishes his required task without deviating from the marked line; just so... ‘At the tip of the nose or at the mouth-sign’: a person with a long nose [focuses] at the tip of the nose; another [person with a short nose focuses] on the upper lip, which has received the name ‘mouth-sign’ because by this the mouth or teeth are covered or concealed.

Idaṃ padhānanti yena vīriyārambhena āraddhavīriyassa yogino kāyopi cittampi kammaniyaṃ bhāvanākammakkhamaṃ bhāvanākammayoggaṃ hoti, idaṃ vīriyaṃ padhānanti phalena hetuṃ dasseti. Upakkilesā pahīyantīti cittassa upakkilesabhūtāni nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanavasena pahīyanti.
