Vitakkā vūpasamantīti tato eva kāmavitakkādayo micchāvitakkā upasamaṃ gacchanti, nīvaraṇappahānena vā paṭhamajjhānādhigamaṃ dassetvā vitakkavūpasamāpadesena dutiyajjhānādīnamadhigamamāha. Ayaṃ payogoti ayaṃ jhānādhigamassa hetubhūto kammaṭṭhānānuyogo payogo. Saṃyojanā pahīyantīti dasapi saṃyojanāni maggapaṭipāṭiyā samucchedavasena pahīyanti. Anusayā byantī hontīti tathā sattapi anusayā anuppattidhammatāpādanena bhaṅgamattassapi anavasesato vigatantā honti. Ettha ca saṃyojanappahānaṃ nāma anusayanirodheneva hoti, pahīnesu ca [V 1.0314] saṃyojanesu anusayānaṃ lesopi na bhavissatīti ca dassanatthaṃ “saṃyojanā pahīyanti anusayā byantī hontī”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ visesoti imaṃ samādhiṃ nissāya anukkamena labbhamāno ayaṃ saṃyojanappahānādiko imassa samādhissa visesoti attho.

‘This is striving’: by which arising of energy the body and mind of a yogī who has aroused energy become workable, suitable for meditation practice; this energy is called ‘striving.’ Thus, it shows the cause by way of the effect. ‘Defilements are abandoned’: the hindrances, which are defilements of the mind, are abandoned by way of suppression. ‘Thoughts are stilled’: thereby, wrong thoughts such as sensual thought are stilled. Or, having shown the attainment of the first jhāna through the abandoning of the hindrances, by the indication of the stilling of thought, it speaks of the attainment of the second jhāna and so on. ‘This is application’: this devotion to the meditation subject, which is the cause for the attainment of jhāna, is ‘application.’ ‘Fetters are abandoned’: all ten fetters are abandoned in sequence by the path, by way of eradication. ‘Latent tendencies come to an end’: similarly, the seven latent tendencies, by being brought to a state of non-arising, come to an end without any remainder, not even a moment of their breaking. And herein, the abandoning of the fetters occurs only through the cessation of the latent tendencies. And to show that when the fetters are abandoned, not even a slight trace of the latent tendencies will remain, it was said, ‘Fetters are abandoned, latent tendencies come to an end.’ ‘This is the distinction’: this attainment, beginning with the abandoning of the fetters, which is obtained sequentially by relying on this concentration, is the distinction of this concentration. This is the meaning.

Yassāti yena. Anupubbanti anukkamena. Paricitāti pariciṇṇā. Ayaṃ hettha saṅkhepattho – ānāpānassati yathā buddhena bhagavatā desitā[M 1.0333], tatheva yena dīgharassapajānanādividhinā anupubbaṃ paricitā suṭṭhu bhāvitā, tato eva paripuṇṇā soḷasannaṃ vatthūnaṃ pāripūriyā sabbaso puṇṇā. So bhikkhu imaṃ attano khandhādilokaṃ paññobhāsena pabhāseti. Yathā kiṃ abbhā muttova candimā abbhupakkilesavimutto candimā tārakarājā viyāti.

‘Yassa’ means ‘by whom.’ ‘Anupubbaṃ’ means ‘sequentially.’ ‘Paricitā’ means ‘practiced.’ Herein, this is the brief meaning: by whomever mindfulness of breathing, just as it was taught by the Buddha, the Blessed One, has been sequentially practiced and well-developed by the method beginning with knowing the long and short breaths, because of that it is perfected through the completion of the sixteen bases, and is completely fulfilled. That bhikkhu illuminates this world of his own, beginning with the aggregates, with the light of wisdom. Like what? Just like the moon freed from clouds, like the moon, the king of stars, freed from the defilement of clouds.

Idhāti kakacūpamāyaṃ. Assāti yogino. Idhāti vā imasmiṃ ṭhāne. Assāti upamābhūtassa kakacassa. Āgatagatavasena yathā tassa purisassa amanasikāro, evaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ āgatagatavasena amanasikāramattameva payojanaṃ.

‘Idha’ means ‘in the saw simile.’ ‘Assa’ means ‘of the yogī.’ Or, ‘Idha’ means ‘in this place.’ ‘Assa’ means ‘of the saw which is the simile.’ Just as that person has non-attention regarding the coming and going [of the saw teeth], so too, regarding the coming and going of the in-breaths and out-breaths, mere non-attention is the purpose.

228. Nimittanti paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Avasesajhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitāti appanāvitakkādiavasesajhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitāti vadanti, vicārādīti pana vattabbaṃ nippariyāyena vitakkassa appanābhāvato. So hi pāḷiyaṃ “appanā byappanā”ti (dha. sa. 7) niddiṭṭho, taṃsampayogato vā yasmā jhānaṃ “appanā”ti aṭṭhakathāvohāro, jhānaṅgesu ca samādhi padhānaṃ, tasmā taṃ “appanā”ti dassento “avasesajhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitā appanāsaṅkhātā ṭhapanā ca sampajjatī”ti āha. Kassaci pana gaṇanāvaseneva manasikārakālato pabhutīti ettha “anukkamato…pe… laṅghanākārappattaṃ viya hotī”ti ettako gantho parihīno.

228. ‘The sign’ means the counterpart sign. Regarding ‘adorned with the remaining jhāna factors,’ they say it means ‘adorned with the remaining jhāna factors beginning with applied thought.’ However, it should be said ‘sustained thought and so on,’ because applied thought, in the direct sense, is not absorption. For in the Pāḷi it is pointed out as ‘placing, applying.’ Or, because jhāna is spoken of in the commentaries as ‘absorption’ due to its association with that applied thought, and because among the jhāna factors concentration is chief, therefore, showing that concentration to be ‘absorption,’ He said, ‘adorned with the remaining jhāna factors, the placement called absorption is also accomplished.’ However, in the passage ‘For some, from the time of attention by way of counting,’ this much of the text is missing: ‘sequentially… as if having reached the state of leaping.’

Sāraddhakāyassa kassaci puggalassa. Onamati paṭṭikādīnaṃ palambanena. Vikūjatīti saddaṃ karoti. Gattānisadakapparādīnaṃ sandhiṭṭhānesu valiṃ gaṇhāti tattha tattha valitaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā sāraddhakāyo garuko hotīti kāyadarathavūpasamena saddhiṃ sijjhamāno oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodho byatirekamukhena tassa sādhanaṃ viya vutto. Oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodhavasenāti anvayavasena tadatthasādhanaṃ. Tattha kāyadarathe vūpasanteti cittajarūpānaṃ lahumudukammaññabhāvena yo sesatisantatirūpānampi lahuādibhāvo, so idha kāyassa lahubhāvoti [V 1.0315] adhippeto. Svāyaṃ yasmā cittassa lahuādibhāvena vinā natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “kāyopi cittampi lahukaṃ hotī”ti.

For a certain person whose body is agitated and weary. It bends down by the hanging of mats, straps, planks, and so on. ‘Vikūjati’ means it makes a creaking sound. It becomes wrinkled in the joints of the limbs, buttocks, elbows, and so on. Why? Because an agitated and weary body is heavy. Thus, the cessation of coarse in-and-out breathing, which is accomplished together with the calming of bodily distress, is spoken of as if it were the means of accomplishing that calming by way of the negative method. The phrase ‘by means of the cessation of coarse in-and-out breathing’ accomplishes that meaning by way of the positive method. Herein, by the phrase ‘when bodily distress is calmed,’ the lightness of the body intended here is that lightness, etc., of the remaining three continuities of matter which arises due to the lightness, softness, and wieldiness of mind-born matter. Since this lightness of body does not exist without the lightness, etc., of the mind, therefore it is said, ‘Both the body and the mind become light.’

Oḷārike [M 1.0334] assāsapassāse niruddhetiādi heṭṭhā vuttanayampi vicetabbākārappattassa kāyasaṅkhārassa vicayanavidhiṃ dassetuṃ ānītaṃ.

The passage beginning with ‘when coarse in-and-out breathing is ceased,’ which contains a method spoken of below, is also brought forth to show the method for investigating the bodily formation that has reached a state requiring investigation.

229. Uparūpari vibhūtānīti bhāvanābalena uddhaṃ uddhaṃ pākaṭāni honti. Desatoti pakatiyā phusanadesato, pubbe attanā phusanavasena upadhāritaṭṭhānato.

229. ‘Manifest ever higher’ means they become manifest higher and higher by the power of cultivation. ‘From the location’ means from the place of natural contact, from the location previously determined by oneself by way of contact.

“Kattha natthī”ti ṭhānavasena, “kassa natthī”ti puggalavasena vīmaṃsiyamānamatthaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā vibhāvetuṃ “antomātukucchiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā udake nimuggassa puggalassa niruddhokāsatāya assāsapassāsā na pavattanti, evaṃ antomātukucchiyaṃ. Yathā matānaṃ samuṭṭhāpakacittābhāvato, evaṃ asaññībhūtānaṃ mucchāparetānaṃ, asaññīsu vā jātānaṃ, tathā nirodhasamāpannānaṃ. Catutthajjhānasamāpannānaṃ pana dhammatāvaseneva nesaṃ anuppajjanaṃ, tathā rūpārūpabhavasamaṅgīnaṃ. Keci pana “anupubbato sukhumabhāvappattiyā catutthajjhānasamāpannassa, rūpabhave rūpānaṃ bhavaṅgassa ca sukhumabhāvato rūpabhavasamaṅgīnaṃ natthī”ti kāraṇaṃ vadanti. Atthiyeva te assāsapassāsā pariyesatoti adhippāyo, yathāvuttasattaṭṭhānavinimuttassa assāsapassāsānaṃ anuppajjanaṭṭhānassa abhāvato. Pakatiphuṭṭhavasenāti pakatiyā phusanaṭṭhānavasena. Nimittaṃ ṭhapetabbanti satiyā tattha tattha sukhappavattanatthaṃ thiratarasañjānanaṃ pavattetabbaṃ. Thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā hi sati. Imamevāti imaṃ eva anupaṭṭhahantassa kāyasaṅkhārassa kaṇṭakuṭṭhāpananayena upaṭṭhāpanavidhimeva. Atthavasanti hetuṃ. Atthoti hi phalaṃ, so yassa vasena pavattati, so atthavasoti. Muṭṭhassatissāti vinaṭṭhassatissa. Asampajānassāti sampajaññarahitassa, bhāventassa anukkamena anupaṭṭhahante assāsapassāse vīmaṃsitvā “ime te”ti upadhāretuṃ, sammadeva pajānituñca samatthāhi satipaññāhi virahitassāti adhippāyo.

In order to clarify by combining into one the matter being investigated by way of place—‘Where do they not exist?’—and by way of person—‘For whom do they not exist?’—the passage beginning with ‘inside the mother’s womb’ was stated. Therein, just as for a person submerged in water in-and-out breaths do not occur due to the space being obstructed, so it is inside the mother’s womb. Just as for the dead they do not occur due to the absence of a mind that can generate them, so it is for those who have become unconscious, for those overcome by fainting, or for those born in the non-percipient realm, and likewise for those who have attained cessation. However, for those who have attained the fourth jhāna, their non-arising is simply by the force of nature; likewise for those endowed with form and formless existence. Some, however, state the reason thus: ‘They do not exist for one who has attained the fourth jhāna due to having successively attained a state of subtlety, and for those endowed with form existence due to the subtlety of material form and the life-continuum in the form realm.’ The intention is: those in-and-out breaths of yours do indeed exist, to be known by the method of elimination; because for one who is free from the seven aforementioned places, there is no place where in-and-out breathing does not arise. ‘By the way of natural contact’ means by way of the place of natural contact. ‘A sign should be established’ means that a firmer perception should be made to arise in that very place by means of mindfulness for the sake of easy progress. For mindfulness has firm perception as its proximate cause. ‘This very one’ means this very method of making it appear for one to whom the bodily formation does not appear, by the method of extracting a thorn. ‘For the sake of the goal’ (atthavasa) means for the cause. For ‘goal’ (attha) is the result, and that by means of which it occurs is ‘atthavasa’. ‘For one of unmindfulness’ means for one whose mindfulness is lost. ‘For one not clearly comprehending’ means for one devoid of clear comprehension. The intention is: for one who, while developing, is devoid of the mindfulness and wisdom capable of investigating the in-and-out breaths that successively do not appear, determining ‘these are they,’ and knowing them perfectly well.

230. Ito aññaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Garukanti bhāriyaṃ. Sā cassa garukatā bhāvanāya sudukkarabhāvenāti āha “garukabhāvana”nti. Uparūpari [M 1.0335] santasukhumabhāvappattito “balavatī suvisadā sūrā ca satipaññā ca icchitabbā”ti vatvā sukhumassa nāma atthassa sādhanenāpi sukhumeneva [V 1.0316] bhavitabbanti dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idāni anupaṭṭhahantānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ pariyesanupāyaṃ dassento “tāhi ca panā”tiādimāha. Tattha gocaramukheti gocarābhimukhe. Anupadanti padānupadaṃ. Caritvāti gocaraṃ gahetvā. Tasmiṃyeva ṭhāneti upanibandhanānimittasaññitaṭṭhāne. Yojetvāti manasikārena yojetvā. Satirasmiyā bandhitvāti vā vuttamevatthamāha “tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne yojetvā”ti. Na hi upameyye bandhanayojanaṭṭhānāni visuṃ labbhanti.

230. A meditation subject other than this. ‘Difficult’ means weighty. And that difficulty of it is due to the extreme difficulty of its cultivation; therefore, he said ‘difficult cultivation.’ Due to having attained a state of tranquil subtlety ever higher, it is said, ‘strong, very clear, and courageous mindfulness and wisdom should be desired.’ And having said this, to show that the means for accomplishing a goal that is subtle must itself also be subtle, the passage beginning with ‘Just as…’ was stated. Now, showing the method for seeking the in-and-out breaths that do not appear, he stated the passage beginning with ‘And by means of those…’. Herein, ‘facing the pasture’ means facing towards the object. ‘They follow’ means they follow step by step. ‘Having roamed’ means having taken the object. ‘In that very place’ means in the place designated as the sign of binding. ‘Having yoked’ means having yoked by means of attention. Or, by ‘having bound with the reins of mindfulness,’ he states this very same meaning with ‘having yoked it in that very place.’ For in the subject of the comparison, the places of binding and yoking are not found separately.

231. Nimittanti uggahanimittaṃ, paṭibhāganimittaṃ vā. Ubhayampi hi idha ekajjhaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tūlapicuādiupamattayaṃ uggahe yujjati, sesaṃ ubhayattha. Ekacceti eke ācariyā.

231. ‘Sign’ (nimitta) means either the learning sign (uggahanimitta) or the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). For indeed, both are spoken of together here. Thus, the triad of similes beginning with cotton fluff is applicable to the learning sign; the remainder is applicable to both. ‘Some’ (ekacce) means some teachers.

Tārakarūpaṃ viyāti tārakāya pabhārūpaṃ viya. Maṇiguḷikādiupamā paṭibhāge vaṭṭanti. Kathaṃ panetaṃ ekaṃyeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ anekākārato upaṭṭhātīti āha “tañca paneta”ntiādi. Suttantanti ekaṃ suttaṃ. Paguṇappavattibhāvena avicchedaṃ, mahāvisayatañca sandhāyāha “mahatī pabbateyyā nadī viyā”ti. Atthabyañjanasampattiyā samantabhaddakaṃ suttaṃ sabbabhāgamanoharā sabbapāliphullā vanaghaṭā viyāti āha “ekā vanarāji viyā”ti. Tenāha bhagavā – “vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge”ti (khu. pā. 6.13; su. ni. 236). Nānānusandhikaṃ nānāpeyyālaṃ vividhanayanipuṇaṃ bahuvidhakammaṭṭhānamukhasuttantaṃ atthikehi sakkaccaṃ samupajīvitabbanti āha “sītacchāyo…pe… rukkho viyā”ti. Saññānānatāyāti nimittupaṭṭhānato pubbeva pavattasaññānaṃ nānāvidhabhāvato.

‘Like the form of a star’ means like the radiance of a star. The similes of a gem-ball, etc., are applicable to the counterpart sign. But how does this one single meditation subject appear in many aspects? Therefore, he stated the passage beginning with ‘And this...’. ‘Suttanta’ means one sutta. Referring to its uninterruptedness due to its fluent progression and its vast scope, he said, ‘like a great mountain river.’ Because it is auspicious in every way due to its excellence in meaning and phrasing, the sutta is like a forest thicket, captivating the heart in all its parts and fully blossomed in all its foliage; therefore, he said, ‘like a single forest range.’ For this reason, the Blessed One said: ‘As in a forest thicket with blossoms at the tips.’ A suttanta with various connections, various elisions, subtle with diverse methods, and having the entrance to many kinds of meditation subjects, should be well resorted to and lived by with care by those who are desirous; therefore, he said, ‘like a cool-shaded… tree.’ ‘By the diversity of perceptions’ means due to the diverse nature of the perceptions that have arisen even before the appearance of the sign.

Ime tayo dhammāti assāso, passāso, nimittanti ime tayo dhammā. Natthīti kammaṭṭhānavasena manasikātabbabhāvena natthi na upalabbhanti. Na ca upacāranti upacārampi na pāpuṇāti, pageva appananti adhippāyo. Yassa panāti vijjamānapakkho vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

“These three things” are: the in-breath, the out-breath, and the sign. “They do not exist” means they do not exist, they are not found, due to not being what should be attended to by way of the meditation subject. “Nor do they reach access” means they do not even reach access; how much less, absorption—this is the meaning. “But for whom…” refers to the side where they are existent, which should be understood according to the stated method.

Idāni vuttasseva atthassa samatthanatthaṃ kakacūpamāyaṃ āgatā “nimitta”ntiādikā gāthā paccānītā.

Now, in order to support the meaning already stated, the verses beginning with “nimitta” that are found in the Kakacūpama Sutta are brought back.

232. Nimitteti [M 1.0336][V 1.0317] yathāvutte paṭibhāganimitte. Evaṃ hotīti bhāvanamanuyuttassa eva hoti. Tasmā “punappunaṃ evaṃ manasi karohī”ti vattabbo. Vosānaṃ āpajjeyyāti “nimittaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ uppādetuṃ, tayidaṃ laddhaṃ, handāhaṃ dāni yadā vā tadā vā visesaṃ nibbattessāmī”ti saṅkocaṃ āpajjeyya. Visīdeyyāti “ettakaṃ kālaṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa nimittampi na uppannaṃ, abhabbo maññe visesassā”ti visādaṃ āpajjeyya.

232. “Nimitta” refers to the counterpart sign as described. “Thus it is” means it is so for the yogī devoted to the practice. Therefore, one should be told, “Again and again, apply your mind in this way.” “He might reach an end” means he might think, “The sign is indeed hard to produce, but this has been gained by me. Come now, I will produce a special attainment at any time whatsoever,” and thus he might fall into complacency. “He might lose heart” means he might think, “For so long have I been devoted to the practice, yet not even the sign has arisen. I think I am incapable of a special attainment,” and thus he might fall into despondency.

“Imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇato muccissāmīti paṭipannassa nimitta”nti vutte kathaṃ saṅkocāpatti, bhiyyoso mattāya ussāhameva kareyyāti “nimittamidaṃ…pe… vattabbo”ti majjhimabhāṇakā āhu. Evanti vuttappakārena paṭibhāganimitteyeva bhāvanācittassa ṭhapanena. Ito pabhutīti ito paṭibhāganimittuppattito paṭṭhāya. Pubbe yaṃ vuttaṃ “anubandhanāya ca phusanāya ca ṭhapanāya ca manasi karotī”ti (visuddhi. 1.224), tattha anubandhanaṃ, phusanañca vissajjetvā ṭhapanāvasena bhāvanā hotīti ṭhapanāvaseneva bhāvetabbanti attho.

When it is said, “the sign for one who practices thinking, ‘By this path, I shall be freed from aging and death,’” how could there be an occurrence of complacency? One should make effort even more exceedingly. Therefore, the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say, “This sign… should be spoken.” “Thus” means: by establishing the meditation-mind on the counterpart sign itself, in the manner stated. “From here onwards” means: starting from the arising of this counterpart sign. Previously, it was said: “One attends for the sake of pursuing, touching, and establishing.” Therein, having abandoned pursuing and touching, the meditation occurs by way of establishing. Therefore, the meaning is that one should develop it only by way of establishing.

Porāṇehi vuttovāyamatthoti “nimitte”ti gāthamāha. Tattha nimitteti paṭibhāganimitte. Ṭhapayaṃ cittanti bhāvanācittaṃ ṭhapento, ṭhapanāvasena manasi karontoti attho. Nānākāranti “cattāro vaṇṇā”ti (visuddhi. 1.219; pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.1.163) evaṃ vuttaṃ nānākāraṃ. Ākārasāmaññavasena hetaṃ ekavacanaṃ. Vibhāvayanti vibhāvento antaradhāpento. Nimittuppattito paṭṭhāya hi te ākārā amanasikaroto antarahitā viya honti. Assāsapassāseti assāsapassāse yo nānākāro, taṃ vibhāvayaṃ, assāsapassāsasambhūte vā nimitte. Sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhatīti tāya eva ṭhapanāya attano cittaṃ upanibandhati, appetīti attho. Ye pana “vibhāvayanti vibhāvento viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto”ti atthaṃ vadanti, taṃ pubbabhāgavasena yujjeyya. Ayañhettha attho – dhitisampannattā dhīro yogī assāsapassāse nānākāraṃ vibhāvento nānākārato te pajānanto vidite pākaṭe karonto, nānākāraṃ vā oḷārikoḷārike passambhento vūpasamento tattha yaṃ laddhaṃ nimittaṃ, tasmiṃ cittaṃ ṭhapento anukkamena sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhati appetīti.

This meaning was stated by the ancients, and thus he spoke the verse beginning “nimitte.” Therein, “nimitte” means on the counterpart sign. “Establishing the mind” means establishing the meditation-mind, attending by way of establishing; this is the meaning. “Of various aspects” refers to the various aspects stated as “the four colors.” This singular form is used because of the commonality of the aspects. “Dispelling” means making disappear, causing to vanish. For, from the arising of the sign, those aspects seem to have vanished for one who does not attend to them. “On the in-breath and out-breath” refers to dispelling the various aspects in the in-breath and out-breath, or to the sign that has arisen from the in-breath and out-breath. “Binds one’s own mind” means that by that very establishing, one binds one’s own mind closely, directs it to absorption; this is the meaning. But those teachers who state the meaning of “dispelling” as “making clear, making what is known manifest,” that would be suitable for the preliminary stage. For this is the meaning here: the wise yogī, being endowed with resolve, making clear the various aspects in the in-breaths and out-breaths—knowing them by their various aspects, making what is known manifest—or, calming and pacifying the various gross aspects, establishes the mind on the sign that has been gained therein, and sequentially binds his own mind, directing it to absorption.

Vaṇṇatoti [M 1.0337] picupiṇḍatārakarūpādīsu viya upaṭṭhitavaṇṇato. Lakkhaṇatoti kharabhāvādisabhāvato, aniccādilakkhaṇato vā. Rakkhitabbaṃ taṃ nimittanti sambandho. Nimittassa [V 1.0318] rakkhaṇaṃ nāma tattha paṭiladdhassa upacārajhānassa rakkhaṇeneva hotīti āha “punappunaṃ manasikāravasena vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ gamayitvā”ti.

“By way of color” means by way of the color that has appeared, as in the case of a cotton ball, the form of a star, and so on. “By way of characteristic” means by way of its intrinsic nature, such as the state of roughness, or by way of the characteristics of impermanence and so on. The connection is: “That sign should be guarded.” The guarding of the sign, it is said, is accomplished only by guarding the access concentration that has been attained therein. Therefore, he said, “by way of repeated attention, having brought it to growth and development.”

233. Etthāti etissaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ. Pārisuddhiṃ pattukāmoti adhigantukāmo, samāpajjitukāmo ca, tattha sallakkhaṇāvivaṭṭanāvasena adhigantukāmo, sallakkhaṇāvasena samāpajjitukāmoti yojetabbaṃ. Nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetīti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā hītiādi kāyassa, cittassa ca assāsapassāsānaṃ samudayabhāvadassanaṃ. Kammāragaggariyāti kammārānaṃ ukkāyaṃ aggidhamanabhastā. Dhamamānāyāti dhamayantiyā, vātaṃ gāhāpentiyāti attho. Tajjanti tadanurūpaṃ. Evamevāti ettha kammāragaggarī viya karajakāyo, vāyāmo viya cittaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānā, karajakāyaṃ pana vinā tesaṃ appavattanato “kāyañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsā”ti vuttaṃ.

233. “Herein” means in this contemplation of the body. “Desiring to attain purity” means desiring to attain and desiring to enter into. Herein, it should be understood as desiring to attain by way of turning away through the discernment of characteristics, and desiring to enter into by way of discerning characteristics. To show in detail the meaning stated briefly—“Having determined name-and-form, one establishes insight”—the passage beginning “How?” was stated. Therein, the passage beginning “Just as...” shows the arising of the in-breaths and out-breaths from the body and mind as their cause. “A blacksmith’s bellows” means the leather bag of blacksmiths for blowing fire in the forge. “When it is being blown” means when it is fanning, or when it is causing air to be taken in; this is the meaning. “Corresponding” means in accordance with that. “Just so”: herein, the body born of action should be seen as the blacksmith’s bellows, and the mind should be seen as the effort. Although the in-breaths and out-breaths originate from the mind, yet because they do not occur without the body born of action, it is said, “Dependent on body and mind are the in-breaths and out-breaths.”

Tassāti nāmarūpassa. Paccayaṃ pariyesatīti “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.50) avijjādikaṃ paccayaṃ vīmaṃsati pariggaṇhāti. Kaṅkhaṃ vitaratīti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) ādinayappavattaṃ soḷasavatthukaṃ vicikicchaṃ atikkamati pajahati. “Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna”nti (ma. ni. 1.347; 361; 3.86; a. ni. 4.181) ādinayappavattaṃ kalāpasammasanaṃ. Pubbabhāgeti paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhipariyāpannāya udayabbayānupassanāya pubbabhāge uppanne. Obhāsādayoti obhāso ñāṇaṃ pīti passaddhi sukhaṃ adhimokkho paggaho upekkhā upaṭṭhānaṃ nikantīti ime obhāsādayo dasa. Udayaṃ pahāyāti udayabbayānupassanāya gahitaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ udayaṃ vissajjetvā tesaṃ bhaṅgasseva anupassanato bhaṅgānupassanaṃ ñāṇaṃ patvā ādīnavānupassanāpubbaṅgamāya nibbidānupassanāya nibbindanto. Muñcitukamyatāpaṭisaṅkhānupassanāsaṅkhārupekkhānulomañāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante uppannagotrabhuñāṇānantaraṃ uppannena maggañāṇena sabbasaṅkhāresu virajjanto vimuccanto. Maggakkhaṇe [M 1.0338] hi ariyo virajjati vimuccatīti ca vuccati. Tenāha “yathākkamena cattāro ariyamagge pāpuṇitvā”ti. Maggaphalanibbānapahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesasaṅkhātassa paccavekkhitabbassa pabhedena ekūnavīsatibhedassa[V 1.0319]. Arahato hi avasiṭṭhakilesābhāvena ekūnavīsatitā. Assāti ānāpānakammaṭṭhānikassa.

Of that: of name-and-form. Seeks the condition: by the method beginning, 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form,' he investigates and comprehends the condition, such as ignorance. Overcomes doubt: he transcends and abandons the sixteen-factored doubt that proceeds in the way beginning, 'Did I exist in the past?' 'Whatever form, past, future, or present': this refers to the contemplation of groups that proceeds in this way. In the preliminary stage: when they have arisen in the preliminary part of the insight into rise and fall, which is included in the purification of knowledge and vision of the way. The corruptions of insight, etc.: these ten are illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, equanimity, mindfulness, and desire. Having abandoned arising: having relinquished the arising of formations grasped by the insight into rise and fall, and by contemplating only their dissolution, having attained the knowledge of dissolution, he becomes disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment, which is preceded by the contemplation of danger. Becoming dispassionate towards and liberated from all formations by means of the path-knowledge that arises immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge, at the culmination of the practice of the knowledges of desire for deliverance, reflection, equanimity towards formations, and adaptation. For at the moment of the path, the noble one is said to become dispassionate and to be liberated. Therefore, he said: 'Having attained the four noble paths in due order.' Of the nineteen kinds, by way of the division of what is to be reviewed, designated as path, fruit, Nibbāna, abandoned defilements, and remaining defilements. For an Arahant, due to the absence of remaining defilements, it becomes nineteen. Of him: of one practicing the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.

234. Visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvanānayo nāma natthi paṭhamacatukkavasena adhigatajhānassa vedanācittadhammānupassanāvasena desitattā. Tesanti tiṇṇaṃ catukkānaṃ.

234. There is no separate method for developing the meditation subject, because for one who has attained jhāna by means of the first tetrad, the practice is taught by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and dhammas. Of them: of the three tetrads.

Pītipaṭisaṃvedīti pītiyā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedanāsīlo, tassā vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedo etassa atthi, taṃ vā paṭi paṭi sammadeva vedayamāno. Tattha kāmaṃ saṃvedana-ggahaṇeneva pītiyā sakkaccaṃ viditabhāvo bodhito hoti, yehi pana pakārehi tassā saṃvedanaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ paṭi-saddaggahaṇaṃ “paṭi paṭi saṃvedīti paṭisaṃvedī”ti. Tenāha “dvīhākārehī”tiādi.

Experiencing rapture: one whose nature is to experience rapture repeatedly and rightly; or, for whom the experience of it exists repeatedly and rightly; or, one who is experiencing it repeatedly and rightly. Herein, the state of having carefully known rapture is indeed indicated by the mere taking of the term 'experiencing'; but to show the ways in which that experiencing is intended, the word 'paṭi' is taken, as in 'one who experiences repeatedly is “paṭisaṃvedī”'. Therefore, he said: 'in two ways,' etc.

Tattha kathaṃ ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti pucchāvacanaṃ. Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjatīti pītisahagatāni dve paṭhamadutiyajhānāni paṭipāṭiyā samāpajjati. Tassāti tena. “Paṭisaṃviditā”ti hi padaṃ apekkhitvā kattuatthe etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Samāpattikkhaṇeti samāpannakkhaṇe. Jhānapaṭilābhenāti jhānena samaṅgibhāvena. Ārammaṇatoti ārammaṇamukhena, tadārammaṇajhānapariyāpannā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇassa paṭisaṃviditattā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā nāma sappapariyesanaṃ carantena tassa āsaye paṭisaṃvidite sopi paṭisaṃvidito gahito eva hoti mantāgadabalena tassa gahaṇassa sukarattā, evaṃ pītiyā āsayabhūte ārammaṇe paṭisaṃvidite sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā eva hoti salakkhaṇato, sāmaññato ca tassā gahaṇassa sukarattāti.

Herein, 'How is rapture experienced with respect to the object?' is a question. Attains the two jhānas with rapture: he successively attains the first and second jhānas, which are accompanied by rapture. Of him (tassa): by him (tena). With reference to the word 'experienced' (paṭisaṃviditā), this is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent. At the moment of attainment: at the moment of entering. By gaining jhāna: by being endowed with jhāna. With respect to the object: by way of the object, the rapture included in the jhāna that has that object is experienced because the object is experienced. What is meant? Just as when one searching for a snake has experienced its lair, the snake itself is as good as experienced and caught, because of the power of spells and antidotes, making its capture easy. Similarly, when the object, which is the basis of rapture, is experienced, that rapture is as good as experienced, because it is easy to grasp it by way of its specific characteristic and its general characteristic.

Kathaṃ asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Vipassanākkhaṇeti vipassanāpaññāya tikkhavisadappattāya visayato [M 1.0339] dassanakkhaṇe. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhenāti pītiyā salakkhaṇassa, sāmaññalakkhaṇassa ca paṭivijjhanena. Yaṃ hi yassa visesato, sāmaññato ca lakkhaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ vidite so yāthāvato vidito eva hoti. Tenāha “asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotī”ti.

“How is rapture experienced without confusion?”—this should be brought forward and connected. At the moment of insight: at the moment of seeing by way of the object with insight-wisdom that has become sharp and clear. By penetration of the characteristics: by penetrating the specific characteristic and the general characteristic of rapture. For when the characteristic of anything, both specific and general, is known, then that thing is as good as known as it really is. Therefore, he said: 'Rapture is experienced without confusion.'

Idāni [V 1.0320] tamatthaṃ pāḷiyā eva vibhāvetuṃ “vuttañheta”ntiādimāha. Tattha dīghaṃ assāsavasenātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Tattha pana satokāritādassanavasena pāḷi āgatā, idha pītipaṭisaṃveditāvasena, pītipaṭisaṃveditā ca atthato vibhattā eva. Apica ayamettha saṅkhepattho – dīghaṃ assāsavasenāti dīghassa assāsassa ārammaṇabhūtassa vasena pajānato sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti sambandho. Cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānatoti jhānapariyāpannaṃ “avikkhepo”ti laddhanāmaṃ cittassekaggataṃ taṃsampayuttāya paññāya pajānato. Yatheva hi ārammaṇamukhena pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti, evaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammāpi ārammaṇamukhena paṭisaṃviditā eva hontīti. Sati upaṭṭhitā hotīti dīghaṃ assāsavasena jhānasampayuttā sati tassa ārammaṇe upaṭṭhitā ārammaṇamukhena jhānepi upaṭṭhitā nāma hoti. Tāya satiyāti evaṃ upaṭṭhitāya tāya satiyā yathāvuttena tena ñāṇena suppaṭividitattā ārammaṇassa tassa vasena tadārammaṇā sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Dīghaṃ passāsavasenātiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

Now, to clarify that meaning with the Pāli itself, he says, 'For it has been said,' etc. Herein, regarding 'by means of long in-breathing,' etc., what should be said has already been said below. But there, the Pāli came by way of showing the state of being a mindful doer, whereas here it is by way of experiencing rapture; and the experiencing of rapture is indeed distinct in meaning. Moreover, this is the concise meaning here: 'by means of long in-breathing'—the connection is that for one who understands by means of the long in-breath, which has become the object, that rapture is experienced. 'Understanding the unification and non-distraction of the mind': for one who understands, by means of the wisdom associated with it, the unification of mind, which is included in jhāna and has obtained the name 'non-distraction.' For just as rapture is experienced by way of the object, so too the dhammas associated with it are indeed experienced by way of the object. 'Mindfulness is established': mindfulness associated with jhāna by means of the long in-breath, being established in its object, is by way of the object said to be established in the jhāna as well. 'By that mindfulness': by that mindfulness thus established, because the object is well penetrated by that knowledge as previously stated, that rapture which has that as its object is experienced by means of that object. Regarding 'by means of long out-breathing,' etc., too, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

Evaṃ paṭhamacatukkavasena dassitaṃ pītipaṭisaṃvedanaṃ ārammaṇato, asammohato ca vibhāgaso dassetuṃ “āvajjato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āvajjatoti jhānaṃ āvajjantassa. Sā pītīti sā jhānapariyāpannā pīti. Jānatoti samāpannakkhaṇe ārammaṇamukhena jānato. Tassa sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotīti sambandho. Passatoti dassanabhūtena ñāṇena jhānato vuṭṭhāya passantassa. Paccavekkhatoti jhānaṃ paccavekkhantassa. Cittaṃ adhiṭṭhahatoti “ettakaṃ velaṃ jhānasamaṅgī bhavissāmī”ti jhānacittaṃ adhiṭṭhahantassa. Evaṃ pañcannaṃ vasībhāvānaṃ vasena jhānassa pajānanamukhena ārammaṇato pītiyā paṭisaṃvedanā dassitā.

Thus, to show the experiencing of rapture, as presented by way of the first tetrad, in detail with respect to the object and without confusion, 'reflecting upon,' etc., has been stated. Herein, 'reflecting upon' means for one who is reflecting upon the jhāna. 'That rapture' means that rapture included in the jhāna. 'Knowing' means for one who knows by means of the object at the moment of attainment. The connection is that for him, that rapture is experienced. 'Seeing' means for one who, having emerged from the jhāna, sees with knowledge that has become the seeing. 'Reviewing' means for one who is reviewing the jhāna. 'Establishing the mind' means for one who establishes the jhāna-mind with the thought, 'I will remain endowed with jhāna for this much time.' Thus, the experiencing of rapture with respect to the object has been shown by means of understanding the jhāna, by way of the five kinds of mastery.

Idāni [M 1.0340] yehi dhammehi jhānaṃ, vipassanā ca sijjhanti; tesaṃ jhānapariyāpannānaṃ, vipassanāmaggapariyāpannānañca saddhādīnaṃ vasena pītipaṭisaṃvedanaṃ dassetuṃ “saddhāya adhimuccato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha adhimuccatoti saddahantassa, samathavipassanāvasenāti adhippāyo. Vīriyaṃ paggaṇhatotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Abhiññeyyanti abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya jānitabbaṃ. Abhijānatoti vipassanāpaññāpubbaṅgamāya maggapaññāya jānato. Pariññeyyanti dukkhasaccaṃ tīraṇapariññāya, maggapaññāya ca parijānato. Pahātabbanti samudayasaccaṃ pahānapariññāya, maggapaññāya ca pajahato. Bhāvayato sacchikaroto bhāvetabbaṃ maggasaccaṃ[V 1.0321], sacchikātabbaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ. Keci panettha pītiyā eva vasena abhiññeyyādīni uddharanti, taṃ ayuttaṃ jhānādisamudāyaṃ uddharitvā tato pītiyā niddhāraṇassa adhippetattā.

Now, to show the experiencing of rapture by way of faith and other qualities—which are included in jhāna and included in the path of insight, and through which both jhāna and insight succeed—it is said, “one who is resolved through faith,” etc. Herein, 'one who is resolved' means one who has faith; the intention is by means of serenity and insight. The same method applies to “exerts energy” and so on. 'To be directly known' means to be known by superior wisdom. 'Directly knowing' refers to one who knows by the wisdom of the path preceded by the wisdom of insight. 'To be fully understood' means for one who fully understands the truth of suffering by means of the full understanding of scrutiny and the wisdom of the path. 'To be abandoned' means for one who abandons the truth of the origin by means of the full understanding of abandoning and the wisdom of the path. 'Developing' means for one who develops the truth of the path that is to be developed. 'Realizing' means for one who realizes the truth of cessation that is to be realized. Some, however, extract “to be directly known” and so on here solely by means of rapture, but that is incorrect, since the intention is to extract the aggregate of jhāna and other factors, and then to determine rapture from that.

Ettha ca “dīghaṃ assāsavasenā”tiādinā paṭhamacatukkavasena ārammaṇato pītipaṭisaṃvedanaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā “āvajjato”tiādīhi pañcahi padehi. “Abhiññeyyaṃ abhijānato”tiādīhi pana asammohato. “Saddhāya adhimuccato”tiādīhi ubhayathāpīti saṅkhepato samathavasena ārammaṇato, vipassanāvasena asammohato pītipaṭisaṃvedanaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā panettha vedanānupassanāyaṃ pītisīsena vedanā gahitā, na sarūpato evāti? Bhūmivibhāgādivasena vedanaṃ bhinditvā catudhā vedanānupassanaṃ dassetuṃ. Apica vedanākammaṭṭhānaṃ dassento bhagavā pītiyā oḷārikattā taṃsampayuttasukhaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ pītisīsena dasseti.

And here, by 'by means of long in-breathing,' etc., the experiencing of rapture is stated with respect to the object by way of the first tetrad; similarly, it is stated through the five phrases beginning with 'reflecting upon.' Moreover, by the phrases beginning with 'by directly knowing what is to be directly known,' it is stated by means of non-confusion. By the phrases beginning with 'by being resolved through faith,' it is stated in both ways; thus it should be understood that, in brief, the experiencing of rapture is stated by means of serenity with respect to the object, and by means of insight with respect to non-confusion. Why here, in the contemplation of feelings, is feeling taken under the heading of rapture, and not in its own nature? It is to show the fourfold contemplation of feelings by dividing feeling by way of its division into planes and so on. Furthermore, in teaching the meditation subject of feeling, the Blessed One presents the happiness associated with rapture under the heading of rapture because of rapture’s grossness, for the sake of the easy grasping of happiness.

Eteneva nayena avasesapadānīti “sukhapaṭisaṃvedī cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃvedī”ti padāni pītipaṭisaṃvedipade āgatanayeneva atthato veditabbāni. Sakkā hi “dvīhākārehi sukhapaṭisaṃveditā hoti, cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃveditā hoti ārammaṇato”tiādinā pītiṭṭhāne sukhādipadāni pakkhipitvā “sukhasahagatāni tīṇi jhānāni, cattāri vā jhānāni samāpajjatī”tiādinā atthaṃ viññātuṃ. Tenāha “tiṇṇaṃ jhānānaṃ vasenā”tiādi. Vedanādayoti ādi-saddena saññā gahitā. Tenāha “dve khandhā”ti. Vipassanābhūmidassanatthanti pakiṇṇakasaṅkhārasammasanavasena vipassanāya bhūmidassanatthaṃ “sukhanti dve sukhānī”tiādi vuttaṃ [M 1.0341] samathe kāyikasukhābhāvato. Soti so passambhanapariyāyena vutto nirodho. “Imassa hi bhikkhuno pubbe apariggahitakāle”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.220) vitthārato kāyasaṅkhāre vutto, tasmā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tattha kāyasaṅkhāravasena āgato, idha cittasaṅkhāravasenāti ayameva viseso.

By this same method, the remaining terms, 'experiencing happiness' and 'experiencing mental formations,' should be understood in meaning just as the term 'experiencing rapture' was explained. For it is possible to understand the meaning by substituting terms like 'happiness' in the place of 'rapture', using such phrases as, 'The state of experiencing happiness occurs in two ways, and the state of experiencing mental formations occurs in two ways—with respect to the object, and so on,' and, 'one attains three jhānas accompanied by happiness, or four jhānas.' Therefore, it is said, 'by way of the three jhānas,' etc. 'Feeling, etc.': by the word 'etc.,' perception is included. Hence it is said, 'two aggregates.' 'For the purpose of showing the plane of insight' means that to show the plane of insight by way of comprehending miscellaneous formations, 'happiness means two kinds of happiness,' etc., was said, because of the absence of bodily happiness in serenity. 'That' refers to that cessation, spoken of as a synonym for calming. Since this was discussed in detail in the section on bodily formations in the passage, 'For this monk, in the time before it was taken up…' (Vism. I, 220), it should be understood in the manner stated there. There, it came by way of bodily formation; here, it comes by way of mental formation—this alone is the difference.

Evaṃ cittasaṅkhārassa passambhanaṃ atidesena dassetvā yadaññaṃ imasmiṃ catukke vattabbaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pītipadeti “pītipaṭisaṃvedī”tiādinā desitakoṭṭhāse. Pītisīsena vedanā vuttāti pītiapadesena taṃsampayuttā vedanā vuttā, na pītīti adhippāyo. Tattha kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Dvīsu cittasaṅkhārapadesūti “cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃvedī passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāra”nti cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃyuttesu dvīsu padesu. “Viññāṇapaccayā [V 1.0322] nāmarūpa”nti (mahāva. 1; ma. ni. 3.126; udā. 1) vacanato cittena paṭibaddhāti cittapaṭibaddhā. Tato eva kāmaṃ cittena saṅkharīyantīti cittasaṅkhārā, saññāvedanādayo, idha pana upalakkhaṇamattaṃ saññā vedanāva adhippetāti āha “saññāsampayuttā vedanā”ti.

Thus, having shown the calming of the mental formation by way of extended application, to show what else should be said in this tetrad, 'furthermore,' etc., was said. Therein, 'in the term on rapture' means in the section taught with 'experiencing rapture,' etc. 'Feeling was stated under the heading of rapture' means that by way of indicating rapture, the feeling associated with it was stated, not rapture itself—this is the intention. The reason for that has already been stated above. 'In the two terms on mental formation' means in the two terms connected with mental formation, namely 'experiencing mental formation' and 'calming the mental formation.' Because of the saying, 'With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form,' they are connected with the mind; therefore, they are called 'mind-connected.' For that very reason, although it is true that perception, feeling, and so on are called 'mental formations' because they are formed by the mind, here, however, perception is only an indicator; only feeling is intended. Therefore, he said, 'feeling associated with perception.'

235. Cittapaṭisaṃvedīti ettha dvīhākārehi cittapaṭisaṃveditā hoti ārammaṇato, asammohato ca. Kathaṃ ārammaṇato? Cattāri jhānāni samāpajjati, tassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānapaṭilābhenātiādinā vuttanayānusārena sabbaṃ suviññeyyanti āha “catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena cittapaṭisaṃveditā veditabbā”ti. Cittaṃ modentoti jhānasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ sampayuttāya pītiyā modayamāno, taṃ vā pītiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattaṃ vipassanācittaṃ tāya eva ārammaṇabhūtāya pītiyā modayamāno. Pamodentotiādīni padāni tasseva vevacanāni pītipariyāyabhāvato.

235. ‘One who experiences the mind’ here means experiencing the mind in two ways: with regard to the object and with regard to non-confusion. How with regard to the object? One attains the four jhānas, and at the moment of attainment, according to the method explained beginning with “by the attainment of jhāna,” everything is easily understood. Thus it is said, “Experiencing the mind should be understood by way of the four jhānas.” “Gladdening the mind” means gladdening the mind associated with jhāna with the associated joy, or gladdening the insight consciousness that arises taking that joy as its object with that same joy that serves as the object. The terms “rejoicing” and so on are synonyms for that very word, being terms for joy.

Sampayuttāya pītiyā cittaṃ āmodetīti jhānacittasampayuttāya pītisambojjhaṅgabhūtāya odagyalakkhaṇāya jhānapītiyā tameva jhānacittaṃ sahajātādipaccayavasena ceva jhānapaccayavasena ca paribrūhento haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāraṃ pāpento āmodeti pamodeti ca. Ārammaṇaṃ katvāti [M 1.0342] uḷāraṃ jhānasampayuttaṃ pītiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānaṃ vipassanācittaṃ tāya eva ārammaṇabhūtāya pītiyā yogāvacaro haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāraṃ pāpento “āmodeti pamodetī”ti vuccati.

‘He gladdens the mind with associated joy’ means that by means of the jhāna-joy, which is associated with the jhāna-mind, which is the enlightenment factor of joy, and which is characterized by uplift, he nourishes that very jhāna-mind by means of co-nascent and other conditions, as well as by means of jhāna conditions, bringing it to a state of delight and rejoicing, and thus gladdens and delights it. ‘Taking it as an object’ means that the meditator, taking the sublime joy associated with jhāna as the object, bringing the insight-mind that arises to a state of delight and rejoicing by means of that very joy which serves as the object, is said to ‘gladden and delight’ it.

Samaṃ ṭhapentoti yathā īsakampi līnapakkhaṃ, uddhaccapakkhañca anupagamma anonataṃ anunnataṃ yathā indriyānaṃ samattapaṭipattiyā avisamaṃ, samādhissa vā ukkaṃsagamanena āneñjappattiyā sammadeva ṭhitaṃ hoti, evaṃ appanāvasena ṭhapento. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhenāti aniccādikassa lakkhaṇassa paṭi paṭi vijjhanena khaṇe khaṇe avabodhena. Khaṇikacittekaggatāti khaṇamattaṭṭhitiko samādhi. Sopi hi ārammaṇe nirantaraṃ ekākārena pavattamāno paṭipakkhena anabhibhūto appito viya cittaṃ niccalaṃ ṭhapeti. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ uppannāyā”tiādi.

‘Establishing it evenly’ means establishing it through absorption in such a way that it does not incline even a little towards a depressed aspect or a restless aspect, being neither bent down nor raised up, and so that, by the balanced practice of the faculties, it is not uneven; or, by the attainment of imperturbability through the exaltation of concentration, it stands quite correctly. ‘By penetrating the characteristics’ means by individually penetrating the characteristics of impermanence, etc., through moment-by-moment comprehension. ‘Momentary one-pointedness of mind’ is concentration that lasts for only a moment. For even it, continuously proceeding in a single mode towards the object, unoverpowered by its opposite, makes the mind unshaken as if in absorption. Hence it is said, “Thus arisen,” etc.

Mocentoti vikkhambhanavimuttivasena vivecento visuṃ karonto, nīvaraṇāni pajahantoti attho. Vipassanākkhaṇeti bhaṅgānupassanākkhaṇe. Bhaṅgo hi nāma aniccatāya paramā koṭi, tasmā [V 1.0323] tāya bhaṅgānupassako yogāvacaro cittamukhena sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ aniccato passati, no niccato. Aniccassa dukkhattā, dukkhassa ca anattakattā tadeva dukkhato anupassati, no sukhato. Anattato anupassati, no attato. Yasmā pana yaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, na taṃ abhinanditabbaṃ. Yañca na abhinanditabbaṃ, na taṃ rañjitabbaṃ. Tasmā bhaṅgadassanānusārena “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti saṅkhāragate diṭṭhe tasmiṃ nibbindati, no nandati. Virajjati, no rajjati. So evaṃ nibbindanto virajjanto lokiyeneva tāva ñāṇena rāgaṃ nirodheti, no samudeti, nāssa samudayaṃ karotīti attho. Atha vā so evaṃ viratto yathā diṭṭhaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ, tathā adiṭṭhaṃ attano ñāṇena nirodheti, no samudeti. Nirodhamevassa manasikaroti, no samudayanti attho. So evaṃ paṭipanno paṭinissajjati, no ādiyati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ayañhi aniccādianupassanā saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilesānaṃ pariccajanato, saṅkhatadosadassanena tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandanato pariccāgapaṭinissaggo pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo cāti vuccati. Tasmā tāya samannāgato yogāvacaro vuttanayena kilese ca pariccajati, nibbāne ca pakkhandati. Tena vuttaṃ “so vipassanākkhaṇe aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāto cittaṃ mocento vimocento [M 1.0343] …pe… paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādānato cittaṃ mocento vimocento assasati ceva passasati cā”ti.

‘Releasing’ means separating and making distinct by way of liberation by suppression; the meaning is that one abandons the hindrances. ‘At the moment of insight’ means at the moment of contemplating dissolution. For dissolution is the highest extremity of impermanence; therefore, the meditator contemplating dissolution, with the mind as the chief instrument, sees all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, not as permanent. Because what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self, one contemplates that same thing as suffering, not as happiness. One contemplates it as non-self, not as self. Furthermore, since that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self should not be delighted in, and that which should not be delighted in should not be lusted after, therefore, in accordance with the vision of dissolution, when conditioned phenomena are seen as ‘impermanent, suffering, and non-self,’ one becomes disenchanted with them, one does not delight. One becomes dispassionate, one does not lust. Thus, becoming disenchanted and dispassionate, one for the time being brings lust to cessation with merely worldly knowledge; one does not cause it to arise; the meaning is that one does not bring about its arising. Alternatively, being thus dispassionate, just as one contemplates the cessation of the conditioned phenomena that are seen, so too one contemplates with one’s own knowledge the cessation of the conditioned phenomena that are not seen; one does not cause them to arise. One attends only to their cessation, not to their arising; this is the meaning. Practicing thus, one relinquishes, one does not grasp. What is said? This contemplation of impermanence and so on—because of the abandoning of the defilements together with the aggregates and formations, and because of plunging into Nibbāna, which is the opposite of the conditioned, through seeing the fault in the conditioned and through inclination towards it—is called both relinquishment-by-abandoning and relinquishment-by-plunging-into. Therefore, the meditator endowed with that, in the way that has been stated, both abandons the defilements and plunges into Nibbāna. For that reason it is said: ‘At the moment of insight, by contemplating impermanence, releasing and liberating the mind from the perception of permanence… by contemplating relinquishment, releasing and liberating the mind from grasping, one breathes in and breathes out.’

Tattha aniccassa, aniccanti vā anupassanā aniccānupassanā. Tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā pavattāya vipassanāya etaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññātoti saṅkhatadhamme “niccā sassatā”ti pavattāya micchāsaññāya. Saññāsīsena cittadiṭṭhīnampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo sukhasaññādīsupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbindanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nanditoti sappītikataṇhāto. Virāgānupassanāyāti tathā virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Tena vuttaṃ “rāgato mocento”ti. Nirodhānupassanāyāti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya. Yathā saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ punabbhavavasena na uppajjanti, evaṃ vā anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Muñcitukamyatā hi ayaṃ balappattā. Tenāha “samudayato mocento”ti. Paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Ādānatoti niccādivasena gahaṇato, paṭisandhiggahaṇato vāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Therein, the contemplation of what is impermanent, or the contemplation ‘it is impermanent,’ is the contemplation of impermanence. This is the name for the insight that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena belonging to the three planes. ‘From the perception of permanence’ means from the wrong perception that proceeds regarding conditioned phenomena as ‘permanent, lasting.’ The inclusion of consciousness and views with perception as the heading should be understood. This is the method in regard to the perception of happiness and so on as well. ‘By the contemplation of disenchantment’ means by the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of becoming disenchanted with formations. ‘From delight’ means from craving accompanied by joy. ‘By the contemplation of dispassion’ means by the contemplation that proceeds similarly in the manner of dispassion. For that reason it is said, ‘releasing from passion.’ ‘By the contemplation of cessation’ means by the contemplation of the cessation of formations. Or, the contemplation in such a way that formations just cease and do not arise again in the future by way of a new existence is the contemplation of cessation. For this is the desire-for-deliverance knowledge that has gained strength. For that reason he said, ‘releasing from arising.’ The contemplation that proceeds in the manner of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment. ‘From grasping’ means from grasping by way of permanence, etc., or from grasping a rebirth-linking; thus the meaning should be understood here.

236. Aniccanti [V 1.0324] anupassī, aniccassa vā anupassanasīlo aniccānupassīti ettha kiṃ panetaṃ aniccaṃ, kathaṃ vā aniccaṃ, kā vā aniccānupassanā, kassa vā aniccānupassanāti catukkaṃ vibhāvetabbanti taṃ dassento “aniccaṃ veditabba”ntiādimāha.

236. One who contemplates 'impermanent,' or one whose habit is to contemplate the impermanent, is called 'one who contemplates the impermanent.' Here, the tetrad—What is this 'impermanent'? How is it impermanent? What is the contemplation of impermanence? And whose is the contemplation of impermanence?—should be clarified. To show this, he said, 'The impermanent is to be known,' and so on.

Tattha niccaṃ nāma dhuvaṃ sassataṃ yathā taṃ nibbānaṃ, na niccanti aniccaṃ, udayabbayavantaṃ, atthato saṅkhatā dhammāti āha “aniccanti pañcakkhandhā. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvā”ti, uppādavayaññathattasabbhāvāti attho. Tattha saṅkhatadhammānaṃ hetupaccayehi uppajjanaṃ ahutvā sambhavo attalābho uppādo. Uppannānaṃ tesaṃ khaṇanirodho vināso vayo. Jarāya aññathābhāvo aññathattaṃ. Yathā hi uppādāvatthāya bhinnāya bhaṅgāvatthāyaṃ vatthubhedo natthi, evaṃ ṭhitisaṅkhātāya bhaṅgābhimukhāvatthāyampi vatthubhedo natthi, yattha jarāvohāro. Tasmā ekassāpi dhammassa jarā yujjati, yā khaṇikajarāti vuccati. Ekaṃsena ca uppādabhaṅgāvatthāsu vatthuno abhedo icchitabbo, aññathā “añño uppajjati, añño bhijjatī”ti āpajjeyya[M 1.0344]. Tayimaṃ khaṇikajaraṃ sandhāyāha “aññathatta”nti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato kathayissāma.

Among these, 'permanent' (niccaṃ) means stable (dhuvaṃ), eternal (sassataṃ), as is Nibbāna. 'Impermanent' (aniccaṃ) means not permanent; it is that which possesses arising and passing away (udayabbayavantaṃ); in essence, it refers to conditioned phenomena (saṅkhatā dhammā). Thus, it is said: 'The five aggregates are impermanent. Why? Because of their state of arising, passing away, and alteration.' The meaning is 'because of the existence of arising, passing away, and alteration.' Therein, for conditioned phenomena, their arising through causes and conditions—their coming into being from a state of not-yet-being, their attainment of an individual essence—is origination (uppādo). For those that have arisen, their momentary cessation (khaṇanirodho), their destruction (vināso), is passing away (vayo). The state of otherness due to aging (jarā) is alteration (aññathattaṃ). For just as there is no difference in the substance (vatthubhedo) in the state of breaking, which is different from the state of arising, so too, in the state facing dissolution, which is called duration (ṭhiti), there is no difference in the substance, wherein the term 'aging' is used. Therefore, aging is applicable even to a single phenomenon; this is called momentary aging (khaṇikajarā). And it must be unequivocally accepted that there is no difference in the substance in the states of arising and breaking; otherwise, one would fall into the error that 'one thing arises, and another breaks apart.' It is with reference to this momentary aging that it is said, 'alteration' (aññathattaṃ). What should be said further on this matter, we will discuss later.

Yassa lakkhaṇattayassa bhāvā khandhesu aniccasamaññā, tasmiṃ lakkhaṇattaye aniccatāsamaññāti “aniccatāti tesaṃyeva uppādavayaññathatta”nti vatvā visesato dhammānaṃ khaṇikanirodhe aniccatāvohāroti dassento “hutvā abhāvo vā”tiādimāha. Tattha uppādapubbakattā abhāvassa hutvāgahaṇaṃ. Tena pākabhāvapubbakattaṃ vināsabhāvassa dasseti. Tenevākārenāti nibbattanākāreneva. Khaṇabhaṅgenāti khaṇikanirodhena. Tassā aniccatāyāti khaṇikabhaṅgasaṅkhātāya aniccatāya. Tāya anupassanāyāti yathāvuttāya aniccānupassanāya. Samannāgatoti samaṅgibhūto yogāvacaro.

Because of the presence of the three characteristics, the designation 'impermanent' arises in the aggregates, and in those three characteristics, there is the designation 'impermanence.' Thus, having said, 'Impermanence is their very arising, passing away, and alteration,' and in order to show that, specifically, the term 'impermanence' refers to the momentary cessation of phenomena, he said, 'or having been, non-existence,' and so on. Therein, the term 'having been' (hutvā) is used because this non-existence is preceded by origination. By that, it shows that the state of non-existence due to destruction is preceded by prior non-existence. 'By that very manner' means by the very manner of its occurrence. 'By momentary dissolution' means by momentary cessation. 'Of that impermanence' means of the impermanence called momentary dissolution. 'By that contemplation' means by the contemplation of impermanence as described. 'Endowed with' means the yogi who is endowed.

Khayo saṅkhārānaṃ vināso, virajjanaṃ tesaṃyeva vilujjanaṃ virāgo, khayo eva virāgo khayavirāgo, khaṇikanirodho. Accantamettha etasmiṃ adhigate saṅkhārā virajjanti nirujjhantīti accantavirāgo, nibbānaṃ. Tenāha “khayavirāgo saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgo, accantavirāgo nibbāna”nti. Tadubhayavasena pavattāti khayavirāgānupassanāvasena vipassanāya, accantavirāgānupassanāvasena maggassa pavatti yojetabbā. Ārammaṇato vā vipassanāya khayavirāgānupassanāvasena [V 1.0325] pavatti, tanninnabhāvato accantavirāgānupassanāvasena, maggassa pana asammohato khayavirāgānupassanāvasena, ārammaṇato accantavirāgānupassanāvasena pavatti veditabbā. “Eseva nayo”ti iminā yasmā virāgānupassī-pade vuttanayānusārena “dve nirodhā khayanirodho ca accantanirodho cā”ti evamādiatthavaṇṇanaṃ atidisati, tasmā virāgaṭṭhāne nirodhapadaṃ pakkhipitvā “khayo saṅkhārānaṃ vināso”tiādinā idha vuttanayena tassa atthavaṇṇanā veditabbā.

Destruction (khayo) is the perishing of formations; fading away (virajjanaṃ), their very dissolution (vilujjanaṃ), is dispassion (virāgo). Destruction itself is fading away; 'destruction-fading away' (khayavirāgo) is momentary cessation. 'Ultimate fading away' (accantavirāgo) is Nibbāna, because when this is attained, formations utterly fade away and cease. Therefore, he said, 'Destruction-fading away is the momentary dissolution of formations; ultimate fading away is Nibbāna.' The occurrence by way of both should be connected thus: the occurrence of insight (vipassanā) by way of the contemplation of destruction-fading away, and the occurrence of the path (magga) by way of the contemplation of ultimate fading away. Alternatively, the occurrence of insight should be understood as proceeding by way of the contemplation of destruction-fading away from the standpoint of the object, and by way of the contemplation of ultimate fading away due to its inclination towards that. The occurrence of the path, however, should be understood as proceeding by way of the contemplation of destruction-fading away from the standpoint of non-delusion, and by way of the contemplation of ultimate fading away from the standpoint of the object. By the phrase 'This is the method,' he refers to the explanation of the meaning such as, 'There are two cessations: cessation by destruction and ultimate cessation,' in accordance with the method stated in the section on the contemplator of fading away. Therefore, by inserting the word 'cessation' in place of 'fading away,' the explanation of its meaning should be understood here according to the method stated, beginning with 'Destruction is the perishing of formations.'

Paṭinissajjanaṃ pahātabbassa tadaṅgavasena vā samucchedavasena vā pariccajanaṃ pariccāgapaṭinissaggo. Tathā sabbūpadhīnaṃ paṭinissaggabhūte visaṅkhāre attano nissajjanaṃ, tanninnatāya vā tadārammaṇatāya vā tattha pakkhandanaṃ pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo.

Relinquishment (paṭinissajjanaṃ), which is the abandoning (pariccajanaṃ) of what is to be abandoned, either by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅgavasena) or by way of cutting off (samucchedavasena), is 'relinquishment by abandoning' (pariccāgapaṭinissaggo). Similarly, the releasing of oneself into the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra), which is the relinquishment of all substrates of existence (sabbūpadhi), or the plunging into that either due to inclination towards it or by making it the object, is 'relinquishment by plunging in' (pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo).

Tadaṅgavasenāti [M 1.0345] ettha aniccānupassanā tāva tadaṅgappahānavasena niccasaññaṃ pariccajati, pariccajantī ca tathā appavattiyaṃ ye “nicca”nti gahaṇavasena kilesā, tammūlakā abhisaṅkhārā, tadubhayamūlakā ca vipākakkhandhā anāgate uppajjeyyuṃ, te sabbepi appavattikaraṇavasena pariccajati, tathā dukkhasaññādayo. Tenāha “vipassanā hi tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajatī”ti.

Regarding 'by way of substitution of opposites': here, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), for instance, abandons the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) by way of abandonment by substitution. And in so abandoning, by way of preventing their occurrence, it abandons all those defilements that would arise from grasping at 'permanence,' the volitional formations rooted in them, and the resultant aggregates rooted in both that might arise in the future. The same applies to the contemplations of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), and so on. Therefore, it was said: 'For insight, by way of substitution of opposites, abandons the defilements together with the aggregates and volitional formations.'

Saṅkhatadosadassanenāti saṅkhate tebhūmake saṅkhāragate aniccatādidosadassanena. Niccādibhāvena tabbiparīte. Tanninnatāyāti tadadhimuttatāya. Pakkhandatīti anupavisati anupavisantaṃ viya hoti. Saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajatīti maggena kilesesu pariccattesu avipākadhammatāpādanena abhisaṅkhārā, tammūlakā ca khandhā anuppattirahabhāvena pariccattā nāma hontīti sabbepi te maggo pariccajatīti vuttaṃ. Ubhayanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ, maggañāṇañca. Maggañāṇampi hi gotrabhuñāṇassa anu pacchā nibbānadassanato “anupassanā”ti vuccati.

'By seeing the fault in the conditioned' means by seeing the fault of impermanence, etc., in the conditioned, which pertains to the three realms and consists of the host of formations. In that which is the opposite of those, having the nature of permanence, etc. 'By inclination towards that' means by being resolved on that. 'Plunges in' means it enters; it is as if entering. 'Abandons the defilements together with the aggregates and volitional formations' is said because when the defilements are abandoned by the path, the volitional formations are said to be abandoned by being rendered incapable of giving fruit, and the aggregates rooted in them are said to be abandoned by being made unworthy of future arising. Thus, it is said that the path abandons all of them. 'Both' means insight-knowledge and path-knowledge. For even path-knowledge is called 'contemplation' (anupassanā) because it sees Nibbāna immediately after change-of-lineage knowledge.

Soḷasavatthuvasena cāti soḷasannaṃ vatthūnaṃ vasenāpi vuccamānasantabhāvādivasenāpīti samuccayattho ca-saddo. “Ānāpānassati bhāvitā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

Regarding 'and by way of the sixteen subjects': the word 'ca' (and) has an aggregative sense, indicating 'also by way of the sixteen subjects, and also by way of the states to be mentioned, such as being peaceful, etc.' The phrase 'mindfulness of in-and-out breathing, when developed' should be brought in and connected.

237. Assāti ānāpānassatisamādhissa. Kāmavitakkādivitakkupacchedasamatthatāyapi mahānisaṃsatā [V 1.0326] veditabbāti sambandho. Ayanti ānāpānassatisamādhi. Uccāvacesu ārammaṇesu pavattiyeva ito cito ca cittassa vidhāvanaṃ.

237. “Of this” means of the concentration of mindfulness of in-and-out breathing. The connection is that its great benefit should be understood also through its capacity to cut off sensual thought and other such thoughts. “This” means the concentration of mindfulness of in-and-out breathing. The running about of the mind here and there is simply its occurrence in relation to diverse objects.

Vijjā nāma maggo. Vimutti phalaṃ. Mūlabhāvo vipassanāya pādakabhāvo. Cattāro satipaṭṭhāne paripūreti kāyānupassanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena tassā bhāvanāya pavattanato. Satta bojjhaṅge paripūrenti bojjhaṅgabhāvanāya vinā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāpāripūriyā abhāvato. Vijjāvimuttiṃ paripūrenti bojjhaṅgabhāvanāya tāsaṃ sikhāppattibhāvato. Carimakānanti antimakānaṃ.

Knowledge is the path. Liberation is the fruit. The state of being the root is the state of being the foundation for insight. It perfects the four foundations of mindfulness because that development proceeds by way of the four contemplations beginning with the contemplation of the body. They perfect the seven factors of enlightenment because without the development of the enlightenment factors, there is no perfection of the development of the foundations of mindfulness. They perfect knowledge and liberation because by means of the development of the enlightenment factors, these reach their peak. “Of the last ones” means of the final ones.

238. Nirodhavasenāti [M 1.0346] nirujjhanavasena. Bhavacarimakāti bhavavasena carimakā nihīnabhavapavattino. Tathā jhānacarimakā veditabbā. Cuticarimakāti cutiyā carimakā cutikkhaṇapavattino sabbapariyosānakā. Tasmāti tīsu bhavesu nihīne kāmabhave pavattanato. Teti assāsapassāsā. Puratoti heṭṭhā. Yasmā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā) rūpadhammānaṃ soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā vibhāvitā, tasmā “soḷasamena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Cuticittassa puratoti vā cuticittaṃ avadhibhāvena gahetvā tato oraṃ soḷasamena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjitvāti evaṃ pana atthe gayhamāne sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukatāva assāsapassāsānaṃ vuttā hoti.

238. “By way of cessation” means by way of ceasing. “The last of existence” means the last by way of existence, which are the inhalations and exhalations that proceed in an inferior existence. Similarly, “the last of jhāna” should be understood. “The last of death” means the last by way of death, those that proceed at the moment of death, being the end of all. “Therefore” means because they proceed in the inferior sensual-sphere existence among the three existences. “They” are the inhalations and exhalations. “Before” means below. Because in the Vibhaṅga commentary the state of having a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments for material phenomena is explained, therefore it is said, “having arisen together with the sixteenth mind.” Or, regarding the text “before the death-consciousness,” taking the death-consciousness as the limit and interpreting it as “having arisen together with the sixteenth mind on this side of that”; however, when the meaning is taken in this way, the state of having a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments for the inhalations and exhalations is said to be the case.

Ime kira imaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuttassa bhikkhuno pākaṭā hontīti ānetvā sambandho. Tattha kāraṇamāha “ānāpānārammaṇassa suṭṭhu pariggahitattā”ti. Tamevatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “cuticittassā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The connection is made by bringing forward the words: “These, it is said, become manifest to a bhikkhu devoted to this meditation subject.” There, he states the reason: “because the object of mindfulness of breathing is well grasped.” To clarify that very meaning, “of the death-consciousness,” etc., was said.

Tattha āyuantaraṃ nāma jīvitantaraṃ jīvanakkhaṇāvadhi. Dhammatāya evāti sabhāveneva, rucivasenevāti attho.

There, “life-interval” means the duration of life, the limit of the life-moment. “Just by its own nature” means just by its inherent nature, that is, just by the power of its inclination.

Candālokaṃ oloketvāti juṇhapakkhe padosavelāyaṃ samantato āsiñcamānakhīradhāraṃ viya gaganatalaṃ, rajatapattasadisavālikāsanthatañca bhūmibhāgaṃ disvā “ramaṇīyo vatāyaṃ kālo, deso ca mama ajjhāsayasadiso, kīva ciraṃ nu kho ayaṃ dukkhabhāro vahitabbo”ti attano āyusaṅkhāre upadhāretvā parikkhīṇeti adhippāyo. Lekhaṃ katvāti caṅkame tiriyaṃ lekhaṃ katvā.

“Having looked at the moonlight” means: in the waxing fortnight, at the time of early night, having seen the surface of the sky like a stream of milk being poured from all around, and the surface of the earth spread with sand like a silver plate, the intention is that, after reflecting, “Oh, delightful is this time, and this place is like my own disposition. How long indeed must this burden of suffering be borne?” he understood his own life-formations to be exhausted. “Having made a line” means having made a line across the walking path.

Anuyuñjethāti anuyuñjeyya, bhāveyyāti attho.

“You should devote yourselves” means one should apply oneself, one should develop.

Upasamānussatikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Recollection of Peace

239. Evanti [V 1.0327] yathāvuttena virāgādiguṇānussaraṇappakārena. Sabbadukkhūpasamasaṅkhātassāti dukkhadukkhādibhedaṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ upasammati etthāti sabbadukkhūpasamoti saṅkhātabbassa.

239. “Thus”—in the manner of recollecting the qualities such as dispassion, as previously described. “Called the stilling of all suffering”—meaning all suffering, which is divided into suffering as suffering and so on, is stilled here; thus, it is to be known as the stilling of all suffering.

“Paññattidhammā”tiādīsu asabhāvopi ñāṇena dhārīyati avadhārīyatīti dhammoti vuccatīti tato nivattento “dhammāti sabhāvā”ti āha[M 1.0347]. Bhavanaṃ paramatthato vijjamānatā bhāvo, saha bhāvenāti sabhāvā, sacchikaṭṭhaparamatthato labbhamānarūpāti attho. Te hi attano sabhāvassa dhāraṇato dhammāti, yathāvuttenaṭṭhena sabhāvāti ca vuccanti. Saṅgammāti paccayasamodhānalakkhaṇena saṅgamena sannipatitvā. Samāgammāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paccayehīti anurūpehi paccayehi. Katāti nibbattitā. Akatāti kehicipi paccayehi na katā. Asaṅkhatāti bahuvacanassa kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Aggamakkhāyatīti aggo akkhāyati, ma-kāro padasandhikaro. So asaṅkhatalakkhaṇo sabhāvadhammo virāgoti paccetabbo, virajjati ettha saṃkilesadhammoti. Nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānena ariyamaggena pahīyamānā mānamadādayo taṃ patvā pahīyanti nāmāti āha “tamāgamma…pe… vinassantī”ti. Tattha “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1121; saṃ. ni. 4.108) maññanāvasena pavatto māno eva mānamado. Purisabhāvaṃ nissāya uppajjanakamado purisamado. Ādi-saddena jātimadādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nimmadāti vigatamadabhāvā. Imameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “amadā”ti vuttaṃ. Madā nimmadīyanti ettha amadabhāvaṃ vināsaṃ gacchantīti madanimmadano. Eseva nayo sesapadesupi. Kāmapipāsāti kāmānaṃ pātukamyatā, kāmataṇhā. Kāmaguṇā eva āliyanti ettha sattāti kāmaguṇālayā. Tebhūmakaṃ vaṭṭanti tīsu bhūmīsu kammakilesavipākavaṭṭaṃ. Esa asaṅkhatadhammo. Aparāparabhāvāyāti aparāparaṃ yoniādito yoniādibhāvāya. Ābandhanaṃ gaṇṭhikaraṇaṃ. Saṃsibbanaṃ tunnakāraṇaṃ. Nikkhamanaṃ, nissaraṇañcassa taṇhāya visaṃyogo evāti āha “visaṃyutto”ti.

In such phrases as “conceptual phenomena,” even that which is without inherent nature is called a “phenomenon” because it is held or discerned by knowledge. Turning away from that, it is said, “phenomena are inherent natures.” Existence is the state of being present in an ultimate sense; this is “being” (bhāva). Because they are together with being, they are “inherent natures” (sabhāvā); the meaning is that they are things whose forms are obtainable in the ultimate sense of direct realization. For they are called “phenomena” (dhammā) from their bearing of their own inherent nature, and they are called “inherent natures” (sabhāvā) in the sense explained. “Assembled” means having come together through assembly, which has the characteristic of a conjunction of conditions. “Gathered” is a synonym for that. “By conditions” means by suitable conditions. “Made” means produced. “Not made” means not made by any conditions whatsoever. As for “unconditioned,” the reason for the plural has been stated below. In “it is declared supreme,” this is split into “the supreme is declared”; the letter ‘m’ is for euphonic conjunction. That phenomenon of inherent nature with the characteristic of the unconditioned should be understood as “dispassion” (virāga), for defiling phenomena fade away (virajjanti) here. It is said, “having come to that… they are destroyed,” because conceit, pride, and so on, which are being abandoned by the noble path that proceeds with Nibbāna as its object, are indeed abandoned upon reaching it. Therein, the conceit that proceeds by way of conceiving such thoughts as “I am better” is itself “conceit-pride” (mānamada). The pride that arises dependent on the male state is “male-pride” (purisamada). By the word “and so on,” the inclusion of pride in birth and so on should be understood. “Devoid of pride” is due to the state of being without pride. Indeed, to show this very meaning, it was said, “without pride.” Because prides are made devoid here, go to a state of non-pride, to destruction, it is the “subduer of pride” (madanimmadano). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. “Thirst for sensual pleasures” is the desire to enjoy sensual pleasures; it is sensual craving. Because beings cling to the qualities of sensual pleasure here, they are “attachments to the qualities of sensual pleasure.” “The round in the three planes” is the round of kamma, defilements, and results in the three planes. This is the unconditioned phenomenon. “For one state after another” means from one plane of existence to another. “Binding” is the making of a knot. “Sewing together” is the act of stitching. Its departure and escape are simply the disjunction from craving; thus, it is said, “disjoined.”

Ye guṇe nimittaṃ katvā madanimmadanādināmāni nibbāne niruḷhāni, te madanimmadanatādike yathāvutte nibbattitanibbānaguṇe eva gahetvā āha “madanimmadanatādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ vasenā”ti, na pana madā nimmadīyanti etenāti evamādike. Te hi ariyamaggaguṇā[V 1.0328]. Bhagavatā upasamaguṇā vuttāti sambandho. Kattha pana vuttāti? Asaṅkhatasaṃyuttādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.366 ādayo). Tattha saccanti avitathaṃ. Nibbānaṃ hi kenaci pariyāyena asantabhāvābhāvato ekaṃseneva santattā aviparītaṭṭhena saccaṃ. Tenāha “ekaṃ hi saccaṃ, na dutiyamatthī”ti [M 1.0348] (su. ni. 890). Pāranti saṃsārassa paratīrabhūtaṃ. Tenevāha “tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”ti (itivu. 69), “appakā te manussesu, ye janā pāragāmino”ti (dha. pa. 85) ca. Sududdasanti paramagambhīratāya, atisukhumasantasabhāvatāya ca anupacitañāṇasambhārehi daṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya suṭṭhu duddasaṃ. Natthi ettha jarā, etasmiṃ vā adhigate puggalassa jarābhāvoti ajaraṃ. Tato eva jarādīhi apalokiyatāya thiraṭṭhena dhuvaṃ. Taṇhādipapañcābhāvato nippapañcaṃ. Natthi ettha matanti amataṃ. Asivabhāvakarānaṃ saṃkilesadhammānaṃ abhāvena sivaṃ. Catūhi yogehi anupaddutattā khemaṃ. Visaṅkhārabhāvena acchariyatāya, abhūtapubbatāya ca abbhutaṃ. Sabbāsaṃ ītīnaṃ anatthānaṃ abhāvena anītikaṃ. Niddukkhatāya abyābajjhaṃ. Sabbasaṃkilesamalato accantasuddhiyā visesato suddhīti visuddhi. Catūhipi oghehi anajjhottharaṇīyatāya dīpaṃ. Sakalavaṭṭadukkhato paripālanaṭṭhena tāṇaṃ.

Taking only those qualities of Nibbāna produced from the aforesaid names, such as 'the state of subduing pride'—names that are established for Nibbāna by making certain qualities their basis—he said, 'by way of the qualities such as the subduing of pride,' and not by way of such instrumental qualities as 'prides are subdued by this.' For those are the qualities of the noble path. The connection is that the qualities of peace were spoken of by the Blessed One. But where were they spoken of? In the Asaṅkhatasaṃyutta and other texts. Therein, 'truth' means unfailing. For Nibbāna, being in every way absolutely peaceful due to the absence of a non-peaceful state, is 'truth' in the sense of being unperverted. Therefore, he said, 'Truth is one, there is no second.' 'The far shore' means being the other shore of saṃsāra. For that very reason, he said, 'Having crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on high ground,' and 'Few are they among humans, those people who go to the far shore.' 'Very difficult to see' means exceedingly difficult to see, due to its extreme profundity, its extremely subtle and peaceful nature, and because it cannot be seen by those who have not accumulated the provisions of knowledge. 'Aging is not here,' or, when this is attained, there is an 'absence of aging' for the person; thus, it is 'ageless.' For that very reason, because it is not destroyed by aging and so on, it is 'permanent' in the sense of being firm. Because of the absence of proliferation such as craving, it is 'non-proliferating.' 'Death is not here,' thus it is 'deathless.' Because of the absence of defiling phenomena that cause what is inauspicious, it is 'auspicious.' Because it is unassailed by the four yokes, it is 'secure.' Because of its nature as unconditioned and its wondrousness, it is 'marvelous.' Because of the absence of all calamities and misfortunes, it is 'free from calamity.' Because of its freedom from suffering, it is 'unafflicted.' Because of its utter purity from all stains of defilements, it is a special purity; thus, it is 'purity.' Because it cannot be overwhelmed by the four floods, it is an 'island.' In the sense that it protects from all the suffering of the cycle, it is a 'refuge.'

“Saccañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādikā pāḷi saṃkhittāti veditabbā. Ādi-saddena anantaanāsavanipuṇaajajjaraapalokitaanidassanapaṇītaacchariyaanītikadhammamuttileṇaparāyaṇagambhīrādivacanehi ca bodhitā idha avuttā guṇā saṅgayhanti, tattha natthi etassa uppādanto vā vayanto vāti ananto, asaṅkhatadhammo. Āsavānaṃ anārammaṇatāya anāsavo. Nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya nipuṇo. Saṅkhatadhammo viya jarāya ajajjaritatāya ajajjaro. Byādhiādīhi apalokiyatāya apalokitaṃ. Acakkhuviññāṇaviññeyyatāya anidassano. Atittikaraṭṭhena paṇīto. Apacuratāya acchariyo. Ītīhi anabhibhavanīyasabhāvattā, anītikabhāvahetuto ca anītikadhammo. Vaṭṭadukkhamuttinimittatāya mutti. Saṃsāraṃ bhayato passantehi nilīyanīyato leṇaṃ. Tesaṃyeva parā gatīti parāyaṇo. Pakatiñāṇena aladdhapatiṭṭhatāya agādhaṭṭhena gambhīro. Katapuññehipi dukkhena kicchena anubujjhitabbato duranubodho. Sacchikiriyaṃ muñcitvā na takkañāṇena avacaritabboti atakkāvacaro[M 1.0349]. Buddhādīhi paṇḍiteheva veditabbato adhigantabbato paṇḍitavedanīyoti evamattho veditabbo.

“I will teach you the truth, O monks,” etc.—this Pali passage should be understood as being abbreviated. By the word 'ādi' (etc.) and by terms such as endless, taintless, subtle, unaging, unimpaired, invisible, excellent, marvelous, calamity-free, liberation, shelter, final resort, profound, and so on, qualities not mentioned here are included.
