“Tatra” (therein) means in that form. “Satto” (attached) means attached, clinging, through greed which has the function of adhering and is synonymous with desire, etc. Or, “tatra” is a locative used in the instrumental sense, meaning: by that desire, etc.

Yadi sattatāya sattā, kathaṃ vītarāgesūti āha “ruḷhīsaddenā”tiādi. Avītarāgesu ruḷhena, avītarāgesu vā pavattitvā indriyabaddhakhandhasantānatāya taṃsadisesu vītarāgesu ruḷhena saddena. Atha vā kiñci nimittaṃ gahetvā satipi aññasmiṃ tannimittayutte katthaci visaye sammutiyā cirakālatāya nimittavirahepi pavatti ruḷhī nāma yathā “gacchantīti gāvo”ti, evaṃ sattasaddassāpi ruḷhībhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Bhūtapubbagatiyā vā vītarāgesu sattavohāro daṭṭhabbo. Satvayogatoti ettha satvaṃ nāma buddhi, vīriyaṃ, tejo vā, tena yogato sattā, yathā “nīlaguṇayogato nīlo paṭo”ti.

If beings are called ‘beings’ (sattā) because of their attachment (sattatāya), how then is this term applied to the passionless? To this, it is said, “by the conventional term (ruḷhīsaddena),” and so forth. It is by a term established among the non-passionless; or, having come into use among the non-passionless, it is applied by an established term to the passionless, who are similar to them due to having a continuum of aggregates connected with the faculties. Alternatively, having taken some characteristic as the basis for a word, its application even in the absence of that characteristic in a certain domain, due to long-standing convention, is called ‘ruḷhī’ (conventional usage). For instance, it is said, “they go (gacchanti), therefore they are cows (gāvo).” In the same way, the status of the word ‘being’ (satta) should be understood as conventional. Or, the designation ‘being’ for the passionless should be understood by way of a past state (bhūtapubbagatiyā). Regarding the phrase “due to connection with essence” (satvayogato), here ‘essence’ (satva) is called intelligence, energy, or heat (tejo). Due to connection with that, they are called ‘beings’ (sattā), just as it is said, “a blue cloth is so called due to its connection with the quality of blue.”

Pāṇanti etenāti pāṇanaṃ, assāsapassāsā, tassa kammaṃ pāṇanatā, tāya, assāsapassāsasampayogenāti attho. Bhūtattāti kammakilesehi jātattā. Pūraṇato, galanato ca puggalāti neruttā. Sattā hi nibbattantā taṃtaṃsattanikāyaṃ pūrentā viya honti, sabbāvatthanipātitāya ca galanti cavantīti attho. Apariññātavatthukānaṃ “attā”ti [M 1.0367] bhavati ettha abhidhānaṃ, cittañcāti attabhāvo, sarīraṃ, khandhapañcakameva vā. Tanti khandhapañcakaṃ[V 1.0346]. Upādāyāti gahetvā upādānaṃ nissayaṃ katvā. Paññattimattasambhavatoti paramatthato asantepi sattasaññite paññattimattena sambhavato.

They breathe (pāṇanti) by this; therefore, they are called ‘breathers’ (pāṇā), which refers to in-breaths and out-breaths. The act of this is breathing (pāṇanatā), and by this is meant the connection with in-breaths and out-breaths. As for ‘having become a being’ (bhūtattā), it means because of being born from kamma and defilements. Because of ‘filling’ (pūraṇato) and ‘falling away’ (galanato), they are called ‘persons’ (puggalā), thus say the etymologists. Indeed, beings, when they arise, are as if filling up their respective classes of beings; and because of their liability to fall in all states, they fall away and pass away—this is the meaning. For those whose substance is not yet fully understood, the designation ‘self’ (attā) and the mind that conceives it arise in this body; therefore, it is called ‘individual existence’ (attabhāva), which refers to the body, or just the five aggregates. ‘Continuum’ (tanti) means the five aggregates. ‘Having taken up’ (upādāya) means having grasped, having made clinging a support. ‘Because of arising merely by designation’ (paññattimattasambhavato) means that although in an ultimate sense it does not exist, it can arise merely by designation as that which is perceived as a ‘being’.

Yathā ca sattāti vacananti yathā satta-saddo yathāvuttenaṭṭhena nippariyāyato padesavuttipi ruḷhīvasena anavasesapariyādāyako. Sesānipīti pāṇādivacanānipi. Tānipi hi rūpārūpabhavūpagacatutthajjhānādisamaṅgīnaṃ assāsapassāsābhāvato avinipātadhammānaṃ pugalanassa abhāvato padesavuttīni. Ruḷhīvasena āropetvā yathāvuttāya ruḷhiyā vasena katthaci visaye avijjamānampi pāṇapuggalabhāvaṃ āropetvā. Yadi sādhāraṇato sattavevacanānīti gahetvā anodhisopharaṇā mettā vuccati, atha kasmā pañcaheva ākārehi vuttāti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “kāmañcā”tiādi. Keci panāhu “na kho panetāni “sattā”tiādīni padāni vevacanatāmattaṃ upādāya gahitāni, yato jantuādīnampi gahaṇaṃ āpajjeyya, atthavisesaṃ pana nimittabhūtaṃ upādāya gahitānī”ti, te sandhāyāha “ye panā”tiādi. Tattha atthatoti sajjanaṭṭhena sattā, pāṇanaṭṭhena pāṇāti evamādiatthato. Tesaṃ taṃ matimattanti dassento āha “anodhisopharaṇā virujjhatī”ti. Kasmā? Keci sattā, keci pāṇā, keci puggalāti āpajjanato. Tathā atthaṃ aggahetvāti sattādisaddā sappadesavisayāti evamatthaṃ aggahetvā pubbe vuttanayena nippadesavisayāti evamatthaṃ gahetvāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “imesū”tiādi. Pañcasu ākāresūti “sabbe sattā”tiādinā pāḷiyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 2.22) āgatesu pañcasu bhāvanākāresu. Aññataravasenāti yassa kassaci vasena.

And just as with the term 'beings' (sattā): just as the word 'satta', although according to the meaning explained, in its primary sense (nippariyāyato) it has a limited application, by way of conventional usage (ruḷhīvasena) it is all-encompassing. So too with the remaining terms, that is, the words 'breathers' (pāṇa), etc. For they too have a limited application: because of the absence of in-breath and out-breath for individuals who have reached the form and formless existences and those endowed with the fourth jhāna, etc., and because of the absence of falling [into states of woe] for noble individuals who are not of a nature to fall away. This is done by superimposing through conventional usage—that is, by superimposing, through the aforesaid conventional usage, the state of being a 'breather' or a 'person' even where it does not actually exist in a certain domain. If, taking them as general synonyms for 'being', mettā is said to be an unlimited pervasion, then why is it spoken of with only five modes? Anticipating this inquiry, it is said, 'If one wishes...', and so forth. Some, however, say: 'These terms, 'beings', etc., are not taken merely as synonyms, for if so, the inclusion of terms like 'creatures' (jantu), etc., would follow. Rather, they are taken based on a special meaning that serves as the cause for the word's usage.' Referring to them, it is said, 'But those who...', and so forth. There, 'by meaning' means: 'beings' (sattā) in the sense of clinging, 'breathers' (pāṇā) in the sense of breathing, and so on according to such meanings. To show that this is merely their opinion, it is said, 'the unlimited pervasion is contradicted.' Why? Because it would follow that some are 'beings', some are 'breathers', and some are 'persons'. 'Not taking the meaning in that way' means not taking the meaning that the words 'beings', etc., have a limited scope, but rather, taking the meaning by the method previously stated, that they have an unlimited scope—this is the intention. Therefore, it is said, 'In these...', and so forth. 'In the five modes' refers to the five modes of development found in the Pāli text beginning with 'All beings...'. 'By way of any one' means by way of whichever one.

257. Idāni dvāvīsatiyā bhāvanākāresu appanā pariggahetvā dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Byāpādarahitāti domanassabyāpādarahitā. Tasmāti yasmā na kevalaṃ yathāvuttaākāravibhāgamattato appanāvibhāgo, tasmā. Imesupi padesūti “sabbe sattā averā hontū”tiādikoṭṭhāsesupi. Yaṃ yaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti yadipi pubbabhāge [M 1.0368] tattha tattha abhinivese anekakoṭṭhāsavaseneva manasikāraṃ pavatteti, bhāvanāya samijjhanakkhaṇe pana tattha yaṃ paguṇataratāya supākaṭaṃ hoti, tassa vasena appanā hoti, yathā taṃ dvattiṃsākāre. Tattha pana ārammaṇaṃ, idha bhāvanākāroti ayameva viseso. Catunnanti catunnaṃ catunnaṃ. Byāpanicchālopena hi niddiṭṭhaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi.

257. Now, in order to show the absorptions by encompassing them within the twenty-two modes of development, the passage beginning 'And here...' was stated. 'Free from ill will' means free from the ill will of mental distress. 'Therefore' means: because the classification of absorption does not come about merely from the classification of modes as stated, therefore... 'Also in these parts' means also in the sections such as 'May all beings be free from enmity...'. 'Whichever becomes clear' means: although in the preliminary stage one directs one's attention by way of many sections, at the moment of the development's success, absorption occurs by way of whichever section among them becomes very clear due to greater proficiency, just as in the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body. But there it is the object, whereas here it is the mode of development—this alone is the difference. 'Of the four' means of four each. It is indicated by the elision of an intervening word. This is the method in the remaining cases as well.

Liṅgavasena [V 1.0347] vuttaṃ tesaṃ pacurato labbhamānattā. Tatiyā pana pakati yadipi paṭhamadukena na saṅgahitā, dutiyadukena pana tikena ca saṅgahitā eva.

It is stated by way of gender because they, males and females, are found in abundance. But the third nature, that of the neuter and the paṇḍaka, although it is not included in the first dyad, is nevertheless certainly included in the second dyad and in the triad.

Iti sabbānipīti anodhisopharaṇe vīsati, odhisopharaṇe aṭṭhavīsati, disāpharaṇe cattāri satāni, asīti cāti evaṃ sabbānipi. Sata-saddāpekkhāya napuṃsakaniddeso.

Thus, all of them: in the unspecified pervasion, twenty; in the specified pervasion, twenty-eight; and in the directional pervasion, four hundred and eighty—thus, all of them. The neuter gender designation is with reference to the word 'hundred' (sata).

258. Evaṃ mettābhāvanaṃ vibhāvetvā idāni tattha ānisaṃse vibhāvetuṃ “itī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha sesā janāti mettāya cetovimuttiyā alābhino. Samparivattamānāti dakkhiṇena passena asayitvā sabbaso parivattamānā. Kākacchamānāti ghurughurupassāsavasena vissaraṃ karontā. Sukhaṃ supatīti ettha duvidhāsupanā sayane piṭṭhippasāraṇalakkhaṇā, kiriyāmayacittehi avokiṇṇabhavaṅgappavattilakkhaṇā ca. Tatthāyaṃ ubhayathāpi sukhameva supati. Yasmā saṇikaṃ nipajjitvā aṅgapaccaṅgāni samodhāya pāsādikena ākārena sayati, niddokkamanepi jhānaṃ samāpanno viya hoti. Tenāha “evaṃ asupitvā”tiādi.

258. Having thus explained the development of loving-kindness, now, in order to explain the benefits therein, the passage beginning 'Thus...' is introduced. There, 'the remaining people' means those who have not obtained the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. 'Turning over and over' means not lying on the right side, but turning over completely. In the passage 'sleeps happily', sleep is twofold: that characterized by stretching out the back on a bed, and that characterized by the occurrence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind unmixed with minds of functional consciousness. Therein, this person sleeps happily in both ways. Because one lies down gently, arranges the major and minor limbs, and lies down in a graceful manner, and even upon falling asleep, one is as if having entered jhāna. Therefore, it is said, 'Not sleeping thus...', and so forth.

Niddākāle sukhaṃ alabhitvā dukkhena suttattā eva paṭibujjhanakāle sarīrakhedena nitthunanaṃ, vijambhanaṃ, ito cito viparivattanañca hotīti āha “nitthunantā vijambhantā samparivattantā dukkhaṃ paṭibujjhantī”ti. Ayaṃ pana sukhena suttattā sarīrakhedābhāvato nitthunanādirahitova paṭibujjhati. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ appaṭibujjhitvā”tiādi. Sukhapaṭibodho ca sarīravikārābhāvenāti āha “sukhaṃ nibbikāra”nti.

Because one did not obtain happiness at the time of sleep and slept with suffering, upon awakening there is groaning, yawning, and turning from side to side due to bodily fatigue; thus, it is said: 'Groaning, yawning, and tossing about, they awaken in suffering.' This person, however, because of having slept with happiness, awakens free from groaning and so on due to the absence of bodily fatigue. Therefore, it was said: 'Thus, not awakening...' and so forth. And a pleasant awakening is due to the absence of bodily distortion; thus, it is said: 'happily, without distortion.'

“Bhaddakameva [M 1.0369] supinaṃ passatī”ti idaṃ anubhūtapubbavasena, devatūpasaṃhāravasena cassa bhaddakameva supinaṃ hoti, na pāpakanti katvā vuttaṃ. Tenāha “cetiyaṃ vandanto viyā”tiādi. Dhātukkhobhahetukampi cassa bahulaṃ bhaddakameva siyā yebhuyyena cittajarūpānuguṇatāya utuāhārajarūpānaṃ.

This statement, 'One sees only an auspicious dream,' was said with this in mind: for this person, due to what has been previously experienced and due to what is presented by deities, there is only an auspicious dream, not an evil one. Furthermore, for this person, even a dream caused by a disturbance of the elements would for the most part be auspicious, since materiality born of temperature and nutriment is generally in conformity with mind-born materiality.

Ure āmuttamuttāhāro viyāti gīvāya bandhitvā ure lambitamuttāhāro viyāti kehici vuttaṃ. Taṃ ekāvalivasena vuttaṃ siyā, anekaratanāvalisamūhabhūto pana muttāhāro aṃsappadesato paṭṭhāya yāva kaṭippadesassa heṭṭhābhāgā palambanto ure āmukkoyeva nāma hoti.

As for 'like a pearl necklace worn on the chest': it has been said by some that this is like a pearl necklace tied at the neck and hanging down on the chest. That may have been said with reference to a single strand of pearls. But in fact, a pearl necklace that is a collection of many strands of gems, hanging down from the shoulder region as far as the lower part of the waist area, is indeed called 'worn on the chest'.

Tatthevāti [V 1.0348] pāṭaliputteyeva. Sakkā nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā desassa khematāya, tassa tassa padesassa ramaṇīyatāya ca.

'There' means in Pāṭaliputta itself. It was possible to sit or lie down because of the safety of the region and the pleasantness of its various places.

Dasāva anto dasanto, vatthassa osānanto.

The fringe (dasā) itself is the end (anto), hence dasanto (fringe-end); it is the final end of the cloth.

Samappavattavāsanti tattha tattha vihāre samappavattavattavāsaṃ. Thero kira attanā paviṭṭhapaviṭṭhavihāre “ahamettha āgantuko”ti acintetvā tattha tattha yathārahaṃ attanā kātabbavattāni paripūrento eva vihāsi. Apare pana bhaṇanti sabbasattesu samappavattamettāvihāravāsaṃ. Ayaṃ hi thero arahattādhigamato pubbepi mettāvihārī ahosi.

'Dwelling with evenly flowing conduct' means dwelling with evenly flowing duties in various monasteries there. The Elder, it is said, in every monastery he entered, without thinking, 'I am a newcomer here,' dwelt only while fulfilling the duties to be done by himself in each place as was suitable. But others say it means dwelling with loving-kindness that flows evenly to all beings. For this Elder was one who dwelt with loving-kindness even before the attainment of Arahantship.

Vanantare ṭhitoti thero kira tathā samappavattavāsavasena caramāno ekadivasaṃ aññataraṃ ramaṇīyaṃ vanantaraṃ disvā tattha aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā yathāparicchedena tato uṭṭhito attano guṇāvajjanahetukena pītisomanassena udānento “yāvatā upasampanno”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “vanantare ṭhito”ti paṭhamagāthā ṭhapitā. Tattha gajjamānakoti sīhagajjitaṃ gajjanto. Guṇamesantoti attano guṇasamudayaṃ gavesanto paccavekkhanto.

Regarding 'standing in the forest': it is said that the Elder, while wandering by way of such an evenly flowing dwelling, one day saw a certain delightful forest-interior. There, at the foot of a certain tree, having entered into an attainment and having arisen from it after the determined period of time, he uttered the verse beginning, 'As far as the fully ordained...' while making an inspired utterance with the rapture and mental joy that had the reflection on his own virtues as its cause. To show that meaning, the first verse, 'standing in the forest,' was placed. There, 'roaring' (`gajjamānako`) means roaring a lion's roar. 'Seeking virtues' (`guṇamesanto`) means searching for and reviewing the collection of his own virtues.

Maṇilarukkhe nivāsitāya taṃ devataṃ “maṇiliyā”ti voharanti, tasmā sā devatāpi “ahaṃ, bhante, maṇiliyā”ti āha. Rukkhadevatānaṃ hi yebhuyyena nivāsarukkhavasena vohāro yathā phandanadevatāti. Tatthevāti cittalapabbateyeva.

Because of her dwelling in the Maṇila tree, they call that deity 'Maṇilī'; therefore, that deity also said, 'Venerable sir, I am Maṇilī.' For the designation of tree deities, for the most part, is by way of their tree of residence, just as in 'the deity of the Phandana tree'. 'There itself' means on Cittalapabbata itself.

“Balavapiyacittatāyā”ti [M 1.0370] iminā balavapiyacittatāmattenapi satthaṃ na kamati, pageva mettāya cetovimuttiyāti dasseti.

By this phrase, 'due to a strong, affectionate mind,' it is shown that even by the mere fact of having a strong, affectionate mind, a weapon does not penetrate; how much more so by the liberation of mind through loving-kindness.

Khippameva cittaṃ samādhiyati kenaci paripanthena parihīnajjhānassa byāpādassa dūrasamussāritabhāvato khippameva samādhiyati. Āsavānaṃ khayāyāti keci. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Ettha ca kiñcāpi ito aññakammaṭṭhānavasena adhigatajjhānānampi sukhasupanādayo ānisaṃsā labbhanti, yathāha –

For a person whose jhāna has been lost due to some obstacle, the mind quickly becomes concentrated because ill will has been driven far away. Some say it becomes concentrated 'for the destruction of the taints.' The rest is easily understood. And here, although benefits such as sleeping happily are obtained even by those who have attained jhāna by way of other meditation subjects than this one, as it is said:

“Sukhaṃ [V 1.0349] supanti munayo, ajjhattaṃ susamāhitā;

Suppabuddhaṃ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā”ti. –

'Happily sleep the sages, inwardly well-composed; Well-awakened they awaken, always the disciples of Gotama.'

Ca ādi, tathāpime ānisaṃsā brahmavihāralābhino anavasesā labbhanti byāpādādīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhāvato brahmavihārānaṃ. Tenevāha “nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa, yadidaṃ mettā cetovimuttī”tiādi (dī. ni. 3.326; a. ni. 6.13). Byāpādādivasena ca sattānaṃ dukkhasupanādayoti tappaṭipakkhabhūtesu brahmavihāresu siddhesu sukhasupanādayo hatthagatā eva hontīti.

and so on. Nevertheless, these benefits are obtained without remainder by one who has obtained the divine abidings, because the divine abidings are the direct opposite of ill will and so forth. For that very reason, it was said: 'This, friend, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness,' and so on. And by way of ill will and so forth, beings experience such things as sleeping in suffering; therefore, when the divine abidings, which are their opposites, are accomplished, benefits such as sleeping happily are as if in one's hand.

Karuṇābhāvanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Development of Compassion

259. Karuṇanti karuṇābrahmavihāraṃ. Nikkaruṇatāyāti vihesāya, “idhekacco pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā daṇḍena vā satthena vā aññataraññatarena vā sattānaṃ viheṭhanajātiko hotī”ti evaṃ vuttaviheṭhaneti attho. Ādīnavanti dosaṃ. Yathā tathā sattānaṃ viheṭhanāya pāpako vipāko idha ceva samparāye ca. Tathā hi yo satte jīvitā voropanena vā aṅgapaccaṅgacchedanena vā dhanajāniyā vā alābhāya vā avāsāya vā anatthāya vā ayasatthāya vā parisaṃsakkanena vā antamaso yathāvajjadassanenapi viheṭheti, tassa so pamādavihāro diṭṭheva dhamme alābhāyapi hoti, laddhassa parihānāyapi hoti, tannimittaṃ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, avisārado [M 1.0371] parisaṃ upasaṅkamati maṅkubhūto, sammūḷho kālaṃ karoti, kāyassa bhedā duggati pāṭikaṅkhā, sugatiyampi manussabhūto dujjaccopi hoti nīcakuliko, dubbaṇṇopi hoti duddasiko, bahvābādhopi hoti rogabahulo, duggatopi hoti appannapāno, appāyukopi hoti parittajīvitoti evamādianekānatthānubandhitā vihesāya paccavekkhitabbā, tappaṭipakkhato karuṇāya ānisaṃsā paccavekkhitabbā. Tena vuttaṃ “nikkaruṇatāya ādīnavaṃ karuṇāya ca ānisaṃsaṃ paccavekkhitvā”ti. “Piyo hī”tiādinā paṭhamaṃ piyapuggalādīsu anārambhassa kāraṇamāha. Piyaṃ hi puggalaṃ karuṇāyitumārabhantassa na tāva piyabhāvo vigacchati, avigate ca tasmiṃ kuto karuṇāyanā. Tenāha “piyaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhatī”ti. Sesapuggalesupi eseva nayo. Liṅgavisabhāgakālakatānaṃ akhettabhāve kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

259. 'Karuṇā' refers to the divine abiding of compassion. 'Nikkaruṇatā' means cruelty (vihesāya), as in: 'Here, a certain person is of a nature to harm beings with the hand, with a clod, with a stick, with a weapon, or with some other thing'—this is the meaning of the harming thus spoken of. 'Ādīnava' means disadvantage (dosaṃ). In whatever way one harms beings, the evil result is in this world and in the next. For indeed, one who harms beings by depriving them of life, by cutting off their limbs major and minor, by causing loss of wealth, for the sake of non-gain, for the sake of homelessness, for the sake of misfortune, for the sake of ill-fame, or by exertion, or even at least by pointing out a fault as it is, for that person, that dwelling in negligence leads to non-gain in this very life, it leads to the loss of what has been gained, and on account of that, an evil sound of their reputation goes forth. They approach an assembly without confidence, downcast; they die bewildered. After the breakup of the body, a bad destination is to be expected. Even if reborn in a good destination as a human, they are of bad birth, of a low family; they are of bad complexion, ugly to see; they have many afflictions, are full of diseases; they are poor, with little food and drink; they are short-lived, with a brief lifespan. Thus, the many disadvantages connected with cruelty should be reflected upon, and, as its opposite, the benefits of compassion should be reflected upon. Therefore, it is said: 'Having reflected on the disadvantage of cruelty and the benefit of compassion...' By the words beginning with 'For a dear one,' he first states the reason for not beginning with beloved persons and so on. For one who begins to generate compassion for a dear person, the state of dearness does not depart. And when that state of dearness has not departed, whence compassion? Therefore, he said, 'It remains in the state of being dear.' For other persons too, this is the method. As for persons of a different sex and those who are dead, the reason for their being an unsuitable field has been stated before.

Yattha [V 1.0350] pana paṭhamaṃ ārabhitabbā, taṃ pāḷinayeneva dassetuṃ “kathañca bhikkhū”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha duggatanti daliddaṃ. So hi bhogapārijuññato sukhasādhanānaṃ abhāvena dukkhaṃ gato upagato duggatoti vuccati. Atha vā duggatanti dukkhena samaṅgibhāvaṃ gataṃ. Durupetanti kāyaduccaritādīhi upetaṃ. Gatikularūpādivasena vā tamabhāve ṭhito duggato. Kāyaduccaritādīhi upetattā tamaparāyaṇabhāve ṭhito durupetoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Paramakicchappattanti ativiya kicchamāpannaṃ mahābyasanaṃ nimuggaṃ. Appeva nāmāti sādhu vata.

Moreover, to show by the method of the Pāḷi itself the person with whom one should first begin, the passage beginning 'And how, monks...' was started. Therein, 'duggata' means destitute. For he, due to the complete destruction of wealth and the absence of the means for happiness, has gone to, has reached suffering; therefore he is called 'duggata'. Or alternatively, 'duggata' means one who has gone to a state of association with suffering. 'Durupeta' means one endowed with bodily misconduct and so on. Or, 'duggata' is one established in darkness by way of destiny, family, form, and so on. 'Durupeta' is one established in having darkness as their destination because of being endowed with bodily misconduct and so on. Thus should the meaning here be understood. 'Paramakicchappattaṃ' means one who has fallen into extreme hardship, sunk in great disaster. 'Appeva nāma' means 'It would be good indeed!'

Vadhetha nanti “ghātetha naṃ cora”nti evaṃ pahitāya rañño āṇāya khādanīyampi…pe… denti “idāneva māriyamāno ettakampi sukhaṃ labhatū”ti. Susajjitoti sukhānubhavane sannaddho.

'Kill him,' meaning, 'Execute that thief!' By the king's command thus dispatched, they give food... thinking, 'Even as he is about to be killed right now, let him get at least this much pleasure.' 'Susajjito' means well-equipped for the experience of pleasure.

Eteneva upāyenāti yena yena vidhinā etarahi yathāvutte paramakicchāpanne āyatiṃ vā dukkhabhāgimhi puggale karuṇāyituṃ karuṇā uppāditā, eteneva nayena. Piyapuggaleti piyāyitabbapuggale. Etarahi vā dissamānaṃ āyatiṃ vā bhāviniṃ dukkhappattiṃ gahetvā karuṇā pavattetabbāti sambandho. Majjhattaverīsupi eseva nayo. Yo hi so karuṇāya vatthubhūto duvidho puggalo vutto, kāmaṃ tattha karuṇābhāvanā sukheneva ijjhati, iminā pana bhikkhunā tattha bhāvanaṃ paguṇataraṃ katvā [M 1.0372] sīmāsambhedaṃ kātuṃ tadanantaraṃ piyapuggale, tato majjhatte, tato veripuggale karuṇā bhāvetabbā. Bhāventena ca ekekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse muduṃ kammaniyaṃ cittaṃ katvā tadanantare tadanantare upasaṃharitabbaṃ. Yassa pana veripuggalo vā natthi, mahāpurisajātikattā vā anatthaṃ karontepi verisaññāva nuppajjati, tena majjhatte me cittaṃ kammaniyaṃ jātaṃ, idāni verimhi upasaṃharāmīti byāpārova na kātabbo. Yassa pana atthi, taṃ sandhāyāha “sace panā”tiādi.

By this very method: by whatever method compassion has now been aroused for a person who has fallen into extreme hardship as described, or for one who will have a share of suffering in the future, by this same method. 'For a beloved person' means for a person who should be loved. Taking up the attainment of suffering that is either seen at present or will be in the future, compassion should be made to proceed; this is the connection. For neutral and hostile persons also, this is the method. For the two kinds of persons who have been mentioned as the basis for compassion, although the development of compassion for them may indeed succeed easily, this monk, having made the development for them more proficient, in order to break the boundaries, should thereafter develop compassion for a beloved person, then for a neutral one, then for a hostile one. And while developing, having made the mind soft and workable in each section, it should be applied to the next one immediately after. But for one who has no hostile person, or for whom, due to being of the nature of a great man, the perception of hostility does not arise even towards one who does harm, for that person, the very exertion, 'My mind has become workable towards a neutral person; now I will apply it to a hostile one,' should not be made. But for one who does have a hostile person, referring to that person, he said, 'But if...' and so on.

Tattha pubbe vuttanayenevāti mettākammaṭṭhānikassa (visuddhi. 1.240 ādayo) vuttanayena. Taṃ mettāya vuttanayeneva. Vūpasametabbanti “athānena purimapuggalesū”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.243), “kakacūpamaovādādīnaṃ anussarato”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.243) ca mettābhāvanāya vuttena nayena taṃ paṭighaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Evaṃ etarahi mahādukkhappatte sukhitepi akatakusalatāya āyatiṃ dukkhappattiyā vasena karuṇāyanavidhiṃ dassetvā idāni katakalyāṇepi taṃ dassetuṃ “yopi cetthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tesanti byasanānaṃ. Vaṭṭadukkhaṃ anatikkantattāti [V 1.0351] sammāsambuddhenāpi akkhānena pariyosāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa anāgatassa āpāyikassa sugatīsupi jātijarādibhedassāti aparimitassa saṃsāradukkhassa anatikkantabhāvato. Sabbathāpi karuṇāyitvāti dukkhappattiyā, sukhappattiyā akatakusalatāya vā katākusalatāya vāti sabbapakārenapi karuṇāya vatthubhāvassa sallakkhaṇena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ puggale karuṇaṃ katvā karuṇābhāvanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā. Vuttanayenevāti “athānena punappunaṃ mettāyantenā”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.243) mettābhāvanāyaṃ vuttena nayena. Taṃ nimittanti sīmāsambhedavasena pavattaṃ samathanimittaṃ. Mettāya vuttanayenevāti yathā mettābhāvanāyaṃ “appakasirenevā”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.253) tikacatukkajjhānavasena appanā “ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.253-254) tassā vaḍḍhanā ca vuttā, evamidha karuṇābhāvanāyaṃ tikacatukkajjhānavasena appanā veditabbā ca vaḍḍhetabbā ca, tathevassā vaḍḍhanāvidhipi veditabbāti adhippāyo. Vuttanayenevāti avadhāraṇena “paṭhamaṃ veripuggalo karuṇāyitabbo”ti idaṃ yathā pāḷiviruddhaṃ, evaṃ yuttiviruddhampīti imamatthaṃ [M 1.0373] dīpeti. Paṭhamaṃ hi veriṃ samanussarato kodho uppajjeyya, na karuṇā. Attāpi sakkhibhāvena karuṇāyanavasena gahetabbo, so kimiti pacchā gayhatīti. “Appanā vaḍḍhetabbā”ti iminā ca appanāppattacittasseva “karuṇāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77, 509; 2.309, 315, 452, 471; 3.230) vuttavikubbanā ijjhatīti ayamattho dassito.

Herein, 'by the method previously stated' refers to the method stated for the person with the loving-kindness meditation subject. This is by the method stated for loving-kindness. 'Should be pacified' means that that resentment should be pacified by the method stated in the development of loving-kindness, with 'Then, for this former person...' etc., and 'by one who recollects the advice in the Simile of the Saw,' etc. Thus, having now shown the method of developing compassion for a person who has attained great suffering, and also for a person who is happy, by way of attaining suffering in the future due to not having done wholesome deeds, now, in order to show that method even for a person who has done good, 'And whoever here...' etc., is said. 'Of them' means of misfortunes. 'Because the suffering of the round has not been transcended' means because of not having yet transcended the immeasurable suffering of saṃsāra—of the future suffering in the woeful states, and also in the fortunate destinations the suffering distinguished as birth, aging, etc.—which even a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One would be unable to bring to an end by description. 'Having had compassion in all ways' means having developed the development of compassion by generating compassion for each and every person, by clearly perceiving the state of being a basis for compassion in all ways, that is, by way of the attainment of suffering, or by way of the attainment of happiness, whether one has not done wholesome deeds or has done them. 'By the method stated' means by the method stated in the development of loving-kindness, with 'Then, by one who pervades with loving-kindness again and again...' etc. 'That sign' means the sign of serenity that has arisen by way of the breaking of boundaries. 'By the method stated for loving-kindness' means: just as in the development of loving-kindness, absorption by means of the three- and four-fold jhānas with 'without difficulty...' etc., and its development with 'having pervaded one direction, one dwells...' etc., were stated, so here in the development of compassion, absorption by means of the three- and four-fold jhānas should be known and should be developed, and likewise the method of its development should be known; this is the meaning. By the emphasis in 'by the method stated,' it shows this meaning: that this statement, 'First, a hostile person should be made an object of compassion,' is contrary to the Pāḷi, and likewise, it is also contrary to logic. For, to one who first recollects a hostile person, anger would arise, not compassion. Oneself, too, should be taken as a witness by way of developing compassion; why is that self taken later? And by this, 'absorption should be developed,' this meaning is shown: that only for one whose mind has attained absorption do the transformations stated with 'with a mind accompanied by compassion, one dwells pervading one direction...' etc. succeed.

Karuṇāpadamattameva cassā pāḷiyā visesoti taṃ anāmasitvā paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttavikubbanā, mettāya vuttaānisaṃsā ca idha labbhantīti dassetuṃ “tato paraṃ…pe… veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha tato paranti “karuṇāsahagatena cetasā”ti (dī. ni. 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77, 509; 2.309, 315, 452, 471; 3.230) vuttavikubbanato upari. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

And, in order to show that, because only the mere term 'compassion' is the distinction in that Pāḷi passage, without touching upon that, the transformations stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and the benefits stated for loving-kindness are obtained here, it is said, 'Beyond that... should be understood.' Therein, 'beyond that' means after the transformations stated as 'with a mind accompanied by compassion...' The rest is just according to the stated method.

Muditābhāvanāvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Development of Sympathetic Joy

260. Piyapuggalādīsūti piyamajjhattaverīsu na ārabhitabbā. Muditābhāvanāti vibhattiṃ pariṇāmetvā yojanā. Na hītiādi tattha kāraṇavacanaṃ. Piyabhāvamattenāti ettha matta-saddo [V 1.0352] visesanivatti attho, tena somanassapaṭisandhikatādisiddhā niccappahaṃsitamukhatā, pubbabhāsitā, sukhasambhāsatā, sakhilatā, sammodakatāti evamādike muditāya padaṭṭhānabhūte visese ulliṅgeti, īdisehi visesehi virahitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Eva-kārena pana piyapuggalassa sukhasamappitatādiṃ, muditāya ca hetubhūtaṃ pamodappavattiṃ nivatteti. Piyapuggalepi hi paramāya sampattiyā pamudite haṭṭhatuṭṭhe bhikkhuno muditokāsaṃ labheyya. Vakkhati hi “piyapuggalaṃ vā”tiādi. Ādito majjhattapuggalaṃ anussarantassa udāsinatā saṇṭhāti, veriṃ samanussarantassa kodho uppajjati. Tenāha “pageva majjhattaverino”ti.

260. 'Among dear persons, etc.' means that the development of sympathetic joy should not be started with dear, neutral, and hostile persons. The connection is to be made by changing the case ending. 'For not...' etc., is the statement of reason for that. 'Merely by being dear': here the word 'merely' (matta) has the meaning of excluding specifics. By that, it indicates the specific qualities which are the proximate cause for sympathetic joy, such as: having a constantly cheerful face, being one who speaks first, having pleasant conversation, being gentle, and being one who causes delight, which are established due to having a joyful disposition, etc. It is said to mean 'devoid of such specific qualities.' However, by the word 'only' (eva), it excludes the state of being endowed with happiness, etc., of a dear person, and the arising of joy which is the cause of sympathetic joy. For, even in the case of a dear person who is delighted and overjoyed with the highest fortune, a monk could find an opportunity for sympathetic joy. For it will be said, 'or a dear person,' etc. For one who recollects a neutral person from the start, indifference is established. For one who recollects a hostile person, anger arises. Therefore, it is said, 'how much more so with neutral and hostile ones.'

Pamodappavattiyā soṇḍasadiso sahāyo soṇḍasahāyo. Muditamuditovāti pasādasommatāya ativiya mudito eva. Pasāde hi idaṃ āmeḍitaṃ. Evaṃ aṭṭhakathānayena ādito muditābhāvanāya vatthuṃ dassetvā idāni pāḷinayena dassetuṃ “piyapuggalaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sukhitanti sañjātasukhaṃ, sukhappattanti attho. Sajjitanti sukhānubhavane sannaddhaṃ paṭiyattasukhasādhanaṃ. Aho sādhūti tassa sattassa sampattiyaṃ [M 1.0374] sampajaññapubbapamodanākāradassanaṃ. Puna aho suṭṭhūti tassa pamodanassa bahulīkāradassanaṃ. Piyaṃ manāpanti ettha manāpa-ggahaṇena pāḷiyampi atippiyasahāyako adhippetoti eke.

A companion who is like a drunkard due to the constant arising of joy is a 'soṇḍa companion.' 'Rejoicing, rejoicing' means exceedingly joyful due to serenity and agreeableness. For this is a reduplication in the sense of serenity. Thus, having first shown the object for the development of sympathetic joy according to the method of the commentary, now, in order to show it according to the method of the Pāḷi, 'or a dear person,' etc., is said. Therein, 'happy' means one for whom happiness has arisen, one who has attained happiness. 'Equipped' means bound for the experience of happiness, having the means for happiness prepared. The words 'Ah, it is good!' are a showing of the manner of rejoicing preceded by clear comprehension at that being's success. Again, the words 'Ah, it is very good!' are a showing of the making much of that rejoicing. 'Dear and agreeable': here, by the inclusion of 'agreeable,' some say that even in the Pāḷi, a very dear companion is intended.

Atīteti tasmiṃyeva attabhāve atīte. Anāgateti etthāpi eseva nayo. Na hi bhavantaragate brahmavihārabhāvanā ruhati. Yadi evaṃ, atītānāgate kathanti? Nāyaṃ doso. “So evāyaṃ datto tisso”ti addhāpaccuppannatāya vijjamānabhāvena gahetabbato. Kathaṃ panassa anāgate sampatti ārammaṇaṃ hotīti? Ādesādito, paccuppannāya vā payogasampattiyā anumānato laddhāya gahetabbato.

'Past' means past in that very same existence. Here too, in 'future,' this is the same method. For the development of the divine abidings does not succeed with regard to a person who has gone to another existence. If so, how does it succeed with regard to the past and future? This is not a fault. Because it is to be taken as actually existing by way of being temporally present, as in 'This is that same Datta, that same Tissa.' But how does future attainment become an object for this one? Because it is to be taken either from prediction, etc., or as obtained by inference from the success of the present effort.

Piyapuggaleti soṇḍasahāyasaññite atippiyapuggale, piyapuggale ca. Duvidhopi cesa idha piyabhāvasāmaññato “piyapuggalo”ti vutto. Anukkamenāti atippiyapuggalo piyapuggalo majjhatto verīti catūsu koṭṭhāsesu ekekasmiṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ paguṇaṃ, muduṃ, kammaniyañca katvā sesesu upasaṃharaṇānukkamena. Kiñcāpi catūsu janesu samacittatāva sīmāsambhedo sīmā sambhijjati etāyāti katvā. Bhāvanāya pana tathā bahuso pavattamānāya purimasiddhaṃ hetuṃ, itaraṃ phalañca katvā [V 1.0353] vuttaṃ “samacittatāya sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā”ti. Yathāvuttasīmābhāvo vā sīmāsambhedoti vuttaṃ “samacittatāya sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā”ti. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

'A dear person' refers to an extremely dear person, one designated as a 'soṇḍa companion,' and also a dear person. Both types are referred to here as 'a dear person' due to their common characteristic of dearness. 'Gradually' means by the sequence of applying the meditation subject to the remaining persons, after having made it proficient, soft, and workable in each of the four categories: an extremely dear person, a dear person, a neutral person, and a hostile person. Although equanimity towards the four types of people is indeed the breaking of boundaries—in the sense that the boundary is broken by it—yet, when the development proceeds frequently in that way, it is said, 'having broken the boundary through equanimity,' by making the previously accomplished equanimity the cause and the other, the breaking of the boundary, the result. Or, the absence of the boundary as described is called 'the breaking of boundaries.' Hence, it is said, 'having broken the boundary through equanimity.' As for the rest that needs to be said here, it is according to the method stated above.

Upekkhābhāvanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Development of Equanimity

261. Upekkhābhāvananti upekkhābrahmavihārabhāvanaṃ. Yasmā purimabrahmavihārattayanissando catutthabrahmavihāro, tasmā vuttaṃ “mettādīsu paṭiladdhatikacatukkajjhānenā”ti. Paguṇatatiyajjhānāti subhāvitaṃ vasībhāvaṃ pāpitaṃ paguṇaṃ, tathārūpā tatiyabrahmavihārajjhānato. Appaguṇaṃ hi uparijhānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ na hoti. Catukkanayavasena cettha tatiyaggahaṇaṃ. Sukhitā hontūtiādivasenāti ādi-saddena “niddukkhā hontū”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sattakelāyanaṃ sattesu mamāyanaṃ [M 1.0375] mamattakaraṇaṃ, tathā manasikārena yogo sattakelāyanamanasikārayuttattaṃ, tasmā. Mettādīnaṃ rāgagehassitadomanassasomanassānaṃ āsannavuttitāya yathārahaṃ paṭighānunayasamīpacāritā veditabbā. Atha vā “sukhitā hontu, dukkhato muccantu modantū”ti hitesitabhāvappattiyā tissannampi anunayassa āsannacāritā. Sati ca tabbipariyāye lohitappakope pubbo viya laddhokāsamevettha paṭighanti avisesena tāsaṃ paṭighānunayasamīpacāritā daṭṭhabbā.

261. 'The development of equanimity' means the development of the divine abiding of equanimity. Because the fourth divine abiding is the result of the preceding three divine abidings, it is said: 'by means of the tetrad of jhānas attained in loving-kindness and the others.' 'From a proficient third jhāna' means from a third jhāna of the divine abidings that is well-developed and brought to mastery, which is called 'proficient.' For an unproficient jhāna is not a proximate cause for a higher jhāna. And here, the mention of the third is by way of the tetrad system. By way of 'May they be happy,' etc.: by the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of such phrases as 'May they be free from suffering' should be understood. 'Affection for beings' is making them 'mine' or the act of making them one's own with regard to beings. The connection with such attention is 'being endowed with attention connected with affection for beings.' Therefore, due to the close occurrence of lust, household-based grief, and household-based joy with loving-kindness and the others, their state of roaming near aversion and affection should be understood as appropriate. Alternatively, through attaining the state of wishing for their welfare—'May they be happy, may they be freed from suffering, may they rejoice'—the state of roaming near affection should be understood for all three. And when the opposite occurs, just as pus finds an opportunity when there is a corruption of the blood, so too aversion finds an opportunity here. Thus, their state of roaming near aversion and affection should be understood generally.

“Somanassayogena oḷārikattā”ti idaṃ tatiyajjhānassa vasena vuttaṃ, tato vuṭṭhitassa idamādīnavadassananti. Mettādivasena pana oḷārikabhāve vuccamāne vitakkavicārapītiyogeneva oḷārikatā vattabbā siyā, tāhipi tāsaṃ samāyogasambhavato, upekkhāya ca tadabhāvato. Na vā vattabbā tatiyajjhānikānaṃyeva mettādīnaṃ idhādhippetattā, taṃtaṃjhānasamatikkameneva ca taṃtaṃjhānikā mettādayopi samatikkantā eva nāma honti, jhānasāmaññena viya mettādisāmaññena vohāramattaṃ. Purimāsūti mettākaruṇāmuditāsu. Santabhāvatoti yathāvuttasattakelāyanādianupasantabhāvābhāvato upekkhāya santabhāvato. “Santabhāvato”ti ca idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sukhumatā paṇītatā vidūrakilesatā vipulaphalatāti evamādayopi upekkhāya ānisaṃsā daṭṭhabbā. Pakatimajjhattoti kiñci kāraṇaṃ anapekkhitvā pakatiyā sabhāveneva imassa bhikkhuno udāsinapakkhe ṭhito. Ajjhupekkhitvāti attanā katakammavaseneva ayamāyasmā āgato gacchati ca, tvampi attanā katakammavaseneva āgato [V 1.0354] gacchasi ca, na tassa tava payogena kiñci sukhaṃ vā upanetuṃ, dukkhaṃ vā apanetuṃ labbhā, kevalaṃ panetaṃ cittassa anujukammaṃ, yadidaṃ mettāyanādinā sattesu kelāyanaṃ. Buddhādīhi ariyehi gatamaggo cesa apaṇṇakapaṭipadābhūto, yadidaṃ sabbasattesu majjhattatāti evaṃ paṭipakkhajigucchāmukhena majjhattatāya samupajātagāravabahumānādaro taṃ puggalaṃ punappunaṃ ajjhupekkhati, tattha ca savisesaṃ upekkhaṃ paccupaṭṭhapeti, tassa tathā paṭipajjato pakatiyāpi udāsinattā sātisayaṃ tattha majjhattatā saṇṭhāti[M 1.0376]. Bhāvanābalena nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāneva honti, kilesā sannisinnā eva honti, so taṃ upekkhaṃ piyapuggalādīsu upasaṃharati. Tenāha “upekkhā uppādetabbā. Tato piyapuggalādīsū”ti. Ekaṃ puggalanti ettha aññattho eka-saddo “ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.27) viya. Ekavacaneneva cettha saṅkhyāviseso siddho, tasmā aññaṃ ekaṃ puggalanti ayamettha attho. Tena attānaṃ nivatteti. “Neva manāpa”nti iminā piyapuggalaṃ, atippiyasahāyakañca nivatteti, attānampi vā attani amanāpatāya abhāvato. “Na amanāpa”nti iminā appiyaṃ, veripuggalañca, pārisesato majjhattapuggalassa gahaṇaṃ āpannaṃ. Iti “ekaṃ puggalaṃ neva manāpaṃ nāmanāpa”nti iminā attano, piyādīnañca paṭikkhepamukhena udāsinapuggalaṃ dasseti.

“Because of its coarseness due to its connection with joy” (somanassayogena oḷārikattā): this is said with reference to the third jhāna; this is the seeing of the danger for one who has emerged from it. However, when the state of coarseness is spoken of with reference to loving-kindness and so on, the coarseness should be said to be due only to the connection with applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), and rapture (pīti), since their combination with those states is possible, whereas equanimity lacks them. Or, it should not be said so, because it is only the loving-kindness and so on associated with the third jhāna that are intended here. And by transcending each respective jhāna, the states of loving-kindness and so on associated with those jhānas are also indeed transcended; the designation is a mere convention based on the commonality of 'jhāna' or the commonality of 'loving-kindness,' etc. “In the former ones” (purimāsu) means in loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy. “Because of its peaceful nature” (santabhāvato) means because of the peaceful nature of equanimity, due to the absence of the unpeaceful state of affection for beings, etc., as previously mentioned. And this phrase “because of its peaceful nature” should be seen as a mere illustration. The benefits of equanimity, such as subtlety, refinement, distance from defilements, and great fruitfulness, should also be seen. “Naturally neutral” (pakatimajjhatto) means one who stands on the side of indifference for this monk by natural disposition alone, without regard to any reason. “Having regarded with equanimity” (ajjhupekkhitvā) means: “This venerable one comes and goes by the power of the kamma he himself has done, and you too come and go by the power of the kamma you yourself have done. It is not possible for you, by your effort, to bring him any happiness or to remove any suffering. This affection for beings through loving-kindness and so on is merely a crookedness of the mind. And this is the path trodden by the noble ones, such as the Buddha, being the unerring practice—that is, neutrality toward all beings.” Thus, having well-arisen respect, great esteem, and reverence for neutrality by way of disgust for its opposite, he regards that person with equanimity again and again, and establishes a special equanimity towards him. For one who practices thus, neutrality is exceedingly well-established towards that person, due to his being naturally indifferent. By the power of the development, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, and the defilements are indeed settled. He then applies that equanimity to the dear person and so on. Therefore, it is said: “Equanimity is to be produced. Then towards the dear person and so on.” “One person” (ekaṃ puggalaṃ): here the word eka has the sense of “another,” as in “some assert thus” (MN 3.27). For here the specific number is established by the singular case ending alone; therefore, the meaning here is “another one person.” By this, he excludes himself. By “neither pleasant” (neva manāpaṃ), he excludes the dear person and the extremely dear companion, or also himself, due to the absence of unpleasantness in himself. By “not unpleasant” (na amanāpaṃ), he excludes the disliked person and the enemy. By elimination, the taking of the neutral person is arrived at. Thus, by this phrase “one person neither pleasant nor unpleasant,” he indicates the indifferent person by way of rejecting himself and the dear persons, etc.

Vuttanayenāti “yvāssa pakatimajjhatto”tiādinā anantaraṃ vuttena nayena. Attasinehassa balavabhāvato veritopi attani majjhattatāya durūpasaṃhārattā “imesu ca attani cā”ti attā pacchā vutto. Pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayenevāti “ayaṃ samāpatti āsannapītipaccatthikā”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.87) pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayena. Yaṃ hi heṭṭhā “paguṇatatiyajjhānā vuṭṭhāyā”tiādi (visuddhi. 1.87) vuttaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā tīsu brahmavihāresu, catutthabrahmavihāre ca ādīnavānisaṃsadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Idaṃ pana tatiyajjhāne ādīnavaṃ, catutthajjhāne ca ānisaṃsaṃ disvā catutthādhigamāya yogaṃ karontassa catutthajjhānassa uppajjanākāradassanaṃ. Tasmā tattha vuttaṃ “pathavīsaddaṃ apanetvā tadeva nimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjatī”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ.

“By the way stated” means by the way stated immediately before, beginning with “one who is naturally neutral,” and so on. Because of the strength of self-love, it is difficult to establish neutrality towards oneself, even more so than towards an enemy; hence, in “among these and in oneself,” ‘oneself’ is stated afterwards. “By the method stated in the earth kasiṇa” means by the method stated in the section on the earth kasiṇa, beginning with “this attainment has joy as a near enemy” (Visuddhimagga 1.87). For what was stated below, beginning with “having emerged from a proficient third jhāna” (Visuddhimagga 1.87), was stated with respect to the three divine abidings below and the fourth divine abiding, by way of showing the drawbacks and benefits. This, however, is the showing of the mode of arising of the fourth jhāna for one who, having seen the drawback in the third jhāna and the benefit in the fourth jhāna, is making an effort to attain the fourth. Therefore, what was stated there should be connected with the passage beginning, “having removed the word ‘earth,’ and having made that very sign the object, mind-door adverting arises,” and so on.

Pathavīkasiṇādīsūti ādi-saddena sesakasiṇāni, assāsapassāsanimittañca saṅgaṇhāti. Kāmaṃ kasiṇānāpānesu uppannassāpi tatiyajjhānassa upekkhābrahmavihārena rūpāvacarajjhānāditāya attheva sabhāgatā, taṃ pana akāraṇaṃ ārammaṇassa visadisatāyāti āha [V 1.0355] “ārammaṇavisabhāgatāyā”ti. Nanu ca aññathāva kasiṇādibhāvanā, aññathā brahmavihārabhāvanāti bhāvanāvasenāpi yathāvuttajjhānānaṃ attheva visadisatāti? Saccametaṃ, bhāvanāvasena pana visadisatā anuppattiyā na ekantikaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Tathā hi aññathāva mettādibhāvanā[M 1.0377], aññathā upekkhābhāvanā. Tathāpi sattesu yathāpavattitaṃ hitesitādiākāraṃ byatirekamukhena āmasantī, tato vinivattamānarūpena ajjhupekkhanākārena brahmavihārupekkhā pavattati. Tathā hi vakkhati “kammassakā sattā, te kassa ruciyā sukhitā vā bhavissantī”tiādi (visuddhi. 1.263). Ārammaṇasabhāgatāpi cettha atthīti mettādivasena paṭiladdhatatiyajjhānassa ijjhati upekkhābrahmavihāro. Tena vuttaṃ “mettādīsū”tiādi. Tattha mettādīsūti mettādīsu nipphādetabbesu, mettādivasenāti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

“In the earth kasiṇa and so on”: by the word “and so on,” he includes the remaining kasiṇas and the sign of in-and-out breathing. Indeed, for the third jhāna arisen in the kasiṇas and Ānāpāna, there is a similarity in nature with the upekkhā-brahmavihāra by way of being a form-sphere jhāna, etc. But that is not a cause, due to the dissimilarity of the object; thus he says, “due to the dissimilarity of the object.” Is it not so that the development of kasiṇas, etc., is one way, and the development of the brahmavihāras is another? Thus, by way of development also, there is indeed a dissimilarity of the aforementioned jhānas. This is true, but the dissimilarity by way of development is not a decisive reason for non-attainment. For the development of loving-kindness, etc., is one way, and the development of equanimity is another. Nevertheless, by reflecting in a contrary manner on the mode of desiring welfare, etc., that has been applied to beings, the brahmavihāra-equanimity proceeds in the mode of looking on with equanimity, in the form of withdrawing from that. For he will say, “Beings are owners of their kamma; by whose wish will they become happy?” and so on (Visuddhimagga 1.263). And since there is also a similarity of object here, the upekkhā-brahmavihāra is accomplished for one who has attained the third jhāna by means of loving-kindness, etc. Therefore, it was said, “in loving-kindness, etc.” and so on. Therein, “in loving-kindness, etc.” means “in cases where loving-kindness, etc., are to be produced,” that is, “by means of loving-kindness, etc.” The rest is by the method stated below.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discourse

262. Brahmuttamenāti ettha sammutibrahmāno upapattibrahmāno visuddhibrahmānoti tividhā brahmāno.

262. Here, in the phrase “by the highest Brahmā,” Brahmās are of three kinds: conventional Brahmās, Brahmās by rebirth, and Brahmās by purification.

“Sampannaṃ sālikedāraṃ, suvā bhuñjanti kosiya;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na ne vāretumussahe. (jā. 1.14.1);

“The rice field is abundant, O Kosiya, parrots are eating it; I report this to you, O Brahmā, I am not able to stop them.”

Paribbaja mahābrahme, pacantaññepi pāṇino”ti. (pāci. 647) –

“Wander forth, O great Brahmā; other beings also cook.”

Ca evamādīsu hi brahmasaddena sammutibrahmāno vuttā.

And in such cases as these, conventional Brahmās are spoken of by the word ‘brahmā’.

“Apārutā tesaṃ amatassa dvārā,

Ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṃ;

Vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ,

Dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme”.

“Opened for them are the doors to the Deathless; let those with ears release their faith. Perceiving vexation, O Brahmā, I did not speak the proficient and excellent Dhamma among humans.”

“Atha kho brahmā sahampatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.71; ma. ni. 1.283; 2.340; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 9) ca [V 1.0356] evamādīsu brahmasaddena upapattibrahmāno vuttā. “Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.148; saṃ. ni. 2.21; a. ni. 4.8; 5.11; paṭi. ma. 2.44) vacanato “brahma”nti ariyadhammo vuccati, tato nibbattattā avisesena sabbepi ariyā visuddhibrahmāno nāma paramatthabrahmatāya. Visesato pana “brahmāti, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti vacanato sammāsambuddho uttamabrahmā nāma sadevake loke brahmabhūtehi guṇehi ukkaṃsapāramippattito. Iti brahmānaṃ uttamo, brahmā ca so uttamo cāti vā [M 1.0378] brahmuttamo, bhagavā. Tena kathite “so mettāsahagatena cetasā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77, 459, 509; 2.309, 315, 451, 471) tattha tattha veneyyānaṃ desite. Itīti evaṃ yathāvuttena bhāvanākkamena ceva atthavaṇṇanākkamena ca viditvā jānitvā. Pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyāti pubbe viya asādhāraṇaṃ taṃtaṃbrahmavihārapaṭiniyatameva atthaṃ aggahetvā sādhāraṇabhāvato tattha tattha pakiṇṇakaṃ visaṭaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā pavattitā pakiṇṇakakathāpi vijānitabbā.

“Then Brahmā Sahampati,” and so on: in such cases, Brahmās by rebirth are spoken of by the word ‘brahmā.’ Based on the saying, “He sets in motion the Brahmā-wheel,” and so on, the noble Dhamma is called ‘brahmā.’ Because they are born from that, all noble ones without distinction are called ‘Brahmās by purification’ due to their ultimate Brahmā-nature. Specifically, however, based on the saying, “Bhikkhus, ‘Brahmā’ is a designation for the Tathāgata,” the Perfectly Enlightened One is called the Supreme Brahmā, because in the world with its devas he has reached the highest perfection through qualities that have become brahmā. Thus, the Blessed One is ‘supreme among Brahmās’ (brahmānaṃ uttamo), or ‘he is a Brahmā and he is supreme’ (brahmā ca so uttamo ca), hence ‘Brahmuttamo.’ When it was taught by him in various places for those to be trained, with the words, “with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness,” and so on. Thus: having known and understood in this way by the aforesaid sequence of development and sequence of commentary on the meaning. As for ‘the miscellaneous discourse should also be understood’: as before, not taking the specific meaning confined only to each respective brahmavihāra, but taking the miscellaneous and widespread meaning in various places due to its common nature, the miscellaneous discourse that has been set forth should also be known.

Mejjatīti dhammato aññassa kattunivattanatthaṃ dhammameva kattāraṃ katvā niddisati. Siniyhatīti ettha sattesu byāpajjanavasena lūkhabhāvassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ hitākārapavattivasena sinehanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na taṇhāyanavasena. Taṃ hi mohapubbaṅgamaṃ lubbhanasabhāvaṃ, idaṃ pana adussanasabhāvaṃ alobhasampayuttaṃ. Nanu ca taṇhāsinehopi byāpādavirodhī tena sahānavaṭṭhānato. Yadipi tena saha ekasmiṃ citte nappavattati, virodhī pana na hoti appahāyakato. Mejjatīti mitto, hitajjhāsayo khandhappabandho, tappariyāpannatāya mitte bhavā, mitte vā ārammaṇabhūte piye puggale bhavā, mittassa esā pavatti mejjanavasena vāti veditabbā.

“He loves” (mejjati): in order to avert an agent other than the mere phenomenon, he indicates the phenomenon itself as the agent. Here, in “he is affectionate” (siniyhati), affection should be understood as that which is the opposite of a harsh state based on ill will towards beings, is preceded by knowledge, and occurs by way of acting for their welfare; it should not be understood as being by way of craving. For that is preceded by delusion and has the nature of greed, whereas this has the nature of non-hatred and is associated with non-greed. Is it not so that affection based on craving also opposes ill will, because it does not stand together with it? Although it does not proceed in one consciousness together with it, it is not an opponent because it does not lead to its abandonment. Because he loves (mejjati), he is a friend (mitto); a continuum of aggregates with a disposition for welfare. It should be known thus: it exists in a friend because of being included in that; or it exists in a dear person who is a friend and has become an object; or this is the activity of a friend by way of affection.

Karotīti karuṇā, kiṃ karoti, kesaṃ, kiṃ nimittanti āha “paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampana”nti. Kampananti ca paresaṃ dukkhaṃ disvā tassa apanetukāmassa asahanākārena cittassa aññathattaṃ. Tayidaṃ sappurisānaṃyeva hotīti āha “sādhūna”nti. Sappurisā hi saparahitasādhanena “sādhū”ti vuccanti. Vināsetīti adassanaṃ gameti, apanetīti attho. Tenettha hiṃsanaṃ apanayananti dasseti. Paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā hi karuṇā. Pharaṇavasenāti [V 1.0357] phusanavasena, ārammaṇakaraṇavasenāti attho. Ārammaṇakaraṇañcettha dukkhitesu dukkhāpanayanākārenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because it acts (karoti), it is called compassion (karuṇā). What does it do? For whom? For what reason? To this, he said: “It is the trembling of the heart of the good when the suffering of others is present.” And “trembling” is the alteration of the mind, in the manner of being unable to bear it, of one who desires to remove that suffering upon seeing the suffering of others. This belongs only to the virtuous; thus, he said “of the good.” Indeed, virtuous persons are called “good” because they accomplish their own welfare and the welfare of others. “It destroys” means it causes to disappear, it removes; this is the meaning. By that, he shows that herein, harming is removal. Indeed, compassion has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of removing the suffering of others. “By way of pervading” means by way of touching, that is, by way of making it an object; this is the meaning. And herein, the making of an object should be understood as occurring only in the mode of removing suffering in those who are suffering.

Modanti tāyāti modanakiriyāya muditāya karaṇabhāvaniddeso, svāyaṃ upacārasiddho, muditāvinimutto natthi tattha koci kattāti tameva kattubhāvena niddisati “sayaṃ vā modatī”ti, ayampi upacāraniddesova. Dhammānaṃ avasavattanatoti vasavattibhāvanivāraṇatthaṃ “modanamattameva vā tanti muditā”ti āha.

“They rejoice by means of it” is an indication of the instrumental state for the action of rejoicing, which is sympathetic joy. This is established by convention. Since there is no agent separate from sympathetic joy who accomplishes that rejoicing, he indicates that very sympathetic joy in the state of an agent, saying, “or one rejoices oneself.” This indication of an agent is also merely an indication by convention. Because phenomena are not subject to one's will, in order to prevent the state of being subject to one's will, he said, “Or, sympathetic joy is merely the state of rejoicing.”

Piyādīsu [M 1.0379] pakkhapātupacchedanamukhena udāsinabhāvasaṅkhātā upapattito ikkhā upekkhā. Tenāha “averā hontū”tiādi. Tattha upekkhatīti kattuniddese kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

Equanimity (upekkhā) is the looking on (ikkhā) that arises fittingly, which is known as the state of neutrality, primarily by way of cutting off partiality towards the beloved and so on. Therefore, he said, “May they be free from enmity,” and so on. Therein, the reason for the indication of an agent in “he is equanimous” has already been stated below.

263. Hito nāma atthacaro, tasmā hitākārappavattilakkhaṇāti sattānaṃ hitacaraṇākārena pavattilakkhaṇā, hitākārassa vā pavattanalakkhaṇā. Hitūpasaṃhārarasāti sattesu hitassa upanayanakiccā, upanayanasampattikā vā. “Anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1237; vibha. 909) pavattanakassa āghātassa vinayanākārena paccupatiṭṭhati, ñāṇassa gocarabhāvaṃ gacchati, yattha vā sayaṃ uppajjati, tattha āghātavinayanaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti āghātavinayapaccupaṭṭhānā. Amanāpānampi sattānaṃ paṭikkūle appaṭikkūlasaññitārūpena, pageva manāpānaṃ yaṃ manāpabhāvadassanaṃ, tathāpavatto yonisomanasikāro, taṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ etissāti manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Byāpādūpasamoti byāpādassa vikkhambhanavasena vūpasamo. Sampattīti sampajjanaṃ sammadeva nibbatti. Sinehasambhavoti taṇhāsinehassa uppatti. Vipattīti vināso. Mettāmukhena hi rāgo vañceti.

263. ‘Beneficial’ (hito) means acting for welfare (atthacaro). Therefore, ‘it has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of benefit’ means it has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of acting for the welfare of beings, or it has the characteristic of causing the mode of welfare to occur. Its function is to bring about welfare, meaning it has the function of bringing welfare to beings, or its accomplishment is bringing it about. It manifests in the mode of dispelling the ill will that arises from such thoughts as, ‘He did me harm,’ etc.; it enters the range of knowledge. Or, wherever it arises, it causes the dispelling of ill will to manifest. Thus, its manifestation is the dispelling of ill will. Its proximate cause is seeing a lovable aspect, for the well-directed attention that occurs as the seeing of a lovable aspect—even in disagreeable beings by perceiving what is not disagreeable in the disagreeable, and how much more so in agreeable beings—is its proximate cause. Its success is the calming of ill will, which is its calming by way of suppression. ‘Success’ is accomplishment, proper completion. Its failure is the arising of affection, which is the arising of affection based on craving. ‘Failure’ is destruction. For lust deceives under the guise of loving-kindness.

Karuṇādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādīsu iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Visesamattameva vaṇṇayissāma. Sattānaṃ pavattadukkhassa apanayanākāro. Apanayanaṃ pana hotu vā mā vā, yo dukkhāpanayanākāro, tathāpavattilakkhaṇā dukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā. Apanetukāmatāya paresaṃ dukkhassa asahanaṃ anadhivāsanaṃ paradukkhāsahanaṃ. Na vihiṃsā avihiṃsā, sattānaṃ aviheṭhanaṃ. Taṃ paccupaṭṭhapeti, vihiṃsāya vā paṭipakkhabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti avihiṃsāpaccupaṭṭhānā. Vihiṃsūpasamoti ettha vihiṃsanti etāya satte, vihiṃsanaṃ vā nesaṃ tanti vihiṃsā[V 1.0358], sattānaṃ viheṭhanākārena pavatto karuṇāya paṭipakkhabhūto paṭighacittuppādo. Karuṇāmukhena soko vañcetīti āha “sokasambhavo vipattī”ti.

The meaning of the characteristics, etc., of compassion and so on should be understood in this way. We will explain only the distinctive points. Its characteristic is occurring in the mode of removing the suffering of beings. Now, whether the removal occurs or not, whatever is the mode of removing suffering, [compassion] has the characteristic of occurring in such a way, that is, it has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of removing suffering. Its function is the inability to bear the suffering of others, meaning the inability to bear or endure it due to the desire to remove it. Its manifestation is non-harming. Non-harming (`avihiṃsā`) is not harming; it is not afflicting beings. It causes that to manifest, or it manifests as the opposite of harming; thus, it has non-harming as its manifestation. Regarding [the manifestation as] 'the calming of harm' (`vihiṃsūpasamo`): herein, 'harm' (`vihiṃsā`) is that by which they harm beings, or it is their harming. This refers to the arising of a mind-state of aversion, which is the opposite of compassion and occurs in the mode of afflicting beings. Sorrow deceives under the guise of compassion; therefore, he said, 'The arising of sorrow is its failure.'

Pamodanalakkhaṇāti parasampattiyā pamodanalakkhaṇā. Anissāyanarasāti issāyanassa usūyanassa paṭipakkhabhāvakiccā. Sattānaṃ sampattiyā, pantasenāsanesu, adhikusaladhammesu ca asahanaṃ aramaṇaṃ aratiicceva [M 1.0380] saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tassā vihananākārena paccupatiṭṭhati, tassa vā vighātaṃ vūpasamaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti arativighātapaccupaṭṭhānā.

Its characteristic is rejoicing, meaning it has the characteristic of rejoicing in the success of others. Its function is non-envy, meaning it has the function of being the opposite of envy and jealousy. Its manifestation is the destruction of discontent. The inability to bear and the lack of delight in the success of beings, in secluded dwellings, and in superior wholesome states, are included under the term 'discontent' (`arati`). It manifests in the mode of destroying that discontent. Or, it causes the destruction and calming of that discontent to manifest. Thus, its manifestation is the destruction of discontent.

Pahāso gehasitapītivasena pahaṭṭhabhāvo uppilāvitattaṃ. Sattesu samabhāvadassanarasāti piyādibhedesu sabbasattesu udāsinavuttiyā samabhāvasseva dassanakiccā, upapattito ikkhaṇato samabhāveneva tesaṃ gahaṇakiccāti attho. Sattesu paṭikkūlāpaṭikkūlākārānaṃ aggahaṇato tattha paṭighānunayānaṃ vūpasamanākārena vuttiyā tesaṃ vūpasamaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti paṭighānunayavūpasamapaccupaṭṭhānā. Evaṃ pavattakammassakatādassanapadaṭṭhānāti ettha “eva”nti iminā byatirekamukhena hitūpasaṃhāradukkhāpanayanasampattipamodanākārena paccāmasanto mettādīnaṃ tissannaṃ pavattiākārapaṭisedhanamukhena pavattaṃ kammassakatāñāṇaṃ upekkhābrahmavihārassa āsannakāraṇaṃ, na yaṃ kiñcīti dasseti.

Mirth (`pahāso`) is a state of being gladdened and elated, a giddiness, by way of joy and delight based on the household life. [Equanimity's] function is seeing beings with equality. This means it has the function of seeing only equality towards all beings who are differentiated as beloved, etc., by maintaining a neutral attitude. Because of looking on fittingly, it has the function of grasping them only with equality; this is the meaning. Its manifestation is the calming of aversion and attachment. Because of not grasping the agreeable and disagreeable aspects in beings, and by occurring in the mode of calming aversion and attachment towards them, it causes their calming and suppression to manifest. Thus, its manifestation is the calming of aversion and attachment. Its proximate cause is seeing the ownership of kamma that occurs thus. Herein, by the word 'thus', he shows that the knowledge of ownership of kamma which arises primarily by way of contrast—that is, by reflecting on the modes of bringing welfare, removing suffering, and rejoicing in success, and then primarily by way of rejecting the modes of occurrence of the three divine abidings beginning with loving-kindness—is the proximate cause of the divine abiding of equanimity, and not just any such knowledge.

264. Vipassanāsukhañceva bhavasampatti cāti ettha diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro cāti vattabbaṃ. Tampi hi nesaṃ sādhāraṇapayojanaṃ. Tathā “sukhaṃ supatī”tiādayo (a. ni. 8.1; 11.15) ekādasānisaṃsā. Te pana heṭṭhā vuttā evāti idha na gahitā.

264. Herein, regarding 'the happiness of insight and success in existence', it should also be said 'and a pleasant abiding in the here and now'. For that too is their common benefit. Likewise, the eleven benefits beginning with 'one sleeps happily' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.1; 11.15). However, since they have already been stated below, they are not taken up here.

Nissarati apagacchati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ, pahāyakaṃ. Kāmañcetehi pañcapi nīvaraṇāni, tadekaṭṭhā ca pāpadhammā vikkhambhanavasena pahīyanti, ujuvipaccanīkadassanavasena pana byāpādādayo pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 3.326; a. ni. 6.13) vuttā. Evañca katvā rāganissaraṇatāvacanaṃ upekkhābrahmavihārassa suṭṭhu samatthitaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It is an escape because by this one goes forth and departs; it is that which abandons. Although by these [divine abidings] the five hindrances and the unwholesome states that share their basis are abandoned by way of suppression, yet ill will and others are stated in the Pāḷi (Dīgha Nikāya 3.326; Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.13) by way of seeing their direct opposite. And for this reason, the statement that the divine abiding of equanimity is the escape from lust should be seen as well-supported.

265. Etthāti etesu brahmavihāresu. Mettā sattesu yathārahaṃ dānapiyavacanādisīlasutādiguṇagahaṇavasena pavattati. Tena vuttaṃ “sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā”ti. Rāgopi [V 1.0359] tattha yathā tathā guṇaggahaṇamukheneva pavattati manāpasaññāpalobhatoti āha “guṇadassanasabhāgatāyā”ti. Tasmā mittamukhasapatto viya tulyākārena dūsanato rāgo mettāya āsannapaccatthiko, so lahuṃ otāraṃ labhati satisammosamattenāpi mettaṃ apanīya tassā vatthusmiṃ uppajjanārahattā[M 1.0381]. Tatoti rāgato, rāgassa vā otāralābhato. Sabhāgavisabhāgatāyāti sabhāgassa, sabhāgena vā visabhāgatāya. Sattesu hi manāpākāragāhino mettāsabhāgassa tabbiparītasabhāvo byāpādo tena visabhāgo. Tasmā so otāraṃ labhamāno cireneva labheyyāti purisassa dūre ṭhitasapatto viya mettāya dūrapaccatthiko. Tatoti byāpādato. Nibbhayenāti anussaṅkanaparisaṅkanena, laddhapatiṭṭhāya mettāya byāpādena duppadhaṃsiyattāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “mettāyissatī”tiādi.

265. 'Here' means among these divine abidings. Loving-kindness proceeds towards beings according to what is fit, by way of apprehending qualities such as giving, kind speech, virtue, and learning. Therefore it is said: '[It has] seeing the agreeable nature of beings as its proximate cause.' Lust, too, proceeds there in one way or another only by way of apprehending qualities, due to the enticement of the perception of agreeableness. Therefore, he said: 'because of sharing the nature of seeing qualities.' Thus, like an enemy with the face of a friend, lust is the near enemy of loving-kindness because it corrupts in a similar manner. It quickly finds an opening, because it is fit to arise in the object of loving-kindness, displacing it even by a mere lapse of mindfulness. 'From that' means from lust, or from lust's gaining an opening. 'Due to similarity and dissimilarity' means due to the dissimilarity of the similar. For ill will, which has a nature contrary to that which is similar to loving-kindness that apprehends the agreeable aspect in beings, is dissimilar to it. Therefore, if it were to find an opening, it would find it only after a long time; thus, like an enemy standing far from a person, it is the distant enemy of loving-kindness. 'From that' means from ill will. 'Without fear' means without suspicion and anxiety; the meaning is that because loving-kindness that has gained a footing is hard to be assaulted by ill will. Therefore he said, 'he will be friendly,' etc.

Iṭṭhānanti piyānaṃ. Kantānanti kamanīyānaṃ. Manāpānanti manavaḍḍhanakānaṃ. Tato eva mano ramentīti manoramānaṃ. Lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānanti taṇhāsannissitānaṃ. Appaṭilābhato samanupassatoti appaṭilābhena ahamime na labhāmīti paritassato. Atītanti atikkantaṃ. Niruddhanti nirodhappattaṃ. Vipariṇatanti sabhāvavigamena vigataṃ. Samanussaratoti anutthunanavasena cintayato. Gehasitanti kāmaguṇanissitaṃ. “Ādinā”ti iminā “sotaviññeyyānaṃ saddāna”nti evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vipattidassanasabhāgatāyāti yesu sattesu bhogādivipattidassanamukhena karuṇā pavattati, tesu tannimittameva ayoniso ābhoge sati yathāvuttadomanassamukhena soko uppajjeyya, so karuṇāya āsannapaccatthiko. Soko hi idha domanassasīsena vutto. Sabhāgavisabhāgatāyāti ettha sattesu dukkhāpanayanakāmatākārassa karuṇāsabhāgassa tesu dukkhūpanayanākāro vihesāsabhāvo visabhāgoti tāya sabhāgavisabhāgatāya sā otāraṃ labhamānā cireneva labheyyāti purisassa dūre ṭhitasapatto viya karuṇāya dūrapaccatthikā vuttā.

'Of the wished-for' means of the dear. 'Of the lovely' means of the desirable. 'Of the agreeable' means of that which enhances the mind. 'Of the delightful' means they delight the mind for that very reason. 'Connected with the baits of the world' means dependent on craving. 'He observes from non-attainment' means of one who is distressed, thinking 'Due to non-attainment, I do not get these.' 'Past' means passed away. 'Ceased' means having reached cessation. 'Changed' means departed through the departure of its nature. 'He recollects' means of one who thinks by way of lamenting. 'Based on the household life' means based on sensual pleasures. By 'etc.', he includes 'of sounds cognizable by the ear,' and so on. 'Because of sharing the nature of seeing misfortune': in those beings in whom compassion proceeds by way of seeing misfortune such as loss of wealth, if there is unwise attention to that very sign, sorrow would arise by way of displeasure as described; that is the near enemy of compassion. For here sorrow is spoken of with displeasure as its head. Here, in the phrase 'due to having a dissimilar nature': for the nature of compassion, which has the aspect of desiring to remove suffering in beings, the state of cruelty, which has the aspect of bringing suffering to them, is dissimilar. Thus, because of that dissimilarity of nature, if it (cruelty) were to find an opening, it would find it only after a long time; thus, like an enemy standing far from a person, it is called the distant enemy of compassion.

Sampattidassanasabhāgatāyāti yesu sattesu bhogādisampattidassanamukhena muditā pavattati, tesu tannimittameva ayoniso ābhoge sati “cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpāna”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.306) vuttasomanassamukhena pahāso uppajjeyya, so ca muditāya āsannapaccatthiko. Pahāso hi idha somanassasīsena vutto. Sabhāgavisabhāgatāyāti bhogādisampattīhi [M 1.0382] muditesu sattesu pamodanākārassa muditāsabhāgassa tattha anabhiramanākārā arati visabhāgāti tāya sabhāgavisabhāgatāya [V 1.0360] sā otāraṃ labhamānā cireneva labheyyāti purisassa dūre ṭhitasapatto viya muditāya dūrapaccatthikā vuttā. Pamudito cātiādi muditāya siddhāya ayampi arati na hotīti laddhabbaguṇadassanavasena vuttaṃ, na idhādhippetaaratiniggahadassanavasena. Kāyacittavivekapaṭipakkhāya vā aratiyā vikkhambhitāya muditāya paṭipakkhā arati suvikkhambhaneyyā hotīti dassanatthaṃ ekadesena arati dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Adhikusaladhammesūti samathavipassanādhammesu.

'Because of sharing the nature of seeing prosperity': in those beings in whom appreciative joy proceeds by way of seeing prosperity such as wealth, if there is unwise attention to that very sign, merriment would arise by way of the joy spoken of in the phrase 'of visible forms cognizable by the eye,' etc.; and that is the near enemy of appreciative joy. For here merriment is spoken of with joy as its head. In the phrase 'due to having a dissimilar nature': for the nature of appreciative joy, which has the aspect of rejoicing in beings who are gladdened by prosperity such as wealth, discontent, which has the aspect of not delighting therein, is dissimilar. Thus, because of that dissimilarity of nature, if it (discontent) were to find an opening, it would find it only after a long time; thus, like an enemy standing far from a person, it is called the distant enemy of appreciative joy. The phrase 'And being joyful,' etc., is stated by way of showing the quality to be obtained—that when appreciative joy is accomplished, this discontent does not arise—not by way of showing the suppression of the discontent intended here. Or, it should be seen that discontent is shown in one aspect in order to demonstrate that when the discontent opposed to bodily and mental seclusion is suppressed, the discontent opposed to appreciative joy becomes easy to suppress. 'In higher wholesome states' means in the states of serenity and insight.

Bālakaradhammayogato bālassa. Attahitaparahitabyāmūḷhatāya mūḷhassa. Puthūnaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādīhi kāraṇehi puthujjanassa. Kilesodhīnaṃ maggodhīhi ajitattā anodhijinassa, odhijinā vā sekkhā odhisova kilesānaṃ jitattā. Tena imassa odhijitabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Sattamabhavādito uddhaṃ pavattanavipākassa ajitattā avipākajinassa, vipākajinā vā arahanto appaṭisandhikattā. Tenassa asekkhattaṃ paṭikkhipati. Anekādīnave sabbesampi pāpadhammānaṃ mūlabhūte sammohe ādīnavānaṃ adassanasīlatāya anādīnavadassāvino. Āgamādhigamābhāvā assutavato. Ediso ekaṃsena andhaputhujjano nāma hotīti tassa andhaputhujjanabhāvadassanatthaṃ punapi “puthujjanassā”ti vuttaṃ. Evarūpāti vuttākārena sammohapubbikā. Rūpaṃ sā nātivattatīti rūpānaṃ samatikkamanāya kāraṇaṃ na hoti, rūpārammaṇe kilese nātivattatīti adhippāyo. Somanassadomanassarahitaṃ aññāṇameva aññāṇupekkhā. Dosaguṇāvicāraṇavasena sabhāgattāti yathā brahmavihārupekkhā mettādayo viya sattesu hitūpasaṃhārādivasena guṇadose avicārentī kevalaṃ ajjhupekkhanavaseneva pavattati, evaṃ aññāṇupekkhā sattesu vijjamānampi guṇadosaṃ acintentī kevalaṃ ajjhupekkhanavaseneva pavattatīti dosaguṇāvicāraṇavasena sabhāgā. Tasmā sā lahuṃ otāraṃ labhatīti brahmavihārupekkhāya āsannapaccatthikā vuttā. Sabhāgavisabhāgatāyāti iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu majjhattākārassa upekkhāsabhāgassa [M 1.0383] tattha anurodhavirodhapavattiākārā rāgapaṭighā visabhāgāti tāya sabhāgavisabhāgatāya te otāraṃ labhamānā cireneva labheyyunti purisassa dūre ṭhitasapatto viya upekkhābrahmavihārassa dūrapaccatthikā vuttā.

Of a fool, due to association with qualities that make one a fool. Of a deluded one, due to being greatly bewildered about one's own welfare and the welfare of others. Of a worldling, because of causes such as generating numerous defilements. Of one who has not conquered the limits, because the limits of defilements have not been conquered by the limits of the path; or, trainees are conquerors of the limits because they have conquered the defilements only by limits. By that, it rejects this person's state of having conquered by limits. Of one who has not conquered the resultant-fruit, because the resultant-fruit that will occur beyond the seventh existence has not been conquered; or, Arahants are conquerors of the resultant-fruit because there is no further relinking. By that, it rejects his state of being a non-trainee. Of one who does not habitually see danger, due to the nature of not seeing the dangers in delusion, which has many dangers and is the root of all evil states. Of one who is unlearned, due to the absence of scriptural learning and realization. Such a person is definitely called a blind worldling; thus, to show his state of being a blind worldling, it is said again, 'of a worldling.' 'Of such a kind' means preceded by delusion in the manner stated. 'It does not transcend form' means it is not a cause for transcending forms; the intention is that it does not transcend the defilements regarding a form-object. Ignorance devoid of joy and sorrow is itself ignorant equanimity. 'It is of a similar nature by way of not investigating faults and virtues': Just as the divine abiding of equanimity, like loving-kindness and so on, proceeds solely by way of looking on with indifference towards beings, not investigating their virtues and faults, so too ignorant equanimity proceeds solely by way of looking on with indifference, not considering existing virtue and fault in beings. Thus, they are of a similar nature by way of not investigating faults and virtues. Therefore, because it quickly finds an opening, it is called the near enemy of the divine abiding of equanimity. 'Due to having a dissimilar nature': for the nature of equanimity, which has the aspect of neutrality towards liked and disliked objects, lust and aversion, which have the aspect of proceeding by way of conformity and opposition, are dissimilar. Because of this dissimilarity of nature, if they were to find an opening, they would find it only after a long time; thus, like an enemy standing far from a person, they are called the distant enemies of the divine abiding of equanimity.

266.
