Kattukāmatā chando ādi “chandamūlakā kusalā dhammā”ti (a. ni. 8.83) vacanato, atha vā sattesu hitesitādukkhāpanayanakāmatādinā anavajjābhipatthanāvasena [V 1.0361] pavattanato “kattukāmatā chando ādī”ti vuttaṃ. Upekkhābrahmavihāropi hi sattesu anirākatahitacchandoyeva “tattha abyāvaṭatā apaṇṇakapaṭipadā”ti ajjhupekkhanākārena pavattati mātā viya sakiccapasute putte. Nīvaraṇādīti ādi-saddena tadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Katthaci sattaggahaṇampi saṅkhāraggahaṇameva hoti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya yathā “sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti (a. ni. 10.27; khu. pā. 4.1), na evamidhāti āha “paññattidhammavasena eko vā satto aneke vā sattā ārammaṇa”nti. Paññattidhammavasenāti paññattisaṅkhātadhammavasena. Kāmañcettha “sukhitā hontū”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.23) bhāvanāyaṃ sukhādiggahaṇampi labbhati. Taṃ pana “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti (dha. pa. 255; theragā. 676; netti. 5) vipassanāya aniccalakkhaṇagahaṇaṃ viya appadhānabhūtaṃ, sattapaññatti eva padhānabhāvena gayhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Upacāre vā patte ārammaṇavaḍḍhanaṃ tatthāpi sīmāsambhedasiddhitoti adhippāyo.

266. The desire to act (kattukāmatā), which is desire (chanda), is the origin (ādi), in accordance with the saying, 'Wholesome states are rooted in desire' (chandamūlakā kusalā dhammā). Or alternatively (atha vā), because it proceeds by way of blameless aspiration (anavajjābhipatthanāvasena), such as the desire for the welfare of beings and the desire to remove their suffering (sattesu hitesitādukkhāpanayanakāmatādinā), it is said, 'the desire to act, desire, is the origin' (kattukāmatā chando ādī'ti vuttaṃ). For (hi) the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhābrahmavihāropi) also proceeds with an attitude of looking on with indifference (ajjhupekkhanākārena), thinking, 'Herein, non-busyness is the unerring practice' (tattha abyāvaṭatā apaṇṇakapaṭipadā'ti), while having a desire for the welfare of beings that has not been rejected (sattesu anirākatahitacchandoyeva), like a mother (mātā viya) towards her son who is devoted to his own duties (sakiccapasute putte). In 'hindrances, etc.' (nīvaraṇādi'ti), by the word 'etc.' (ādi-saddena), the inclusion (saṅgaho) of defilements that share the same basis (tadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ) should be understood (daṭṭhabbo). Sometimes (katthaci), the taking of 'beings' (sattaggahaṇampi) is just the taking of formations (saṅkhāraggahaṇameva hoti), in a teaching established on a person (puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya), as in 'All beings subsist on nutriment' (sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā'ti). It is not so here (na evamidhā'ti); thus, he said (āha), 'By way of a conceptual state, one being or many beings are the object' (paññattidhammavasena eko vā satto aneke vā sattā ārammaṇa'nti). 'By way of a conceptual state' (paññattidhammavasenā'ti) means by way of the state called a concept (paññattisaṅkhātadhammavasena). And it is true (kāmañca) that here (ettha), in the development (bhāvanāyaṃ) of phrases such as 'May they be happy' (sukhitā hontū'tiādinā), the taking of happiness, etc., is also obtained (sukhādiggahaṇampi labbhati). However (pana), that (taṃ) is of secondary importance (appadhānabhūtaṃ), like the grasping of the characteristic of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇagahaṇaṃ viya) in insight meditation (vipassanāya) with 'All formations are impermanent' (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā'ti). It should be understood (daṭṭhabbaṃ) that the concept of a being (sattapaññatti) is what is grasped as primary (padhānabhāvena gayhati). Or (vā), when access concentration is reached (upacāre patte), there is the expansion of the object (ārammaṇavaḍḍhanaṃ). The intention (adhippāyo) is that even there (tatthāpi), it is due to the accomplishment of the breaking of boundaries (sīmāsambhedasiddhito).

Ekamāvāsaṃ paricchinditvāti ettha “satte mettāya pharissāmī”ti evaṃ ñāṇena paricchedaṃ katvā ekā racchā paricchinditabbāti yojanā. Racchāgahaṇena racchāvāsino sattā gahitā yathā ekaṃ disanti. Evaṃ sabbattha.

Regarding 'having delimited a single dwelling' (ekamāvāsaṃ paricchinditvā'ti): here (ettha), having made a delimitation with knowledge (ñāṇena paricchedaṃ katvā), thinking, 'I will pervade the beings with loving-kindness' (satte mettāya pharissāmī'ti), the construction is (yojanā): 'a single street should be delimited' (ekā racchā paricchinditabbā'ti). By the taking of 'street' (racchāgahaṇena), the beings dwelling on the street (racchāvāsino sattā) are taken (gahitā), just as in 'one direction' (ekaṃ disaṃ'ti). It is the same everywhere (evaṃ sabbattha).

267. Kasiṇānaṃ nissandoti kasiṇajjhānānaṃ nissandaphalasadisā āruppā arūpajjhānāni, kasiṇajjhānānaṃ pāripūriyāva sijjhanato. Tehi vinā asijjhanatoti keci. Samādhinissandoti rūpajjhānasamādhīnaṃ, heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ arūpajjhānasamādhīnañca nissando paṭipāṭiyā te adhigantvāva paṭilabhitabbato[M 1.0384]. Vipassanānissando vipassanānubhāvena laddhabbato, vipassanāvaseneva ca samāpajjitabbato. Samathavipassanānissando nirodhasamāpatti. Yathāha “dvīhi balehi samannāgatattā”tiādi (visuddhi. 2.868). “Purimabrahmavihārattayanissando”ti iminā mettādivasena tīṇi jhānāni adhigantvā ṭhitasseva upekkhābrahmavihāro, na itarassāti dasseti. Tamevatthaṃ upamāya pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

267. 'The result of the kasiṇas' (kasiṇānaṃ nissando'ti): the formless attainments (āruppā), that is, the formless jhānas (arūpajjhānāni), are similar to the resultant fruit (nissandaphalasadisā) of the kasiṇa jhānas, because they are accomplished only through the fulfillment (pāripūriyā eva sijjhanato) of the kasiṇa jhānas. Some (keci) say it is because they are not accomplished without them (tehi vinā asijjhanato). 'The result of concentration' (samādhinissando'ti) is the result of the concentrations of the form jhānas (rūpajjhānasamādhīnaṃ) and of the three lower formless jhānas (heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ arūpajjhānasamādhīnañca), because it is to be obtained (paṭilabhitabbato) only after having attained them (te adhigantvāva) in sequence (paṭipāṭiyā). The result of insight (vipassanānissando) is so called because it is to be obtained through the power of insight (vipassanānubhāvena laddhabbato) and is to be entered by way of insight (vipassanāvaseneva ca samāpajjitabbato). The result of serenity and insight (samathavipassanānissando) is the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). As was said (yathāha): 'Because of being endowed with two powers...' and so on (dvīhi balehi...tiādi). By this phrase, 'the result of the first three divine abidings' (purimabrahmavihārattayanissando'ti iminā), he shows (dasseti) that the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhābrahmavihāro) is only for one who is established (ṭhitasseva) having attained the three jhānas by way of loving-kindness, etc. (mettādivasena tīṇi jhānāni adhigantvā), and not for another (na itarassa). To show that same meaning (tamevatthaṃ... dassetuṃ), having made it clearer (pākaṭataraṃ katvā) with a simile (upamāya), 'Just as...' and so on (yathā hī'tiādi) was said (vuttaṃ). Whatever should be said here (yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ), that has already been said below (taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva).

268. Siyāti vuccamānākārena siyā kassaci parivitakko. Etthāti etesu mettādīsu brahmavihāratā veditabbā, itarakammaṭṭhānāni attahitapaṭipattimattāni. Imāni pana “sabbe [V 1.0362] sattā sukhitā hontū”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.22) parahitapaṭipattibhūtāni. Tasmā sattesu sammā paṭipattibhāvena seṭṭhā ete vihārā. Brahmānoti upapattibrahmāno. Te hi idha jhānabhāvanāya vinīvaraṇacittā hutvā brahmaloke uppannā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ vinīvaraṇacittāva honti. Tasmā “niddosacittā viharantī”ti vadanti. Brahmānoti vā sakalabuddhaguṇahetubhūtānaṃ dānapāramitādīnaṃ buddhakaradhammānaṃ paripūraṇavasena brūhitaguṇā mahāsattā bodhisattā. Te hi sabbasattānaṃ hitesanena, ahitāpanayanena, sampattipamodanena, sabbattha vivajjitāgatigamanamajjhattabhāvādhiṭṭhānena ca niddosacittā viharanti. Evanti yathā te upapattibrahmāno, mahābodhisattabrahmāno vā, evaṃ etehi brahmavihārehi sampayuttā samaṅgībhūtā.

268. By `Siyā` is meant: a thought might arise for someone in the manner being spoken. Here, among these states of loving-kindness and so on, their nature as divine abidings should be understood. Other meditation subjects are merely practices for one's own welfare. But these, through thoughts like 'May all beings be happy,' and so forth (Paṭis. 2.22), are practices for the welfare of others. Therefore, these abidings are the best because they are right practice toward beings. By `Brahmā` is meant the Brahmās by rebirth. For they, having become of mind free from hindrances through the development of jhāna here, are reborn in the Brahmā world and remain there with minds free from hindrances for as long as they live. Thus, it is said they 'dwell with faultless minds.' Alternatively, by `Brahmā` is meant the great beings, the bodhisattas, who have developed virtues by fulfilling the perfections such as generosity, which are the causes of all the Buddha's qualities and the qualities that make one a Buddha. For they dwell with faultless minds through seeking the welfare of all beings, removing what is not their welfare, rejoicing in their success, and being established in a state of impartiality, having abandoned going to a wrong course everywhere. By `Evaṃ` is meant: just as those Brahmās by rebirth, or the great bodhisatta-Brahmās, so too are those who are associated and endowed with these divine abidings.

269. Catassovātiādipañhassāti catassotiādikassa tividhassa pañhassa. Visuddhimaggādivasāti ettha byāpādasaṃkilesādito visujjhanupāyo visuddhimaggo. Ādi-saddena hitūpasaṃhārādimanasikāravisesā saṅgahitā. Āsaṃ mettādīnaṃ. Appamāṇeti pamāṇarahite. Yenāti yena kāraṇena. Tanti tasmā. Da-kāro padasandhikaro.

269. By `Catassovātiādipañhassa` is meant: of the threefold question beginning with 'four,' and so forth. By `Visuddhimaggādivasā` (by way of the path of purification, and so forth) is meant: here, the path of purification is the means of purification from the defilement of ill will, and so forth. By the word `ādi` (and so forth) are included special kinds of attention such as that of bringing about welfare, and so forth. `Āsaṃ` means: of loving-kindness and so forth. `Appamāṇe` means: in the immeasurable, that is, devoid of measure. `Yenā` means `yena kāraṇena` (by which reason). `Tad` means `tasmā` (therefore). The letter 'd' is a word-joining particle.

Byāpādabahulassa visuddhimaggoti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ, ujuvipaccanīkabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Pakkhapātavasena anābhujanamanābhogo majjhattākāroti adhippāyo. Yvāyaṃ catubbidho sattesu [M 1.0385] manasikāro vutto, tameva upamāya dassetuṃ “yasmā ca yathā mātā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vuttassāpi hitūpasaṃhārādiatthassa upameyyabhāvaṃ upanetvā dassetuṃ atthupanayanattho “yasmā cā”ti ca-saddo. Pariyāyeti vāre, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kiccavasena parivattanakkameti attho. Abyāvaṭāti anussukkā. Tathāti yathā mātā daharādīsu puttesu, tathā sabbasattesu mettādivasena mettāyanādivasikena bhavitabbanti yojanā. Tasmāti yasmā sabbepi saṃkilesadhammā yathārahaṃ dosamoharāgapakkhiyā, tehi ca visujjhanupāyo appamaññā, hitūpasaṃhārādivasena catubbidho ca sattesu manasikāro, tasmā visuddhimaggādivasā catassova appamaññā. Catassopi etā bhāvetukāmena na ekekanti adhippāyo. Sati hi sabbasaṅgahe kamena bhavitabbaṃ. Hitesitā mettāyananti āha “evaṃ patthitahitāna”nti. Sambhāvetvā vāti “imāya paṭipattiyā ayaṃ nirayādīsu nibbatteyyā”ti parikappetvā vā. Dukkhāpanayanākaārappavattivasena [V 1.0363] paṭipajjitabbanti sambandho. Tato paranti tato hitākārappavattiādito paraṃ. Kattabbābhāvatoti catutthassa pakārassa kattabbassa abhāvato. Ayaṃ kamoti ayaṃ imāsaṃ appamaññānaṃ yebhuyyena pavattanakkamoti katvā vuttaṃ, na “imināva kamena etāsaṃ pavatti, na aññathā”ti. Mettādīnaṃ hi tissannaṃ bhāvanānaṃ kamaniyamo natthi, yaṃ vā taṃ vā paṭhamaṃ bhāvetuṃ labbhā, desanākkamavasena vā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

It should be brought and connected as: 'the path of purification for one with much ill will'; the meaning is that it is the direct opposite. This is the method for the rest as well. The meaning is: `anābhoga` is not paying attention due to partiality; this is the state of impartiality. To illustrate with a simile this fourfold attention to beings that has been spoken of, it is said, 'Because, just as a mother,' and so forth. Here, to present the already-mentioned meaning of bringing about welfare and so on as the object of comparison, the particle `ca` in `yasmā ca` has the function of introducing the topic. `Pariyāyeti` means 'in turns'; the meaning is 'in the sequence of revolving according to this or that duty.' `Abyāvaṭā` means 'unconcerned.' `Tathā` means: the connection is that just as a mother is towards her young sons and so on, so one should be towards all beings by way of loving-kindness and so on, dwelling by way of developing loving-kindness and so on. `Tasmā` means: because all defiling states, as appropriate, are on the side of aversion, delusion, and greed, and the means of purification from them are the immeasurables, and there is a fourfold attention to beings by way of bringing about welfare, and so forth, therefore, the four immeasurables are by way of the path of purification, and so forth. The meaning is that one who wishes to develop all four of these should not do so one by one. For when there is the inclusion of all, it should be done in sequence. 'Desiring welfare' (`hitesitā`) is the development of loving-kindness (`mettāyanaṃ`); thus, he said, 'thus for those whose welfare is desired.' `Sambhāvetvā vā` means 'or having conceived thus: "By this practice, this one might be reborn in hell, and so forth."' The connection is that one should practice by way of the arising of the aspect of removing suffering. `Tato paraṃ` means beyond that, i.e., beyond the arising of the aspect of welfare, and so forth. `Kattabbābhāvato` means because of the absence of a fourth kind of thing to be done. `Ayaṃ kamo` is said having considered it as 'this is the general sequence of occurrence for these immeasurables,' not having considered that 'their occurrence is only in this order, and not otherwise.' For, of the three developments—loving-kindness, and so forth—there is no fixed sequence; whichever one may be developed first. Or, it was said thus by way of the sequence of teaching.

Ekasattassāpīti ekassāpi sattassa. Appaṭibhāganimittattā paricchedaggahaṇaṃ natthi, na ca sammutisaccavasena pavattaṃ sattaggahaṇaṃ paricchinnarūpādiggahaṇaṃ hotīti appanāppattiyā aparāmāsasattaggahaṇamuddhabhūtānaṃ mettādīnaṃ ekasattārammaṇānampi appamāṇagocaratā vuttā. Evaṃ pamāṇaṃ aggahetvāti yathā uddhumātakādīsu atirekuddhumātakādibhāvappatte padese nimittaṃ gayhati, evaṃ pamāṇaṃ aggahetvā. Sakalapharaṇavasenāti niravasesapharaṇavasena.

`Ekasattassāpi` means 'even of one being.' Because there is no counterpart sign, there is no grasping of a boundary; and the grasping of 'being,' which proceeds by way of conventional truth, does not become a grasping of limited form, and so forth. Thus, for loving-kindness and so on—which, upon reaching absorption, become the pinnacle of the grasping of 'being' without misapprehension—their immeasurable scope is stated, even when they have a single being as their object. `Evaṃ pamāṇaṃ aggahetvā` means: just as in the meditation on a bloated corpse, and so forth, the sign is grasped in a part that has reached a state of excessive bloatedness, and so forth, so too, without grasping a measure. `Sakalapharaṇavasena` means `niravasesapharaṇavasena` (by way of pervading without remainder).

270. Nissaraṇattāti ettha yaṃ yassa nissaraṇaṃ, taṃ tassa ujupaṭipakkhabhūtameva hoti. Yathā kāmānaṃ nekkhammaṃ, rūpānaṃ āruppā, saṅkhārānaṃ nibbānaṃ[M 1.0386], evaṃ domanassasahitānaṃ byāpādavihiṃsāratīnaṃ nissaraṇabhūtā mettākaruṇāmuditā na somanassarahitā honti. Nissaraṇaggahaṇeneva ca pubbabhāgiyānaṃ tāsaṃ upekkhāsampayogopi anuññātoti daṭṭhabbaṃ anissaraṇabhāvato. Tathā hi aṭṭhavīsatiyā cittuppādesu karuṇāmuditānaṃ pavattiṃ ācariyā icchanti. Na hi brahmavihārupekkhā upekkhāvedanaṃ vinā vattati pārisuddhiupekkhā viya. Na hi kadāci pārisuddhiupekkhā vedanupekkhaṃ vinā vattatīti.

270. Here, in `nissaraṇattā` (because it is an escape): whatever is an escape from something is indeed its direct opposite. Just as renunciation is the escape from sensual pleasures, the immaterial attainments are the escape from forms, and Nibbāna is the escape from formations, so loving-kindness, compassion, and appreciative joy—being the escape from ill will, cruelty, and discontent which are accompanied by displeasure—are not devoid of joy. Moreover, by the very mention of 'escape,' it should be understood that for these meditations in their preliminary stage, association with equanimity is also permitted, because they (the preliminary stages) are not the escape. For so the teachers accept the occurrence of compassion and appreciative joy in twenty-eight types of consciousness. For the equanimity of the divine abidings does not occur without neutral feeling, just like the equanimity of purity. For the equanimity of purity never occurs without feeling-equanimity.

271. Sātasahagatanti sukhasahagataṃ. Tasmāti yasmā “tato tvaṃ bhikkhū”tiādikāya (a. ni. 8.63) desanāya catunnampi appamaññānaṃ savitakkādibhāvo viya upekkhāsahagatabhāvopi viññāyati, tasmā. Catassopi appamaññā catukkapañcakajjhānikāti codakassa adhippāyo. Evañhi satīti yadi mūlasamādhimhi vuttamatthaṃ anantaraṃ vuttatāya brahmavihāresu pakkhipati, evaṃ sante kāyānupassanādayopi catukkapañcakajjhānikā siyuṃ, na pana honti vipassanāvasena desitattāti adhippāyo, hontu kāyānupassanādayo ānāpānabhāvanāvasena catukkapañcakajjhānikāti vadeyyāti āsaṅkanto āha “vedanādīsū”tiādi. Byañjanacchāyāmattaṃ gahetvāti “mettā me cetovimutti bhāvitā bhavissatī”tiādīhi [V 1.0364] byañjanehi pakāsito eva cittasamādhi “ajjhattaṃ me cittaṃ ṭhitaṃ bhavissatī”tiādīhipi byañjanehi pakāsitoti byañjanato labbhamānasamādhicchāyāmattaṃ gahetvā ubhayattha labbhamānaṃ adhippāyaṃ aggahetvāti attho. Suttatthaṃ hi aññathā vadanto ayathāvāditāya satthāraṃ apavadanto nāma hoti. Tenāha “mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhī”ti.

271. 'Accompanied by pleasure' (`sātasahagataṃ`) means 'accompanied by happiness' (`sukhasahagataṃ`). 'Therefore' (`tasmā`): Because in the teaching beginning with 'Then you, monks,' and so forth (AN 8.63), a state of being accompanied by equanimity is understood for the four immeasurables just like the state of being with initial and sustained thought, and so forth, therefore... The questioner's intention is that the four immeasurables are of the fourfold and fivefold jhāna. For if this is so: If one includes the meaning stated in the root concentration and places it among the divine abodes due to its being stated immediately after, then in that case, the contemplations of the body, and so forth, would also be of the fourfold and fivefold jhāna. But they are not, because they are taught by way of insight—this is the intention. Anticipating that one might say, 'Let the contemplations of the body, and so forth, be of the fourfold and fivefold jhāna through the development of mindfulness of breathing,' he says, 'in feelings, and so forth.' 'Taking only the shadow of the expression' (`byañjanacchāyāmattaṃ gahetvā`) means taking only the shadow of concentration obtainable from the expressions—without grasping the intended meaning obtainable in each case—on the grounds that the concentration of mind revealed by expressions like 'my liberation of mind through loving-kindness will be developed,' and so forth, is also revealed by expressions like 'my mind will be internally settled,' and so forth. This is the meaning. For one who speaks contrary to the meaning of the sutta, by speaking not as it was said, is in fact one who disparages the Teacher. Therefore, he said: 'Do not misrepresent the Blessed One.'

272. “Tayimaṃ dosaṃ pariharitukāmena na sabbaṃ suttaṃ nītatthameva, tasmā garukulato adhippāyo maggitabbo”ti dassento “gambhīraṃ hī”tiādiṃ vatvā tattha ādito paṭṭhāya adhippāyaṃ dassetuṃ “ayañhī”tiādimāha. Āyācitā dhammadesanā etenāti āyācitadhammadesano, taṃ āyācitadhammadesanaṃ. Evamevāti garahane nipāto, mudā evāti attho. Ajjhattanti gocarajjhatte, kammaṭṭhānārammaṇeti attho[M 1.0387]. Yasmā cittekaggatā nāma sasantatipariyāpannā hoti, tasmā atthavaṇṇanāyaṃ “niyakajjhattavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Cittaṃ ṭhitaṃ bhavissatīti bahiddhā avikkhippamānaṃ ekaggabhāve ṭhitaṃ bhavissati. Tato eva susaṇṭhitaṃ, suṭṭhu samāhitanti attho. Uppannāti avikkhambhitā. Pāpakāti lāmakā. Akusalā dhammāti kāmacchandādayo akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena akusalā dhammā. Cittaṃ pariyādāya pavattituṃ okāsādānena kusalacittaṃ khepetvā na ca ṭhassantīti yojanā. Iminā yathāvuttassa samādhānassa kāraṇamāha.

272. “Wishing to avoid this fault, one should not take the entire sutta as having a definitive meaning only; therefore, the intended meaning should be sought from the teacher.” Thus showing this, he says, “For it is deep,” and so forth, and then from the beginning onwards, to explain the intended meaning, he says, “For this,” and so forth. He is 'one for whom the teaching of the Dhamma was requested' (āyācitadhammadesano) because 'the teaching of the Dhamma was requested by him' (āyācitā dhammadesanā etena). (The text refers to) him, the one for whom the teaching of the Dhamma was requested. 'Just so' (evameva) is a particle in the sense of censure; the meaning is 'just in vain'. 'Internally' (ajjhattaṃ) means within the range of the object, that is, the meditation object. Since one-pointedness of mind is included in one’s own continuity, therefore in the explanation of the meaning it is said, “by way of one’s own internal state.” “The mind will be settled”—meaning, not being distracted externally, it will be settled in a state of one-pointedness. From that, it is very well-settled, meaning well-concentrated. “Arisen” (uppannā) means not suppressed. “Evil” (pāpakā) means bad. “Unwholesome states” (akusalā dhammā) means sensual desire and so forth are unwholesome states because they arise from unskillfulness. The connection is as follows: by not giving an opportunity for them to arise, take over the mind, and exhaust the wholesome mind, they will not remain. By this, he states the cause of the concentration as described.

Cittekaggatāmattoti bhāvanamanuyuttena paṭiladdhamattaṃ nātisubhāvitaṃ samādhānaṃ. Taṃ pana upari vuccamānānaṃ samādhivisesānaṃ mūlakāraṇabhāvato “mūlasamādhī”ti vutto. Svāyaṃ cittekaggatāmatto “ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmī”tiādīsu viya khaṇikasamādhi adhippeto. Yatheva hi aññatthāpi “āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhikkhave, vīriyaṃ ahosi asallīnaṃ…pe… samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekagga”nti (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 11) vatvā “vivicceva kāmehī”tiādivacanato (a. ni. 8.11) paṭhamaṃ vuttacittekaggatā “khaṇikasamādhī”ti viññāyati, evamidhāpīti. So eva samādhīti mūlasamādhimāha.

“Merely one-pointedness of mind” (cittekaggatāmatto) is a concentration that is merely attained by one devoted to development, a concentration not yet very well developed. That, however, being the root cause of the special concentrations to be mentioned later, is called “root concentration.” This mere one-pointedness of mind is intended as momentary concentration, as in passages such as “‘I establish my mind internally, quiet it, make it unified, concentrate it.’” For just as elsewhere, after saying, “My energy, O monks, was roused, unflagging… my mind was concentrated, one-pointed” (A.N. 8.11; Pārā. 11), the one-pointedness of mind mentioned first is understood as “momentary concentration” because of the statement, “Secluded from sensual pleasures,” and so forth (A.N. 8.11), so too is it understood here. By “that very concentration,” he refers to the root concentration.

Assāti bhikkhuno, assa vā mūlasamādhissa. Bhāvananti vaḍḍhanaṃ. Ayaṃ samādhīti ca mūlasamādhiyeva adhippeto. Evaṃ bhāvitoti yathā araṇisahitena uppādito aggi gomayacuṇṇādīhi [V 1.0365] vaḍḍhito gomayaggiādibhāvaṃ pattopi araṇisahitena uppāditamūlaggītveva vuccati, evamidhāpi mūlasamādhi eva mettādivasena vaḍḍhitoti katvā vuttaṃ.

“Of this” (assa) refers to the monk, or to this root concentration. “Development” (bhāvanā) means growth. “This concentration” also refers specifically to the root concentration. “Thus developed” (evaṃ bhāvito): just as fire produced with a fire-drill set, though developed by cow-dung powder and the like into a cow-dung fire, is still called the 'original fire produced with a fire-drill set,' so too here, it is said because the root concentration itself is developed by way of loving-kindness and so forth.

Aññesupi ārammaṇesu pathavīkasiṇādīsu. Tattha yathā mettābhāvanāpubbaṅgamena bhāvanānayena pathavīkasiṇādīsu savitakkādibhāvavasena catukkapañcakajjhānasampāpanavidhinā mūlasamādhissa bhāvanā vuttā, evaṃ karuṇādibhāvanāpubbaṅgamaṃ pathavīkasiṇādīsupi bhāvanāvidhiṃ dassetvā pacchā kāyānupassanādipubbaṅgamaṃ bhāvanāvidhiṃ dassento āsavakkhayāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tena vuttaṃ “karuṇā me cetovimuttī”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ dhammānupassanāpariyosānāya desanāya arahattādhigamāya kammaṭṭhānassa [M 1.0388] kathitattā puna “tato tvaṃ, bhikkhu, imaṃ samādhiṃ savitakkampī”tiādi (a. ni. 8.63) kasmā vuttanti? Dhammānupassanāya matthakappattidassanatthaṃ. Sā hi saṅkhārupekkhābhāvena vattamānā yathāvuttajjhānadhamme sammasantī visesato matthakappattā nāma hoti. Phalasamāpattibhūmidassanatthaṃ vuttanti keci.

Also in other objects, such as the earth kasiṇa and so forth. Therein, just as the development of the root concentration has been taught by the method of development preceded by the development of loving-kindness—by means of the procedure for attaining the fourfold and fivefold jhānas through the state of having initial thought, etc., in the earth kasiṇa and other objects—so too, after showing the method of development preceded by the development of compassion, etc., in the earth kasiṇa and so forth as well, and afterwards, while showing the method of development preceded by the contemplation of the body, etc., he taught the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. Therefore it is said, “My liberation of mind is compassion,” and so forth. If so, since the meditation subject for the attainment of Arahantship has been taught by the teaching that culminates in the contemplation of phenomena, why was it said again, “Then you, monk, this concentration with initial thought…” and so forth (A.N. 8.63)? To show the attainment of the peak of the contemplation of phenomena. For that contemplation, proceeding by way of equanimity towards formations, while comprehending the jhāna-factors as described, is said to have especially reached the peak. Some say it was stated to show the plane of the attainment of fruition.

Puna yato kho tetiādi arahattappattito uddhaṃ laddhabbaphāsuvihāradassanaṃ. Tattha gagghasīti gamissasi. Tasmāti yasmā “savitakkampī”tiādikā desanā mettādīnaṃ ārammaṇato aññasmiṃ ārammaṇe samādhiṃ sandhāya vuttā, na appamaññā, tasmā. “Tathevā”tiādinā ganthantarenapi tamevatthaṃ samattheti. Tattha tathevāti tikacatukkajjhānavaseneva. Abhidhammeti cittuppādakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 251 ādayo), appamaññāvibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 684 ādayo) ca tattha tattha abhidhammappadesesu.

Furthermore, the words beginning with “from when…” are the demonstration of the pleasant abiding to be attained above the attainment of Arahantship. Therein, gagghasi means “you will go.” As for tasmā (therefore): because the teaching beginning with “with initial thought…” was spoken in reference to concentration on an object other than the objects of loving-kindness and so forth, not the immeasurables, therefore. By the words beginning with “Just so,” he confirms that very same meaning even with another text. Therein, “just so” means simply by way of the triple and quadruple jhānas. As for “Abhidhamma,” it refers to the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 251 ff.), the Analysis of the Immeasurables, and so forth (Vibhaṅga 684 ff.), and in those various sections of the Abhidhamma.

273. Subhaparamādivasenāti subha-saddo “subhanteva adhimutto hotī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.212; a. ni. 8.66) evaṃ vuttasubhavimokkhaṃ sandhāya vutto uttarapadalopena. Parama-saddo ukkaṃsattho. Subho subhavimokkho paramo ukkaṃso paramā koṭi etissāti subhaparamā, mettācetovimutti, tato paraṃ tāya sādhetabbaṃ natthīti attho. Asādhāraṇassa atthassa adhippetattā vipassanāsukhādayo idha anavasarā. Itaretaravisiṭṭhāpete visesā, pageva parehi. Tenāha “aññamaññaṃ asadiso ānubhāvaviseso veditabbo”ti. Visesetvāti aññamaññaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ katvā.

273. Regarding “by way of supreme beauty, etc.”: the word “beautiful” (subha) is stated in reference to the beautiful liberation spoken of thus, “He is resolved only upon the beautiful” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.212; Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.66), with the omission of the latter word (vimokkha). The word “supreme” (parama) has the meaning of excellence. For this (liberation), the beautiful—the beautiful liberation—is the supreme excellence, the highest limit; hence it is subhaparamā, the mind-release of loving-kindness. The meaning is that beyond it, there is nothing further to be accomplished by it. Because an uncommon meaning is intended, insight-happiness and so forth have no place here. These special qualities are also mutually distinct, how much more so from others. Therefore, he said, “The special power, dissimilar from one another, should be understood.” As for “having distinguished” (visesetvā), it means having made them mutually distinct.

Tassa [V 1.0366] tassa upanissayattāti subhavimokkhādikassa tassa tassa vimokkhassa pakatūpanissayavasena upanissayapaccayabhāvato. Idāni tamatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ “mettāvihārissā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Assa mettāvihārissa cittaṃ upasaṃharatoti sambandho. Appaṭikkūlaparicayāti mettābhāvanāvasena sattasaññite yattha katthaci ārammaṇe appaṭikkūlākāreneva gahaṇassa paricitattā. Tassa saṅkhārabhūtampi yaṃ kiñci ārammaṇaṃ appaṭikkūlākāreneva paccupatiṭṭhati, pageva sabhāvato. “Appaṭikkūla”nti [M 1.0389] tatthassa cittaṃ abhirativasena nirāsaṅkaṃ pavattati, paccanīkadhammehi ca sukhena, suṭṭhu ca vimuccati, yatassa jhānassa vimokkhapariyāyo vutto. Tenāha “appaṭikkūlesū”tiādi. Yathāvutto ca attho anatthacaraṇādiadhippāyena sacetane ārammaṇe āghātaṃ uppādentassa paṭikkūlaparicayā acetanepi vātātapādike āghātuppattiyā vibhāvetabbo. Na tato paranti tato subhavimokkhato paraṃ kassaci vimokkhassa upanissayo na hotīti attho.

“Because of being a support for each of these” means because of being a supporting condition by way of natural support for each of those liberations, such as the beautiful liberation, etc. Now, to show that meaning more clearly, “for one dwelling in loving-kindness,” etc., was said. The connection is: “of this one dwelling in loving-kindness… directing the mind.” As for “familiarity with the non-repulsive”: because of being familiar, through the development of loving-kindness, with grasping in a non-repulsive manner any object designated as a being. For him, any object, even if it is conditioned, appears in a non-repulsive manner, how much more so that which is naturally so. As for “non-repulsive”: therein his mind proceeds in delight without aversion, and it is liberated from opposing states easily and well, wherefore for this jhāna the term “liberation” is spoken. Therefore, he said, “in non-repulsive things,” etc. And the meaning as stated should be clarified by the arising of aversion even towards an inanimate object like wind, heat, etc., which occurs for one who, due to familiarity with the repulsive, generates aversion towards an animate object with the intention of acting harmfully, etc. “Not beyond that” means that beyond that beautiful liberation, it is not a support for any liberation.

Abhihananti etenāti abhighāto, daṇḍo abhighāto yassa taṃ daṇḍābhighātaṃ, taṃ ādi yassa taṃ daṇḍābhighātādi, daṇḍābhighātādi rūpaṃ nimittaṃ yassa taṃ daṇḍābhighātādirūpanimittaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “sattadukkha”nti, daṇḍappahārādijanitaṃ karajarūpahetukaṃ sattānaṃ uppajjanakadukkhanti attho. Rūpe ādīnavo suparividito hoti karuṇāvihārissa rūpanimittattā, dukkhassa karuṇāya ca paradukkhāsahanarasattāti adhippāyo. Tattha ākāse. Cittaṃ pakkhandati sabbaso rūpānaṃ abhāvo vivaramapagamoti.

“They strike with this,” thus it is an “assault” (abhighāta). A rod is the assault for it, thus it is “rod-assault” (daṇḍābhighāta). That is the beginning for it, thus it is “rod-assault and so forth” (daṇḍābhighātādi). Form that is rod-assault and so forth is the sign for it, thus it is “having form beginning with rod-assault as its sign” (daṇḍābhighātādirūpanimittaṃ). But what is that? He says, “the suffering of beings,” meaning, the suffering that arises for beings, which is caused by the body born of kamma, and is generated by being struck with a rod and so forth. The danger in form is well understood by one dwelling in compassion, because suffering has form as its sign, and because compassion has the function of not being able to endure the suffering of others; this is the intention. There, in space, the mind leaps in, adverting: “The complete absence of forms is an opening, a departure.”

Tena tenātiādīsu ayaṃ yojanā – tena tena bhogasampattiādinā pāmojjakāraṇena pamuditānaṃ sattānaṃ uppannapāmojjaviññāṇaṃ samanupassantassa yogino “sādhu vatāyaṃ satto pamodatī”ti muditāya pavattisambhavato pamuditaviññāṇassa dassanena viññāṇaggahaṇaparicitaṃ cittaṃ hotīti.

In the texts beginning with “by this and that,” this is the connection: For a yogi who observes the arisen consciousness of joy in beings who are joyful due to this or that cause of joy, such as the accomplishment of wealth, etc., because of the possible occurrence of sympathetic joy from thinking, “It is good indeed that this being is joyful,” the mind becomes, through seeing the joyful consciousness, familiar with grasping consciousness.

Anukkamādhigatanti ākāsakasiṇavajje yattha katthaci kasiṇe rūpāvacarajjhānādhigamānukkamena rūpavirāgabhāvanāya adhigataṃ. Ākāsanimittaṃ gocaro etassāti ākāsanimittagocaraṃ, tasmiṃ ākāsanimittagocare paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe. Cittaṃ upasaṃharatoti dutiyāruppādhigamāya bhāvanācittaṃ nentassa, tathā bhāvayatoti attho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ [V 1.0367] paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe. Cittanti viññāṇañcāyatanacittaṃ. Pakkhandatīti anupavisati vimokkhabhāvena appeti.

“Gradually attained” means attained by the development of dispassion towards form, through the sequence of attaining the form-sphere jhānas in any kasiṇa except the space kasiṇa. “The space-sign is its object,” thus it is “having the space-sign as its object”; in that first immaterial consciousness which has the space-sign as its object. As for “directs the mind”: for one directing the meditation-mind for the attainment of the second immaterial state; the meaning is, “thus one develops.” “Therein” means in that first immaterial consciousness. “The mind” means the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness. “Plunges into” means it enters, it attains by way of liberation.

Ābhogābhāvatoti “sukhitā hontū”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.23) sukhāsīsanādivasena ābhujanābhāvato. Sattānaṃ sukhāsīsanādivasena pavattamānā [M 1.0390] mettādibhāvanāva paramatthaggahaṇamukhena satte ārammaṇaṃ karoti, upekkhābhāvanā pana tathā appavattitvā kevalaṃ ajjhupekkhanavaseneva satte ārammaṇaṃ karotīti āha “upekkhāvihārissa sukhadukkhādiparamatthaggāhavimukhabhāvato avijjamānaggahaṇadukkhaṃ cittaṃ hotī”ti. Nanu ca “kammassakā sattā, te kassa ruciyā sukhitā vā bhavissantī”tiādinā paṭikkhepavasenapi paramatthaggahaṇamukheneva upekkhābrahmavihāropi satte ārammaṇaṃ karotīti? Saccametaṃ, taṃ pana bhāvanāya pubbabhāge, matthakappattiyaṃ pana kevalaṃ ajjhupekkhanavaseneva satte ārammaṇaṃ karotīti savisesaṃ paramatthato avijjamāne eva visaye tassa pavatti. Avijjamānaggahaṇadukkhatā ca ajjhupekkhanavasena appanāppattiyā aparāmāsasattaggahaṇamuddhabhūtatāya veditabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

“Because of the absence of adverting” means because of the absence of turning the mind to by way of wishing for happiness, etc., with phrases like “May they be happy!” The development of loving-kindness and so forth, which proceeds by way of wishing for the happiness of beings, takes beings as its object by way of grasping the ultimate reality. The development of equanimity, however, not proceeding in that way, takes beings as its object solely by way of observing with equanimity. Thus he says, “For one dwelling in equanimity, the mind has difficulty in grasping the non-existent, due to being turned away from grasping ultimate realities such as happiness and suffering.” Is it not the case that the divine abiding of equanimity also takes beings as its object by way of grasping the ultimate reality, even by way of rejection, as in “Beings are owners of their kamma; by whose preference will they be happy?” This is true. However, that is in the preliminary stage of development; but upon reaching the culmination, it takes beings as its object solely by way of observing with equanimity. Its occurrence is in a domain that is ultimately non-existent, but with a distinction. And the difficulty of grasping the non-existent should be understood as being due to its being the pinnacle of grasping the concept of beings without misapprehension, through reaching absorption by way of observing with equanimity. The rest is as already explained.

274. Sabbāpetāti sabbāpi etā appamaññā. Dānādīnanti pāramibhāvappattānaṃ dānādīnaṃ buddhakaradhammānaṃ. Sabbakalyāṇadhammānanti sabbesaṃ anavajjadhammānaṃ, samatiṃsāya pāramitānaṃ, tannimittānaṃ buddhayāniyānañca, sabbehi vā sundarasabhāvānaṃ. Na hi lokiyadhammā buddhakaradhammehi ānubhāvato ukkaṭṭhā nāma atthi, buddhadhammesu vattabbameva natthi. Paripūrikāti parivuddhikarā. Adhiṭṭhānāni viya hi appamaññā sabbāsaṃ pāramitānaṃ pāripūrikarā. “Hitajjhāsayatāyā”tiādinā mettābrahmavihārādīnaṃ upekkhābrahmavihārassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvadassanamukhena catūhi appamaññāhi attano santānassa pageva abhisaṅkhatattā mahābodhisattā dānādipāramiyo pūretuṃ samatthā honti, nāññathāti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Imassa dātabbaṃ, imassa na dātabbanti nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, “idaṃ dātabbaṃ, idaṃ na dātabbanti ca vibhāgaṃ akatvā”ti vattabbato. Deyyapaṭiggāhakavikapparahitā hi dānapāramitā. Yathāha –

274. “Sabbāpetā” means all these immeasurables. “Dānādīnaṃ” refers to giving and so on, which have attained the state of perfections and are Buddha-making qualities. “Sabbakalyāṇadhammānaṃ” means of all blameless qualities, of the thirty perfections, and of the qualities connected with the Buddha-vehicle which are their cause, or of all those with a beautiful nature. For indeed, worldly qualities are not called more excellent in power than the Buddha-making qualities; regarding the Buddha's own qualities, there is nothing at all to be said. “Paripūrikā” means they bring to full growth. For the immeasurables, like the foundations of resolve, are fulfillers of all the perfections. Through the phrase beginning with “through the disposition of wishing for welfare,” by showing how the divine abodes, from loving-kindness to equanimity, serve as a foundation, it demonstrates this meaning: because their own mental continuum has already been prepared by the four immeasurables, the great bodhisattvas are able to fulfill the perfections of giving and so on, and not otherwise. The lack of distinction—'To this one it should be given; to this one it should not be given'—is to be understood, because it is said that one gives 'without making a distinction that “this should be given, this should not be given.”' For the perfection of giving is free from conceptualization regarding the gift and the recipient. As it is said:

“Yathāpi kumbho sampuṇṇo, yassa kassaci adhokato;

Vamatevudakaṃ nissesaṃ, na tattha parirakkhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.118);

“Just as a pot filled full, overturned by anyone, empties out its water completely, and nothing there is kept back.”

“Sabbasattāna”nti [V 1.0368] idaṃ “sukhanidāna”nti imināpi sambandhitabbaṃ, “dentī”ti iminā ca. Tena deyyadhammena viya dānadhammenāpi mahāsattānaṃ lokassa bahūpakāratā [M 1.0391] vuttā hoti, tathā tassa pariṇāmanato. Tadatthadīpanatthaṃ hi “vibhāgaṃ akatvā”ti vatvāpi “sabbasattāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tesanti sabbasattānaṃ. Upaghātanti etthāpi “vibhāgaṃ akatvā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ hettha padayojanā – vibhāgaṃ akatvā upaghātaṃ parivajjayantā sabbasattānaṃ sukhanidānaṃ sīlaṃ samādiyantīti. Sattakālavikapparahitā hi sīlapāramitā, lokatthameva cassa phalaṃ pariṇamīyati. Nekkhammaṃ bhajantīti pabbajjaṃ upagacchanti. Pabbajitassa hi sabbaso sīlaṃ paripūrati, na gahaṭṭhassa. Idhāpi “vibhāgaṃ akatvā sabbasattānaṃ sukhanidāna”nti idaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Na hi bodhisattā kālavibhāgaṃ katvā pabbajjaṃ anutiṭṭhanti, sīlaṃ vā samādiyanti, nidassanamattañcetaṃ jhānādinekkhammabhajanassāpi icchitabbattā. Sabbasattānaṃ sukhanidānatā heṭṭhā vuttanayāva. Esa nayo sesesupi. Hitāhitesūti atthānatthesu. Asammohatthāyāti sammohaviddhaṃsanāya. Paññaṃ pariyodapentīti yogavihitaṃ vijjāṭṭhānādiṃ assutaṃ suṇantā sutaṃ vodapentā ahaṃkāramamaṃkārādiṃ vidhunantā ñāṇaṃ visodhenti. “Ahaṃ mamā”ti vikapparahitā hi paññāpāramitā. Hitasukhatthāyāti sattānaṃ hitasukhādivuddhiyatthameva. Niccanti satataṃ avicchedena paṭipakkhena avokiṇṇaṃ. Vīriyamārabhantīti yathā sattānaṃ anuppannaṃ hitasukhaṃ uppajjati, uppannaṃ abhivaḍḍhati, evaṃ parakkamaṃ karonti. Saṅkocavikkheparahitā hi vīriyapāramitā. “Vīrabhāvaṃ pattāpī”ti iminā aparaddhānaṃ niggahasamatthataṃ dasseti. Nānappakārakaṃ aparādhaṃ khamantīti mammacchedanākārena attani pavattitaṃ nānāvidhaṃ aparādhaṃ sahanti. Attaparavikappavirahitā hi dosasahanā khantipāramitā.

This term “sabbasattānaṃ” (for all beings) should be connected with “sukhanidānaṃ” (the source of happiness), and also with “denti” (they give). By that, it is said that the great beings are of great benefit to the world of beings, not only through the gift itself but also through the act of giving, because of dedicating it in that way. For, to clarify that meaning, even after saying “without making a distinction,” it is also said “for all beings.” “Tesaṃ” (of them) means of all beings. Here too, with “upaghātaṃ” (harm), one should bring in and connect “vibhāgaṃ akatvā” (without making a distinction). Here this is the connection of the words: without making a distinction, avoiding harm, they undertake virtue, which is the source of happiness for all beings. For the perfection of virtue is free from conceptualization regarding beings and time, and its fruit is dedicated only for the welfare of the world. “Nekkhammaṃ bhajanti” (they pursue renunciation) means they approach the state of going forth. For one who has gone forth, virtue is completely fulfilled, not for a householder. Here too, this phrase “without making a distinction, a source of happiness for all beings” should be brought in and connected. For bodhisattvas do not undertake the going forth or undertake virtue by making a distinction of time. And this is merely an illustration, because the cultivation of renunciation through jhāna and so on is also desirable. The state of being a source of happiness for all beings is as explained above. This method applies to the rest as well. “Hitāhitesu” (in the beneficial and the harmful) means in what is advantageous and disadvantageous. “Asammohatthāya” (for the sake of non-delusion) means for the destruction of delusion. “Paññaṃ pariyodapenti” (they purify wisdom) means: hearing what was unheard regarding the fields of knowledge established by practice, clarifying what was heard, shaking off the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ and so on, they purify their knowledge. For the perfection of wisdom is free from the conceptualization of “I” and “mine.” “Hitasukhatthāya” (for the sake of welfare and happiness) means solely for the increase of beings' welfare, happiness, and the like. “Niccaṃ” (constantly) means perpetually, without interruption, unmixed with opposition. “Vīriyamārabhanti” (they arouse energy) means they make an effort in such a way that for beings, unarisen welfare and happiness arises, and what has arisen increases. For the perfection of energy is free from contraction and distraction. By this phrase “vīrabhāvaṃ pattāpi” (even having attained the state of a hero), it shows the ability to subdue wrongdoers. “Nānappakārakaṃ aparādhaṃ khamanti” (they endure various kinds of offenses) means they endure various kinds of offenses committed against themselves, even in a manner like cutting vital spots. For the perfection of patience, which is the endurance of offenses, is free from the conceptualization of self and other.

Paṭiññaṃ na visaṃvādentīti avisaṃvādanasāmaññena sabbassapi anariyavohārassa akaraṇamāha. Paṭiññāte, apaṭiññāte ca diṭṭhādike micchāvikapparahitā hi saccapāramitā. Avicalādhiṭṭhānāti yathāsamādinnesu dānādidhammesu niccalādhiṭṭhāyino acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānā, samādinnesu ca buddhakaradhammesu sammadeva avaṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramitā. Tesūti sattesu. Avicalāyāti paṭipakkhena akampanīyāya. Evanti yathāvuttena sattesu hitajjhāsayatādiākārena. Yathā ca brahmavihārādhiṭṭhānā pāramiyo, evaṃ adhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānāpi. Tathā hi yathāpaṭiññaṃ parānuggahāya pāramīnaṃ [M 1.0392] anuṭṭhānena saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tappaṭipakkhapariccāgato [V 1.0369] cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ, pāramīhi sacittupasamato upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tāhi parahitūpāyakosallato paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ paccekampi pāramitāsu yathārahaṃ netabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana pāramitāsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paramatthadīpaniyaṃ cariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ, ativitthārabhayena na vitthārayimha. Tathā dasabalañāṇādiketi. Etāva hontīti etā honti evāti yojanā.

“Paṭiññaṃ na visaṃvādenti” (they do not break their promise): by the commonality of not deceiving, this speaks of the non-doing of all ignoble speech. For the perfection of truth is free from wrong conceptualization regarding things seen, etc., whether they are declared or undeclared. “Avicalādhiṭṭhānā” (of unshakable resolve) means they are of unshakable resolve in the qualities of giving, etc., that have been undertaken, having a foundation of immovable undertaking. And the perfection of resolve is the proper establishment in the Buddha-making qualities that have been undertaken. “Tesu” (in them) means in beings. “Avicalāya” (unshakable) means unable to be shaken by opposition. “Evaṃ” (thus) means in the manner already stated, such as having a disposition for the welfare of beings. And just as the perfections have the divine abodes as their foundation, so too do they have the four resolves as their foundation. Indeed, by undertaking the perfections for the benefit of others as promised, there is the resolve of truth. By abandoning their opposites, there is the resolve of relinquishment. By the calming of one's own mind through the perfections, there is the resolve of tranquility. Through them, by skill in the means for the welfare of others, there is the resolve of wisdom. In this way, it should be applied to each of the perfections accordingly. This is the summary here. But in detail, what should be said about the perfections should be known by the method stated in the Cariyāpiṭaka commentary called the Paramatthadīpanī. We have not elaborated for fear of being too extensive. Likewise regarding the ten powers of knowledge, etc. The connection of “Etāva honti” (they are of this extent) is “etā honti eva” (these are indeed thus).

Brahmavihāraniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Divine Abodes is completed.

Iti navamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the Commentary on the Ninth Chapter.

10. Āruppaniddesavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Exposition of the Immaterial

Paṭhamāruppavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the First Immaterial Attainment

275. Uddiṭṭhesūti [M 1.0393][V 1.0370] “cattāro āruppā”ti evaṃ uddiṭṭhesu, niddhāraṇe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Tenevāha “catūsu āruppesū”ti. Tattha rūpavivekena arūpaṃ, arūpameva āruppaṃ jhānaṃ, idha pana tadatthaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Taṃ bhāvetukāmo catutthajjhānaṃ uppādetīti sambandho. Rūpādhikaraṇanti rūpahetu. Hetuattho hi ettha adhikaraṇa-saddo “kāmādhikaraṇa”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.168-169) viya. Daṇḍanaṭṭhena daṇḍo, muggarādi. Parapīḷādhippāyena tassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ. Sattānaṃ sasanaṭṭhena satthaṃ, āvudhaṃ. Bhaṇḍanaṃ kalaho. Virodho viggaho. Nānāvādo vivādo. Etanti yathāvuttaṃ daṇḍādānādikaṃ. Sabbasoti anavasesato. Āruppe arūpabhāve, āruppe vā bhave. Rūpānaṃyevāti diṭṭhādīnavānaṃ rūpānaṃyeva, na arūpānanti adhippāyo. Nibbidāyāti vikkhambhanavasena nibbindanatthāya. Virāgāyāti virajjanatthāya. Nirodhāyāti nirujjhanatthāya. Sabbametaṃ samatikkamaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Daṇḍādānādīnanti ādi-saddena adinnādānādikaṃ sabbaṃ rūpahetukaṃ anatthaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, na idha pāḷiyaṃ āgatamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Karajarūpeti yathāvuttādīnavādhikaraṇabhāvayogyaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, oḷārikarūpeti attho. Ādīnavanti dosaṃ. Tassāti rūpassa. Ālokoti vaṇṇaviseso evāti tattha pavattaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ ugghāṭetvā siyā ākāsanimittaṃ uggahetuṃ, na pana paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā. Tassa hi ugghāṭanā nāma rūpanimitteneva siyāti āha “ṭhapetvā paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ navasū”ti. Keci pana “ālokakasiṇampi ṭhapetvā aṭṭhasū”ti vadanti, tassa pana ṭhapane kāraṇaṃ na dissati, karajarūpaṃ atikkantaṃ hoti tassa anālambanato.

275. Uddiṭṭhesu means “among those enumerated,” as in “the four immaterial attainments”; and this is a locative of determination. Therefore it is said, “in the four immaterial attainments.” There, through seclusion from form, the formless is attained; the formless itself is the immaterial jhāna. Here, however, the meditation subject for that purpose is intended. One who wishes to develop it arouses the fourth jhāna—this is the connection. Rūpādhikaraṇa means “on account of form,” i.e., “form as cause.” For here the word adhikaraṇa has the meaning of “cause,” as in “kāmādhikaraṇa” (on account of sensual desire) and so forth. A stick (daṇḍa) is so called because of its function of beating (daṇḍana); a club (muggara) and so forth. Taking it up with the intention of harming others is daṇḍādāna (taking up a stick). A weapon (sattha) is so called because of its function of harming (sasana) beings; it is an instrument of violence. Bhaṇḍana is quarreling. Virodha is opposition. Nānāvāda is disputation. Etanti refers to what has been described, such as taking up a stick and so forth. Sabbaso means “entirely,” without remainder. Āruppe means “in the formless state” or “in the immaterial existence.” “Of forms alone” means that the dangers that are seen pertain to forms alone, not to the formless—this is the meaning. Nibbidāya means “for disenchantment,” i.e., for the purpose of becoming disenchanted through suppression. Virāgāya means “for dispassion,” i.e., for the purpose of becoming dispassionate. Nirodhāya means “for cessation,” i.e., for the purpose of ceasing. All this is said with reference to transcendence. Daṇḍādānādīni: by the term ādi (and so forth), this includes all detriment rooted in form, such as taking what is not given. It should be understood that this does not include only what has come down in the Pāli text here. Karajarūpa is said to indicate that which is fit to be a basis for the aforementioned dangers; it means “gross form.” Ādīnava means “fault.” Tassa means “of form.” Āloko means “a particular color”—thus, having removed the counterpart sign that arises there, one might take up the space sign, but not after removing the limited space kasiṇa. For its removal would only be possible by means of the form sign. Hence it is said, “except for the limited space kasiṇa, in the nine cases.” Some, however, say, “except for the light kasiṇa also, in the eight cases.” But no reason is seen for excluding it, for the corporeal body is transcended by not taking it as an object.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā “catutthajjhānavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu paṭhamajjhānādīnipi tassa anālambanavaseneva pavattanti paṭibhāganimittārammaṇattā? Saccametaṃ, oḷārikaṅgappahānato pana santasabhāvena [V 1.0371] āneñjappattena catutthajjhānena atikkantaṃ suṭṭhu atikkantaṃ nāma hotīti “catutthajjhānavasenā”ti vuttaṃ[M 1.0394]. Keci “assāsapassāsānaṃ nirujjhanato, kāmadhātusamatikkamanato cā”ti vadanti, taṃ akāraṇaṃ, itaresaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ sambhavato, heṭṭhimajjhānānañca akāmadhātusaṃvattanīyato. Tappaṭibhāgamevāti karajarūpapaṭibhāgameva nimittaggāhasambhavato. Sadisañca nāma taṃ na hoti, tasmā kiṃ tassa samatikkamanenāti anuyogaṃ sandhāya “kathaṃ? Yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kathanti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Yathāti opammatthe nipāto. Lekhācittanti kāḷavaṇṇādinā kataparikammāya lekhāya cittaṃ. Phalitantaranti vivaraṃ. Disvāti dūrato disvā. Samānarūpasaddasamudācāranti sadisarūpasaṇṭhānasarappayogaṃ.

If so, why is it said, “by means of the fourth jhāna”? Do not the first jhāna and so on also proceed by not taking that as an object, since their object is the counterpart sign? This is true. However, by the fourth jhāna, which has reached a peaceful and imperturbable state through the abandoning of coarse factors, when it is transcended, it is called “well transcended.” Therefore, it is said, “by means of the fourth jhāna.” Some say, “Because the in-breaths and out-breaths cease, and because it transcends the sense-sphere.” But that is not a valid reason, because other mind-produced forms can still arise, and the lower jhānas are also not conducive to rebirth in the sense-sphere. Tappaṭibhāgameva means: it is indeed the counterpart of the corporeal body, because of the existence of the grasping of the sign. And a likeness is not the thing itself. Therefore, what is the use of transcending it? With reference to this question, it is said, “How? Just as…” Here, kathaṃ is a question indicating a desire to explain. Yathā is a particle in the sense of a simile. Lekhācitta refers to a variegated drawing with lines prepared with black and other colors. Phalitantara means “an opening.” Disvā means “having seen from a distance.” Samānarūpasaddasamudācāra means “having a similar form, shape, and vocal expression.”

Ārammaṇavasenāti “mama cakkhu sobhanaṃ, mama kāyo thiro, mama parikkhārā sundarā”ti evaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena. Karajarūpasamaṅgikāloti attano attabhāvarūpena ceva ārammaṇarūpena ca samannāgatakālo. Tampīti kasiṇarūpassapi. Sāmiatthe hi idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Bhayasantāsaadassanakāmatā viya samatikkamitukāmatāti yojanā. Idañca yathāvuttānaṃ nibbidāvirāganirodhānaṃ sādhāraṇavacanaṃ. Te hi tayo apekkhitvā bhayasantāsaadassanakāmatā vuttā. Eko kira sunakho vane sūkarena pahaṭamatto palāto, so arūpadassanavelāya bhattapacanaukkhaliṃ dūrato disvā sūkarasaññāya bhīto uttasanto palāyi, pisācabhīruko puriso rattibhāge aparicite dese matthakacchinnaṃ tālakkhandhaṃ disvā pisācasaññāya bhīto uttasanto mucchito papati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sūkarā…pe… veditabbā”ti.

Ārammaṇavasena means “by way of making it an object,” as in: “My eye is beautiful, my body is firm, my requisites are lovely.” Karajarūpasamaṅgikāla means the time when one is endowed with both the form of one's own being and the form of the object. Tampīti means “of the kasiṇa form also.” For here this is a word used in the sense of possession. The connection is: the desire to transcend is like the desire not to see out of fear and terror. And this is a statement common to the aforementioned disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation. For with reference to those three, the desire not to see out of fear and terror is spoken of. It is said that a certain dog, having been struck once by a boar in the forest, fled. Later, at a time when forms are not clearly seen, seeing a cooking pot from a distance, it fled in fear and terror with the perception that it was a boar. And a man fearful of demons, at nighttime in an unfamiliar place, seeing a palm trunk with its top cut off, with the perception that it was a demon, fainted and fell down in fear and terror. With reference to this, it was said: “The boar… should be understood.”

276. Evanti yathāvuttaṃ opammatthaṃ nigamento āha. Soti yogāvacaro. Tasmiṃ jhāne ādīnavaṃ passatīti sambandho. Rūpanti kasiṇarūpaṃ. Santavimokkhatoti arūpajjhānato. Tāni hi “ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe āruppā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.72; 10.9) santavimokkhāti āgatā. Santatāsiddhi cassa anussutito daṭṭhabbā. Yathevāti eva-kārena yena pakārena etaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ duvaṅgikaṃ, evaṃ āruppānipīti [M 1.0395] upekkhācittekaggatāvasena duvaṅgikattaṃ dasseti, na tatiyajjhāne viya duvaṅgikatāmattaṃ. Nanu cetthāpi duvaṅgikatāmattameva bhūmibhedatoti? Nāyaṃ doso upamopameyyabhāvassa bhinnādhikaraṇato.

276. Evaṃ: desiring to conclude the meaning of the aforementioned simile, he speaks. So means “the yogī.” The connection is: he sees the danger in that jhāna. Rūpa means “the kasiṇa form.” Santavimokkhato means “from the immaterial jhāna.” For these are called “peaceful liberations” in passages such as, “Those peaceful liberations, the immaterial attainments, which transcend forms…” etc. (A.N. 8.72; 10.9). And the establishment of its peacefulness should be understood from oral tradition. Yathā eva: by the particle eva, it shows that in whatever way this fourth form-realm jhāna is twofold, in that same way the immaterial attainments are also twofold, by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—not merely the state of being twofold as in the third jhāna. But is it not merely the state of being twofold here also, because of the difference in plane? This is not a fault, because the simile and that which is illustrated have different bases.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne. Nikantinti apekkhaṃ. Pariyādāyāti ādīnavadassanena [V 1.0372] tasmiṃ jhāne khepetvā, anapekkho hutvāti attho. Santato manasikaraṇeneva paṇītato, sukhumato ca manasikāro siddho hotīti āha “santato anantato manasi karitvā”ti. Pattharitvāti pageva vaḍḍhitaṃ, tadā vaḍḍhanavasena vā pattharitvā. Tenāti kasiṇarūpena. Ugghāṭeti kasiṇanti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ pathavīkasiṇādikasiṇarūpaṃ apaneti. Ugghāṭanavidhiṃ pana dassento “ugghāṭento hī”tiādimāha. Tattha saṃvelletīti paṭisaṃharati. Aññadatthūti ekaṃsena. Neva ubbaṭṭatīti neva uṭṭhahati. Na vivaṭṭatīti na vinivaṭṭati. Imassāti imassa kasiṇarūpassa. Amanasikāranti manasi akaraṇaṃ acintanaṃ. Manasikārañca paṭiccāti “ākāso ākāso”ti bhāvanāmanasikārañca nissāya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ kasiṇarūpaṃ na sabbena sabbaṃ manasi karoto, tena ca phuṭṭhokāsaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti manasi karoto yadā taṃ bhāvanānubhāvena ākāsaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, tadā so kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭeti nāma, tañca tena ugghāṭitaṃ nāma hotīti. Tenāha “kasiṇugghāṭimākāsamattaṃ paññāyatī”ti. Sabbametanti tividhampetaṃ ekameva pariyāyabhāvato.

Tattha means “in that fourth jhāna of the form realm.” Nikanti means “longing.” Pariyādāya means “having exhausted,” i.e., by seeing its drawbacks, having exhausted attachment for that jhāna, having become without attachment; this is the meaning. By peaceful attention itself, the attention is accomplished as refined and subtle, therefore he said, “having attended peacefully and boundlessly.” Pattharitvā means “having spread out,” i.e., having already developed it beforehand, or having spread it out by way of development at that time. Tena means “by means of the kasiṇa-form.” Ugghāṭeti kasiṇaṃ means “he unfastens the kasiṇa,” i.e., he removes the kasiṇa-form such as the earth kasiṇa, which is the object of the fourth jhāna of the form realm. Then, showing the method of unfastening, he said, “unfastening it, indeed,” and so on. Therein, saṃvelleti means “he retracts.” Aññadatthu means “certainly.” Neva ubbaṭṭati means “it does not rise up.” Na vivaṭṭati means “it does not turn away.” Imassa means “of this kasiṇa-form.” Amanasikāra means “non-attention,” i.e., not placing in the mind, not thinking. Manasikārañca paṭicca means “and relying on attention,” i.e., relying on the meditative attention of “space, space.” This is what is said: for one who does not attend at all to the kasiṇa-form, which is the object of the fourth jhāna of the form realm, and who attends to the space pervaded by it as “space, space,” when, through the power of meditation, it appears having become space, then he is said to unfasten the kasiṇa, and it is said to have been unfastened by him. Therefore, he said, “the unfastening of the kasiṇa is discerned as mere space.” Sabbametaṃ means “all this,” i.e., these three are one and the same, due to being synonyms.

“Nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhantī”ti kasmā vuttaṃ? Nanu rūpāvacarapaṭhamajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāni, tato paṭṭhāya cassa na nesaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ. Yadi siyā, jhānato parihāyeyya? Yaṃ paneke vadanti “attheva sukhumāni arūpajjhānavikkhambhaneyyāni nīvaraṇāni, tāni sandhāyetaṃ vutta”nti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Na hi mahaggatakusalesu lokuttarakusalesu viya odhiso pahānaṃ nāma atthi. Yo pana rūpāvacarehi āruppānaṃ uḷāraphalatādiviseso, so bhāvanāvisesena santatarapaṇītatarabhāvena tesuyeva purimapurimehi pacchimapacchimānaṃ [M 1.0396] viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Vikkhambhantī”ti pana vacanaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanavasena vuttaṃ. Tathā hi aññatthāpi heṭṭhā pahīnānaṃ upari pahānaṃ vuccati. Ye pana “sabbe kusalā dhammā sabbesaṃ akusalānaṃ paṭipakkhāti katvā evaṃ vutta”nti vadanti, tehi dutiyajjhānūpacārādīsu nīvaraṇavikkhambhanāvacanassa kāraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ. Sati santiṭṭhatīti ākāsanimittārammaṇā sati sammā sūpaṭṭhitā hutvā tiṭṭhati. Satisīsena cettha upacārajjhānānuguṇānaṃ saddhāpañcamānaṃ sakiccayogaṃ dasseti. Upacārenāti upacārajjhānena. Idhāpīti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ sandhāya sampiṇḍanaṃ. Taṃ hi upekkhāvedanāsampayuttaṃ. Sesanti “sesāni kāmāvacarānī”tiādi. Yaṃ idha vattabbamavuttaṃ, taṃ pana pathavīkasiṇaniddese (visuddhi. 1.51 ādayo) vuttanayānusārena [V 1.0373] veditabbanti āha “pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayamevā”ti.

“Why is it said, ‘They suppress the hindrances’? Are not the hindrances suppressed even at the moment of access of the first jhāna of the form realm, and from then on, for that person, there is no manifestation of them? If there were, he would fall away from the jhāna. As for what some say, ‘There are indeed subtle hindrances to be suppressed by the formless jhānas; referring to them, this was said,’ that is merely their opinion. For in the exalted wholesome states, there is no such thing as abandonment by limitation, as there is in the supramundane wholesome states. However, whatever distinction of the formless jhānas over the form realm jhānas there is, such as having a more magnificent fruit, that should be seen as being due to a distinction in meditation, through being more peaceful and more sublime, just as is the distinction of the later ones over the former ones among those very jhānas. The statement “they suppress” is, however, said by way of praise. For indeed, elsewhere too, the abandonment above of what has already been abandoned below is spoken of. But those who say, ‘It was said thus because all wholesome states are the opposite of all unwholesome states,’ should state the reason for not mentioning the suppression of hindrances in the access to the second jhāna and so on. ‘Mindfulness stands firm’ means mindfulness, having the sign of space as its object, stands, having become well-established. And here, with mindfulness as the head, he shows the application to their own function of the five faculties ending with faith, which are suitable for access jhāna. ‘By access’ means by access jhāna. ‘Here too’ is an inclusion referring to the fourth jhāna of the form realm. For it is associated with equanimous feeling. The rest means ‘the remaining sense-sphere states,’ and so on. What should be said here but was not said, that should be understood according to the method stated in the exposition of the earth kasiṇa. Therefore he said, ‘It is the same method as stated in the earth kasiṇa.’

Evaṃ yaṃ tattha avisiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ atidisitvā idāni visiṭṭhaṃ dassetuṃ “ayaṃ pana viseso”tiādimāha. Yānapputoḷi kumbhimukhādīnanti oguṇṭhanasivikādiyānānaṃ mukhaṃ yānamukhaṃ, putoḷiyā khuddakadvārassa mukhaṃ putoḷimukhaṃ, kumbhimukhanti paccekaṃ mukha-saddo sambandhitabbo. Ākāsaṃyeva yānamukhādiparicchinnaṃ. Parikammamanasikārenāti parikammabhūtena manasikārena upacārajjhānena. Parikammaṃ anulomaṃ upacāroti ca anatthantarañhetaṃ. Pekkhamāno arūpāvacarajjhānacakkhunā.

Thus, having made an extension for what was not distinct there, now, in order to show what is distinct, he says, “But this is the distinction,” and so on. Yānapputoḷikumbhimukhādīnaṃ means: the opening of vehicles such as covered litters is yānamukha; the opening of a small door of a basket (putoḷī) is putoḷimukha; kumbhimukha is the opening of a pot. Thus the word mukha (opening) should be connected with each one individually. The space itself is defined by the openings of vehicles and the like. Parikammamanasikārena means by the mental attention that is the preliminary work, by access jhāna. And parikamma (preliminary work), anuloma (conformity), and upacāra (access)—these are not different in meaning. Observing with the eye of the formless-sphere jhāna.

277. Sabbākārenāti rūpanimittaṃ daṇḍādānasambhavadassanādinā sabbena rūpadhammesu, pathavīkasiṇādirūpanimittesu, tadārammaṇajjhānesu ca dosadassanākārena, tesu eva vā rūpādīsu nikantippahānaanāvajjitukāmatādinā. Rūpajjhānampi rūpanti vuccati uttarapadalopena “rūpūpapattiyā maggaṃ bhāvetī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 160; vibha. 625) yathā rūpabhavo rūpaṃ. Rūpīti hi rūpajjhānalābhīti attho. Ārammaṇampi kasiṇarūpaṃ rūpanti vuccati purimapadalopena yathā “devadatto datto”ti. Rūpāni passatīti kasiṇarūpāni jhānacakkhunā passatīti attho. Tasmāti yasmā uttarapadalopena, purimapadalopena ca yathākkamaṃ rūpajjhānakasiṇarūpesu rūpavohāro dissati, tasmā. Rūpe rūpajjhāne taṃsahagatā saññā rūpasaññā. Tadārammaṇassa cāti ca-saddena yathāvuttaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ sampiṇḍeti, tena [M 1.0397] pāḷiyaṃ “rūpasaññāna”nti sarūpekasesena niddeso katoti dasseti. Virāgāti jigucchanato. Nirodhāti tappaṭibandhachandarāgavikkhambhanena nirodhanato. Vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “kiṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassa sabbākārena virāgā anavasesānaṃ nirodhāti evaṃ vā ettha yojanā kātabbā.

277. Sabbākārena means: by the mode of seeing faults in every way in form-dharmas, in form-signs such as the earth kasiṇa, and in the jhānas that have them as object—a seeing of faults such as the liability to the taking up of sticks; or, in those very forms, etc., by way of abandoning delight, unwillingness to advert, and so on. The form-jhāna is also called “form” (rūpa) by elision of the final word, as in “he develops the path for rebirth in the form-realm,” where rūpabhava (form-existence) is called rūpa. For rūpī means “one who has obtained a form-jhāna.” The object, the kasiṇa-form, is also called “form” by elision of the first word, just as “Devadatta” is called “Datta.” “He sees forms” means he sees kasiṇa-forms with the jhāna-eye. Therefore, because the designation “form” is seen applied to the form-jhāna and the kasiṇa-form respectively—by elision of the final word and elision of the first word—the perception associated with that rūpa, the form-jhāna, is rūpasaññā (form-perception). And in tadārammaṇassa ca (and of that which has it as object), by the word ca (and), he includes the aforesaid form-sphere jhāna. Thereby he shows that in the Pāli, the designation rūpasaññānaṃ (of form-perceptions) is made by sarūpekasesa (ellipsis of a similar term). Virāgā means because of disgust. Nirodhā means because of cessation by suppressing the desire and lust connected with it. To make the stated meaning clearer, “What is said?” etc., was stated. Or, the connection here should be made thus: “through dispassion in every way, comes the cessation of the remaining perceptions without exception.”

“Ārammaṇe avirattassa saññāsamatikkamo na hotī”ti idaṃ yasmā imāni jhānāni ārammaṇātikkamena pattabbāni, na aṅgātikkamenāti katvā vuttaṃ. Yasmā panettha saññāsamatikkamo ārammaṇasamatikkamena vinā na hoti, tasmā “samatikkantāsu ca saññāsu ārammaṇaṃ samatikkantameva hotī”ti āha. Avatvā vuttoti sambandho. Samāpannassātiādīsu [V 1.0374] kusalasaññāvasena samāpannaggahaṇaṃ, vipākasaññāvasena upapannaggahaṇaṃ, kiriyāsaññāvasena diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraggahaṇaṃ. Arahato hi jhānāni visesato diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro. Yadi saññāsamatikkamassa anunipphādiārammaṇasamatikkamo vibhaṅge ca avutto, atha kasmā idha gahitoti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Ārammaṇasamatikkamavasenāpi ayamatthavaṇṇanā katā, “tadārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacana”ntiādinā vibhaṅge viya saññāsamatikkamameva avatvāti adhippāyo.

This—'For one not dispassionate towards the object, there is no transcending of perception'—was said because these jhānas are to be attained by transcending the object, not by transcending the factors. Furthermore, since the transcending of perception here does not occur without transcending the object, he said, 'And when perceptions are transcended, the object is also transcended.' The connection is: what was unstated is stated. In the passage beginning with 'for one who has attained,' the taking of 'attained' is by way of wholesome perception; the taking of 'arisen' is by way of resultant perception; and the taking of 'a blissful abiding in the present life' is by way of functional perception. Indeed, for an Arahant, the jhānas are especially a blissful abiding in the present life. Addressing the inquiry, 'If the transcending of the object, which is a consequence of the transcending of perception, is unstated in the Vibhaṅga, then why is it taken up here?' he said, 'But because…' etc. The intention is that this explanation of the meaning is also made by way of transcending the object, and not, as in the Vibhaṅga with passages such as 'and this is a designation for that object,' by stating only the transcending of perception.

278. Paṭighātenāti paṭihananena visayīvisayasamodhānena. Atthaṅgamātiādīsu purimaṃ purimaṃ pacchimassa pacchimassa atthavacanaṃ, tasmā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamo jhānasamaṅgikāle anuppattīti tassa idheva gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ anuyogamukhena dassetuṃ “kāmañcetā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ussāhajananatthaṃ paṭipajjanakānaṃ. Etāsaṃ paṭighasaññānaṃ. Ettha paṭhamāruppakathāyaṃ. Vacanaṃ atthaṅgamavasena.

278. 'By resistance' (`paṭighātena`) means by striking, by the conjunction of the sense faculty and its object. In the passage beginning with 'cessation' (`atthaṅgamā`), each succeeding term explains the meaning of each preceding term. Therefore, the cessation of perceptions of resistance is their non-arising at the time one is endowed with jhāna. To show, by way of inquiry, the reason for this being taken up right here, the passage beginning 'Though these...' (`kāmañcetā`) was stated. This was for the purpose of generating diligence in those who are practicing. The statement concerning the cessation of these perceptions of resistance is made here in the discourse on the first formless attainment.

Kiṃ vā pasaṃsākittanena, paṭighasaññānaṃ pana atthaṅgamo idheva vattabbattā vuttoti dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabhāvadhammassa abhāvo nāma paṭipakkhena pahīnatāya vā paccayābhāvena vā. Tesu rūpajjhānasamaṅgino paṭighasaññānaṃ abhāvo paccayābhāvamattena, na paṭipakkhādhigamenāti dassento āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Tattha tāti paṭighasaññā[M 1.0398]. Rūpāvacaranti rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ. Samāpannassāti samāpajjitvā viharantassa. Kiñcāpi na santīti yojanā. Na pahīnattā na santīti na tadā paṭighasaññā pahīnabhāvena na santi nāma. Tattha kāraṇamāha “na hi rūpavirāgāya rūpāvacarabhāvanā saṃvattatī”ti. Nanu ca paṭighasaññāpi arūpadhammā evāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “rūpāyattā ca etāsaṃ pavattī”ti. Ayaṃ pana bhāvanāti arūpabhāvanamāha. Dhāretunti avadhāretuṃ. Idhāti arūpajjhāne. Āneñjābhisaṅkhāravacanādīhi āneñjatā. “Ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe āruppā”tiādinā (a. ni. 8.72; 10.9) santavimokkhatā ca vuttā.

Or what is the use of praise and commendation? To show that the cessation of perceptions of resistance is stated because it should be stated right here, the passage beginning 'Or else...' was stated. Herein, the absence of a state in its own nature is due to either its abandonment by an opposing factor or the absence of its conditions. Among these, for one endowed with a form jhāna, the absence of perceptions of resistance is merely due to the absence of conditions, not due to the attainment of an opposing factor. To show this, he says, 'Even though...' etc. Herein, 'those' refers to the perceptions of resistance. 'Form-sphere' means the form-sphere jhāna. 'For one who has attained' means for one who, having attained it, is abiding therein. The connection is 'even though they are not present.' It is not that they are not present because they are abandoned; that is, at that time, perceptions of resistance are not absent by way of being abandoned. Herein, he states the reason: 'For the cultivation of the form-sphere does not lead to dispassion toward form.' Anticipating the objection, 'But are not perceptions of resistance also formless phenomena?' he says, 'And their occurrence is dependent on form.' 'This cultivation,' however, refers to the cultivation of the formless. 'To hold' means to ascertain. 'Here' means in the formless jhāna. Its imperturbability is stated through terms such as 'imperturbable formations.' And its nature as a peaceful liberation is stated in passages such as, 'Those peaceful liberations that, transcending forms, are formless.'

279. Dosadassanapubbakapaṭipakkhabhāvanāvasena paṭighasaññānaṃ suppahīnattā mahatāpi saddena arūpasamāpattito na vuṭṭhāti. Tathā pana na suppahīnattā sabbarūpāvacarasamāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ siyā, paṭhamajjhānaṃ pana appakampi saddaṃ na sahatīti taṃ samāpannassa saddo kaṇṭakoti [V 1.0375] vuttaṃ. Āruppabhāvanāya abhāve cutito uddhaṃ uppattirahānaṃ rūpasaññāpaṭighasaññānaṃ yāva attano vipākappavatti, tāva anuppattidhammatāpādanena samatikkamo, atthaṅgamo ca vutto. Nānattasaññāsu pana yā tasmiṃ bhave na uppajjanti ekantarūpanissitā, tā anokāsatāya na uppajjanti, na āruppabhāvanāya nivāritattā, anivāritattā ca kāci uppajjanti. Tasmā tāsaṃ amanasikāro anāvajjanaṃ apaccavekkhaṇaṃ, javanapaṭipādakena vā bhavaṅgamanassa anto akaraṇaṃ appavesanaṃ vuttaṃ.

279. Because perceptions of resistance are well abandoned by means of cultivating the opposing factor, which is preceded by seeing the fault, one does not emerge from a formless attainment even with a loud sound. However, because they are not so well abandoned, emergence from any form-sphere attainment may occur. Furthermore, since the first jhāna cannot tolerate even a slight sound, it is said that for one who has attained it, sound is a thorn. In the absence of the cultivation of the formless, the transcending and cessation of perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance—which are liable to arise after death—are spoken of by way of bringing them to a state of non-arising for as long as its own result occurs. Furthermore, among perceptions of diversity, those that are exclusively dependent on form do not arise in that formless existence; they do not arise because there is no opportunity, not because they are prevented by the cultivation of the formless. And some do arise because they are not prevented. Therefore, for them, what is stated is non-attention, non-adverting, non-reviewing, or, by means of that which produces impulsion, the non-doing and non-allowing-to-enter within the life-continuum.

Tena ca nānattasaññāmanasikārahetūnaṃ rūpānaṃ samatikkamā samādhissa thirabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “saṅkhepato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Apica imehi tīhi padehi ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā vaṇṇo kathito sotūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ, palobhanatthañca. Ye hi akusalā evaṃgāhino “sabbassādarahite ākāse pavattitasaññāya ko ānisaṃso”ti, te tato micchāgāhato nivattetuṃ tīhi padehi jhānassa ānisaṃso kathito. Taṃ hi sutvā tesaṃ evaṃ bhavissati “evaṃ santā kirāyaṃ samāpatti evaṃ paṇītā, handassā nibbattanatthaṃ ussāhaṃ karissāmī”ti.

And by this, to show the stability of concentration that comes from transcending forms—which are the cause for attending to perceptions of diversity—the passage beginning 'In brief...' was stated. Moreover, by these three terms the excellence of the attainment of the base of infinite space is described, for the purpose of generating diligence in the listeners and for enticing them. For those unskilled ones who hold such a view, thinking, 'What is the benefit of a perception occurring in space devoid of all that is worthy of respect?'—to turn them away from that wrong view, the benefit of the jhāna is described in three terms. For, having heard that, they will think, 'Indeed, this attainment is so peaceful, so sublime! Come now, I will make an effort to produce it.'

280. Assāti [M 1.0399] ākāsassa. Uppādo eva anto uppādanto, tathā vayanto. Sabhāvadhammo hi ahutvā sambhavato, hutvā ca vinassanato udayavayaparicchinno. Ākāso pana asabhāvadhammattā tadubhayābhāvato ananto vutto. Ajaṭākāsaparicchinnākāsānaṃ idha anadhippetattā “ākāsoti kasiṇugghāṭimākāso vuccatī”ti āha. Kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭīyati etenāti kasiṇugghāṭo, tadeva kasiṇugghāṭimaṃ. Manasikāravasenāpīti rūpavivekamattaggahaṇena paricchedassa aggahaṇato anantapharaṇākārena pavattaparikammamanasikāravasenāpi. Anantaṃ pharatīti aggahitaparicchedatāya anantaṃ katvā parikammasamphassapubbakena jhānasamphassena phusati. Yathā bhisaggameva bhesajjaṃ, evaṃ ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ saṃyogaparassa ta-kārassa ca-kāraṃ katvā. Jhānassa pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato ārammaṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena “āyatanamassā”ti vuttaṃ, adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhe āyatana-saddassa dassanato. Kāraṇākarasañjātidesanivāsatthepi āyatana-saddo idha yujjateva.

280. Assa means 'of space' (ākāsassa). Arising itself is the limit (anto), the limit of arising (uppādanto); similarly, the limit of passing away (vayanto). Indeed, a conditioned phenomenon (sabhāvadhammo), from coming to be after not having been and from perishing after having been, is delimited by arising and passing away. But space (ākāso), because of its nature as an unconditioned phenomenon and due to the absence of both of these, is said to be limitless (ananto). Because unentangled space and delimited space are not intended here, he said, “By ‘space’ is meant the space of the removed kasiṇa.” By this the kasiṇa is removed (ugghāṭīyati), hence it is kasiṇugghāṭa; that very thing is kasiṇugghāṭima. “Also by way of mental attention” means: also by way of the preliminary mental attention that occurs in the manner of limitless pervasion, due to not grasping the limit by grasping only the seclusion from form. “It pervades the limitless” means: having made it limitless by way of the ungrasped limit, one touches it with the jhāna-contact that is preceded by the preliminary-practice contact. Just as bhisagga itself is bhesajja, so ākāsānanta itself is ākāsānañca, having made the letter 't' which is after a conjunct consonant into the letter 'c'. Because it is the place of occurrence for the jhāna, the object is called “its base” (āyatanam assā) in the sense of a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna). This is because the word āyatana is found in the sense of a foundation. The word āyatana is also suitable here in the senses of cause, mine, place of origin, and residence.

Viññāṇañcāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Base of Infinite Consciousness

281. Ciṇṇo [V 1.0376] carito paguṇikato āvajjanādilakkhaṇo vasībhāvo etenāti ciṇṇavasībhāvo, tena ciṇṇavasībhāvena. Rūpāvacarasaññaṃ anatikkamitvā anadhigantabbato, taṃsahagatasaññāmanasikārasamudācārassa hānabhāgiyabhāvāvahato, taṃsamatikkameneva tadaññesaṃ samatikkamitabbānaṃ samatikkamasiddhito ca vuttaṃ “āsannarūpāvacarajjhānapaccatthikā”ti. Vīthipaṭipannāya bhāvanāya uparūparivisesāvahabhāvato, paṇītabhāvasiddhito ca paṭhamāruppato dutiyāruppaṃ santatarasabhāvanti āha “no ca viññāṇañcāyatanamiva santā”ti vakkhati hi “suppaṇītatarā honti, pacchimā pacchimā idhā”ti (visuddhi. 1.290). Anantaṃ anantanti kevalaṃ “anantaṃ ananta”nti na manasi kātabbaṃ na bhāvetabbaṃ, “anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ, anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti pana manasi kātabbaṃ, “viññāṇaṃ viññāṇa”nti vā.

281.
