One by whom mastery (vasībhāvo) characterized by adverting and so on has been practiced (ciṇṇo), frequented (carito), and made proficient (paguṇikato) is one of 'practiced mastery' (ciṇṇavasībhāvo); by that one of practiced mastery. Because it is unattainable without transcending the form-sphere perception, because the occurrence of perception and mental attention associated with that leads to a state of decline, and because only by transcending that is the transcending of other things that should be transcended accomplished, it is said, “it has the near enemy which is the form-sphere jhāna.” And because the meditation that has entered the path brings about progressively higher distinction, and because of the accomplishment of a refined state, the second formless attainment has a more peaceful nature than the first formless attainment; thus, he said, “but not as peaceful as the base of infinite consciousness.” For it will be said, “Herein, the later, later ones are exceedingly refined.” As for “infinite, infinite,” one should not merely give attention to or develop “infinite, infinite.” But rather, one should give attention to “infinite consciousness, infinite consciousness,” or “consciousness, consciousness.”

Tasmiṃ nimitteti tasmiṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇasaṅkhāte viññāṇanimitte. Cittaṃ cārentassāti bhāvanācittaṃ pavattentassa. Ākāsaphuṭe viññāṇeti [M 1.0400] kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ pharitvā pavatte paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe ārammaṇabhūte. Appetīti appanāvasena pavattati. Sabhāvadhammepi ārammaṇasamatikkamabhāvanābhāvato idaṃ appanāppattaṃ hoti catutthāruppaṃ viya. Appanānayo panettha vuttanayenevāti ettha dutiyāruppajjhāne purimabhāge tīṇi, cattāri vā javanāni kāmāvacarāni upekkhāvedanāsampayuttāneva honti. “Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vā arūpāvacara”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.276) paṭhamāruppajjhāne vuttena nayena, atha vā appanānayoti sabhāvadhammepi ārammaṇe jhānassa appanānayo ārammaṇātikkamabhāvanāvasena āruppaṃ appanaṃ pāpuṇāti, “appanāppattasseva hi jhānassa ārammaṇasamatikkamanamattaṃ tattha hotī”ti maraṇānussatiniddese (visuddhi. 1.177) vuttanayena veditabboti attho.

“In that sign” means: in that sign of consciousness which is designated as the first formless consciousness. “For one who makes the mind occur” means: for one who makes the meditation-mind occur. “In the consciousness that has pervaded space” means: in the first formless consciousness which has become the object, having arisen by pervading the space of the removed kasiṇa. “It enters” means: it occurs by way of absorption. Even though it is a conditioned phenomenon, because it is a meditation that transcends its object, this reaches absorption, like the fourth formless attainment. As for “The way of absorption here is by the way already stated”: here, in this second formless jhāna, it is by the way stated in the first formless jhāna with the text beginning, “In the preliminary part... the fourth or fifth is formless-sphere...” Or alternatively, “the way of absorption” means that the way of absorption for the jhāna in its object, even though it is a conditioned phenomenon, should be understood by the way stated in the Exposition of Mindfulness of Death: “...for it is only the transcending of the object that occurs there for a jhāna that has reached absorption.” This is the meaning.

282. Sabbasoti sabbākārena paṭhamāruppe “āsannarūpajjhānapaccatthikatā, asantasabhāvatā”ti evamādinā sabbena dosadassanākārena, tattha vā nikantipahānaanāvajjitukāmatādiākārena, sabbaṃ vā kusalavipākakiriyābhedato anavasesanti attho. Svāyamattho heṭṭhā vuttanayena ñātuṃ sakkāti āha “sabbasoti idaṃ vuttanayamevā”ti. Jhānassa ākāsānañcāyatanatā bāhiratthasamāsavasena heṭṭhā vuttāti āha “pubbe vuttanayena jhānampi ākāsānañcāyatana”nti[V 1.0377]. Ārammaṇassa pana samānādhikaraṇasamāsavasenāti sandassetuṃ “ārammaṇampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “purimanayenevā”ti idaṃ “nāssa anto”tiādinā vuttapadasiddhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yathā adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena, evaṃ sañjātidesaṭṭhenapi āyatana-saddena idha attho yujjatīti dassetuṃ “tathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sañjāyati etthāti sañjāti, sañjāti eva deso sañjātideso. Jhānaṃ appavattikaraṇena. Ārammaṇaṃ amanasikaraṇena. Ubhayampi vā ubhayatā yojetabbā. Jhānassapi hi anāvajjanaṃ, javanapaṭipādakena vā bhavaṅgamanassa anto akaraṇaṃ amanasikaraṇaṃ, ārammaṇassa ca ārammaṇakaraṇavasena appavattanaṃ appavattikaraṇanti atthassa sambhavato ekajjhaṃ katvā sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā.

282. “In every way” (sabbaso) means: with respect to the first formless attainment, in every way of seeing faults, beginning with “the state of having the near form-sphere jhāna as an enemy” and “the state of having an unpeaceful nature”; or, in the manner of abandoning craving for it, the desire not to advert to it, and so on; or, “all” means without remainder, according to the division into wholesome, resultant, and functional. This is the meaning. Because this meaning can be known by the way stated previously, he said, “As for sabbaso, this is the way already stated.” Because the jhāna’s being the Base of Infinite Space was stated previously by way of an external-referent compound, he said, “By the way previously stated, the jhāna too is the Base of Infinite Space.” But to show this by way of a co-referential compound of the object, the words beginning “the object too...” were said. Therein, the words “by the previous way” were said in reference to the derivation of the term stated with the words beginning “it has no end.” To show that just as the meaning is suitable here with the word āyatana in the sense of a foundation, so too it is suitable in the sense of a place of origin, the words beginning “similarly...” were said. Therein, sañjāti means “it arises here” (sañjāyati ettha); sañjāti itself is the place (deso), hence sañjātideso (place of origin). The jhāna by not causing it to occur; the object by not giving attention to it. Or both should be connected in both ways. For, in the case of the jhāna, not adverting to it, or the non-making within the life-continuum mind which is the basis for impulsion, is “not giving attention.” And in the case of the object, its non-occurrence by way of taking it as an object is “not causing it to occur.” Because this meaning is possible, it is stated comprehensively by way of a general indication or by way of the ekasesa method.

Pubbe [M 1.0401] anantassa ākāsassa ārammaṇakaraṇavasena paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ attano pharaṇākāreneva “ananta”nti manasi kātabbattā “anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti vuttanti puna “manasikāravasena vā ananta”nti vuttaṃ, sabbaso manasikaraṇavasenāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “anavasesato manasi karonto ‘ananta’nti manasi karotī”ti. Jhānavibhaṅgepi ayamevattho vuttoti dassento “yaṃ pana vibhaṅge vutta”ntiādimāha. Tassā pāḷiyā evaṃ vā attho veditabbo – taṃyeva ākāsaṃ phuṭaṃ viññāṇaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaviññāṇena manasi karotīti. Ayaṃ panattho yutto viya dissati, taṃyeva ākāsaṃ viññāṇena phuṭaṃ tena gahitākāraṃ manasi karoti. Evaṃ taṃ viññāṇaṃ anantaṃ pharatīti. Yaṃ hi ākāsaṃ paṭhamāruppasamaṅgī viññāṇena anantaṃ pharati, taṃ pharaṇākārasahitameva viññāṇaṃ manasi karonto dutiyāruppasamaṅgī anantaṃ pharatīti vuccati.

Because the first formless consciousness—by way of making the previously infinite space its object—should be attended to as 'infinite' through its own mode of pervasion, it is called 'infinite consciousness.' And again, it is said, 'or infinite by way of attention.' The meaning is: by way of attending to it completely. Therefore, he said: 'Attending to it without remainder, one attends to it as "infinite."' To show that this very meaning is stated in the Jhānavibhaṅga, he said, 'But what is stated in the Vibhaṅga,' and so on. Alternatively, the meaning of that Pāḷi text should be understood thus: one attends to that very space, pervaded by the first formless consciousness, with the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness. This meaning, however, appears to be suitable: one attends to that very space, pervaded by the first formless consciousness, in the mode grasped by it. Thus, that consciousness pervades it as 'infinite.' For, whatever space the one endowed with the first formless attainment pervades as 'infinite' with the first formless consciousness, the one endowed with the second formless attainment, while attending to that very consciousness together with its mode of pervasion, is said to pervade it as 'infinite.'

Manasikāravasena anantapharaṇākārena idha anantatā, na ākāsassa viya uppādantādiabhāvenāti “nāssa antoti ananta”nti ettakamevāha. “Ruḷhīsaddo”ti iminā “viññāṇānañca”nti etassa padassa atthe viññāṇañca-saddo niruḷhoti dasseti, yathāvuttaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ dutiyāruppajjhānena añcīyati vuttākārena ālambīyatīti viññāṇañcanti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ vuttatthamevāti āha “sesaṃ purimasadisamevā”ti.

Here, infinity is by way of attention, by the mode of pervading as 'infinite'; not, like space, by the absence of a beginning, limit, and so on. Therefore, he said only this much: 'It has no end, thus it is infinite.' By 'it is a conventional term,' he shows that in the meaning of this term 'viññāṇānañca,' the word 'viññāṇañca' is established. Alternatively, the aforesaid consciousness is approached (añcīyati) by the second formless jhāna, that is, it is taken as an object (ālambīyati) in the aforesaid manner; therefore, it is called 'viññāṇañcaṃ.' Thus also, the meaning should be understood here. The rest has the meaning already stated; therefore, he said, 'The rest is just like the preceding.'

Ākiñcaññāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Base of Nothingness

283. Tatiyāruppakammaṭṭhāne yaṃ heṭṭhā vuttasadisaṃ, taṃ vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ, apubbameva [V 1.0378] vaṇṇayissāma. Tattha tassevāti yaṃ ārabbha viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ pavattaṃ, tasseva. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇassā”ti. Etena tato aññaṃ tatiyāruppajjhānassa ārammaṇaṃ natthīti dasseti. “Ārammaṇabhūtassā”ti iminā tassa anārammaṇabhūtaṃ dutiyāruppaviññāṇaṃ nivatteti. Abhāvoti natthitā. Suññatāti rittatā. Vivittākāroti viveko. Tīhi padehi paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa apagamameva vadati. “Manasi kātabbo”ti vatvā [M 1.0402] manasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ viññāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha amanasikaritvāti sabbena sabbaṃ manasi akatvā acintetvā. Vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena tīsu pakāresu ekenapi atthasiddhīti dasseti.

283. In the meditation subject of the third formless attainment, whatever is similar to what was said before should be understood according to the method already stated; we shall comment only on what is new. Therein, as to 'of that very thing': it means of that very thing with reference to which the base of infinite consciousness arose. What is that? He says: 'of the consciousness of the base of infinite space.' By this, he shows that there is no other object for the third formless jhāna than that. By 'of that which has become the object,' he excludes the second formless consciousness which has not become its object. 'Absence' means non-existence. 'Emptiness' means voidness. 'Secluded aspect' means seclusion. With these three terms, he speaks only of the passing away of the first formless consciousness. Having said, 'should be attended to,' he stated 'that consciousness,' etc., to show the method of attention. Therein, 'not attending' means not placing in the mind at all, not thinking. The word 'vā' has the meaning of indefiniteness; by that, he shows that the purpose is accomplished by even one of the three modes.

Tasmiṃ nimitteti tasmiṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa abhāvasaṅkhāte jhānuppattinimitte. Ākāse phuṭeti ākāsaṃ pharitvā pavatte. “Ākāsaphuṭe”ti vā pāṭho. Suññavivittanatthibhāveti suññabhāve, vivittabhāve, natthibhāve cāti yena ākārena bhāvitaṃ, tassa gahaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Atha vā suññavivittanatthibhāveti suññavivittatāsaṅkhāte natthibhāve, tena vināsābhāvameva dasseti, na pure abhāvādike.

As to 'in that sign': in that sign for the arising of the jhāna, designated as the absence of the first formless consciousness. As to 'pervades in space': having pervaded space, it proceeds. Or, the reading is 'ākāsaphuṭe' (pervaded in space). As to 'in the state of emptiness, seclusion, and non-existence' (suññavivittanatthibhāve): it is said for the purpose of grasping that mode by which it was developed, namely, in the state of emptiness, the state of seclusion, and the state of non-existence. Alternatively, as to 'in the state of emptiness, seclusion, and non-existence': in the state of non-existence designated as emptiness and seclusion. By that, he shows only absence due to destruction, not a prior absence and so on.

Tasmiṃ hi appanācitteti ākiñcaññāyatanajjhānasampayutte appanāvasena pavatte citte, tasmiṃ vā paṭhamāruppassa apagamasaṅkhāte natthibhāve yathāvutte appanācitte uppanne. So bhikkhu abhāvameva passanto viharatīti sambandho. Puriso katthaci gantvā āgantvā suññameva passati, natthibhāvameva passatīti yojanā. Taṃ ṭhānanti taṃ sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ. “Parikammamanasikārena antarahite”ti iminā ārammaṇakaraṇābhāvena tassa antaradhānaṃ na naṭṭhattāti dasseti. Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – yathā so puriso tattha sannipatitaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā gato, tato sabbesu bhikkhūsu kenacideva karaṇīyena apagatesu āgantvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhikkhūhi suññameva passati, na bhikkhūnaṃ tatopi apagatakāraṇaṃ, evamayaṃ yogāvacaro pubbe viññāṇañcāyatanajjhānacakkhunā paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ disvā pacchā natthīti parikammamanasikārena tasmiṃ apagate tatiyāruppajjhānacakkhunā tassa natthibhāvameva passanto viharati, na tassa apagamanakāraṇaṃ vīmaṃsati jhānassa tādisābhogābhāvatoti. Sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

As to 'in that absorption-consciousness': in the mind that proceeds by way of absorption, associated with the jhāna of the base of nothingness; or, when the aforesaid absorption-consciousness has arisen in that state of non-existence designated as the passing away of the first formless consciousness. The connection is: 'That bhikkhu dwells seeing only the absence.' The application is: 'A person, having gone somewhere and returned, sees only emptiness, sees only the state of non-existence.' 'That place' means that meeting place. By the phrase 'when it has disappeared through preliminary-work attention,' he shows that its disappearance is due to the absence of making it an object, not due to its having been destroyed. Herein, this is the application of the simile: just as that person, having seen the assembled community of monks there, departed, and then, after all the monks had left on some business, he returned and saw that place as empty of monks, not seeing the reason for the monks' departure from there; so too this yogī, having previously seen the first formless consciousness with the jhāna-eye of the base of infinite consciousness, and afterwards, when that consciousness has passed away through the preliminary-work attention 'it is not,' he dwells with the jhāna-eye of the third formless attainment seeing only its state of non-existence, not scrutinizing the reason for its passing away, because the jhāna lacks such an inclination. Regarding 'having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness,' whatever should be said here is to be understood according to the method stated before.

284. Natthitā [V 1.0379] pariyāyāsuññavivittabhāvāti “natthī”ti padassa atthaṃ vadantena suññavivittapadānipi gahitāni. Āmeḍitavacanaṃ pana bhāvanākāradassanaṃ. Vibhaṅgepi imassa padassa ayamevattho vuttoti dassetuṃ “yampi vibhaṅge”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha taññeva viññāṇaṃ abhāvetīti yaṃ pubbe “anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti manasi kataṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ, taṃyevāti attho[M 1.0403]. Taṃyeva hi ārammaṇabhūtaṃ paṭhamena viya rūpanimittaṃ tatiyenāruppenābhāvetīti. Khayato sammasananti bhaṅgānupassanamāha. Sā hi saṅkhatadhammānaṃ bhaṅgābhāvameva passantī “viññāṇampi abhāvetī”tiādinā vattabbataṃ labhatīti adhippāyenāha “khayato sammasanaṃ viya vutta”nti. Assāti pāṭhassa. Puna assāti viññāṇassa. Abhāvetīti abhāvaṃ karoti. Yathā ñāṇassa na upatiṭṭhati, evaṃ karoti amanasikaraṇato. Tato eva vibhāveti vigatabhāvaṃ karoti, vināseti vā yathā na dissati, tathā karaṇato. Teneva antaradhāpeti tirobhāvaṃ gameti. Na aññathāti imissā pāḷiyā evamattho, na ito aññathā ayujjamānakattāti adhippāyo.

284. The states of voidness and seclusion are synonyms for the state of non-existence. Therefore, by explaining the meaning of the word 'natthī', the words 'suñña' and 'vivitta' are also included. The repetition, however, shows the mode of development. To show that this very meaning of the word is also stated in the Vibhaṅga, it is said, 'and also what is in the Vibhaṅga,' etc. Therein, 'it makes that very consciousness non-existent' means that very first immaterial consciousness which was previously attended to as 'infinite consciousness.' For, just as the form-sign is made non-existent by the first immaterial attainment, so that very consciousness which has become the object is made non-existent by the third immaterial attainment. 'Contemplating as destruction' refers to the observation of dissolution. For it, seeing only the non-existence which is dissolution of conditioned phenomena, obtains the state of being expressible by 'it makes even consciousness non-existent,' etc. With this intention, it is said, 'it is stated as if contemplating as destruction.' 'Assa' refers to the reading. Again, 'assa' refers to the consciousness. 'Abhāveti' means 'it makes non-existent.' It acts in such a way that it does not appear to knowledge, due to not attending to it. For that very reason, 'vibhāveti' means it makes it a gone state, or 'vināseti' means it destroys it, because of acting in such a way that it is not seen. For that very reason, 'antaradhāpeti' means it causes it to disappear, it makes it go to a state of concealment. 'Na aññathā' means: the meaning of this Pali passage is thus, not otherwise than this, because it would be unsuitable. This is the intention.

Assāti paṭhamāruppaviññāṇābhāvassa. Kiñcananti kiñcipi. Sabhāvadhammassa appāvasesatā nāma bhaṅgo eva siyāti āha “bhaṅgamattampi assa avasiṭṭhaṃ natthī”ti. Sati hi bhaṅgamattepi tassa sakiñcanatā siyā. Akiñcananti ca viññāṇassa kiñci pakāraṃ aggahetvā sabbena sabbaṃ vibhāvanamāha. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

‘Assa’ refers to the non-existence of the first immaterial consciousness. ‘Kiñcanaṃ’ means anything whatsoever. The state of having no remainder of a phenomenon with intrinsic nature would be precisely dissolution; therefore, it is said, 'Not even a mere dissolution remains for it.' For if even a mere dissolution were present, there would be a state of 'having something' for it. And by 'akiñcanaṃ', he states the complete making non-existent of the consciousness, without grasping any mode of it. The rest is according to the method already stated.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Base of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception

285. No ca santāti yathā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattiyā savisesā santā, evamayaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpatti no ca santā tadabhāvato. Yā ayaṃ khandhesu paccayayāpanīyatāya, rogamūlatāya ca rogasarikkhatā, dukkhatāsūlayogādinā gaṇḍasarikkhatā, pīḷājananādinā sallasarikkhatā ca, sā saññāya sati hoti, nāsatīti vuttaṃ “saññā rogo, saññā gaṇḍo, saññā salla”nti. Sā cettha paṭukiccā pañcavokārabhavato oḷārikasaññā veditabbā. Na kevalaṃ saññā eva, atha kho vedanācetanādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Saññāsīsena pana niddeso kato. Etaṃ santanti etaṃ asantabhāvakararogādisarikkhasaññāvirahato santaṃ. Tato eva paṇītaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “nevasaññānāsaññā”ti[V 1.0380]? Tadapadesena [M 1.0404] taṃsampayuttajjhānamāha “ādīnava”nti. Ettha rogādisarikkhasaññādisabbhāvopi ādīnavo daṭṭhabbo, na āsannaviññāṇañcāyatanapaccatthikatāva. Uparīti catutthāruppe. Sā vāti sā eva. Vattitāti pavattitā nibbattitā vaḷañjitā.

285. ‘And it is not peaceful’: Just as the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful in a special way by having reached the state of being subtle with residual formations, so this attainment of the base of nothingness is not peaceful, due to the absence of that. That which, in the aggregates, is like a disease because it is sustained by conditions and is the root of disease; like a boil because of its connection with suffering, pain, etc.; and like a dart because it generates affliction, etc.—that exists when perception is present, and does not exist when it is absent. Therefore it is said: 'Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart.' And here, this should be understood as the gross perception with a distinct function, pertaining to the five-constituent existence. Not only perception, but rather the inclusion of feeling, volition, etc., should also be seen. However, the exposition is made with perception as the heading. ‘This is peaceful’: This is peaceful because of the absence of the perception which resembles disease, etc., which causes a state of not being peaceful. For that very reason, it is sublime. But what is that? He says, 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' By this designation, he refers to the jhāna associated with it. Here, the very existence of perception, etc., which resembles disease, etc., should be seen as a disadvantage, not merely its being inimical to the nearby base of infinite consciousness. ‘Above’ means in the fourth immaterial attainment. ‘That’ means just that. ‘Occurred’ means arisen, produced, practiced.

Tasmiṃ nimitteti tasmiṃ tatiyāruppasamāpattisaṅkhāte jhānanimitte. Mānasanti cittaṃ “mano eva mānasa”nti katvā, bhāvanāmanasikāraṃ vā. Taṃ hi manasi bhavanti mānasanti vuccati. Jhānasampayuttadhammānampi jhānānuguṇatāya samāpattipariyāyo labbhatīti āha “ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattisaṅkhātesu catūsu khandhesū”ti, ārammaṇabhūtesūti adhippāyo.

“In that sign” means in the jhāna-sign designated as the third immaterial attainment. “Mental” means the mind—taking it as “the mind itself is mental”—or the attention of development. For that which is in the mind is called “mental.” Because the states associated with the jhāna are in conformity with the jhāna, the synonymous term “attainment” is obtained; thus it is said: “in the four aggregates designated as the attainment of the base of nothingness.” The intention is that they have become the object.

286. Yathāvuttaṃ ākiñcaññaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhāvato āyatanaṃ kāraṇamassāti jhānaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, ākiñcaññameva ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ jhānassa kāraṇanti ārammaṇaṃ ākiñcaññāyatananti evaṃ vā attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

286. The jhāna is the 'base of nothingness' because, as has been said, nothingness is its base and cause by way of being an object-condition. Or the meaning should be understood thus: nothingness itself, having become the object-condition, is the cause of the jhāna; therefore, the object is the 'base of nothingness.' The rest here should be understood according to the method stated previously.

Yāya saññāya bhāvatoti yādisāya saññāya atthibhāvena. Yā hi sā paṭusaññākiccassa abhāvato saññātipi na vattabbā, saññāsabhāvānātivattanato asaññātipi na vattabbā, tassā vijjamānattāti attho. Tanti taṃ jhānaṃ. Taṃ tāva dassetunti ettha tanti taṃ sasāpaṭipadaṃ, yathāvuttasaññaṃ, tassā ca adhigamupāyanti attho. Nevasaññīnāsaññīti hi puggalādhiṭṭhānena dhammaṃ uddharantena saññāvantamukhena saññā uddhaṭā, aññathā nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti uddharitabbaṃ siyā. Sā pana paṭipadā yattha pavattati, yathā ca pavattati, taṃ dassetuṃ “ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasi karoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāvetī”ti vuttaṃ. Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ hi catutthāruppabhāvanāya pavattiṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti pavattiākāroti. Yatra hi nāmāti yā nāma. Natthibhāvampīti viññāṇassa suññatampi, evaṃ sukhumampīti adhippāyo. Santārammaṇatāyāti santaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etissāti santārammaṇā, tabbhāvo santārammaṇatā, tāya, na jhānasantatāya. Na hi tatiyāruppasamāpatti catutthāruppajjhānato santā.

‘By the existence of which perception’ means by the existence of such a perception. For that perception, because of the absence of the function of acute perception, cannot be called ‘perception’; yet because it does not transcend the nature of perception, it cannot be called ‘non-perception,’ due to its existence. This is the meaning. ‘That’ means that jhāna. In the phrase ‘He shows that first,’ ‘that’ means that perception along with its practice, the aforesaid perception, and the means for its attainment. This is the meaning. For in the expression ‘one with neither perception nor non-perception,’ when setting forth the Dhamma with the person as the basis, perception is set forth by way of one who possesses perception; otherwise, it would have to be set forth as ‘the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ But to show where that practice proceeds and how it proceeds, it is said: ‘He attends to the base of nothingness as peaceful; he develops the attainment of residual formations.’ For the base of nothingness is the ground of occurrence for the development of the fourth immaterial attainment, and the attainment of residual formations is the mode of occurrence. ‘Yatra hi nāma’ means ‘whatever.’ ‘Even the state of non-existence’ means even the emptiness of the consciousness, and thus its subtlety; this is the intention. ‘Because it has a peaceful object’: It has a peaceful object, thus it is ‘one with a peaceful object’; its state is ‘having a peaceful object.’ Because of that, not because of the peacefulness of the jhāna. For the third immaterial attainment is not more peaceful than the fourth immaterial jhāna.

Codako [M 1.0405] “yaṃ santato manasi karoti, na tattha ādīnavadassanaṃ bhaveyya. Asati ca ādīnavadassane samatikkamo eva na siyā”ti dassento “santato ce manasi karoti, kathaṃ samatikkamo [V 1.0381] hotī”ti āha. Itaro “asamāpajjitukāmatāyā”ti parihāramāha, tena ādīnavadassanampi atthevāti dasseti. So hītiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ karoti. Tattha yasmiṃ jhāne abhirati, tattha āvajjanasamāpajjanādipaṭipattiyā bhavitabbaṃ. Sā panassa tatiyāruppe sabbaso natthi, kevalaṃ aññābhāvato ārammaṇakaraṇamattamevāti dassento “kiñcāpī”tiādimāha.

The objector, showing that “In that which one attends to as peaceful, there would be no seeing of disadvantage. And when there is no seeing of disadvantage, there could be no transcending,” said: “If one attends to it as peaceful, how can there be transcending?” The other gave the reply: “Because of the desire not to attain it,” thereby showing that the seeing of disadvantage also exists. With “For he…” and so on, he makes the aforesaid meaning clearer. Therein, in whatever jhāna one delights, there must be the practice of adverting, attaining, and so on. But for this person, this is entirely absent in the third immaterial attainment; showing that there is only the mere making of an object because of the absence of another, he says “Although…” and so on.

Samatikkamitvāva gacchatīti tesaṃ sippīnaṃ jīvikaṃ tiṇāyapi amaññamāno te vītivattatiyeva. Soti yogāvacaro. Tanti tatiyāruppasamāpattiṃ. Pubbe vuttanayenāti “santā vatāyaṃ samāpattī”tiādinā vuttena nayena santato manasi karonto. Tanti yāya nevasaññīnāsaññī nāma hoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāvetīti vuccati, taṃ saññaṃ pāpuṇātīti yojanā. Saññāsīsena hi desanā. Paramasukhumanti ukkaṃsagatasukhumabhāvaṃ. Saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattinti ukkaṃsagatasukhumatāya saṅkhārānaṃ sesatāmattaṃ samāpattiṃ. Tenāha “accantasukhumabhāvappattasaṅkhāra”nti. Antamaticca accantaṃ. Yato sukhumatamaṃ nāma natthi, tathāparamukkaṃsagatasukhumasaṅkhāranti attho. Paṭhamajjhānūpacārato paṭṭhāya hi tacchantiyā viya pavattamānāya bhāvanāya anukkamena saṅkhārā tattha antimakoṭṭhāsataṃ pāpitā, tato paraṃ nirodho eva, na saṅkhārappavattīti. Tena vuccati “saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattī”ti.

“Having transcended, he goes”: not esteeming the livelihood of those craftsmen even as much as a blade of grass, he just passes them by. “He” means the yogi. “That” means the third immaterial attainment. “In the way previously stated” means attending to it as peaceful in the way stated with the words, “Oh, how peaceful is this attainment!” and so on. “That”: the construction is that he attains that perception by which one is called ‘one with neither perception nor non-perception’ and is said to ‘develop the attainment of residual formations.’ For the teaching is headed by perception. “Extremely subtle” means the state of subtlety that has reached the peak. “The attainment of residual formations” means the attainment that is the mere remainder-state of formations due to their extreme subtlety. Hence he says: “formations that have reached the state of ultimate subtlety.” “Ultimate” means having gone beyond the end. The meaning is: formations that have reached such a peak of subtlety than which there is nothing subtler. For beginning from the access to the first jhāna, by the development proceeding gradually like a carpenter's adze, the formations are brought to their final portion there. Beyond that there is only cessation, not the proceeding of formations. Therefore it is called “the attainment of residual formations.”

287. Yaṃ taṃ catukkhandhaṃ. Atthatoti kusalādivisesavisiṭṭhaparamatthato. Visesato adhipaññāsikkhāya adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ idhādhippetanti āha “idha samāpannassa cittacetasikā dhammā adhippetā”ti. Oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvatoti yadipi catutthāruppavipākasaññāya catutthāruppakusalasaññā oḷārikā, tathā vipassanāmaggaphalasaññāhi, tathāpi oḷārikasukhumatā nāma upādāyupādāya gahetabbāti pañcavokārabhavapariyāpannāya viya catuvokārepi heṭṭhā tīsu bhūmīsu saññāya viya oḷārikāya abhāvato. Sukhumāyāti saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattiyā sukhumāya saññāya bhāvato vijjamānattā. Nevasaññāti ettha [M 1.0406] na-kāro abhāvattho, nāsaññanti ettha na-kāro aññattho, a-kāro abhāvatthova, asaññaṃ anasaññañcāti attho. Pariyāpannattāti ekadesabhāvena antogadhattā. Etthāti catutthāruppe. Dutiye atthavikappe nevasaññāti ettha na-kāro aññattho. Tathā nāsaññāti ettha na-kāro, a-kāro ca aññattho evāti tena dvayena saññābhāvo eva dassitoti dhammāyatanapariyāpannatāya [V 1.0382] āyatanabhāvo vuttovāti “adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhenā”ti vuttaṃ nissayapaccayabhāvato.

287. “That which is the four aggregates.” “In reality”: from the point of view of ultimate reality distinguished by special qualities such as the wholesome. He says that what is intended here is especially that which has become the basis for the training in higher wisdom: “Here, the mind and mental factors of one who has attained are intended.” “Because of the absence of coarse perception”: although the wholesome perception of the fourth immaterial attainment is coarse in relation to the resultant perception of the fourth immaterial attainment, and likewise in relation to the perceptions of insight, path, and fruition, nevertheless, coarseness and subtlety are to be understood relatively. It is because of the absence of a perception that is coarse like the perception included in the five-constituent existence, or like the perception in the three lower planes within the four-constituent existence. “Because of the subtle”: because of the existence of a subtle perception that has reached the subtle state of residual formations. In “neither-perception” (nevasaññā), the particle ‘na’ has the meaning of absence. In “nor-non-perception” (nāsaññā), ‘na’ has the meaning of otherness, while ‘a’ has the meaning of absence; the meaning is ‘without perception and not without perception.’ “Included” means being included as a part. “Here” means in the fourth immaterial attainment. In the second alternative meaning, in “neither-perception,” ‘na’ has the meaning of otherness. Similarly, in “nor-non-perception,” both ‘na’ and ‘a’ have the meaning of otherness. Thus by these two the very state of being perception is shown. Its nature as a base is stated because of its inclusion in the mind-object base. It is said “in the sense of foundation” because of its being a support condition.

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ, yenettha saññāva edisī jātāti anuyogaṃ sandhāyāha “na kevala”ntiādi. Saññāsīsenāyaṃ desanā katā “nānattakāyā nānattasaññino”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.341, 359; a. ni. 9.24) viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ esa atthoti kañci visesaṃ upādāya sabhāvato atthīti vattabbasseva dhammassa kañci visesaṃ upādāya natthīti vattabbatāsaṅkhāto attho.

Referring to the question, “But what is the reason why such a perception has arisen here?” he says, “Not only…” and so on. It should be seen that this teaching is given with perception as the heading, as in such passages as “beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions.” Thus this is the meaning: with respect to a certain distinction, it can be said of a phenomenon that it exists by its intrinsic nature; but with respect to another distinction, it can be said of that same phenomenon that it does not exist. This is the designated meaning.

Atithokampi yaṃ telamatthi bhanteti āha akappiyabhāvaṃ upādāya, tadeva natthi, bhante, telanti āha nāḷipūraṇaṃ upādāya. Tenāha “tattha yathā”tiādi.

With reference to its unsuitability, one says, “There is oil, venerable sir,” of what is just a very little. With reference to filling a measure, one says of that very same thing, “There is no oil, venerable sir.” Therefore he said, “Therein, just as…” and so on.

Yadi ārammaṇasañjānanaṃ saññākiccaṃ, taṃ saññā samānā kathamayaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti āha “dahanakiccamivā”tiādi. Saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattiyā eva hesā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, tato eva ca ñāṇassa sugayhāpi na hoti. Tenāha “nibbidājananampi kātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. Akatābhinivesoti akatavipassanābhiniveso appavattitasammasanacāro. Pakativipassakoti pakatiyā vipassako. Khandhādimukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisitvā dvārālambanehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattadhammānaṃ vipassako sakkuṇeyya tabbisayaudayabbayañāṇaṃ uppādetuṃ, yathā pana sakkoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “sopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kalāpasammasanavasenevāti catutthāruppacittuppādapariyāpanne phassādidhamme avinibbhujja ekato gahetvā kalāpato samūhato sammasanavasena nayavipassanāsaṅkhātakalāpasammasanavasena. Phassādidhamme vinibbhujjitvā visuṃ visuṃ sarūpato gahetvā aniccādivasena sammasanaṃ anupadadhammavipassanā[M 1.0407]. Evaṃ sukhumattaṃ gatā yathā dhammasenāpatināpi nāma anupadaṃ na vipassaneyyāti attho.

If the function of perception is to perceive an object, how is it that this perception, being a perception, cannot perform it? To this it is said: “like the function of burning,” etc. It is because it has reached a state of subtlety as residual formations that it cannot perform the function of keen perception, and for that very reason it is not easily graspable by knowledge. Therefore it is said: “It cannot even generate disenchantment.” “One who has not undertaken the application” means one who has not undertaken the application to insight, whose practice of comprehension has not been set in motion. “A natural insight meditator” means one who is an insight meditator by nature. An insight meditator who, having undertaken insight by way of the aggregates, etc., contemplates the phenomena occurring at the doors together with their door-objects, would be able to generate knowledge of arising and passing away with that attainment as its object. To show how he is able, it is said: “even he,” etc. “By way of comprehending in groups” means by way of the insight of method called ‘comprehension of groups,’ which is to comprehend as a group, as a collection, by taking together without distinguishing them the phenomena of contact, etc., included in the mind-moment of the fourth immaterial attainment. Insight into phenomena one by one is the comprehension of the phenomena of contact, etc., as impermanent, etc., after having distinguished them and taken them up individually according to their own nature. The meaning is that they have become so subtle that even the General of the Dhamma, so to speak, could not practice insight into them one by one.

Therassāti aññatarassa therassa. Aññāhipīti ettha ayamaparā upamā – eko kira brāhmaṇo aññataraṃ purisaṃ manuññaṃ mattikabhājanaṃ gahetvā ṭhitaṃ disvā yāci “dehi me imaṃ bhājana”nti. So surāsittataṃ sandhāya “nāyyo sakkā dātuṃ, surā ettha atthī”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo [V 1.0383] attano samīpe ṭhitaṃ purisaṃ uddissa āha “tena hi imassa pātuṃ dehī”ti. Itaro “natthayyo”ti āha. Tattha yathā brāhmaṇassa ayogyabhāvaṃ upādāya “atthī”tipi vattabbaṃ, pātabbatāya tattha abhāvato “natthī”tipi vattabbaṃ jātaṃ, evaṃ idhāpīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Of the elder’ means of a certain elder. ‘By others too’: Here there is another simile. It is said that a certain brahmin, seeing a man standing holding a pleasing earthen vessel, begged him: ‘Give me this vessel.’ Referring to the fact that it was filled with liquor, the man said: ‘Sir, it cannot be given; there is liquor in it.’ The brahmin, addressing a man standing near him, said: ‘Well then, give it to this man to drink.’ The other replied: ‘There is none, sir.’ Just as in that case, with reference to the brahmin's unsuitability it had to be said ‘there is,’ and because there was nothing suitable for drinking in it, it had to be said ‘there is not,’ so too should it be seen here.

Kasmā panettha yathā heṭṭhā “ananto ākāso, anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ, natthi kiñcī”ti tattha tattha bhāvanākāro gahito, evaṃ koci bhāvanākāro na gahitoti? Keci tāva āhu – “bhāvanākāro nāma sopacārassa jhānassa yathāsakaṃ ārammaṇe pavattiākāro, ārammaṇañcettha ākiñcaññāyatanadhammā. Te pana gayhamānā ekassa vā pubbaṅgamadhammassa vasena gahetabbā siyuṃ, sabbe eva vā. Tattha paṭhamapakkhe viññāṇassa gahaṇaṃ āpannanti ‘viññāṇaṃ viññāṇa’nti manasikāre catutthāruppassa viññāṇañcāyatanabhāvo āpajjati. Dutiyapakkhe pana sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanadhammārammaṇatāya jhānassa ‘ākiñcaññaṃ ākiñcañña’nti manasikāre ākiñcaññāyatanatā vā siyā, abhāvārammaṇatā vā. Sabbathā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabhāvo na labbhatī”ti. Tadidamakāraṇaṃ tathā jhānassa appavattanato. Na hi catutthāruppabhāvanā viññāṇamākiñcaññaṃ vā āmasantī pavattati, kiñcarahi? Tatiyāruppassa santataṃ.

Why is it that here no mode of development is taken up, in the way that below, for each respective case, a mode of development was taken up, namely, ‘space is infinite,’ ‘consciousness is infinite,’ ‘there is nothing’? Some say: ‘The mode of development is the mode of occurrence of the jhāna with access in its respective object. And here the object is the phenomena of the base of nothingness. When these are being grasped, they might be grasped by way of a single preliminary phenomenon, or all of them. In the first alternative, the grasping of consciousness is entailed; thus, by attending ‘consciousness, consciousness,’ the fourth formless attainment would become the base of infinite consciousness. In the second alternative, since the jhāna has the phenomena of the base of nothingness as its object in their entirety, by attending ‘nothingness, nothingness,’ it might become the base of nothingness or have non-existence as its object. In no way is the state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception obtained.’ This is not the reason, because the jhāna does not occur in that way. For the development of the fourth formless attainment does not proceed by touching upon consciousness or nothingness. What then? It is the peacefulness of the third formless attainment.

Yadi evaṃ, kasmā pāḷiyaṃ “santa”nti na gahitanti? Kiñcāpi na gahitataṃ sutte (dī. ni. 2.129; saṃ. ni. 2.152), vibhaṅge (vibha. 606 ādayo) pana gahitameva. Yathāha – “taññeva ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasi karoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāvetī”ti (vibha. 619). Atha kasmā vibhaṅge viya sutte bhāvanākāro na gahitoti? Veneyyajjhāsayato, desanāvilāsato ca. Ye hi veneyyā yathā heṭṭhā tīsu [M 1.0408] āruppesu “ananto ākāso, anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ, natthi kiñcī”ti bhāvanākāro gahito, evaṃ aggahite eva tasmiṃ tamatthaṃ paṭivijjhanti, tesaṃ vasena sutte tathā desanā katā, suttantagatikāva abhidhamme suttantabhājanīye (vibha. 605 ādayo) uddesadesanā. Ye pana veneyyā vibhajitvā vutteyeva tasmiṃ tamatthaṃ paṭivijjhanti, tesaṃ vasena vibhaṅge bhāvanākāro vutto. Dhammissaro pana bhagavā sammāsambuddho dhammānaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ jānanto katthaci bhāvanākāraṃ gaṇhāti, katthaci bhāvanākāraṃ na gaṇhāti. Sā ca desanā yāvadeva veneyyavinayatthāti ayamettha desanāvilāso. Suttantadesanā vā pariyāyakathāti tattha bhāvanākāro [V 1.0384] na gahito, abhidhammadesanā pana nippariyāyakathāti tattha bhāvanākāro gahitoti evampettha bhāvanākārassa gahaṇe, aggahaṇe ca kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

If so, why is ‘peaceful’ not taken up in the Pāḷi? Although it is not taken up in the Suttas, it is indeed taken up in the Vibhaṅga. As it is said: ‘He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful and develops the attainment that has residual formations.’ Then why is the mode of development not taken up in the Suttas as it is in the Vibhaṅga? Because of the disposition of the disciples and the grace of the teaching. For those disciples who penetrate the meaning even when it is not taken up—just as the mode of development was taken up in the three lower formless attainments as ‘space is infinite,’ ‘consciousness is infinite,’ ‘there is nothing’—for their sake the teaching was given thus in the Suttas; and the exposition by way of summary in the Suttantabhājanīya of the Abhidhamma follows the Sutta method. But for those disciples who penetrate the meaning only when it is stated analytically, for their sake the mode of development is stated in the Vibhaṅga. The Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, knowing the way the teachings should be expounded, sometimes takes up the mode of development and sometimes does not. And that teaching is solely for the purpose of training the disciples; this is the grace of the teaching here. Or, the Sutta teaching is a discourse with an indirect meaning, so the mode of development is not taken up there; but the Abhidhamma teaching is a discourse with a direct meaning, so the mode of development is taken up there. Thus the reason for the taking up and not taking up of the mode of development should be understood here.

Apare pana bhaṇanti – “catutthāruppe visesadassanatthaṃ sutte bhāvanākārassa aggahaṇaṃ, svāyaṃ viseso anupubbabhāvanājanito. Sā ca anupubbabhāvanā pahānakkamopajanitā pahātabbasamatikkamena jhānānaṃ adhigantabbato. Tathā hi kāmādivivekavitakkavicāravūpasamapītivirāgasomanassatthaṅgamamukhena rūpāvacarajjhānāni desitāni, rūpasaññādisamatikkamamukhena arūpajjhānāni. Na kevalañca jhānāniyeva, atha kho sabbampi sīlaṃ, sabbāpi paññā paṭipakkhadhammappahānavaseneva sampādetabbato pahātabbadhammasamatikkamadassanamukheneva desanā āruḷhā. Tathā hi “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.8, 194) sīlasaṃvaro, “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.213; ma. ni. 1.411, 421; 3.15, 75) indriyasaṃvaro, “neva davāya na madāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23, 422; 2.24; 3.75; saṃ. ni. 2.63; a. ni. 6.58; mahāni. 206; vibha. 518) bhojane mattaññutā, “idha bhikkhu micchājīvaṃ pahāya sammāājīvena jīvikaṃ kappetī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.8) ājīvapārisuddhi, “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.217; ma. ni. 1.412, 425; 3.16, 75) jāgariyānuyogo, “aniccasaññā bhāvetabbā asmimānasamugghātāya, aniccasaññino, meghiya, anattasaññā [M 1.0409] saṇṭhāti, anattasaññī asmimānasamugghātaṃ gacchati, āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī”tiādinā paññā paṭipakkhadhammappahānavaseneva desitā. Tasmā jhānāni desento bhagavā “vivicceva kāmehī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123) pahātabbadhammasamatikkamadassanamukheneva desesi. Tena vuttaṃ “kāmādivivekavitakkavicāravūpasamapītivirāgasomanassatthaṅgamamukhena rūpāvacarajjhānāni desitāni, rūpasaññādisamatikkamamukhena arūpajjhānānī”ti. Tattha yathā rūpāvacaraṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ bhāvanāvisesādhigatehi vitakkādīhi viya saddhādīhipi tikkhavisadasūrasabhāvehi dhammehi samannāgatattā kāmacchandādīnaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ, tadekaṭṭhānañca pāpadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanato uttarimanussadhammabhāvappattaṃ [V 1.0385] kāmāvacaradhammehi saṇhasukhumaṃ, santaṃ, paṇītañca hoti; dutiyajjhānādīni pana bhāvanāvisesena oḷārikaṅgappahānato tato sātisayaṃ saṇhasukhumasaṇhasukhumatarādibhāvappattāni honti. Tathā arūpāvacaraṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ rūpavirāgabhāvanābhāvena pavattamānaṃ ārammaṇasantatāyapi aṅgasantatāyapi pākatikaparittadhammehi viya sabbarūpāvacaradhammehi santasukhumabhāvappattaṃ hoti. Ārammaṇasantabhāvenāpi hi tadārammaṇadhammā santasabhāvā honti, seyyathāpi lokuttaradhammārammaṇā dhammā.

But other teachers say: 'The non-mention of the mode of development in the Sutta concerning the fourth formless jhāna is for the purpose of showing a distinction. This distinction is generated by gradual development. And that gradual development is generated by the sequence of abandoning, since the jhānas are to be attained by transcending what is to be abandoned. For indeed, the form-sphere jhānas are taught by way of seclusion from sensual pleasures, the stilling of thought and examination, dispassion for rapture, and the disappearance of joy; and the formless jhānas are taught by way of transcending perceptions of form, etc. And not only the jhānas, but since all virtue and all wisdom are to be perfected solely by the power of abandoning opposing states, the teaching is presented solely by way of showing the transcending of states to be abandoned. Thus, moral restraint is taught with such phrases as: 'Having abandoned the destruction of life, he abstains from the destruction of life'; restraint of the sense faculties with such phrases as: 'Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features'; moderation in eating with such phrases as: 'not for amusement, not for intoxication'; purity of livelihood with such phrases as: 'Here, a bhikkhu, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood'; the practice of wakefulness with such phrases as: 'Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind devoid of covetousness'; and wisdom is taught by way of abandoning opposing states with such phrases as: 'The perception of impermanence should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit “I am.” For one with the perception of impermanence, O Meghiya, the perception of not-self is established. One with the perception of not-self attains the uprooting of the conceit “I am,” and through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.' Therefore, when teaching the jhānas, the Blessed One taught solely by way of showing the transcending of states to be abandoned, with such phrases as: 'Secluded from sensual pleasures…' Hence it was said: 'the form-sphere jhānas are taught by way of seclusion from sensual pleasures… and the formless jhānas are taught by way of transcending perceptions of form, etc.' Herein, just as the first form-sphere jhāna—being endowed with states such as faith, etc., that have become sharp, clear, and vigorous, like thought and examination, which are attained through a distinction in development, and because it suppresses the hindrances of sensual desire, etc., and the unwholesome states that share their foundation—has attained the state of a superhuman phenomenon and is subtle, peaceful, and sublime in comparison with sense-sphere states; and the second jhāna and the others, because of the abandoning of the grosser factors through a distinction in development, attain states that are successively more subtle and sublime than that. Similarly, the first formless jhāna, occurring through the development of dispassion towards form, attains a state of peacefulness and subtlety in comparison with all form-sphere states—just as it does in comparison with ordinary sense-sphere states—due to both the peacefulness of its object and the peacefulness of its factors. For by the peaceful nature of the object, the states that have that as their object also have a peaceful nature, just as the states that have the supramundane as their object.

Satipi dhammato, mahaggatabhāvenāpi ca abhede rūpāvacaracatutthato āruppaṃ aṅgatopi santameva, yatassa santavimokkhatā vuttā. Dutiyāruppādīni pana paṭhamāruppādito aṅgato, ārammaṇato ca santasantatarasantatamabhāvappattāni tathā bhāvanāvisesasamāyogato, svāyaṃ bhāvanāviseso paṭhamajjhānūpacārato paṭṭhāya taṃtaṃpahātabbasamatikkamanavasena tassa tassa jhānassa santasukhumabhāvaṃ āpādento catutthāruppe saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvaṃ pāpeti. Yato catutthāruppaṃ yathā anupadadhammavipassanāvasena vipassanāya ārammaṇabhāvaṃ upagantvā pakativipassakassāpi nibbiduppattiyā paccayo na hoti saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattito, tathā sayaṃ tatiyāruppadhammesu pavattamānaṃ te yāthāvato vibhāvetuṃ na sakkoti, yathā tadaññajjhānāni attano ārammaṇaṃ. Kevalaṃ pana ārabbha pavattimattamevassa tattha hoti[M 1.0410], tayidaṃ ārammaṇabhāvenāpi nāma vibhūtākāratāya ṭhātuṃ appahontaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇe kiṃ pahoti. Tasmā tadassa avibhūtakiccataṃ disvā satthā heṭṭhā tīsu ṭhānesu bhāvanākāraṃ vatvā tādiso idha na labbhatīti dīpetuṃ catutthāruppadesanāyaṃ sutte bhāvanākāraṃ pariyāyadesanattā na kathesi.

Although there is no difference from the fourth form-sphere jhāna by way of associated states and by way of being exalted, the formless jhāna is indeed peaceful also in terms of its factors, for which reason its state as 'peaceful liberation' is stated. But the second formless jhāna and the others, in terms of their factors and object, attain states of being peaceful, more peaceful, and most peaceful in comparison with the first formless jhāna and the others, because of their conjunction with such a distinction in development. This distinction in development, starting from the access concentration of the first jhāna, while bringing about the peaceful and subtle state of each respective jhāna by the power of transcending each respective thing to be abandoned, leads to the subtle state of the mere remainder of formations in the fourth formless jhāna. Since the fourth formless jhāna, just as having approached the state of being an object for insight by way of insight into successive phenomena, does not become a condition for the arising of disenchantment even for a practitioner of ordinary insight, due to its having attained the subtle state of the mere remainder of formations; similarly, it, while occurring with the states of the third formless jhāna as its object, is not able to make them clearly known as they really are, as other jhānas are able to do with their own object. But for it, there is only a mere occurrence with respect to them. This jhāna, being unable to stand in a distinct manner even as an object, what is it capable of in making something an object? Therefore, seeing this indistinct function of it, the Teacher, having spoken of the mode of development in the three lower instances, did not state the mode of development in the Sutta when teaching the fourth formless jhāna, in order to show that such a mode is not obtained here, because it is an indirect teaching.

Yasmā pana sārammaṇassa dhammassa ārammaṇe pavattiākāro atthevāti atisukhumabhāvappattaṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “taṃyeva ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasi karotī”ti (vibha. 619) vibhaṅge vuttaṃ yathādhammasāsanabhāvato, pubbabhāgavasena vā vibhaṅge “santato manasi karotī”ti vuttaṃ tadā yogino tassa vibhūtabhāvato. Appanāvasena pana sutte bhāvanākāro na gahito avibhūtabhāvato. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ hi kiñci ādito avibhūtaṃ hoti, yathā taṃ? Buddhānussatiādi. Kiñci majjhe, yathā taṃ? Ānāpānassati. Kiñci ubhayattha, yathā taṃ? Upasamānussatiādi. Catutthāruppakammaṭṭhānaṃ pana pariyosāne avibhūtaṃ bhāvanāya matthakappattiyaṃ [V 1.0386] ārammaṇassa avibhūtabhāvato. Tasmā catutthāruppe imaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ satthārā sutte bhāvanākāro na gahito, na sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvatoti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Furthermore, because the mode of occurrence of a phenomenon with an object in its object indeed exists, to show that mode, which has reached a state of extreme subtlety, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful” (Vibh 619). This is stated in the Vibhaṅga because it is in accordance with the teaching of the Dhamma, or it is stated in the Vibhaṅga by way of the preliminary part, “he attends to it as peaceful,” because at that time it is manifest to the yogi. However, in the Sutta, the mode of development is not taken up by way of absorption because it is not manifest. For some meditation subjects are not manifest at the beginning, such as the recollection of the Buddha, etc. Some are not manifest in the middle, such as mindfulness of breathing. Some are not manifest in both places, such as the recollection of peace, etc. But the fourth formless meditation subject is not manifest at the end, when the development has reached its peak, because the object is not manifest. Therefore, to show this distinction in the fourth formless attainment, the mode of development was not taken up by the Teacher in the Sutta—not because it is entirely absent. This is the conclusion to be reached here.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on Miscellaneous Topics

288. Asadisarūpoti dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāketumālādīhi rūpaguṇehi aññehi asādhāraṇarūpakāyo, sabhāvattho vā rūpa-saddo “yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; vibha. 203) viya. Tasmā asadisarūpoti asadisasabhāvo, tena dasabalacatuvesārajjādiguṇavisesasamāyogadīpanato satthu dhammakāyasampattiyāpi asadisatā dassitā hoti. Itīti evaṃ vuttappakārena. Tasminti āruppe. Pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyāti pubbe viya asādhāraṇaṃ tattha tattha jhāne patiniyatameva atthaṃ aggahetvā sādhāraṇabhāvato tattha tattheva pakiṇṇakaṃ visaṭaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā pavattā pakiṇṇakakathāpi vijānitabbā.

‘Of incomparable form’ (asadisarūpo) means having a physical form that is not shared with other individuals, by means of the qualities of form such as the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, the crowning radiance, and so on. Or, the word ‘form’ (rūpa) has the meaning of ‘nature,’ as in such passages as, “whatever in the world is of a pleasing nature, of an agreeable nature” (Dī. Ni. 2.400; Ma. Ni. 1.133; Vibh. 203). Therefore, ‘of incomparable form’ means ‘of incomparable nature.’ Through that, because it shows the connection with special qualities such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, etc., the incomparability of the Teacher's accomplishment of the Dhamma-body is also shown. ‘Thus’ (iti) means in the manner thus stated. ‘In that’ (tasmiṃ) refers to the formless attainment. ‘The miscellaneous discussion should also be understood’ means that the miscellaneous discussion—which proceeds by taking the scattered and diffused meaning in each respective jhāna due to its common nature, not grasping the uncommon, specifically fixed meaning in each respective jhāna as before—should also be known.

289. Rūpanimittātikkamatoti [M 1.0411] kasiṇarūpasaṅkhātassa paṭibhāganimittassa atikkamanato. Ākāsātikkamatoti kasiṇugghāṭimākāsassa atikkamanato. Ākāse pavattitaviññāṇātikkamatoti paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa atikkamanato, na dutiyāruppaviññāṇātikkamanato. Tadatikkamato hi tasseva vibhāvanaṃ hoti. Dutiyāruppaviññāṇavibhāvane hi tadeva atikkantaṃ siyā, na tassa ārammaṇaṃ, na ca ārammaṇe dosaṃ disvā anārammaṇassa vibhāvanātikkamo yujjati. Pāḷiyañca “viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ sato samāpajjati…pe… sato vuṭṭhahitvā taṃyeva viññāṇaṃ abhāvetī”ti vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “taṃyeva viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ abhāvetī”ti, “taṃyeva abhāvetī”ti vā. “Anantaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajjā”ti ettha pana dvayaṃ vuttaṃ ārammaṇañca viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanañca. Tasmiṃ dvaye yena kenaci, yato vā vuṭṭhito, teneva padhānaniddiṭṭhena taṃ-saddassa sambandhe āpanne “ayañca ārammaṇātikkamabhāvanā”ti viññāṇañcāyatanassa nivattanatthaṃ viññāṇavacanaṃ. Tasmā paṭhamāruppaviññāṇasseva abhāvanātikkamo vutto.

288. ‘By transcending the form-sign’ (rūpanimittātikkamato) means by transcending the counterpart sign, which is designated as the kasiṇa-form. ‘By transcending space’ (ākāsātikkamato) means by transcending the space that is the remover of the kasiṇa. ‘By transcending the consciousness that has occurred in space’ (ākāse pavattitaviññāṇātikkamato) means by transcending the first formless consciousness, not by transcending the second formless consciousness. For by transcending that, there is the disappearance of that very thing. Indeed, in the case of the disappearance of the second formless consciousness, that very second consciousness would be transcended, not its object. Moreover, it is not fitting to transcend by causing the disappearance of the subjective consciousness after seeing a fault in the object. And in the Pāḷi it is said, ‘…having arisen mindfully, one causes that very consciousness to cease’ (taṃyeva viññāṇaṃ abhāvetīti); it is not said, ‘one causes that very base of infinite consciousness to cease’ (taṃyeva viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ abhāvetīti), nor ‘one causes that very thing to cease’ (taṃyeva abhāvetīti). However, in the passage, ‘He attains the base of infinite consciousness, (perceiving) “Consciousness is infinite”’ (anantaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajjā), two things are mentioned: the object, which is consciousness, and the base of infinite consciousness. In those two, although the word ‘that’ (taṃ) could be connected with either one, when it is connected with that very one from which one has arisen—which is the primary referent—the word ‘consciousness’ (viññāṇa) is used for the purpose of turning away from the base of infinite consciousness, with the understanding that ‘this is the development of transcending the object.’ Therefore, it is the transcendence by causing to cease of the first formless consciousness alone that is spoken of.

290. Evaṃ [V 1.0387] santepīti aṅgātikkame asatipi. Suppaṇītatarāti suṭṭhu paṇītatarā, sundarā paṇītatarā cāti vā attho. Satipi catunnaṃ pāsādatalānaṃ, sāṭikānañca tabbhāvato, pamāṇato ca samabhāve uparūpari pana kāmaguṇānaṃ, sukhasamphassādīnañca visesena paṇītatarādibhāvo viya etāsaṃ catunnaṃ samāpattīnaṃ āruppabhāvato, aṅgato ca satipi samabhāve bhāvanāvisesasiddho pana sātisayo uparūpari paṇītatarādibhāvoti imamatthaṃ dasseti “yathā hī”tiādinā.

289. ‘Even so’ (evaṃ santepi) means ‘even though there is no transcending of factors.’ ‘Exceedingly exquisite’ (suppaṇītatarā) means ‘very much more exquisite,’ or the meaning is ‘more beautiful and more exquisite.’ Just as, although the four palace floors and cloths are of the same nature and equal in measure, there is, one above the other, a state of being more exquisite through the distinction of sensual pleasures, pleasant contacts, and so on, so too, with these four attainments, although there is equality on account of their formless nature and in terms of their factors, there is, however, a superior state of being more exquisite one above the other, which is accomplished through the distinction of development. This meaning is shown by the passage beginning ‘Just as…’ (yathā hi).

291. Nissitoti nissāya ṭhito. Duṭṭhitāti na sammā ṭhitā, dukkhaṃ vā ṭhitā. Tannissitanti tena nissitaṃ, ṭhānanti attho. Tannissitanti vā taṃ maṇḍapalaggaṃ purisaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ purisanti attho. Maṇḍapalaggañhi anissāya tena vinābhūte vivitte bahi okāse ṭhānaṃ viya ākāsalaggaviññāṇassa viveke tadapagame tatiyāruppassa ṭhānanti.

290. ‘Reliant’ (nissito) means ‘standing in reliance.’ ‘Badly stood’ (duṭṭhitā) means ‘not standing well,’ or ‘standing with difficulty.’ ‘Reliant on that’ (tannissitaṃ) means ‘relied upon by him’; the meaning is ‘place.’ Alternatively, ‘reliant on that’ (tannissitaṃ) means ‘the man who is standing in reliance on that man attached to the pavilion’; the meaning is ‘man.’ For just as there is a standing in a secluded, outer space, separate from him and without relying on the man attached to the pavilion, so too is the standing of the third formless attainment in the seclusion from—in the departure of—the consciousness attached to space.

292. Ārammaṇaṃ [M 1.0412] karoteva, aññābhāvena taṃ idanti “āsannaviññāṇañcāyatanapaccatthikarūpāsannākāsārammaṇaviññāṇāpagamārammaṇaṃ, no ca santa”nti ca diṭṭhādīnavampi taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ idaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanajjhānaṃ aññassa tādisassa ārammaṇabhāvayogyassa abhāvena alābhena ārammaṇaṃ karoti eva. “Sabbadisampati”nti idaṃ janassa agatikabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttinti jīvikaṃ. Vattatīti jīvati.

291. It indeed makes that its object. Due to the absence of any other, it is said: 'Its object is the disappearance of the consciousness that has space near form as its object, which is hostile to the base of infinite consciousness; and it is not peaceful.' And even having seen the danger in that base of nothingness, this jhāna of neither-perception-nor-non-perception makes it its object, due to the absence and non-attainment of any other such suitable object. The phrase ‘sabbadisampati’ is stated to show the state of beings having no place to go. ‘Vutti’ means livelihood. ‘Vattati’ means 'he lives'.

293. Āruḷhotiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yathā koci puriso anekaporisaṃ dīghanisseṇiṃ āruḷho tassa uparimapade ṭhito tassā nisseṇiyā bāhumeva olubbhati aññassa alābhato, yathā ca paṃsupabbatassa, missakapabbatassa vā aggakoṭiṃ āruḷho tassa matthakameva olubbhati, yathā ca giriṃ silāpabbataṃ āruḷho paripphandamāno aññābhāvato attano jaṇṇukameva olubbhati, tathā etaṃ catutthāruppajjhānaṃ taṃ tatiyāruppaṃ olubbhitvā pavattatīti. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ uttānameva.

293. In the texts beginning with 'āruḷho,' this is the concise meaning: Just as a certain person who has climbed a long ladder of many persons' height, standing on its highest rung, clings only to the side-rail of that ladder due to not getting anything else; and just as one who has climbed to the summit of a mountain of soil or a mountain of mixed earth and rock clings only to its peak; and just as one who has climbed a rocky mountain, trembling due to the absence of anything else, clings only to his own knee—so too does this fourth immaterial jhāna proceed by clinging to that third immaterial jhāna. Whatever herein is not distinguished in meaning is indeed obvious.

Āruppaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the immaterial attainments is concluded.

Iti dasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus ends the commentary on the tenth chapter.

11. Samādhiniddesavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Exposition of Concentration

Āhārepaṭikkūlabhāvanāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Development of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Food

294. Uddeso [M 1.0413][V 1.0388] nāma niddesattho mudumajjhimapaññābāhullato, āgato ca bhāro avassaṃ vahitabboti āha “ekā saññāti evaṃ uddiṭṭhāya āhāre paṭikkūlasaññāya bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto”ti. Tatthāyaṃ saññā-saddo “rūpasaññā saddasaññā”tiādīsu (mahāni. 14) sañjānanalakkhaṇe dhamme āgato, “aniccasaññā dukkhasaññā”tiādīsu vipassanāyaṃ āgato, “uddhumātakasaññāti vā sopākarūpasaññāti vā ime dhammā ekatthā udāhu nānatthā”tiādīsu samathe āgato. Idha pana samathassa parikamme daṭṭhabbo. Āhāre hi paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇaṃ, tappabhāvitaṃ vā upacārajjhānaṃ idha “āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā”ti adhippetaṃ. Tattha yasmiṃ āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā bhāvetabbā, tattha nibbedavirāguppādanāya tappasaṅgena sabbampi āhāraṃ kiccappabhedādīnavopammehi vibhāvetuṃ “āharatīti āhāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

294. A summary exposition (uddesa) has the purpose of a detailed exposition (niddesa) due to the abundance of persons with tender and middling wisdom; and since a burden that has come must certainly be borne, it was said: 'The detailed exposition on the development of the perception of repulsiveness in food, which was indicated thus as "one perception," has now been reached.' Therein, this term 'perception' (saññā) is found in the sense of a state characterized by perceiving, as in 'perception of form, perception of sound,' etc.; it is found in the sense of insight, as in 'perception of impermanence, perception of suffering,' etc.; and it is found in the sense of serenity, as in 'Are the perception of a bloated corpse... and the perception of a livid corpse the same or different?' etc. Here, however, it should be understood in the context of the preliminary work for serenity. For 'perception of repulsiveness in food' is intended here to mean the grasping of the aspect of repulsiveness in food, or the access concentration developed from that. Therein, regarding the food in which the perception of repulsiveness is to be developed, in order to produce disenchantment and dispassion, the section beginning with 'It brings (āharati), thus it is food (āhāro)' was undertaken to explain all food in connection with that by way of function, divisions, dangers, and similes.

Tattha āharatīti āhārapaccayasaṅkhātena uppattiyā, ṭhitiyā vā paccayabhāvena attano phalaṃ āneti nibbatteti pavatteti cāti attho. Kabaḷaṃ karīyatīti kabaḷīkāro, vatthuvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, lakkhaṇato pana ojālakkhaṇo veditabbo, kabaḷīkāro ca so yathāvuttenatthena āhāro cāti kabaḷīkārāhāro. Esa nayo sesesupi. Phusatīti phasso. Ayaṃ hi arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇe phusanākāreneva pavattati. Tathā hi so phusanalakkhaṇoti vuccati. Cetayatīti cetanā, attano sampayuttadhammehi saddhiṃ ārammaṇe abhisandahatīti attho, manosannissitā cetanā manosañcetanā. Upapattiparikappanavasena vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Evamettha sāmaññatthato, visesatthato ca āhārā veditabbā. Kasmā panete cattārova vuttā, aññe dhammā kiṃ attano phalassa paccayā na hontīti? No na honti, ime pana tathā [V 1.0389] ca honti [M 1.0414] aññathā cāti samānepi paccayabhāve atirekapaccayā honti, tasmā āhārāti vuccanti.

Herein, 'it brings' (āharati) means that by way of the food condition, as a condition for arising or for subsistence, it brings, generates, and maintains its own fruit—this is the meaning. It is called 'morsel-made' (kabaḷīkāra) because a morsel (kabaḷa) is made (karīyati); this is said in terms of the physical basis, but in terms of characteristic, it should be understood as having the characteristic of nutritive essence. And it is that which is made into a morsel and it is food (āhāra) in the aforesaid sense; thus it is 'morsel-made food' (kabaḷīkārāhāra). This same method applies to the others as well. It is called 'contact' (phassa) because it contacts (phusati). For this, though an immaterial state, occurs only in the mode of contacting an object. Indeed, it is said to have the characteristic of contact. It is called 'volition' (cetanā) because it wills (cetayati); the meaning is that it directs its associated states towards the object. Volition associated with the mind is 'mental volition' (manosañcetanā). It is called 'consciousness' (viññāṇa) because it cognizes (vijānāti) by way of origination and conceiving. Thus, these foods should be understood here in both a general and a specific sense. But why are only these four mentioned? Do other states not act as conditions for their own fruit? It is not that they do not, but these are so in that way and also in another way. Therefore, even when the nature of being a condition is the same, they are pre-eminent conditions, and thus they are called 'foods'.

Kathaṃ? Etesu hi paṭhamo sayaṃ yasmiṃ kalāpe tappariyāpannānaṃ yathārahaṃ paccayo hontova ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ āharati, dutiyo tisso vedanā āharati, tatiyo tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhiṃ āharati, catuttho paṭisandhikkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ āharati. Tenāha “kabaḷīkārāhāro”tiādi. Ettha ca kammajādibhedabhinnā ojā sati paccayalābhe dve tisso paveṇiyo ghaṭentī ojaṭṭhamakarūpaṃ āharati, sukhavedanīyādibhedabhinno phassāhāro yathārahaṃ tisso vedanā āharati, puññābhisaṅkhārādibhedabhinno manosañcetanāhāro kāmabhavādīsu tīsu bhavesu yathārahaṃ saviññāṇaṃ, aviññāṇañca paṭisandhiṃ āharati, viññāṇāhāro yathāpaccayaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe nāmaṃ rūpaṃ, nāmarūpañca āharatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā upatthambhakaṭṭhena ime eva dhammā āhārāti vuttā. Yathā hi kabaḷīkārāhāro rūpakāyassa upatthambhakaṭṭhena paccayo, evaṃ arūpino āhārā sampayuttadhammānaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “kabaḷīkāro āhāro imassa kāyassa āhārapaccayena paccayo, arūpino āhārā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ āhārapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.15). Aparo nayo – ajjhattikasantatiyā visesapaccayattā kabaḷīkārāhāro, phassādayo ca tayo dhammā āhārāti vuttā. Visesapaccayo hi kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ sattānaṃ rūpakāyassa kabaḷīkārāhāro, nāmakāye vedanāya phasso, viññāṇassa manosañcetanā, nāmarūpassa viññāṇaṃ. Yathāha “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko, āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati, anāhāro no tiṭṭhati (saṃ. ni. 5.183). Tathā phassapaccayā vedanā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti (udā. 1; mahāva. 1; netti. 24).

How? Among these, the first, while itself being a condition as appropriate for the states included within whatever material group it is in, brings forth material form having nutritive essence as its eighth factor. The second brings forth the three feelings. The third brings forth rebirth-linking in the three existences. The fourth brings forth name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking. Therefore, it was said, 'Edible food,' and so on. Herein, nutritive essence, which is of various kinds such as kamma-originated, etc., upon obtaining its conditions, connects two or three lineages and brings forth material form having nutritive essence as its eighth factor. The food of contact, which is of various kinds such as that accompanied by pleasant feeling, etc., brings forth the three feelings as appropriate. The food of mental volition, which is of various kinds such as meritorious formations, etc., brings forth rebirth-linking with consciousness and without consciousness in the three existences, such as the sense-sphere existence, as appropriate. The food of consciousness, according to conditions, brings forth name, form, and name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking; thus it should be understood. Alternatively, these very states are called 'foods' because of their meaning of supporting. For just as edible food is a condition for the material body by way of supporting it, so the immaterial foods are for their associated states. For thus it is said: 'Edible food is a condition for this body by way of the food condition. The immaterial foods are a condition for their associated states and for the material form originated from them by way of the food condition.' Another method: Edible food and the three states beginning with contact are called 'foods' because of being a special condition for the internal continuity. For edible food is a special condition for the material body of beings who consume edible food; in the mental body, contact is for feeling, mental volition is for consciousness, and consciousness is for name-and-form. As it was said: 'Just as, monks, this body is sustained by food, depends on food to persist, and without food does not persist, so too feeling arises with contact as its condition, consciousness arises with formations as its condition, and name-and-form arises with consciousness as its condition.'

Kabaḷīkārāhāreti kabaḷīkāre āhāre nikanti taṇhā, taṃ bhayaṃ anatthāvahato. Gadhitassa hi āhāraparibhogo anatthāya hoti. Hetuatthe bhummaṃ. Evaṃ sesesu. Nikantīti nikāmanā chandarāgo[M 1.0415]. Bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, nikanti eva bhayaṃ nikantibhayaṃ. Kabaḷīkārāhārahetu imesaṃ sattānaṃ chandarāgo bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ diṭṭhadhammikādibhedassa anatthassa sakalassāpi vaṭṭadukkhassa hetubhāvato. Tenevāha “kabaḷīkāre ce, bhikkhave, āhāre atthi rāgo, atthi nandī, atthi taṇhā, patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ viruḷha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.64; kathā. 296; mahāni. 7). Upagamanaṃ [V 1.0390] appahīnavipallāsassa ārammaṇena samodhānaṃ saṅgati sukhavedanīyādiphassuppatti bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ tīhi dukkhatāhi aparimuccanato. Tenāha “sukhavedanīyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā (saṃ. ni. 4.129), tassa vedanāpaccayā taṇhā…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti (udā. 1). Tattha tattha bhave upapajjati etenāti upapatti, upapajjanaṃ vā upapatti, khipanaṃ bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ upapattimūlakehi byasanehi aparimuttato. Tenāha “avidvā, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo puññañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, puññupagaṃ bhavati viññāṇaṃ. Apuññañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, apuññupagaṃ bhavati viññāṇa”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.51). Paṭisandhīti bhavantarādīhi paṭisandhānaṃ, taṃ bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ paṭisandhinimittehi dukkhehi avimuccanato. Tenāha “viññāṇe ce, bhikkhave, āhāre atthi rāgo, atthi nandī, atthi taṇhā, patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ viruḷha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.64).

Regarding physical food: in physical food, 'delight' (nikanti) is craving (taṇhā). That craving is a 'danger' (bhaya) because it brings what is unbeneficial. Indeed, for one who is attached, the consumption of food is for what is unbeneficial. The locative case is used in the sense of cause. Likewise in the remaining cases. 'Delight' (nikanti) means fondness, lustful desire. One fears on account of this, thus it is 'danger' (bhaya); delight itself is a danger, hence 'the danger of delight' (nikantibhaya). Because of physical food, for these beings, lustful desire is a danger, a terror, because it is the cause of what is unbeneficial—distinguished as visible in this life, etc.—and of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths. Therefore, He said: 'If, monks, in physical food there is lust, there is delight, there is craving, consciousness is established there and grows,' and so on. Approaching—which for one with unabandoned perversions is the meeting and coming together with an object—and the arising of contact to be felt as pleasant, etc., are a danger, a terror, because of not being freed from the three kinds of suffering. Therefore, He said: 'Monks, conditioned by contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises. For that person, with feeling as condition, craving arises… the origin of this whole mass of suffering occurs.' One is reborn in various existences by means of this, thus it is 'rebirth' (upapatti); or, being reborn is rebirth. The casting down is a danger, a terror, because of not being freed from the calamities rooted in rebirth. Therefore, He said: 'Monks, if an uninstructed ordinary person generates a meritorious formation, consciousness becomes one that goes to merit. If he generates a demeritorious formation, consciousness becomes one that goes to demerit,' and so on. 'Rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) is the connecting with another existence, etc. That is a danger, a terror, because of not being freed from the sufferings caused by rebirth-linking. Therefore, He said: 'If, monks, in the nutriment of consciousness there is lust, there is delight, there is craving, consciousness is established there and grows,' and so on.

Puttamaṃsūpamena ovādena dīpetabbo nicchandarāgaparibhogāya. Evaṃ hi tattha nikantibhayaṃ na hoti. Niccammā gāvī yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ upagacchati, tattha tattheva naṃ pāṇino khādantiyeva. Evaṃ phasse sati vedanā uppajjati, vedanā ca dukkhasallādito daṭṭhabbāti phasse ādīnavaṃ passantassa upagamanabhayaṃ na hotīti āha “phassāhāro niccammagāvūpamena dīpetabbo”ti. Ekādasahi aggīhi sabbaso ādittā bhavā aṅgārakāsusadisāti passato upapattibhayaṃ na hotīti āha “manosañcetanāhāro aṅgārakāsūpamena dīpetabbo”ti. Corasadisaṃ viññāṇaṃ anatthapātato, pahārasadisī vedanā duradhivāsatoti sammadeva passato paṭisandhibhayaṃ na hotīti āha “viññāṇāhāro sattisatūpamena dīpetabbo”ti.

It should be shown by the admonition with the simile of the son's flesh, for the sake of consumption free from lustful desire. Indeed, in this way, the danger of delight does not arise in that regard. A flayed cow, whatever place it approaches, in that very place living beings devour it. Similarly, when there is contact, feeling arises, and feeling should be seen as suffering, a dart, and so on. For one who sees the danger in contact thus, the danger of approaching does not arise. Therefore, he said: 'The nutriment of contact should be shown by the simile of the flayed cow.' For one who sees that existences, being completely ablaze with the eleven fires, are like a pit of embers, the danger of rebirth does not arise. Therefore, he said: 'The nutriment of mental volition should be shown by the simile of the pit of embers.' Consciousness is like a thief because it falls into what is unbeneficial; feeling is like a blow from a spear because it is difficult to endure. For one who sees rightly thus, the danger of rebirth-linking does not arise. Therefore, he said: 'The nutriment of consciousness should be shown by the simile of the hundred spears.'

Evaṃ [M 1.0416] kiccādimukhena āhāresu ādīnavaṃ vibhāvetvā idāni tattha yathādhippetaṃ āhāraṃ niddhāretvā paṭikkūlato manasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “imesu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upādāyarūpaniddesepi “kabaḷīkāro āhāro”ti (dha. sa. 595) āgatattā tato visesento “asitapītakhāyitasāyitappabhedo”ti āha, bhūtakathanaṃ vā etaṃ. Tattha asitapītakhāyitasāyitappabhedoti asitabbapātabbakhāyitabbasāyitabbavibhāgo kālabhedavacanicchāya abhāvato yathā “duddha”nti. Kabaḷīkāro āhāro vāti avadhāraṇaṃ yathā phassāhārādinivattanaṃ, evaṃ ojāhāranivattanampi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Savatthuko eva hi āhāro idha kammaṭṭhānabhūto, tena āharīyatīti [V 1.0391] āhāroti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Āharatīti āhāroti ayaṃ panattho nibbattitaojāvasena veditabbo. Imasmiṃ attheti imasmiṃ kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte atthe. Uppannā saññāti saññāsīsena bhāvanaṃ vadati. Tathā hi vakkhati “paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇavasena panā”tiādi (visuddhi. 1.305).

Thus, having clearly shown the danger in the nutriments with function, etc., as the principal point, now, having determined the intended nutriment among them, in order to show the method of mental attention from the perspective of repulsiveness, 'But among these...' and so on was said. Also in the exposition of derived matter, because it comes as 'physical food is nutriment,' distinguishing from that, he said, 'differentiated as that which is eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored'; or, this is a statement of fact. Therein, 'differentiated as that which is eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored' means the division into what is to be eaten, to be drunk, to be chewed, and to be savored, because there is no intention to express a difference in tense, just as in 'duddhaṃ' (milked). The emphasis in 'physical food is nutriment' should be understood to exclude the nutriment of contact, etc., and likewise to exclude the nutriment of nutritive essence. Indeed, only nutriment together with its physical basis is the meditation subject here; therefore, 'it is consumed, thus it is nutriment'—this is how the meaning should be understood here. But this meaning, 'it brings, thus it is nutriment,' should be understood by way of the produced nutritive essence. 'In this matter' means in this matter designated as a meditation subject. 'Perception has arisen' speaks of the development of meditation with perception as the principal factor. For so it will be said: 'But by way of grasping the aspect of repulsiveness...' and so on.

Kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvāti kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyattidhammato, atthato ca suggahitaṃ sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ katvā. Tenāha “uggahato ekapadampi avirajjhantenā”ti. Tattha uggahatoti ācariyuggahato. Ekapadampīti ekampi padaṃ, ekakoṭṭhāsampi vā, padesamattampīti attho. Dasahākārehīti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu antimajīvikābhāvato, piṇḍapātassa alābhalābhesu paritassanagedhādisamuppattito, bhuttassa sammadajananato, kimikulasaṃvaddhanatoti evamādīhipi ākārehi āhāre paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā? Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolyaṃ, abhisāpoyaṃ, bhikkhave, lokasmiṃ ‘piṇḍolo vicarasi pattapāṇī’”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.80), “aladdhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ paritassati, laddhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ gadhito mucchito ajjhosanno anādīnavadassāvī anissaraṇapañño paribhuñjatī”ti (a. ni. 3.124), “bhutto ca āhāro kassaci kadāci maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ āvahati, ukkocakādayo, takkoṭakādayo ca dvattiṃsa dvattiṃsa kulappabhedā kimayo ca naṃ upanissāya jīvantī”ti.
