'Having learned the meditation subject' means having well learned, well attended to, and well retained the meditation subject from the perspective of the scriptural teaching and from the perspective of the meaning. Therefore, he said, 'by not deviating even one word from what was learned.' Therein, 'from what was learned' means from the method of meditation learned from the teacher. 'Even one word' means even one word, or one part, or just a small portion. Why was it said 'in ten aspects'? Should not the repulsiveness in food also be reflected upon in such aspects as: because of its being the lowest livelihood; because of the arising of longing, greed, and so on, on the non-receipt and receipt of almsfood; because of its causing drowsiness when eaten; and because of its breeding families of worms? For this was said: 'This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods, that is, the alms-round. This, monks, is a curse in the world: "You wander for alms with a bowl in your hand."' And, 'Not receiving almsfood, one longs for it; and having received almsfood, one consumes it greedily, confusedly, voraciously, not seeing the danger, without the wisdom for escape.' And, 'The food, when eaten, sometimes brings death or suffering equivalent to death to someone; and worms of thirty-two different families, such as the ukkocaka and takkoṭaka, live depending on it.'

Vuccate [M 1.0417] – antimajīvikābhāvo tāva cittasaṃkilesavisodhanatthaṃ kammaṭṭhānābhinivesato pageva manasi kātabbo “māhaṃ chavālātasadiso bhaveyya”nti. Tathā piṇḍapātassa alābhalābhesupi paritassanagedhādisamuppattinivāraṇaṃ pageva anuṭṭhātabbaṃ suparisuddhasīlassa paṭisaṅkhānavato tadabhāvato. Bhattasammado anekantiko, paribhogantogadho vā veditabbo. Kimikulasaṃvaddhanaṃ pana na saṅgahetabbaṃ, saṅgahitameva vā “dasahākārehī”ti ettha niyamassa akatattā. Iminā vā nayena itaresampettha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo yathāsambhavamettha paṭikkūlatāpaccavekkhaṇassa adhippetattā. Tathā hi gharagoḷikavaccamūsikajatukavaccādikaṃ sambhavantaṃ gahitaṃ, na ekantikanti. Tathā pariyesanādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ vattabbaṃ.

It is said: For the purpose of purifying the mind's defilements, the state of having the most inferior livelihood should be kept in mind right from the initial application to the meditation subject, with the thought, 'May I not be like one who burns corpses.' Likewise, for one of perfectly pure virtue and endowed with reflective knowledge, the prevention of the arising of craving, greed, and so on, even in the non-obtaining and obtaining of alms-food, should be undertaken right from the start, owing to the absence of those states. Intoxication from food should be understood as not being certain, or as being included within consumption. The breeding of families of worms, however, should not be included; or it is indeed included, because no fixed rule is made here in the phrase 'in ten ways.' Or, by this method, the inclusion of other aspects herein should also be seen, as the contemplation of repulsiveness is intended here as far as possible. For thus, what is included is that which may occur, such as house-lizard droppings, mouse droppings, bat droppings, and so on, but not as a certainty. Likewise, regarding searching and so on, it should be spoken of as far as possible.

Gamanatotiādīsu paccāgamanampi gamanasabhāgattā gamaneneva saṅgahitaṃ. Paṭikkamanasālādiupasaṅkamanaṃ [V 1.0392] viya pariyesane samānapaṭikkūlaṃ hi asuciṭṭhānakkamanavirūpaduggandhadassanaghāyanādhivāsanehi. Gamanatoti bhikkhācāravasena gocaragāmaṃ uddissa gamanato. Pariyesanatoti gocaragāme bhikkhatthaṃ āhiṇḍanato. Paribhogatoti āhārassa paribhuñjanato. Ubhayaṃ ubhayena āsayati, ekajjhaṃ pavattamānopi kammabalavavatthito hutvā mariyādavasena aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarato sayati tiṭṭhati pavattatīti āsayo, āmāsayassa upari tiṭṭhanako pittādiko. Mariyādattho hi ayamākāro, tato āsayato. Nidadhāti yathābhutto āhāro nicito hutvā tiṭṭhati etthāti nidhānaṃ, āmāsayo, tato nidhānato. Aparipakkatoti gahaṇīsaṅkhātena kammajatejena aparipakkato. Paripakkatoti yathābhuttassa āhārassa vipakkabhāvato. Phalatoti nibbattito. Nissandatoti ito cito ca vissandanato. Sammakkhanatoti sabbaso makkhanato. Sabbattha āhāre paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbāti yojanā. Taṃtaṃkiriyānipphattipaṭipāṭivasena cāyaṃ gamanatotiādikā anupubbī ṭhapitā, sammakkhanaṃ pana paribhogādīsu labbhamānampi nissandavasena visesato paṭikkūlanti sabbapacchā ṭhapitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In 'by going,' and so on, 'returning' is also included under 'going' because it has the same nature as going, just as approaching a rest-house after the alms-round is included in 'searching.' For it is equally repulsive through having to endure treading on impure places, seeing distorted forms, and smelling bad odors. 'By going' means by going towards an alms-resort village for the sake of the alms-round. 'By searching' means by wandering for alms in the alms-resort village. 'By consuming' means by consuming the food. It is called 'āsaya' (receptacle) because, although occurring together, each is established by the power of kamma and, by way of its boundary, lies, stands, and proceeds without mixing with the other; such as the bile, etc., that stands above the stomach (āmāsaya). Indeed, this 'ā' has the meaning of 'boundary'; hence 'āsaya.' It is called 'nidhāna' (repository) because the eaten food, having been gathered, lies there; this is the stomach (āmāsaya); hence 'by the repository.' 'By being undigested' means by not yet being cooked by the kamma-born fire element called the digestive fire. 'By being digested' means by the state of the eaten food having been cooked. 'By the result' means by its production. 'By secretion' means by oozing out from here and there. 'By smearing' means by being smeared all over. The connection is: 'the repulsiveness in food should be contemplated in all these ways.' And this sequence beginning with 'by going' is established according to the successive accomplishment of each respective action. 'Smearing,' however, although found in 'consuming,' etc., is placed last of all because it is especially repulsive by way of secretion; this should be understood.

295. Evaṃ mahānubhāveti idāni vattabbapaṭipattiyā mahānubhāveti vadanti, sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānapariharaṇādisiddhaṃ vā dhammasudhammataṃ purakkhatvā yogāvacarena [M 1.0418] evaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti dassento “evaṃ mahānubhāve nāma sāsane”tiādimāha. Tattha nāma-saddo sambhāvane daṭṭhabbo. Pabbajitena gāmābhimukhena gantabbanti yojanā. Ayañca gamanādito paccavekkhaṇā yogino na attuddesikāva, atha kho anuddesikāpīti dassento “sakalaratti”ntiādinā dhuradvayaṃ pariggahesi. Pariveṇanti pariveṇaṅgaṇaṃ. Vīsatiṃsavāreti ettha santatipaccuppannavasena vāraparicchedoti keci, apare pana “uṇhāsanenā”ti vadanti. Nīvaraṇavikkhambhanañhi appattā bhāvanā pharaṇapītiyā abhāvato nisajjāvasena kāyakilamathaṃ na vinodatiyevāti iriyāpathacalanaṃ hotiyeva. Vīsatiṃsaggahaṇaṃ pana yathāsallakkhitabhikkhācaraṇavelāvasena. Atha vā gamanato yāva sammakkhanamanasikāro eko vāro, evaṃ vīsatiṃsavāre kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karitvā. Nijanasambādhānīti janasambādharahitāni, tena appākiṇṇataṃ, appasaddataṃ, appanigghosatañca dasseti. Tato eva pavivekasukhāni janavivekena iṭṭhāni, pavivekassa vā jhānānuyogassa upakārāni. Yasmā chāyūdakasampannāni, tasmā [V 1.0393] sītalāni. Yasmā sucīni, tasmā ramaṇīyabhūmibhāgānīti purimāni dve pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ kāraṇavacanāni. Ariyanti niddosaṃ. Vivekaratinti jhānānuyogaratiṃ.

295. Regarding 'thus of great power,' they say this means 'of great power through the practice about to be described.' Or, showing that 'a yogī should practice thus,' having placed foremost the excellence of the Dhamma, which is accomplished through such things as undertaking the universal meditation subject, he said, 'in such a dispensation of great power...' and so on. There, the word 'nāma' should be seen in the sense of esteem. The connection is: 'a renunciant should go facing the village.' And showing that this reflection, starting from 'going,' is for the yogī not only directed towards himself but can also be undirected, he took up the two duties with the words 'the entire night,' etc. 'Pariveṇa' means the grounds of the monastery. Regarding 'twenty or thirty times,' some say the division of rounds is by way of the continuous present. Indeed, meditation that has not reached the suppression of the hindrances does not dispel bodily fatigue by way of sitting, due to the absence of pervading joy; thus a change of posture occurs. The taking up of 'twenty or thirty' is by way of the observed time for the alms-round. Alternatively, from the contemplation of 'going' up to the contemplation of 'smearing' is one round; in this way, having applied the mind to the meditation subject for twenty or thirty rounds. 'Free from the confines of people' means devoid of crowds of people; by this, he shows a state of not being crowded, of little sound, and of no clamor. For that very reason, they are 'pleasant with solitude,' desired for their seclusion from people, or they are helpful for solitude, that is, for the practice of jhāna. Because they are endowed with shade and water, they are cool. Because they are clean, they are delightful portions of ground. Thus, the first two phrases are causal statements for the latter two. 'Noble' means faultless. 'Delight in seclusion' means delight in the practice of jhāna.

Kiñcāpi yogāvacarānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma sujaggitaṃ susammaṭṭhameva hoti, kadāci pana jagganato pacchā evampi siyāti paṭikkūlatāpaccavekkhaṇāya sambhavadassanatthaṃ “pādarajagharagolikavaccādisamparikiṇṇa”ntiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha paccattharaṇanti bhūmiyā chavirakkhaṇatthaṃ attharitabbaṃ cimilikādiattharaṇamāha. Jatukā khuddakavagguliyo. Upahatattāti dūsitattā. Tatoti tato tato. Appekadā ulūkapārāvatādīhīti idhāpi “appekadā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Udakacikkhallādīhīti ādi-saddena kacavarādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Pariveṇato vihāraṅgaṇappavesamaggo vihāraracchā.

Although a yogī's dwelling place is indeed well-tended and well-swept, it should be understood that the words 'strewn with foot-dust, house-lizard droppings, and so on' were said to show the possibility for the contemplation of repulsiveness, because sometimes, after being tended to, it might become like this. Therein, by 'paccattharaṇa' (ground-covering), he refers to a covering such as a coarse cloth mat to be spread for the protection of the ground's surface. 'Jatukā' are small bats. 'Upahatattā' (being affected) means because of being defiled. 'Tatoti' means from here and there. In the phrase 'sometimes by owls, pigeons, and so on,' the word 'sometimes' should be brought in and connected here as well. In 'by water, mud, and so on,' the word 'and so on' includes rubbish and the like. The path leading from the monastery grounds into the monastery courtyard is a 'vihāraracchā' (monastery lane).

Vitakkamāḷaketi “kattha nu kho ajja bhikkhāya caritabba”ntiādinā vitakkanamāḷake. Gāmamagganti gāmagāmimaggaṃ. Khāṇukaṇṭakamaggoti khāṇukaṇṭakavanto maggo. Daṭṭhabbo hotīti dassanena gamanaṃ upalakkheti.

In 'vitakkamāḷake' (in the pavilion of thought): in the pavilion for thinking, with such thoughts as, 'Where indeed today should I wander for alms?' 'Gāmamaggaṃ' (the village path) means the path leading to the village. 'Khāṇukaṇṭakamaggo' (a path of stumps and thorns) means a path possessing stumps and thorns. In 'it should be seen,' he indicates going by means of seeing.

Gaṇḍaṃ [M 1.0419] paṭicchādentenātiādi evamajjhāsayena nivāsanādi kātabbanti vattadassanaṃ, gaṇḍaroginā vātātapādiparissayavinodanatthaṃ gaṇḍaṃ paṭicchādayamānena viya. Atha vā gaṇḍaṃ viya gaṇḍaṃ paṭicchādayamānenāti ekaṃ gaṇḍa-saddaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ bhavati. “Gaṇḍoti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti (a. ni. 9.15; saṃ. ni. 4.103) vacanato gaṇḍoti attabhāvassa pariyāyo, visesato rūpakāyassa dukkhatāsūlayogato, asucipaggharaṇato, uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātakapakkapabhijjanato. Vaṇacoḷakanti vaṇapaṭicchādakavatthakhaṇḍaṃ. Nīharitvāti thavikato uddharitvā. Kuṇapānipīti pi-saddo garahāyaṃ evarūpānipi daṭṭhabbāni bhavantīti, sambhavadassane vā idampi tattha sambhavatīti. Adhivāsetabboti khamitabbo aññathā āhārassa anupalabbhanato. Gāmadvāreti gāmadvārasamīpe, ummārabbhantare vā. Gāmaracchā vinivijjhitvā ṭhitā oloketabbā honti yugamattadassināpi satāti adhippāyo.

“Concealing a sore,” and so on. This shows the practice that wearing robes and so forth should be done with such an intention, like a person with a sore concealing it to ward off the dangers of wind, sun, and so forth. Or alternatively, by bringing in one word “sore,” it should be connected as “concealing the body, which is like a sore.” Because it is said, “Monks, ‘sore’ is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging” (AN 9.15; SN 4.103), “sore” is a synonym for existence, especially for the material body, because of its connection with the affliction of the three kinds of suffering, its oozing of impurities, and its swelling, ripening, and bursting due to arising, aging, and dissolution. “A bandage for the wound” means a piece of cloth for covering a wound. “Having taken it out” means having taken it out from the bag. In “even corpses,” the particle “pi” is used in the sense of censure, meaning “even such repulsive things must be seen,” or in the sense of showing possibility, meaning “this too may occur there.” “Should be endured” means it should be tolerated, because otherwise food would not be obtained. “At the village gate” means near the village gate, or inside the threshold. The meaning is that the village streets, which stand penetrating right through, should be looked at, even by one who is accustomed to seeing only a yoke’s length ahead.

Paccattharaṇādīti gharagolikavaccādisaṃkiliṭṭhapaccattharaṇādikaṃ. Anekakuṇapapariyosānanti ettha [V 1.0394] dunnivatthaduppārutamanussasamākulānaṃ gāmaracchānaṃ olokanampi ānetvā vattabbaṃ. Tampi hi paṭikkūlamevāti. Aho vatāti garahane nipāto. Bhoti dhammālapanaṃ. Yāvañcidaṃ paṭikkūlo āhāro yadatthaṃ gamanampi nāma evaṃ jegucchaṃ, duradhivāsanañcāti attho.

“Floor coverings, and so on” refers to floor coverings and so forth soiled by things like house-lizard droppings. Here, in the phrase “ending in many corpses,” the seeing of village streets crowded with people who are poorly dressed and robed should also be brought in and mentioned. For that too is indeed repulsive. “Alas!” is a particle used in the sense of censure. “Bhoti” is a term of address in a Dhamma context. The meaning is: For the sake of which food even the act of going is so loathsome and hard to endure, how very repulsive this food is!

296. Gamanapaṭikkūlanti gamanameva paṭikkūlaṃ gamanapaṭikkūlaṃ. Adhivāsetvāpīti pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena “ettakenāpi mutti natthi, ito parampi mahantaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ sakalaṃ adhivāsetabbamevā”ti vakkhamānaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Saṅghāṭipārutenāti saṅghāṭiyā kappanapārupanena pārutasarīrena. Yatthāti yāsu vīthīsu. Yāva piṇḍikamaṃsāpīti yāva jaṅghapiṇḍikamaṃsappadesāpi. Udakacikkhalleti udakamisse kaddame. Ekena cīvaranti ekena hatthena nivatthacīvaraṃ. Macchā dhovīyanti etenāti macchadhovanaṃ, udakaṃ. Sammissa-saddo paccekaṃ sambandhitabbo. Oḷigallāni ucchiṭṭhodakagabbhamalādīnaṃ sakaddamānaṃ sandanaṭṭhānāni, yāni jaṇṇumattaasucibharitānipi honti. Candanikāni kevalānaṃ ucchiṭṭhodakagabbhamalādīnaṃ sandanaṭṭhānāni[M 1.0420]. Yatoti oḷigallādito. Tā makkhikāti tattha saṇḍasaṇḍacārino nīlamakkhikā. Nilīyantīti acchanti.

296. “The repulsiveness of going” means the going itself is repulsive, the repulsiveness of going. In “even after having endured,” the particle “pi” has the meaning of combination; by it, it combines the repulsiveness that will be spoken of, thus: “Even with this much there is no release; beyond this, the great, entire repulsiveness must still be endured.” “Clad in the saṅghāṭi” means with the body covered by the patched outer robe. “Where” means in which streets. “Even up to the calf-flesh” means even up to the region of the calf muscle. “In water and mud” means in mud mixed with water. “With one, the robe” means holding up the worn robe with one hand. “Fish are washed with this,” thus it is fish-washing water. The word “mixed” should be connected to each individually. “Gutters” are places where water from washing leftovers, fetal impurities, and so on, together with mud, flow; these can be filled with impurities up to the knee. “Cesspools” are places where only water from washing leftovers, fetal impurities, and so on, are discarded. “From which” means from the gutters and so on. “Those flies” means the bluebottles that move about in swarms there. “They settle” means they stay.

Dadamānāpītiādi satipi kesañci saddhānaṃ vasena sakkaccakāre paṭikkūlapaccavekkhaṇāyogyaṃ pana asaddhānaṃ vasena pavattanakaasakkaccakārameva dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ. Tuṇhī honti sayameva riñcitvā gacchissatīti. Gacchāti apehi. Reti ambho. Muṇḍakāti anādarālapanaṃ. Samudācarantīti kathenti. Piṇḍolyassa antimajīvikābhāvenāha “kapaṇamanussena viya gāme piṇḍāya caritvā nikkhamitabba”nti.

The passage beginning “Even when giving” is stated in order to show only the disrespectful actions that occur due to the faithless—which are suitable for contemplating the repulsive—even though there is respectful action on the part of some faithful people. “They are silent” means they think, “Becoming weary, he will go away by himself.” “Go” means depart. “Re” means friend. “Shaveling” is a disrespectful term of address. “They converse” means they speak. Because alms-gathering is the lowliest livelihood, he says, “one must wander for alms in the village and depart like a wretched person.”

297. Tatthāti tasmiṃ pattagate āhāre. Lajjitabbaṃ hoti “ucchiṭṭhaṃ nu kho ayaṃ mayhaṃ dātukāmo”ti āsaṅkeyyāti, sedo paggharamāno āhārassa vā uṇhatāya, bhikkhuno vā sapariḷāhatāyāti adhippāyo. Sukkhathaddhabhattampīti sukkhatāya thaddhampi bhattaṃ, pageva takkakañjikādinā upasittanti adhippāyo. Tena sedena kilinnatāya paṭikkūlataṃ vadati.

297. “Therein” means in that food that is in the bowl. One should be ashamed, as one might suspect, “Does this person want to give me leftovers?” The meaning is that sweat drips, either because of the food’s heat or because of the monk’s own heat. “Even dry, hard rice” means rice that is hard due to dryness; what more of rice that has been sprinkled with buttermilk, gruel, and so on? This is the meaning. He speaks of its repulsiveness because of its being moistened by that sweat.

Tasminti piṇḍapāte. Sambhinnasobheti sabbaso vinaṭṭhasobhe. Vemajjhato paṭṭhāyāti jivhāya majjhato paṭṭhāya. Dantagūthako dantamalaṃ. Vicuṇṇitamakkhitoti ubhayehi dantehi vicuṇṇito [V 1.0395] kheḷādīhi samupalitto. Evaṃbhūtassa cassa yāyaṃ pubbe vaṇṇasampadā, gandhasampadā, abhisaṅkhārasampadā ca, sā ekaṃsena vinassati, raso pana nasseyya vā na vāti āha “antarahitavaṇṇagandhasaṅkhāraviseso”ti. Suvānadoṇiyanti sārameyyānaṃ bhuñjanakaambaṇe. Suvānavamathu viyāti vantasunakhachaḍḍanaṃ viya. Cakkhussa āpāthaṃ atītattā ajjhoharitabbo hotīti ukkaṃsagataṃ tassa paṭikkūlabhāvaṃ vibhāveti.

“In that” means in that almsfood. “With its beauty destroyed” means with its beauty completely ruined. “Starting from the middle” means starting from the middle of the tongue. “Tooth-filth” is tooth grime. “Ground and smeared” means ground by both sets of teeth and smeared with saliva and so on. Of this food which has become like this, whatever excellence of color, excellence of scent, and excellence of preparation it had before, that is completely destroyed. As for the taste, it may be destroyed or it may not; for this reason, he said, “with its distinction of color, scent, and preparation having disappeared.” “In a dog’s trough” means in the eating trough of dogs. “Like a dog’s vomit” means like the discarded vomit of a dog. The statement that it has to be swallowed because it has passed beyond the range of the eye reveals the extreme degree of its repulsive nature.

298. Paribhoganti ajjhoharaṇaṃ. Esa āhāro anto pavisamāno bahalamadhukatelamakkhito viya paramajeguccho hotīti sambandho. Antoti koṭṭhassa abbhantare. Nidhānamanupagato āmāsayaṃ appattoyeva āhāro pittādīhi vimissito hotīti āha “pavisamāno”ti. Āmāsayapakkāsayavinimutto koyamāsayo nāmāti [M 1.0421] āsaṅkaṃ sandhāyāha “yasmā”tiādi. Pittamevāsayo pittāsayo. Adhiko hotīti vuttaṃ mandapuññabāhullato lokassa. Evaṃ āsayatoti jeguccho hutvā anto paviṭṭho jegucchatarehi pittādīhi vimissito ativiya jeguccho hotīti evaṃ āsayato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

298. “Consumption” means ingestion. The connection is: this food, upon entering inside, becomes extremely repulsive, as if smeared with thick honey-oil. “Inside” means inside the stomach. The food, not yet having reached its storage place, not yet having arrived in the stomach, is mixed with bile and so on; for this reason, he said “entering.” Anticipating the doubt, “Distinct from the stomach and intestines, what is this thing called a ‘receptacle’?” he said “Because,” and so on. The bile itself is the receptacle, the bile-receptacle. It is said to be “excessive” because of the abundance of people with little merit in the world. Thus, from the perspective of the receptacle: having become repulsive, upon entering inside, it is mixed with even more repulsive things like bile and becomes exceedingly repulsive. In this way, its repulsiveness should be contemplated from the perspective of the receptacle.

299. Nidhānatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Soti āhāro. Dasavassikenāti jātiyā dasavassena sattena. Okāseti āmāsayasaṅkhāte padese.

299. Regarding the phrase 'from the receptacle,' here too, this is the same method. 'It' refers to the nutriment. 'By a ten-year-old' means by a being who is ten years old by birth. 'It occupies a place' means in the region designated as the stomach.

300. Evarūpeti edise, dasavassāni yāva vassasataṃ adhotavaccakūpasadiseti attho. Nidhānanti nidhātabbataṃ. Yathāvuttappakāreti sace pana “dasavassikenā”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.299) yathāvutto pakāro etassāti yathāvuttappakāro, tasmiṃ. Paramandhakāratimiseti ativiya andhakaraṇamahātamasi. Atiduggandhajegucche padese paramajegucchabhāvaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhatīti sambandho. Kattha kiṃ viyāti āha “yathā nāmā”tiādi. Kālameghena abhivuṭṭhe āvāṭe bahuso vassanena ekaccaṃ asucijātaṃ uppilavitvā vigaccheyyāti akālamegha-ggahaṇaṃ. Tiṇapaṇṇakilañjakhaṇḍa-ggahaṇaṃ na asubhassāpi asubhena sammissatāya asubhabhāvappattidassanatthaṃ. Kāyaggisantāpakuthitakuthanasañjātapheṇapubbuḷakācitoti gahaṇitejena pakkuthitanippakkatāya samuppannapheṇapubbuḷanicito. Aparipakkatoti aparipakkabhāvato.

300. 'Of such a kind' means of this sort; the meaning is, like an unwashed cesspool for ten years, up to a hundred years. 'As a deposit' means the state of being deposited. 'Of the characteristic as described' means: if, as stated in the phrase beginning 'by a ten-year-old,' the characteristic is as described, it is 'of the characteristic as described'; in that. 'In extreme darkness and gloom' means in extremely great darkness that causes blindness. The connection is: it remains, having reached a state of extreme repulsiveness in a place of extreme foul odor and disgust. When asked, 'Where? Like what?' he said the passage beginning 'Just as...' The taking of 'seasonal rain cloud' is because if a seasonal rain cloud were to pour down heavily on a pit, some of the collected impurity might float up and be carried away by the repeated raining. The taking of 'grass, leaves, and pieces of matting' is for the purpose of showing the attainment of an impure state by the mixing of that which is not impure with the impure. 'Piled with foam and bubbles produced from the seething and cooking by the heat of the body-fire' means heaped with well-arisen foam and bubbles due to being boiled and cooked by the heat of digestion. 'Because it is undigested' means due to the state of being undigested.

301. Suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo viyāti yathā suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo vidhinā tāpiyamānā suvaṇṇarajatādike [V 1.0396] muñcantiyo suvaṇṇarajatādibhāvaṃ upagacchantīti vuccanti, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana āhāro kāyagginā paripakko pheṇapubbuḷake muñcanto saṇhaṃ karonti etthāti “saṇhakaraṇī”ti laddhanāmake nisade pisitvā nāḷike khuddakaveḷunāḷikāyaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānamattena pakkhippamānapaṇḍumattikā viya karīsabhāvaṃ upagantvā pakkāsayaṃ pūreti, muttabhāvaṃ upagantvā muttavatthiṃ pūretīti yojanā. Gahaṇiyā indhanabhāgo viya kimibhakkhabhāgo ca apākaṭova[M 1.0422]. Rasabhāgo phalato pakāsīyati, aparipakkasabhāgā ca teti te anāmasitvā karīsamuttabhāgā evettha dassitā.

301. 'Like ores of gold, silver, etc.' means: just as ores of gold, silver, and so on, when smelted according to a method, are said to release gold, silver, etc., and attain the state of gold, silver, and so on, this nutriment is not so. This nutriment, however, when digested by the body-fire, releasing foam and bubbles, is like pale-colored fine clay being placed in a small bamboo tube only in terms of color and form, after being ground on a grinding slab named 'that which makes fine.' Having reached the state of feces, it fills the receptacle for digested food; having reached the state of urine, it fills the bladder—this is the connection. The portion that is fuel for the digestive fire and the portion that is food for worms are indeed unmanifest. The portion of essence is made manifest by its result. And those portions have a nature similar to the undigested portion. Therefore, without mentioning them, only the portions of feces and urine are shown here.

302. Paṭikkūlassa nāma phalena paṭikkūleneva bhavitabbanti dassento “sammā paripaccamāno”tiādimāha. Nakhadantādīnīti ādi-saddena na kevalaṃ tacādīni eva dvattiṃsākārapāḷiyaṃ (ma. ni. 3.154; khu. pā. 3.dvattiṃsākāra) āgatāni, atha kho akkhigūthakaṇṇagūthadantamalajallikāsambhavādīni dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsavinimuttāni asubhāni saṅgaṇhanto “nānākuṇapānī”ti āhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

302. Wishing to show that 'The result of what is repulsive must indeed be repulsive,' he stated the passage beginning 'When being properly digested...' Regarding 'nails, teeth, etc.,' it should be understood that by the word 'etc.,' he includes not only things like skin and so on that are mentioned in the Pāli text on the thirty-two parts of the body, but rather, wishing to include impure things that are separate from the thirty-two parts—such as eye-secretion, earwax, tooth-dirt, bodily grime, and semen—he said, 'various kinds of corpses.'

303. Nissandamānoti vissavanto, paggharantoti attho. Ādinā pakārenāti ettha ādi-saddena nāsikāya siṅghāṇikā, mukhena kheḷo, kadāci pittaṃ, semhaṃ, lohitaṃ vamati, vaccamaggena uccāro, passāvamaggena passāvo, sakalakāye lomakūpehi sedajallikāti evaṃpakāraṃ asuciṃ saṅgaṇhāti. “Paṭhamadivase”ti idaṃ nissandadivasāpekkhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “dutiyadivase nissandento”ti. Vikuṇitamukhoti jigucchāvasena saṅkucitamukho. Tenāha “jegucchī”ti. Maṅkubhūtoti vimanakajāto “imampi nāma posemī”ti. Rattoti vatthaṃ viya raṅgajātena cittassa vipariṇāmākārena chandarāgena ratto. Giddhoti abhikaṅkhanasabhāvena abhigijjhanena giddho gedhaṃ āpanno. Gadhitoti dummocanīyabhāvena ganthito viya tattha paṭibaddho. Mucchitoti rasataṇhāya mucchaṃ mohaṃ āpanno. Virattoti vigatarāgo. Aṭṭīyamānoti dukkhiyamāno. Harāyamānoti lajjamāno. Jigucchamānoti hīḷento.

303. 'Flowing out' means oozing, trickling out. In the phrase 'by other means,' the word 'etcetera' includes such impurities as: nasal mucus from the nose, saliva from the mouth; sometimes one vomits bile, phlegm, or blood; feces from the anal passage, urine from the urinary passage, and sweat and bodily grime from the hair-pores all over the body. The phrase 'on the first day' is stated with reference to the day of flowing out. For that reason, he said, 'flowing out on the second day.' 'With a contorted face' means with a face contracted by way of disgust. For that reason, he said, 'being disgusted.' 'Disheartened' means having become disheartened, thinking, 'I am nourishing even this!' 'Impassioned' means attached by sensual passion, which is a transformation of the mind, like cloth dyed with color. 'Greedy' means greedy with intense longing, having fallen into avarice. 'Ensnared' means bound to it, as if knotted, with the quality of being hard to undo. 'Infatuated' means having fallen into confusion and delusion through craving for tastes. 'Dispassionate' means devoid of passion. 'Distressed' means feeling pain. 'Ashamed' means feeling shame. 'Despising' means scorning.

Navadvārehīti pākaṭānaṃ mahantānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, lomakūpavivarehipi sandatevāti. Nilīyatīti attānaṃ adassento nigūhati, saṅkucati vā. Evanti ekena dvārena pavesanaṃ anekehi dvārehi anekadhā nikkhāmanaṃ, pakāsanaṃ pavesanaṃ, nigūḷhaṃ nikkhāmanampīti somanassajātena [V 1.0397] pavesanaṃ, maṅkubhūtena nikkhāmanaṃ, sārattena pavesanaṃ, virattena nikkhāmananti imehi pakārehi.

'Through the nine openings' is said with respect to the manifest and large openings; it should be understood that it also flows out from the openings of the hair-pores. 'It lies hidden' means it conceals itself, not showing itself, or it contracts. 'Thus' means in these ways: entry is through one door, while exit is through many doors in many ways; entry is manifest, while exit is concealed; entry is with gladness, while exit is with dejection; entry is with attachment, while exit is with detachment.

304. Paribhogakālepīti [M 1.0423] pi-saddena paviṭṭhamattopi nāma pavesadvāraṃ jegucchaṃ karoti, pageva laddhaparivāso paripākappatto itaradvārānīti dasseti. Esa āhāro. Gandhaharaṇatthanti vissagandhāpanayanatthaṃ. Kāyaggināti gahaṇitejānugatena kāyusmānā. Pheṇuddehakanti pheṇāni uṭṭhapetvā uṭṭhapetvā. Paccitvāti paripākaṃ gantvā. Uttaramānoti uppilavanto. Semhādīti ādi-saddena pittādike saṅgaṇhāti. Karīsādīti ādi-saddena sedajallikādike. Imāni dvārāni mukhādīni. Ekaccanti passāvamaggaṃ sandhāya vadati. Cokkhajātikā pana mukhādīnipi dhovitvā hatthaṃ puna dhovantiyeva. Puna ekaccanti vaccamaggaṃ. Dvattikkhattunti dvikkhattuṃ, tikkhattuṃ vā. Ettha ca āhāratthāya gamanapariyesanānaṃ paṭikkūlatā āhāre paṭikkūlatā vuttā. Paribhogassa tannissayato, āsayanidhānānaṃ taṃsambandhato, itaresaṃ tabbikāratoti ayampi viseso veditabbo. Kimibhakkhabhāvopi hissa vikārapakkheyeva ṭhapetabboti.

304. Regarding 'Even at the time of consumption': by the particle 'pi' (even), it is shown that the nutriment, merely upon having entered, makes the door of entry repulsive; how much more so the other doors, once it has found its lodging and reached the state of digestion? This is that nutriment. 'For the purpose of removing odor' means for the purpose of dispelling the raw, fleshy smell. 'By the body-fire' means by the body's heat which is accompanied by the heat of digestion. 'Causing foam to rise' means causing foam to rise up again and again. 'Having been cooked' means having undergone digestion. 'Rising up' means floating up. 'Phlegm, etc.': by the word 'etcetera,' he includes bile and so on. 'Feces, etc.': by the word 'etcetera,' he includes sweat, bodily grime, and so on. These doors are the mouth and others. 'A certain one' is said referring to the urinary passage. People of clean habits, however, after washing the mouth and other parts, wash their hands again. 'Again, a certain one' refers to the fecal passage. 'Two or three times' means twice or thrice. And here, the repulsiveness of going and searching for the sake of food is called 'repulsiveness in food.' This distinction should also be known: the repulsiveness of consumption is due to dependence on it; the repulsiveness of the receptacles and deposits is due to connection with it; and the repulsiveness of its transformations is also called 'repulsiveness in food.' Indeed, its state as food for worms should be placed only in the category of its transformation.

305. Taṃ nimittanti yathāvuttehi ākārehi punappunaṃ manasi karontassa paṭikkūlākāravasena upaṭṭhitaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārasaññitaṃ bhāvanāya nimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, na uggahapaṭibhāganimittaṃ. Yadi hi tattha uggahanimittaṃ uppajjeyya, paṭibhāganimittenapi bhavitabbaṃ. Tathā ca sati appanāppattena jhānena bhavitabbaṃ, na ca bhavati, kasmā? Bhāvanāya nānākārato, sabhāvadhammabhāvena ca kammaṭṭhānassa gambhīrabhāvato. Tenāha “kabaḷīkārāhārassa sabhāvadhammatāya gambhīrattā”ti. Ettha hi yadipi paṭikkūlākāravasena bhāvanā pavattati. Ye pana dhamme upādāya kabaḷīkārāhārapaññatti, te eva dhammā paṭikkūlā, na paññattīti paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇamukhenapi sabhāvadhammeyeva ārabbha bhāvanāya pavattanato, sabhāvadhammānañca sabhāveneva gambhīrabhāvato na tattha jhānaṃ appetuṃ sakkoti. Gambhīrabhāvato hi purimasaccadvayaṃ duddasaṃ jātanti. Yadi upacārasamādhinā cittaṃ samādhiyati, kathaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ “saññā” icceva voharīyatīti āha “paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇavasena panā”tiādi.

305. “That sign” (taṃ nimittaṃ): the object of meditation, which arises by way of the repulsive aspect for one who repeatedly gives attention to the morsel-food with the characteristics as stated, is the sign of the meditation (bhāvanāya nimittaṃ), its object; it is not the learning sign (uggahanimittaṃ) or the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimittaṃ). For if the learning sign were to arise there, there would also have to be a counterpart sign. And that being so, there would have to be jhāna that has reached absorption, but this does not happen. Why? Because of the various aspects of the meditation, and because of the profundity of the meditation subject due to its being an intrinsic phenomenon. Therefore, it was said: “because of the profundity of morsel-food due to its being an intrinsic phenomenon.” For here, although the meditation proceeds by way of the repulsive aspect, the very phenomena upon which the concept of ‘morsel-food’ depends are themselves repulsive, not the concept. Thus, since the meditation proceeds by taking as its object only the intrinsic phenomena even when approached through grasping the repulsive aspect, and because of the profundity of the intrinsic phenomena by their very own nature, one is not able to apply jhāna there. For, due to its profundity, the first two truths have become difficult to see. If the mind is concentrated by access concentration, how is the meditation subject designated merely as “perception”? To answer this, he said, “But by way of grasping the repulsive aspect,” etc.

Idāni imissā bhāvanāya ānisaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ “imañca panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Rasataṇhāyāti madhurādirasavisayāya taṇhāya. Patilīyatīti saṅkucati anekākāraṃ tattha paṭikkūlatāya [V 1.0398] saṇṭhitattā. Patikuṭatīti apasakkati [M 1.0424] na visarati. Pativattatīti nivattati. Kantāranittharaṇatthikoti mahato dubbhikkhakantārassa nittharaṇappayojano. Vigatamadoti mānamadādīnaṃ abhāvena nimmado, madābhāvaggahaṇeneva cassa davamaṇḍanavibhūsanādīnampi abhāvo gahitoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kabaḷīkārāhārapariññāmukhenāti vuttanayena paṭikkūlākārato kabaḷīkārāhārassa paricchijja jānanadvārena. Pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgoti anativattanaṭṭhena pañcasu kāmaguṇesu niyutto, tappayojano vā rāgo. Pariññaṃ samatikkamaṃ gacchati. Rasataṇhāya hi sammadeva vigatāya rūpataṇhādayopi vigatā eva honti bhojane mattaññutāya ukkaṃsagamanato. Sati ca visayisamatikkame visayo samatikkanto eva hotīti āha “so pañcakāmaguṇapariññāmukhena rūpakkhandhaṃ parijānātī”ti. Rūpāyatanādīsu hi pariññaṃ gacchantesu tannissayabhūtāni, taggāhakā pasādā ca sukheneva pariññaṃ gacchantīti. Aparipakkādīti ādi-saddena āsayanidhānānampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha aparipakkaṃ tāva udariyameva. Āsayaggahaṇena pittasemhapubbalohitānaṃ, paripakkaggahaṇena karīsamuttānaṃ, phalaggahaṇena kesādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ pariggaho siddho hotīti āha “kāyagatāsatibhāvanāpi pāripūriṃ gacchatī”ti. Asubhasaññāyāti asubhabhāvanāya, aviññāṇakaasubhabhāvanānuyogassāti attho. Anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇena kāyassa asuciduggandhajegucchabhāvasallakkhaṇato. Imaṃ pana paṭipattinti imaṃ āhāre paṭikkūlasaññābhāvanaṃ. Amatapariyosānatanti nibbānaniṭṭhitaṃ āhāre paṭikkūlasaññābhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ upacārajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nibbānādhigamanti attho.

Now, to show the benefits of this meditation, it is said, “And this…” etc. ‘Craving for flavors’ (rasataṇhāya) means craving for the object of sweet and other flavors. ‘It shrinks back’ (patilīyati) means it contracts, because of being well-established in the repulsiveness there in many ways. ‘It recoils’ (patikuṭati) means it moves away, it does not spread. ‘It turns away’ (pativattati) means it turns back. ‘Desiring to cross the wilderness’ (kantāranittharaṇatthiko) means having the purpose of crossing the great wilderness of famine. ‘Free from intoxication’ (vigatamado) means without intoxication due to the absence of pride, etc.; and by grasping the absence of intoxication, the absence of his playfulness, adornment, and embellishment should also be understood as having been grasped. ‘Through the full understanding of morsel-food’ (kabaḷīkārāhārapariññāmukhena) means through the door of knowing by defining morsel-food by way of its repulsive aspect, according to the method stated. ‘Lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure’ (pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo) means lust that is engaged in the five strands of sensual pleasure in the sense of not transcending them, or lust that has them as its purpose. It is transcended through full understanding. For when craving for flavors has been rightly removed, cravings for forms and so on are also removed, because of reaching the culmination of moderation in eating. And when the subject is transcended, the object is also transcended. Thus he said, “Through the full understanding of the five strands of sensual pleasure, he fully understands the form aggregate.” For when the form base, etc., go to full understanding, the sensitive faculties that are dependent on them and that grasp them also easily go to full understanding. ‘Unripe, etc.’ (aparipakkādi): by the word ‘etc.’ (ādi-saddena), the inclusion of the receptacle (āsaya) and what is stored (nidhāna) should also be understood. Therein, ‘unripe’ is just the stomach contents. By grasping the receptacle, the inclusion of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood is accomplished; by grasping the digested, the inclusion of feces and urine; and by grasping the fruit (phala), the inclusion of all parts such as hair, etc., is accomplished. Thus he said, “The development of mindfulness directed to the body also reaches completion.” ‘For the perception of foulness’ (asubhasaññāya) means for the development of foulness; the meaning is, for the practice of developing foulness in that which is without consciousness. He has entered upon the conformable practice by grasping the repulsive aspect, because of marking the state of the body as impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting. ‘This practice’ (imaṃ pana paṭipattiṃ) means this meditation on the perception of repulsiveness in food. ‘Ending in the deathless’ (amatapariyosānatanti) means culminating in Nibbāna; the meaning is the attainment of Nibbāna by having made the access concentration—called the meditation on the perception of repulsiveness in food—a foundation, and having developed insight.

Āhārepaṭikkūlabhāvanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Meditation on Repulsiveness in Food is concluded.

Catudhātuvavatthānabhāvanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meditation on the Defining of the Four Elements

306. “Ekaṃ vavatthānanti evaṃ uddiṭṭhassa catudhātuvavatthānassa bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto”ti uddeso nāma niddesattho mudumajjhapaññābāhullato[M 1.0425], āgato ca bhāro avassaṃ vahitabboti katvā vuttaṃ. Tattha satipi visayabhedena vavatthānassa bhede vavatthānabhāvasāmaññena pana taṃ abhinnaṃ katvā vuttaṃ “ekaṃ vavatthāna”nti, pubbabhāge vā satipi visayabhede atthasiddhiyaṃ [V 1.0399] tassa ekavisayatāvāti “ekaṃ vavatthāna”nti vuttaṃ. Yathā hi dvattiṃsākāre kammaṃ karontassa yogino yadipi pubbabhāge visuṃ visuṃ koṭṭhāsesu manasikāro pavattati, aparabhāge pana ekasmiṃ khaṇe ekasmiṃyeva koṭṭhāse atthasiddhi hoti, na sabbesu, evamidhāpīti. Tattha siyā – yathā paṭikkūlabhāvasāmaññena dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhāne abhedato manasikāro pavattati, evaṃ idha dhātubhāvasāmaññena abhedato manasikāro pavattatīti “ekaṃ vavatthāna”nti vuttanti? Nayidamevaṃ. Tattha hi paṇṇattisamatikkamato paṭṭhāya paṭikkūlavaseneva sabbattha manasikāro pavattetabbo, idha pana sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇato dhātuyo manasi kātabbā, na dhātubhāvasāmaññato. Tenevāha “sabhāvūpalakkhaṇavasena sanniṭṭhāna”nti. Kiṃ vā etena papañcena, aññehi ekūnacattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānehi asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ catudhātuvavatthānaṃ nāma ekaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti dassetuṃ “ekaṃ vavatthāna”nti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Catudhātuvavatthānassa bhāvanāniddeso”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu catudhātuvavatthānaṃ bhāvanāva? Saccaṃ bhāvanāva, sakiṃ pavattaṃ pana vavatthānaṃ, tassa bahulīkāro bhāvanāti vacanabhedena vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ pana bhāvanā niddisīyati tassā vacīgocarātikkantabhāvatoti? Nāyaṃ doso bhāvanatthe bhāvanāvohārato. Bhāvanattho hi kammaṭṭhānapariggaho idha “bhāvanā”ti adhippeto.

306. “The exposition of the development of the four-element determination, which has been indicated thus as ‘one determination,’ has been reached”—this designation is for the purpose of exposition, due to the abundance of those with soft and medium wisdom, and it is stated having considered that a burden that has come must certainly be borne. Herein, although there is a division of the determination by way of the difference of object, yet by way of the commonality of the state of being a determination, it is spoken of as undivided: ‘one determination.’ Alternatively, in the preliminary stage, although there is a difference of object, upon the accomplishment of the purpose, it has the nature of a single object—thus it is called ‘one determination.’ For just as for a yogī practicing on the thirty-two parts, although in the preliminary stage attention proceeds separately on each part, yet in the later stage, at one moment, the accomplishment of the purpose occurs on just one part, not on all—so too here. Herein, one might think: just as in the meditation subject of the thirty-two parts, attention proceeds undividedly by way of the commonality of the state of repulsiveness, so here attention proceeds undividedly by way of the commonality of the state of being an element—hence it is called ‘one determination.’ But this is not so. For there, starting from the point of transcending concepts, attention should be made to proceed everywhere solely by way of repulsiveness. Here, however, the elements are to be attended to by their own nature, essence, and characteristic, not by the commonality of the state of being an element. For that very reason, he said: ‘conclusion by way of observing the intrinsic nature.’ Or, what is the use of this elaboration? It should be understood that ‘one determination’ was stated in order to show that the four-element determination is one meditation subject, unmixed with the other thirty-nine meditation subjects. Why was it said, ‘the exposition of the development of the four-element determination’? Is not the four-element determination itself development? True, it is development. However, the determination is what has occurred once; the frequent practice of that is development. Thus, it was stated with a difference in terms. But how is development expounded, since its nature is to transcend the sphere of speech? This is not a fault, because of the convention of using the term ‘development’ for that which has the purpose of development. For the grasping of the meditation subject, which has the purpose of development, is intended here by ‘development’.

Sabhāvūpalakkhaṇavasenāti kakkhaḷattādikassa salakkhaṇassa upadhāraṇavasena. Idaṃ hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇādikammaṭṭhānaṃ viya na paṇṇattimattasallakkhaṇavasena, nīlakasiṇādikammaṭṭhānaṃ viya na nīlādivaṇṇasallakkhaṇavasena, nāpi vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ viya saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatādisāmaññalakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena pavattati, atha kho pathavīādīnaṃ sabhāvasallakkhaṇavasena pavattati. Tena vuttaṃ “sabhāvūpalakkhaṇavasenā”ti, kakkhaḷattādikassa salakkhaṇassa upadhāraṇavasenāti attho. Sanniṭṭhānanti ñāṇavinicchayo veditabbo, na yevāpanakavinicchayo, nāpi vitakkādivinicchayo[M 1.0426]. Dhātumanasikāroti dhātūsu manasikāro, catasso dhātuyo ārabbha bhāvanāmanasikāroti attho. Kātabbato kammaṃ, yogino sukhavisesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato ṭhānañcāti kammaṭṭhānaṃ, catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ sabhāvasallakkhaṇavasena pavattaṃ yogakammaṃ. Tenāha “dhātumanasikāro, dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ, catudhātuvavatthānanti atthato eka”nti. Tayidaṃ catudhātuvavatthānaṃ. “Dvidhā āgata”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu dhātuvibhaṅge nātisaṅkhepavitthāravasena āgataṃ, tasmā “tidhā āgata”nti vattabbanti? Na, tatthāpi ajjhattikānaṃ dhātūnaṃ pabhedato anavasesapariyādānassa katattā, bāhirānañca dhātūnaṃ pariggahitattā[V 1.0400]. Atha vā dvidhā āgatanti ettha dvidhāva āgatanti na evaṃ niyamo gahetabbo, atha kho dvidhā āgatamevāti, tena tatiyassāpi pakārassa saṅgaho siddho hoti. So ca nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayo “saṅkhepato ca vitthārato cā”ti ettha āvuttivasena, ca-saddeneva vā saṅgahoti daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā yo nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayena atisaṅkhepapaṭikkhepamukhena labbhamāno vitthārabhāgo, taṃ vitthāranayantogadhameva katvā vuttaṃ “dvidhā āgata”nti. Evañca katvā “nātitikkhapaññassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa vasena vitthārato āgata”nti idañca vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. “Mahāsatipaṭṭhāne”ti ca idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, satipaṭṭhāna(dī. ni. 2.378 ādayo; ma. ni. 3.111 ādayo) kāyagatāsatisuttādīsupi (ma. ni. 3.153 ādayo) tatheva āgatattā. Rāhulovādeti mahārāhulovāde (ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo). Dhātuvibhaṅgeti dhātuvibhaṅgasutte (ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo), abhidhamme dhātuvibhaṅge (vibha. 172 ādayo) ca.

By way of observing intrinsic nature—that is, by way of noting the individual characteristic of hardness, etc. For this meditation subject does not proceed by way of merely marking a concept, like the earth-kasiṇa and other meditation subjects; nor by way of marking a color like blue, etc., like the blue-kasiṇa and other meditation subjects; nor does it proceed by way of marking the general characteristics of impermanence, etc., of formations, like an insight meditation subject. Rather, it proceeds by way of marking the intrinsic nature of the earth element, etc. Therefore, it was said, ‘by way of observing the intrinsic nature’; the meaning is: by way of noting the individual characteristic of hardness, etc. ‘Conclusion’ should be understood as the discernment of knowledge, not conventional discernment, nor the discernment of thought, etc. ‘Attention to the elements’ means attention on the elements; the meaning is: meditative attention taking the four elements as its object. Because it is to be done, it is ‘work’ (kamma); and because it is a basis for the yogī’s special kinds of happiness, it is also a ‘basis’ (ṭhāna). Thus, it is ‘kammaṭṭhāna’—the yogic work that proceeds by way of marking the intrinsic nature of the four great elements. Therefore, he said: ‘Attention to the elements, the meditation subject of the elements, and the determination of the four elements—these are one in meaning.’ This is that determination of the four elements. Why was it said ‘it comes in two ways’? Does it not come in the Dhātuvibhaṅga in a way that is neither too brief nor too detailed? Therefore, should it not be said ‘it comes in three ways’? No, because even there, the internal elements have been completely taken up by way of classification, and the external elements have also been comprehended. Alternatively, here in ‘it comes in two ways,’ a fixed rule should not be taken that it comes only in two ways; rather, it should be taken that it does come in two ways. By that, the inclusion of the third method is also established. And that method of neither too brief nor too detailed should be seen as included here in ‘briefly and in detail’ by way of repetition, or by the word ‘ca’ itself. Alternatively, whatever detailed portion is obtained by the method of neither too brief nor too detailed, which has as its principal feature the rejection of excessive brevity, having considered that as simply included within the detailed method, it was said ‘it comes in two ways.’ And having done so, this statement is also justified: ‘it comes in detail for the benefit of one practicing the element meditation who is not of very sharp wisdom.’ And this ‘in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna’ should be seen as just an example, because it comes in the same way also in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, and other suttas. ‘In the Rāhulovāda’ means in the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta. ‘In the Dhātuvibhaṅga’ means in the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta and in the Dhātuvibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma.

Kāmaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhāne atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā desanā āgatā, upamā ca nāma yāvadeva upameyyatthavibhāvanatthāti upamaṃ tāva dassetvā upameyyatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “seyyathāpī”tiādinā pāḷi ānītā. Kasmā panettha dhātuvasena, tatthapi catumahābhūtavasena kammaṭṭhānaniddeso katoti? Sattasuññatāsandassanatthaṃ, ettha dhātuvasena, tatthāpi oḷārikabhāvena supākaṭatāya, ekaccaveneyyajanacaritānukulatāya ca mahābhūtavasena kammaṭṭhānaniddeso katoti veditabbo. Tattha pathavīdhātūtiādīsu dhātuttho nāma sabhāvattho, sabhāvattho [M 1.0427] nāma suññatattho, suññatattho nāma nissattattho. Evaṃ sabhāvasuññatanissattatthena pathavīyeva dhātu pathavīdhātu. Āpodhātuādīsupi eseva nayo. Pathavīdhātūti sahajarūpadhammānaṃ patiṭṭhā dhātu, tathā āpodhātūti ābandhanadhātu, tejodhātūti paripācanadhātu, vāyodhātūti vitthambhanadhātūti evamettha samāso, bhāvattho ca veditabbo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana parato āgamissati.

Although in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna the teaching has come encompassing the simile by way of the meaning to be compared, a simile is for the sole purpose of clarifying the meaning of what is to be compared. Therefore, having first shown the simile, in order to clarify the meaning to be compared, the Pāḷi text is brought forth with the words beginning 'Just as...'. Now, why here is the instruction on the meditation subject made by way of the elements, and among them, by way of the four great elements? For the purpose of showing the state of being void of a being. It should be understood that here the instruction on the meditation subject is made by way of the elements, and among them, by way of the great elements, due to their coarse nature and because they are very evident, and because it is suitable for the temperament of certain trainable individuals. Therein, in 'earth element' and so on, the meaning of 'element' is the meaning of intrinsic nature; the meaning of intrinsic nature is the meaning of voidness; the meaning of voidness is the meaning of non-being. Thus, by the meaning of intrinsic nature, voidness, and non-being, the earth itself is an element, the earth element. This is the same method for the water element and so on. 'Earth element' is the element of support for co-arisen material phenomena. Similarly, 'water element' is the element of cohesion, 'fire element' is the element of maturing, and 'wind element' is the element of supporting. Thus, here the compound and the intended meaning should be understood. This here is the summary; the detailed explanation, however, will come later.

Evaṃ tikkhapaññassātiādīsu evanti yathādassitaṃ pāḷiṃ paccāmasati. Nātitikkhapaññassa vitthāradesanāti katvā āha “tikkhapaññassā”ti. Yathā vatthayugaṃ arahatīti vatthayugiko, evaṃ dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ arahati, dhātukammaṭṭhānapayojanoti vā dhātukammaṭṭhāniko, tassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa.

In the passages beginning with 'evaṃ tikkhapaññassa', by the word 'evaṃ' one reviews the Pāḷi text as has been shown. Thinking, 'The detailed teaching is for one whose wisdom is not very sharp,' he said, 'for one with sharp wisdom.' Just as one who is worthy of a pair of cloths is a 'vatthayugika' (cloth-pair recipient), similarly, one who is worthy of the element meditation subject, or has the element meditation subject as his purpose, or applies himself to the element meditation subject, is a 'dhātukammaṭṭhānika' (practitioner of element meditation); for that practitioner of element meditation.

Chekoti [V 1.0401] taṃtaṃsamaññāya kusalo, yathājāte sūnasmiṃ naṅguṭṭhakhuravisāṇādivante aṭṭhimaṃsādiavayavasamudāye avibhatte gāvīsamaññā, na vibhatte, vibhatte pana aṭṭhimaṃsādiavayavasamaññāti jānanako. Goghātakoti jīvikatthāya gunnaṃ ghātako. Antevāsīti kammakaraṇavasena tassa samīpavāsī tassa tannissāya jīvanato. Vinivijjhitvāti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne aññaṃ vinivijjhitvā. Mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāteti catunnaṃ mahāpathānaṃ tāya eva vinivijjhanaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte. Yasmā te cattāro mahāpathā catūhi disāhi āgantvā samohitā viya honti, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ catumahāpathānaṃ, tasmiṃ catumahāpathe. Vilīyanti bhijjanti vibhajjantīti bīlā, bhāgā, va-kārassa ba-kāraṃ, i-kārassa ca ī-kāraṃ katvā. Tameva hi bhāgatthaṃ dassetuṃ “koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi ṭhita-saddo “ṭhito vā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.28) viya ṭhānasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamaṅgitāya, gatinivattiatthatāya vā ṭhā-saddassa aññattha ṭhapetvā gamanaṃ sesairiyāpathasamaṅgitāya bodhako, idha pana yathā tathā rūpakāyassa pavattiākārabodhako adhippetoti āha “catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathāṭhita”nti[M 1.0428]. Tattha ākārenāti ṭhānādinā rūpakāyassa pavattiākārena. Ṭhānādayo hi iriyāsaṅkhātāya kāyikakiriyāya pavattiṭṭhānatāya “iriyāpathā”ti vuccanti. Yathāṭhitanti yathāpavattaṃ. Yathāvuttaṭṭhānamevettha paṇidhānanti adhippetanti āha “yathāṭhitattāva yathāpaṇihita”nti. Ṭhitanti vā kāyassa ṭhānasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. Paṇihitanti tadaññairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. Ṭhitanti vā kāyasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe sakiccavasena avaṭṭhānaparidīpanaṃ. Paṇihitanti paccayakiccavasena tehi tehi paccayehi pakārato nihitaṃ paṇihitanti evamettha attho veditabbo. Dhātusoti dhātuṃ dhātuṃ pathavīādidhātuṃ visuṃ visuṃ katvā. Paccavekkhatīti pati pati avekkhati ñāṇacakkhunā vinibbhujitvā passati.

‘Skilled’ (cheko) means one who is expert in the respective designations; one who knows that in the case of a cow as it is found, with its dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, horns, and so on, when the aggregate of parts such as bones, flesh, etc., is undivided, there is the designation ‘cow’; but not when it is divided. When it is divided, however, there is the designation of the parts such as bones, flesh, etc. ‘Butcher’ (goghātako) means a killer of cows for the sake of a livelihood. ‘Apprentice’ (antevāsī) means one who lives near him by way of doing work, because he lives by depending on him. ‘Having pierced through’ (vinivijjhitvā) means having pierced through another in one place. ‘At the place called the middle of the great roads’ means at the place called the middle, precisely because it is the place of intersection (vinivijjhanaṭṭhāna) of the four great roads. Because those four great roads, coming from the four directions, are as if they have converged, that place is called a ‘four-great-road junction’ (cātumahāpatha); at that four-great-road junction. ‘Bīlā’ means they are dissolved (vilīyanti), broken (bhijjanti), divided (vibhajjanti); they are portions (bhāgā), this being formed by changing the ‘va’ to ‘ba’ and the ‘i’ to ‘ī’. Indeed, to show that very meaning of ‘portion,’ it was said, “having made into portions” (koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā). Although the word ‘ṭhita’ (established), as in passages such as “standing or…”, indicates being endowed with the posture called standing, or, due to the meaning of the root ‘ṭhā’ as the cessation of movement, it indicates being endowed with the remaining postures after setting aside going elsewhere, here, however, it is intended to indicate the mode of occurrence of the material body in any way whatsoever. Thus, he said, “‘As it is established’ (yathāṭhitaṃ) means because it is established in any manner whatsoever among the four postures.” Therein, ‘by the manner’ (ākārena) means by the mode of occurrence of the material body, such as standing, etc. Standing and so on are called ‘postures’ (iriyāpathā) because they are the basis for the occurrence of the bodily activity called ‘iriyā’. ‘As it is established’ (yathāṭhitaṃ) means as it occurs. Because the intention here is that ‘placing’ (paṇidhāna) is just the state as described, he said, “‘As it is placed’ (yathāpaṇihitaṃ) is just as it is established.” Or, ‘ṭhitaṃ’ is the elucidation of the body’s connection with the posture called standing. ‘Paṇihitaṃ’ is the elucidation of the connection with the other postures. Or, ‘ṭhitaṃ’ is the elucidation of the abiding, at each and every moment, of the material phenomena called ‘body’ according to their respective functions. ‘Paṇihitaṃ’ means placed (nihitaṃ) in a specific way (pakārato) by these and those conditions according to the function of the conditions; thus the meaning should be understood here. ‘Element-wise’ (dhātuso) means having separated each and every element—the earth element, etc. ‘He reflects’ (paccavekkhati) means he looks at each one individually; he sees by discerning with the eye of wisdom.

Yathā chekotiādinā pāḷiyā saddatthavivaraṇavasena vuttamevatthaṃ idāni bhāvatthavibhāvanavasena dassetuṃ “yathā goghātakassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha posentassāti maṃsūpacayaparibrūhanāya kuṇḍakabhattakappāsaṭṭhiādīhi saṃvaḍḍhentassa. Vadhitaṃ matanti hiṃsitaṃ hutvā mataṃ. Matanti ca matamattaṃ. Tenevāha “tāvadevā”ti. Gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyati yāni aṅgapaccaṅgāni upādāya gāvīsamaññā, matamattāyapi gāviyā tesaṃ sannivesassa avinaṭṭhattā. Bilāsoti bilaṃ bilaṃ katvā. Vibhajitvāti aṭṭhisaṅghātato maṃsaṃ vivecetvā, tato vā vivecitaṃ [V 1.0402] maṃsaṃ bhāgaso katvā. Tenevāha “maṃsasaññā pavattatī”ti. Pabbajitassapi apariggahitakammaṭṭhānassa. Ghanavinibbhoganti santatisamūhakiccaghanānaṃ vinibbhujanaṃ vivecanaṃ. Dhātuso paccavekkhatoti yathāvuttaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā dhātuso paccavekkhantassa. Sattasaññāti attānudiṭṭhivasena pavattā sattasaññāti vadanti, vohāravasena pavattasattasaññāyapi tadā antaradhānaṃ yuttameva yāthāvato ghanavinibbhogassa sampādanato. Evaṃ hi sati yathāvuttaopammatthena opameyyattho aññadatthu saṃsandati sameti. Tenevāha “dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhatī”ti.

Just as the meaning was explained in the Pāli passage beginning with ‘Yathā cheko’ by way of clarifying the literal sense, now, to show the meaning by way of revealing the essential meaning, the passage beginning with ‘Yathā goghātakassā’ is stated. Therein, ‘posentassa’ means of one who fattens a cow with broken rice, cotton seeds, and so forth, for the purpose of increasing and nourishing its flesh. ‘Vadhitaṃ mataṃ’ means killed, that is, having been harmed, it is dead. And ‘mataṃ’ means merely dead. For that reason, he said, ‘tāvadeva’ (just so). The perception ‘cow’ does not disappear because the arrangement of the limbs and parts, with reference to which the designation ‘cow’ arises, is not destroyed even when the cow is merely dead. ‘Bilāso’ means having made it portion by portion. ‘Vibhajitvā’ means having separated the flesh from the mass of bones, or having divided the separated flesh into portions. For that reason, he said, ‘the perception of flesh arises.’ This is also for one who has gone forth but has not grasped a meditation subject. ‘Ghanavinibhoga’ means the breaking up and analysis of the compactness of continuity, mass, and function. ‘Dhātuso paccavekkhati’ means for one who, having performed the breaking up of compactness as stated, reviews it element-wise. ‘Sattasaññā’—they say this is the perception of a being that proceeds by way of the view of self; yet even the perception of a being that proceeds by way of convention fittingly disappears at that time, due to accomplishing the breaking up of compactness in accordance with reality. For when this is so, the meaning of what is to be compared truly connects and agrees with the meaning of the simile as stated. Therefore, he said, ‘the mind becomes established only by way of the elements.’

307. Evaṃ dhātukammaṭṭhānassa saṅkhepato āgataṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā idāni vitthārato āgataṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ “mahāhatthipadūpame panā”tiādi [M 1.0429] vuttaṃ. Evanti iminā rāhulovāda- (ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) dhātuvibhaṅgesu (ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo; vibha. 172 ādayo) dhātukammaṭṭhānassa vitthārato āgamanameva upasaṃharati, na sabbaṃ desanānayaṃ aññathāpi tattha desanānayassa āgatattā.

307. Having thus shown in brief the source of the element meditation subject, now, to show its source in detail, the passage beginning with ‘mahāhatthipadūpame panā’ is stated. By this word ‘Evaṃ,’ he summarizes only the detailed presentation of the element meditation subject in the Rāhulovāda Sutta and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, not the entire method of teaching, since the method of teaching there has also been presented in other ways.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ yathādassite mahāhatthipadūpamapāṭhe. Ajjhattikāti sattasantānapariyāpannā. Ajjhattaṃ paccattanti padadvayenāpi taṃtaṃpāṭipuggalikadhammo vuccatīti āha “ubhayampi niyakassa adhivacana”nti. Sasantatipariyāpannatāya pana attani gahetabbabhāvūpagamanavasena attānaṃ adhikicca pavattaṃ ajjhattaṃ. Taṃtaṃsantatipariyāpannatāya paccattaṃ. Tenevāha “attani pavattattā ajjhattaṃ, attānaṃ paṭicca paṭicca pavattattā paccatta”nti. Kakkhaḷanti kathinaṃ. Yasmā taṃ thaddhabhāvena sahajātānaṃ patiṭṭhā hoti, tasmā “thaddha”nti vuttaṃ. Kharigatanti kharīsu kharasabhāvesu gataṃ tappariyāpannaṃ, kharasabhāvamevāti attho. Yasmā pana kharasabhāvaṃ pharusākārena upaṭṭhānato pharusākāraṃ hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pharusa”nti. Tenāha “dutiyaṃ ākāravacana”nti. Upādinnaṃ nāma sarīraṭṭhakaṃ. Taṃ pana kammasamuṭṭhānataṃ sandhāya upādinnampi atthi anupādinnampi, taṇhādīhi ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhavasena sabbampetaṃ upādinnamevāti dassetuṃ “upādinnanti daḷhaṃ ādinna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “mama”nti gahitaṃ “aha”nti parāmaṭṭhanti yojanā. Seyyathidanti kathetukamyatāpucchāvācīti āha “taṃ katamanti ceti attho”ti. Tatoti pacchā. Tanti taṃ ajjhattikādibhedato dassitaṃ pathavīdhātuṃ. Dassentoti vatthuvibhāgena dassento. Kiñcāpi matthaluṅgaṃ aṭṭhimiñjeneva saṅgahetvā idha pāḷiyaṃ visuṃ na uddhaṭaṃ, paṭisambhidāmagge [V 1.0403] (paṭi. ma. 1.4) pana vīsatiyā ākārehi paripuṇṇaṃ katvā dassetuṃ visuṃ gahitanti tampi saṅgaṇhanto thaddhabhāvādhikatāya pathavīdhātukoṭṭhāsesuyeva “matthaluṅgaṃ pakkhipitvā vīsatiyā ākārehi pathavīdhātu niddiṭṭhāti veditabbā”ti āha. “Yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñcī”ti vā iminā pāḷiyaṃ matthaluṅgassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā idha “yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñcī”ti idaṃ pubbāparāpekkhaṃ “matthaluṅgaṃ pakkhipitvā vīsatiyā ākārehi pathavīdhātu niddiṭṭhāti veditabbā, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñcī”ti vacanato. Puna yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñcīti avasesesu tīsu koṭṭhāsesūti [M 1.0430] yojetabbaṃ. Tīsu koṭṭhāsesūti tippakāresu koṭṭhāsesu. Na hi te tayo koṭṭhāsā.

‘Therein’ refers to that passage on the Great Elephant-Footprint Simile as shown. ‘Ajjhattika’ (internal) means included within the continuity of a being. ‘Ajjhatta’ (internal) and ‘paccatta’ (personal)—by both these terms, the individual phenomenon pertaining to each individual is meant. Thus, it is said, ‘both are terms for what belongs to oneself.’ However, because it is included within one’s own continuity and regarded as something to be taken as oneself, it is called ‘ajjhatta’ as it occurs in oneself. Because it is included within each individual continuity, it is called ‘paccatta’. Thus, it is said: ‘Because it occurs in oneself, it is internal; because it occurs repeatedly in dependence on oneself, it is personal.’ ‘Kakkhaḷa’ (hard) means solid. Because it serves as a foundation for coexisting phenomena due to its stiffness, it is called ‘thaddha’ (stiff). ‘Kharigata’ (harsh-natured) means gone into harsh states, pertaining to harshness, having a harsh nature—this is the meaning. Moreover, because a harsh nature appears in a rough manner, it is called ‘pharusa’ (rough). Hence, it is said: ‘The second term refers to its characteristic.’ ‘Upādinna’ (grasped) refers to bodily materiality. However, regarding that which arises from kamma, there is both what is grasped and what is not grasped. But to show that all of this is grasped in the sense of being seized, clung to, and misapprehended by craving and the like, it is said: ‘Upādinna means firmly taken,’ and so on. Here, ‘mine’ means seized, and ‘I’ means misapprehended—this is the interpretation. ‘Seyyathidaṃ’ (for example)—this is a particle expressing a question arising from the desire to speak. Thus, it is said: ‘The meaning is, “What is that?”’ ‘Tato’ (therefrom) refers to what follows. ‘Taṃ’ (that) refers to the earth element, classified as internal and so forth, as previously shown. ‘Dassento’ (showing) means showing through the analysis of the object. Although the brain is included here along with the bone marrow and not separately distinguished in the Pāli text, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is separately taken to be fully described in twenty aspects. Including that as well, due to its predominance in stiffness, he said that having included the brain in the very portions of the earth element, ‘it should be known that the earth element is specified by twenty aspects.’ Alternatively, the inclusion of the brain in the Pāli text should be seen by this phrase, ‘Or whatever else there might be.’ Therefore, here this phrase ‘Or whatever else there might be’ looks to what precedes and follows: ‘having included the brain, it should be known that the earth element is specified by twenty aspects,’ because it is said, ‘Or whatever else there might be.’ Again, ‘Or whatever else there might be’ should be connected with the remaining three portions. ‘In the three portions’ means in the three kinds of portions. For those portions are not three.

Vissandanabhāvenāti paggharaṇasabhāvena. Appotīti visarati. Pappotīti pāpuṇāti, sasambhāraāpavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. So hi vissandanabhāvena sasambhārapathavīsaṅkhātaṃ taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ visarati, pāpuṇāti ca, lakkhaṇāpavaseneva vā. Sopi hi sahajātaaññamaññanissayādipaccayatāya sesabhūtattayasaṅkhātaṃ taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ dravabhāvasiddhena vissandanabhāvena ābandhattaṃ, āsattattaṃ, avippakiṇṇañca karontaṃ “appoti pappotī”ti vattabbataṃ arahatīti.

‘Vissandanabhāvena’ (by its flowing nature) means by its trickling nature. ‘Appoti’ means it spreads. ‘Pappoti’ means it reaches. And this is said by way of the water element with its constituents. For that water element spreads to and reaches each of those places designated as the earth element with its constituents by its flowing nature. Or else, this is said only by way of the characteristic water element. For that characteristic water element also, due to its being a condition such as co-nascence, mutuality, and dependence, while bringing about the state of being bound together, the state of clinging together, and the state of being unscattered in those places designated as the remaining three primary elements through its flowing nature which is accomplished by fluidity, is worthy of being called ‘appoti pappoti.’

Tejanavasenāti nisitabhāvena tikkhabhāvena. Vuttanayenāti kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena “nānāvidhesū”ti āpodhātuyaṃ vuttanayena. Kupitenāti khubhitena. Usumajātoti usmābhibhūto. Jīratīti jiṇṇo hoti. Tejodhātuvasena labbhamānā imasmiṃ kāye jarāpavatti pākaṭajarāvasena veditabbāti dassetuṃ “indriyavekallata”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sarīre pakatiusumaṃ atikkamitvā uṇhabhāvo santāpo, sarīrassa dahanavasena pavatto mahādāho paridāhoti ayametesaṃ viseso. Yena jīrīyatīti ca ekāhikādijararogena jarīyatītipi attho yujjati. Satakkhattuṃ tāpetvā tāpetvā sītudake pakkhipitvā uddhaṭā sappi “satadhotasappī”ti vadanti. Asitanti bhuttaṃ. Khāyitanti khāditaṃ. Sāyitanti assāditaṃ. Sammā paripākaṃ gacchatīti samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā vasena vuttaṃ, asammāparipākopi pana visamavepākiniyā tassā eva vasena veditabbo. Rasādibhāvenāti rasarudhiramaṃsamedanhāruaṭṭhiaṭṭhimiñjasukkavasena. Vivekanti puthubhāvaṃ aññamaññaṃ visadisabhāvaṃ. Asitādibhedassa hi āhārassa pariṇāme raso hoti, taṃ paṭicca rasadhātu uppajjatīti attho. Evaṃ “rasassa pariṇāme rudhira”ntiādinā sabbaṃ netabbaṃ.

By 'the force of heat' (tejanavasena) is meant its keenness and sharpness. By 'as explained' (vuttanayena) is meant in the way described in the exposition of the water element, such as 'arising from kamma' and 'in various ways'. By 'agitated' (kupitena) is meant disturbed. By 'overheated' (usumajāto) is meant overwhelmed by heat. By 'decays' (jīrati) is meant becomes old. To show that the process of aging occurring in this body by way of the heat element is to be understood as manifest aging, it is said, 'the impairment of the faculties,' and so forth. When the natural heat in the body is exceeded, the state of being hot is a burning sensation (santāpo); the great burning that arises by way of scorching the body is a great conflagration (paridāho)—this is the distinction between them. And the phrase 'by which one decays' (yena jīrīyati) can also suitably mean 'one is made feverish by an aging-illness such as a one-day fever'. Ghee that has been heated a hundred times, then placed in cold water and taken out, is called 'hundred-washed ghee' (satadhotasappi). By 'eaten' (asita) is meant consumed. By 'chewed' (khāyita) is meant masticated. By 'tasted' (sāyita) is meant savored. The phrase 'reaches proper digestion' (sammā paripākaṃ gacchati) is said with reference to the evenly digesting faculty (gahaṇī); but improper digestion should also be understood by way of that same faculty when it is unevenly digesting. By 'in terms of nutritional essence, etc.' (rasādibhāvena) is meant by way of nutritional essence, blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, bone marrow, and semen. By 'separation' (viveka) is meant the state of being distinct, the state of being dissimilar from one another. For in the transformation of food of the 'eaten' and other kinds, nutritional essence arises; the meaning is that, dependent on that, the nutritional essence element arises. Similarly, everything should be understood by way of the phrase 'from the transformation of nutritional essence, blood arises,' and so forth.

Vāyanavasenāti [V 1.0404] samudīraṇavasena, savegagamanavasena vā. Uggārahikkādīti ettha ādi-saddena uddekakhipanādipavattanakavātānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo[M 1.0431]. Uccārapassāvādīti ādi-saddena pittasemhalasikākevaladuggandhādinīharaṇakānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Yadipi kucchi-saddo udarapariyāyo, koṭṭha-saddena pana antantarassa vuccamānattā tadavasiṭṭho udarappadeso idha kucchi-saddena vuccatīti āha “kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā”ti. Samiñjanapasāraṇādīti ādi-saddena ālokanavilokanauddharaṇātiharaṇādikā sabbā kāyikakiriyā saṅgahitā. “Assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānāvā”ti etena assāsapassāsānaṃ sarīraṃ muñcitvā pavatti natthīti dīpeti. Na hi bahiddhā cittasamuṭṭhānassa sambhavo atthīti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ “passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikavāto, dīghanāsikassa nāsikaggaṃ, itarassa uttaroṭṭhaṃ phusanto pavattatī”ti vacanaṃ? Taṃ nikkhamanākārena pavattiyā cittasamuṭṭhānassa, santāne pavattautusamuṭṭhānassa ca vasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbatthāti āpodhātuādīnaṃ tissannaṃ dhātūnaṃ niddesaṃ sandhāyāha. Tattha āpodhātuniddese “yaṃ vā panañña”nti iminā sambhavassa, tejodhātuniddese sarīre pākatikausmāya, vāyodhātuniddese dhamanijālānusaṭassa tattha tattha cammakhīlapīḷakādinibbattakavāyuno saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Samiñjanādinibbattakavātā cittasamuṭṭhānāva. Yadi evaṃ, kathaṃ “purimā pañca catusamuṭṭhānā”ti vacanaṃ? Na hi samiñjanādinibbattakā eva aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā, atha kho tadaññepīti natthi virodho.

By 'by way of movement' (vāyanavasena) is meant by way of impelling, or by way of moving with momentum. Here, by the word 'etc.' in 'belching, hiccups, etc.' (uggārahikkādi), the inclusion of winds that cause actions such as vomiting and sneezing should be understood. By the word 'etc.' in 'feces, urine, etc.' (uccārapassāvādi), the inclusion of those that expel bile, phlegm, lymph, and just plain bad smells, etc., should be understood. Although the word 'belly' (kucchi) is a synonym for the abdomen (udara), since by the word 'koṭṭha' the area within the intestines is meant, the remaining part of the abdomen is here referred to by the word 'belly.' Hence, it is said: 'The winds that dwell in the belly are the winds outside the intestines.' By the word 'etc.' in 'bending, stretching, etc.' (samiñjanapasāraṇādi), all bodily actions such as looking straight ahead, looking sideways, lifting, and stepping are included. By the statement 'in-breaths and out-breaths are mind-originated' (assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānā), it is shown that in-breaths and out-breaths do not occur apart from the body. For there is no possibility of a mind-originated phenomenon existing externally. If that is so, how is the statement 'out-breath is the wind exiting through the nose, touching the tip of the nose for one with a long nose, or the upper lip for others' to be understood? It should be understood that this is said with reference to the occurrence in the manner of exiting of the mind-originated phenomenon, and of the temperature-originated phenomenon that occurs in the continuum. By 'in all cases' (sabbattha), he speaks with reference to the exposition of the three elements: the water element, and so forth. Therein, in the exposition of the water element, by the phrase 'or whatever other...' (yaṃ vā panaññaṃ), the inclusion of semen should be understood; in the exposition of the heat element, the natural heat in the body; in the exposition of the wind element, the inclusion of winds that spread along the network of vessels, producing things like skin-stakes, boils, etc., here and there, should be understood. The winds that produce bending, etc., are only mind-originated. If that is so, how is the statement 'the first five are of fourfold origin' to be understood? For it is not that only the winds that produce bending, etc., are the winds that course through the major and minor limbs; but rather, others also are. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Itīti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Tenāha “vīsatiyā ākārehī”tiādi. Etthāti etasmiṃ vitthārato āgate dhātukammaṭṭhāneti attho. Tena ayaṃ vaṇṇanā na kevalaṃ mahāhatthipadūpamasseva (ma. ni. 1.300 ādayo), atha kho mahārāhulovāda- (ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) dhātuvibhaṅgasuttānampi (ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo) atthasaṃvaṇṇanā hotiyevāti dassitaṃ hoti. Bhāvanānayepi eseva nayo. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “evaṃ rāhulovādadhātuvibhaṅgesupī”ti.

The word 'thus' (iti) refers back to the manner already described. Therefore, he said, 'with twenty aspects,' and so forth. The meaning of 'here' (ettha) is: in this meditation subject of the elements that has been presented in detail. By this, it is shown that this commentary is not merely an explanation of the meaning of the Great Elephant Footprint Simile, but is indeed also an explanation of the meaning of the Great Discourse of Advice to Rāhula and the Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements. In the method of development also, this is the same method. For so it was said: 'Thus also in the Discourse of Advice to Rāhula and the Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements.'

308. Bhāvanānayeti bhāvanāya naye. Yena kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā ijjhati, tasmiṃ bhāvanāvidhimhīti attho. Etthāti dhātukammaṭṭhāne. Yasmā yesaṃ “tikkhapañño nātitikkhapañño”ti imesaṃ duvidhānaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ dvidhā āgataṃ dvidhā desitaṃ, tasmā kammaṭṭhānābhinivesopi tesaṃ dvidhāva icchitabboti taṃ tāva dassetuṃ “tikkhapaññassa bhikkhuno”tiādi [M 1.0432] āraddhaṃ. Lomā pathavīdhātūtīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho[V 1.0405]. Evaṃ vitthārato dhātupariggahoti “kesā pathavīdhātu, lomā pathavīdhātū”tiādinā evaṃ dvācattālīsāya ākārehi vitthārato dhātukammaṭṭhānapariggaho. Papañcatoti dandhato saṇikato. Yaṃ thaddhalakkhaṇanti kesādīsu yaṃ thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ kakkhaḷabhāvo. Yaṃ ābandhanalakkhaṇantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ manasi karototi vatthuṃ anāmasitvā evaṃ lakkhaṇamattato manasikāraṃ pavattentassa. Assāti tikkhapaññassa. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti yogakammassa pavattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ tadeva lakkhaṇaṃ vibhūtaṃ hoti, tassa vā lakkhaṇassa suṭṭhu upaṭṭhānato taṃ ārabbha pavattamānaṃ manasikārasaṅkhātaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ vibhūtaṃ visadaṃ hoti, tikkhapaññassa indriyapāṭavena saṃkhittarucibhāvato. Sabbaso mandapaññassa bhāvanāva na ijjhatīti āha “nātitikkhapaññassā”ti. Evaṃ manasi karototi vuttanayena saṅkhepato manasi karoto. Andhakāraṃ avibhūtaṃ hotīti anupaṭṭhānato andhaṃ viya karontaṃ apākaṭaṃ hoti kammaṭṭhānanti yojanā. Purimanayenāti “kesā pathavīdhātū”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayena. Vatthuāmasanena vitthārato manasi karontassa pākaṭaṃ hoti kammaṭṭhānaṃ, nātitikkhapaññassa akhippanisantitāya vitthārarucibhāvato.

308. The phrase 'bhāvanānaye' means 'in the method (naye) of development (bhāvanāya)'. The meaning is: in that method of development by which the development of the meditation subject succeeds. 'Ettha' (here) means in the meditation subject of the elements. Because this meditation subject was taught in two ways according to two types of individuals—'one of sharp wisdom' and 'one not of overly sharp wisdom'—therefore, the initial application to the meditation subject should also be desired as twofold for them. To show this, the passage beginning with 'for a bhikkhu of sharp wisdom' is introduced. Here, in the phrase 'lomā pathavīdhātūti' (body hair is the earth element), the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on'. Thus, 'the detailed comprehension of the elements' is the detailed comprehension of the element meditation subject through forty-two aspects, beginning with 'head hair is the earth element, body hair is the earth element'. 'Papañcato' (diffusely) means slowly, gradually. 'Yaṃ thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ' (the characteristic of hardness) means the characteristic of hardness, which is roughness, in head hair and so on. The same method applies to 'yaṃ ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ' (the characteristic of cohesion), and so forth. 'Evaṃ manasi karoti' (attends in this way) refers to one who directs attention merely to the characteristic in this way, without touching upon the object. 'Assa' (for him) means for the one of sharp wisdom. 'Kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti' (the meditation subject becomes clear) means: either that very characteristic, which is the basis for the yogic practice, becomes evident; or, due to the clear manifestation of that characteristic, the meditation subject called 'attention' that proceeds taking that characteristic as its object becomes evident and distinct, because of the sharpness of the faculties and the preference for brevity of one with sharp wisdom. Because for one of dull wisdom development does not succeed at all, it says 'for one not of overly sharp wisdom'. 'Evaṃ manasi karoti' (attends in this way) refers to one who attends briefly in the manner described. 'Andhakāraṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti' (it becomes dark, unmanifest): the connection is that due to its non-appearance, the meditation subject becomes unclear, as if making one blind. 'Purimanayena' (in the former method) means in the way previously stated, beginning with 'head hair is the earth element'. For one who attends in detail by touching upon the object, the meditation subject becomes clear; this is for one not of overly sharp wisdom, due to an inability to investigate quickly and a preference for detail.

Idāni yathāvuttamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā dvīsu bhikkhūsū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha peyyālamukhanti peyyālapāḷiyā mukhabhūtaṃ dvārabhūtaṃ ādito vāraṃ, vāradvayaṃ vā. Vitthāretvāti anavasesato sajjhāyitvā. Ubhatokoṭivasenevāti tassa tassa vārassa ādiantaggahaṇavaseneva. Oṭṭhapariyāhatamattanti oṭṭhānaṃ samphusanamattaṃ. Yathā ganthaparivattane tikkhapaññassa bhikkhuno saṅkhepo ruccati, na vitthāro. Itarassa ca vitthāro ruccati, na saṅkhepo, evaṃ bhāvanānayepīti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, to clarify the aforesaid meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with 'Just as with two bhikkhus' is stated. Therein, 'peyyālamukhaṃ' (the beginning of the repetition) means the initial section, or two sections, which serve as the opening or doorway of the repetitive passage (peyyālapāḷi). 'Vitthāretvā' (expanding) means reciting it completely without leaving anything out. 'Ubhatokoṭivaseneva' (just by the two ends) means just by grasping the beginning and end of each respective section.
