'Oṭṭhapariyāhatamattaṃ' (merely the touching of the lips) means just the contact of the lips. Just as, in reviewing the texts, a bhikkhu with keen wisdom prefers brevity, not elaboration, while the other prefers elaboration, not brevity, so too is it in the method of development. This should be understood as the application of the simile.

Tasmāti yasmā tikkhapaññassa saṅkhepo, nātitikkhapaññassa ca vitthāro sappāyo, tasmā. Yasmā kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitukāmassa sīlavisodhanādipubbakiccaṃ icchitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbākārasampannaṃ heṭṭhā vuttamevāti idha na āmaṭṭhaṃ. Yasmā pana vivekaṭṭhakāyassa, vivekaṭṭhacittasseva ca bhāvanā ijjhati[M 1.0433], na itarassa, tasmā tadubhayaṃ dassento “rahogatena paṭisallīnenā”ti āha. Tattha rahogatenāti rahasi gatena, ekākinā bhāvanānukūlaṭṭhānaṃ upagatenāti attho. Paṭisallīnenāti pati pati puthuttārammaṇato cittaṃ nisedhetvā kammaṭṭhāne sallīnena, tattha saṃsiliṭṭhacittenāti attho. Sakalampi attano rūpakāyaṃ āvajjetvāti uddhaṃ pādatalā, adho kesamatthakā, tiriyaṃ tacapariyantaṃ sabbampi [V 1.0406] attano karajakāyaṃ dhātuvasena manasi karonto yasmā cātumahābhūtiko ayaṃ kāyo, tasmā “atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū”ti catumahābhūtavasena samannāharitvāti attho. Idāni tāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ lakkhaṇato, upaṭṭhānākārato ca manasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “yo imasmiṃ kāye”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Therefore: because brevity is suitable for one of sharp wisdom, and detail for one not of overly sharp wisdom, therefore. Because for one who wishes to apply themself to a meditation subject, the preliminary duties beginning with the purification of virtue should be desired, and that, being complete in all aspects, has already been stated below, it is not touched upon here. But because development succeeds only for one whose body is in seclusion and whose mind is in seclusion, not for another, therefore, to show both of these, it is said: 'by one who has gone into solitude, withdrawn' (rahogatena paṭisallīnena). Therein, 'rahogatena' (gone into solitude) means having gone to a solitary place, alone, having reached a location favorable for development; this is the meaning. 'Paṭisallīnena' (withdrawn) means having restrained the mind from various individual objects and being absorbed in the meditation subject; the meaning is having a mind that clings well to that. 'Having reflected on one's entire physical body' (sakalampi attano rūpakāyaṃ āvajjetvā) means attending to one’s own entire body born of action in terms of the elements—upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the tips of the hair, and across, bounded by the skin—and the meaning is comprehending it in terms of the four great elements thus: 'Because this body is composed of the four great elements, therefore, in this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element'. Now, to explain the method of attention to those elements in terms of their characteristic and their mode of manifestation, the passage beginning with 'whatever in this body' is stated.

Tattha thaddhabhāvoti lakkhaṇamāha. Thaddhattalakkhaṇā hi pathavīdhātu. Kharabhāvoti upaṭṭhānākāraṃ, ñāṇena gahetabbākāranti attho. Dravabhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ āpodhātuyā paggharaṇasabhāvattā. Ābandhanaṃ upaṭṭhānākāro. Uṇhabhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ tejodhātuyā usmāsabhāvattā. Paripācanaṃ upaṭṭhānākāro. Vitthambhanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātuyā upatthambhanasabhāvattā. Samudīraṇaṃ upaṭṭhānākāro, upaṭṭhānākāro ca nāma dhātūnaṃ sakiccakaraṇavasena ñāṇassa vibhūtākāro. Kasmā panettha ubhayaggahaṇaṃ? Puggalajjhāsayato. Ekaccassa hi dhātuyo manasi karontassa tā sabhāvato gahetabbataṃ gacchanti, ekaccassa sakiccakaraṇato, yo rasoti vuccati. Tatrāyaṃ yogī dhātuyo manasi karonto ādito paccekaṃ salakkhaṇato, sarasatopi pariggaṇhāti. Tenāha “yo imasmiṃ kāye thaddhabhāvo vā kharabhāvo vā…pe… evaṃ saṃkhittena dhātuyo pariggahetvā”ti. Tattha pariggahetvāti pariggāhakabhūtena ñāṇena dhātuyo lakkhaṇato, rasato vā paricchijja gahetvā. Ayaṃ tāva saṃkhittato bhāvanānaye kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso.

Therein, by 'the state of hardness' (thaddhabhāvo) he states the characteristic. Indeed, the earth element has hardness as its characteristic. By 'the state of roughness' (kharabhāvo) he states the mode of manifestation; the meaning is the aspect to be apprehended by knowledge. The state of fluidity is the characteristic of the water element, due to its nature of flowing. Cohesion is the mode of manifestation. The state of heat is the characteristic of the fire element, due to its nature of warmth. Maturing is the mode of manifestation. Supporting is the characteristic of the wind element, due to its nature of upholding. Impelling is the mode of manifestation. The mode of manifestation, it should be known, is the distinct appearance to knowledge of the elements in terms of their performance of function. Why here is there a twofold apprehension? Due to the inclinations of individuals. Indeed, for some, when attending to the elements, they become apprehendable by their intrinsic nature; for others, by their performance of function, which is called 'function' (rasa). Therein, this yogi, attending to the elements, at the outset comprehends them individually by their own characteristic and also by their own function. Therefore, he said: 'whatever in this body is the state of hardness or the state of roughness... (etc.)... having thus comprehended the elements in brief'. Therein, 'having comprehended' means having grasped the elements after defining them either by their characteristic or by their function, with the knowledge that is the means of comprehension. This, for now, is the initial application to the meditation subject in the method of development, in brief.

Evaṃ pana dhātuyo pariggahetvā “atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu thaddhabhāvo vā kharabhāvo vā, āpodhātu dravabhāvo vā ābandhanabhāvo vā, tejodhātu uṇhabhāvo vā paripācanabhāvo vā, vāyodhātu vitthambhanabhāvo [M 1.0434] vā samudīraṇabhāvo vā”ti evaṃ lakkhaṇādīhi saddhiṃyeva dhātuyo manasi karontena kālasatampi kālasahassampi punappunaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ, takkāhataṃ vitakkapariyāhataṃ kātabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ manasi karoto yaṃ lakkhaṇādīsu supākaṭaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, tadeva gahetvā itaraṃ vissajjetvā tena saddhiṃ “pathavīdhātu āpodhātū”tiādinā manasikāro pavattetabbo. Evaṃ manasi karontena hi anupubbato, nātisīghato, nātisaṇikato, vikkhepapaṭibāhanato, paṇṇattisamatikkamanato, anupaṭṭhānamuñcanato, lakkhaṇato, tayo ca suttantāti imehi dasahākārehi manasikārakosallaṃ anuṭṭhātabbaṃ.

Furthermore, having thus comprehended the elements, one should attend to them together with their characteristics and so on, thinking: 'In this body there is the earth element, the state of hardness or roughness; the water element, the state of fluidity or cohesion; the fire element, the state of heat or maturation; the air element, the state of supporting or moving.' This should be adverted to and attended to again and again, a hundred times, a thousand times; it should be made struck by reasoning and thoroughly pervaded by thought. For one attending in this way, whatever among the characteristics and so on appears, having become very clear, one should take hold of just that. Abandoning the other, one should proceed with attention together with that in the manner of 'earth element, water element,' and so on. Indeed, for one attending in this way, skill in attention should be developed through these ten modes: gradually, not too quickly, not too slowly, by warding off distraction, by transcending concepts, by abandoning what is not manifest, by way of the characteristic, and by the three suttas.

Tattha anupubbatoti anupaṭipāṭito ācariyassa santike uggahitapaṭipāṭito, sā ca desanāpaṭipāṭiyeva[V 1.0407]. Evaṃ anupubbato manasi karontenāpi nātisīghato manasi kātabbaṃ. Atisīghato manasi karoto hi aparāparaṃ kammaṭṭhānamanasikāro nirantaraṃ pavattati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ pana avibhūtaṃ hoti, na visesaṃ āvahati. Tasmā nātisīghato manasi kātabbaṃ. Yathā ca nātisīghato, evaṃ nātisaṇikatopi. Atisaṇikato manasi karoto hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ na gacchati, visesādhigamassa paccayo na hoti. Atisīghaṃ atisaṇikañca maggaṃ gacchantā purisā ettha nidassetabbā. Vikkhepapaṭibāhanatoti kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cetaso vikkhepo paṭibāhitabbo. Bahiddhā vikkhepe hi sati kammaṭṭhānā parihāyati paridhaṃsati. Ekapadikamaggagāmī puriso cettha nidassetabbo. Paṇṇattisamatikkamanatoti “yā ayaṃ pathavīdhātū”tiādikā paṇṇatti, taṃ atikkamitvā lakkhaṇesu eva cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ.

Herein, 'gradually' means in sequence, in the sequence learned from the teacher; and that sequence is indeed the teaching sequence. Thus, even when attending to it gradually, one should attend to it not too quickly. For if one attends too quickly, successive attention to the meditation subject proceeds uninterruptedly, but the meditation subject remains unclear and does not bring about any special attainment. Therefore, one should attend to it not too quickly. And just as one should not attend too quickly, so too one should not attend too slowly. For if one attends too slowly, the meditation subject does not reach completion, and it is not a condition for the attainment of any special distinction. Men going on a road too quickly and too slowly should be shown as an example here. 'Warding off distraction' means that the distraction of the mind towards various external objects, abandoning the meditation subject, should be prevented. For when there is external distraction, one declines and falls away from the meditation subject. A man going on a path one footstep wide should be shown as an example here. 'Transcending concepts' means that having transcended concepts such as "this is the earth element," the mind should be established only on the characteristics.

Evaṃ paṇṇattiṃ vijahitvā kakkhaḷalakkhaṇādīsu eva manasikāraṃ pavattentassa lakkhaṇāni supākaṭāni suvibhūtāni hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Tassevaṃ punappunaṃ manasikāravasena cittaṃ āsevanaṃ labhati. Sabbo rūpakāyo dhātumattato upaṭṭhāti suñño nissatto nijjīvo yantaṃ viya yantasuttena aparāparaṃ parivattamāno. Sace pana bahiddhāpi manasikāraṃ upasaṃharati, athassa āhiṇḍantā manussatiracchānādayo sattākāraṃ vijahitvā [M 1.0435] dhātusamūhavaseneva upaṭṭhahanti, tehi kariyamānā kiriyā dhātumayena yantena pavattiyamānā hutvā upaṭṭhāti, tehi ajjhohariyamānaṃ pānabhojanādi dhātusaṅghāte pakkhippamāno dhātusaṅghāto viya upaṭṭhāti. Athassa tathā laddhāsevanampi cittaṃ yadi accāraddhavīriyatāya uddhaccavasena vā atilīnavīriyatāya kosajjavasena vā bhāvanāvidhiṃ na otareyya, tadā adhicittasuttaṃ (a. ni. 3.103), anuttarasītibhāvasuttaṃ (a. ni. 6.85), bojjhaṅgasuttanti (saṃ. ni. 5.194-195) imesu tīsu suttesu āgatanayena vīriyasamādhiyojanā kātabbā. Tena vuttaṃ “tayo ca suttantā”ti. Evaṃ pana vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā tasmiṃyeva lakkhaṇe manasikāraṃ pavattentassa yadā saddhādīni indriyāni laddhasamatāni suvisadāni pavattanti, tadā asaddhiyādīnaṃ dūrībhāvena sātisayaṃ thāmappattehi sattahi balehi laddhūpatthambhāni vitakkādīni jhānaṅgāni paṭutarāni hutvā pātubhavanti, tesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāniyeva honti saddhiṃ tadekaṭṭhehi pāpadhammehi. Ettāvatā cānena upacārajjhānaṃ samadhigataṃ hoti dhātulakkhaṇārammaṇaṃ[V 1.0408]. Tena vuttaṃ “punappunaṃ pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti…pe… upacāramatto samādhi uppajjatī”ti.

Thus, having abandoned concepts, for one who makes attention proceed only on the characteristics of hardness and so forth, the characteristics appear, having become very clear and very distinct. Through this repeated attention, the mind obtains familiarity. The entire physical body appears as mere elements—empty, not a being, lifeless—like a machine, revolving successively by means of its strings. Furthermore, if one directs attention externally as well, then for that person, wandering humans, animals, and so on, having abandoned the appearance of a being, appear only by way of a collection of elements. The actions done by them appear as if being set in motion by a machine made of elements. The drinks, food, and so on consumed by them appear like a collection of elements being put into a collection of elements. Then, if the mind of that person, though having gained such familiarity, should not enter the path of development due to having excessively aroused energy, by way of restlessness, or due to having very sluggish energy, by way of laziness, then the yoking of energy and concentration should be done in the manner that has come down in these three suttas: the Adhicittasutta, the Anuttarasītibhāvasutta, and the Bojjhaṅgasutta. For that reason it was said, "and the three suttas." Furthermore, having thus balanced energy and concentration, for one who makes attention proceed on that very characteristic, when the faculties of faith and so forth proceed, having obtained balance and being very pure, then, due to the farness of faithlessness and so on, the jhāna factors of initial thought and so on, having obtained support from the seven powers which have reached exceeding strength, manifest, having become sharper. Due to their being the direct opposite, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, together with unwholesome states that have the same foundation. And by this much, access concentration with the characteristics of the elements as its object is well attained by this person. For that reason it was said, "Again and again, 'earth element, water element'... and so on... concentration that is mere access arises."

Tattha dhātumattatoti visesanivattiattho matta-saddo. Tena yaṃ ito bāhirakā, lokiyamahājano ca “satto jīvo”tiādikaṃ visesaṃ imasmiṃ attabhāve avijjamānaṃ vikappanāmatteneva samāropenti, taṃ nivatteti. Tenevāha “nissattato nijjīvato”ti. Āvajjitabbanti samannāharitabbaṃ. Manasi kātabbanti punappunaṃ bhāvanāvasena dhātumattato dhātulakkhaṇaṃ manasi ṭhapetabbaṃ. Paccavekkhitabbanti tadeva dhātulakkhaṇaṃ pati pati avekkhitabbaṃ, bhāvanāsiddhena ñāṇacakkhunā aparāparaṃ paccakkhato passitabbaṃ.

Therein, in the phrase 'mere elements,' the word 'mere' has the meaning of eliminating a special quality. By it, whatever special quality such as 'a being,' 'a soul,' which does not exist in this individual existence, that outsiders from this Dispensation and the great mass of worldly people superimpose merely by way of conjecture, that it eliminates. For that very reason, it was said 'as being without a being, without a life-principle.' 'Should be adverted to' means it should be well and repeatedly brought to mind. 'Should be attended to' means that again and again, by way of cultivation, the characteristic of the elements as mere elements should be placed in the mind. 'Should be reviewed' means that very characteristic of the elements should be looked at intently, individually, and repeatedly; it should be seen successively and directly with the eye of wisdom accomplished through cultivation.

Tassevaṃ vāyamamānassāti tassa yogino evaṃ vuttappakārena bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjantassa, tattha ca bhāvanāanuyoge sakkaccakāritāya, sātaccakāritāya, sappāyasevitāya, samathanimittasallakkhaṇena, bojjhaṅgānaṃ anupavattanena, kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhavuttitāya, antarā saṅkocaṃ anāpajjantena bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ussoḷhiyaṃ avaṭṭhānena [M 1.0436] sammadeva vāyāmaṃ payogaṃ parakkamaṃ pavattentassa. Dhātuppabhedāvabhāsanapaññāpariggahitoti pathavīādīnaṃ dhātūnaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇāvabhāsanena avabhāsanakiccāya bhāvanāpaññāya ādimajjhapariyosānesu avijahanena sabbato gahito mahaggatabhāvaṃ appattatāya upacāramatto sikhāppatto kāmāvacarasamādhi uppajjati. Upacārasamādhīti ca ruḷhīvasena veditabbaṃ. Appanaṃ hi upecca cārī samādhi upacārasamādhi, appanā cettha natthi. Tādisassa pana samādhissa samānalakkhaṇatāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Kasmā panettha appanā na hotīti? Tattha kāraṇamāha “sabhāvadhammārammaṇattā”ti. Sabhāvadhamme hi tassa gambhīrabhāvato asati bhāvanāvisese appanājhānaṃ na uppajjati, lokuttaraṃ pana jhānaṃ visuddhibhāvanānukkamavasena, āruppaṃ ārammaṇātikkamabhāvanāvasena appanāppattaṃ hotīti maraṇānussatiniddese (visuddhi. 1.177) vuttovāyamattho.

‘While he is striving thus’: for that yogi who is practicing meditation in the manner thus described, and in that practice of meditation—by acting respectfully, acting persistently, resorting to what is suitable, properly discerning the sign of serenity, maintaining the factors of enlightenment, maintaining an attitude of non-concern for body and life, not shrinking back in the middle, having made an effort in meditation and standing firm with extreme exertion—thus rightly causing effort, endeavor, and exertion to arise. ‘Grasped by the wisdom that illuminates the analysis of elements’: because it has not reached the exalted state, a sense-sphere concentration that is merely access and has reached its peak arises, which is grasped from all sides by the meditation-wisdom whose function is to illuminate through the illumination of the inherent characteristics of the elements such as earth, etc., and which does not abandon it at the beginning, middle, and end. And it should be known as ‘access concentration’ by way of conventional usage. For, concentration that proceeds by approaching absorption is access concentration, and here there is no absorption. However, it is so called because of having a similar characteristic to such a concentration. Why is there no absorption here? Therein, the reason is stated: ‘Because its object is a natural phenomenon.’ For, due to the profundity of a natural phenomenon, absorption-jhāna does not arise when there is no special development. However, supramundane jhāna reaches absorption by means of the sequence of the development of purification, and the formless attainment reaches absorption by means of the development of transcending the object. This meaning has been stated in the exposition on mindfulness of death.

Evaṃ rūpakāye avisesena catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ pariggaṇhanavasena dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā idāni tattha aṭṭhiādīnaṃ vinibbhujanavasena saṅkhepato sutte āgataṃ dhātumanasikāravidhiṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ye ime cattāro koṭṭhāsā vuttāti sambandho. Yathāpaccayaṃ ṭhitā sannivesavisiṭṭhā kaṭṭhavallitiṇamattikāyo upādāya yathā agārasamaññā, na tattha [V 1.0409] koci agāro nāma atthi, evaṃ yathāpaccayaṃ sannivesavisiṭṭhāni pavattamānāni aṭṭhinhārumaṃsacammāni paṭicca sarīrasamaññā, na ettha koci attā jīvo. Kevalaṃ tehi parivāritamākāsamattanti dasseti. Desanā sattasuññatāsandassanaparāti imamatthaṃ vibhāvento “nissattabhāvadassanattha”ntiādimāha. Tattha aṭṭhiñca paṭiccāti paṇhikaṭṭhikādibhedaṃ paṭipāṭiyā ussitaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ atirekatisatabhedaṃ aṭṭhiṃ upādāya. Nhāruñcāti tameva aṭṭhisaṅghāṭaṃ ābandhitvā ṭhitaṃ navasatappabhedaṃ nhāruṃ. Maṃsanti tameva aṭṭhisaṅghāṭaṃ anulimpitvā ṭhitaṃ navapesisatappabhedaṃ maṃsaṃ. Cammanti macchikapattakacchāyāya chaviyā sañchāditaṃ sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ bahalacammaṃ paṭicca upādāya. Sabbattha ca-saddo samuccayattho. Ākāso parivāritoti yathā bhittipādādivasena ṭhapitaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ, tasseva ābandhanavalli, anulepanamattikā, chādanatiṇanti etāni kaṭṭhādīni anto, bahi ca parivāretvā ṭhito ākāso [M 1.0437] agārantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, gehanti paṇṇattiṃ labhati, evameva yathāvuttāni aṭṭhiādīni anto, bahi ca parivāretvā ṭhito ākāso tāneva aṭṭhiādīni upādāya rūpantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, sarīranti vohāraṃ labhati. Yathā ca kaṭṭhādīni paṭicca saṅkhaṃ gataṃ agāraṃ loke “khattiyagehaṃ, brāhmaṇageha”nti vuccati, evamidampi “khattiyasarīraṃ brāhmaṇasarīra”nti voharīyati, natthettha koci satto vā jīvo vāti adhippāyo.

Having thus shown the meditation subject on the elements by way of comprehending the four elements in the physical body without distinction, now, in order to show the method of attention to the elements that comes in the Sutta in brief, by way of analyzing the bones and so forth, the passage beginning ‘Or else…’ is started. Herein, the connection is with ‘these four parts that were mentioned.’ Just as, depending on conditions, from wood, vines, grass, and clay that are established and distinctively arranged, there is the designation ‘house’—though no thing called a ‘house’ exists therein—so too, depending on the bones, sinews, flesh, and skin that are proceeding, established, and distinctively arranged according to conditions, there is the designation ‘body.’ Here, there is no self or living being. It is shown that it is merely space surrounded by them. This discourse is chiefly for showing the emptiness of a being; clarifying this meaning, he said what begins with ‘for the purpose of seeing the state of non-being.’ Herein, ‘depending on the bones’ refers to the over three hundred kinds of bones, such as the heel bone, etc., that stand erected in sequence. ‘And the sinews’ refers to the nine hundred kinds of sinews that stand binding that very collection of bones. ‘The flesh’ refers to the nine hundred pieces of flesh that stand plastering that very collection of bones. ‘The skin’ refers to the thick skin that covers the entire body, which is itself covered by the epidermis that has the likeness of a fish's scale. The word ‘and’ in all places has the meaning of collection. ‘Space is surrounded’ means that just as the space that stands surrounded inside and out by these things—wood placed by means of walls and posts, the vines for binding it, the clay for plastering, and the grass for thatching—is reckoned as a ‘house’ and gets the designation ‘home’; just so, the space that stands surrounded inside and out by the aforementioned bones, etc., depending on those very bones, etc., is reckoned as ‘form’ and gets the designation ‘body’. And just as a house, which is reckoned depending on wood, etc., is called in the world ‘a khattiya's house’ or ‘a brahmin's house,’ so too this is designated ‘a khattiya's body’ or ‘a brahmin's body.’ The intention is that no being or life exists herein.

Teti te cattāro koṭṭhāse vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvāti yojanā. Taṃtaṃantarānusārināti aṭṭhinhārūnaṃ nhārumaṃsānaṃ maṃsacammānanti tesaṃ tesaṃ koṭṭhāsānaṃ vivarānupātinā ñāṇasaṅkhātena hatthena. Vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvāti anekakkhattuṃ viniveṭhetvā. Atha vā vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvāti paccekaṃ aṭṭhiādīnaṃ antarānusārinā ñāṇahatthena vinibbhogaṃ katvā. Etesūti sakalampi attano rūpakāyaṃ catudhā katvā vibhattesu yathāvuttesu aṭṭhiādīsu catūsu koṭṭhāsesu. Purimanayenevāti “yo imasmiṃ kāye thaddhabhāvo vā”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayeneva. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ bhāvanāvidhānaṃ, taṃ anantaranaye vuttākāreneva vattabbaṃ.

The construction is: ‘those four parts, having divided and divided them.’ ‘Following each of their intervals’: with the hand called knowledge that follows the openings of those respective parts—of bones and sinews, of sinews and flesh, of flesh and skin. ‘Having divided and divided’: having unwrapped them many times. Or else, ‘having divided and divided’: having made a separation of each of the bones, etc., with the hand of knowledge that follows their interior. ‘Among these’: among these four aforementioned parts—bones, etc.—after having divided one's entire physical body into four. ‘By the previous method’: by the method previously stated, beginning with ‘Whatever in this body is hardness…’ etc. As for the method of development that should be stated here, it should be understood in the same manner as stated in the immediately preceding method.

309. Vitthārato āgate pana “catudhātuvavatthāne”ti ānetvā yojanā. Evaṃ idāni vuccamānākārena veditabbo bhāvanānayo. “Dvācattālīsāya ākārehi dhātuyo uggaṇhitvā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu ādito dvattiṃsākārā dhātuyo na hontīti? Vatthusīsena dhātūnaṃyeva uggahetabbattā [V 1.0410] nāyaṃ doso. Vuttappakāreti “gocaragāmato nātidūranāccāsannatādīhi pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgate”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.53) vuttappakāre. Katasabbakiccenāti palibodhupacchedādikaṃ kataṃ sabbakiccaṃ etenāti katasabbakicco, tenassa sīlavisodhanādi pana kammaṭṭhānuggahaṇato pageva siddhaṃ hotīti dasseti. Sasambhārasaṅkhepatoti sambharīyanti etena buddhivohārāti sambhāro, tannimittaṃ. Kiṃ panetaṃ? Pathavīādi. Kesādīsu hi vīsatiyā ākāresu “pathavī”ti buddhivohārā pathavīnimittakā thaddhataṃ upādāya pavattanato. Tasmā [M 1.0438] tattha pathavīsambhāro nāma savisesāya tassā atthitāya kesādayo saha sambhārehīti sasambhārā. Āpokoṭṭhāsādīsupi eseva nayo. Sasambhārānaṃ saṅkhepo sasambhārasaṅkhepo, tato sasambhārasaṅkhepato bhāvetabbanti yojanā. Saṅkhepato vīsatiyā, dvādasasu, catūsu, chasu ca koṭṭhāsesu yathākkamaṃ pathavīādikā catasso dhātuyo pariggahetvā dhātuvavatthānaṃ sasambhārasaṅkhepato bhāvanā. Tenāha “idha bhikkhu vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesū”tiādi.

309. Furthermore, regarding that which is presented in detail, the connection should be made by bringing in the phrase 'in the analysis of the four elements.' Thus, the method of development should be understood in the manner now being explained. Why is it said, 'having learned the elements by means of forty-two aspects'? Is it not so that from the beginning the thirty-two aspects are not the elements? Because, by way of the subject matter, only the elements themselves are to be learned, this is not a fault. 'In the stated manner' refers to the manner stated in the passage (Vism. 1.53) beginning, 'in a dwelling endowed with the five factors, such as not being too far or too near the alms-resort village.' 'By one who has completed all duties' means: all duties, such as the cutting off of impediments, have been completed by him, thus he is 'one who has completed all duties.' By this, it is shown that for him, the purification of virtue and so on has already been accomplished even before taking up the meditation subject. 'By way of summarization with constituents' (`sasambhārasaṅkhepato`): By this, intellectual understanding and verbal expression are produced; therefore, it is called a 'constituent' (`sambhāro`). It is the cause for them. What is this? It is earth, etc. Indeed, in the twenty aspects beginning with hair, the intellectual understanding and verbal expression 'earth' have earth as their cause, because they arise by depending on hardness. Therefore, therein, the earth element is called a 'constituent.' Because of its existence with its specific quality, the aspects beginning with hair, etc., exist 'together with the constituents' (`saha sambhārehi`); therefore, they are called 'with constituents' (`sasambhārā`). The same method applies to the parts of the water element, etc. The summarization of those things that are 'with constituents' is `sasambhārasaṅkhepo`. From that, the connection is: 'it should be developed by way of summarization with constituents.' The development by way of summarization with constituents is the analysis of the elements by grasping the four elements—earth, etc.—respectively in the twenty, twelve, four, and six parts. Therefore, he said, 'Here, a monk, in the twenty parts,' etc.

Sasambhāravibhattitoti sasambhārānaṃ kesādīnaṃ vibhāgato kesādike vīsati koṭṭhāse pubbe viya ekajjhaṃ aggahetvā vibhāgato pathavīdhātubhāvena vavatthāpanaṃ. Āpokoṭṭhāsādīsupi eseva nayo. Salakkhaṇasaṅkhepatoti lakkhīyati etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, dhammānaṃ sabhāvo, idha pana thaddhatādi. Tasmā thaddhalakkhaṇādivantatāya saha lakkhaṇehīti salakkhaṇā, kesādayo dvācattālīsa ākārā. Tesaṃ saṅkhepato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kesādike vīsati koṭṭhāse ekajjhaṃ gahetvā tattha thaddhatādikaṃ catubbidhampi lakkhaṇaṃ vavatthapetvā bhāvanā salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato bhāvanā. Esa nayo āpokoṭṭhāsādīsupi. Salakkhaṇavibhattitoti thaddhalakkhaṇādinā salakkhaṇānaṃ kesādīnaṃ vibhāgato kesādīsu dvācattālīsāya ākāresu paccekaṃ thaddhatādīnaṃ catunnaṃ catunnaṃ lakkhaṇānaṃ vavatthāpanavasena bhāvanā.

By way of analysis with constituents (`sasambhāravibhattito`): This is the determination, as the earth element, of the twenty parts beginning with hair, etc., which are 'with constituents,' by analyzing them—not taking them together as one, as before. The same method applies to the parts of the water element, etc. By way of summarization with characteristics (`salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato`): That by which one marks is a 'characteristic' (`lakkhaṇa`); it is the intrinsic nature (`sabhāva`) of phenomena. Here, however, it is hardness, etc. Therefore, because they possess the characteristic of hardness, etc., they exist 'together with characteristics' (`saha lakkhaṇehi`), hence they are called `salakkhaṇā`; this refers to the forty-two aspects beginning with hair. By way of their summarization. This is what is meant: taking the twenty parts beginning with hair together as one, and therein determining the fourfold characteristic of hardness, etc.—this is development by way of summarization with characteristics. This same method applies to the parts of the water element, etc. By way of analysis with characteristics (`salakkhaṇavibhattito`): This is the development by way of determining, for each of the forty-two aspects beginning with hair, the four characteristics such as hardness; this is done by analyzing the parts beginning with hair, which are 'with characteristics' due to the characteristic of hardness and so on.

Evaṃ catūhi ākārehi uddiṭṭhaṃ bhāvanānayaṃ niddisituṃ “kathaṃ sasambhārasaṅkhepato bhāvetī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Ettha ca yathā tikkhapañño puggalo tikkhatāya paropariyattasabbhāvato tikkhindriyamudindriyatāvasena duvidhoti. Tattha tikkhindriyassa vasena saṅkhepato paṭhamanayo vutto, mudindriyassa vasena dutiyo. Evaṃ nātitikkhapaññopi puggaloti. Tattha yo visadindriyo puggalo, tassa vasena sasambhārasaṅkhepato, salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato ca bhāvanānayo niddiṭṭho. Yo pana nātivisadindriyo, tassa vasena sasambhāravibhattito, salakkhaṇavibhattito ca bhāvanānayo niddiṭṭhoti [V 1.0411] veditabbo. Tassa evaṃ vavatthāpayato eva dhātuyo pākaṭā honti savisesaṃ dhātūnaṃ pariggahitattā. Bhāvanāvidhānaṃ panettha heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Thus, to explain in detail the method of development that was indicated in brief in four ways, the passage beginning, 'How does one develop by way of summarization with constituents?' was commenced. And here, just as a person of sharp wisdom—due to the manifest existence of maturity or immaturity in their sharpness—is of two kinds by way of being sharp-facultied or dull-facultied, so therein, for the one with sharp faculties, the first method is stated by way of summary, and for the one with dull faculties, the second. Likewise, a person not of very sharp wisdom is also of two kinds. Therein, for the person who has clear faculties, the method of development is explained by way of summarization with constituents and by way of summarization with characteristics. But for the one whose faculties are not very clear, the method of development is explained by way of analysis with constituents and by way of analysis with characteristics; thus it should be understood. For one determining thus, the elements become manifest, because the elements have been grasped with their specific qualities. The procedure of development here should be understood according to the method stated previously.

310. Yassāti [M 1.0439] nātivisadindriyaṃ puggalaṃ sandhāya vadati. Evaṃ bhāvayatoti sasambhārasaṅkhepato bhāventassa. Yena vidhinā uggahetvā kusalo hoti, so sattavidho vidhi “uggahakosalla”nti vuccati, tannibbattaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ. Evaṃ manasikārakosallampi veditabbaṃ. Dvattiṃsākāreti dhātumanasikāravasena pariggahite kesādike dvattiṃsavidhe koṭṭhāse. “Dvattiṃsākāre”ti ca idaṃ tejavāyukoṭṭhāsesu vaṇṇādivasena vavatthānassa abhāvato vuttaṃ. Sabbaṃ tattha vuttavidhānaṃ kātabbanti “vacasā manasā”tiādinā vuttauggahakosalluddesato paṭṭhāya yāva “anupubbamuñcanādivasenā”ti padaṃ, tāva āgataṃ sabbaṃ bhāvanāvidhānaṃ kātabbaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Vaṇṇādivasenāti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena. Ayañca vaṇṇādivasena manasikāro dhātupaṭikkūlavaṇṇamanasikārānaṃ sādhāraṇo pubbabhāgoti nibbattitadhātumanasikārameva dassetuṃ “avasāne evaṃ manasikāro pavattetabbo”ti vuttaṃ.

310. The word `yassa` is spoken in reference to a person whose faculties are not very clear. 'Developing thus' means: for one developing by way of summarization with constituents. The sevenfold method by which one learns and becomes skilled is called 'skill in grasping' (`uggahakosalla`), or the knowledge produced thereby. In the same way, 'skill in attention' (`manasikārakosalla`) should also be understood. 'In the thirty-two aspects' (`dvattiṃsākāre`) means: in the thirty-two kinds of parts beginning with hair, which are comprehended by way of attention to the elements. And this phrase 'in the thirty-two aspects' is said because in the fire-element parts and the air-element parts, there is no determination by way of color, etc. 'All the procedure stated therein should be done' means: all the procedure of development that has been presented, starting from the exposition of the 'skill in grasping' which was stated with 'by speech, by mind,' etc., up to the phrase 'by way of gradual release, etc.,' should be done, should be accomplished. 'By way of color, etc.' means by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. And this attention by way of color, etc., is a preliminary part common to the attention to the elements, the attention to repulsiveness, and the attention to the color kasina. To show only the attention to the elements that has been produced, it is said, 'At the end, attention should be directed thus.'

311. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammāti ete “sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacammaṃ kesā”ti evaṃ vohariyamānā bhūtupādāyadhammā “mayi kesā jātā, mayamettha jātā”ti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇasuññā. Iminā kāraṇassa ca phalassa ca abyāpāratāya dhātumattataṃ sandasseti, tena ca ābhogapaccavekkhaṇānampi evameva abyāpāratā dīpitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi tāni, tesaṃ kāraṇāni ca tathā tathā ābhujitvā, paccavekkhitvā ca uppajjanti, paccayabhāvaṃ vā gacchantīti. Itīti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Acetanoti na cetano, cetanārahito vā. Abyākatoti abyākatarāsipariyāpanno. Suññoti attasuñño. Tato eva nissatto. Thaddhalakkhaṇādhikatāya thaddho. Tato eva pathavīdhātūti evaṃ manasikāro pavattetabboti sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha.

311. ‘These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection’ means this: these phenomena, which are primary elements and derived matter, referred to as ‘the thick skin that wraps around the skull’ and ‘hairs,’ are empty of mutual consideration and reflection, [as if thinking,] ‘Hairs have grown on me,’ or ‘We have grown here.’ By this, it shows the state of being mere elements through the non-activity of the cause and the effect. And by that, it should be understood that consideration and reflection are likewise shown to be non-active. For they and their causes do not arise by being inclined towards and reflected upon in such and such a way, nor do they become conditions. The word ‘iti’ (thus) refers to the manner described. ‘Acetana’ (non-volitional) means not volition, or devoid of volition. ‘Abyākata’ (indeterminate) means included in the group of the indeterminate. ‘Suñña’ (empty) means empty of a self. From that very reason, it is ‘nissatta’ (without a being). ‘Thaddha’ (hard) means it is hard due to the predominance of the characteristic of hardness. From that very reason, it is the ‘pathavīdhātu’ (earth element). The connection is that attention should be directed in this way. So it is in all cases.

312. Suññagāmaṭṭhāneti ettha suññagāmaggahaṇaṃ paramatthato vedakavirahadassanatthaṃ kāyassa.

312. In the phrase ‘in the simile of an empty village,’ the mention of an empty village is for the purpose of showing the body's absence of an experiencer, in an ultimate sense.

313. Madhukaṭṭhiketi madhukabījāni.

313. ‘Madhukaṭṭhika’ means licorice seeds.

314. Gehathambhānaṃ [M 1.0440][V 1.0412] ādhārabhāvena ṭhapitasilāyo pāsāṇaudukkhalakānīti adhippetāni.

314. The stones placed as a base for the house pillars are intended to mean stone mortars.

315. Duggandhādibhāve cassa sadisabhāvadassanatthaṃ allagocammaggahaṇaṃ.

315. Furthermore, the mention of a wet cowhide is for the purpose of showing the similarity of this [human skin] in its state of having a foul smell and so on.

316. Yebhuyyena maṃsapesīnaṃ bahalatāya mahāmattikaggahaṇaṃ.

316. The mention of a large lump of fine clay is mostly due to the thickness of the muscle tissues.

317. Kuṭṭadārūsūti dārukuṭṭikāya kuṭiyā bhittipādabhūtesu kaṭṭhesu.

317. ‘Kuṭṭadārūsu’ refers to the pieces of wood that form the base of the wall of a hut with a wooden wall-base.

318. Paṇhikaṭṭhiādīnaṃ ādhārabhāvo viya gopphakaṭṭhiādīnaṃ ādheyyabhāvopi asamannāhārasiddhoti dassanatthaṃ “paṇhikaṭṭhigopphakaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita”ntiādiṃ vatvā puna “sīsaṭṭhigīvaṭṭhike patiṭṭhita”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

318. To show that just as the state of the heel bone, etc., as a support, so also the state of the ankle bone, etc., as what is supported, is accomplished without deliberation, having said, ‘The heel bone is situated holding up the ankle bone,’ etc., it is then said again, ‘The skull bone is established on the neck bone,’ etc.

319. Sinnavettaggādīsūti seditavettakaḷīrādīsu.

319. ‘Sinnavettaggādīsu’ means on steamed cane shoots and so on.

321. Uraṭṭhisaṅghāṭo pañjarasadisatāya “uraṭṭhipañjara”nti vutto. Tassa athirabhāvadassanatthaṃ jiṇṇasandamānikapañjaraṃ nidassanabhāvena gahitaṃ.

321. The collection of chest bones is called the ‘chest-cage’ due to its resemblance to a cage. To show its unstable nature, a decayed, rickety cage is taken as an illustration.

322. Yamakamaṃsapiṇḍeti maṃsapiṇḍayugaḷe.

322. ‘Yamakamaṃsapiṇḍa’ means a pair of lumps of flesh.

323. Kilomakassa setavaṇṇatāya “pilotikapaliveṭhite”ti pilotikaṃ nidassanabhāvena vuttaṃ. Evameva na vakkahadayāni sakalasarīre ca maṃsaṃ jānātīti ettha na vakkahadayāni jānanti “mayaṃ paṭicchannakilomakena paṭicchannānī”ti, na sakalasarīre ca maṃsaṃ jānāti “ahaṃ paṭicchannakilomakena paṭicchanna”nti yojetabbaṃ.

323. Due to the white color of the pleura, a coarse cloth is mentioned as an illustration in the phrase ‘wrapped in a coarse cloth.’ In the phrase ‘Thus the kidneys and heart and the flesh in the entire body do not know,’ the connection should be made as follows: the kidneys and heart do not know, ‘We are covered by the covering pleura,’ and the flesh in the entire body does not know, ‘I am covered by the covering pleura.’

324. Koṭṭhamatthakapassanti kusūlassa abbhantare matthakapassaṃ.

324. ‘Koṭṭhamatthakapassaṃ’ means the upper side inside a granary.

325. Dvinnaṃ thanānamantareti dvinnaṃ thanappadesānaṃ vemajjhe, thanappadeso ca abbhantaravasena veditabbo.

325. ‘Between the two breasts’ means in the middle of the two breast regions; and the breast region should be understood in terms of the inside.

327. Ekavīsatiantabhogeti [V 1.0413] ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu obhaggobhagge antamaṇḍale.

327. ‘In the twenty-one intestinal coils’ means in the circle of the intestinal coil which is bent and folded in twenty-one places.

328. Āmāsaye [M 1.0441] ṭhito paribhuttāhāro udariyanti adhippetanti āha “udariyaṃ udare ṭhitaṃ asitapītakhāyitasāyita”nti.

328. The consumed food situated in the stomach is intended as ‘udariyaṃ’ (stomach contents); therefore, it is said: ‘Udariyaṃ is what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored, situated in the stomach.’

331. Abaddhapittaṃ saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ viya, kāyusmā viya ca kammajarūpapaṭibaddhavuttikanti āha “ābaddhapittaṃ jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhaṃ sakalasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhita”nti. Paṭibaddhatāvacanena cassa jīvitindriye sati sabbhāvameva dīpeti, na jīvitindriyassa viya ekantakammajatanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pittakosaketi mahākosāṭakīkosasadise pittādhāre. Yūsabhūtoti rasabhūto.

331. Unbound bile, like circulating blood and the body's heat, has its occurrence connected with kamma-born matter; therefore, it is said: ‘Unbound bile, connected to the life faculty, is situated pervading the entire body.’ And by the statement of its connectedness, it shows its existence only when the life faculty is present; it should be understood that it does not show that it is exclusively kamma-born, like the life faculty. ‘In the gall bladder’ means in the receptacle for bile, which is similar to the gourd of a large sponge gourd. ‘Being like juice’ means being in a liquid state.

332. Ucchiṭṭhodakagabbhamalādīnaṃ chaḍḍanaṭṭhānaṃ candanikā, tassaṃ candanikāyaṃ.

332. A cesspool is the place for discarding water used for washing leftovers, impurities of the womb, and so on. ‘In that cesspool’ [means in that cesspool].

333. Pubbāsayo mandapaññānaṃ kesañcideva hotīti katvā asabbasādhāraṇanti adhippāyenāha “pubbo anibaddhokāso”ti.

333. Considering that a basis for pus exists only for certain individuals of little wisdom, with the intention that it is not common to all, it is said: ‘Pus has no fixed location.’

334. Pittaṃ viyāti abaddhapittaṃ viya. Sakalasarīranti jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhaṃ sabbaṃ sarīrappadesaṃ. Vakkahadayayakanapapphāsāni tementanti ettha yakanaṃ heṭṭhābhāgapūraṇena, itarāni tesaṃ upari thokaṃ thokaṃ paggharaṇena ca temetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Heṭṭhā leḍḍukhaṇḍādīni temayamāneti temakatemitabbānaṃ abyāpāratāsāmaññanidassanatthaṃ eva upamā daṭṭhabbā, na ṭhānasāmaññanidassanatthaṃ. Sannicitalohitena hi temetabbānaṃ kesañci heṭṭhā, kassaci upari ṭhitatā kāyagatāsatiniddese (visuddhi. 1.206) dassitāti. Yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgaṭṭhānaṃ “mayi lohitaṃ ṭhita”nti na jānāti, vakkādīni “amhe temayamānaṃ lohitaṃ ṭhita”nti na jānantīti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

334. ‘Like bile’ means like unbound bile. ‘The entire body’ means every bodily region connected to the life faculty. In the phrase ‘it moistens the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs,’ it should be understood that it moistens the liver by filling its lower part, and it moistens the others by dripping a little upon them. The simile ‘like... moistening clods of earth, etc., below’ should be seen only for the purpose of indicating the commonality of non-activity between the moistener and the moistened, not for indicating a commonality of location. For it is shown in the exposition of mindfulness directed to the body that, of the things to be moistened by the collected blood, some are situated below and some are situated above. The connection should be understood in this way: The liver's lower part does not know, ‘Blood is situated in me,’ and the kidneys and so on do not know, ‘Blood is situated moistening us.’

336. Patthinnasinehoti thinabhāvaṃ ghanabhāvaṃ gatasineho. Sakalasarīre maṃsanti yojanā, tañca thūlasarīraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Medassa satipi patthinnatāya ghanabhāve maṃsassa viya na baddhatāti vuttaṃ “patthinnayūso”ti. Tenevassa āpokoṭṭhāsatā.

336. ‘Solid fat’ means fat that has reached a state of viscosity and solidity. The connection is with ‘flesh in the entire body,’ and this is said with reference to a fat body. Although solid fat is in a solid state due to its viscosity, it is not firm like flesh; therefore, it is called ‘thickened juice.’ For that very reason, it is a part of the water element.

337. Udakapuṇṇesu [M 1.0442][V 1.0414] taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakesūti nātipariṇatānaṃ sajalakānaṃ aggato chinnānaṃ tālasalāṭukānaṃ vivarāni sandhāya vuttaṃ.

337. ‘In water-filled cavities of young palmyra nuts’ is said with reference to the openings of young, unripe, water-containing palmyra fruits that have been cut at the top.

338. Vasāya attano ādhāre abhibyāpanamukhena abyāpāratāsāmaññaṃ vibhāvetabbanti ācāmagatatelaṃ nidassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

338. It should be understood that oil in rice gruel is given as an example in order to make clear the commonality of non-activity of tallow, by way of its pervasion in its own receptacle.

339. Kheḷuppattipaccaye ambilaggamadhuraggādike.

339. In the conditions for the arising of saliva, such as things with a predominantly sour or predominantly sweet taste.

343. Kesādīsu manasikāraṃ pavattetvā tejokoṭṭhāsesu pavattetabbo manasikāroti vibhattiṃ pariṇāmetvā yojetabbaṃ. Yena santappatīti yena kāyo santappati, ayaṃ santappanakicco. Tejoti tassa pariggaṇhanākāro eva paccāmaṭṭho. Yena jīrīyatītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

343. Having caused attention to arise regarding the hair and so forth, attention should be caused to arise regarding the parts of the fire element; thus, the connection should be made by changing the case ending. As for 'by which it is heated,' this means 'by which the body is intensely heated'; this has the function of intense heating. Regarding the fire element, only its mode of being grasped is reviewed. In 'by which it decays' and so forth, this is the same method.

344. Assāsapassāsavasenāti antopavisanabahinikkhamananāsikāvātabhāvena. “Evaṃ pavattamanasikārassā”ti iminā vuttākārena sasambhāravibhattito pavattakammaṭṭhānamanasikārassa. Dhātuyo pākaṭā hontīti vitthārato pariggahitattā dhātuyo vibhūtā honti. Idhāpi bhāvanāvidhānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

344. 'By way of in-breaths and out-breaths' means by the state of being the nostril-wind that enters within and exits without. 'Of one whose attention proceeds thus' means of one whose attention to the meditation subject proceeds in this stated manner, by way of analyzing the parts together with their components. 'The elements become manifest' means the elements become distinct because they have been grasped in detail. Here also, the method of development should be understood only by the method stated below.

345. Tatthevāti tesuyeva vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu. Paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ vitthambhanalakkhaṇanti etthāpi “tatthevā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

345. 'Therein' means in those very twenty parts. In the passage 'the characteristic of digestion... the characteristic of supporting,' here too, the term 'therein' should be brought forward and connected.

Puna tatthevāti tesuyeva dvādasasu koṭṭhāsesūti attho. Ettha ca kesādikoṭṭhāsānaṃ saṃviggahatāya tattha vijjamānā āpodhātuādayo nhāniyacuṇṇādīsu udakādayo viya suviññeyyāti “tattheva ābandhanalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Again, 'therein' means in those very twelve parts. And here, because the parts beginning with hair have a physical substance, the water element and other elements existing therein are easily knowable, like water and so forth in bathing powder and the like. Therefore, the passage beginning 'therein, the characteristic of binding' is stated.

Santappanāditejokoṭṭhāsesu pana vāyodhātuādayo na tathā suviññeyyāti katvā “tena avinibhutta”nti vuttaṃ, na tatthevāti. Yadi evaṃ, vāyukoṭṭhāsesu kathaṃ tatthevāti? Vāyukoṭṭhāsāpi hi uddhaṅgamavātādayo piṇḍākāreneva pariggahetabbataṃ upagacchanti, na pana santappanāditejokoṭṭhāsāti [V 1.0415] nāyaṃ doso. Tattha tenāti tena tejena. Avinibhuttanti avinābhūtaṃ, taṃtaṃkalāpagatavasena vā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vavatthāpayatoti vuttākārena salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato dhātuyo vavatthāpentassa[M 1.0443]. Vuttanayenāti “tassevaṃ vāyamamānassā”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.308) heṭṭhā vuttanayena.

However, in the parts of the fire element, such as that which heats, the wind element and others are not so easily knowable; therefore, it is stated 'inseparable from that,' and not 'therein.' If so, why is 'therein' stated in regard to the parts of the wind element? Because the parts of the wind element, such as the upward-going wind, also reach a state of being graspable only as a mass, whereas the parts of the fire element, such as that which heats, do not. Therefore, this is not a fault. Therein, 'by that' means by that fire element. 'Inseparable' means not existing without, or it is stated thus by way of being included in their respective material groups. 'Of one who thus determines' means of one who determines the elements concisely with their characteristics in the stated manner. 'By the stated method' means by the method previously stated in the passage beginning 'Of one striving thus' (Vism. I, 308).

346. Evampi bhāvayatoti salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato dhātuyo pariggahetvā bhāventassāpi. Pubbe vuttanayenāti sasambhāravibhattito bhāvanāyaṃ vuttena nayena. Evanti yathā kese, evaṃ. Sabbakoṭṭhāsesūti ekacattālīsabhedesu sesasabbakoṭṭhāsesu evamettha aṭṭhasaṭṭhidhātusatassa pariggaho vutto hoti. Bhāvanāvidhānaṃ panettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

346. 'Even thus one develops' means even of one who develops after having grasped the elements concisely with their characteristics. 'By the method previously stated' means by the method stated in the development by way of analysis with components. 'Thus' means just as in the case of the hair, so too. 'In all parts' means in all the remaining parts of the forty-one divisions. Thus, herein, the grasping of one hundred and sixty-eight elements is stated. The method of development here is just the method stated previously.

Idāni vacanatthādimukhenapi dhātūsu manasikāravidhānaṃ dassetuṃ “vacanatthato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vacanatthatoti yasmā sabbapaṭhamaṃ kammaṭṭhānassa uggahaṇaṃ vacanavasena hoti vacanadvārena tadatthassa ādito gahetabbato, tasmā vacanatthatopi dhātūnaṃ manasikātabbatā vuttā. Kalāpatoti vacanatthavasena visesato, sāmaññato ca dhātuyo pariggahetvā ṭhitassa yasmā tā piṇḍaso pavattanti, na paccekaṃ, tasmā kalāpatopi manasikātabbatā vuttā. Te pana kalāpā paramāṇuparimāṇā hontīti tappariyāpannānaṃ pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ ekasmiṃ sarīre parimeyyaparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ cuṇṇato manasikātabbatā vuttā. So panāyaṃ tāsaṃ cuṇṇato manasikāro saṅghāṭavasena hotīti nibbaṭṭitasarūpameva pariggahetabbaṃ dassetuṃ lakkhaṇādito manasikāro vutto. Lakkhaṇādito dhātuyo pariggaṇhantena salakkhaṇavibhattito kammaṭṭhānābhinivese yasmā dvācattālīsāya koṭṭhāsānaṃ vasena dhātūsu pariggayhamānāsu “ettakā utusamuṭṭhānā, ettakā cittādisamuṭṭhānā”ti ayaṃ vibhāgo ñātabbo hoti, tasmā samuṭṭhānato manasikāro vutto.

Now, to show the method of attention to the elements by way of definition and so on, the passage beginning 'by way of definition' is stated. Therein, 'by way of definition' means: since the meditation subject is first apprehended by means of words—because its meaning must be grasped from the outset through the gateway of words—therefore, the need for attention to the elements by way of definition is stated. 'By way of groups' means: for one who stands having grasped the elements specifically and generally by way of their definitions, since those elements proceed in masses and not individually, therefore the need for attention by way of groups is stated. Furthermore, since those groups are of the measure of ultimate particles, to show the measurable delimitation of the earth element and so forth included within them in a single body, the need for attention by way of minute particles is stated. Furthermore, since this attention to them as minute particles occurs by way of aggregation, to show that only their manifested nature which is to be grasped should be grasped, attention by way of characteristics and so on is stated. Since, for one who is grasping the elements by way of characteristics and so on, while applying oneself to the meditation subject by way of analysis of individual characteristics, and while the elements are being grasped by way of the forty-two parts, this distinction—'so many are temperature-originated, so many are mind-originated, etc.'—must be known, therefore attention by way of origination is stated.

Evaṃ pariññātasamuṭṭhānānampi tāsaṃ saddānusārena vinā visesasāmaññapariggaho kātabboti dassetuṃ nānattekattato manasikāro vutto. Lakkhaṇavisesato vinibhuttarūpāpi etā aniddisitabbaṭṭhānatāya padesena avinibhuttāti ayaṃ viseso pariggahetabboti dassetuṃ [M 1.0444] vinibbhogāvinibbhogato manasikāro vutto. Satipi avinibbhogavuttiyaṃ kācideva kāsañci sabhāgā, kāci visabhāgāti ayampi viseso pariggahetabboti dassetuṃ sabhāgavisabhāgato manasikāro vutto. Sabhāgavisabhāgāpi dhātuyo ajjhattikā īdisakiccavisesayuttā, bāhirā tabbiparītāti [V 1.0416] ayaṃ viseso pariggahetabboti dassetuṃ ajjhattikabāhiravisesato manasikāro vutto. Sajātisaṅgahādiko dhātusaṅgahavisesopi pariggahitabboti dassetuṃ saṅgahato manasikāro vutto. Sandhāraṇādīhi yathāsakakiccehi aññamaññūpatthambhabhāvatopi dhātuyo pariggahetabbāti dassetuṃ paccayato manasikāro vutto. Abyāpāranayato dhātuyo pariggahetabbāti dassetuṃ asamannāhārato manasikāro vutto. Attano paccayadhammavisesato, paccayabhāvavisesato ca dhātuyo pariggahetabbāti dassetuṃ paccayavibhāgato manasikāro vuttoti evametesaṃ terasannaṃ ākārānaṃ pariggahe kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ākārehīti pakārehi, kāraṇehi vā.

To show that, even for those elements whose origination is fully understood, the grasping of their specific and general aspects should be done without following the words, attention by way of diversity and unity is stated. To show that this distinction must be grasped—that although these elements are distinct by way of specific characteristics, they are inseparable by location due to their place being unspecifiable—attention by way of separability and inseparability is stated. To show that this distinction also must be grasped—that even while being inseparable in their occurrence, some are similar to certain others, while some are dissimilar—attention by way of similarity and dissimilarity is stated. To show that this distinction must be grasped—that similar and dissimilar elements that are internal are endowed with such and such specific functions, while external ones are the opposite—attention by way of the distinction between internal and external is stated. To show that the specific grouping of elements, such as grouping by similar kind, must also be grasped, attention by way of grouping is stated. To show that the elements must be grasped also by their state of mutually supporting one another through their respective functions, such as sustaining, attention by way of conditionality is stated. To show that the elements must be grasped by the method of non-volition, attention by way of non-deliberation is stated. To show that the elements must be grasped by their specific conditioning phenomena and by the specific nature of their state as a condition, attention by way of the analysis of conditions is stated. Thus, the reason for the grasping of these thirteen modes should be understood. 'By modes' means by types, or by reasons.

347. Tattha patthaṭattāti puthuttā, tena puthubhāvato puthuvī, puthuvī eva pathavīti niruttinayena saddatthamāha. Patthanaṭṭhena vā pathavī, patiṭṭhābhāvena patthāyati upatiṭṭhatīti attho. “Appotī”ti padassa attho heṭṭhā vutto eva. Āpīyatīti sosīyati, pivīyatīti keci. “Ayaṃ panattho sasambhārāpe yujjatī”ti vadanti, lakkhaṇāpepi yujjateva. Sopi hi pharusapācanavisosanākārena sesabhūtattayena pīyamāno viya pavattatīti. Appāyatīti brūheti. Paribrūhanarasā hi āpodhātu. Tejatīti niseti, tikkhabhāvena sesabhūtattayaṃ usmāpayatīti attho. Vāyatīti samīreti, desantaruppattihetubhāvena bhūtasaṅghātaṃ gametīti attho.

347. Therein, regarding patthaṭattā, it means because of its vastness (puthuttā). By that, because of its state of being vast (puthubhāvato), it is called puthavī. Puthavī itself is pathavī; thus he states the meaning of the word according to etymology. Alternatively, it is called pathavī because of the meaning of spreading out (patthanaṭṭhena); the meaning is that it is manifest and serves as a foundation (patiṭṭhābhāvena patthāyati upatiṭṭhati). The meaning of the word appoti has already been stated below. Āpīyati means it is dried up (sosīyati); some say it means 'it is drunk' (pivīyati). They say, 'This meaning is suitable for composite water,' but it is also suitable for characteristic water. For that too proceeds as if being drunk by the remaining three elements in the manner of coarsening, maturing, and drying. Appāyati means it augments (brūheti). Indeed, the water element has the function of causing increase. Tejati means it sharpens (niseti); the meaning is that by its sharp nature, it heats up the remaining three elements. Vāyati means it impels (samīreti); the meaning is that by being the cause for arising in another place, it causes the aggregate of elements to move.

Evaṃ tāva visesato vacanatthaṃ vatvā idāni sāmaññato vattuṃ “avisesena panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Salakkhaṇadhāraṇatoti yathā titthiyaparikappito “pakati attā”ti evamādiko sabhāvato natthi, na evametā. Etā pana salakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyo. Dukkhādānatoti [M 1.0445] dukkhassa vidahanato. Etā hi dhātuyo kāraṇabhāvena vavatthitā hutvā ayalohādidhātuyo viya ayalohādiṃ anekappakāraṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ vidahanti. Dukkhādhānatoti anappakassa dukkhassa vidhānamattato avasavattanato, taṃ vā dukkhaṃ etāhi kāraṇabhūtāhi sattehi anuvidhīyati, tathāvihitañca taṃ etāsveva dhīyati ṭhapīyatīti evaṃ dukkhādhānato, dhātuyo. Apica “nijjīvaṭṭho dhātuṭṭho”ti vuttovāyamattho. Tathā hi bhagavā “chadhāturoyaṃ bhikkhu puriso”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.343-345) jīvasaññāsamūhananatthaṃ dhātudesanaṃ akāsīti. Iti vacanatthamukhenapi asādhāraṇato, sādhāraṇato ca dhātūnaṃ sarasalakkhaṇameva vibhāvīyatīti āha “evaṃ visesasāmaññavasena vacanatthato manasi kātabbā”ti. Manasikāro pana vacanatthamukhena dhātuyo pariggahetvā ṭhitassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Having thus first explained the etymological meaning specifically, now, in order to state it generally, the passage beginning with 'But without distinction...' was spoken. 'Because they bear their own characteristic': just as that which is conceived by heretics, such as 'primal nature' and 'self,' does not exist in its own nature, it is not so with these elements. Rather, these elements bear their own characteristic, their own nature; therefore, they are called 'elements' (dhātuyo). 'Because they give suffering' (dukkhādānato): this means because they ordain suffering. Indeed, these elements, being established as causes, just as mineral elements like iron ore produce iron, etc., ordain the manifold suffering of saṃsāra. 'Because they are a basis for suffering' (dukkhādhānato): this is because they are merely the arrangement of much suffering, and because they are not subject to one's will. Or, that suffering is arranged by beings through these elements which have become the cause; and that suffering, so arranged, is placed and established in these very elements. Thus, because they are a basis for suffering, they are called 'elements'. Furthermore, this meaning has been stated: 'The meaning of "element" is "lifeless."' For so indeed, the Blessed One, in teachings such as, 'This person, O monk, is of six elements,' gave the teaching on the elements for the purpose of eradicating the perception of a living being. Thus, because through the etymological meaning both the particular and the general intrinsic characteristics of the elements are made clear, he said, 'Thus they are to be contemplated by way of the etymological meaning according to the specific and general sense.' As for the contemplation for one who stands having grasped the elements through their etymological meaning, it should be understood in the same way as stated below.

348. Ākārehīti [V 1.0417] pakārehi. Atha vā ākarīyanti dissanti ettha dhātuyoti ākārā, koṭṭhāsā. Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānāti yathāvuttānaṃ paccayavisesena visiṭṭharūpānaṃ vaṇṇādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ dhammānaṃ samavadhānato sannivesavisesavasena sahāvaṭṭhānato taṃ upādāya. Kesāti sammuti samaññāmattaṃ hoti. Tesaṃyeva vinibbhogāti tesaṃyeva vaṇṇādīnaṃ vinibbhujanato. Yathā hi vaṇṇādayo aṭṭha dhammā paññāya vinibbhujjamānā aññamaññabyatirekena paramatthato upalabbhanti, na evaṃ vaṇṇādibyatirekena paramatthato kesā upalabbhanti. Tasmā ye ca dhamme samudite upādāya “kesā”ti sammuti, tesu visuṃ visuṃ katesu natthi “kesā”ti sammuti, vohāramattanti attho.

348. By 'aspects' (ākārehi) is meant by types (pakārehi). Or alternatively, because the elements are seen (ākarīyanti dissanti) herein, they are called aspects (ākārā), which are the parts (koṭṭhāsā). 'By the convergence of eight phenomena' (aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā): depending on the co-existence, by way of the distinction of being assembled together, of the eight phenomena beginning with color, which are distinct material phenomena due to specific conditions as mentioned, the convention, the mere designation 'hair' comes to be. 'By their very analysis' (tesaṃyeva vinibbhogā): this means by analyzing those very phenomena beginning with color. For just as the eight phenomena beginning with color, when being analyzed by wisdom, are found in an ultimate sense in distinction from one another, so 'hair' is not found in an ultimate sense in distinction from those phenomena beginning with color. Therefore, depending on which phenomena are assembled together, the convention 'hair' arises; when those phenomena are made separate, the convention 'hair' does not exist. The meaning is that it is merely a term of usage.

“Aṭṭhadhammakalāpamattamevā”ti idaṃ kesapaññattiyā upādāyabhūte vaṇṇādike ekattena gahetvā vuttaṃ, na tesaṃ aṭṭhadhammamattabhāvato. Kammasamuṭṭhāno koṭṭhāsoti kesesu tāva kesamūlaṃ, evaṃ lomādīsupi yathārahaṃ veditabbaṃ. Dasadhammakalāpopīti ettha asitādiparipācako tejokoṭṭhāso navadhammakalāpopīti vattabbo. Yadime kesādikoṭṭhāsā yathārahaṃ aṭṭhanavadasadhammasamūhabhūtā[M 1.0446], atha kasmā pathavīādidhātumattato manasi karīyantīti āha “ussadavasena panā”tiādi. Yasmā ayaṃ dhātumanasikāro yāvadeva sattasaññāsamugghāṭanattho, dhammavinibbhogo ca sātisayaṃ sattasaññāsamugghāṭāya saṃvattati, tasmā koṭṭhāsesu evaṃ dhammavibhāgo veditabbo. Ettha hi udariyaṃ karīsaṃ pubbo muttañca utusamuṭṭhānā, asitādiparipācakatejo kammasamuṭṭhāno, assāsapassāsavāto cittasamuṭṭhānoti cha ekasamuṭṭhānā, sedoassu kheḷo siṅghāṇikāti cattāro utucittavasena dvisamuṭṭhānā, sesā dvattiṃsa catusamuṭṭhānā.

This statement, 'Merely a group of eight phenomena,' was said having taken the phenomena beginning with color, which are the basis for the concept 'hair,' as a single unit, not because they are merely eight phenomena. As for the part originated from kamma, in the case of hair, it is the root of the hair; similarly, it should be understood accordingly for body hair and the rest. Here, regarding 'also a group of ten phenomena,' the heat-part that digests what is eaten, etc., is also to be called a group of nine phenomena. If these parts beginning with hair are, as appropriate, groups of eight, nine, or ten phenomena, then why are they contemplated merely as the earth element and other elements? To this, he said the passage beginning with 'But by way of predominance...'. Because this contemplation of the elements is for the very purpose of uprooting the perception of a being, and the analysis of phenomena conduces exceedingly to the uprooting of the perception of a being, therefore, the analysis of phenomena in the parts should be understood in this way. Herein, stomach contents, feces, pus, and urine are originated from temperature; the heat that digests what is eaten, etc., is originated from kamma; in-breaths and out-breaths are originated from mind—thus, six are of single origination. Sweat, tears, saliva, and mucus—these four are of dual origination by way of temperature and mind. The remaining thirty-two are of fourfold origination.

Tesu asitādiparipācake tejokoṭṭhāse eko kalāpo jīvitanavako, aññesu ekasamuṭṭhānesu utusamuṭṭhāno, cittasamuṭṭhāno vā ekeko aṭṭhako, dvisamuṭṭhānesu utucittavasena dve dve aṭṭhakā, catusamuṭṭhānesu utucittāhārasamuṭṭhānā tayo tayo aṭṭhakā, utucittasamuṭṭhānesu saddanavakā, aṭṭhasu tejovāyokoṭṭhāsesu aṭṭha jīvitanavakā, sesesu catuvīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu kāyabhāvadasakadvayasahitā, cakkhādisaññitesu maṃsakoṭṭhāsesu cakkhusotaghānajivhāvatthudasakasahitā cāti paripuṇṇāyatanake rūpakāye bhedaṃ anāmasitvā ekattavasena gayhamānā sattacattālīsādhikasatarūpakalāpā rūpavibhāgato sādhikaṃ diyaḍḍharūpasahassaṃ hoti, koṭṭhāsānaṃ pana avayavavibhāgena tadavayavakalāpānaṃ bhede gayhamāne rūpadhammānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyabhedatā veditabbā[V 1.0418]. Evaṃ dhammavibhāgato anekabhedabhinnāpi ime dvācattālīsa koṭṭhāsā ussadaggahaṇena catudhātuvaseneva vavatthapetabbā. Tenāha “ussadavasena pana…pe… manasi kātabbā”ti. Tattha manasikāravidhi vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Among these, in the fire-element part that digests what is eaten, etc., one kalāpa is the life-nonad. In other parts with a single origin, whether temperature-originated or mind-originated, each is an octad. In those with two origins, due to temperature and mind, there are two octads each. In those with four origins, originated from temperature, mind, and nutriment, there are three octads each. In those originated from temperature and mind, there are sound-nonads. In the eight fire and air parts, there are eight life-nonads. In the remaining twenty-four parts, there are kalāpas together with the pair of the body-decad and faculty-decad. In the flesh parts designated as eye, etc., there are kalāpas together with the eye-decad, ear-decad, nose-decad, tongue-decad, and heart-basis-decad. Thus, in the material body with complete sense-bases, without considering the division but taken as a unity, there are one hundred and forty-seven material kalāpas. By way of the division of materiality, it amounts to one thousand five hundred and one material units. However, when the division of the parts into their constituents is considered, and the division of the kalāpas of those constituents is taken, the divisions of material phenomena should be understood as innumerable. Thus, although these forty-two parts are divided into many distinctions by the analysis of phenomena, they should be established only by way of the four great elements by taking what is prominent. Therefore, he said: 'By way of prominence...pe... should be kept in mind.' Here, the method of attention should be understood in the way already explained.

349. Majjhimena pamāṇenāti ārohapariṇāhehi majjhimasarīre labbhamānena majjhimena parimāṇena. Pariggayhamānāti paññāya paritakketvā gayhamānā. Paramāṇubhedasañcuṇṇāti ettha yathā “aṅgulassa aṭṭhamo bhāgo yavo, yavassa aṭṭhamo bhāgo ūkā, ūkāya [M 1.0447] aṭṭhamo bhāgo likkhā, likkhāya aṭṭhamo bhāgo rathareṇu, rathareṇussa aṭṭhamo bhāgo tajjārī, tajjāriyā aṭṭhamo bhāgo aṇu, evaṃ aṇuno aṭṭhamo bhāgo paramāṇu nāmā”ti keci. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 515) pana “sattadhaññamāsappamāṇaṃ ekaṃ aṅgulaṃ, sattaūkāpamāṇo eko dhaññamāso, sattalikkhāpamāṇā ekā ūkā, chattiṃsarathareṇuppamāṇā ekā likkhā, chattiṃsatajjārippamāṇo eko rathareṇu, chattiṃsaaṇuppamāṇā ekā tajjārī, chattiṃsaparamāṇuppamāṇo eko aṇū”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā aṇuno chattiṃsatimabhāgamatto paramāṇu nāma ākāsakoṭṭhāsiko maṃsacakkhussa agocaro dibbacakkhusseva gocarabhūto. Taṃ sandhāyāha “paramāṇubhedasañcuṇṇā”ti, yathāvuttaparamāṇuppabhedena cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhūtā. Sukhumarajabhūtāti tatoyeva ativiya sukhumarajabhāvaṃ gatā.

349. "By a medium measure" means by a medium measure obtainable in a body of medium stature in terms of height and girth. "Being grasped" means being grasped after having reflected with wisdom. Herein, in the phrase "pulverized into the division of ultimate particles," some say: "Just as an eighth part of a finger-breadth is a barleycorn, an eighth part of a barleycorn is a louse, an eighth part of a louse is a nit, an eighth part of a nit is a chariot-dust, an eighth part of a chariot-dust is a lint-speck, an eighth part of a lint-speck is an atom, thus an eighth part of an atom is called an ultimate particle." However, in the commentary it is said: "One finger-breadth is the measure of seven grains of paddy; one grain of paddy is the measure of seven lice; one louse is the measure of seven nits; one nit is the measure of thirty-six chariot-dusts; one chariot-dust is the measure of thirty-six lint-specks; one lint-speck is the measure of thirty-six atoms; and one atom is the measure of thirty-six ultimate particles." Therefore, what is called an ultimate particle is about the thirty-sixth part of an atom; it is a constituent of space, not an object for the physical eye, being an object for the divine eye only. Referring to that, he said, "pulverized into the division of ultimate particles," meaning having become pulverized by the aforesaid division of ultimate particles. "Having become fine dust" means for that very reason, having gone to a state of exceedingly fine dust.

Doṇamattā siyāti soḷasa nāḷimattā. Idhāpi “majjhimena pamāṇenā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Tena “pakatiyā catumuṭṭhikaṃ kuḍuvaṃ, catukuḍuvaṃ nāḷi, tāya nāḷiyā soḷasa nāḷiyo doṇaṃ, taṃ pana magadhanāḷiyā dvādasa nāḷiyo hontī”ti vadanti. Saṅgahitāti yathā na vippakirati, evaṃ ābandhanavasena sampiṇḍitvā gahitā. Anupālitāti yathā paggharaṇasabhāvāya āpodhātuyā vasena kilinnabhāvaṃ, picchilabhāvaṃ vā nāpajjati, evaṃ anurakkhitā. Vitthambhitāti saṅghātavāyunā ativiya vitthambhanaṃ pāpitā. Na vikirati na viddhaṃsatīti sukhumarajabhūtāpi pathavīdhātu ābandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇakiccāhi āpotejovāyodhātūhi laddhapaccayā sinehena temitā tejasā paripakkā vāyunā vitthambhanaṃ pāpitā piṭṭhacuṇṇā viya na ito cito ca vikirati na viddhaṃsati, atha kho piṇḍitā ghanabhūtā hutvā nānappakārena gahetabbataṃ āpajjati. Tenāha “avikiriyamānā”tiādi. Tattha vikappanti vibhāgaṃ. Yadipi tejovāyodhātuyopi saviggahā rūpadhammabhāvato, yādiso pana ghanabhāvo pathavīāpodhātūsu labbhati[V 1.0419], na tādiso tejovāyodhātūsu labbhatīti meyyabhāvābhāvato tattha cuṇṇabhedo na uddhaṭo. Tathā hi sasambhāratejovāyūsupi meyyabhāvo na labbhateva.

"It would be the measure of a doṇa" means the measure of sixteen nāḷis. Here too, the phrase "by a medium measure" should be brought in and connected. Therefore, they say: "By nature, four handfuls are a kuḍuva; four kuḍuvas are a nāḷi; by that nāḷi, sixteen nāḷis are a doṇa; that, however, is twelve nāḷis by the Magadhan nāḷi." "Gathered" means taken, having been amassed by way of binding, in such a way that it does not scatter. "Preserved" means protected in such a way that it does not reach a state of being moist or a state of being sticky, by the power of the water element which has the nature of oozing. "Held firm" means made to reach a state of being very firm by the cohesive wind. "It does not scatter, it does not get destroyed"—even though it has become fine dust, the earth element, having received the condition from the water, fire, and wind elements, which have the functions of binding, maturing, and impelling—being moistened by moisture, matured by heat, and made firm by wind—does not scatter here and there like flour-powder, nor does it get destroyed; but rather, having become amassed and solidified, it reaches a state of being able to be taken in various ways. Therefore, he said, "not scattering," etc. Therein, 'vikappanti' means division. Although the fire and wind elements also have substance, due to being material phenomena, the kind of solidity that is found in the earth and water elements is not found in the fire and wind elements; due to the absence of measurability, the distinction of being pulverized is not shown there. For indeed, even in the fire and wind elements together with their components, measurability is not found at all.

Yūsagatāti [M 1.0448] yūsabhāvaṃ dravabhāvaṃ gatā. Tato eva ābandhanākārabhūtā. Na paggharatīti na ogaḷati. Na parissavatīti na vissandati. Pīṇitapīṇitabhāvaṃ dassetīti āpodhātuyā brūhanarasatāya vuttaṃ.

"Having become broth" means having reached a state of being broth, a liquid state. For that very reason, it has the characteristic of binding. "It does not ooze" means it does not drip down. "It does not flow around" means it does not flow out. "Showing a state of being plumped up" is said because of the water element's nature of causing growth.

Usumākārabhūtāti etena kāye pākatikausmāpi gahaṇīsaṅkhātāya tassāyeva tejodhātuyā vasena hotīti dasseti. Paripācetīti santejeti. Sā hi yathābhuttassa āhārassa sammā pariṇāmanena rasādisampattiyā hetubhāvaṃ gacchantī imaṃ kāyaṃ paripāceti santejetīti vuccati. Tenevāha “na pūtibhāvaṃ dassetī”ti. Kammūpanissayāya, cittappasādahetukāya ca sarīre vaṇṇasampadāya tejodhātu visesapaccayo, pageva utuāhārasamuṭṭhānāya rūpasampattiyā yathāvuttatejodhātūti āha “vaṇṇasampattiñcassa āvahatī”ti.

"Having the characteristic of heat"—by this it is shown that even the natural heat in the body, known as the 'digestive fire,' occurs by the power of that very fire element. "It matures" means it heats well. For it, by properly transforming the food that has been eaten, becomes a cause for the attainment of taste, etc., and is said to mature and heat this body. For that very reason, he said, "It does not show a state of putrefaction." The fire element is a special condition for the excellence of complexion in the body, which has kamma as a decisive support and is a cause for mental clarity. How much more so is the aforesaid fire element for the excellence of material form arising from temperature and nutriment. Therefore, he said, "and it brings excellence of complexion to it."

Samudīraṇavitthambhanalakkhaṇāti ettha samudīraṇaṃ anupellanaṃ, visosananti keci. Vitthambhanaṃ sesabhūtattayassa thambhitattāpādanaṃ, uppīlananti eke. Tāyāti vitthambhanalakkhaṇāya vāyodhātuyā. Aparāyāti samudīraṇalakkhaṇāya. Sā hi pellanasabhāvā. Tenāha “samabbhāhato”ti. Samabbhāhanañca rūpakalāpassa desantaruppattiyā hetubhāvo. Avaghaṭṭanaṃ āsannataruppattiyā. Lāḷetīti parivatteti. Idāni yadatthaṃ cuṇṇato manasikāro āgato, taṃ nigamanavasena dassetuṃ “evameta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dhātuyantanti suttena viya yantarūpakaṃ asatipi kattubhūte attani cittavasena dhātumayaṃ yantaṃ pavattati, idhāpi manasikāravidhi vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

In the phrase 'the characteristic of impelling and supporting,' 'impelling' means urging on; some say it is drying up. 'Supporting' means causing the state of being propped up for the remaining three primary elements; some say it is pressing down. 'By that' means by the air element with the characteristic of supporting. 'By the other' means by that with the characteristic of impelling. For it has the nature of pushing. Therefore, it is said, 'thoroughly struck.' And 'thorough striking' is the state of being a cause for the arising of the material group in another location. 'Striking' is for arising in a very near location. 'Stirs' means it turns around. Now, to show by way of conclusion the purpose for which attention by way of analysis into particles has come about, 'thus this,' etc., is said. Therein, 'the element-machine' means that just as a puppet-machine operates by means of a string, even though there is no agent-self, so the machine made of elements operates by the power of the mind. Here too, the method of attention should be understood in the same way as described.

350. Yadipi catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ lakkhaṇādayo heṭṭhā tattha tattha vuttā eva, tathāpi te anavasesato dassetvā visuṃ kammaṭṭhānapariggahavidhiṃ dassetuṃ “lakkhaṇādito”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha lakkhīyati etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, kakkhaḷattaṃ lakkhaṇametissāti kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā. Nanu ca kakkhaḷattameva pathavīdhātūti? Saccametaṃ, tathāpi viññātāviññātasaddatthatāvasena abhinnepi dhamme kappanāsiddhena bhedena evaṃ niddeso kato. Evaṃ hi atthavisesāvabodho hotīti. Atha vā [V 1.0420] lakkhīyatīti [M 1.0449] lakkhaṇaṃ, kakkhaḷattaṃ hutvā lakkhiyamānā dhātu kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesāsupi eseva nayo. Patiṭṭhānarasāti sahajātadhammānaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvakiccā. Tato eva nesaṃ sampaṭicchanākārena ñāṇassa paccupatiṭṭhatīti sampaṭicchanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Padaṭṭhānaṃ panettha aññadhammatāya na uddhaṭaṃ, sādhāraṇabhāvasabbhāvato vā dūrakāraṇaṃ viya. Yathā vā dhammuddesavāravaṇṇanādīsu rasādinā aññesaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ dassetvā paccayavantatādassanatthaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ uddhaṭaṃ, na evamidha. Idha pana dhātūnaṃ anaññasādhāraṇavisesavibhāvanaparāya codanāya aññadhammabhūtaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ na uddhaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Brūhanarasāti sahajātadhammānaṃ vaḍḍhanakiccā. Tathā hi sā nesaṃ pīṇitabhāvaṃ dassetīti vuccati. Saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhānāti bāhiraudakaṃ viya nhānīyacuṇṇassa sahajātadhammānaṃ saṅgahaṇapaccupaṭṭhānā. Maddavānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānāti bāhiraggi viya jatulohādīnaṃ sahajātadhammānaṃ mudubhāvānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Abhinīhāro bhūtasaṅghāṭassa desantaruppattihetubhāvo, nīharaṇaṃ vā bījato aṅkurassa viya.

350. Although the characteristics and so forth of the four elements have indeed been stated in various places below, nevertheless, to show them without remainder and to show separately the method of grasping the meditation subject, the passage beginning 'from the characteristic,' etc., is commenced. Therein, 'characteristic' is that by which something is characterized. 'Having the characteristic of hardness' means that hardness is its characteristic. But is not hardness itself the earth element? This is true. Nevertheless, although the phenomenon is undivided, this indication is made with a conceptual distinction, by way of the meaning of the term being known or unknown. For in this way, there is an understanding of the special meaning. Alternatively, 'characteristic' is that which is characterized; the element, being hardness, that is being characterized, has the characteristic of hardness—thus the meaning should be understood here. This is the same method for the remaining elements as well. 'Its function is to be a foundation' means its task is to be the state of a foundation for co-arisen phenomena. From that itself, it manifests to knowledge in the manner of receiving them, thus its manifestation is receiving. Herein, the proximate cause is not pointed out because it is a different phenomenon, or because of the existence of its common nature, like a remote cause. Or, just as in the explanations of the Dhammuddesa section and so on, the proximate cause is pointed out to show the conditionality of other phenomena by way of function, etc., and to show the state of having a condition, it is not so here. Rather, it should be understood that here, in accordance with the exhortation which has as its chief aim the explanation of the special, non-common characteristics of the elements, the proximate cause, being a different phenomenon, is not pointed out. 'Its function is to augment' means its task is to increase co-arisen phenomena. For so it is said: 'It shows their state of being plump.' 'Its manifestation is cohesion' means it manifests by cohering co-arisen phenomena, like external water for bath powder. 'Its manifestation is providing softness' means it manifests by providing a state of softness to co-arisen phenomena, like an external fire for lac, metal, and so on. 'Carrying forward' is the state of being a cause for the arising of the compact mass of primary elements in another location, or it is bringing forth, like that of a sprout from a seed.

351. Utusamuṭṭhānāva kammādivasena anuppattito. Utucittasamuṭṭhānā kadāci ututo, kadāci cittato uppajjanato. Avasesāti vuttāvasesā kesādayo catuvīsati, ādito tayo tejokoṭṭhāsā, pañca vāyokoṭṭhāsā cāti dvattiṃsa. Sabbepīti te sabbepi kammādivasena uppajjanato catusamuṭṭhānā. Kesādīnampi hi maṃsato avimuttabhāgo kammāhāracittasamuṭṭhānova hotīti.

351. They arise only from temperature, because of their non-arising by way of kamma, etc. They arise from temperature and mind, because they arise sometimes from temperature, sometimes from mind. 'The rest' means the remaining twenty-four parts beginning with hair of the head, from what has been said, and the three parts of heat and five parts of air from the beginning—thus, thirty-two parts. 'All of them' means all those parts also have four origins, because they arise by way of kamma, etc. For indeed, the part of hair, etc., that is not separate from the flesh arises only from kamma, nutriment, and mind.

352. Nānattekattatoti visesasāmaññato. Dhammānaṃ hi aññamaññaṃ visadisatā nānattaṃ, samānatā ekattaṃ. Sabbāsampīti catunnampi. Salakkhaṇāditoti sakaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ salakkhaṇaṃ, tato salakkhaṇādito. Ādi-saddena rasapaccupaṭṭhānānaṃ viya mudusaṇhapharusabhāvādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. “Kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena nānattabhūtāna”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ ekattaṃ hoti sādhāraṇattāti? Na, “aññā eva dhātuyo kammasamuṭṭhānā, aññā utuādisamuṭṭhānā”tiādikaṃ bhedaṃ sandhāya tathā vacanato. Etāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ ruppanasabhāvaṃ. Kimpanetaṃ ruppanaṃ nāma? Yā sītādivirodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti, tasmiṃ vā sati yo vijjamānasseva visadisuppattiyā [M 1.0450] hetubhāvo, taṃ ruppanaṃ. Anatītattāti apariccajanato.
