352. 'From diversity and unity' means from particularity and generality. For, the mutual dissimilarity of phenomena is diversity; their similarity is unity. 'Of all' means of all four. 'From their own characteristic, etc.': 'own-characteristic' is one's own characteristic; 'from that' means from their own characteristic, etc. By the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of states such as softness, smoothness, and roughness, as well as function and manifestation, should be understood. Why was it said, 'being diverse by way of origin from kamma, etc.'? Is it not the case that by way of origin from kamma, etc., there is a unity of the four elements due to their commonality? No. It was said in that way with reference to the distinction such as: 'The elements originating from kamma are quite different; those originating from temperature, etc., are different.' Of these elements, the characteristic of being afflicted is the nature of being afflicted. What, then, is this 'being afflicted'? It is the dissimilar arising on the conjunction of opposing conditions such as cold, etc.; or, when that conjunction exists, it is the state of being a cause for the dissimilar arising of what already exists—that is 'being afflicted.' 'Due to not having passed beyond' means because of not abandoning.

Mahantapātubhāvo [V 1.0421] cettha sasambhāradhātuvasena veditabbo, tathā mahāvikāratā mahābhūtasāmaññalakkhaṇadhātuvasena, mahāparihāratā, mahattavijjamānatā ca ubhayavasenāti. Bhūtasaddāpekkhāya “etānī”ti napuṃsakaniddeso. Mahantāni pātubhūtāni anekasatasahassa rūpakalāpasaṅghāṭatāya samūhavasena, santativasena ca aparimitaparimāṇānaṃ, anekayojanāyāmavitthārānañca uppajjanato. Cattāri nahutānīti cattāri dasasahassāni. Devadānavādīnaṃ tigāvutādisarīravasena mahantāni pātubhūtāni.

And here, the great manifestation should be understood by way of the element with its constituents; likewise, the great variation. The commonality with the great primaries should be understood by way of the characteristic-element. And the state of being maintained by many causes, and the state of being great and manifest, should be understood by way of both. The neuter indication 'etāni' is with reference to the word 'bhūta'. They have greatly manifested because of being a conglomeration of many hundreds of thousands of material groups, by way of being a collection and by way of continuity, and because of the arising of immeasurable quantities and of things having a length and breadth of many yojanas. 'Four myriads' means forty thousand. They have greatly manifested by way of the bodies of devas, dānavas, and others, such as those with bodies of three gāvutas.

Tatthāyaṃ vacanattho – mahantāni bhūtāni jātāni nibbattānīti mahābhūtānīti. Anekābhūtavisesadassanena, anekabbhutadassanena ca anekacchariyadassanavasena mahanto abbhuto, mahantāni vā abhūtāni etthāti mahābhūto, māyākāro. Yakkhādayo jātivaseneva mahantā bhūtāti mahābhūtā, niruḷho vā ayaṃ tesu mahābhūtasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Pathavīādayo pana vañcakatāya, aniddisitabbaṭṭhānatāya ca mahābhūtā viya mahābhūtā. Bhūtasaddassa ubhayaliṅgatāya napuṃsakatā katā. Tattha vañcakatā sayaṃ anīlādisabhāvāni hutvā nīlādisabhāvassa upaṭṭhāpanaṃ, anitthipurisādisabhāvāneva ca hutvā itthipurisādiākārassa upaṭṭhāpanaṃ. Tathā aññamaññassa anto, bahi ca aṭṭhitānaṃyeva aññamaññaṃ nissāya avaṭṭhānato aniddisitabbaṭṭhānatā. Yadi hi imā dhātuyo aññamaññassa anto ṭhitā, na sakiccakarā siyuṃ aññamaññānuppavesanato, atha bahi ṭhitā vinibbhuttā siyuṃ. Tathā sati avinibbhuttavādo hāyeyya, tasmā na niddisitabbaṭṭhānā. Evaṃ santepi patiṭṭhānādinā yathāsakaṃ kiccavisesena sesānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ upakārikā honti, yena sahajātādinā paccayena paccayā honti. Tenāha “na ca aññamaññaṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhantī”ti. Manāpehīti manoharehi cāturiyavantehi. Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavikkhepehīti kāḷasāmatādivaṇṇehi, puthulavivarakisatādisaṇṭhānehi, hatthabhamukādivikkhepehi ca. Sarasalakkhaṇanti sabhāvabhūtaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ, sakiccakaṃ vā sabhāvaṃ.

Herein, this is the word-meaning: Because they are great (mahantāni) and have come into being (bhūtāni)—that is, have been born (jātāni) and produced (nibbattāni)—they are called 'great elements' (mahābhūtāni). By showing many unreal distinctions and by way of showing many marvels, one is a 'great being' (mahanto bhūto). Or, because 'great unreal things' (mahantāni abhūtāni) are in him (ettha), he is a 'mahābhūto', a magician. Yakkhas and others, by the power of their birth alone, are 'great beings' (mahantā bhūtā), hence they are called 'mahābhūtā'. Or, this term 'mahābhūta' should be understood as established usage regarding them. The earth element and others, however, are like the 'mahābhūtā' (i.e., magicians, yakkhas) because of their deceptiveness and their un-indicatable location; therefore, they are called 'mahābhūtāni'. The word 'bhūta' is made neuter because it has two genders. Therein, 'deceptiveness' is that, while not being of a nature that is blue, etc., they manifest the nature of blue, etc.; and while not being of a nature that is female, male, etc., they manifest the appearance of female, male, etc. Likewise, 'un-indicatable location' is due to their standing in dependence on one another while not being established either inside or outside one another. For if these elements were established inside one another, they could not perform their own functions due to mutual interpenetration. And if they were established outside, they would be separate. In that case, the doctrine of inseparability would fail. Therefore, they do not have an indicatable location. Even so, by means of their respective specific functions, such as providing a foundation, they are helpful to the other three elements each, whereby they are conditions for one another through co-nascence and other relations. Therefore, it is said: 'And they do not stand without depending on one another.' 'By pleasing' (manāpehi) means by charming and graceful means. 'By variations of color, shape, and gesture' (vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavikkhepehi) refers to colors such as black and golden-brown; shapes such as broad, hollow, and thin; and gestures such as those of the hands and eyebrows. 'Essential characteristic' (sarasalakkhaṇa) means the characteristic that is its intrinsic nature, or its intrinsic nature together with its function.

Mahāparihāratoti [M 1.0451] ettha vacanatthaṃ vadanto āha “mahantehi…pe… bhūtāni, mahāparihārāni vā bhūtānī”ti. Tattha pacchimatthe purimapade uttarapadassa parihāra-saddassa lopaṃ katvā “mahābhūtānī”ti vuttaṃ.

Herein, stating the word-meaning of 'mahāparihāratoti', he said: 'Beings maintained by great ones... (etc.)... or beings of great maintenance (mahāparihārāni).' Therein, regarding the latter meaning, the term 'mahābhūtāni' is stated by having elided the word 'parihāra', the latter part of the compound, in the preceding term.

Tathā hīti tato eva vikārassa mahantattā evāti taṃ vikāraṃ dassetuṃ “bhūmito”tiādi [V 1.0422] vuttaṃ. Tattha accimatoti aggissa. Koṭisatasahassaṃ ekaṃ koṭisatasahassekaṃ cakkavāḷanti taṃ sabbaṃ āṇākhettabhāvena ekaṃ katvā vadati. Vilīyatīti vipattikarameghābhivuṭṭhena khārudakena lavaṇaṃ viya vilayaṃ gacchati viddhaṃsati. Kupitenāti khubhitena. Vikīratīti vidhamati viddhaṃsati.

Thus indeed, because of the very greatness of that alteration, 'from the earth,' etc., is said in order to show that alteration. Therein, 'from the flame' (accimato) means of fire. 'A hundred thousand crores, one hundred thousand crores of world-systems'—by this, he speaks of all of it, having made it one by way of being a sphere of command. 'It dissolves' (vilīyati) means: like salt, by the saline water rained down from a destruction-causing cloud, it goes to dissolution, it is destroyed. 'By the enraged' (kupitena) means by the agitated. 'It is scattered' (vikīrati) means it is blown away, it is destroyed.

Anupādinnesu vikāramahattaṃ dassetvā upādinnesu dassento “patthaddho”tiādimāha. Tattha kaṭṭhamukhena vāti vā-saddo upamattho. Yathā kaṭṭhamukhena sappena ḍaṭṭho patthaddho hoti, evaṃ pathavīdhātuppakopena so kāyo kaṭṭhamukheva hoti, kaṭṭhamukhamukhagato viya patthaddho hotīti attho. Atha vā vā-saddo avadhāraṇattho. So “pathavīdhātuppakopena vā”ti evaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbo. Ayañhettha attho – kaṭṭhamukhena ḍaṭṭhopi kāyo pathavīdhātuppakopeneva patthaddho hoti, tasmā pathavīdhātuyā aviyutto so kāyo sabbadā kaṭṭhamukhamukhagato viya hotīti. Vā-saddo vā aniyamattho, tatrāyamattho – kaṭṭhamukhena ḍaṭṭho kāyo patthaddho hoti vā, na vā hoti mantāgadavasena, pathavīdhātuppakopena pana mantāgadarahito so kāyo kaṭṭhamukhamukhagato viya hoti ekantapatthaddhoti.

Having shown the greatness of alteration in the unappropriated, wishing to show it in the appropriated, he said 'stiff,' etc. Therein, in 'kaṭṭhamukhena vā', the word 'vā' has the meaning of comparison. Just as one bitten by a snake called Kaṭṭhamukha becomes stiff, so too, due to the affliction of the earth element, that body becomes stiff as if it had gone into the mouth of the Kaṭṭhamukha snake—this is the meaning. Alternatively, the word 'vā' has the meaning of emphasis. It should be brought and connected thus: 'pathavīdhātuppakopena vā'. Herein, this is the meaning: even a body bitten by the Kaṭṭhamukha snake becomes stiff only because of the affliction of the earth element. Therefore, that body, not being separate from the earth element, is always as if it had gone into the mouth of the Kaṭṭhamukha snake. Or, the word 'vā' has the meaning of uncertainty. Therein, this is the meaning: a body bitten by the Kaṭṭhamukha snake may or may not become stiff, depending on the power of mantras and antidotes; but due to the affliction of the earth element, that body, being devoid of mantras and antidotes, becomes utterly stiff as if it had gone into the mouth of the Kaṭṭhamukha snake.

Pūtiyoti kuthito. Santattoti sabbaso tatto samuppannadāho. Sañchinnoti samantato chinno paramāṇubhedasañcuṇṇo āyasmato upasenattherassa sarīraṃ viya. Mahāvikārāni bhūtānīti mahāvikāravantāni bhūtāni mahābhūtānīti purimapade uttarapadalopena niddeso daṭṭhabbo. “Pathavī”tiādinā sabbalokassa pākaṭānipi vipallāsaṃ muñcitvā yathāsabhāvato pariggaṇhane mahantena vāyāmena vinā na pariggaṇhantīti duviññeyyasabhāvattā “mahantānī”ti vuccanti. Tāni hi suviññeyyāni. “Amahantānī”ti mantvā ṭhitā tesaṃ duppariggahataṃ disvā [M 1.0452] “aho mahantāni etānī”ti jānātīti mahābhūtekadesatādīhi vā kāraṇehi mahābhūtāni. Etā hi dhātuyo mahābhūtekadesato, mahābhūtasāmaññato, mahābhūtasannissayato, mahābhūtabhāvato, mahābhūtapariyosānato cāti imehipi kāraṇehi “mahābhūtānī”ti vuccanti.

'Putrid' (pūti) means rotten (kuthito). 'Scorched' (santatto) means completely burnt, with burning having arisen. 'Shattered' (sañchinno) means cut all around, pulverized to the extent of atomic particles, like the body of the Venerable Upasena Thera. The phrase 'mahāvikārāni bhūtāni' means 'beings possessing great alteration'; the term 'mahābhūtāni' should be understood as an explanation by elision of the latter part in the former word. By 'earth,' etc., although they are evident to the whole world, when one tries to grasp them according to their true nature, having abandoned distorted perception, they are not grasped without great effort. Thus, because of their nature of being difficult to discern, they are called 'great' (mahantāni). For one who stands thinking, 'They are easy to discern; they are not great,' upon seeing how difficult they are to grasp, knows, 'Oh, how great these are!' Or, they are 'mahābhūtāni' for reasons such as being a part of the great elements, etc. For these elements are also called 'mahābhūtāni' for these reasons: because of being a part of the great elements (i.e., the five aggregates); because of being designated as great elements; because of being a support for great beings; because of having the nature of many elements; and because of culminating in the great element (i.e., the Arahant).

Tattha mahābhūtekadesatoti “bhūtamidanti, bhikkhave, samanupassathā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.401) hi avisesena khandhapañcakaṃ “bhūta”nti vuccati. Tattha yadidaṃ kāmabhave, rūpabhave, pañcavokārabhave, ekacce ca saññībhave pavattaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ, taṃ mahāvisayatāya “mahābhūta”nti [V 1.0423] vattabbataṃ arahati. Pathavīādayo pana catasso dhātuyo tassa mahābhūtassa ekadesabhūtā “mahābhūtā”ti vuccanti. Samudāyesu hi pavattavohārā avayavesupi dissanti yathā “samuddo diṭṭho, paṭo daḍḍho”ti ca. Mahābhūtasamaññatoti tadadhīnavuttitāya bhavanti ettha upādārūpānīti bhūtāni, pathavīādayo catasso dhātuyo. Sā panāyametāsu bhūtasamaññā anaññatthavuttitāya upādārūpānaṃ aviparītaṭṭhā, lokassa cetā bahūpakārā, cakkhusamuddādīnaṃ nissayabhūtā cāti mahantāni bhūtānīti samaññāyiṃsu. Mahābhūtasannissayatoti mahantānaṃ mahānubhāvānaṃ mahāsammatamandhātuppabhutīnaṃ raññaṃ, sakkādīnaṃ devānaṃ, vepacittiādīnaṃ asurānaṃ, mahābrahmādīnaṃ brahmānaṃ, guṇato vā mahantānaṃ buddhānaṃ, paccekabuddhānaṃ, sāvakānaṃ upādāyupādāya vā sabbesampi bhūtānaṃ sattānaṃ nissayabhūtatāya mahantā bhūtā etesūti mahābhūtā. Cātumahābhūtiko hi nesaṃ kāyoti. Mahābhūtabhāvatoti bahubhūtabhāvato. Ayaṃ hi mahā-saddo “mahājano sannipatito”tiādīsu bahubhāve dissati. Pathavīādayo ca dhātuyo ekasmimpi attabhāve aparimeyyappabhedā pavattanti. Tasmā mahantā bahū anekasatasahassappabhedā bhūtāti mahābhūtā. Mahābhūtapariyosānatoti mahābhūtassa vasena pariyosānappattito.

Here, regarding the reason 'because of being a part of the great existent' (mahābhūtekadesato): Indeed, in passages such as, “Do you see this as ‘that which has come to be’ (bhūta), monks?” (M I 299), the five aggregates are generally called 'bhūta'. Therein, whichever five aggregates exist in the sense-sphere existence, the fine-material existence, the five-aggregate existence, and in some conscious existences, those five aggregates, due to their vast scope, are worthy of being called 'mahābhūta' (the great existent). However, the four elements beginning with earth, being a part of that 'mahābhūta', are called 'mahābhūtā' (the great elements). For designations current for composites are also seen for their components, as in “the ocean was seen” or “the cloth was burnt”. Regarding the designation 'mahābhūta': because derived matter exists dependent on them, they—the four elements beginning with earth—are called 'bhūtāni'. Furthermore, this designation 'bhūta' for these elements is unfailing in meaning because derived matter does not occur elsewhere; and because these are of great benefit to the world and are the basis for the eye, ocean, etc., they were designated as 'great bhūtas' (mahantāni bhūtāni). Regarding 'because of being the support for great beings' (mahābhūtasannissayato): because they are the support for great beings—that is, for great and powerful kings such as Mahāsammata and Mandhātu; for gods such as Sakka; for asuras such as Vepacitti; for brahmās such as Mahābrahmā; or for those who are great in terms of virtue, such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples; or, by extension, because they are the support for all beings whatsoever—great beings (mahantā bhūtā) exist in relation to them (etesu), hence they are 'mahābhūtā'. For their body is composed of the four great elements. Regarding 'because of being many existents' (mahābhūtabhāvato): this is because of being a multitude of existents. Indeed, this word 'mahā' is seen in the sense of 'many' in passages such as “a great crowd (mahājano) has gathered”. And the elements beginning with earth exist with innumerable variations even in a single individual existence. Therefore, because they are 'bhūtas' that are great, many, and of more than a hundred thousand variations, they are called 'mahābhūtā'. Regarding 'because of culminating in the great existent' (mahābhūtapariyosānato): this is because of reaching the end by means of the 'mahābhūta' (i.e., the Arahant).

“Kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā;

Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto, sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacī”ti. (jā. 1.2.190) –

“Time devours all beings, together with itself; and that being who is the devourer of time, he 'cooks' that which 'cooks' beings.”

Hi [M 1.0453] evamādīsu khīṇāsavo “bhūto”ti vutto. So hi ucchinnabhavanettikatāya āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikattā ekantato “bhūto”ti vuccati, na itare, bhavissantīti vohāraṃ anatītattā. Bhūto eva idha pūjāvasena “mahābhūto”ti vutto yathā “mahākhīṇāsavo, mahāmoggallāno”ti ca. Imāsañca dhātūnaṃ anādimati saṃsāre pabandhavasena pavattamānānaṃ yathāvuttassa mahābhūtasseva santāne pariyosānappatti, nāññatra. Tasmā mahābhūte bhūtā pariyosānaṃ pattāti mahābhūtā purimapade bhūta-saddassa lopaṃ katvā. Evametā dhātuyo mahābhūtekadesatādīhi mahābhūtāti veditabbā. Pathavīādīnaṃ kakkhaḷapaggharaṇādivisesalakkhaṇasamaṅgitā apariccattadhātulakkhaṇānaṃyevāti āha “dhātulakkhaṇaṃ anatītattā”ti. Na hi sāmaññapariccāgena viseso, visesanirapekkhaṃ vā sāmaññaṃ pavattati. Tathā hi vadanti –

Indeed, in such passages, the one whose taints are destroyed is called 'bhūto' (one who has become). For because he has severed the guide-rope of existence and has no relinking in the future, he is definitively called 'bhūto'; not so others, because they have not gone beyond the designation 'they will become'. Here, it is the 'bhūto' (the Arahant) who, by way of veneration, is called 'mahābhūto', just as in 'the great one whose taints are destroyed' or 'the great Moggallāna'. And for these elements, which have been occurring by way of continuity in beginningless saṃsāra, their culmination is reached only in the continuum of the aforementioned 'mahābhūta' (the Arahant), and not elsewhere. Therefore, because 'in the mahābhūta, the bhūtas (elements) have reached their end' (mahābhūte bhūtā pariyosānaṃ pattā), by eliding the word 'bhūta' from the first part of the phrase, they are called 'mahābhūtā'. Thus, these elements should be understood to be 'mahābhūtā' for reasons such as being a part of the great existent. The fact that earth and the other elements are endowed with specific characteristics such as hardness, flowing, etc., applies only to them insofar as they have not abandoned the general characteristic of an element; therefore, it is said: 'because of not transcending the characteristic of an element'. For a specific characteristic does not exist by abandoning the general, nor does a general characteristic exist without regard for the specific. Thus they say:

“Tamatthāpekkhato [V 1.0424] bhedaṃ, sasāmaññaṃ jahāti no;

Gaṇhāti saṃsayuppādā, samevekatthakaṃ dvaya”nti.

“Considering that (general) meaning, one does not abandon the specific difference that is together with the general; due to the arising of doubt, one grasps the pair (the specific and the general), which has a single meaning, as being equal.”

Salakkhaṇadhāraṇena cāti yena salakkhaṇadhāraṇena “dhātuyo”ti vuccanti, teneva “dhammā”tipi vuccanti ubhayathāpi nissattanijjīvatāya eva vibhāvanato. Tenevāha – “chadhāturoyaṃ bhikkhu puriso, dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”ti ca. Arūpānaṃ khaṇato rūpānaṃ khaṇassa nātiittaratāyāha “attano khaṇānurūpa”nti. Dharaṇenāti ṭhānena, pavattanenāti attho. Khayaṭṭhenāti khaṇabhaṅgutāya. Bhayaṭṭhenāti udayavayapaṭipīḷanādinā sappaṭibhayatāya. Asārakaṭṭhenāti attasāravirahena.

And by 'bearing their own characteristic': by whichever bearing of their own characteristic they are called 'elements', by that very same reason they are also called 'dhammas', because in both cases, it is simply the state of being without a being and without a life-principle that is made clear. Therefore it is said: 'This person, monk, is of six elements', and 'he dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas'. Because the duration of a moment of matter is not exceedingly shorter than that of a moment of non-matter, it is said: 'in accordance with its own moment'. 'By bearing' means by standing, by occurring. 'In the sense of decay' means because of momentary destruction. 'In the sense of fear' means because of being perilous through the oppression of arising and ceasing, etc. 'In the sense of being essenceless' means due to the absence of a core of self.

353. Sahuppannāva etāti etā catasso dhātuyo saha uppannāva saha pavattamānāva samānakāle labbhamānāpi avakaṃsato sabbapariyantime utucittāhārasamuṭṭhānesu suddhaṭṭhake, kammajesu jīvitanavaketi ekekasmiṃ suddhaṭṭhakādikalāpepi padesena avinibbhuttā visuṃ visuṃ aniddisitabbaṭṭhānatāya. Yattha hi tissannaṃ dhātūnaṃ patiṭṭhāvasena [M 1.0454] pathavī, tattheva tassā ābandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇavasena itarā. Esa nayo sesāsupi.

353. By 'they arise together': these four elements, arising together, occurring together, and being found at the same time, are—even in the very least and most basic pure octad in the case of those originated by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, and in the vital nonad in the case of those produced by kamma; that is, in each and every kalāpa such as the pure octad—inseparable by region, because their location cannot be pointed out separately. For wherever the earth element exists as the foundation for the three other elements, right there the others exist by way of binding, maturing, and impelling it. This same method applies to the remaining elements as well.

354. Purimā dve garukattā sabhāgā aññamaññanti adhippāyo. Ettha ca nanu pathaviyāpi lahubhāvo atthi. Tathā hi sā “kakkhaḷaṃ mudukaṃ saṇhaṃ pharusaṃ garukaṃ lahuka”nti niddiṭṭhā, āpepi lahubhāvo labbhatevāti? Na, nippariyāyagarubhāvassa adhippetattā. Garubhāvo eva hi pathavīdhātuyā garutaraṃ upādāya lahubhāvoti pariyāyena vutto sītabhāvo viya tejodhātuyā. Yadi evaṃ rūpassa lahutāti kathaṃ? Ayampi vuttanayā eva lahutākāraṃ upādāya labbhanato. Na hi paricchedavikāralakkhaṇāni paramatthato labbhanti nipphannarūpānaṃ avatthāvisesasabhāvato. Tasmā paramatthasiddhaṃ garubhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “purimā dve garukattā sabhāgā”ti. “Tathā”ti padena “sabhāgā”ti imamatthaṃ upasaṃharati. “Dve”ti pana idaṃ yathā “purimā”ti ettha, evaṃ “pacchimā”ti etthāpi ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Visabhāgā garukalahukabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Yathā ca garukalahukabhāvehi, evaṃ peyyabhāvāpeyyabhāvehi ca sabhāgavisabhāgatā yojetabbā.

354. The first two, due to heaviness, are similar to each other—this is the intended meaning. And here, is there not also a light aspect in the earth element? For it is described as 'hard, soft, smooth, rough, heavy, and light,' and is lightness not also found in water? No, because what is intended is heaviness in an unqualified sense. Indeed, with respect to the earth element, what is heavy is figuratively called 'lightness' by reference to what is heavier, just as coolness is in the fire element. If so, how is 'the lightness of matter' to be understood? This too is obtained by reference to the aspect of lightness in the way already stated. For the characteristics of delimitation, alteration, and sign are not found in an ultimate sense, because they are the nature of specific states of derived matter. Therefore, with reference to heaviness established in an ultimate sense, it was said: 'the first two, due to heaviness, are similar.' By the word 'thus,' he concludes this meaning of 'similar.' But this word 'two' should be brought and connected with 'the latter' here, just as with 'the first' here. The intended meaning is that they are dissimilar due to being heavy and light. And just as with heaviness and lightness, so too similarity and dissimilarity should be applied with regard to measurability and immeasurability.

355. Ajjhattikā [V 1.0425] heṭṭhā vuttaajjhattikā, sattasantānapariyāpannāti attho. Viññāṇavatthu viññattiindriyānanti cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ viññāṇavatthūnaṃ, dvinnaṃ viññattīnaṃ, itthipurisindriyajīvitindriyānañca. Ye pana “viññāṇavatthūti hadayavatthu gahita”nti vadanti, tesaṃ indriya-ggahaṇena aṭṭhannampi rūpindriyānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Vuttaviparītappakārā”ti idaṃ bāhirānaṃ dhātūnaṃ yathā sabbaso viññāṇavatthuviññattiindriyānaṃ anissayatā ca iriyāpathaviraho ca vuttavipariyāyo, evaṃ catusamuṭṭhānatāpīti katvā vuttaṃ, na lakkhaṇarūpassa viya kutocipi samuṭṭhānassa abhāvato utusamuṭṭhānatāya tāsaṃ. Lahutādinissayatāpi ajjhattikānaṃ dhātūnaṃ vattabbā, na vā vattabbā. Viññatti-ggahaṇaṃ hi lakkhaṇanti.

355. Internal elements are the internal elements previously mentioned; the meaning is that they are included in the continuum of a being. 'Bases of consciousness, expression, and faculties' refers to the six bases of consciousness beginning with the eye, the two expressions, and the faculties of femininity, masculinity, and life. But as for those who say, 'By "basis of consciousness," the heart-basis is taken,' for them, it should be understood that by the taking of 'faculty,' the taking of all eight material faculties is meant. The phrase 'of a nature contrary to what was stated' is said because for the external elements, just as their not being a support for the bases of consciousness, expression, and faculties, and their lack of postures, is the opposite of what was stated, so too is their not having four origins. This is not said because of an absence of any origin whatsoever, like characteristic-matter, for they have temperature as their origin. Also, the fact that the internal elements are a support for lightness, etc., should be stated, or it should not be stated. For the inclusion of expression is a characteristic.

356. Itarāhīti āpotejovāyudhātūhi. Ekasaṅgahāti sajātisaṅgahena ekasaṅgahā. Samānajātiyānaṃ hi saṅgaho sahajātisaṅgaho. Tenāha “samuṭṭhānanānattābhāvato”ti.

356. 'By the others' means by the water, fire, and air elements. 'Of a single inclusion' means of a single inclusion by way of inclusion with the same kind. For the inclusion of those of a similar kind is inclusion of the same kind. Therefore, it is said, 'because of the absence of diversity in origination.'

357. Tiṇṇaṃ [M 1.0455] mahābhūtānaṃ patiṭṭhā hutvā paccayo hotīti yehi mahābhūtehi sampiṇḍanavasena saṅgahitā, paripācanavasena anupālitā, samudīraṇavasena vitthambhitā ca, tesaṃ attanā sahajātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ patiṭṭhā hutvā tato eva sandhāraṇavasena avassayo hoti, vuttanayena vā patiṭṭhā hutvā sahajātādivasena paccayo hotīti. Esa nayo sesāsupi.

357. 'Having become the support for the three great elements, it becomes a condition' means: having become the support for those three great elements co-arisen with itself—by which elements it is held together by way of cohesion, maintained by way of maturing, and propped up by way of impelling—it becomes a reliance for them by way of supporting. Or, having become the support in the way stated, it becomes a condition by way of co-nascence, etc. This method applies to the remaining elements as well.

358. Yadipi aññamaññaābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammāti heṭṭhā dhātūnaṃ asamannāhāratā dassitā eva, athāpi imināva nayena visuṃ kammaṭṭhānapariggaho kātabboti dassento “pathavīdhātu cetthā”tiādimāha. Tattha pathavīdhātu cetthāti ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena ayampi eko manasikārappakāroti dīpeti. Etthāti etāsu dhātūsu. Ahaṃ “pathavīdhātū”ti vā “paccayo homī”ti vā na jānātīti attani viya attano kicce ca ābhogābhāvaṃ dassetvā upakārakassa viya upakattabbānampi ābhogābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “itarānipī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbatthāti sabbāsu dhātūsu, tatthāpi attakiccupakattabbabhedesu sabbesu.

358. Although it was already shown previously that 'these phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection,' and thus the elements' lack of mutual application was shown, nevertheless, showing that 'by this very method, a separate grasping of the meditation subject should be done,' he said, 'the earth element here,' etc. Therein, in 'the earth element here,' the word 'ca' has the meaning of combination; by it, he indicates, 'this too is one type of attention.' 'Here' means among these elements. Having shown the absence of advertence towards itself and its own function, as in '[it] does not know "I am the earth element" or "I am a condition,"' in order to show the absence of advertence also for those things to be benefited, just as for the benefactor, it was said, 'the others too,' etc. 'In all' means in all elements, and there too, in all the divisions of one's own function and what is to be benefited.

359. Paccayavibhāgatoti paccayadhammavibhāgato ceva paccayabhāvavibhāgato ca. “Paccayato”ti hi iminā pathavīādīnaṃ aññāsādhāraṇo patiṭṭhābhāvādinā sesabhūtattayassa paccayabhāvo vutto. Idha pana yehi dhammehi pathavīādīnaṃ uppatti, tesaṃ pathavīādīnañca anavasesato [V 1.0426] paccayabhāvavibhāgo vuccatīti ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ ākārānaṃ viseso. Kammanti kusalākusalaṃ rūpuppādakaṃ kammaṃ. Cittanti yaṃ kiñci rūpuppādakaṃ cittaṃ. Āhāroti ajjhattiko rūpuppādako āhāro. Utūti yo koci utu, atthato tejodhātu. Kammamevāti avadhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānasaṅkarābhāvadassanatthaṃ, tena akammajānampi kesañci kammassa pariyāyapaccayabhāvo dīpito hoti. Tathā hi vakkhati “kammapaccayacittasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādi. Nanu ca kammasamuṭṭhānānaṃ kammato aññenapi paccayena bhavitabbanti? Bhavitabbaṃ, so pana kammagatikovāti paṭiyogīnivattanatthaṃ avadhāraṇaṃ kataṃ, tenāha “na cittādayo”ti. Cittādisamuṭṭhānānanti etthāpi ayamattho yathārahaṃ vattabbo. Itareti cittādito [M 1.0456] aññe. Janakapaccayoti samuṭṭhāpakataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, paccayo pana kammapaccayova. Vuttaṃ hi “kusalākusalā cetanā vipākānaṃ khandhānaṃ kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.427).

359. 'By division of condition' means by way of both the division of conditioning phenomena and the division of the state of being a condition. For by the term 'by way of condition,' the state of being a condition for the remaining three primary elements by way of being a foundation, etc.—which is not shared by others—of the earth element, etc., was stated. Here, however, the division of the state of being a condition is spoken of without remainder for those phenomena by which the arising of the earth element, etc., occurs, and for the earth element, etc., themselves. This is the distinction between these two modes. Kamma means wholesome and unwholesome kamma that produces matter. Citta means any consciousness that produces matter. Āhāra means internal nutriment that produces matter. Utu means any temperature, that is, the fire element in essence. The emphasis in 'kamma only' is for the purpose of showing the absence of a mixture of origins; by that, the state of being an indirect condition of kamma is shown even for some things not born of kamma. For thus it will be said, 'consciousness-originated by kamma-condition,' etc. But should not those originated by kamma also be by a condition other than kamma? It should be. But that other condition is of the same nature as kamma. Therefore, the emphasis was made to exclude a rival; hence he says, 'not by consciousness, etc.' Also in 'of those originated by consciousness, etc.,' this meaning should be applied as appropriate. 'Others' means other than consciousness, etc. 'Generative condition' is said with reference to its function as an originator, but the condition is only the kamma-condition. For it is said, 'Wholesome and unwholesome volition is a condition for the resultant aggregates and for matter produced by kamma by way of kamma-condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.427).

Sesānanti cittādisamuṭṭhānānaṃ. Pariyāyato upanissayapaccayo hotīti paṭṭhāne (paṭṭhā. 1.1.9) arūpānaṃyeva upanissayapaccayassa āgatattā nippariyāyena rūpadhammānaṃ upanissayapaccayo natthi. Sutte pana “puggalaṃ upanissāya vanasaṇḍaṃ upanissāyā”ti vacanato suttantikapariyāyena vinā abhāvo upanissayapaccayoti veditabbo. Cittaṃ janakapaccayo hotīti sahajātanissayāhārādivasena paccayo hontaṃ cittaṃ samuṭṭhāpakataṃ upādāya “janakapaccayo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Āhārautūsupi eseva nayo.

As for 'the rest,' it refers to those originated by mind and so on. Figuratively, it is a condition by way of decisive support—as stated in the Paṭṭhāna—because the decisive support condition is mentioned only for immaterial phenomena. Literally, there is no decisive support condition for material phenomena. However, in the Suttas, because it is stated, “relying on a person, relying on a forest grove,” it should be understood that, according to the Suttanta method, the state of indispensability is the decisive support condition. As for 'Mind is a generating condition,' it means that mind, being a condition by way of co-nascence, dependence, nutriment, and so on, is called a 'generating condition' on account of its being an originator. The same method applies to nutriment and temperature.

Evaṃ kammādīnaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ vasena dhātūsu paccayavibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ dhātūnampi vasena paccayavibhāgaṃ dassento paṭhamaṃ tāva “kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ mahābhūta”ntiādinā uddisitvā puna “tattha kammasamuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātū”tiādinā niddisati. Tattha kammasamuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātūti “kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ mahābhūta”nti ettha sāmaññato vuttā kammajapathavīdhātu. Kammasamuṭṭhānānaṃ itarāsanti kammajānaṃ āpodhātuādīnaṃ tissannaṃ dhātūnaṃ sahuppattiyā attano upakārakānaṃ tāsaṃ upakārakato, ādhārabhāvato, uppādato yāva bhaṅgādharaṇato, vigamābhāvato ca sahajātaaññamaññanissayaatthiavigatavasena ceva patiṭṭhāvasena ca paccayo hoti, hontī ca kammaṃ viya attano, tāsañca na janakavasena paccayo hoti asamuṭṭhāpakattā tāsaṃ. Kāmañcettha nissayapaccaya-ggahaṇeneva patiṭṭhābhāvo saṅgahito, pathavīdhātuyā pana anaññasādhāraṇakiccaṃ sahajātānaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvoti imaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ [V 1.0427] “patiṭṭhāvasena cā”ti visuṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Ābandhanavasena cātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tisantatimahābhūtānanti utucittāhārasamuṭṭhānānaṃ catumahābhūtānaṃ aññamaññaṃ avokiṇṇānaṃ, avicchedena pavattiṃ upādāya santatīti santatiggahaṇaṃ. Pathavīdhātuyā patiṭṭhābhāvo nāma sahajātānaṃ dhammānaṃyevāti āha “na patiṭṭhāvasenā”ti. Na ābandhanavasenātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Etthāti [M 1.0457] etesu kammasamuṭṭhānamahābhūtesu. “Cittasamuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātu cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ itarāsa”ntiādīsu sukaro tantinayo netunti “cittaāhāra…pe… eseva nayo”ti atidisati.

Having thus shown the classification of conditions among the elements by way of conditioning states such as kamma, etc., now, to demonstrate the classification of conditions by way of the elements that arise from them, he first enumerates with 'The great elements are originated by kamma,' etc., and then expounds with 'Therein, the earth element is originated by kamma,' etc. Herein, 'the earth element originated by kamma' refers to the earth element born of kamma, which was stated generally in 'the great elements are originated by kamma.' For the other elements originated by kamma—that is, for the three elements born of kamma, the water element and so on, which are helpful to oneself by co-arising—the earth element is a condition. It is a condition because it is helpful to them, because of its state as a support, because it endures from arising to dissolution, and because of the absence of disappearance; it is a condition by way of co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance, and also by way of foundation. However, although it is a condition, unlike kamma, it is not a condition by way of generation for itself or for those others, because it is not their originator. Although the state of being a foundation is indeed included here by the taking up of the dependence condition, to show this distinction—that the unique function of the earth element is to be a foundation for its co-nascent states—it is stated separately as 'and by way of foundation.' The same method applies to such phrases as 'and by way of binding,' etc. The term 'continuity' is used with reference to the uninterrupted occurrence of the four great elements arising from temperature, mind, and nutriment, which are unmixed with one another. The state of being a foundation of the earth element pertains only to its co-nascent states; hence, it is said, 'not by way of foundation.' The same method applies to such phrases as 'not by way of binding,' etc. 'Herein' refers to these great elements originated by kamma. Because in such passages as 'The earth element originated by mind is a condition for the others originated by mind,' the textual method is easy to apply, he extends the principle by stating, 'mind, nutriment... this is the same method.'

Sahajātādipaccayavasappavattāsu ca panāti ettha ca-saddo samuccayattho, pana-saddo visesattho, tadubhayena ca yathāvuttasahajātādipaccayehi pavattamānā dhātuyo iminā visesena pavattantīti imamatthaṃ dīpeti.

In the phrase 'Sahajātādipaccayavasappavattāsu ca pana,' the word 'ca' has the meaning of conjunction, and the word 'pana' has the meaning of distinction. By both of them, it is indicated that the elements that occur through the aforesaid conditions such as co-nascence, etc., occur with this particular distinction.

Idāni taṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ “ekaṃ paṭiccā”tigāthamāha. Tattha ekaṃ dhātuṃ paṭicca tisso dhātuyo catudhā sampavattanti, tisso dhātuyo paṭicca ekāva dhātu catudhā sampavattati, dve dhātuyo paṭicca dve dhātuyo chadhā sampavattantīti yojanā. Attho pana pathavīādīsu ekekissā paccayabhāve itarāsaṃ tissannaṃ tissannaṃ paccayuppannatāti ayameko catukko, tissannaṃ tissannaṃ paccayabhāve itarāya ekekissā paccayuppannatāti ayamaparo catukko, paṭhamadutiyā, tatiyacatutthā, paṭhamatatiyā, dutiyacatutthā, paṭhamacatutthā, dutiyatatiyāti imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ paccayabhāve tattha tattha itarāsaṃ dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ paccayuppannatāti ayameko chakko. Evaṃ paccayabhāvena catudhā, chadhā ca pavattamānānaṃ ekakadvikatikavasena tikadukaekakavasena ca yathākkamaṃ paccayapaccayuppannatāvibhāgo veditabbo. Ayañca paccayabhāvo sahajātaaññamaññanissayaatthiavigatapaccayavasena, tatthāpi ca aññamaññamukheneva veditabbo. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ paṭiccavāre “ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca tayo mahābhūtā, tayo mahābhūte paṭicca ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ, dve mahābhūte paṭicca dve mahābhūtā uppajjantī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.53).

Now, to show that distinction, he states the verse beginning 'depending on one.' Therein, the connection is as follows: dependent on one element, three elements occur in four ways; dependent on three elements, one element occurs in four ways; dependent on two elements, two elements occur in six ways. But the meaning is this: among earth, etc., when any one serves as a condition, the other three are conditioned—this is one tetrad. When any three serve as conditions, the remaining one is conditioned—this is another tetrad. For the pairs—first and second, third and fourth, first and third, second and fourth, first and fourth, second and third—when any two serve as conditions, in each case the other two are conditioned—this is one hexad. Thus, for those occurring in four ways and six ways by being a condition, the classification of condition and conditioned should be understood respectively by way of singles, pairs, and triads, and by way of triads, pairs, and singles. And this state of being a condition should be understood by way of co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions; and even among those, it should be understood primarily through mutuality. It is with reference to this that it was stated in the Chapter on Conditional Relations: “Dependent on one great element, three great elements arise; dependent on three great elements, one great element arises; dependent on two great elements, two great elements arise” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.53).

Abhikkamapaṭikkamādīti ādi-saddena ādānavissajjanādikāyikakiriyākaraṇassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Uppīḷanassa paccayo hoti ghaṭṭanakiriyāya pathavīdhātuvasena sijjhanato. Sāvāti pathavīdhātuyeva. Āpodhātuyā anugatā āpodhātuyā tattha appadhānabhāvaṃ, pathavīdhātuyā ca [V 1.0428] padhānabhāvanti patiṭṭhābhāve viya patiṭṭhāpanepi sātisayakiccattā tassā patiṭṭhāpanassa pādaṭṭhapanassa paccayo hotīti [M 1.0458] sambandho. Avakkhepanassāti adhonikkhipanassa. Tattha ca garutarasabhāvāya āpodhātuyā sātisayo byāpāroti āha “pathavīdhātuyā anugatā āpodhātū”ti. Tathā uddhaṅgatikā tejodhātūti uddharaṇe vāyodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo vutto. Tiriyaṃ gatikāya vāyodhātuyā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu sātisayo byāpāroti tejodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo gahito. Tattha ṭhitaṭṭhānato abhimukhaṃ pādassa haraṇaṃ atiharaṇaṃ, purato haraṇaṃ. Tato thokaṃ vītikkamma haraṇaṃ vītiharaṇaṃ, passato haraṇaṃ.

In 'going forward, returning, etc.' (abhikkamapaṭikkamādi), by the word 'etc.' (ādi), the inclusion of performing bodily actions such as taking and releasing should be understood. It is a condition for pressing down, because of its accomplishment by means of the earth element in the action of striking. That is the earth element itself. Being followed by the water element—and because in that place there is the non-dominant state of the water element and the dominant state of the earth element—just as in the state of being established, so also in the act of establishing, due to its having a superior function, it is a condition for the establishing, for the placing of the foot. This is the connection. 'Of placing down' (avakkhepanassa) means of placing downwards. And therein, because there is a superior activity of the water element, which has a particularly heavy nature, it is said: 'The water element is followed by the earth element.' Similarly, because the fire element has upward movement, in lifting, its state of following the air element is stated. Because the air element, which has lateral movement, has a superior activity in carrying forward and carrying beyond, its state of being followed by the fire element is taken. Therein, from a standing position, moving the foot forward is 'carrying forward' (atiharaṇa), that is, moving to the front. Moving a little beyond that is 'carrying beyond' (vītiharaṇa); moving to the side is also a kind of carrying.

Ekekena mukhenāti “patthaṭattā pathavī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.347) vibhattesu terasasu ākāresu ekekena dhātūnaṃ pariggaṇhanamukhena. Svāyanti so ayaṃ upacārasamādhi. Kathaṃ panassa vavatthānapariyāyoti āha “catunnaṃ dhātūna”ntiādi.

'By each aspect' means: by way of grasping the elements one by one through each of the thirteen aspects which are differentiated by 'earth, because of its spread-out nature,' etc. This is that access concentration. But how does this get the name 'determination'? To answer this, he said 'of the four elements,' etc.

360. Idāni imissā bhāvanāya ānisaṃse dassetuṃ “idañca panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Suññataṃ avagāhatīti dhātumattatādassanena rūpakāyassa anattakataṃ vavatthāpayato tadanusārena nāmakāyassāpi anattakatā supākaṭā hotīti sabbaso attasuññataṃ pariyogāhati tattha patiṭṭhahati. Sattasaññaṃ samugghātetīti tato eva “satto poso itthī puriso”ti evaṃ pavattaṃ ayāthāvasaññaṃ ugghāteti samūhanati. Vāḷamigayakkharakkhasādivikappaṃ anāvajjamānoti sasantāne viya parasantānepi dhātumattatāya sudiṭṭhattā khīṇāsavo viya “ime sīhabyagghādayo vāḷamigā, ime yakkharakkhasā”ti evamādivikappaṃ akaronto bhayabheravaṃ sahati abhibhavati. Yathāvuttavikappanāpajjanaṃ hi bhayabheravasahanassa kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ugghāto uppilāvitattaṃ. Nigghāto dīnabhāvappatti. Mahāpañño ca pana hoti dhātuvasena kāye sammadeva ghanavinibbhogassa karaṇato. Tathā hidaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ buddhicaritassa anukūlanti vuttaṃ, sugatiparāyaṇo vā indriyānaṃ aparipakkatāyanti adhippāyo.

360. Now, to show the benefits of this meditation, 'And this...' etc., was said. 'He plunges into emptiness' means: for the yogi who determines the not-self nature of the material body by seeing its nature as mere elements, in accordance with that, the not-self nature of the mental body also becomes very clear. Therefore, he completely penetrates the emptiness of self and becomes established therein. 'He eradicates the perception of a being' means: for that very reason, he uproots and eradicates the incorrect perception that occurs as 'a being, a person, a woman, a man.' 'Not falling into conceptual proliferation concerning beasts of prey, yakkhas, rakkhasas, etc.' means: because the nature of being mere elements is well seen in others' continuities just as in one's own, like one whose cankers are destroyed, not creating conceptual proliferations such as 'These are beasts of prey like lions and tigers; these are yakkhas and rakkhasas,' he endures and overcomes fear and terror. For it is said that not falling into the aforementioned conceptual proliferation is the cause for enduring fear and terror. Ugghāta is the state of being agitated. Nigghāta is the attainment of a state of wretchedness. And he becomes one of great wisdom because of correctly making the analysis of the solid mass in the body by way of the elements. For this meditation subject has been called suitable for one of intellectual temperament. Or, when his faculties are immature, he is bound for a good destination. This is the meaning.

Ekūnavīsatibhāvanānayapaṭimaṇḍitassa

Adorned with the nineteen methods of meditation,

Catudhātuvavatthānaniddesassa līnatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the hidden meaning of the Exposition of the Determination of the Four Elements is concluded.

361. “Ko [M 1.0459][V 1.0429] samādhī”tiādinā sarūpādipucchā yāvadeva vibhāgāvabodhanatthā. Sarūpādito hi ñātassa pabhedo vuccamāno suviññeyyo hoti saṅkhepapubbakattā vitthārassa, vitthāravidhinā ca saṅkhepavidhi saṅgayhatīti “samādhissa vitthāraṃ bhāvanānayañca dassetu”nti vuttaṃ. Atha vā “ko samādhī”tiādināpi samādhisseva pakārabhedo dassīyati, bhāvanānisaṃsopi bhāvanānayanissito evāti adhippāyena “vitthāraṃ bhāvanānayañca dassetu”nti vuttaṃ. Sabbappakāratoti palibodhupacchedādikassa sabbassa bhāvanāya pubbakiccassa karaṇappakārato ceva sabbakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāvibhāvanato ca.

361. The question about its nature, etc., beginning with 'What is concentration?' is solely for the purpose of understanding the classification. For when the classification of something that is known by its nature, etc., is stated, it is easy to understand, because the detailed explanation is preceded by the summary, and the summary method is included by the detailed method. Therefore, it was said, 'to show the detailed explanation of concentration and the method of meditation.' Alternatively, by the question 'What is concentration?', etc., the classification of the types of concentration itself is shown. And with the intention that the benefit of the meditation is also dependent on the method of meditation, it was said, 'to show the detailed explanation and the method of meditation.' 'In every way' means: both from the manner of performing all the preliminary duties of meditation, such as the cutting off of obstacles, and from the clear explanation of the meditation on all meditation subjects.

“Samattā hotī”ti vatvā tameva samattabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “duvidhoyevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idha adhippeto samādhīti lokiyasamādhiṃ āha. Dasasu kammaṭṭhānesūti yāni heṭṭhā “upacārāvahānī”ti vuttāni dasa kammaṭṭhānāni, tesu. Appanāpubbabhāgacittesūti appanāya pubbabhāgacittesu aṭṭhannaṃ jhānānaṃ pubbabhāgacittuppādesu. Ekaggatāti ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ, nānāvajjanavīthiyañca ekaggatā. Avasesakammaṭṭhānesūti “appanāvahānī”ti vuttesu tiṃsakammaṭṭhānesu.

Having said 'it is complete,' in order to explain that very state of completeness, 'it is of two kinds,' etc., was said. By 'the concentration intended here,' he speaks of mundane concentration. 'In the ten meditation subjects' means: in those ten meditation subjects that were stated below as 'conducive to access concentration.' 'In the minds of the preliminary part of absorption' means: in the minds of the preliminary part of absorption, in the mind-arisings of the preliminary part of the eight absorptions. 'One-pointedness' means: one-pointedness both in a cognitive series with a single determining consciousness and in one with various determining consciousnesses. 'In the remaining meditation subjects' means: in the thirty meditation subjects stated as 'conducive to absorption'.

Samādhiānisaṃsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Benefits of Concentration.

362. Diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkhabhūto attabhāvo, tattha sukhavihāro diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro. Kāmaṃ “samāpajjitvā”ti etena appanāsamādhiyeva vibhāvito, “ekaggacittā”ti pana padena upacārasamādhinopi gahaṇaṃ hotīti tato nivattanatthaṃ “appanāsamādhibhāvanā”ti vuttaṃ. Na kho paneteti ete bāhirakabhāvitā jhānadhammā cittekaggatāmattakarā. Ariyassa vinaye buddhassa bhagavato sāsane “sallekhā”ti na vuccanti kilesānaṃ sallekhanapaṭipadā na hotīti katvā, sāsane pana avihiṃsādayopi sallekhāva lokuttarapādakattā.

362. The directly visible state of existence is called 'the present life' (diṭṭhadhamma); therein, pleasant abiding is 'pleasant abiding in the present life' (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra). Although by the phrase 'having attained' (samāpajjitvā) only absorption concentration is clarified, since by the term 'with a one-pointed mind' (ekaggacittā) the inclusion of access concentration also occurs, it is stated as 'the development of absorption concentration' in order to exclude that. However, these jhāna states, cultivated by outsiders, only produce one-pointedness of mind. In the Discipline of the Noble One, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, they are not called 'effacement' (sallekha), because they are not the practice for effacing the defilements. In the teaching, however, non-harming and other such states are indeed effacement, because they are a basis for the supramundane.

Sambādheti taṇhāsaṃkilesādinā saṃkiliṭṭhatāya paramasambādhe ativiya saṅkaṭaṭṭhānabhūte saṃsārappavatte. Okāsādhigamanayenāti atthapaṭilābhayoggassa navamakhaṇasaṅkhātassa okāsassa adhigamanayena. Tassa [M 1.0460] hi dullabhatāya appanādhigamampi anadhigamayamāno saṃvegabahulo puggalo upacārasamādhimhiyeva [V 1.0430] ṭhatvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karoti “sīghaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ samatikkamissāmī”ti.

It is constricted in the continuation of saṃsāra, which is an extremely constricted place, an extremely confined location, because of being defiled by craving, defilements, and so on. 'By the way of attaining an opportunity' means: by the method of obtaining the opportunity called the ninth moment, which is suitable for gaining the supramundane benefit. Indeed, because of the rarity of this moment, a person with a great sense of urgency, not waiting to attain absorption, remains in access concentration itself and undertakes the work of insight, thinking, 'I will quickly overcome the suffering of saṃsāra.'

Abhiññāpādakanti iddhividhādiabhiññāñāṇapādakabhūtaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Hotīti vuttanayāti ettha iti-saddo pakārattho, tena “iminā pakārena vuttanayā”ti sesābhiññānampi vuttappakāraṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sati sati āyataneti purimabhavasiddhe abhiññādhigamassa kāraṇe vijjamāne. Abhiññādhigamassa hi adhikāro icchitabbo, yo “pubbahetū”ti vuccati. Na samāpattīsu vasībhāvo. Tenāha bhagavā “sati sati āyatane”ti (ma. ni. 3.158; a. ni. 3.102). Abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassāti vakkhamānavibhāgāya abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya sacchikātabbassa. Dhammassāti bhāvetabbassa ceva vibhāvetabbassa ca dhammassa. Abhiññāsacchikiriyāya cittaṃ abhininnāmetīti yojanā. Tatra tatrevāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃyeva sacchikātabbadhamme. Sakkhibhāvāya paccakkhakāritāya bhabbo sakkhibhabbo, tassa bhāvo sakkhibhabbatā, taṃ sakkhibhabbataṃ.

'A basis for higher knowledge' (abhiññāpādakaṃ) means: being a basis and foundation for the knowledge of higher powers such as psychic power. In the phrase 'it is, in the way spoken of' (hotīti vuttanayā), the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'manner'. By this, it includes the manner taught for the remaining higher knowledges as well, meaning 'in the way taught in this manner'. 'When there is the basis' (sati sati āyatane) means: when the cause for attaining higher knowledge, accomplished in a previous existence, is present. Indeed, for the attainment of higher knowledge, a special condition is to be desired, which is called 'the prior cause' (pubbahetu). It is not mastery in the attainments. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'when there is the basis'. 'Of that which is to be realized by higher knowledge' (abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassa) means: of that which is to be realized by the distinguished wisdom that has the analysis that will be spoken of. 'Of the Dhamma' (dhammassa) means: of the Dhamma that is to be developed and to be made manifest. The connection is: 'he inclines the mind for the sake of realization by higher knowledge'. 'In this and that very place' (tatra tatreva) means: in just that very Dhamma to be realized. 'Sakkhibhabbo' means one who is capable of becoming a witness (sakkhibhāvāya), of being one who realizes directly (paccakkhakāritāya). The state of that is 'sakkhibhabbatā' (witness-capability); 'taṃ sakkhibhabbataṃ' means to that witness-capability.

Taṃ taṃ bhavagamikammaṃ ārabbha bhavapatthanāya anuppannāyapi kammassa katūpacitabhāveneva bhavapatthanākiccaṃ sijjhatīti dassento āha “apatthayamānā vā”ti. Saha byeti pavattatīti sahabyo, sahāyo, idha pana ekabhavūpago adhippeto, tassa bhāvo sahabyatā, taṃ sahabyataṃ.

Showing that, with respect to whatever kamma leads to a particular existence, even if an aspiration for that existence has not arisen, the function of the aspiration for existence is accomplished simply by the kamma having been done and accumulated, he said, 'or without aspiring' (apatthayamānā vā). 'Sahabyo' is so called because 'it proceeds together' (saha byeti); it means a companion. Here, however, one who partakes in the same existence is intended. The state of that is 'sahabyatā' (companionship); 'taṃ sahabyataṃ' means to that state of companionship.

Kiṃ pana appanāsamādhibhāvanāyeva bhavavisesānisaṃsā, udāhu itarāpīti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “upacārasamādhibhāvanāpī”tiādi.

Now, does only the development of absorption concentration have the benefit of a special existence, or does the other [development of access concentration] also have it? Having taken this question to mind, he said, 'Even the development of access concentration…' and so on.

Nibbānanti tissannaṃ dukkhatānaṃ nibbutiṃ. Rūpadhamme pariyāpannā vijjamānāpi saṅkhāradukkhatā cittassa abhāvena asantasamāva. Tenāha “sukhaṃ viharissāmā”ti. Soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhīti aniccānupassanādukkhaanattanibbidāvirāganirodhapaṭinissaggavivaṭṭānupassanāti imāhi aṭṭhahi, aṭṭhahi ca ariyamaggaphalañāṇehīti evaṃ soḷasahi. Navahi samādhicariyāhīti [M 1.0461] pañcannaṃ rūpajjhānānaṃ, catunnaṃ arūpajjhānānañca vasena evaṃ navahi. Keci pana “cattāro rūpajjhānasamādhī, cattāro arūpajjhānasamādhī, ubhayesaṃ upacārasamādhiṃ ekaṃ katvā evaṃ navā”ti vadanti.

'Nibbāna' means the quenching of the three kinds of suffering. Even though the suffering of formations, which is included in material phenomena, exists, due to the absence of mind, it is as if non-existent. Therefore, he said, 'We will dwell happily.' 'By sixteen practices of knowledge' means: by these eight—contemplation of impermanence, suffering, non-self, disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and turning away—and by the eight noble path and fruition knowledges; thus by sixteen. 'By nine practices of concentration' means: by way of the five form jhānas and the four formless jhānas; thus by nine. Some, however, say: 'The four form jhāna concentrations, the four formless jhāna concentrations, and making the access concentration of both into one; thus there are nine.'

Samādhibhāvanāyogeti [V 1.0431] samādhibhāvanāya anuyoge anuyuñjane, samādhibhāvanāsaṅkhāte vā yoge. Yogoti bhāvanā vuccati. Yathāha “yogā ve jāyatī bhūrī”ti (dha. pa. 282).

'In the application to the development of concentration' (samādhibhāvanāyoge) means: in the constant application to, the engagement in, the development of concentration; or in the application designated as the development of concentration. Application (yoga) is called development (bhāvanā). As it is said: 'Indeed, from application wisdom arises' (Dhp 282).

363. Samādhipīti pi-saddena sīlaṃ sampiṇḍeti.

363. In the word 'samādhipi', the particle 'pi' also includes virtue (sīla).

Samādhiniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of concentration is finished.

Iti ekādasamaparicchedavaṇṇanā.

Thus, the commentary on the eleventh chapter.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is finished.
